Male athletics is one of the most competitive atmospheres, if not the most. Knowing this, coaches always want to put the best and most athletic players on the field or court. Growing up I have never been the biggest or strongest person that could be used for sports. So, in today’s world, I would not be a good fit to be on the field during a game. Football was always a hardship for me, starting back in middle school. I still remember today the words that came out of the coach during tryouts. He said to a group of us, “Sorry, I will not be able to keep you all on the team because of the size difference.” To me, it was extremely unnecessary for him to say that about us. He could have told us to practice harder and come back next year to tryout. Instead, hegemonic masculinity standards were put into place and could have been easily avoided with a different choice of words.
chunks.label: Cut from middle school football
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up playing sports, but during middle school football tryouts, the coach cut the student and a group of others specifically citing their small size.
chunks.people: middle school coach, group of peers

chunks.text: Life went on and I tried not to think about the time in middle school. It was not until high school when another standard was put onto me. Unfortunately, it was another incident involving football. In high school, I hit a growth spurt, but have never been able to gain as much weight as I needed to, even to this day. It was junior year of high school when our football coach asked a question that was like the statement of my middle school coach. He said to me, “When is your body going to get wider?” This remark was made by my coach because the day after I did good at practice the day before, but it still did not help because of the size of my body. I went to a high school where people were favorited in sports due to their last names. So, no matter how good I did in practice or how muscular I was, it was hard to get a starting spot because of my last name compared to other last names, where they sponsored the school and had more money than my family did.
chunks.label: High school football body comments and favoritism
chunks.what_happened: During junior year of high school football, the coach questioned when the student's body would get wider despite performing well at practice, and wealthier students were favored for starting spots based on their family names.
chunks.people: high school football coach, teammates, student's family

chunks.text: There were times when I asked what I could do to get better and hopefully get a starting spot on the team. I did not get many answers, so I started to work out every weekday at school. Working out is one of the main things to do to fit in with hegemonic standards. When everybody expects a guy to be muscular, it pushes you to want to work out so you can fit in. Unbelievably, working out was the one solution that helped me get the starting spot, but it only came during my senior year. I did not have a huge transformation, but it was good enough to help me out with athletics. Football was my only issue when it came to body size. My skills were good enough in baseball to put myself over others. I know I am not the best, but I always looked at where practice beats talent.
chunks.label: Working out to earn a starting spot
chunks.what_happened: The student began working out every weekday at school to meet muscular standards and finally earned a starting football spot senior year, while having better success in baseball through practice.

chunks.text:
Brett Stoudt was able to explain the “School Violence, Peer Discipline, and

the (Re)Production of Hegemonic Masculinity” in his article, “You’re Either In or You’re Out” (Stoudt, 2006). The concept was that hegemonic masculinity is the dominant idea of how a many should act and carry himself. The idea was practiced at a privileged educational school, called Rockport. It consisted of “mostly white, independent boys’ school located in an upper-middle to upper-class suburban region” (Stoudt, 2006). Stoudt argues that hegemonic masculinity was beneficial for the boys of privilege and gave them new opportunities. Even though it is beneficial for the boys, hegemonic masculinity becomes a problem for society because it reinforces toxic masculinity and is normalized in their group, but not in society. Hegemonic masculinity also plays a part in how men expect women to act and look.
chunks.label: Stoudt's study on hegemonic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Brett Stoudt's article about how hegemonic masculinity is reproduced among privileged boys at Rockport and how it harms society.

chunks.text: The standard that these women must meet from men is known as the beauty myth. The beauty myth is a concept that switches roles of gender. It is where women must have an image of beauty for their identity. Not only do men look for the beauty in women, but women themselves compete against each other. This competition between each other has caused female advancement to lack because they have not been able to form a community with each other without the competitiveness of beauty standards placed on them. Women may be suppressed by men, but there are things that goes on by both genders that should not be happening. There should be no beauty standards and no specific way a person should look or act. Everybody was made to be different and not perfect, but the way people are raised could influence how they react to these scenarios about hegemonic masculinity or the beauty myth.
chunks.label: The beauty myth and female competition
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the beauty myth, how beauty standards force women to compete against each other, and argues that such standards should not exist.

chunks.text: Stereotypes are made every day about cultural norms that should be portrayed, and I feel like stereotypes were made about me. My coaches did not see me as the right fit because I was not big enough to compete with others around me. To me, they used it as an advantage to not let me play as a starter. I practiced hard every day, but never got the chance to because hegemonic masculinity confirmed their beliefs that I was not “big enough” to play. My school was like Rockport, instead we were not an all-boy school. Even with both genders at our school, we had the upper-class individuals that had the privilege of playing over others. Privileges play a part in hegemonic masculinity, and in the beauty myth, which was another reason I felt like I did not get the playing time I deserved.
chunks.label: Connecting school sports experience to theory
chunks.what_happened: The student connects personal experiences of being denied playing time to hegemonic masculinity, comparing their high school's class privileges to Rockport.

chunks.text: People are compelled to fit into cultural norms that are created by both parties. Both genders try to escape these stereotypes, but in today’s world it is harder than it sounds. These scenarios played out exactly how it is explained in my own life. People may not think it influences a person, but until it happens to them, these stereotypes should not be made about men or women. Both genders should start to accept each other the way they are, and one gender should not bash the same gender over standards being made. Change should start to show up soon because if not, the world will stay exactly how it is now, divided.
chunks.label: Call for change regarding stereotypes
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that cultural norms and gender stereotypes harm people and calls for mutual acceptance and change to avoid a divided world.

chunks.text: Irving Goffman, however, introduced the theory of the front stage versus backstage self when trying to understand social interaction and perception. The front stage mainly represents the public image that an individual will present to other people intentionally. This side of the self-portrays the way we might act as a way to conform to the current social normalities and expectations of the current culture. The backstage, however, touches more on private and true self-expressions and actions where individuals feel they can act completely real and raw and get away from impression management they may deal with in front of others. This theory deals with a more fake vs. real approach when it comes to self-perception and authenticity. Even in the name itself, one might imagine the side of the self behind the curtain verses the side broadcast on stage for all to see. This theory suggests those are the two options of the self and emphasizes the skill of “reading the room”.
chunks.label: Goffman's front stage versus backstage theory
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Erving Goffman's sociological theory of the front stage and backstage self, discussing impression management, social norms, and authenticity.

chunks.text: Imagine a real-world scenario to illustrate these two theories. We will use a job interview. When applying for a job and going in for an interview, the applicant would most likely apply their front stage self by consciously picking and choosing what they decide to say, what they wear, and the demeanor with which they present themselves to impose favor on the interviewer to get the job. They will most likely discuss all their positive qualities and the positive things that they can do to meet the expectations of the job. This is an example of the social self as an individual and the way we navigate professional environments by choosing who we want to show up as and which role to play. This is also an example of front stage self. A very real possibility in this situation is that during the preparation for this, the person getting interviewed, could discuss how they feel they may not be good enough for the job and their insecurities regarding it to a friend on the phone. This shows their authentic backstage setting. In this setting, the person getting interviewed does not feel the need to impress or sway anyone and they can just show their true feelings which is also aligned with the spiritual self-concept from Williams.
chunks.label: Hypothetical job interview scenario
chunks.what_happened: The student presents a hypothetical scenario of a job interview to illustrate the front stage self during the interview and the backstage self when talking candidly with a friend.
chunks.people: an applicant, an interviewer, a friend

chunks.text: In conclusion, I see accurate parts to both theories. William James’ three selves theory does a good job of not keeping self-perception into one concise real versus fake box and for that reason I feel like it’s a more inclusive and realistic way to paint out self-perception. However, Erving Goffman’s front versus backstage gives a more closed approach that only allows a fake and real self. I personally believe that there is a lot more than fake versus real, and I align more with William James' three options because it allows for the ability to be real but selective. Both theories are well thought out and do a good job of explaining perception.
chunks.label: Comparing theories of self-perception
chunks.what_happened: The student compares William James' theory of the three selves with Erving Goffman's front and backstage theory, expressing an alignment with James' perspective.

n4811bebf.title: Analyzing Gender Dynamics in Popular Television

chunks.text:
Hegemonic Masculinity and Women as “The Other” in “Sex and the City”

In the show “Sex and the City” Carrie writes a column that delves into her, and her friends struggles with finding eligible bachelors in Manhattan. As a young woman myself, I can attest to the fact that it’s nice to be taken care of and not have to worry about things in the company of a man. While that is true for most of the women in “Sex and the City”, these women work hard for their lives and don’t like it when they’re not validated for their careers. Living alone in New York City takes a lot of hard work and each of these women clearly put in the work to do so. Simone de Beauvoir wrote about women being regarded as “the other” because the man is the absolute which makes the women the object. Men are expected to have a successful career and become the provider for their family and women are just supposed to sit there and look pretty. One of the characters, Charlotte, is an art dealer. Naturally working in the city, she meets many famous artists. One day she met a big-time artist who invited her to his home upstate to see some of his new work. Charlotte makes the trip and soon realizes the artist is painting various women’s body parts and wants her to model. De Beauvoir states men view women's body as an obstacle and is instantly burdened by everything it touches. A woman becomes “the other” because the man is the absolute and therefore society allows men to disregard women’s ideas and opinions. This happens quite often on the show and in the real world. De Beauvoir states women have always been subordinated to men because men felt they were more essential to society. Charlotte was shocked by the artist's actions and decided to leave; causing the male artist to change his view on her from “the other”. Women are frequently viewed as having “too many” emotions and hormones which society says makes them less equip to make real-world decisions. Clearly the women in this show are very successful and do not need men to tell them otherwise.

Many women would say some men can be regarded as having large egos and little regard for women. This is true when it comes to hegemonic masculinity; which is the practice of upholding the dominant nature of men. This concept is showcased in season one, episode two of the show “Sex and the City”. In this episode, Carrie’s doing research on men who only sleep with models. One of her friends, Barkley is what the women call a “modelizer”, or a man who only sleeps with models. This is regarded as hegemonic masculinity because people are just allowing this behavior to happen, as if it isn’t degrading not only to the models but to average women. In this episode, Barkley talks about meeting the models and he mentions “you gotta treat them like they’re regular girls” (Barkley), as if they’re a different bread than any other woman. This behavior is absolutely unacceptable because as mentioned above, this also makes women viewed as “the other”. Hegemonic masculinity is also displayed in season one, episode five. Carrie sleeps with a man from France while he’s in town on business. When she wakes up the next morning after he left the hotel, she finds an envelope with one thousand dollars in it. While some women may appreciate this, Carrie was appalled at the fact that he thought that was necessary. By this man paying Carrie, it put him in a dominant position over her and made her feel inferior to him. She felt disappointed because besides their physical lust for each other she felt like they had a great connection. Carrie didn’t know “whether to take it as an incredible compliment or as an incredible insult” (Bradshaw). In the writing by Brett Stroudt, he feels hegemonic masculinity can help men appreciate women for the “mothering” love they give men. This statement could be true, but also men should recognize women bring much more to their lives than acting as their mother. In general, men have this invisible power over women, and they exercise this power by participating in hegemonic masculine behaviors such as being assertive and aggressive.

Women have come so far in being able to accomplish their hopes and dreams over the years. Men tend to view women as “the other”, but the women in the show “Sex and the City” withstand this stereotype as they are all very successful without the guidance of a man. A lot of men in the show also participate in hegemonic masculinity behaviors. Carrie, Charlotte, Samantha and Miranda all have their fair share of interactions with these men, and they realize they’re let down consistently by this behavior. The women in this show discover how these concepts affect typical women and they ultimately try to do everything in their power to resist hegemonic masculine behaviors and being viewed as “the other”.
chunks.label: Analyzing Sex and the City through gender theory
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes episodes and themes from the television show 'Sex and the City' through sociological theories of hegemonic masculinity and Simone de Beauvoir's concept of women as 'the other'.

n3faa2958.title: Examining Modern Consumerism and Exploitative Labor

chunks.text:
We almost all have an iPhone. Most likely we have all had a few and have upgraded every few years. We chase what's new to boost our perceived social status regardless of economic background. We often don’t notice where the products we buy come from. Look at iPhones, predominantly produced in China and under unethical practices and mining techniques. Production has increased at exponential rates due to consumer demand. As demand increases prices become more affordable. These technologies are an example of how McDonaldization has affected other aspects of production technology outside of fast food. Worker surveillance and assembly have exponentially expanded the capabilities of product creation. Alienation is the concept that keeps workers working by subjecting them to unfulfilling tasks that take personal expression out of mass production. Examples of this include assembly lines. A McDonald's assembly station or drive-through keeps employees focused on one task at a time while making individuals work parts to a production line. Factory workers, similarly, to McDonald's employees, are tasked and taught to work on a limited number of tasks, making each step impersonal. Taking self-expression out of production. These practices oppress worker creativity and move away from self-fulfilling goals. This cycle has been created to number the market and force producers to produce and those producers to continue consuming. In class, we watched a commercial for GMC. The Christmas commercial involved a couple buying new cars before the holidays and advertising what seemed to be affordable prices. These prices are marketed to normalize and promote commercial spending. Creating a norm that everyone should be able to buy new cars whenever they want. The promotional advertisement was created to increase spending. Money is power in our society. Through modern technology and marketing strategies, consumerism normalizes and adopts a spending cycle that keeps us spending more.

What makes meaning? What gives us as humans satisfaction? Consumerism is the narrative that has been socially adopted to bring us enjoyment. Looking at Holidays shows us prime examples of American consumerism in mass accepting quantities. For example, Christmas, gift giving was an almost ancient part of the traditional holiday but recently almost exclusively what surrounds this time of year. During 2023 in the United States, it was estimated that holiday retail sales would reach new levels projected to be around 957 billion dollars (Smith, P.). These figures are outstanding, showing direct relevancy between consumer-based holidays and projected spending levels. But where are these items coming from? Most are made in China with few worker protection programs in place. Looking at kids' toys, more and more easily produced wheeled, scale models, and puzzle toys are coming from China. Toys like this and similar products saw a drastic increase, valued at 17.8 billion dollars in 2021 (Mileva, Geri). Commodity Fetishism increases the consumer's likelihood of purchasing a product to identify with the in-group of consumerism. Manufacturing techniques have created things at rates never seen in previous timeframes. Society has normalized consumer production methods and has created a norm that to find meaning and take part in traditions and holidays we are required to spend money.

Meaning is all subjective and marketable. Companies will stop at nothing to get ahead of the curve on trends and automated assembly techniques. In the media, we are bombarded with advertisements for new products making every new thing better than the last. This is done on purpose. Large corporations want us to keep buying. Through the creation and concept of McDonaldization, we can see how technology is advancing at alarming rates. These new practices are also taking away personal value from the employees and instilling a mentality of consumption. We often overlook unsafe and unethical treatment of employees by focusing on the promised outcome the product will give us. These practices have forever changed our country's marketplace through the idealization of consumption and demand for popular products.

Work Cited

Mileva, Geri. “What Does the U.S. Import from China? Statistics to Know in 2024.” RSS, Threecolts, 12 Dec. 2023, www.threecolts.com/blog-articles/what-usa-import-china.

Smith, P. “Topic: U.S. Christmas Season Shopping.” Statista, www.statista.com/topics/991/us-christmas-season/#topicOverview. Accessed 2 May 2024.
chunks.label: Reflections on consumerism, McDonaldization, and alienation
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on consumerism, iPhone production, McDonaldization, alienation among assembly line workers, and how holiday marketing pushes people to spend money.

nb414c5c1.title: Facing Gender Stereotypes in the Gym

chunks.text: Do women truly get treated with the same respect as men? Women are often discriminated against in the workplace, in schools, and in other areas of society. They may be paid less for the same work as men, have fewer opportunities for promotion, and be subject to sexual harassment or other forms of discrimination. Women are often stereotyped as being emotional, weak, or irrational, while men are seen as strong, rational, and in control. This can lead to women being underestimated or overlooked in certain situations. Women are often objectified in the media and popular culture, reducing them to their physical appearance and sexual desirability. This results in women being seen as less valuable or worthy of respect than men. These patterns of unequal treatment are systemic and widespread, and they can have a negative impact on women's lives and opportunities. Due to women’s physical appearance, they are often undervalued, which results in them getting less respect than men and being treated as less than.
chunks.label: Gender inequality and respect for women
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the systemic unequal treatment, discrimination, stereotyping, and objectification of women in society.

chunks.text: I work at a gym, here at the University of North Carolina Wilmington, and in my hometown. There, my job is to observe the patrons and make sure no one gets hurt while working out. I am also required to spot anyone if they ask for assistance. However, if I am working with another male, men tend to ask them for a sport rather than me because I am a female. This is because men tend to perceive women as weaker just because the common stereotype defines men as more well-built and muscular compared to the stereotype of women, who are identified as nurturing and tender. Most men do not realize that women can be just as strong as men. I lift weights every day and am much stronger than most people realize because of my physical appearance. I am only 5’3 and 135 pounds so men may think I look incapable of spotting them because of my appearance. In reality, I am very strong and capable of spotting a male.
chunks.label: Working as a gym monitor and being underestimated
chunks.what_happened: The student works at gyms at UNCW and in her hometown where male patrons avoid asking her for a spot because she is female and petite, despite her being strong.

chunks.text: Not only have I experienced being judged based on my physical appearance while working at the gym, but I have also experienced objectification by men while working out at the gym. I have had many experiences where I will catch men staring at me or other people will tell me they saw someone creepily staring at me. I have also had men, some much older, come up and flirt with me. Men have followed me around the gym just to stare at me and tried to engage with me in an unwanted way. Men have also made unsolicited comments about my body and appearance in the gym. They have invaded my personal space by standing too close to me or, specifically, one time a man came up behind me while I was squatting and spotted me even though I did not ask for a sport nor did I need one. I have also witnessed these same exact scenarios happen to other females in the gym. All of these go unreported, which allows men to continue to get away with this behavior.
chunks.label: Objectification and harassment while working out
chunks.what_happened: While working out at the gym, the student experienced men staring at her, following her, flirting, making unsolicited comments, and invading her space by spotting her unasked.
chunks.people: male gym patrons, other female gym patrons

chunks.text: Naomi Wolf explains the beauty myth as the idea that women's value and worth are primarily based on their physical appearance and that there is a narrow, often unattainable standard of beauty that women are expected to conform to. The beauty myth creates unrealistic expectations for women to achieve a particular body type, skin tone, and facial features, often by using makeup, cosmetic procedures, and restrictive diets. According to Wolf, the beauty myth is perpetuated by various industries, including the fashion, beauty, and diet industries, as well as the media. These industries profit from promoting the idea that women must look a certain way to be successful, desirable, and happy. The beauty myth has been criticized for placing unrealistic and harmful expectations on women, which can lead to low self-esteem, body image issues, and even eating disorders. These beauty standards are created by men to objectify all women.
chunks.label: Naomi Wolf's beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Naomi Wolf's concept of the beauty myth and how industries and societal standards harm and objectify women.

chunks.text: Women are not the only ones expected to meet high standards, men are also required to be tough, dominating, and aggressive according to hegemonic masculinity. Men who embody these traits are seen as more masculine and are often rewarded with social status and power. For example, a study was done at an all-boy school called Rockport, to see if hegemonic masculinity was beneficial or problematic for these boys. They benefited from hegemonic masculinity because it influenced them into how men are supposed to behave, disciplined them, and gave them a common bond. Men can also use hegemonic masculinity to make women feel less than them by reinforcing traditional gender norms, asserting their dominance, and treating women as objects rather than individuals. Men who treat women as objects to be admired or desired are using hegemonic masculinity to reinforce traditional gender roles. They are perpetuating the idea that women exist primarily for men's pleasure or entertainment, rather than as individuals with their own desires and needs.
chunks.label: Hegemonic masculinity and gender dominance
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses hegemonic masculinity, cites a study on an all-boys school, and explains how men use it to assert dominance over women.

chunks.text: People often assume that I am physically incapable of certain tasks, such as spotting them in the gym, due to my physical appearance. In the gym, men tend to presume that I am not as strong as a male because of the beauty myth. This is because men perceive women as weaker due to traditional gender roles and societal expectations. Women are also expected to look a certain way, and I feel as though I fit into the stereotypes that are associated with the beauty myth. This results in me being treated a certain way by men because of my physical appearance. Women who conform to traditional beauty standards may receive more attention and compliments from others, particularly men. Men stare at me, follow me, flirt with me, invade my personal space, and make comments about my physical appearance in the gym, which is one example of the effects of the beauty myth. In these instances, men have also used hegemonic masculinity to make me feel like an object. Men can use hegemonic masculinity in the gym towards women to reinforce traditional gender norms, assert their dominance, and treat women as objects rather than individuals.
chunks.label: Applying sociological concepts to gym experiences
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how the beauty myth and hegemonic masculinity explain why men underestimate and objectify her at the gym.

chunks.text: Men often treat women differently because of the beauty myth and hegemonic masculinity. I have personally experienced this in my place of work and while working out. Men have made assumptions about my capabilities because of my appearance and common stereotypes created by the beauty myth. While at work, men tend to ask another male working for a spot rather than me because they assume that women are weak when women can be just as strong as men. Men have also objectified me in the gym by staring, following me, making sexual comments, and unwanted physical contact. By reinforcing traditional gender norms, asserting their dominance, and treating women as objects rather than individuals, men are using hegemonic masculinity to make women feel less than. Standing up to the men that partake in the beauty myth and hegemonic masculinity, would be one step toward preventing men from continuing these acts toward women. We can also speak out against these beauty standards that promote unrealistic body types, skin tones, or other physical features. By not accepting the standards of the beauty myth and hegemonic masculinity, we can put a stop to these stereotypes and unwanted acts committed toward women.
chunks.label: Conclusion on resisting stereotypes and objectification
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes her main points and argues for challenging hegemonic masculinity and unrealistic beauty standards.

n3963da3d.title: Labor and Value at Duck Donuts

chunks.text:
Capitalism, in its design is one of the most controversial topics in society today with people constantly examining the pros and cons. Capitalism values labor and products differently which can fluctuate with time. As an individual that has worked since starting high school, it is evident that humans in ourselves are commodities. To understand how capitalism works you have to understand that the commodities in our society are operated by a “free” market, which means that there is no regulation to them.

Karl Marx explains the concept of alienation through “Estranged labor”. In this article Marx better relates that an individual worker works for products that is not theirs because society deems it for survival. This relates to the concept of a “free” market because the labor of the worker is a commodity, the value of the work is determined by the market. Max Weber in the “Spirit of Capitalism and the Iron Cage”, relates the protestants to the modern-day society of capitalism. He proclaims that for the protestant’s capitalism was predestined because of their work ethic. This work ethic led to the “iron cage” which contributes to the “free” market by demonstrating that there is no regulation and no escape from it. Both of what Marx and Weber preached can be shown in modern day society through the minimum wage worker.
chunks.label: Theories of capitalism and labor
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses capitalism, commodities, and the free market, referencing theories of alienation by Karl Marx and the iron cage by Max Weber in relation to modern minimum wage workers.

chunks.text: I can relate to the capitalistic society and am familiar with how the ideology works. Being a minimum wage worker at Duck Donuts, I’ve realized that the value of the product that I produced goes fluctuates throughout the year. At the beginning of the year business is slow, because of new year resolutions and people are trying to get in shape for summer. The value of my job changes from month to month because it a mainly labor-induced job. What sets myself apart from the theories of Marx and Weber, is that I don’t work for survival in society. If that were not the case, the value of my labor would need to be higher than the exchange value that I put out.
chunks.label: Working at Duck Donuts
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on their personal job as a minimum wage worker at Duck Donuts, noting how business and labor value fluctuate throughout the year and how their situation compares to Marx and Weber's theories.

chunks.text: In conclusion, it can be stated that through the commodity of labor, the value of a product is exclusive to the amount of effort. The relationship between the commodities makes the supply and demand for a variety of items. Along with supply and demand is the creation of a social hierarchy that promotes only individuals with high revenue value.
chunks.label: Conclusion on labor value and social hierarchy
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes on how the commodity of labor, supply and demand, and product value create a social hierarchy favoring high-revenue individuals.

n880fbb51.title: Confronting Social Media and Beauty Standards

chunks.text: How often do you compare yourself to others as you scroll through Instagram, Facebook, or other social media platforms? Most people could say very often, especially teenage girls and young women. By comparing their physical appearances or even fashion choices to others, young girls are falling victim to societal beauty standards and accepting them. Although social media was created with the intention of bringing people together, it has caused a lot more issues than expected. Constantly seeing other females with the “perfect” body, hair, clothes, and life can cause young girls to feel very insecure about themselves. They may even feel like something is wrong with them because they do not look like the skinny Instagram model or the pretty girl from their high school that seems to get all of the boys. This leads to negative thoughts about one’s appearance or self as a whole, and can even lead to eating disorders, anxiety, and depression. Such ideas of what the “perfect” female should look like and the obsession females have with their appearances stems from the beauty myth. As if the beauty myth was not bad enough on its own, social media makes it impossible to escape the grips of comparison while displaying unrealistic societal beauty standards.
chunks.label: Social media and societal beauty standards
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how social media causes teenage girls and young women to compare themselves to unrealistic beauty standards, leading to insecurity and mental health issues.

chunks.text:
I can personally speak to how social media has affected me in a negative way and caused me to always compare myself to others. About two years ago, at the end of my junior year of high school, I noticed that I really started paying attention to what I looked like, and what the girls I followed on Instagram looked like. I would overanalyze everything about the pictures they posted and compare their appearances to mine. Were they prettier than me? Were their stomachs flatter than mine? Did they always have some sort of cute hairstyle? Were their clothes nicer and more fashionable than mine? And much more. These thoughts started to consume me and take up way more of my time and energy than they should have.

It is probably not a coincidence that this was happening at the same time the COVID-19 pandemic began. Since there was nothing else to do but sit at home, I was spending a lot more time on social media than I previously had been. This gave me more time to scroll and compare myself to these girls that I had never even met in real life. Were the bikini pictures they posted what they really looked like, or did they only look like that because they were posing and spent hours editing the picture? To me it did not matter and was not even something I had considered. All I was thinking was “I wish I looked like that”. After all of this started and a beach trip with my parents was quickly approaching, I decided to start working out a lot. It was not like I never exercised or did any physical activity to begin with, because it was actually quite the opposite. I played soccer from the time I was 4 years old all the way through high school, and I even ran cross country one year in addition to soccer. While most would have considered me an active person, I felt like I needed to exercise more, not for fun or for the sport I loved, but to change my body.

I began waking up every morning during the week and going for runs in my neighborhood, then doing additional workouts in my garage. While I told my parents and friends that I was doing this to stay in shape and because, well, “the whole world is shut down so what else and I going to do?”, my motives were a little different. My goal by exercising five days a week was to become thinner. Some mornings I genuinely enjoyed my runs, while others it was the last thing I wanted to do, but I made myself go anyway. For the entire summer I ran and did at home workouts hoping to look like the girls I was always comparing myself to.
chunks.label: Comparing oneself on Instagram and excessive exercising
chunks.what_happened: During high school and the COVID-19 lockdown, the student spent hours comparing herself to girls on Instagram and began intensely running and exercising five days a week to become thinner before a beach trip.
chunks.feelings: consumed, wished they looked like the girls, enjoyed runs on some mornings, reluctant on other mornings

chunks.text:
Today I still run and workout, but my motivation has completely changed. I work out to be healthier, to see growth, and as a stress reliever; not just to lose weight and look skinnier. The reason all of this occurred in the first place is due to the beauty myth. While I had no idea at the time, I was letting social media and the beauty myth control my life.

The beauty myth refers to the idea that women’s value comes from their appearance and from being attractive. Societal beauty standards came into existence because of the beauty myth. Naomi Wolfe explains that the beauty myth is a result of feminism and the advancements women have made in society. Women now have a lot more freedom and power than they once did, making the beauty myth the only remaining old feminine ideology that still has serious control over women today. Wolfe also discusses how men use the beauty myth to maintain their dominance over women. If women did not feel constant pressure about their looks and feel the need to be considered beautiful by men, then men would lose their power over women.

A common way that the beauty myth is used to control and oppress women can be seen in almost any business. When a woman works her way up to a position of authority or a high-level position, she often faces a lot of criticism. Men may make comments like, “She only got the job because of her looks” or “She’s not actually qualified she's just hot”. These comments show how deeply rooted the beauty myth is in society. Men will not be happy for a woman who has power, but if it were another male in the same position, they would likely be happy for them. When a woman holds significant power, she is attacked and ridiculed constantly because men feel threatened and jealous. Women feel they must be beautiful and fit into societal standards to be attractive and valued, but at the same time, beauty can also be used to disqualify them. Women are in a lose-lose situation because of this.

When it came to my experience with social media causing me to feel like I needed to change the way I looked, the beauty myth was largely at play. Although my family always told me I was “skinny”, the beauty myth was telling me that I wasn’t skinny “enough”. I felt that my value was in my appearance and that I needed to change how I looked in order to prove myself to others. Looking back now, I see that by comparing myself to every girl I saw on social media, I also felt like I was competing against them. I would see someone who looked a certain way and wished that I looked like that, but at the same time I disliked them for having what I considered to be a better physical appearance than me. Women seeing other women as competition is sadly another normal aspect of society that stems from the beauty myth. Competition between women only reinforces the beauty myth and prolongs the oppression women face. Previously I was unaware that the beauty myth even existed, but now it makes sense to me why I went through the things I did.

Ultimately, social media heavily reaffirms the beauty myth and makes it nearly impossible to not compare oneself to others, especially in the case of young girls and young women. Additionally, societal beauty standards are a result of the beauty myth and portray unrealistic expectations of what women should look like to be considered beautiful. The beauty myth causes a lot of emotional hardship for young women, and as I have personally experienced, can cause negative thoughts and views about oneself.
chunks.label: Analyzing experiences through the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Naomi Wolf's concept of the beauty myth, describes how it impacts women in workplaces and fuels competition, and reflects on how it influenced their own past insecurity and behavior.

n845b3a49.title: Performing on the Modern Global Stage

chunks.text: The Presentation of Self highlighted the idea that many of life’s interactions mirror a stage-actor relationship. The individual is the actor and the stage is society. Every actor presents him or herself on a stage, wether that stage be before friends, acquaintances or strangers. Goffman saw this as an extremely common situation, which everyone participate in unconsciously or consciously. In his view, behaviors were shaped around responses to performances. More specifically, other’s perceptions of us begin to form a collective impression of who we are in society.
chunks.label: Goffman's presentation of self concept
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Erving Goffman's concept of the presentation of self, describing how social interactions mirror theater and how individuals perform for others to shape social impressions.

chunks.text: Goffman was groundbreaking in his ideas in the Presentation of Self. Harari further expounded upon the ties between Goffman’s ideas and modern technological advances. With this insight, we can see a clear indication of small community degradation due to global communities beginning to uptick. Moreover, modern individuals have invested significant time and energy into their personal performance on global stages such as social media. The question still appears as, will we use new technology to increase community or watch as traditional communities degrade due to modern performances of individuals on the global stage?
chunks.label: Applying Goffman's ideas to modern technology and community
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Harari's connection between Goffman's theories and modern technology, questioning how online performances affect traditional and global communities.

chunks.text:
Inequalities and discrimination within genders have persisted long throughout history in not only the United States, but around the world. These inequalities occur in many aspects whether it be in culture, politics, or within occupation. What all women have in common is that they can all relate to feeling some sort of discrimination and being treated unfairly, solely because of the biases that come from gender, at some point in their lives. These inequalities between men and women have persisted within communities and throughout society for as long as anyone can remember. While forms of discrimination can come in various forms and in various settings, one setting in particular is in the workplace. Regardless of what that workplace is, they are all notorious for practices that involve countless forms of unfair policies towards women which affect their employment, salaries, and the length of training. These policies, which have occurred for centuries, are too often seen as societal norms further implementing a false idea stating that men and women are not created equal.

While it is true that over the years, we, as a society, have gotten closer to achieving gender equality. Nonetheless, it is still an imperative issue that needs to be resolved and we still have much growing to do. Women are constantly subject to discrimination and getting the “short end of the stick” when it comes to their careers specifically. Within this course, we learned about the endless inequalities between genders and how men and women are not treated equally. When it comes to discrimination towards women, it would simply be a disservice to not mention those discriminatory events that occur within the walls of their workplaces. Gender inequalities in the workplace are important to recognize because they lead to discriminatory treatment, unequal payment, and sex labeled careers.

This semester, we learned about gender and discussed many topics surrounding this module. Author of “The Beauty Myth”, Naomi Wolf, discusses in her writing that women are constantly objectified and required to uphold certain beauty standards. Wolf begins her reading by stating “The affluent, educated, liberated women of the First World, who can enjoy freedoms unavailable to any women ever before, do not feel as free as they want to. During the past decade, women breached the power structure; meanwhile, eating disorders rose exponentially and cosmetic surgery became the fastest-growing medical specialty” (Wolf 1990). Wolf provides the information that proves the fact that women are notoriously expected to uphold traditional feminine values and ideas. This expectation of upholding feminine values relates to how women are often discriminated against in their professional careers. Wolf also presents that women struggle with confidence by expressing “It is no accident that so many potentially powerful women feel this way. We are in the midst of a violent backlash against feminism that uses images of female beauty as a political weapon against women’s advancement: the beauty myth. As a woman released themselves from the feminine mystique of domesticity, the beauty myth took over its lost ground, expanding as it waned to carry on its work of social control” (Wolf 1990). Wolf provides proof that women who are discriminated against lack confidence due to the inappropriate treatment they generally receive. Women are often inclined to be the “nurturing mother” and be the main caretaker, given no room for exploration or individuality, that of which is in plethora for men. This assumption feeds into employers, impacting their actions on ideology to prefer hiring men over women. The false beliefs that society has allowed employers to believe brings in an idea of women’s supposed “lack of time”. Gender inequalities bombard every aspect of women's lives and are a huge issue in the workplace especially. Naomi Wolf helps to bring awareness to this unjust treatment.

Women are often treated in inequitable ways in the workplace. “Women encounter discrimination in hiring and are less likely to be perceived as capable and committed to the occupation than men” (Friedman 2015). This discrimation comes about because of the stereotypes created in society. Those stereotypes often perceive women as having “womanly duties” which include the idea that mothers should solely take care of the kids, cook, and clean. On the other hand, there are also stereotypes towards men that state that the man of the house should be the “breadwinner”. While these stereotypes have declined in the 21st century, they are still valid within occupational environments. These assumptions that women should stay home while men make money cause the view that women have less time and commitment for higher authority jobs and that they simply are not suitable for some careers. This is something that absolutely should not be assumed based on the gender of someone. Because women are expected to be in charge of family care and childcare, they are often in need to take time off to do so. “Because women are more likely to anticipate interruptions in paid employment, they may be unwilling to make the long-term commitment to an employer that a position of authority often entails'' (Wolf and Fligstein 1979). To employers, not being able to work long hours is a disadvantage, making it more likely for a man to be hired over a woman. While one should obviously be hired due to their knowledge, skill, and cooperation within the workplace, employers should not conclude these qualities based on the stereotypes of women.

For years, the gender pay gap has been a very controversial topic because many believe that it is a myth. Regardless of some beliefs, a gender pay gap has been proven time and time again. The gender wage gap is “cited at 77 cents to every dollar” (Friedman 2015). This means that on average, males in the US receive twenty-three cents per dollar higher than the average female. Although this gap has decreased overtime, it has been stable for quite some time now. Most of this gap occurs due to factors such as job training and education, but there is still an unexplained 9% of the wage gap. This 9% is believed to occur solely because of discrimination. Over 50 years ago, the United States passed the Equal Pay Act, requiring that employers pay men and women equally for doing the same work. If two employees are doing the same work, they should be paid the same, but unfortunately this is not always the case. For example, in professional athletics, men are usually paid more than women. This is done because men’s sports achive higher revenue, allowing them to receive higher earning. Mariq states “90% of sports television hours have been devoted to men’s sports, whereby women’s sports are viewed as less significant for media coverage” (Marig 2020). Women’s sports can be just as engaging as men’s sports which is why the media coverage for men and women in the same sport should equal. Overall, pay should be duplicate for men and women because it should be based solely off of skill and nothing else.

We often think of specific jobs as predominantly achieved by a male or female. “Gendered organizations are workplaces where advantage and disadvantage, corrupt and control, action and emotion, meaning and identity patterned through and in terms of a distinction between male and female, masculine and feminine” (Mastracci and Arreola 2016). Gender norms have constantly been a pattern for years and is based solely on stereotypes of men and women. Like mentioned earlier career paths and pay should not be justified by gender, but by skill and hard work. Studies show that “Women predominantly major in fields that steer them into lower-paid occupations such as humanities, education, and social sciences such as psychology, while men major in fields, such as science, engineering, and business, that lead to higher-paying jobs” (Kugler, Tinsley and Ukhaneva 2021). This segregation is an issue causing women to be too intimidated to break the pattern of male predominant jobs. Men are also more likely to be given positions of authority over women. “Recent research has shown that women are much less likely than men to be in positions of authority, even when they have the same level of education and occupational status, and that this difference cannot be explained by the fact that men are more likely to be self-employed” (Wolf and Fligstein 1979). Something must be done to create careers to be sexually unbiased. Research shows that this process has been “stalled” and as a whole we must stop the segregation of female and male career paths. Cross‐national research suggests that an even greater focus on men's roles and movement into historically “feminine” domains is necessary for ultimately dismantling the persistent gender gap and “installing” the gender revolution (Friedman 2015). Because men are primarily working the higher paying jobs, they are less likely to want to be a part of the female prevalent jobs, due to the lower income. Like Friedman stated, to “unstall” the gender revolution we must mix the genders practicing these sex labeled careers to provide a fair workspace for both genders.

Throughout history, women have been treated as “less than” in all aspects of life but particularly the workforce. While the list of these inequalities is a lengthy one, just a few include that of unequal pay, discriminatory treatment, and sex labeled careers. It is important to note that inequalities occur all around us. Women and men see gender inequalities within their homes and communities every day. Some men still see women as caregivers and responsible for the household when they need to start seeing women for who they are today. Today's women are self-sufficient, independent, and powerful. They are highly educated, strong, reliable, and persistent. By keeping women from various aspects of the workforce, it is simply just a disservice to the economy. What this issue truly boils down to is that we, collectively, men and women, need to do more to improve gender equality. By educating communities of the disparities between genders, we can break down the barriers of inequality and change societal norms. It is time to see more women in positions of power. There should be no discrepancy towards females in the workplace, or even in life. Men and women should be observed and valued the same. Gender should not be the characteristic that defines us or separates us from our fellow coworkers.

Works Cited

Friedman, S. (2015). Still a “Stalled Revolution”? Work/Family Experiences, Hegemonic Masculinity, and Moving Toward Gender Equality. Sociology Compass, 9(2), 140–155. https://doi.org/10.1111/soc4.12238

Kugler, A. D., Tinsley, C. H., & Ukhaneva, O. (2021). Choice of majors: are women really different from men? Economics of Education Review, 81, 102079. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.econedurev.2021.102079

Marig, M. (2020). Women in Sports - Issue on Pay Gap, Media Coverage and Women Representation in Sports.

Mastracci, S., & Arreola, V. I. (2016). Gendered Organizations: How Human Resource Management Practices Produce and Reproduce Administrative Man. Administrative Theory & Praxis, 38(2), 137–149. https://doi.org/10.1080/10841806.2015.1130523

Wolf, N. (2015). The beauty myth: how images of beauty are used against women. Vintage Books.

Wolf, W. C., & Fligstein, N. D. (1979). Sex and Authority in the Workplace: The Causes of Sexual Inequality. American Sociological Review, 44(2), 235. https://doi.org/10.2307/2094507
chunks.label: Gender inequality in the workplace
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes gender discrimination, wage gaps, stereotypes, and occupational segregation in the workplace, citing academic sources and calling for equality.

n5e8f710f.title: Theoretical Delineations of the Metaphysical Self

chunks.text:
The human experience is entirely centered around the person, themselves. At first glance this sounds fairly obvious, yet there is a time in everyone’s life where they question the essential origin of who they are. The question of “Who am I?”, is a core component of true self-actualization and proves to be a valuable part of every human’s experience. To effectively answer questions such as these, there must be a delineation and separation between what role the physical body plays and what the self, or metaphysical being plays in who a person is. In addition to this delineation, the Self has been further broken down into components that aide in understanding the role that the Self carries out.

Mead sought to delineate between the Self and the body in which the Self resides. He specifically advocates for the idea that the Self and the organism are completely distinguishable. The body refers to the organism, or the physical portrayal of the Self. Simply stated, the body is the anchor to which the self adheres. The Self refers to the metaphysical attributes that compose every persons’ being. These two, separate components are what collaborate to form the person or the being. Complimentary to Mead’s work, James brought an even more specific approach to the understanding of what the Self is. He believed that there are four components of the Self: the natural self, social self, spiritual self, and the Ego. The natural self is said to be what one possesses in material goods, and in companionship or close relationships. The social self is composed of the ideas and perceptions that others have about someone. The spiritual self is the totality of someone’s moral and ethical actions and beliefs. And finally, the Ego is the personality of one’s being. These four components directly compose the metaphysical self, as described my Mead. From these explanations, it is evident that all aspects of the Self collaborate to form the metaphysical being. The four components of James’s Self are equally important, and interface with Mead’s delineation seamlessly.

The question of who one is, will never be answered completely. However, Mead and James’s work towards answering that question provides significant insight into how everyone can view themselves more accurately. By breaking down the Self, one can understand the areas in which they are unique. Those qualities of Self, in conjunction of the understanding that the body is separate, gives a well-rounded picture as to what essentially a being consists of. These ideas are revolutionary to the understanding of how every being or person is composed, and their concepts may prove to be increasingly valuable through human development.
chunks.label: Theories of the Self by Mead and James
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on questions of identity and self-actualization, examining Mead's distinction between the physical body and the metaphysical Self as well as James's four components of the Self.

n411aef4d.title: Performing the Self on Social Media

chunks.text:
Goffman breaks down “the self” into two main parts; the performance and the character. Before we get into the separate parts, it’s important to understand “the self” as a whole. According to Goffman, there is no “true self,” but instead it’s a consolidated illusion we’re constantly changing and putting on. “The self” provides us with the necessary resources to act suitably when presented with a stimulus. While “the self” provides us with these assets, it can also be a product of the performance we’re putting on. With that said, the performance is the production we put on and maintain while presenting ourselves to diverse audiences. The performance also varies depending on who the spectators are. For example, we typically act differently at school or work compared to when we’re with our friends. This brings us into the character, which is the outcome of the performance. “The self” includes the psychobiology of our personality whereas the character is the way we perform to leave a certain impression on people. The character allows us to control how the audience will react to us because we attempt to produce reactions as if we’re an outsider looking in. With these parts of the self-production working simultaneously, it allows us to correctly acknowledge a stimulus.

While Goffman breaks “the self” into two parts, James divides it into four main parts; the material self, social self, spiritual self and the pure ego. James feels the total of a man’s self consists of everything he can call his. Not just his body or thoughts, but everything he physically owns and anything that gives him some type of emotion. The Material self is the physical aspects of one’s life they identify with, such as their clothes, cars, house, etc. The Social self is how peers view us and our role in a specific context. The Spiritual self consists of our beliefs or values, consistency in our reaction to stimulus and our relative emotions or behaviors. The Pure Ego is the most comfortable we can get; it’s our unseen essence and how an individual views themself. Using these four categories, James divides aspects of our personality into being a part of the “me” or the “I”. The “me” is our response to external stimuli, and how our interactions create the experience of the self. The “me” is also referred to as our social self; how we act in social situations. While the “I” is our answer to how others view us and what we’ve learned subconsciously from interactions with people.

Between Goffman’s and James’ concepts, we’re able to use several aspects of each to reply to stimuli accordingly depending on what type of social situation we’re in. Goffman believes we adjust our behaviors to act a certain way in social settings while James feels we use our own emotions to react to an event. By using these techniques together, we can appropriate the correct response to any factors we encounter outside or inside the body. For example, social media has a huge influence on everyone, and it’s where people seek the approval of others. When anyone makes a post on social media, they first embody the performer; posting something they feel others will enjoy. Then the character and social self come into play because depending on the feedback we get; we’ll act in response to that. The character and social self are concerned with how others view us, and they generate our justification of our actions. Next comes the pure ego, which will help us connect what we’ve learned from this interaction to our past, present and future presence on social media. We may not realize it, but we’re constantly enduring social and emotional stimuli to determine our response based on how we feel others will perceive it.

Interacting with and reacting to people is part of our day-to-day life, even if we don’t realize it. As much as humans try not to, we care about what others think of us, and we’re constantly trying to act the way we want others to perceive us. Overall, the evidence shown throughout Goffman and James’ work provides us with an appreciation for our reaction to social and emotional stimuli. Using a combination of Goffman and James’ concepts, we can better understand how we form connections with others based upon our actions.
chunks.label: Goffman and James on the self
chunks.what_happened: The student explains and compares theories of the self from Erving Goffman and William James, using examples like social media to show how people manage impressions and respond to stimuli.

n2f84c3db.title: Performing in Interviews and Everyday Life

chunks.text: Erving Goffman has this idea that when we interact with people it is as if we are on a stage. By the word “stage” we are always putting on a performance around everyone. We might act differently in different scenarios based on evaluating the circumstance. From there we have a back stage and a front stage personality. We perform differently in front of certain people which is what separates the back from the front stage. The backstage is how we act to the people we are the closest and most comfortable with. While the front stage is the people that we put our main performance on for.
chunks.label: Goffman's front and back stage
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Erving Goffman's concept of social interaction as a performance on a stage, distinguishing between front stage and back stage personalities.

chunks.text: Then we have Charles Cooley's idea of the “Looking Glass-Self” in which we view ourselves based on how we think other people see us. We use other people’s opinions and thoughts on us as a reflection of who we are. We then take those opinions and judgments to refine how we act, portraying how we want them to see us. First someone might think about what others are thinking about them. Then they might imagine what the other person’s judgement of their appearance. Lastly you react and respond based on what you think their judgements are.
chunks.label: Cooley's looking-glass self
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces Charles Cooley's concept of the looking-glass self, explaining how individuals view and alter themselves based on imagined judgments from others.

chunks.text: According to Goffman, when we are out in the real world searching for a job and attending a job interview we put on our front stage. Going into a job interview you want to be as professional as you can be. When you walk into the room of a job interview your mannerisms change, you say things differently and act accordingly for the situation. For example you shake their hand, you dress more professional than you would be in your back stage. You use appropriate formal etiquette and grammar, for instance you wouldn’t use any type of “slang” words to come off unprofessional. Your body language is going to change by sitting up right, your going to smile and nod your head. By doing all of these things you are putting on your front stage on because it is as if you are putting you best foot forward.
chunks.label: Job interview as front stage
chunks.what_happened: The student describes a hypothetical job interview scenario to illustrate how people present their professional front stage.

chunks.text: Now I want you to think of the times that you are having a game night with your friends and family, this would be where your backstage comes out. When you are with your friends and family you might make more jokes then you would in your front stage. Let’s say you are having a game night and you win the game, you might yell, scream, jump up and down, etc. This is an example of your backstage because you wouldn’t do these types of things in your front stage. The way you dress might also be different in that you would wear more ‘comfy’ clothes like sweatpants, sweatshirts, shorts, t-shirts. Your backstage comes our with the people you are most comfortable around. Some people refer to the back stage as your comfort zone or your true self.
chunks.label: Game night as backstage
chunks.what_happened: The student describes hypothetical situations with friends and family during game nights to illustrate backstage behavior.

chunks.text: You can compare the scenarios from a front stage and back stage from the moment you enter till the moment you leave. When you walk into a job interview you are most likely to shake their hand, smile, and introduce yourself. While if you walk in to you friends house to hangout you might hug them and say a more informal hello. Then during the middle of an interview you might talk in a very formal tone, good posture, and keep smiling. While if you are in the middle of hanging out with you friends you might say some dumb things or laugh a lot. Lastly by the end of your interview you would most likely get up and shake their hand and leave. If you are saying goodbye to your friends you might give them a hug good bye and talk while you are leaving.
chunks.label: Comparing interview and friendship scenarios
chunks.what_happened: The student contrasts typical actions during a job interview with hanging out at a friend's house to demonstrate front stage versus backstage behavior.

chunks.text: The looking glass self could also be portrayed in an interview. When entering the interview you start to think about what the person conducting the interview is thinking. Then from there we respond to them based on what we think their judgements are. For example if you walk into an interview you might be thinking that they think you look presentable and well respected. From there you are going to continue to answer the questions from the interview in a well presented and respectable way. We tend to think that the person conducting the interview sees us that way because that is how we want to be seen. If we think that they believe we are respectable and well presented then we are more likely to act that way.
chunks.label: Looking-glass self in an interview
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how Cooley's looking-glass self applies in a job interview setting through imagined judgments and reactions.

chunks.text: Lastly, another example of the looking glass self could be getting embarrassed when giving a speech. Imagine you are up on a stage or platform and you are giving a speech. When all of the sudden you look into the audience and you see some people giving you a look of disapproval. From there you are more likely to take that judgement in and you could possibly mess up your speech. We start by thinking what they are thinking about us. Therefore we might start to think that we are incompetent in our speech. Then we act upon it which might end up making us incompetent.
chunks.label: Looking-glass self during a speech
chunks.what_happened: The student describes an example of giving a speech and perceiving disapproval from an audience to explain the looking-glass self.

chunks.text:
Have you ever felt as if you are playing a role in life? According to Erving Goffman, everyone is viewed as a character and a performer. In life, you have to play different roles to make everyone happy. By playing these roles, this is how society judges you. If you play a good role, society will like you. If not, you will be disliked by society. These roles are also looped into the collective consciousness where people with similar beliefs are put in this stereotype of their type of person. Playing a role in life causes people to get through unneeded stress and makes them feel as if they have to make up a character to be around people when we should genuinely escape this collective consciousness let people live the life they want to.

Playing a role is the basis of how society judges you. Through your roles, you define to everyone the person you are. Goffman stated, "the very structure of the self can be seen in terms of how we arrange for such performances in our Anglo-American society." (Goffman 256) When he talks about the self, he is talking about the image you portray out into society. The self is something that is housed inside someone's body that allows them to play this role. Many people have this happen in their life and never realize. Our roles constantly judge us, and if you break your role, the whole thought of you will be different throughout society.

In your life, your role has two main parts the character and the performer. The charter is stated as "a figure, typically a fine one, whose spirit, strength, and other sterling qualities the performer was designed to evoke." (Goffman 256) I take this statement as the character is the person you become due to what the performer wants. The performer is defined as "a harried fabricator of impressions involved in the all-too-human task of staging a performance." (Goffman 256) In my mind, this is saying that we are not our true selves. We are just trying to make everyone believe that the "performance" is the real you and that you are different from what you are.
chunks.label: Goffman's roles and the self
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Erving Goffman's sociological theory of roles, performers, characters, and the self, explaining how society judges individuals based on the roles they play.

chunks.text: In my life, I have had this happen numerous times. I catch myself changing who I am to fit in. I never really knew what this was called until I learned about roles. The one significant time in my life I noticed me playing a role to make people like me, and I had to become a completely different person. This time in my life was my freshman year of high school. I had these friends from middle school who were considered popular kids. I tried so hard to change who I am to fit in with them, and it worked. I had them all fooled that I was exactly like them, a kid that pushed their parent's boundaries. I eventually had to give up the role. It became too much to handle. I could not put up with the act anymore, so I dropped it. This action caused me to lose many friends, but it was the best thing for my mental health. It allowed me to become my authentic self again.
chunks.label: Faking a persona to fit in with popular friends
chunks.what_happened: During their freshman year of high school, the student changed who they were to fit in with popular middle school friends by acting like a kid who pushed parental boundaries. Eventually finding the act too difficult to handle, the student dropped the role, losing friends but regaining authentic mental health.

chunks.text: Another time I have done this in my life was when I was younger. My parents had this idea that I needed to be the perfect child and never mess up, so I took this role to the extreme and made them believe that I was as great as they wanted me to be. This standard made my life very hard. I had to get straight A's, or I thought they would be disappointed in me. I took any time I got a bad grade on a quiz to heart and would think about it over and over again, which caused me to start doing terribly in school. This role of the perfect child also carried over into sports. My family is a huge sports family. My older sister was a star softball player, and I felt I had to live up to her shoes. I was practicing 20 to 30 a week to be able to perform this role. This role had terrible effects on my body. I hurt my arm many times and did not tell anyone because I did not want to disappoint my parents. It took me until I turned 15 to realize that my parents only wanted me to be happy, and I was not disappointing them as long as I gave 100 percent effort.
chunks.label: Trying to be the perfect child in school and sports
chunks.what_happened: Growing up, the student tried to be the perfect child by striving for straight A's and excessively practicing sports to live up to their older sister's athletic success. The student hid physical injuries out of fear of disappointing their parents, until realizing at age fifteen that their parents only wanted them to be happy.

chunks.text:
Through these experiences, this is what allowed me to realize that roles are a real thing that happens in everyone's life. If you say you had never played a role in your life, you are lying. You may not notice that this is a thing that has been happening, but you are playing a role, and society is judging you on every move you make. Society is a very judgmental crowd. You cannot do anything without it judging you. You may believe that everyone likes the role you are playing, but there will always be someone who does not like it. You have to learn that you should not try to make society happy and focus on yourself.

Throughout life, you will always play a role, whether to get a job or in a relationship. We do things to make everyone happy at the expense of ourselves. This causes people to have mental illnesses. We have this pressure of people watching every move we make so that people in society will accept us, which causes us to put way too much stress on ourselves. This is where depression and anxiety come from because we walk on theoretical eggshells, trying not to mess up and get judged by society. The advice I would give from someone that has been through this is that you need to live your life and only worry about what you think of yourself. Life is a journey that only you will be around to see yourself to the end at the end of the day. You have to live with the person you are. Society will eventually forget everything you have done when something more significant happens. However, you will be there with all the things you have done on your conscience.

Another topic that I believe ties into the roles of life is the collective conscious. The collective conscious is defined as "a set of shared beliefs, ideas, and moral attitudes which operate as a unifying force within society." (Durkheim Collective Consciousness slides) I take this as society believes that everyone should be grouped by the way they think, such as people with similar political views or religious beliefs. This and the roles are very similar because your collective consciousness is based on the role you play.

The collective consciousness allows you to find what you believe in and be grouped with people who have a similar outlook on the same things. This could be through institutions such as schools where everyone is there for the same fundamental reason to better their lives by getting a degree. This is something that you have to accept. You are always going to be in a group that has the same ideals as you.
chunks.label: Societal roles and collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how everyone plays roles in society and connects this to Durkheim's concept of the collective consciousness, where individuals are grouped based on shared beliefs and institutions.

chunks.text: In my life, this is always there. In high school, I hung out with athletes because I was an athlete and had similar views on life. This also links into the roles because I was playing a role in my school as an athlete; thus, I was grouped into this collective consciousness that I was meant to hang out with people like me.
chunks.label: Hanging out with high school athletes
chunks.what_happened: In high school, the student hung out with athletes because of playing sports and sharing similar views on life, which fit them into the collective consciousness of the athlete role.

chunks.text:
This is where I believe society is messed up. Society has this way of making everyone believe that you have to be exactly what society wants, which is not valid. You can have your views on things and still get along with people. We need to be individuals, not a group that society thinks they can push around.

Another example that I have noticed in my life is school. Here at college, I have noticed that everyone has this same ideal about college, and this ideal is that you will not have a successful life if you do not attend college. Going to college has become a stereotype that you have to go or are a less than worthy person in society. This has caused all of us to have this collective consciousness that we have to go to college to get a good job and live a happy life which is not valid. We need to start pushing away from this and not let society have such a stronghold in our lives.

The collective consciousness is everywhere in society. I believe that this is outdated, and we need to push away from it. This pushes unneeded stress on the younger generations of society. You are already falling into it from a young age where we are placed around people with similar beliefs to use. Life nowadays is much different than it used to be. If we started pushing out of this way of thinking, we would move much further as a society. We need to learn to listen to each other and learn new things from different beliefs. This will allow us to see things from many different points of view, and this with ultimately allow us to leave things behind and have a more innovative and more well-rounded society.

The collective consciousness has a hold on society. It has been engraved into our minds that this is how the world should be. You stay around people that are similar to you. This thinking causes people to be stereotyped into groups.
