In school, just because you played sports, you got put into this group of jocks that people disliked because they are known as the people who think they are better than everyone else. The collective consciousness lets people group you without actually knowing who you are, which causes the group to live up to the stereotype.

With all this information, you can see how you are always playing a role in society no matter who you are. Society has caused people to believe that they are not a meaningful part of society if they are not playing a good role. This role has worn me down mentally, and I believe that we need to push away from people playing roles. They should be who they are, not whom society wants them to be. The collective consciousness also plays a role in this people have been told for so long that you have to be around people like you are you will not get along. This made-up stereotype makes people feel that they will be judged if they push out of the group they belong to. In all, I believe that we need to push away from our older ways and accept everyone for who they are. Life is too short to allow society to make us scared and play a role so that people will like us and want to be around you.
chunks.label: Critique of collective consciousness and societal roles
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the negative consequences of collective consciousness and social roles, arguing that society forces harmful stereotypes and expectations, such as feeling compelled to go to college or fit into jock cliques, and advocates for individuality and acceptance.

chunks.text:
The only people reading this essay are going to be Dr. Elliott and my peers of UNCW. Being a Male Asian-American that can afford college and has the resources to be successful shows an incredible amount of predisposed privilege. I have come to recognize this privilege and have realized that social standing is in direct correlation with how society sees you.

This concept can be better understood through the eyes of Peggy McIntosh’s “White Privilege”. McIntosh discusses the white privilege that she has, of which including how she can watch tv and she can see white people being positively symbolized. This puts strain and mental frustration over time on the oppressed groups of people. In reference to George Herbert Mead’s theory, the conceptualization of ourselves is dignified by symbolic interactions within a community. This corresponds with each other because as the oppressed community observes how negatively society sees them, it makes the notion that they are looked down upon.

“White Privilege” shows that you are not taught to see white privilege, moreover you are taught that racism is individual acts of rather than your initial status. This perception that the oppressed groups experience shapes their status and what they can accomplish in society. All privileged members of society must recognize their privilege, for the oppressed people to have fair opportunities.
chunks.label: Reflecting on privilege and sociological theories
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on their own privilege as an Asian-American college student and analyzes privilege and oppression through Peggy McIntosh's concepts and George Herbert Mead's theory.
chunks.people: Dr. Elliott, peers of UNCW, Peggy McIntosh, George Herbert Mead

nd27662af.title: Analyzing Sociological Perspectives on Harari's Lessons

chunks.text:
In the book 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, written by Yuval Noah Harari, there are a variety of different topics covered. These topics include discrimination, nationalism, the dubiousness of individuality, and groupthink, among other things. Many of the topics that Harari covers in his books can be related to the topics that were discussed in our class, earlier on in the semester. Some of them may complement each other well. They may also disagree with each other, and there may be contradictions between concepts. In this essay, I hope to analyze the differences and similarities between the concepts and ideas presented in 21 Lessons for the 21st Century and the ideas that we have previously learned about in this class.

Something that Harari brings up in the “Ignorance” chapter of his book is the idea that individuality is a myth. In his words “Humans rarely think for themselves. Rather, we think in groups.” (Harari, 222). Harari says that it is humanity's ability to think as a group that has set us apart from all other species on the planet. This is called “groupthink”. To Harari, groupthink is not inherently bad, but depending on the circumstance, it can be dangerous. On one hand, humans being able to put their knowledge together has helped us to become smarter collectively. It allows us to complete complex tasks that we may not have otherwise been able to do, had we acted as individuals. However, on the other hand, groupthink can be harmful, or even detrimental. For example, imagine if someone proposed an idea that is damaging to a certain group of people. If the majority of people not belonging to that group are convinced that this idea is a fact, then it could cause them to become prejudiced towards that group. In some cases, that belief could become institutionalized, leading to generations of harm done to the group. The concept of groupthink is interesting, as it shares similarities with concepts that have been discussed earlier in the semester, while also contradicting some of the other concepts that we have learned about. The idea of groupthink has some similarities to the concept of collective consciousness, a concept that was developed by Émile Durkheim, a sociologist, in the late 1800s. The term “collective consciousness” refers to a set of shared morals, ideas, or beliefs that unify a group of people in some way. Similarly to groupthink, collective consciousness is not presented as inherently good or evil, and the benefits and drawbacks of collective consciousness can depend on the situation. Whether or not it is harmful depends on the unifying idea or moral. Much like with groupthink, if the idea is one that is oppressive and institutionalized, it can cause harm to the specific group that the idea in question targets. However, if the belief is beneficial, it could allow humanity to become more advanced in a number of ways. Although groupthink has some similarities to collective consciousness, Harari’s belief that individuality is a myth directly contradicts concepts that were discussed very early on in the semester, specifically the ideas originated by William James, Charles Horton Cooley, and George Herbert Mead, which were discussed in Module 2. William James proposed that an individual’s identity can be divided into three parts, including the spiritual, social, and material self. Charles Horton Cooley argued a similar point, putting forward that people have a “looking glass” self, in which people change the way that they behave based on how others perceive them. Finally, George Herbert Mead, similarly to James, suggests that a person’s identity is split into three parts, those being the Self, the I, and the Me. Although these three people present different interpretations of identity, they share one thing in common. They all believe that people are individuals, with different views of the world around them, and that their identities are multifaceted. However, Harari argues that because humans rarely, if ever, think as individuals, and only really think as a group, and it is because of this that individuality is a myth. The tension between these two arguments comes from their core components. Both of these arguments can be applied to many different situations, and not all of them will contradict each other. However, the argument of whether or not people can be individuals is what creates the conflict between these points. I don’t think that any one person in this argument is right or wrong. As I said before, any of these concepts could be applied to many different sets of circumstances. I think that both arguments make good points, and have validity. How applicable the argument is just depends on the situation.

In the chapter “Nationalism”, Harari discusses many aspects of nationalism. Nationalism is defined as having extreme loyalty and devotion to one’s own nation, usually to the extent of looking down upon other nations. People who are nationalists tend to look down upon other cultures, as they consider theirs to be the “right one”. When faced with other cultures or beliefs, nationalists may react negatively or aggressively. Harari describes how these behaviors start to occur, talking about how “benign patriotism morphs into chauvinistic ultranationalism. Instead of believing that my nation is unique - which is true of all nations - I might begin feeling that my nation is supreme, that I owe it my entire loyalty, and that I have no significant obligations to anyone else'' (Harari, 112). This way of thinking is described further in the chapter “Immigration”. Harari describes how “though globalization has greatly reduced cultural differences across the planet, it has simultaneously made it far easier to encounter strangers and become upset by their oddities” (Harari, 140). Nationalists that view others in this way may feel like they don’t need to respect other cultures or people different from them. They see these people as beneath them, and feel no obligation to treat them with much consideration. This way of thinking is complimentary of racism. Extreme nationalism shares many similarities with racism, and can often be the source of racism. Earlier in the semester, racism and the different ways it can manifest were discussed, especially in module 4, where job discrimination was discussed. A key example of job discrimination can be found with the Pager discriminaiton study. The study was performed by Devah Pager and Bart Bonikowski, both from Princeton University, as well as Bruce Western from Harvard University. This study addressed the question of how racial discrimination impacts the job market. The study involved a number of job applicants, all men between the ages of 22 and 26. All of the applicants presented themselves as being of the same education level, and having equal job experience. The applicants were all either Black, White, or Latino. Some of the applicants were instructed to disclose a criminal record when asked. The results show just how widespread job discriminaiton is. Among the group that included participants that didn’t have a criminal record, the white applicants had the most positive responses, with 31% of the callbacks. Latino applicants followed with 25.2% of the positive responses, and Black people had 15.2% of the positive responses. This part of the study shows how race can have an impact on the job application process. In the group that included participants who were given a criminal record, white applicants still had the highest amount of positive responses, with 17.2% of the job offers. Latino and Black participants followed with 15.4% and 13% of the positive responses respectively. Overall, this study shows that, even though progress has been made, racial discriminaiton, especially in regards to job applications, is still very much alive. The act of judging someone based on something like their race or culture is what connects job discrimination and extreme nationalism. People who participate in extreme nationalism believe that those who are different from them are less deserving of certain opportunities or rights. When an interviewer turns down an applicant based on their race, similarly to extreme nationalists, it shows that they believe that people of a certain race are less deserving of the opportunities that other people get.

The Pager discrimination study also has similarities to another topic covered by Harari in the “Equality” chapter of his book. In this chapter, the topic of economic disparities and class discrimination are covered. Similarly, the Pager discrimination study deals with the economic effects of racism. In 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, the history of inequality is discussed. Harari describes how economic inequality can date back to the Stone Age, and talks about how some members of hunter-gatherer communities were buried with expensive jewelry and clothing, and others were buried with nothing at all. Even back then, people’s status depended on their wealth. Harari also mentions that throughout history wealth is the only thing that determines high social status, and that “throughout history the rich and the aristocracy always imagined that they had skills superior to everybody else’s, which was why they were in control. As far as we can tell, that wasn’t true” (Harari, 75). The Pager discrimination is almost like a continuation of this chapter. It shows how economic inequality has persisted into the modern day, and the ways in which it manifests.

In conclusion, Harari’s book covers many topics that both complement and contradict topics that have been covered in the past in this class. These topics include the comparison of economic disparity in the past and modern day, the similarities between extreme nationalism and racial discrimination, and the similarities and differences between the collective consciousness, the different “selves” that make up a person’s identity, and individuality being a myth. Having many different perspectives on an issue is important, which is why it’s essential to think critically about people’s opinions. Having different views on a topic is one thing among many that makes our experiences unique.

SOURCES

Harari, Yuval N. 21 Lessons for the 21st Century. Spiegel & Grau, 2018.

Pager, Devah, et al. Discrimination in a Low-Wage Labor Market: A Field Experiment. American Sociological Review, Oct. 2009.
chunks.label: Analyzing Harari's concepts and course sociology topics
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes and compares ideas from Yuval Noah Harari's book with sociological concepts and studies learned in class, including groupthink, nationalism, racism, and inequality.

n7987f5e2.title: Applying Dramaturgy to Perceptions of Terrorism

chunks.text:
The ideas that people have about terroism and the presence of terrorists is very different from the actual presence of terorism and terrorists. Terorims is a mind game played by terrorists in such a way that they can do absolutely nothing but their mere presence is enough to instill massive amounts of fear and worry. The idea of what they are doing on the outside and what everyone can see versus what they are doing behind the scenes is similar to a “frontstage and backstage” outlook about the presentation of the self. What terrorism does without activly doing anything is very similar to how humans present themselves to the world.

The ideas of a front stage and a backstage can really be applied to any human being and any social situation. The specific instance of terrorism is a great example of this because the entire idea of terrorism is the idea that they are playing a role for everyone to see. Goffman created his ideas about the presentation of the self specifically talking about human beings but like most things in life, it is a simple property or theory that can be applied to many different mediums.
chunks.label: Applying Goffman's frontstage and backstage concepts to terrorism
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on terrorism as a psychological mind game and compares it to Erving Goffman's sociological theories of the presentation of self, specifically frontstage and backstage behavior.

n0e4dc0f1.title: Critique of Modern American Economic Inequality

chunks.text:
In twenty-first century America, equality is something that is seen as a luxury and it is something that has separated us from other countries. The reality is that for the past few decades we are constantly being told about the great strides made toward equality, but when you look at the big picture of America, it is far from equal. One of the largest gaps of equality in twenty-first century America is between the economic classes, which can also be referred to as the rift between rich and poor. Economic equality does not exist in America and the class system is so one sided that it is possible to be looked at as a hierarchy. The economic hierarchy in twenty-first century America can be heavily related to beliefs about the existence of a “Power Elite” in America.

Harari’s ideas about the 1% and Domhoff’s ideas on the “Power Elite” can come together and represent what this economic hierarchy is. The 1% and the “Power Elite” would be at the top of your hierarchy like a king and in this role they are governing over and making decisions for the people in the levels below them. When taking these two ideas into considerations there is no possible way to see twenty-first century America as equal, specifically in the economic sense. A society cannot be equal if there is one small group ruling over another group, especially not when the margin between these two groups is as wide as it is.
chunks.label: Economic inequality and the Power Elite
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the reality of economic inequality in twenty-first century America, arguing that concepts from Harari and Domhoff illustrate how a small 'Power Elite' or 1% creates an unequal social hierarchy.

chunks.text:
The issue of alienation is more significant in today's world. Workers feel disconnected from their work, products, colleagues, and even themselves due to the way production works under capitalism. This disconnection leads to feelings of powerlessness, estrangement, and a sense of being removed from society. Moreover, this feeling extends beyond economics to affect cultural aspects, contributing to a sense of being culturally adrift and losing one's identity in an increasingly globalized society. Technology plays a role in intensifying feelings of alienation today. While technology has connected people from all over the world, it has also caused division and loneliness. People may get lost in worlds and lose touch with the natural world, leading to feelings of detachment and alienation from reality.

Apart from alienation, social alienation is also widespread nowadays. Social media platforms may seem like they bring people together, but they often result in relationships that deepen feelings of loneliness and isolation. There can be pressure on individuals to present an image online, which can lead to feelings of inadequacy and disconnect from human interactions. While Domhoff's theory, Marx's idea of commodity fetishism, and the concept of alienation offer insights, they come with some limitations. Domhoff's theory might not fully acknowledge the role of individuals and social movements in challenging power structures. Critics argue that Marx's focus on commodity fetishism is too narrow, overlooking forms of oppression like those based on gender and race. Moreover, while the idea of alienation is impactful, it may not completely capture the complexities of today's socio landscape, calling for a nuanced analysis of social relationships.

In summary, Domhoffs power elite theory, Marx's concept of commodity fetishism, and the notion of alienation serve as frameworks for understanding society. By applying these perspectives to real-world scenarios, scholars and activists can deepen their insights into issues like power dynamics, exploitation, and feelings of estrangement. However, it is crucial to approach these concepts and acknowledge their limitations to develop sophisticated analyses of contemporary socio-economic realities.

When exploring the concept of alienation in today’s world, it is worth considering whether all professions involve some level of detachment. According to Marx, alienation refers to individuals feeling disconnected from the fruits of their labor, their colleagues, at work, and even themselves. In the realm of work, this feeling of alienation shows itself in forms, adding to an issue of disconnection within society.

Modern work often involves tasks and specialized roles, which can result in a feeling of monotony and detachment from the work itself. In fields, workers might find themselves doing tasks without fully grasping how their efforts contribute to the final product or service. This lack of understanding can breed feelings of alienation and disinterest.

Additionally, the hierarchical setup in workplaces can worsen this sense of alienation among employees. In these structures, decision-making power tends to be concentrated at the top, leaving lower-level employees with little autonomy and control over their tasks. This power disparity can lead to a feeling of helplessness and alienation among workers who feel cut off from decision-making processes that impact their daily work lives. Furthermore, the increase in employment situations like contracts and gig jobs has added to feelings of alienation in today's workforce. Precarious workers often lack job security, benefits, and chances for career growth, creating a sense of instability and uncertainty. The uncertainty in job security can make workers feel disconnected, trying to find stability and a sense of belonging at work.

Technology's widespread presence at work also contributes to employees feeling detached. While technology has made work more efficient, it has also increased isolation among workers. Virtual communication tools and remote work setups can hinder interactions, leading to loneliness and detachment from coworkers. Moreover, how labor is treated as a commodity under capitalism makes workers feel alienated from their work results. In a system, labor is viewed as something to be bought and sold rather than a form of self-expression or satisfaction. This commodification can lead to workers feeling dehumanized and objectified, reduced to cogs in the production wheel.

In summary, alienation seeps into aspects of work life and contributes to a broader sense of disconnection in society. Many employees experience alienation in their jobs due to tasks, hierarchical workplace structures, precarious job conditions, or technological impacts. By acknowledging and dealing with these types of disconnection, we can strive to establish work settings that are more satisfying and purposeful for everyone.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of alienation
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological concepts of alienation, Marx's theories, Domhoff's power elite theory, and how technology, modern workplace structures, and capitalism impact workers and society.

chunks.text:
In this reflection essay, my goal is to compare Yuval Harari’s arguments in 21 Lessons for the 21st Century to sociological topics from this course. In a broad sense, Harari has similar perspectives to many sociology points mentioned previously in this class, but this essay will serve as a more detailed synthesis of two differing perspectives. While Harari focuses on the 21st century and the lessons of history we should head advice from, much of sociology reveals lessons and understandings of human behavior from the past that are still relevant today. Yuval Harari is a historian and philosopher who forms his arguments to convey that type of perspective, while sociology describes social relationships and human behavior in relation to those historical perspectives. In Yuval Harari’s book, Chapter 6’s lesson is about civilization in which he talks about community, culture, and religion in relation to historical and geographical perspectives. Going forward, I will compare this chapter to sociological perspectives on similar topics from module 1 such as “The Neurology of Religion” by Maryanski and Turner, “Microfoundations” by Fligstein and MacAdams, and “The Cultural Logic of Collective Representation” by Durkheim.

In module 1, “The Neurology of Religion” by Maryanski and Turner describes religion not by what each individual religion believes, but rather the mechanisms that are behind the formation of religion in humans. Maryanski and Turner’s perspective comes from an evolutionary standpoint, where they identified reasons for religious expansion through diving back in history to when humans had the brain capacity for religion but did not yet collectively believe. The authors argue against recent tendencies to view religion as simple neurological forces, and instead explain religion to be a complex compilation of many driving factors. Religion does not happen because humans have a “God gene” or cognitive “nodules” in the brain to enable their capacity for religious belief. Religion may partially be caused by neurology like that, but those perspectives leave out the evolutionary reasons for religion that formed from the evolution of neurology along with cognitive and emotional dynamics. According to Maryanski and Turner, religion itself is not just belief in the supernatural; it is communities of individuals with shared beliefs of sacred and supernatural powers, engaging in emotional rituals, and organizing those rituals within social structures in the community. Religion evolved while ancient humans evolved the capacity to believe in the supernatural. No other species on Earth has the capacity for collective religious belief and that ultimately stems from human consciousness and human’s capacity to maintain social connections. Maryanski and Turner illustrate the importance of behavioral adaptations, such as stronger social groupings, that has allowed religion to have longevity in human societies.

“Microfoundations” by Fligstein and MacAdams talks about rational choice theory and the social behavior of humans compared to other primates. Humans have the capacity for abstract thought, which distinguishes them from other primates such as chimpanzees or gorillas. Humans can make things meaningful but can also make things seem meaningless. This reason explains what Fligstein and MacAdams mean when they describe human abstract thought as “double-edged.” Just as humans can find inspiration and assign meaning to our goals and achievements, we can also doubt that our lives have any meaning at all. This distinguishes us from other primates who follow their social structure and follow their natural instincts rather than draw inspiration from abstract thought. Fligstein and MacAdams coined the phrase “the existential function of the social.” According to them, the social (or society) provides coordinated, meaningful activity; allowing us to collectively make each other’s lives meaningful (or meaningless). Behavioral evolution of the human species around 45,000 years ago created the kind of humans we see today. During this time, humans developed various sorts of communication that were beneficial to survival such as language, art, and burial traditions. Humans had the capacity to do this before, but through collective meaning making projects, we began to evolve into more social creatures who assigned symbolic reality to have true meaning.

“The Cultural Logic of Collective Representation” by Durkheim illustrates the importance of religion in society. It is important to study religion in society, according to Durkheim, because shared beliefs and religions shape different societies and cultures. “Collective effervescence” refers to feeling together in society. Society and community are therefore the fundamental principles of religion. “Collective representations” are symbols, artifacts, or narratives that embody the collective beliefs and values of a group. Although these are not always religious, they certainly can be. For example, a nation’s flag is an example of a collective representation, and the ideals and values of the flag establishes some type of community. These representations are how collective consciousness manifests in society. Durkheim believes that collective ideals provide us with truth and stability. With joint individual effort and understanding, comes collective rationality and truth. Individual thoughts and experiences are variable, but when collective thought was introduced to society, impersonal thought was also unveiled. This change in human consciousness allowed for new understanding of situations and perspectives that they could have never known without communication and collective thought. This created morality in society.

Yuval Harari speaks of religion and culture from a philosophical and historical context. For example, he mentions Orthodox Jews of today and how they refrain from images and depictions of women and girls in society and often segregate them from men and boys in their sacred spaces. Harari argues that this is a fault of some religions and cultures, because instead of adapting their collective beliefs to be inclusive in today’s standards, they uphold outdated standards from history that are not entirely accurate. According to some Orthodox Jews of today’s standards, the Jews in early Israeli history (who did not segregate people based on gender) would be blasphemous and disrespectful to their [ancient] culture… that they consider themselves to be a part of. This illustrates a blatant disregard to the cultural changes of human society that were for the better. According to Harari, humans have social systems, but they are not genetically determined. Chimpanzees and gorillas also have distinct social structures, but unlike humans, those are genetically determined. Gorillas cannot decide to behave socially as chimpanzees do, and chimpanzees cannot decide to adopt the social structure of gorillas. Both animals have the capacity for intelligent thought, but they lack the consciousness and group communication that humans have. If humans wanted to behave in social structures like chimpanzees or gorillas, we could observe the behavior of the animals and collectively communicate how we wanted to behave. Those animals are limited to their own neurology, and since humans are a more complex species, we have evolved from our ancient ancestors to behave completely different than in the past. Humans are one species but have many different cultures, beliefs, and social identifiers. People around the world speak different languages, believe in different supernatural powers, and learn from different historical outcomes. Human structures and religions constantly change, because humans can look at the recorded past and make adequate changes for the future. Other animals do not have the same cognitive abilities.

While Harari analyzes human behavior and achievement throughout history, the sociological perspectives mentioned previously find the root of that behavior and achievement. Harari criticizes human history to make a more inclusive tomorrow, while Maryanski and Turner, Fligstein and MacAdams, and Durkheim all explain the fundamental reasons for the behaviors. Harari sees the flaws of humans and points the readers in the moral right direction to correct those mistakes. Just as Fligstein and MacAdams describe abstract thought as “double-edged,” Harari reaffirms this belief in 21 Lessons for the 21st Century. Fligstein and MacAdams focus on the collective meaningful developments of humans, while Harari focuses on the contrary beliefs and the negative impacts that come from meaningless thought. Regarding religion, Harari focuses on the negatives of religion and what that conveys to society, while Maryanski and Turner focus on what led to the development of religion and what has kept religion in society. Both texts talk about the causes and effects of religion on humans, but Harari focuses on the growth that society can have, without disregarding the importance of religion. Regarding Durkheim and collective representations, Harari similarly finds the importance of collective beliefs on truth and stability. What differs between the two texts is which side of truth they are on. Durkheim reiterates how collective ideals lead to clearer beliefs in society, while Harari illustrates how collective ideals can be harmful to the overall society if not everyone shares the ideals.

In modern society it is hard to have collective beliefs that align with everyone, but upholding beneficial beliefs is important for the future. Yuval Harari’s text combines many cultures, just as our nations of today do. The sociological ideas talked about previously mostly refer to general human behavior of the past and how that affects us today, but Yuval Harari’s specific lessons for the 21st century tie history with how we want society to look in the future. Just as Harari listed many lessons for us to learn from, we can equally learn from sociological perspectives of the past. Collectively, humans need to take Harari’s lessons and combine them with the sociological lessons from the past, to accurately understand how history continues to affect civilization today.
chunks.label: Comparing Harari's arguments to sociological theories
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes and synthesizes Yuval Harari's arguments from '21 Lessons for the 21st Century' alongside sociological readings on religion, social structure, and collective representations.

ne38b19d9.title: Understanding Hierarchies in Gender and Society

chunks.text:
The Matrix of Domination is a symbolic order and used to show or determine something in society. A simple example could be an old, white, male using statistics and data to prove his points and support his arguments on equality. What this matrix really means is that in all categories of society and life, there is going to be a ranking of these groups where one is seen as superior to the rest. The Matrix of Domination can be seen in gender roles as through history people have fought for the matrix to shift but its reality has not wavered.

When thinking about gender roles in society as it pertains to the matrix of domination, Simone de Beauvoir does a really good job explaining this hierarchy between men and women. She explained that men were seen as the “subject and absolute” and that women were the supporting characters for whatever a man may need. Women were not treated as equal and did not have the same status as men, so much so that they were compared to African Americans and Jews, as far as how society saw them. This is where we can see the matrix because it is very obvious that in the category of gender the matrix put men first and women second, as men had all the power over women.

The matrix of domination is a hierarchy within a societal category where one group in this category is going to have supreme power over the other groups. In the matrix of gender the group that has this overarching power of the rest is men, and their power extends over women. How this matrix is going to be seen to society is that men are granted more roles, more opportunities, greater salaries, etc. simply because, compared to their female counterparts, they are a man and therefore seen as superior. In this society everyone just expects women to go along with this idea because it is the way things have always been so things will stay this way, and do to people thinking this way, the matrix is just enforced that much more.

The Matrix of Domination is the symbolic order and intersection used to show or determine something in a society. What this matrix means is that in many categories of life and society, there is going to be a hierarchy within these groups where one is seen as superior to the rest. The Matrix of Domination as seen in gender roles has shown little change in history because this idea that men are above women is all that most people have known. The Matrix of Domination has heavily impacted the flow of society for a long time, most prevalently in categories like gender, race, religion, and social class.
chunks.label: The Matrix of Domination and gender hierarchy
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the concept of the Matrix of Domination, referencing Simone de Beauvoir to discuss how patriarchal hierarchies place men above women in society.

n060f51fc.title: Navigating Phases of the Social Self

chunks.text:
The sociability of humans is at the center of Mead's ideas on the self. He proposes that the self is not something innate or predetermined, but emerges through social interaction. One of Mead’s many contributions to social psychology is his concept of the “I” and the “me.” Mead refers to these two states as phases of the self. This distinction highlights the mutual exchange between individual agency and social influence in the construction of the self. There are times when the “I” emerges and creates new responses that do not align with the “Me” that has been created. The intersection of these two states occurs through reflection.

“I” represents the spontaneous and creative aspect of the self. The “I” reflects the self as a subject of experiences. Mead describes the “I” as being a response to the “Me”. “I” is not immediately aware of itself. Imagine you’re at a dinner party with colleagues. As you engage in conversation with one of your work friends, they remind you of a funny memory. This causes you to feel the uncontrollable urge to laugh out loud. This is an example of the “I” taking precedence. You momentarily lose awareness of the social norms dictating that setting and express yourself without regard for external expectations.

We can describe the "Me" as the objective that we experience when we reflect on our actions. While you were at that dinner party laughing loudly, you suddenly engaged in your “Me” aspect. You remembered the context of the social situation and regained your composure. You become aware of what is expected of you and make the conscious decision to suppress the urge to laugh, aligning your behavior with societal norms. “Me” is not a static state. It is a phase of your existence that is constantly transforming.

William James, an American philosopher, produced work that contributed to the understanding of the self in a social context. Similarly to Mead, James separates the self into “Me” and “I”. However, James argues that the “Me” can be divided into subcategories- the social self, the material self, and the spiritual self. The division of the self into these categories supports both James’ and Mead’s claim that human identity is multifaceted and influenced by one’s environment and personal thoughts.

The social self is the aspect of the self that relates to an individual’s identity with others. The social self is shaped by social interaction and the roles expected in society. For James, people act based on who they are with. For example, a person may have an entirely different personality at work than the personality they have at home with their family.

The material self relates to the physical body, possessions, and the immediate environment that surrounds someone. The possessions that compose someone's material self are tied to their identity. Things like the body, family, clothing, wealth, and other tangible possessions constitute the material self. According to James, the cornerstone of the material self rests upon the physical body. Following the body, attire holds significance. He claims that clothing serves as a way for individuals to express their perceived identity or social status, thereby contributing to the creating and maintaining one’s self-image. Furthermore, money and family play pivotal roles in the material self. The loss of a family member often results in a corresponding loss of one’s identity. A substantial financial loss could prompt a fundamental shift in an individual’s sense of self. Cell phones have grown to become large parts of a material identity. There is a large dependency on cell phones, as they have become indispensable tools for sociality. Individuals rely on their phones to stay connected with others.

The spiritual self is the innermost core of a person’s existence. Thoughts, feelings, and consciousness make up this state of being. The spiritual self represents one’s unique identity beyond their physical and social dimensions. The spiritual self motivates reactions. Reactions are based on emotions, thoughts, and intentions. The spiritual self includes introspection and looking inward. The religious self is used to explore profound spiritual, moral, or intellectual questions free from the influence of others.

James and Mead propose that developing the self is not entirely an individual process. Both share common ground in their emphasis on the social nature of identity formation and the dynamic interplay between individuals and their social environments. The self relies heavily on social interactions. We are aware of this because of the large contributions James and Mead made to sociology.
chunks.label: Mead and James's theories of the self
chunks.what_happened: The student explains George Herbert Mead's concepts of the 'I' and the 'Me', using hypothetical dinner party examples, and compares them with William James's theories on the social, material, and spiritual self.

chunks.text:
Men are considered to have preeminence over relationships, home-life, and occupations in society today. However, since this is the social speculation of men, it brings the idea of unfairness and oppression towards women behind it. As shown in Gilman’s The Yellow Wallpaper, men have controlled her life and explain how men control the nation’s economic standards. The authority that men use over women which society derives from the norms of superiority form a component in the Matrix of Domination, which symbolizes the oppression women face based on men’s dominance.

Gilman displays her story in her article of The Yellow Wallpaper, which entails her being told that she is not sick or ill when she believes otherwise. But since her husband and brother were doctors and male, she did not have the personal decision on her well-being. She later talks about how men rule over the economic income in families, and that women’s only duties are to take care of the family, where the man is the working character. This shows the overwhelming side of women being oppressed by men in society, and how the norms are restricting women to exercise their rights to be human. Women are being bound to the house and taking care of kids every single day just to please the husband, just because of society’s rationale of the Matrix of Domination.

The Matrix of Domination, written by Patricia Collins, describes the complete meaning of what the Matrix of Domination is. The Matrix of Domination is the components of gender, race, ethnicity, environment, age, and many more that show the correlation of the oppressed and the oppressors according to society. Even with the Matrix, the oppression develops a way to resist the dominance, like stated by Collins, the oppressed group finds ways of empowerment to reject the dimensions of knowledge of the system of oppression. This means that with empowerment, groups of oppressed people will create new value for themselves, new images of themselves, and new restrictions that pertain to their likings. This shows that the Matrix of Dominations models who is superior and whom do they oppress, but the people of oppression have capabilities to counteract the social perception put on them from the people of dominance.

In conclusion, the Matrix of Domination symbolizes the meaning behind the Yellow Wallpaper, where women are less dominant compared to men, so women are being oppressed by men because they are controlled physically, emotionally, and economically by them. The Matrix of Domination does not just pertain to gender, but also race, ethnicity, and other socially specific things. Race is something that people of color get oppressed every day and needs to be more universally known to society so we can lessen the effects of oppression with knowledge of the issue and empowerment of all the oppressed races.
chunks.label: The Yellow Wallpaper and the Matrix of Domination
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses male dominance, Gilman's 'The Yellow Wallpaper', and Patricia Hill Collins's concept of the Matrix of Domination, explaining how systems of oppression function and can be resisted through empowerment.

n00d28d70.title: Tracing the Power of Collective Consciousness

chunks.text:
Community is something that can create influential order and make certain ideas powerful if it has the right amount of affinity behind it. For instance, the social norms of today's world are based on the collective consciousness, which is the shared ideology or reality of a community. Collective consciousness is formed by manifesting certain ideas through rituals or certain repeated human cooperation and can be examples of art, symbols, artifacts, or narratives of cultural beliefs. The idea of collective consciousness is the rooted basis of almost all social norms today, but it what is the origin of this manifested ideology and how influential is it.

Collective consciousness has been around since the era of Neanderthals, and according to Fligstein and MacAdams, Microfoundations, sociologists used the collective aspect for survival from Neanderthal's one of the earliest fundamental concepts of collective consciousness. The Neanderthals created tools and art which symbolized evolutionary development and coordinated symbolic activities. The idea of collective consciousness also is shown to be the representation of religions and folklore. As Durkheim describes in The Cultural Logic of Collective Representations, religious origins are the motive for the fundamental categories of thought and therefore science. Religion is essentially the main example of the collective consciousness because religion itself is a system of beliefs for people with common values to practice similar experiences. Religion has an influential capability in today’s society, however, the power of lore is also just prominent. In the podcast Black Stockings by Aaron Mahnke, he states that the power of fear or the unknown is very powerful and uses the Lore of the Irish legend “changelings” as an example. Aaron Mahnke explains how this lore of changelings plagued the Irish’s mind so severely that they would burn babies, kill, and do inhumane rituals based on superstitions of changelings. This shows the extraordinary measure collective consciousness can accomplish.

Everything today's society believes in or does is originally the conspectus of collective consciousness and has impacted humanity throughout history. From the collaborative effort of the Neanderthals to religions to folklore, collective consciousness in its nature influences everything we know today. It forms the social norms that we believe in and the way people teach things, and it explains why community is so influential.
chunks.label: Collective consciousness and community influence
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on collective consciousness, discussing how it shapes social norms, citing Neanderthals, Durkheim's theories on religion, and a podcast about Irish folklore.

chunks.text:
The world today is plagued with social norms that are against women. For example, the collective consciousness norm that women must look pretty, as summarized in Naomi Wolf’s Beauty Myth. Women have been judged on the way they looked, and have been told by men how to act, what to wear, and what to think. It is important to understand the subjective ideology that follows women’s history so we can learn and help change the roles they are supposed to be, and so we can see the consequences that follow the social roles.

In the Yellow Wallpaper, by Gilman, she encapsulates the story of a woman getting told by her husband and brother that nothing is wrong with her when she develops this mental ailment. This is an example of how men, have a social superiority over women on how they are supposed to think. She is driven crazy because she is cannot make her own choices or thoughts and she slowly drown in her inner thoughts which was the ultimate consequence. Men also have control over how women are believed to look. In Beauty Myth, Wolf states that women have been made to believe that “beauty” is something valuable which is the highest social factor for them, and that the power lies in how pretty, skinny, or sexually attractive they are. The results from these social norms caused thirty-three thousand women in the past decade to want to achieve weight loss and caused pornography to rise double. These consequences conclusively resulted in other norms that degrade women and change the way they live.

These readings showcase all the ways men and society has impacted women's sexuality and the norms have not stopped coming. But knowing the consequences and norms that result in this problem we can collectively change the roles and change the gender inequality to equality.
chunks.label: Social norms, gender inequality, and literature analysis
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on social norms against women, discussing readings like Naomi Wolf's 'The Beauty Myth' and Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 'The Yellow Wallpaper' to explain how men and society control women's thoughts, appearances, and roles.

ne9049688.title: Being the Only Girl in Weightlifting

chunks.text: When I was in my senior year of high school I had an open spot in my schedule, I did not have to take a math class which I was incredibly happy about but then I was tasked with the decision of filling a spot I wished I could have just left empty. I was dreading choosing a class until I came upon a weight training class, I was ecstatic! I had been working out for a while at that point but I did not belong to a gym and did not own any home weights and I liked the idea of getting my work out over with during school hours so I wouldn't have to worry about it when I got home when I was already worried about getting homework done and spending time with my friends and other chores I had to get done around the house. I knew I was not going to go in there and lift super heavy, but I was a little disappointed that to start with I could only lift the bar. I could often hear other classmates laughing at me as I did my sets and making jokes about it being pointless for me to even try and some of the guys would say I was taking up their time to lift. I was the only girl in the class. I told them I was a beginner, and I knew I could not lift much weight, but I told them that I truly wanted to improve and get stronger and more muscular and that I did not take the class to joke around, waste their time or take up their workout time, I truly wanted to become good at weight lifting. Nobody seemed to care that I had good intentions. I am considered to be quite petite so I was judged even before they saw I could only lift the bar. We were all paired as two-person partner groups. My partner seemed very upset to be paired with me and he would talk to the other guys in class but then when it was time for us to lift weights together he would put in his AirPods and refuse to talk to me and was very reluctant to take out his earbuds when I was waving at him to get his attention which I rarely did only if needed. One day in class I was lifting the bar for a bench press when he spotted me and I was struggling, it was obvious I needed his help lifting the bar back onto the rack, I said: “I cannot get it, can you help?” He looked me straight in the eyes and saw me struggling and refused to help me lift it onto the rack, I dropped it on my chest, and it rolled down my ribcage onto my stomach. I always felt like an outsider in that class, it was although they all had a supportive and healthily competitive community, and I was the “other.” Around this time, I started seeing videos of female weightlifters on social media, I was envious of their bodies, and it made me feel even worse that I could not lift anywhere close to what they could. It very negatively affected my self-esteem and my relationship with food and my body image.
chunks.label: High school weight training class experiences
chunks.what_happened: The student enrolled in a high school weight training class as the only girl. Male classmates and her lifting partner excluded and judged her, culminating in her partner refusing to help her rack a bench press bar, while social media weightlifters made her feel worse about herself.
chunks.feelings: incredibly happy, dreading, ecstatic, a little disappointed, felt like an outsider, envious, felt even worse
chunks.people: classmates, guys in class, lifting partner, female weightlifters on social media

chunks.text:
De Beauvoir described women as being categorized as the other as society viewing women as weak and as an incomplete man whose body has no meaning without being in reference to a man’s body. Society deemed women and their attributes to be non-essential and different than the majority and therefore did not belong. Men were deemed the sovereign of society. A woman's body is then seen as an object rather than a useful human being with potential. Women are judged by their anatomy and are accused of acting certain ways because of their hormones, women as the other are seen as obstacles for men. De Beauvoir says women are called “the sex” and that men see her essentially as a sexed being and that is all. De Beauvoir says women are inessential in front of the essential, men are the subject, the absolute and women are the other. Women are not a minority in the traditional sense there are equal number of men and women on Earth, however, women are treated as a minority and as weak incomplete beings that are meant to be tools or playthings for men. We as women are outsiders in our own society. Women have always been seen as subordinates to men. Women are designated as the other by men who posited themselves as the one or the subject.

The weight training class I took was certainly a hegemonic masculinity environment and, in my situation, it was damaging. Hegemonic masculinity encourages men to act hyper-masculine and shuns those who do not fit that mold. This encourages men to be “manly men.” Hegemonic masculinity is meant to legitimize men as the dominant force in society and that men are dominant over women.
chunks.label: Beauvoir's concept of the other and hegemonic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Simone de Beauvoir's theory of women as the other and explains the sociological concept of hegemonic masculinity.

chunks.text: The most obvious way I was blatantly put into the category as other and was made to feel as though I did not belong was one day, we had a substitute in class, he looked me up and down and his face twisted with annoyance and disgust, and he asked me “ do you even lift anything in here?” I felt truly angry and isolated. I kept getting the same message that I was the other and I was in everyone else's way. The message that I was weak, and incomplete was repetitively sent to me in different ways. The boys in my class and the substitute teacher supported treating women as other and a hegemonic masculine environment.
chunks.label: Substitute teacher's insulting comment in class
chunks.what_happened: A substitute teacher in the student's weight training class looked at her with disgust and asked if she even lifted anything in there.

chunks.text: Women are often excluded or judged in male dominated sports. I experienced this treatment firsthand in the weight training class I took. The way my other classmates treated me and the way the substitute teacher spoke to me supported a hegemonic masculinity environment where I was made to feel like I did not belong, and I was made to feel like I was weak, not capable of improvement. Everyone should make efforts to disrupt and dismantle this system of treating women as the other and it should be known that hegemonic masculinity is not okay. I should have stood up to my classmates and the substitute teacher or even reported the rude comment he made to me to someone of a higher position at the school. Men should give women equal opportunity and be patient and accepting when they themselves are also looking to improve. Allowing women into male sports and maybe doing away with a separation between sports such as the WNBA and NBA may be a viable solution as well.
chunks.label: Exclusion in sports and dismantling hegemonic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the exclusion of women in male-dominated sports, how she should have stood up to her peers and the substitute, and potential solutions to dismantle hegemonic masculinity.

chunks.text: I lift weights with my husband, and I also occasionally lift weights with one of our male mutual friends and neither of them judge me and they are both incredibly supportive during our workouts, so I know it is possible for men to not be toxic towards women in the gym.
chunks.label: Lifting weights with husband and friend
chunks.what_happened: The student lifts weights with her husband and a mutual male friend, who are supportive and do not judge her.

chunks.text:
I would urge everyone not to play into or accept hegemonic masculinity as okay and to treat women as equals rather than subordinates or the other.

Work Cited

Beauvoir, S. de. (2015). The second sex. Vintage Classics.

(Originally published 1949)
chunks.label: Call to action and citation
chunks.what_happened: The student urges everyone to reject hegemonic masculinity and treat women as equals, concluding with a work cited entry for Simone de Beauvoir.

n3f1cc7ca.title: Performing Different Roles for Different Audiences

chunks.text: One Question I repeatedly hear from my roommate is, “Why are you always so hard on yourself?” For example, I complain about my grades if they are less than an A, as well as if I make a perfectly normal mistake. However, despite my errors, she accepts me the way I am in these instances, mainly because roles such as academia and responsibility are not what I am required to prove to her.
chunks.label: Roommate questioning my high standards
chunks.what_happened: The student's roommate repeatedly asks why the student is so hard on themselves, such as when complaining about receiving less than an A or making normal mistakes. Despite these errors, the roommate accepts the student without requiring proof of academic perfection.

chunks.text: Throughout different “scenes” over the course of our lives, we put on new costumes, act as different characters, and engage in different roles the best we can. However, it is only natural that like in any performance, we forget our lines or trip on stage. This has the potential to disrupt the balance within the production. Upon this occurring, it can embarrass and make others uncomfortable. So, why do we take ourselves so seriously? I believe this is a question that us as humans do not analyze enough. At the end of the day, maybe our best performances are improv.
chunks.label: Life as theatrical performance and expectations
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the metaphor of life as a theater production where people perform different roles, occasionally slip up, and wonder why humans take themselves so seriously.

chunks.text: Throughout my personal life, my specific roles and characters change immensely from situation to situation. When I was growing up, I noticed that in every friend group, I played the role of the “dumb” one, frequently being teased for my awkward jokes or irrelevant comments. I have always been told that I am an “easy target” for teasing, as well as “we aren’t laughing at you, we are laughing with you” a countless number of times. Although this was true sometimes, it does not mean it did not offend me. This trend additionally followed me into middle school as well as high school within the friend groups I would weave through. If I would get upset from the “playful” teasing, then I would be taking it too seriously and take the fun out of the joke. This ties back to the role I played among my friend groups. My role is making silly mistakes for the purpose of others laughter and entertainment. I have accepted that this is my role and that it is this way because that is what my friends expect from me and accept me for. However, in other scenarios, such as my family and academics, playing the role of the “easy target” would be disappointing.
chunks.label: Being teased as the dumb one in friend groups
chunks.what_happened: Growing up and through middle and high school, the student routinely played the role of the 'dumb' one and easy target for teasing in friend groups. Although offended at times, the student accepted making silly mistakes for their friends' laughter and entertainment.

chunks.text: If I am performing the role of daughter, I am expected to be responsible, independent, and live up to the expectations of my older sister. In order to do these things, I have to hold myself accountable for my grades, actions, expenses, and other things that come with being grown up. This means always working hard to supply myself with money, always getting straight A’s, and handling my real-world issues on my own. This role of the put-together, smart, independent girl is far from what I experience around my friends. I am required to transform from the silly bubblehead girl to the smart and sophisticated women. Being all these things and not slipping up is very difficult and trust me, I have fallen out of character many of times before. When this happens, I get hit with an “how could you” attitude. When my role is questioned, others around me do not know how to react. When the critics does not like the performance, they will be sure to let you know in the reviews.
chunks.label: Performing the role of the responsible daughter
chunks.what_happened: In the family setting, the student is expected to be responsible, independent, get straight A's, earn money, and match an older sister's expectations. Slipping out of character leads to disapproval and confusion from those around them.

chunks.text:
In Erving Goffman’s piece, “Presentation of Self”, he illustrates the idea of us as humans, presenting ourselves as though we are performers on a stage, and these performances make up the self. He states, “the very structure of the self can be seen in terms of how we arrange for such performances in our Anglo-American society” (Goffman). Face to face interactions give us a role to fill and stage where we preform them. We gain a sense of self and identity through social encounters and preforming these roles. “A correctly staged and preformed scene leads to audience to impute a self a preformed character” (Goffman). We take our characters very seriously because they give us a role in the social world. Therefore, living up to these expectations is very important to us.

We are constantly searching for meaning in our lives. Humans strive to find a place in this society. This is why we participate in collaborate meaning-making processes like religion, clubs, activist group, etc. We have seen this trend in our world for thousands of years. We appeal to the collective conscious to fit in so that we can relate to one another and give meaning to this life. We live in the ideas of narratives to give explanation to the external world and create roles for ourselves to play. With all this being said, it is only natural that we want to play our roles the best we can in order to feel fulfilled in life.

I feel as though I, as well as others, take my roles very seriously because without them, I feel as though I have no purpose. We strive to appeal to the standards that the social creates. Through these standards and expectations, the self emerges and is shaped through trial and tribulation. When I am with my friends, I know the type of person they expect me to portray. I know what to say, the jokes to make, and the way to act. With my family, I know how to turn myself into the responsible, academic, and mature daughter they raised me to be. I know what jokes to slide into the conversations and when to be silly at the right time, without breaking my reputation. Breaking our character means breaking our reputation, which leaves us in the world with an unfilled purpose and lack of meaning.

So why do we take ourselves so seriously? As described throughout this paper, it is to find and create meaning for us. We want to feel fulfilled in our interactions and contribute positive meaning to the world around us. Like we see in religion, organizations, and many other things, we want meaning to explain our purpose in this world. All of this is very understandable and reasonable ways to think. Society has engraved in our minds the type of people we are supposed to be and the characters we are expected to portray. In my own life, I demonstrate needing to find meaning within social interactions. I allow myself to play a role that I am not always comfortable with because it gives me a purpose in my friend group. In my family, I let them hold me up to higher standard because I want them to be proud of me. I need to fulfil that role the best I can in order to feel like I have meaning to them.

As humans, we are bound to take ourselves too seriously. This idea has been constructed and enforced by the social for a very long time. I think striving for meaning in our lives is a trend we will never break out of. However, I think instead of taking ourselves so serious in our roles, we should learn to break out of character sometimes. If we didn’t limit ourselves to what is expected of us, we can discover more about ourselves as people. Also, if we criticized less when people stepped out of their roles, everyone would feel more accepted when they cannot live up to others standards. Overall, I think we all need to be less hard on ourselves about meeting the expectations of others and ourselves. Being authentic in all circumstances may lead to a happier and better state of mind.
chunks.label: Goffman's presentation of self and seeking meaning
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Erving Goffman's concept of the presentation of self, analyzes how social roles provide human life with purpose and meaning, and concludes that people should be less hard on themselves and more authentic.

chunks.text: A problem is developing in my generation as well as the upcoming one, where kids and young adults are becoming addicted to their electronic devises.
chunks.label: Issue of device addiction in younger generations
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on a growing problem of device addiction developing in their generation and the upcoming one.

chunks.text: A prime example is this past weekend, I was at the local Chipotle in Wilmington and as I ate my delicious burrito, I noticed an older teen was watching a YouTube vide while eating dinner with his mother. The experience looked awkward as the mother was trying to make conversation, which can be explained by Erving Goffman and Yuval Harari.
chunks.label: Observing a teen and mother at Chipotle
chunks.what_happened: While eating at a local Chipotle in Wilmington, the student observed an older teen watching a YouTube video instead of conversing with his mother.

chunks.text: Chapter five of “21 Lessons for the 21st century”, Harari talks about how the community is slowly being taken over by the algorithms of technology. He criticizes Mark Zuckerberg on the way he is trying to “connect” people through Facebook. In reality it is dividing people and stopping the interaction of shared experiences, which can be further explained by Goffman. In “The Presentation of Self”, Goffman explains that in a performance of an interaction each member needs to actively play the role that they are expected to be, or the situation fails. He explains this through the idea of the front stage and backstage, where individuals prepare for the front stage of acting as the collective role they are supposed to play.
chunks.label: Sociological perspectives on technology and interaction
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Harari's criticism of technology dividing community interaction and Goffman's concept of front stage and backstage roles.
chunks.people: Yuval Harari, Mark Zuckerberg, Erving Goffman

chunks.text: The awkward chipotle relates in the fact that the mother was ready and on the frontstage, whereas the teen was still in the backstage. Through Harari it is identified that technology is a barrier to the front stage which keeps individuals in the backstage. This creates awkwardness in situations because there isn’t communication amongst the “actors”.
chunks.label: Analyzing the Chipotle interaction using Goffman and Harari
chunks.what_happened: The student applies Goffman's frontstage and backstage concepts and Harari's ideas to explain why the Chipotle interaction was awkward.

nce21ba60.title: Unrealistic Standards and the Beauty Myth

chunks.text:
The Beauty Myth is a phenomenon by Naomi Wolf explaining the ways modern society restricts women. In the past ideologies set up women as caretakers, homemakers, and mothers. Women were property of their fathers and then their husbands. If their husbands died, their sons oversaw them. Now, women are not married off to settle debts, or are married to old men to create political bonds or for social status. They are seen as equal to men in the eyes of society and the law. So, then what makes Wolf believe that women are still restricted in society? Her answer is the overwhelming obsession with physical perfection forced into modern women. It is mental aberration that has never been seen before and formed by inconspicuous psychological pressures placed throughout everyday life.

Women haven’t always been seen as beneath men. In hunter-gather days, the men would hunt large game and women would gather, and later farm. This system allowed both genders to place food on the table and provide for the family, by playing to their own strengths. However as technology, agriculture, medicine, and society has advanced, women were placed into more and more of an oppressed role. Finally, in the early 1900s, women began fighting for gender equality again and gained the right to vote. Ever since, women have slowly gained a more equal status with men in society and law. However, with the rise of this status, the “ideal woman” has become an impossible goal. Beauty standards for women no longer represent what real women look like. It would be more accurately described as a sexualized girl than a woman.

These “perfect women” have been placed all throughout society, creating a fake idea in men's minds. These advertisements make men believe that these 'perfect’ women exist and are all over the world. Because men so often see these fake girls, who smile at them and are advertised to be available to men, real women and the real world doesn’t meet their standards. These standards can lead to mentally unstable men, like Elliot Rodgers, feel rejected when women don’t smile, flirt, or have sex with them. Rodgers was a twenty-two-year-old who killed six people and injured twenty two more during a rage. Before his rage he proclaimed in videos and a manifesto that he was the closest thing there was to a living god and could not comprehend why women didn’t want to have sex with him. The “perfect” women in advertisements, tv shows, movies, and social media convinced him that women were supposed to simply be available for men to have. These platforms don’t just twist the minds of men, but also twist the minds of women. Advertisements which include a photoshopped “perfect” girl and say to women that their product can make you look like her.

The beauty standards placed into the minds of every young girl are very strict; 1. Your hair must be long, pin straight, and blonde. 2. You must have clear skin with big eyes, long lashes and a small nose and chin. 3. Your body must be toned, but not too muscular. 4. You can’t have any visible fat, but you must have a nice sized butt and breast. 5. You must be natural, not have surgery, because scars are ugly. 6. You can’t have stretch marks from growing, you can’t be too tall or too short, and you shouldn’t have any body hair. 7. The ideal measurement for your body is an hourglass shape with a bust of 36 inches, a waist of 24 inches, and hips of 36 inches. 8. You must always be smiling, friendly and talkative, but not fake, sexual, or loud. This list is a small percentage of the standards placed on women. Women have been flogged the idea that to be beautiful or no one will love us. This fake ideal woman made up in society's mind is constantly reinforced in society. These platforms don’t simply make women try to be ‘prettier’, but they enforce the idea upon women that it is possible to look like this.

The idea of these ‘perfect’ women don't simply trick the minds of men and women about how they should act and look, but they disrupt the natural order of what girls and boys should act like at different ages. Beer ads often show smiling women flirting with a man at the bar or scantily clad women on a river. These companies are taking the idea of the ‘perfect’ woman and using girls from the ages of 17 to mid-twenties to try and fit this idea. These young girls used in advertisements tell older men to be more attracted to younger women. It then makes the women in the same age range as the men feel much older than they are. This system tells men they are allowed to have fun, party, and sleep around from their teenage years until their early thirties, and forces women to think they should be married and settled down in their mid-twenties. The Beauty Myth causes women to age, socially, faster than men.

The beauty Myth doesn’t just affect teenage and adult women. The infiltration of this way of thinking begins while a mother is still pregnant. Many girl baby clothes include sayings like, “my daddy can fight”, making the girl already subject to the idea saying she should grow up to be pretty enough so her dad must fight boys away from her. As the girl grows up, she is given dolls which are not made to represent her or real women, but the ideal woman. Girls in their early teenage years are given makeup and told to start shaving. This is the start of wanting to change their natural body to fit a certain look. These small, seemingly insignificant details of a girl's life are the brainwashing of women to look a certain way. Women are not only told to look a certain way for men or by society. They place themselves and other women under extreme scrutiny.

It is well known that the way we see ourselves is very different from the way others see us, because of our sensations and feelings, we see ourselves in a far more detailed way than anyone else could ever see us. We can hold on to a single memory of our mothers pointing out acne on our face as a preteen, and the embarrassment and shame we felt along with it, and scrutinize every pore on our face for the rest of our lives. These feelings along with this memory can develop bad habits like obsessive compulsive skin picking disorder. For the rest of our life, every time they feel embarrassed or anxious, we will scratch at our skin. This scratching can cause deep scars and ruin the chances of ever getting the ‘perfect skin’, causing more embarrassment. Another example of the distress caused by the beauty myth is the development of body dysmorphia. This mental disorder is the inability to perceive what you actually look like and often shows up in things like picking sizes in clothes and causes eating disorders.

Naomi Wolf believes that beauty is the "last, best belief system that keeps male dominance intact". It pitches women against each other in a race to achieve the impossible. The Beauty Myth affects how women view themselves, how women view other women, and how men view women. The rise in rebranding of famous toy brands, like Barbie, is a step in the right direction in eliminating the Beauty Myth from a young age. Barbie now has four different body types for their doll and include many different races. Savage X Fenty is a clothing brand which has put lots of effort into designing clothes for all body types and showing many races as the faces of their brand. Many brands are taking steps in the right direction with body positivity and racial inclusion. However, brands need to include girls with less makeup, scars, acne, and different facial structures.
chunks.label: The Beauty Myth and its societal effects
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Naomi Wolf's concept of the Beauty Myth, historical gender roles, media-driven beauty standards, and their harmful psychological impacts on men and women.

chunks.text:
Both of this week's readings focus primarily on Capitalism and the ideas of two theorist,

Max Weber and Karl Marx. The first reading titled The Spirit of Capitalism by Max Weber portrays his idea of capitalism and the theoretical concept of “the iron cage”. This concept refers to the principles of social structure and bureaucracy that had evolved while the system of capitalism remained. He suggests the idea that money is prolific, comparing it to nature, essential for shaping life. The economic relationships within capitalism that essentially shape social life is proved with his idea of the iron cage.
chunks.label: Weber's views on capitalism and the iron cage
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes Max Weber's 'The Spirit of Capitalism', discussing the iron cage, bureaucracy, and how money shapes social life.

chunks.text: The second reading titled Estranged Labour by Karl Marx portrays his own view of capitalism under an economic system. His idea is that society tends to divide itself into two classes. He refers to these two classes as “property owners and property-less workers”. These two classes face considerable differences and the workers often experience an estrangement and alienation from the word. Marx theory states that this alienation occurs in several ways. One way is because the workers' lives are devoted to the products they are working on and the outside world, that of which they do not belong. One other way is because the workers' lives are consumed by that product, it exists outside of them and signifies a loss of self.
chunks.label: Marx's views on estranged labour and alienation
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Karl Marx's 'Estranged Labour', detailing class divisions between property owners and workers as well as forms of worker alienation.

chunks.text: These two theorists' arguments on capitalism relate in many ways. They both believe that there is a greater factor in shaping social life. Weber believes this factor is the economy while Marx believes it is social class. However, both theorists agree that the basis of class division relies on ownership versus non ownership. While one group continues to prosper, the oher will lag behind. This idea continues to grow and become increasingly more relevant within society.
chunks.label: Comparing Weber and Marx's theories
chunks.what_happened: The student compares how Weber and Marx view the forces shaping social life and their shared focus on ownership versus non-ownership.

chunks.text: The economic impacts of the coronavirus pandemic and unemployment rates are comparable to these ideas. It unfortunately proved what class people really were in. You saw huge corporations with wealth continue to grow, prosper, and stay that way all throughout the past year. While those businesses stayed in theoretical “power”, small businesses with not as much standing fell apart, alienated from the rest of the world.
chunks.label: Applying theories to the coronavirus pandemic
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how the economic impacts of the coronavirus pandemic and unemployment rates reflected these theories through the prosperity of large corporations versus the alienation of small businesses.

chunks.text:
