On the other hand, Karl Marx's study of the "conscious self" delves thoroughly into the notion that the superstructure—which consists of institutions, politics, and culture—is essentially shaped by the economic foundation of society, which consists of the mode of production and class relations. Marx held that a person's social circumstances mold their consciousness, and that by altering these circumstances, people might grow a class consciousness that propels societal change. This theory draws attention to the possibility of human action within a capitalism system that frequently appears to be unchanging and unbreakable. This Marxian idea of rising consciousness leading to organized resistance and potential transformation is seen, for instance, in the modern labor movement and its growing understanding of workers' rights and collective bargaining.

By contrasting these views, a nuanced understanding of contemporary capitalism is revealed. On the one hand, it appears that corporate models constantly impose inflexible patterns on many facets of life, reducing human connections to transactions—the mechanistic dehumanization that Ritzer warned against. Marx's optimism, however, about the conscious self's capacity for change offers a counterbalance, implying that these same circumstances can provoke a collective awakening and reclaim of personal agency. In the digital age, this tension between the limiting forces of McDonaldization and the liberating possibilities of Marxian consciousness is most apparent. In addition to providing activists and marginalized communities with previously unheard-of means for communication and organization, technology is also frequently used by companies to increase productivity and control. This dual character is demonstrated by social media platforms' worldwide reach, which may both mobilize social movements and promote cross-border solidarity while simultaneously serving as a vehicle for the commercialization of personal data and interactions. The continuous conflict between the impersonal forces of capitalism and the persistent human need for independence and significant change is captured by this dichotomy.

In summary, examining Karl Marx's "conscious self" and George Ritzer's "McDonaldization" offers important new perspectives on how structure and agency interact in capitalist society. Marx's idea underscores the possibility of a conscious awakening and societal reform, while McDonaldization emphasizes the ubiquitous effects of efficiency and standardization on human creativity and autonomy. This contrast highlights the constant conflict between pursuing individual and group emancipation and complying to structural demands, while also enhancing our comprehension of contemporary capitalism. Analyzing these theories critically promotes more in-depth thought about how we fit into these dynamics and how to move toward a society that is more egalitarian.
chunks.label: Analyzing Marx's conscious self and Ritzer's McDonaldization
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Karl Marx's theory of consciousness and collective resistance, compares it with George Ritzer's concept of McDonaldization, and examines how these theoretical perspectives apply to contemporary capitalism, technology, and social change.

n673ccb9e.title: Women Climbing Into the Power Elite

chunks.text:
How Women Fought for Their Spot into The Power Elite

When we look at how feminism over time combines with the power elite, we see the growth of society. These women at one point were not allowed to work and were only thought of as someone to care for children and take care of the house. Now not only do some women have a job in a primarily male position, but a position of power in that job. This is a significantly positive change in society. The first women power elite CEO in the United States was Anna Bissell. In 1889, Anna Bissell became the CEO of Bissell Carper Sweeper Company. A little under 100 years later, Katharine Graham became the first female CEO of a Fortune 500 company, The Washington Post. These two women made history by holding a position of power after fighting for gender equality. While this history being made is very exponential, in some areas of life, feminism, and the power elite correlation still needs improvement. We can see this in the scenario of promotion and paying a CEO for let’s say a car company, and two applicants, one man, and one woman. If both applicants have equal elite schooling, equal past experience and training, the man would still be more likely to be promoted. If both applicants were promoted to be Co-CEO’s, the women would be getting paid less than the man. Both of these situations of becoming a power elite go against the feminist advancements. To go along with this scenario, the fact that the company is a car company, and the women is getting less credit for her role shows that there are certain things that people see as interesting for men versus women. While it is great to see that women are able to work and get jobs as power elites, it is sad to know that there are still some things that the current feminist waves need to advocate for.

The feminist movement has changed the lives of women in a significant amount of ways. Women are considered in a more respectable manner, can vote, seen as more than the person who cares for the children and house, and work in positions of power. Simone De Beauvoir said that society viewed men as a subject and women as an other. This meant that society viewed men as purposeful and powerful, and women as meaningful only when referenced to a man. The second feminism wave knocked this societal view down some, and feminist movements now continue to fight this. Women being able to become part of the power elite inspires other women as well as closes the difference in the discrimination between them and men. While instances like the gender wage gap and employer preference for certain jobs still exist, women have made substantial improvements in almost everything else. Women today continue to reach dreams of being a CEO, or other power elite jobs, especially because women in the past weren’t allowed to get anywhere close to that power. As women strive to climb the ladder at the job, they also want to continue to gain equality and continue the feminist ways.
chunks.label: Feminism and women in the power elite
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the history and progress of women entering the power elite, discussing early female CEOs, ongoing gender inequality in promotions and wages, and the impact of feminist movements.

chunks.text:
Beauty myths are societal standards of beauty that are based on individual cultures and can have many different elements. In every culture, however; a beauty myth describes what a certain group of people should look like. Although many different people can beautiful, the standards are always set by the dominant group in society. This generally means that men set standards for how women should look, with complete disregard to each woman’s physical or emotional strengths. Every standard is set through gender norms that have been widely accepted in that culture. There can also be many different gender norms, so depending on where or who is a part of the society, there are traits and qualities that each gender is supposed to have or develop.

In today’s United States society, all people have equal rights. This does not mean that beauty myths are no longer present. We have many standards that are expected, and only time can help this trend crumble. Since the United States is such a diverse country, with people from around the world calling it their home, there are many different standards that have prevailed. In nearly every civilization throughout history, a single group has controlled the power, which almost always has led to discrimination and “othering.” Othering and defensive othering are both ways to label some person or some group as other. If you are labeled as other, you are not only subjected to discrimination and/or oppression, but also held to different and unrealistic standards.

The term “beauty myth” was coined by Naomi Wolf in 1990. In her book, she talked about societal pressure to conform to certain beauty standards, particularly placed on women in the West. The age of new feminist ideas previously brought freedom, but Wolf argues that also brought preconceived notions of beauty standards, self-hatred, physical obsessions, terror of aging, and other “political weapons” used against women’s advancement in society. Once women gained the same rights as men, they were still thought less of, which meant that men saw a woman’s value solely based on looks, rather than their actions. This cultural shift subjected women to unrealistic standards, and men belittled women who could not achieve the beauty standards already set in place.

Women are subjected to this beauty myth, according to Naomi Wolf, as a form of retaliation or backlash against 2nd wave feminism. During this time, the objectification of women was taken to a new level with new forms of media. Men had previously controlled society, so subjecting women to these standards seemed like a natural way to gain back cultural control. For example, women felt discriminated against as they aged, while men were thought of as wise, powerful, and successful as they aged. In some areas, this type of disparity is still found today. Throughout history and various cultures, strong men battled for beautiful women. It was thought that beautiful women were the most reproductively successful, although that has never had scientific-backing. According to Naomi Wolf, male dominated institutions are fearful of strong independent women having equal freedoms, which led to more discrimination and additionally turned women against each other.

Men are also held to standards, but it has never been institutionalized in Western cultures. Toxic masculinity is a standard that has been perpetuated by men to other men, and scientists conceived the term “hegemonic masculinity” to explain this. For example, men are told they need to be strong, wealthy laborers who provide for their families while never showing emotion. Additionally, men are subjected to certain physical standards, primarily height, which can be comparable to a beauty myth, but these standards cannot be institutionalized since women are not superior to men today. Men were once legally superior to women in the United States and many countries in the West, so it is not a comparable standard. However, in the Mediterranean from around 25,000 BCE to 700 BCE, women controlled the power in their society. In this culture, powerful women controlled the economy and often had many expendable male lovers. This example would be an accurately comparable beauty myth for men, but this is an outlier over many generations and geographical locations.
chunks.label: Sociological perspectives on beauty myths and gender norms
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses beauty myths, gender norms, othering, Naomi Wolf's theories, and standards applied to men and women throughout history.

chunks.text: I have experienced and observed many examples of the beauty myth playing out in society. There are many preconceived notions of how women are supposed to look and dress even in 2021. Growing up in the Charlotte area, I noticed how people thought my sister and my mother should act and present themselves. My mom is a strong and beautiful woman, now 51 years old, so she is experiencing the criticism from society particularly as she is aging. For the last few years, she has clearly been aging, as she should be, but rather than people complimenting her for any of her amazing qualities, she gets criticized or joked about for having new wrinkles and/or grey hair. My father on the other hand gets complimented for looking young, even though my parents are the same age.
chunks.label: Parents aging and societal double standards
chunks.what_happened: Growing up in Charlotte, the student observed their mother facing criticism and jokes about aging, while their father was complimented for looking young.

chunks.text: Since I was a pre-teen, I have seen a lot of discrimination in how men are treated compared to how women are treated, and even though we are all equal in today’s culture, women are still thought less of by many people. In school I would always hear my friends and classmates degrade women who were attractive by only referring to them with sexual innuendos rather than for their personality. I do not believe it is unfair to judge someone for their looks (since everyone is attracted to looks), but I do believe it is wrong if those judgements continue to name calling or discrimination. There are many beauty standards in our culture that I have been aware of, and even thought myself, but belittling anyone for traits and qualities that are completely incontrollable is unfair and only continues this trend of inequality.
chunks.label: Classmates degrading attractive women in school
chunks.what_happened: In school, the student regularly heard friends and classmates reduce attractive women to sexual innuendos instead of appreciating their personalities.

chunks.text: Just as I have seen beautiful women belittled, I have seen many more women discriminated against for not meeting our society’s beauty standards. If a woman is too overweight or too skinny, they were made fun of and never given the attention that “barbie doll” women got from men. If a woman does not have the most attractive smile, or even dress a certain way, they are also thought to not conform to the norms of society. No matter which facet of beauty is criticized, women almost always start with a disadvantage.
chunks.label: Reflections on discrimination for not meeting beauty standards
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how women who do not fit societal ideals of weight, smile, or clothing are ridiculed and placed at a disadvantage.

chunks.text: Growing up with only an older sister, I also got to see many ways that young women were discriminated against, even if they are beautiful. My sister is a beautiful 24-year-old now, so three years older than me. Even though many people thought she was a good-looking girl, she was frequently targeted by toxic men who had closed minds. My sister is not the slim, blonde haired, blue-eyed model that many men expect their ideal women to look like. If she dyed her hair any color, she was criticized. If she gained any weight, she was made fun of. If she liked certain sports, like basketball and golf, she was labelled a tom-boy. My sister is very independent and has never relied on her significant other to take care of her, which has made long term relationships hard for her. Yet this quality of hers is one that I personally respect the most.
chunks.label: Sister being scrutinized and judged by toxic men
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up watching their older sister face criticism for her hair color, weight, and interest in sports, as well as difficulty in relationships due to her independence.

chunks.text: While I grew up, I was certainly picked on for not conforming to every gender norm, but since I am a man, much of that discrimination came from other men.
chunks.label: Being picked on for not conforming to gender norms
chunks.what_happened: The student was picked on by other men while growing up for failing to conform to every male gender norm.

chunks.text: For as long as I can remember, women have been expected to look their best in every situation, while men are not held to that same standard. Women in modern cultures are pushed to wear makeup, provocative clothing, and act “lady-like.”
chunks.label: Unequal societal expectations placed on women
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the expectation for women to always look their best and behave ladylike, unlike men.

chunks.text: I went to middle school and high school with many people who did not conform to the traditional gender roles, so I frequently saw them targeted by (mostly) men who expected them to look a certain type of way. For example, my friend Thalia in middle school always dressed very neutral and would wear clothes that were not particularly women’s style, and she was criticized. If she had to dress up for a presentation, she would wear nice clothes, but would never wear a dress and heels. This type of attire is not rare to see in society, but because our parents and older friends perpetuated these gender norms, it is still a prevalent criticism today. Fast forward to Thalia in late high school and she was thought of as an icon for her style, because she did try to look presentable and trendy, she just did not conform to traditional women’s attire.
chunks.label: Friend Thalia's style scrutinized and later praised
chunks.what_happened: In middle school, the student's friend Thalia was criticized for dressing in gender-neutral clothes, but later in high school she was seen as an icon for her style.

chunks.text:
Although the beauty myth is still ongoing today, I believe that society is progressing, and women are beginning to be treated as true equals in society. Just as religion and ethnicity are still criticized, gender norms and beauty myths will still be placed on women for some time. This does not mean that we stop pushing back against these standards, because that is the only way to truly rid these standards from society. Women are just as human as men, so I hope that toxic men will start to realize the negative impacts their ideals have on women and society. Beauty has always been held to a high standard, and I doubt that will change, but beauty is in the eye of the beholder. Beauty can be found in everything; we just need to start opening our eyes and ears to find the beauty in everyone.

I believe that most gender norms and beauty myths are carried out primarily by young men and women, so proper parenting is very important to get rid of these problems in our society. Society has always placed pressure on certain groups to act or look a certain way, but in the United States in 2021 I believe that we have the most freedom of any culture throughout history. This has allowed us to break many barriers that have held back human civilizations of the past. As a collective society, everyone wants equality, even though politics of today have divided us greatly. Just as racism and slavery has been prevalent in many cultures throughout history, so are some of these beauty myths. The United States has allowed for the most advancement in human history, for women and other groups, so I have hope for the future.
chunks.label: Hope for future progress and gender equality
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on societal progress toward equality, the need to challenge beauty myths, the importance of parenting, and reasons for optimism.

nfb62c2e9.title: Navigating Racial Hierarchies as an Immigrant

chunks.text:
Overcoming the Urge to Reracialize by Building a Multicultural Community

How can a non-white immigrant to the United States fit in? I was born in Lebanon and moved to the United States when I was four years old, and thus I had the experience of trying to acclimate to a change in culture coupled with the attempt to make friends and fit in at school. My desire to fit in led to embarrassment concerning various aspects of myself and my life, including my skin color and my last name, which is difficult to pronounce. Furthermore, I ended up placing myself within the racial hierarchy which is in place in the U.S, striving to be considered white as a way to feel accepted. However, as I grew older, I was fortunate enough to find friends from other cultures who inspired me and gave me the courage I needed to be myself. Overall, for a non-white immigrant moving to the U.S, befriending people from other cultures is critical to oppose the pressure to place oneself and others within a racial hierarchy.
chunks.label: Introduction on immigrant assimilation and racial hierarchy
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces their background moving from Lebanon to the United States and reflects on how befriending people from diverse cultures helps counter racial hierarchies.

chunks.text: Being an only child and a relatively insecure one at that, I felt desperate to fit in and to be liked. Through my attempts to do so, I found myself attempting to repress my culture as much as possible and I tried to avoid standing out because I did not want to be labeled as “other”. As a consequence, I felt embarrassed about various aspects of myself. For instance, I would get uncomfortable when waiters at restaurants could not understand what my parents said due to their accent. Furthermore, I would wince when thinking of people struggling to pronounce my last name at awards ceremonies and when teachers would ask me to pronounce my last name. Now, I try to say it in the easiest way possible for Americans to pronounce, even though this is not how I would pronounce it in Arabic. Moreover, after moving to the U.S, I would visit Lebanon once or twice a year. In order to make the trip worthwhile over Christmas break, I would skip a few days of class and as such would be asked to make an educational presentation on my trip to Lebanon to share with the class when I returned. This would also lead to embarrassment because I was the only person in class who did such presentations.
chunks.label: Childhood insecurity and repressing Lebanese culture
chunks.what_happened: Growing up as an immigrant, the student felt embarrassed by their parents' accents, struggled with teachers mispronouncing their last name, and felt singled out presenting about trips to Lebanon.
chunks.feelings: desperate to fit in, insecure, embarrassed, uncomfortable

chunks.text: After the tenth grade, I went to the North Carolina School of Science and Mathematics (NCSSM), which had a far greater level of diversity and which had several multicultural events occurring throughout my time there. At NCSSM, I was not as worried about standing out because there were lots of my peers from different cultures.
chunks.label: Attending NCSSM among diverse peers
chunks.what_happened: The student attended the North Carolina School of Science and Mathematics, which had multicultural events and a diverse student body.

chunks.text: Tomás Almaguer described the process of the reracialization of Latino populations in the United States. Reracialization is when a group fuses the racial divisions and hierarchies of their country of origin with those of the country they immigrated to; each group will position itself in relation to the other in the newly formed racial hierarchy. For example, a white immigrant from Iceland might conduct reracialization upon arriving in the U.S, thus positioning themselves higher up in the racial hierarchy than a black immigrant from Kenya.
chunks.label: Concept of reracialization
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Tomás Almaguer's sociological concept of reracialization and gives an example of how immigrants position themselves in racial hierarchies.

chunks.text: I have been told that I appear ethnically ambiguous and have observed that my physical appearance and skin color are similar to those of people from various parts of the world. Moreover, I have been mistaken for a Hispanic person on multiple occasions by Hispanics. When I was little, I wished that I had a lighter skin tone so that I would appear to be more white. I thought that I was “almost” white. In the summer, I would be saddened by the fact that my skin would get darker, pushing me further away from the race I wanted to be. Thus, after I moved to the U.S., I began the process of reracialization, not only of the people I met but of myself as well. In Lebanon, race was not something I thought of because most people looked like me. Here, there is a clear racial hierarchy which pervades media and social interactions in both subtle and striking ways, placing white people on top and black people on the bottom. When growing up, I had friends, the majority of whom were white; this was due to the fact that my school was predominantly white and that I held stereotypes about the black students, which led me to avoid attempting to start friendships with them. Maybe I wanted to be accepted by white people to feed into my hope of being perceived as white.
chunks.label: Wishing to be white while growing up
chunks.what_happened: The student was mistaken for Hispanic and wished for lighter skin, avoiding friendships with Black classmates while striving for acceptance from white peers.
chunks.feelings: saddened, hope of being perceived as white

chunks.text: Nowadays, I feel more comfortable spending time with people who are from other cultures. Somehow, I feel closer to them than to white people because it is like we are in the same boat. We have parallel experiences which, even though they are not identical, serve to bring us closer. At UNCW, I have been fortunate enough to join multicultural clubs and to meet people who have immigrated to the U.S like I did.
chunks.label: Connecting with multicultural peers at UNCW
chunks.what_happened: At UNCW, the student joined multicultural clubs and made friends with other immigrants and people from different cultures.

chunks.text: Forming close ties and bonds with people from other cultures is an effective way to oppose the strong pressure to reracialize the self and others. Even though my friends are not Lebanese, the fact that they are not afraid to be a race other than white gives me the courage to accept myself as being different and yet still feel like I fit in. Arguably, the inverse is true as well. Even if there is no ill will or intent to exclude amongst the majority in a population, people in the minority will end up feeling pressure to reracialize according to the racial hierarchy unless they are able to form bonds with other minority members.
chunks.label: Reflecting on minority bonds against reracialization
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how forming close bonds with non-white peers gives courage to accept differences and counter systemic racial hierarchies.

chunks.text: At NCSSM, I went to several multicultural events, allowing me to learn more about the cultures of which my peers were a part and to have fun doing so by eating food, listening to music, and playing games which came from those cultures. Comparing NCSSM to my previous high school, Gray’s Creek High School (GCHS), I can see stark differences in the amount of pressure I felt to place myself within a racial hierarchy. At GCHS, since most people were white and the second largest group was black, I felt drawn to the former because I looked more white than black and because of the pre-existing racial hierarchy. Thus, my internalized reracialization drove which groups of people I ended up spending time with, who I wanted to be friends with, who I had a crush on, and how I would approach interactions with various people and myself. On the other hand, at NCSSM, the culturally diverse environment served to counter my urge to reracialize because it reduced my need to be associated with the majority racial group in order to fit in. I was able to fit in by just being myself despite the fact that none of my friends were Lebanese or even Arabic. Simply knowing that my friends were not the majority meant that I felt a sense of shared experience with them and thus I grew strong bonds with them through empathy.
chunks.label: Contrasting high school environments at GCHS and NCSSM
chunks.what_happened: The student compares attending Gray's Creek High School, where they felt pressure to align with white peers, to NCSSM, where diverse multicultural events fostered empathy.

chunks.text: In conclusion, reracialization in immigrants is spurred by the pervasive pre-existing racial hierarchy in the U.S, yet it can be opposed through the formation of connections among people of various minorities. Becoming friends with people who are from different cultures can help immigrants reduce the power of racial stereotyping and can help them fit in despite the fact that they are a minority. Moreover, having an environment where various cultures are constantly being celebrated and represented can help immigrants feel more comfortable about their own culture, even if their culture is not being celebrated directly. This works because people from minority groups face similar difficulties in their daily lives and can thus relate to one another and empathize despite not being from the same culture.
chunks.label: Conclusion on cross-cultural connections and inclusion
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that celebrating diverse cultures and building empathy across minority groups effectively counters the pressures of racial hierarchies.

n05721633.title: Analyzing the Beauty Myth in Society

chunks.text:
The Beauty Myth is a book written by Naomi Wolf in 1990 where she formulates an ideology about women and beauty. In this book she talks about the different ways that women have progressed throughout society and the ways they have fought for the rights that they have. She discusses how even though they have broken into positions of power that have not existed for women in the past, there are new issues that arise with each breakthrough. She mentions all the ways that women will tear down their bodies and go through strenuous dieting, physical activity, and surgery just to look in the mirror and see a body that pleases them. (Wolf 9) These are some of the ideas that lead her to come up with the beauty myth. She defines the beauty myth as the apparent or assumed want of women to look beautiful due to the belief that this beauty is going to lead them to more success. (Wolf 10)

The beauty myth is both very simple and very complex and in terms of modern feminism there are different ways to look at it. History has gone through two major waves of feminism that have broken down many barriers for women, but there will always be things left to fight for. This is where the third wave of feminism can be seen in the present day. The beauty myth and Modern Feminism go hand and hand and can be looked at and applied to many ideas and modern problems. The beauty myth and its existence in society have major negative effects on Modern Feminism and the ways that women are treated. The beauty myth is seen affecting women with eating disorders and their economic effects, prescriptive beauty norms and its hierarchy, as well as feminizing and controlling women and their racial constructs.

In the last 30 years the rates of eating disorders and obesity in women and girls has exponentially increased to dangerous levels and the outlining reasons behind these increased rates can be tied back to the beauty myth. Well known eating disorders like anorexia nervosa and bulimia have risen roughly 3%, from 1% to 4%, in females in the United States. Rates of bulimia nervoasa in college and high school females are estimated to be about 20%, but when representative testing and sampling is done, it is closer to 5%. The likely cause of the inflation of these numbers is seen as consciousness-raising efforts brought on by Wolf’s Beauty Myth. There has also been increased rates of obesity where a very negative social stigma has been created around being overweight. (Averett 304-305) What these statistics are able to explain is the truths about the existence and severity of eating disorders and obesity in females. While numbers like 4% and 5% don’t seem exceptionally high, it means that standing in a room with 100 females, 4 of them are going to suffer from anorexia nervosa or bulimia and 5 of them suffering from bulimia nervosa. What the beauty myth has done with numbers like these is inflate them for people to see, and create a stigma around the diseases. It does this with the intention to scare women into taking better care of their body and encouraging unhealthy mindsets that ultimately cause more harm than good.

After examining the reasons for the increased rates of eating disorders and obesity another problem can be looked at, which is the statistics that detail the economic losses that these women are suffering from due to having an eating disorder or being obese. The economic status of someone suffering from an eating disorder or someone who is obese can suffer for manny reasons both simple and complex. A simple, surface level reason is to say that these people are not physically able to work some jobs, thus preventing them from being able to work. Not to say that these people don’t exist, but when looking at the people who are perfectly able to work and are working, these people are making significantly less money. Averett says, “In employment-selectivity corrected wage equations, the pay differential is minus 12 percent for obese women and minus 5 percent for obese men.”, which shows the blatant discriminatin against obese people and even more so, obese women. (306) Averett goes on to list more specific statistics of different age groups that have suffered economic losses do to the fact that they are obese. The statistics are simple and direct and they show a direct correlation between economic losses being greater in obese women than in obese men or men and women of a standard weight class. Where the beauty myth comes into this is when you apply the definition of the beauty myth to the employers who are making these wage decisions. Employers expect that someone who is physically fit or more appealing to the eye is going to work better and is worthy of more money. The beauty myth is able to showcase that if a woman who is obese and a woman who is not obese applied for the same job with the same exact resume, then the woman who is not obese will get the job and get a hihger salary becaus her appearance gives the idea that she will be a better worker.

Prescriptive Beauty Norms can be defined as ways that women will spend time, money, and effort to attain the level of beauty seen in society, and these norms affect many aspects of modern day feminism and do a great deal to hinder women’s progress. A lot of women have the ability to take beauty norms like dressing up and wearing makeup and genuinely enjoy them and gain a sense of empowerment from feeling beautiful and put together. It is not that easy for everyone as some women will either not have the resources, not have the money, or not have the capabilities to do these things on a regular basis. This is where the beauty norms start to be taken as disempowering as Ramati-Ziber writes, “However, when intense social pressure turns pursuing beauty into a mandate (rather than a freely chosen activity), beauty practices become socially coercive, an obligation women must fulfill or risk being “. . . deemed uncivilized and immoral”(Fredrickson & Roberts, 1997, p. 182)”. (318) The disempowerment comes when these beauty norms are being forced and not seen as an option. This broadcasts a feeling to women where they believe that they have to be fully out together to go out for the day or society is going to make negative opinions about them. The Beauty Norm is seen as the push to enjoy these norms and feel empowerment from them, but in reality the too heavy push toward empowerment turns into disempowerment.

After defining Prescriptive Beauty Norms, also known as PBN, they can be applied to the beauty myth and the way this is done is through the built in Hierarchy-Enhancing effects of the beauty myth. In Wolf’s books she further defines the beauty myth through many different lenses and goes on to explain that it is more about types of behavior that is encouraged and not solely appearance. What this means is that there is a gender hierarchy that becomes enforced showcasing the different body types and how they are seen in society. Ramati Ziber describes the main three components of the beauty myth as, “(a) beauty ideals, which Toledano (2012) suggests include both “biological,” less easily modified, bodily standards (e.g., youth, thinness) and “performed,” more malleable, grooming standards (e.g., wearing make-up and high heels); (b) attainability beliefs, believing that beauty ideals can be reached via beauty practices; and (c) the PBN, which prescribes women to intensively strive for and prioritize attainting beauty.” (319) These different components are what push the hierarchy as each component has certain things that make someone more desirable and are going to put them higher up in the hierarchy. Someone who did not have the good traits from these components is going to be lower down on the hierarchy. The beauty myth pushes people into categories based on how many of these components they satisfy.

Burcar analyzes the beauty myth through the lens of Toni Morrison’s The Bluest Eye and she breaks down the ways that the Myth has made gendered beauty norms into a way of feminizing and controlling women. The Bluest Eye is about a woman who decides to leave her domestic confinement and head to Hollywood To pursue a career in cinema. Very quickly she discovers the intense representations in cinema that cater to, “Feminine beauty and whiteness”, and explains how these things made it difficult for her. (Burcar 141) Women in Hollywood are seen simply as a body that is available for manipulation, and even though all they want is bodies that can be decorated at their disposal, there is only a specific group of bodies that is going to please them. Being successful in Hollywood and having a career in front of a screen all comes down to if they can fit the mold of what is deemed to be beautiful, and can this beauty be used and capitalized off of. The beauty myth very obviously fits the mold of Hollywood because just like the beauty myth, in Hollywood if you are beautiful you are going to be successful and if you are not their idea of beautiful then you will not be successful.

Bucar also analyzes the effects of the beauty myth in The Bluest Eye as it pertains to the racial constructs of beauty. Racism and the Racialized constructs of beauty go hand and hand and have come about and developed at the same time. Racism alone is a social construct used to divide people into groups that simply do not need to exist, and the same can be seen with beauty. Beauty in itself dissects people into who is conventionally beautiful and not beautiful, and these groups can be further broken down with race. A student from a 2016/2017 seminar provided this analysis of The Bluest Eye, “Pecola is black and because of that she is not just ugly in the eyes of Mr. Yacobowski, she is not even worth his glance. He does not want to look at her. It seems as if he is looking through her as if she were invisible. This invisibility is even worse than just hatred or disgust, because even if you are hated at least you are perceived as a person.” (Burcar 148) This analysis of The Bluest Eye details the intense effect of racism within the beauty myth. Not only was the teacher outwardly racist doward Pecola, but due to this racism he would never even consider her to be beautiful and fit into beauty norms. The beauty myth ties directly into racial constructs and people's perception of what is beautiful, and shows a further step into someone's analysis of what is beauty.

The beauty myth can be defined many ways and throughout daily life it could be stumbled upon 100 times without even realizing it. Naomi Wolf defined the beauty myth in 1990 but that is not to say that it did not exist before. The reality is that it has likely always existed and her book in 1990 only brought to light a fraction of the way that it affects women. In the twenty-first century as society is moving through the third wave of feminism, it is the first major femenism movement since the existence of Naomi Wolf’s book. What this means is that, as modern feminists fight for more rights, equal treatment, equal respect, better wages, and more representation, the beauty myth can be dissected in these fights. The beauty myth and its existence in society have had major negative effects on Modern waves of Feminism and the ways that women are treated. The beauty myth is seen majorly affecting women suffering from eating disorders and obesity and their economic effects, prescriptive beauty norms and the hierarchies enforced, as well as feminizing and controlling women and their racial beauty constructs.
chunks.label: Analysis of Naomi Wolf's beauty myth and feminism
chunks.what_happened: The student presents an academic essay analyzing Naomi Wolf's concept of the beauty myth and its intersection with modern feminism, eating disorders, wage gaps, prescriptive beauty norms, and racial constructs.

chunks.text: Gender has given people the ability to define who they are and the way that they act, but gender has also been used against people for as long as the idea has existed. Women have had their gender used against them and been used for their stereotype as being described as the “other” as well as the drawbacks from the “beauty myth”. It has taken a long time for society to take women as seriously as they do, but there will likely never be a time when men and women are truly equal. Society will likely never give women the same opportunities, and the same level of respect that men get, because that was never the norm.
chunks.label: Gender inequality and societal treatment of women
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how gender defines people and is used against them, noting concepts like the 'other' and the 'beauty myth'. The student asserts that society will likely never truly treat men and women equally or give women the same opportunities and respect.

nb786db3e.title: Perceptions of Power and Social Division

chunks.text: Civilization refers to a society built upon government, communication, social organizations as well as urban development. Within civilization forms a society in which social classes are incorporated, causing that civilization to become socially divided. These divided social classes lead to an imbalance in feelings of power and superiority. While many refuses to believe this idea of social class, it is very apparent and with factors such as income and social appearance, the formation of classes is almost inevitable.
chunks.label: Social class and division in civilization
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the concept of civilization and reflects on how social classes divide society and inevitably create imbalances in power and superiority.

n26515d1c.title: Perceiving Actors Beyond Their Famous Roles

chunks.text:
In tv entertainment I get caught up in an actors life so much that when I see them in different program it catches me off guard. For example, John Krasinski, he plays Jim Halpert from the office as well as Jack Ryan from Tom Clancy’s Jack Ryan. For the longest time whenever I saw Mr. Krasinski in any film, I always gave him the persona as Jim from the office. This briefs the idea of the conception of self and how an individual sees themselves from a third- and first-person point of view.

Erving Goffman proclaims that the self is collectively produced and that for the self to be defined the “collective” third person needs to interact with the first-person. This interaction expands the idea that the social aspect is an important factor in the thought of self. In correspondence to George Mead, the “I” is the reaction because of the environment and the “me” is a reaction in response to the “I”. The “Me” is autonomous feelings towards self that contextualizes from the consciousness. Both philosophers communicate the concept that conversation, whether it be from an outside source or within yourself, is key to understanding the idea of self.

The example with John Krasinski; when people meet him in person is becomes confusing for the audience because they are not used to that type of role with Mr. Krasinski, but rather with Jim or Jack. John’s acting assimilated to the “I” in Mead’s theory then, on the outside his personal life could be seen as the “me”. This is present in daily life with your peers, meaning that everyone has differently roles and it becomes confusing, even awkward, if the roles are not met.
chunks.label: The sociological conception of self and acting roles
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on perceiving actor John Krasinski only as his characters, connecting this to theories by Erving Goffman and George Herbert Mead regarding the 'I', the 'me', and social roles.
chunks.people: John Krasinski, Erving Goffman, George Mead

nf00dcaa9.title: Religious Influence and Expanding Individual Liberties

chunks.text:
No matter if you believe in God, Yahweh, Buddha, or blue flying fish as a divine power, religion is eminent in composing societies’ ethics and norms. Religion influences everything that constructs societies today, from social interactions to laws. According to Emile Durkheim, religion is the reasoning behind all great social institutions in society, however, without the collective representation of society, there would be no religion. Although religion has had such a massive impact on society, Yuval Harai believes that the social concepts are becoming less religious and more human.

The collective consciousness is a mass of people having the same ideas or morals and doing similar rituals that result in a common social concept within the collective group. Religion, according to Durkheim, is the collective representation of most social concepts today, meaning that without religion being the fundamental ideas, then the principle of collective consciousness would not exist in the social setting. Religion has been important in many things in the world, for example, “In God, We Trust” is printed on every American currency. The religion-based collective consciousness also affected the constitutional paper in America like the Declaration of Independence, where multiple remarks relate to God. However, these collective representations were made in the 18th century, which means the religious ideas in the papers could be possibly different from the collective social norms made today.

Harai explains in 21 Lessons for the 21st Century that, individuals’ free will and liberties used to be neglected by the collective belief that divine laws come from a higher power, before modern times. This idea is still being used in certain societies today across the globe, from third-world tribes to radical Christianity. Society used to be solely religious but now people are starting to become more spiritual. Today, social institutions are created by a collective of individual liberties of free will, which Harai believes is the collective idea of liberalism shaping our minds to live more freely. More liberties in America have become less religious, in the sense of choosing what to study, whom to marry, or which candidate or party to vote for, wherein some societies are all based on religious values and rules.

The idea of collective consciousness from Durkheim was the basis of the conceptualization of Harai’s “Part 3: Liberty” in 21 Lessons for the 21st Century. The concept of the collective believes today have brought more liberalism in our common practices like the personal choice of university studies, marriage, and political beliefs, which used to be religiously demonstrated. Durkheim’s concept of collective consciousness was used in today’s socially updated; by Harai to explain what our Liberties in society are based on.
chunks.label: Religion and collective consciousness in society
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological perspectives on religion and collective consciousness, comparing Emile Durkheim's theories with Yuval Harari's ideas about modern liberties and secularism.

na7499f4a.title: Analyzing Hegemonic Masculinity and Doing Gender

chunks.text:
When we look at the term hegemonic masculinity, we can also interpret it as doing gender. The term hegemonic masculinity is this behavior that men have the power within society over women. While the concept of doing gender is within the way we carry ourselves and feeling like we need to act a certain way based on our sex. Hegemonic masculinity is a prime example of men “doing gender”.

Then we have the term “hegemonic masculinity” who is coined from the sociologist R.W. Connell. Hegemonic masculinity is a behavior that supports the power of men in society, and the subordination of women, other oppressed male identities, and the general male population. It is the practice of supporting male domination, the dominant form of masculinity, violence, and aggression. Men often feel that hegemonic masculinity benefits them when in reality it is hurting society. In the reading “You’re Either In or You’re out” the boys asserted their dominance through bullying other people. Men want to assert their dominance because they have always been the ones in the most power, when that feels threatened they tend to use hegemonic masculinity. Hegemonic masculinity is the standard for what a man should be as it is seen within society. The sense that men are aggressive, strong, that they provide, and overall an alpha.

A real world example that could be used in both terms is when a husband feels like they need to be working more and making more money than his wife. Society has made it a social norm that men are the ones that are providing for their family. They are the ones that are supposed to be working the most and making the most money. Men want this feeling of having male domination over women, so if the wife is making more money than them then they tend to feel insecure and threatened. This is a prime example of doing gender because society makes men feel like they have to work more than women. When they indulge in that they are considered doing gender. They are the “breadwinner” in the family. The gender roles in society is that men are the one providing for their family and the wife is more of a stay at home mom. It is also a prime example of hegemonic masculinity because they are asserting male dominance by having this power over women that they are the ones making more money than their wife. They feel dominant because they feel as if they are better than their wife in that sense. In society's standards men are supposed to be smarter and work harder than women.

Another unfortunate real world example would be domestic violence. When a man hits a woman it is usually because they are insecure and their masculinity feels threatened in some way. It is known that society has this norm that when men get angry they get aggressive. Therefore, say a couple is arguing and the woman says something that questions a man's masculinity, the man might feel the need to hit the woman in order to feel like he has power over her. This shows doing gender because of the fact that men get angry which escalates to being aggressive. It is doing gender because men are supposed to feel masculine and they are proving to themselves that they are by acting in aggression. The body is often used as a tool for expressing our gender. In this case they use their body to feel strong against the women. It is also an example of hegemonic masculinity in the fact that they feel this need to prove their masculinity. They try to assert their dominance by hitting the women so they feel this sense of power. When the woman says something that makes them insecure they want to still feel like they have their masculinity. They get aggressive and violent to reclaim their masculinity.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of hegemonic masculinity and doing gender
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the concepts of hegemonic masculinity and doing gender, discussing general hypothetical examples such as breadwinning dynamics and domestic violence.

nedf94361.title: Intersections of Race and Middle Class

chunks.text:
Everyone has heard of the term white privilege and the term middle class so much so that they might even be living both of them to the fullest. While it is easy to assume that each person’s definition is the correct one and that the benefits of each outweigh the history; perhaps some have no clue about what each of these terms truly mean along with how they are interconnected. The middle class has a very broad range of families including some who make fifteen thousand dollars a year to others who make well over two hundred thousand dollars a year. Are these families that are on the upper end of the middle class living out the perfect white privilege scenario without even noticing? White privilege is a term that simply means that people who are white are granted certain aspects of life due to their skin color which other skin colors wouldn’t be able to indulge in. White privilege and the middle class have a significant correlation that many may have never thought about or noticed but is an issue that needs to be addressed.

White privilege, having an invisible package of unearned assets that can be cashed in every day to help out a white human. This means that every day, due to skin color, white people have a safer advantage than others who may have a different color of skin. This is a systematic approach that developed due to racism. Throughout the years, white people have fed into racism and constantly perpetuated it meaning that all it takes is one act of meanness for racism to come back in spiraling. The white privilege concept goes on to treat race as a property of the body rather than anything else such as a characteristic of someone. White privilege operates on both conscious and unconscious levels, challenging various aspects of life, including education, employment, housing, healthcare, and the criminal justice system for people who aren’t white. While this doesn't mean that all white individuals live privileged lives or do not face hardships throughout their lives, it does acknowledge that race is not a barrier to their success or safety in the same way it is for people who have different skin colors.

Middle class is a very broad term for which people see themselves on the spectrum of how they live and the money they make/spend. This is the middle term for the broad term of social class which is a particular collective consciousness that is produced through wealth. Social class shapes the experience of social reality through the collective consciousness. The collective consciousness is what shapes your values, and beliefs, and also provides context for the self to experience external domains. Within the middle class, it is found that families send their children to public school and have social activities in which they indulge. While some people are born into the middle class, others work their way up from the bottom by providing for themselves and taking opportunities that come their way. It is found that race, parents, and gender are all aspects that affect the class that people grow up to be a part of.

White privilege and class privilege are intertwined particularly in the middle-class era. Not only does this highlight the complexities of social advantages and disadvantages, but it also shows just how the white privilege invisible package is put into place within the real world. Although all individuals from any race or gender can be part of the middle class, white middle-class people are often the ones who continue to live out and experience the additional perks of privilege due to their race. They may benefit from their families' inherited wealth or family connections which ties in with the factor that everyone is affected by their parents or how they were raised. This results in different opportunities coming to different people due to connections from parents and families who continue helping their children and shaping their futures. This leads them to be more likely to reside in neighborhoods with better schools and resources, have access to higher-paying jobs, and encounter fewer problems when seeking loans or investments. Even within the middle class, racial disparities are still encountered although white individuals do still experience greater advantages and better opportunities simply because of their race.

In conclusion, it is easier for people who are white to experience the perks of living in the middle status and accept opportunities that come within. While not everyone who experiences middle class is white, it is still easier for white people to get jobs, gain experience, and get better connections than someone with a different skin color who may have more barriers that are preventing them from something that they are trying to do. The middle class is a very broad term that a lot of people within the United States fall under and get to experience but with that may come scenarios where racism, rights, and even opportunities are not being provided fairly among all skin colors. This has been an ongoing problem for generations due to most people feeding into and constantly perpetuating mean actions toward people who are different than them. While it would be very hard to reverse racism, the world would be a much better place if everyone treated each other with respect and disregarded skin color, class differences, and differing opinions.
chunks.label: Interconnection of white privilege and middle class
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses and analyzes the concepts of white privilege and the middle class, explaining how they intersect to provide systemic advantages to white individuals.

nad0f8f05.title: Performing Roles on the Social Stage

chunks.text:
Why do people feel the need to change how they act based on the situation that they are in? The feeling that one has to behave differently depending on the situation is an almost universal one. Many people will keep their true selves hidden, with their real thoughts and feelings concealed behind a facade. They can only be revealed when the person is in a private setting. But what is it that drives people to be so self-conscious? In Sociology, there is a concept that explains this type of behavior. Originated by Erving Goffman, this is known as front and back stage behavior, the study of which is sometimes called dramaturgical analysis. Goffman introduced this concept in his book ,“The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life”, published in 1956. In this book, Goffman describes social interaction between people as being similar to the interaction of roles in a theater play, which explains the front and back stage comparison. The “front stage” is the way that people behave in front of an “audience”. The audience is usually a person or a group of people. Someone may make themself seem more confident, smart, or sociable than they actually are in order to make a good impression on their audience. Backstage behavior is the opposite - it is the behavior that one exhibits when there is no one else around to see it. There is no pressure to look or act presentable, so the person is able to truly let themself relax. This concept introduces the idea that everyone has a role that they are expected to play, and failure to do so will result in humiliation and ridicule from your audience.

The main question that I have is “why?”. Why do people feel so inclined to hide who they are? Is fitting in and playing your role really this important? What makes people so willing to change who they are just to please everyone else? One possible solution to this conundrum is impression management. Impression management, as defined by Erving Goffman in the same book that he introduced front stage and backstage behavior in, is the act of trying to present yourself or behave in a way that is considered acceptable by your audience. It is connected to front and back stage behavior, specifically front stage behavior, because it concerns the way that someone acts in front of their audience. An example of impression management could be someone making an effort to dress and speak formally when going into a job interview, even though in their day to day life they could act completely differently. The book “Impression Management Theory and Social Psychological Research” by James T. Tedeschi references a great example of impression management and why people are concerned with front stage behavior in the section “Avoiding Blame and Getting Credit” (pgs. 5-10). This section explains how many people are concerned with both getting credit for their positive actions and averting criticism for their negative actions. In figure 1.1 on page 6, the many different paths someone may take to either claim responsibility or innocence when faced with the consequences of their decisions is shown.When faced with the consequences of a poorly thought out choice, people may try to distance themselves from their actions in order to avoid punishment or blame for that action, thus avoiding any damage to their public image. They may also try to justify their actions by minimizing the impact of their outcome. When faced with the positive outcomes of a choice, someone may try to enhance the benefits of their decision to make their choice seem more admirable, or they could try to make themselves seem more responsible for the outcome. This type of impression management can be seen in our society in many different cases. For example, when someone does something harmful, they may apologize in a way that seems disingenuous. They may try to place some sort of blame on the people that they hurt with their decision by saying things like “I am sorry that you feel that way”, where the person is placing blame on the upset party for feeling hurt, rather than taking responsibility for causing the hurt. This is impression management because the person who did the harmful thing is trying to absolve themself of blame or guilt by transferring it onto another person, making them look better. This is also called blame-shifting. On page 7, the types of excuses that someone may use to preserve their self-image are listed, and they include the denial of bad intentions, lack of bodily control, and denials of agency. These are all excuses meant to distance a person from their actions. They are intended to convince others that the person who committed these actions did not have as much control over the situation as everyone thought, whether or not that is actually true. They are meant to make the person look better to their audience.

Societal expectations are also a big reason for why front stage and backstage behavior exists. These affect both front stage and backstage behavior. One’s front stage behavior “reflects internalized norms and expectations for behavior shaped partly by the setting, the particular role one plays in it, and by one’s physical appearance” (Cole, Goffman’s Front Stage and Back Stage Behavior). Concerning the front stage, the way that people are expected to act has a lot to do with how they present themselves. For example, customer service workers are expected to be courteous to all of their customers, even the ones that are unkind to them. If they don’t fulfill this expectation, they may be met with scorn from their audience, and could lose their job. Business people are expected to be professional at all times, and in every aspect of their life, such as their speech and appearance. If they fail to do so, they too could lose their job. Students in a school are often expected by their peers to keep up with certain trends or they will be met with bullying. Clearly, a lot of importance is placed upon front stage behavior, so much so that the consequences of not playing your role can be catastrophic. Societal expectations can also influence a person’s backstage behavior. For example, a student feeling pressured to follow certain trends at school may spend their time at home organizing outfits to wear to school, or a businessman concerned with looking professional may spend the hours after his shift is done rehearsing a presentation or an interview so that he does not embarrass himself in front of his coworkers. Societal expectations can differ from culture to culture, but one thing is certain. If someone fails to adhere to expectations, then they have failed to play their role, and the results can range from humiliating to devastating. There is a lot depending just on someone playing their role, including self-esteem and employment, which could also explain why keeping front stage and backstage behavior separate is important to many.

In conclusion, front stage and backstage behavior defines how people will behave differently depending on the situation that they are in. This concept was introduced by Erving Goffman, in his book “The Presentation of Self in Everyday Life”, which used theater terms to describe social behaviors. Front stage behavior refers to how someone acts when they are in front of an “audience”. When engaging in front stage behavior, a person will often make themselves act differently in order to please their audience. Backstage behavior is the way that a person acts when no one is around to judge them. Although the person isn’t expected to think about their front stage personas at this time, many will often spend this time preparing for the next time that they are in front of an audience. There are a couple of different reasons why someone would want to hide their true selves in order to please their audience. One of those reasons is impression management. Impression management is when someone presents themself in a way that makes them seem more pleasing to the audience. There are many different ways that impression management can manifest, several of those being in reaction to an action, good or bad. Depending on the consequences of the action that they took, a person may try to overstate their responsibility in the situation, distance themself from the action overall, or justify the decisions that they made. Another reason why someone would choose to behave differently in front of an audience is societal expectations. In all different cultures, and in all different situations, people have a lot of expectations placed upon them by society. Failure to live up to these expectations could result in embarrassment or ridicule from one’s audience. Many are pushed to behave or present themselves in a certain way in order to live up to these expectations. The reasons why many want to keep their front stage and backstage separate are numerous, but they all come down to one main point - people want to look good for those who are paying them attention, just as actors want to put on a good performance for their audience.

n609e5d71.title: Analyzing Mental Health and Social Media

chunks.text:
Mental Health Degradation: The Effect of Extensive Social Media Use

Social contact, an intrinsic aspect of human existence, has been changed forever. Traditional human soapily contact has been recorder throughout history and is often see in the context of rituals and cultural experiences. While traditional roles have and always will be a staple in society, the creation of social media has drastically affected the behaviors that humans express in social settings. Social media was intended to foster more close-knit relationships and robust social structures, yet through research as startling discovery is found. Social media is diminishing the mental health of its users, especially the younger and emerging adult populations. Mental health issues such as Depressive Disorders , General Anxiety, Body Dysmorphic Disorder, High-Risk Sexual Activities, and addictive behaviors are all exacerbated through the use of social media. What was once a tool to bring global sociology to the individual scale, is now creating an insurmountable mental health pandemic.

This also mirrors the class discussion on the stage that people present themselves on. The social media is used constantly and that’s provided a new stage for users to present themselves on, but they tend to be more socially anxious when removed from social media. Other studies have been performed in similar fashion, over a brow scale of participants and have found very similar results as states previously. (Shensa, Sidani, Dew, Escobar-Viera, & Primack, 2018) This means that the idea that anxiety and anxiety disorders are dire results of extended social media use, is being proven consistently. In conjunction with general anxiety, social anxiety has also been researched respect to its correlation with social media use. Research shows that altho social media was intended to foster community and group cooperation, it has resulted in an innately for users to feel comfortable in a live setting when interacting with other humans. Females were specifically found to feel more anxious on average over their male counterparts and also felt as if their privacy was a significant concern on social media. (Alkis, Kadirhan, & Sat, 2017) This is extremely detrimental to cultural ties and society in general, where real-life is a constant reality what all must be able to navigate without the help of social media. Privacy is no longer a mutual respect, and physical relationships are imperative to humanity’s existence. Social media has been found to risk that reality.

Another risk that extends past social medias risk to society itself, is that social media may be linked to behavior and mental disorders that rick the health of its users. Body Dysmorphic Disorder (BDD) and the broad topic of body image issues, is a growing issue in the social media realm. BDD is typically characterized by the following habits and/or symptoms: perfectionist tendencies, belief that the subject had unseen defects in appearance, social situation avoidance, constant grooming or cosmetic hiding habits, etc. (2019) What this disorder does is target how individuals perceive themselves among the group, particularly in how they physically appear. The very nature of social media is that users post photos of themselves and activities they perform in order to gain recognition. This has proven to be destructive in many cases, where users become entrapped in the false idea that everyone else in their feed or their life looks a certain way or has certain physical attributes. This is where body image comes into the scene. Time and time again, body-shaming and buying n the rounds of physical appearance is an all too common occurrence. Naturally, the more time users spend on social media, the more they come into contact with this occurrence. Adolescence in particular have been targeted by social media use, and express heightened body dysmorphia in general. (Behm-Morawitz & Lewallen, 2016) This issue is not as common in real-life where there is a far greater array of body types, shapes, and sizes and none of which are put on a social pedestal quite like social media. Women have been the target of anti-body dysmorphia campaigns that aim to defeat the hard reality that social media promotes, but men are often forgotten. Studies have been conducted, where men are affected in a very similar way to women in this realm. (Hobza, Walker, Yakushko, & Peugh, 2007) Social media has no boundaries where users can hide or de-categorize themselves. BDD and body image issues will continue to be a great concern and a great downfall in modern social media history.

Body Dysmorphic Disorder has recently been highlights by social media stars and the media alike, however, darker and more dangerous complimentary issue is high-risk sexual behavior. High-Risk Sexual Activity (HRSA) has begun to emerge as a result of extensive social media use by teen and younger adults. Some examples of HRSA include, unprotected sex (oral/anal/vaginal), multiple sex partners, sex before the age of 18, sex work, and others. (Healthwise Staff, 2020) All of these activities pose a significant threat to young adults that are captivated by social media trends and subsequently normalized potentially dangerous activities. One study specifically looked into the affects that social media has on Latino populations in this context. Researchers found that a significant portion of subjects actively “sexted” boyfriends or girlfriends on a regular basis. Parental oversight of social media use was found to not only lower the risk for HRSA such as sexting, but all restore normal family function. (Landry, Turner, Vyas, & Wood, 2017) In this case, the Latino culture was a specific concern but this can be used for cross-cultural analysis in a sociological context. In a more broad study, researchers found that not only text messaging but social media had a specific impact on the extremely high percentage of young adults (15-24 yrs) that report contracting a sexually transmitted disease. Young adults make up an all-time high of 48% of all cases. (Jones, Eathington, Baldwin, & Sipsma, 2014) When viewed in the context that social media influencers are pushing sexually based agendas and promiscuity to gan recognition, this is to be the expected result. Every beyond a correlation, there is a causative effect with exposure to sexual content on social media and participation in HRSA. (Bleakley, Hennessey, Fishbein, & Jordan, 2008) The issue with social media in this sense is that it is giving particularly vulnerable populations access to content that thy would otherwise be unable to access. This is causing a sharp incline in risky behavior and has spiked rates of STDs and STIs across the globe. Not only is this an epidemic among developed countries, but this is a pandemic and is on track to influence human culture and group behavior overall.

In a cascade of negative effects that social media has on mental health, the nagging result that is often overlooked by its users is addiction. Addiction, whether that be to HRSA, body image, or to social media itself. Addiction in the form of social media overuse, constantly checking ones phone for notifications or new social media posts, and abusing time spent on social media to the point where it impedes everyday life. (Hilliard, 2021) This addiction extends to other addictive habits scubas substance abuse. Substance abuse has been linked to social media, where groups that promote addictive behavior with illicit substances are found. Moreover, the simple act of posting about substance abuse may normalize its existence and result in addictive behavior in the future. (Kim et al., 2017) College students as a sub culture of the human race are experiencing heightened issues with addictive behavior. College in general is an open door to substances and experiences that are often unique to the college experience. Parties, clubbing, and diverse friendships have a new dynamic who social media is introduces. (D’Arienzo, Boursier, & Griffiths, 2019) Social media accounts highlighting such scenes to college students normalizes potentially detrimental social practices and when combined with addiction to social media itself, may result in addiction to substances and the Fear of Missing Out (FOMO). This goes back the self-esteem issue earlier, where self-esteem is lower with extended social media use and results in addiction to the positive feedback loop that social media employs. This takes time away from studying for exams and leads to a general decimation of college grades and self-efficacy. (Hou, Xiong, Jiang, Song, & Wang, 2019) This too is a pandemic that extends to a global scale. Populations of college students an young adults are faced with defeating addictions to trends or social media itself. This undoubtedly affects future generations, and may end up affecting groups of people that are surrounded with substance abuse issues due to low socioeconomic status.

The mental health crisis the world is facing today has always existed throughout human history. The change in how mental health is viewed has largely been exposed through modern media coverage and through social media use. The negative effects of social media use are costly, and have resulted in global outcry for research on remedies to the problems it can create. From depression and anxiety, to BDD and addiction; social media presents a significant challenge to vulnerable populations. Teens and young adults are the most notable, however, any population or group of people that overuses social media is at risk for the variety of factors presented above. As social media continues to grow into new facets of human life and social structures, a significant uptick in mental health issues will be experiences. If humans have survived through tens of thousands of years with traditional social structures and behaviors, will the exponentially growing invasion of social media into life itself finally drive mankind mad?

n012f53b1.title: Reflecting on Alienation in Modern Work

chunks.text: Every society has its detrimental aspects. What seems to nag Western society is the relationship that workers have with the work they perform. Society can often times be overly individualistic and too focussed on material wealth, that many people forget the rewards that their work can ultimately yield: fulfillment. I believe that Marx was right in that there is a general, unnatural relationship that is promoted within work and life. That is facilitated by bureaucracy, and exploited by economic gate-keepers. It is a sad reality, but it can be fixed by finding the true nature and rewards of work and Capitalism which is so often forgotten. Twenty-five to thirty years is a long relationship, so it ought to be a healthy one.
