n25690534.title: Analyzing Systemic Racism in American Institutions

chunks.text:
Racism is a major topic in America today with the murders of innocent citizens, social justice movements, and accusations of systemic oppression within the health care field. This fast-growing, social-civil issue has risen back to the platform of importance due to the recent controversial actions within the U.S government. What exactly defines the system of “racism”? "Race" is a social construct created by the majority entirely based on racial differences (Hutto and Green 2016). Looking back to the early days of American history, we can see that racism has been rooted in America's upbringing since its beginning. With slavery being one of the main foundations of America during the colonial era, up until the Civil War, it has systematic roots buried into almost every government system or institution. However, people believe that the 1960s when the Jim Crow laws were abolished and more Civil Rights Laws were added was the last time America could be considered a racist nation. Despite the judicial legal rights African Americans gained from this era, these laws could not stop the racial background of the U.S.’s government systems who would counter-act their rights. Throughout this paper, I will discuss the current systematic racism that is affecting the justice system and health care systems in the U.S, and how it was structurally created.

To begin to see how systematic racism still exists in today’s America, we will have to understand the framework of racism. The beginning of these racial schemes could be explained best by using one of the articles used in class, Estranged Labour by Karl Marx. The Marxian idea of capitalism is the complex framework that allows racism to carry into current-day society. Capitalism is summed down into two parts: the small capitalist class who own the means of production, and the working class who uses their labor to provide their money (Hutto and Green 2016). In simpler terms, the rich are the capitalist class, and the middle to poor class was the working. Back when capitalism first started, only the Caucasians could be the capitalist class, and the working class was predominantly African American. The capitalist class also systematically exploited the working class, which later brought oppression and suppression towards the working class. With Caucasians controlling the African Americans in early America’s capitalist society, this prompted the social ideology of racism to start snowballing into other systems in America.

Even after attempts by some American governmental powers to stop the systematic racism so it will not corrupt the American governance. America’s governmental systems still found a way to counteract them, for example, the creation of the KKK (Ku Klux Klan), who lead racially charged lynching, and other horrific actions towards African Americans. This white-supremacist ideology --made by the capitalist class-- would weaken and oppress the working class even more. With this new racist ideology, the capitalist class’s efforts would subconsciously be ingrained into the minds of other whites (Hutto and Green 2016). This process is comparable to the formation of the collective consciousness, which was talked about in the first module of this course. The collective consciousness in white Americans started to slowly become more aligned with oppression towards the black Americans, due to the new racial ideology slowly furnishing American’s minds. This one ideology became collective consciousness due to the fact it slowly infested a large population of white Americans which shaped these people to have a racist mindset. Whenever the capitalist class created this new national ideology, it made their system of capitalism stronger and the working class weaker and easier to exploit.

And since the working class became so easy to exploit, other systems of the U.S came to escalate the exploitation including racial police brutality, intimidation, and murder which all directly benefited the function of capitalism (Hutto and Green 2016). This led to racial ideals being anchored in some police forces, which later proved to be systematic racism at its prime. Police brutality has been around for a while and is still a dangerous culture that exists in today’s America. In this culture, police have a predisposed reaction to generate greater readiness to use lethal force whenever faced with a person of color. Police brutality also includes the misconduct of treatment towards people with disabilities. This results in distrust towards the legal system from Americans and creates this battle of social justice between the police force and citizens fighting for justice.

Some specific instances that police systems in America are discriminating and targeting black Americans are found in Prince George County. Where the police department created an undercover task force titled “Death Squad” that would target African American men to entrapment for robbery to arrest them. Their brutality does not stop there, in 1969, this same police department killed an unarmed black man, which resulted in a large protest. The Prince George County Police Department also shot and killed an unarmed black man who was attempting to steal two 7-dollar country hams, on Christmas day. Police brutality has not changed at all since the late 1960s, and we are facing more police brutality ever more often. With the vociferous death of George Floyd, the issue of system racism in our police force has been revitalized and seen as an important topic for social injustices today. Many riots have resulted in police brutality in the 21st century due to the long-drawn-out issue that centers around police discrimination. So it is very understandable why African American communities have distrust in the American police system.

People of color have also distrusted the U.S government health care system, due to discrimination in the health field. Black Americans are more likely to trust black doctors, according to Evans et al., and research shows that a black man will receive better care from a doctor who is racially concordant compared to a doctor that is racially discordant. There is an element of structural racism in America’s medical workforce, in which black Americans are less likely to become doctors compared to any other race. African Americans are found to face serious health inequities and a lack of support for health care coverage, along with a lower chance, compared to any other race to find a racially concordant doctor (Evans et al., 2020). This shows that people of color are discriminated against based on preventative measures, access to treatments, and other resource needs to ensure the health of these patients. Wingfield also states that discrimination occurs in the scientific research field as well, due to algorithms are designed to make decisions for health care incorporates biases that prevent the amount of care for African American patients.

This systematic racism in our health institutions creates more health disparities in our world, which is a racial disparity. This health disparity determines the difference in treatment of races. This can affect the quality and quantity of care for African American patients, and negatively affects the overall health of the race entirely. Studies have also shown that white applicants of grant programs ran by the U.S. National Institutes of Health received more money, compared to their black counterparts. This goes to show how inequality in our health care systems truly exists and need to be further fought against.

Social justice movements that include BLM (Black Lives Matter) have been created to start the fight for racial equality from police discrimination to healthcare. With fighting America will continue to have corruption and systemic racism in its Police departments and health care systems.

chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes systemic racism in the United States, examining how capitalism, historical oppression, police brutality, and healthcare inequities affect African Americans, supported by course concepts and citations.

n95ffd8ba.title: Reflecting on Religion, Race, and Freedom

chunks.text:
Religion has a great and powerful influence in today’s society and always have for many years. A society formed by strong shared origins in religion can be a powerful unity if it wants to be. Religion was introduced in the first human society and has remained a part of human society ever since. Religion in some way defines individuals and gives them characteristics be ever discovered, it can be either positive or negative. I was inspired to do more research about religious concepts after reading the neurology of religion. It differentiates religion and culture. In class, we talked about the start of religion and what led to the expansion. Which has a huge impact on Race too because they kind of go hand-in-hand. You cannot talk about the origin of religion and not bring in “race” because every religion started within a specific environment with the same kind of people. There are more chances of them agreeing on a specific belief than a diverse community.

American religion missionaries’ determination led them to other continents of the world, where do you make the word of God known to many. African-Americans were are highly known achieved in forming their churches, calling in the memberships, which increase the spread of Christianity. Enslavement of Africans and their descendants, as well as captured Native Americans, demonstrated the power of white Europeans and they used slavery as an economical profit. African descendants changed and adjusted their belief systems to local conditions and rules of the white man. Christian religious groups performed an influential role, and most tried to impose strict religion on slaves.

Now when we look at the different types of beliefs people have, this just clarifying how opinionated and unnecessary religious people became. Let’s first start with the beliefs of atheists and agnostics, that there is or is not a god, and ethics do not necessarily matter. So are they a religion? The concept of religion can be very hard and tricky. Most people are familiar with different kinds of religion. The most critical part is when people basically share the same concept but have different ways of going about it. Most of us would say that agnostics are not because we view religion as something that has something to do with God. New Age is sometimes called a religion, but in reality, they embrace whatever appeals to them the most and add them to an existing religious order. We claim certain religions and we don’t even practice them right at the end of the day. Is it because religion creates a sense of community and some people join a religion in order to feel included in a smaller subsection of a larger society. We see that a lot in society nowadays, and I don’t even blame religious people when they get offended by that. That’s a very high level of disrespect in my opinion. Not all societies offer religious freedom, with some countries demanding the practice of one religion and others going to war to create a religious dominance.

However, for American society and other societies that allow religious freedom, the ability to practice a religion when and where someone likes helps to protect other freedoms, such as speech and expression. This gives some people the wrong expression of religious practices. Most people choose certain beliefs because they fit better with their societies and others don’t even have that choice. They have to live with that burden and sadness until they gain freedom from their superiors. Talking from an Islamic perspective, modern freedom doesn’t exactly line up with their religious perspective. People find out new things about them every day. Today’s societies gave youths the right to change whatever they are unhappy about since it’s their life. I’m in full support of human rights and the “it’s your body your choice” saying. But when it comes to religions, they have their own teachings and that’s what defines and differentiates them.
