n248bbc04.title: Unrealistic Beauty Standards and Eating Disorders

chunks.text:
As women continue to make remarkable strides toward equality, they are constantly being judged, they are constantly being valued based on their appearance. Despite the advancements in equality, power, and position, women still face obstacles such as being valued based on their physical appearance and ability to become fertile. The stigma arose in the 1900s, when the Beauty Myth was prevalent. According to the author, Naomi Wolf, the beauty myth is not solely based on beauty, but also “it is composed of emotional distance, politics, finance, and sexual repression” (Wolf 1991). The beauty myth focused so much on women’s appearance for advancement in gender hierarchy, not just for respect within the community, but also for political advancement. Men also faced social pressure to pursue a ‘beautiful’ woman to gain more political power. According to Wolf (1991), “strong men battle for beautiful women, and beautiful women are more reproductively successful.” Essentially, men and women were both defined by women’s beauty.

As we learned in class, the collective conscious is an unspoken, unwritten, set of rules and standards that society unknowingly follows. Each individual’s collective conscious, during the beauty myth period, focused so evidently on beauty and appearance. There was so much pressure on both genders to be physically attractive. According to Wolf, “many [women] are ashamed to admit that such trivial concerns to do with physical appearance, bodies, faces, hair, clothes – matter so much” (1991). Even though women are becoming more powerful within society, their collective conscious will always remind them that there is an unspoken expectation to be beautiful. Insecurities, mental illnesses, and even health issues became more extensive to women. There was a high standard to fit in with society for women, and women worked hard to be within these irrational standards.

Did you know that “More than 1 million American teenagers and preteens live with an eating disorder—about 3 percent of that population” (Cooperman 2009)? Currently, in the United States, eating disorders have become increasingly popular. Interestingly enough, it is more common in women than in men. So, is it possible that the beauty myth from the 1900s, that focused so highly on women’s physical attraction for political advancement acted as a precursor to current eating disorders?

What is the Beauty Myth?

Naomi Wolf, author of “The Beauty Myth”, discusses the importance of the beauty myth stigma and defines the political movement. As women socially and politically advance within society, Wolf elucidates the decline in mental health. Women in society were constantly being compared to old photographs of what society considered beautiful women. In order to meet society’s expectations, women were constantly focusing on their exterior. How women portrayed themselves to society was crucial for political advancement for both themselves and for the men in society. There were unspoken expectations for men to pursue beautiful women in order to become more politically powerful. How each gender was perceived by society mattered. These irrational standards for physical attraction increased numerous kinds of mental illnesses and, more importantly, eating disorders.

According to Wolf, “During the past decade, women breached the power; meanwhile, eating disorders rose exponentially and cosmetic surgery became the fastest growing medical specialty” (1991). During the rise of feminism and the fight for equality, women believed that a necessity that contributes to political power was to be beautiful. Back then, women were constantly forced to look at photographs of provocative, thin women. Because of the beauty stigma, women constantly would strive to look just like these provocative women. It was important to have a youthful face, but not too youthful, and to be skinny. It was just as important to dress up appropriately to society’s standards. Women were defined not only by physical looks, but also by the clothing that they chose to wear. Women’s body shape should be the same as the women in the photographs, which led to unnecessary dieting. The pressure for women to appropriately portray themselves to society was uncanny and unfair. Women were vulnerable to outside approval which, in turn, consequently led to self-esteem issues, mental disorders, and most importantly eating disorders.

What is an Eating Disorder?

What exactly is an eating disorder? An eating disorder can be defined as “...medically and psychiatrically recognized illnesses...they are complex conditions involving mental, physical, and social issues” (Cooperman 2009). An eating disorder is serious and potentially fatal. Eating disorders are so important to understand because they encompass both unhealthy eating behaviors and also mental illnesses. In order to be diagnosed with an eating disorder, the individual must have serious disturbances in their eating behavior. This can include an extreme or unhealthy reduction of food intake, severe over-eating, or feelings of distress or extreme concern about body shape or weight (Cooperman 2009).

Eating disorders begin when an individual is unhappy with their appearance. There are numerous types of eating disorders such as anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and binge-eating disorder. Each disorder is serious and can become fatal because of the biological and physical detrimental effects. For example, anorexia nervosa is the most prevalent eating disorder. Anorexia nervosa includes feelings of low self-esteem, lack of eating, and an intense fear of gaining weight. Due to this fear of gaining weight, individuals are usually below the healthy body mass index average. Body Mass Index (B.M.I) is defined by the person’s weight in comparison to their height. Unfortunately, being below the BMI average indicates lack of healthy eating and lack of healthy physical involvement. Without proper eating styles, the individual will lack the proper nutrients that enable the body to function properly. Without appropriate physical activity, the individual will lack metabolic movement, and the body will become slower in almost every anatomical aspect. The second most common eating disorder is bulimia nervosa. This eating disorder isn’t as serious as anorexia nervosa, but it still can become unhealthy. Bulimia Nervosa can be triggered by life’s stressors. An individual with bulimia nervosa will binge-eat for an unhealthy period of time, and then later, want to reverse the effects of eating too much. This individual will purge the calories that they just ate by either self-inducing vomit or by excess exercise. This purging stage can become dangerous for the individual but is a hard action to treat due to the positive emotional effects that the reversal can have on the individual. The individual will have these positive emotions because they feel proud that they reversed the caloric gain. An individual with bulimia nervosa likes feeling in control of their purge making this disorder hard to treat. (Cooperman 2009)

Lastly, the third most common eating disorder is binge-eating. Unlike the other two disorders, binge-eating does not correlate with weight-loss. These individuals will eat an excessive amount but will not purge their weight. Interestingly, despite the individual’s lack of reversal of the caloric intake, these individuals will still have low self-esteem. Each eating disorder has one thing in common and that is low self-esteem and / or poor image issues. Statistically, women are more prone to eating disorders than men. So, did the beauty myth stigma leave such a detrimental impact that still effects millions of women today?

Beauty Myth and Eating disorders

Did you know that at least, approximately, 7 million women are diagnosed with an eating disorder (Kramer 2021)? During the beauty myth stigma time period, women constantly compare themselves to photogprahs of what society considers beautiful. Women strive to look just like the provocative women in these photographs. Similarily, to this day, women are still constantly comparing themselves to photogprahs of models. This has become more evident in shopping centers. When women shop at malls or clothing stores, or even beauty counters, they are constatnly faced with beauty selections for specifically youthful women. In both generations, it has been important for women to have a youthful face and to be skinny. For example, clothing stores are oriented for skinnier women because sizing is emphasized in shopping centers. In beauty counters, the ‘in-style’ look is to be youthful, to cover-up any flaws. Do these expectations for women to fit into these unrealistic standards of beauty correlate with the high statistic of women with eating disorders?

Did you know that “approximatey 0.5 percent to 1 percent of young women will suffer from anorexia...?” (Kramer 2021). Anorexia is the lack of self-esteem, fear of gaining weight, and insufficent food intake. Anorexia emphasizes insecurities about the woman’s body figure. Anorexia can be correlated with the idea that girls and women need to be beautiful. Society’s idea of beautiful involves the expectation to be skinny. Individuals with anorexia may try to fit in by purging caloric intake and by avoiding proper nutrients just to fit in with society’s expecations. In concldusion, as Kramer discusses in her article, “the empahsis in American society on physical beauty, thinnness, dieting, and exercise plays a role in the prevlance of eating disorders...” (2021).

There are too many irrational expecations placed upon women. Women are not only facing inequality in social injustice, but also facing judgements based on physical appearance. Women suffer from eating disorders because of society’s standards of beauty. Just because women are politically more powerful than they were centuries ago, women are still struggling with mental illnesses and eating disorders. These illnesses are crucial because they can become fatal. The collective conscious of each society has an unjust, unfair, high standard for women to be beautiful in order to fit in with soicety. These societal pressures lead to these illnesses, so it is important to spread awareness about eating disorders before it becomes too late. Early intervention, such as therapy, is one of the best practices to prevent eating disorders from becoming suicidal or unhealthy. Not only does therapy prevent suicide, but it will also help build self-esteem and confidence in women. Moreoever, it is important to not ignore the constant pressure that women face politically, physically, and internally.
chunks.label: Analysis of the beauty myth and eating disorders
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Naomi Wolf's concept of the beauty myth and examines how societal beauty standards contribute to eating disorders among women.

chunks.text: In the mountains of North Carolina, there are about one thousand acres of land owned by two men. This place is called Turtle Island Preserve. In the summers, Turtle Island Preserve hosts summer camps for young men from the ages of ten to eighteen. These camps last two weeks and place an emphasis on the skills they teach young men about traditional survival skills. I attended these camps for four years and was exposed to a culture that I would have never found if I had not attended the camps. However, the culture which Turtle Island proudly boasts as one of inclusivity and acceptance, is much more prone to the pitfalls of hegemonic masculinity and the hierarchical pyramid of domination that accompanied this culture.
chunks.label: Introduction to Turtle Island Preserve and hegemonic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces Turtle Island Preserve's summer camps for young men and reflects on its culture of hegemonic masculinity and domination.

chunks.text:
To give you a better idea of the exact circumstances that bred this culture of hegemonic masculinity, allow me to explain the demographic that this camp typically attracted. During my four summers attending the camp, I never saw a single camper or counselor that wasn’t white. Any women that were living or working on the land were kept far away from the campers. This included them eating at different times. So while there were women living on the land during the boys two week camp, our exposure to them was limited as much as possible. All of the counselors were ex-campers that were over eighteen and therefore not technically allowed to be campers. This concoction of all male, all white campers and counselors formed a sort of singular culture within the camp that was based around hedgemonic values.

Turtle Island Preserve challenges young men to face their fears via a set of challenges. These challenges include slaughtering pigs, running 3 miles with a mouth full of water, spending a night alone in the woods, taking a polar plunge (jumping into a freezing cold pond) at dawn, and a night hike. The camp also had trouble with campers becoming violent with one another. Nobody was ever seriously hurt but there were at least one or two fights per summer between campers. These fights were the result of campers trying to exert dominance over eachother and move up the pyramid of hedgemonic masculinity.

When campers first arrive at Turtle Island they are exposed to a hierarchy of command and told to obey that chain of command. This included meeting all of the staff on site and learning who all of the counselors are. The campers are then divided into four groups asked to pick a speaker or leader for their group. The leader the group elects remains the leader for the rest of the camp. This would immediately cause problems within some groups because multiple people wanted to be leader. The role of leader usually fell to the oldest person in the group as they were trusted to be the most reposonible. However, having a leader become appointed based on very little to no real merit caused problems. The leaders were trusted by the counselors and would settle disputes between campers. The leaders almost always showed favoritism to their friends or the people they liked the most.

The establishment of leaders within groups also allowed for bullying and a sort of hive mind to be born within the camp. If a camper had a weak stomach and couldn’t stand the sight of pigs blood they would be teased. If a camper was scared of the dark and had a hard time falling asleep outdoors at night they would be teased. This mentality amongst campers forced the idea of hedgemonic masculinity onto the social structure of the camp.
chunks.label: Demographics, hierarchy, and teasing at summer camp
chunks.what_happened: The student spent four summers at an all-male, all-white survival camp where women were separated, campers elected group leaders who showed favoritism, and boys were challenged and teased if they showed fear.
chunks.people: campers, counselors, women living/working on the land

chunks.text: I specifically remember a game called gladiator that we were playing during my second year. The game consists of two people standing on a log and trying to push eachother off. The last person standing on the log wins and a new challenger approaches. This game exonerated the hedgemonic value of being tough and capable of dispatching multiple opponents by yourself. However, this game led to a small selection of mostly older campers that were bigger and stronger completely dominating the younger and often smaller campers by quite literally throwing them to the ground. At the time, the game just seemed like fun. But now I know that this activity reinforced this social hierarchy predicated on how well each person fits the hedgemonic values of the camp.
chunks.label: Playing the gladiator log game
chunks.what_happened: During their second year, the student played a game called gladiator where older, bigger campers threw smaller campers off a log to exert dominance.

chunks.text: The camp utilized this pressure to be hegemonic as a way to get young men to face their fears. One activity in particular was the most infamous for establishing who was and was not worthy of praise and respect. The activity was called the ‘night hike’, but that makes it sound too simple. It was an activity in which our counselor would march the group about a mile into the woods in a random direction and make the campers wait until the sun went down. The counselor would then confiscate any flashlights the campers had brought with them and would make the campers navigate their way back to the camp by themselves with no light. Without fail, someone would be unable to complete this task and start crying for help. Ironically, these cries were always met with snickering and comparisons to a frightened animal by the other campers. The people who could not complete this challenge were seen as weak and were often picked on for the remainder of the camp. Those who could complete the challenge without any sort of fear or hesitation were seen as brave and their social status was vaulted. So in a way, these challenges became a way for campers in less than desirable social positions to improve their status through a literal test of mental fortitude.
chunks.label: Surviving the night hike challenge
chunks.what_happened: Camp counselors marched campers into the woods at night without flashlights to navigate back alone, leaving those who cried to be mocked while successful campers gained status.

chunks.text: The same logic applies to the other challenges. If you couldn’t take the polar plunge you were considered a coward. If you couldn’t run three miles with a mouth full of water you were weak. If you couldn’t spend a night along in the woods alone you were deemed as lesser than those who could. So while we were learning traditional survival skills, the camp was also reinforcing this idea of independence and a toughness-over-all mentality. Those that were established as weak or less masculine than the rest of the camp were picked on relentlessly until the proved themselves in one of the challenges. Then the ridicule would switch to some other camper who was unable to complete the challenges. It was this type of toxic mindset that caused the campers to face their fears. No camper ever did these challenges out of want. They did them out of necessity and to avoid bullying by the rest of their group. So though the idea behind these challenges is a pure one, and facing your fears can be healthy, the way in which each camper’s performace dictated their status meant that people felt forced to complete the challence or suffer the consequences.
chunks.label: Camp challenges and peer bullying
chunks.what_happened: Campers engaged in grueling tests such as the polar plunge and running with water in their mouths to avoid relentless teasing and prove their masculinity.

chunks.text:
The hedgemonic values of being tough, independent, dominant, and brave were all taught and reinforced over and over again during my four years at Turtle Island. The survival skills were really a secondary education when you compare just how much the camp is centered around making young boys into young men. The methods may seem extreme but they work pretty well as long as you can handle the violence and bullying aspects of the method. However it’s not all bad.

The time I spent at Turtle Island preserve exposed me to the hedgemonic lifestyle and allowed me to understand that hierarchy in a more forgiving atmosphere than the ones I encountered later in life. I also think that similar to the boys in Rockport, the boys at Turtle Island Preserve end up forming very tightly knit friendship for the duration of their stay and leaving camp always feels more sad than it should. When you consider that most fo the camp is just one test after then other in an effort to dominate those you call friends, I’m surprised that anyone got along at all. I believe that this connection between domination and kinship comes from out biological programmedness to dominate and protect. Men want to feel valued and feel important and are willing to do abnormal things in order to earn that respect. But, on the flipside, once we prove our strength, we select others who have not proven themselves and pressure them into proving their own masculinity.

I know that the conditions and the activities that took place at Turtle Island may seem cruel and unusual but I agree with the author of the Rockport reading when he says that the boys ultimately benefit from their experience in this type of hedgemonic culture. Though I feel no need to create my own subculture of hedgemonic values, I think being exposed to that kind of hyper masculine system was good for me and is an integral part of who I am today. But, I’m sure not everyone that attended Turtle Island benefitted from their experience.

The bullying was constant for those who could not prove themselves and the effects of being othered by a group of people that don’t respect you is potentially very dangerous. Looking back on it now, I feel lucky to have mostly avoided the ridicule of my cabinmates. And I feel real remorse for not standing up for people who were being bullied. The biggest downside to the hedgemonic lifestyle is the complete lack of empathy. When people are judged on skill and dominance and everything becomes a competition, the humanity of each person begins to fade. Everyone is trying to dominate each other which sadly means that someone has to be dominated.

I think the hedgemonic lifestyle is inherently problematic and should not be the sole provider of worth in a society. Though I got through my time at Turtle Island relatively unscathed, I think it’s important to note that I have mostly rejected the hedgemonic values espoused by the camp. A lifestyle based in the domination of everyone around you can breed deep resentment and sadness. Not to mention how unhealthy it is to never let your guard down and just be comfortable in your own skin. To feel like you constantly have to prove your worth to both yourself and your peers is an incredibly stressful way to live and may lead to substance abuse later in life. Though some things can be learned from hedgemonic masculinity, relying on it as a sort of one-size-fits-all approach to being a man is dangerous and causes people to lose their humanity in chasing social recognotion.
chunks.label: Reflecting on hegemonic masculinity and camp impact
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the lasting effects of the camp's hyper-masculine culture, the bond and competition between boys, course readings, and their feelings about avoiding bullying and lacking empathy.
chunks.feelings: sad, surprised, lucky, real remorse, stressful

chunks.text: Durkheim’s theory of the collective consciousness explains that within a society, there is a sort of unspoken set of beliefs, values, behaviors, patterns, and other likenesses that set the expectations and guide life for its members. They are universally accepted and play a huge role in the formation of individual identities as well. Such a strong force of cohesion provides peace and tranquility, and also purpose for the people. Such beliefs can then be sort of divided into smaller categories and identities, creating even more intricate groups and communities. For example, you may be a part of a specific religious group with others who share very specific ideas with you. However, there is also a larger presence of religious belief in society altogether and a (somewhat) mutual respect of those groups. Solidarity is found in likeness and we achieve a sense of comfort by surrounding ourselves with those who either reflect or support or roles in society. We interpret these roles by understanding them in the context of the collective consciousness that we all share. This is made evident through archetypes. We see many examples of the collective consciousness in all different aspects of life. Things as simple as what we consider to make a person “well mannered,” our senses of humor, what emotions we assign to what connotation… These are all things that have a very specific interpretation to all of us because of their existence in our society’s collective consciousness. Another huge influence on what exists in that consciousness is social institutions. Simply being a member of a country alone gives you a very strong sense of identity that you share with everyone around you. On top of that, politics create even more opportunities for unity and shared opinion. News, popular, and social media set the stage for how we should look, talk, and act and we all undoubtedly find ourselves attempting to conform to that. Law enforcement and the justice system create expectations for not only our behavior but our morality, influencing how we act every single day and how we consequently judge others for acting. Simply put, we accept the truths of society, whatever they may be, simply because everyone else does. What holds value to others then holds value to us. The collective consciousness is such a simple thing to achieve, but such a strong tie that glues people together without any question of why.
chunks.label: Durkheim's theory of collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Durkheim's theory of collective consciousness and examines how shared beliefs, values, and social institutions unify society and shape individual identity.

chunks.text: This sort of blind acceptance can be explained by Fligstein and MacAdams’ idea of the existential function of the social. Their theory provides that the “social” or a society/group of some sort creates activity that creates meaning, resulting in meaning in people’s lives. Basically, without others, we would be meaningless, but in a like-minded group, we create value for ourselves and others. Without the role that we provide to others, we view ourselves as having no purpose. A collective belief about the role we play in a problem that is also a problem to other people makes us a significant player in that problem, therefore giving meaning to the people involved. Also, by people choosing a problem to work on collectively, it then assigns value to that problem simply because we choose it to. It could be something that we may usually have deemed insignificant, or unimportant in the grand scheme of things, but once society or a group holds it as so, it becomes of the utmost importance. We as humans essentially define our beliefs ourselves, and whatever we tell ourselves is important, it absolutely is. Sports are a great example of this. As an average person with no money invested or potential for personal gain from the outcome of a football game, it seems as if there should be no devout investment in the outcome. However, team rivalries and the passion for the game is one of the strongest pieces of identity that you may find in a lot of American households. This ability to give ourselves, our actions and interests, and others significant meaning is extremely powerful because it allows for people to explicitly shape our societies. People participate in practices that correlate to those beliefs then validate them and start to form groups that unite around the shared identity of stakeholding interest in that specific ideal.
chunks.label: Existential function of the social
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Fligstein and McAdam's theory on how society and collective action provide individuals with meaning and purpose, using sports fandom as an example.

chunks.text: These two theories both offer very strong insight into how societies are formed and how beliefs become set. Durkheim explains that everyone shares an identical understanding at the core which is how we form societies, and Fligstein and MacAdams explain that our significance comes from other people. Essentially, they both rely on the principle of fitting in. We do what others do and accept what others think as being true. We allow the ideas of others to become our own and let them shape our identities without any hesitation. The fear of being different then the group ultimately leads us to become one of the group, making the group and their beliefs that much stronger. The group is society, and the habit of following along as others do creates a very strong foundation of beliefs, morals, and expectations that we all share. While we do have individual significance, it is explained that you don’t mean anything without what you mean to others, and therefore, other people and external factors have the biggest influence on your identity. While we may think that we have our own personalized values, society shows us that it's all a game of follow the leader, whether that be for better or for worse.
chunks.label: Synthesis of sociological theories on conformity
chunks.what_happened: The student synthesizes both theories to conclude that human identity and social norms are driven by conformity and a need to fit in with the group.

chunks.text:
Mental health is extremely significant in American society as it constitutes part of an individual's identity. Although there is a consensus that mental health is very important, many groups in society have considerable barriers to accessing comprehensive health care. This begs the question: If mental health is so crucial to our society, why doesn’t everyone have equal access to it? According to Community of Hearts, an advocacy for the importance of mental health care, “1 in 4 people live with a mental health issue” (Community of Hearts). However, not all people who suffer with their mental health get appropriate care, especially minorities in America. This paper identifies how the mental health stigma, an individual's culture, and lack of resources discriminate in the mental health care system and create barriers to equitable access to proper care for minorities compared to non-Latino whites.

In The Matrix of Domination, Patricia Hill Collins depicts how African American women have a perspective that should be utilized by society to advocate for change. By using an oppressed groups perspective, institutions are able to assess what needs to be changed to create a more inclusive mental health care system. The Matrix of Domination will be addressed throughout the paper to show that by focusing on oppressed groups, the American mental health care system can give minorities the accessibility and attention they deserve.

The stigma of mental health leads to a lack of people getting help for their mental illness because the stigma creates an illusion that it is something to be embarrassed about. Some people even feel like it is something you can’t talk about without negative repercussions. Factors of these repercussions could be judgment from society, how they feel about getting help, and how their family and friends view mental health care. For example, an individual may be more hesitant to address their problems to a family member or friend on account of the backlash they might receive. The stigma can have extremely detrimental effects on an individual, as it prevents them from getting the help they need. A 2017 study by the APA proved, “greater self-stigma was associated with poorer recovery from mental illnesses after one and two years” (American Psychiatric Association). What this study by the APA indicates is that less people are getting the help they need as a result of the stigma associated with mental health harming your identity. Some effects of this harmful stigma can be strains on relationships, a negative self attitude, withdrawal from beloved activities, and so much more. Furthermore, the data shows that attributing a negative connotation to getting help for a mental illness is actively contributing to making the individual’s mental health worse.

Due to the negative connotation of receiving care for your mental health, groups in America fear the judgment of the public. These groups already receive judgment in the United States due to their race and culture, why would they want more? Throughout United States history, minorities in American have been segregated from non-Latino whites and stripped of respect. Fear is prevalent in their lives as they have to fight for equality every single day. Wiley Online Library states, “The fear of experiencing double discrimination- from mental illness and from being black- was a significant barrier to care” (Alang). The double discrimination expressed by Alang indicates how African Americans are scared that they will have one more thing to be discriminated against. The persistent discrimination against minorities in America for decades has instilled fear in them that the discrimination has the potential to get even more severe.

A lack of understanding for one’s culture has also constructed a barrier in certain groups in America from receiving proper mental health care. Cultures all have different rituals, narratives, and artifacts that form them, which are called collective representations. These factors can influence racial/ethnic groups not to seek help. According to Sage Journals, “Variation in cultural orientations, adherence to social norms, and location in the system may generate variation in self-labeling across racial/ethnic groups” (Villatoro). Villatoro describes in the Sage Journals article that certain groups will restrain from seeking help for a mental illness due to the beliefs their culture has instilled in them. For example, The American Psychiatric Association states, “in some Asian cultures, seeking professional help for mental illness may counter cultural beliefs of a strong family, emotional restraint, and avoiding shame” (American Psychiatric Association). The assertion made by The American Psychiatric Association illustrates that some Asian Americans are not willing to get help due to the collective representations their culture has embedded in them, such as it being shameful to seek help. Cultures around America differ in their beliefs and the way they carry themselves, which can influence their stance on whether they seek help for their mental health.

Alongside cultural barriers, If an individual cannot find someone proficient in their language for their mental health needs, it can create a barrier from receiving proper help as well. Language allows individuals and groups to communicate with one another in a plethora of ways; however, individuals speaking different languages can cause misunderstanding and affect the conversation immensely in a negative way. According to Psychiatry Online, “previous studies have shown that psychiatric patients with limited English proficiency underutilized specialist outpatient services and that those who did receive such services were less likely to participate in psychotherapy than fluent English speakers” (Alegria). The Psychiatry Online quote describes the difficulty those who do not speak English have in finding proper mental health care. Non-English speaking individuals have a hard time trying to navigate how to get help when they can’t engage in a conversation about their needs.

The lack of respect in American institutions towards minorities has caused oppressed groups to avoid seeking help from them, which reduces the resources available to them. According to the American Psychiatric Association, “only one-in-three African Americans who need mental health care receive it” (American Psychiatric Association). The policies, regulations and employment positions in American institutions have left oppressed groups feeling under-represented and unheard which alter their appeal to mental health care treatment. The Wiley Online Library conducted a study which showed an immense lack of trust in United States institutions from minorities. The study conveyed how “black people have gone into the mental health care system to get help, but have lost things that are important to them” (Alang). The conclusion made by the study shows how mistreatment in American systems has made oppressed people frightened to go back to them. In other words, the fear instilled in minorities due to oppression in American institutions is drastically reducing their urge to get the help they need.

Resources are a vital aspect to acquiring proper care for an individual’s mental health. The link discovered between race and availability to resources proved to stagger the opportunity of getting proficient help. Villatoro states,“the benefits of educational and economical resources for the identification of need for treatment and its response may not extend to racial/ethnic minority populations in the same way it benefits non-Latino whites” (Villatoro). Villatoro is concluding the benefits non-Latino whites have in accessing resources and being able to use them proficiently. Resources may conclude facilities and programs embedded in the community to connect people with information on how to seek help. The resources in your community allow easier access for help, but what if there is none? According to the Psychiatry Service article, “research has found that the more behavioral health specialists there are in a community, the more likely individuals are to use these services” (Alegria). The research states in the previous article that this is often seen with marginalized races or ethnicity, as well as within those experiencing poverty or homelessness. Non-Latino whites have an advantage over other races/ethnicity who do not commonly have the access to those crucial resources.

The sources throughout this essay conclude Collins' discussion in The Matrix of Domination on how oppressed people in our society have a beneficial perspective that should be looked at. When white men are the focus point of so many US institutions, the institutions are listening to the group that is the least oppressed in America. A black resident took note of this in the Wiley Online Library article by stating, “if the board of directors are all white, they should be asking themselves why” (Alang). This retort suggests a reexamining of the people in charge of making the policies. When the least oppressed group is controlling the situations, it allows for unfair treatment towards minorities to be suggested.

For Collins, African American women show a perspective that can illustrate where in the system inequalities are shown between minorities and non-Latino whites. By looking at this perspective, institutions can contribute to decreasing the stigma in communities. Decreasing stigma in communities can be attributed to evaluating where the stigma is stemming from and how the oppressed groups think it can be nurtured. The knowledge obtained from these groups when creating new policies and regulations in the mental health institutions is crucial for reducing the stigma in communities.

Discussing an oppressed group's culture from their point of view allows a universal understanding of their needs. Not everyone will accept different cultures, but it is important to get members of mental health institutions to understand where their clients are coming from and how to help them to the best of their knowledge. The oppressed groups' knowledge is obtained from personal experience and is a direct correlation of how their culture has impacted them. Educating others on a culture has to come from an individual in that culture because those who are not oppressed cannot fully comprehend what it is like for them.

Mental health care institutions can assess where they need more mental health care resources by attributing Collins theory. Primarily focusing on oppressed groups and services they lack, will lead to an increasing number of the population receiving proper mental health care. Collins summarizes the importance of community oppressed groups, such as African Americans, have sparked. Communities built by oppressed groups provide strength in fighting injustices. The communities need accessible resources for mental health that allow them to use their strength to help others and themselves.

Learning from the current issues, such as the stigma, culture barriers, and lack of resources, we can ensure that the prominence of discrimination in our system can change for the better. Change can be attributed by placing those who are oppressed in the center of focus, so mental health institutions can identify factors that are wrong with the system. Mental health affects individuals everyday life and it is crucial to ensure proper care for it is taking place. In American society, individuals and systems need to influence change on expanding accessibility of mental health care resources. This change will not be an easy one; however, with reduction to the mental health stigma, cultural understanding, and proper allocation of resources, a definite improvement can be achieved in American society with equitable access for all.
chunks.label: Disparities in mental health care for minorities
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how mental health stigma, cultural differences, language barriers, institutional mistrust, and lack of resources create inequities in mental health care for minorities, drawing on Patricia Hill Collins's Matrix of Domination.

chunks.text: McIntosh picked up where Omi and Winant left off. She sought to explore the idea of white privilege and social superiority of Whites in modern society. She argued that much like male privilege, white privilege is the product of denying the existence of a social hierarchy that was set up in the distant past. Much like the abuse of Natives by White settlers, McIntosh argues that the prevalent social reinforcers are here to stay and are consistently used as a political tool. She also proposed the idea of the hierarchy being a result of Whites not acknowledging their inadvertent oppression of non-Whites. She seems to advocate for educating Whites on their elevated status as to aid them in realizing that they are privileged. Her early research into this topic suggests that racism and lower-class mentalities are a direct result of centuries of white superiority. Where Omi and Winant focus on the historical perspective of racial issues, McIntosh is more interested in the current state of these issues and their qualifying parameters.
chunks.label: McIntosh's arguments on white privilege
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses McIntosh's ideas on white privilege, social hierarchy, and the inadvertent oppression of non-Whites, contrasting her focus with Omi and Winant.

chunks.text: Modern thought and discussion revolving around race relations and the formation of races that we see today is an ongoing process of research and deliberation. The results of these particular formations have long-standing impacts on human social norms and play a role in nearly every facet of human life. From the economy to cultural statistics, there seems to be a distinct difference in each race’s human experience. What those core differences are and why they exist are socially reinforced is a debate with many unanswered questions. Omi and Winant made substantial headway in researching a possible origin of these race formations, while McIntosh shared her opinion on what modern implications are with political reinforcement. With research and discussion such as this, the modern world has a substantial probability of improving overall race relations and fixing disparities, due to a deeper understanding in humanity’s races.
chunks.label: Impact of racial formations and ongoing research
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on modern discussions of race relations, the widespread impacts of racial formations, and how sociological research can help improve disparities.

chunks.text:
Émile Durkheim, a renowned French sociologist, explored the societal dispositions caused by collective thought. By first defining collective representation as a symbol, artifact, or narrative that embodies collective belief, Durkheim had a reasonable explanation for the objective unification of a society. For example, America is united by the symbol of the American flag, and Christians are united by various Christmas traditions. Durkheim, however, still had to do some research into the effects of collective representation on the individual.

Shortly afterwards, Durkheim discovered the related concept of collective consciousness. The collective consciousness is essentially the shared and intertwined sense of reality we all experience because of shared collective representations. Its purpose is to provide universal truths and values we can all understand, accept, and follow as individuals. Individuals collectively fabricated our society with the help of collective representations, thus creating a collective consciousness, in order to justify our own daily thoughts and actions. Traditions and objects were created and celebrated so that humans had a sense of meaning and a sense of unity. These traditions and objects, over generations, invented a collective mindset we all today share. For example, the tradition of gift-giving at Christmas time began as a way to pay respect to and honor the three kings that brought gifts to Jesus Christ. It gave citizens a sense of meaning and purpose, and brought the society together in humility and gratitude. After becoming a tradition, or norm, the act brought people together in likemindedness. The action of exchanging presents brought people together physically, and was then followed by a mental and emotional unification. The collective consciousness was formed thanks to collective representation. The mindset was created because of the accepted “object”.

Yuval Noah Harari, an Israeli historian and author, explored the related topic of the 2 versions of God. The first God is the “cosmic mystery”, the God that makes us ponder the purpose of life and the mysteries of the world. This God is the mystic aura that explains the deepest riddles of the universe. The first God is pretty much universally agreed upon and accepted. Many believe that there is some greater force, a greater being that knows all and watches over all. Though it may be vague, it is still an idea that universally connects our society.

The second God is the “worldly lawgiver”. This is the God that blurts out rules about dress, language, diet, appearance, sexual behavior, daily conduct, etc. This God is more controversial, more disagreed upon. In fact, this second God is what split up the Christian religion into dozens of denominations, creating rivalries and even hatreds of opposing groups. The first God is more of a general belief, while the second God creates daily rituals and practices. In reality, the two have no logical correlation. For example: why do the mysteries of the universe determine what length of dress a woman can wear? However, followers use various holy books that teach rituals and food taboos to justify the connection.

Most people began with a general belief in a greater force, or higher being. But thanks to newly instituted (at least in the span of time) religious rituals, or collective representations, the mindset, or collective consciousness, has thus shifted. We, as humans, long to be a part of something bigger. We need a purpose, a higher reason, and we want to feel supported in it. We seek unity. Therefore, overtime, different groups have instituted different practices in order to coordinate our social lives. The shared goal to discover more about the “greater force” causes us to create shared plans, practices, etc. But obviously, sometimes people disagree. Different groups stuck together on different topics, and a variety of different religions were born. Even those basic religions broke off several more times to create different branches and denominations. As time goes on, more groups are created. Objects and habits, such as the Bible and its teachings, were created as physical structures to glue the institutions together. The Bible is an example of a collective representation. The variety of representations created, such as the Bible, the Tipitaka, the Quran and the Hadiths, and the Tanakh and the Talmud, paved the way for dozens of new mindsets, or collective consiousnesses, such as Christianity, Buddhism, Islam, and Judaism.

In other words, collective representation is to scripture as collective consciousness is to religion. The second God that Harari describes creates these divisions as new symbolic objects and belief systems integrate themselves into the world. The more divisions created in scripture and teachings, the more extreme the different collective consciousnesses become. The mindset of religion, defined as the first God, or collective consciousness, is formed thanks to collective representation, or the object of scripture or worship. The first God was originally a much broader topic, but as generations have instituted and accepted new collective representations, the first God has been redefined. There are now many new versions of this first God, based on any given specific belief system, which is why we now see so much rivalry and competition in religion rather than worship. In the effort to uncover truths and individual value systems, we have forgotten the basic, shared foundation in our first God.

In order to recultivate our shared curiosity and love for the greater forces in the universe, and unify ourselves once again in vague belief, we must reevaluate the importance we place upon our various collective representations. Is it more important that we feel justified in our dress length and word usage, or that we are a unified society? At the very least, we should take just a few steps back, far enough where we can be civil, become educated about, and respect specific religions. Just as bloodshed is never the answer, convention will never bring peace. Rather than pushing practices onto people, we as a society should celebrate and worship the greater forces together and unite in the common goal for the betterment of society.
chunks.label: Durkheim, Harari, and religious collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Émile Durkheim's concepts of collective representation and collective consciousness alongside Yuval Noah Harari's two versions of God, analyzing how religious practices divide society and calling for shared unity.

n2c658bd8.title: Examining Alienation in Modern Rationalized Labor

chunks.text:
Alienation is a relatively new concept in human history. For the majority of our existence as a species, humans existed for a purpose. In our labor and work experience, we have felt connected to what we are doing, and the products produced by our labor. Our societies were not so focused on production, but rather survival. However, since the onset of the industrial revolution, humans have shifted to become a resource rather than a producer. The industrial revolution brough the introduction of rationalization. The movement towards a society that is more efficient, calculable, and predictable. This has caused humans to become detached from their work, as they only see a part of the process to the product. This essay will cover how alienation has derived from the shift to a more rationalized society.

Alienation started to become a concept with the introduction of industrialization. When the industrial revolution came into effect, people were not valued as much for their skills, but for their labor. Just their ability to work and create a product or a piece of said product. For example, factory workers. When factories were first implemented, they of course needed workers. However, they did not need specialized skills. So, men came to work in factories, but the work was not enjoyable. It did not help that labor laws were not yet invented, so the workplace was likely dangerous, as well as alienating. The reason jobs like these are alienating is because you get no say in what you would like to do. Given a required task and told to complete it. This caused the beginnings of alienation. Workers were starting to be seen as a resource of labor, rather than something of value.

The industrial revolution is a prime example of rationalization. It is the very beginnings of the concept. Societies began to move towards consumerism. This shift required products to be produced at an increasing rate and speed. This meant the necessity of a more predictable product, which would be similar or the same after each production. Assembly lines are a good example of rationalization. They produce the same exact item each time, at each station. They also cause the workers who are a part of them to feel more alienated from their job. The job an individual partakes in might be a pillar of one's self, in today’s world, as well as in past eras. The reduction of the job as meaning to an individual may cause them to feel alienated from it.

As societies have become more rationalized and more geared towards being as efficient as possible, alienation has become more widespread. This is especially seen in capitalist economies, such as the United States. Large industries and corporations with tens of thousands of employees have taken rationalization and extracted it to its truest form. Making their products and companies as efficient and predictable as possible. To do this, however, the same is required of their employees, which are quite abundant.

To do this, employers give employees specific tasks and guidelines which they cannot break. For example, factory or warehouse workers follow very exact schedules and rules. They often do not even see the final product of what they work towards. This may cause workers to become detached from their job. They are only being seen by large industries as sources of labor, and are not as cared for as in the past. Rationalization practiced by many large corporations has created alienation, especially in today’s world. Corporations such as Amazon, Walmart, and McDonalds are all examples of forerunners of rationalization. Amazon warehouses are another great example of rationalization, and resulting alienation of employees. Warehouses have very set rule, time clocks, conveyor belts, etc, which all run in a certain way for maximum efficiency. It is necessary for the company to survive and continue to make a massive profit. The workers, in some cases, do not feel like they matter in their job. Yes, they earn a living, however they may find no meaning in their work outside of money. Because humans want to have purpose and work, doing something you don’t want to do for someone else, for a product you will never see, can be detrimental.

In conclusion, the continual shift and leaning into rationalization over the past several hundred years has brought forth more alienation in our capitalistic society. Starting from the industrial revolution, and the introduction of the extraction of labor from humans to today, which is a more refined version of this. Because much of our society has become so focused on efficiency and max productivity, alienation is a common byproduct. It had not been seen as frequently or at all in previous societies, because each laborer existed for their purpose. Stonemasons, blacksmiths, textile workers, artisans, all had a certain purpose and a role to fill. Today, with a very consumer-based economy, the focus is on products. Rationalization is the best way to produce products. Many laborers do not see their final product, which may cause them to be alienated from their job, which can really only be seen in more modern western societies.
chunks.label: Rationalization and alienation in capitalist societies
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the historical shift toward rationalization starting with the Industrial Revolution and explains how modern capitalist corporations and assembly-line work lead to worker alienation.

n4de2c981.title: Analyzing Power in the American Racial Hierarchy

chunks.text:
As society in America grows and is constantly evolving, the dominance that individual people hold remains uniform. If you asked a random stranger on the street if they were to describe someone who has the most powerful socioeconomic status, they would describe a white heterosexual man. Why is that the immediate answer that the majority of people come to? What is the relationship between social class, financial class, and racial class? When did this power system start? The prejudice that people have toward other minority groups forms a caste system that is equal to the power that they hold. This system forms groups that tend to band together because of similar social status that they share. Social ques and day-to-day encounters are present in all environments that show that there is an unequal distribution of power amongst racial groups. Many have researched this concept and have found that racialization is collectively formed by individuals who discriminate against other groups that are below them. In this paper, I will talk about the discrimination against minority groups and address how it negatively affects the opportunities people will have in their lives.

In module four of class, we talked about race vs. ethnicity and the difference between the two. Race, being a top-down process where a dominant group utilizes their power to give meaning to a specific group. Ethnicity, being a bottom-up process where a specific group had a uniform identity formed by the history of their region. Specifically, Omni and Winant’s “Racial Formations”, talks about the idea of how being a person of color has changed its’ meaning through time. Through their research they developed the concept that the meaning of an individual’s race is constructed by someone that is at the top of this social caste. Over time this has evolved into racism, serotypes and microaggressions, which has left prejudice against minority groups in modern society.

Society as a whole understands that racialization is formed predominantly involuntary in most situations. The point of interest is when this prejudice or classification towards groups of specific people start. An experiment was done with primary school students which aimed to prove that instinctively they have already racialized all of society. In the study, children were asked to class depictions of families on who they think is the wealthiest and which one they would want to live with. The four families drawn were, a business-working family, a middle-class working family, an intellectual looking family, and a working-class family. All are white heterosexual families. Within these families, the clothes that each person had on ranged from business suits to casual wear for the adults and respectively for the children.

The results were not surprising as ninety-five percent of children guessed that the business working family made the most money and they wanted to live with them the most. The working-class family was the family they were least likely to live with, given the choice. “The fact that young children already demonstrate master of such schemata, on the basis of a limited social trajectory and, indeed, even before lengthy formal education and the development of literacy, suggests other sources than the direct experience of class inequality and cross-class interactions.”. (Vandebroeck) It is amazing how children can pick up on these things without anyone telling them the average salary for people that wear business suits to work. In correspondence to race, this study was only done with white families, if the study was done with black families would they be ranked lower than the working-class families? To further explain this, children are already aware of the social caste that they are put in. It is evident that they know who holds more power and money within the groups of solely the white families. Adding black families into the experiment would result in having the white working-class families, higher on the scale.

In the experiment that Vandebroeck, conducted it not only showed that children are already aware of the social caste, but they are also aware of the advantages of living with the white business-class family. Focusing more on how the white business family got to the top of list, can be explained by “White Privilege” by Peggy McIntosh. Simply put, McIntosh illuminates that white privilege is the system where white people have unearned benefits exclusively because of their skin color. In society today, it is evident that white communities are better funded, whereas black communities are underfunded. This being said, white people have a better chance at education, job opportunities, and quality of life, immensely proportional to those of black communities. A specific example would be the difference between private and public schools. The majority of students enrolled at private schools are white, why is that? White families, because of the privilege they have, are more able to afford to send their kids to private schools because they were born into families that did the same for them. The process repeats itself over and the children will have more opportunities for jobs which will recycle into the production of more revenue.

White people can use the privilege that they have to change the system and help equalize the opportunity that black people lack. Today, movements such as Black Lives Matter, show efforts specifically in trying to eliminate and exemplify racial discrimination. White privilege is associated with ‘White guilt’ which is the concept that white people are starting to recognize the privilege they have and try to take action against injustices. Research was done on youth adults that show white guilt is a motivator to take action, yet at the same time if it were low social responsibility there would be less action. “Future research investigation the link between White guilt and civic action should pay close attention to measures of civic engagement that differentiate between all forms civic engagement and social-justice related action.” (Dull) This being said, someone who identifies white privilege does not mean they will take social-justice action because many are absent in civic engagement. Furthermore, this explains white privilege even better because they have the opportunity yet choose to not engage because it does not directly relate to them.

In response to this study, it can be found that there is a correlation between white people and racism. Although indirect, white people can only benefit from the social placement they are put in. Placed at the top of the social caste means that they have hidden opportunities that they are not aware of. In this social structure only certain groups of people are granted privilege, where you get half the privilege of the social structure preceding you. This goes so on and so on taking into the account of race, gender and sexual orientation, until you get to the very bottom of the pyramid. While privilege comes naturally, the lower you are ‘ranked’ the more you are affected by the privilege of the latter. The distribution of this power by categorizing individuals by what they were born into is called the “Matrix of Domination”

In module four, as a class we read an excerpt from Patricia Hill Collins, ‘Black Feminist Thought’, which talks about the matrix of domination and the effects it has on oppressed individuals. As we studied Collins, we discovered that within the matrix of domination an individual will become ingrained into their social order and become an agent to the process. She explains that what defines these levels can be a multitude of different things including, race, gender, sexuality, cultures, nations, etc. For the United States, from the birth of the country in 1776, the matrix began and has stayed present sociologically to present day. Specifically, it is evident that the Matrix of Domination is evident through education institutions, media, churches and markets. These manifest into the dominant point of interest and everything else is seen as foreign. What makes these standards is one group which is at the top of the matrix, resulting in racism, microaggressions, and attacks on everyone that does not fit the standard at the top of the matrix.

The most important factor that Collins describes it that through this social hierarchy; everyone has an advantage or disadvantage, not just over the color of your skin, but also your gender. In terms of color, individuals who are lighter skinned will have the most power. In terms of gender, men will always be ranked higher over women every time. The white male will remain at as the foundation of power because it has been fused into society. Another point of interest is that whenever a group tries to relegate a topic for reform, it directly affects another group. This is shown when Collins talks about how white woman urge for female rights in the workplace, where a lot of black woman were working, by which would lower their power. Further pushing the point when a shift happens at the top of the matrix it becomes a domino effect, toppling down the levels of power.

To better understand the matrix of domination, examining Donald Trump’s first election highlights how and why people, specifically people of color, were scared. In the 2016 election Trump attracted the votes from the majority of the white working class. He conformed to what the white working class wanted in a candidate, in response to that collectively they felt as if they were losing power as a class. These class ‘anxieties’ are a huge deception and become politicized off the fact that in reality that equality was becoming present not only in the workplace, but the media and the public. These voters became selfish and looked only at notions the ex-president made to help better their class, paying no attention to how the black community would be affected. This directly alters the matrix of domination by shifting the power that the black community were slowly gaining. Trump’s election made it difficult for many groups of people because the matrix conformed them into an even more state of preference by white people.

Eduardo Bonilla-Silva, a sociologist from Duke-University, deeper analyzed the effects of the Trump election through a sociological lens. He concluded that racism has returned a more “old-fashioned” (Bonilla-Silva), in return has formed more activist groups to combat them. Although Trump had huge negative effects on the racial issue in the United States it forced different groups of people to band together. In essence, shifting the power within the “Matrix of Domination”, so that there will be a more equal level that is inclusive. “We must become sociologically driven citizens concerned with building a more democratic, inclusive, and just society.”(Bonilla-Silva) Eduardo creates a statement to establish urgency in the dying democracy that we live in today. Society in America is fading away from democracy because there is real no change in power, thus no change in societal issues. Taking Eduardo’s warning to heart will cure America of the disease we have put it through, yet at the same time lessening the power of the “Matrix of Domination”

In conclusion, racism as a whole has baked into society to the point where it has become a norm which can’t be escaped from. It is seen all over the media, schools, and tv shows where black people are often portrayed as bad, and white people are seen as good. One of the products of this is that black communities are often underfunded and do not have the opportunities that white people would otherwise get. This sets off into an eternal loop of generations where families are stuck in their class which limits their power in society. In turn, this bands people of similar treatment together creating levels of belonging where they feel most accepted. To truly abolish racism, society as a whole must break these levels and must rebuild an inclusive society that accepts individuals for who they are.
chunks.label: Racialization, privilege, and the Matrix of Domination
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological concepts of race, ethnicity, white privilege, and Patricia Hill Collins' Matrix of Domination, citing course readings, studies, and political events.

chunks.text:
Growing up as a woman, I have viewed life much different than a man would. You might be thinking, how is that? Many women in the world are treated different and have different expectations upon them. They might be told that they only need to do 20 pushups, while a man has to do 40 pushups, or that woman have to be the cook in the family. These expectations show the opposing views that are placed on men and women throughout the globe. For example, in many countries, especially the Middle East, women are talked down to, as to say that she deserves the same treatment as a dog. At the same time, men are treated as they are superior and deserve to have more respect. So, why are women treated with less respect than men are? Are women not as deserving of the same respect as men in society?

In dealing with the complexity of the roles of men and woman in the world, we have to take a look at what how society view this. Society believes this to be the norm. There are certain unwritten rules that people follow, so everyone can calmly follow their role in life. But are these roles starting to change as the world becomes more modern? People are starting to do different tasks because of modernization and more acceptance with others.

To take it back to better understand the changes that we are seeing now in the modern world, let us take a look to what it was like in the early 1900s. In the early 1900s though, the roles between the two genders had not changed. The roles were always the men worked and the women would stay home. Women were expected to help take care of the children, cook all the meals, and clean the house. This was their “job.” They were not allowed outside of the home, like in today’s societies. You never saw a woman out of the house doing something besides her job of being a mother. As the years went on, women started gaining more rights. They started to change the history. The first time the world saw this change was in the 1920s. The 1920s was when women were able to fight for their voting right and gained the right to participate in elections. This was just the beginning the women’s movement. As one can see, women starting fighting for more freedom and demanding more change. This change started to be seen in the movies and shows that were produced. It showed the gender roles being flipped from what they had been where women went to work and the man would stay home.

This change in the roles of men and women are now prevalently seen in the modern world. I have watched the different roles in life change. One thing I have observed is fathers are staying home more, while the women are going out to make the money. There are different reasons why this might be. It might be better financially better for the family or it might just suit the family dynamic better this way. My family has not experienced this, but I recently watched a movie The Interns that speaks to this situation. The two characters that are in this are Jules, the mom, and Matt, the father. Jules recently started up her company called “About the Fit,” which is an online fashion website. Since the company is such a big hit, Matt stayed home to help take care of their daughter, Paige. He helped take Paige to school, birthday parties, had tea time with her, and so much more to be there for their daughter.

The Intern shows how the roles of men and women are depicted differently than how society had demonstrated them to be. In society, the mom is typically the one that stays at home but for this family, it made since for the dad to stay home to watch the daughter. This is one of example of how peoples gender roles are changing.

Another example this is the show Full House. This show is about Danny Tanner (the dad) and how he raises his three daughters. He has help from his brother-in-law, Joey Gladstone and Uncle Jesse watches the daughters as well. This shows was filmed in the early 90s, so it marked the beginning where we started seeing men stay at home.

Even though roles have significantly changed as seen in the show, there is another problem that women are faced with. Women are judged everyday for their physical appearance by men and society, in general. They are expected to look perfect. Their body size must be small. This view of women makes women out to be less important and only fit just to reproduce.

It is made to seem that women’s only contribution to society is just for reproductive purposes only. And, it also underlines the myth that beauty is subjective to the end. Thus, we can see that women have made quite a progression in certain areas, while in other areas, things have not changed at all.

The same thing can be seen in the workplace. Men and women’s salaries are not always equal. Men are usually always paid more than women are for doing the same job. This has given men more advantages. They do not have to prove their worth to the boss or to society as a whole in the same way that women do. Men can more easily get a job and do not have to go through the same inspection of the interview process to prove that they are qualified to have the job. It has created an unequal divide regarding the paychecks, occupations, and how the views of the genders are changing.

Another issue that we have seen in society is the LGBTQ+ society. This is an issue as the genders are not given the same rights. They also have to fight for the rights that are given to other individuals. This can be seen in a worldly fashion. LGBTQ+ in many parts of the world are being punished for what they believe to be who they are and what they deserve. An example of how mistreated LGBTQ+ people are in the world. Let us take a look at what happens in the Middle East for being gay. In Middle East, they are killed for being who they are. Just like women are. Both groups of people are being scrutinized for being who they are.

These examples of my own personal family dynamics, the movie, The Interns, and Full House, and other examples have demonstrated how the family roles have changed over the years. The women’s movements from the early 1900s to modern day reflects how much progression and change we have gone through as a society. Women are able to participate in virtually every aspect of society and do not have to just be a stay-at-home mom. This fight for women’s rights can also be seen in the LGBTQ+ group fighting for their rights. Even though women and the LGBTQ+ have attained many more freedoms, we are still seeing a constant battle to equal out the playing field among the two genders and LGBTQ+.
