chunks.label: Gender roles, historical changes, and equality
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the changing gender roles from the 1900s to modern times, citing movies like The Intern and shows like Full House, and discusses workplace inequality and LGBTQ+ rights.

n0507cc4f.title: Experiencing Double Standards in College Hookups

chunks.text: Slaps on the back, fist pumps in the air, cheering, and hair ruffling. This is the exact reaction I have seen time and time again when a male walks in the room from a suggested sexual encounter. However, women lose girl friends, and make plenty of new guy friends, thanks to their new title as a “whore”. The morning after is comical for men, yet embarrassing, and creates feelings of guilt for women. Society celebrates men, but criticizes women, for the same sexual encounters because of the construct of gender roles, defined by the collective consciousness, and the role of anatomy in performing these roles.
chunks.label: Double standards in reactions to sexual encounters
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on societal double standards celebrating men and criticizing women for sexual encounters due to gender roles and collective consciousness.

chunks.text:
Countless examples come to mind when considering this argument. I recently walked into a room with a guy, whom we will refer to as Kevin, from a late dinner on campus, but the image of us walking in together created a different idea. All of Kevin’s friends, particularly his roommate, were extremely excited. They exemplified the previously stated symptoms of celebration - the fist pumps and “ahhh I see you’s”. Watching this unfold, my face reddened from embarrassment, even though I knew that nothing had happened.

Throughout the entire night, every time Kevin made his way to specifically talk to me, or touch me on the arm, or make any sort of “move”, cheers from the other men began. However, not a single girl spoke to me the rest of the night. I had officially won the unwanted title. I was made to feel guilty and outcast for something I did not even pursue. This is one of many, many similar experiences I have encountered in my relatively short lifespan.
chunks.label: Assumed encounter after walking in with Kevin
chunks.what_happened: The student walked into a room with Kevin after campus dinner, leading his friends to cheer and assume a hookup, while girls ignored the student.
chunks.people: Kevin, Kevin's friends, Kevin's roommate, other girls

chunks.text:
Additionally, I have heard the gossip and the truth to many comparable experiences. Just a few nights ago, a girl, whom we will refer to as Carla, sent a photo of her and a guy to my dorm’s group chat. Only about half of their faces were visible, but because of the messiness of Carla’s hair, it was immediately assumed they “hooked up”. This girl had recently moved into our dorm, and only a few nights into meeting new people, she was automatically labeled a whore. Her ability to make her own positive impression disappeared.

I was in the room with most of the people in the group chat, and the guys were shocked, impressed, yet also disgusted with her behavior. “Damn, he got with Carla?” was asked repeatedly. Her sexuality was discussed, and decided to be readily available and unwanted. Many of the women listening to the debate were just as disgusted as the men by her assumed actions, however, my roommate and I happen to be friends with Carla. My roommate reached out to her and told her what was being discussed. Carla was, understandably, extremely upset. She responded, explaining that she hadn’t even kissed the guy. Similar to my experience, Carla was made to feel guilty and outcast for something she had not even done.
chunks.label: Carla's photo in dorm group chat
chunks.what_happened: Carla sent a photo to the dorm chat, leading people in the room to assume a sexual encounter and slut-shame her despite her having done nothing.
chunks.feelings: shocked, impressed, disgusted, extremely upset, guilty, outcast
chunks.people: Carla, guys in room, women in room, roommate

chunks.text:
While sex is assigned at birth, gender is a societal construction dictating how the male versus female should behave. Everyone is expected to “do gender” by conforming to their assigned, socially learned set of acceptable behaviors. This set of actions is created by the collective consciousness - a system in which the population creates a set of uniform ideals and standards based on overarching values, experiences, and practices. “Doing gender” is following these standards, and can be exemplified by women wearing longer hair and shorter shorts, while men do the opposite. Men “do gender” by acting tough and strong, while women submit to their dominance. Gender is an achieved status, in which one can become successful or fail, depending on the way each individual chooses to behave (West & Zimmerman). Our ability to perform these expected actions is specifically dictated by our physical bodies.

Each gender has been defined to have a specific body for a specific purpose. The male’s body is viewed as a direct and normal link to the world. However, for centuries, women have been seen as imprisoned, or held captive, by their bodies. Supposedly, women only think with their hormones, are held back by their ovaries and uterus, and are seen as incomplete. The woman is viewed only as a sexed being. The collective consciousness has defined a woman's purpose to make use of these hormones and internal organs and find a partner to complete them. Men, however, have been defined as perfectly complete by themselves, with the ability to think rationally and make decisions free of anatomical inhibition. Both men and women have hormones, yet our society has created the idea that women are completely dictated by these hormones, while men are completely unaffected (de Beauvoir).

This idea is also related to the toxic institution of hegemonic masculinity. This cultural practice legitimizes men’s dominance in society by celebrating the male gender role. Men are defined as strong, competitive, initiative-taking providers. The practice of these roles hurls men up the world’s socio-economic ladder, with new job opportunities and respected reputations. The beneficial outcome reestablishes the idea that men are the dominant, successful gender, and encourages men to continue being strong and independent (Stroudt).

Because the male is defined by strength and independence, sexual encounters are seen as an active choice. In other words, men can control their emotions and passions and reactivate these drives when they want to. They are celebrated for being strong, for leading the act with a level head, and for being independent. However, dictated by their hormones, women are viewed as “out of control” when acting on their emotions and participating in sexual behaviors. De Beauvoir’s exploration of the difference in purposes of the male and female body explains the expected actions and reactions of “the act”.

Additionally, the idea that men supposedly control themselves, and consciously, actively engage in sexual activity reestablishes the idea that they are mentally, emotionally, and physically strong, and are dominant because of their self-control. This cycle furthers the institution of hegemonic masculinity, and thus furthers the idea that women need support and are too mentally weak to fight their emotions. The guilt and embarrassment women feel when accused of a sexual encounter stems from this idea. Women feel like they have done something wrong, that they should have been stronger, should have controlled themselves differently, should have presented themselves better, even when they did not participate in anything at all.

Men are celebrated, while women are criticized, for the exact same sexual actions, or even assumed sexual actions, in the exact same context. Sexual encounters reestablish men’s strength, independence, and dominance defined by their gender role. Becoming successful in this role grants men overall respect, and countless opportunities in the “real world”. This celebrated dominance instantly labels women as “the other” and treats half of the population as a weaker minority.

As our society begins to shift to accept “girl-bosses” and female empowerment, it becomes even more embarrassing and frustrating for “slutty” actions to be assumed. Women desire to be respected, to be accepted for who they are, and to be viewed as controlled, intentional beings, who are more than just a sexed body. The assumptions that women are “too eager”, have “let their guard down”, have “lost control”, or just don’t have a desire for a sexual partner to “complete them”, invalidates the real emotions and intelligence hiding behind the hyperfocus on women’s hormones and uterus. In order to continue progression into a more equal and just world, we have to begin recognizing that men and women can both cultivate self-control, and both deserve respect, not punishment.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of gender roles and hegemonic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes gender construction, biological essentialism, de Beauvoir's ideas, and hegemonic masculinity to explain sexual double standards and argue for equality.

n3f05d15b.title: Masculinity at a Military Boarding School

chunks.text:
While our culture has begun to place a greater emphasis on mental health issues, the impact mental health has on men is sometimes overlooked. Men's mental health is becoming increasingly stigmatized, according to societal norms, religious, and cultural views. Hegemonic masculinity is a term used to describe this phenomenon. Hegemonic masculinity is a means for a society to force men to fit into the mold they desire. Telling them that they cannot express emotion, that they must be powerful and aggressive, and that they must adhere to these rules in order to be “cool and popular”. Hegemonic masculinity is a toxic mold in our culture that must be acknowledged, and the community must work to change for the welfare of all.

Hegemonic masculinity is often everywhere in a growing boy and adult man's life. Yet, why and how do societal standards within military or leadership schools effect the development of young men? The most prominent area to affect growing boys, however, is schools. As boys develop and get older, they are pushed into a system that will change who they are. They need to play sports and be muscular, wear cool clothes and have a kind personality but not too kind.

In today's society, hegemonic masculinity has been demonstrated in a variety of texts and other ways. In the text "You're either in or out," the author discusses how hegemonic masculinity impacts young boys in a private school setting. The boys are bound to a societal hegemonic masculinity structure. "Obviously [you're]... the coolest man ever if you're dating the lead cheerleader in a coed school, but... because there are no girls, that's simply one less way for guys to... prove themselves, so they have to find other methods" ( pg.275). The passage also mentions how the guys are shamed for expressing emotion and are always competing with one another. Though the teachers and adults are very satisfied with the boys' behavior, they earn high grades, which helps them get into excellent schools; their athletics are above and beyond typical standards, and the teachers believe it makes them feel more connected to the boys. While the hegemonic masculinity system pushes boys further in life and everyone around them admires how they act, the system's impact on the boy as an individual is negative. The guys will grow up believing that they must prove themselves in various ways, such as having the newest automobile, the prettiest woman, being the best athlete, or owning the largest home. However, their brains are conditioned to believe that human emotions are unacceptable and that a guy must constantly be put together and provide for others in order to be a man.

"Bias" is defined as "prejudice in favor of or against one thing, person, or group when compared to another, usually in an unjust fashion" (oxford languages). Negativity bias explains why bad events have a greater psychological influence. This could explain why it's so difficult to get past "initial impressions." This explains why we recall negative experiences more easily than good recollections, and why trauma flashbacks are more common than joyful flashbacks. This bias can be acquired throughout one's life; it can be forced on people by societal standards or incorporated into one's childhood to make one believe that this is how things should be. A negative bias is commonly created in many schools where hegemonic masculinity impacts growing boys. This would be a voice in the boys' brains asking them to do better in this or that so that they can outperform other males, and if they don't, the negativity bias would focus on that moment and they will believe they are not good enough.
chunks.label: Hegemonic masculinity and negativity bias in schools
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how hegemonic masculinity harms men's mental health and uses literature and concepts like negativity bias to analyze its impact on boys in school settings.

chunks.text: For high school, I went to a private boarding school where the boys were in the military and the ladies were in leadership. I am more passionate about the topic of why hegemonic masculinity is wrong and negatively effects guys now that I've witnessed it myself. When boys first arrive at Culver, they go through a process known as "new cadet," in which they must clean and memorize "common knowledge" about the school in order to pass boards at the end. Board is a three-day test in which they must have a spotless room and be able to answer difficult common knowledge questions at random while being shouted at. New cadets are treated with contempt and ridiculed until they pass. Whenever you go to Culver, you see the bright young males go in on orientation day and almost completely transform into a new person. You wouldn't recognize them if you saw them from their first day of high school to their last. You see kids participate in sports and you see everything about who they disappear and they become a whole new person. While they do excel in academics and athletics the personal effect on the boys is negative.
chunks.label: Witnessing cadet hazing at boarding school
chunks.what_happened: The student attended Culver, a private boarding school, and witnessed how male cadets were subjected to rigorous new-cadet testing, shouting, and ridicule, completely changing who they were.

30% of men between the ages of 18-24 suffer from mental health issues, the percentages are only going up as age goes up. Mental health is a growin probelm throughout the world and becoming a very publzied and prominent issue. Many organization and people are focusing on overcoming this problem and working to help people through their mental health issues. Something our society often ofrgets about though is menal halt problems effect men also and not only women. While there is not as large of a group of men with mental health problems as there is women there is alot of people that still need help. Many times men will nto reach out foe help because they do not want to be seen as weak and not “manly” enough. Society has created such a stigma around emotions for men and that they should not cry and more. Hegmonic masculinity is to blame for many mental health problems. Men feeling like they have to do certain things or they will be critzied and ridiculed, feeling like they can never show emotion, must provide for others and be strong and athletic, love sports and outdoors. This negatively effects the mental health of men heavily. They go from being care free and living life however they want to living life inside a world of standards and conformitys they must fit into. This is why hegemonic masculinity negatively effects men in such a bad way, especially in growing boys because their brains are still malleable and when this is pushed onto them it is just what they assume is normal.

Hegemonic masculinity has transformed what it means to be a man over history, but many aspects have remained the same. Despite the changes and chances that come, hegemonic masculinity continues to have a negative impact on men's mental health. Growing boys' mental health deteriorates whenever they are exposed to rigorous societal expectations, whether they show it or not. They are pressured to meet societal standards in order to gain status in their schooling system and in life; they try to be viewed as cool and popular and to be better than everyone else. Athletics and academics are utilized as a means of determining who is the best.

nce774312.title: Analyzing America's Obsession with Light Skin

chunks.text:
Sixty years ago, most would question a man who darkened his skin. Surprisingly, skin-darkening is essential to 21st-century white Americans. To such claim, one may argue that “white people aren’t dark-skinned, so what have they done?”. Counterarguments are ironically self-damaging, for skin alteration is so commonplace that it camouflages itself as beauty. Bronzer, tanning booths, and sunbathing are beautifying practices, though they are also manifestations of society’s adolescent fixation with olive skin. Truly, black people’s culture is interpreted by many as “cool”, though black people’s struggles are undesired. As non-black Americans want not to be black, but rather black-adjacent, corporate America monetizes olive skin. Using James Cooley’s concept of the “looking-glass self”, Americans of all races internalize society’s “light-skin” obsession, which we measure our value with.

Romil Hemnani, producer for rap group Brockhampton, once said, “I want to live in the White House”. Here, Hemnani is not referring to the office of the President, but rather to a figurative structure that exclusively benefits white people. For clarity, Hemnani is a brown-skinned Pakistani man. In expressing his reservations for those who are racially privileged, Hemnani conveys a belief that is shared by millions of American minorities: fair skin makes life easier. Needless to say, slavery’s horrors are not still existent, and the days of pre-1964 are behind us. Yet, public schools remain largely segregated, incarceration is racially disproportionate, and low wages primarily affect minority workers. America’s racist policy is blatant. Simultaneously, ignorance must be bliss, for the whole of white Americans are current participants of skin-darkening practices. These practices include tanning, bronzer application, and sunbathing. Lip fillers, butt lifts, braids, and other Afrocentric features are occasionally assumed by non-black women. A general population of non-black Americans don articles of clothing that are associated with hip-hop culture. Attempts, by non-black people, to present themselves as black are ever-present in both suburbia and high-profile circles; celebrities like Madonna, Kylie Jenner, and Kim Kardashian-West have publicly presented themselves as black-adjacent. The list of culture offenders is never-ending.

For many non-black Americans, particularly those who are neither non-black nor a separate minority, privilege is one hell of a drug. Considering America’s racist policy, one would concede Romil Hemnani’s argument that fair skin eases life’s societal burdens, though a population of non-black Americans seemingly want to be black. Meanwhile, many dark-skinned people undergo surgeries to disassociate themselves from others who look similar. In both cases, Americans want to appear “light-skinned”, which implies a black complexion that is light when compared to dark-skinned black complexions. American beauty standards are so olive-toned that they are expected, but other countries encourage Eurocentric standards of beauty. American magazines are significantly “white”, but general media tells a different story, one that includes racial ambiguity. American society’s obsession with a light-skinned aesthetic may be explained by Charles Cooley’s “looking-glass self”. Cooley was an American sociologist who developed numerous theories of societal effects on one’s self, but the “looking-glass self” remains his most famous concept. The “looking-glass self” refers to a self-perception that is based on how one is perceived by others. This concept is dependent on how one’s self appears in another’s mind, similar to psychologist William James’ “social self”. According to Cooley, we decide our peers’ opinions regarding us, and we base our self-confidence, self-worth, and self-value on these imaginations. Subsequently, we either dislike ourselves or like ourselves. With relation to society’s focus on racial ambiguity, the “looking-glass self” places value on olive skin. This particular “looking-glass self” is accredited to several factors, and efforts of non-black people’s to be associated with blackness are proof.

Prior to its collapse, the Roman Empire admired Egypt for its giftedness in science, technology, engineering, and math. Such international relationship would shock today’s Americans, for the federal government has ties to few African countries. Furthermore, we undoubtedly discourage black citizen’s advancement via policy, culture, and legal loopholes. That said, individuals cannot alter systems in a similar manner that is used to alter town-wide trends. Social media has supplied youth with additional influence on fashions, styles, and trends. Youth’s proximity to aesthetics is much, much closer than their proximity to anti-black institutions, and the former is how a light-skinned ideal has fogged millions of non-black minds. Simultaneously, visually multiracial beauty standards communicate value, which defines the “looking-glass self” at hand. In most cases, the “looking-glass self” is regarded as a basis for one’s satisfaction with himself/herself that is, in-and-of itself, based on other’s opinions of him/her. The “looking-glass self” is a concept comparable to American psychologist George Mead’s “social self”, which assumes we internalize other’s opinions. The social self is popular as a sociological concept, and it concedes that our identities are conceived using socialization. The “looking-glass self” is, essentially, cousins with Mead’s “social self” because it advocates that an individual’s self-value is correlated with widely-held beliefs regarding him/her.

Described by the “looking-glass self” is a cognitive process that utilizes perception to interpret social contexts. That said, social ability is vital to one’s understanding of the world. In 2021, for example, users of Instagram recognize a relationship between popularity and monetary value. Influencers may gain popularity by posting photos that alter their skin tones to match those of mixed-race people. Money is earned when influencers pander society, and photo manipulation becomes survival. The “looking-glass self” encourages humans to decide other’s opinions of them, and it punishes, or rewards, us for deciding how we are perceived.

Non-black celebrities, influencers, and youth’s audacity to assume a light-skinned aesthetic is enabled by accessibility to social media, spin, and popular culture, but rationale for such appropriation is embedded in the “looking-glass self”. As previously mentioned, American society’s “looking-glass self” uses a racially ambiguous standard to encourage appropriation of black culture by non-black people. As black musicians, black athletes, and black actors have overcome enormous obstacles of racist policy, mainstream culture is more diverse than it was fifty years ago, and even white nationalists view black culture as “cool”. Many white people have even attempted passing as African American. In 2015, former NAACP president Rachel Dolezal received backlash for claiming to be half black. In 2020, activist Sean King received online criticism for performative activism as he, too, pretended to be black. Also in 2020, author Jessica Krug’s European roots were uncovered, despite Krug’s self-prescribed Afro-Latina identity. Efficacy of society’s mulatto-favoring “looking-glass self” is evidenced by dark-skinned Americans, as well. Famous cases of skin-bleaching include Michael Jackson, Sammy Sosa, and Blac Chyna, all dark-skinned at birth. Black casts like those of Black-ish, Grown-ish, and #BlackAF are predominantly light-skinned. Most notably, influencers like Emma Hallberg, Jesy Nelson, and Kylie Jenner have been accused of “blackfishing”, which describes the act of an influencer using skin-darkening filters on photos to receive likes and, by default, gain sponsorships. Not only does the “looking-glass self” value black culture, but it is also recognized by 21st-century workers as a method of accumulating wealth. For black Americans exists an added “looking-glass self” that rewards assimilation, which partly configures a double consciousness within such Americans. Regarding both appropriation and assimilation, all Americans are overwhelmed with a “self” that generates from the “looking-glass”, which places both societal value and monetary value on olive-tone skin. In this case, the “looking-glass” refers to positive views of light-skinned Americans, and those not succumbing to light-skinned beauty are either void of monetary gain or insecure physically; black people are vulnerable to both negatives of dissatisfaction with their looking-glass selves.

To be mixed is desirable, according to American youth, American influencers, and American celebrities, whose appearances decide trends. Demand for tans, hairstyling, and plastic surgery is monetized under a capitalist economy. To be unaware of racial ambiguity’s desirability, one must live under a rock. America’s “mixed” economy produces both satisfaction and dissatisfaction in Americans of all races regarding their “looking-glass selves”. Specifically, white Americans seek social, cultural, and financial gain through appropriation of black culture. Simultaneously, black Americans experience additional effects, namely pressure to avoid adversity of racist institutions. Light-skinned privilege pales in comparison to white privilege, but it also poses a threat to dark-skinned Americans. Effects of the “looking-glass self” on opportunistic non-black Americans who determine their actions by a fetishizing society’s views of them are damaging. To be black in America will never be easy, yet passing for light-skinned in a community that oppresses is no different than passing for white in a community that enslaves.
chunks.label: Racial ambiguity, skin-darkening, and the looking-glass self
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the monetization of racially ambiguous and olive-toned aesthetics in American culture, using sociological concepts such as Charles Cooley's 'looking-glass self' and George Mead's 'social self' to analyze cultural appropriation and beauty standards.

chunks.text:
Who defines gender? We, as a society, have a subconscious set of guidelines for the expression of gender and how individuals that identify with a specific gender should portray themselves, but who is coming up with these concepts and social expectations of gender expression? The definition and social construct of gender is constantly changing and being redefine in society. However, society knows these guidelines we subconsciously have for gender, but how do we formulate those common expectations?

Throughout much of history, women were seen as the inferior gender. Women were considered to be weak, frail, emotional, and their purpose was to take care of the house, children, and serve their husband. Women were seen as needy, and they were expected to get married and rely on their husband to provide them with basic needs. However, men were thought of as the providers or supporters of the family. It was the man’s duty to work, put food on the table, and put a roof over their family’s head. Men were considered to be tough, emotionless, and superior. Men were the head of the household, the ones making all of the decisions for the family as a whole. These ideas within the gender roles have begun to change over the past few decades as individuals begin to challenge these roles and standards. Women are becoming more independent of men, obtaining a higher level of education, working towards equality in the job market, both genders making money along with providing for the family, sharing responsibilities at home, and more. There is still progress to be made in changing the gender roles from what they used to be, however, there is a lot of change that has already taken place and continues to grow in providing opportunities for change and equality for women.

Society has set expectations on what is believed to be “normal” expression of male and female genders. We apply society’s expectations of gender expression subconsciously with every person we meet. Think about it this way, when we see an individual walking past us on the sidewalk, wearing a dress, has on makeup, has long and curly hair, is wearing heels, and is carrying a purse, we automatically assume that the gender of that individual is female just based on what we observe initially before we have even met that individual. This assumption is made due to the fact that the characteristics they are expressing are consistent with societal norms of expression for the female gender. When we see an individual walking past us on the sidewalk, wearing a suit, a tie, dress shoes, wearing a nice watch, has very short hair, and is carrying a briefcase, we automatically assume that the gender of that individual is male simply based on what we can observe in that brief interaction. This assumption is made due to the fact that the characteristics that they are expressing are consistent with societal norms of expression for the male gender. However, if we see an individual walking past us on the sidewalk, wearing a skirt, floral blouse, has very short hair, has facial hair, is wearing tennis shoes, and is carrying a bookbag, we will be a little confused and not sure quite what their gender is exactly, just based on the characteristics they are expressing, since they are not completely consistent with a specific gender as determined by societal norms.

This idea behind gender expression roles occurs due to society having an unspoken standard for the way that individuals should conduct themselves based on which gender they want to portray to the rest of the world around them. When discussing the “Doing Gender” reading by West and Zimmerman in class, we came up with a list of traits that society associates with a specific gender. The traits that were outlined as being associated with the female gender include having long hair, wearing dresses, wearing makeup, being overly emotional, and being subservient. These are some of the traits that individuals wanting to portray a feminine gender would “need” to display, according to society. The traits that were outlined as being associated with the male gender include having shirt hair, wearing suits or button up shirts, not wearing any makeup, being stoic, and being dominant. Again, these are some of the traits that individuals wanting to portray a masculine gender would “need” to display to others, according to societal norms. Gender is said to be a routine accomplished in everyday interaction; it is not considered a property of individuals. The idea of gender is a social construct and society sets a sort of “rubric” for individuals to follow when “doing gender.” We also discussed that the second wave of feminism, which occurred in the 1950s, challenged the cult of domesticity and had the goal of working towards things like equality in the workplace, changes in gender roles, and more. Society is coming to a point now where individuals are challenging the idea of gender and making it more of a fluid concept, meaning that gender can change depending on the intended expression of the individual. This is obviously a huge shock to the older population in society who are used to the gender roles that existed many years ago and the younger population challenging these ideas is receiving a lot of backlash due to the resistance to change most people have. West and Zimmerman also discuss the idea that gender is an ongoing accomplishment, reinforcing the idea that gender is a fluid concept and is constantly changing. Society is having to unlearn and relearn the idea of gender as it changes, like the introduction of male to female transexuals as well as female to male transexuals.

As a society, we know and understand the subconscious standards that exist for gender expression. Although gender is becoming more and more fluid as the definition changes according to societal standards and norms, collectively, we all know and understand the roles we play in society and how we are supposed to portray ourselves towards others based on the gender we identify as. In Durkheim’s passage about “The Cultural Logic of Collective Representation,” the concept of “collective consciousness” is explored. This is a very important concept in sociology and when trying to grasp how society forms the norms and standards that are commonly understood among citizens. The collective consciousness is defined as the norms, beliefs, and ideas that characterize a social system. Different social systems have different collective consciousnesses, which is why gender norms and expectations differ from place to place throughout the world. The collective consciousness of a group represents the ideas or values of that group that are commonly shared and accepted. We define gender based on how the collective consciousness of society views gender. The collective consciousness is constantly changing as the values, beliefs, norms, and ideas of a society change. We can see this very prominently in today’s society as the fight to change gender expression and gender norms is ongoing, especially in the younger generation.

There are many different sociological concepts that tie into the formation and implementation of gender roles, norms, and expression. The collective consciousness of a society has the biggest impact on how society collectively views gender and what the accepted norms are for gender and expression. This concise representation of the ideas behind gender are constantly changing and being rewritten. The collective consciousness is constantly being challenged in a way that gender is becoming more and more fluid. Individuals are able to express their gender identity in a more widely acceptable way, especially if it does not align with the strict gender roles/ representation of the past that some members of society still value. Gender is something that is constantly changing as society changes the standards, norms, ideas, and beliefs that it has towards gender, expression, roles, and characteristics.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of gender expression and collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how society defines and constructs gender roles and expectations historically and currently, referencing hypothetical street scenarios, class discussions on West and Zimmerman's 'Doing Gender', feminism, and Durkheim's theory of collective consciousness.

chunks.text:
Despite its name, the theory of McDonaldization actually spread in to a variety of other industries other than just fast food. Industries like banking, news papers, grocery shopping, schooling have all started to implement the ideals of McDonalization into their businesses. With each new generation we seem to be growing more and more impatient as a society with the expectation of instant satisfaction being at an all time high. The continuous evolution of the tech industry has become the biggest driving factor in all this as things like streaming services, online shopping, and social media continuing to fill our need for instant gratification. And in a world with 7 billion people and counting who expect all tasks to be performed with near perfect execution the theory of McDonalization has flourished.

Growing up there are very few sights that are more beloved than that of seeing two golden arches in the horizon while on a long road trip. Its the most gourmet meal you have ever had, the pinnacle of all restaurants, your yelling and pleading becomes more intense the closer you get, with the exit nearing you can almost taste those golden French fries, only to have your heart broken by your parents passing it by uttering the most heart breaking phrase “we have food at home”. While there were fast food restaurants before it and continue to be more after it McDonalds has truly perfected the formula when it comes to fast food. The speed at which their food was made, the low price making it seemingly affordable for everyone, and the entertainment for the kids in happy meal toys and play grounds built into the establishment were all firsts with in the food industry. This was something that no restaurant before them had done before and catered perfectly to new ‘on the go’ family lifestyle that was beginning to be popularized.
chunks.label: McDonaldization in society and fast food
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the spread of McDonaldization to various industries, society's desire for instant gratification, and the appeal and formula of McDonald's.

chunks.text: However, as we continue to grow up there comes a time in all our lives where our tastes begin to change and allure of the golden arches starts to fade. For me this time was right before I started middle school, the happy meals no longer filled me up like they once did and I had started to get to big for the play place.
chunks.label: Outgrowing McDonald's before middle school
chunks.what_happened: Right before starting middle school, the student found that Happy Meals no longer filled them up and they were getting too big for the play place.

chunks.text:
It is at this point in life that we start to see the ideals from the McDonaldization theory being put in practice inside of the stores. There are four main ideals that the McDonaldization theory puts into practice, efficiency, calculability, predictability and standardization, and control. Efficiency is the choosing of means to reach and end rapidly and is usually portrayed as a benefit to the consumer but in reality is in the interests of the company. For example, drive thru windows and filling your own drink are both ways fast food restaurants cut costs as their employees are doing less work and making sure all the food is pre-made helps to speed up wait times letting the restaurants serve more customers faster. Calculability emphasizes the companies desire to have things like money and supplies calculated and accounted for as this lets companies know exactly how much each aspect of their product costs. Predictability and standardization refer to companies attempts to make sure that their products are all the same no matter where a consumer may buy them from. The best example of this comes from the fast food industry as you could go to any two McDonalds and a Big Mac would taste the exact same at both locations. The final ideal is control, which is what these companies want to have over their customers. Any company using the McDonaldization theory has a set way of doing things which is made abundantly clear to the customer as soon as the walk in the door. Take any fast food restaurant for example, it is expected of you to know what you want when you reach the register, money already out to pay, and then you stand off to the side while you wait.

The theory of McDonaldization was developed by sociologist George Ritzer in his book “McDonaldization of Society” which he released in 1993. Throughout this book, Ritzer is providing the reader with insightful knowledge about how the principles predominately found in the fast food industry are working their way into other aspects of society. Ritzer’s main basis for this argument comes from the theory of rationalization which was developed by Max Weber. In essence the theory of McDonaldization is the process of rationalization as one of its fundamental aspects is that any task should and can be rationalized. Rationalization is a sociology term that refers to the replacement of traditional decision motivators with the ideals of efficiency and rationality instead. As a result of this the user is left with an easily controllable process of efficient and logical tasks that can be completed in the same manner each time to produce the same outcome without fail.

Outside of the obvious in McDonalds, on of the biggest corporations to adopt the McDonaldization theory is Amazon. With its continuous digital growth and focus on stream lined efficiency with their customers, Amazon has been able to use the McDonaldization method to create on of the most successful business to date. Its most basic principle being that of efficiency as Amazon has developed a straight forward direct to consumer sales approach that allows its customers to buy any product they need from their couch. There is also an aspect of predictability and calculability when shopping through Amazon because there are clear steps you need to follow when placing your order and when you do you know exactly how much it is all going to cost as the prices of products are clearly marked on the website.

Another major industry that has seen more of a reliance on the McDonaldization method is banking. Going to the bank used to be an ordeal that could last you hours but now with the advancements in technology the whole process has become for more efficient and calculated. Some of the biggest ways that the banking industry has become more efficient is through ATMs, mobile deposits, direct deposits, and the ability to automatically pay your bills. The efficiency in banking has grown drastically through the use of ATMs allowing use to withdraw money at any given time and the development of mobile deposits which allows us to cash checks with just a few photos. Auto bill pay has also helped with efficiency as customers can now have their bills automatically paid straight out of their account each month instead of having to deal with paying bills manually. Calculability has also seen a sharp increase now that we banks have developed their own apps, allowing us to see exactly how much money is in our accounts at all times.

The media has also been affected by the McDonaldization theory as news outlets are producing more stories that, like the food found at McDonalds, are fast easy reads that lack any true substance for the consumer. Many of the stories now are written with the hopes of reaching as wide of an audience as possible and usually are very cheap to produce maximizing profits. The biggest form of media that utilizes the McDonaldization method is social media. Social media has a focus on quick content that are meant to keep the audiences attention for long periods of time. Prime examples of this are the apps Tik Tok and Instagram as they produce short meaningless clips that use the simple act of swiping to keep the audience engaged.

Overall the McDonaldization theory has seen continued success in a variety of different industries over the years with many more industries starting to adopt its ideals. Its focus on the four main ideals of efficiency, calculability, predictability, and control make it easy for any company to adopt and helps to satisfy our ever growing need for instant satisfaction as a society. As our society continues to grow and as technology continues to advance, the theory of McDonaldization will grow as well finding its way into even more industries in the future.
chunks.label: Core principles and examples of McDonaldization
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the four principles of McDonaldization and rationalization, detailing examples in Amazon, banking, and media.

n6c2a51c6.title: Persistent Influence of Racism in Society

chunks.text: Although racism has evolved due to societal forces and is rarely shown in the traditional format anymore, it is extremely important to keep working to make racism less influential in our society. With the underlying theme of racism still being prevalent in American culture, we are unable to escape the racist realms that hold us back from truly being united.
chunks.label: The persistence and impact of racism in society
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how racism has evolved and remains prevalent in American culture, emphasizing the importance of working to lessen its influence.

nf25b091a.title: Intersections of Class and Workplace Discrimination

chunks.text: In the United States a large majority of the population is made up of the working class, similarly a large majority of the country is also made up of people who have experienced a form of discrimination. While the working class experiences economic oppression, the group of people who have dealt with challenges of discrimination often face societal oppression along with various other forms of subjugation. Domhoff's idea of the working class takes the time to dissect many groups within capitalist societies. The concept of discrimination offers insights into how social society forms deep suppression and prejudice. However, with an understanding of these two concepts people still often fail to realize how frequently these two notions tend to cross paths. After analyzing Domhoff's take on the working class and the concept of discrimination, it is evident that these two classes have many daily similarities. Understanding of the similarities and variations of these theories allows individuals to gain a broader comprehension of what many people around the country experience daily.
chunks.label: Intersections of the working class and discrimination
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces Domhoff's concepts of the working class and discrimination, explaining that the two groups frequently intersect and face similar daily struggles.

chunks.text: An eye opening example of these two concepts colliding is the explanation of a simple norm for families all around the United States. To provide better clarity, there is a hypothetical yet realistic story about a woman named Maria. Maria happens to be a single, Latina mother who is currently working numerous jobs to support herself and her children. Everyday Maria experiences multiple acts of discrimination in the workplace due to many factors. She was being judged for many characteristics like her ethnicity, her gender, her clothes looking cheaper than others, and more. This discriminatory behavior is part of the reason why she faces limited career improvement opportunities, and is paid a lower wage compared to her white and male coworkers. Discrimination is known as the unjust treatment of people based on certain characteristics. Domhoff's view of the working class puts emphasis on the role it plays as a subordinate group in capitalist societies. This example of Maria shows how these two subjects can intertwine and leech off of eachother in many negative ways. Maria is unable to get a higher paying job due to the reasons she is discriminated against. However, a significant reason why she is discriminated against is for not having an extremely well paying job. In the end, the process comes full circle. The intriguing example provided showcases the disadvantages faced by these groups. The expectations are set impossibly high for people in these minorities and within the working class. As there are so many opportunities available, but all of them lack a sense of reality and attainability. Maria struggles everyday to keep her family financially stable as she is stuck in this perpetual rotation of inequality. Race, gender, socioeconomic examples of discrimination in the working class are all very prime examples. However, there are even more ways that these two concepts can intersect. This same concept also applies to those who are in the working class and the LGBTQ+ community, society often fails to accept them and treat them with the same respect they would treat a heterosexual with. This also goes for those who struggle with disabilities. Lastly, a more hidden form is discrimination in the workplace can be age! Many who achieved goals young, or work into their older years, are often judged or misvalued. Because of these issues, there is also an issue within job security. The large majority of wealth in our country is held within a very small amount of people on the large scale of population. Why are we treating the majority of our country disrespectfully just because the top one percent holds the most wealth? The system often feels backwards. Overall, all of these representations of discrimination in the workplace contribute to the difficulty with advancement opportunities. These individuals struggle daily within society because they are stuck between a rock and hard place due to things they often have no control over.
chunks.label: Hypothetical example of Maria and systemic discrimination
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes a hypothetical scenario of a single mother named Maria to illustrate how race, gender, class, sexual orientation, disability, and age create cycles of discrimination and lack of job mobility.

chunks.text: Domhoff's approach of the working class, and the concept of discrimination overall show deep connections through the daily similarities that these two groups face. Gaining a broader insight of the similarities and variances of these two concepts allows individuals to grow a deep comprehension of the loops and twists of our society's economic system and social systems. Our country has learned how to use personal characteristics that are out of an individual's control and vilanize them in society. Overall, Domhoff explains the details of the working class and numerous forms of discrimination in an informative way that is eye opening. The widespread effect of these boundless walls, created for individuals that fit the profile to be discriminated against, is something that people around the country fail to understand. In total, the working class and the discriminated class share more similar struggles and intersections than many often realize.
chunks.label: Conclusion on social systems and economic inequality
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that society vilifies personal traits out of an individual's control, reiterating that the working class and discriminated groups share closely intertwined struggles.

n0d6a593e.title: Constructing Gender and the Workplace Division

chunks.text:
Our personal beliefs and morals are heavily influenced by society and the people in it. As a society, we have determined that gender is dichotomous and an important social identity. This means our conception of gender is part of our collective consciousness. The collective consciousness is the shared beliefs and values that connect individuals in a society. In other words, we view society through a group consciousness. In his article “The Cultural Logic of Collective Representations,” Emile Durkheim explains this phenomenon in terms of religion. He writes, “Thus the collective ideal which religion expresses is far from being due to a vague innate power of the individual, but it is rather at the school of collective life that the individual has learned to idealize.” In this quote, Durkheim explains that our values do not stem from individuals, but that individuals learn to idealize certain values. According to Durkheim, these shared ideas are manifested through collective representations in the form of rituals, artifacts, symbols, and values. This is true for gender, as it is represented in art, advertisements, language, celebrations, institutions, etc. The idea of two distinct genders is a common belief that is deeply rooted in our society. The gender binary stems from the concept of sex. This comparison is inaccurate, however, as there are some key differences. According to authors Candace West and Don H. Zimmerman in “Doing Gender,” sex is determined by biology, anatomy, and hormones. Gender, in contrast, is achieved through psychology, culture, and social means. The two are connected through a concept known as sex category, or the identifying features that categorize someone as male or female. West and Zimmerman argue that because of this, gender is something we “do” when we align our outward appearance and behavior with those expected of a specific sex category. For this reason, western society believes that men and women are inherently different, with phycological and behavioral discrepancies that can be determined based on reproductive organs. This aspect of our collective consciousness has been used to justify the social consequences of assuming “gender roles.”

Throughout history, the female gender has been considered inferior. In the article “Women as Other,” author Simone de Beauvoir argues this is because women have always been considered the “other” in society while men are considered absolute. Beauvoir argues that this ideology didn’t just appear, as women have always been treated as subordinates. Women often submit to this point of view because they do not have a history, religion, or community of their own separate from men. Women have always been tied to men, and therefore have been unable to separate from their oppressors. This historical mistreatment of women is evident when examining the unequal division of labor in western society. In the article “Two worlds of female labour: gender wage inequality in western Europe 1300-1800,” authors Alexandra de Pleijt and Jan Luiten Van Zanden examine the underutilization of women in European labor markets from 1300-1800. Pleijt and Zanden argue that for women to be autonomous and remain single, they must be able to earn a living wage. Additionally, women participating in labor increased the human capital formation, but required women to be educated, skilled, or limit their fertility, all of which were undesirable for the time. For this reason, opportunities for women to work were not comparable to that of men. Following the Black Death, poor economies and low population required more women to join the workforce. In southern Europe, the gender wage ratio was approximately 0.5. In northern Europe, however, the gender wage ratio was much higher at 0.8. In medieval England, there were legal constraints that discouraged young, single women from working casually, and many were not allowed to work enough days to earn a livable wage. The sixteenth century market a time of labor market slack, in which the demand for labor was less than supply. This resulted in the gender wage ratio decreasing rapidly, with women making less than half of that of men. This trend continued through the nineteenth century. By examining these statistics, it becomes clear that gender has played a key role in determining who can participate in the labor market. This was a strategic decision to prevent women from making a living wage and becoming independent from men.

Because women were often unable to make a living wage, they were forced to marry young. A consequence of this is that women were often unskilled and uneducated. This allowed the traditional gender roles to remain intact as women became reliant on their husbands. Women were valued in society only for their fertility and were often patronized by their husbands. An example of this can be seen in Charlotte Gilman’s “The Yellow Wallpaper.” In this story, the main character’s husband, who is a physician, refuses to believe she is sick and insists that she is just hysterical. For this reason, she spends many hours in her room, unable to write or work. The woman feels guilty for not feeling more grateful for her husband, but she cannot deny her feelings of resentment. She directs this resentment towards her yellow wallpaper, a metaphor for the oppression she experiences as a woman. This demonstrates the struggle many women faced in the ninetieth and twentieth centuries. During this time, many women were unable to work or pursue an education. This often left women at the mercy of their husbands, who considered them hysterical for expressing resentment towards their gender roles. This power dynamic can also be seen in the cult of domesticity.

Throughout history, women have been denied career opportunities and burdened with domestic duties such as childbearing, cooking, and cleaning. This reflects the cult of domesticity, or the belief that women should embrace these duties and create a loving home. As a result, women complete approximately 2/3 of all domestic work. Women are primarily responsible for the tasks that must be completed daily, while men complete scheduled maintenance. Domestic responsibilities are time consuming, especially raising children. This can prevent women from pursuing careers and fulltime jobs, often leaving them unemployed or employed part time. Women who work fulltime are not exempt from these duties, however, as many are involved in a junior partner/senior partner relationship. These relationships exist when both partners have careers, but the woman has a “second shift“ in which she must also complete domestic work. This issue has only worsened recently due to the covid-19 pandemic. In the article titled “A gendered pandemic: Childcare, homeschooling, and parents’ employment during COVID-19,” authors Richard Pettes, Daniel Carlson, and Joanna Pepin explain that the availability of domestic support like daycare and school are important for mother’s labor force participation, while father’s participation is generally unaffected. As a result of daycares and schools closing due to covid and the domestic labor that follows, mother have been significantly more likely to reduce their work hours. According to Petts, Carlson, and Pepin as of April 2020, the beginning of lockdowns, the unemployment rate for women was 16.2% and 13.5% for men. This is an example of traditional gender roles in which women are responsible for childcare and housework and men for breadwinning. The responsibilities associated with each gender are harmful to women, as they are often unable to participate in the workforce due to responsibilities at home.

Though women have made many advancements in the workforce, there are still many obstacles. One example is the gender pay gap. In the article “The Gender Wage Gap: Extent, Trends, and Explanations,” authors Francine Blau and Lawrence Kahn examine why and how the pay gap has changed. According to Blau and Kahn, there are several reasons why the pay gap exists. Firstly, familial attitudes and gender norms often reduce women’s work life and discourage them from pursuing formal schooling. Secondly, women tend to gravitate towards lower paying college majors like art as opposed to science. Thirdly, it is often difficult for women to make advancements in the workplace due to bias. In the early twentieth century, women made approximately 60% as much as their male counterparts. Around 1980, however, women’s wages rose, and the gap changed to around 67%. This trend has continued at around 79% today. Blau and Kahn argue that this improvement is due to the shrinking education and experience gaps. In 1981 only 15.3% of women had a bachelor's degree and 13.5 years of work experience, with men at 18.1% and 20.3 years. These gaps have shrunken, with 24.7% of women in 2011 having a bachelor’s degree and 16.4 years of experience, with men at 26.2% and 17.8 years. The gender wage gap reveals that women often receive less opportunity for advancement and higher paying jobs based solely on the concept of gender. These statistics show the division of labor between genders.

Gender is a social construct embedded in our collective consciousness. As a society, we have come to believe that there are two inherently different genders who assume different roles. This idea is ingrained in our institutions and affects many aspects of our society. This is extremely evident when examining the workforce. Throughout history, it has been difficult for women to find and maintain job opportunities because of traditional ideas of gender, as women are mostly responsible for domestic labor. This made women reliant on their husbands and has kept them as the “other” in society. Though women have made advancements, the gender wage gap and the unequal unemployment caused by the covid-19 pandemic are continuous reminders that there is still progress to be made. By adjusting our understanding of gender, we can create equal opportunities for everyone in society.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of gender and labor division
chunks.what_happened: The student presents an academic essay analyzing gender as a social construct within the collective consciousness and examines historical and modern gender inequalities in labor, wages, and domestic responsibilities through various sociological texts.

chunks.text:
The collective consciousness is a critical aspect of studying Sociology when developing theories of race and ethnicity. Race and ethnicity are two different concepts symbolizing different aspects of the United States’ society. Studying the differences between race and ethnicity are crucial components to spreading awareness of racism, as spreading awareness is the first step to liberties for every matrix. Author, Patricia Hill Collins, portrays the subconscious hierarchies of oppression. She discusses the structure of domination within the country’s society through a rank-ordered preference. Collins explains how the United States structures power and authority, the way in which the country is run. Similarly, the podcast “Get Back to Where You Once Belonged” highlights the oppression black women faced through personalized stories. The story focused on a specific family and the struggle the family endured based on their race. It’s important to talk about how the collective consciousness developed a structured society based on a hierarchy of domination, with components such as race and ethnicity, and Collins illustrates the controversial themes of oppression.

Patricia Hill Collins paints a picture of ranking within society -- ranking based off of order of a specific, unfair, preference. There were multiple levels of domination based on three levels. These levels are: level of personal biography, group or community level of the cultural context created by race, class and gender, and the systemic level of social institutions. Each level plays a role in symbolic privilege, this unspoken advantage that certain ‘categories’ of people have over other types of people. Patricia Collins advocates that the known studies of systematic disadvantage have been biased, only one race has studied the effects of racism on communities. Because of this biased research, she believes that scientists should approach the study in a different manner. She believes that the first step to freedom and rights for every group, even those considered minorities, begins with acknowledging intersectionality, the combination of different race and ethnic groups, including the different genders. Once awareness of different personal, cultural, and institutional knowledge is spread, scientists will be able to gain a better understanding of inequality. The Podcast “Get Back to Where You Once Belonged” is a prime example of spreading awareness.

“Get Back to Where You Once Belonged” was an interview with a woman of African descent. She talks about the struggles she faced as an African American, light skinned, woman. She illustrates the feelings of unease, the feeling of being out of place. At a young age, Lily was faced with unfair stereotypes and cruel comments. Unknowingly, she would defend the perpetrators with the defense that these kids were just ‘ignorant’. She held high spirits, she chose to see the good in the people causing social unjust. Lily lived in Russia with her family because, although Russia wasn’t considered Utopia for racism, Russia stood by the fact that they were less racist than the United States during World War II. African Americans stood by the Soviet Union in hopes for a better, more free life. Lily’s family took the option to move to Russia, but still faced hardships, and although Lily chose to have good faith in her society, she was still oppressed. She talked about her damaged self-esteem, the feeling of loneliness, and the lack of trust in her community. Lily tried to date a Russian boy, but instead, she was faced with a cruel racist nickname, she even believed that the Russian boy was only dating her to see what it was like to date a black woman. She became more self-conscious of her skin as she grew older, but she also grew wiser. She talks about her philosophical beliefs about facing racism as a woman of color. She believes that in order to live a satisfying life of a minority, it is important to stop listening to the voice in her head blaming every little wrong on the color of her skin. She believes that she, and people like her, should just live their life, they should stop wasting time trying to change to conform to society and instead, drop the racist people who segregate, and continue to live life with people who aren’t threatening. She ended up living a satisfying life as she grew older, she learned how to adjust to the oppression in order to be happy.

“Get Back to Where You Once Belonged” is an important illustration of racialization. Racialization is the process that became ethnic identity, it’s the process of counting and defining immigrants because they went against the norms of society -- the norms that the collective consciousness created. As society grew and advanced, the creation of community formed. Ethnic identities were based on commonalities. Lily, from “Get Back to Where You Once Belonged” faced racialization living in a community unlike the people of her own culture. She felt lonesome due to lack of commonalities with her community, she felt out of place because her identity was outnumbered by people of different identities. Lily had to adapt to a social hierarchy, as discussed by Collins in “Black Feminist Thought in the Matrix of Domination” that went against her ethnic identity. It’s important to spread awareness, to acknowledge institutionalized differences in order to create liberation for every community, including minorities. It’s important to fight for freedom for everyone in society, to help those oppressed. More specifically, it’s important to find ways to advocate for freedom for those oppressed.
chunks.label: Analyzing Collins's theories and the podcast on racialization
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on sociological theories of race, ethnicity, and hierarchies of domination proposed by Patricia Hill Collins, and examines the podcast story of Lily facing racism in Russia.

chunks.text:
The Concept of McDonaldization which was created by George Ritzer, is about the process through which methods of fast food restaurants, particularly exemplified by McDonald's, procreates through our various aspects of society. McDonaldization is made up of four key characteristics: efficiency, calculability, predictability, and control. All of these dimensions permeate through the fast food chains and outwards into greater society. McDonaldization also involves the change of traditional, human-centered methods with rationalized, systematized approaches aimed at maximizing efficiency and minimizing costs. This phenomenon results in the proliferation of standardized procedures, the prioritization of speed and convenience over quality, and the commodification of experiences. While McDonaldization facilitates convenience and expediency, it also engenders consequences such as homogenization, loss of individuality, and the erosion of traditional social interactions and cultural practices.

These two concepts, albeit holding similarities, do have some glaring differences in that they have completely different goals. The main idea of rationalization is that is reaching for one common goal and being rational all the time, its entire goal is to come to what is believed to be the best outcome and that people will be completely rational for the sake of others. This is contradicted by the belief of McDonaldization which in a way is entirely different in that it seeks to gain an increasing large stake in peoples lives by making everything simple and efficient via proven principles of specifically fast food everything is to be productive, etc. Another difference between these two is the approach in formality, the concept of Rationalization is deeply suited in formality and through old means of control such as things like governmental bureaucracy, etc. While its counterpart McDonaldization is informal and controls through newer means such as corporate control and that everything can and should be controlled and it wishes to spread through every aspect of life which it has.

despite their apparent disparities these two concepts are far closer than anything as in logical sense they form branches on the same family tree of sociological, ideological family tree with McDonaldization and both of these concepts use similar points being those of Efficiency, Calculability, Predictability and Control. Efficiency, the cornerstone of both rationalization and McDonaldization, dictates the relentless quest for optimal resource utilization and output maximization. Whether in bureaucratic procedures or fast food assembly lines, while calculability shows the measurement of inputs, outputs, and the like and leads to a process of standardization. Predictability entails the establishment of clear guidelines, protocols, and routines to minimize uncertainty and ensure consistency, and control which is the most important of these two imposes rules, hierarchy and order whether it benefits societal or corporate interests. In the end, both the ideals of Rationalization and McDonaldization harness these shared principles to rationalize and optimize processes, whether for the collective benefit of humanity or the narrow interests of profit-driven entities and that is what makes them the same yet different.

nba47c25b.title: Debunking Myths of American Class Mobility

chunks.text:
There are many myths circulating our collective consciousness regarding class and whether it truly exists. For example, as highlighted by Mantsios, many believe that class is not relevant, as everyone has an equal opportunity to succeed. Another misconception, as highlighted by Domhoff, is that because we live in a democracy, we all have power in the government. In reality, the upper class is advantageous because they have more opportunities and influence in government and policy making. Mantsios explains that class affects where you live geographically and therefore what education you receive. Mantsios provides statistics showing that low-income students often score lower on standardized tests. This then translates into fewer job opportunities and a less optimistic outlook on life. Lower class individuals also have a higher mortality rate caused by health issues and less access to medical treatment. For these reasons, it’s often difficult to ascend between classes. Domhoff also supports that the upper class receive more opportunities on an institutional level because of their heavily influence in economics and government. Nonprofit organizations often share many directors with large corporations. These nonprofits provide money to education, research, and political campaigns resulting in tax cuts, subsidies, and less regulations on business. Overall, they can leverage their wealth to support ideas that are compatible with their goals and set the standards by which the working class must operate.

Though many fail to realize, one’s class heavily influences their experience and what opportunities they receive. Authors Mantsios and Domhoff attempt to refute common misconceptions about class in America by highlighting the many ways the wealthy benefit from our capitalist society on both a personal and institutional level. The class system is very much alive in America and by recognizing its effects, we can lessen the ever-growing gap between the rich and the poor. By doing this, we can provide everyone with equal opportunities despite the family they’re born into.
chunks.label: Myths and realities of social class in America
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological readings by Mantsios and Domhoff to explain how social class shapes opportunity, education, health, and political power, arguing against common myths of equality.

nad96604b.title: Observing Prejudice Across Minority Soccer Teammates

chunks.text:
Why do individuals of color face racism and prejudice from all angles of society? Judgment based upon race and ethnicity is omnipresent within contemporary society and extends much farther than the traditional discussion. Often, when discussing the plight of individuals of color, it can seem that these individuals are solely oppressed by the dominant social group. This dominant social group is said to be well-to-do white individuals, who are primarily male. However, people of color face judgment and prejudice from not only the dominant social group but also those in their own social group and those of similar ethnicities. Individuals of color and of various ethnicities face this racialization from other minorities as well as the individuals within their own race or social class. Why is it that minorities face this hardship from not only the dominant group but also other minorities? It is a complex issue that has a complex reasoning behind it. While it may be easy to assume that individuals of the same race or similar minority status would have a shared empathy for one another, this is often not the exact reality.

The roots of this issue are based on the fact that there is a ‘matrix’ nature to social status and privilege. This matrix is known as the ‘Matrix of Domination’ which explains the varying levels of privilege in society by acknowledging how the characteristics of race, ethnicity, gender, and sexuality all intersect. This matrix gives way for varying levels of privilege and can often pose minority groups against one another, creating prejudice and racialization from all sides. This phenomenon can be observed in various situations within the lives of individuals in contemporary society.
chunks.label: Introduction to the Matrix of Domination and interminority prejudice
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the topic of prejudice among minorities and explains Patricia Hill Collins's concept of the Matrix of Domination.

chunks.text: Throughout my own childhood, I have seen the levels of privilege and reracialization amongst minorities take form in many situations. This has primarily been observed through my involvement in the sport of soccer. I have played soccer throughout my entire life, beginning when I was around 5 years old. I have continued on to play soccer in middle school, high school, and still today while in college. Along the way, I have made many Hispanic friends who are deeply engaged in the culture of the sport. Due to our similar passions, I have built a strong connection with the Hispanic community throughout my childhood. Many of my current friends are Hispanic and frequently invite me to cultural gatherings and family events. I even currently play on an adult league soccer team that is exclusively Hispanic aside from myself. This team, made up of many of my best friends, plays and practices together every week and often go out for dinner together.
chunks.label: Playing soccer and connecting with Hispanic teammates
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up playing soccer and developed close friendships and connections with the Hispanic community, eventually joining an adult league soccer team where they are the only non-Hispanic player.

chunks.text: One of my many experiences with this team came several months ago when we had an open practice that anyone could attend. As usual I arrived early with one of my best friends, Adrian, and a few others on the team. When we arrived at the park, the field we normally practice on was taken up by a large group playing flag football. The rest of the team and I all waited by our cars as more and more people showed up for our upcoming practice. As the time for practice arrived, the field was still occupied and everyone on my team started to get a bit frustrated. As we all stood around, some of the Hispanic players began to talk to each other about the people taking up the field in a very crude way. These people playing football were primarily black and the Hispanic individuals started using racial slurs amongst each other and making many racist comments. I was shocked that they were so disgusted and offended by these black individuals doing absolutely nothing wrong. Eventually, we were able to practice and these comments eventually stopped. However, this was not the last time I saw this happen.
chunks.label: Teammates making racist comments toward Black football players
chunks.what_happened: At an open practice, the soccer field was occupied by a group of primarily Black players playing flag football, prompting Hispanic teammates to use racial slurs and make racist comments about them while waiting.
chunks.people: Adrian, teammates, Black individuals playing flag football

chunks.text: Not only did I see this type of racial judgment and prejudice applied to individuals of another race, I also saw Hispanics do this within their own ethnicity. Many of the hispanics who come to practice are Mexican or Honduran, while some come from other backgrounds. During one game in particular, we played against a primarily Columbian team who were made up of individuals of a different heritage and slightly different complexion. After the game, several slurs were used between players of my team and the Columbians. Both seemed to be very resentful of each other and judge each other based on their complexion and heritage.
chunks.label: Racial conflict with a Colombian soccer team
chunks.what_happened: During a soccer match, the student's predominantly Mexican and Honduran team played against a primarily Colombian team, and players exchanged slurs and judged each other based on complexion and heritage after the game.

chunks.text:
Patricia Collins explains this phenomenon in relation to the concept of the “matrix of domination”. The matrix of domination is made up of various levels and determines an individual's privilege based on their race, gender, sexuality, etc. In this matrix, each individual has a position determining their privilege. Collins states the following, “Depending on the context, an individual may be an oppressor, member of an oppressed group, or simultaneously oppressor and oppressed” (Collins 405). The dominant group made up of white, well educated, male individuals are positioned at the top while subordinate groups fall beneath. Amongst these subordinate groups, there are differences in heritage, education, race, etc that determine their level of privilege in relation to the matrix. All social aspects of an individual intersect to determine a person's “position” in this hierarchy of perceived status.

In relation to my personal experiences, the Hispanic individuals on my team have a position on the matrix of domination. Being that they are Hispanic, they are often oppressed by the dominant group on both a systemic and personal level. Not only are they oppressed due to their race but also their ethnic background.
