However, they see themselves as positioned higher on this matrix than black individuals. It is almost as if subordinate groups seek to position themselves closer to the dominant group and distinguish themselves from other subordinate groups. In an effort to position themselves as not completely subordinate, the Hispanic individuals in my personal example choose to oppress another minority group. Thus, Blacks face prejudice from not only the dominant group but also other minorities who seek to impose the same oppression as the dominant group in an effort to advance their social position. There is almost a mindset amongst the Hispanic community that while they are oppressed, they are not at the lowest position on the matrix of domination.

Not only does oppression occur across different minority groups, it can also occur within a particular minority or amongst a certain ethnic group. This concept is discussed in Tomas Almaguer’s piece, “Race, Racialization, and Latino Populations in the United States”. Almaguer states, “these groups [Mexicans and Puerto Ricans] then reracialize each other under the discursive logic that structures the meaning of race in the United States' ' (63). This means that minority groups apply similar patterns of racism as the dominant groups amongst their own ethnicity/race. This reracialization occurs as race is a symbolic concept and there is an established logic of a racial hierarchy which individuals seek to perpetuate. Not only is racism applied from the dominant group but also across the individuals of a particular subordinate group.

The Mexican individuals of my soccer team exemplify this instance of reracialization amongst the Latino community. The Columbians and Mexicans that I met, have similar cultural backgrounds and experiences of oppression. However, the Mexican individuals attempt to position themselves higher on the ‘racial hierarchy’. To do so, these individuals apply the same patterns of racism as the dominant group does. In turn, a structure of hierarchy is created amongst their own ethnicity. Through applying racism amongst their own ethnicity, these individuals seek to position themselves as a dominant group within their own Latino community. The negative ideas of blackness that are present within the United States are imposed amongst individuals within the Hispanic community as well, explaining why these Mexican individuals have a negative outlook on the ‘darker skinned’ Columbians on the opposing team. The same structures of racism that oppress the Hispanic community are utilized by Hispanics to oppress other Hispanic individuals and establish a separate social hierarchy where one group is dominant to the other.

The plight of individuals of color is complex as there is not only systemic racism that they face but also a reracialization by other individuals of color. Each individual in contemporary society seeks to improve or maintain a particular status. No one wants to be considered to be at the very bottom of the matrix of domination. Thus, oppressed individuals seek to oppress others in an effort of self advancement and placement in a higher social status. The logic of a racial hierarchy is not only perpetuated by the individuals with the most privilege, but also those who are oppressed. This makes for an experience of racism and prejudice that is very complex for individuals of color in contemporary society.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of interminority oppression and conclusion
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes their teammates' behavior using Patricia Hill Collins's matrix of domination and Tomás Almaguer's concept of reracialization, concluding on the complexities of racial hierarchy.

n982368c9.title: Analyzing Misinformation and Political Polarization Online

chunks.text:
The influence of social media and “fake news” on the spread of ideas across society

Mollie Clary

University of North Carolina Wilmington

The rapid development of technology has changed the way we live in countless ways. One way is the increase in the spread of ideas and connectivity of the world through social media. According to Statista, in 2020, social media users included over 3.6 billion people worldwide. An implication of the prevalence of social media is the significant amount of false information that is spread throughout the population and perceived as truth by thousands, if not millions of people. In the United States, this issue came to light during the 2016 presidential election when Donald Trump utilized the phrase “fake news!” throughout his campaign and presidency. “Fake news,” or false information disguised as truth, can be difficult to distinguish from credible news information. Additionally, an increasing number of people are turning to social media as an avenue for consuming news, where anyone has the freedom to post whatever they want. This is why it is so important to recognize and identify this dangerous force as it relates to the spread of ideas, beliefs, and the development of a collective consciousness.

Durkheim argued for the existence of collective belief and idea systems throughout society. He believed that religion contributed to this collective consciousness which can be observed through collective representations. Collective representations are symbols that exist in society and have meanings placed upon them that have become fabricated and prevalent through the development of society. The concept of the collective consciousness is important to acknowledge because it can explain a lot about our society and can help us understand why certain behaviors and ideas are popular among the general population and among certain groups. In our current American society, there are various groups that have strong belief systems that are consistent among members of the group. For example, the groups of this kind that get the most attention are Democrats and Republicans. The belief systems of these groups have become more and more solidified and polarized through the use of social media. Fake news is important to fit into this narrative because it can help explain some of the tension between these two groups in the United States.

A study conducted in 2018 by Pennycook and colleagues sought to examine the relationship between exposure to fake news headlines and perceived accuracy of these headlines. There is a previously proven idea in psychology called the “illusory truth effect” which is the process of being exposed to information and therefore being more likely to perceive the information as accurate, solely based on the fact that one was exposed to it, sometimes even only subconsciously exposed. This theory says that there is a positive relationship between amount of exposure to information and perceived accuracy of the information. Pennycook and colleagues (2018) attempted to understand whether or not the illusory truth effect would apply to fake news headlines that seem less plausible than the information used in previous research that examined this effect. In order to do this, they conducted three studies with slightly different conditions. The first study included “trivia” statements that were easily identifiable as highly implausible. Researchers concluded that exposure/repetition to these statements had no impact on perceived accuracy due to the high implausibility of the statements.

The second study conducted by Pennycook and colleagues in 2018 included fake news headlines which included warnings about the possible inaccuracy of the information being presented. The results of the second study indicated that exposure to these headlines, (whether true or false, regardless of whether there was a warning indicating possible false information, and regardless of whether the information agreed with the person’s political identity) increased perceived accuracy of the information. The third study found that exposure positively influences perceived accuracy of information, even with a week-long delay. Researchers pointed out that these findings have significant implications related to everyday life. For example, when politicians repeatedly communicate an idea to the public, based on these findings, people will be more likely to accept it; and the same applies to other ideas that may be impossible to definitively confirm or deny, such as religious beliefs (Pennycook et al., 2018). This study reinforces the idea that a high amount of exposure to information through social media, regardless of whether it is true, has a significant impact on the evolution of our collective consciousness and belief systems.

The social aspect of this issue is highly important to acknowledge because our belief systems are highly influenced by our environment. “Groupthink” is a phenomenon in psychology that occurs as a cycle, when group members’ beliefs are strengthened through the influence of the group (Groupthink, n.d.). Individuals in society often classify themselves and are perceived to be included in many groups whether these groups are imaginary or institutional. According to Psychology Today, Groupthink is similar to the concept of conformity, but exclusively occurs during decision-making processes related to a group. The Psychology Today article explains that Groupthink can have dangerous implications when it occurs in parts of society that contain large scale groups such as politics. This is because the phenomenon of Groupthink can cause people to dismiss ethics and morals in favor of conforming to their group’s priorities. According to Psychology Today, “(“an ‘us versus them’ mentality”)… can prompt members to accept group perspectives, even when those perspectives don’t necessarily align with their personal views.” This displays the high impact of Groupthink on individuals. This phenomenon is important to note in the context of fake news and its impact on societal beliefs because it definitely seems to play a role in the perceived accuracy of fake news. For example, when Donald Trump and some media outlets downplayed the Coronavirus pandemic, it appears that many Republicans went along with these ideas. This was very dangerous because it prompted many people to disregard important CDC community safety guidelines; some even protesting important aspects of these guidelines such as mask-wearing. The simple use of the phrase “fake news” adds to a general mistrust of the media which could lead to issues for our society.

Research conducted by Colliander in 2019 examined the relationship between fake news on social media and individuals’ conformity to its ideas through two studies. The first study included 3 experimental conditions in which participants were exposed to fake news social media posts. In the first condition, these posts included comments from social media users that expressed support for the information. The second condition included fake social media posts with comments that expressed disbelief or the acknowledgement of the post as fake news. The third condition included both types of comments: supportive and critical. The findings of this study indicated that the comments from other social media users influenced the likelihood that participants would share and/or comment on the posts. The second study was designed similarly to the first study but included a condition with no comments and another condition where there was a warning from the social media platform about the possible inaccuracy of the information. Based on the results of the second study, Colliander (2019) states, “Social media users seem to use the comments of other people as a guide for how to respond to disinformation online rather than disclaimers.” This finding emphasizes the significant impacts of social influence on beliefs and perceptions of information, even false information.

A study published in 2021 by Michael and Breaux aimed to examine whether political affiliation has an impact on the perception of fake news. Three almost identical studies were conducted, one in 2017, the second in 2018, and the last in 2020. Researchers hypothesized that people would trust news that agreed with their beliefs, and distrust news that disagreed with their beliefs. Participants were given a list of news sources and asked to rate them based on level of trustworthiness using the categories “real news,” “fake news,” and “propaganda.” Participants were also asked to define the terms “real news,” “fake news,” and “propaganda.” Researchers grouped participants based on “self-reported political identification.” (Michael & Breaux, 2021) The results of the study suggest that in general, more conservative people would view the news sources included in this study as less trustworthy than more liberal people. The two additional studies yielded similar results although there were some changes in the results due to the passage of time. Overall, researchers found that news sources that were rated as more trustworthy by liberals were likely to be rated as “fake news”/” propaganda” by conservatives and vice versa. Steps were taken to rule out level of familiarity as an explanation for perceived trustworthiness of the news sources. The findings of this study raise questions surrounding the influence of political groups on media consumption among the general public. Personal belief systems evolve over time partly due to the consumption of new information, therefore, with a high level of information absorption among individuals in society due to the current prevalent use of social media, it is important to acknowledge the influence of political ideologies on the acceptance and sharing of information.

Allen and colleagues (2020) argued that the spread of fake news may not be an urgent crisis due to the actual prevalence of this type of media compared to other media types. Through their research study, they sought to understand the prevalence of fake news based on the ideas that people use various platforms to consume media and that there is a high variety of types of media and news content. In order to do this, they measured TV consumption and consumption of media through desktop and mobile devices. They found that on average, Americans spend over 7.5 hours per day consuming media (Allen et al., 2020). The results also demonstrated that news constitutes only a fraction of individuals’ total daily media consumption, therefore, fake news must constitute a tiny fraction (about one tenth). Researchers noted that according to Google Scholar, between 2017 and 2020, 2210 English publications with “fake news” in the title emerged, while before this there were only 73. Although fake news is not widespread when compared to total media consumption, the increasing magnitude of the conversation surrounding it is enough to constitute an issue.

In conclusion, societal influences have a huge impact on personal values, beliefs, perceptions, and ideas. Social media is a new way that this has been occurring over the last ~25 years. Social media is the perfect tool for spreading misinformation over a large audience. This is why it is so important to acknowledge, identify, and fight the spread of fake news, other misleading propaganda and inaccurate information. To the naked eye, it might seem as though fake news is easy to avoid and will not become a huge problem. However, based on the research, fake news is not always as easy to reject as one might expect. As a society, we need to learn to be cautious among the constant flood of information that we are being exposed to.
chunks.label: Fake news, social media, and collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the sociological and psychological impacts of social media and fake news, reviewing sociological concepts like collective consciousness as well as various empirical studies on groupthink, political polarization, and misinformation.

n17230bfe.title: Navigating the Rise of Artificial Intelligence

chunks.text:
Humans are frequently viewed as a type of working machine. We get up every day and stick to a routine; most individuals work like clockwork and don't recognize the drawbacks. Similarly, advances in A1 systems have led to predictions that our lives would one day be governed by algorithms; many individuals do not see this as a problem, while others do. Both Harari and Durkhiem are concerned with A1 systems and how people will react to something new.

Harari discusses the growing problem of A1 systems, the strength of algorithms, and how they dominate our life in his book 21 lessons for the 21st century. While we currently have control over our daily lives, this may not be the case in the future. An algorithm would control our life, telling us things like "how to react in a breakup," "when to smile," and other things. While this may help our world function more smoothly, we would lose the very thing that makes us human: our emotions. Everyone should not react the same way to a split; some people may cry, while others may be fine, and still others may become enraged; but, this should be a personal choice, not one dictated by a system that does not know you. A1 systems are already invading our lives through different aspects. Many people often will say “my phone is spying on me” while it definitely is not in the way most people assume it is in a small aspect. Each website you go onto tracks your searches; such as amazon if you were searching for a rug you are more likely to start seeing ads for rugs than anything else because companies know you are more likely to buy that than something else. With the growing problem of A1 jobs are effected too. Harari says that not having a job right now may be beneficial in the long run. Because we don't know what the "work market" will look like in 2050, not having a job for a while may be beneficial. According to Harari, and as we all know, technical advancements and electronic takeover are destined to replace many manual jobs with "robots." So, if you don't know what career you want or what to commit to in the long run, it's best to avoid committing to something that will no longer require people in 10 years, and you'll have wasted time and money on something you won't be able to pursue.

Durkheim wrote that people feel better when they are in groups, and when they all agree upon the same thing. He concluded that “society exists because unique individuals feel a sense of solidarity with each other” (Cole, Nicki Lisa, Ph.D).This is how many social standards are established; if one person believes something and the rest of the group agrees, it appears to be more acceptable because the entire group agrees. This could be advantageous to A1 systems in both good and bad ways; it could help everyone embrace the takeover of A1 while also helping everyone reject it. A1 has a lot of advantages, but it also has a lot of disadvantages. Many people in society say things like "we shouldn't let technology dictate our life," and we should really listen to them. Allowing A1 to control our life would be giving up the very thing that makes each of us unique, akin to surrendering our freedom. What freedom do you really have if you can't make decisions for yourself in your daily life? When a parent or sibling dies, or when you get your favorite dish, an algorithm can't predict how you'll feel because these events are unique every time. You wouldn't respond the same way to every breakup, so there's no reason for an algorithm to know because you don't.
chunks.label: Reflections on AI systems, algorithms, and human emotions
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the ideas of Harari and Durkheim, discussing how AI systems and algorithms could control daily life, the impact on human emotions and jobs, and the importance of preserving human uniqueness and decision-making.

n8da24b2a.title: Perceptions of Class and Power Inequality

chunks.text:
Class is an aspect of our society that influences how certain people live their lives. It is seen through commercials, television shows, school, and other institutions in our society; however, it is not always depicted correctly. There are myths about our perception of class ingrained in our collective consciousness, that we may not even be aware of.

Although the middle class is a term used commonly in society, the opposite ends of the class spectrum do not use the term ‘class’ as often. In Class In America, Mantsios discusses how the middle class in America does not occupy most of the nation's wealth. This is misconstrued in society because most of the commercials on television advertise towards the nation's middle class, which leads us to believe that the middle class has a large portion of money that is increasing, but it is actually decreasing. A large portion of Americans fall under this category; however, the upper class obtains the largest amount of money in our society. Domhoff discusses, in The Class Domination Theory of Power, that the upper class holds a dominant amount of power, although the United States is a democratic society. As a society, we have believed that since we have free speech and can vote and have rights that we are all equal; however, Domhoff emphasized the fact that the upper class possessed much more power in practical terms, because they have more revenue into the federal government and the corporations that rule the country.

Class is a term that can make people feel uncomfortable because as a society we all want to feel equal. There are differences shown in the media and in our society as a whole that affect our collective consciousness about how we view the impact of class in society. We must address the reality of the situations in order to convey change and stand for equal rights.
chunks.label: Reflecting on social class perceptions and inequality
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological concepts of class, citing works by Mantsios and Domhoff to reflect on wealth distribution, media portrayals, and power inequalities in American society.

chunks.text:
Politics has become such an essential power that controls society. Politics organizes each community so that there is organization. Without organization, there would be chaos. However, politics has become competitive, especially between differing countries. Harari discusses the terrorism in his book, 21 Lessons for the 21 Century. The goal of terrorism is to change a political situation by conducting fear in a country’s enemy. Terrorism is ruthless and destructive. Terrorism threatens the heart of each society, the government. Government stems from politics. Society places the government on a high pedestal of importance. This stems from the collective conscious. The collective representation of government is authority, control, and law-making. Harari’s description of terrorism is emphasized because of differing collective representations of politics between countries.

Harari describes the impact terrorism has to each society. For each country under attack of terrorism, threats to security and safety become a pressing issue. Each country has to scramble for resources to protect themselves from terrorism. Terrorism occurs due to differing collective conscious representations. Each society runs their government differently which, consequently, can cause a rift. This rift can become so evident that terrorism arises.

It is important to understand the collective conscious to understand why issues like terrorism occurs. The collective conscious shapes society’s views, norms, expectations, and more. Each society is different, and differing opinions can often clash causing a disagreement or altercation. This can sometimes lead to terrorism which is often alarming and threatening towards the safety of the society being under attack.
chunks.label: Politics, terrorism, and the collective conscious
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the role of politics and government in society, analyzes Harari's perspective on terrorism from his book, and discusses how differing collective conscious representations between societies lead to conflict and terrorism.

nf79bfb45.title: Facing Gender Pay Disparity at Work

chunks.text: Are women truly given a fair shot to make money compared to men? Millions of women are in the workforce today but make significantly less money than men. There is a wage gap that exists in America, and currently, it is eighty-two cents to every dollar a man makes. Women have already overcome many obstacles when it comes to oppression. The wage gap is another obstacle that must be overcome. The wage gap is not a problem that begins when women are in the workforce later in their careers it starts right when they enter. Not only is it difficult for women to make fair wages, women of color struggle much more when it comes to making fair wages in the workforce. There is a societal standard or view of women that their worth stems from their beauty rather than their qualifications. A lot of these standards can be tied to the concept of the beauty myth and doing gender.
chunks.label: Introduction to wage gap and beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the gender wage gap in America, racial pay disparities, and how societal standards connect beauty and gender performance to women's workplace value.

chunks.text: When I was 16 years old, I got my first job at a local Panera Bread. I was quickly trained and became one of the most dependable employees they had. I was the first one they always called to cover shifts, train people, and handle mishaps at the cash register. All the while I was working there, I was paid $9 an hour. I was training boys my age who were making more than I was. When I brought this up to management, they denied that there was a gap in my pay with the boys I was training. I knew that this was quite fishy so everything I did following that was done contemplating what management's plans were. Management tended to hire a lot of “pretty” people, but these people were not good at their job. The people they hired tended to fit into the norm and beauty myth. They just needed to be conventionally attractive to get the job it seemed. After all of my hard work, some of the managers started to realize, after a year, that I was a good employee to have around. They started to promise me a promotion and raise, but that never did happen. In my attempt to try and resolve the problems that existed at Panera, I spoke with managers on multiple occasions about the promotion, promises of a raise, and harassment from a male co-worker with nothing to be changed. The constant feeling of having no power was solidified and confirmed with all of the power that men had in the chain.
chunks.label: Experiencing pay disparity and inaction at Panera
chunks.what_happened: The student worked at Panera Bread at age 16 as a dependable employee, but found out that younger male trainees earned more than her. Management denied the disparity, broke promises of raises and promotions, and ignored harassment from a male coworker.

chunks.text: The power struggle can be explained by Naomi Wolf’s “beauty myth.” The concept of the beauty myth is that women are judged purely on their appearance and nothing more. In the “beauty myth,” Wolf states, “Feminism gave us laws against job discrimination based on gender; immediately case law evolved in Britain and the United States that institutionalized job discrimination based on women's appearances.” (Wolf 2). The appearance of women takes an abnormal precedent when it comes to hiring decisions and the compensation between men and women. There is an inherent bias when it comes to men and women in the workplace. Women are at a disadvantage when it comes to pay equality. The current pay gap is 82 cents to a dollar which tends to relate to the beauty myth. A large portion of the gap comes from the basis of judging women and placing their value on their looks. For example, a man and woman who are hired at the same time with similar qualifications and work history will commonly have a wage gap. This can often be attributed to the “beauty myth” within the working communities.
chunks.label: Naomi Wolf's beauty myth in the workplace
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Naomi Wolf's concept of the beauty myth, explaining how hiring decisions and pay disparities stem from evaluating women based on appearance rather than qualifications.

chunks.text: The concept of “doing gender” also ties into the wage gap currently. “Doing gender” is a concept that refers to conforming to a certain gender type whether that be with clothes, mannerisms, or actions. Often women in the workforce do not get the same opportunities that men do. Women can certainly aim for jobs that are higher in the chain of working but sometimes they are not awarded those jobs. Women can be guided or coerced into job positions that are more “fit” for women. Some of those jobs include receptionists and assistants as opposed to leaders within their realm of work. The coercion for women in certain roles does not fall just into the corporate world it is everywhere, it is in college majors too. For example, gendered expectations say that women should major in more feminine things like nursing or teaching which is the opposite for men. The gender expectations for college majors can be an immediate disadvantage to how much money in a career path women can make. The “doing gender” concept highlights the wage gap and the gendered expectations that loom over women especially.
chunks.label: The concept of doing gender
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses the sociological concept of doing gender, detailing how women are guided into lower-paying gendered positions and college majors.

chunks.text: To summarize, the gender wage gap is a complex issue that is influenced by many factors, including discrimination, workplace segregation, and differences in education and experience. However, the concepts of the “beauty myth” and "doing gender" shed light on how gendered expectations and norms can play a significant role in extending the wage gaps existence. The “beauty myth” reinforces the idea that women must meet certain physical standards to be considered valuable and successful, which leads to discrimination in the workplace and limits women's earning potential. Similarly, "doing gender" focuses on how gendered expectations can influence the types of jobs that men and women pursue and how they negotiate for pay, which can also contribute to the wage gap. Overall, addressing the gender wage gap requires a wide-focused approach that recognizes and challenges the ways in which gendered expectations and norms can limit women's earning potential at any age. By promoting gender equality in all areas of life, we can create a more just and equal society where all individuals have the opportunity to succeed and thrive.
chunks.label: Summary of wage gap factors
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes how discrimination, workplace segregation, the beauty myth, and doing gender perpetuate the wage gap, advocating for broad societal solutions.

chunks.text: In conclusion, women are not given a fair shot to make money compared to men in the workplace. My own experience while working at Panera Bread is an example of the unfair and unequal pay between men and women in the workforce. Men have a leg up on fair wages because of certain fields they dominate in career paths as well as negotiations for pay ranges. While working at Panera I can now say that the “beauty myth” and “doing gender” largely contributed to the people that worked there. The “beauty myth” was utilized quite often as how people would be compensated. The conventionally attractive employees were the ones who made more money regardless of their skill set and ability to do their job well. As for “doing gender” among the employees at Panera it was something that was also commonly seen. Management would oftentimes try to get more of the male employees to higher ranks or work in the kitchen as line cooks whereas female employees would be recruited to work in the bakery or as a cashier. These opportunities are not equal and give a clear view into the inner workings of how the wage gap remains and is encouraged today. The wage gap is still very much something that currently and historically affects our pay which is an obstacle that must be overcome.
chunks.label: Conclusion connecting Panera to sociological concepts
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by reflecting on how the beauty myth and doing gender explain employee pay and gendered job segregation at Panera Bread and the wider workforce.

nb1ea8e61.title: Analyzing Collective Consciousness in Modern Politics

chunks.text:
How does the collective conscious relate to politics? How does disillusionment correlate with the collective consciousness? Author, Yuval Noah Harari, discusses in part one of his novel, 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, the importance of advancing technology and how it plays a role in politics, more specifically, liberalism. Views on politics have been construed from the collective consciousness. Similarly to Emile Durkeim’s idea that religion gave birth to society, society places politics on a high pedestal. Without politics and government, there wouldn’t be another form of organization and control. This need for government and politics stems from the collective conscious.

To begin, Emile Durkeim explains collective consciousness and collective representations. He believed that society is made up of individuals with ideas. These ideals are unspoken rules that organize the society of individuals. The collective consciousness forms collective representations which are symbols that define a specific thought, idea, or object. Emile Durkeim felt strongly about religion being one of the most highly viewed upon moral forces. Essentially, Emile Durkeim viewed religion as the reasoning behind society’s morals and ethics. Similarly to Emile Dukeim’s view on religion and how it shaped society’s morals, Yuval Noah Harari believed that politics and liberalism shaped society.

Society places a high value on liberalism. These expectations create situations when political agendas fall through, a concept known as disillusionment. Harari emphasizes the idea that individuals tend to think in stories rather than in facts. He believed that society’s current political situation is not progressing, it is not working. He believed that it’s not working because individuals fear the concept of change. Like Emile Durkeim’s view of how religion shaped morals, change behind a solidified concept is a hard idea to grasp. It is hard to accept and adapt to change. He believes that society should be working to welcome disruption in technologies, accept advantage objective realities, and reduce suffering and brutality. Harari sees that society places a high value on government, but unlike Durkeim, he feels negatively towards the way it has shaped society. He believes that reform is needed because this story has started to become problematic for society. However, he does recognize that society needs democracy and free markets in order to function.

In conclusion, both Durkeim and Harari have similar views that religion and government shape society. However, as life progresses, it is important to keep up to date with technology and society. Society constantly advances itself, so it is important to accept change and adapt in order to not be left behind. It is important to recognize that this story of disillusionment of liberalism is not working for society. It is important to start looking towards change even though the collective conscious created unspoken rules, generations ago, and representations that society is unknowingly expected to follow.
chunks.label: Collective consciousness, religion, politics, and disillusionment
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological ideas from Emile Durkheim and Yuval Noah Harari, exploring how collective consciousness, religion, and politics shape society and why society must adapt to change.

n49129b88.title: Sociological Perspectives on Religion and Immigration

chunks.text:
Do all sociologists interpret social constructs such as religion and racism in similar ways? Since these topics can be abstract and there are many ways of viewing them, sociologists often disagree. However, they also agree on the implications of some of these social institutions. In Yuval Noah Harari’s book, 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, he explores many different problems which he sees to be the most relevant for today’s dynamic society. In this essay, I will specifically be focusing on his chapters about religion and immigration. I plan to compare them with a piece from Émile Durkheim and one by Patricia Hill Collins.

Religion is a topic that many sociologists have explored. They try to determine why religion was a unifier, specifically in primeval societies. They also explore the trajectory that religion took and how it came to play the role it does today. Émile Durkheim is a French sociologist from the late 19th century-early 20th century who is considered to be one of the founders of modern-day sociology. In one of his papers, The Cultural Logic of Collective Representations, he explored how religion was developed. His main argument to explain the development of religion is that it was a way to unify groups of similar people to form a collective consciousness. Collective consciousness is an idea developed by Émile Durkheim and is defined as, “a group or society’s commonly shared fundamental beliefs, customs, norms, and values” (Bell).

Durkheim talks about how religion was essential to societies forming because they needed something to believe in. When societies were first forming, they revolved entirely around religion. In the collective consciousness, the ideas or beliefs that are unique to a certain group are called the collective representations. They help differentiate people’s identities. Since religion became the foundation of these collective consciousnesses, all of the collective representations in each society were tied to the religion that they believed in. Durkheim argues that without religion, society would not exist, and he believes that religion is essential for its functioning. He says that the collective consciousness of a group provides the group members with stability. When someone is surrounded with people who have similar beliefs, then they feel supported, so it is easier for them to see these beliefs as the truth. Religion became the foundation for all the important social institutions within a society, so Durkheim’s main idea when writing this piece is that society and religion are heavily intertwined.

In the chapter about religion, Yuval Noah Harari discusses the uses of religion in the past versus the present. He acknowledges that religion used to play a big part in society, but its hold on people’s lives has loosened since it is not relevant to important aspects of life such as medicine, science, and economics. In the past, when people’s lives revolved around religion, it did control these fields. However, as knowledge adapts and we learn more about the world around us, religion becomes increasingly insignificant. In short, Harari’s argument is that although religion still has the power to unify and divide people, it is no longer necessary for our sense of community nor for us to develop as a society. He asserts that religion is essentially worthless in today’s society.

Although they have different takes on religion, both authors make good points. Durkheim focuses on the past and why religion came to play such an important role while Harari explores the present functions of religion. Harari makes good points about why religion is not as important and does not have as much power over people’s lives, but it seems like he allows some of his biases to seep into his writing. He calls religion a problem and says that it cannot be part of the solution. While some religious practices are problematic and have the tendency to ostracize people, they still have a way of gathering people together. In the midst of tragedy and despair, many people turn to the gods they believe in for hope. Most religious rituals include an aspect of community, or they bring people together, so I would argue that the positive impact religion has on people’s lives outweighs the negatives. This is not to disregard the negative experiences that people have had with religion. Instead, it is to offer a more neutral view that considers multiple perspectives.

One topic that was discussed in class is racism and how people are treated based on their unchangeable characteristics. Patricia Hill Collins wrote The Matrix of Domination. In it, she explained how people are either oppressed or oppressors based on their situation. She also argues how people can exist in both of these positions depending on the system of oppression. For example, a black man could be oppressed because of his race, but also be an oppressor because of his gender. She argues that the way people experience oppression and fit into the matrix of domination is very fluid and is subject to changes. The systemic level that racism functions on is one of the main factors in how the dominant group maintains control. On this level, social institutions such as schools or churches will only expose people to the ideas of their group, and they encourage thinking that coincides with their own. These institutions also require people who are not in the dominant group to be submissive, and they discourage any media that challenges their rhetoric. This essentially means that the dominant group often uses its power to continually oppress the submissive group.

The chapter that Harari wrote on immigration ties in well with Collins’ argument. He talks about how people are treated differently in various cultures because of their appearance. He uses immigration as the primary example of this and goes into multiple debates surrounding this issue. The debates primarily revolve around immigrants assimilating to a country. For example, how much should immigrants have to assimilate. Or, at what point have they fully assimilated and can then be considered citizens? The anti-immigrant side argues that immigrants should have to assimilate to all aspects of European culture, but they also believe that Europe should not let in too many immigrants for fear that they are intolerant. They say that their society cannot manage an abundance of illiberal people. Some will even go as far to say that national community is the most important European value, so immigrants should go as far as to change their culture. This is where the debate of when someone fully assimilates comes into play. There still lies the question of what extent do immigrants need to go to if they want to become full citizens of a country. Some would argue that they have to change everything about themselves and their beliefs while the pro-immigration side would favor a faster acceptance. Nonetheless, it still takes a long time for immigrants to be considered a part of society instead of outsiders, and are they really ever fully accepted by the people they are surrounded by?

He concludes this chapter by discussing the switch from racism to culturism and how they are similar yet different forms of oppression. Historically, racism was more biologically based, so people were treated differently because of their DNA and their physical appearance, but it has evolved to be more a reflection on the places they are from. Harari says that the degrading comments people make about people of color are more about their culture instead of their biology. This is how the term culturism came to be. Since there is so much variation between cultures, they are the root of the differences in humans. He also discusses how their standing in a country change how they are treated. Regardless of political party, people often find immigrants to be a threat. Not only are they seen as outsiders, but many people also believe that they came to take something from them. Despite there being no real evidence to support this claim, it still instills a negative attitude toward immigrants. When immigrants are portrayed as a threat or as the other, then citizens of the country are more likely to react badly when encountering them. It also subjects immigrants to higher rates of racism.

Collins’ theory that someone can be an oppressor, oppressed, or function on both levels depending on the situation can be applied to immigration. Although Harari and Collins do not have the exact same argument in their writings, their ideas are complementary. On one hand, Collins talks about the different levels that racism can exist on, and she discusses the implications of the institution that is perpetuating the racism. On the other hand, I would argue that Harari uses immigration as an example of the different functions of racism. Instead of directly stating how immigrants suffer from the racist ideas and actions that are perpetuated against them, he describes the tension surrounding immigration and discusses the effects of it. His explanation of culturism, or modern-day racism that focuses more on a person’s culture than their biology, directly correlates to Collins’ theory. For example, if a Muslim man immigrated to England, then he would most likely face hate, exclusion, and oppression from the people who live there. Alternatively, if an American man immigrated to somewhere with high populations of Muslims in the Middle East, he would be seen as a threat and untrustworthy. The Muslim man would then occupy the position of an oppressor instead of the oppressed. Therefore, one person could be both oppressed and an oppressor depending on the situation.

Whether religion is still important or has become a trivial institution is something that sociologists could debate. There is strong evidence for it being essential in the past, but Harari believes that the past is where it should stay. For this reason, Harari and Durkheim’s arguments are contradictory. However, the one concept that most sociologists can agree on is racism and that it is still a problem on a global scale. Both Harari and Collins give examples of how it is still present and creates injustices for the oppressed, but neither offers a solution. Their arguments have the same basis, so they are complimentary. All three writers offered good support for their conclusion and make a strong argument in favor of their position. Now, it is up to us to determine what we see to be the truth.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of religion, racism, and immigration
chunks.what_happened: The student compares the sociological theories of Yuval Noah Harari, Émile Durkheim, and Patricia Hill Collins on the functions and evolution of religion, racism, and immigration.

na994e4f3.title: Challenging Traditional Gender Roles and Expectations

chunks.text: Unknowingly, there are numerous expectations and standards that men and women incessantly face in society just because of their gender. There are unspoken rules implemented that women and men follow to ‘fit in’ with their community, if these rules aren’t followed, those men and women are seen as outcasts. Within society, genders have roles. Men are supposed to be dominant, to be superior, while women are supposed to be inferior to men. Fortunately, in the 19th and 20th century, a concept known as feminism, rose. Feminism is a political movement in which the goals are to reduce the stigma of gender roles.
chunks.label: Gender roles and the rise of feminism
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces societal gender expectations and discusses the rise of feminism as a political movement to reduce gender role stigmas.

chunks.text: In regard to gender and sexism, gender differs because it is a set of roles put in place through the collective consciousness. Sexism is biologically based; sex differentiates men and women based off of physical features. Interestingly enough, author of “Women as Other”, Simone de Beauvoir, illustrates the roles that women should play in society. She emphasizes the differences anatomically between men and women. Men view women as ‘obstacles’, as their ‘other’ because of their anatomical parts. Men are expected to be of authority because they are built to be stronger, forcing women to be submissive, to live in their shadow. Women were not expected to speak up, they were expected to follow society’s idealism of gender roles. Simone de Beauvoir validates the argument that gender is just assigned rules thought up through the collective consciousness.
chunks.label: Simone de Beauvoir on gender and sexism
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the distinction between gender and sex, discussing Simone de Beauvoir's arguments on anatomical differences and women as the 'other'.

chunks.text: Similarly to Simone de Beauvoir, Naomi Wolf, author of “Beauty Myth” speaks about how women should behave. Just like de Beauvoir’s argument that men should be assertive, women were expected to not only act a certain way but look a certain way. Although there was a rise of women empowerment in this timeframe, Wolf illustrates the negative mental illnesses that women of this century faced. Women were expected to be beautiful, to be youthful, and thin. In the 1840s, the first nude photograph of a prostitute emerged. This photograph was of a woman considered ‘beautiful’, which resulted in society’s women striving to look like the woman in the photograph. Wolf highlights the increase in cosmetic surgeries, eating disorders, consumer spending, and pornography during this timeframe because of how intense the yearn to be beautiful was for women.
chunks.label: Naomi Wolf and the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Naomi Wolf's arguments about beauty standards, mental illnesses, cosmetic surgery, and the historical pressures women faced to look youthful and thin.

chunks.text: Fortunately, despite the gender roles implemented in this century, feminism and reproductive rights came to surface giving more freedom to both genders. Feminism forces people to have a broader perspective on gender roles, to challenge the negative stigmas. This movement enabled women to have more rights and freedom within society. Reproductive Rights gave women the power to control their own body. Even though there is still a prominent stigma with how genders should behave, look, or act within society, society is slowly becoming more progressive.
chunks.label: Impact of feminism and reproductive rights
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by discussing how feminism and reproductive rights expanded women's bodily autonomy and freedom, noting that society is gradually progressing.

chunks.text:
Meaningless Work and Corporate-Owned Data: Comparing and Contrasting Marxist Theory with Yuval Harari’s 21 Lessons for the 21st Century

Movies Back to the Future, Meet the Robinsons, and Robots portray the future as a utopia, perhaps because history has only credited humans’ capacity for evolution. Today, however, society takes a rather ominous path toward the future. Karl Marx’s theory of estranged labor has proven itself in 2021, and it will continue to do so until capitalism is replaced by an economic system that prioritizes workers’ needs. Frighteningly, advanced technology legitimizes a need for employee relations. Modern technology also restricts humans to a livelihood that, under capitalism, is no different from that of feudal serfs. As an increasing number of humans’ basic needs become monetized, our self-autonomy is slowly undermined by large corporations. Who is to say that humans’ future selves will not be at executives’ mercy through technological forces? When assessing economic circumstances of the present, which match Marx’s theory of estranged labor, one may predict a future that aligns with Yuval Harari’s corporate-owned, employee-harming outlook.

With the exception of humans, every species may thrive only in a particular environment. Humans are unique from other species because our imaginations enable us to adapt to a variety of environments. Humans are the universe’s most valuable resource, and our advanced capabilities materialize our thoughts. Historically, humans have used our imaginations to establish civilizations, create industry, and discover agriculture, all of which further our chances of survival. In accordance with Marx, labor perverts unique activity by enforcing production of goods that are unnecessary for humans’ longevity. Coinciding with Marxist theory, the market assigns monetary value to all things, and human energy is commodified. Prior to the 1800s, which is when the Enlightenment birthed liberalism, labor was interpreted as a means to survive. A village that existed in Europe at this time consumed all of its produced goods. For instance, a farmer who lived in 18th century Europe may have supplied his village’s most popular “restaurant” with ingredients. In return, he/she paid no amount for food. Ultimately, relationships incentivized villagers to labor, and villagers knew who consumed their goods. Pre-modern societies are reproduced using exchange of goods, services, and resources that occurs within a singular net. Market societies are reproduced using goods that are provided to consumers by third parties. Markets are third parties that estrange laborers from their “fruits”. Thus, the theory of estranged labor is born.

MFW, also known as meaningful work, weakens alienation of labor. To lose a job in effect of technological advancement is rather beneficial, according to author Yuval Harari. In his book 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, Harari argues that if humans lose jobs to algorithms, then we may be able to pursue meaningful careers. Specifically, “losing our jobs to algorithms might actually turn out to be a blessing”, for doing so may motivate us to pursue our interests. Chapter 2 of 21 Lessons for the 21st Century warns humans of a future composed of “artificial” labor. In such a future, scientists will have studied the brain enough to influence formation of algorithms. Resolutely, artificial intelligence will possess abilities of determining various situations’ maximum outcomes, driving, and performing surgery. In addition to pursuing meaningful careers, humans may generate little human errors, should A.I. overtake job markets. Human error includes car crashes, doctor shortages, and employee discrimination.

Although Harari acknowledges in 21 Lessons for the 21st Century that fears of an A.I. uprising “have never materialized”, his opinion that for an algorithm to overtake one’s job is a blessing contradicts the theory of estranged labor. Harari insists that an economic safety net would replace the market, if A.I. supplants manual labor. Marx warns that capitalism separates property-owners from propertyless workers. Present-day consumers are often unable to afford their own products, justifying need for an economic safety net. Contrarily, A.I. requires management. Harari’s image of a picturesque, jobless universe is inspiring, particularly as we exist in modern society. Still, an economic safety net does not answer to those who manage algorithms. Marx states in Estranged Labor that all functions of human survival begin with human action. Again, Harari contradicts the theory of estranged labor by disregarding concern for employees’ invulnerability. Sure, opportunity for humans to pursue meaningful work at welfare’s hands may still be attained, but what economic system will replace capitalism so that those operating A.I. are better-recognized for their labor?

Estranged Labor spotlights dangers of a society that is too immersed in the market to repair itself should humans become alienated from their customers. Class is a large aspect of Marx’s worry that for-profit labor removes propertyless workers from property-owners. Today, the “free market” controls every aspect of humans’ lives between Europe and the United States. However, a low class would be impossible without neoliberalism, specifically. As evidenced by the Occupy Wall Street movement, which began in 2011, every-day Americans are upset with the top 1 percent of earners. Marxist fears of an unchecked class have finally boiled over. Previously, for-profit labor was means to an end; initial uprisings indicated boundaries past which executives were not permitted to travel. Coupled with ministries of Richard Nixon, Ronald Reagan, and Margaret Thatcher, 1970s stagflation ushered an era of corporate dominance, which has yet to conclude.

Today, humans’ lives are not only affected by modern technology, but also entangled with it. As modern society is defined by corporate-dominated markets, large corporations may only gain power over humans. Chapter 4 of 21 Lessons for the 21st Century concerns data, which is presently used by Facebook, Google, and Amazon to procure customers. Technology advances so quickly that humans may not regulate distribution of data before large corporations obtain such data. Deregulation of the market may empower large corporations to withhold data by dominating competitors. Already, gas, internet, and other necessities have been monopolized. Harari cites the “liberal story” as a primary reason for humans’ inevitable imprisoning livelihoods. Full ownership of incomprehensible—yet fundamental—technology by large corporations is certain to dictate societal function.

In his research, Marx uncannily predicts the future. The market is not only a method of obtaining land, but also a necessity for modern society’s functioning. Between McCarthyism, Reaganomics, and general conservatism, many civilians of the global West cannot remove the “free market” from freedom. Advanced technology, which Harari alludes to when reprimanding large corporations, is no less than a part of this functioning. Wherein algorithms outline increasing parts of humans’ lives, large corporations face no difficulty controlling narratives. Harari states that, in the future, algorithms will decide what humans eat, where we buy groceries, and how we commute to work. To predict humans’ every-day decisions, algorithms retain data that they have already collected. Were private companies to access human data, much of which they already do, humans would have no choice but to pay for actions that we currently consider to be second nature. In a technology-dominated future, the top 1 percent of earners may oversee not certain resources, but humans’ entire lives. Neoliberalism has managed to negatively alter human existence, but one aspect of life that it has not affected is technology. Humans already live in generally dire economic conditions, considering numerous recessions that have crashed markets regarding housing, employment, and other goods. Contrarily, there once stood a time at which point working-class citizens had stake in their job benefits. Fortunately, a similar time still remains for technology. Yes, Silicon Valley is composed of privately-owned enterprises. Simultaneously, Apple, Google, and Facebook are unique from State Farm, Food Lion, and CVS Pharmacy. Before humans are unable to determine reality from virtuality, we must reevaluate our economic system. In Harari’s words, “it is unclear what [private ownership of data] actually means”. A government-run system of distribution regarding data may sound unappealing, but so does big business’ control of humans’ lives. It is entirely possible for data-dependent functions to “stagflate” and charge more than that which laborers earn.

2050 may be defined by A.I. doctors and data-generated algorithms. Dissimilarly, 2050 will still include markets, which—if we aren’t careful—may decide limits of human decision regarding technologically composed activity. If A.I. executes future labor, then working-class people might foresee rather nongreen pastures, for even robots must be upkeeped. Even with presence of a safety net, those who operate A.I. find themselves ever-trapped in meaningless pursuits. Likewise, one can assume that large corporations will eventually control human data. If algorithms that humans currently use are updated for buying groceries, dining out, and transportation, then large corporations will be first to decide at which restaurants we eat, what groceries we buy, and how we commute. The future toward which humans are headed is a terrifying one. Technology advances too quickly for modern society to match. If humans refuse to rework the world’s dominant economic system, then we will seal our own fates.
chunks.label: Marxist theory and Harari's technological outlook
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes and compares Karl Marx's theory of estranged labor with Yuval Harari's predictions about artificial intelligence, corporate data ownership, and capitalism.

n550b843d.title: Performing the Self in Social Settings

chunks.text:
George Herbert Mead’s concept of the self is a challenge to itself as according to Mead the self is not inherent to itself and is its own unique set of characteristics and experiences that separate itself from one’s body. The Self vs Body is one of the key aspects of his philosophy as the Self relies on the physical aspect while the latter does not rely on the former. With the body being the propulsion or machine for the self, it is not unlike how the body would be the stage for Erving Goffman’s principles.

One of the most important aspects of the self in Mead’s eye is similar to Cooley’s “looking glass self” where in individuals imagine how others perceive them and adjust their self-concept, accordingly, usually based on the specific group. Though this pails in comparison to his primary point of language or communication, individuals learn to interpret symbols and meanings within their cultural context, contributing to the ongoing development of the self. The fluidity of oneself, according to Mead, arises from the continuous negotiation and reinterpretation of social experiences, shaping our identities and our lifespan. Though the main issues of Mead’s philosophy come in that he hardly provides any notion of how emotions and conflict shape one’s personality rather than focusing on the language and group setting even so his persuasive argument is compelling.

This is all further supported by Erving Goffman's dramaturgical approach which complements Mead's ideas by portraying social life as something akin to a theatrical performance with how we as the actors play roles in settings, people must navigate through life’s many different social situations by portraying aspects of their identity deemed appropriate for the context such as how one would seem studious and observant around a teacher while acting more of oneself and relaxed around close friends at recess. This self-presentation shows how fluid oneself, as individuals actively move to conform to societal expectations while navigating the intricate social stage though, this is not so true in every case as the stage is divided into a fore-and-back where one shows different levels of who they truly are.

One of the faults of Goffman’s view as it does not account for how social media affects one’s performance as people fake their backstage view and spew out a highly curated slop of a front stage with social media not being a truly collective work where people can build and react off one another as they would. Making this an empty husk of oneself.

A Proper example of how these two concepts would work in synchronization in the average day would be this; Imagine being a new employee joining a corporate team. In the initial weeks, they would engage with colleagues and superiors. Through this one would begin to see how others view them and with feedback, this contributes to the self-concept. If their ideas are well-received, and they successfully integrate they may act one way or if it is seen negatively, they will adjust their behavior to fit in more appropriately. While Goffman’s work would be more suited for day-to-day actions this comes up most apparently within meetings as one has to manage to appear professional, choosing what and when to say things. This strategic self-presentation is influenced by the desire to be perceived as competent, cooperative, and aligned with organizational goals. The dynamic nature reflects the fluidity of the self as individuals adapt their self to fit the social concept circle setting.

The combination of Mead and Goffman's perspectives on identity construction shows a comprehensive understanding of the ever-changing social-based nature of the self. The ongoing negotiation of social experiences, as emphasized by Mead, intertwines with Goffman's theatrical metaphor, illustrating the performative aspect of one’s identifiable self within society. Though these two both add they also have many negative spots as they imply that we as people have no identity or self perfectly set in stone, nor do they explain what factors properly affect and cause the growth and change in our identities throughout our life as mentioned earlier with how mead mostly overlooks emotions and conflict within one’s personal life.
chunks.label: Theories of Mead and Goffman on self-presentation
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes and compares George Herbert Mead's concept of the self and Erving Goffman's dramaturgical approach, illustrating their ideas with a hypothetical scenario of a new corporate employee.

chunks.text:
There are many different sociologists and historians who have many different views and ideas. Each sociologist focuses on a different area of study and are working in a different time period, which means that there are many different ways to look at sociological concepts. In addition, as time passes, new problems and ideas arise that lead to new ways to understand sociology and our society today. As a result, different sociologists will have some similar, but also some differing views and explanations for different aspects of sociology. Yuval Noah Harari, for example, will have some similar and different ideas compared to past sociologists such as Émile Durkheim and George Mead.

Yuval Noah Harari is an Israeli historian and philosopher, and the author of the book 21 Lessons for the 21st Century. In this book, he addresses our current global climate and looks at big questions faced by today’s society. He thinks about these pressing questions and then addresses them throughout the book. Many of the topics addressed in his book relate to concepts that have been discussed by sociologists. One of the points that Harari argues in his book is that religion is completely irrelevant to policy and technical problems and should not be used to solve them. The examples that he provides for these problems include ideas such as what measures governments should take and how farmers should deal with droughts. In the past, religion was consistently used to solve these problems because people didn’t have the same knowledge that we have today. Given what we now know with modern science and technology, religion would have no way to help solve these problems, and so it should be left out completely. However, Harari states that religion is relevant for problems surrounding identity, and that it contributes to a big part of the problem rather than the solution. Identity problems include things like what we should care about and how we should feel about certain topics. Harari explains how all religious traditions unite the people who follow and distinguishes them from the other people around them that don’t follow the same religion. Religion is what provides people with a template for how they should live their lives and what they should believe in, which creates one group with the same views. He also explains how some religions encourage more kindness and charitability, while others fill the world with more ugliness and cruelty. He is demonstrating how the unity created through religion can be harmful rather than beneficial.

Émile Durkheim was a French sociologist who studied religion and how it influences our social interactions. Durkheim believed that religion was important to study and understand because he thought that all fundamental categories of thought and science have religious roots. This meant he believed that religion was the backbone for thinking and provided a sort of template for how science and thought were created. He also believed that all great institutions were born in religion. Religion is what helped form our modern institutions and provide them with the foundation to grow into what they are today. In addition, Durkheim believed that religion created a collective representation and consciousness among those who practiced a similar religion. The collective consciousness is the set of common ideas or beliefs held by a certain group. These beliefs that are the same among the whole group act to unify the group. It also works to shape the individual’s perspective on how they should live their life. It guides what someone perceives as meaningful, dangerous, good, or evil. A collective representation is a symbol, artifact, or narrative that articulates and embodies the collective beliefs, sentiments, and values of a certain group. This includes examples such as the idea of giving at Christmas, a cross, or wedding rings. The collective representation is the symbol or identifying factor of the collective consciousness. Durkheim believes that society is then created through the collective conscious. We work together as a group to collectively produce a shared sense of reality and morals. In Durkheim’s mind, religion is a crucial part of how society is created and run.

Harari and Durkheim both argue that religion is an important aspect for uniting people and creating a common belief system. However, their differences are evident in whether they believe this collective consciousness is beneficial or harmful to society. Durkheim believes that having a collective consciousness is important in creating a cohesive society. He argues that it is essential to have similar beliefs and values so that you have a way to relate to those around you. The collective consciousness is what allows us to form our society. He also believed that religion was important in creating our modern institutions and ways of thinking, and that without it, we wouldn’t have modern science or thinking. On the other hand, Harari is arguing that this collective consciousness created from religion often goes too far and creates more problems than solutions. Harari believes that when religion becomes involved, there are strong divisions created between individuals as well as groups. Because religion creates such strong beliefs, it often means that the two opposing groups have even stronger divisions. Each person is expected to act exactly how their religion says they should, and no one should sway from this path. This can lead to problems with the two groups working together or finding ways to keep the peace. When neither group is willing to compromise or hear the other groups perspective, a solution will never be reached. In addition, Harari explains how problems can arise when our identity clumps together beyond our sense of experience.

George Mead was another sociologist who had ideas that related to Harari’s. Mead worked to develop an idea of how the human self arises. He believed that the self is experienced through internal dialogue between the “I” and the “me”. The “I” and the “me” are both cognitive elements of the mind, but they have different influences. The “I” is the subjective reaction of the mind to stimuli in the environment and comes from emotional responses or actions. It is almost like your reflex or instincts in response to some event. The “me” is the objective evaluation of the “I” reactions and comes from what has been learned about the particular social setting. Mead also believed that the self is experienced indirectly but completely, while the body is experienced directly but incompletely. When we put these factors together, we have a full, conscious experience of our self. We are reacting to our environment and then evaluating that reaction. Mead believed that this conscious experience was important for humans to understand. It is important that we are fully aware of our “self” and the different pieces that influence our self.

In addition to the role of religion in society, another issue Harari addresses in his book 21 Lessons for the 21st Century is the dangers of algorithms and technology in our society. He argues that technology will eventually take over jobs that are currently occupied by humans. Eventually, machines and technology will be able to complete almost all of the jobs that humans are responsible for. This means that many people will be out of jobs and will have to train for new, higher-level jobs that technology will not yet be capable of completing. Another major problem that arises through the development of technology is that it will eventually be able to know you better than you know yourself. Once technology understands us better than we understand ourselves, it will be able to monitor and manipulate our feelings. One example Harari provides for this is how companies will be able to use data and technology to target ads specifically towards you. Your preferences will be used to target ads to you in order to help the companies make the maximum profit. Technology takes away our conscious experiences, and simply replaces it with artificial intelligence. Harari stresses that there is a difference between consciousness and intelligence, and it is important that we continue to have conscious experiences.

Both Mead and Harari have a similar view in how it is important to have an overall conscious experience. Mead believed that it was important to have a conscious experience of the self through the “I” and the “me”. He argued that in order to fully experience something, all of the different aspects of your “self” had to interact and work together. Understanding the different influences on your overall experience is crucial in having a conscious experience. Similarly, Harari argues how it is important to maintain a conscious experience rather than simply relying on artificial intelligence. Technology can take over our lives and know us better than we know ourselves, but it cannot create a conscious experience. Technology simply has intelligence while humans are the only ones capable of having a true conscious experience. Therefore, Harari is stressing the importance of preventing technology from taking over every aspect of our lives. Consciousness is too important to humans to let technology take it over.

There are many concepts in sociology that remain consistent over time, while others seem to change. As our society grows and develops, new problems will arise that will lead to new concepts and understandings to be created. This means that while some sociologists and historians will have similar views, there will be times when they disagree or have ideas that are inconsistent with one another. However, this does not mean that one view is necessarily better than another. Each sociologist can develop an idea that is completely correct, and that doesn’t automatically discredit another person’s idea. We must take into account all concepts and viewpoints when thinking about sociological concepts.
chunks.label: Comparing Harari to Durkheim and Mead
chunks.what_happened: The student compares the sociological and philosophical views of Yuval Noah Harari with Émile Durkheim and George Mead regarding religion, consciousness, and technology.

nf5aed9dd.title: Confronting Hegemonic Masculinity at Frat Parties

chunks.text:
What does it mean to be a woman in America, or what does it mean to be a member of the LGBT community? To put it another way, what does it mean to be considered unequal to the ordinary male? In America, gender roles and stereotypes are often founded on taught actions and conditions that are used to give one another authority. Despite the fact that American ideals are built on a patriarchal controlling position of men, it causes men to be more prejudiced against particular groups of people, displaying hegemonic masculinity. Hegemonic masculinity is clinging to life in a way that feminine and heteronormative values aren't. Many people, on the other hand, see a common ground between homosexuality and femininity, putting persons who fall into any of these categories in a major inherent deficiency.

Women, like others who belong to various sexually oriented groups, are more likely to be considered as permanent outsiders. For a variety of reasons, gay men constitute a special risk to hegemonic masculinity. To compensate for their lack of masculinity, gay men frequently surround themselves with a female presence in mitigate negative opinions toward their sexuality. They represent a threat to the average male by demonstrating their dominance over women. Men are "protective othering" in response to a threat to hegemonic masculinity. Men care to remove themselves from anything that devalues their own identity and collective consciousness.
chunks.label: Gender, sexuality, and hegemonic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological concepts of gender roles, hegemonic masculinity, and protective othering regarding women and gay men.

chunks.text:
In my own personal experience, I had overheard constant discussions and a noticeable obsession with "fraternities and frat parties" when I arrived at UNCW for my first year. Of course, any female going to college is thrilled to meet a massive amount of people and to put the high school boy image everyone all had in their heads to the test. I was drawn to the problem of hypermasculinity in fraternities as an exaggerated organization of men. As a woman who demonstrates many loving and sensitive traits it would be an interesting mix. So, when I attended to my first frat party with my new college mates, it commenced right away.

After dollishly getting ready for hours to impress a group of strangers we had never met, my friends and I ordered an Uber. When we arrived, there were five older college boys in front of the house, seated on filthy lawn chairs. All five of them stood up as we approached in a group of four. That was the first thing that caught my eye; they were exerting their control, and it reminded me of castle guards. They assessed our "beauty" by looking at all of us up and down, then turned around and talked for a few seconds. My friends and I stood there, uneasy but curiously anxiously anticipating these boys' approval. One of the boys asked for my friend's phone number and asked if she wanted a drink, but she refused, and the boy gave her an odd and disturbed expression. With an irritated tone, he welcomed everyone except her to the event. We certainly couldn't go without her, so we left the party. "Don't ever come back," one of the boys said as we walked away.
chunks.label: Turned away from first frat party
chunks.what_happened: The student and three female friends went to their first college frat party, where fraternity boys evaluated their appearance; after one friend rejected a boy's request for her number and drink offer, he excluded her and told the group never to come back as they all left together.
chunks.feelings: thrilled, drawn, uneasy, curiously anxiously anticipating
chunks.people: college mates/friends, five older college boys

chunks.text: This particular incident reminded me strongly of Simone de Beauvoir's Woman as Other. These males had no regard for us because their parties were exclusively female.
