They needed us more than we needed them, in order to establish a position of condescending service. They encouraged us to have a great time, but they really wanted us to be grateful for their approval, and in doing so, they conceptualized women's subordination in this brief encounter. Furthermore, in that situation, our bodies were the only thing that defined us. Because we individualized ourselves in a position of power by saying no, we were perceived as an inconvenience. We were portrayed as the Other because he was the Subject, the Absolute. We were firm and distinctive, and then we were viewed as inessential since men are viewed as virtues, while we, as women, were merely seen as pillars in their party fantasies.
chunks.label: Analysis of party using Beauvoir's theory
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the party incident through Simone de Beauvoir's 'Woman as Other,' analyzing how the fraternity men attempted to subordinate and objectify women.

chunks.text:
Of course, I'd been to a lot of other parties like this, and when I stepped inside, I saw a lot of girls standing around waiting for men's approval to have a nice time. The next example, which demonstrated hegemonic masculinity's anti-homosexual bias, touched near to home. In a similar situation, one of my best friends at UNCW who is gay asked if he could join us for a frat party one night. We made the decision to give it a shot. All boys are welcome to attend these gatherings only one week out of the year, at the start of the semester, even if they are not members of a fraternity.

We reasoned that our friend would enjoy himself and would be able to spend time with us girls. When 7 of my friends and I arrived, including my gay friend, we approached the boys, and a similar, but even more heated situation ensued. The boys rose up and looked about, wondering, "What is this?" referring to my friend, who was dressed in girl shorts and a cropped t-shirt. My friend, who was too shocked to speak, simply let it go. As we began to walk in, some of the boys began to come at us, forcing my friend away. He informed us that individuals like him are not allowed to attend these events. We asked several questions and tried to come up with a solution.

People like him, the boys continued, pull the females away from the very premise of the gathering. In this instance, their self-assurance and aggressiveness told us that any conventional values they held could not be shattered by someone who did not fit the stereotype. We were also thrown out of this fraternity as a result of this.
chunks.label: Gay friend rejected from frat party
chunks.what_happened: The student attended a fraternity party with seven friends, including a gay male friend; the fraternity members questioned the friend's outfit, aggressively forced him away, stated people like him were not allowed, and threw the whole group out.
chunks.people: best friend who is gay, seven friends, fraternity boys

chunks.text:
As discussed in the paper "Doing Gender," many of the social expectations of "sex" related to this circumstance in a perplexing way. Our biological differences, which in this case were purely physical, identify our sex. If there are 100 straight boys and one gay boy, they should be treated equally. However, homosexuals do not seem to behave in the same way or have the same societal standards that heterosexual boys appear to perceive as acceptable to their institutions in the area of behaving as expected.

College boys, in my opinion, are predicated on hegemonic masculinity. In a weak position, this concept might be seen as a marginalized version of what it is to be a man from a social standpoint. The fact that this idea is articulated for a single gender of male demonstrates how Zimmerman and West revere "Doing Gender." Hegemonic masculinity is a historical idea, and how we shape gender shapes social structures in the same way that the scenarios I discussed previously in this paper do. It is hypothesized in this essay that I fell into the trap of promoting toxic masculinity. I was willing to participate in activities that are well-known for demonstrating my own oppression and surface-level prejudice towards my gender, as well as others I care about who didn't fit into the stereotype of this concept. When hegemonic masculinity is clearly produced, males are complicit in the physical rewards of women's subordination through a fantasy of a place and time in which they have authority. What women want is dependent on what men can supply, and men's acceptance and enjoyment of having a system of servitude is what keeps them on the margins.

To conclude, the argument provided in this study discusses what Brett Strout observed in his work "In or Out" for the reproduction of toxic masculinity. Similarly, males who exhibit the characteristic are able to shame others in order to express their compliance and avoid engaging in "feminine" activities in public. As one of my examples and personal stories reveals, certain masculinities in this culture "find masculine femininity in homosexuality and then use it to discipline masculinity"(Stoudt, 2006). Even if it's in jest, from Stoudt’s article, a man who calls someone a "faggot" or refers to someone as "gay" conveys that he isn't, establishing his innate privileged masculinity by subduing and ostracizing another's masculine identity. It can be frowned upon and against the norm to be gay. After witnessing how effortlessly misogynistic or homophobic remarks elicit embarrassment and avoidance, I know can look at oppressive situations of homophobic and anti-feministic as something I do not want to contribute to; not giving men the ego they want so badly.
chunks.label: Reflection on toxic masculinity and readings
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes the experiences using sociological texts ('Doing Gender' and Brett Stoudt's work), reflecting on toxic masculinity, homophobia, and their own past participation in these spaces.

chunks.text:
I wish I were Heather. In the beginning of 2020, I heard this lyric countless times. I would scroll for hours on end on TikTok, watching girls compare themselves to celebrities, influencers, models – any woman who they believed to be perfect; any woman they deemed a Heather. This was a trend that had taken off on TikTok rather quickly. Given that this was the beginning of quarantine, teenagers spent much of their time online to make up for the lack of social interaction. In doing so, women began to closely follow the lives of beautiful and famous models and celebrities, which bred comparison. Young girls found comfort in each other, creating an environment where they could speak freely about their insecurities and self-image issues with no fear of judgement. This trend allowed women to display their despair about feeling inferior to other woman, feeling as though they weren’t, and could never be as beautiful, as skinny, as tan, as popular as these women; that I could never be Heather.

After watching so many of these videos, I began to feel the same way: How could anyone ever think I’m beautiful, when there are women who look like that?! Although there were many different women who were deemed Heathers, all of them had an indescribable quality. Everything about them was beautiful – and everything they had was something I felt I lacked in myself. When looking at these girls, I couldn’t help but envy them. The beauty standard for women is regarded as completely unattainable, but somehow, they were able to perfectly embody it.

Not only were these women beautiful, but they were popular, rich, and famous – more things I could never be. Although I knew some of them spent thousands of dollars on plastic surgery and continued to pay for injections, that didn’t affect how I felt. I still wanted to be them. I still wanted to be free from insecurity and the thought that I could never be worthy of anything.

I continued to watch the videos, and after some time, I noticed something. The women who originally posted these videos were Heathers. They were the women that others were scrupulously comparing themselves to. As I continued to watch these videos and notice this pattern, I began to feel differently. Being Heather wouldn’t keep me from feeling insecure or stop me from comparing myself to other women. Women that I felt were the beauty standard still felt the same insecurity that I did, and still found women who they deemed to be perfect.

In reading comments, I found that many other women had reached the same conclusion. So many girls felt that they were so below what was considered perfect, when others found them to surpass that.
chunks.label: Watching TikTok trends and feeling insecure
chunks.what_happened: During quarantine in 2020, the student scrolled TikTok watching girls compare themselves to ideal women deemed 'Heather.' Over time, watching these videos and reading comments made the student realize that even women considered ideal felt insecure.
chunks.feelings: despair, inferior, envy, insecure, lacking, unworthy
chunks.people: girls on TikTok, celebrities, influencers, models

chunks.text:
Naomi Wolf explains the reason why women think this way about themselves. Wolf describes women being judged based off their appearance as the beauty myth. The beauty myth is defined as, “An obsession with physical perfection that traps the modern woman in an endless spiral of hope, self-consciousness and self-hatred as she tries to fulfill society’s impossible definition of the flawless beauty.” This concept is a violent backlash against feminism because it uses images of female beauty as a political weapon against women’s advancement. Wolf argued that the beauty myth affected women in multiple categories such as work, religion, sex, violence, and hunger. This myth established by the mind of men has carried its way into the mind of women immensely which has caused a mass amount of competition between women. Due to the competition women face with one another, because of a man’s idea of a perfect woman, has prohibited the ability for women to create a community. Men have been able to hold onto their power over women because of this. Women must learn and start to oppose of the beauty myth and see their worth through more than just their looks.

Every woman wants to be Heather because that’s what men have deemed as perfect. The unrealistic beauty standard that women try to achieve doesn’t necessarily reflect their own personal beliefs, rather, the ideal woman that men have defined. While men are not the ones who are the targets of the standard of beauty for women, they still are the primary influence for what it is.

Why do women stare at celebrities every day idolizing their looks? Why do women constantly compare themselves to unrealistic standards of beauty? Why do I want to be anyone but myself? The beauty myth, created by the minds of men, has taken over the way women perceive their worth. The beauty myth has convinced a lot of women that they need to be flawless or else they aren’t worthy of love, or respect.
chunks.label: Naomi Wolf and the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Naomi Wolf's concept of the beauty myth and explains how male-defined standards create competition among women and harm women's self-worth.

chunks.text: Many women have begun to believe that when they get cheated on, it’s because they weren’t pretty enough, or they just weren’t enough in general for their boyfriend at the time. This was a sentiment I shared. I believed that I got cheated on because I wasn’t pretty enough for him. But now, I realize I can’t blame myself or my looks for the wrongdoing of a man. I recognized that I blamed my looks because the beauty myth created by men was engraved into my mind regarding my self-worth. The beauty myth explains why I’m sometimes unaware of what I deserve because I’m so wrapped around the idea that I wasn’t perfect enough for him; that he cheated on me because the other girl was much prettier, and I should’ve done better.
chunks.label: Blaming looks after being cheated on
chunks.what_happened: The student experienced being cheated on by a boyfriend and believed it happened because they were not pretty enough compared to the other woman.
chunks.feelings: unaware of what I deserve, feeling not pretty or perfect enough

chunks.text:
The beauty myth has rerouted the minds of women into thinking that they are the problem. That they weren’t pretty enough for their boyfriend to remain loyal to them. Wolf states, “It is no accident that so many potentially powerful women feel this way.” The beauty myth impacts so much of a women’s own worth and respect. Women need to come together to take down the power men hold over their self-worth. They need to break the unrealistic cycle of beauty created by men that has gone on for countless years.

Women put so much pressure on themselves to seek out perfection due to the beauty standard created by men in society. I see this everywhere on social media and specifically through “the Heather” trend on TikTok. Beautiful women and girls comparing themselves to other beautiful women. Beautiful women blaming themselves for the disloyalty of a man. Beautiful women suppressing their worth because of their looks. The beauty myth has disrupted the raw understanding of the world, that everyone deserves the best in life no matter who you are or what you look like. Women must come together to fight the unrealistic standards created by men and men must stop putting so much pressure on women to fit such unrealistic standards of beauty. Women must learn to believe that they are deserving of everything and anything no matter their looks. There shouldn’t continue to be a beauty standard through the eyes of men, there should be a beauty standard created by a woman for that woman and no one else. Every woman is Heather, and every woman should fight to break the unrealistic beauty standard and take their power back.
chunks.label: Calling for women to reject beauty standards
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how the beauty myth harms women's relationships and self-worth, arguing that women must unite to dismantle male-created beauty standards.

nc649e667.title: Comparing Views on Religion and Society

chunks.text:
Emile Durkheim and Yuval Harari both talked about religion and its role in society. Some of their ideas lined up but others were contradictory. Durkheim believed that everything circled back to religion, that fundamental categories of thought and science had religious roots and all great social institutions were born from religion. Harari believed religion brought people together but had no role in government or political decisions. Harari thought that different societies with different ideas created conflict and made it harder to come to solutions. I will be focusing on the similarities and differences between their thoughts in order to fully understand how religion and society are connected.

First, Durkheim wrote about the cultural logic of collective representation, in which he talks about how social institutions, thoughts, and sciences all come from religion. The collective consciousness is a collection of beliefs, ideas, and sentiments shared by the community. Those thoughts and ideas shape collective representation, which is defined as a symbol, artifact, or narrative that embodies the collective beliefs of a specific group. An example of collective representation could be the American flag, it represents all the values that our country was formed on. There is a shared sense of reality, morality, and identity based on common or shared experiences. He also stated that the collective shapes the individual’s perspective on how life should be lived. Durkheim believed that religion brings the community together through a shared belief and in turn, furnishes us with both stability and truth. This truth and stability give access for social institutions to be formed through the collective consciousness and religion. These social institutions could be the government, politics, education, healthcare, and so many more things.

Furthermore, When talking about the role religion plays in society Harari says we need to focus on three main societal problems: technical, economic, and identity. Religion used to be helpful in solving technical problems in areas like agriculture, as they would use divine calendars to decide when to plant and when to harvest. Temple rituals also helped by securing rainfall to prevent pests, and when there was an agricultural crisis, farmers would turn to priests who talked to the gods. Religion is no longer a solution to technical problems because even those who are religious know that scientists have better answers for agricultural and medicine evolution. Harari states that the whole world is a single civilization because when one thing works everyone just uses that method. Religion cannot be used to solve policy issues because your religious status does not always line up with your political views. Even though one might use the bible or Quran to defend their position on a subject, the real source comes from scientific theories and political movements. An example of this is in cars, as evangelical’s may drive gas-powered cars, while Catholics will drive electric cars. They might claim it's because of their beliefs, but the decision is really rooted in their scientific beliefs to save the earth. The one issue religion has an impact on is identity issues. Harari believes that religion is made up of a series of false truths or myths but he says that our identities are made from fictional stories rather than science or economics. We learned that trying to scientifically assign identities is dangerous after Nazis and communists attempted to. Since those events, scientists have decided not to give out natural identities to people. Harari says that the one thing religion does is tells us who we are, some religious traditions fill the earth with joy and love, while others fill the earth with anger and ugliness. Even though Harari does not think religion is real, he does believe it brings people together.

However, It is important to know exactly what religion is and how it functions. Religion is defined as the belief in or worship of a higher power, usually a god or multiple gods. This higher power gives life a new meaning to people, it gives morals and values so people know how they should live their lives. We learn from Durkheim that religion shapes the individual, without a higher power to rely on it could be harder to make your own values for your life. Religion also helps people through hard times, it gives people a reason to why things happen and answers some existential questions no one really has the answers to. Of course, many people also don’t have a religion they find self and form morals in other things, which also works as it is all based off of personal preference, which leads us into the similarities and differences between Durkheim and Harari.

Harari and Durkheim both believe one thing, that religion brings people together through shared beliefs, values, and morals. Durkheim said that religion has three major functions in society, as one of those is to provide social cohesion to help maintain social solidarity through shared rituals and beliefs. Harari said that people are brought together through religious myths and fallacies. These two ideas, although stated very differently mean the same thing. In pre-modern eras society needed religion but in todays world a society can still thrive without religion. If religion did not exist there would be less discrimination, which would possibly cause less wars and maybe less deaths. There could also be complete anarchy though with no morals or beliefs, if people aren’t held up to a moral standard then they would pay no mind to how their actions affect other people.

Both Durkheim and Harari would also argue that religion gives people a purpose in life. Many people need a purpose to believe that doing anything is really worth it and religion gives that to them. Harari does not explicitly state that religion gives purpose, but he implies that it gives meaning to people's lives, he believes it is a false meaning, but it's one, nonetheless. Durkheim talks about how the collective consciousness and collective representation, which are rooted by religion, give meaning to people’s life. An example of this is Christianity, from my personal experience in church, the bible says that God will love you no matter what. Even though he has eternal love for all his children they still strive to not disappoint him and devote their lives to following his word. There is also the belief that God has a plan for all of us and that gives Christians a sense of hope that even when they are lost and confused and do not have a foreseeable plan for where their life is heading, they can trust that God has one and they do have a purpose on this Earth.

The difference between Durkheim and Harari’s beliefs lies in if religion should play a role in government, politics, and policy making. When Durkheim talks about the collective consciousness, he says that religion forms great social institutions, two of those institutions being government and politics. Unlike Harari, Durkheim believes religion is real and is an expression of society as a whole. The second function he gave of religion in his reading was that it provides social control to enforce religious-based morals to help maintain conformity and control in society. Since he believes that religion brings control he believes that policy and government decisions should be made with the thought of religion in mind. According to Durkheim, the collective consciousness makes the self, therefore, the self gives the power to make meaningful decisions. That being said those in the power to make decisions and determine policies should stick with their religious morals. On the other hand, Harari thinks religion is fake and all it creates differing viewpoints that make it harder to come to a decision. He believes that religion is based on emotions and myths and policy making should be based on science-based theories. He states that religion and nationalism divide our nation into hostile parts when it comes to making decisions, which defeats the original purpose to bring people together. As I mentioned earlier according to Harari, technical and economic problems can’t possibly be solved by religion so there is no way policies that decide how people live their lives should be taken with religion into account.

Another main difference between Durkheim and Harari’s beliefs is two important words, reason and excuse. Durkheim tells us that religion helps create the self because we find a reason as to why things happen and why we are on this Earth. His last function of religion that he mentioned was that it offers meaning and purpose to answer many existential questions. Without this meaning we could lose ourselves, whether that’s our self-worth or our drive to be successful, you could completely forget who you are. Humans try to get answers to questions they don’t know, especially questions like, ‘what happens after we die?’ Religion answers some of these questions to give stability in individual lives, and in-turn, stability in societies. Harari mentions multiple times that religion is an excuse, it’s a made-up reason for questions we can’t answer. Since Harari does not think religion is real he believes it is an excuse to cope with the fact that we can’t answer all the questions. An example of this was when he mentioned pre-modern times when agriculture was solved through religion, it was not real but they needed some form of solution so the farmers went to the one thing they knew would give them an answer, their religion, and their gods. Harari still believes that religion gives a purpose, but he uses the word excuse because that purpose is based off of myths according to him.

Durkheim and Harari have many similarities and differences regarding religion. Both of them believe that religion brings society together through beliefs, morals, and values. They also both believe that religion gives people a purpose in life. In contrast, Durkheim believes that religion should have a role in policy making, while Harari believes that religion should be completely left out of decision making. The other difference is that Durkheim believes religion is a reason, meanwhile Harari believes religion is an excuse. This shows us that even though there are so many different religions out there and so many different beliefs, we know for sure that religion has the power to bring people together for better or for worse, and that our society revolves around the aspect of religion.
chunks.label: Comparing Durkheim and Harari on religion
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes and compares the sociological perspectives of Emile Durkheim and Yuval Harari regarding the role and function of religion in society.

n30388bfa.title: Social Media and the Beauty Myth

chunks.text:
Social media has easily taken over the minds of many as it has become more accessible and easier to use. Since social media is open for anyone, people can post whatever they want and can post as much as they want. There are no guidelines for what people are allowed to post which creates a free-for-all environment. This being said, social media can create a toxic environment as people tend to flash their perfect lives which leads others to believe a false persona. These face-tuned pictures make viewers feel bad about their bodies, and they become envious of these strangers because they have what seems to be a perfect body. Women tend to only post pictures where they look beautiful in the eyes of today’s standards so they can be praised and feel like they too fit the “perfect body type.” The most recent issue that social media has harmed is women’s body image. People are seeing pictures of half-naked women who have the “perfect body” and the comment sections are flooded with questions about how to get that figure, praises of how perfect their life looks, and comments about how jealous people are of them. Today women are pressured to look a certain way because all they see on social media are pictures of skinny women who have the “perfect body.” Throughout this paper, I will discuss how social media is negatively affecting women’s body images and introducing widespread insecurities and set back in women’s progression for feminisms.

During the semester we talked about Naomi Wolf and the Beauty Myth which discussed how images of beauty are used against women. The literature emphasizes how women’s appearance makes women inferior to men in society and how women are held to an unreasonably high beauty standard. This beauty standard has harmed women and how they perceive themselves as comments are made about how they should look and dress in public. Wolf says that women are held to these standards because women are held too old, devaluing traits like being known as a household helper, or a mother. Social media has contributed to the idea of women needing to look a certain way and this affects women’s thoughts about their bodies and how they see themselves.

Social media is so powerful because there is so much distance between the viewer and the poster. This distance allows for many messages to be misinterpreted as the interaction is solely online. People also believe that because they are behind a screen, they can post anything they want. The people who post on these platforms don’t see how their content affects their viewers which gives them the power to keep posting what they want. If the people who post don’t know they are hurting anyone then why would they stop posting?

Another factor that makes mass media a culprit of women’s body issues is the interactivity involved in it (Perloff 2014). Anyone is allowed to interact with the post and leave a comment saying whatever they please. Words on a screen aren’t always perceived how the writer intended them to sound which is where many people tend to get hurt. Social media is also an “immensely more personal outlet than conventional impersonal mass media” (Perloff, 2014). People can relate posts to their life and take the words said more personally. This opens the door for self-comparison and the creation of body insecurities. Social media platforms are also open for viewing and posting 24/7, which gives women the opportunity to constantly compare their bodies to others and feel discomfort in their own skin (Perloff, 2014).

According to Hogue’s and Mills’ study (2019), when people interact with “attractive peers’ appearance-based social media” posts they are more likely to have a worsened self-body image. Interaction is a key part of this because it shows that people are actively trying to compare themselves to the person in the post. Many people interact when they come across body image posts because they want to know how a person looks a certain way so they can try to achieve that ideal body too. This comparison is detrimental to one’s health because it brings feelings of self-doubt and inadequacy. The downside of social media is the secrecy behind it. Certain posts could be photoshopped and touched up in a million different ways to make the women look “beautiful,” but the viewer would never know. Without this knowledge, the viewer will feel insecure and have a poor mindset about how she looks.

In “The Beauty Myth” Wolf talks about “beauty pornography” which links commodified beauty to sexuality. Wolf (1991) claims that this concept has entered into mainstream media and is undermining “women’s new and vulnerable sense of sexual self-worth.” According to Peter and Valkenburg (2017), sexual content in the media has grown bigger in the most recent decades which means more people are being exposed to these unrealistic beauty standards. Social media is the perfect platform for people to post their bodies and show off their figures for anyone to see. However, more women are photoshopping and altering their pictures to fit social media’s beauty standards. This is what is creating the commodified beauty that Wolf is talking about. Some social media posts promote eating disorders and “invasive, potentially deadly "cosmetic" surgeries” that will help women get the perfect body (Wolf, 1991). Without knowing it our society is connecting manufactured beauty with sexuality and body image disorders. These sexual posts create negative body image thoughts in women’s heads because all they see in the media are skinny perfect women. Additionally, when women view such posts, they think that this is the way all women look, yet this is quite incorrect. Women tend to collectively think that they are larger than all the other women around them, but this is far from true. All women, if not most, feel the same insecurities about wanting to change their body, no matter their weight. Unfortunately, all women are in the same boat about wanting to change to fit into the media's beauty standards. Even the skinny models that are being highlighted by the media feel pressure to be skinnier so they can still fit into the beauty standard. If all women feel the same about wanting to look appealing in the eyes of the media, then all women should understand that everyone is different, and everyone should be able to be comfortable in their own skin.

Social media has also started to objectify women, reducing their importance to their “sexual appeal in terms of their outer appearance” (Peter & Valkenburg, 2017). Our society has also put women’s sexual activities as the most important criteria for their attractiveness and has made women out to be “sexual playthings waiting to please men’s sexual desires” (Peter & Valkenburg, 2017). Most media content today displays women’s bodies in a way where certain body parts are emphasized which sends an underlying message. Social media tends to define women by their looks and advertising that women’s bodies should look a certain way so that males find them attractive. Wolf (1991) notes that we are using “images of female beauty as a political weapon against women’s advancement.” By putting out the idea that women’s bodies need to look a certain way so that other people, especially men, will find them attractive makes people feel insecure about their looks. Women are even pushing this notion on to other women as they post sexualized pictures of their skinny, perfect bodies on social media. Wolf (1991) believes that we are halting our progression of feminism by letting this beauty myth “poison our freedom” and letting women believe that they need to look a certain way to be appealing to others.

In a study done by Grabe et al. (2008) it was said that body dissatisfaction has risen as a “core aspect of women’s physical and mental health.” This study also points to the media as the culprit of body insecurities as it shoves images of thinness onto our society. The images of women that are being shown in today’s media are thinner than in the past, thinner than the actual female population, and thinner than the criteria needed for anorexia (Grabe et al., 2008). This is creating an unattainable goal that is starting to become fanaticized. This study also discovered that media exposure is linked to decreased levels of body satisfaction in women. Moreover, it was concluded that exposure to the thin body type has become more present in the 2000s than it was in the 1990s (Grabe et al., 2008). Social media is a predominant factor in this claim as it allows for the fast-paced spread of ideas and creates a toxic environment. Even Wolf (1991) states that women would “rather lose ten to fifteen pounds than achieve any other goal.” Women nowadays have more power, money, and legal status than they have ever had in the past, yet they physically feel worse about themselves now than any woman before them has ever felt (Wolf, 1991). It’s unfortunate to hear that women have come so far in their struggle for gaining rights and respect just to be brought back down because of the way their bodies look.

Social media has evolved into a toxic environment that pushes unattainable and unrealistic body images on women today. Naomi Wolf’s literature perfectly complements the ideas of the negative impacts that social media has on women’s body satisfaction. Wolf believes that women’s beauty is being used as a weapon against them and their progression in feminism is being halted as women are again being reduced to their bodies. Women have come so far in their fight for equality and now their main roadblock is their own bodies. Female beauty is a weapon that is being used against all women and the worst part is, is that women are doing this to other women (Wolf, 1991). Social media enables this by allowing anyone to post whatever content they want for all to see. The lack of connection between the poster and the viewer brings upon miscommunication and secrets which creates an untruthful and negative environment. This is vital because social media is distorting how people look which creates confusion among the female community. Women have started to post more about their bodies and the images of women being shown by the media are more sexualized and show off the thin perfect body type. People are becoming envious of other body types and are developing insecurities and dissatisfactions with the ways they look. Today’s notions of beauty are getting out of hand and leading women to go to extreme measures just to fit into today’s beauty standard. Social media is evidently the leading factor in women’s insecurities as it is using women’s beauty as a weapon against women as a whole and is setting back feminism progression.
chunks.label: Social media's negative impact on women's body image
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological research, Naomi Wolf's 'The Beauty Myth', and various studies to explain how social media promotes unrealistic beauty standards, objectification, and body dissatisfaction among women.

n28d1de7e.title: Facing Gender Bias as a Lifeguard

chunks.text:
Are men and women truly equal in America? Although it may appear so when considering the country’s laws, the social power structure and culture that exists gives men a big advantage over women. In essentially every profession in America, women make less money than men. Despite women being far more likely to have a higher educational degree than their male counterparts, women on average make 80 cents to each dollar paid to men. There are many initiatives and state-level policies that are trying to combat this problem, but the root of it lies in the societal view of women and how their value is determined. In western society, women’s value is generally based more off their appearances than their achievements. They are expected to fit into a mold based off stereotypes perpetuated by men.

Since women are often judged based on their appearance, they are subjected to stereotypical beauty standards created by men. To gain back their power, women must oppose the beauty myth and use their traits that are considered ‘weak’ to overcome the male-enforced stereotypes.
chunks.label: Gender inequality and the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on gender inequality, wage disparities, and how societal beauty standards are used to suppress women.

chunks.text: I am a lifeguard at a pool, and I have been told that I look weak, so people often assume that I am not very good at my job. Despite what people say, I believe that I am competent, and I believe that I determine my own worth. To give some background, there are two managers at my work, Megan, and Marco. I have also been working there for multiple years. When Megan is managing, she just asks me to do various jobs around the pool because she knows that I can handle it. She even had me teach the new lifeguards how to vacuum at the beginning of last summer. However, I started noticing that whenever Marco was working, he favored the boys. He would always make comments about the girls’ capabilities. We have to carry stacks of chairs across the pool deck every Thursday, so he used to get upset when only girls were scheduled for that shift, saying things such as, “I wish the guys were here” or “We would have had this done in 10 minutes if there were no girls working”.
chunks.label: Lifeguard work dynamic under two managers
chunks.what_happened: The student describes working as a lifeguard under two different managers, Megan and Marco, noting Marco's consistent favoritism toward male guards and remarks demeaning female guards' capabilities.
chunks.people: the student, Megan, Marco, male lifeguards, female lifeguards

chunks.text: One day when I was working, Marco asked me to finish vacuuming the pool. I vacuumed the whole pool, then one of my guy friends who was also working came over. He said that Marco told him to come help me take out the vacuum because he did not think that I could do it myself. My friend tried to convince him that I was capable enough to take it out, but he still thought that I needed the help. Later, my friend told me that our manager was making jokes about me to the other guards and saying that I was probably too dumb to understand them. Not only was he questioning my physical capabilities, but he was also degrading my intellect. Now that I think back on the summer, it was not an isolated event. Every time that Marco asked me to sweep under the pavilion, he would come with me and watch me to make sure I was doing it right. He would even take the broom and dustpan out of my hands and show me what he thought was the ‘right’ way to sweep. Another girl that I work with tried to defend my abilities to Marco, but she took it too far and ended up calling him a “cunt”. Our boss is also a white male, so he trusts Marco’s opinion over everyone else. Knowing this, he used it to his advantage and threatened to get my friend fired. Since then, everyone else has been scared to defend themselves or their friends to him.
chunks.label: Marco's micro-management and threats
chunks.what_happened: Marco questioned the student's physical ability and intelligence while she was vacuuming and sweeping, and later threatened to fire a female coworker who defended the student.
chunks.people: the student, Marco, guy friend, another female coworker, boss

chunks.text: In an attempt to resolve our problems with Marco, my friends and I talked to the other manager, Megan, one day about how he was making us feel. We told her that he would belittle us in front of the other lifeguards and make sexist remarks. My friend even confided in her about how he tried to have her fired for standing up to him. Megan, having never experienced this side of him or heard about what was happening, was very surprised. She told us that our descriptions do not fit into her experiences with him and that we should not let what he says get in our heads. While it may seem like she was trying to silence our experiences, she was just protecting herself. Since she was offered the position as manager, no one on the board has shown her any respect, and they do not think that she is competent enough to run the pool without help. So, the culture of men having power over women is perpetuated throughout the whole chain of command at the pool.
chunks.label: Reporting Marco's behavior to Megan
chunks.what_happened: The student and her friends talked to Megan about Marco's sexist remarks and threats, but Megan was surprised and advised them not to let it get to them.

chunks.text:
Naomi Wolf explains why women are judged based on their appearance as the beauty myth, “a social construct that uses images of female beauty as a political weapon to combat female advancement” (Wolf 1). The idea that a woman’s identity must be based on their beauty puts women in a competition with each other, so they are unable to form a community. The only way for women to gain more power is for them to realize that they are being suppressed, come together for a common cause, and stand up against the male-enforced beauty standard. However, it is not possible if women are constantly in competition. This structure keeps men in power and creates a specific beauty standard that is controlled by them. Although women often play into this standard, the beauty myth is a product of men’s institutions and the power they hold, not what women believe.

The idea that men are expected to be strong and not show emotions is at the root of the concept of hegemonic masculinity. Hegemonic masculinity is when a man portrays stereotypical masculine traits that fit into the cultural norms. For example, men are expected to be strong, be the ‘bread-winner’ for their family and take care of women. These are all stereotypes that people often associate with males, especially ‘many men’. When society validates these beliefs, then it gives men a more dominant social role, and further suppresses women. This form of masculinity is often portrayed in the media as the ideal traits of a man. The setting that we were raised in also affects how we participate in these misconceptions. Someone who grew up in a homogenous environment, or one that lacks diversity and encourages one specific set of beliefs, would be more attune to certain stereotypes because they were never exposed to opposing ideas. If a male was raised in an environment where he was surrounded by other rich, white men and was exposed to media that also enforces the same rhetoric, then he would be much more inclined to believe it.
chunks.label: The beauty myth and hegemonic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Naomi Wolf's concept of the beauty myth, hegemonic masculinity, and how homogenous environments reinforce these gendered stereotypes.

chunks.text: I often feel like I play into the stereotypes that go along with the beauty myth because my physical appearance is consistent with the conventional beauty standard in America. Therefore, people often make assumptions that I am not smart or that I am not strong enough to do my job. My manager used this beauty myth to justify his opinion that I need help completing tasks that require physical strength or other skills. When my manager made a male lifeguard help me with vacuuming, a physical task that I had done countless times before, his thinking coincided with hegemonic masculinity. He believed that a woman was supposed to be weak and need a big, stronger man to help her. He also Along with this, Marco judged my intellect based on my appearance, so he thought that I was too dumb to know how to sweep. If he did not buy into the beauty myth, then he would have a similar mindset to Megan, so he would just give me tasks to do without supervision.
chunks.label: Applying sociological concepts to lifeguard experiences
chunks.what_happened: The student connects her own physical appearance and experiences with Marco's behavior to the concepts of the beauty myth and hegemonic masculinity.
chunks.people: the student, manager (Marco), male lifeguard, Megan

chunks.text: The environment at my pool is an example of a homogeneous environment. The community is almost entirely made up of white families, and most of them are in the upper-middle class. Therefore, the members of the board, my managers, and the people who supervise the pool are also of that socioeconomic and racial status. Since they are generally not exposed to diverse ideas, their beliefs are encouraged by everyone in their community. The board is comprised almost entirely of men, except for one or two women, but the women do not hold any power. Their beliefs are never challenged, so they can continue to do what they want. Their ideas are also perpetuated in the way that the pool runs. This explains why they treat Megan in the way they do. Although she is the manager and Marco is the assistant manager, the board members tell Marco important information about the pool instead of her. They also only trust him with repairs to the pool and solving problems. Marco also perpetuates their beliefs. He knows that since he is a white male, the board and our supervisors favor him. That’s why he can say what he wants and if anyone threatens him, he knows that he can easily get them fired. Essentially, his actions are supported by the homogenous community at the pool and by the stereotypical traits of hegemonic masculinity.
chunks.label: Analyzing the pool's homogeneous environment
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes the upper-middle-class, predominantly white structure of the pool community, board, and management, explaining how it enables Marco's behavior and diminishes Megan's authority.

chunks.text: Women are often forced into beauty standards that were created by men to keep their power, and these standards are often encouraged by their surroundings. I saw this play out in the way the male manager treated me compared to how the female manager treated me as well as in the standards that are created in the male-dominated, predominantly white community. So, how can we change the standard to make the workplace equal for both men and women? Standing up to the men who oppress us is a start, but it would make more of an impact by talking to their superiors. Although there are many equal opportunity plans being started, they do not account for the microaggressions and bias against women in various workplaces. Creating government-endorsed initiatives to change these conditions is a step that can be taken. However, these are just ideas. The biggest way to create change in one person’s life is to not buy into the hegemonic masculinity and beauty myth stereotypes that engulf society today.
chunks.label: Conclusion on resisting gender stereotypes
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes how societal standards manifest in the workplace and suggests ways individuals and society can resist hegemonic masculinity and beauty myth stereotypes.
chunks.people: the student, male manager (Marco), female manager (Megan)

nd03af185.title: Confronting Gender Bias in Club Volleyball

chunks.text: Do you think women and men are treated the same in America? Most people would say yes just because of what year it is and how much we have developed as a society, but even with that being said women are treated very differently from men even if some men don’t even realize it. On this subject, there is a large gender divide. Only around half of males believe that men and women are treated equally in society, while only 34% of women agree. Approximately half of women believe society favors men over women, compared to 36% of men. With that being said some men do not realize it in the same way that women do just because they overlook it and don’t really understand that no matter what women have always been looked at as inferior.
chunks.label: Gender divide on equality
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on societal perceptions of gender equality and how men and women view the treatment of women differently.

chunks.text:
Something that I have personally experienced with this was actually here at UNCW. My first semester here I was deciding if I wanted to play club volleyball here at UNCW because volleyball has always been something that I love playing and I thought that it would be very good for me and even a way to make some friends. The first day that I went it everyone was just playing king of the court and pick up games and it was really fun. About 30 minutes into playing the boys club volleyball team showed up and wanted to play pick up with us. I did not think anything of it and thought “oh this is going to be fun because I bet they are good”. Whenever the boys team came up to us they started acting kind of weird and I did not think anything of it just because I thought oh well maybe they don’t really know who we are yet. They ended up sitting on the sidelines and just watching us play. Shortly after they came back up to us and were like can we play with you guys and make teams. Of course we said yes and none of us thought anything about it until about 20 minutes into playing one of the boys came up to me and said “I didn’t expect you to be that good at volleyball”. I was really confused because I had no idea who he was and thought to myself well did he expect me to be bad or not know how to play. I kept playing with them and they were constantly complimenting me and saying things like wow you are really good for your height. I know that they did not think anything about that but to me it felt like a backhanded compliment because they were straight up telling me that they didn’t think I was going to be good and I know it was just because I was a girl.

Eventually, I put two and two together and realized that they just expected me to not be as good or be able to keep up and actually play a good game with them just because I was a girl. I know that mens volleyball is a lot different than women at the professional level but anything other than that girls can usually keep up with a boys team or at least everytime I have played a boys team I have been able to. The boys team looked at us girls as weak and did not expect us to be good so they just were not even going to play with or ask us to play with them only until they saw us play. That honestly bothered me so much just because the boys came in and just assumed that we were not going to be good I guess and looked at us as inferior to them just because we were girls. It is just crazy to me how the boys do not even realize what they are saying because they don’t look at it the same way girls do just because they are boys and automatically assume that they will be better at sports and don’t think that girls can keep up with them.
chunks.label: Playing pickup volleyball at UNCW
chunks.what_happened: During pickup volleyball at UNCW, the boys club team hesitated to play, watched from the sidelines, and gave backhanded compliments about the student's skills after joining.

chunks.text: ​​Darwin upheld the gender stereotypes of his period in print, most prominently in "The Descent of Man." In that 1871 research of sexual selection, he concluded that a man achieves "a higher eminence, in whatever he takes up" than a female. Meanwhile, he argued that a woman's intuitive abilities are "typical of the lower races." We have talked about gender in society a lot in class and also about different scientists who talk about it and have theories. We read “The Yellow Wallpaper” by Charlotte Perkins Gilman, which is a story based on the nineteenth centuy, for questions in class and that article really stood out to me just for the sole fact that the wife in this story was just looked at as women and not even a person just because of her gender and her husband sees himself as more powerful than her. The narrator was married to a man who dominated her and treated her like a child. Her husband was the primary decision maker, and she lived in a society where women were not permitted to dispute their husbands' judgments. He loves and cares for his wife, but their unequal connection stops him from genuinely understanding her and her issues. He contributes to her destruction by treating her as a "case" or a "wife" rather than a person with a free choice, which is the last thing he wants. The husband in the story did not even realize the way that he was treating her was not fair and because of that the wife was miserable and felt like she had no power and could not do anything. ​​Although the narrator perceives John as cautious and kind at times, she also sees him as arrogant and manipulating at other times. The narrator eventually regards John as her jailer. While prevailing over her supposed escape from the nursery wallpaper, she eventually loses her sanity. I think that this story really expresses gender roles the best just because her husband truly did love her but just because of society and because he was a man he did not realize that he was treating her unfairly and gave her no say in their relationship.
chunks.label: Darwin and 'The Yellow Wallpaper'
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Darwin's views on gender stereotypes and analyzes Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 'The Yellow Wallpaper' regarding unequal gender roles in marriage.

chunks.text: We also read “ Women as Other” by Simone de Beauvoir which has the same concept about women being treated differently than men. De Beauvoir claims that the fundamental concept of 'woman' is a male concept. Woman is always 'other' because the male is the 'seer' which means he is the subject and she is the object. Beauvoir's focus on the necessity for women to have access to the same activities and projects as men positions her in the liberal, or second-wave feminism tradition. She insists that women be regarded on an equal footing with men, and that laws, practices, and education be changed to support this. This article also stood out to me because men look at women kind of like objects and just as something fun for them, which is the reason why women get objectified so much by men or looked at as weak and not having power.
chunks.label: Simone de Beauvoir's 'Women as Other'
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes Simone de Beauvoir's writings on women being treated as the 'other' and objectified by men.

chunks.text: In conclusion, men may believe that women are treated the same as women just because of where we are today in society and how things actually have changed so much, but in reality there are still some underlying assumptions about men being superior to women even when they do not realize it. I have personally experienced this in college and definitely have many more times than that. Perkins and Beauvoir explain about it very well in their narratives and writings by talking about things that have actually happened and even giving numbers and percentages to prove their points. I think that in today's society the way women are treated is way better than it used to be, but we still are not treated completely equal like we should be even if men think that we are. Women have always been looked at as inferior to men even if men do not even try to think about it like that. Women are looked at as weak and just as something for mens entertainment which is why they objectify women all the time without even trying. No matter what happens women will be looked at inferior just because of how women used to be treated and that is not fair because women can do anything that a man can and should be recognized for all the things that we can do instead of just being looked at as an object and someone who is weak and powerless.
chunks.label: Conclusion on gender inequality
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that despite progress, women are still treated as inferior, weak, and objectified in society.
chunks.people: Charlotte Perkins Gilman, Simone de Beauvoir

chunks.text:
Religion and its Effects on the Formation of Society and Politics

Religion has always been a topic that is dangerous; whoever you are talking with, you are always walking on ice. Whether you are religious or not, everyone has been involved or witnessed religious-like interactions; decisions, confessions, lifestyle, etc. In attempts to understand the “why” of religion in physiological aspects, Maryanksi and Turner discuss the changes in parts of the brain that in turn enhance emotional intelligence. In support of Maryanski and Turner, Durkheim connects religion to the origins of social institutions - through emotional application - and the cultural logic of collective representation. Harari discusses the role of religion in policy making and whether or not it should be a relevant factor to politics. The following is going to show the logistics behind authors and how their ideals can be compared and contrasted.

Starting off with Maryanski and Turner, the neurological differences were spotted within apes. What Turner and Maryanski concluded was that the Morotopithecus apes were more socially advanced due to the expansion of emotion centers of the brain and the postcranial skeleton. The postcranial skeleton allowed the adaptation for hanging and propelling the body, furthering social organization when food was needed. Those with low sociality didn’t organize with other apes, were independent, and considered not a part of a society. Emotions were important for the expansion of cognition due to natural selection eliminating those with smaller emotional centers. The increase in size of the subcortical structures caused an increase in connections within the emotion centers and the neocortex - otherwise known as the prefrontal cortex - where decision making occurs. More importantly, the decisions needed that concerned fight or flight. The amygdala is the part of the brain that controls fight or flight responses, and with an emotional response to a certain stimulus creates memories. By having an apes’ memories enhanced, it created rationality depending on how much emotion was attached to the decision. This expansion of emotions made it possible to read the emotions of others. The ability to read the emotions of others created a language between the apes. With this, a greater capacity for symbolic thought is created and coordination develops between the apes.

Continuing on this emotional intelligence tangent, Durkheim finds similar results as Maryanksi and Turner, but with humans. The emotional application takes place when a certain amount of cognitive capacity (emotional centers) is developed. According to Durkheim, a general concept of the social needs a collective consciousness and representation. When collective consciousness is established within a society, morals and legality are established. When morals and legality is established, then truth and stability are found. Collective representation is created due to a body of people being in agreement or close to agreement enough where everyone feels comfortable with the ideals they’re associated with.

With Maryanski, Turner, and Durkheim, it can be inferred that religion is created within societies as sort of a union and commonality. Harari established the negatives with religion and how it has controlled policy decisions in history. For instance, different societies idolize and practice different religions in comparison to other societies. This difference in religion creates conflict and makes it more difficult to come to solutions between societies and countries. Over time, solutions have become increasingly difficult to come to due to the flexibility religion has in newer political situations. Harari claims that religion is only helpful with identity problems, in addition to justifying and legitimizing the social order. Identity is based on fixed positions in this hierarchy where there is not much change or movement after your position has been established. Industrial society and group identity concerns the feelings and wants of humans to be a part of the group. Because of this want, societies are only deemed as powerful if they control and manipulate identities.

Harari breaks down 3 problems with religion being involved in politics: technical, policy and identity. Technical problems concern things such as agriculture, world disasters, global warming, etc. This is where religion is seen to cross the line to become medicine. Treatment of these huge problems with religion was popular until technology and science came into play. Now, people are relying more on science instead of religious beliefs. With this Harari revealed his stance by concluding that priests further their presence and validity within politics through more excuses. Harari’s remark on scientists remains positive; evidence can be twisted and trials can fail, but scientists will further experiment in order to find a solution. Policy problems revolve around the measures that should’ve been taken to prevent problems. Examples include actions to prevent global warming before the effects are irreversible, being prepared for natural disasters, etc. Identity problems represent the lack of consideration and perspective to others due to selfishness. In addition, identity problems include the cognitive dissonance of being considerate of others or to be selfish.

The ideals of unity and how unity is formed explained by Durkheim, Turner, and Maryanski can be compared to the political ideals of unity expressed by Harari. For instance, Durkheim explains that when collective consciousness is created, morals and legality - along with trust and stability - are established. This association of morals and legality goes in hand with how religion is included in policy making. Morals and legality creates a base to which each country is run politically. Different morals between societies make it harder to come to solutions.

Similar to Harari, Turner and Maryanski determine that expanded emotional centers create language and a bond between apes in a societal form. Due to this emotional expansion established, it can be connected to how religion can control and manipulate identities expressed by Harari. If there is an emotional attachment to a symbol, a government can use that symbol as a reason for a policy to be or not to be enacted. When that reason is used, the society that revolves around that religious symbol is automatically manipulated to agree with that decision due to prior beliefs and identity.

As easy as these concepts can be compared, they can also be contrasted. For instance, Durkheim, Turner, and Maryanski have a very positive or an intriguing outlook when it comes to societal formation surrounding emotional attachments and religion. The neurological aspects made societal formations seem fascinating and applauded for. The enhancement of emotional intelligence aided in the formations of common ideologies and morals. On the other hand, Harari views this as a very negative thing. Harari believes that unity and identity is why there are little to no solutions between societies because of their beliefs. Harari describes the 3 problems with religion that have a negative influence on politics. How identity found within one country aids with being inconsiderate of other countries and a lack of unity. How the problems affecting the world such as climate change, are being handled with traditional and religious beliefs as opposed to science.

In conclusion, religion can be found as both a positive and negative influence on society in many different forms. Maryanski, Turner, and Durkheim portray more of the positive and scientific reasoning for why the results of unity and commonality support society. The discovery of emotional attachments to symbols - the spark of religion - and which parts of the brain interacted in order to create languages. In other perspectives, Harari shows how it can be detrimental as a global population and how independent and limiting religion can be towards political ideals and how countries are running today. Because of both of these stances on religion, it is why there is such a feeling of walking on ice whenever it is discussed.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of religion and politics
chunks.what_happened: The student compares and contrasts theories on religion, emotional evolution, and politics from Maryanski, Turner, Durkheim, and Harari.

na0c62369.title: Navigating High School Cafeteria Racial Divisions

chunks.text: If we all took a minute and thought back to what our high school cafeterias looked like, I fully believe we would all be seeing the exact same patterns. I remember the first time I stepped foot in the cafeteria at my high school. There were about three hundred or so students there, and they were all grouped off. I noticed that there was not much integration; the black people were sitting with other black people, Latinos were sitting with other Latinos, and the white people were sitting with other white people. Of course, there were some outliers, but this was the most common theme. These outliers were generally the mixed-race kids who did not fit the exact mold anywhere. They kind of broke this pattern and would sit with whomever they wanted. I immediately began to wonder why it was like this. My school was centered in a large district filled with diversity; it pulled kids from the wealthiest parts of town to the poorest parts and every other socioeconomic status. This puzzled me and made me wonder why people feel the need to segregate themselves and have these tendencies that seem racist even when they themselves are not racist?
chunks.label: Observing racial segregation in high school cafeteria
chunks.what_happened: The student stepped into their high school cafeteria for the first time and observed that students were grouped by race, with mixed-race students being the main exception.

chunks.text:
In society, race has always been a topic that lots of people try to stay away from in order to not offend anyone. While in actuality, race is a very interesting and complex topic that has influenced society as we know it. If you look like me you have probably always been asked the question, where are you from?” or “What are you mixed with?” and after a while, you just start to expect it. I think the reason that people always ask this is because of a concept called ethnocentrism: people who look and have similar cultures to each other tend to stick together. So when people don’t quite fit into a set group, they get questioned about it a lot, so others can know how or if they can relate to them.

As I stated earlier, the best example of this theory would be a school cafeteria, which is the epitome of ethnocentrism. If you look closely, most of the time the cafeteria will be split into about three or four groups, but there will be a few outliers (like myself) who will sit with any group. The African American kids will usually all sit together on one side, along with the Hispanics and Latinos. Then there are the white kids who would all sit together, but the last group, which is not always there, is the group of people of all different races sitting together. Which brings up the question: What has changed in these kids to value friendships over staying with the people who look similar to them?

Are children raised to value people and to judge off of character instead of judging by skin tone or by appearances? Or do people just like to stick with what they know? This inherent quality that humans have of making a tribe of similar people can be broken if they are taught that everyone is equal, and instead of sticking with people that look like you, you should surround yourself with diversity. This way you can learn as much as you can about other people’s cultures and values. This also brings me to believe that, while humans naturally want to be with people who are familiar, the idea of racism and that another race could be inferior to you is completely a taught or learned behavior. If you allow children to choose for themselves, without the influence of their parents, they will most likely choose to be inclusive and just judge people based on their character.

Even though racism is taught, the people who spread this concept capitalize from the nature of humans to be afraid or leery of things that are different. While this mechanism probably developed into humans as a safety precaution for our ancestors to stay away from poisonous food and dangerous predators, it has evolved as an excuse to explain away hatred, or the fear of the unknown. Some people try to twist the minds of ignorant and uneducated people to convince them to hate what they hate, and they have a few different methods of doing so. They may try to relate it to something that they value highly, like their religion, or something that favored their particular group, like slavery in the south. They may even try to disguise their hatred as love (possibly backed up by the Bible). Even though this does not happen as much today, people still believe that other races are inferior. This is a twisted cycle, because the more racist parents there are, the more people are passing those toxic beliefs down to their children who will continue to facilitate hate in our society. I believe this cycle is slowly starting to break, because today the idea of stopping hate and being an anti-racist is running ramped through big cities, and people are finally being educated and taught that everyone is equal and that no one person is better than another.

Even with our society starting to make little changes and trying to teach people that everyone is equal, it is a very slow process that takes even longer the further south you venture in the United States. It has historically always been this way, because it takes longer to change the minds of southern people (as they are more likely to still be reaping the rewards of slavery and continued racism both financially and socially). It is also due to modern black diaspora out of the south, as this further facilitates ethnocentric rituals and behaviors in the south that have long been removed from other states which are more diverse. This is why I think that anti-racism literature and teachings should not only be included, but mandated in all school curriculums (especially in the south) due to the lack of education on those subjects. Children in public schools should be learning exactly how this nation came to be, and there needs to be an end to white-washing textbooks and only giving little pieces of the truth. The fact that there are still people who are currently trying to block out and ignore the parts of their history that makes them look bad or show the true colors of the leaders of their states is beyond concerning. A famous quote by Winston Churchhill states, “Those who do not learn from history are doomed to repeat it.” This reinforces my belief that if you do not teach about what happened in the past, it can and will eventually, happen again.

Sociologists have conducted multiple studies regarding racism and racist behaviors and more recently they have studied ethnocentrism in relation to those ideologies. This term was supposedly coined by Polish sociologist, Ludwig Gumplowicz, in the nineteenth century and the term ethnocentrism derives from two Greek words: "ethno,” meaning culture, and "kentron,” meaning center, that basically explains that individual human beings put their culture at the center of their own world view. People who heavily lean into this theory see all of these other cultures and people through their biased view and firmly believe that their culture is the “correct” way. Ethnocentric people see other cultures through a warped lens which can make them believe that they are better and other cultures are less than. This is dangerous, as it can cause them to see people of other cultures as wrong, bad, or less human. This increases the chances of justifying the dehumanization of specific cultures that are different, and they may try to exploit them or even defend or perpetuate violence. This goes hand in hand with the study of racism. They are very similar on the surface, but the biggest difference between the two is that racism is taught and ethnocentrism is more of a natural instinct. Everyone is born with some degree of ethnocentrism, considering the fact that when most people are adolescents their day-to-day routines and meals rely heavily on their parents’ customs. It is only natural to become used to and even prefer the things you grew up with, but growth is all about learning that just because it is the most comfortable or preferred for you, does not make it the best overall. As long as people are able to respect other people’s customs and learn to appreciate their differences, ethnocentrism is not a bad thing. However, I also believe that it can get more extreme if you are surrounded by other, like-minded people, who feed into those thoughts and switch from thinking, “I like this way” to “This is the best and only way people should do this.” That mindset just reinforces those thoughts and behaviors, so eventually, ethnocentrism could turn into racism if you are surrounded by those ideals and taught that it is okay.

This brings me back to my original point, the reason people tend to segregate themselves, and the reason that people are always so curious about what race others are, is because they are looking to see what they have in common with them. This is ethnocentrism: the mechanism that makes people want to be with people that are similar to them in either looks or culture or both. This is normally cultivated during childhood, and kids learn to seek out people who look like their parents because they associate that look with safety. When they are first introduced to people of other races it can be a shock to them; one exception to this is mixed-race people. Usually, mixed-race people have something in common with everyone, so they can bypass the ethnocentric views of others by relating to them in some way. Whether it is being a part of the same race or of the same culture as them, mixed-race people have found a loophole where they have adapted to relate to everyone in some way or another. Other people feel like they can relate to them on a personal level, and they do not have their guard up around them like they might with others. This is because people see mixed-race people as somewhat familiar and have common interests or hobbies. On the other hand, if someone of a different race tried to connect with someone else like a mixed person does, they could be met with either hostility or just be blatantly ignored. People instantly have their guard up with people of another race or culture because they automatically think that they are different, while if they would just see people as people and ignore race and color they would probably have more in common with others than they think.
chunks.label: Reflecting on race, ethnocentrism, and societal attitudes
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses why people ask about mixed-race backgrounds, explains ethnocentrism versus learned racism, and advocates for inclusive education and anti-racist history curriculums.

chunks.text: It is a common experience between women to be ignored when your pain is at an all time high. Whether it is menstrual cramps or an undiagnosed chronic illness, women are repeatedly ignored and brushed to the side for being “too much” and “overdramatic” when it comes to pain. After hearing these phrases over and over, a woman may start to believe this and push their pain to the sides; complying with the stereotype that women are indeed too dramatic and that they really have nothing to be complaining about. In modern day times, women are told that their pain is not as bad as it seems, due to the place they have been put into by men as the “others” or secondary counterparts.
chunks.label: Women's pain dismissed by society
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how society minimizes women's pain, treating women as dramatic counterparts to men.

chunks.text:
Women must push past these boundaries to make themselves heard as individuals.

This argument continued until the nurse finally gave in and tested Mary for a kidney infection. While nurses are usually supposed to take the sample and then move to another room to test, the nurse gathered the sample, looked Mary in the eyes and said, “I’m going to test this in front of you to prove that there is nothing wrong with you.” The nurse tested the sample, and of course, Mary had a kidney infection. After the results came back, the nurse still acted cold and unsympathetic towards Mary, even though Mary was right about her own symptoms. She had to fight a nurse, someone whose job it is to help people and believe their patients to even get a test and receive the medical care she needed to feel better and to get the medication she needed. To make matters even more confusing, the nurse was a woman, but because she was educated and trained by a system that favors men, she still brushed Mary off. If Mary had perhaps been a man, her symptoms would have immediately been listened to, and she would have been tested and treated promptly. This situation explains the way that women are treated as “others” and overlooked because they aren’t considered individuals, but rather counterparts to their men.
chunks.label: Mary dismissed by nurse during infection
chunks.what_happened: Mary had to argue with a dismissive nurse to get tested for a kidney infection, which came back positive, yet the nurse remained cold and unsympathetic.

chunks.text: In Woman as Other, Simone DeBeauvoir explains the position of women in comparison to men. As a feminist and a student of social theory and modern philosophy, she can understand the female struggle, and why that struggle exists in almost every social situation. DeBeauvoir lived through this type of oppression through the scope of a upper class perspective. She interprets the roles of women and men in the modern world thoroughly and states, “He is the Subject; he is the Absolute. She is the Other” (DeBeauvoir 260). This is a perfect explanation of women when they are compared to men. DeBeuvoir explains the role of women in society within her writing, especially as simply a counterpart to men. She also explains that women often play into these roles, as they have been convinced by societal norms that they are the “others”, and their opinions have no relevance.
chunks.label: Simone de Beauvoir's Woman as Other
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Simone de Beauvoir's theory regarding women being designated as the 'Other' in relation to men.

chunks.text: Women find breaking out of this entrapment to be difficult.
