As explained in Woman as Other, women tend to have no shared stories, religion, past, or sense of community like other communites such as African Americans, those of Jewish descent, and immigrant workers. A woman is completely alone in her own world, and while different women might be experiencing the same situations, they would never know because it has been instilled in modern women that they should not be complaining about their issues, but instead staying quiet and subdued for the men around them. DeBeauvoir states, “They live dispersed among men, tied by homes, work, economic interests, and social conditions to certain men – fathers or husbands – more closely than to other women” (DeBeauvoir 261). Women are so disconnected from their own selves that they become disconnected from the women around them, even though most women suffer from the same oppression daily.
chunks.label: Isolation and lack of shared community among women
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on de Beauvoir's idea that women lack a unified community and remain isolated by their ties to men.

chunks.text: While the way that Mary was treated in a place of medical care is inexcusable, it is expected. Since the nurse was a women pushed into a career typically controlled by men, she is so disconnected from her patients (especially women) that she can’t believe a woman fully when they say they are in extreme pain. When women play into this stereotype, this enforces their role as the “other”. Playing into this stereotype also continues to allow men to stand on the pedestal of being the “Absolutes”. Men’s words are law, as show throughout history, and when they say that a woman is overreacting to pain, they must be right. It is often difficult to not play into this stereotype unfortunately. I find that even I do it when talking about an injury because, often, a man in the conversation will counter the pain with the question of “But have you even had this happen to you?” or something similar. After hearing this so many times, it is easier for women to just stay silent in the way that men want them to be rather than expressing more pain or discomfort and sticking up for themselves.
chunks.label: Connecting healthcare bias and personal minimization to theory
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Mary's experience through gender stereotypes and notes their own tendency to stay quiet when men downplay their injuries.

chunks.text: It is a common tactic for men to push women to the side, especially when they are talking about their own personal pain. Simone DeBeuvoir explains it best when she labels women as “others”. Healthcare is a place in which a woman can be completely brushed off when she should be listened to and taken care of, which puts women into this “other” position. It is not “over dramatic” to complain about pain, men do it all the time. To tell women that they need to stop complaining about something that isn’t that bad is to play into the stereotype that women should be silent and submissive, the perfect woman for a man or their “One”. While Mary’s story may seem unbelievable, women suffer from this sort of treatment every day in the medical field. Whether their pain is mild or the most excruciating feeling they have every felt, women deserve to feel heard and cared for in the world today.
chunks.label: Need for women to be heard in healthcare
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that women's pain must not be brushed aside as overly dramatic and calls for women to be heard and cared for in medicine.

chunks.text: The collective consciousness is so powerful that it makes communities believe things and engage in things that may be abnormal but is shows that one small concept can hold a society together. Both Durkheim and the Lore podcast explain that societies are built on common beliefs which help create the collective consciousness. According to Durkheim, religion is essentially social and according to Lore superstition brought the community together. Evidently, factors like these are influential enough to strongly glue a community together and add to the creation of the collective consciousness.
chunks.label: Collective consciousness and shared beliefs in society
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how collective consciousness, religion, and shared superstitions bind communities together, drawing on ideas from Durkheim and the Lore podcast.

nb4eea9f1.title: Growing Up in the Working Class

chunks.text:
Is an NFL Quarterback more valuable than a paramedic saving lives? While the impulse reaction for most would be to claim the paramedic is more important, looking at wages tells a different story. In fact, compared to a North Carolina paramedic averaging $38,270 per year, the NFL’s top 10 quarterbacks earn an average of $33.5 million per year, a whopping 875 times that of the average paramedic. Despite paramedics providing life saving service, judged in the terms of capitalism, they are approximately 875 times less important than the stars on the television screen. Is this fair? These two roles and their disparity in wealth and power provide a clear example of the class system. In America, the class system provides too much power and control to those at the top while leaving barely anything left for those below them.

The disparity in power and wealth in America’s class system is not exclusive to the comparison of professional athletes and medical workers.
chunks.label: Wealth disparity between quarterbacks and paramedics
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the wage disparity between NFL quarterbacks and paramedics as an example of power imbalance in the American class system.

chunks.text:
Growing up, I’ve witnessed and experienced the pitfalls of the class system firsthand. I was raised in a family that would probably be most closely defined as lower middle class, and both of my parents worked very hard. My dad worked as a mechanic doing serious physical labor every day, and my mom worked late hours as a nurse. Despite all their hard work, this was still only enough to provide the necessities to our family, which I’m very grateful for. I have had to take out loans for college and I hope to pay them off as soon as I can after graduation.

Witnessing my mom come home on weekends past 2 am and dad clearly exhausted after every shift left a strong impression on me. While our financial situation wasn’t strong, the effort they put into their jobs was admirable. I know I’m not alone in this struggle, as I have friends who relate. Many of the families in my community struggled to make ends meet, and as a kid we were never able to splurge on lavish vacations or cars like our fellow classmates. I am super appreciative of my parents’ hard work, but my family’s situation has been a strong indicator of a major issue with America’s class system.

Seeing how hard my parents worked and how little return on their labor was given was frustrating, to say the least, and inevitably made me somewhat bitter towards the class system in America.
chunks.label: Growing up in a lower middle class family
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up watching their parents work exhausting hours as a mechanic and a nurse to cover necessities, and took out college loans while observing that neighbor families also struggled.
chunks.feelings: grateful, admirable, super appreciative, frustrating, somewhat bitter
chunks.people: the student's mom, the student's dad, friends, classmates

chunks.text:
Ever since I was a kid, the American Dream has always been preached to me, promising infinite possibilities if I work hard. The longer I’ve lived though, the more I’ve learned that it’s those at the top who have the greatest freedom and power. Wealthy “super-celebrities” like Mark Zuckerburg, Elon Musk, and Jeff Bezos are frequently on the news, announcing new acquisitions, ventures, or even going to space. Measuring income, the richest 0.1% earn 196 times as much as the bottom 90%(inequality.org, 2020). These elite and their counterparts have so much power, as well as financial and informational control, that their continued domination seems unavoidable.

William Domhoff discusses the class system, specifically the class-domination theory of power in his article. Those at the top of the class system, as referenced in my experiences, are referred to by Domhoff as the social upper class. Within the upper class, leaders of subgroups in this category are referred to as the “power elite”. These power elites are able to ensure their continued domination in America by controlling the organizations they lead to benefit themselves. This level of control is one of the ways the upper class maintain their place and continue to oppress the working class in America.

In addition to control over businesses and organization from Domhoff’s power elite, another way they have control over the country is through the government. Those in the top of the class system have tremendous funding and resources to push policies beneficial to themselves through lobbying, gifts, and promises. While heavily frowned upon, this practice is very successful at implementing the upper class’s ideal policies into the government. When rules and structures are put into place that keep power in the elite’s hands, all lower classes suffer as a result.

Through these strategies the power elite Domhoff describes employ, it’s clear why inequality is only rising in America, and why it’s so prevalent. Families like mine can work very hard, but will simply never have the tools or control to prosper like the upper class does. While any level of success requires effort, the disparity in wealth in America is not even remotely about who’s working harder. Under the current class system in America, unfairness and mass inequality is an inevitable outcome that will oppress anyone not on top.

Another topic Domhoff discusses is the weakness of the working class in America. The working class make up a vast majority of the country’s population, yet have relatively little power. Domhoff notes that historically, despite the country making lots of social progress, including civil rights, feminism, and support for the lgbt community, the power of the working class has regressed. In fact, between 1962 and 1990, the ratio of business executive pay to that of their workers skyrocketed from 41 to 1 to 300 to 1. While many factors influence policy in the United States, the working class simply is overmatched in terms of finance. In America, those with the money have the resources to keep it. The working class has to make ends meet with their small share, and often there is little remaining after necessities are purchased.

While some inequality is a healthy part of any economy, I believe that the degree America has reached under the class system has crossed a line. The top 1% making more than a hundred times that of the bottom 90% reflects the two ends of a spectrum, where some don’t have enough things to buy, while many families including mine struggle with bare necessities.

In the case of NFL Quarterbacks making tens of millions of dollars, they very quickly find themselves in the top tier of the upper class. They can then use this money to invest and build even greater wealth. On the other end of the spectrum, paramedics are being worked to death and likely barely make enough to survive. While the professional athlete isn’t necessarily working harder, or striving towards the American dream any more than the paramedic, the two occupations provide two opposite outcomes in terms of compensation. Under the American class system, the gap between these two workers will only grow with each consecutive year.

The 875 to 1 ratio between NFL quarterbacks and paramedics provide just one example of wealth disparity in America. The class system in America creates unfair income inequality that keeps the top living lucrative lives while the working class struggles to make ends meet. As long as the class system still exists in the way it currently operates, quality of life for families like mine will continue to be very poor. I think that it’s impossible to eliminate all inequality, but we can make changes to allow the working class to be able to work for improvement, and make the upper class play by the rules instead of controlling the entire country. Overall, while taking down the class system is a daunting task, it’s clear America needs to change in order for it to truly be the land of the free.
chunks.label: Analysis of the class system and power elite
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the myth of the American Dream, critiques extreme wealth using Domhoff's theory of the power elite and class domination, and argues for systemic change.

n08e5b68e.title: Analyzing Technology and American Class Power

chunks.text:
Harari also said that, “for every job Artificial Intelligence takes from humans, it creates one new job in its place.” While in the past this may have been true and exciting for “robots” to take the boring jobs to allow humans to focus on more important jobs. In reality, with how far technology has progressed, the future could look much different than we previously thought. Technology could take millions or billions of jobs from people leaving a new useless and jobless class. This new class could cause major financial problems not only for itself, but for the government that now has to support this new class of people. This situation would be one of the most expensive things that our government would have had to deal with in a very long time. Depending on how this potential situation is handled will determine the future of America and its people.

Harari also says that there are some potential solutions to prevent job loss. While stopping the loss of jobs altogether is almost impossible, if it were to happen, we would lose the possibility of AI filled jobs that could help humanity. He says, “Although just because something can be done does not mean that it must be done.” So governments may choose to integrate AI slowly to lessen the effect that it will have on people that lose their jobs and this will also give the government an opportunity to try and create new jobs to make up for the ones that were lost. In this situation, humans will not be needed as producers or consumers because AI would be producing everything that the economy needs. They would not be needed as consumers because the American economy would evolve to not need the consumption of its citizens. If nothing is done to prepare for the time when AI is introduced it could be catastrophic. One solution for this model that Harari discussed is not meant to protect jobs, but to protect humans themselves; he called this UBI (universal basic income). The government would tax both the extremely wealthy individuals and corporations to provide a stipend for people who may need it to cover their basic needs. The other option is UBS (universal basic services) where the government would pay a certain group of people who would go and provide necessary services to citizens who need them. They would do things such as child care, caring for the elderly, cooking etcetera. The usefulness of UBI and UBS is a hot topic in America because those systems are very similar to Communism and Socialism, which America has been conditioned to not like.

Harari believes that the lower class in America has little to no power in the decisions that are made in the country. There are many reasons for this imbalance including that the rich and powerful do everything in their power to manipulate the system to create the illusion of choice for the lower class. Some of the ways that are used to facilitate this illusion of choice are gerrymandering and the electoral college so the individual’s vote counts for very little overall. Most of the choices that are made for this country are heavily influenced by a minority of people with the majority of the wealth. This is very unfair for the rest of the people in this country that are middle or low class whose vote becomes meaningless in the big picture.

Mantsios has quite a different view on class than Harari, the main difference is the fact that Mantsios is more focused on the present and how the class system is now, while Harari is centered on what the class system will turn into in the coming years. Mantsios believes that there are four main myths about the class system in America. The first myth is the thought that America is a classless society and people can move between classes freely. The second myth is that everyone in America is middle class, while the majority of Americans are middle class, there is a huge leap between the bottom of the middle class and the top. A family that makes three hundred thousand dollars a year is considered middle class, but so is the family that makes sixty thousand dollars a year. The third myth is that everything one has, has come from smarts or hard work. This is false, as America is the epitome of “old” money because America has had a huge economic boom in the last two hundred years that has produced generational wealth. Individual people and/or families that experienced that economic boom had a big influx of cash, which they used to establish themselves. This “found” wealth led to things like buying lots of land or to running a successful business that generated even more money. So the people with a family that established themselves early in America, on average, became very wealthy. This inherited wealth got passed down for many generations which essentially gave those select people a head start. This phenomenon is referred to as generational wealth. The last myth that Mantsios discusses is that the economy is growing for everyone. Realistically, the economy is influenced most by other countries and the very wealthy people in America, who know how to use the economy and society to their advantage, in turn making themselves even more money.

Domhoff has a theory that there are people who control and have great influence over the economy. These people are referred to as the power elite; the power elite is the top of the social upper class. This group includes CEOs, boards of directors, and the board of trustees of banks and large companies. These select few have a significant amount of power in the United States because they are the group with the most economic sway due to the mass amount of capital their positions control. The power of this elite group is that they have congruent class consciousness. They actively work to splinter the potential for any polarizing class consciousness to form. So if another person or group is spreading ideas that the powerful don’t agree with, they will do everything in their power to stop them from spreading their ideals. This is done through media, movies, TV, and commercials; they portray the world through presumptions of the elites that actively defund projects that may challenge their main view. They also have most media outlets under their influence so they perpetuate their ideas even further. In addition, there is a very clear policy that they follow which is anti-tax, anti-union, and anti-workers rights. This group also supports deregulation so that they can do as they please without having any restrictions.

Social and financial class is a very complex subject and can be hard to understand. Although these three authors have a deep understanding of society and class they present some very profound ideas about what it needs or what might happen in the future, they agree that there are many detrimental flaws within the class system in America. Harari believes that this class system can not withstand the current rate of technology innovation. Classes will not be stable in the future without preparation beforehand and the creation of a cushion for the people who will need it. Mantsios instead focuses on the wage disparity within the class system, especially the middle class. Being the biggest class in America, there are “middle class” people that vacation outside of the country seasonally and send their kids to private schools and ivy league colleges. While people in this same “middle class” have never even been out of their home state or town and have to work on the holidays just to keep food on the table for their families. It is not justifiable to have such disparity between people in supposedly the same class. On the other hand, Domhoff centers on the fact that classes and society are controlled by the power elite. His other main point is the fact that the working class and the “normal” American citizen has little to no power in the say of things that happen in the United States. Overall, these three authors offer thoughtful insight into the very complex and intricate society in which we all live. Taken together as a study for positive social and economic change, there is great value in moving toward a future that considers each viewpoint.
chunks.label: Analysis of class perspectives by Harari, Mantsios, and Domhoff
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on and compares theories of class, technology, and economic power presented by authors Harari, Mantsios, and Domhoff.

ne4562e95.title: Analyzing Corporate and Political Power Elites

chunks.text:
In any type of society, as learned through studying Sociology over the course of this semester, there is a hierarchy of power. In each society, the roles and functions of the so-called “power elite” differ, but the concept of power remains the same. Regardless of the time period, race, gender, or age, each individual experiences the effects of the “power elite”. This statement is proven by the works of Doffhom and Harari, as each describes what power looks like in different time periods and how power is established. While both authors discuss the same initial topic, the smaller factors that make up their individual definitions of power are described in different ways. Doffhom describes the “power elite” in America as the upper class that consists of active workers for-profit or nonprofit organizations while Harari argues that big corporations are continuously increasing in power, and will hold the most power over America in the near future.

Each author discusses the concept of power in different ways. In Doffhom’s argument, he describes political power of the elites over the lower class members of society, while Harari discusses the technological power that big corporations hold over the rest of society. The “power elites” are able to work their way into the government through their social and economic status, which allows them to make decisions for the country that directly contributes to their socioeconomic group. Harari explores how big corporations use their technological power to expand their own companies. For example, when Apple releases a new product, people wait outside in extreme temperatures for extended amounts of time hoping to be the first to snag the new iPhone. There are videos of customers trampling each other to get inside the building to spend a pretty penny on a device not much different from the last one. The ability to control hundreds of thousands of people with the release of a new product is baffling, and Harari explores how this type of situation is only the beginning of big corporations using their power to advance society in a way that benefits them.

Doffhom’s argument is focused around the upper class, “snobby” individuals that have money and a strong educational background. This elite group consists of CEOs, socialites, and executives that execute their power in the government. Although it seems that the government would have more control than a group of “daddy’s money Harvard alumni”, these individuals are able to intertwine themselves in the government system by becoming lawyers, judges, and even friends of individuals inside the government, and are able to tip the hat in a direction that directly benefits the elite group. Even research shows that members of the senate and congress for both political parties consist of members of the elite. Although the government claims to be “for the people, by the people”, it truly is to benefit the elite, by the elite. By tricking citizens to believe they are choosing who goes into office, what decisions are made, and more, citizens willingly give up their power, and hand it to the elite.

Harari argues that the advancement of technology has allowed large companies to create an unspoken power of the citizens of America due to the fact that they are the most technologically advanced, and Americans have become obsessed with the new advancements granted by the creation of new algorithms. These algorithms essentially force individuals to give up their ability to make their own choices and allow AI to begin possessing the power of decision-making. Now more than ever, technology is advancing at a rapid pace, which in return, allows companies to make these large leaps towards an AI-centered lifestyle. Harari discusses how these corporations creating AI models of doctors and homes are removing the concept of free will from the lives of Americans. By interacting with these new forms of technology, Americans cannot be certain how much power is truly being stolen. As interaction with AI increases, the more that these models learn about individuals, and over time, will replace the individuals’ own conscious and begin making decisions for them. For example, Harari discusses how AI will eventually take over most jobs in society, ranging from cashiers to doctors. With no jobs available, individuals are forced into using their time doing other activities, however, this decision was not based upon free will, but technically, by force. Although having an AI model in homes or workplaces has it benefits, the more closely that individuals interact with these models, the more the models are able to learn about human consciousness, giving them more information to modify themselves, and essentially, know humanity more than humanity knows itself.

In both scenarios, the lower class citizens are being robbed of their own sense of free will, and are being controlled by whoever is in power. The concept of power is not something that can be eliminated in society, as it is an essential factor for advancement, however, as the power is continuously being granted to the elite groups, the more they are able to advance. This is a vicious cycle that is almost impossible to escape, and the lower class groups are unaware of how they are fueling this hierarchy of power.

Another obvious difference between the two author’s arguments about power is that Doffhom discusses how the government and corporations (and or business owners) are divided, while Harari explores how technological advancements could possibly grant corporations all the power, or that they could work together with the government as a unit. Doffham explores how many business leaders feel powerless in the face of the government, and how they feel unheard. There is an obvious rift between political leaders and business leaders, which fuels the government even more, because members are aware of how other groups feel threatened by the government. On the other hand, Harari explores how corporations and the government could possibly work hand in hand. Because AI is expected to take over many jobs in the future, it is not surprising that the government could potentially be controlled by AI models, which are controlled by big corporations, furthermore, gaining more power for these said corporations. By implementing AI in every aspect of individuals lives, the corporations that create them will gain power exponentially until houses, cars, and even individuals’ thoughts are controlled, monitored, and used for further advancements.

Although both situations from each author is different, individuals are still trapped in the cycle that is power in America. Doffhom describes how socialites are able to sneak their way into government, but this process happens very publicly, and the people still believe that it is their decision. For example, by electing Donald Trump as President of the United States, the people believed they were making this choice, while in reality, Trump was already an individual of high status with the financial stability and connections that already included him somewhat in politics. Electing him as President was merely the last step to the plan to include the elites in the government. Soon after, it was released that Trump had elected some of his personal friends to serve in different areas of government, which supports Doffhom’s argument.

Both Doffhom and Harari discuss how power allows individuals to believe they are making decisions for themselves, but in reality, individuals are forced to make a certain decision that has been provided by the ones in control. As Doffhom explains in his work, many members of the “power elite” are able to run for political office due to their connections and status. When the ballet is provided during the election season, Americans are able to choose between several different options of candidates, and between more than two political parties. However, each individual is typically one of these “power elites”, and therefore, the decision has already been made. An example of this is that every few years, Apple products begin to become glitchy and suddenly stop working. However, this typically occurs during two different events; either there was just a new software update or a new product is soon being released. Apple is able to force their users to buy new products when their old ones stop working. This is not by coincidence, but by the fact that Apple is such a large and successful company that it’s customers do not mind buying the “latest and greatest” product that they are offering.

Regardless of time period, the hierarchy of power exists in any sort of functioning society. Doffhom and Harari show how generalizable the concept of power is in society, and provides two different examples of how power can be created and exerted upon the individuals not included in the group with power. Doffhom explains how the “power elites” have their power due to their wealth and status, and are able to exert this power by either becoming CEOs or members of the government, where they exert their power to benefit themselves. Harari discusses how big corporations are currently the most powerful due to their access to technological advances, and how the world will be effected by these new algorithms. While companies like Apple and Microsoft are now the most current technological “crazes” in the world, every day they are modifying these products to become better and better, which will result in these companies having the power to control every aspect of an individual’s life. With the rise of smart homes and talks of robots delivering UPS packages to front doors, I have no doubt in my mind that within 30 years, AI will have almost completely taken over inside the workplace. There will be Siri like robots that talk through devices catching people shoplifting, or diagnosing someone with cancer. There is a possibility as well that the concept of power will shift away from technology and towards another concept. Regardless of how it is presented and exerted, the concept of power will remain the same throughout any society.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of power elites and technology
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes and compares theories by Domhoff and Harari regarding power elites, political control, technological advancement, and corporate influence over society.

nbae8d379.title: Stuck in a High School Role

chunks.text: Accepting change, whether it’s as small as throwing away a favorite old shirt or as drastic as moving to a new city, can be extremely challenging. Change can be scary as we often don’t know what to expect. There is no way to know exactly what will happen in every new situation. We get comfortable in our current situation and changing that constant routine can be stressful and even scary. Once we find something that makes us feel comfortable, we don’t want to try anything else and risk having it be worse than what we had before. This uncertainty that comes with new adventures has produced a society where change is difficult to initiate and often prevented altogether. As members of society, we each develop a certain role to play, and we often stick to that role. Once we find our role, the fear and uncertainty surrounded by change makes it difficult for us to shift into a new role. Our concern about creating potential problems or embarrassment in a situation often prevents us from accepting these changes and allowing people to move between roles. Stopping each other from changing roles in turn prevents our society from seeing any real change with social issues.
chunks.label: The difficulty of change and social roles
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how change is challenging and scary, and how societal roles and the fear of embarrassment prevent individuals from changing.

chunks.text: Growing up, and even still today, I have always been a more introverted person. I love to spend time with friends, but I always tend to be quieter and more reserved when I’m around people I don’t know very well. When I’m at home it’s like I’m a completely different person: I crack jokes and I don’t mind being silly. I’m more comfortable around my close friends and family, so I’m not embarrassed to act like myself while I’m with them. In public, though, I’m never the friend doing crazy things or the first one to shout something out in class. I have always been so worried everyone was going to judge me or make fun of me if I acted how I did at home. However, as I have started to get older, and especially towards the end of high school, I noticed that I was becoming more confident and was shifting into a more outgoing person. I learned that I didn’t need to feel embarrassed for acting like myself or being the person I truly am. Once I realized this, I was able to apply it to all aspects of my life and show a different side of myself that not many people had seen before. Even when I was around people I didn’t know as well, I found that I was beginning to have a different attitude and I wasn’t afraid to truly be myself.
chunks.label: Becoming more outgoing and confident
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up introverted and reserved around unfamiliar people while acting silly at home, but gradually became more confident and outgoing near the end of high school.

chunks.text: I saw the most significant change in my personality while I was at softball. I have been playing softball since I was around 8 years old. From growing up playing tee ball in the yard, to playing in my first travel game, to playing on the varsity team in high school, a significant portion of my life has been devoted to softball. The softball field is like my second home, and my teams have always felt more like family than just friends. After playing for so many years I was more comfortable and confident in myself when I was on the softball field. Also, when you spend hours practicing and playing together, you form a bond with your teammates greater than just friendship. It was a shock, then, when I realized that high school softball was actually the hardest setting to act like myself in. Even though I considered those teammates to be close friends, I slowly realized that I wasn’t acting like myself while I was at practice.
chunks.label: Playing softball growing up
chunks.what_happened: The student played softball from age eight through high school varsity, forming strong bonds with teammates, but discovered that high school softball was the hardest place to act like themselves.

chunks.text: In my town, softball was completely run by politics. If you didn’t have the right last name you weren’t going to play, and I certainly did not have the right name. From the very first day of tryouts freshman year, I could tell that I was not one of the popular girls. The coach loved the girls in one friend group who were showing off and acting like they owned the place. I quickly realized that I would not be one of those favorites and accepted my place as the quiet freshman. At that point in time, I was completely terrified to be playing with the upperclassmen and felt like I shouldn’t be there at all. I stuck to myself and was too scared to even try to be more outgoing. Even as the years passed, I noticed I was still stuck as the shy underclassmen. Despite growing and changing as a person, I realized that my teammates were not open to the same kind of change, preventing me from being myself when I was there. At school before practice, I was able to be myself, but the second I arrived to practice it was like a switch flipped and I was back to my quiet, freshman self. I didn’t realize this was happening for a long time, but by senior year I really began to notice that I was a completely different person around my teammates than while I was with my other friends. The confident, more outgoing personality that shined most of the time was suddenly gone whenever I was around my teammates.
chunks.label: Stuck in a quiet role during high school softball
chunks.what_happened: During high school softball tryouts and practices, the student felt excluded from the popular group favored by the coach and remained stuck in a quiet, shy role through senior year.

chunks.text: One sociological concept I have been able to observe throughout my own experiences (and especially at softball) is Goffman’s presentation of the self. Erving Goffman, a Canadian sociologist, suggested the idea that the self is collectively produced. What he meant by that was that as a society we live life on a stage and are actors performing different roles. Our interactions with everyone else performing are what defines our own role and performance in the situation. The different factors like setting, environment, and people involved all work together to create the overall performance. In any interaction, each and every one of us has a certain role to play. For example, a student’s role is to prepare for, attend, and participate in class, and to complete any assigned work outside of class. The teacher’s role is to prepare the lesson, lead class discussions, and prepare students to complete assignments. Together, the students and teacher are actively giving a performance in the classroom. The teacher’s actions and attitude affect how the students act, and how the students are acting impacts how the teacher teaches the class. Additionally, the role we play is greatly influenced by the situation we are in. In a social interaction, if one person does not take part and play their role, then the rest of the performance is thrown off. As the actors in the performance, we take cues from our environment and others around us to determine what our role is in a certain situation. For example, if we are surrounded by close friends and family, we might act more comfortable and informally; a greeting in this setting might be a hug. In contrast, when we meet someone new or are in a business setting, we might act in a more professional manner; a greeting in this situation will most likely be a firm handshake. How we act and the role we play greatly depends on the conditions created by everyone involved. One of the most important aspects of these social performances is a collective understanding of the situation and each other’s roles. Everyone must be aware of the definition of the situation, or the role that each person involved is trying to achieve. It is an expectation that everyone involved is invested in making everyone else’s role appear credible. If a role is discredited or someone misunderstands a role, that is when embarrassment occurs.
chunks.label: Goffman's presentation of the self
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Erving Goffman's sociological theory that the self is collectively produced through social performance, roles, and the avoidance of embarrassment.

chunks.text:
All our different interactions and performances are unique, which requires us to work together to validate everyone’s roles and ensure a smooth performance.

This idea of validating roles and preventing embarrassment is one of the biggest factors that affected my experience playing softball in high school. As I got older and throughout my time in high school, I changed as a person, which ultimately meant my role in softball should change accordingly. However, this change did not occur. When I was at softball, I had tried a few times to change my role and become the outgoing person I was outside of practice. I quickly realized two different things were happening that were combining to prevent me from really stepping into my new role at softball. The first was that my own fear of embarrassment was preventing me from continuing to try to be myself at practice. I was worried that because I had held a certain role for so long, that my new role would be discredited, leading to me becoming embarrassed. The second thing I noticed was that the other people involved weren’t letting me change my role within the context of softball. My teammates had also grown to expect a certain role from me and changing their understanding of my role could have caused an overall misunderstanding and embarrassment. Because of this, it was easier for them to trap me in a certain role rather than take the risk of allowing a new role and potentially creating a problem in the overall situation.

Since my teammates weren’t open to change, I was unable to shift into a new role. Our group collectively defined my personal role in our overall performance, which in turn prevented change in that performance from occurring.
chunks.label: Inability to shift roles on the softball team
chunks.what_happened: The student attempted to act more outgoing at high school softball practice, but both fear of embarrassment and teammates expecting a certain role prevented any shift.

chunks.text: My personal example from softball is just one of many instances where society has made it difficult for change to occur. Considering Goffman’s idea that the self is collectively produced, it is essential that everyone involved in a certain situation allows for change to occur. Thinking about larger issues in our society such as racism and gender bias, it is clear that change has been difficult and prolonged. For example, racism has always been evident in the United States. Even though we have progressed to abolish slavery and grant rights to African Americans, they still face oppression and injustices in everyday life. Not everyone in society is open to a change in roles for minority groups which makes it extremely challenging for any change to occur. Despite a number of people being open to change, and even fighting in favor of it, if everyone involved is not fully invested in these changing roles, problems will arise. It is very common in our world today for us to collectively prevent someone’s role from changing in order to avoid any possibility of embarrassment or overall problems in the social setting. If, as a society we want significant change to occur, we must first understand that our social interactions have a significant impact on our own self-identity. We must learn how our own actions and beliefs influence how others feel and act when we are with them. Continuing to prevent others from changing their role will stop any sort of progress or change from occurring in our society.
chunks.label: Connecting social roles to societal change
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how collective definitions of roles restrict change broadly, applying the concept to larger social issues like racism and gender bias.

nc1bf7712.title: Examining Power and Class in America

chunks.text:
In our society today we have equated money with power and social standings. The more money one has the higher up they are social class wise, and therefore the more power they possess. This thought process has now created a class system in our society. At its core, the class systems can be broken up into three categories: the upper class, the middle class, and the lower class. In Domhoff’s “Power in America,” the upper class is called the “power elite” and they control the institutions of authority and all the power in the society. Gregory Mantsios examines the division of the economy in America in her writing titled “Class in America” as he believes the concept of societal classes is pushed under the rug and not payed attention to.

Mantsios believes that classes aren’t discussed because some people choose to ignore the issue and other are just simply ignorant to it. Throughout the literature Mantsios stresses the fact that the gap between the middle and upper class is growing at an alarming rate. It is also said that class differences have a profound impact on the way people live. Differences in class determine where people live, what jobs they have, who they socialize with, and how they are educated. Mantsios also states that class standings are largely determined at birth. This illustrates the fact that class mobility is extremely rare, meaning that the gap between the middle class and upper class is large and can’t be overcome. Overall, people don’t choose to be a part of the middle class, they are confined to the opportunities that society grants or shields from them because of the social class they are a part of. This ideal creates the gap between social classes which creates divisions in our societal.

Domhoff’s literature focuses on the power elite and how they rule America. Most simply stated, Domhoff believes that the people who have the money hold the most power in society. However, he believes that the power network of the United States is rooted in the economy which means that the CEO’s and big companies of the world yield all the power. Since these institutions hold all the power, the working-class people have the least amount of power. Structure wise, the “upper class” is commonly agreed upon by member of the society to be the “top” or “elite” class, according to Domhoff. Because the social hierarchy gives these people such an exclusive title such members think of themselves as “special” or “superior” to everyone else. Domhoff also says that “the rich” come together to develop institutions by which the members children are socialized into an “upper-class worldview.” This concept can be connected to Mantsios’s ideas as both pieces state that people are born into such high classes which shows that people can only go so far with the opportunities they are given. Because the children of the “elite” are already born into a higher status they are able to achieve so much more than children of the lower class. This head start allows the higher-class children to stay in the “elite” class because they are excelling in their life from the start unlike the children of the lower class.

The collective consciousness also creates a concept of the social hierarchy. In this social hierarchy moving between social classes is a more accepted concept than in Domhoff and Mantsios’s writings. The collective consciousness wants people to disregard the thought of having different social class in its entirety. This concept pushes the idea of having no material conditions, like money or job titles, shape one’s class category. The perfect idea is to have everyone believe that class changes are based on individuals’ abilities and not what material items or titles they have. Overall, class structure should be determined by one’s world views, beliefs, and/or values.

Domhoff and Mantsios believe that the upper class and middle class are separated by a huge gap. People are put into the right class based on their jobs and wealth. It is also thought that people are born into certain social classes and will reside there for life because of the limitations or advantages they receive from their designated class. These thoughts are challenged by the collective consciousness view on social class structure as the consciousness doesn’t believe people are put into different class for the same reasons. The collective consciousness believes that people have the ability to move through the social structure and one’s class position should be based off of them as a person and not their wealth or titles they have.
chunks.label: Social class and power in America
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological readings by Domhoff and Mantsios regarding social class, the power elite, and mobility, comparing their views to concepts of collective consciousness.

chunks.text:
The “Beauty Myth” and its Effects on a Woman’s Life

Before a child is even born, there are already plans and standards created for the child. The standards for each child differs around the sex of the baby. For instance, little girls are raised around the standard that if a boy is mean to you, he likes you - that it is just dandy to absorb insults from a male. Why is it that boys aren’t raised in the same manner? To be constantly thinking about the interactions they have with girls, to live up to women’s standards?

For women, the standards end up being more costly in comparison to men. Women end up sacrificing their lives in order to please a man; to raise a family, to feed the family, clean up after a family, not to go to school, to dress properly, to not act provocatively, to judge others that act out of character - those who are not womanly - it’s seen as a competition. The saying that women live in a man’s world is correct, slowly adapting to change, but is still valid in today’s circumstances. Still valid in my life directly.
chunks.label: Gender standards and the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the differential standards imposed on boys and girls from birth, arguing that women sacrifice their lives to please men and live in a man's world.

chunks.text: My family pushed classic feminine and masculine traits on my siblings and I. My mother didn’t go to college and she met my father at a job. After they got married and had my brother, Jack, my mother was deemed the one to stay home and raise Jack while my father worked. Growing up watching my mother take care of us, I thought that this is what I was supposed to do in life. That taking care of my husband and kids is all that I would do. At the time, I thought that the purpose of life was that - now, I am absolutely terrified of falling into that trap. My mother didn’t have much say during political discourse over dinner; how women should live their lives, what is a respectable woman, how men should be the ‘man of the house,’ etc. My brother usurped these ideologies from my father and my mother didn’t reject anything, encouraging him through silence.
chunks.label: Family gender roles growing up
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up watching her mother stay home and remain silent during political discussions while her father worked and her brother adopted their father's patriarchal ideologies.

chunks.text: Growing up, I was definitely pushed to do girlier things. My neighbor that I had playdates with, Cecelia, decided to stop hanging out with me because I was too boyish. I played soccer for the majority of my life and she thought that I should be partaking in girlier sports like cheerleading. Because I played soccer competitively, I was very fit and muscular. Being muscular, more than some of the boys, I would be seen as masculine and not attractive. Boys in elementary school were not a fan of girls who were confident and beat them in sports or P.E. games. The boys would then draw a liking to the classic feminine girls. No one in elementary school likes playing the part of the odd girl out. That said, I moderated my life to still play soccer and look the way that I did, but I acted more feminine; more flirty, paying my attention to boys and if they liked me or not. As soon as I started acting that way, I started gaining popularity.
chunks.label: Elementary school soccer and feminine expectations
chunks.what_happened: After being rejected by a neighbor for being too boyish and muscular from competitive soccer, the student moderated her behavior in elementary school to act more flirtatious and feminine to gain popularity.

chunks.text: As I got older, things changed. In middle school, I started becoming a woman; I got my period, I developed breasts, I was taller than some of the boys, the whole shabang. Because of this, I matched the current beauty standard that derived from the Kardashian/Jenner family. I became curvy and I was “distracting” the boys in my class. I was told to wear more than our uniform required. When I physically matured, I was socially acceptable by the boys in my grade. I was the hot topic of seventh and eighth grade due to my breasts. Since middle school, I have endured more instances similar and worse to those growing up; however, now that I am in college, I am able to conceptualize them.
chunks.label: Middle school maturation and sexualization
chunks.what_happened: During middle school, the student physically developed early, leading to boys paying attention to her, being told to cover up her uniform, and becoming the subject of school gossip.

chunks.text:
Naomi Wolf and her concept of the “beauty myth” surrounds the reproductiveness of women. The ideology that men go and fight in wars for beautiful women or their current wife(s). Competition between women changes as the beauty standard changes - this includes behavior, women have to behave in such a manner to achieve beauty. The value of women is based on the looks, or beauty of women.

Why are women subjected to this “beauty myth?” The concept of competition between women allows for a hatred to form amongst others that are deemed socially threatening (beautiful). This hatred advocates against forming communities or support of each other, as women. The lack of support and communities formed between women allowed for the dominance of men and manipulation of women. Marketing of preferred images of women or beauty standards of women was used as political ammunition to control women and keep them submissive.

Now that there’s an establishment that men are the reason for the “beauty standard,” the next question is why? What sort of myth is holding men hostage to oppressing women? The only identifiable causes are hegemonic masculinity and the beauty myth. A simple definition of hegemonic masculinity surrounds the stereotype of men being strong, providing for the family (“man of the house”), not showing emotion in front of others, etc. This domination creates a ‘split household’ where women are silenced and are servants of men. Men played the role of maintaining this role of women through abuse, psychological and physical. The continuation of hegemonic masculinity is generational, but also economical. The economy benefits from the underpayment of women.
chunks.label: The beauty myth and hegemonic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Naomi Wolf's concept of the beauty myth and how hegemonic masculinity economically and socially oppresses women and creates intra-female competition.

chunks.text: My family pushed feminine and masculine traits on me and my siblings due to hegemonic masculinity. My mother played the submissive role to my father, and my brother played the generational aspect. My sister and I hope to play the role of not being economically oppressed, of course that is still being worked on as we obtain education. My brother is psychologically a genetic replication of my father, following all of his footsteps - purposefully. My father never wanted to cry in front of me or my family. I have seen him cry once in all my life, he usually releases his emotions through anger. My brother also refuses to cry and has anger management issues. My sister ironically has anger issues as well, but cries more and is still deemed to be “weak.” My mother is emotional and not taken seriously if she is mad, and I am in a similar position to my mother.
chunks.label: Gendered emotional expressions in family
chunks.what_happened: The student observed how hegemonic masculinity manifested at home, with her father and brother suppressing tears and showing anger, while her mother and sister were viewed as emotional or weak.

chunks.text: Being forced to change my personality in elementary school created competition. All the other girls had flirty personalities and their lives revolved around boys. When I decided to join the party, drama started. Hard to believe, but my school maintained the same 60 people from kindergarten to high school. Due to competition identified within the beauty myth, I was considered a threat because more of the boys had crushes on me. The other girls in my class started to spread rumors about me in attempts to make the boys stop liking me. Even as children, the boys hindered the advancement of girls being friends with each other due to their standards. The boys controlled the standards of our grade and anything else was considered undesirable. By growing up this way, learning how to impress or live by a certain standard created by men, causes this domino effect that takes place for the majority of your life. Personally the domino effect didn’t end for me until my junior year of high school.
chunks.label: Elementary school rivalry over boys
chunks.what_happened: When the student changed her behavior to gain attention from boys in elementary school, other girls in her small cohort viewed her as a threat and spread rumors about her.
chunks.people: girls in class, boys in class

chunks.text: Due to the physical maturity that took place in middle school, a newfound value was created. I was valued as a person, as a young woman, due to hormones and development. I was overly sexualized in middle school and distracting because I was wanted and showed means of reproduction. During middle school, and still to this day, there was a certain beauty standard that was starting to be portrayed by the media that I fit into. Physically I am curvy, short, and I look submissive. Those were some physical features that were wanted then and are still wanted now. Because of the personality change I had in fifth grade, that carried on in middle school. Even behaviorally I was wanted. I was never rude to any boy - I let them walk all over me. I was liked by the majority - insinuating that I kept a good reputation for myself. I was innocent, I was pure and they wanted to ruin that. I was considered to be exotic. My behavior and physicality in middle school portrayed me to be the perfect woman. It kept me to be the perfect woman in a man’s eye for a long time. My beauty was accessible to men, fulfilling the beauty myth.
chunks.label: Middle school sexualization and submissive behavior
chunks.what_happened: In middle school, the student was sexualized due to her early physical development and behaved submissively toward boys, letting them walk all over her so she could remain liked.

chunks.text: Overall, women are conditioned to live in society as objects of men. We sleep under the stars known as the beauty myth. We were not the creators of the standards and expectations, we could not change them. We were forced inside this bubble before we were even born by others already oppressed by it. The value of a woman, how successful she is or liked is dependent on how beautiful she is physically and behaviorally. The image of a woman is created by a man and is used as political ammunition to limit women’s advancement in society. Men continue to create standards for women based on their own standards and roles as a man. Women are expected to live in a man’s world, and it’s because of this that women have standards of living that are more costly than men.
chunks.label: Societal objectification of women
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by summarizing how women are conditioned to live as objects of men under the beauty myth and face costly standards created by men.

n2aa4a7ae.title: Social Media and the Beauty Myth

chunks.text:
Social media has developed into a widely used platform of communication and connection between individuals around the world. The accessibility to online platforms has allowed for many adolescents and young women to interact with multiple applications that display the cultural norms on the appearance of females. What are the implications of the perception of beauty and body stereotypes? How does this affect individual body image of young women? Social media portrays the cultural norms and expectations that adolescents and young women are expected to maintain in relation to their physical appearance. The constant society pressure placed on women negatively impacts their physically and psychological well being. While social media is a benefit of access to information and quicker communication, it negatively impacts the identity of women on a consistent basis. This paper discusses how social media impacts promotes the standards of physical attractiveness leading to body dissatisfaction, a negative impact on identity, and increases the likelihood of eating disorders.

The topic of gender is discussed in “The Beauty Myth,” which seeks to reveal the social expectations for women to be physically beautiful. Wolf explains that female liberation is often hindered by a shift towards a feeling of negativity towards physical appearance. Despite women becoming more successful and gaining power throughout the feminist movements, many still felt hindered by feelings of self hatred and physical obsessions. As these ideas became more prevalent in society and through the development of technology, mass media campaigns created a significant force of societal pressure for women to conform to unrealistic standards. Due to the societal pressure, many women become preoccupied with these expectations, leading to the rise of eating disorders and plastic surgery in order to compete with the unattainable standards set by society. The rise of modern society lead to a display of images depicting how women are desired to look, thereby controlling women through ideals and stereotypes.

The pressure for women to conform to societal ideals of aesthetics means that there is constantly an expectation that women are forced to achieve. However, this is an unobtainable reality and leads to an attack on a young woman’s sense of self. This leads to dangerous implications in which young women become constantly dissatisfied with their physical appearance and oftentimes leads to drastic measures. Social media enhances the impact on women’s identity by amplifying the cultural perception of women across all applications such as Facebook, Pinterest, and Instagram. Access to these forms has created a whole new world of interactions, except this time it is through a screen. Being behind a screen distorts the reality of the “beauty” that women are trying to achieve. Societal expectations are amplified because women are conditioned to believe that what is present on the screen is true. While this is oftentimes not the case, women misunderstand that the images on the screen are a distorted sense of reality. Without the understanding that many images presented on social media are often photoshopped or edited, women often believe that they must do what it takes in order to match the image on the screen.

The idea that “beauty is pain” leads to the perception in young women to implement extreme measures in order to combat struggles with self-image. These implications often come from examples of mass media that influence women’s perceptions of their own physical appearance. The “cultural icon of female beauty” for adolescents and women is the “Barbie doll” (Dittman 2009). The mass production of a toy often given to young girls represents an image of an ultra-thin woman. This leads to a desire to have a “thin” and perfect ideal body. As an individual continues to grow up, these ideas are amplified through social media depicting images of real-life women who look identical to the doll they once played with as a child. These ideas are also shown in magazines such as Sports Illustrated and Playboy, in which models epitomize the ideal female body shape. These real-world examples often lead to body dissatisfaction and a negative factor in relation to perceived body image. The idea often leads to women projecting negative feelings towards physical attributes of themselves and comparing themselves to peers who resemble these types of mass media images.

Another impact of body expectations presented through social media is through body image. Women often project a negative self attitude towards their size, shape, and physical aesthetics in relation to the norms presented by society that women are expected to obtain. These emotions are directed by how each woman’s self-perceived physical attributes relate to the negative evaluation of their overall appearance. In relation to the topic of gender, women often are dissatisfied and have a negative body image as they often view themselves as overweight, despite maintaining an average weight level. This perception is discussed in “The Looking Glass Self,” in which James Cooley describes the idea that how you feel about yourself is based on how you think others perceive you. Through social media, societal norms and expectations often lead to judgements on others that do not match the ideal standard of beauty. As mentioned previously, social media exists as a screen distorting that distorts the realities of life. Since the perceptions of oneself depends on the social context one is in, because social media translates these negative connotations of body image, women feel as though they do not conform to societal norms and therefore have a negative image of themselves.

Another aspect of social media that creates a negative impact on women’s identity is that apps design feeds that reflect individual preferences specific to each user. This has developed the capacity to bring the user into a new world, separate from reality. Because social media has become personal and sites shape to each individual user, one who is likely to look at models on Instagram is likely going to see those types of images everytime the app is accessed. This leads to an obsessive quality in which the user feels as though they should be engaged with the app constantly and indirectly, creating a negative impact on self worth. In addition, social media involves following peers, acquaintances, and influencers. While seeing models presented with a “perfect” body often leads to women feeling less happy with themselves, however, seeing individuals you know embody the societal norms often has a greater impact on negative self image. Social media has become the domain of peers in which women find it functional to compare themselves to others, likely those they often see in the hallways at school. The idea of comparison in these situations often leads to a negative affect. Everytime one posts on Instagram, yet the post has fewer “likes” when compared to others, one often feels as though they are not enough which decreases self worth. This leads to a poor perception of self as one sees themselves based on what others might think and leads to destruction in their identity.

A study conducted in 1997 discussed the idea of a “model trap,” which proposed that young girls often compare their physical attractiveness with that of advertising models. Being challenged by unrealistic expectations impacts self-perceptions of physical attractiveness and leads to individuals having a desire to become models. These concepts are often implemented in advertisements and tv commercials that convey the idea that female bodies are considered “objects” and their physical beauty determines their overall value. This idea is related to three viewpoints in which women find themselves when struggling with body image issues. The first is self evaluation, the judgment of value of one’s abilities and personal traits. Because women consider models to have “superior” physical attractiveness, one often compares themselves to individuals who are shaped to represent the ideal body image. This directly relates to negative self-perceptions and self-esteem. Secondly, one may focus on self-improvement. This is defined through an individual’s inspiration to better oneself through a particular attribute. Even as a child, individuals often compared themselves to a peer when learning how to perform tasks or reach a certain goal. This translates to women working to reach the same weight as a friend or comparing with others to reach a goal rather than focusing on their individual health and well-being. The last viewpoint is self enhancement, which is an individual's attempt to maintain positive views of oneself to protect self-esteem. These comparisons to others are often made in a downward connotation, meaning that individuals put down others in order to make them feel better about themselves. This is a very negative concept as many individuals often cyberbully others through social media because there is a screen blocking them from the hurtful words displayed. The response of self greatly impacts the extent of the negative nature women feel when they are fighting the battle of body dissatisfaction.

Another implication of the effects of social media and its negative impacts on women is the development of eating disorders. While this is not a common result for most women, those who exhibit vulnerable characteristics such as low self-esteem, depression, perfectionism and internalization of physical expectations. This leads to an amplification in the desire to reach the “thin” level of ideal physical characteris. These negative thoughts can potentially lead to eating disorders in which women maintain unhealthy lifestyles hoping that they can reach the ideal body type. This can be found through the refusal to eat and maintain the appropriate body weight for age and height. Others often experience patterns of binging followed by fasting and overexercising to lessen caloric intake. These unhealthy lifestyles often stem from the unrealistic body image type displayed on social media.

In conclusion, the online world of social media often influences the self perception of women in terms of physical appearance. As new technology continues to advance, powerful industries have created a massive impact on culture to reinforce these ideas of the “perfect” body. These articles show that “The Beauty Myth'' explains the underlying relationship of women with societal expectations to be physically beautiful. Throughout history, women have been subjected to a system of beliefs that controls women into maintaining aesthetic qualities that are unobtainable. The role of social media enhances these psychological and physical hardships on women by establishing a force of cultural pressures women have to maintain. Because of these ideals, women are willing to go to extreme measures and even maintain unhealthy lifestyles in order to achieve a “perfect body.” These implications often lead to severe negative effects on women’s mental health and sense of self worth.

Sources

Perloff, R.M. Social Media Effects on Young Women’s Body Image Concerns: Theoretical Perspectives and an Agenda for Research. Sex Roles 71, 363–377 (2014). https://doi.org/10.1007/s11199-014-0384-6

Cusumano, D. L., & Thompson, J. K. (1997). Body image and body shape ideals in magazines: Exposure, awareness, and internalization. Sex Roles, 37(9), 701-721. Retrieved from https://search-proquest-com.liblink.uncw.edu/scholarly-journals/body-image-shape-ideals-magazines-exposure/docview/225375527/se-2?accountid=14606

Martin, M. C., & Gentry, J. W. (1997). Stuck in the model trap: The effects of beautiful models in ads on female pre-adolescents and adolescents. Journal of Advertising, 26(2), 19-33. Retrieved from https://search-proquest-com.liblink.uncw.edu/scholarly-journals/stuck-model-trap-effects-beautiful-models-ads-on/docview/236566548/se-2?accountid=14606

Cash, T. F., Ancis, J. R., & Strachan, M. D. (1997). Gender attitudes, feminist identity, and body images among college women. Sex Roles, 36(7), 433-447. Retrieved from https://search-proquest-com.liblink.uncw.edu/scholarly-journals/gender-attitudes-feminist-identity-body-images/docview/225383519/se-2?accountid=14606

Garner, David M., et al. “Cultural Expectations of Thinness in Women.” Psychological Reports, vol. 47, no. 2, Oct. 1980, pp. 483–491, doi:10.2466/pr0.1980.47.2.483.
chunks.label: Social media's impact on female body image
chunks.what_happened: The student presents an academic essay and references examining how social media and cultural beauty standards negatively impact young women's body image and self-esteem.

chunks.text:
‘The Looking-Glass self’ is a biological pseudo-mechanism that prevents us from truly fulfilling our natural existential function of social. These reactions, natural or not end up setting humans more complex and true relationships back due to the tendency to authenticate a more consumable or pleasurable outward persona. It ends up preventing true connection within our groups, also known as fulfilling our existential function to form true social connections.

The Looking-Glass self is the biological tendency to rearrange one’s true self into a more socially accepted person. People shape their perceptions of themselves on how other individuals or groups perceive their outward persona. This habit can make an entirely new personality for a person. Changing small or big aspects of someone’s character to then perfect the outermost persona is essentially basing yourself on a lie or reaction. Thus, this persona is inherently fragile, seeing that it can be built up by lies and false persona. This is the explanation for how people nowadays find they’re different around different types of people. Everyone finds a way to adjust to different groups, strangers, authority figures versus friends, and being alone. Different groups require different necessities, whether it be an honest person, a comedian, a supportive friend, a worker, etc. These different necessities are observable to humans. They pick up on these social queues and in turn, adapt to that group. Some people are better than others at this, practically chameleon-like with their ability to jump from group to group and fit in seamlessly. People also find themselves being naturally withdrawn, calm, polite, and the best version of themselves according to the society that specific person was raised in. Another clear distinction of attitude is the reaction of peers versus an authority figure. When a person is amongst peers they trust or feel they can relate to, they relax in turn. Very laid back and calm in response to their surrounding stimuli. Now at the other end of that spectrum is the authority figure. A person’s attitude will become rigid, perfected, and attentive. This is another reaction nobody thinks about, it is drummed into you at an early age and only progresses clearer as one matures. Finally, there’s being alone. This is where all the other relationships combine and form what one perceives as the true ‘them.’ People will combine all of their roles in their lives, or their multiple mirrors formed by their social reaction to determine their true self. In reality, this is solely the culmination of reactions to certain social stimuli and can change based on minute situational alterations. Each of these reactions are all very natural; they are practically reflexes to the masses of people across the world. Some differentiation in mannerisms is obviously common and possible but the majority conforms to their instincts.

“The existential function of social” is humanity’s unique tendency to be more aware of social surroundings and the meaning of life. It’s the search for the meaning of life but also knowing that they are not likely to find it. There are many subdivisions that apply to this function, such as collection collaboration capacity, individual vs group thinking, and group morals and values. Humanity has the habit of finding a group, a social setting to belong to. This is the “collective collaboration capacity”, an ability in which humans naturally organize themselves within groups and find their places. When people find their groups or those whom they align with, they adapt to group thinking. It becomes a group affair, the exchange of knowledge, habits, cautionary information, and more. This can also implement a routine for group members. The final aspect of this function is conforming to the group’s values, morals, and definition of meaning. When groups find each other, they work together. They help each other piece together aspects of the world into their meanings. Each person’s experience gets put into the group and in turn, affects the final product of the group. The culmination of all of these subgroups within this function has numerous benefits such as taking stress off an individual, helping the mental function of an individual, putting a mind at peace, and having a sense of community for a social creature. When humans are solely individual and have to continuously function alone, this puts stress on the brain. The brain constantly interprets surrounding stimuli and is constantly working to understand and take in everything around them. Being on high alert 24/7 is a huge burden on the brain. This coincides with mental function in the sense that the brain being by itself and taking on that much work continuously will also tire the brain out. Its ability to function, let alone function well, is better within a group. Loneliness tires the brain and body out quickly. The group takes this burden from the individual. Finally, there’s putting the mind at peace from the sense of community. The group helps put the individual’s mind at ease by determining meaning along with giving each group member a sense of purpose and belonging. Since humans are social creatures, they find peace while fulfilling that need. The feeling that they know what they are doing for the group is good and worth it. Meaning is needed to define reality and the group aids that necessity.

The problem with defining oneself based on puzzle-piecing one’s persona only around the reactions to different social settings is that many aspects of a person will get lost. Such aspects include the material self and pure ego. The material self-comprised of physical aspects or possessions that you identify with can be lost in different groups. Those pieces of oneself will deteriorate away, leaving a hole in one’s persona. The other, is pure ego, the soul or essence of a person. This central component of a person is lost when outward perception is the only thing taken into consideration. People will lose these aspects and more to adapt to a group where they feel they belong. Although this is a natural process, it is also a cheat code that eventually can set you back in more complex and developed relationships. Changing small aspects of oneself and then later being more comfortable to then reveal the true desires, opinions, etc. can confuse the dynamic between the individual and the group. Collective Collaboration Capacity being where humans naturally find a place, due to their constructed personality (looking-glass self) can be set back when one adapts to a group or person, the relationship has that honeymoon phase or that start of a friendship, you change small aspects of yourself to better fit with that person or group dynamic. It’s a cheat that ends up pushing you further away from those who can truly become close to you.
