Because in the end those outward personas become chipped away, leaving the true core of a person’s nature.

In conclusion, the attempt to form true social connections is hindered by the instinct to form the best outward version of yourself to others. So, people should attempt to disregard their instincts to falsify the outside and be their truest selves. Let the culmination of their other selves beyond the looking-glass self shine.
chunks.label: The Looking-Glass self and social connections
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological concepts including the Looking-Glass self, the existential function of social, and how adapting outward personas affects genuine human connection.

chunks.text: For many people, getting hired at their first job is one of the most exciting experiences. You’ve filled out the application, put down all your assets, recommendations, and now, you await a response. Getting the phone call that you’ve received your desired position makes you feel accomplished, especially while juggling high school and extracurriculars, and you realize that all your hard work has paid off. Receiving the position initially is impressive, while typically you are competing against others, however, maintaining your position at the same workplace is even more impressive than emerging victorious throughout the hiring process.
chunks.label: getting hired and keeping a job
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the excitement of getting hired for a first job and the challenge of maintaining employment while in high school.

chunks.text: I have worked at my school’s after school program for four years throughout highschool. Most of my tasks once I clock in after the final school bell rings include helping children with homework and communicating with parents over the phone or in person while simultaneously making sure children aren’t shoving each other down while they play. Because of my many years of experience, I was able to participate in training new workers, and having some input on new applicants to the program. Recently, I discovered shocking news that is unsettling to myself and should be unsettling to society’s collective consciousness (Durkheim) as well. Although I have worked with this program longer than any of my other coworkers, I am getting paid $1.20 less than some of my fellow coworkers. This information truly puzzled me, and I began to ask myself “Why am I receiving less pay for all the time I have spent here, when I’ve been here the longest and have barely received a raise?” After conversing with the only other female that works alongside me, we realized that the two of us were being paid the exact same amount, while our male coworkers were receiving $1.20 higher. Why are the women of this establishment being treated unequally while possessing either the same tasks as the males, or even more than them?
chunks.label: discovering gender wage disparity
chunks.what_happened: While working at an after-school program, the student discovered she was being paid less than her male coworkers despite having worked there longer, learning that she and the only other female coworker were earning less.

chunks.text: The only disgusting conclusion that I have been able to muster regarding this situation is that I have been “other[ed]” (de Beauvoir) inside my workplace without even realizing it. As de Beauvoir discusses in her essay, “The Second Sex”, about women being “other[ed]” throughout history. Throughout this essay, she criticizes the collective consciousness of society, and how with regards to women, the same beliefs about female inferiority have been collectively held since the beginning of time, starting with religion. De Beauvoir quotes Poulain de la Barre, who discusses how male Jews thank God during their prayers that they were not born a woman. This prayer places so many questions in my mind. Why would these men not want to be a woman so badly that they thank their God for being a male? Is it because they realize as a whole, men are subjugating women?
chunks.label: de Beauvoir and the othering of women
chunks.what_happened: The student connects her workplace experience to Simone de Beauvoir's writings on how women are 'othered' and subjugated in society's collective consciousness.

chunks.text: After finding out this information, I immediately went to my boss in case the unequal pay was a mistake, or perhaps something that was accidentally overlooked. I approached my female boss after work, asking to speak with her in private with the hope that I could resolve this issue occurring at my workplace. However, to my astonishment, the conversation was shut down immediately when I expressed that I was inquiring about unequal pay. I was not even given the opportunity to express my thoughts on the matter, and was told to not discuss my pay with my coworkers again. During this conversation with my boss, I saw a side of her that I had not seen before. This conversation proved to me in a more personal light how the collective consciousness can truly transform a person’s belief, and this especially shocked me since my boss is a woman. I truly would have thought she could relate to me, and realize something unfair was happening, however I was proven wrong by this conversation.
chunks.label: confronting boss about unequal pay
chunks.what_happened: The student spoke privately with her female boss to ask about the unequal pay, but her boss immediately shut down the conversation and told her not to discuss pay.

chunks.text: Afterwards, I felt defeated. I felt as if my voice didn’t matter, but I recognized that my rights were not being respected. I could not figure out why, and I didn’t understand why me not getting the pay I deserved was being shoved under the rug. I could only assume that I was being paid less because I am a woman. I do my job, arguably better than my other coworkers, and never cause any trouble. De Beauvoir quotes Montaigne in her text, “It is easier to accuse one sex then to excuse the other”. I believe that it is easier to punish female coworkers inside the workplace than to change the ideals of the collective consciousness. It is more convenient for those in control of the ideas held in the collective consciousness to allow society to punish women in every aspect of their lives.
chunks.label: reflecting on boss's reaction and gender bias
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on feeling defeated and silenced, considering how the collective consciousness makes it easier to punish women than to address inequality.

chunks.text: The issue of unequality for women is not a new topic in society’s collective consciousness. There have always been laws, “traditions”, or ideals that have subjugated women, and there was no way for women to defend themselves. Like in my situation, I felt as if there was no way I could defend myself. After being shut down by my boss, I contemplated giving up or not. I feared that me speaking my feelings again would lead to me losing my job. Half of me wanted to stay quiet, but the other half knew that staying quiet is what my workplace wanted me to do. They wanted to get away with the inequality occurring, and not have to change their beliefs about equal pay.
chunks.label: fear of retaliation and societal inequality
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the history of women's subjugation and her internal conflict over whether to speak up again or stay silent out of fear of losing her job.

chunks.text: Oddly enough, in my history class, we were discussing feminism during the time these events were happening. I expressed what was happening to my entire class, and my male teacher, who was enraged by the fact I was getting paid less. My other coworker who was also getting paid less was in this class, and she told her side of the story to him as well. What angered my teacher the most was the fact that when my boss was approached, she denied my request. After talking with us in private after class, he told us he was going to the principal to discuss this matter because she overlooked the summer camp and after school program. He recognized the inequality and admitted it, while my boss refused to.
chunks.label: discussing pay in history class
chunks.what_happened: During a history class discussion on feminism, the student and her female coworker shared their unequal pay situation, prompting their male teacher to report the issue to the principal.
chunks.people: classmates, male teacher, female coworker, boss, principal

chunks.text: A few weeks go by, and my boss approaches my friend and I, asking to talk after work. Honestly, I assumed she was going to fire us, and tell us that we crossed some sort of boundary by discussing our pay amongst ourselves and with faculty members. However, this meeting truly resolved nothing. The only thing my boss was able to offer us is that she would talk with our administrator, and see what she could do about getting our issue resolved. This did not give me much hope, because I was not sure if this would actually happen, or if she would even attempt to resolve this issue . However, the fact that my teacher had gone to the principal about our issue did give me some sort of hope that this could possibly be resolved, or that it would act as an example for future females in the workplace at school. Even after all of this, I was still left with the question: Why is this happening? Why are women being treated unfairly, and why is no one doing anything about it?
chunks.label: follow-up meeting with boss
chunks.what_happened: A few weeks later, the boss called the student and her coworker into a meeting, offering only to speak with an administrator, which left the pay issue unresolved.

chunks.text: There is no found explanation as to why women and men are treated unequally in society. People might say “that’s just how it has always been”, but for me, that is not an explanation at all. Simply saying “that’s how life works” just seems like a lousy excuse for people that do not want to fight the beliefs of the collective consciousness and truly dissect why these types of things are happening to women. De Beauvoir quotes Dorothy Parker in The Second Sex, “Men as well as women, should be regarded by human beings”. There should be no superior or comparison, when in reality, we are all human. De Beauvoir says herself, “[Women] do not authentically assume a subjective attitude”, but it is something that society has conformed to believing themselves. It is evident that my boss has conformed to these ideas about women because she sees no problem with paying my friend and I less than the males that we work with.
chunks.label: lack of explanation for gender inequality
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on societal excuses for gender inequality using de Beauvoir's concepts and notes that her boss conformed to these beliefs.

chunks.text: The issue of my friend and I’s unequal pay was never resolved. We were never provided with more information as to why we were being paid unequally, and we were never spoken to about it again. After this past summer, I quit working at the summer camp. I refuse to work someplace where I have dedicated more time and energy than any of my other coworkers, and still be denied an explanation as to why I am being denied the pay I deserve. If this issue was due to a behavioral problem, or my inability to provide work to the program’s standards, I would have been asked to leave instead of getting paid less. I would have been spoken to about my inadequacy for the job, and been asked to leave. I almost wish that this had instead been the reason I was receiving a lesser pay, but because this issue was never resolved and the response from my boss when I first approached her, I know that I was being paid less because I am a woman. It was almost too coincidental that the two women at the program were being paid less than the men for it to not have been the reason. I was “othered” in my workplace, then refused an explanation. I can also infer that this situation was gender based because my male teacher was able to bring attention to this situation, but I was not, when I was actively being victimized and “othered”, yet my opinion was not enough to cause a change. De Beauvoir comments throughout her text that there really has never been an explanation as to why the collective consciousness supports the idea that women are inferior, and every time that there is an attempt at an explanation, the explanation has been “dictated by men’s interest”. This statement in itself raises too many questions for me to even begin to discuss, but supports the statement that those in the superior position, which just so happens to be men, are able to dictate the gap between men and women.
chunks.label: unresolved issue and resigning
chunks.what_happened: The student explains that the pay issue was never resolved, leading her to quit the summer camp, and reflects on gender-based power dynamics.

chunks.text: The idea that men and women are unequal will not change until the beliefs of the collective consciousness change. It is this reason that women are still being paid less, not receiving equal job opportunities, and our rights are being thrown around in congress by men who do not have a say. The inequality between genders is an ongoing argument fueled by the collective consciousness that is trapped in a vicious cycle.
chunks.label: the cycle of collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how gender inequality remains trapped in a vicious cycle until collective consciousness changes.

chunks.text: When I turned in my two weeks notice, I informed my boss I was quitting due to my rights not being fulfilled at this workplace. I hope that in the future, my step towards equality for women will be appreciated, and not viewed as a cowardly exit to those in society, and it will force them to question the catalysts that led to my resignation.
chunks.label: submitting two weeks notice
chunks.what_happened: The student submitted her two weeks' notice to her boss, explaining that she was resigning because her rights were not being respected.

chunks.text:
Will Men ever see Women as their Equals? Women have been making significant strides to balance workplace inequalities, as we will always deal with the fact that Men will always be paid more. The top female dominated professions are relating to childcare or aiding a medical professional. The fact that many top female-dominated professions are related to childcare or medical aid is certainly interesting, and it speaks to the societal expectations placed on women to be caregivers. Men will continue to see Women as the “other sex” as they consider themselves to be alpha in the workplace and will promote the ideology of the “beauty myth” how women should act, dress, work, take care of the children, etc.

In the workplace, women are frequently under pressure to conform to specific beauty norms, such as being slender, having flawless skin, and donning cosmetics. This can pose a major obstacle since they may believe that meeting these criteria is essential to earning respect or climbing the career ladder. Furthermore, promoting the idea of the "beauty myth" can result in women being objectified and seen as desirable objects, rather than multifaceted individuals with distinct viewpoints and innovative concepts.
chunks.label: Gender inequality and the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on workplace inequalities, expectations for women to be caregivers, and how the beauty myth objectifies women.

chunks.text: I have worked many small part-time jobs, ice cream scooper, server, babysitter, volleyball coach, feed shop warehouse worker, farm hand, and most recently a metal worker for a golf company. I never really thought much about my past work experiences and specific interactions I had, but after reading the beauty myth and the article about othering I quickly reflected and understood what was happening and how it was playing into my life.
chunks.label: Reflecting on past work experiences
chunks.what_happened: The student lists various past jobs and explains how course readings prompted reflection on them.

chunks.text: I was sixteen at the time and had applied for a part time job at a local feed store as a warehouse hand. I was raised on Black Angus Family Farm, so I am used to labor intensive jobs, and throwing feed bags and hay bales. Upon turning my application into the owner of the feed store who was a middle-aged man, he quickly questioned me and asked me if I meant to apply for the warehouse position. I told him yes, that I was a farm hand, and I would prefer that to be opposed to being behind a counter all day. He in turn asked me if I could lift a feed bag; I demonstrated by lifting a 75-pound bag of grass seed. The owner simply just smiled at me and said I would look better behind the counter and unless I worked the counter, he would not offer me a job because the warehouse is for men, and it would not be right to have a “little girl” back there.
chunks.label: Applying for a feed store job
chunks.what_happened: At age sixteen, the student applied for a warehouse job at a feed store and demonstrated lifting a 75-pound bag, but the owner refused to hire her for the warehouse because she was female.

chunks.text: I faced a similar challenge when I worked in the metals department of a golf company where I was the only female among male colleagues. During my interview, they asked if I was okay with getting my hands dirty and emphasized that the job required physical labor. Despite this, I was hired. Working there opened my eyes to how men think and talk about women, sometimes as objects or in ways I never imagined. For instance, while washing a metal pan, a colleague told me to stay in the kitchen because that is where I belonged, and to come in only when the real work was done, so I could clean up the mess, and that I look too good to be doing dirty work. Recently, we had a project with 650 metal ball markers, I completed three in the time it took my male colleagues to finish one. They make jokes about needing to give me directions on where to drop off shipments, even asking if they needed to draw me a map, because they know women are dictionally challenged. I am even reminded of how to do basic tasks I perform every day by my supervisor. Despite their belittling comments, I know my worth and am confident in my abilities.
chunks.label: Working at a golf company
chunks.what_happened: The student worked in the metals department of a golf company, where male colleagues and a supervisor made sexist remarks, belittled her capabilities, and told her to stay in the kitchen.

chunks.text:
The feed store experience highlights the issue of othering and gender discrimination in the workplace. My gender was the store owners only grab. He made assumptions about my abilities and suitability for the job. The owner actively stereotyped me and made assumptions about women's competence and value in the workplace. After reading Naomi Wolfs “The beauty Myth” which says that women are constantly pressured to conform to narrow and unrealistic standards of beauty, it made me reflect on these experiences, which can have negative effects on our self-esteem, health, and overall well-being. This myth is perpetuated by various industries, including fashion, beauty, and media, and serves to reinforce gender inequality by objectifying women and limiting their opportunities in society.

The concepts that I connected to these puzzles are othering and the beauty myth. Othering is the social concept of viewing or treating people or groups are different or less valuable than oneself or one's own group. Othering This can lead to people diminishing or belittling other groups and people, simply just because they are different. Othering can happen due to differences of race, gender, sexuality, nationality, religion, and many other characteristics. Othering contributes to social inequities and is a form of discrimination. The beauty myth is the idea that women are frequently under pressure to conform to specific beauty norms, such as being slender, having flawless skin, and donning cosmetics, just to achieve proper status in society. These concepts relate to my work experiences because the experiences described in both examples relate to the beauty myth and othering because they prove how society has constructed certain gender roles and expectations that limit women's opportunities and potential.

In my first puzzle the feed store owner assumed that I could not handle the physical demands of the job simply because of my gender, and even denied me of the job because I am woman. I am other, despite my experience. He told me that I “would look better behind the counter.” This is an example of the beauty myth limiting opportunities for women such as myself and othering me as weaker or less capable than men in physical labor.

In my second puzzle, my male colleagues at the golf company treated me the only female employee differently, making sexist comments and belittling my abilities, even when I proved that I was capable and efficient in my work. This is another example of othering and the beauty myth, as the men in this case saw the me as an outsider, an object to be looked at or a lower-class worker, rather than an equal colleague with skills and abilities.

The problem with othering and the beauty myth is that it is deeply ingrained in our society and in the way we view others. These concepts also play a role in how we view and value each other in the workplace. Even though women have come a long way in society in terms of equal opportunity and rights, we are still not valued or view the same way men are when it comes to the workplace. Society has beliefs and stereotypes that women are not capable of doing labor intensive jobs.

The beauty myth reinforces the idea that the value of a women lies in their physical appearance, regardless of their skill, intelligence, or abilities. The myth also holds the idea that women should be “seen and not heard.” The myth is reflected by social media, advertising, pop culture, because all of these portray women as objects for men's desire, rather than personal individuals, with interests, skills, intelligence, and personalities.

As you can see from my personal experience women that choose to pursue a career in male dominated fields, will often be subjected to discrimination, harassment, and stereotyping. In my experience I was denied a job opportunity because I was the “other” sex, so women might be subjected to loss job opportunities, promotions, and we also may be paid less than our male colleagues.

The issues of othering and the beauty myth are interconnected, and both contribute to the discrimination and belittling of women in society but especially in the workplace. I hope as a woman one day we will challenge these beliefs and stereotypes to create a more equal workplace for ourselves. I also hope that women who work in male dominated fields know that they are there because of their skills, not their beauty. Worth does not derive from beauty. One day we should have a society where people are valued and respected for themselves regardless of gender or appearance.
chunks.label: Analysis of othering and the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student connects the feed store and golf company experiences to the sociological concepts of othering and the beauty myth, concluding with hopes for a more equal society.

n17596984.title: Examining Systemic Racism and White Privilege

chunks.text:
Do all lives matter? One may answer, without hesitation, and out of the goodness in their heart, “Yes, of course they do”. However, ask a black American who avoids certain neighborhoods in fear of being harassed and killed in the year of 2021 what they think. Ask any member of a Native American tribe, that is still alive and active today, and living on a reservation what they think. Ask the Mexican American children who are separated from their parents because ice arrested them, what they think? To say all lives matter would imply that there is equal respect and care for citizens of every race. Yet, there is not and there never was. At least not in the United States.

It may be hard to believe that racial injustice as we all learned about in history class is still occurring even though we may not experience it personally. Even so, it is unfair to discredit racial minorities and claim that they are not oppressed if one is not aware of it. Therefore, the statement, “all lives matter” is an invalid one that does not allow for racial minority groups to speak up about their issues and educate the public. Whether the protests are peaceful with sadness or violent with anger, the feelings of oppressed groups are still valid. The root behind most issues facing minority groups in the United States is race and the existence of White privilege. Throughout this essay, I will further explain what White privilege is, its’ origin in the United States of America, the ways in which it is still present today and how it puts racial minority groups at a societal disadvantage.

White privilege refers to the societal bias set towards White citizens. Being a white U.S citizen means that there is a systematic advantage to ensure that white people are being given first priority for most aspects in life. This may mean being hired over a person of color regardless of job qualifications, being the majority race at an institution due to historical segregation and racial biases, and having politicians and laws cater solely to one’s own demographic. Such things create cases of injustice for people of color who have been subject to lesser opportunities and un-deservingness.

Racism is a motive behind white privilege as most white Americans may fear that the progression of rights and opportunities for another racial group or demographic may mean less for them. Therefore, as long as wealthy, white citizens have been in a position of power, they have been able to restrict the number of rights and power given to people of color. Simply put, systemic racism created white privilege, and white privilege enforces oppression on other racial groups. The problem is that this issue has existed for as long as the U.S has existed. Therefore, we as a society have to dissect how racism became institutionalized and identify the ways that these practices have evolved with time.

In the United states, race has always been heavily distinguished. One was either white or “colored”. Even as a person of color, some individuals experienced more humane treatment with being visibly “white passing”. A clear indicator of racial privilege is the way in which ethnically ambiguous people were able to bypass racial discrimination. In being a racially divided nation, there was a lack of education on different cultures. Therefore, society functioned off of their knowledge on ignorance and stereotypes.

The United States was built on colonization and racial division. According to the Stanford Encyclopedia, colonialism is, “a practice of domination, which involves the subjugation of one people to another...colonialism usually involved the transfer of population to a new territory, where the arrivals lived as permanent settlers while maintaining political allegiance to their country of origin” (Kohn, Margaret; Reddy, Kavita 2017). The issue mentioned in the definition here is that colonialism shares similarities with imperialism which involves taking over and taking command of. The similar trait between colonialism and imperialism is that it involves political and economic control over a dependent territory.

Not only were European settlers colonizing indigenous lands, but they were also taking control over the indigenous people. This practice instilled a supremacist mindset as European migrants used dominance to enforce their culture on other ethnic groups. White supremacy is the mindset and belief that white people are the superior race. This mindset controlled who the U.S government felt was deserving and undeserving of certain rights. Therefore, first priority and privilege were granted to white citizens.

The early European settlers went on to force the Native American tribes to either conform to a Eurocentric lifestyle or to live in designated terrain so not to interfere with the settlers. This portion of U.S history instilled the belief that Native Americans were living incorrectly and that they were “savages”. Thousands of Native people were killed and subject to live within specified parameters on their own native continent. In prioritizing the European settlers over the native people, it left an eternal stain on the way in which our country operates today. Native reservations continue to decrease in size and lose access to clean water as the United States Government takes more of the land for construction and oil pipelines.

Another historical event that influenced race and led to white privilege is slavery. The enslavement of African people further supported the idea of white supremacy because it permitted settlers and early white citizens to treat black people as animals and objects. Black people were chained up like prisoners, bought and sold like cattle, separated from their loved ones, starved, and physically abused. Some received a very small compensation to buy themselves out of slavery with time and others were only compensated with another day of life. Those who escaped slavery were hunted down and returned to slavery or sometimes even killed. Slavery created this idea that it was necessary to punish black people and limit their rights so that they could not live a life of equal quality to that of white people. Even following the abolishment of slavery, black Americans continued to be beaten, wrongfully imprisoned and lynched as “free” U.S citizens.

In discussing Jim Crow and the civil rights movement, it is apparent that in the 20th century, black people were still being treated unfairly. They were forced to attend segregated churches, schools, and restaurants. There were, and still are many individuals who do not feel that black people, or POC in general are deserving of a qualitative life. Therefore, cases of implementing white privilege continue to occur and will not cease until they are called publicly acknowledged and parties are held accountable.

Knowing the origins of racial discrimination and white supremacy provides a foundation for understanding institutionalized racism and white privilege. The article, Raciontologies: Rethinking Anthropological Accounts of Institutional Racism and Enactments of White Supremacy in the United States explains the concept of racism in both the individual and institutional sense. The article favors the belief that racism in the United States is an institutionalized issue. It states that racism is a ‘system of structural inequalities’ and a ‘historical process’”. The article makes note of the fact that the racial conflict that racial minorities face today started during the colonial times and has not ceased but instead evolved. The author references Avram Bornstein in explaining that, “patterns in housing policies that (re)produce segregation and socioeconomic stratification, as well as education policies that structure school funding in relation to local property taxes and impose high‐stakes assessments. In all of these cases, “‘institutional policies operate with or without conscious or unconscious bias, although there is a reinforcing connection between the two’”.

In observing the existence of white privilege today, A modern example of white privilege is prevalent in politics. As mentioned in the article White Privilege, White Poverty: Reckoning with Class and Race in America. The article uses the 206 presidential election to explain the mindset behind those who still enforce a white supremacist and white privilege mindset. During former president Donald Trump’s campaign, he tried to promote the idea of restoring a “great America” in creating more job opportunities for U.S citizens while simultaneously removing illegal immigrants who were “stealing” these job opportunities away. Trump’s election generated four years of meritocracy. With white Americans being the majority population, such ideals seemed only to benefit their demographic. The wealthy and the white working class. Furthermore, it established a period of blatant hatred towards people of color as they were the targeted out to be the obstacle for the success of white Americans. The article explained it as being “social status anxiety” and “racialized economics” which is the fear of one’s own demographic falling behind with the progression of another demographic (Blacksher, Valles 2021). Therefore, the election and time period following brought attention to the fact that citizens based their presidential vote on personal advantage and that white Americans and politicians purposefully sought out to suppress minority groups. Therefore, reinforcing institutionalized racial prejudice.

In sending ICE to track down “illegal immigrants”, a stigma was created against Mexican Americans. In not openly supporting the Black Lives Matter movement, supporters of former president Donald Trump disapproved with the movement and protested against it labeling protestors and supporters as “thugs “in the president’s words. His responses alone, as a white person in power is enough to influence his followers to inflict disdain towards ethnic minority groups. This disdain translates into action when laws and decisions are made in favor of white people and against people of color ultimately permitting white privilege.

A second modern day example would be in healthcare. Racial health disparities are the differences in statistics between white and nonwhite individuals with mortality, health insurance coverage and access to healthcare facilities. The article, An Empirical Analysis of White privilege, Social Position and Health discuses a study done on predominantly White neighborhoods of differently social class. The purpose behind the study was to determine if there was a correlation between health and inequality. The speculation comes from the fact that predominantly white neighborhoods typically have access to healthful resources while black neighborhoods feature sources that are detrimental to one’s health such as liquor stores and even fast-food chains. Therefore, the experiment done through survey questions, would determine if predominantly white neighborhoods experienced better health on the basis of economic status and neighborhood diversity.

The study found that in some respects there was a decreased welcome for black residents in the neighborhoods when it came to having high dentalcare and healthcare (Kwate, Goodman 2014). The article concluded that in doing the experiment, participants form the lesser diverse neighborhoods may not have answered truthfully about how welcoming their neighborhood would be towards black people due to their personal knowledge on how likely it realistically is for a black family to move in. Furthermore, the question of whether the participants were answering because they and their neighbors acknowledge the existence of racism is still questionable. The experiment not only showed the prominence of better healthcare for racially exclusive communities, but also that there is ignorance on the part of the white neighbors in terms of how welcoming their neighborhoods are to black people, given that there was only a small population of black people living in each of the neighborhoods.

Acknowledgement is a crucial part in abolishing white privilege because it first brings the issue to light and allows those involved to put a stop to it. As Peggy McIntosh mentions in White Privilege: Unpacking The Invisible Knapsack, “As we in Women’s Studies work to reveal male privilege and ask men to give up some of their power, so one who writes about having white privilege might must ask, “having described it, what will I do to lessen or end it?” (McIntosh 1988). It is not enough for people of color to speak out on their own struggles. It is crucial for white citizens as well to hold themselves and their peers accountable. For as long as the United States has dealt with racism and the existence of white privilege, it is evident that the issue needs to be addressed from the inside. As Dr. McIntosh explains, while they were not being actively racist, they grew up unaware of how society catered to them as a white individual. By simply educating oneself and passing the same information along, white citizens can help advance and secure the social rights for POC. This would guarantee them fair opportunities at improved physical health, education, job opportunities and overall safety. This country was originally designed with only White people in mind; therefore, the former laws and practices have become outdated with the increasingly diverse population. U.S citizens of all ethnic backgrounds must share the collective effort of speaking out on racial discrimination and holding oneself accountable for benefiting off of racial privilege if we want to coexist in a peaceful America.
chunks.label: White privilege and institutional racism in America
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the concept of White privilege, its historical origins in colonialism and slavery, and modern examples in politics and healthcare based on academic articles.

n8483c143.title: Critiquing the Rise of Artificial Intelligence

chunks.text:
Technology is on the rise in today’s modern world, aiming to conquer and work its way deeper into the everyday lives of human beings. There will always be technological advancements in the works. Whether those are the brand new smartphones expected to hit stores, a smart home that can fully function on its own, or self driving and flying vehicles. But as Apple continues to release a brand new phone every year, and Dubai now only has to perfect their already mastered idea of a self-flying helicopter, there is an even bigger advancement that also grows by time: Artificial Intelligence. Artificial Intelligence or AI has in fact been around for quite some time. Behind doors, scientists experiment, build, and test new structures including AI’s in order to release them into the world. Artificial Intelligence is being designed to properly mimic and recreate algorithms in everyday functions of humans. AI’s take science, formulas, chemical makeups, and neurological discoveries into consideration in order to replicate the basic functions necessary, and then work to expand those with hopes of mastering them. Many people applaud the possibility of artificial intelligence. AI’s can offer a high quality of help and aid in basic tasks they are programmed for. As AI’s can be deemed helpful, there is still a threat they pose to the evolving world. If artificial intelligence systems are allowed to grow into most societies, the need for work performed by regular humans will no longer be a necessity, leading to a world that can be controlled and ruled by engineered intelligence. With AI’s invading the routine system society has made for themselves, issues are bound to occur, even if artificial intelligence systems could improve areas significantly.

When it comes to artificial intelligence systems, people automatically think robots. Although robots are a large part of AI’s, there is a much more complex and intricate network to the AI name. Artificial intelligence is the promising replication of human thoughts and interactions that will be incorporated into AI systems used to take the place of human beings. Areas such as the workforce, government, medical fields, and basic everyday life will soon be affected by the rise of artificial intelligence if not done so already. Behind the scenes of AI systems are often not considered. In order for these AI’s to be brought to life, scientists must figure out how to master the Polyheirarchich Model of Intelligence as described in Keith Stearne’s article “The Polyheirarchich Model of Intelligence: A Critique of the Future of Intelligence Biological and Artificial.” Stearne states that the way scientists have previously been creating these complex systems is through general strategic coordination which is achieved through “the mechanism of a ‘zone of highest general connectivity’ which moves round the strategic region, partly under the direction of the appetitive system, providing the necessary extra input to trigger selected potential responses in the motorium to the current sensory input” (Stearne 158). Scientists have to first figure out how the human brain functions, and responds to actions and demands. With that knowledge a similar electronic system must be created and then programmed to act the same way. As this is the basis for artificial intelligence, scientists must follow up and incorporate feelings and other human functions in order to properly replicate human functionality. Yuval Noah Harari, an Israeli historian, notes in his book 21 Lessons for the 21’st Century that society “usually [fails] to realize that feelings are in fact calculations, because the rapid process of calculation occurs far below our threshold of awareness” (Harari). Once again scientists must come to properly understand the way the body and mind functions, including when dealing with emotions and other important human ideals. Overall it comes down to the mastering of biology and anatomy before artificial intelligence can properly be mastered to where it is authentic and useful.

In the world of science, artificial intelligence has always peaked raging interest. As the years go on, the idea of an artificially intelligent world is starting to appeal to everybody. According to Joshue Eckroth in his article “Evolution of a Robust Artificial Intelligence System: A Case Study of the Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence’s AI-Alert” even “the popularity of #artificialintelligence Twitter hashtag has grown so much that now AITopics’ news content is strongly dominated by stories posted on Twitter” (Eckroth 27). This shows that the idea of artificial intelligence is on people's minds, and growing popular by the minute. The appeal is the general idea of what AI’s can do. In the article “Human Digital Thought Clones: The Holy Grail of Artificial Intelligence for Big Data” written by Jon Truby and Rafael Brown, it is expressed “When humanity’s unquenchable thirst for understanding human behaviour, decision making, and the human mind are coupled with economic incentives, the idea of a digital thought clone is not surprising” (Truby & Brown 167). It is the general idea of a different and technological society that draws the public into praising and recommending the increase in AI’s. As interesting as the idea of robots running around Earth, and functioning the way humans do is, people must look at the future outcome of supporting the rise of artificial intelligence before fully supporting it.

There are a lot of speculations regarding the future of artificial intelligence. As there is no sure outcome of what could come out of the widespread use of AI systems, the possibilities should still be heavily considered. For starters, “An individualised digital thought clone can be used first to predict how a person would behave in a given set of parameters based on very precise behavioural patterns” (Truby & Brown 147). The human mind has already been studied enough for scientists to mimic the functionality into intricate softwares. With knowledge of the human behavioral patterns and how the human mind reacts to certain situations, the basic human algorithm can be completely replicated to where future generations could be shaking hands with robots that will easily be mistaken for real human beings. Eckroth states in his article that “AI algorithms and models trained by ML are often highly tuned to the specific nature of the data on which the algorithm was developed and model was trained” (Eckroth 25). What Eckroth is telling us is that AI’s have been and will continue to be created for specific reasons and for tackling certain objectives. In the future, an AI could easily be created for anything desired, which will eventually work its way into the workforce and take important tasks from real human beings.

Yuval Noah Harari describes the future of AI’s best. Dedicating half a chapter to the current and future development of artificial intelligence, Harari notes how “Once AI makes better decisions about careers and perhaps even relationships, our concept of humanity and of life will have to change” (Harari). The way society will need to function in the future will soon revolve around AI technology. So much that Harari also states “When the biotech revolution merges with the infotech revolution, it will produce Big Data algorithms that can monitor and understand my feelings much better than I can, and then authority will probably shift from humans to computers” (Harari). If artificial intelligence continues to grow more popular, the future might be strictly run off of AI systems in mostly AI environments. This is not as beneficial or amazing as it seems. As the work put into designing such systems is ordinary and interesting, the increase of a computerized society can give the government more ways to control us. Harari says “As algorithms come to know us so well, authoritarian governments could gain absolute control over their citizens..” (Harari). If the book Nineteen Eighty-Four has ever been read, the future of AI systems can be compared to what George Orwell wrote. A computer could eventually be used to monitor everyday actions, thoughts, and words from citizens. This type of control is exhausting and violates privacy that citizens are promised in the U.S Constitution. But the possibility of a ‘Big Brother’ scenario due to AI’s taking over society is not the only problem that could be faced.

Every artificial intelligence system starts somewhere. A team or specialist has to be the one to make the effort to bring one of these ideas to life. What if the one in control means harm? The AI to come from a creator with mal intention will start numerous issues and pose a risk to mankind. According to Harari, “The real problem with robots is not their own artificial intelligence, but rather the natural stupidity and cruelty of their human masters” (Harari). As AI’s start to populate more than ever, people need to be aware of the bad that can come from the wrong hands. If AI’s can be programmed to be useful, they can most definitely be programmed to cause harm and fear. “Any AI system that processes human generated content must be carefully watched because people will often find ways to influence the system” says Joshua Eckroth (Eckroth 27). There will always be somebody with the mal intention of harming society. This gives them a sense of power and supreme priority over others. If systems can be hacked now, then AI systems can risk being hacked as well. It could only take one bad person to create an AI that will endanger society, and there will not be a way to know that until it is too late. As Keith Stearne says in his article, “we could never know for sure whether or not intelligent beings we create ‘self-aware’ as we are, especially if their construction is radically different from our own” (Stearne 157). Scientists may be able to understand the human genome well enough to replicate it, but once AI’s start to populate, there won’t be enough knowledge from regular citizens to notice wrong behavior fast enough to stop it. They most likely won't know how to stop it. Not only would this increase the risk of harm, but it can also lead to many other complications. Harari believes “the philosophical algorithms will never be perfect. Mistakes will still happen, resulting in injuries, deaths, and extremely complicated lawsuits” (Harari). On top of injuries and pain, AI’s can lead to possible lawsuits that will stress out and mess up a lot of people's lives. Lives of people who might not have wanted or approved for AI’s to be so heavily incorporated into everyday life, either. If the strength of the argument for Artificial Intelligence increases, it could potentially end up that artificial cloning of one person will slowly become less of a choice, and more of a demand. Keith Stearne also makes a point to say that he personally would not be happy if a replica of himself were cloned and created into an AI (Stearne 157). The arguments against the increasing popularity of AI systems are powerful, but it would be wrong to ignore the potential benefits.

As Harari mainly talks about the downfalls of an artificially intelligent future, he also brings up some good viewpoints on how society can be benefitted from AI systems. He starts off by saying “there is no reason to assume that algorithms won’t be able to outperform the average human even in ethics” (Harari). It is no secret that when given the chance, AI systems can and will outperform humans in the work given. This is the biggest argument for Artificial Intelligence, as it does limit the possibility for work that will not be completed to its fullest potential. It can also limit labor costs as AI’s can handle more than one person's work at a time, but it is important to note that this will take away possible jobs for people who need them. Another interesting argument Harari brings up, is that AI’s could reduce discrimination in scoeities. “If we allow a computer to evaluate job applications, and program the computer to completely ignore race and gender, we can be certain that the computer will indeed ignore these factors” (Harari). The idea of programming and using AI’s to ignore race and gender when making decisions will indeed limit the amount of dicrimination that takes play currently. Harari also compares AI systems to the future of war. By replacing soldiers with AI robots, the main goal of a soldier will be carried out proficiently with little error. By error, Harari is talking about the previous cases where soldiers have not been able to control their rage and go off on unnecessary killing and rape sprees. “Since robots have no emotions, they could be trusted to always adhere to the dry letter of the military code, and never be swayed by personal fears and hatred” (Harari). By using robots in these settings, there would be limited defiance and risk of violent outbursts that will negatively impact the world.

It is hard to hear about the incorporation of AI’s into everyday life and side against it. These technological advancements have the potential to do good in society, but when weighing all the negative outcomes to the positive ones, it is clear that a future mostly run by AI’s is not a future worth encouraging. There is too much of a risk of a controlled world that will come from the increase in AI usage and demand. People could also end up hurt in irreversible or non-curable ways. AI’s could also lose control any minute with no way of knowing how to properly handle those situations. AI’s could even be programmed to negatively lose control and harm others. In the end, it is better for society to continue to operate with manual labor as done now. If freedom is promised in the land of America, the threat to our freedom and privacy should be annihilated. Artificial intelligence systems should not be allowed to take control of the world.
chunks.label: Risks and consequences of artificial intelligence
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the rise of artificial intelligence, citing various authors and sources to analyze both its potential benefits and severe dangers regarding control, labor, privacy, and ethics.

n2002aab5.title: Transitioning to a Predominantly White University

chunks.text: Racialization is the top-down political process where a dominant group decides the symbolic values of subordinate groups. In this day and age racialization is higher than ever, with immigrants coming in and the constantly changing society that we live in. This is a downward spiral, as racialization creates a social hierarchy based on skin color and essentially defines people by their race. The concept of systemic racism connects to racialization because with racialization you are defining people by their skin color and creating a hierarchy. Racism is not to be confused with ethnocentrism though, which is the tendency to trust or lean on people in your culture. Because of ethnocentrism, most people have a slight bias toward people of other races and ethnicities, but it is not inherently racialization.
chunks.label: Defining racialization, systemic racism, and ethnocentrism
chunks.what_happened: The student defines racialization as a top-down process creating social hierarchies based on skin color and compares it to systemic racism and ethnocentrism.

chunks.text: I grew up near a military base, in a very diverse area, my high school had a minority rate of 62%. Due to the increased diversity of the area, no one really thought about race or classified people based on their race. Through my eyes, there was no dominant group it was all very inclusive. There were some neighborhoods growing up that were more black and some that were more white but it wasn’t to the point where it was dangerous to go there if you were the opposite race.
chunks.label: Growing up in a diverse military area
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up near a military base in a diverse area where high school had a high minority rate and neighborhoods did not feel segregated or hostile.

chunks.text: Then I came to UNCW, which is a primarily white institution and it really surprised me how much they lack diversity and some of the stories I have heard from people of color about how they were mistreated and how they feel like an outcast here. It really opened my eyes to how much racialization there is before I never even thought about it because all my childhood everyone came together as one. This made me think, “why is systemic racism still so prevalent in our country”
chunks.label: Attending UNCW and hearing peers' experiences
chunks.what_happened: The student came to UNCW, noticed the lack of diversity compared to home, and heard stories from students of color about feeling mistreated and cast out.

chunks.text:
Systemic racism is caused by many things, first, some believe minorities don’t deserve the same rights because of discriminatory policies. There used to be policies put in place, such as black not being able to own a house any of these policies do exist today but they s o minorities and now they have the reputation of living in low-income areas . The media representation is another thing still expanding racism, whether it’s a book, movie, or news story, the media tends to represent people of color in a negative light. This causes people to be engrained with the fact that all of them act like that in real life. Even though slavery was abolished on December 18, 1865, there is still underground trafficking going on forcing minorities into labor because the stigma of slavery still exists, that People of color were made to do hard labor.

The hierarchy created by racialization causes white to make it out on top as the dominant group and other races to be looked down upon and go through all these challenges just to get where white people are. A lot of white people don’t realize their privilege and in turn, don’t realize how hard other races have it to live everyday life. This lack of acknowledgment only . If white people in power took a step back and realized what was truly going on, they could make some changes, the country does not have to be this way. Of course, you cannot do anything about specific internalized racism among individuals, but we can change policies and fire people who go against them. This is supposed to be a free country for all, yet some people are still fighting for their spot.

There are many ways to combat systemic racism in healthcare, the criminal justice system, housing, and politics. It starts within the education system, for medical school, law school, or even a management degree. If we learn how to identify our implicit biases and control them or learn from them, won’t make it into these systems. The best place to learn this is at the root of the problem when you begin learning the technical things. We can also make set-in-stone changes to public policy and industry the systemic racism flows all the way into the concrete practices that already exist. Some states opted out of using Medicaid which left 46% of black working adults without some kind of insurance. Hospitals and physicians could start excepting Medicaid, which is a health insurance that helps people with low-income. Within the criminal justice system, it is important to remain aware of police brutality, this way we can hold the system accountable. Addressing the inequality in the police system and in court settings would eventually lead to change as well. Some ways to stop inequality in the housing industry are investing in segregated communities, create affordable rental housing for low-income families, and increase the opportunities for black homeownership.

One of the major reasons a lot of the inequality that is very obvious is not being solved is due to white privilege. White privilege is the privilege white people have in everyday life that they don’t recognize as an advantage. The thing about white privilege is the fact that it causes some whites to be oblivious to the problems other races face. White people have the freedom to walk around in a grocery store without being followed, have a civilized run-in with the police, apply for jobs easily, and many other things. These are things that minorities have a hard time with, they could simply just be grocery shopping with their kids, and someone might suspect them of stealing, solely based on the color of their skin. Many white people aren’t just oblivious, they don’t believe it's real and get mad at those who think it is. The problem with this belief is that we can’t help stop one race from becoming superior to another, thus racialization will continue to grow even more. Of course, having privilege does not mean you don’t have struggles or get discriminated against in other aspects, it simply means you’re struggles are not due to your race. America could be a much better place if we used our white privilege to help others, such as standing up for a minority when it may be more dangerous for them.

So why does white privilege exist? The Civil Rights Act of 1964 was supposed to prohibit discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or nationality. As a country, the Act did help some discrimination, but discrimination of race still strongly persisted. This is when the term “white privilege” came about when people started to realize that it was psychological and less of a choice. Sme still believed white privilege was due only to conscious action, which is not inherently true because it is both conscious and unconscious. Some aspects of white privilege are surface deep, and others are embedded in the culture throughout the years. This is why Peggy Macintosh defined it as “an invisible knapsack,” it's hard to see and even harder to get rid of.

It is important to note that there is a big difference between racism and white privilege. History has caused white privilege to exist, biases exist all throughout time periods. Racism is something you choose to believe, that one race is better than another. It is not true that everyone with white privilege is racist, they interlock whenever one with white privilege does not recognize or rejects the fact that they have it and use it against those of other races. The concept of racialization is embedded in our culture and is also not just about racism, it is about whites being on top throughout history and our culture hasn’t changed. White people hold more wealth, have higher government positions, and gain better opportunities.

Racialization depends on where you are how extreme it is but it exists everywhere. Even though where I grew up there was not a lot of racism, there was still white privilege so white people were still on top because of their race. This is due to systemic racism in our country, dating all the way back to before 1964 when the thirteenth amendment passed that outlawed slavery. America is known as a free country, everyone, in theory, has the same freedoms but when you combine those with the fear people of other races face of persecution, then everyone is not free. The roots of this country still lie under the fact that white men are on top and until that changes the systemic racism will still be more prevalent than ever. Some things like white privilege you can’t just get rid of after all this time, it will always exist to an extent, but we can recognize it and learn from it. That is the important thing about America’s history, it is not always the best but as a country, we can learn from our mistakes and increase the equality this country holds. So back to the question, why is systemic racism still so prevalent in our country? The answer is simpler than we think, it's because we lean on racialization to help us understand people and why people do things. Unconscious bias and ethnocentrism are rooted not only in our country but in everyone’s minds. That is holding back a change that could occur.
chunks.label: Reflecting on causes and solutions for systemic racism
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes the causes of systemic racism, white privilege, media representation, historical policies, and ways to combat racial inequalities in institutions.

ndc9845c5.title: Reflecting on Learned Hate and Morality

chunks.text:
When reading and understanding “The Cultural Logic of Collective Representations Durkheim'' and realizing humans have this collective consciousness might be a little intimidating for some. So in the reading “The Matrix of Domination” thinking white people look at African American women as being a subordinate: do you think this just happened naturally? Or was it a societal thought which evolved into collective consciousness.

“By objectifying African American Women and recasting our experiences to serve the elite white men, much of the Eurocentric masculinist fosters Black women's subordination”. To think white people have been taught to look down upon another sex as less than but a race also might not sit well with most Americans. While these not only women but men were oppressed in history on disgusting levels we have to understand why? This happened because of something bigger. I'm not talking about physically enslaving people to gain wealth but let's look into the brain.

In “The Cultural Logic of Collective Representations Durkheim” we learned a quick overview of collective consciousness. This has caught my attention on every reading, lecture and essay we have done at some point. Racism is taught. Prejudice is taught. Hate is mostly taught, because I feel you can develop hatred feelings towards things later once the brain has developed. What i'm trying to say in all of this is our collective consciousness has been the downfall of civilization since we can recall. Starting in North America with Christopher Columbus, looking at his journal and him saying We could take this land and enslave these people, because of their ignorance in western civilization. That was over five hundred years ago and it was seeded into the brains of humans then and was passed down generation by generation.

Collective consciousness is the reason for genocide, slavery, racism and all terrible things humans have done. It is also terribly good. With giving one morals of how they are raised. So when they are faced with right and wrong decisions they know how to feel and how to decide. Humans can be evil. But I hope we have learned from history and are passing down new morals to give the next generations a better collective consciousness.
chunks.label: Collective consciousness and historical oppression
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on course readings regarding collective consciousness and the matrix of domination, analyzing how racism, prejudice, and oppression are socially taught and passed down through generations.

n1ab1cc85.title: Analyzing Power Elite Control Over Consumers

chunks.text:
The Domination Over the Collective Consciousness by the Power Elite

Within the realm of the American market, there will always have to be those in higher standards of power due to the highly neoliberal structure of the United States. It is said that those with money have power over the minds of consumers, and therefore the collective consciousness that resides within the everyday consumer. The amount of influence the Power Elite has over consumers collective consciousness’ has allowed them to manipulate market trends and have dominance over the media and consumer propaganda.

The Power Elite, the semi-minority group of CEO’s and high wealth individuals naturally find themselves with lots of voice in the media and society as a whole. Their large net worth legitimately allows them to do more things than the average middle-class citizen. And because of this inherent power they already have, oftentimes that is abused to gain them even more profits and market share. Most trends in social media that are related to the market are more often than not due to the influence of the Power Elite whether it’s tons of funding towards marketing or using their typically large follower base on social media platforms to shift the general consensus towards a desired ideology.

The collective consciousness is simply the shared beliefs and ideologies that reside within a certain group of people or an entire society. In a way, social media platforms can be seen as having their own collective consciousnesses, as the members that use those platforms all intake the same content that can influence their beliefs and views. And like social media, the capitalist market also has a collective consciousness that contains all the common interests of consumers and market trends at that time. This means that somewhere along the line someone or something must go in and usher their desired trends into the shared consciousness that those with less voice will have to intake and accept as the new trend.

This aforementioned group of people influence the collective consciousness within the market is none other than the Power Elite. Their immense amount of money and sheer power allows them to effortlessly manipulate and modify the collective consciousness to cast their intended visions onto most consumers who also find themselves inside this same collective consciousness. An example of this working is that those with lots of money can market a new product or service to the point where it’s virtually impossible for consumers to not notice this new product. Now that the majority of consumers within that space are aware of this new product, it not only can render other products in that same space as “worse” or “useless”, but it gains revenue for the Power Elite’s that are on funding this market manipulation.

One example that is quite relevant to today’s market is the newfound use of Artificial Intelligence in Big Tech’s services like Google and Meta. This AI craze started when OpenAI released GPT3.5 as the ChatGPT service. This opened the window to endless possibilities for companies with lots of money to expand their regions into the AI space. Soon enough, Google created Gemini, their ChatGPT equivalent, and this now creates a dominance in the AI space by Big Tech companies.

It may seem unrelated, but the reason AI is related to the Power Elite and the collective consciousness is quite simple. It takes a lot of machinery and money to train AI models and market them, something which only these large Power Elite companies have access to. These large companies can now fund all this research and technology to increase their dominance in the AI space, and because AI is so common now in all products seen in the common consumer market, that means that the majority of this market is dominated by said Power Elite companies. Essentially this means that whatever these Power Elite says goes as nobody has the ability to have a counterview.

A slightly different approach to this comparison between the two can be indirectly seen in the Barbie movie. The Barbie movie aimed to emphasize the oppression of women in modern day society and the normalization of the patriarchy. The interesting thing about this is that patriarchy nowadays is fueled by marketing techniques by the Power Elite who have lots of say and voice in the collective consciousness in society. So while the Barbie movie was indeed portraying the objectification of women and the patriarchy being the main influencer of that, the patriarchy is actually backed by the Power Elite’s influence of this collective consciousness.

The Power Elite is so effectively able to influence consumers by basically shaping the collective consciousness to their desires at will. This means that all the advertising, trends, and lot of pop culture is sparked by the Power Elite wanting to shift the focus in their favor. Even if people disagree with them in their choices, the majority of people simply don’t have enough money or power to have much of a say in the war against the greedy Power Elite vs. the consume collective consciousness. As morbid as this all seems, not all the Power Elite are bad, however it is often seen that with money and power comes corruption and manipulation. For the foreseeable future, the Power Elite will remain in dominance over the market and the collective consciousness that resides within it, which will continue to influence the minds and beliefs of all consumers.
chunks.label: The Power Elite's dominance over collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological concepts regarding how the Power Elite manipulates market trends and collective consciousness through wealth, social media, artificial intelligence, and pop culture like the Barbie movie.

n77ded799.title: Religion and Authority in Modern Society

chunks.text:
Harari explains how societies across the globe have previously used religion as a basis of governing. They go into depth on how certain individuals, political groups and countries are very against the idea of liberalism and view it strictly as the opposite of being conservative. The author explains that it is more traditional to put faith in the law of higher and divine authority. This concept can be related to collective consciousness and the way in which one's ideals are based on their upbringing or environment. Harari writes, “For thousands of years people believed that authority came from divine laws rather than from the human heart, and that we should therefore sanctify the word of God rather than human liberty” (Harari 58). This is a demonstration of collective consciousness within a time period. Religion is a global practice and has served as a method of governing in many nations throughout history. In The Cultural Logic of Collective Representations, Durkheim explains the religious order is the basis for both governing and cultural morals in some societies. The author writes, “Now in order that these principal aspects of the collective life may have commenced by being only varied aspects of the religious life, it is obviously necessary that the religious life be the eminent form and, as it were, the concentrated expression of the whole collective life. If religion has given birth to all that is essential in society, it is because the idea of society is the soul of religion” (Durkheim 72).

Through both readings, the answer as to why religion has been used in this way, is because it is one of the oldest forms of community that humans developed. People will find likeminded individuals through church or religious organizations. It allows them to have a safe space to express their ideals and lifestyle. However, religion being used to control citizens has been practiced for hundreds of years. Rulers and political figures will use the fear of God to instill order within a society. Even on a smaller scale, groups and clubs still practice this hierarchical order of having set rules and leaders. In the same way that it is in human nature to flock to those one relates to, we are also used to the ordered form of having a set person in charge that is above us. In religious households, it is God, and, in every household, it is our parental guardians and then our teachers, employers and so on. Unfortunately, religion in politics has created more harm than good in societies that practice it. This is due to the fact that modern societies are more culturally diverse. Therefore, one moral perspective cannot be used as law and enforced on all citizens. The ultimate solution to ensuring that everyone’s beliefs and feelings are respected is in liberalism as Harari explains in chapter 3. It promotes taking feelings into account and not limiting citizens on the basis of personal beliefs.
chunks.label: Religion, collective consciousness, and liberalism
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses readings by Harari and Durkheim regarding religion as a basis of governance and collective consciousness, arguing that liberalism provides a better framework for diverse modern societies.

chunks.text:
Is hegemonic masculinity benefitting society’s youth? While current media and mainstream culture in recent western society are perpetuating the notion or practice of dominant, assertive, strong, and competitive masculine traits; moreover, it brings up the question, how is it affecting society’s youth? There are some in society that tends to belong to a higher social class who have certain racial, societal, gender-based, economic, and other privileges that would state that the messages or teachings of hegemonic masculinity towards the youth bring out breadwinners and overall successful men into functioning society. In contrast, another side of society states that hegemonic masculinity is destructive to young boys and men because it maintains a toxic form of masculinity that not only affects men negatively but also women. After all, they can become victims of men who have been guided or influenced by the effects of this masculinity.

Young men and boys who don’t fit into the direct mold that is placed for the type of man this masculinity maintains, are now put into a category lesser than the “ideal man”. I argue that those same men who are put in a lesser category because they aren’t the stereotypical dominant, controlling, and overachieving men that hegemonic masculinity expects; they become victims in society due to this idea of thought.
chunks.label: Impact of hegemonic masculinity on youth
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the debate surrounding hegemonic masculinity and argues that boys who do not fit its mold become societal victims.

chunks.text: One summer evening while Tita Carol was away doing some shopping, my Uncle Fred got drunk and started talking to us boys, my cousins, and me about “manly stuff”. He ended up discussing women in excruciating detail by vulgarly sexualizing and even degrading them and saying things such as, “You guys need to get women with meat on her bones, that’s how you’ll know she’ll feed you right” or “You guys need to gain a woman who’s a 6 or 7 because women who are 9’s and 10’s don’t stay too long”. Uncle Fred continued in a drunken stupor about how a woman’s ass is more important than boobs. While listening I ended up having a disgusted look on my face which my Uncle quickly called out. I explained to him that his comments didn’t feel right to me and how it asserts and perpetuates that women should be practically servants to men. He quickly responded by laughing at my face and told me that I’ll learn one day that he’s right, how I need to learn how to engage in locker-room talk and do more manly activities with them. My cousins sat there in silence while I listened to their father’s comments.
chunks.label: Uncle Fred's drunken locker-room talk
chunks.what_happened: During a summer evening while his aunt was away, Uncle Fred got drunk and made vulgar, degrading comments about women to the student and his cousins. The student expressed disagreement and was mocked by Uncle Fred.

chunks.text: Another similar event happened while staying at their house, on my 13th birthday we all decided to host a big Filipino party at my Tita’s. The party was going well until my Uncle Fred started drinking. I was outside playing with my cousins and other kids till he stopped drinking to strangely comment how my testicles would grow in and I’d start feeling certain ways toward women. I became so embarrassed because all the other kids and even their parents heard him talk to me that way. I soon went over to my mother and my Tita Carol tearing up and explaining what happened and they excused it by saying it was the alcohol talking and that he loves me. Both my mother and my Tita Carol are married to men who I know married them due to Asian fetishization and due to the effects of hegemonic masculinity. I truly believe both men do not think of them as equals. I soon went back outside wiping the tears off my face which my Uncle noticed and said, “Man up John. Men don’t cry” as he was rummaging through the garage fridge for more beer. I have been surrounded by a culture of hegemonic masculinity ever since my days as a young boy, and it is being perpetuated by not only the powerful men in my family but also the women who are victims of it as well.
chunks.label: Uncle Fred's comments at 13th birthday
chunks.what_happened: At the student's 13th birthday party, Uncle Fred drank and made inappropriate comments about the student's body and feelings toward women. When the student cried, his mother and aunt excused the behavior, and Uncle Fred told him to man up.
chunks.people: Uncle Fred, cousins, other kids, mother, Tita Carol

chunks.text: Brett Stoudt discusses in his article how these wealthy, upper-class white boys who attend a rich all-boys private school named Rockport and their experiences of violence in relation to the concept of hegemonic masculinity. For instance, the author concluded that hegemonic masculine attributes are beneficial to the privileged boys because it directly creates a culture of competition between all of the boys which motivated them to improve. However, while this form of masculinity can be beneficial, it is only beneficial to the young men who are surrounded by the environment, fit the mold, and are privileged enough to reap the benefits. Furthermore, this formation of competition rewards men who are privileged enough to be able to compete at the top, as the ideal successful man. Although, there is certainly a sense of impunity in place towards the men who fit the mold of hegemonic masculinity and their words and actions towards “lesser categories of people”.
chunks.label: Brett Stoudt's article on privileged boys
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Brett Stoudt's reading about privileged boys at Rockport school and how hegemonic masculinity rewards those who fit the mold.

chunks.text: As I have stated before, my cousins have been more privileged than I have. They have had more economic advantages, social advantages, educational advantages, and other privileges than I ever will. Both of them have always worked well with the plans of my Uncle Fred and they especially check out all the categories for hegemonic masculinity.
