Moreover, like the Rockport boys, my cousins have benefitted due to the competitive effects of hegemonic masculine attributes they have learned from their father. My older cousin James always followed his Father’s words as if they are absolute and has become a man with hegemonic masculine values and attributes. He has always stayed consistent in his beliefs imparted to him from my Uncle Fred, that men must be at the very top, must be dominant, non-emotional, tough, competitive, and overall superior to women. It is the same for my younger cousin, Fred Jr. as I watch him grow up into his freshman year of high school. Their beliefs are perpetuated because they aren’t challenged by diverse mindsets and when they are exposed to those different mindsets they push them away.
chunks.label: Cousins adopting Uncle Fred's masculine values
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how his cousins have enjoyed more privileges, aligned with Uncle Fred's expectations, and adopted hegemonic masculine beliefs.

chunks.text: The youth of society who are inharmonious with the culture of hegemonic masculinity can grow up believing they are “lesser than” because they are forced into a position of a “lesser category” by these hegemonic masculine men and those who perpetuate this form of masculinity. Now, what can the people put these lesser categories do to stop this cycle? It is through educating oneself about these harmful stereotypes and how toxic they can be to others who don’t fit the mold of hegemonic masculinity, only then we can start working to create change.
chunks.label: Breaking the cycle of hegemonic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by reflecting on the harmful effects of hegemonic masculinity on marginalized youth and the need for education to break the cycle.

chunks.text:
“The self, the I and Me” and “The self and its selves” sound close in title but turn out to be different in explanation of our mind. Introducing mind body duality and comparing it with having four different categories making up our brain are two different theories completely. Is one more correct or believable in their depiction of your brain?

Having a mind and body relationship and knowing which reaction you're having in your brain seems virtually self explanatory while material self, social self, personal identity and pure ego seem to compartmentalize the theory of our brain but doesn't touch on the body or our physical being. When mentioning material self and having a reaction to a family member or close friend being hurt for example; empathizing with them and wanting to help or do something to help would sound like a body reaction exactly how George is describing in his writings. Sounds like a body reaction to me. Is one more right than the other? Dun, Dun, Dun..

It's subjective, but the philosophy behind “The self, the I and Me” help me understand the mind while relating to the body. For example while writing this essay and re-reading my sentences and thinking “man that sounds dumb, im going to look like and idiot.” But knowing he is a much more educated human than myself shows you how I am having mind duality and using both my I and Me brain.
chunks.label: Reflecting on theories of the self and mind
chunks.what_happened: The student compares two theories regarding the mind, self, and body duality, reflecting on their own internal thoughts and reactions while writing the essay.

chunks.text:
Have you ever felt like you were being watched through your technological devices? Most individuals who live in America use a wide variety of electronics and most of the devices include some type of surveillance. In today’s world of technology advancements, it is a common feeling for tech users to sense they are being watched constantly and almost always under some type of surveillance. Foucault proposed an experiment in a prison that allowed him to focus on prisoners and their behaviors through a control mechanism. I argue that surveillance has a strong connection with the behaviors of humans. The monitoring presence can even control the way people act in a negative way.

Surveillance monitors are found in numerous different types around the world in a variety of locations. One of the most common examples of monitors is security cameras. Security cameras are found in almost all grocery stores, banks, parking decks and common spaces. The cameras can be visible to the human eye or completely hidden. Homeowners have access to purchase house cameras for the inside and outside of their home. The cameras specialized for a home can be created to connect to an iPhone, they can be wired directly into a house, be wireless or battery powered. Computers, iPhones, and cars are also monitors that are connected to a camera of some sort.

Cameras can be super beneficial and helpful in some cases. For example, cameras are useful in places of business if stealing occurs. The recordings from the cameras are often used as evidence for police officers in many different situations. Most security cameras can also pick up on voices in the recordings. Customers who are aware that cameras are in an area of a store may act different or try to conform to normal actions because they realize they are being watched. A con that elaborates on this example could be that the customers are conforming to the norm and not showing their true personality since they are on camera.

Another large issue that exists with the significant amount of security cameras being installed is that people no longer have privacy in their lives. Humans are constantly being watched on surveillance in some way, shape or form.
chunks.label: Surveillance and behavior reflection
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the prevalence of surveillance technologies, security cameras, and how surveillance influences human behavior and privacy.

chunks.text: I have experienced a form of surveillance in my personal life with my smart phone. One day I was shopping in Old Navy, and I found a sweater that I wanted to purchase. The second I walked outside of the store and looked on my Facebook account there was an Old Navy ad on my page for the exact same sweater that I had just purchased. I immediately felt like I was being watched and that people were listening to me speak as I shopped and looked around the store. I have experienced several other incidents like this story with ads popping up on my computer of the exact same item that I previously had searched for.
chunks.label: Old Navy targeted ad experience
chunks.what_happened: The student bought a sweater at Old Navy and immediately saw a Facebook ad for the exact same sweater upon leaving the store, which made them feel watched.

chunks.text:
Do you ever wonder where the idea of surveillance becomes too much? Adults and teenagers can be spied on through their cameras on the technological devices that they use. I find it very creepy and invasive that people can watch us at any given time. An article online mentioned that trackers can collect data about a user. The data can include the users phone number, email address, street address and the IP address that is connected to the Internet. Trackers are even able to access the precise location of a user. The information that trackers can find is very personal therefore it is frightening that they are able to easily get into human’s phones.

Behaviors of people change when they feel like they are being watched. Surveillance over abnormal behavior is one of the topics we focused on in Sociology. Studies have shown that people may try to change their behaviors to fit what the social norms are when they are under surveillance. People also may try to act more kind than they usually are because they are wanting to make a good impression to the people who are watching them.

Social media makes it very accessible for people to play different roles and to not show their true self and who they are in real life. Many social media platforms create negativity because they portray images that seem to be perfect, and all put together. Their images were created with filters to cover up all their imperfections and it only shows a highlight reel of their daily life. This connects to the idea of being different from expectations constituting a ground for punishment. Many people are worried that if they stand out or look different then they will be put down and made fun of.

Social media influencers are a great example of a person trying to change their behaviors to fit a social norm. Influencers spend a generous amount of time picking out different outfits, finding locations to take pictures and planning out their next Instagram post or Tik-tok video that they are going to create. People who are influencers on Instagram or YouTube often change their self-identity to represent for a brand so that they can make money. Privacy can be difficult to achieve for people who are social media influencers because in order to influence people you must show your life to the world. Influencers post blogs and videos that go into many details about their personal life. Hackers are also more likely to be able to get influencers information because in most cases their accounts are made public so they attract a higher amount of viewers.

Video surveillance is also used to show abnormal behaviors. Abnormal behaviors can be behaviors that are described as uncultured or different than the normal standard behavior. A term that explains this particular behavior would be “deviance”. Deviance can be defined as a behavior that does not conform to norms and expectations. Society is often so afraid to act in a way that does not fit the social norms. Many people believe that every person should dress the same way, have the same style, and act the same. Deviance can change depending on what activities and interests become popular for a specific year or what is relevant to culture. Finally, deviance is determined by the social context that it is used in.

Surveillance is predominantly used to control the behaviors of people. Behaviors that are being watched can become more under control in a way. Foucault experienced behavior control through the experiment that he proposed. A “controlling mechanism” is a sophisticated way of describing Foucault’s theory that he experienced through observing the prison. The design technique that was instilled in the prison was called “Panopticon.” This layout forced the prisoners to be spread out and away from each other. While the experiment was taking place there was no time for communication or interacting with others. During the experiment the guards of the prison were able to see inside each cell because they were centered at a tower that had a high viewpoint. The entire experiment allowed Foucault to focus on systems of social control and people in disciplinary situations and how they react. Lastly, he was able to study the “power-knowledge concept.”

Foucault describes the “power-knowledge concept” as, the more a person observes a particular situation the more knowledge they will gain. Therefore, having more knowledge and background information about a circumstance can make people feel like they have more power. He also found through his experiment that there is a penetration of power that comes through to individuals. While there are many mechanisms for observation of humans, power definitely becomes more systematic as more knowledge is gained. Oppression also is a fear that is in place when only specific groups of people understand knowledge. Most people like to find out who is watching them on a camera or even who is listening to the recordings. Knowing who is watching people can make humans feel like they know who is in control and they can understand which people have authority and power.

Power can be a difficult topic to speak about for humans because we do not always have control and authority over our lives. Most people have probably been in a situation in their life where they felt as if they had no control over a circumstance. This feeling can be uncomfortable, scary, sad and can even cause anxiety for many people. While the idea of surveillance over humans lives is not going to dissapear it is important that people realize they do not have to conform to the norms of society. Our whole scope of our life can be potentially under watch but we can still have originality and a want to be different than others and to stand out in life.

In conclusion, surveillance strongly relates to the behaviors and the way people act when they are being watched. Being different from what is expected can often constitute grounds for punishment, but it does not always have to be this way. Society has made surveillance over behaviors a normal and accepted part of life. People are so used to being under surveillance, being watched and conforming to the norms of society that it is so comfortable for them. Often people want to do exactly what other people are doing because they fear trying something new and possibly failing at meeting the standards of society. They also may be scared to dress differently or to behave in a way that most people do because other people may not accept them. I would like to challenge the readers to standout, make a difference in the world and try to not conform to the ways of the world. Strive to show positivity in your daily life because negativity can be tiring and draining to you and the other people around you. Always remember that it is beneficial to show others kindness, love others and to not let surveillance control your life behaviors in a negative way.
chunks.label: Surveillance, deviance, and Foucault's Panopticon
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on online tracking, social media conformism, sociological deviance, Foucault's Panopticon and power-knowledge concepts, and concludes with advice to not conform.
chunks.feelings: creepy, invasive, frightening, uncomfortable, scary, sad, anxiety

chunks.text:
Capitalism is a system based on 5 core principles: private property, supply & demand, competition, freedom, and incentive. Private property can be anything from something physical like a house to something intangible like a patent or a brand. Supply & demand is the economic system put into place where there is a direct relationship between a price and how much is produced based on sales. Competition is related to the working field and any other possible jobs in which the best people rise to the top. Everyone wants to be at the top so it is a constant struggle to get there. Freedom is connected to a person's right to autonomy and choices. Finally, incentive regards to profit and making people strive to get that profit. People and companies will work harder and be more innovative and efficient to achieve that improved profit. A society that exists of these 5 aspects is a self-serving one. People within the society are encouraged to be independent and look out for themselves so that they can compete to be on top. This makes a series of impersonal exchanges and an excess of intangible assets. The depersonalization of an economy and those within it go hand-in-hand with McDonaldization and Rationalization. Both systems rely on anything but humanity and interpersonal communication. Though Capitalism has more equity seeing the more you wear the more you get, it does have the habit of developing systems in which people do not interact. Isolation is a key component of Capitalism.

Marxism mixed with Capitalism finalizes the concept that isolation is inevitable when people are exposed to the 5 pillars of Capitalism. The Marxist idea that humans are so susceptive to change based on what they are surrounded by makes Capitalism the key to coding someone's manner and habits. Each of the five pillars affects social habits in different ways, but competition and incentives are more likely to cause isolation and self-serving behavior. Competition causes people to directly go up against one another and struggle to get to the top. There can only be so many on top, so it causes tension and individualism. Incentive has many forms, money, success, and any other kinds of profit available. So, different people will strive and improve things for different reasons, so what one person does for their incentive might oppose another person's way of receiving their incentive. The culmination of the two creates the ultimate individualist structure in this bigger society. Marxism is a smaller scale of a big society/economy where people can be connected to their work and surroundings more easily. This encourages a herd mentality and community, versus a competitive struggle to determine who will be on top.

In conclusion, human nature is easily changed and can be rewired based on the necessity to survive and thrive. Capitalism has specific aspects in which they can isolate all the natural survival instincts to then cause people to be more self-interested and individualistic. Though Capitalism is effective, it does oppose the groupthink aspect of social nature.
chunks.label: Principles of capitalism and Marxist views on isolation
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes the five core principles of capitalism, explaining how competition and incentives foster isolation, depersonalization, and individualism compared to Marxist concepts of community.

n97b817e5.title: Living with Society's Skinny Shaming Double Standard

chunks.text:
A large majority of individuals have been told this sentence by someone in their lifetime: “do not make fun of someone because of their weight.” Usually, when this sentence is uttered, it is in response to someone making remarks about a person that is overweight. I have lived my entire life as a substantially underweight human being, I have been picked on harshly about my “scrawniness” by friends, family members and even complete strangers. If I had a dollar for every time someone told me I “need some meat on my bones” or “somebody get this boy a cheeseburger,” I would not be attending college right now, due to my fortune. A sentence I have never been heard uttered is “you need to take some meat off them bones” or “somebody get this boy a salad.” Why is that? Why is it the case that making remarks to a person who is struggling with obesity so extremely frowned up in society although it is perfectly normal to make remarks on someone is struggling with their weight at the opposite extreme? That is what we are going to attempt to answer.

What part of our society allows skinny shaming to happen and believes this type of behavior is okay and does not harm any party? It is almost as if this form of behavior is a collective conscious in our society. Others in our society have deemed these actions as okay and others begin joining in, soon creating a new norm on what is allowed to be said involving an individual’s weight.
chunks.label: Double standards in weight-based comments
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the societal double standard of condemning fat shaming while permitting skinny shaming.

chunks.text: Growing up as a young kid, I noticed this behavior all the time. Many of my friends in grade school only weighed maybe 20 to 30 pounds more than me, yet I was always singled out regarding my weight. Grownups, people I was supposed to look up to and respect, poked fun at me about my body and I could never make sense of it. I knew that what they did hurt my feelings, what I just could not understand was that if I made a remark talking about someone’s weight, I was scolded, it felt like a double standard. This has been something that I have constantly dealt with and when I told my parents the topic of this paper, they themselves were taken by surprise at how true the double standard truly is. They had gone my whole life never knowing the issues that I had with constantly being criticized by others regarding my weight. This does not make my parents bad people for not seeing this sort of thing, it just simply shows how big of a hold it has on the world and not many people are even aware of it.
chunks.label: Being skinny shamed while growing up
chunks.what_happened: Growing up, the student was singled out and teased about his underweight body by friends and adults, and later spoke with his parents about how they were unaware of this lifelong criticism.

chunks.text:
I believe that what has happened in our society is an example of the social learning theory.

The social learning theory as we’ve discussed in class is basically just learning from others. Seeing what others do, seeing the reaction it brings, and then determining whether this behavior is accepted by others. It is like how a child learns and develops throughout their life. They first learn to talk by mimicking the sounds he or she hears from others, soon after, learning how to form these words into coherent sentences. A child learns all of this based on repetition and listening to what other people are saying. Then the next step of their life as they grow older is learning what is right and wrong, how does the child achieve this? Through the help of their parents of course, but also by seeing what the adults around them are doing. So, in other words if these children are growing up and seeing that it is wrong to curse, wrong to take things from others, wrong to bully people because they are overweight, however, never being told that it is wrong to bully those that are underweight, they will spend their entire lives believing this harmful behavior is okay. This results in them intentionally or unintentionally bestowing these same values into their own kids and the never-ending cycle continues.

It is no secret that many people in our society struggle with self-image and body consciousness. This is a popular topic among females due to the beauty myth that instructs them to maintain an impossible standard of physical beauty to adhere to the women that are seen commercially and are deemed “beautiful” or “ideal.” It is only recently that there has begun to be a push back on this sort of culture although there is still much more ground to make up. You are now seeing plus sized models advertising clothes and more women with a wide array of body types and physiques being televised allowing for women of the public to see these women and say, “I look like her, and people think she’s beautiful, that means I am too.” I also believe that this beauty myth is fuel for people to give excuse to their behavior towards people that are underweight. It is viewed as ideal to be skinny; skinny is the goal for many people in America. It seems that the public has decided that if you are skinny then you are happy with your body; this is not always the case though. People that struggle with gaining weight are just as unhappy with their failed results as overweight people attempting to lose weight.
chunks.label: Social learning theory and the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how social learning theory and the beauty myth contribute to normalized skinny shaming and body image struggles.

chunks.text: My girlfriend is the first person to ever explain, using this reason, as to why people believe it is okay to skinny shame. First, it is a mixture of people believing that individuals are happy with their bodies when they are super skinny because it is deemed ideal; the belief that they have no shame in their looks. Secondly, these remarks are a reflection on the bully’s own insecurities; their jealousy that they were not born with society’s “perfect body.”
chunks.label: Girlfriend's explanation of skinny shaming
chunks.what_happened: The student's girlfriend explained to him why people feel it is acceptable to skinny shame, citing assumptions about satisfaction and projection of personal insecurities.

chunks.text:
Regardless of the latter, I believe that the beauty myth has not only destroyed women’s ideology about the perfect figure, but everyone’s idea of it, no matter the gender. As I stated above, if the entire world thinks that you are the perfect weight because you are skinny, and they make fun of you for it, then there really is no harm, plus, they have seen everyone else do the same thing throughout their life and have been convinced it is not an issue.

As a person that has spent their whole life hearing about how small I am and constantly being underestimated, believing I am not strong enough to do something or I am too weak to fight, it takes a toll on my self-image. I have proved people wrong within these categories a vast number of times, but there have also been times where I let myself down and was even further ridiculed. I just cannot understand how the collective conscious of our society and the social learning that has been instituted has made people believe that this type of behavior is normal and/or okay. My whole life I have heard to not comment on people’s obesity and it frustrates me when no one will do the same for my side of the spectrum. I understand that there are societal values beyond my scope of understanding that have caused this issue but if I had to point to a root cause for this, it would be the sociological concepts I have discussed above. I also believe that if we took the time to make this a more well-known topic as we have done regarding fat shaming, we could work towards progression of fixing this issue. There will always be bullies in the world that will tarnish our self-image, but I believe that a majority of the people who have skinny shamed me never did it to cause me harm, they just believed, because society told them so, that it was okay.
chunks.label: Reflection on self-image, society, and progression
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the emotional toll of being underestimated, the frustration over social double standards, and hopes for greater awareness.

chunks.text:
Race is a modern concept in the eyes of sociologists. It was invented to put one group above another and provide a base for diminishing and demeaning the group it is being used against. Race is based on skin color and tends to be used as a weapon by the ones with lighter or fairer skin. This concept was used to justify slavery from the 17th through the 19th centuries. Now it is used to justify discrimination and separation. In my time, I have witnessed this in every aspect of society, stemming from school to life in the outside world. This brings us to the question of whether racism is still around today. An inquiry based in part on how our ancestors passed down their beliefs, and how they got instilled into people’s brains over time. Yes, the concept of race and racism is printed into everyone’s collective consciousness, though mostly unnoticed, and still plays a major part in everyday critical decisions.

A pattern that seems to occur a lot in the United States is a modern version of segregation. It is not forced segregation, but more of a voluntary separation that happens because of the imprinted concepts and ideologies in our minds. Personally, I have noticed this throughout all aspects of my life, but the most noticeable spot has been in school. When you walk around school, you tend to see everyone cliqued up with the people that they hang out with and most of the time they look the same with similar cultural backgrounds. The collective consciousness is in some way at fault for this way of living because people of differing ethnicities have lived separately for the majority of the United States’ existence. This causes static in the growth of society because without mixing cultures, there will be no advancement towards peace in humanity.

This puzzle starts with the sociological concept of race vs ethnicity. The definition of race is the categorization of humans that share the same physical appearance and social qualities. The definition of ethnicity is belonging to a group of people with the same cultural background. People tend to mix these two concepts up or think they are the same thing. The government uses them to categorically divide the nation by sending out the census where you are required to lay claim to a certain race and ethnicity. This makes it possible to put certain cultural groups to be above others in the social aspect. This leads to things such as workplace discrimination and residential segregation.

This residential segregation tends to divide the youth which as time goes on, grows and keeps people separate. As it says in an article by Think “Racial residential segregation in the United States is the mechanism by which people are sorted into neighborhoods and communities that offer opportunity and deny it.” This tends to mean that people of color in the lower or middle class usually reside in lower-opportunity areas (Think). While middle-class white families are able to live in better neighborhoods. Bringing them more and better opportunities in life. This separates us in many ways as people go to different churches and schools and play sports in different places. This just starts the segregation between races because you make acquaintances and friends that you stick with for the rest of your life.

Devah Pager did a study on the hiring process discrimination. It showed many ways how jobs and managers treated and responded to different cultural groups when trying to obtain a job. The people who applied to these jobs all had the same resume, background, and social and communication skills. The research conducted that white interviewees were twice as likely to have a positive response from the job as a black interviewee and 5% more likely than a Latino interviewee. Similar results happened when people with felonies applied. White felons were 2% more likely to get a positive response than Latinos and 4% more likely than black felons. This is known as subtle discrimination as it is printed into everyone’s collective consciousness to have certain biases and prejudices that often go unnoticed even by the person doing them. It is the result of years of racism trickling down through society over time, making it impossible for anyone to not have a drop of racism in their mind.

Racism has been a part of the United States since the founding of the country. The concept of the matrix of domination, explains that white supremacy, patriarchy, and capitalism all work together to reinforce each other. From the beginning of the country, the rich white slave owners were building their wealth and power while the black people were being held as slaves, making it impossible to grow wealth and status. The power elite holds the economic power in America and uses this power to exploit the marginalized communities that don’t have access to good economic opportunities. They also held the power to exclude minorities and marginalized groups from getting good access to healthcare and education.

My experience with seeing the separation of races throughout society and specifically in school really didn’t make me think much at the time. But these concepts we go over in class opened my eyes to the causes and repercussions of this separation. The concept of race gives people an excuse to degrade another group of people that don’t fit the same physical image and social concepts as them. The way the government uses race and ethnicity to segregate the people of the nation through residency, access to needs like education and healthcare, and workplace discrimination. Systemic racism plays a huge part in many people’s lives, and it is important to find the roots of these problems. Finding the roots is the only way to find a solution.

The nation is in a split and it goes back to way before any of us were born. The teachings and ideologies of our ancestors have been passed down and imprinted in our minds. This is a case of collective consciousness working against the people of the world. It is the fact that everyone has an underlying way of thinking that is not even noticed by the person thinking most of the time. This is how the youth becomes divided and continues to grow apart as they get older. Concepts like race, and ethnicity, and how sociologists view and research them show us how racism and discrimination run our system here in the United States. The youth of this country need to use this knowledge and listen to the older generation to see where they messed up and how we can fix it. With the way society is now our generation is on a path to finally overcoming racism. Youth nowadays are gaining an awareness of racism that hasn’t been seen yet, on top of the awareness youth today are stepping up and protesting and speaking out on racism. Instead of sitting around and talking about what problems are occurring people are stepping up and fixing the world one problem at a time.

Work Cited

Collins, Patrica. “Matrix of Domination.” Wikipedia, Wikimedia Foundation, 3 Sept. 2014, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_of_Domination.

Western, Bruce. “The Inspiring Life and Career of Devah Pager.” The Marshall Project, The Marshall Project, 14 Nov. 2018, https://www.themarshallproject.org/2018/11/13/the-inspiring-life-and-career-of-devah-pager#:~:text=Conducting%20the%20experiment%20in%20Milwaukee,rate%20was%20only%2017%20percent.

Menendian, Stephen. “Opinion | Why Neighborhoods Are More Segregated Now than They Were a Generation Ago.” NBCNews.com, NBCUniversal News Group, https://www.nbcnews.com/think/opinion/u-s-neighborhoods-are-more-segregated-generation-ago-perpetuating-racial-ncna1276372.

Omi, M. Racial Formations.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of race and racism
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological definitions of race and ethnicity, citing concepts like residential segregation, hiring discrimination studies, and the matrix of domination, concluding with thoughts on generational awareness and citing sources.

n2e19804f.title: Critiquing Religion and the Future of Labor

chunks.text: In his book, 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, Harari analyzes many different aspects of society and provides his input on why he believes they either contribute to or diminish aspects of society. Some of his ideas include ideas about religion, Artificial Intelligence (AI), terrorism, and many more. He provides an interesting perspective on these ideas and goes into depth about each one. Two of Harari’s main points are about religion and its effect on societal issues and the role it plays in society as well as the work ethic/ introduction of AI into society and how that changes the way people work. Both topics are commonly talked about in sociology, as well as in the readings we did in class. Those are the topics that will be focused on throughout this essay.
chunks.label: Introduction to Harari's sociological perspectives
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces Yuval Noah Harari's book '21 Lessons for the 21st Century' and explains that the essay will focus on religion and AI in relation to work.

chunks.text: Durkheim, Maryanski, and Turner evaluate the essence of religion in our earliest time in society. Together, they analyze the point that religion was needed in society to develop emotional intelligence, cognitive ability, and the fundamental categories of thought as well as forming the first social groups in society. Religion played a key role in forming the fundamental categories of thought in our society by forcing the earliest humans to form their own beliefs about something and create a structure in which to live their lives. Durkheim describes this concept as collective effervescence. Religions were created from this fundamental category of thought since multiple people believed in the same ideas. Once they formed these religious ideas, social groups were then formed based off religious beliefs and understandings. This helped to shape society in the earliest time because people were put into social groups and social standings which in turn created social hierarchies. In the earlier periods of society, this was important because it created structure, showed people the “way of life”, and basically told them where they belonged in society. Over time, religious social groups have been questioned as to whether they help society or hurt it.
chunks.label: Durkheim, Maryanski, and Turner on religion
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological perspectives from Durkheim, Maryanski, and Turner on the foundational role of religion and collective effervescence in early human society.

chunks.text: Harari believes that these religious groups have over time hurt society and caused hostility within it, leading to conflict and instability. While Harari does agree with Durkheim, Maryanski, and Turner that religion does create social groups and hierarchies in a society, he does not agree with the idea that they are necessary or beneficial for a society in the twenty-first century. On page 138 of his book, he states that “unfortunately, all of this [issues within religion and economic problems] really makes traditional religions part of humanity’s problem, not part of the remedy.” He elaborates on this by stating that religions have been turned to be used against the people in government, rather than for the people. They are used to separate people, not unify them. This is where he would begin to disagree with Durkheim, Maryanski, and Turner because they believed that religion was a necessary part of society to create structure. While Harari wouldn’t completely disagree with this, he also wouldn’t completely agree. He states that, “…nationalism and religion still divide our human civilization into different and often hostile camps.” Harari believes that religion has been turned into a negative construct that causes hostility rather than a unifying subject in society. However, he does say that religion isn’t all negative because it can help country leaders to make economic decisions based on their belief systems. Harari would probably disagree with Durkheim, Maryanski, and Turner in their broad idea that religion is a positive aspect of society because he believes that overall, it causes more negativity in society than it does positivity.
chunks.label: Harari's critique of religion's modern impact
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Harari's perspective that religion creates division and hostility in the 21st century, contrasting his view with Durkheim, Maryanski, and Turner.

chunks.text: The second commonly talked about idea in sociology is work. In Karl Marx’s “Estranged Labour”, he states that work under capitalism is not beneficial to society because in time it causes people to give up their true self and be forced into labor. He says that they become forced to be a part of competition rather than working for themselves, like they used to in earlier times of society. Because of the competition created by work under capitalism, people tend to lose their true identity and work ethic. They work for societal approval, rather than approval by themselves and their belief system. He would also say that the nature of human beings has become unique because people almost willingly give up themselves and their beliefs to fit into society and become a product of labor under capitalism. Marx states that over time, this causes alienation within a society and withing your essence of self because people give away their happiness and true self to fit in with the ideas of capitalism and work under capitalism.
chunks.label: Marx's views on alienated labor and capitalism
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Karl Marx's theory of estranged labor under capitalism and how it causes alienation from one's true self.

chunks.text: Harari believes something like Marx, but not because of capitalism. In his book, Harari discusses the future of labor due to the implementing of Artificial Intelligence systems in our society. He attempts to warn the reader that AI systems will take away jobs and take away motivation to work. Harari believes that once AI systems can take over jobs, this will cause panic and chaos because people won’t have to work anymore. This in turn will lead to a lack of motivation and the want to work. On page 55, Harari states, “Once AI makes better decisions than we do about careers and perhaps even relationships, our concept of humanity and of life will perhaps have to change.” This is an important idea to bring up because this summarizes Harari’s main point of AI’s and the work environment in society. A good example from class that relates to this view is the Jarus video, which is about a family that allowed an AI system to completely control their lives, such as chores, locations, TV time, etc. Harari would not support this lifestyle because the children will be raised to believe everything is done for them and they can rely on an AI system about when to do certain things and what is right and wrong. If the AI systems are implemented into society in this type of way, no one will be able to think for themselves anymore, causing their true self to be the ‘true self’ of the AI system, not their own.
chunks.label: Harari's views on artificial intelligence and labor
chunks.what_happened: The student describes Harari's predictions about AI altering human labor and sense of self, referencing a class video about a family controlled by an AI system.

chunks.text: While Harari and Marx discuss different aspects of work in society, they have similar or complementary beliefs about societies view of work. In Marx’s viewpoint, he believes that humans have lost their true selves while working under capitalism. In Harari’s viewpoint, he believes that humans will have to reevaluate their sense of self if AI’s take over human jobs. These viewpoints are similar and complementary because both change the sense of self that humanity has and will cause a huge shift in society. Marx would say that capitalism caused the shift in the sense of self of society and Harari would say the same about AI’s. Both believe that these interferences in society led to negative outputs rather than positive outputs. They would also both say that the work in society should not be influenced by these factors because society will not be the same with this occurring. If the true self of the people is put at risk, humanity will completely change and not be able to turn around to revert to the old ways of the work force.
chunks.label: Comparing Marx and Harari on work and self
chunks.what_happened: The student compares the viewpoints of Marx and Harari, noting how both analyze how outside economic or technological forces negatively alter humanity's true sense of self.

chunks.text: Harari would support the concept of work brought about by Marx but not the concept of religion brought about by Maryanski, Turner, and Durkheim for a few reasons. For one, the concept of Marx is more modernized, and Harari continuously suggests lessons throughout his book to try to prepare us for the future of the twenty-first century. Marx’s idea about work in society is like Harari’s because he relates it to what can happen in the future. The idea about religion by Maryanski, Turner, and Durkheim doesn’t necessarily grow with the future of society, but rather acts as one idea over time. They’re idea about religion doesn’t provide a modern viewpoint and suggests one main idea, rather than relating it to the future of society or modernizing it to how society is today. This makes a major impact on Harari not fully agreeing with their stance on religion because his stance relates more to the current and future impacts of society.
chunks.label: Contrasting Harari's reception of Marx versus classical religion theorists
chunks.what_happened: The student argues why Harari aligns more with Marx's view on work than with the classical theorists' views on religion due to Harari's focus on future societal impacts.

chunks.text: In conclusion, while Harari does not completely agree with the ideas brought about by Durkheim, Marynaski, and Turner regarding religion, he would agree with the ideas brought about by Marx regarding the work system in society. Harari believes that religion is not completely benefitting society, and in the long run could damage the way that society works because it creates hostility and negative social groups in our society. He also believes that the work system in society could be completely damaged by AI’s, which in turn would damage the idea of our true self and would cause our true self to be thoughts created by an algorithm program rather than our own thoughts. Harari brings many interesting points into common ideas discussed in sociology and causes readers to question ideas that they thought they stood firmly on. The sociologists mentioned (Durkheim, Marx, Maryanski, and Turner), all have very sound and traditional views on society, while Harari comes in to question these sound views and provide a more updated side to them. Harari questions these views in an effort to predict and assist humanities future and provide a modern stance on many issues and situations occurring in society. Overall, Harari would agree with many perspectives of sociologists, however, also would disagree, and challenge many perspectives of sociologists, which is not traditionally seen in society nowadays.
chunks.label: Conclusion on Harari's contributions to sociology
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes the essay by summarizing Harari's modern challenges and contributions to classical sociological perspectives on religion and labor.

n7455174f.title: Censorship and Resistance in High School

chunks.text: Although many people like to claim that feminism belongs in the past, there are many legitimate reasons why fighting for women’s rights is a current and pressing issue. This discrimination starts young and continues to affect women throughout their lives. As a high school student, I want to discuss how stereotypes and bias influence young women enrolled in secondary schools. From a young age, girls are taught to be ashamed of their bodies and are shamed for using their power to assist themselves and others. Women are kept from working with each other towards a common goal.
chunks.label: Introduction on feminism and discrimination in schools
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the ongoing importance of feminism and how stereotypes and bias affect young women from an early age.

chunks.text: Before diving into the sociological concepts that explain the prevalence of hegemonic masculinity and the toxic putting-down of young women, I need to explain my own experiences within an institution in my school. For all four years of high school, I have been a part of the Women’s Empowerment through Education, or WEE, club. For the past two years, I have served as secretary of the school. Since I am very involved in this operation, and have been for quite some time, I have experienced many different types of discrimination. I have witnessed both men and women inside and outside the organization shame the club and put it down.
chunks.label: Involvement with the WEE club
chunks.what_happened: The student served as secretary and member of the Women's Empowerment through Education club throughout high school, witnessing shaming and discrimination directed at the organization.
chunks.people: the student, club members, men and women inside and outside the organization

chunks.text:
The first example I would like to speak of involves a feminine product drive that WEE Club put on, in partnership with a feminist club at another nearby high school. This drive was advertised as a feminine product drive and the posters listed the items that the club would be collecting. This included bras, tampons, pads, underwear, and other items for feminine hygiene. The plan was for all these items to be donated to a domestic violence shelter. Our advertiser hung up the posters and was called to the principal’s office, along with our president.

They were told that we were not allowed to use certain words and descriptions in our advertising because of their “graphic nature.” WEE club was ordered to take down all our signs as well as our donation boxes until we would change the posters to include less inflammatory language. Our principal argued that words such as tampon and bra would distract the young men in our school. He argued that boys may not have been introduced to the concept of a period, and therefore the language we were using was harmful. Since our club focused on feminism and women’s empowerment, we fought back against this censorship. This refusal to change our wording caused the donation drive to be shut down completely. In comparison, our sister club was able to continue the fundraiser with the same wording as us.
chunks.label: Principal shutting down the feminine product drive
chunks.what_happened: The student's club organized a feminine product drive, but the principal forced them to take down posters and ultimately shut down the drive because he deemed words like 'tampon' and 'bra' graphic and distracting to boys.
chunks.people: the student, club advertiser, club president, principal, sister club

chunks.text:
One of the issues surrounding how young women are treated in high school is the ideas and opinions of the men surrounding them. Hegemonic masculinity creates in men the idea that women are weaker and less than. These ideas are approved by the continuous belief in hegemonic masculinity. Male teachers and administrative officers perpetuate the standard by treating female students differently than male ones. Because of the prevalence of hegemonic masculine ideas, types of harmful beliefs have bled into the collective consciousness. This incorrectly displays the thought that men are dominant, and women are subservient. A high school is a dangerous place because it is where these ideas become embedded in the minds of young students, both male and female.

Simone de Beauvoir discusses many of the concepts that I will be discussing in her article titled “Woman as Other.” In this article the author debates how women are thought of as secondary to men, and what, if anything, can be done to combat this. De Beauvoir discusses how because a woman has ovaries and a uterus, she is inferior and subject to rule by the male. Men see their bodies and anatomy as normal and even empowering, whereas a woman’s body is a prison.

Simone de Beauvoir’s theory of women as others as well as the theory of hegemonic masculinity, explains my story of the principal banning the use of words such as period or tampon because it might harm young men’s learning and thought processes. In this scenario, the principal thinks that he and his anatomy are superior and the baseline for how all bodies work. This explains his condescending behavior and belief that speaking or writing about menstrual cycles is inappropriate for a school setting. Speaking of bras and tampons breaks down the mental barrier of thought that creates the idea that women are held back by their anatomy.
chunks.label: Connecting principal's actions to hegemonic masculinity and De Beauvoir
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on hegemonic masculinity and Simone de Beauvoir's 'Woman as Other' to analyze the principal's censorship of feminine hygiene words.

chunks.text:
Although I have witnessed and experienced discrimination based on sex by men, there are also many situations where the club faced barriers from other women. I would like to focus on a conflict with our teacher sponsor. Unfortunately, between my junior and senior year, our former teacher sponsor left the school and our club. My school is small, so we were left with a limited number of teachers to choose. We wanted a female representative that would be able to assist us and relate to our mission. We found a new female teacher representative and began my senior year. This female teacher was quite hard to work with and opposed us at every move. At the start of the year, we held meetings in her classroom, and she would argue with us the entire time. She fought against our feminist values and refused to help us in our mission to gain equality for all genders. Because of this teacher, we started losing members, and by the time the first semester had passed, we barely had any people attending our meetings.

Although this was annoying and unnecessary, the board was prepared for opposition. However, we were not prepared for what was going to happen next. Our teacher sponsor started trying to shut down our club because she did not believe in our mission or effectiveness. She talked with the principal without informing us and then shut down tbe club for a semester until we could “get our act together.” Our board tried everything from scheduling a meeting with the principal to holding meetings without the authority of our teacher sponsor, but we kept getting shut down. This is a prime example of how other women can oppose modern feminism and cause internal conflict within a movement.
chunks.label: Conflict with a new female teacher sponsor
chunks.what_happened: A new female teacher sponsor argued with the club during meetings, opposed their feminist values, drove away members, and went to the principal to shut down the club for a semester.
chunks.people: the student, former teacher sponsor, new female teacher sponsor, club board members, principal

chunks.text:
This story concerning the teacher sponsor who tried to shut down the club can be explained through defensive othering and inequality between women. This is all discussed in the article titled “Barbie Dolls on the Pitch” by Matthew Ezzell. Ezzell discussed how in defensive othering, a person who is part of a devalued and discriminated group thinks that although certain stereotypes do belong to the group that they are a part of, they do not fit into the same characteristics. They use these thoughts to put themselves on a pedestal while perpetuating the stereotypes that have been forced onto the rest of the group.

Ezzell’s article discussing hetero sexy fit and defensive othering play into women devaluing women in many ways. Our teacher sponsor saw that our club was beginning to struggle. Instead of focusing on working with the members and the board to improve the current conditions, she shed her identity as a fellow woman and feminist in favor of the winning side. She denounced the ideals that we were fighting for, which became very destructive to our club’s survival.
chunks.label: Analyzing teacher sponsor's actions through defensive othering
chunks.what_happened: The student applies Matthew Ezzell's theory of defensive othering to explain why the female teacher sponsor undermined and denounced the club's feminist mission.

chunks.text: My two personal experiences involving my high school principal and my teacher sponsor clarify sociological concepts such as hegemonic masculinity, woman as other, and defensive othering. These ideas create a harmful environment for young women in high school because they diminish the woman’s identity and force her into submission. These ideas are so prevalent that young women will often create conflict within themselves, furthering the damage caused. This shame and control keep girls from realizing their full potential and coming into themselves. High school is still a toxic environment for young women, and much needs to be done to fix this. A first step is to understand the concepts that are inhibiting people from working together, and slowly breaking down barriers. Then, we can work towards making a more understanding and inclusive society.
chunks.label: Conclusion on high school environments and societal change
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes how the experiences illustrate sociological concepts and calls for breaking down barriers to create a more inclusive society.

chunks.text: In America, we are trained under the impression that all people of all classes are equal in the eyes of the law and have the same rights. This couldn’t be further from the truth. In reality, one’s class means more than one’s character, and money does so many more things than we realize. In this short essay, I will talk about the differences between what we are taught about class in society and what the readings from class said about the importance of class in the USA.
chunks.label: Introduction on class equality myths
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the essay, stating that people are taught everyone is equal despite class actually mattering more, and outlines their plan to discuss course readings about class in America.

chunks.text: Growing up, everything was about money. Even if I saw a nickel on the ground, I picked it up because I didn’t want to “Be poor”. Although I was only 6, and overvalued those five cents more than life, I still understood the potential consequences of not having money to pay for things.
chunks.label: Picking up nickels as a child
chunks.what_happened: Growing up at age six, the student picked up nickels from the ground because they did not want to be poor and understood the potential consequences of lacking money.

chunks.text:
From the youngest ages, Americans are indoctrinated with the idea about the division between rich and poor, and we are taught that money is the key to happy living. After reading the excerpts, I was further convinced (I already had some kind of idea) that money isn’t everything. While it is important for living, we don’t need to live in an excess of money to be happy.

In the first reading, George Mantsios gives myths and contradicting realities about classism that were really meaningful. The most impactful myth that he gave was that everyone has the equal chance to succeed, given enough work. I liked this because it brought out the obvious stupidity found in so many myths about class and privilege. Not everyone has an equal shot at success, because success in America is based on your education and family, and those contribute to your income. A lot of people don’t get that access to education and strong family, so the majority of them start off at a heavy disadvantage. In the third reading, “From Colonialism to the Coup”, there was a statistic that showed the percentage of the national income that the top 0.1% own. If it was an equal distribution, it would have shown that they have less than 1%, but in 2010, they owned about 10% of the national income. This means that the top 1% must own even more. I did my own research, and it turns out that the top 1% of wealthy Americans owned a shocking 38.5% of the national wealth in 2016. I don’t think I can explain how shocking this is. It’s crazy that there is that much of a disparity in the top 1% from the other 99%. They didn’t teach us that in economics, all I heard was the importance of money for success.

The readings disproved every myth I had ever heard about the equal rights of all classes, and now it is quite apparent to me the importance of class in America. We run on a system dependent on the working class, who are so much lower in the eyes of the law and of other people.
chunks.label: Reflections on readings, wealth inequality, and class
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes course readings on myths about classism and wealth disparity, details their own research into the top 1% wealth share, and concludes that the readings disproved societal myths about equality.

n7fdaf0b4.title: Evolution of Language and Symbolic Thought

chunks.text:
Human development overtime has been more profound than any other animal in the world. Collective consciousness is what makes humans so special. Humans have developed the ability to share and create ideas in order to maintain stable groups which is beneficial for survival. In both mircofoundations and Alexandra Maryanski and Jonathan H. Turner ideas, we can compare the idea that language has endowed humans with art and symbolic thought which has lead humans to develop beliefs.

In Mircofoundations, it states that around 45,000 years ago the symbolic revolution must have been triggered by a random genetic mutation. This mutation improved the organization of the brain by affording humans the capacity for language and enhanced symbolic activity. Language increased sociality for group formation among human ancestors. By linking sociological concepts to sociability, humans are able to think symbolically to make things meaningful. Unlike animals, humans were able to develop strong emotional attachments to others and groups. According to Maryanski and Turner, cognitive, emotional and behavioral properties that evolved during the hominoid evolution are responsible for religious behavior and organization. Durkheim concluded that religion provided people with an explanation of their place in this world and allowed humans to cope with the uncertainties of life and provided affirmation and expression of the collective group.

The collective consciousness of humans has greatly expanded our ideas and beliefs. We began by creating languages and forming collaborative activity. The hominin brain was able to increase emotions and create meaningful symbolic thought. Overtime, humans created beliefs and religion from symbolism, and by creating groups, humans have utilized their collective consciousness to share beliefs, ideas and behavior.
chunks.label: Human evolution, collective consciousness, and religious beliefs
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the evolutionary development of language, symbolic thought, and collective consciousness in humans, referencing sociological theories from Maryanski, Turner, and Durkheim regarding religion and group formation.

n42d74d63.title: Gender Pay Gaps in the Workplace

chunks.text:
Are women and men truly being paid equally in current-day America? It would be easy to say the answer is yes, they are paid equally, especially after the Equal Pay Act of 1963 was passed and enforced, however, if you really dig deep into some companies you would be surprised to see this is not always upheld. While there are many different variables and circumstances that can play a role in a person's average income different studies have shown that women and men are in fact not paid equally at all companies. On average a woman completing the same job that a man is, holding the same level of degree, would only be paid about 80% of what that man would be paid. However, because of the vast number of variables that can affect a person’s salary the issue regarding equal pay in America has not been an easy battle to fight.

The biggest misconception regarding equal pay discrimination is that it does not occur in America and only happens in other countries. Another common misconception about equal pay discrimination is that it only affects people who work full-time at large companies. Research has shown that the smallest gender pay gap is for both part-time and full-time workers between the ages of 25 and 34. Women who are between the ages of 25 and 34, on average, make 93 cents for every dollar that a man in this age group makes, whereas workers age 16+ (excluding ages 25-34) on average make 84 cents for every dollar a man of the same age makes. To make matters worse, Black and Latina women in America make even less than white women in America.
chunks.label: Gender wage gap misconceptions and statistics
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses the gender wage gap in America, dispelling misconceptions about where and how it occurs, and citing statistical data regarding age and race.

chunks.text: My mom’s friend, who will be named Emily, experienced a similar situation except unlike me, Emily was working at her company full-time receiving a salary rather than hourly pay. Emily had been working at this company for 19 years when she got promoted from “team member” to manager after her previous manager left. Her previous manager was a man who had only been with this company for about 5 years before he left. Emily had her master's, a higher degree in school than her previous manager who only had a bachelor's degree. When Emily got promoted to manager, she expected to be getting the same salary her previous manager did when he started working as a manager. This however was not the case. Emily found out she was making 30,000 dollars less than what her previous manager made annually, even though she had been at the company for 14 more years than he was and she even had a higher level of education than he possessed. Both of these situations go to show that not only do women who work full-time and receive a salary get discriminated against when it comes to equal pay, but part-time hourly pay workers do as well.
chunks.label: Emily's unequal managerial pay
chunks.what_happened: The student's mother's friend Emily got promoted to manager after 19 years at a company with a master's degree, only to discover she made $30,000 less than her male predecessor who had less tenure and a lower degree.
chunks.people: Emily (student's mother's friend), previous male manager

chunks.text: Discrimination against women regarding equal pay most of the time spawns from men who believe, or have been taught, that the male sex is more powerful and is placed higher than women in a social hierarchy. Brett G. Stoudt conducted research regarding hegemonic masculinity in an all-boys school to see if the lack of women and women as authoritative figures had an effect on the way these young boys viewed women. This study was taken place in an all-boys school called Rockport, located in an upper-middle to upper-class region. This study was distributed to 148 boys who attended Rockport. Hegemonic masculinity as described in this research paper is the idea and practice that validates the idea that men belong above women in a social hierarchy. Stoudt's research concluded that at Rockport hegemonic masculinity was taught and reinforced through their schooling curriculum. The effect of this on the teenage boys who attend this school was shown through a conversation with David and Brian, two boys who went to school at Rockport. Both David and Brian claimed they viewed girls as a mother or a friend because they were better at the emotional and caring aspects of life. This unfortunately places women in a subordinated position in these teenage boys' minds without them even realizing it.
chunks.label: Hegemonic masculinity research at Rockport
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how hegemonic masculinity reinforces social hierarchies placing men over women, referencing research by Brett G. Stoudt at an all-boys school named Rockport.

chunks.text: As mentioned above the teaching of hegemonic masculinity is very common throughout society and plays a major role in the social hierarchy which places men above women. This hierarchy is one of the major issues that have caused this unequal pay between men and women. If I were to have had a female supervisor who was in charge of the hourly pay it is much more likely that I would have received the pay I was promised while I was being interviewed. There is a small chance that she would have started women lifeguards out at the base pay because she believed “men are stronger than women so in conclusion men are more capable and proficient in this job” just like my male supervisor believed.
chunks.label: Reflecting on supervisor bias in lifeguarding
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how male dominance in the social hierarchy leads to pay disparities, hypothesizing that having a female supervisor at their lifeguard job might have prevented the unequal pay they experienced.

chunks.text:
The discussion of equal pay amongst men and women has been an ongoing topic ever since the first wave of feminism. As the social hierarchy of men being placed above women has decreased so has the gap between the average pay of men and women, however, there is still a fairly large difference. Women making on average 93 cents for every dollar a man makes may not seem like a huge gap in pay, but over time this pay difference adds up. The average annual wage in America is about 51,916 dollars. If a man made that amount in a year a woman would only make around 48,281 dollars. That is a 3,635 dollar difference and when women have to raise children every dollar makes a difference in the mom's life and the child's life. The first step to abolishing this gap in pay is to get rid of the hegemonic masculinity and/or the idea that men are better and harder workers than women, so as result, they should be paid more. Once this idea has been erased from everyone's heads there will not be as noticeable of a gap in pay based on gender, it will be solely based on worth ethics, and experience as companies nowadays say it is.

Word Count: 1643
chunks.label: Eliminating hegemonic masculinity to close wage gap
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses the persistence of the gender pay gap and argues that society must eliminate hegemonic masculinity so that pay is based strictly on work ethic and experience.

chunks.text:
When beginning to think about class, we usually break it up into three main categories: lower, middle and upper class. Although today, class identity has been stripped away from popular culture. In the readings of Class in America by Mantsios and The Power of Elite by Domhoff, we can separate their ideas of class between what our present collective consciousness is about class rankings in the United States.

The middle class in the United States holds a very small share of the nation's wealth, the gap between the lower class and rich and middle class and rich is larger than it’s ever been. Mantsios states that we do separate ourselves, but we don’t identify as our class ranking. The middle class is so large that associating yourself with 60% percent of the population doesn’t really give one much of an identity they can call their own. Domhoff argues that the social upper class enjoys associating themselves with their status-quo. He believes that through institutions young members of the upper class and those who are new to wealth develop a shared understanding of how to be wealthy. Most, but not all, live expensive and exclusive lifestyles.

In my own experiences and some of our collective consciousness is that we do not associate ourselves with class. The middle class is so large, that it is difficult to distinguish between what is considered to be rich or poor throughout the United States. I do believe that wealth within the upper class does provide them with more power than people below them. We do not identify ourselves with a class ranking, but the class we live in does have an impact on developing our own identity.
chunks.label: Reflections on social class and identity
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological readings by Mantsios and Domhoff, analyzing class categories, wealth disparity, and how individuals generally do not identify directly with their class ranking despite its impact on identity.

na2a53d7e.title: Analyzing Power and the Working Class

chunks.text:
Years of inequality has created a divide in America’s social classes. The American working class is relatively powerless in a county that prides itself on its history of pluralism and elections. In “The Class-Domination Theory of Power” by G. William Domhoff and Chapter 4 (Equality) of “21 Lessons for the 21st Century” by Yoval Noah Harari, connect the idea that the weakness of the American working class is a potential reason of an enlarged rift between classes.

Domhoff states that the weakness of the working class began during the Industrial Revolution, when the black/white split between the working class was reinforced, causing conflicts between “skilled” and “unskilled” workers. These workers had no luck organizing themselves through unions, employees had no power unlike their employers who had great influence with politicians. The history of internal division, political frustration and union defeat caused American workers to continue their individualistic ideology. This left the working class with very little social power unless they were a part of the power of elite. Harari shares similar ideology, he believes that the industrial revolution created industrial economies that relied on masses of common workers. The history of the twentieth century revolved to a large extent around the reduction of inequality between classes, races, and genders. Although, the weakness of the working class is the reason that the gap of inequality has grown between social classes. There are signs of growing inequality both between and within societies. Today, the richest 1 percent own half the world’s wealth, and the richest one hundred people together own more than the poorest four billion.

Both Domhoff and Harari could both agree that the working class fuels the power of elite. The 21st century might cause the most unequal societies in history. Just as Americans unify themselves, they begin to separate themselves from each other once again.
chunks.label: Working class weakness and growing inequality
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on readings by Domhoff and Harari regarding how the historical weakness of the American working class has driven growing social class inequality.

chunks.text:
Throughout history, there have been groups of people that have been discriminated against due to race or gender. No group of people has experienced this more than african american women. From being enslaved for being african, directly into having rights very limited just for being a woman, they’ve never had it easy.

The matrix of domination is essentially an explanation of oppression. This explains how somebody could be being oppressed, while also oppressing someone else. For example, white women were oppressed by white men, but at the same time they would oppress african-americnas. This is brought to attention with afican american women because they never have really been the oppressor; between being oppressed by white people for being african american, and then being oppressed by men for being women. With the three levels of oppression being personal biography, group/community (race, class, gender), and social institutions, african american women were oppressed in nearly all three.

Due to historical collective consciousness, many groups of people have been oppressed. African american women are among one of the most oppressed groups of people throughout history because of the two main collective consciousnesses against african americans, and against women. The matrix of domination goes into detail about why different groups of people were oppressed and different levels of resistance to this oppression.
chunks.label: The matrix of domination and oppression of African American women
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses historical discrimination against African American women and explains the sociological concept of the matrix of domination across personal, community, and institutional levels.

chunks.text: This fear brought upon a whole country can be related back to the collective consciousness. When total fear is brought upon a select few then projected onto the whole country by them, everyone is taught to be scared of whatever the fear is coming from. This is not to take away from the tragedy of these attacks, but to merely put them in perspective. With technology having as big of a presence in society today, word, video, and feelings spread much more quickly than ever before. With the 9/11 attacks being publicly broadcasted on as many news channels as you can think of, this feeling of fear and sorrow was brought upon the whole country in almost the snap of 2 fingers. And now with the collective conscious feeling of fear/sorrow from any mention of terrorism, anyone that disagrees would be looked at as crazy.
chunks.label: Collective consciousness and fear following 9/11
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how fear and sorrow from the 9/11 attacks were rapidly projected across the entire country through broadcast media, shaping society's collective consciousness around terrorism.

nefbb1849.title: Performing Frontstage and Backstage in College

chunks.text:
Goffman’s theory of stage is an analogy in which each individual is merely an actor performing on a stage that represents society. The instant the curtain rises, an actor’s goal is to convince their audience that they are not just playing a character, but rather, that they are the character. The hope is that the audience will react positively to the performance. This is frontstage behavior. When the curtain closes, they are stripped of all falsified identity. Now, the actor is forced to re-enter their reality. They can now engage in backstage behavior, like listening to their favorite song during the commute home. Goffman believed that an individual in society is perfectly represented by an actor on stage. For example, a college student arrives late to class and quietly finds her seat. She is being watched by her peers, or at least she feels like she is, so she quickly attempts to adjust herself to fit in. She usually types notes on her laptop, but when she sees everyone else taking handwritten notes, she quickly decides to pull out her notebook instead. This is an example of frontstage behavior. After class, the student heads back to her dorm to catch up on the notes she missed. There is no longer any external pressure on her to handwrite her notes, so she opens her laptop and begins to type without hesitation. This is an example of backstage behavior. Goffman’s theory of stage outlines the effects of societal pressure concerning an individual’s actions, often guiding the individual to lose sight of their true self in high-pressure settings.

James and Goffman’s theories are underscored by the simple idea that humans have an inherent need to be liked. This desire for reassurance is stronger than a genuine sense of self, causing the self to often become overpowered by superficial selves. Individuals, when found amongst peers, are simply projecting a reflection of their understanding of societal expectations. James’ theory of the social self explains the constant stream of information the brain receives from its surroundings to assimilate a temporary self that has the highest chance of being accepted. Goffman’s theory of the stage builds on the social self, as he claims that one’s genuine self will indeed emerge when one feels as if no one is watching. James would refer to the emergence of one’s genuine self as their pure ego. James’ theory of self and Goffman’s theory of stage are merely extensions of one another, best understood when providing each other context.
chunks.label: Goffman and James theories of self and stage
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Goffman's frontstage and backstage theory and James' theory of the social self, illustrating them with a hypothetical example of a student in class and comparing how both theories address the desire for acceptance.

chunks.text:
Today, social media has strong influences on a person's online social self. Young adults are highly impacted by social networking sites. People can change or update their personalities to create friendships. Social media provides an outlet for people to illustrate themselves by self-presentation. Social media users then manifest their identities to join other communities to increase their sociality. Although, we begin to wonder how someone's online social self may differentiate from their offline social self. Also, how social media effects ourselves and manipulates our personality. Do we create our own identity or are we influenced by social media? Throughout this paper, I will cover multiple concepts that connect the idea that social media plays a crucial role in developing our online social self.
