In class, we studied Cooley and Mead’s argument of social self. Coming to a mutual conclusion that a man's self is the sum total of what he can call his own. Things such as body, clothes, house, friends and family. Man can have multiple social selves, as there are individuals who recognize him and carry a certain image of him in their mind. We create different social selves because we associate ourselves with multiple groups, and man’s social self is made by the recognition he receives in those groups. We divide up ourselves in all sorts of different selves with reference to our acquaintances, the social process itself is responsible for the appearances of oneself. Therefore, we can argue that social networking sites are partially responsible for the creation of an online social self throughout multiple groups. We being to dive into the social media that allows us to create our online personality.

Firstly, we will begin discussing how selfies operate as a ubiquitous mode of sociality. (Cambre 2019). Media and mobile culture often present social media and selfies which then allow active self-creation. We may take selfies for control, to be visible/invisible or just for fun. The practices of “selfie culture”, which consist of posting and receiving selfies, allows us to receive affirmation from others and builds our self-esteem. Overtime replacing old selfies with new ones allows us to create a new social identity. Keeping up with the social stigma makes people believe they must look a certain way over social media in order to develop relationships with new friends and communities. “As such, pictures of the self are understood as the self but also illustrate how personal identity is increasingly rooted in commodifying and objectifying epistemologies. Narrative forms of identity stressing how the self is continuously rewritten and revised within a dialectics of continuity and rupture seem displaced by the selfie” (Cambre 2019). Social media post such as selfies are the beginning of what influences us to keep up with the most present stigma. It is the foundation of developing one's own social self over social media. Next, we consider how our offline self-impacts our online identity.

In the last few years, the internet has become one of the prime places for social interaction among peers. Young adults have a strong need for online socialization, as being offline can sometimes be more difficult. We begin to understand why offline identities influence young people's online interaction, behavioral and cognitive (Helsper 2014). We answer the question, “Does awareness of certain identity aspects influence how teenagers feel about themselves and act in online environments?” (Helsper 2014). We begin by getting greater background knowledge of how adolescents begin to develop their own identity. Interaction and communication are important to develop at this stage in order to build a social network and create a sense of self. Researchers argue a shift as occurred, and now this stage is being done over the internet (Davis 2012). Teenagers have the need to identify with certain social groups and have strong desires to be romantically involved. This begins the idea of belonging influence, and how teenagers think about themselves and who they interact with. “What is clear is that offline personality and identity aspects are used by teens to determine how to present themselves and interact online” (Helsper 2014).

The Social Identification and Deindividuation (SIDE) is a framework that argues that social identity influences individual's self-perceptions and behaviors according to social norms (Helsper 2014). SIDE builds upon the self-categorization theory, which supposes that recognizing oneself as a member of a social group depends on the awareness of the group as part of the self. Identification within the group therefore leads to behaviors and self-perceptions to conform to group norms. SIDE frameworks have become an explained link between social identity and online interactions. SIDE often researchers about teen identity development in online interactions, or the content of the interaction in relation to one aspect of identity (mostly gender). There have been experiments about how the prominence of gender, ethnicity and generational aspects are manipulated in an online environment. One experiment consisted of 220 students from 15 secondary schools in the United Kingdom, schools were selected based on the ethnic makeup of their student body (Helsper 2014). All participants were seated behind their own computer, they could not interact with other students unless it was online. “The findings presented here suggest that offline social group norms related to gender and ethnic identities influence how teenagers think about themselves in online interactive contexts and that the way in which they are addressed can change the importance of different identity aspect” (Helsper 2014). This confirms that identities influence how teenagers see themselves and the way they act online. Now that we understand that our offline selves develop our online identities, we now dive deeper into how teenagers develop friendships and communities.

After discussing self-presentation and our online identities, we can argue that these two things can create friendship development among young adults. The concepts of media richness, perceived functionality and openness lead to friendship development on social media sites such as Instagram (Lee and Borah 2020). Social networking sites have become an outlet for identity expression amongst teenagers. Instagram, an image sharing, and self-presentation application has attracted more than one billion monthly users and is the fastest growing mobile media, social networking sites around the world. From creating personal profiles and posting videos, photos, liking and commenting has created multiple chances for young adults to manifest their identities. This helps strengthen their need for belongingness to their communities. Instagram gives self-expressive opportunities, and this impacts interpersonal dynamics such as developing friendships. Most studies focus on intrinsic factors such as personality traits. “Regarding self-expression, personality trait of openness has been examined under other media contexts and the trait was found to play an influential role” (Lee and Borah 2020). Openness, for example creating blogs and vlogs, has made attention for the explication of self-presentation on Instagram. Media Richness theory illustrates that media platforms are built on; immediate interaction, cues such as texts, images, symbols and gestures, focus on personal interest, and communication with natural languages. This theory is considered a fitting tool because Instagram works towards visualization, and this enhances natural communication.

Self- presentation in social networking sites such as Instagram give users expressive opportunities to contribute to their self-presentational behaviors. Instagram provides new features such as animated stickers and creative fonts which help users better express themselves. Users would perceive Instagram as more functional for self-presentation, and it allows them to be more expressive. This being said, an hypothetical assumption can be made, self-presentation on Instagram is positively related to friendship development (Lee and Borah 2020). Friendship development is one of the most critical forms of social capital that can be created through the self-presentation. We can conclude that perceived media richness, perceived functionality and the personality trait of openness leads to self-presentation, which is positively associated with friendship development. (Lee and Borah 2020).

Cooley and Mead argued that we have multiple social selves depending how others perceive us. Social media platforms allow us to creatively express ourselves, and according to Mead, a person's social self is the recognition which they get from their peers. Social media platforms give people the opportunity to self-present themselves to others. We can use things such as selfies for control and to keep up with social stigmas. We can choose what parts of us we want to make visible and invisible to viewers, or it can be just for fun. We update photos to demonstrate our new social selves to others. Social media post such as selfies are the foundation of self-expression. Then we dived deeper into what creates our online social selves. Young adults have a need for online socialization, and that our identities offline greatly impact the way we act online. Teenagers seem to follow the offline social norms of identity and bring those norms into online scenarios. Personal identities influence teenagers and the way they act online. Then while teenagers utilize social networking sites such as Instagram, three things become a driving factor when developing online friendships. Media richness, openness and perceived functionality. These three concepts are what create self-presentation, which then leads to the development of friendships. It begins with a social media post, such as a selfie. Then it leads to online interactions with others. Lastly, social networking users begin to develop a online social self and begin the develop friendships and create communities. Social networking sites are the reason we have created online social selves.

Work Cited

nac645728.title: Navigating Comparison and Identity on Social Media

chunks.text:
In any social scene there’s going to be some people that have higher status than others, on social media this is especially relevant and not the most ideal situation. While users gain their popularity and climb to the top of the applications fame, they can be viewed as role models and can inspire people to improve themselves, help others, and do good in the community. Other popular users don’t utilize their reach for good and end up promoting products, goods, and services that will make them money but then the rest of us then feel like we need to be more like them. Oftentimes these promoted items are out of the general population's reach, making us feel as though we won’t be able to become more like them resulting in us feeling down on ourselves. With these users being so easily accessible, these feelings become increasingly common.

Other pressures of social media don’t even come from the top users, but from common users feeling like they have to present their absolute best self on their own profile for others to see. In Christian Baccarella’s article Social Media? It's Serious! Understanding the Dark Side of Social Media he describes this as “oversharing photos of positive experiences unintentionally causing anxiety among those who live less glamorous”. This includes anywhere from the pressures of posting the perfect picture in order to get the much desired validation from “friends” and “followers”; to scrolling through your own feed and seeing your friends and others posts of that crazy international vacation they’re on, or that fancy restaurant downtown that everyone wants to go to, or some crazy party that you didn’t hear about in time inducing quick feelings of spite and jealousy. With everyone putting on their best fronts for social media it’s easy to come across posts like these and feel down on yourself.

The American sociologist Charles Cooley’s concept of the “Looking Glass Self” fits perfectly into the role that social media plays in our daily lives. The “Looking Glass Self” is Cooley's concept of how individuals view themselves based on two things; how we directly view ourselves in our own company, and how we perceive others view us. This concept was created in the early 1900’s, prior to any advanced technology, but is still relevant in the fact that through social media, the thought “what will everyone that sees this think of me” goes through any users prior to posting anything. “Presenting one's identity is a central aspect of social media” (Baccarella), although more often than not, the “identity” presented to that social media platform is the one that they want everyone to see; not the most genuine and realistic to that person's actual identity. This is because it is a part of human nature to think about how others will perceive them based on what they are doing, or in this case posting. In fact, prior to posting anything nobody has seen it, so we are basing our view of ourself off of how we think others will perceive what they are about to see. This is exactly what Cooley explains as the second part of how we view ourselves, based on how we believe that others will think of us.

Having most social media applications typically involve heavy photo-sharing by both peers and celebrities (Burnette), the users with big followings are able to visually show off how they’re living and how they look, usually widely believed to be more attractive with near perfect physique. This combined with being backed by their social reputation, which “can be indicated by the number of followers someone has, the sentiments of the comments expressed about that user, the view and like counts for a user's post, or the status some platforms award to users” (Baccarella), leads to their lifestyle being extremely sought after but near impossible to reach. The photo-heavy social media platforms nowadays lead to general users being more exposed to upward appearance comparisons, which can cause users to develop poorer body image (Burnette). The american philosopher George Mead had a similar concept of self-conception to that of Cooley, but was more general. His concept of “The Self, The I, and The Me” was that “The Me” is how the general society as a whole views someone, “The I” is who that person is and how they act according to this view, and “The Self” is the balance between both “The I” and “The Me”. This is prevalent in social media because with the popular users having such positive comments to a body image post, this can exert influence on young adults’ perceptions of an ideal body and their own body perception (Kim). Making them not want to post pictures of themselves because they think society's view of their “Me” won’t be good compared to those of the popular users.

The popular users having positive comments to body image posts isn’t always a bad thing though. Because “Social media comments provide users with the ability not only to express their own opinion but also to monitor the other viewers’ collective reactions” (Kim), this allows for the ideal body image to be commonly believed among the social media community, giving some people a goal to work towards as opposed to an image used as comparison. This is more common in users with lower self-discrepancy due to the ideal body being believed to actually be achievable. Users with higher self-discrepancy are more likely to use these ideal body images as means of self comparison/evaluation due to the huge discrepancy and gap they already have (Kim).

Social media's influence on society and how people view each other is as dominant as ever, which causes many people to put up a front to blend in with the crowd. When viewing these famous social media stars’ profiles it can be easy to get caught up in what to aspire for and end up comparing yourself to them, and everyone does it from time to time. The pressures of showing off your best self on social media will also always be around, but remembering that other peoples profiles are also fronts of their best life can help users to not feel as jealous or self-conscious of themselves when scrolling through their feed. It is and always will be in human nature to care about what others will think of you, but not focusing on this and being confident in yourself will lead to more enjoyable social media experiences.
chunks.label: Social media influence, self-presentation, and sociological theories
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how social media impacts self-esteem and body image, applying Cooley's Looking Glass Self and Mead's concept of the self to online behavior.

chunks.text: Why is physical appearance the main measurement of self-worth for the majority of women? Who decided that what a woman looked like determined how valued they would be within society? What enables the power difference between men and women within society? These questions and more have been asked over and over by women trying to come up with logical solutions to the disparities that they face compared to men. One logical reason is the idea that women’s value is based more on what they look like versus their accomplishments in life. The “ideal woman” is based on stereotypes that men place upon women. This idea is known as the beauty myth. To stop the perpetuation of these degrading standards, women need to take back their power by straying from these unrealistic beauty ideals.
chunks.label: Introduction to the beauty myth and gender disparities
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the concept of the beauty myth and questions why women's self-worth and power are determined by their physical appearance.

chunks.text: Being a woman myself, I have experienced events of being looked down upon only because of the gender I am. There have been times when I have been mansplained only because I present as female. Or times when men think that I am incapable of doing something just because I am a girl. A common experience that I think many girls can relate to is not being picked on to stack chairs. Throughout school, I was told I wouldn’t be able to pick up as many chairs as the boys or told that I was unable to do something because it was a “boys’ job.” The girls are just supposed to sit around and “look pretty” while the boys do the “hard work.” I remember always being mad because I knew that I could’ve done anything the boys did. I just didn’t understand how much being a girl and trying to “fit in” would affect me until I grew up.
chunks.label: Gendered expectations and stacking chairs in school
chunks.what_happened: Throughout school, the student experienced being mansplained, seen as incapable, and excluded from physical tasks like stacking chairs because she was a girl.

chunks.text: As I aged and moved to the Northeast, I found myself being more and more worried about what I looked like. I had never really cared growing up because I had lived in Colorado where all the girls were just as much a tomboy as I was. They played outside just as much as I did. They wore baggy clothes and had dirt all over their faces after a day of playing just as I did. These normal experiences for me completely changed however when I moved to Massachusetts. In Massachusetts, the beauty myth was in full effect. You didn’t fit in with the girls unless you wore makeup, wore pink, and tried to impress the boys. This culture shock was a major change for me as I had never been a girly girl. I spent most of my life playing outside with my brother and his friends. Now, I was being forced to like playing with makeup, doing my hair, and wearing tighter clothes.
chunks.label: Culture shock moving from Colorado to Massachusetts
chunks.what_happened: After growing up playing outside as a tomboy in Colorado with her brother and his friends, the student moved to Massachusetts and faced pressure to wear makeup, do her hair, and dress feminine.

chunks.text: This ideal to look feminine has been prominent in my life ever since that time. I have felt the need to show off my body to get male attention. This concept is so disturbing as I am forced to wear uncomfortable clothing and gross makeup so that a guy will look at me two seconds longer than normal. It’s, even more, overwhelming in college as it seems as though every girl is looking for male validation in any way they can. This has led to some of my friends not eating as much as they should or revealing too much of themselves so that guys can find them attractive. It’s not only women in the real world who seem to act, dress, and just be for male validation.
chunks.label: Pressure for male validation in college
chunks.what_happened: The student felt pressured to wear uncomfortable clothing and makeup for male attention, and witnessed college friends restricting food or dressing revealingly for male validation.

chunks.text:
Women in video games, tv shows, and movies all adhere to femininity for men. In video games, tv shows, and movies women are normally side characters. They are seen as the weak side characters who need the help of a big strong male character to fix their problems. They are also normally always dressed in a sexual way—tight and revealing clothes. There are very few movies in which a female character is an independent woman who doesn’t need a man to prove her worth. Even the ones that are produced and sent to movie theatres often do a lot worse with critics and with the overall money that they generate. Society doesn’t like to see women who aren’t living their lives with the intent of pleasing men.

The idea of women needing to feel beautiful to feel worthy/have value is known as the “beauty myth.” This concept was introduced by Naomi Wolf in the 1990s. She explains that women are judged on their appearance which creates a societal standard affecting their behavior. This societal standard is enforced by men who want women to be a specific size, a specific shape, and act a specific way. By creating this structure of who and what women can be, men can stay in power. They can pin women against each other in an attempt to have women compete to prove who the “perfect woman” is. However, the problem is that there is no “perfect woman.” The concept is socially constructed. It isn’t what women believe, but it is instead what is forced onto them through media. If the media shows skinny, (normally) white models then most women are going to try to obtain that same look. This is why plastic surgery, as well as the number of eating disorders, have shot up immensely after the introduction of social media. Women are trying to obtain bodies that will play into the male gaze with devastating consequences.

I take this theory of the beauty myth and place it into the context of all of the experiences that I talked about earlier, we see an obvious connection. Girls from a young age are taught that men need to take care of them. They are too weak and small to do anything physical. Men are supposed to take care of them and protect them. Not only does this further perpetuate the beauty myth, but it also creates a corollary myth for men. If society believes that men are around to protect and take care of women, this creates pressure on men. They are taught to be tough, don’t cry, and always be strong. This ideology adds to why toxic masculinity is such a prominent problem within our society. If men are measured by their possession of women, men with little to no women believe as though women owe them themselves. They are men and therefore get to “have” women. When women don’t give in to this, men can become violent and aggressive toward women in general.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of beauty standards and toxic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes media representation of women, Naomi Wolf's beauty myth theory, social media's impact on eating disorders, and how expectations on men fuel toxic masculinity.

chunks.text: If we apply the concept of the beauty myth to my experience growing up, we can see the obvious correlation. As I got older, I felt the beauty myth placed upon me even more. I could feel that I wouldn’t be seen as valuable to not only men but society as well if I didn’t fit in the mold. I needed to be skinny, have my hair and makeup done, and behave appropriately toward men. If I didn’t, I would be ostracized from society. Men wouldn’t find me attractive; therefore, making me worthless. However, because I want to fit in with society, I decided to do my hair and makeup. I changed my appearance so men could find me appealing. I gave in to the beauty myth.
chunks.label: Giving in to beauty standards to fit in
chunks.what_happened: As she got older, the student chose to alter her appearance by doing her hair and makeup to fit societal expectations and be appealing to men.

chunks.text: Women are forced to fit into unrealistic beauty standards in today’s society to be seen as worth anything. We have to change ourselves in all ways both physically and mentally to fit the mold that the media and men place upon them. We have to fit the stereotypes that are perpetuated—pretty and subservient to men. If I and other women want to escape from the abomination that is the beauty myth, we need to take back our bodies. We, collectively, need to stop giving in to the pressures of the media. We need to take back the power that was ripped away from us. Men have kept us away from male-dominated spheres like politics and STEM. They have placed women against each other when we should be coming together to get rid of this corrupt societal standard. If we want things to get better, we need to show everyone the truth. The beauty myth is anything but a myth. It’s a real and pressing matter that will continue to devalue women for generations to come unless we come together and make our needs a reality.
chunks.label: Call for women to reject beauty standards
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by urging women to unite, stop submitting to media pressures and male-dominated standards, and dismantle the beauty myth.

chunks.text: In my life and the lives of others, I have noticed the harmful effects of social media on self-confidence and body image. From friends sharing their insecurities to countless posts advocating unrealistic beauty ideals, the pressure to be perfect is evident. The widespread presence of these images and their impact on people's self-worth presents a puzzle that can be examined through the lens of Wolf's "The Beauty Myth."
chunks.label: Introduction to social media and beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the harmful effects of social media on self-confidence and frames this issue through Naomi Wolf's 'The Beauty Myth.'

chunks.text: One day, while studying in Randall with my best friend, we decided to take a break and catch up on each other's lives. As we were talking, she pulled out her phone to check her social media. She was scrolling through Instagram when I noticed her expression change, and a sadness washed over her. I asked her what was wrong, but she just shrugged it off, saying it was nothing. I couldn't help but notice that my friend became quieter and more withdrawn after that moment. I knew she had encountered something on social media that had affected her. Finally, after a bit of gentle prodding, she admitted that she had seen photos of influencers promoting an unattainable body image. The images made her feel insecure about her own appearance and fueled her self-doubt.
chunks.label: Friend becoming insecure while studying at Randall
chunks.what_happened: While taking a study break at Randall library, the student's best friend scrolled through Instagram and became visibly sad and withdrawn. After gentle prodding, the friend admitted feeling insecure after seeing photos of influencers promoting unattainable body standards.

chunks.text: It’s really profound how immediate and deep an impact a screen can affect a human being. Something that is so obviously fake, can influence our emotions on a serious level. These algorithms are specifically designed to make you feel a certain way. To garner your attention, and there is no intention within it that is good.
chunks.label: Impact of screens and algorithms
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the immediate emotional impact of screens and the morally unacceptable predation of algorithms designed to manipulate emotions.

chunks.text:
On a moral level, there is no reality where this predation is acceptable.

This instance highlighted how the unrealistic beauty standards perpetuated by social media, as described by Naomi Wolf's "The Beauty Myth," could have immediate and profound effects on individuals like Sarah. Her self-confidence was shaken, and she began questioning her self-worth, wondering if she wasn't attractive enough to be valued by society.
chunks.label: Friend questioning self-worth after seeing standards
chunks.what_happened: The student recounts how the friend, Sarah, experienced shaken self-confidence and questioned her self-worth and attractiveness following the encounter with social media beauty standards.

chunks.text:
Naomi Wolf's idea of "The Beauty Myth" suggests that society's beauty standards are an oppressive force, maintained to keep women under control. According to Wolf, these standards are impossible to achieve and always changing, making sure women continuously strive for an ideal they can never truly reach. To better understand this concept, think about the fashion industry's promotion of extremely thin models as the ultimate beauty standard in the 1990s. This ideal was then replaced by a more athletic and toned appearance in the 2000s, leaving women trying to adapt to the new standard.

Using Wolf's concept of "The Beauty Myth," we can now analyze the effects of social media on beauty standards and self-esteem. The constant flood of images on social media platforms, often digitally edited or filtered, strengthens the idea that perfection is achievable. This false belief increases the pressure to fit into these unrealistic standards, leaving people feeling not good enough and always chasing an unattainable goal. Moreover, social media algorithms often keep this cycle going by promoting content that aligns with these beauty ideals, reinforcing the myth's power.

Through the lens of "The Beauty Myth," we can also understand how beauty has become a product on social media. Influencers and celebrities often take advantage of this myth by promoting beauty products and treatments that promise to help people achieve the "perfect" look. This commercialization of beauty creates a culture of consumption that makes money from people's insecurities, further embedding the power of the beauty myth in society.

Additionally, the beauty myth perpetuates harmful gender stereotypes that are detrimental to both women and men. For women, it reinforces the idea that their worth is primarily based on their physical appearance, while for men, it promotes toxic masculinity and the notion that they must adhere to specific body types and appearances. The perpetuation of these stereotypes on social media platforms contributes to a culture that values conformity over individuality and exacerbates the harmful impact of the beauty myth.

By understanding the role that social media plays in maintaining and promoting the beauty myth, we can raise awareness of the issue and encourage individuals to critically evaluate the images and messages they consume. Creating open conversations about the unrealistic standards perpetuated by the media can help empower individuals to challenge these ideals and promote a more inclusive and diverse representation of beauty.

Naomi Wolf's idea of "The Beauty Myth" offers valuable insights into the puzzle of unattainable beauty standards pushed by social media platforms. By understanding how these standards are oppressive and ever-changing, we can start to see the negative effects they have on people's self-esteem and mental well-being. Furthermore, recognizing the commercialization and consumer culture surrounding beauty on social media allows us to question the systems that profit from our insecurities.

The importance of this analysis goes beyond the world of social media, as the beauty myth is deeply rooted in society as a whole. By critically examining and questioning these standards, we can start to break down the oppressive structures that perpetuate them and work towards a more inclusive and empowering definition of beauty. In doing so, we can ultimately create a more just society that celebrates and values diversity in all its forms.

One potential way to challenge the beauty myth is through the promotion of body positivity and self-love. Encouraging individuals to embrace their unique appearances and focus on their personal strengths can help counteract the negative effects of unrealistic beauty standards. By sharing diverse images and stories on social media platforms, we can create a more inclusive online environment that reflects the true variety of human beauty.

Moreover, educating young people about the harmful effects of the beauty myth and the manipulation of images on social media can help build resilience against the pressure to conform to unrealistic standards. Providing tools for critical thinking and media literacy can empower individuals to navigate the digital landscape with a more discerning eye and a greater understanding of the constructed nature of beauty ideals.

Lastly, advocating for greater transparency and responsibility from social media platforms and the advertising industry can help mitigate the harmful impact of the beauty myth. By holding these entities accountable for the content they promote, we can push for a more ethical and inclusive representation of beauty that reflects the diversity of our society.

In summary, applying Naomi Wolf's concept of "The Beauty Myth" to social media allows us to better understand the pressure of unrealistic beauty standards and their impact on individuals' self-esteem and mental health. By acknowledging the oppressive nature of these standards and the role of social media in perpetuating them, we can work towards dismantling the structures that support the beauty myth and create a more inclusive and diverse understanding of beauty. By doing so, we can foster a more equitable society that values and celebrates the uniqueness of every individual.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis using Wolf's Beauty Myth
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Naomi Wolf's concept of 'The Beauty Myth,' discussing how social media and algorithms commercialize beauty, reinforce stereotypes, and harm self-esteem, while proposing solutions like media literacy and body positivity.

nc7b980e0.title: Questioning Religion and Finding Personal Spirituality

chunks.text: Have you or someone you know ever questioned religion or what religion means to you? I have. Religion is something that many people consider a top priority in their lives. It gives people a way to frame their morals and a way to direct the choices that they make throughout their lives. It can act as a pathway to guide your life. However, religion is something that many people also question. People who are very religious and grounded by religion can sometimes judge those who question religion or aren’t as grounded by it. This idea was something I was worried about when I began to question religion. My whole life I was surrounded by family and friends who put religion as one of the top priorities in their life. They questioned me when I began to ponder the importance of religion in my own life.
chunks.label: Questioning religion surrounded by religious family
chunks.what_happened: The student began questioning religion and felt worried about being judged because their family and friends prioritized religion. Their family and friends questioned them when they started reconsidering religion's importance.

chunks.text:
Religion is one of the founding principles of sociology and arguably is one of the biggest influences in one’s life; from day-to-day conditions to pathways in which one guides their life. Religion throughout the timeline of society has continuously developed and gained more and more importance. At the beginning of society, religion helped shape language and create social groups as well as being something that didn’t make you lesser-than or different than someone else. Currently, religion still creates social groups but can also play a role in the creation of stereotypes and in “othering” people who don’t have the same beliefs as you may. In earlier periods of society, religion was more important to define social groups than it currently is now

Religion has been an important aspect of society for centuries and continues to grow with society as society develops. You may be wondering why religion is so important and what exactly religion has done for society. In present-day society, there are many different religions as well as different groups formed out of a broader religion. For example, Christianity has many different branches. There’s Presbyterian, Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, and many more. Most religions have different branches based on one broad idea. While each one has similarities, they are all separated by smaller beliefs that categorize people into groups of religion within a religion. Religion today has grown into something that is more than a personal belief; it is involved in government, politics, and protests. In the earlier periods of society, religion was something that was used to create languages and cognition as well as being used as a tool to create groups within a society. So, while religion has changed and developed over time, the founding principle of social group creation still exists.

At the beginning of society, religion was analyzed as a tool that helped to create social groups and develop language and cognition. In the essay, Neurology of Religion, by Alexandra Maryanski and Jonathan H. Turner, they go into depth about the effects of religion in earlier society. They argue that religion helped to “work on a facility…on the hominin brain to increase sociality and capacities for group formation among humans’ ancestors. (Pages 113-114)” Religion played an interesting role in organizing rituals and increasing religious behavior and social groups. The largest effect of religion as argued by Maryanski and Turner is the social group forming factor. In the period of society discussed in the essay, religion wasn’t used in a group form to create social standards or stereotypes, but rather provide individuals with a proper place to fit into society. It helped to create a deeper level of cognition, and over time has changed into a way to be categorized in society.

As argued by Durkheim, religion “provides social cohesion to help maintain social solidarity through shared religious beliefs.” This means that religion was a form of unity and played a major role in shaping society as we know it today. I believe that without the formation of religious groups, society would not be the same. Without the formation of religion, society wouldn’t have a unifying factor that allowed people to find their social group and expand their beliefs. Religion acts as a form of expression, and that is one idea that hasn’t changed as society has developed throughout the centuries.

Religion has continuously shifted throughout society. As stated previously, religion acted as a tool for the formation of social groups and aided in increasing cognition. Currently, religion still creates social groups, but in a different way than in earlier periods.
chunks.label: Sociological perspectives on religion and society
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the historical role of religion in forming social groups, developing language, and fostering cohesion, citing sociologists and scholarly works.

chunks.text: My experience with religion hasn’t always been smooth sailing. I grew up in a Christian household, with a mom who took my brother and I to church every Sunday and even some Wednesdays for small group studies. I also went to a Christian school from kindergarten to third grade. I didn’t begin to question religion until I went through a traumatic experience. After this, I began to wonder why God would allow such a bad thing to happen to me and my family at such a young age, so I started looking into other religions or even into spirituality. I eventually settled on more of a belief of spirituality rather than a specific religion, and it was at first something very hard for my mother to understand. Once I voiced to her why I questioned it, however, she began to become more understanding and respect my new beliefs. I know quite a few people who have gone through something similar in regards to questioning religion and I think it is a very interesting thing to occur when someone begins to question it. While I do not belong to a specific religion when meeting and interacting with other spiritual people I feel that I am a part of a social group. This is something important to analyze because religions are very specific groups in society and if you don’t fit into one of those groups, you can be seen as an outsider. I have only felt this way a few times, but for the most part, I do still feel like I belong to a group in society, whether or not religious people would view me as an “other”.
chunks.label: Shift from Christianity to spirituality after trauma
chunks.what_happened: Growing up attending church and Christian school, the student began questioning religion after a traumatic experience and turned to spirituality. Their mother initially struggled to understand but eventually respected the student's beliefs, and the student found belonging among other spiritual people.

chunks.text:
Another major way that religion has shifted in society over time is through the way that it is used and how it affects people in society. While religion was once used as a tool for belonging in society, it is now used in government and politics as well as creating a sense of belonging in society. People in the government, as well as politicians, have come to realize the power that religion has over people, and have started using it against people in things like trying to gain a vote in an election. This is also something that I think is important to analyze because, in the earlier periods of society, religion was seen as a positive aspect of society that captured ones’ beliefs and morals. While this is still true, it is also used as a tool against people in present-day society. Religion has gone from something with such a positive connotation to something with a slightly negative connotation.

I believe that religion was a more important aspect of society during the earlier time periods because it is now used as a tool against people, rather than something that solely helps to create social groups. As argued throughout the essay, religion does continue to aid in the creation of social groups, but often is not a positive thing and can push people to be considered “others” of society if they do not agree with the majority of people’s religious beliefs. The evidence that supports this is mainly involved with government and politics.
chunks.label: Reflection on religion in modern politics
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how religion has shifted from a unifying social tool into a political instrument that can manipulate and 'other' people.

chunks.text: People involved in the government now use religion as a way to get people to follow them, not as something that is ones’ thoughts. It has shifted from being a social group created to a way to categorize people, but not always in a positive way. This is shown with my situation when I questioned religion and changed my religious beliefs from the ones’ of my parents to my own beliefs. Much of my family still doesn’t know that I do not belong to a specific religious group because they wouldn’t support this change that I decided. I was very lucky to have supportive parents that don’t think religion is the most important part of someones’ life and that respected my new beliefs as I grew up and developed my own beliefs and morals.
chunks.label: Hiding non-religious beliefs from extended family
chunks.what_happened: The student kept their departure from traditional religion a secret from most of their family out of fear they would not be supportive, while appreciating their supportive parents.

chunks.text:
This is relevant in present-day society because as stated before, there have been more and more people who question their religious beliefs.

In conclusion, I believe that religion has shifted throughout society to be something that hurts society more than it helps it. Society was built on the principles of individual thought, however, when someone begins to question religion society sees it from a negative point of view rather than a positive point of view. I also believe that religion should be something that people should be able to decide for themselves and not experience pressure from society to conform to a specific religion.
chunks.label: Conclusion on personal freedom in religion
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that people should be allowed to decide their religious beliefs for themselves without facing societal pressure or negative judgment.

n71648608.title: Unlearning Expectations of Femininity Through Fiction

chunks.text:
The Concept of the Beauty Myth and Othering of Women in Fiction:

Application in Selected Fictional Media

The idea of the beauty myth has been around for centuries in one form or another particularly in fictional media. There has always been an idea of what a “woman” should look, talk, think, and act like that changes from one generation to another. With the goalposts of womanhood changing over the course of time and generations, the pressures surrounding and pushing for conformity have to change with the times. The emergence of social media and the increasing interconnectedness of people to each other has only served to heighten the societal pressure to adhere to the ideas of what a woman is in different situations. This affects fiction in all forms and provides a blueprint for reality and the people in the real world to follow.

Gillian Flynn is a popular fiction writer whose works focus on women's relationships with the beauty myths that surround their roles in their worlds and how that affects them and the people around them. I chose to use two of her novels ``Gone Girl” and “Sharp Objects'' as I have a close connection with both pieces. I feel like they demonstrate how the beauty myth is unobtainable in a concrete way and only serves to enforce rules onto women's presence in the world that keep them separate from themselves and their relationships. By changing the goalposts for what a woman is supposed to be, there is no way to “become” a woman and then stay one in the eyes of the collective society. It is a never ending push to conform to constantly changing standards and diffrening situations.

This idea of femininity encompasses every aspect of a person. The film and novel “Gone Girl” , has a monologue where the leading woman, Amy Dunne, is talking about what makes up a “Cool Girl” , the girl that every guy wants as opposed to the person she actually is when she is by herself; “Cool Girls are above all hot. Hot and understanding. Cool Girls never get angry; they only smile in a chagrined, loving manner and let their men do whatever they want.” This idea encompasses what she looks like, how she talks, how she acts, how she thinks, her relationships with men, and how she lets people treat her. This is the beauty myth under another name and with a different face but it's the beauty myth all the same. The presence of the beauty myth is so strong that it sinks into fiction and for this specific example, is part of the reason Amy sets the events of the novel into motion.

Her resentment for the role she feels she has to play, as the Cool Girl her husband wants her to be in spite of his affair and his increasing poor attitude twords her, leads her to frame her husband for her murder as an act of revenge. Amy even goes as far to tell her husband at the end of the novel that he made her this way and that he wouldn't have wanted her any other way, she goes on to say she wouldn't be capable of loving if she wasn't exactly the way he made her. This supports the beauty myth as she not only conformed to the “cool girl” her husband wanted; she was also the dutiful wife, the tragic murder victim, the suffering victim when she returned home, and the scheming women her husband is stuck with out of spousal obligation. The beauty myth rewards women that can perform femininity and the roles each situation provides for them but will punish them for the slightest deviation outside the established lines.

To further add to the idea that the beauty myth can be used to push the idea that beauty myth is a consequence in fiction, in “Sharp Objects”, femininity is rewarded and deviance from the norm is punished. The novel is about Camille Preaker, a conventionally attractive journalist, coming back to her hometown to write about a series of murders of children whose teeth are then removed. Her being seen as a “pretty woman” is used by her to get information she needs about the dead girls and their families for her story and she is shamed when her scars, scars she gave herself that “ruin” the idea of what she should look like, are revealed to her romantic interest and her younger half sister, Amma Crellin. Her mother punishes her for having the scars and for her career, as a journalist which is viewed as improper for a woman, in front of Amma, reinforcing the belief to the sister that looks, particularly feminine looks and attitude are everything and are used as bargaining chips in the world. It is shown over the course of the book that all the little girls who were killed were “tomboys”, were known as troublemakers, and all had a history of biting people.

The climax of the book shows that Camille's younger half sister, Amma Crellin, murdered the girls to punish them for being different and taking more of her mothers attention because of their differences. Amma would then remove the girl's teeth to make a marble floor in her dollhouse that was a replica of her own home. She would murder the girls as punishment for not being “good little girls”, remove their one form of protection, and then use that to play house where Amma was the leading role. Amma used the beauty myth as reasoning for the deaths of these girls, providing severe consequences for inability to conform.

In Gone Girl, the beauty myth is something that Amy comes to resent because of how much it affects her life and her relationships. In Sharp Objects, Amma uses the idea of how she should look and behave as a girl as a weapon to harm and kill other girls to punish them. Both stories paint the idea of femininity as a looming presence over women, waiting for a mistake or a slip up, and then punishment of some sort will follow. Obviously the real world is not like this, with murderous little girls and scheming housewives waiting in the wings to punish those who act outside the norms, but there is the presence of what you should look, talk, and act like as a woman always at the back of your mind. This idea has to come from somewhere and fiction is as good a place as any for this to spring from.

Margaret Atwood is quoted as saying “You are a woman with a man inside watching a woman. You are your own voyeur." That there will always be a person watching you inside of you, judging you based on the standards shown to you as you grow up. I used Sharp Objects and Gone Girl for fictional examples as they are pieces of media I found at a time in my life where I was struggling with the idea of the beauty myth.
chunks.label: The beauty myth in fiction and media
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the concept of the beauty myth and examines how it is portrayed and subverted in Gillian Flynn's novels Gone Girl and Sharp Objects.

chunks.text: I was raised in a very strict no makeup, no “girly” things household where more masculine traits were praised. I remember being jealous of the other girls my age doing ballet when I did martial arts instead. In high school I envied my best friend going out with her boyfriend on the weekends when I was competing in fighting tournaments. I grew up with no idea how to perform femininity the way I say other girls grow into. My mom never taught me how to do my makeup and my dad never gave my boyfriend the “You hurt my daughter, I hurt you” speech. I felt like I was watching all the girls my age through a glass plane, I could see them but they were totally alien to me.
chunks.label: Growing up without performing traditional femininity
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up in a strict household where girly things were not allowed, did martial arts instead of ballet, and felt disconnected from other girls and typical feminine rituals.

chunks.text:
Then I found Gone Girl, where the main character resents the way she was brought up into the beauty myth with all her heart. Amy hates the idea that she's supposed to be the perfect wife by other people's standards. This was the first time I had seen media that didn’t endorse the perfect little girl idea of the beauty myth. In the second act of the book Amy goes into hiding by cutting her hair poorly, dying it patchy and uneven, and gaining weight. The novel makes a point in saying she enjoys the rebelling against what she was raised to be. That was so shocking to me at the time. Amy did exactly what you're told not to do from a young age as a girl and not only that, she enjoyed it. As the story goes on, Amy's distaste for other women and their conformity to the beauty myth is shown and her true colors as a person very comfortable with immoral actions that benefit her are brought to light, but seeing a woman deliberately go against the beauty myth so dramatically showed me that there were other options to how I could inhibit the world without necessarily conforming to femininity to the letter.

The thing that struck me so much about Amy and Camille is that they were allowed to be mean, ugly, and bitter. They resented the people that made them that way and looked out for themselves first. They were not caring or nurturing to anybody but themselves outside of self benefit. They both were so directly opposite to the idea of the loving mother or dutiful girlfriend/wife archetype. They both have goals that directly oppose the leading men of their stories; Amy wants to punish her husband for making her something she doesn’t want to be and Camille wants to find out who the killer is on her own and is at odds with the male detective on the case. At the end of both of their stories, they are both respectively freed from the demands of the idea of femininity by bending the typical roles of women to their own benefit. Amy returns to her husband and is carrying his child, but she makes it clear she is in control of the relationship now and encourages his resentment of her. Camille’s mother is in prison for abusing her and Amma is in prison for murder; freeing Camille from both the bonds of motherhood and daughterhood. This is her breaking away from both roles typically assigned to women in fiction.

Both novels praise and punish conformity to the beauty myth in about equal measure. Camille is praised for being a good sister but punished for being a bad daughter. Both stories paint pictures of complicated ideas around the beauty myth and being a woman at all. Amy and Camille are bitter and angry but they both are shown to have the capacity to care about others. These stories show that the idea of the beauty myth is inherently flawed, it's never that simple but at the same time, a standard that can ever be reached is not simple. It's damning for whoever tries a lifetime of resentment and anger. “Gone Girl” and “Sharp Objects” both end with Amy and Camllie rejecting what was laid out for them and changing it to fit them instead. They changed the narrative of their story and how they are seen in that context. I can only hope more fiction follows this idea that rejecting what “should” happen to a female character bleeds over into real life and helps lessen the stigma around turning your back on what a “woman” should be, think, do, and say.
chunks.label: Impact and analysis of Flynn's female characters
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on reading Gone Girl and Sharp Objects, analyzing how characters like Amy and Camille rebel against feminine archetypes and how fiction impacts perceptions of womanhood.

n7be64cbb.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Class System

chunks.text:
America has an unspoken, unacknowledged class system. With the one percenters owning most of the wealth in America, there’s not much for anyone else. The middle class system splits a portion of the rest of the wealth and the working class divvy up the rest. With artificial intelligence (ai) becoming more and more advanced what does this mean for everyone?

In today's society we are seeing AI be advanced at faster rates than ever before. This is due to the one percenters seeing more and more potential for revenue through them. But the trade offs for this start with having working class citizens losing their jobs to technology and are making everyone much more lazy. With self driving cars on the rise, people aren’t even going to have to drive themselves where they need to go. This is good in terms of less risk to the passengers because of the vehicles being a part of the same algorithm and having much less chance for miscommunication. The downside to this is people not seeing how much technology is taking over our lives. It’s projected that by 2050 computers will be able outperform human psychiatrists and even bodyguards.

With AI advancing at unacknowledged fast rates this could be the downfall to the class system in America. People need to acknowledge what is happening with technology and/or find alternative ways for people and technology to thrive together. Also, with technology becoming more and more accessible we should be utilizing this to eliminate the class system throughout America.
chunks.label: AI advancements and the American class system
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the wealth disparity in the American class system and discusses the implications of advancing artificial intelligence and technology on jobs, daily life, and society.

chunks.text:
Religion, Cultural Development, and Dehumanization Through the Military Industrial Complex: Second Reflection Essay

The book 21 Lessons for the 21st Century by Yuval Noah Harari covers a number of topics ranging from the role of religion in society to the future of war in the modern age. This also lines up with a number of other readings from this sociology course such as Estranged Labor by Karl Marx and The Spirit of Capitalism by Max Weber. However there are differences and similarities between how these three authors view the world and this allows their work to be looked at critically and analyzed.

Religion exists, as posited by Harari, as a framework humans have made to give meaning to the world and their choices. Morality has evolved to fit in the framework religion has been created around. By following this logic, the only place religion has in policy is in its spirit of unity. He states that human nature is to come together one way or another, religion is an extension of that. Therefore, the religion of a region is built on the preexisting cultural norms and ideas, creating different religions and value systems by location. By bringing people together under a fairly consistent moral framework, it serves its purpose that way. In short, this idea states that religion serves people first and foremost and varies based on the cultures of the area. For example, Buddhism and Catholicism are vastly different, in part based on where they were developed and in part based on the cultures they originated around. This is a key facet of Harari’s ideas about religion, it exists to serve the people within it, not the other way around.

Religious faith was often a key reason people and groups immigrated to America in the first place as England was rife with religious discrimination against any kind of dissent from the established norms. Protestantism was an offshoot of the practiced Christanity in England at the time that was being punished for stepping outside the norms for religious practice. This led to many people who followed this way of life to immigrate to America in the hopes of religious freedom and a fresh start.

Weber argued that the Protestant work ethic was a very solid base for the rise of capitalism in the west with the presence of the Protestant work ethic. The idea that having to work very hard to earn a place in the society and furthermore Heaven was a grounding point in the Protasnat faith. Weber states that having this framework built so heavily into the Western society with early Pilgrim settlers bringing their faith to the colonies with them and building their new world with these ideas almost baked in. From this base, as time progressed and technology increased this religious belief was taken for granted as part of the American fabric of life.

The conflict here between both arguments is the nature of what religion is used for and how it comes to be. Weber states that the groundwork laid by the existence of Protatasmt, modern day capitalism was able to grow and thrive in the West. Harari argues that religion is created to serve the people who create it as a point of unity. While it can be said that the settlers that came to America were united under the idea of having religious freedom in the new world, there were strict dividing lines between religious groups of all sorts, sometimes even within the same religious groups. Furthermore capitalism developed in various ways and at various places all over the world. There is almost no way to argue that, beyond a shadow of a doubt, the Protastant background of America is what allowed modern day capitalism to spring up the way it has.

Marx argues that in modern day capitalism products made by the laborer don't belong to the laborer. They work on an assembly line for 16 hours a day but the end products belong to the boss of the factory or the government at large. This separates the worker from their labor and their products. This product is now completely separate from the worker and what made it. This leads to the dehumanization of the person through the denial of the human capacity for conscious production. As industrialization becomes more and more complex and infiltrates every aspect of human life, particularly in a political and social sense, this sense of dehumanization will spread to every aspect of the human condition.

Industrialization has had leaps and bounds over the past few centuries as advancements compound on each other. The steam engine opened up trade in new and exciting ways, which brought in more resources, which allowed for more advancement and so on and so forth. One of the biggest pushes for advancement has always been war and the drive to be the best in the world at war. In the past, war was more about how many bodies could be thrown at a problem, which is its own kind of dehumanization, but as time advances the roles the individual can take in the framework of a society at war have changed and opened up new avenues for duminization within the framework of capitalism.

The idea of what the roles that should be filled in society change over time. The cultural consciousness has always dictated the roles of the individuals within the society: based on race, gender, age, and class standing. During the past, military enlistment was a point of pride. During World War 2, almost every aspect of American individual life revolved around the war and the war effort. If the individual did not serve, they were expected to provide for the war effort in some way, such as working on the factory line. The people who did not fit within this were considered outsiders and not part of the social fabric.

Harari states that the previous idea of war for profit is no longer financially viable in the modern day and age, that the wars of the future are being fought in more abstract ways than outright battlefields and trenches. The wars of the future are increasingly being fought over cyber security, technological advancements, and over resources with increasing scarcity. In turn instead of being pushed towards military service, more and more people are being pushed to higher education and jobs in the private sector.

According to the Department of Defense only about 2% of the 20.6 17-21 years olds are even capable of enlisting to serve. ( Bloomberg.com, Bloomberg, 12 July 2021 ) However College enrollment rates have increased 195% since 1970, when 3.5% of the U.S. population were college students. ( Education Data Initiative, 22 Nov. 2021,) This is adding further to Harai’s point that the future wars are going to be fought in the realm of technology as time passes.

Novels such as Ender's Game, Ready Player One, and The Ghost Fleet are recommended reading for enlisted members of the Marine Corps of all ranks. (“Commandant's Professional Reading List (Foundational).” MCA, 3 June 2021,) These novels are all written about futures where wars are fought in the realms of technology and over resources, with a focus on how the idea of wars being physically fought has too much of a physical cost or this cost being completely negated by being capable of fighting the entire war from the comfort of your own country, further adding to Hararis point that the direction of future war is going to be more and more impersonal as technology advances what we can do from the safety of our own homes. These fictional wars all illustrate the point within the text that the people involved are largely superfluous. In most of these stories, a point is made to show that at the end of the story, the individual's choices were laid out within a framework that did not allow for much choice on their end. They were acting out a script, without being aware of what their actions cost, separating them from their labor. The message is as war further develops, the dehumanization brought to the individual under capitalism has no choice but to spread to other aspects of the human experience, taking away other freedoms to express human desires, regelaging the indivdal to express aminal desires instead.

In conclusion, Harai’s work covers a number of topics with a level of grace applied to them. He posits that religion exists to serve the people within it, not the other way around and that modern day wars will be fought in the realms of technology rather than in the physical world. Max Weber argued that within the foundations of the Protastant in America, modern day capitalism would not have the same spread and hold on the world today that it does now. This is somewhat at odds with what Harari says about religion and what its role within a society is and should be. On the other hand, Karl Marx talks about how the modern industrialization of labor serves to dehumanize the people within the system, this lines up with what Harari writes about modern war and the wars of the future.
chunks.label: Analysis of Harari, Weber, and Marx on religion and modern war
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes and compares sociological theories from Yuval Noah Harari, Max Weber, and Karl Marx regarding the purpose of religion, the rise of capitalism, and the dehumanization of labor and modern warfare.

n07efcd8c.title: Performing at a Significant Other's Dinner

chunks.text:
Goffman offers “The Presentation of Self” and draws upon the stage to describe oneself. He uses this stage to create a comparison between an actor in a play to the conscious creation of one’s personality towards others. Goffman states, “A correctly staged and performed scene leads the audience to impute a self to a performed character, but in this imputation—this self—is a product of a scene that comes off, and is not a cause of it.” Goffman uses this evidence to elaborate on how the self that others see is more or less the product of an act. He goes on to mention that the way we conduct ourselves in front of others is purely for the conformity of those others. The stage creates a movement that can be discredited as easily as it can be credited. This is in pure contrast to the way we live, think, and breathe. We are one, singular, living being. However, the actions we choose to take within social settings are forged in the moment to suit the conditions of those around us. This, in turn, creates the act to which Goffman refers.

Cooley and Goffman both draw on the basic fact that humans, truly and subconsciously, care what others think. This idea is in direct tandem with the passages from both authors. The looking glass self is an idea established on assuming what others think, while the stage is the action of changing the way you act around others to suit what they think of you. Afterall, it would take a thorough analysis of how you are seen in order to act properly. Let’s say, for example, you go to your significant other’s house for a dinner, and the father is constantly looking at you with furrowed eyebrows. This, in one’s mind, might generate an uneasy feeling. It would be clear to see that the father does not like you. This reaction may involve you bringing up possible real-world achievements. Maybe you might mention that you are pursuing a medical degree to impress him. You will use better manners at the table. These are prime examples of both the looking glass self and Goffman’s stage. You are assuming the way the father is perceiving you, even though he hasn’t actually said anything about not liking you. You are also changing your act, civility, and speech patterns based on your lack of comfort around this individual.

Both Goffman and Cooley work hand-in-hand to show how individuals change the way they act around others based on how they are viewed. These authors are highly effective in their views because they directly build upon each other. Cooley proposes the original view of others, while Goffman proposes the way we shape ourselves to correlate to these viewpoints. This is why we feel certain emotions towards how others view us, and it is why we try to adhere to or correct those emotions in the real world. Both Goffman and Cooley essentially display that the way we act is not truly the way we are, since we live in a world of constant judgement. Any action may be seen by others as positive or negative, and subsequently corrected or embraced.
chunks.label: Analyzing Goffman and Cooley's sociological theories of self
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Goffman's presentation of self and Cooley's looking glass self, using a hypothetical example of meeting a significant other's father to illustrate how people alter their behavior based on perceived judgment.

chunks.text:
Have you ever thought about the importance of the people in your life? Do you like having lots of friends or just a few quality friends? Do you value human connection in your everyday life? All of these questions establish a human need for contact with others and how that can have an impact on someone’s everyday life. Recognizing that not all human connection is beneficial for you is also important. The way we act around everyone is different and is based upon the setting we are in. This piques the question: are all types of friendships essential for survival, or just some, if any?

There are many arguments for both sides of this topic. Lots of studies have shown the importance of human interactions, while others have shown that you can survive as an independent. Goffman explores the idea of “self” through an analogy of comparing it to a stage. When there are performers on a stage, each of them has a role they play. They all understand their roles and contribute something to the storyline. He believes that depending on who you are with, you will act a certain way. Essentially, each interaction we have is compared to acting or a “show” we are putting on for an “audience.” The use of “backstage” is where someone may “prepare” for a “performance.” This is the analogy he uses to explain how someone may prepare their personality to match how they feel they should act with specific people. This could be based on how the person thinks others think they should act, or what the person has concluded on how they should act based on group or friendship dynamics they have observed. When comparing the self to a stage, it almost makes it sound as though all of our interactions are ingenuine. This leads to the part of Goffman’s theory that says that we are never truly ourselves unless we are alone.

That is one side of Goffman’s theory which would make it seem like the people around you do not have any impact on your sense of “self.” However, because you act a certain way in front of others, they are in turn impacting your personality. As humans, we choose how to act in different scenarios based on how we feel as though we should act, not necessarily how we want to act. Awkwardness can occur if someone does not recognize their “role” in a certain group of people. In other words, if you act differently than normal in a situation, it may cause people to be confused or uncomfortable. We all have defined personalities based upon our environment and surroundings. Because making connections with people is important to our ability to navigate the world, friendships and relationships are essential to our survival.

Personally, I feel as though I have many roles in each of my friend groups. While I feel as though I am being “myself” when I am with each of my close friends, I can see some differences in how I act. It is impossible to act the same way in all settings. I feed off my friends' energies and not all of them have the same energy. It is also based on what “roles” need to be filled in each setting or friendship dynamic. For example, I find myself being quieter and observant in some groups, while in other groups I am more outgoing and energetic. Even though I feel comfortable with all of these friends, I have noticed my role in each group leading me to act a certain way. They are all versions of myself that I have modified slightly to fit the energy of who I am with. Being able to fit a “role” in each setting of your life is a skill that humans must learn to be successful.

I had never thought about this concept much before learning about how we are never truly ourselves unless we are alone. When we are alone, there is no judgment, no rules, and no outside influences causing us to want to act one way or another. There is no one to react to, therefore, you are completely and utterly “yourself.” No one but yourself can see what is going through your mind or what you are thinking and understand it with the full complexities you can. While this is the true reflection of “ourselves,” it is not realistic to be able to act this way in front of others. Finding people who make you feel as close to this version of yourself as possible is the best way to measure a friendship.

Reflecting back on the question about if you need friends to survive or not, I would have never said that you do not need friends to survive. Friends have always been something I value and feel is a necessity in my life. Without human interaction and genuine connection, I feel alone and like I am lacking something. I believe it is part of my personality to surround myself with others and feed off their energies. While this is technically altering my sense of “self,” I do not see it as a negative thing. I see it more as an opportunity to expand my thoughts and gain new opinions and views on topics I might not have seen differently otherwise.

Looking back at the early ancestors of humans, the great apes, they were not very social. According to the reading from Maryanski and Turner, The Neurology of Religion, adolescent apes would leave their units after puberty, which then placed them with apes that they did not know. No bonds were formed between these apes, leaving them to be more independent. So, how did we go from having low sociality to forming family units with strong bonds? The formation of language was key in this shift. When language was formed, so was the ability to feel emotions and create memories. This connected humans to each other more, and bonds were easier to make. The formation of language made it nearly impossible to not be able to connect to others, as it allowed us to communicate with anyone who spoke the same language as us. Imagine not being able to talk to your friend. How would you be able to know anything about them? How would you be able to know if they like the same things as you? It is harder to form bonds with people when you cannot communicate properly with them. Language also helped form communities of people who come from the same area, have the same interests or values, or who want to learn more about people different from themselves. Language was able to expand the minds of humans and led to great innovation in the world.

Nowadays, connections are key to making it in society. While our society has shifted to be more independent, you still need to have interactions with people in order to make it as an individual. In order to find a job, you need good social skills to be able to form bonds with employers and get them to hire you. These skills stem from social interactions that take place in our everyday lives. This is a key reason why having friends surrounding you that you feel comfortable with is beneficial. If you are constantly around those that support you, and you feel most closely to your true “self,” these relationships will be beneficial to you.

Lastly, not only does friendship and bonds help us with social skills and connecting, but it also impacts a part of our brain. Have you ever lost a good friend and been extremely upset by it? Did being reminded of them hurt you and made you think about all the good memories you shared? This is because all the good chemicals in your brain are released when you are with friends. This is what keeps you going back to those relationships you have formed, and what prevents us from hopping around from person to person, without getting to know them. I think most people would say they would rather have a few quality friends over lots of friends that they kind of know. Humans value learning about others and wanting to hear from them. There is such an importance to learning about others and from them. We can take their experiences and apply them to our own and vice versa. Along with our brain releasing chemicals like dopamine and serotonin when we are with friends, friends and social interactions, in general, can also do wonders for our physical and mental health. According to a Fader article, Why We Need Friends, According to a Scientist, people who have friends are less likely to die of heart disease. The article also reveals that having friends around is a big comfort. From personal experience, I would say that that is true. Many times, when I have been in uncomfortable situations, having a friend or friends with me has helped calm my nerves. It is almost like having a barrier there to help break up some of the awkwardness. I know that I can trust them and that they will help me if I need it.

Overall, social interactions play a key role in shaping who we are. While you may find yourself in situations where you do not feel like how you are presenting yourself is truly “you,” it is a version of you that you have created. You can learn from each version of “you” and apply the reactions you get from your “audiences” to other settings and situations. Having friends and forming connections with people is key to our ability to navigate society and the world. Without bonds, we are just existing as an individual. It is harder to be able to relate to others and find out more about yourself without building social skills and forming friendships with those you feel most comfortable with.
