Everyone should value the friends and people they have in their lives because they are an opportunity for growth, support, and overall positive physical and mental health.
chunks.label: The necessity of friendships and social roles
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological theories and readings regarding friendship, roles, language evolution, and the benefits of social connection.

chunks.text: The two articles fell in line with one another beautifully, ultimately explaining all of the contributors to self-concept. Our material possessions influence how we look at ourselves because it makes other people look at us a certain way (the social self). The Personal identity allows us to be individuals based on who we are and who we choose to be based on unique character traits. The pure ego is our deepest, most unknown aspect, one that we can’t ever change, but it contributes highly to the conception of self.
chunks.label: Contributors to self-concept
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses two articles and explains contributors to self-concept, including material possessions, personal identity, and the pure ego.

chunks.text:
A popular concept throughout history is that men are stronger, smarter, and simply better than women, and that women are just a lesser subcategory of men. Some may argue that this is because men are more genetically superior as men do not suffer from periods or pregnancy, while others may argue that men are supposed to be in control because that is how God intended it to be. Due to this unfortunate bias, women have always been separated from men and labeled as “other.” While we are all human, gender has divided us into 2 groups, lesser and superior; the One and the Other.

The truth is men are not superior to women. While men may be better at some things than women, men and women are equally capable of doing most things. This can be intimidating and threatening to men because they have always considered themselves the superior gender. While we are approaching a more equitable society, sexism and misogyny are complex issues that will certainly not be resolved in the near future. Due to this slow progression, women will remain the other in the eyes of some men and suffer because of it.

In “Women as Other” by Simone de Beauvoir, she poses a theory about how women are presented as “other” and men are the main idea and self. An example would be two separate village tribes each thinking of themselves as the main tribe and the other tribe as the “others.” She starts off by saying, “If I want to define myself, I first have to say, ‘I am a woman’; all other assertions will arise from this basic truth.” Gender is an essential part of human identity. Once you are confident about your gender identity, your inner, true self will become more clearly revealed to yourself and the world. Men do not have to navigate the world as men, the world has already been carved out for them to insert themselves into. Women on the other hand have to forge their own paths because not only do they have to prove themselves in their abilities but they also have to prove their worth.

Beauvoir also claims that “Women are the negative, to such a point that any determination is imputed to her as a limitation, without reciprocity.” By saying this, it is implied that women are not really a positive, contributive part of a society. Any aspirations that a woman has will be ignored or negatively received and will not be reciprocated by men. A woman’s determination and ambition is considered to be a handicap. We can see this is the real world when certain women are reprimanded for their confidence and accomplishments, while men doing the same tasks are awarded and praised.

With the topic of women as “other” arises the question “How did this happen?” In early history it seems that men had chosen that they were to be the dominant ones and women just decided to follow. But why and how did men decide this? They viewed women’s bodies as a complex, disturbing system. Eve was made from Adam’s rib and she became a subcategory of man; an incomplete man. Even the famous ancient philosopher Aristotle said that “We should regard women’s nature as suffering from natural defectiveness.” It is human nature to fear the unknown, therefore it is understandable that men would form their societies around subjugating women rather than give up their advantage and appear weak.

To put it in more simple terms, men are afraid of what they do not understand. With this fear comes a need for power to control the unknown and resilient nature of women. The problem with that idea is women were not really made to be controlled. Women are free thinkers with brilliant ideas. Beauvoir talks about how men will tell her “You think such and such a thing because you’re a woman” and the only reply she can think of is “I think it because it is true.” This is an example of men separating themselves from women and classifying them as “other”. In a man’s head he is right because he is superior and will not allow a woman to go against him or prove him wrong.

The whole point of othering is to dehumanize another group to make yourself or the group you belong to seem more appealing. This othering has taken many different forms throughout history. For one, the concept of marriage seems, on the surface, to be an act of partnership and love. However, marriage often confines women to predetermined roles rather than allowing them to choose their own. Certain marital traditions are used to obtain women’s power and submission. For example, when a woman marries a man, she takes his last name which essentially means she becomes part of his identity and erases a little of her own. It is presented as unity but symbolizes control.

In the past, a woman's responsibilities included cleaning, housemaking, child rearing, educating children, etc. Men would go to work while women would stay home to watch the kids, clean the house, do the laundry and cook dinner for the husbands when they got home. About a hundred years ago, women began fighting to become more than that. They wanted to be part of the workforce and make their own money. Of course, this threatened men. If women were making their own money and providing for themselves, why would they need to rely on men any longer? To appease women they allowed them to work, but the jobs weren’t as legitimate as mens. They were receptionists for a company run by men or sewed clothes for a company run by men. By doing this, men believed they were in control by “letting” women work but they were also able to keep their power.

While the majority of the workforce is dominated by men, one industry that has almost always been dominated by women is education. When schools in the United States began to be established, the teachers used to be all men who did not really know how to teach, they were just intelligent. Because of this, men did not make very good teachers for young children. As public schooling became a more widespread idea throughout the country, the need for teachers and school staff increased. Women were brought in as teachers not just because it was considered a lesser field, but because they put affection over reason. This is very important when dealing with developing minds because children need to be nurtured in order to learn and grow properly. And so, the feminization of teaching developed and prospered. Women dominating the education field seems to imply that women are in fact superior to men at teaching. But if women are “other” how can they be better than men at something?

It is because while women may be “other” it should not be in a negative connotation. Being outcasted by men has brought women together to form a sisterhood. They look out for each other by walking home in groups, comforting each other when they are upset, and lending strangers tampons. Women have to stick together because it still is a male dominant world. Men make decisions and laws on women’s bodies, controlling what they can and cannot do with them. There is a saying that “boys will be boys” and it is a terrifying saying. It is used to excuse male actions, including violence against women. Women understand the fear of not being believed and believe in each other. The female gender has always come together and fight for what is just for them, whether it’s the right to vote or the #MeToo movement.

In “Women as Other”, Beauvoir also says that “Women’s actions have never been more than a symbolic agitation; they have won only what men have been willing to concede to them; women have taken nothing; they have only received.” In this she means that women only really have what has been given to them by men. That men are the ultimate decision makers in women's lives. But with what they have been given they have redefined and improved. They stand up for what they believe in, defend one another, and challenge what is unjust. Women’s actions are no longer just a symbolic agitation.

To be a woman is to be “other”, but to be a woman is not to be an outcast. Women understand each other because they share the same experiences. By othering women, men simply created a united front who stand up for and support each other. As each year passes and humanity progresses, there are more and more victories for women's rights. But, if men and women ever do achieve absolute equality, women will still be different. Being a woman is an experience and it is shared between women all over the world. Womanhood is an essential intimacy. Women are other, not because they are lesser, but because they are connected.
chunks.label: Reflections on Beauvoir, gender inequality, and womanhood
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the historical subjugation of women as 'the Other' through Simone de Beauvoir's theory, discussing patriarchal control, marriage, labor, teaching, and female solidarity.

chunks.text: For decades, scholars have debated the importance of Gregory Mantsios’ and Max Weber’s ideas in sociology. On one hand, Gregory Mantsios in his article Class in America reveals how one’s social class influences their experiences and opportunities in life. On the other hand, in George Ritzer’s monograph The McDonaldization of Society, Ritzer describes Max Weber’s ideas of rationalization as a process where the world, especially bureaucracies, becomes based on efficiency, predictability, calculability, and control. Although these writings discuss different conversations, Mantsios and Weber’s ideas can be synthesized to understand funerary services in America. Therefore, the purpose of this paper is to evaluate how Mantsios’ idea of class and Weber’s idea of rationalization relate to understanding why Americans choose cremation over other funerary services.
chunks.label: Paper introduction comparing Mantsios and Weber on funerals
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces their essay, explaining how Gregory Mantsios' ideas on class and Max Weber's concept of rationalization can be synthesized to analyze funerary services and cremation in America.

chunks.text: In Mantsios’ article Class in America, he debunked four myths about the American lifestyle: that America is classless, that America is a middle-class nation, that all Americans are getting richer, and that everyone has an equal chance to succeed. Mantsios exposed the falsity of these myths by revealing the lives of three individuals, Harold S. Browning, Bob Farrel, and Cheryl Mitchell, who are all considered middle-class in America. In examining the different lives of these individuals, he revealed that there existed large economic disparities between each of the individuals from the moment they were born that persisted throughout their lives, shaping their experiences and opportunities. Thereby, Mantsios exposed seven realities to American life. To summarize these realities, Mantsios underlines how there are extreme differences in the economic standing of American citizens as the middle class owns a small percentage of the nation's wealth. This disparity affects Americans’ lifestyles, educational opportunities, chance for survival, and success.
chunks.label: Mantsios' analysis of American class myths and realities
chunks.what_happened: The student outlines Mantsios' article debunking four myths about American class and explains the persistent economic disparities in American society.

chunks.text: An example of where this economic disparity affects American lifestyles is when an American is selecting a funerary service for themselves or their loved ones. Relating to Mantsios’ myths and realities of the American social classes, Mantsios exposes how although the United States is not a country of equal opportunity, Americans still embrace the American dream, which he represented through the myths of American social class. Pertaining to funeral services, there exists a myth about funeral services, which can be showcased in American movies. Once a character dies in a movie, they are depicted lying in an open casket with guests and family lined up in front of the casket weeping and dressed in all black. In reality, most Americans do not hold funerals as 59% of Americans who died in 2022 were cremated according to the Cremation Association of North America (“Industry Statistical Information”). Around 41% of those Americans chose to do a direct cremation (“What the Latest Stats”), which is when an individual is cremated without a memorial service, making it the most cost-effective funerary service. Furthermore, this cremation rate is expected to reach 80% by 2045. This increase in cremation rates is largely due to America's inability to afford funerals. However, other reasons come into play for some Americans, such as environmental concerns about casket burials or preference (“U.S. Cremation Rate”). A survey of 1,500 Americans run by Anthony Martin in 2021 found that “73% of respondents don't have enough money set aside to cover the cost of the average funeral” (Martin). In regards to Mantsios’ ideas of class and economic differences in America, these statistics about cremation rates reveal that most Americans do not have the opportunity to have an open casket funeral or memorial service to celebrate the death of their loved ones. Thereby, the myth of the American dream depicted in movies of grandiose funeral services is debunked by the reality that most Americans cannot afford it. As Mantsios states, Americans' economic disparity is increasing and their wealth is largely dependent on the social class they are born into. This helps to highlight why there is an expected increase in dead cremated in forthcoming years. Ultimately, Mantsios’ ideas of economic disparity between social classes in America can be observed through American's choice of funerary services as most Americans are cremated because it is the least costly funerary service.
chunks.label: Applying Mantsios' class ideas to American cremation trends
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how economic disparities make traditional funerals unaffordable for most Americans, debunking the movie myth of grandiose funerals through rising cremation statistics.

chunks.text: Furthermore, Mantsios’ ideas of economic disparity between social classes in funerary services can be further observed by its relation to Weber’s idea of rationalization. In Ritzer’s monograph The McDonaldization of Society, he describes Weber’s idea of rationalization as the shift in how institutions are built, focussing on efficiency, predictability, calculability, and control, which is done in bureaucracies and Ritzer’s McDonaldization. This shift from pre-modern institutions to modern institutions changes the focus of the institutions from acting out of social meaning to acting out of social purpose. Institutions that act out of social meaning prioritize a symbolic shift and collective understandings, such as transformative baptism in churches to represent religious values. On the other hand, institutions that act out of social purpose prioritize accomplishing a purposeful, collective task, such as exchanging money to purchase goods in banks. This shift in rationalization gets rid of spontaneous interactions; replaces traditions, values, and emotions; and causes individuals, such as consumers and employees to be allowed few choices to their means to an end. These effects of rationalization are often dehumanizing for people affected by it, expressing Weber’s idea of the “iron cage.”
chunks.label: Explaining Weber's rationalization and the iron cage
chunks.what_happened: The student defines Weber's rationalization and Ritzer's McDonaldization, discussing the shift toward efficiency, predictability, calculability, control, and the resulting dehumanizing iron cage.

chunks.text: As highlighted above in funerary services, cremation is the most cost-effective funerary service. This is because the process of cremation exhibits the characteristics of Weber’s rationalization: efficiency, predictability, calculability, and control. Cremation is an efficient process because it takes between an hour and a half to two hours for a body to get cremated while funeral service takes long hours of planning and executing; cremation is predictable as the outcome, receiving a loved one’s ashes, is guaranteed; cremation is calculable as the service is relatively cheap with a relatively constant cost everywhere unless an individual wants a memorial service with the cremation, which increases the cost; and cremation is controlled as it primarily only needs a cremation chamber to conduct and is primarily the only choice for most Americans as the only affordable option. Although the cremation process is efficient, predictable, calculable, and controlled, it faces the problems of dehumanization explained in Weber’s idea of the iron cage. As most Americans get cremated without a memorial service, the tradition of a funeral, the value of celebrating a person’s death, and the emotions of grief and acceptance that result from traditional funerary services have to be experienced in different manners, which result from the cremation being the only means to an end for most Americans. All in all, cremation exhibits the characteristics of rationalization through its efficiency, predictability, calculability, and control, which in turn causes it to become an iron cage as it is the only affordable option for most Americans.
chunks.label: Analyzing cremation through Weber's rationalization and iron cage
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes cremation as an efficient, predictable, calculable, and controlled process that acts as an iron cage by stripping away traditional mourning rituals due to affordability.

chunks.text: Ultimately, Mantsios’ ideas of social class in America and Weber’s ideas of rationalization can be synthesized to understand why most Americans choose cremation over other funerary services. This is due to the fact that cremation is the only affordable or cost-effective funerary service because it exhibits the characteristics of Weber’s rationalization, which in turn becomes the only option for most Americans because of the economic disparity between social classes in America as explained by Mantsios. It is important to understand this connection between Mantsios’ and Weber’s ideas because it underlines the dehumanizing nature of cremation when Americans cannot afford the expected funeral service depicted in movies, expressing the American dream or myth of funerary services.
chunks.label: Conclusion synthesizing Mantsios and Weber on cremation
chunks.what_happened: The student synthesizes Mantsios and Weber to conclude that economic disparity forces Americans into rationalized, dehumanizing cremation over traditional funerals.

chunks.text:
A western concept known as “gender binary” claims that there are only two gender options; male or female. It is also believed in some collective groups that sex and gender are the same, but in sociological terms they are very different. Sex is assigned at birth from the appearance of Gentelia while gender is a role. West Zimmerman argues that both gender role and display focus on behavioral aspects of being a woman or a man, not biological aspects.

It has been perceived that “men are men and women are women”, to be natural and rooted to biology, which over time has produced psychological, behavioral and social consequences. Now it is commonly believed that gender has to act a certain way. Gender roles are situated identities, but many roles are already gender marked. For example, nurses have been identified with a female role. In the short story The Yellow Wallpaper, written by Charolotte Perkins Gilman, the wife is trapped inside of her mind. She believes she is ill, although her husband (a physician) does not believe her. Her husband tells her not to speak of her problems, saying that it will make her “feel worse”. They are playing a doctor, patient role instead of the role of husband and wife. Because of her gender, she is treated unequally. As the husband he is taught to act masculine and controlling, and the wife has to act as the submissive. Gender has been created to be this social expectation, but in reality, gender role can be anything we want it to be.

The concept of gender is a socially learned set of behaviors associated with assignment. Gender does not have to correlate to the sex stereotype. Men don’t have to masculine, and women don’t have to be feminine. Gender is a choice developed by different groups of the collective consciousness.
chunks.label: Sociological concepts of gender binary and gender roles
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the distinction between sex and gender, societal expectations of gender roles, and illustrates these concepts using the story 'The Yellow Wallpaper'.

chunks.text:
People are born with an innate sense of right and wrong. Where does this come from? Are we born knowing not to steal, lie, and cheat, but do so anyway? Do we know not to hit other kids, or take their toys? What are we told and how do we feel when we do? Where do our ethical and moral choices come from? Harari discusses possible answers to these questions in his book, 21 Lessons for the 21st Century in the sections labeled, Secularism, God, Religion, and Post-Truth World. To discover the truth, we must first ask the question, what is truth? Is it simply something we know to be true? Is truth the same for all people?

Religion is not something uncommon, or new. It can be seen throughout all corners of the earth, through all different languages, cultures, and societies. Religion is so important, that there are hundreds upon hundreds of differing beliefs, gods, spiritualities, and more. “Religion is a universally and uniquely human phenomenon in that all human societies possess recognizably religious beliefs and practices, but (as far as we can tell) only human societies do so. Together, these observations suggest that religion is closely related to human nature, and perhaps explicable as a function thereof. At the same time, the indubitably social enactment and implications of religion, as well as the socially determined nature of its contents, ensure that any meaningful attempt to explain religion must simultaneously be a sociological exercise.” (Marshall, 2016)

There are many different ways to define “truth.” There is a spiritual or meditative sense of truth, and then there is personal truth. Lastly there is just truth, in the sense that it aligns with given facts or reality, such as “The sky is blue.” “Of course the cosmic mystery doesn’t help us at all in maintaining the social order. People often argue that we must believe in a god that gave some very concrete laws to humans, or else morality will disappear and society will collapse into primeval chaos.” (Harari, 2018)

Earlier this semester in this class, there were readings and discussions of the Matrix of Domination and Power in America. Both of these can correlate to the previously mentioned sections of Harari’s book by looking at how religion was used to enforce these beliefs and ideas. Harari believes that Religion or God is not actually about “god” but about humans and that religion is all about stories that give legitimacy and validation to a previously established authority. Also correlating to the collective consciousness, people take this idea of religion and use it to control or have authority over an enormous mass of people.

Other important topics by Harari that come into play when discussing these topics are the ideas of “Truth” and living in a “Post-Truth” world, as well as how that affects how people live their lives ethically and morally today. Without a higher authority, or set of given rules and beliefs to follow, how does society and its people function? We are currently living in a world where truth is more and more often seen as being relative. “What’s true for me is not necessarily true for you.” I have my beliefs, you have yours, and that’s that.

Is it possible that these collective beliefs and ideas can be harming us? Are they dangerous to this new generation that questions and defies everything because of the media that is presented to them? Why is the truth so important? At first, that may sound like a dumb question. But every day, more and more, little by little, the truth is changing. Government officials lie, companies lie about what's in their food and products, even teachers lie about the subject matter of their choice. Along with the rise of technology and therefore, science, the “truth” is changing more and more. Everything I was raised to believe as “True” has now been challenged, and things that I was told were “lies” are now making much more sense than what I was originally taught to believe growing up.

In contrast to Harari, Emile Durkheim believed that the societal formation of the collective consciousness furnishes us with both stability and truth. Because the collective consciousness is not artificial, made by an unspoken agreement of a multitude of groups of people, it is deemed trustworthy. It is embraced because of the fear of being left out, or different, or alone. It is only aware of what it needs to establish authority. Additionally, religion is used as a sort of resource to give meaning or purpose to life.

Another large matter when it comes to the importance of religion and truth, is “meaning” or “purpose.” Durkheim's theory of religion is approached from the perspective of his lifelong concern with the question of meaning and moral order in modern society. Really thinking about the reason people exist, and why and how life, community, and the world works scientifically and down to the design of a hummingbird or toucan, or life cycle of a butterfly is extremely important to think about.

For Durkheim, the religion of society was important to study because he believed that religion provided social cohesion to help maintain social solidarity through shared rituals and beliefs, social control to enforce religious based morals, and an atmosphere to help maintain conformity and control in society. It has become increasingly likely that religion nowadays is used as a fear tactic to scare people and control them and their actions. For example, “You don’t believe in God? You’re not a christian? Aren’t you scared of hell?” And rather than basing any of their beliefs in fact and/or truth, they use fear and threats to get the collective consciousness to obey their “God given rules.”

To sum up, truth is astronomically important, but we can not use religion as a basis of truth as a force to control others. While Durkheim and Harari both make good points, neither have any one perfect answer to the various questions that are so important. With today's constant and ever-changing technology, media, and ideas and beliefs, truth is something to both be consistently challenged, and researched.

Sources

21 Lessons for the 21st Century- Yuval Noah Harari, 2018

https://philosophiatopics.files.wordpress.com/2018/09/yuval-noah-harari-21-lessons-for-the-21st-century.pdf

Durkheim on Religion and Moral Community in Modernity- Lise Anne Tolle, January 1993

https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1475-682X.1993.tb00199.x

The Moral Origins of God: Darwin, Durkheim, and the Homo Duplex Theory of Theogenesis. Douglas A. Marshall, 31, August 2016

https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fsoc.2016.00013/full
chunks.label: Reflections on truth, religion, and sociological theories
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on morality, religion, and the definition of truth by discussing theories from Yuval Noah Harari and Émile Durkheim, as well as course topics and sources.

nd9db057e.title: Contrasting Opportunities Across Class and Race

chunks.text:
Economic class is a systemic hierarchy within America that determines a citizen’s power status. In “Class in America,” Gregory Mantsios addresses concerns regarding inequality the system promotes. In “Discrimination in a Low-Wage Labor Market: a Field Experiment,” authors Devah Pager, Bruce Western, and Bart Bonikowski address an experiment led to detect discrimination in the modern workforce. All these authors cohesively present evidence that addresses the concerns of racial bias throughout the classes of America.

Gregory Mantsios writes of his findings revolving around an experiment conducted between families of different financial standings. In the result of the preceding experiments, Mantsios notes that there is a direct correlation between high school students’ SAT scores and the wealth of their parents. This finding exhibits the context of control. Those who have more money are more likely to be able to afford a solution to the problems of their children’s educations. The parents who were more likely to find value in their children’s educations, likely to uphold the image of being considered “better” than the general public, were the ones to impart those shared values to their children.

The discrimination experiment, on the other hand, was conducted to show the difference between an employer’s biases based on race. In the experiment, a group of several men with no outstanding qualifications than the others involved. These men all had impressive backgrounds, all with the same skills and qualifications. The results showed that the white men were far more likely to get a call back from the interviewers. This result showed the basis of race in America and how employers will, even unconsciously, rely on predetermined bias to make decisions.

Both these sources detail a system of inequality in the United States, though these sources work in tandem to illustrate the inequality of race in modern working America. Those who maintain the working, middle class in America are seen as those who work. The American ideals lead to the belief that hard work can lead one to the top. While this idea may or may not lead to a system of power, the discrimination experiment shows that those of minority races are less likely to be hired for working positions by employers. This result, coupled with the fact that power is distributed to those of higher economic status, insists that minorities are far less likely to hold positions of American power.

In the modern United States, black Americans have essentially been forced to live in poor areas and living conditions. Since Mantsios elaborates on correlating wealth and SAT scores, black Americans living poor lifestyles are less likely to get a high score on the SAT. This, in turn, leads to a lack of college acceptance and future jobs. Black Americans are dealt a lower likelihood to advance to a position of power in the United States. This position of power, naturally, is one based off economic wealth, with the power elite being the richest in America.
chunks.label: Analyzing readings on economic class and racial discrimination
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses readings by Gregory Mantsios and Devah Pager et al., analyzing how wealth, SAT scores, and racial discrimination limit minority advancement to positions of power.

chunks.text:
In my experience, I come from a well-off household, on the upper end of the middle class. I was taught the values of hard work and professionalism from a very young age by my father, who held and maintained a job in a stable, professional working environment. These values were instilled in me because it is what my father deemed important enough to pass to me. While in his position, he clearly held the wish for me to do the same in the future. This carried on to me, as I am pursuing a master’s degree in electrical engineering. My friend, Justin, on the other hand, was raised in a considerably poor household. His parents came from Mexico and then started a life of hard work. This hard work meant little because they didn’t have an American education, nor could they speak perfect English. His mother was a nurse and worked long hours just to make ends meet.

I went to high school with Justin, and I asked him what job he wanted to do when he graduated college. He told me that college was not part of his plans. He intended to get out of high school and work hard for the rest of his life because that is what he knows.
chunks.label: Comparing upbringing and plans with friend Justin
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up in an upper-middle-class home where their father instilled professionalism and the pursuit of advanced education. In contrast, their high school friend Justin came from a working-class immigrant family and explained that college was not part of his plans.
chunks.people: father, friend Justin, Justin's parents, Justin's mother

chunks.text:
When it comes to my father, there is much more than hard work. He knows how to talk to people, how to propose new ideas, and how to cater towards other white males’ interests. From this perspective, it is very easy to see how the white male is set up for more success, being taught the values of other white males, which then get passed to newer generations. This act assists in the matter of keeping less wealthy minorities, what deBeauvoir would deem as the “other,” out of any positions of power and financial standing.

Each of the authors proposed above uses their corresponding experiments to prove that American minorities are withheld from positions of economic power. While minorities tend to maintain positions of lower finances, the values of hard work are taught to their children. This, coupled with the results of the discrimination experiment, proves a difficult concept. The reason is this: minorities maintain the instilled values of hard work, but not that of appealing to the white man. Starting a business is not always the best option, so working to the top is more likely the method to success. How can minorities make their way to the top when employers refuse to hire them? Hard work means little when you are denied any opportunity to show it, maintaining the reason that there is a distinct correlation between minorities and lower economic American classes.
chunks.label: Reflecting on white male advantage and systemic barriers
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the cultural and professional advantages passed down through white males and concludes that systemic discrimination prevents hardworking minorities from attaining power and financial standing.

chunks.text:
The argument I will use to explain Peggy McIntosh’s argument is the idea of “Collective Consciousness” from Emile Durkheim. From Durkheim and collective consciousness, we see “Collective Representation,” which to me seems to be the best explanation for the arguments in the reading for this week. Collective Representation can only be created from the group of people who believe it to be so—this belief held by a group of people forms from human interaction patterns over time. From McIntosh, we see that the white privilege is very real to everyone except white people. Still, white people and the question of racism will not be answered until white people realize that there is a distinct privilege given to them based on their skin color.

This week, we focused on the Sociology of Race and, like collective consciousness, the idea of race is socially constructed. From the times of ancient Rome, we first see “racism” at a “local” level because the Romans got along with the Egyptians and the Persians, two groups of people with a darker complexion and on the other hand, we see the lack of respect towards the Germanic people because they were seen as uncivilized. Racism during ancient times was based on if your civilization had laws and wasn’t running wild. From Rome, we move into European cities, which saw the term “whiteness” as a ranking in society. This idea that “whiteness” had a higher social standing then turned into the idea that anyone who was not white had no social place, and it was questioned if they should be deemed human or not. Racism is a collective consciousness created hundreds of years ago to put white people at an advantage over black people. We see this argument presented in Peggy McIntosh’s “White Privilege: Unpacking the Invisible Knapsack”. In this essay, we know how the author compares male privilege to white privilege using the fact “whites are carefully taught to not recognize white privilege, as males are taught not to recognize male privilege.” I believe that the idea of Collective Consciousness and Collective Representation is responsible for this unspoken fact that white people have a leg up in a society based on the ancient ideology that communities can be uncivilized and civilized.

Considering the fact that white people created the Collective Conscious and Collective Representation for white people. White people have created a society for white people, and black people have created a society for black people, but somehow a white person took the “foreign” society and said, “that’s wrong” therefore white people must force this ‘foreign” society to conform into the white culture for it to be civilized—that is the collective consciousness of racism and white people are responsible for this consciousness. Suppose you compare the population's size for white people to the population of black people and many other races found in a community, the number of white people in a given society most likely outnumbers any other race; therefore, assimilating the races to conform to the idea that unless your white, you do not have a chance to earn the high ranking. This ideology is responsible for racism still be present in 2021; until white people realize that white privilege is real, society stands no chance at defeating the disease of racism.
chunks.label: Analyzing race and white privilege through collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Peggy McIntosh's essay on white privilege and Durkheim's concepts of collective consciousness and collective representation, tracing the social construction of race and racism from ancient Rome to modern society.

chunks.text: I thought that temple was extremely boring when I started going. Other than the oneg, which is the part after the service where you get free food, I saw no good reason to be there. It felt like I was just going to sit and listen to someone talk in a different language for an hour and a half. As I kept going, it did not get any more fun, but I did start to observe how everyone that attended seemed very content, and everybody got along with each other quite well. This is the first time I had seen such a large community of people united under a set of moral beliefs that were designed to improve the lives of everyone they touched.
chunks.label: Starting temple attendance
chunks.what_happened: The student began attending temple services, initially finding them boring before noticing how content and united the community was.

chunks.text: After attending weekly services for a while, the idea of becoming a Bar Mitzvah was introduced to me. I decided I would do it. Mainly, I was interested in the afterparty and the gifts that would come my way as a result. Once I committed to my decision, I started attending Hebrew school on Thursdays and Sunday school on, well, Sundays. Learning Hebrew was the first part of Judaism up to that point that I truly enjoyed. It was fun learning how to read a mysterious-looking language, and there were other kids my age there with me going through the same thing. In Sunday school, I sat with the same kids and learned about the history and principles of the religion. I started to get to know many of the people that I had seen at services and build solid relationships.
chunks.label: Deciding on Bar Mitzvah and attending classes
chunks.what_happened: The student decided to become a Bar Mitzvah and began attending Hebrew school and Sunday school, enjoying learning Hebrew and connecting with peers.
chunks.feelings: interested in the afterparty and gifts, truly enjoyed, fun

chunks.text: Once I had gotten into this routine of Hebrew school on Thursday, service on Friday, and Sunday school on Sunday, things began to get a little more intense. I began to meet with the Rabbi in my free time. I would go into her office and we would sit for an hour each session and study prayers and readings in Hebrew to prepare for my event. Becoming a Bar Mitzvah almost felt like a job at this point. I remember the Rabbi getting upset with me one time because I was reading the English transliteration of the prayer instead of the Hebrew. I was becoming tired of all the hard work.
chunks.label: Studying with the Rabbi
chunks.what_happened: The student began meeting weekly with the Rabbi to study prayers and readings, experiencing pressure and fatigue as the work intensified.
chunks.feelings: tired of all the hard work

chunks.text: Of course, even more work came on top of this. I was told I needed to complete a Bar Mitzvah project, which is essentially a social action project that encourages students to combine their talents and hobbies with an act of community service. I have played piano for many years, so I decided to play for senior citizens at retirement homes. I figured that this would serve the community well since many people living in these homes did not have the option to go out to events or see live music. While this was a fun thing to do and it felt good to make people happy, it was even more work that I had to do apart from school and other extracurriculars.
chunks.label: Performing piano for senior citizens
chunks.what_happened: The student completed a Bar Mitzvah community service project by playing piano for residents at retirement homes.

chunks.text: There was a final aspect of my studying on top of everything else. This was a Hebrew tutor, who helped me learn the prayers I had to learn in between my meeting times with the Rabbi. I knew my tutor personally and we got along very well, so this was also a good time, but again, it was more work that I had to do in preparation for what was once just an idea. It was at this point that I began to ask myself what the point of this was. Who was I doing it for? It was not for my parents, my friends, or my teachers. I never answered this question for myself until months later.
chunks.label: Working with a Hebrew tutor
chunks.what_happened: The student worked with a Hebrew tutor to study prayers, questioning why they were doing all the preparation.

chunks.text: Emile Durkheim, a French sociologist, explained the idea of the collective consciousness and collective representations. The collective consciousness is the shared values, beliefs, and viewpoints of a group. A collective representation is something that represents the common beliefs and ideals of a society. For example, a collective representation from American society would be the American Flag. The flag is for all Americans and symbolizes the common American belief system and dream. Rather than being individual people leading completely separate lives and completely forming our own beliefs, the collective consciousness gives us an opportunity to have a group to share knowledge with.
chunks.label: Durkheim's collective consciousness and representations
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Emile Durkheim's sociological concepts of collective consciousness and collective representations using the American flag as an example.

chunks.text:
This is what I realized once I reflected on my experience of becoming a Bar Mitzvah. All of the things I had done to work towards a seemingly pointless goal had done something bigger than I could have imagined. It introduced me to a new community of people to share values and beliefs with. I had not been indoctrinated into a belief system, I had been welcomed into a community. I understood that it was actually preparing me to decide to what extent religious values shared by my community would affect and direct my later life, and realized that decisions I make regarding my involvement and participation in the community are fully voluntary, and should come from a place of genuine care.

Once I truly considered these things, everything that had once seemed like a job started to become parts of a whole. The connection to all of these people and ideas that I made through my work bound me to my faith. I now carry the values and lessons I have learned with me and allow them to influence my life and decisions in positive ways. Being a Jew means being part of a unique collective consciousness. A Bar Mitzvah is more than just the rote memorization of various prayers and readings, it is a celebration of an individual taking their place in the community.

In conclusion, the true meaning of religion took me a while to understand. From attending temple, to Hebrew school, to Sunday school, to studying prayers and readings, I am grateful for the community that I have become a part of, even if I did not understand what was happening in the moment. I am very close with the people that I got to know through my experiences. Although I only have experience with one religion, I can extrapolate that all religions and belief systems have rituals that may not be understood by outsiders. However, these rituals serve a purpose in bringing a certain group of people together under shared values. It goes even further than religion. This system of shared values happens with entire countries. Being a part of the collective consciousness provides meaning in one’s life.
chunks.label: Reflecting on Bar Mitzvah and community
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how their Bar Mitzvah connected them to a Jewish community and how shared rituals and collective consciousness provide meaning across religions and societies.

chunks.text:
In Harari’s “21 Lessons for the 21st Century,” he shares his views on the many controversial problems of the global society. Harari shares personal viewpoints and experiences, historical references, and social science to deeply explain where he stands. Harari’s text provides an updated view of sociology, compared to the most popular dated sociologists. This essay will highlight and explore contradictions between Harari and Durkheim on the topic of religion in a society and moral compasses. Next, the essay will dive into the many similarities between Harari and Mantsios regarding their views on hierarchal structures in societies and equality.

In Durkheim’s “The Cultural Logic of Collective Representations,” he argues that religions were important in creating the many ways that a society functions. Durkheim credits religion with developing the peak of societal function. Durkheim stated, “In fact, we have seen that if collective life awakens religious thought on reaching a certain degree of intensity, it is because it brings about a state of effervescence which changes the conditions of psychic activity” (Durkheim 73). Durkheim describes the vast power religion has in conjunction with the intensity of socialization and group thought. Durkheim goes on to explain morals and human thought, “Hence the individual at least obscurely takes account of the fact that above his private ideas, there is a world of absolute ideas according to which he must shape his own; he catches a glimpse of a whole intellectual kingdom in which he participates, but which is greater than he.” Durkheim believed that religions provide people with the collective consciousness of “truth”. The individual has the power to interpret the truth, but they can’t truly choose and decide what the truth is. Durkheim credits religion heavily for being the moral compass of people, guiding individuals in their beliefs of what is wrong or right in any situation.

Harari has a far different take on how religion functions in a society, and how individuals form a moral compass. Harari explains, “﻿There are no “Muslim” or “Jewish” positions here. Humankind is likely to be divided into two main camps—those in favor of giving AI significant authority, and those opposed to it. Muslims and Jews are likely to be found in both camps, and to justify whichever position ﻿they espouse through imaginative interpretations of the Quran and the Talmud” (Harari 119). Harari does not believe that religion spawns individuals’ beliefs and morals. As he explained, there will always be people from all religions on both sides of any given political debate. Furthermore, Harari argues that people’s moral compasses do not come from religion. Harari also goes on to argue that science and medicine is the key to successful human evolution, not organized religion. People from all places and cultures will all come to similar conclusions of what is truly important in life. Harari gives credit where is due and explains how religion has positives such as bringing people together in positive ways. Harari also explains some negatives to religion, “﻿Other religious traditions fill the world with a lot of ugliness and make people behave meanly and cruelly. There is little to be said, for example, in favor of religiously inspired misogyny or caste discrimination” (Harari 121). Harari uses both pros and cons of religion as a whole, to demonstrate that society and individuals can easily operate efficiently without the need for organized religion.

Durkheim believed that religion was pivotal in shaping societal structures and human evolution, as Harari believes religion was only a byproduct of the evolving individuals and societies. Durkheim highlighted how collective consciousnesses and collective representations create culture and community in a society. On the contrary, Harari explains how religion is more so just a story, behind the true reality. The things that shape reality are science, medicine, and politics. Harari views the effects of religion on society with an open mind, while still being critical of its darkest aspects. On the contrary, Durkheim explains how religion shaped and pushed societies into growth.

Gregory Mantsios and Harari have very similar views on class hierarchy systems in the global society. In Gregory Mantsios’ “Class in America,” he explains a common myth “Rich or poor, we are all equal in the eyes of the law, and such basic needs such as health care and education are provided to all regardless of economic standing.” (Mantsios 183). Mantsios debunks this myth early in the reading, to show how we are supposed to view the United States. He explains that American values want us to believe that everyone is equal even though that is far from reality. We are taught about the American dream growing up, and this idea is meant to make people feel like everyone has an equal deck of cards dealt to them. Mantsios uses statistics to show how unequal the United States really is, such as 1 in 5 children ages 1-6 are living in poverty. This stat was a clear example of how unequal circumstances are in America, debunking the myth very easily. Mantsios also explains how the United States is notorious for wealth inequality. He explains how the country has very rich people, and very poor people. Mantsios states, “The income gap between rich and poor in the United States (measured as the percentage of total income held by the wealthiest 20 percent of the population versus the poorest 20 percent) is approximately 12 to 1, one of the highest ratios in the industrialized world.” (Mantsios 185). Mantsios wants readers to be aware of how glaringly obvious income in equality is in the country, our middle class is very sparce. He goes on to illustrate 3 different lifestyles, using characters. One character represents upper class with many privileges such as knowing powerful people, growing up rich, and attending private schools. The next character is from a middle/working class family and attended public schools with people of a similar background. This Character went on to trade school and graduated in 2 years. The final character is from the lower class from a family that struggles to make ends meet. This character attends the worst schools of the 3, and eventually had to drop out of trade school due to poverty. The 3 different lifestyles accurately represent how unfair financial circumstances and opportunity are. In America we are taught that we all have an equal opportunity at success, but this is far from reality. Harari would agree with Harari that we live in an unequal world.

In the “Equality” chapter of Harari’s book, he explains how even though the world is more equal than it was before 1900, it is still tremendously unequal financially. Harari explains some very similar stats to Mantsios, “﻿Today, the richest 1 percent own half the world’s wealth. Even more alarmingly, the richest one hundred people together own more than the poorest four billion” (Harari 72). These statistics and the statistics used by Mantsios show the clear similarities in the 2 authors’ views on wealth inequality. Harari ties in the current landscape of global wealth inequality to the imminent danger of artificial intelligence. Harari makes it clear in earlier chapters that AI will one day help the richest powerful people do what they do today, on a larger scale. This means that inequality will likely become even more drastic than today! Harari explains one of his fears regarding the elite utilizing AI in the future, “﻿While up until now they have only been able to ﻿buy little more than status symbols, soon they might be able to buy life itself. If new treatments for extending life and upgrading physical and cognitive abilities prove to be expensive, humankind might split into biological castes” (Harari 72). If this hypothetical from Harari becomes true, the global issue of wealth inequality would become even more intense.

Harari and Mantsios both prove how crippling wealth inequality is in the United States and the global society. Both Mantsios and Harari address how these inequalities are extremely apparent and real, regardless of if we were intended to see. Powerful elite people obtained wealth through power and opportunity, not necessarily from pure hard work and grit. In the future, AI and advanced technology may aid the powerful elite in becoming even more powerful. If medicinal advances and technology combine to extend life, the elite will be the first to reap the benefits of the new privileges. This will lead to even more unequal opportunity across societies, bridging the gaps between classes even bigger. It would be very interesting to see hypothetical characters similar to Mantsios’. But instead, the rich character has even more layers of privilege such as the best medical care including robotic organs. As Harari stated, things are more equal today, but we may be headed in the wrong direction.

Harari’s “21 Lessons for the 21st Century” navigates the main global societal problems. We found that his views both aligned and contradicted other sociologists. Harari had very critical views on religion, as he compared it to the oldest form of “fake news”. As on the contrary, authors like Durkheim credited religion with shaping the successful societies of the world. Harari acknowledges religion for sometimes bringing people together in a positive light, but he views the cons such as oppression to be far worse. Also, Harari believes all religions their cultures/societies to very similar end points. Harari was still able to align with modern sociologists like Gregory Mantsios on the issue of wealth inequality. The 2 authors had very consistent views on the causes and depth of the issue, and Harari took it a step further by hypothesizing and expressing concern for how the problem could worsen in the future. Harari’s lessons went very in-depth, inevitably meaning that he would find consistent and inconsistent bases with other renowned sociologists.

References

Harari, Y. N. (2019). 21 Lessons for the 21st Century. Vintage.

Mantsios , G. (2006). Class in America- 2006.

Durkheim, E. (1912). The Cultural Logic of Collective Representations.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of Harari, Durkheim, and Mantsios
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes and compares the sociological perspectives of Harari, Durkheim, and Mantsios regarding religion and wealth inequality.

nd1727a52.title: Conforming to Unrealistic Female Beauty Standards

chunks.text: As children grow older, they become more aware and self-conscious of themselves and their bodies. Many times, this is a negative experience, as children begin to compare themselves against their peers, models in magazines, and modern beauty standards. This can be damaging to both mental and physical health, as such comparisons can lead to the development of eating disorders like anorexia, bulimia, and binge eating. Despite being subjected to similar media and peer groups, eating disorders disproportionately affect young women and girls as opposed to young men and boys. (This is not to say that males are not affected by eating disorders). This brings many to raise the following question: Why do women, young women particularly, get diagnosed with eating disorders so much more frequently than men? The answer to this question is based on how society highly values the way that a woman looks, above all other personal aspects, and does not hold men up to the same standard. Because a woman’s value is seemingly determined by her looks, a phenomenon known as the beauty myth, eating disorders plague younger women and girls and can cause severe mental and physical consequences.
chunks.label: Eating disorders and beauty standards
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how societal beauty standards disproportionately affect young women and lead to eating disorders.

chunks.text: In my personal experience, eating disorders are incredibly common in my peers. I have distinct memories of sitting at the lunch table with friends in my middle and high school years discussing how we could lose weight, apply makeup, or utilize a number of other beauty treatments. This was characterized by normal “girl talk”, while boys in the seats across the room were more concerned with whose soccer team they would be on at recess than anything else. Even now as a college student, I frequently witness similar interactions among my peers, specifically in the swim team locker room. Before anyone that I knew was ever diagnosed with an eating disorder, it was commonplace for us all to despise and attempt to improve upon our naturally growing and changing bodies.
chunks.label: Body talk in school and swim locker rooms
chunks.what_happened: The student recalls discussing weight loss and beauty treatments with friends at lunch in middle and high school, and witnessing similar interactions in the college swim team locker room.

chunks.text: This age and time period are universally awkward for children as they go through puberty and their body transitions into something new and unknown. This is an incredibly vulnerable and developmentally important time period and the diagnosis of an eating disorder prevents children from maturing in a healthy way. With this being said, eating disorders are also detrimental to the health of people past the age of puberty. Eating disorders frequently prohibit those affected from getting the nutrients that they need to maintain good health. Also related to this is the concept of diet culture. Diet culture is the societal belief that physical appearance is more important than physical and mental well-being. This concept was widely accepted by my peers by the time I entered middle school, and this culture enabled and continues to enable the development of eating disorders in young women.
chunks.label: Puberty and diet culture
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses the vulnerability of puberty and explains the concept and societal impact of diet culture.

chunks.text: Around the time I turned eighteen, I was diagnosed with bulimia. Growing up, I was always taller and lankier than my peers, and I always stuck out in a crowd. I was incredibly self-conscious about this, so as I got older and my body started to change, I wanted to do everything that I could in an attempt to fit society’s ideal beauty standard. Being tall is typically considered to be unfeminine, and because I was very involved as a competitive swimmer, I was also muscular with broad shoulders, adding to my masculine traits. Many of my friends, and lots of girls my age regularly made fun of me for this, causing me to do everything in my power to prove my femininity and fit the male gaze in other ways. Namely, I started experimenting with makeup, clothes, and weight loss. During this time, I was a healthy weight for my gender and age, but I found myself comparing my body type to the edited pictures of models in bikinis in the media, as well as my more petite peers. Because of this, I certainly felt the pressure to work to conform to society’s beauty standards. There were many factors that eventually led to my bulimia diagnosis, all centered around conforming to society’s beauty standards, and this is something that I still struggle with even today, despite knowing these expected standards of beauty are totally unrealistic.
chunks.label: Bulimia diagnosis and pressure to conform
chunks.what_happened: The student experienced teasing from friends and peers for being tall and muscular from competitive swimming, which led them to experiment with weight loss and receive a bulimia diagnosis around age eighteen.

chunks.text: In order to further understand this, it seems pertinent to examine the work of Namoi Wolf and the concept of the beauty myth. The beauty myth is essentially the standard of the physical appearance of women, and the idea that a woman’s value is determined based on whether or not she meets this standard. It is a sexist ideal that runs our society in an attempt to control women’s bodies and self-esteem. The phrase “it’s a man’s world” is incredibly relevant here, as women are subjected to the beauty myth because our culture is dominated by men’s power and institutions. This is seen in our daily lives, as the beauty myth is perpetuated by social media, advertisements, and other platforms that project unrealistic body expectations for women. The beauty myth is determined by politics and is designed to keep male dominance intact. Since men are trying to maintain dominance, women are forced into society’s standards in order to fight against each other for the resources that men have appropriated for themselves. Additionally, we see that as a woman’s social power increases, so does the beauty standard that she is expected to fulfill. Frequently, this pressure prevents women from reaching their full potential and being the most effective they can be. A different example of how the beauty myth is seen in our society is plastic surgery. The practice of plastic surgery has increased in relatively recent years, but specifically cosmetic surgery is primarily performed on women. Women who undergo breast augmentation, facial lifts, rhinoplasties, or a number of other procedures do so even when it is not medically necessary, but instead, fit society’s definition of beauty. This myth is a travesty in and of itself, but what makes it even worse is that there is no corollary myth for men. While it is true that men strive to have good looks, they simply do not face the same pressures women have to be attractive. Conclusively, the beauty myth is a belief system studied by Wolf that ensures male dominance stays intact in every aspect of society, but actively diminishes the worth of women by judging them solely off of appearance.
chunks.label: Naomi Wolf and the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Naomi Wolf's concept of the beauty myth, male dominance, and societal practices like cosmetic surgery.

chunks.text: Overall, today’s widespread problem of eating disorders, particularly in young women and girls can be explained by the concept of the beauty myth. Because women are only valued in society if they are beautiful in the eyes of men, many women are pushed to attempt to achieve these unattainable standards in extremely unhealthy ways. The idea of the beauty myth is ingrained in the minds of women starting at a very young age, meaning that these unhealthy coping mechanisms frequently develop early, leaving girls with lifelong insecurities as well as worrying mental and psychical health conditions, like eating disorders. It is important to note that driving women to such lengths is simply a sadistic control method to keep men in positions of power and to ensure that women compete with each other instead of with men. It is despicable that this misogynistic belief rules our society, and that young women and girls are forced to suffer the consequences of male insecurity.
chunks.label: Conclusion on the beauty myth and eating disorders
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that the beauty myth acts as a misogynistic control mechanism driving young women into eating disorders.

nef7698fc.title: Hesitating to Speak in the Classroom

chunks.text:
When a professor asks a question in class and one feels confident enough to think “I know this, I can answer this 100%” what is the determining factor in whether that person raises their hand to answer the professor’s question in front of the whole class? That factor in which we as humans always seem to lose faith in ourselves in fear of somehow getting the question that you know is correct wrong is called the Conception of Self. The first reading I am going to use is George Herbert Mead’s “The Self, The I, and the Me”. In the reading it becomes three different concepts; the “I” is the part of our brains that responds to stimuli being presented to us from the environment (like the example used previously) knowing the answer to a question when asked. The “Me” is the part of our brains that evaluates what this stimulus is and how it will be affecting us, the “What if it’s wrong, don’t raise your hand”. The “Self” is the part of our brains that exerts the emotions from the conversation between the “I” and the “Me” part of our brains. The self in the classroom situation would be feeling unconfident/nervous to answer the question due to the argument between the “I” and “Me”.

Now take the “I”, “Me”, and “Self” and consider Erving Goffman’s “The Presentation of Self”. In Goffman’s “The Presentation of Self” we see that the performance of the “I”, “Me” and “Self” depends on the type of interaction we are having. The literal presentation of one’s self solely depends on the audience. For example, my thought process for driving to school and my thought process driving home from school are two totally different fields.

Those two concepts are responsible for the way we create a standard for ourselves in different settings. By using the Conception of Self-concept, we as humans have created a safety net for our own thoughts and actions. When we are with our families, we are going to act a lot different than we would if we were with friends, or if we were in the presence of our teachers or our employers, our brains have created different “modes” based on the constant internalized conversation we have with ourselves every second of every day when we make decisions.
chunks.label: Analyzing Mead's and Goffman's theories of self
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on George Herbert Mead's concepts of the 'I', 'Me', and 'Self', as well as Erving Goffman's 'The Presentation of Self', to explain how people alter their behavior and thoughts depending on social contexts and audiences.

n69d7343c.title: Critiquing Modern Lessons on Religion and Media

chunks.text:
In his book called the “21 Lessons for the 21st Century”, Harari goes over many relevant topics that happened in this time period and gives his thoughts on how we should individually. He lists many controversial things that we should be aware of and more importantly, presents information to us that is very useful. From what I read, I thought that most of what was written was consistent from what was being said and found these ideas to be true. However, there was one idea on the science fiction chapter that I disagree with and found myself to be confused at his point.

Now onto the consistencies. The topic I wanted to talk about is the religion chapter because it ties in together with their relevancy and importance. The book itself is about modern lessons about certain topics and this is one of the controversial ideas that have lasted since forever. Moving on, religion has lasted seemingly ever since humans came about. What Harari talks about now is that religion is irrelevant towards current complications and is no longer useful to modern society. He states that present issues related to more scientific data such as climate change and drought prevention can not be solved by religion. Religions like Christianity were utilized in medieval times where science has not been found to work, so people turned to religion. It made sense that people during previous eras would turn into things like faith in order to have a chance at survival. However, times have changed and now religion’s ideas are not very applicable to today. The main idea of the chapter was that humans past that time period had made many achievements scientifically and now we know that religion has no impact in our lives anymore.

In terms of economics, religion seemed to play a similar role here with science. For instance, in countries such as Israel or Iran when a religious figure has power in a given decision, Harari points out that these rabbis will turn to people who are known to have intelligence in economics, such as Karl Marx as opposed to using religion first. He also tells us that rabbis have little understanding of how economics work and the possible consequences for an unaware mistake. It is clear to the reader that religion serves a different purpose in these specific scenarios and they not nearly accurate enough for even religious figures to make a defined statement that is solely based on old scripture.

The reason I wanted to talk about religion is how it ties to the overall message about the book, and it does so with numerous chapters. In the work chapter, Harari goes on to say that artificial intelligence is something to think about with many positives and negatives. He says that AI was a major breakthrough in human progression and has seen a lot of promise because of its capabilities. Noting that self-driving cars are almost a thing now, job positions could be taken over, and even chess players are being outplayed. The reason why I think it is similar to the religion chapter is the way Harari tries to inform the audience about these modern topics. Harari wants us to learn about the future pros and cons these ideas can have and what a person in this time period can look forward to. In terms of religion, he wants us to figure out that religion has been dwindling over the past centuries and specifically now. He does this by giving us fundamentals about the overall perspective and how that plays into why this certain event is happening if not informed already.

What was religion about, and could it be used to solve current objectives? Harari gives us a fully fleshed answer and provides many examples, but basically says no unless we adapt it. How does religion impact society and where can it be used today? He gives a pro example, Japan, and a negative example, North Korea. What is AI and could it be used to solve current objectives? Again, tells us briefly, but down to the point that AI can do such things. How does AI impact society and how could it be used today? AI has the potential to change a lot of things from different aspect in good and bad ways. He wants us to take this information and calculate that based on a reader’s current situation, which was why I fell in love with this book. As a person living in the 21st century after reading this book, will I turn to religion? After hearing what religion is really about, probably not. Will I investigate artificial intelligence? Given the information, probably. He shows importance in upcoming events and how they mold into the current world. This shows us that he wants the reader to think critically about what is happening and what we take from it. Another thing to note about his writing is that everything he writes is pretty much open-ended. There is no real main idea of each chapter, instead he simply tells us the information we need along with the observations he found and how that plays individually that supports this learning process.

Alternatively, Harari wants us to have our own individual perspective on ideas previously shown to us but were shaped by other factors like school. For example, school taught us about the red scare along with how communism was not successful and actually lead to horrible things. But to the author, he actually credits Karl Marx as an economic intellectual in the religion chapter and possibly wants us to look more into such ideas. He is telling us information that could be used by us, but it has to be looked at properly and rationally. It is kind of saying that “good” things can be taken from “bad” things. It seems that this whole book is a learning process that is interpreted by the individual. Just because Karl Marx created an idea that sprouted fear and war among countries. That does not necessarily mean that what he wrote was intentionally evil. I am trying to say that school could have shaped students to think that everything communistic was bad, but Harari shows a different perspective that makes the reader ponder. This was an important thing he went over in the education chapter where he stressed critical thinking.

As for the inconsistencies, I disagreed with the science fiction chapter as it did not seem to have that impact compared to the religion and work chapter and sounded confusing because of how it was interpreted by the author. He starts off by saying movies such as the Matrix do not have accurate representations of the realistic future and because of that lead to false misinterpretations by society. Personally, I did not consider that fact at all, not because it was something incorrect, but more of that I had no idea people thought these movies literally depicted the near future. To me, anything science fiction is a what if scenario. For example, the Matrix shows a specific event that humans become enslaved by intelligent robots and live in a separate false reality. From my point of view, I see the Matrix as a possibility of the outcome of humans unable to control AI and end up being inferior to them, a “what if” scenario. The way Harari interpreted it was very technical. He states that “very little people look at the latest breakthroughs in technology but learn about AI from movies like the Matrix” (Chapter 18). It seems like Harari knows a lot about what is happening in the Matrix from a realistic perspective. But that does not always mean that is should be changed to suit those something real. A great way to display those ideas the author shared is to show data about how many people really believe these movies to be true and then go off on his statements. Instead, he goes off an assumption that people really believe these things true and causes a lot of confusion.

The word fiction in science fiction is there for a reason and I think Harari missed the point of these movies. Another example would be Marvel movies. Marvel movies have a bit of science fiction added to them specifically with Iron Man, everybody’s favorite character. People watch these awesome movies over and over again, not because they depict reality. But because they hold values that are important to us that is exaggerated in the Marvel universe. People dress up as Iron Man all the time. Do these people actually think in the near future they could literally become their favorite Marvel figure? I just personally do not think people really believe that. They might think it could happen in the long future, but not really. The point was that these movies are a fantasy of what could happen in the next centuries and, I repeat do not explain our future hence the word fiction.

Moving on, he adds on to this chapter with a movie with a very realistic approach called Inside Out. This movie was amazing because it took the newest neurological progresses in science and was able to blend that into a good kid friendly movie. I have not watched it myself; I am sure it is a great movie, but this goes on again to what a movie is supposed to achieve. From my perspective movies teach moral lessons that fit the collective conscious in a positive way, which is why many like Marvel movies. Harari thinks movies should be responsible for their realistic approach, but he explains it in not the best way possible. Sure, this movie is very accurate as the representation of the human brain and its emotions, but it is a darn kid’s movie. Do not get me wrong, it is great to have realistic ideas in a movie, but what is a kid going to learn from that movie? Of course, the children will be more understanding of what is happening on a biological level and may continue that practice. But to justify the main idea being that “movies should be realistic” (Chapter 18) is a great idea coming from bad examples. Not only that, but it does not quite fit with the other chapters. Other chapters were focused on serious current events and their information, and then the science fiction chapter comes out of nowhere. This all reminded me of that one time when the popular game GTA was found by the news, and they ended up sourcing this game to real life crime events like shootings and grand theft auto. I really doubt people who play GTA think they can do that in real life and I see something similar in his statements towards science fiction.

The overall objective of this book was to inform readers about the current situation they live in and how that plays into their individual scenario. I thought that religion along with many other chapters did and very good job at staying with that idea, while also doing well in educating the audience. However, with the science fiction chapter, I thought that it could be scraped for the information that was given due to an awkward meaning with little evidence and inadequate example choice.
chunks.label: Critique of Harari's 21 Lessons for the 21st Century
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on and evaluates Yuval Noah Harari's book '21 Lessons for the 21st Century', comparing chapters on religion and work with the chapter on science fiction.
chunks.feelings: confused, fell in love with this book

n0e971b25.title: Analyzing the Self in Violent Behavior

chunks.text:
