chunks.text:
The two readings I am going to compare are Emile Durkheim’s The Cultural Logic of Collective Representations and Yuval Noah Harari’s One Dollar to Rule Them All. I believe these two reading both reflect the meaning of a collective consciousness by both mentioning religion as a common similarity among cultures and both also mentioning how humans view the natural world through indifferences with science. Collective consciousness and collective representation are both found in social institutions which is why they are responsible for the rituals we see in our everyday lives. Not only do these two concepts allow societies to function as one unit, but it is also these two products of society that allow people to have a sense of belonging.

Emile Durkheim strived to explain why certain values, traditions, and beliefs remain the same through an entire community. His theory is that religion is responsible for the idea of a collective consciousness. “The formation of the ideal world is therefore not an irreducible fact which escapes science: it depends upon conditions which observation can touch; it is a natural product of social life,” (p.73) The conditions of which that are shared are created from a group of people using the same daily traditions. A collective conscious was created by individuals who wanted to achieve a community. By holding certain values and traditions at a high standard among everyone in the community, the ability to achieve a common goal is more successful. This is further explained by Harari in his “One Dollar to Rule Them All”.

I was able to connect this to Harari because he was able to portray the same thought process of Durkheim through his description of similarities between the views shared by humans, “Yet the homogeneity of contemporary humanity is most apparent when it comes to our view of the natural world and of the human body,” (p.113). Like Durkheim, Harari continues to further analyze how humans are not so different after all when describing more realistic values instead of beliefs and traditions, Harari goes as far as comparing how the process of government is similar also, “But when it comes to the practical stuff—how to build a state, an economy, a hospital, or a bomb—almost all of us belong to the same civilization,” (p.115). These two reading share one main topic and that is how similar we as humans really are, from the moment we are born to the moment we die, the societies we are placed in allow us to learn and generate traditions, values, and beliefs to the overall “whole” of society.
chunks.label: Comparing Durkheim and Harari on collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student compares readings by Emile Durkheim and Yuval Noah Harari, discussing collective consciousness, religion, and the shared values and institutions that connect humans in society.

nab61ca04.title: Growing Up in an Interracial Family

chunks.text: It is not often that a person has the chance to experience and observe the workings of white privilege from both sides of the equation. Growing up in an interracial family has opened my eyes to exactly how my fair skin benefits me in life, and how my siblings’ dark skin disadvantages theirs. White privilege is often not realized or willingly acknowledged by many people of the Caucasian race. As Peggy McIntosh states in White Privilege: Unpacking the Invisible Knapsack, “White privilege is like an invisible weightless knapsack of special provisions, maps, passports, codebooks, visas, clothes, tools and blank checks.” (30) I never fully comprehended the amount of advantages I had growing up in the dominantly white United States until the adoption of my siblings, who are both from Ethiopia, Africa, and are currently middle and high school age. Hearing the experiences and concerns of my siblings opened my eyes to the following: white privilege does indeed have a concrete existence in our everyday lives, created through the systemic racism present in American society, and our unwillingness to recognize such privilege only fuels that system further.
chunks.label: Introduction to white privilege and adoption
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the concept of white privilege and quotes Peggy McIntosh, explaining how having adopted Ethiopian siblings opened their eyes to racial advantages in America.

chunks.text: A distinct memory I have from when I was around eight or nine years old is constantly being praised for adopting my brother and sister. When sharing that I have two adopted siblings to someone new, I was often told something along the lines of, “That is so great of your family!” or, “I bet they are so thankful for what you’ve done for them.” Even from such a young age, I always found the comment strange. In recent years I realized it was because it is coming from a privileged and “white savior” perspective, whereas I never saw their adoption through that lens. The adults who praised me most likely did so because, in their eyes, my siblings were lesser and needed our saving. White it is true that they came from a poor country with less opportunity, there are many people living in Ethiopia under the same circumstances who have never known any different. My parents did not adopt with the intentions of being praised or receiving thanks, but rather felt that their faith called them to expand our family through the adoption process. This viewpoint was the beginning of my realization of how much privilege white people receive in our country, to the extent that we place ourselves on a pedestal for opening our homes to those of a different race.
chunks.label: Being praised for siblings' adoption
chunks.what_happened: When the student was eight or nine years old, adults repeatedly praised their family for adopting their brother and sister from Ethiopia, which the student later recognized as a privileged 'white savior' perspective.
chunks.people: brother, sister, parents, adults who praised the family

chunks.text: Another example of this privilege is that I’ve never realized that I have been surrounded by people of my race for my entire life. My parents sent me and each of my siblings to private school for most of our education, and I never realized that there virtually no students of color in the school until my brother or sister would mention it. The school setting made them feel different and outside of the normal, whereas I never gave it a second thought because almost every other peer looked like me. I recall my sister being sad because the only other black girl in her grade was not playing basketball, so she was the only person of color on the team. Nearly all of my siblings’ friends are white as well, taking away that shared experience of being the same race that can create a special connection. While it is of course a good thing to have a diverse friend group, I have never had the issue of not having any friends of the same race as me, something that I would surely miss if that was the case. I have always had the privilege of being within the dominant racial group in the United States, making it easy for me to be surrounded people who are also white. We are taught from a young age that, in our society, skin color has meaning and is a means of interconnection between people of a like race. Whereas I have always had access to that connection, my siblings have not, and therefore feel isolated and abnormal at times because of it.
chunks.label: Racial isolation at private school
chunks.what_happened: The student and their siblings attended a private school with virtually no students of color, leaving the student's sister sad at being the only person of color on her basketball team and making both siblings feel isolated.

chunks.text: The final example is one many people of all races have finally begun to pay attention to, and that is the often unfair treatment of black people by law enforcement and other authorities in the United States. My parents have had to initiate talks with my brother and sister about exactly how to behave when within the same area as law enforcement, especially when driving. Sentences such as “Never move your hands from the wheel,” and, “Announce every action you are about to perform, so they don’t think you are trying to run or pull out a weapon,” have been told to both siblings many times. My sister just obtained her driver’s license very recently, and once again had to be given the same talk. It might seem tedious and dramatic to some, but it is a real fear for black people every day. This fear is something I have never had to experience or be warned about. These fears carry over into other aspects of my siblings’ everyday life. My brother must be told not to act foolish with his white friends, even if they are behaving that way, in case he gets singled out by a person of authority, such as a police officer, or even a teacher. As he gets older, he is not supposed to walk or ride his bike around our predominantly white neighborhood alone, for fear of having someone call the police for trespassing despite our family living there for over seven years. I get in the car to drive, or take my dogs for a walk, without a second thought of how the color of my skin could put me in a position of danger. This is yet another example of the seemingly invisible privilege white people have simply due to their race.
chunks.label: Family warnings about police and neighborhood
chunks.what_happened: The student's parents had to repeatedly give instructions to the brother and sister on how to act around law enforcement and warned the brother not to walk alone in their predominantly white neighborhood.

chunks.text:
How do we know that this is white privilege and not just a handful of random experiences? Peggy McIntosh better explores these advantages in her previously mentioned text, White Privilege: Unpacking the Invisible Knapsack. In her writing, she provides a self-made checklist of assumptions and benefits she feels she inherently receives a right to because of her whiteness. This checklist was made based off of observing what freedoms and things assumed to happen in everyday life that McIntosh’s African American women coworkers did not have access to.

Many of these checklist points correlate to the paralleled experiences between me and my siblings, showing that their experiences and my advantages are not just random or individual. For example, my brother and sister feeling alienated at school corresponds with the privilege McIntosh describes when stating, “I can go home from most meetings of organizations I belong to feeling somewhat tied in, rather than isolated, out of place, outnumbered, unheard, held at a distance, or feared.” (33) I have always had the comfort of being surrounded by people of the same race as me in nearly all settings of my life, whereas my siblings do not often have that assurance.

Several other points on Mcintosh’s list also coincide almost directly with the extra obstacles put in place for my siblings because of their dark skin. These inherent advantages are “I can be pretty sure that my neighbors in a new location will be neutral or pleasant to me the day I move in,” (31) and, “If a traffic cop pulls me over […] I can be sure I haven’t been singled out because of my race.” (33) As previously mentioned, my siblings have to take extra precautions when performing simple tasks such as driving or walking in our neighborhood, just to be seen as a nonthreat to certain people. While these advantages white people receive seem like they should be the normal standard for all (and often are assumed to be afforded to all by white people), this is actually not the case.

Mcintosh begins to expand on how United States systems of government attempt to keep these unearned privileges hidden from white people, as a means to keep them blissfully ignorant in order to continue to support and stand by white-controlled institutions through “conferred dominance.” (34) This gives whites power over other racial groups due to unequal distribution of wealth and assets. Because this realization of the privileges white people receive has been kept from those of the Caucasian race for so long, accepting that such advantages exist becomes a difficult concept to grasp.

There are many white people, such as my grandparents, who have grown up in poor communities with little opportunity. To get out of the situation they were born into, many have had to work hard for what they have in life, following the classic “American dream” and “bootstraps mentality.” Because of this, white people in such a position often deny having such privilege, because they assume privilege only comes from a place of wealth and material possession when, in reality, they were already at an advantage to pull themselves out of poverty because of the color of their skin.

McIntosh also describes a feeling similar to what I experienced when first discovering my inherent privilege, that makes the concept even harder to grasp. Growing up in America, we are taught that we live in a democratic society that provides equal opportunity for all, despite religion, race, age, and many other attributes. With the full acknowledgement of white privilege, Mcintosh states the all too familiar feeling of discovering the hidden truth, saying, “If these things were true, this was not such a free country; my life was not what I had made it; many doors opened for my people through no virtues of our own.” (33) This is what can make the acceptance of the existence of white privilege so daunting, because citizens of the United States are told one streamlined version of history, often leaving out the ugly truths and systemic inequalities that led to the creation of the nation. While people of color realize these inequalities from a young age, white people have often never had to reflect on them because we have no prior experience or knowledge of the inconsistencies within our society.

Without listening to and observing the experiences of my siblings, as well as the behavior and opinions directed towards my brother and sister by white people, I would have most likely remained blissfully ignorant of the privileges I have access to in my everyday life due to my skin color. This is why it becomes extremely important for white people to willingly listen and acknowledge the experiences of people of color in our countries, because it can be a vital way to understand and recognize the privileges we as white people inherently receive in our systemically racist society. However, McIntosh relays one important message in her writing: “Disapproving of these systems won’t be enough to change them.” (35) The first step to redesigning the systems of American society that put white people at an advantage is to accept that such systems and advantages exist in the first place.

In conclusion, the existence of white privilege in the United States is not just an opinion, but rather a tangible concept. This privilege provides white people with advantages, as well as access to basic rights and freedoms, that people of color in the nation are not awarded. Recognizing these privileges can be difficult, because American society attempts to keep white people unaware and denying of such advantages in order to maintain white dominance over other racial groups. Through the simple act of paying attention and being inclined to listen to those who are oppressed by white privilege, it can become quite clear that it does indeed exist. Acceptance of this concept is the first step in attempting to redefine the racially discriminatory systems white privilege was built within.
chunks.label: Reflecting on McIntosh's knapsack and systemic privilege
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Peggy McIntosh's checklist of white privilege, connects it to their family experiences and grandparents' background, and argues that society must acknowledge systemic racism to enact change.

n5644023e.title: Analyzing Modern Capitalism Through Coffee Culture

chunks.text:
In sociology, two known concepts, commodity fetishism and McDonaldization, offer interesting perspectives on modern society. While both ideas deal with characteristics of modern capitalism and its impact on society, they do so from different perspectives, focusing opposite tendencies in the trade of things and the rationalization of social processes. A comparison review of these ideas and a real-world scenario allows us to better comprehend their consequences and judge how effective they are in explaining current events.

Commodity Fetishism: According to Karl Marx's ideas, commodity fetishism is the social trends in which goods have meaning in addition to their physical worth. Goods carry social meanings and wants in capitalist countries in addition to being useful items. This obsession hides the social context of production, making people mistakenly believe that goods possess magical qualities instead of being the result of labor produced by humans..

McDonaldization: George Ritzer, a sociologist, developed the term "McDonaldization" to refer to the process of simplifying and reducing procedures, especially in relation to fast-food restaurants such as McDonald's. It means using effective and controllable methods to a range of areas of life, including food service, healthcare, and education. McDonaldization is a symbol of the success of efficiency and reason over feeling in modern social structures.

Comparisons: While both ideas develop in the context of capitalism, they differ in their focus and level. Commodity fetishism is concerned primarily with the meaning associated with things, emphasizing the creation of value in consumer society. In contrast, McDonaldization focuses on process simplification and standards, emphasizing experience equality and the development of efficiency-oriented systems.

Contrasts: One key distinction between the two concepts lies in their treatment of agency. Commodity fetishism underscores the agency of consumers in attributing value to commodities through their consumption choices and cultural practices. On the other hand, McDonaldization emphasizes the role of institutional structures in shaping social processes, often leading to the disenchantment and standardization of everyday life.

Real-World Scenario: Consider the rise of coffee culture in the 21st century. Coffee, originally considered a simple beverage, has grown into a symbol of status, personality, and lifestyle for many people. The growth of specific coffee shops, each with their own blends, brewing processes, and atmosphere, shows commodity fetishism. Coffee is no longer viewed just as a caffeine source, but rather as an experience to be enjoyed, shared on social media, and connected with specific identities.

Simultaneously, the coffee sector has become McDonaldized, particularly with the rise of global coffee franchises such as Starbucks. These businesses simplify the coffee-drinking experience with the same menus, store layouts, and service processes around the world. Starbucks' efficiency-driven approach, which focuses on speed, consistency, and convenience, illustrates simplified structure.

Despite its flaws, commodity fetishism and McDonaldization continue to be popular concepts for understanding modern society's complexities. Commodity fetishism raises questions about the social creation of value, as well as how consumer culture impacts identities and relationships. Recognizing the symbolic elements of goods allows us to better understand how people interact with their social environment through buying habits.

McDonaldization, focuses on reason and standard of social processes, highlighting the broad impact of things being simplified in modern organizations. While McDonaldization might ignore the wide range of human experiences, it provides important insights into the techniques used by modern capitalism to streamline our daily lives. By combining these viewpoints and analyzing with their effects, we could create deeper views of capitalism's difficult relationship with culture and social organization in the twenty-first century.

Both commodity fetishism and McDonaldization offer valuable insights into contemporary society, yet they have their limitations. Commodity fetishism effectively highlights the cultural and symbolic dimensions of consumption, shedding light on how commodities become repositories of social meaning. However, it may overlook structural inequalities in the production and distribution of goods, focusing primarily on consumer behaviors and cultural practices.

Similarly, McDonaldization provides a compelling framework for understanding the rationalization of modern institutions and the proliferation of efficiency-driven systems. Yet, it tends to oversimplify complex social phenomena, reducing them to calculable and predictable processes. Moreover, McDonaldization overlooks the diversity of human experiences and the potential for resistance against rationalized systems.

In conclusion, while commodity fetishism and McDonaldization offer valuable perspectives on the dynamics of modern capitalism, they should be viewed as complementary rather than competing theories. A nuanced understanding of contemporary society requires integrating insights from both concepts, recognizing the interplay between symbolic meanings and institutional structures in shaping social life. By critically evaluating these concepts and applying them to real-world scenarios, we can deepen our understanding of the complexities of consumer culture and societal organization in the 21st century.
chunks.label: Analyzing commodity fetishism and McDonaldization
chunks.what_happened: The student compares and contrasts Karl Marx's concept of commodity fetishism and George Ritzer's concept of McDonaldization, applying them to the real-world example of modern coffee culture.

ne49054ac.title: Unpacking Hegemonic Masculinity and Emotional Isolation

chunks.text:
In western cultures, hegemonic masculinity is highly valued. This is the classic idea of what a man should be. Hegemonic masculinity refers to a man being physically and mentally strong, providing, wealthy, and emotionless or grounded. This idea of the perfect western man has shaped the way men act in their everyday lives. Men in the western world hold the positions of power, make the most money, but are still often unhappy. Men also lead the statistics in suicide rates and cheating within long-term relationships and marriages. A newer trend shows that young men are having less sex than ever. Are these signs of truly strong people? Many problems that affect men specifically, would be greatly improved by men adopting feminine qualities and behaviors.

In an attempt to deal with these societal problems, right- leaning parties have advocated for men to become more masculine in order to fight the issues. Masculinity and femininity can be measured on a spectrum. Trying to force men to act more masculine is no more than putting on a facade. This only leads to a further lack of authenticity of character in men, making matters worse.

Boys in the western world are taught to act masculine very early on in childhood. Young males are pushed in the directions of interests such as toy cars, guns, and other manly activities. It would be very interesting to see how something as simple as toy selection would be different if all outside factors were taken out.
chunks.label: Hegemonic masculinity and early childhood conditioning
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the negative impacts of hegemonic masculinity in Western culture and how gendered expectations begin early in childhood.

chunks.text: For example, I grew up with a sister, and toy dolls were just as interesting to me as the toys made for boys.
chunks.label: Growing up playing with sister's dolls
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up with a sister and found toy dolls just as interesting as toys intended for boys.

chunks.text: Furthermore, many extracurricular activities that kids engage in are split up by gender. Scouts organizations, sports, and even play groups are often split up by the sexes. We do not see many young boys being signed up for dance classes, yet many men wonder why they feel awkward on a dance floor in their adult lives. In schools, there are awkward dynamics between the sexes.
chunks.label: Gender segregation in youth activities
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how extracurricular activities, sports, and school dynamics are rigidly separated by gender.

chunks.text: I have memories of fears such as the “cooties” early in school, which embedded in kids to not associate with the other sex.
chunks.label: Childhood fear of cooties
chunks.what_happened: The student recalls experiencing childhood fears of 'cooties' in early school years, which discouraged associating with the other sex.

chunks.text:
Kids in the western world are conditioned early on to stick to their gender role in society.

By the time boys reach adolescence, they view the opposite sex as the “other”.
chunks.label: Conditioning boys to view women as other
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how gender conditioning leads adolescent boys to view the opposite sex as the 'other'.

chunks.text: Looking back at my highschool experience, many boys including myself found it very difficult to talk to girls, even when there was no romantic interest. We were indirectly conditioned to view women as the “other”, not just people.
chunks.label: High school difficulty talking to girls
chunks.what_happened: During high school, the student and other boys found it very difficult to talk to girls because of conditioning to view women as 'other'.
chunks.people: the student, high school boys, girls

chunks.text: Many kids have friend groups of one sex. In the case of adolescent boys, they often have superficial relationships with their best friends. It is not uncommon for friend groups of guys to not know major parts of one another’s lives.
chunks.label: Superficiality in male adolescent friendships
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how adolescent male friend groups often have superficial bonds and do not know major personal details about each other.

chunks.text: For example, one of my closest friends did not inform me of his mother having a serious health incident, for weeks. Even when he informed me of the news, it was talked about very briefly and casually.
chunks.label: Friend hiding his mother's illness
chunks.what_happened: A close friend of the student did not mention that his mother had a serious health incident for weeks, and discussed it only briefly and casually when he did.
chunks.people: the student, the student's close friend, friend's mother

chunks.text:
It seems men have difficulty in expressing emotions and feelings with each other. On the contrary, many friend groups of girls know everything about each other. As there is sometimes an issue with this, overall, men would greatly benefit from having deeper friendships with people because they would be able to offer the proper emotional support for one another when times get hard.

For a very long time in western society, men’s strongest relationships are with their spouse. Our society tells us that men are meant to save the intimacy and emotional talks for their wives or girlfriends. When have you seen a man crying on his friend's shoulder, aside from someone dying? This can often create unbalanced relationship dynamics, because women often have close friends to share emotions with outside of the romantic relationship. It seems it is very common for moms to have friend groups, but not dads.
chunks.label: Emotional expression and male relationship imbalances
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how men struggle to share emotions with friends and tend to rely solely on female romantic partners for emotional intimacy.

chunks.text: If I examine my parents’ social lives, my mom has far more friends than my dad. Furthermore, the friends my dad has are either from work, family, or through my mom’s friends.
chunks.label: Comparing parents' social circles
chunks.what_happened: The student observes their parents' social lives, noting that their mother has far more friends while their father's friends are limited to work, family, or his wife's friends.
chunks.people: the student, the student's mother, the student's father

chunks.text:
This can create an imbalance in a relationship or marriage because the woman often has more emotional outlets to vent to. Men’s social lives would be greatly improved if they had more platonic friends to spend time with and share emotions with.

If we examine the dynamics of men’s romantic relationships in today’s landscape, things have become even worse. In addition to men lacking platonic supportive friendships, young men are failing to establish and maintain romantic sexual relationships. According to The Washington Post, the amount of men under 30 years old who have reported no sex in the last year, has skyrocketed to nearly 30% (Ingraham). Because people meet online more than in person these days, this trend can possibly be blamed on the dynamics of online dating applications. Apps like Tinder reward people based on the “matches” they get based on purely looks. Unfortunately, it has been theorized that a small percentage of the men on these applications receive the vast majority of all “matches”. This not only leaves men feeling defeated, but it also reinforces hegemonic masculinity by rewarding the good-looking strong men. If men are struggling to establish romantic relationships , and their platonic friendships are often superficial, how can they properly meet their emotional needs?

The final piece of the puzzle in the unhappy man is the way men work for a living. In our western society, men are expected to be the breadwinners for the family. This inevitably leads to men entering tough professions that they may not enjoy. Allocating the majority of one’s time to something they do not enjoy and receive fulfillment from is a recipe for disaster. When this is paired with lacking relationships, the potential for happiness is greatly reduced. Why is it that women are expected to stay home with the kids, yet many of them would like to pursue a career? The gender roles of society put people in lifestyles that are not suited for the individual. Men would be happier if they engaged in projects they truly cared for, with people they want to work with. In recent news, MMA fighter Jon Jones got arrested for domestic violence and damaging a police vehicle. Jones supposedly does what he loves for a living, but is clearly mentally ill and has an unbalanced life. He is the pinnacle of masculinity as he is strong, large, rich, and can literally end almost anyone's life with his hands. However, he is clearly a very unhappy and unsuccessful man. Happy successful people are in touch with their emotions, have a great support system, and engage in activities they truly enjoy. Toxic masculinity standards do not strengthen people, it puts them in shackles from reaching their own destiny.

As stated earlier, the early years of a kid's life is very important in how the gender roles are enforced subconsciously. In order for boys in society to adopt more healthy feminine behaviors, it will be beneficial to teach these early on. The example of gendered toys was used earlier, but the issue is much deeper rooted. We must teach young boys the importance of building emotional management skills. Boys need to know that it is healthy to express emotions, even if this means crying or “appearing weak”. It will also benefit children when they are taught to socialize with the other sex. Splitting up the sexes does more harm than good as it creates strange dynamics early on that are hard to break.

Next, we must teach children the importance and skills of building friendships. We learn how to treat others with respect as kids, but it rarely goes much deeper than this. Young boys must learn how to share emotions with friends and family, instead of being taught to toughen up, which just teaches people to keep emotions bottled up. This extra education would hopefully lead to male students building meaningful relationships with peers, where they can freely share their emotions.

These healthy relationships must carry into adolescence and adulthood for men. When school, careers, and social aspects get harder as we get older, the relationships become more important than ever. Healthy platonic relationships lead to healthier and happier men, who are more effective in society.

Finally, men must engage in activities and possibly careers that are mentally fulfilling to them. In a perfect world, finance and gender roles will have minimal influence on the decision someone makes. However, more realistically we can hope that men pick careers that are sustainable mentally. We want to shift the paradigm away from teaching men that they must run themselves into the ground in order to provide for the family. People must engage in more healthy lifestyles with balance, in order to be socially productive in society.

In conclusion, toxic masculinity creates many issues for men and the people around them in society. As many believe this is due to men being weak or too feminine, more femininity may actually be the key. Gender role conditioning begins at a very young age, so if we focus less on these roles, and more on mental/emotional health and social skills, we will raise more socially efficient people. Also, it will be beneficial to let kids explore interests they actually enjoy and are drawn too, rather than grouping activities by the sexes. This way, kids can try multiple things and get new perspectives on who they truly are. Moving into adolescence and adulthood, men must continue to build social and emotional skills. Many men struggle to share emotions and keep things bottled up until it is too late. Women seem to socialize and support one another far more often, so men should follow their lead. Finally, we must inspire men by getting them to see the value of doing things that are fulfilling to them as individuals. This will shift some stress away from men, leading to a happier overall society.
chunks.label: Fixing male social isolation and toxic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses modern dating challenges, career pressures, the negative influence of toxic masculinity, and how educating young boys on emotional and social skills can improve society.

n030c1874.title: Performing Roles in Life and Online

chunks.text: In today’s world, everything is seen through a screen and returns to the situation. With the rise of technology throughout the past few centuries, individuals have expressed the idea of putting on a show. This may be for a TV series, movie, social media, or YouTube. However, I think social media has had the most significant effect on individuals and the way that they act to express themselves in front of others. These individuals express themselves in a way that receives more likes and views. This idea goes hand-in-hand with Goffman’s concept of “The Presentation of Self.” This essentially states that individuals present themselves as on a “stage” performing to the world in different situations. Depending on the situation, a different need must be met. Everyone plays a part in collectively forming a situation. With so many different roles to fill, Charles Cooley’s idea of “The Looking Glass Self” shapes the way that individuals see themselves as a single living being through the eyes of others. This relates to the idea that individuals present themselves in a sense that fits the needs of other people. With society’s functioning on the line, everyone’s characters must line up to create a single, flawless symphony, which creates the life and world we know today.
chunks.label: Goffman and Cooley on presentation of self
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces social media and connects it to Goffman's presentation of self and Cooley's looking glass self.

chunks.text: For as long as I can remember, my mom has told me to understand and read my audience. Until about a year ago, I had absolutely zero clue as to what she meant deep down by saying it. It was when I began maturing when I really understood the deeper meaning behind this. I have a role to play, and depending on the situation, my role will vary. For instance, in a professional conversation at work, I must be attentive, clear, concise, and direct. Opposed to when I am hanging out with my friends, where I can act any way that I want, within boundaries. In terms of Goffman, I will present a part of me that is shown through my respected audience providing the character that best fits the situation. It is a simple idea, but in a social setting, it can really make the difference as to who I am looking to impress.
chunks.label: Mom's advice to read the audience
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on their mother's recurring advice to read the audience and discusses how roles vary across work and friends.

chunks.text: For instance, I want to undergo a profession in healthcare, and I thankfully live in an area where healthcare workers happen to also live. When I have spoken to, say, physicians, I must play my part as an intelligent, young individual looking to pursue a similar career as them. However, this is not where that ends. The physician I am speaking to must play the role of a provider, a lifesaver, and a respected individual without flaw.
chunks.label: Role playing when speaking to physicians
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the roles adopted when conversing with physicians in their neighborhood about pursuing healthcare.

chunks.text: Going back to the idea that social media has shaped our world into the way that people perceive information along with give it off, each person is given a role based on what they post about. For instance, models have the job of posting images that make them look good to support and to promote clothing companies. Opposed to me, where I post videos of me riding a scooter. No matter the content that an individual puts out in the world, the idea behind it is to be seen posing as someone that will attract views and likes. This goes into the idea of “The Looking Glass Self.” One quote stated by Cooley proposes the idea that “The thing that moves us to pride or shame is not the mere mechanical reflection of ourselves, but an imputed sentiment, the imagined effect of this reflection upon another’s mind” (Cooley). This really speaks towards a lot of the emotions that one possesses. The idea behind this is to provide a positive image of yourself in the eyes of the people around you. An individual will change the way they are to fit the social structure of a group of people to answer three questions. How will they appear to others? What will people think of them? Are they liked?
chunks.label: The looking glass self and social media
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how people present themselves on social media and Cooley's concept of the looking glass self.

chunks.text: Humans are defined as social creates, and embarrassment drives a lot of factors in our lives. One emotion that is portrayed through Goffman’s stage representation is embarrassment. Depending on the social situation, the embarrassment may come from anyone in a group of people. Goffman states that embarrassment occurs when an individual’s role has been discredited. This relates to the idea that each person in a situation is promoting the roles of every other person to collectively create a stage that flows well.
chunks.label: Goffman's concept of embarrassment
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Goffman's ideas about embarrassment occurring when a social role is discredited.

chunks.text: I particularly remember the day we showed up to class, and Dr. Elliott showed up without his notes. The role of the teacher had essentially been failed. The students in the room played the role as individuals ready to learn from the professor. All the roles were there, but the role of the professor was not played as intended. For this example, the class did not know what to do next as the situation was not played correctly. With one role having been played incorrectly, everyone felt embarrassed for the awkward interaction.
chunks.label: Professor arriving without notes
chunks.what_happened: Dr. Elliott showed up to class without his notes, leaving students unsure of what to do next because his role was not played as intended.

chunks.text: I have had multiple hobbies in my life, switching from scootering, to diving, and to, now, weightlifting. Therefore, the content that I post on social media has varied over the past few years. Every time I post something unlike the previous post, I feel off about posting it. Is this something I want my followers to see? Will I get the same amount of likes and view? Will I lose followers? All of these things are irrelevant, but to the importance society has placed on numerical values on social media, it means everything.
chunks.label: Posting changing hobbies on social media
chunks.what_happened: The student switched hobbies from scootering to diving to weightlifting and worried about audience reactions whenever posting new content.

chunks.text: Social media, however, influences the lives of individuals by posing as another audience to please. Cooley states “Each to each a looking-glass Reflects the other that doth pass” (Cooley). In terms, this reflects the idea that people look at others as a mirror as to who they are as a person. Each interaction possesses the ability to shape the way we view our role and beliefs in the world. This backs the idea that identity comes from within. Social media, in this sense, reflects the way we see ourselves. As we receive more views, likes, and positive comments, we understand that our roles are being fulfilled. Going along with Cooley’s quote, Goffman states that “the means for producing and maintaining selves do not reside inside the peg; in fact, these means are often bolted down in social establishments” (Goffman). With such an important idea behind producing and maintaining the self in a social establishment. In terms of preventing embarrassment, the stage is then broken up into two parts. The backstage along with the front stage. The backstage, according to Goffman, refers to the social places where people prepare to be on the front stage. The front stage is the production of a social situation, in which each person plays a point.
chunks.label: Social media, looking-glass self, and front/backstage
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes social media validation through Cooley's mirror concept and Goffman's front stage and backstage concepts.

chunks.text: Instagram and all these other means of social media have been a driving factor in the shaping of today’s society. Both Cooley’s idea of the “Looking Glass Self” and Goffman’s “Presentation of the Self” correlate to the way that individuals act in a social situation. In my opinion, the attitudes and representations in which people perform have changed significantly from life before technology. There are more social standards that must be followed along with the high need for reinforcement. The “Looking Glass Self” plays a part in all waking function human beings perform today. How will this affect me? Will I gain attraction? But, at the end of the day, all anyone is looking for is an applause for their performance.
chunks.label: Conclusion on social media and performance
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that social media shapes human performance, noting that people ultimately desire applause for their performance.

chunks.text:
Throughout time and as we develop our economy and as a society more and more as years go by, we have always faced an issue of inequality, specifically when it comes to issues that Harari mentions throughout 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, such as issues between the way the economy has been set up and the divide that it has caused throughout the socioeconomic classes that we have. Another issue Harari discusses that is causing inequality against the people through the internet and larger corporations.

As we are constantly electing new candidates into a seat in office, the divide between our socioeconomic classes is growing further and further apart from each other. The idea of a middle class is slowly fading away due to the rich getting richer and the poor getting poorer. As Harari puts it, “ Some groups increasingly monopolize the fruits of globalization, while billions are left behind.” This is caused by the rich employing and paying very little to the hard labor workers so while they are stuck in the bottom class, the rich corporation owners are making millions off of the underpaid laborers.

Another economic issue that we are facing that is causing inequality in the United States, and throughout the rest of the world is the problem between the privacy of consumers and corporations. Large corporations are taking private personal information from their consumers and using that information to be sold to other companies, specifically for marketing purposes. The problem with this is that companies preach that they are there for the people and that all of your information is safe with them. Have you ever noticed how you will look something up or be interested in buying something, and then shortly after you see advertisements and posts geared towards the product you are interested in? This is because of those companies selling your personal data and search history to other countries.

Harari discusses this with the example of Mark Zuckerburg when it comes to Facebook. He talks about how Mar Zuckerburg was focusing on using the information from people’s accounts and putting them into groups through Facebook based on their common interests. Although some people might like this, Facebook is still using the information you are putting into the private parts of your account and sending it out and grouping you with other people. What does not help this cause is that Zuckerburg and the Facebook brand already have a lack of trust from society due to information being stored in Facebook getting accessed by third-party companies to then manipulate elections. The other problem with this situation is that like Hariri states in 21 lessons for the 21st century, that we should not be using this form of technology to fix the issues that this country and world are facing socially.

As stated before, one main issue that causes a divide and inequality throughout the country and the rest of the world is the large class divide between the upper and lower classes. Harari says in his book how the top 1% own half of the world's entire wealth. He also shows how large this divide is by stating that the top 100 richest people combined have more money than four billion people of the entire population.

Marx had a similar look towards this issue as Harari when it comes to how capitalism is affecting the divide between the classes. Marx describes that the worker becomes all the poorer the more wealth that he gains, and the more his production increases in power and range. He discusses how the product of labor is labor which is congealed in an object making it become a material. He also discusses that with the conditions dealt with by political economy and this realization of labor appears as a loss of reality for the workers. Basically stating how the lower class works these very intense, high-demanding labor jobs for countless amounts of hours making the minimum amount. When he talks about the worker becoming poorer the more wealth that he gains he is talking about that divide because the more wealth and product being produced is all going towards the higher-ups in the company, allowing them to make a large amount of profit off of the underpaid laborers.

Both Marx and Harari are on the same page when it comes to their thoughts on the class divide due to the corrupt system we have between the corporations and laborers due to the capitalistic economy that we have established in the United States. It is almost like a never-ending cycle that is very unlikely for you to escape from due to the rarity in moving up classes. Most people will end up making a similar amount to their parents due to if the parents were in a lower social class, some might not be able to afford that college education for their children, making it a lot harder for them to escape the cycle that their parents have established for them.

Overall, there is a big issue that we face throughout the world when it comes to inequality particularly between the economy that we have established and the power that has been given to corporations and large company owners. Whether it is because of them making profits off of hard-working under paid laborers, or selling private information given to them by their consumers, it is causing a widespread issue between people and socioeconomic status. The other issue that we have due to these corporations is that it establishes almost a sandtrap for generations to come because you get stuck in a cycle of underpaid hard-working jobs due to the inability to afford your way into an upper-class.
chunks.label: Inequality, capitalism, and corporate power
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on economic inequality, class divide, and consumer data privacy by discussing ideas from Yuval Noah Harari and Karl Marx.

n1653ae32.title: Comparing Conceptions of the Social Self

chunks.text:
What constitutes the “self” within a person’s stream of consciousness has always been a debated topic among Sociologists for centuries. Some believe that the “self” is merely a way for the body to capture experiences and is merely constructed from two separate ideas. Others share the belief that the “self” is a part of something much greater and can be divided into several different parts which each specialize in one of three categories. Among these sociologists are William James and George Herbert Mead who both spent much of their lives organizing their views on the topic and although they have a fair amount of differences, their ideas on the self are still quite comparable. This comparison can be shown through Mead’s concept of experience and Jame’s concept of the “social self.”

George Herbert Mead is among the sociologists who define the self as working in balance with the body in a construct known as “mind-body duality.” This idea revolves around experiences and the way that an individual experience is interpreted and taken in by both the body and mind separately. An experience of the body is considered to be done directly because when the body is exposed to a stimulus it is able to directly capture the experience. An experience of the mind/self is considered to be done indirectly because when the self is exposed to a stimulus it is only able to experience it through the body, however, the self is able to reflect on the overall experience and think about it later. So although the body is able to feel things directly, the experience is incomplete and even though the mind is able to experience a stimulus completely, it is done indirectly through the body. This idea of the self displays Mead’s concept in how the self is merely an extension of the mind that helps us reflect on our outside environments in a more complete manner so that we can learn and grow from our experiences.

William James believed that the self is such a complicated construct that it must be divided into three separate parts: the material self, the social self, and the spiritual self. His rationale for this idea is that a human being can have so many materialistic and interpersonal connections throughout their life that it becomes hard to distinguish themselves from what they own. In summary the material self refers to a person’s property and body, the social self refers to how they are perceived and accepted by others, and the spiritual self is their emotions and inner thoughts. Although the material self and emotional self are both essential parts of James’ overall construct, the social self is the most relevant in terms of comparison to Mead’s ideas. In general the social self can be seen best through the differing personalities one expresses based on the environment they are in or who they are currently around. For example if someone is with a trusted partner or friend they know intimately then they will tend to be a bit more vulnerable and open. However, if they are among strangers they may be less open and therefore perceived as standoffish and quiet. Both examples showcase instances of the social self as well as how it is easily influenced and changed based on a stimulus or environment.

Although Mead’s and James’ opinions and explanations of the self differ greatly in definition and example I believe that their concepts are still comparable and coexist. This comparison can be displayed through Mead’s overall concept of experience through the mind and James’ concept of the “social self.” In Mead’s article The Self The I and The Me he states that “What determines the amount of the self that gets into communication is the social experience itself.” What Mead is trying to express in this quote is that the way we express ourselves based on our previous experiences and that whether we allow ourselves to come through fully or not depends on how comfortable we are at a given time/conversation. This concept is extremely comparable to James’ specific connotation of the “social self” with both ideas referring to how we express ourselves and are perceived by others based on experiences. “The amount of the self that gets into conversation…” can be viewed as the differing degrees of personality we express at any given time based on the conversation and comfortability.

So even though James and Mead have very differing definitions of the self and how it can be divided, both sociologists believe that the social aspects of the self can be influenced and displayed differently based on our interactions and experience. Mead states that our environment determines the amount of the self we express while James argues this expression is merely a third of the overall construct. Either way these similarities in ideas shows that although the two sociologists have differing ideas on the self, their concepts can still go along with and support the other if analyzed properly.
chunks.label: Comparing Mead and James on the self
chunks.what_happened: The student compares George Herbert Mead's concept of experience and mind-body duality with William James's concept of the social self.

chunks.text:
Max Weber’s The Spirit of Capitalism and the Iron Cage and Karl Marx’s Estranged Labor provide a thorough analysis of how capitalism came to be. In Weber’s piece we see how this contribution to capitalism can be linked back to religion specifically under the Protestant branch. Under the Protestant religion, a group of people called Calvinists believed that their fate was predetermined by whether or not they would go to heaven or hell after their death. Due to this belief, it was believed that if one was already saved, the monetary benefits and material success would reap throughout their lives as God’s way of showing who had been saved. Seeking profit was seen as virtuous because if you had been saved, God would provide you with the means to become wealthy. However, in Marx’s piece, we see the downside of capitalism in the working class. The working class has slowly become estranged from the work because they are not reaping the benefits and are now “abandoning” their work because they are not able to keep the profit they are creating. This environment between the workers and the property owners becomes hostile because they are not working to earn, they are working to distribute. Just like in Weber’s The Spirit of Capitalism, when profit was earned, workers believed they had been saved because of “Gods will” they are able to succeed therefore they were motivated to work. In Marx’s Estranged Labor, the workers feel alienated from their work because they are not succeeding, they are working for someone else and not achieving any personal gain.

Something I see in modern life to illustrate these arguments is college… The connection I made to Marx’s piece is many students do schoolwork 4-6 days a week and still receive low grades and harsh comments from professors even though they did the work. They are not seeing any benefit but instead a depletion in moral therefore becoming estranged from the work. Although, without doing the work in college (which collectively will benefit the economy with students that are ready to work) students will not be able to benefit the “whole” which is the economy by being able to go out and work. The connection that I can also make to college using Weber’s argument is the opposite of the argument I made for Marx’s. When students work 4-6 days a week and receive positive feedback and, in some cases, even praise for their work, students have a high moral and a replenished sense of confidence because they were praised by their “higher up”. Good work is rewarded with good feedback and I can speak personally for this effect, motivation peeks because of that lingering feeling of “profit” and the profit being a good grade and personal achievement.
chunks.label: Analyzing Weber and Marx regarding capitalism and college
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Max Weber's and Karl Marx's perspectives on capitalism and connects their ideas about reward, motivation, and alienation to college students' academic experiences.

chunks.text: My personal experience to illustrate this is very current. Earlier this semester I got feedback on a history essay that I worked on for 9 days. I worked so hard on this essay, day and night, I spent hours researching and find sources and going through my notes to ensure that I had references and evidence to support my claims. I felt so confident on this paper… I got the grade back and my professor literally failed my paper and suggested that I see someone at the writing center. Safe to say my morale was on the floor and was not going to be picked up anytime soon. I felt defeated and out of spite I didn’t attend my class for two weeks. It wasn’t until my professor reached out with concern that I attended the class again but the question that I can connect to Marx’s argument is ‘why should I attend the class when I was attending the class and asking for help on my assignments just to be failed and told to seek help on my writing?” Like the workers began to question why they should do the work if they were not going to be commissioned.
chunks.label: Failing a history essay and skipping class
chunks.what_happened: After spending nine days working hard on a history essay, the student received a failing grade and a recommendation to visit the writing center. In response, the student felt defeated and skipped the class for two weeks until the professor reached out with concern.
chunks.feelings: confident, morale was on the floor, defeated, spiteful

chunks.text: Now onto the more positive side of Weber’s argument, an example I have is also for this semester. I am very passionate about English because I want to pursue a career in writing/journalism (hence why I was so butthurt about my History Professors comment). On the first assignment I completed for my English class this semester, my professor reached out and asked if I was comfortable with her using my work as an example for her to show to the class and others in the English department. I felt starstruck because something I had done had been recognized, this can be connected by the benefits reaped in the Calvinists religion for being chosen by God and the benefits that were seen monetarily in the lives of those who had been “saved”.
chunks.label: Receiving praise on an English assignment
chunks.what_happened: The student completed an assignment for an English class, and the professor asked if she could use the student's work as an example to show the class and the English department.

chunks.text: The two arguments this week analyze the origin and understanding of capitalism through a positive and negative viewpoint. Capitalism can be referred to through many different lenses of how it is received or how it is not received. Those who see physical commission are more likely to strive for even more commission because their hard work is being seen. Those who do not see the physical recognition are less likely to strive for more because their work is not be accepted or commissioned. Capitalism is perceived differently by the different individuals in how they are being recognized for the work they are doing from the person “in charge” or overseeing them.
chunks.label: Summary of recognition and capitalism
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how people's motivation and perception of capitalism depend on whether their work is recognized and rewarded by those in charge.

nd8fb6c9c.title: Reflecting on K-Pop and Collective Consciousness

chunks.text: In my time in this class, we have talked about many cool concepts ranging from what a persons’ character is made up of to how evolution caused the human race to become more advanced. But the one concept that was most relevant to me was the one about the collective conscious and how that plays a role in society. The society I am interested in is the society where I come from, which is Korean. I remember enjoying many things from Korean society, but I wanted to focus on K-pop because artists in that profession face many societal issues that will help understand Korean society and how toxic it can be.
chunks.label: Introduction to collective consciousness in Korean society
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces concepts from class, specifically focusing on the collective consciousness and how it applies to toxicity in Korean society and K-pop.

chunks.text: I remember enjoying listening to K-pop when I was younger. There was this group at the time called BIGBANG that was making these huge hits that I loved. My family had this projector in our basement that I would always go down to watch BIGBANG with their flashy outfits and upbeat music. So, most K-pop groups have choreographed dances to go with the song, which was why it was so exciting to see a new song from that group. And I would turn on my favorite song, MONSTER and try to learn the dance in secret because I had so much fun doing so.
chunks.label: Watching BIGBANG and dancing in basement
chunks.what_happened: When younger, the student loved listening to K-pop and would go down to their family's basement to watch BIGBANG on a projector and secretly practice their choreography.

chunks.text:
But in 2015, the group had disbanded for some odd reason, and I always wondered what happened to them. Up until now, I saw online that the group members had been caught smoking weed and now their whole label, YG who also owns other K-pop groups is hated by the public from one mistake.

Basically, in Korea, smoking weed or doing any recreational drug is considered taboo and they ended up getting ten months because of it. Not only that, but the fanbase ended up turning on the group members by throwing horrible comments at them and it was bad enough to where one of the members attempted suicide. I thought the whole situation was very unforgiving along with being completely undeserved knowing how much fans loved the group before this incident and how they simply threw them away. To make things even worse, because of the war, men in South Korea are required to be in the army at least once in their lifetime. This meant that members of BIGBANG, including the one that attempted suicide are now unable to make music and need to serve their country. The whole situation is very unpleasant, but this drove me to find out why this was happening to them and hopefully try to explain it utilizing what was learned from sociology.

Korean culture can be viewed as toxic mainly because of how their society is based too much off the collective conscious. Going on with K-pop, if a specific idol, or member of a group does not meet a specific beauty standard. They are usually shamed with a sense of worthlessness for not appealing to the collective consciousness. A quick google search brought me to a site of K-pop idols who essentially “defy” Korean beauty standards and how they are treated by fans. I slowly realized that what happened to BIGBANG is not necessarily new and that other groups are often narrowly criticized for even smaller things. I want to emphasize the word toxic in my introduction to describe their society because these performers that are thought to be “ugly” are often ridiculed from mean comments on their videos to straight up death threats for something that artist cannot change. To anyone, it sounds disgusting to call out an artist who makes music to also expect these performers to be models and on top of that, know how to dance well. I think what is expected of these idols is extremely absurd and the Korean fanbase needs to tone it down at least a notch.

What I think is happening is that the collective conscious for Korea is very opinion-based and less individual compared to American values. It feels like the Korean collective conscious tells people to become absolute perfection and has little regard for that person’s quality of life if they are not meeting specific ideals. A slight slip up on what a person’s actions and that person is now deemed “unworthy” and that is a lot of what I am seeing. Going back to that perfectionism, it seems there is a big sense of worthlessness to an individual if they are not a hundred percent and that is shown with all the criticism these entertainers receive. I think this really demonstrates how powerful the collective conscious can be on a society. It is hard to receive good feedback from people in general and even more difficult from a tough crowd that has outrageous expectations. What I am saying is that these performers have little say into a society that has these certain values making it very tough for diversity to occur. It makes sense because a lot of Korean music sounds similar to each other and does not have many genres compared to American music. Most of K-pop consists of usually a group of three to twelve that pretty much produces only mainstream pop music, which proves my point.

Another thing that adds on to the toxicity, is the Korean beauty standard. It is a superficial aspect of their society that is based off that unrealistic perfection that was mentioned before. I felt this needed to be added was because of these absurd requirements that idols are criticized more often than they should. To put it briefly, for women, it is preferred they have a small face, big unproportioned eyes, and a very slim body with a particular weight of about a hundred-and-ten. And for men, they need smooth skin, good hair, have double eyelids, and appear androgyne. Both genders face difficulty and it causes that lack of individuality in their society when fixed attributes are preferred. From an American standpoint, this can seem unachievable because women have to be very thin no matter their height, and men are required to be a little more feminine-sided, which sounds like the opposite from how we see it. It is just very different from our society. On top of that, most Americans would not opt for plastic surgery as it can be extremely expensive and seen as something not needed. A bigger problem with their beauty standards is how far some people are willing to fit into the Korean collective consciousness with the help of plastic surgery. South Korea has the highest rate of plastic surgeries in the world and is also the best at it. Apparently, some estimates suggest that every one in three women in Korea get some sort of surgery, while some say at least fifty percent. Their most popular surgeries are the blepharoplasty, or double-eyelid surgery, rhinoplasties, or nose jobs, and glutathione injections, which slows pigmentation in the skin, giving a brighter tone. expensive and can come with negative side effects.

How does that tie in with Korean society? The whole beauty standard appears to be the root of the problem where people feel pressure to apply themselves to these characteristics. With the example of plastic surgery, clearly Korean women desire to look more beautiful as at least one in three opt to pay for facial surgery. Again, the collective conscious demonstrates how important people’s opinions are to the Korean individual and how surgery can completely change a viewpoint on a person solely based on their attractiveness. By doing so, an individual could possibly have higher social status among peers, get complimented more often, and most importantly, be part of the collective that everyone in that society thinks are positive. Once these social responses are discovered by the individual, it probably leads to a much happier and more welcoming lifestyle if many people accept these looks. On the contrary, say if you do not meet these requirements, then people will probably have some type of prejudice towards that person and perhaps even look down upon them. This is why I describe this society as toxic because not everyone is going to achieve these standards, which attributes to one of the reasons why Korea is one of the top ten countries for suicide.

After everything, how does sociology explain Korean society in how it can be characterized as toxic? I believe that the sociology concept of the collective conscious described by Durkheim allows us to dive deeper into the problem. It helps explain the tragedy of the group BIGBANG and how this scenario is not specific to this group, but a bigger problem of Korean standards along with beauty.
chunks.label: Analysis of BIGBANG's fallout, Korean beauty standards, and collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on BIGBANG's disbandment, drug scandal, public backlash, military service, and broadens the analysis to Korean beauty standards, plastic surgery, and Durkheim's collective consciousness.

chunks.text:
The Erosion of the Human Experience: Estranged Labor and McDonaldization

The innate nature of human beings has always been a prevalent topic discussed among sociologists for centuries with many focusing on the idea of how our environment itself may shape our relationships. Among these sociologists some believe that human beings are inherently social creatures with the capability of expressing cooperation and collective action, yet this is not something commonly seen within today's society. One man who researched this disconnect between our nature and our actions was Karl Marx with his famous writings on “estranged labor.” Much later in time another sociologist by the name of George Ritzer focused on a similar topic, named McDonaldization, which is more in tune with modern occurrences and examples. Although these separate ideas were built nearly a century apart, both McDonaldization and estranged labor come together in order to highlight the dehumanizing effects of capitalist production as well as the loss of autonomy that comes with it.
chunks.label: Introduction to estranged labor and McDonaldization
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces sociological perspectives on human nature and connects Karl Marx's concept of estranged labor with George Ritzer's theory of McDonaldization.

chunks.text: According to Karl Marx, human beings are incredibly unique creatures due to their capacity to interact and produce labor both creatively and socially. He argues that this production of labor is exactly what helped individuals develop their identities and later shape society. However, Marx states that in capitalist societies, workers become disconnected from the products of their labor, from the process of labor itself, and from their own humanity. This separation is referred to as “estranged labor” or “alienated labor.” This estrangement occurs because workers do not have control over what they produce, how they produce it, or the conditions under which they work. Instead, they are often reduced to mere cogs in a machine, performing repetitive tasks without any sense of fulfillment or connection to their work. Overall, work under capitalism subverts Marx’s view on human nature because it alienates individuals from each other which enforces a rigid division of labor with the entire process undermining the intrinsic satisfaction of work and limits individual potential.
chunks.label: Marx's theory of estranged labor
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Karl Marx's ideas regarding human labor and how capitalism alienates workers from their labor, products, and humanity.

chunks.text: Ritzer's idea of "McDonaldization" builds on Marx's concept of alienation but applies it specifically to the context of fast-food restaurants, particularly McDonald's. McDonaldization refers to the process by which principles of fast food, such as efficiency, calculability, predictability, and control are prioritized through automation. However, Ritzer also argues that these key aspects of McDonaldization are increasingly dominating various aspects of society beyond the realm of food service and beginning to seep into other foundations such as retail chains, education facilities, and even social media. This growing concept is referred to as rationalization which describes the transformation of social and economic life from traditional and value driven systems to those based on efficiency, calculation, and control.
chunks.label: Ritzer's concept of McDonaldization
chunks.what_happened: The student explains George Ritzer's concept of McDonaldization and how principles of efficiency and control spread across various institutions through rationalization.

chunks.text: The connection between Marx's concept of estranged labor and Ritzer's theory of McDonaldization is rooted in their shared emphasis on the dehumanizing consequences within the capitalist system of production and consumption. Both feature individuals, whether as workers or consumers, being stripped of their intrinsic humanity and reduced to mere components within a larger mechanized apparatus. Instead, they become mere instruments in the pursuit of profit, engaged in repetitive tasks that divorce them from any genuine connection to the products they create or the process of labor itself. Similarly, Ritzer's idea of McDonaldization extends this dehumanization to the realm of consumption, particularly within the fast-food industry but also across broader domains. The overall focus on efficiency underlines the systematic detraction of agency as well as the commodification of human existence.
chunks.label: Connecting estranged labor and McDonaldization
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses the shared dehumanizing effects of estranged labor and McDonaldization on workers and consumers within capitalist systems.

chunks.text: In conclusion, while theories have varied, one consistent theme on the evolution of human nature is the tension between the potential for cooperation inherent in human beings and the realities of societal structures that often inhibit such tendencies. Karl Marx's concept of estranged labor sheds light on how capitalist modes of production alienate individuals from the fruits of their labor, leading to a loss of autonomy and a sense of disconnection from their work and fellow human beings. This notion, rooted in Marx's analysis of capitalism, resonates with George Ritzer's theory of McDonaldization, which highlights how the principles of efficiency and predictability in fast-food culture have permeated various aspects of contemporary society, further eroding human agency and individuality.
chunks.label: Conclusion on alienation and McDonaldization
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by summarizing how capitalism and McDonaldization inhibit human potential and erode agency.

n9824b698.title: Evolution of Language and Early Religion

chunks.text:
In the essay, “Microfoundations,” the writer points out that ritual burial began happening some point after the 50,000-45,000 years ago mark as evidenced by the Sungir site in Russia that dates a ritual burial that occurred 28,000 years ago for two young people and a 60-year-old male. The significance of this is the evidence of large groups working together for the complex ornamentation of the bodies, each with 3,000 ivory beads that appeared to have taken over an hour to make one single bead, and large mammoth tusks that were boiled to be straightened out on either side of all the bodies. The complex ornamentation and ritual burial then also point to the concept of religion at this time, which is something is not evidenced before the 50,000-year mark for early humans. This essay points to language perhaps being the catalyst for Humans creating the first early animist religions. As in both essays they cite religion as a type of refuge for social beings and in, “The Neurology of Religion,” it is seen that religion is responsible for the organizing of rituals, burials in the case of the last essay, within a community. Which to carry out such complicated, coordinated efforts, it is likely that language would have had to come first to create a religion to become a collective for either tribes or groups of early Humans to rally behind so as to become a part of it.

Prior to 50,000 years ago humans did not have a capacity for complex speech that modern humans had that kept them in the same playing field as Neanderthals and other Hominids. But when the capacity was gained for complex speech, a rise in early Humans’ abilities to form animist religions sparked the beginning of the complex collective consciousnesses that would eventually make up modern human civilization and put Humans ahead of other Hominids.
chunks.label: Language, ritual burials, and early religion
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological readings regarding early human ritual burials, explaining how the development of complex language likely catalyzed animist religions and social coordination.
