nc7046132.title: Challenging Generational Views on Service Workers

chunks.text:
How Technology Controls the Collective Consciousness of Gen Z Today

What seems to be the general consensus among people above the age of at least forty-five everywhere is that “Kids spend too much time on their phones. Everything that goes wrong is the doing of this new-fangled technology.” When discussing the collective consciousness of today, the inclusion and analysis of social media, the Internet, and technology must be included. If enough people come together to share a piece of land, and breathe the same air, as well as all following similar or the same rules, beliefs, and ideas, that counts as a society. Hence, the collective consciousness of one people. Social Media has done this to Gen Z by the rise of technology, and luckily we are breaking cycles through the use of Social Media as an advantage to our Collective Consciousness.

The acronym I.D.E.A by Nathaniel Turner from TED x Hobart High School can help us understand. Impatient. We have the ocean of the world at our fingertips, any information in the world in less than 0.5 milliseconds. We are “Addicts of instant gratification.”

Distracted by all the things we feel that we have to do because no one else will. Global Warming, Race and Gender discrimination, no job or home security. Where does one even start?

Entitled to our inalienable rights as people, the self evident truths given to us by the declaration of independence, which many older generations seem to think we don’t deserve.

Apathetic because of our lack of education on physical and mental health, as well as the rise in anxiety, depression, and other mental health issues and disabilities. Anxiety is on the rise, because of our levels of dopamine being triggered by likes and follows constantly. This generation began to rely on a consistent stream of posts, videos, likes, followers, and any other kind of digital and social media.

As the most suicidal generation in history we joke about EVERYTHING. School shootings, depression, and death. In our generation, depression has also been romanticized. Shows like 13 Reasons Why unfortunately, are a big contributor to that. A lot of the music that is produced now can be found discussing depression, the daily school shootings in our classrooms, the suicidal thoughts and feelings of a whole entire generation. Jon Bellion’s “Morning in America” for example, discusses how the expectations of parents are too heavy, and we try to keep up with all the “great expectations, so I keep on faking. We’re secretly out of control, and everyone knows.” But, no one, at least not the parents, teachers, or counselors tend to do anything about it. The term “depression” is used very loosely, and that results in dangerous thoughts and ideas for this generation. We maladaptive daydream, and question the government and take things into our own hands. Around more than half our life, we have not been seen or treated as our own human beings by the adults around us. Parents, teachers, the older people around us often refuse to see things the way that Generation Z does.

It’s all about connections. As Gary Vee, a popular TikToker and Inspirational Speaker says, “You may not like the way they’re communicating, but they’re more social than we’ve ever seen them.” The tools we have access to, allow us to make these issues mainstream and bring much more awareness. Those who did not grow up with the same experience however, cannot understand and place the blame on the thing they despise, rather than looking at their own actions. Technology is now just a huge plethora of opinions and beliefs and because you don’t need to be a published author to share your ideas anymore the media‘s role as the gatekeeper of truth is gone. Anyone can share anything on the Internet regardless of its accuracy or truthfulness. Lies in fact do have a tendency to spread faster than truth does especially on the Internet. False claims are over 70% more likely to be shared on Twitter than true claims. Over 2/3 of adults receive at least part of their news on social media and of the demographic under half specified Facebook as a “reliable” source. Known as Confirmation Bias, it elicits tendencies of users to select information adhering to their own system of beliefs, using an algorithm of the user instead of stating proof and facts. The groups of like minded people whose view is already polarized because the only information they know is that which proves are already conceived notions. The revolution of social media has both helped and destroyed our way of social activity in different ways. Being the most obese country in the world could partially be due to the fact that most people would prefer to stay inside on their devices instead of get out and move around.

Bo Burnham said it best when he said that it was “a bad idea to allow giant media corporations to exploit the neuro-chemical drama of children in America.” (Bo Burnham, Inside Netflix)

Ever since middle school for most kids my age, and even now from the age of two years old, technology is the only thing that exists and is constant around us nowadays. When sharing everything online, every little detail of life, what you choose to show and what you choose not to show to the world all affects the emotional and mental space in people's minds today. it takes form in movements, trends, and even fashion. From the Black Lives Matter movement, to the Backyardigans trend on Tik Tok, even to what kinds of jeans and shoes are popular. The proof of the collective consciousness comes from this constant peer pressure.

And then there is time to bring in moral absolutes, thoughts and ideas, and the decision of who will be in power. Typically in the past everything has been controlled by Old, White, Cisgendered men. Nowadays though, the younger generations are beginning to question that authority, as they are right to do so. With the mixed ideas of race, gender, and much any quality not only in the workplace but also throughout life, whether it be in a grocery store, dealing with the law and the police, or even just places like restaurants or the service industry, people are no longer seeing people that are differently than them as people.
chunks.label: Technology and Gen Z's collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how technology, social media, and instant gratification shape Gen Z's collective consciousness, mental health, and social awareness compared to older generations.

chunks.text: For example, my father tends to look down on employees who work at restaurants such as McDonald’s or Taco Bell. He has always accused me of becoming like one of those types of people. This past weekend during fall break I brought it up to him that he seems to treat those people as lesser than, as if they are not people with their own lives and problems. He seemed taken aback by this, which I thought was good to point out.
chunks.label: Confronting father about service workers
chunks.what_happened: During fall break, the student confronted their father about his habit of looking down on fast food workers and treating them as lesser people.

chunks.text:
It is so completely normal to ridicule those that are different from us and those who divert from the social norms. The collective Consciousness of Gen Z works through Social Media to change that.

Luckily with the addition of technology and fast spreading information, this is quickly changing. Information and ideas can be spread faster than ever now thanks to social media sites like TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat, and even Facebook. One or two videos that may talk about something such as spiritual deconstruction, capitalism, or even ADHD can be seen by over 5 million people within the span of one day. Another example includes Noodle the pug, the pug with bones or no bones. It has become a game among the TikTok community, as if it is some form of card reading or prediction telling us how our day will go depending on if Noodle the pug has bones. As I write this, it makes me laugh, what a ridiculous thing to think. But so many people that have seen those videos will completely understand the joke and agree. Opinions are another thing that can both spread quicker than wildfire fire, and quickly deter the thoughts, opinions or ideas of many young people today. Spiritual deconstruction is a large conversation amongst the TikTok community, and all it takes is one comment or one share of that video and everyone in your life feels about it.

Even the way the different generations get their news has changed. My parents still read newspapers and watch Fox News. All of my friends and I get our news mainly from Twitter, TikTok, and Instagram. Another difference between my parents' generation and mine is that my generation tends to listen to, appreciate, and even accept that everyone has different points of view. Media literacy….It comes down to deciding which information is valuable, and valid, and safe to rely on. With hundreds of thousands of different opinions, ideas, thoughts, and information flying at you at all times, it takes serious work and time in order to decipher what the truth is.

Even our consumption of media, from movies, to musicals, to books and movies now contains these ideas. The recent My Little Pony movie even has come up with commentary on communism, racism, and even gender, now including the first ever male main character in a My Little Pony series. Cartoons such as Steven Universe, The Owl House, as well as She-Ra are breaking homophobic and gender stereotypes left and right, with multiple LGBTQ and non-binary characters, with large emphasis on representation. The world is changing fast, and the audience, or at least half of it prefers to change right along with it.

ne85a5d90.title: Performing Nonbinary Identity in a Binary World

chunks.text: Humans by nature are binary thinkers, we like having a box or category to fall into; black or white, gay or straight, rich and poor, etc. However, when the subject of gender identity comes up, the mold isn’t always so clear. Even the “strict” definitions of sex have some flexibility, while it may seem obvious to have the binary categories of male and female be applicable, where does that leave intersex people with ambiguous genitalia? Furthermore, what does this strict binary mode of thought mean for people who fall outside of the binary of the categories of man or woman? Based off my lived experience as a nonbinary-identifying individual, paired with my studying of sociological writings about gender, I conclude that even in today’s progressive western society, it is nearly impossible to perform a gender identity outside of the binary given the unspoken “rules” of how gender is performed.
chunks.label: Binary thinking and performing gender outside the binary
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces how humans think in binaries, how this affects sex and gender, and poses their thesis that performing a gender identity outside the binary is nearly impossible.

chunks.text: Despite always having a sense of confusion regarding my gender identity, I don’t believe I heard the term “nonbinary” until I was around fifteen years old when the famous pop singers Sam Smith and Demi Lovato came out as nonbinary to the public. Despite my young age and lack of knowledge about the world, I still considered myself to be a fairly progressive individual, but I knew that I really had no grasp on what this term meant. All I knew was that some people had the preference to be referred to by a set of gender-neutral pronouns and names, but I didn’t understand why, or how this worked. I couldn’t figure it out at the time, but the feelings I had about my gender were persistent, I felt too masculine to fit into what I thought was the standard female mold, but I didn’t feel like I was anything close to being a man either. It wasn’t until I was eighteen and a freshman in college that the label of “nonbinary” started to resonate with me, and at the time it made sense. I didn’t feel as though I could force myself into either category of male or female, so identifying as something outside of these strict categories felt the most comfortable and liberating for me. However, these feelings were short-lived, as it didn’t take long for me to start realizing a troubling pattern was forming, and it caused me to question the foundations of my beliefs about sex and gender.
chunks.label: Realizing and adopting the nonbinary label
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up confused about their gender identity, first heard the term nonbinary around age fifteen, and eventually found that identifying as nonbinary resonated with them during their freshman year of college.

chunks.text: When I first started identifying publicly as nonbinary at nineteen, I assumed rather naively that the transition would be an easy one. I informed my social circle of my new pronouns and changed nothing else about myself. It was at this point that I started to realize just how few people understood the label of nonbinary, the same way that I didn’t understand what it meant just a few years prior. I was never maliciously misgendered by anyone, so I wasn’t too hurt when people would still refer to me as a woman, but deep down I started to feel a mounting internal pressure to change aspects of myself to fit what I thought would be the ideal image of androgyny, to be “successfully” nonbinary, and I became obsessed with this concept. I started dressing more masculine on purpose, even if it made me uncomfortable, shortened my name to something I thought to be more gender-neutral, and I cut my hair short. Much to my dismay this decision proved to be a counterintuitive overcorrection, as people began to perceive my masculine gender display to be congruous with male-identification. I backpedaled and regressed to a more feminine fit; I dressed the same and kept my name, but I started wearing more makeup and growing my hair out, and it had the opposite effect. Once again people assumed that the more feminine display, despite my attempts at keeping some aspects of androgyny, must have meant I identified as a woman. I felt more than a little disheartened at this, but I was truly more curious than offended. How were people not perceiving me as a nonbinary individual? Was it a failing on my part, or was society to blame? I turned to West and Zimmerman’s article “Doing Gender” for the answers for these questions and drew an interesting conclusion.
chunks.label: Navigating gender presentation and being misgendered
chunks.what_happened: The student publicly identified as nonbinary at nineteen, informed their friends, and altered their appearance between masculine and feminine styles to achieve androgyny, but found that people consistently perceived them as either male or female.
chunks.feelings: internal pressure, obsessed, uncomfortable, dismay, disheartened, curious

chunks.text:
Professors at the University of California Santa Cruz and Santa Barbara respectively, Candace West and Don. H. Zimmerman co-wrote the article “Doing Gender” to explain the sociological concept of the same name. Essentially, the concept of “doing gender” consists of the daily social interactions and behaviors that constitute one’s gender expression. While the original purpose of this article was to explain how the process of performing gender is an ongoing accomplishment and it generates “further means to create and maintain differences between women and men,” I feel this same concept can be applied to the puzzle of performing genders outside of the binary and how the corresponding gender displays are so frequently misconstrued (West & Zimmerman, 138). According to their article, one’s sex and gender identity are connected in a way that is composed of three main parts. The first, sex, is made up of the biological differences and is socially designated at birth. The second part, sex category, is the theoretical bridge connecting sex and gender; your sex category is the sex that you claim through external identifiers such as clothing, hair, and makeup. The third and final component is gender, which is comprised of the “routinely fashioned” social expectations of how one should act according to their sex and sex category (West & Zimmerman, 128). It is through the process of “Doing Gender” that the behaviors one performs either align with their sex and sex category, or clash and cause social confusion.

In my case, I believe West and Zimmerman would explain my dilemma as having to do with the growing gap of differences between men and women as well as the overcompensation that gender non-conforming people must perform in order to convey a gender display that matches their sex category. In the instance of their analysis of Garfinkel’s study of the transgender teenage girl Agnes, they found that Agnes claimed to be “120 percent female” with her having to study the other women in her social circles in order to learn how to “pass,” or have her gender display match the sex category she was laying claim to (West & Zimmerman, 134). In the example of my three displays, I was either “doing gender” too much or too little on the masculine and feminine sides, which resulted in other people misreading my displays. By cutting my hair short and dressing differently, I was performing too masculine of a gender, but by wearing makeup and having long hair I was performing the feminine equivalent, which made it appear that the sex category I was laying claim to matched my sex assigned at birth. However, it wasn’t entirely my fault that this happened, as another possible explanation comes from West and Zimmerman’s claim that the ongoing performance of gender and its subsequent roles results in the creation of differences between men and women. As these gaps between male and female gender continue to grow, trying to perform a gender display outside these two categories becomes increasingly difficult, as these perceived differences perpetuate and validate the strict binary of gender, making it nearly impossible to perform a gender outside of this binary without having it misread by one’s peers.

Based on my experiences with having my gender being mislabeled despite my multiple attempts at displaying an androgynous gender identity, along with West and Zimmerman’s possible explanations that the sociological concept of “doing gender” offered as to why this was happening, I can derive from my experiences and readings that in a society where a strict gender binary is enforced by the performance of gender roles and the “gendering” of objects such as clothing, makeup, and haircuts; that it isn’t truly possible to perform a gender outside of the set parameters of what defines a man or woman. It isn’t in the nature of our collective conscious to understand that a number of options could exist besides strictly male and female. The only way I could see a reformation of this strict viewpoint is through a collective effort in deconstructing the binary by a conscious effort of our society to not reenact and further perpetuate gender roles, opening the way for multiple identities to be valid options of gender displays.
chunks.label: Analyzing gender performance through Doing Gender theory
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes their experiences using West and Zimmerman's sociological concepts from 'Doing Gender', examining Agnes's case study, how androgynous displays are misread, and concludes that society must dismantle binary gender roles.
chunks.people: Candace West, Don H. Zimmerman, Harold Garfinkel, Agnes

n12714408.title: Debunking the American Classless Society Myth

chunks.text:
The current established belief in America is that if there were classes, the middle class, or the people of America, hold the power of the economy, the government and have equal access to all opportunities. This is a belief that the majority holds more power than the minority, the top 1% of Americans, in all aspects of life. This however, as both Mantsios and Domhoff have written extensively about, is not the reality of our world. As both writers in their articles, “Class in America,” and “Domination Theory of Power,” respectively, debunk and connect data to reveal that wealth and opportunity distribution is not equal among the social classes. Mantsios debunks this myth by going over several different “cases” of middle-class Americans that each make vastly different amounts of money but would consider themselves “middle class.” The most striking difference is the difference in opportunities for success and wealth given to the man that made 300k a year and came from a wealthy family vs that of the opportunities given to the man that came from a family that made more than 50% of Americans, and the opportunities that a black woman from just above the poverty line had. The richest man had several properties and went to prestigious private schools where he grew up with the sons and daughters of prominent figures and made it into an Ivy League school and managed to end up an executive at a corporation in New York City. While the other two that went to public school in the less well off parts of New York City never had access to the tutoring and job opportunities that the well off man had. Proving that the true upper class of society, the 1%, is able to maintain their position over the majority of American people via the opportunities they are provided in their lives. While in “Domination Theory of Power,” Domhoff continues to prove this point on the monopoly of opportunities by showing how many people in the top 1% of society are a part of the same clubs, organizations, and send their children in the same school so the wealthy stick with the wealthy in terms of education and social spheres. Further showing how difficult it is to break into that class from the outside looking in, especially when both writers reveal that this system is supported not by a third of the country’s wealth, like what might be expected of the 1% to own, but of almost 40% of America’s wealth is held by the upper class of American society proving that the power does not belong with the majority, but with the minority in terms of wealth and opportunities.

The United States holds a shared belief perpetuated in our collective consciousness that we live in a classless, equal, society where power is held by the majority middle class. This, is far from the truth as both opportunities for education and careers and the distribution of wealth is skewed greatly towards the 1% of America that truly hold the power.
chunks.label: Debunking the myth of middle-class power
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses readings by Mantsios and Domhoff to explain that wealth, opportunity, and power are concentrated in the top 1% rather than held equally by the middle class.

nb1051bbf.title: Growing Up Under Unrealistic Beauty Standards

chunks.text: Societal pressures and unrealistic beauty standards take a toll on women’s lives from the day that they are born. We have watched the beauty standards shift and change throughout time for centuries, but the one thing that never changes is the feelings women go through every day as they strive to live up to those impossible standards. The invention of cell phones and social media has turned beauty standards into a whole different kind of monster. The Beauty Myth by Naomi Wolf is a book about how beauty standards came to be and how they have been perpetuated over time. The beauty myth is a concept that says women become obsessed with their physical appearance and how they are perceived. This myth says that the only way you can matter or be a woman of substance in any way is to be beautiful in the eyes of society and it is what causes so many women to develop eating disorders and many other damaging daily habits.
chunks.label: Introduction to beauty standards and Naomi Wolf's book
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces how societal beauty standards and social media impact women, referencing Naomi Wolf's book 'The Beauty Myth'.

chunks.text: I was born in 2003 and I was able to see how social media morphed into what it is now, in 2022. Everything that I can remember from when I was young includes some sort of technology or social media surrounding me. I remember being in elementary school and feeling so stressed and upset because I looked different from the popular girls.
chunks.label: Childhood insecurity compared to popular girls
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up surrounded by technology and social media, and remembers feeling stressed and upset in elementary school because they looked different from the popular girls.

chunks.text:
I can guarantee you that every woman can remember a specific age or time period in their childhood where things changed. They most likely started with comparing themselves to other girls at school and things like that or wanting to act or look different to impress boys. As women get older it only gets worse and worse because you know and have more things to worry about that include the beauty standards that only increase as you become a teenager or adult.

There are many things that the beauty myth entails but one obvious example is that women’s value is based off their appearance. In turn when men are able to say that they have a beautiful woman they are seen as successful. Society has always told women from an extremely young age that their life goal should be finding a man to love them and to remain beautiful. Women are constantly striving to catch up to the unrealistic beauty standards of our society, but when they finally reach those standards, if they even do, the standards have shifted or changed. This cycle is what Naomi Wolf dissects and explains throughout her book.

Women and girls have the idea that beauty and looks should be the most important thing engrained into them from birth. In my personal experience social media has dramatically increased the amount of influence that young girls and women feel to look and be a certain way. Influencers and celebrities are the people that everyone looks up to and people strive to be like them. But when these people are perpetuating fake looks weather it is plastic surgery or simply editing their photos, it becomes a huge issue. If regular women and girls just like me grow up being taught and shown that women are supposed to look like that, they will constantly be striving for an appearance that is utterly impossible.
chunks.label: Societal expectations, male validation, and social media
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how childhood comparisons escalate with age, explaining how women's value is tied to appearance, male approval, and unrealistic social media standards.

chunks.text: Almost every one of my female friends and even some males have said they deal with some sort of eating disorder or body dysmorphia.
chunks.label: Friends disclosing eating disorders and body dysmorphia
chunks.what_happened: Almost all of the student's female friends and some male friends told the student that they deal with an eating disorder or body dysmorphia.

chunks.text:
Body dysmorphia is a serious condition that so many people have without even realizing it. People with body dysmorphia see themselves completely different than they really look. It is usually displayed by people viewing themselves as weighing a lot more than that really do. But it can also come across as seeing your face in a completely different way than others do. When people become so hyper fixated on the way they look you cannot blame them for blurring the lines. Unrealistic beauty standards support and perpetuate this hyper fixation on being the skinniest and the prettiest that you can be according to what that looks like to society at the time being.

Another way that the beauty myth has affected modern day beauty standards is by perpetuating the idea that women should always submit to the eyes of the male gaze. Acting and looking appealing for the male gaze is something that so many girls experience from such a young age because it is what they are taught.
chunks.label: Reflections on body dysmorphia and male gaze
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses the nature of body dysmorphia and how unrealistic beauty standards and socialization direct young girls to cater to the male gaze.

chunks.text: I can remember how girls as young as elementary school age used to change themselves completely, weather it was their personality or looks all for a boy.
chunks.label: Observing elementary school girls altering themselves
chunks.what_happened: The student remembers seeing girls in elementary school change their looks or personalities completely for a boy.

chunks.text:
This kind of ideology follows women as they get older. When women dress for the male gaze it is often come across as being more revealing clothes. But as we get older men only seem to desire women with less and less clothes. But when women follow this standard of less and less clothes and they for example say no to a man, they are showered with hateful words and in some cases even violence. Women are told that they were asking for it after they have been assaulted because what they were wearing was “too revealing”. But if the woman was wearing more clothes they would be seen as undesirable and a prude. There are so many other examples and ways that you could go with this analogy, and you can obviously see that it is a horrible cycle of confusion and hurt for women.

The beauty myth has affected modern day society in many ways including perpetuating things like unrealistic beauty standards, eating disorders, body dysmorphia, and many others. The beauty myth is the idea that women should live for their looks and that their value is based on how well they fit into the perfect standard of beauty that society has in mind at that moment. It is obvious that it is completely impossible for women to keep up with all of these things, because they are changing every single day. It is so harmful to young girls and women to focus on and base their worth on how society perceives them. Social media influencers and celebrities have brought so much more negativity and even more unrealistic standards into women’s lives. Young girls and women are fed these images of fake beauty and told that they should try their best to be just like them. Women are also told that their purpose in life should be to find a man willing to love them and if they cannot they should do everything they can to appeal better to men. We are told that is it our fault if men do not want us or even if they do want us, but we say no. Men are told they can take what they want from women no matter what the women have to say about it and women are often blamed because of things like the way that they looked when it happened. Overall, the unrealistic beauty standards that girls and women face every day have been out of control for long enough and they are only getting more out of control. Something needs to be done because the beauty myth has taken such a toll on women for so long. As I said before it is so detrimental to women’s both physical and mental health. There is no reason why women should base their own value and worth on the way that they look alone. We need to change the way that everyone sees beauty as a whole society.
chunks.label: Double standards, victim blaming, and concluding thoughts
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the damaging double standards regarding women's clothing, victim blaming in sexual assault, and concludes that society must urgently change its definition of beauty.

n59b46638.title: Performing Character and Freezing After Concert

chunks.text:
The Sociological Concept of “The Stage” and How it is used to Demonstrate The Presentation of Self

Why do we act the way we do in social situations and how can the presentation of self be illustrated? “The Stage'' is an analogy presented by the Sociologist Erving Goffman, as a means to demonstrate the presentation of self. Life is just one big series of performances. Through this concept, the presentation of self becomes as simplistic as understanding the different components of theatre. In essence, the way any one person acts is based on what they believe their audience wants to see from them. It is essential for everyone to keep their “character” intact through each and every performance, and for them to assist others in their performances. For these reasons, “The Stage” is a very straightforward way to illustrate the presentation of self. We act the way we do because we are the performers on stage, and we must do what we believe the audience wants us to do given our character and the props available to us. Understanding why we do what we do is the first step in improving the way social interactions are carried out, and result in the formation of new interpersonal relationships. Through this concept we can gain understanding in how identity is self made and interaction based.

The goal of the performer is to please their audience and stay in character while on stage.

Whether it is genuine or not, it is the performers duty to give their audience a specific impression. In my case, I strive to give others the impression that I am a caring person who can and will be there for almost anyone. Although this is a pretty conscious effort that I make through social interactions, I feel that it is a facet of my true self. I genuinely care for others and want to give anyone a shoulder to lean on, just as I would hope others would do for me. However, for some people keeping up their character involves less than authentic interactions. There are times when it can be apparent to others that their reasoning is not genuine. For myself and many others, detecting such actions has become almost second nature- although some people are better at hiding their true intentions than others. This skill is very useful when distinguishing genuine actions from ingenuine actions, thus preventing negative outcomes from social interactions. It is especially useful when making interpersonal and/or romantic relationships.

Many social interactions are ridden with embarrassment, misunderstanding, and unnecessary aggressions because we do not understand why we ourselves and others do and say what they do. So, if this inability to understand other reasoning for their actions is eliminated from the equation, we are left with viable social interactions that result in the understanding of one another and the formation of relationships. For example, embarrassment occurs when someone strays from the contents of their “character”. According to Goffman it is our duty to assist others in keeping their character intact, and that embarrassment feels awkward for all involved. Knowing why embarrassment occurs will allow us to assist others and ourselves with staying in character, and commending the emergence of our true selves when someone becomes embarrassed in social interactions. Because acting on the stage is an effort which is made through any and every social interaction, it can become tiring. Although it can and is an unnoticed human practice by many, it still requires mental effort, and therefore it will be mentally tiring. The solution to this is as simple as assisting and comforting others while socially interacting. By helping others avoid embarrassment or misunderstandings, you help yourself avoid such occurrences too. I myself make efforts to comfort others when they feel embarrassed, or are involved in some sort of misunderstanding. Even if I do not consider myself a friend of that person, I believe that it is possible to relate myself to almost anyone, and find the compassion to help them in a time of need. How can I better understand this person's actions? How can I put myself in their shoes? By asking these questions and interacting we can better understand others' reasoning behind their actions which leads to less embarrassment and misunderstandings. According to Goffman, it is our duty to assist others in their performances, and it is important that all performers are able to recognize the types of roles that each performer is trying to achieve.

Identity is self made and interaction based. According to Goffman, it is the coalition of all performances made by the performer, even performances that stray from their character. It is proven that the way people act “front stage” or present in a collectively produced social situation, contrats from the way they act “backstage” or not present in a collectively produced social situation. Identity is also the outcome of the props a performer has available to them, or the circumstances that they perform under. For example, if someone’s character consists of being generous with all they have, and being a supporter and a provider for others, but they’re financials are lacking, they may not be able to perform as consistently with their character as they or others believe they should. It is also heavily influenced by societal expectations and the collective consciousness. What does society expect from someone who plays their role? What are more specific expectations for their character? These expectations are derived from the collective consciousness. An example of this is the role of the Mother. It is widely thought that Mothers are the caretakers and the nurturers. Society expects Mothers to play this role at all times. Although a Mothers character involves much more specific qualities than these qualities alone, straying from this role is seen as immoral. Identity is the formulation of one's actions when performing and the expectations placed upon them which they are expected to adhere to when performing.

In my opinion, “The Stage '' is the best way to illustrate the presentation of self. This analogy is a good means to visualize the roles we take on in various social situations. There have been multiple occasions where I have questioned my own, and others actions in a specific situation, and this concept has allowed me to gain understanding of these actions.
chunks.label: The stage concept and presentation of self
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Erving Goffman's concept of the stage, discussing how identity, performance, embarrassment, and social roles function in interpersonal interactions.

chunks.text: For example, I attended a concert recently and when it came to an end my boyfriend and I walked outside to wait for our ride. I walked over to the band’s bus to see them while my boyfriend looked for our ride. As soon as I left his presence an intoxicated man with a bottle of liquor in hand approached me in a way that made me very uncomfortable. He attempted to convince me to come with him and made comments about my appearance. He did not seem to notice my discomfort through the interaction. Instead of doing what I should have done, I froze. I didn’t become combative when he made inappropriate comments, I simply tried to end the conversation and walk away but the man blocked me from leaving. I eventually managed to get away, but I felt as though I hadn’t acted in the way I should have. Normally, I would have tried to be very stern and get away quickly from the interaction, but at times when I am on my own- I do not have the will to carry myself out of such dangerous situations. I felt a sort of embarrassment knowing that I should have acted differently, and that the situation could have become much worse. A sense of loneliness washed over me as I fled the situation because I realized that no one had come to assist me.
chunks.label: Uncomfortable encounter outside a concert
chunks.what_happened: While waiting for a ride after a concert, the student walked toward a tour bus and was approached and blocked by an intoxicated man making inappropriate comments, but eventually managed to get away.

chunks.text:
By using the concept of “The Stage”, I can form an understanding of why I felt the way I did when straying from my self made character. I believe that it is because my character resides in social interactions that I am unable to defend myself against such interactions when I am on my own.

In conclusion, “The Stage” is the most fitting concept that can be used to demonstrate the presentation of self. It is a means to simplify and illustrate the presentation of self using the different roles involved in theatre. This concept provides simplistic visuals of the various roles played in social situations. “The Stage '' is an interaction based concept used to illustrate the presentation of self. According to the concept, identity is the coalition of performances the performer carries out through social situations. It is collectively produced by everyone involved in helping it emerge and grow. The goal of the performer is to keep their character intact by acting in a way that pleases their audience, and to support others' roles when performing. By supporting and understanding others, we in turn help ourselves. Using this concept to understand the presentation of self can improve social interactions and create new interpersonal relationships. This knowledge can be used in various social situations, and lead to further understanding others and why we do what we do. If we can understand one another, we can avoid or reduce embarrassment, misunderstanding, and unnecessary aggression in social interactions. By helping others avoid these occurrences, we also help to avoid them for ourselves. Social interactions are what keeps society moving and turning, I would even say they are the essence of society. This is why decreasing the occurrence of misunderstanding, embarrassment and unnecessary aggression is so important. In theory, the knowledge of this concept and its application to the real world could improve the fluidity of the inner workings of society.
chunks.label: Reflections on performance and conclusion
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes their reaction to the confrontation using the stage concept and concludes with broad reflections on the importance of social interaction and understanding others.

n41f2389a.title: Disillusionment and Class Division in America

chunks.text:
Yuval Noah Harari is the writer of the book 21 Lesions for the 21st Century. He begins the book with the concept of Disillusionment. He claims that as things get more convoluted and complicated, people stop paying attention. We like simple stories. This goes with the concept of Ockham’s Razor; the simplest explanation is probably the correct one. For Harari, this is one of the explanations for why people just don’t seem to be active in solving the world’s problems, we just don’t know where to start. Also, we have much more immediate personal pressing matters. We must pay bills; we have mouths to feed. So why would we care and pay attention to Class in America when we are just trying to get by?

The few who take time to dissect and pay attention to how the class system is meant to provide heavily to the power elite and leave table scraps throughout the middle class who are too preoccupied with other things that the power elite dish out to them to realize that something is terribly wrong with the class system. The people in power realize that if the working class wanted to overthrow them, they very easily could. The key is to divide the working class along any means necessary to prevent them from organizing and uniting against the unjust class system and the power elite. To Liberal America, conservatives are the enemy and vise versa. As long as they can prevent open and free dialogue from between the isle from happening, they will. This will keep the working class disillusioned with the real problem of class in America. Keep them distracted and complicate the problems as much as you can so they throw their hand up in the air and give up on trying to understand and solve the problem.

Havari’s concept of Disillusionment applies to many other aspects of life. The formula is simple. Those in positions of power and create untrue and confusing narratives and as a result people will stop paying attention, or grasp onto the most simple and easy explanation.
chunks.label: Disillusionment and class division in America
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Yuval Noah Harari's concept of disillusionment and analyzes how the power elite use distraction, division, and complexity to keep the working class from uniting against class inequality.

ne2ea2f7b.title: Analyzing Media Polarization in Contemporary Politics

chunks.text:
The rise of social media has fundamentally changed the way we perceive and take in information. This coupled with the endlessly improving technology creates an interesting relationship between social media and politics. It is common knowledge at this point that most people get their news from some form of social media, predominantly twitter. This is interesting given 20 years ago traditional media was still unchallenged in its monopoly over stories and coverage. First let us define what the traditional media is. It includes television, radio, newspapers, magazines, newsletters, tax press, and other print publications. Compare this to new media, this definition is not as concrete as the other, but it includes blogs, podcasts, websites, and any internet related form of communication. I want to compare the two in the current age where a viral tweet will get more views than CNN and discover how this has impacted current Global politics.

Traditional media has been on the decline since the invention of the internet. The true nail in the coffin was the events of the 2016 American election. As David Morris puts it in his article, Twitter Versus the Traditional Media: A Survey Experiment Comparing Public Perceptions of Campaign Messages in the 2016 U.S. Presidential Election, “Prior to the 2016 presidential election, the assumption was that campaign messages sent through the traditional media are perceived as more influential, believable, and motivating by the public” (Morris). People had an attraction to hearing what a candidate had to say directly from the source as opposed to hearing a perhaps misleading interpretation of what they said. They found it more credible to see what the candidates were tweeting themselves. In this particular instance we see that the amount of information taken in was not limited by “by the hour” shows or stories that were predetermined to be ran in a television broadcast. Someone who followed Hillary Clinton on twitter could find out exactly what she was saying the minute she said it. This also cuts down on any amount of spin that any news station could put onto a tweet of a candidate to promote an agenda with disinformation. To further break down how the primary forms of how voters would get their information, compare the two most popular forms of media in new and traditional, twitter and television. According to a study done by Gottfried and Shearer in 2016, 90% of adults use the internet and social media sites are used by a vast majority of Americans. Of the 90%, 16% had an active twitter account. Of the 16%, 60% reported primarily getting their news information from twitter when it came to the election. However, “most Americans still view traditional media outlets as the most useful and effective conduits to get information on presidential races” (Morris). To connect this to our class, Harari talks about the importance of information and technology and the specific effects it has on the autonomy of the individual. On the surface the ability to choose the type of media you would like to receive seems like it would increase your autonomy. However, if you chose what you want to read, most are only going to choose what agrees with them which can increase political polarization through confirmation bias and echo chambers. This might ultimately cause a decrease in individual autonomy.

The last two decades have seen a revolution in information. The rise of applications such as Facebook and Twitter have massively changed the way that people think and organize specifically when talking about politics. For example, in his journal; New Media, New Civics?, Ethan Zuckerman opens his piece with an example from Egypt,

“For some, this photo was proof positive that the Internet had helped oust Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and was showing its power in allowing people to organize for political change. For others, it was evidence that the self‐importance of Internet advocates had gotten out of hand. After all, the Arab Spring in Egypt had far more to do with economic factors and popular dissatisfaction than with any specific communications technology” (Zuckerman).

The photo referring to an Egyptian man holding a sign that says “Facebook”. Whether you believe in that specific cause or not, it is inarguable that new media had a hand in the action that happened. This touches on an important advantage that new media has over traditional media; its flexibility and accessibility. You can create a group of people who all think the same thing and organize a movement. This movement does not even have to be a physical location or place, it can be a purely online movement full of posts that can gain ground and more followers. This can also be a disadvantage and may offer an answer to why most people still trust traditional media more than they do new media. A malicious online movement can create discourse and confusion with misinformation campaigns. When people know that they cannot argue against something that they disagree with, they will make online noise to disrupt the true meaning of whatever it is they are trying to disrupt. Again, to connect to Harari, being a citizen in the 21st century can be very difficult because we must wade through all this online fluff to get to what we really want.

How has people view and engagement in politics changed? Specifically due to the rise of new media. For the most part I think had has created a more polarized political climate specifically in America. People wither wear a red or blue jersey and act accordingly to what people who they align with politically act, even if they do not agree with a particular issue. People are willing to put aside their personal view to feel like they belong to a group. This again connects to Harari’s claim of loss of autonomy. Say you are a conservative republican who is pro-choice and make it very clear of that on social media. The conservatives will oust you for not aligning with all their conservative views and the liberal will not accept you for not aligning with all of their liberal views. This leads to a feeling of isolation in the political world.
chunks.label: Traditional versus new media and political polarization
chunks.what_happened: The student compares traditional and new media, discusses their impact on politics and the 2016 election, examines the Arab Spring and misinformation, and reflects on political polarization and loss of autonomy drawing on class readings.

chunks.text:
Racial inequalities and racial disparities can be seen in lots of things in the United States. You can see racial inequalities in the education system, in the economy, and in the government. There have been multiple recent reminders of racial discrimination and its existence all over the world. For example how society tends to view minorities in a negative way compared to whites. The prison system is a great example of racial disparity.

Today there is a clear racial disparity in the United States prison system. There is a disproportionate amount of African Americans that are incarcerated. This is a serious problem considering that the United States has the largest prison population in the world. This racial disparity in the prison system has many contributing factors. In the past there has been crime policies put in place to target blacks and other minorities. Another factor is that minorities tend to receive more harsh sentences in criminal trials. These racial disparities can also be seen with our court and justice system and how different people are sentenced. As well as in our police system by how different people are stopped and questioned by police officers.

The United States prison population is much larger than any other country in the world. The majority of inmates that are incarcerated are African American. Hetey states, “Blacks are the most imprisoned of all groups. Though they comprise only 12% of the U.S. population, Blacks are nearly 40% of the nation’s inmates, with some researchers estimating that more than one in four Black men will spend time behind bars (Bonczar & Beck, 1997; Western, 2006).” This number is disproportionate considering that black people are a minority in America. This shows that there is racial disparity in the prison system and the court system.

Everyone in the United States has the right to a fair trial. But blacks are more likely to receive a longer sentence for the same crime than whites. This racial bias has been implemented in the court system for a long time. Ingraham states, “Black men who commit the same crimes as white men receive federal prison sentences that are, on average, nearly 20 percent longer, according to a new report on sentencing disparities from the United States Sentencing Commission (USSC).” The sentence that is given to the criminal is almost always determined by the judge. Which means that judges play a large part in why African Americans are given longer sentences than whites. This being said almost all of the state and federal judges are white men. Ingraham also states, “Judges are less likely to voluntarily revise sentences downward for black offenders than for white ones, in other words. And even when judges do reduce black offenders' sentences, they do so by smaller amounts than for white offenders.” This harsher sentencing towards blacks leads to more black people being incarcerated and for long amounts of time. These racial disparities can also be seen in the parole and release program. With whites having a better chance of getting released from prison on parole than blacks and other minorities. This shows racial disparity because of the larger number of African Americans that are incarcerated. Also that white people are more likely to get probation instead of prison time than black people.

African Americans and other minorities are more likely to be stopped by the police. This can include being stopped and questioned on the street and being stopped by police while driving. There is clear evidence that shows that blacks or other minorities are more likely to be involved in a police stop. Kovera states, “For example, in North Carolina, which has collected data on traffic stops since 1999, the odds of being stopped by police while driving were higher for Blacks than for Whites or Hispanics (Baumgartner, Epp, & Shoub, 2018). Moreover, the odds of a Black driver appearing in the NC traffic stop data were 60–70% higher than the odds of a Black driver in the population in which the traffic stop occurred.” This higher rate of police stops for African American is due to the racial bias that some people have.

The racial bias that people have is a negative stereotype that black people are violent and dangerous. This negative stereotype can be seen all over the world. Mitchell states, “For example, Devine (1989) in an early study found that respondents regardless of their level racial prejudice as measured by the Modern Racism Scale were knowledgeable about racial stereotypes, and respondents noted that blacks were stereotyped as “hostile” and “criminal-like” (p. 9).” The racial stereotype can also be seen in reports of people calling the police on African Americans for doing nothing wrong, to the multiple incidents where African Americans have been shot by police at traffic stops. For example Kovera states, “Experimental studies confirmed that unarmed Black men face a greater risk of being shot by mistake than do unarmed White men, a phenomenon known as shooter bias (Correll, Park, Judd, & Wittenbrink, 2002).” That bias is why some black men and women fear for their lives when they encounter police. This is because the police tend to have two different meanings for most black and white people. For most white people the police are there to keep you and your community safe, while for some black people the police are there to interrogate you and suspect you of a crime. These two different perspectives of how the police are viewed is from what people have experienced today and in the past.

Another variable that led to mass incarceration of African Americans was the war on drugs. The war on drugs was a movement started by president Nixon and then later led by president Reagan that focused on stopping the illegal use of drugs. This movement implemented more harsh and longer sentences for minor drug charges. The war on drugs targeted blacks and other minorities in particular. By making known illegal drug use was a serious issue, minor drug charges turned into major prison sentences. Mitchell states, “Americans of all racial backgrounds have been affected by the current War on Drugs; yet, minorities, particularly African-Americans, have borne the brunt of the war (Tonry, 1995, 2011). In 1980, prior to the latest War on Drugs, the drug arrest rate for African-Americans was 554 per 100,000 and the rate for whites was 190 per 100,000—a ratio of roughly 3 to 1. Less than 10 years later, at the height of the drug war, these rates had climbed to 2,009 and 363 per 100,000 for blacks and whites, respectively (Human Rights Watch, 2009)—a ratio of 5.5 to 1.” This mass incarceration from the war on drugs also pushed the stereotype of black people as criminals and drug dealers. Which led to more police stereotyping and more unlawful searches and stops of African Americans. Mitchell states, “Such stereotypes appear to be particularly strong when it comes to drug offending. One study found when respondents were asked to close their eyes and envision a drug user more than 95% of respondents described a black person, and when the same respondents also perceived those involved in drug sales as typically being black (Burston, Jones, & Roberson-Saunders, 1995).” While some of these harsh drug sentences have been lessened, many are still in place today.

In Collins article “The Matrix of Domination” she talks about oppression and how it impacts certain races and genders. Collins talks about how society judges people based on certain variables such as age, race, and gender. For example how minorities are discriminated against because of their race, how women are often oppressed by men, and how older people are often discriminated against because of their age. She talks about intersectionality and how people face oppression from multiple things, rather than just one particular thing. For example how Collins as an African American can face oppression from society because of her race. While also as a woman she has to face oppression from society because of her gender. She explains that in order to truly understand how someone is being oppressed you must consider all of the different things that play a part in the oppression.

Collins' ideas can be seen in relation to the racial disparity in the prison system. We can see that in prison people can be discriminated against for multiple variables. How African Americans and other minorities are discriminated against in the courtroom and are more likely to receive a harsher and longer sentence than white people. Also how African Americans and other minorities can be discriminated against when trying to receive parole or probation because the judge is less likely to grant parole or probation to minorities than white people. Another example would be how black people and other minorities are discriminated against and are more likely to be stopped or pulled over by the police than a white person. Also how black people are discriminated against and are looked at as criminals and violent and dangerous people.

Many recent events of racial discrimination against African Americans and other minorities have reminded us that racism hasn’t gone away. This can be clearly seen in the court and prison system. The statistics show the racial disparities that exist in the prison system. That African Americans are a minority in the United States, but are a majority in the worlds largest prison system. The mass incarceration of African Americans is from many factors. The minor drug charges that were changed to have harsh and long sentences because of the war on drugs. Also that black people and other minorities are more likely to get a prison sentence than white people and that black people and other minorities are more likely to get a longer sentence for the same crime than white people. This mass incarceration of African Americans also comes from the police system and how they tend to treat different races. How black people and other minorities are more likely to be stopped and questioned or pulled over by the police than white people. As well as the negative stereotype that black people are given. The stereotype that all black people are dangerous criminals that sell drugs. All of these factors show how African Americans and other minorities are racially discriminated against in this country. The racial discrimination and racial inequality that minorities face in the United States should make people push for a serious change in this country. Hopefully with the reform of our justice and police system the number of black people that are incarcerated will start to decrease.
