n14f9a1c7.title: Class Divides Between Trades and Business

chunks.text:
In modern society, an individual is defined by their career. Careers determine if one is educated, successful, or just another machine in society. The crossing of alienation and social class reflects society and its perception of an individual. In modern society, individuals look down upon people who work blue-collar jobs and idolize those who are millionaires with their own businesses. The correlation between social class and alienation reflects the imbalance of power and opportunities that shape individuals’ experiences and identities.

Social class divides society into economic groups, resulting in resource discrepancies and shaping overall life experiences. In the historical and modern world, labor workers experience a different lifestyle to those of wealth and status. Labor workers have worked endless hours to make ends meet, make insufficient salaries, and work in harsh conditions yet receive no recognition. Those of wealth, however, receive all recognition of the work of the labor workers. Praised by all in society, the wealthy class receives all the economic benefits that result in access to education, the ability to move up the socioeconomic ladder, and guarantee a successful lifestyle for their children.

A prime example of the discrepancies in lifestyles in today's society is the family of a trade worker and the family of a businessman. Social media has allowed society to view different lifestyles, especially TikTok. TikTok has allowed individuals to post their day to day lives, allowing viewers to get the reality of their life. In a day to day of trade worker, the day begins at seven am and ends at five pm. In between their days, trade workers are expected to work in the blazing heat and meet job expectations with little to no help outside of their work crew. Alongside many trade workers work under 1099. They are expected to buy the tools and necessities to complete the job but receive no benefits from their jobs. Trade workers are required to search for and pay for healthcare on their own and at times for their families as well resulting in the need to work countless hours. Whereas the life of a businessman sounds bliss compared to the life of a trade worker. They can work a nine-to-five job, have access to healthcare, and receive an abundance of benefits. This is later reflected in the interactions they have with their own families.

As trade workers work countless hours to make ends meet for their families, their jobs become their identifying factors. There are no longer any separating factors between who the trade worker is as a person and his job. Children begin to view their parents as concrete workers rather than fathers or mothers. Trade workers start to invest in their careers in hopes of economic prosperity resulting in the lack of quality family time. Business owners, however, have the luxury to separate themselves from their jobs. They can practice hobbies, cut time out of their day to spend time with their family, and invest in their family rather than their careers. Business owners do not have the need to alienate themselves for their jobs and have it be a describing factor to who they are as a person. They now instead can focus on obtaining resources that guarantee long-lasting economic success for their children whether it's an investment in their education or hobbies. They have the privilege of becoming known as the family man rather than the working man. However, this success of identification is only granted through the imbalance of power between the two.

The trade worker does not have the luxury of working on their own time and merit compared to the businessman. In the capitalist world, there must always be a worker generating revenue for the ‘boss’. The ‘boss’ will take the revenue generated and distribute a portion of it to pay their workers. Though the ‘boss’ did not partake in any of the labor, they gained all the means and the labor workers must now rely on the generosity of their boss. The trade worker no longer works for themselves, creating work that they are passionate about, but instead, work to create products for the ‘boss’ further alienating themselves. Thus, resulting in greater power and economic imbalance between the two classes.

The relationship between alienation and social class reveals the complex ties between the imbalance of power and opportunities that lead to the individuals' identity. Through the difference in lifestyles, the identities of trade workers are vastly different from the businessman. With the businessman having access to an abundance of resources that guarantee economic prosperity, allowing them to find identifying factors outside of their career. Whereas the trade worker does not have economic security, forcing them to revolve their lives around their job. The difference in economic security further perpetuates the power imbalance between the two. As one has more economic freedom than the other, allows the businessman to work for themselves in comparison to the trade worker working for the businessman. Recognizing the imbalance of power and opportunities allows the potential to demand change and move toward an equal society, in which one does not have to alienate themselves for their career, and social class does not determine the long-lasting success of an individual.
chunks.label: Social class, alienation, and career disparities
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how careers, social class, and alienation shape an individual's identity, comparing the harsh realities of blue-collar trade workers shown on TikTok with the privileged lifestyles of businessmen and bosses in a capitalist society.

nd53742a5.title: Challenging Gender Norms and Facing Violence

chunks.text:
For centuries, society has had gender norms. The men were in power, the women were beneath them, and most of the time, submitted to the man and his needs. Even thousands of years later, the foundations of the United States only had a group of men writing the Constitution, the foundation of a country, allowing for a bias that has now been normalized in societies. In the past couple decades, the world has been working on correcting the systemic racism, stigma in mental health, women in power, and with finding better ways of accepting those who identify in the LGBTQ2+ community. People in the LGBTQ2+ community often act and look differently than the gender roles and norms that society puts on them. This often results in upset and angry people who believe in tradition and are uncomfortable with change. These people are often hiding their homophobia, sexism, and other forms of hatred and end up hurting people in this community. There are several types of abuse that are often seen to be more prevalent for teens in the community than those who are straight. Most common, sexual trauma. Sexual trauma is reported by many to be a much higher percentage by those who identify in the community, and most of them also admitting it happened in their young, crucial, formative years. For clarity, there is no significant correlation that sexual trauma will not determine a person’s sexuality, but instead that those in the community are more vulnerable to these types of abuse. In this paper, I will be explaining the effect on teens who are in the community that have defied and stood up against gender norms, and the consequences that many teens, who are still children, are facing daily, just because of who they are. These teens who are still trying to figure out life in general are also fighting to figure themselves out, while also having to live by the traditional gender norms and “doing gender”.

“Doing Gender” is the idea that you will live your life while being assessed by society and the people that surround you, even if they don’t know you. This is often associated with gender norms and the stereotypes that men and women are separately supposed to fulfill. Activities and outward appearances with masculine features, like walking people across the street or carrying something heavy are considered a man’s job, while sitting and looking pretty is more for a female. Females aren’t expected to be loud or dress a certain way because it seems manly, but skirts aren’t correct for men because its “feminine”. These types of gender roles seem minimal, but since it has been engrained in our brains and society, it has become a tradition that many people are unwilling to change, leading to different types of violence. Next, I will be sharing a couple of personal stories of those I know in the community who have been abused and witnessed violence because of the fact that they were subject to gender norms.

*Names have been changed to protect the privacy of those who allowed me to use their stories*
chunks.label: Introduction to gender norms and LGBTQ2+ abuse
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces historical gender roles, the concept of 'doing gender', and the abuse and sexual trauma experienced by youth in the LGBTQ2+ community.

chunks.text: Annie’s Story: Annie had grown up in a very Christian conservative household. No sex, no lying, no cussing, waiting until marriage until you could marry a man. She had a hard time going out on dates because her parents worried about how she may get hurt while she goes out. They were hard on her and expected her to keep up with their strict expectations. Before high school, she had only dated 2 guys. Both of which she didn’t connect too much with, but she thought it may be just because she couldn’t see them often. She went to a private Christian school where she was extremely sheltered. She then transferred to a public high school where the transition was difficult and a brutal culture shock later learning she couldn’t trust everyone she thought she could. She still believed she needed guys for validation because of an abusive home life and not really knowing herself. She trusted one guy who ended up blackmailing her to sexually assault and rape her for over a year. She felt like she couldn’t tell anyone because her offender was black, and her parents were racist. Her parents would not support her, and she couldn’t tell an adult without getting the parents involved since she was still a minor. Her coach noticed her panic attacks when her offender would walk in and figured there was something wrong. Throughout the time, she had to find peace and a home somewhere else. She allowed vulnerability with dating women and is now bisexual. She has told me that this is where she feels safe. She is now in college, away from her parents, where her roommates accept her, and she has noted how much better her mental health has been since she has been in college. I asked her if she ever acted differently or dressed differently around men to keep herself safe, and she didn’t hesitate with saying yes. She will dress more masculine some days or be “one of the boys” so that they won’t try and do what happened to her during her freshmen and sophomore year of high school. She has stated that there have been men who harass her for not being feminine and polite like many women are expected to do.
chunks.label: Annie's story of trauma and identity
chunks.what_happened: The student shares the story of Annie, recounting her upbringing, sexual assault, transition to college, coming out as bisexual, and her conversations with the student about dressing masculine to feel safe.
chunks.people: Annie, Annie's parents, Annie's offender, Annie's coach, Annie's roommates

chunks.text: Reagan’s Story: Reagan had grown up in a very broken home. She grew up in an African cultured home where the father had many wives and felt as though he could do anything at the demise of the women. While growing up in Islam, her father molested her as a child. She was and witnessed being abused and her mother being abused as well. I personally knew her well for the past couple years and have had to pick her up from her home because she didn’t feel safe. Reagan identifies as lesbian and has for as long as she can remember. She also dresses masculine because that’s what is comfortable, and how she feels safer. She has been through several therapists, medications, and attempts to end her life. Her family does not accept her for not being feminine and not dating men and it something she struggles with every day. She has had sisters who have had arranged marriages with men and is hoping to break this cycle of the gender norm that the female is expected to submit to the man and live to work for his pleasure at home.
chunks.label: Reagan's story of abuse and identity
chunks.what_happened: The student describes Reagan's abusive childhood, her identity as a lesbian, and how the student personally knew Reagan and picked her up when she felt unsafe at home.
chunks.people: Reagan, Reagan's father, Reagan's mother, Reagan's sisters

chunks.text:
In history, those who did not follow the standard of being straight and doing what traditions told them to, have been redefining gender roles, but against a brutal force. Many people in the community have been seen as not real men or women due to the fact they don’t follow the set gender roles that are aligned with their genitalia. Many gender transgressors are marked in society and deal with intense abuse including verbal and physical violence, scrutiny, and community gossip. Many of those who enforce gender norms often have an “anti-gay attitude”. According to Delores Smith, who works in the Department of Child and Family Studies in Tennessee, found that things like this can cause the allowance of “corrective rape”, specifically for lesbians, to be subject to forced sex with a man to “cure” them of their sexual identity. Adults and supervisors who are supposed to be protecting these youth have found that there has been a downplay of harassment of lesbians. A study done where they interviewed several lesbians and their experience showed they have gone against gender norms, but some will change just so that they “pass” as straight. Michael Ferrera, a Clinical Director of Group Homes for Gay and Lesbian Adolescent Social Services says that “The girls who can pass have an easier time…The lipstick lesbians are objectified, but the butch girls ger challenged all the time. The butch lesbians have the hardest time”. The Human Right Watch found that the majority of girls, regardless of their sexual orientation are sexually harassed, making bisexual or lesbian females feel as though they cannot turn to school officials for not protecting girls from the sexual harassment by boys in school. However, with who did turn to other students or service providers, it was consistently noted that girls who failed to conform to the gender stereotypes and normality’s set on them were the most targeted. There was a theory offered as an explanation to why these girls are not accepted, and it was called the inversion theory. Inversion theory is mostly self-explanatory, where there was inborn reversal of gender traits among that person or group of people. This, however, is something that is not accepted among people that follow the traditions of the past, and don’t feel comfortable in the changes of society and the growing acceptance and destigmatizing of the LGBTQ2+ community.

With the stories and evidence above, there is personal and statistical evidence that sexual assault is common throughout the community. While sexual assault happens to every type of person, studies have shown that the frequency of the events happens higher in the LGBTQ2+ community. According to the CDC, lesbian, gay, and bisexual people experience sexual violence at similar and higher rates than straight people. The CDC’s conducted a study and found that 44% of lesbians and 61% of bisexual women have experienced some form of sexual violence including rape, physical violence, or stalking compared to the 35% of straight women. Bisexual women have the highest percent of rape being at 46% compared to 17% of straight women and 13% of lesbians. Another survey found that LGBQ teens and those who are questioning their sexuality face twice the risk of physical violence compared to straight teens. Not only were these stats much higher, but studies have also delved into child sexual abuse for women and men in the community. Prevalence ranged as high as 76% of women and 59% of men who identified as gay or bisexual. These numbers are all comparatively high to straight men and women.

LGBTQ2+ teens have experienced several forms of abuse, many have challenged the gender norms, and are fighting to stay safe. As stated before, many admit to the fact that sometimes they will change just so that they “pass” to avoid being harassed by other people. In the article we read in class “Doing Gender”, the authors talked about what doing gender was, and ongoing accomplishments among people who didn’t fit the gender norms, but still adjusted to society. One example they gave was of someone named Agnes. Agnes was born with male genitalia, but she believed that she was born as a female in a male body. She studied the female and wanted to be undeniably female to society. She had to study what were the “not talked about ruled” for females in society and would have to learn what to do even making sure not to overstep. She had bottom surgery and learned the way of life as a female which is why the authors considered her a gender accomplishment - she became “passing”.

Gender norms have been an influence on society for centuries, and is not destined to change much soon. With society destigmatizing mental illness, women in power, people in the community, and several other things, there will always be a group against it. They believe in traditions and would like to keep it that way. Many people are uncomfortable with change and having the awkward conversations about the bias that flows through society and our brains since it was systematically built into the foundations of our country. With this, they act violently, and do whatever it takes to stop others from being what is outside of the gender norms of society. However, “Doing Gender” shows that no matter who you are, society will set the stereotypes on you even when you are doing daily tasks, so while keeping yourself and loved ones safe, there’s no point of being no one else but who you want to be, and how you best feel comfortable and confident.
chunks.label: Analysis of gender roles, statistics, and conclusions
chunks.what_happened: The student reviews sociological research, statistics on sexual violence against LGBTQ2+ individuals, the case of Agnes from class readings, and concludes with thoughts on gender norms.

nc8ac92af.title: Reflecting on Gender and Female Roles

chunks.text:
Whether you are male, female, transgender, or a mixture of all three, you have experienced, and will continue to experience, the concept of gender as it pertains to the Western collective consciousness. Gender roles affect us all, and while they might not be as stark and suffocating as a few decades ago, they are certainly still there. Whoever you are and whatever you chose to identify as, you are subjected to attitudes and subconscious decisions that will determine how you feel about your own femininity or masculinity. Therefore, your gender expression determines what behavior is appropriate, and even if you decide to go against the grain, you are still doing so because you are conscious that it is an invisible barrier that you must overcome.

Gilman’s “The Yellow Wallpaper” takes a stance on the role of women within a marriage, and how women are relegated to this simple caregiver. In this instance, as all control is taken away from her, she is forced to make up a fantasy in which she has some semblance of control over her life. The stereotype of women being the caregivers and stay-at-home mothers was not perpetuated by women but born out of necessity. As men entered the work force and the capitalistic 9-5 work week became the norm, women were relegated to the home. Men decided to be the breadwinners, and women had to become the other. Even today, as women are an important part of the work force, the wage gap reinforces that even though women have proven time and time again that they are as intelligent and hardworking as men, they are still seen as less in the eyes of their employers and the work force as a whole.

The female experience is one that involves fighting against a norm and being hailed as a ‘trend setter’ or ‘trail blazer,’ going along with a norm for a comfortable life in which you at the very least have control of a household, or somehow blending together the two. Each is as inherently female as the other and should be respected as a decision that is ours alone to make. With the modern feminist movement reaching a peak, women are fighting for the chance to be seen as anything other than “other.” The road is long but is paved by each and every person who decides they are a woman and refuse to be seen as anything other than.
chunks.label: Reflections on gender roles and feminism
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the pervasive influence of gender roles, discusses Gilman's 'The Yellow Wallpaper' and the historical relegation of women to caregiving roles, and examines contemporary feminist struggles regarding the wage gap and female agency.

nc498ac33.title: Gender Dynamics in Local Surf Culture

chunks.text: Growing up in a beach town you tend to be drawn towards the ocean and surfing. That's just what happens and what makes sense. Personally, I have a dad who is a big character in the surf community near me. So for me of course I was going to surf but I was also going to fit into the surf community with no effort. I did not have to prove anything. For me, it was a birthright.
chunks.label: Growing up with surfing access
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up in a beach town with a father who was well known in the local surf community, giving the student easy entry and acceptance into surfing.

chunks.text: However, it doesn't work out like that for all people who end up surfing especially if you are a female. Back in the day, females had to fight for respect in the water. This gender difference was apparent. However, today, surfing is making moves to include the female population. Even though there is movement in the right direction for gender equality, there are still differences that exist. Surfing throughout the years has always been more of a masculine sport and the guys have always been the people to do it. Back when my dad was starting to surf in the late 80s there were very few females in the water. There would be about ten males per every one female out in the water. Even when females would paddle out they would never get the best waves. They were seen by other surfers as a joke and did not get any respect for the sport. This was not only obvious to the surfers but was also evident when surf videos were released. Lost, a board company, put out many videos such as Lost Across America. These videos did not show females surfing. Girls were shown in bikinis on the beach. There wasn’t a market for women surfers. Even in the professional surfing world, women professional surfers were not recognized. There was not a large crowd when a woman was competing and when there was publicity, it was more about how they look then what they could do in the water. Then came Lisa Anderson. Although she did not wear a bikini in the water, she was still pretty and femanine. Interviewing my dad, he believes that if Lisa Anderson was not pretty, she would not have made such an impact on surfing culture. Her parents did not support her surfing either. She ended up running away. One would have to think was this because she was a girl in a male sport? Would she have her parents' support if she were a boy? She was an aggressive surfer who started to get attention around 1997 and was bringing female surfing to life. Lisa Anderson still looked like a girl and did not change her appearance for surfing. She was not trying to fit into a man’s sport but was trying to be a woman in the sport of surfing. Even though Lisa Anderson started to get attention and could surf, she still carried the stereotype, she is “good for a girl”. She was not looked at to be on the same level as the guys and in all honesty she was not nearly as good of the male professionals at the time. During the early 90’s, there was even a time that women’s surfing was cancelled but the men's competition and the bikini contest still happened (Girls Can’t Surf, 2020). I would argue this would not happen today.
chunks.label: History of gender inequality in surfing
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses the masculine history of surfing, the lack of respect and media coverage for women surfers in past decades, and the pioneering role and stereotypes surrounding Lisa Anderson.

chunks.text: My brother and I grew up in a different era but in the same surf culture. When we began surfing, we were young and there were not a lot of surfer girls. However, by the time I turned 13, this had changed. There were girls and boys in the water and we surfed together without any issues or ill feelings. We did not tell the girls they were bad and did not belong here. On the contrary, we welcomed them and enjoyed having them out in the water. We were raised with girl surfers in the water. They are a part of the surfing community. They have been backed by sponsorships and compete at high levels. The girls are just as aggressive as the boys. Locally, there is not much difference between a boy and girl surfer. It is evident now how surfing is more accepting to females.
chunks.label: Surfing alongside girls as a teen
chunks.what_happened: The student and their brother grew up surfing and saw more girls join the lineup by the time the student turned 13, surfing together welcomingly.
chunks.people: the student, brother, local girl and boy surfers

chunks.text: Gender inequality is evident in all cultures. In West and Zimmerman’s article, Do Gender, men and women have differences, “differences seemingly supported by the division of labor into women’s and men’s work...men are men and women are women” (p. 128). There are stereotypes for women and men in our society. Women are not supposed to compete in a “men’s sport”. Men are strong while women do not have the same ability. As we talk in class about the ranks of the people you have, the white male leads everything and that is like being in first place. Then you have black males and white women. Then the last is black women. This is kind of the list for everything and just how people look at other people. Although gender differences do exist, the rank between men and women is starting to shrink as well as the gender roles are changing everyday in the surf world. In the surfing world, men were dominant. Women were not welcomed and treated negatively. In a 2017 op-ed for The Guardian, the seven-time world champion Layne Beachley described how from her first days of learning to surf to her years on the pro circuit in the 1990s, she and other women were heavily harassed, discriminated against, and paid a fraction of what their men competitors earned. “I was teased, cut off, told to get out of the water because I was a girl, advised that girls don’t surf, and to go mind the towel on the beach,” Beachley wrote of her early years surfing. “These encounters taught me to stand up and fight for what I believed in. (Baird, 2019) Many times when a sport has a women’s division, they are thought of outside of their gender roles. “Men positioned athletic women as dangerous and masculines lesbians” (Essell, p.115). This is a common thread when men look at women athletes. Essell discusses in Barbie Dolls that the Rugby players felt they needed to show their femininity since the rules of the game were the same for both male and females and the sport is tough. “Rugby is unique among women’s sports in having the same rules and equipment as the men’s game. The sport offered identity resources for the women, as athletes, because of its hypermasculine structure and style of play” (p. 112). Surfing also follows the same rules no matter what gender you are. When women first started to surf, they did not show their femininity but focused on being tough and masculine to fit into the surfing world. The men surfers did not accept women surfers and made it clear in interviews and out in the water (Girls Can’t Surf, 2020). Lisa Anderson started to change women’s surfing. She showed that beautiful women can be surfers. She did not wear a bikini but still showed her beauty. Now there are a lot of female professional surfers that do not have that hypermasculine side to them. They dress like women and act like women. They are aggressive in the water. That may be compared to being masculine but they are not. However, the surfing world started to use beauty as an identity for women. The surf culture did not think women had a place in surfing and should look attractive. Magazines took pictures of women’s butts for ad campaigns not there surfing. Rebecca Woods' sponsor even dropped her because she did not fit the profile. “In a 2016 piece on Australia’s ABC, the former pro surfer Rebecca Woods detailed how she was dropped by her sponsor Billabong because, she said, they favored surfers who wore bikinis and looked like models” (Baird, 2019). As a result, the gender in-equality continued by using women who “looked like models” instead of women who surfed. Male surfers made comments like about the women surfers never being as good as men and needing to look like women. (Girls Can’t Surf, 2020) Surfing is making efforts in gender equality. Locally and in the professional world. In 2019, the World Surf League (WSL) established equal prize money for men and women surfers. The greatest surfer of all time, Kelly Slater supported the movement for women by saying, “The women on the tour deserve this change. I'm so proud that surfing is choosing to lead sports in equality and fairness. The female WSL athletes are equally committed to their craft as the male athletes and should be paid the same” (WSL, 2018). Slater is an icon to surfing and his support shows surfers the respect women are getting. WSL also made more changes than just the prize money. CEO Sophie Goldschmidt explained, “This is the latest in a series of actions the League has undertaken to showcase our female athletes, from competing on the same quality waves as the men, to better locations, and increased investment and support” (WSL, 2018). The organization has moved women’s events to combine with the men or to better surf spots. The sport has begun to show women as athletes not supermodels. Sponsors and magazines are showing women surfing and not focusing on what they are wearing. They are earning respect for the sport and women’s ability. However, there are still some differences. Women are still not on the same level as the males when competing. You can really see it through the highschool surf team. National Scholastic Surfing Association (NSSA) does not allow girls to have the same number of surfers. A NSSA high school surf team consists of two female surfers, 6 male surfers and one long board surfer who can be male or female. Even if you have females that are better than the males and are willing to surf on the men’s team, NSSA high school national competition will not allow for this change. They are concerned that boys will want to join the girls' event. This shows that there is still room to grow where gender is concerned.
chunks.label: Sociological concepts and surfing gender dynamics
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on sociology concepts regarding gender and race hierarchies, comparing surfing culture to women's rugby, media objectification, and institutional league rules.

chunks.text: The skill level between males and females are different and as a result, there is still a gender separation. This has hurt my high school surf team. When I joined the surf team 5 years ago, the girls' competition was about standing up on a board. The girls were not good surfers. My Sophomore year, a freshman girl joined the team and she was a decent surfer. An even better surfer joined the surf team my junior year. By my senior year, we had too many girls who could surf and the surfer who competed my sophomore and junior year, who placed each year, had to sit out of the state competition due to the talent of the girls on our team. This is even more challenging this year. There are 4 girls who could compete but only 2 are permitted. Throughout this time, in 5 years, I have seen the change and respect for the girl surfers. Truly we were trying to get them to surf with the boys due to the talent they have. I witnessed a change at the NSSA competition. Girls are getting better and gaining respect. The girls are not just able to stand up, they are good surfers. One can see the respect and how surfing has grown on females through the talent and how much better the females are at surfing then the females that surfed a while ago.
chunks.label: High school surf team girl members
chunks.what_happened: Over five years on the high school surf team, the student saw talented female surfers join and improve, though NSSA rules restricted their team roster spots.
chunks.people: the student, high school teammates, female surfers

chunks.text:
The talent level has also grown not just on a small scale of a highschool surf team but also at the professional level. Women surfers are getting better and better. The boys have been throwing airs in contests for years and it is one of the most entertaining things about surfing. Carissa Moore landed the first air in female pro surfing April 9, 2021. This was being talked about in the surfing world and was a great accomplishment. This shows a step and improvement in women's surfing. The male surfers also praised her when she did this. They did not mock her accomplishment or make fun of her like Layne Beachley experienced in 1990 instead they congratulated her. Women surfers have been publicly recognized by their male peers. In John John Florence’s instagram, he congratulates Carissa on winning the world tour. He even posts her wave during the competition. This shows that women are also getting more respect from their male peers at the highest level of surfing. The difference in men and women pro surfing is the judging of the waves and the scores that the women get compared to the men in competitions. The women scoring criteria is easier than the men. A perfect example is going back to Carrissa Moore and landing an air reverse. She got a 9.9 but if a male surfer were to do that in a contest it would not be looked at as special. However, if a guy did the air Carissa did he wouldn’t get any praise. Actually, he would not get any recognition. I do believe we will see this change as more female surfers start to do more radical moves in the water. For now, this difference continues to separate the genders and provide inequality. As the girls get better, so do the boys so the gap in ability continues to exist and expand. WIth the WSL supporting women surfers and making a stance financially for equality, the gender inequality gap should shrink. This shows that the highest level of competition for surfers believes that female surfing is important. There has also been a change for surf clinics for girls. The WSL has added clinics to the tour for girl surfers and is going to clear the beach for these clinics. This shows progress from the late 80’s early 90’s when women were treated poorly in the water and not recognized for their surfing ability. Surfers are more respectful now and more welcoming. It will be nice to see the movement in the future. Unfortunately, the gap still exists since there are more male than female competition. As stated throughout this paper, the gender difference in surfing is moving in the right direction. There are more female surfers at the local level, more opportunities with female clinics for young surfers and equal pay for those that surf professionally. The male counterparts are recognizing female surfers as talented. They are congratulating them and supporting them instead of telling them to get out of the water. When professionals make change, so do the more local communities. Female surfers are continuing to be more and more accepted in the surf culture. Although there is still work to do in the surfing world between the male and female population, surfing is moving to close the gender inequality gap. nb8c8063a.title: Experiencing the Realities of Racial Inequality

chunks.text: Race plays a big role in your life in today's world. Your race can impact every aspect of your life, it can affect you positively and negatively. In particular as a minority in the United States it often affects you in negative ways. Minorities are looked at differently, they deal with discrimination and racial inequalities on a daily basis. While on the other hand white people don't have to deal with the same discrimination and unfair treatment. This idea of races being treated differently is from the racial formation.
chunks.label: The impact of race and racial formation
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how race affects life in modern society, discussing how minorities face discrimination while white people do not, stemming from racial formation.

chunks.text: Omi and Winant start out their argument with the discovery of the new world and Native Americans. The discovery of a type of people who were different from what Europeans were used to normally encountering, made them challenge their beliefs of creation and what man looked like. This meant there had to be a distinction for white Europeans between themselves, and the “other” that had been so unfamiliar to them. Fast forwarding through time to the period after Reconstruction and the development of the different expectations of what it meant to be “black,” or “latino,” or even “white” were created at this time. What this brought with it was a certain level of expectations for how people of a certain race would act in scenarios and what their standing in society and economy was expected to be. The formation of racial stereotypes is a direct application of Erving Goffman’s “Presentation of Self” in a way. This is seen in that where each actor comes to the stage with expectations for how the other actors will perform their roles. This is applied in that how media and past experiences can form stereotypes for people about other races, such as that of white people being expected to hold higher socio-economic positions to that of black or latino people, forcing preconceived notions onto minorities trying to get out of their current socio-economic positions as people who they really aren’t and when do not act in the way they are expected to, can lead to confusion, or suspicion of them for no reason.
chunks.label: Racial stereotypes and sociological theories
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Omi and Winant's arguments regarding the origins of racial distinctions, and connects the formation of racial expectations and stereotypes to Erving Goffman's concept of the presentation of self.

ne73f041e.title: Artificial Intelligence and Consciousness of Self

chunks.text:
The Effects of Artificial Intelligence on the Consciousness of Self

In modern society, the advancements of artificial intelligence are developing at an exponential rate. Micheal Haenlein and Andreas Kaplan define artificial intelligence as “a system’s ability to interpret external data correctly, to learn from such data, and to use those learnings to achieve specific goals and tasks through flexible adaptation”. As this artificial intelligent technology evolves, children are growing up in a world where it is not uncommon to rely on computers for everyday needs. Because of this, people are becoming more reliant than ever on machines. The reliance on AI is a newly found concept that continues to grow, becoming more powerful than we can imagine. With a world becoming so dependent on highly intelligent technology systems, one could consider what the outcome would be if this technology were to disappear. One could also consider what the outcome would be if technology were to completely take over. What would happen to humanity's ability to function?

As time goes on, and the electronic world flourishes, an individual's ability to be self-aware is being quickly depreciated. The consciousness of self is the idea that one is not only aware of their surroundings, but they are aware of how they feel, how they are perceived, and who they are in general. The consciousness of self can be interpreted in many different ways from many different theorists. It is important for one to be connected to their consciousness of self because it helps to express one's individuality. With artificial intelligence developing to the vast size that it is today, great change is happening without humanity even knowing. Artificial intelligence has negative effects on one’s perception of self because it limits one's ability to have original ideas, puts individuals at risk of job loss, makes one blindly reliant, causes one to be unaware of their surroundings, and decreases the amount of social interaction in general.

Individuality is one aspect that is heavily affected by the growth of artificial intelligence. One can argue that today, there is less original thought being provoked because everybody is fed the same information. Being fed the same information makes it extremely difficult for people to form their own ideas and opinions simply because they are given the right answer with no additional thought. As the world is being rewritten by AI, the human race adapts, because that is our nature. In Our Identities in The Age of Artificial Intelligence, Jun Wu states “These impacts will prompt us to adapt. In the process, our identities will shift. For example, workers who thrived performing repetitive tasks will see their jobs being replaced by AI systems. In those instances, the workers’ identities and how they perceive themselves will need to shift with their changing environment… we will need to naturally shift our own social identities to adapt to this new world.” (Wu 3) This shows that people will adapt to whatever the circumstances may be. In this case, individuals will adapt to a society with no original thought. With no individuality, it would not only directly affect the way a society would function, but would essentially strip people of their identities and everyone will be the same.

With the advancements of artificial intelligence, social interaction is put at high risk. If society fully replaced human to human interaction, with human to artificial intelligence interaction, society would lack real, personal connections. In Can Social Interaction Constitute Social Cognition, Hanne De Jaegher, Ezequiel Di Paolo, and Shaun Gallagher states “A definition of social interaction should capture these intuitions concerning the engagement of at least two agents in a complex co-regulated pattern. Engagement can correspond to fluctuating feelings of connectedness with the other – whose meaning sometimes seems transparent and sometimes opaque – and of increasing and decreasing possibilities for participation. This experience sometimes turns into that of being taken up in the flow of the interaction” (Jaegher et al. 442) This shows that an interaction should provide a sense of connectedness. By connecting and building strong ties with family, friends and the community, people tend to feel a sense of security, support, and purpose. George Herbert Mead believed that the conceptualization of ourselves can be broken into two parts: the “me” and the “I”. The “me” regulates our behavior based on how we think that others perceive us, while the “I” is the reaction caused from the attitude of a community. Mead believes the conceptualization of ourselves are defined through the interactions encountered in the social realm. Adolescence is an important time to build social skills and form identity, but with the substitution of AI interaction for real-life interaction, teens will experience major impacts on their social and emotional development.

Human interaction is extremely important for one to understand and perceive their own self. Erving Goffman discovered that the self is collectively produced in the Presentation of Self. He proves that human interaction is so complex that roles are created within a society to provide purpose. Presentation of Self elaborated on the idea of roles in a set society by directly dividing an individual into two parts: the performer and the character. “...the very structure of the self can be seen in terms of how we arrange for such performances in our Anglo-American society” (Goffman 256). This entails that the social world is made up through an abundance of performances by an enormous amount of actors, in a variation of settings. Erving Goffman proposes that we find our identities through the process of performing and observing the way we execute the performance. In “How AI will rewire us”, Nicholas A. Christakis states “But adding artificial intelligence to our midst could be much more disruptive. Especially as machines are made to look and act like us and to insinuate themselves deeply into our lives, they may change how loving or friendly or kind we are—not just in our direct interactions with the machines in question, but in our interactions with one another.” (Christakis 1) This directly shows the potential threat that artificial intelligence brings upon a community. Adding AI to a social environment can only cause humans to behave differently, whether it be shown through daily social skills or something as simple as productivity.

The current technological improvements regarding AI, have created a widespread fear of job loss. After looking at whose specific job is at risk it is important to consider the numbers, how many jobs are being taken? Arto Baltayan, technology writer and technical documentations specialist stated in his article, “Robots, Automation and Technology Taking Over-- Is Your Job At Risk?”, “Between 2000 and 2010, the United States lost over five-and-a-half million jobs in the manufacturing sector,” (Baltayan 1) This shows that the amount of jobs being lost in the United States is extremely high, on top of that, all this evidence is only talking about one sector. Moreover, artificial intelligence technology is not just affecting employees in manufacturing, but has a significant effect on all jobs. William M. Rodgers, professor of public policy at Rutgers University stated “Yet most analysis tends to be prospective in nature, and estimates of future impacts on employment vary widely, with some studies predicting that as many as 50 percent of all workers are at risk of losing their jobs to automation.” (Rodgers 1) This shows that the integration of artificial intelligence does not only impact the manufacturing sector, but has a broader effect on all aspects of the workforce contributing to the predicted 50 percent of all workers losing their jobs to artificial intelligence technology. Without a given purpose, an individual faces the threat of a perception and identity crisis. If artificial intelligence learns how to possess a higher consciousness to function with human behaviors and habits, the people will be forced to learn how to adapt to a new technological world.

Human beings are conscious not only of the world around them but also of themselves: their activities, their bodies, and their mental lives. Changes to consciousness can result in changes in perception, thinking, understanding, and interpretations of the world. In “Society, consciousness and change—An inquiry into Pentti Malaska's futures thinking”, Markku Malaska states “The dynamics of development, where extensive and intensive stages alternate at the same time as regenerative growth forces development into a specific direction.” (Malaska 61) This can be applied to the effects of artificial intelligence because these technological advancements are a major change that will bring upon an inevitable outcome. Adding artificial intelligence to a social environment, will eventually lead to a change in the way society performs. This initially starts with a single individual and their cognition processes being altered by the outside factor. One may ask, if the addition of AI will only bring upon questionable change, why do it? In The impact of artificial intelligence on human society and bioethics, Michael Cheng-Tek Tai states “History tells us that human is always looking for something faster, easier, more effective, and convenient to finish the task they work on; therefore, the pressure for further development motivates humankind to look for a new and better way of doing things.” (Tai 1) This is able to explain the motives behind developing a human society. As the human race has the ability to raise their consciousness higher, they tend to strive for more, without consideration of the possible consequences.

Overall, it can be shown that artificial intelligence can have negative effects on one’s perception of self due to a multitude of reasons. One being the limitations placed on one’s ability to create their own ideas and opinions. Without the influence of others original thoughts and ideas, there would be no free expression and individuality. Individuality is very important when it comes to the consciousness of one’s self. This is because one feels a sense of reassurance in knowing that they have an idea of who they are, or what their identity consists of. A major contributing factor to one’s sense of purpose, that should not go unmentioned, would be the type of job or position that one hold’s. When an individual lacks a sense of purpose, they become susceptible to a loss of self-awareness. Artificial intelligence is not able to raise it’s consciousness like humans, but once it is able to expand its potential, many will fear for their jobs. This will essentially lead to a dependence on artificial intelligence. With a society reliant on AI, many traits of independence and self-sufficiency will deteriorate. The consciousness of self is heavily affected by the surrounding community. One may even say, the consciousness of self can develop solely from the environmental factors one is exposed to. With a heavy reliance on artificial intelligence, social interaction will eventually lose the personal connection and meaning. We find our identities through the process of performing and observing the way we execute our performance.
chunks.label: Effects of AI on consciousness of self
chunks.what_happened: The student presents an academic essay analyzing how artificial intelligence negatively affects individuality, original thought, social interaction, and employment, referencing various sociological theorists.

chunks.text:
Religion is a very complex concept and is interpreted differently by all people within the collective consciousness. Many could even consider religion to be an effect of the collective consciousness. In “Microfoundations”, Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdams can be closely analyzed and compared to Yuval Noah Harari’s book, 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, to show how humans have evolved consciously, leading to further exploration of religion, bringing upon new questions that examine the intentions and purpose.

McAdams and Fligstein propose the theory that humans can raise their consciousness to further grasp and understand the meaning of human existence. Religion, in many cases, tries to define a purpose in an individual’s life. This can be seen as a result of the collective consciousness because religion was formed throughout society as a way to explain a higher consciousness. People tend to gravitate towards order and direction because of their nature. Harari is able to explain the causes of this human nature by stating that people look for this so-called order through institutions such as religion.

All in all, religion is a result of the collective consciousness because of people’s need to justify and explain daily issues. Moreover, religion is used to help humans cope and understand things that cannot be explained by math or science. The existence of religion influences modern day society as a whole by providing answers to many unanswerable questions.
chunks.label: Religion and collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how religion is an effect of the collective consciousness and examines ideas from Fligstein, McAdams, and Harari regarding human consciousness and the search for order.

chunks.text:
In the media, we are exposed to jaw dropping, terrifying news that is hard for an adult, but also teenagers and children to watch. We have all been drug into endless talk about the market, the biggest busts about religion, and we have heard it all, how do we know what is right? Yuval Noah Harari’s 21 Lessons for the 21st Century covers several topics including working, artificial intelligence, social justice, community, several belief systems, war, terrorism, nationalism, education, and several other topics. While heading straight on to several controversial and confusing ideas, some sociologists may agree with things he said, or some may have come to different conclusions. A couple of these a sharing of opinion when it comes to capitalism and now this country is being run with workers and employees and include differencing in opinion over religion. In this paper I will be analyzing how Harari believed capitalism affected the workers along with Weber and Marx, as well as how religion impacted society versus Durkheim, Maryanski, and Turner.

One of the things that Harari wrote about was the idea of capitalism. Harari believed that the economy and how jobs were run in the first place was something that would be drastically changing in the years to come. Machines would take over jobs, new jobs would be created, but the economy and working class would not be able to keep up. Harari believed that the system was just too complex for one man to understand. In the end, artificial intelligence would be able to take over any job and there may be a worthless class of people who are not educated for the next job above. Harari states, “Nevertheless, in the long run no job will remain absolutely safe from automation (26).” From programs made to detect human emotions, to software that can increase knowledge to each individual AI worker, the need for the limited human mind will decrease. When it comes to the current working class, Harari believes that this system is destroying its workers by basically chewing them up and spitting them back out once they are done working. We have made a piece of paper have a respected value, become enslaved to it, and are constantly putting ourselves to work just to survive. This means that corporations are being selfish and money greedy. Corporations build their structure based on their own religion and/or morals. This could actually be hurting employees that do not exactly agree with this. For example, for holidays, what days are breaks and when do people still need to come in even if it is another employee’s holiday. This also can hurt someone’s self esteem by enforcing rules of how they dress, look, act, or perform in general. Not only this, but it trains the employee’s brain to figure out what is best for the buyer before themselves. The corporation will not only use its employees, but also cookies and data on other websites to see how to attract more people to buy their products. Harari believe data is knowledge, knowledge is power, and power is expensive – but worth the pretty penny. Corporations are able to create ads targeted at a specific group of people who they know will see it and invest in their product. This idea of taking advantage of the knowledge of the public, it’s utter hardships on employees, and possibility of being overturned by artificial intelligence, is why Harari does not approve or favor the capitalist society that runs our country.

Several other sociologists are also perplexed over the idea of capitalism and the burden it creates for its employees. Max Weber, in the Spirit of Capitalism, found the idea peculiar because while many people find joy in being able to work toward a common goal, accomplish things, and receive reward for the work they put in, people are still giving up much of their time and happiness for it. In fact, Weber believes that people give up the chance of spontaneity, freedom, and become a completely different person in their work field. The worker’s “outside life” is considered a separate life, and one that becomes something a worker would look forward to because of their job being so terrible. Karl Marx was also someone who empathized with the workers who were put under the capitalist economy. He called it “Estranged Labor”. He believed that people who worked under capitalism was basically turned into an animal and used for profit. Because of the need for money to survive, Marx says that people are coerced into labor, not for the satisfaction of completing or accomplishing anything, but just to make ends meet for themselves and/or their families. The worker becomes solely focused on survival instead of life and having fun, being spontaneous, or just enjoying the moment. Marx believed that capitalism does not help the workers, just the large CEOs of corporations, and the person becomes the tool to the end product, destroying the idea of the purpose of humans. While he admits humans are easily adaptable to life threatening situations, he believes that the market lowers us to the value of an animal. The labor becomes objectified because the value comes from your product and what you are able to produce. Why do people get raises or fired? – their outcomes at work.

Marx also talks about how there are 4 dimensions of alienation. People can be alienated from the process of labor, from the product, from other workers, or just from yourself. He believes that working in this environment makes it hard to avoid these types of alienation. From the process and product was how much you are valued because of your work, from other workers due to the fact that no one shares the same fate, and last from yourself and how you value and make your work meaningful to you, even if that is challenging in a workplace you do not enjoy. Harari, Weber, and Marx all at least were skeptical of the process of capitalism, but all can see that it does not put a worker first and can harm them individually when putting them into the work force. Harari was the one to think further ahead to see that even as employees are not being treated correctly now, it may get worse as we progressively move forward with artificial intelligence.

Even with some in agreement, some of the things Harari argued have not been completely agreed upon among other sociologists. One of these differences was the impact that religion had on a group of people, a society, a definition of a way of life. Harari did admit to being a religious person himself, but he was objective toward how it may have affected society. Harari believed it brought false teaching, fake news, and different ideas of how history came about. He believed that religion was basically a guideline for society and a way to live. It helped to cope with questions that they couldn’t answer, but many didn’t ever know if this “God” was a creator or a lawmaker. Societies will use the story of divine mystery to legitimatize social order, even when no one really has all the answers. Secularism can even be an issue according to Harari because he believes that it is not prepared for the issues of the 21st century. Because of our corrupt justice system, it is hard to enforce that every person has intrinsic value.

Along with the struggle for people to be treated of equal value, he learned that those with different religious backgrounds will have different teachings about history. Not even just as a timeline of when the earth and universe was created, but also with who had great discoveries, inventions, or began different things. For example, Harari used the example of yoga, while known to be a Buddhist tradition, some believe that someone from the Bible actually created it as a gift to a society. Lastly, Harari also believes that we are in a post-truth era. Although he says it has been that way from the Stone Age, he believes that this has allowed for fake news, births of other false religions and teaching, and false power obsessions. He believes that this allows for a concept called group think which can limit a person's individuality and lead them to be loyal to a cause blindly, without doing their own research. He believes that a society has actually gotten dumber due to the fact that the collective consciousness has gotten smarter, but individually we are weaker. We know someone who can fix or make something that we cannot do. Not only this, but many of us will accept the “truth” that we can see on television or on the internet because of our lack of knowledge and research ourselves. We trust that those who are supposed to do their jobs correctly, will do them. As stated earlier, however, it is apparent that corporations will do what they must to bring in the most amount of money. This can set a perfect pathway for false advertising, teaching, and news. Many people in power, who have the money to bend or cut the truth from the public, will do what they need to stay in good standing to make money. Harari states that people in power that do this is what makes up politics, but if it happens over hundreds or thousands of years, it becomes a religion. These point Harari states makes religion out to be where there may be less good and more corrupt and messiness.

However, in past units, there would be other sociologists that would disagree with Harari. Maryanski and Turner studied that adaptation of early Morotopithecus, a type of ape that was able to thrive over other types of apes. They found that emotions were important for the expansion of cognition in early species, and with that came religion. Their memory was enhanced, they were able to make more rational decisions, and they gave things meaning and connections. Without that, they would not have been able to survive and thrive as well, according to Maryanski and Turner. Durkheim also believed that religion was actually important to study and it made strong societies. He believed that all the great social institutions are born in religion. A religion was able to impact the collective consciousness of the society with making symbols, artifacts, a narrative, a day, or really anything has meaning and value to a society. With this said, religion was believed to be crucially important to societies.

Harari believed that the economy and capitalism could crush an individual self, and religion would question an individual self. Which was right, what was wrong, and if you are completing life as you are supposed to. While Harari believed having questions you could not answer was better than answers you could not question, it gives hard direction for someone completing life. Several sociologists agreed with Harari and his findings with a couple also disagreeing. However, there could be a third perspective that something could have been good back then, but without change, it does not work for society now. This is a point that Harari was making. Societies are constantly changing, growing, and upgrading. If traditions do not change and reform, then our society may crumble by unknowns, artificial intelligence, and violence. Both capitalism and religion will make an individual question their self-worth, just depends – where do you see yourself belonging?

Sources:

Harari, Y. (2019). 21 lessons for the 21st century. Vintage.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of capitalism and religion
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on and compares views from Harari, Marx, Weber, Maryanski, Turner, and Durkheim regarding capitalism, labor, alienation, and religion.

n30c97a06.title: Analyzing Systemic Racism in Criminal Justice

chunks.text:
The rate of imprisonment in the United States has seen a five times increase since 1972 and 40% of those prisoners are Black. This may come as a surprise since Black Americans make up only 13% of the population, but there is evidence to suggest that those numbers are engineered by a corrupt Criminal Justice system. For every 100,000 Black Americans, 2,306 of them are incarcerated. Compare that to white Americans, where for every 100,000 there are 450 incarcerated individuals, and you begin to see a trend (Sakala 2014). In light of recent events in the news, like the trial of Derek Chauvin for the murder of George Floyd, more people than ever are talking about police brutality and the Criminal Justice system. The racism goes farther than police brutality, however, and it infects even the deepest roots of our prison system. The American Criminal Justice System does not just passively perpetuate systematic racism in the United States through the personal prejudices of a few police officers, but rather it is founded and based upon discrimination as an inherent mechanism by which it operates. The War on Drugs, mass incarceration, police brutality, and wrongful convictions are all integral to the oppression seen by this system.

White Privilege by Peggy McIntosh outlines several things, 26 to be exact, that are daily occurrences of White Privilege that white people rarely think about being a privilege. White people have the privilege of not having their communities ravaged during the War on Drugs. White people have the privilege of simply existing around police officers without fearing for their safety because of the color of their skin. White people have the privilege of not losing their mothers, fathers, brothers, and sisters all to a prison system that incarcerates them at a higher rate than people of different skin color. White people have the privilege of having a fair and just trial, where they do not know in the back of their minds that people of their skin color are being wrongfully put to death and imprisoned at a higher rate than any other skin color. These things are all happening behind the scenes, but are very purposeful in their effect on Black communities.

“We knew we couldn’t make it illegal to be either against the war or black, but by getting the public to associate the hippies with marijuana and blacks with heroin, and then criminalizing both heavily, we could disrupt those communities. We could arrest their leaders, raid their homes, break up their meetings, and vilify them night after night on the evening news. Did we know we were lying about the drugs? Of course, we did” (Baum 2016). This quote said by John Ehrlichman, who was the Assistant to Domestic Affairs of President Richard Nixon, shows how deep racism runs in the War on Drugs. The War on Drugs was not the first or only instance of Black people being wrongly blamed for an ongoing drug problem in the United States (Lusane, and Desmond 1991). In the late 1880s, cocaine was being included in everything from medicine to soft drinks and cigarettes. By 1906, the Pure Food and Drug Act was passed which required any product manufacturer to tell consumers that their products contained addictive drugs or substances. A few years later in 1909, Dr. Hamilton Wright would be chosen by President Theodore Roosevelt to lead a campaign to stop the opium trade in Asia. In 1910, he would release the Report on the International Opium Commission, which proved to employ racist imagery and scapegoating to appeal to the racism of white Americans. The report would include lies about Black people, even going as far as to propose that cocaine use made them bulletproof, gave them unimaginable strength, and, worst of all, encouraged them to rape women. This was a blatant lie, as no evidence at the time suggested that Black men used cocaine at a higher rate than any other demographic. These lies had disastrous effects, resulting in the “Red Summer” of 1919 where almost seventy lynchings were recorded (Lusane, and Desmond 1991).

Over the next decade, many more decisions would be made to undermine Black communities in America. The Mafia, with their ever-growing power in the 1950s, decided to sell hard drugs almost exclusively to Black Americans. This decision created a Heroin addiction epidemic of intense proportions which disproportionally affected Black communities. Over many years of struggling with addiction, Black communities would turn to drug dealing and gangs to at least make some money off of their growing drug problem. The government’s solution to this problem was vastly more destructive than helpful. Instead of understanding the root of the drug problem in Black neighborhoods, the solution was to build prisons and fill them with said Black neighborhoods (Lusane, and Desmond 1991). This leads to the next mechanism used by the criminal justice system to undermine Black communities in the United States: mass incarceration.

According to a report released by The Sentencing Project in 1994, one in three Black American men ages 20-29 is under the control of the criminal justice system, meaning in prison, on parole, or on probation (Mauer, and Huling 1995). As stated previously, Black Americans make up 40% of the prison population while only making up 13% of the American population. The logical conclusion is not that Black Americans do more crime, but rather that the laws are affecting them disproportionately. The cities that regularly house the poorest and most vulnerable citizens are also the most paroled, and as a result, produce more incarcerations. The judgment cannot necessarily be made that these neighborhoods have more crime happening in them, just that preconceived notions influence increased rates of police intervention (Fagan et al. 2003). As much of the effect incarceration has on the actual individuals being incarcerated, it is also worth noting that families of these individuals may bear more of the hardships of their families being ripped apart from the inside out. When you take into account fathers and mothers leaving children to grandparents, children going into the foster system, and children turning to sell drugs as a way to survive, the cycle continues exponentially (Braman 2003). It was previously determined that drug laws disproportionately affect Black Americans, and these drug laws are working to strip defendants of their rights to a fair trial. The judicial system works to ‘overcharge’ defendants to effectively scare them into waiving their rights to trial by pleading guilty. This causes the majority, more than 90% in some cases, of drug-related cases being ended by guilty pleas rather than a trial (Roberts 2008).

Mass incarceration leads to a disproportionately high number of Black felons. Felons are stripped of their rights to vote or bear arms. Felons also may not be able to travel freely, are barred from employment in some fields, and may lose parental rights to any children they may have and may not participate in many forms of public aid like food stamps and public housing ("What Rights Do Convicted Felons Lose?"). In modern prison systems, all felons are stripped of these rights, but it wasn’t always this way. In the late 1860s, some Southern states passed laws to punish crimes by removing their rights to vote, but they were assigned to crimes like burglary, thievery, adultery, and those convicted of domestic violence, all of which were mainly committed by Black people. Those convicted of murder, however, were not stripped of their right to vote. It can only be assumed that is because more white people were convicted of murder than Black people (Roberts 2008).

There is yet another angle to view this from, however, if we consider that Black Americans are being incarcerated and prosecuted at a higher rate than white Americans, we can also infer that there is a higher percentage of Black Americans being wrongfully accused as well. As of October 2016, Black Americans make up 47% of exonerations listed in the National Registry of Exonerations (Gross et al. 2017). This is not even taking into account the 1,800 people who were framed for crimes as a part of several large scandals, later set straight with “group exonerations.” Innocent Black Americans are seven times more likely to be falsely accused of murder and three-and-a-half times more likely to be falsely accused of sexual assault. They are also five times more likely to be arrested for illegal drug-related crimes, despite using drugs at the same rates as white Americans. Black people are more likely to be stopped and searched concerning drug crimes than white Americans, which is already determined to be deadly in some cases of police brutality. There have even been cases of police officers blatantly lying to incarcerate Black people for drug-related crimes. In 1999 Tom Coleman, an undercover narcotics officer, framed 39 people, most being Black, for selling cocaine. In 2003, 35 of those people were found innocent and Coleman was found guilty of perjury. The cocaine that he proposed was being sold by these people came from cocaine that he owned and bought (Gross et al. 2017).

Police officers have long brought violence to Black communities and often serve as judge, jury, and executioner for many. The media representation of the Derek Chauvin trial has thrown police brutality into the minds of more American’s than ever, but his trial is something that many Black Americans do not have the privilege to be a part of. The criminal justice system works hard to convince the American public that these are isolated events of bad people doing bad things, rather than inherent and systematic racism ingrained in the very fibers of every police uniform worn in this country. Police officers choose to protect other police officers, rather than choosing to protect and serve the people they promised they would, this is often called “the blue wall of silence” (Roberts 2008). If we cannot trust the very people who are entrusted to uphold and enforce our laws to not allow their prejudices to influence who they arrest, who can we trust? The answer is that we should have never trusted these officers in the first place because they are products of an entire system that was built to produce people with the power over life and death and to give them those prejudices.

After outlining four distinct ways the criminal justice system strives to undermine and poison Black communities in America, it is obvious that the system has less of a passive role in systematic racism and more of a foundational and oppressive role. The War on Drugs, dating back to far before Nixon or Reagan’s presidency, simultaneously spread horrible rumors about Black Americans and their role in the growing drug problem in the early 1990s, and later got Black communities dependent on heroin. Mass incarceration put many Black Americans back into the exploitive prison labor system, reminiscent of slavery work conditions, tore apart their families and communities, and lead to the over-policing of Black neighborhoods that we still struggle heavily with. Black Americans who were convicted of felonies also lose a lot of their rights, most devastatingly, the right to public aid that would help to support their families as well as being able to be employed in several fields. This further ruins Black communities and allows young Black people to grow up in unstable situations, completely out of their control. Wrongful convictions affect Black Americans at a higher rate than white Americans and therefore contribute in their own way to the destruction of Black communities and their ways of life. Police officers are allowed and encouraged by the criminal justice system to assume that Black people are violent and a danger to them and others. This must be recognized as a system that was built on the oppression of Black people and not just an unfortunate byproduct. As slavery was made illegal, America turned to “separate-but-equal.” As that was outlawed, lawmakers and public officials found entirely new ways to ensure that Black Americans would never be equal. These have no place in modern America and the system by which they are allowed to continue happening has to be reformed or abolished before any more damage is done to Black communities in America.

References

Baum, Dan. "Legalize It All: How To Win The War On Drugs". Harper's Magazine, 2016, https://harpers.org/archive/2016/04/legalize-it-all/. Accessed 28 Apr 2021.

Braman, Donald. Families And Incarceration. U.S. Department Of Justice, 2003, https://www.ojp.gov/pdffiles1/nij/grants/202981.pdf. Accessed 28 Apr 2021.

Gross, Samuel et al. RACE AND WRONGFUL CONVICTIONS IN THE UNITED STATES. National Registry Of Exonerations, 2017, http://www.law.umich.edu/special/exoneration/Documents/Race_and_Wrongful_Convictions.pdf. Accessed 28 Apr 2021.

Lusane, Clarence, and Dennis Desmond. Pipe Dream Blues. South End Press, 1991, pp. 32-35, 38-39, 44.
