chunks.label: Systemic racism in the criminal justice system
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes systemic racism within the American criminal justice system, discussing mass incarceration, the War on Drugs, police brutality, wrongful convictions, and includes academic references.

nafbb3613.title: Serving Wealth as a Working Student

chunks.text:
How skewed is the distribution of wealth really in America? Everyone is taught that this country gives everyone equal opportunities as long as you work hard. But the truth is, no matter how hard you work the likelihood of growing up the class system is close to none. Most people don’t know this, but the 1% of Americans own 40% of the country's wealth, which is around 21.6 trillion dollars. The top 80-99% own 53%, leaving the bottom 80% of the country with only 7% (3.78 trillion). This distribution of wealth is extremely unjust, and it is hidden from most people to hide the motives of this country.

The key word people in the public eye use to hide this is “middle class.” Everyone who has a job is considered middle class. But why are they held to the same standard? Someone who works as a doctor makes enough money to go on unlimited vacations, splurge on unessentials, and never has to worry about debt. Yet someone who works as a teacher struggles to pay rent, has a side job, and is still paying off her student loans from school. These two people should not be categorized together, but they are. The majority of people place themselves in the general term of “middle class,” because they are afraid to admit that the country's wealth is favored towards making the rich richer.
chunks.label: Wealth inequality and the myth of the middle class
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the skewed distribution of wealth in America and how the label 'middle class' hides inequality.

chunks.text: I have experienced this unequal distribution of wealth first hand. I am a lower middle class student, and my parents worked hard to make me live an average life. I work in a restaurant here in Wilmington, where I make a $4 hourly salary. I work hard, sometimes finding myself catching my breath and seeing burn marks, bruises, and sweat covering my body after each shift. Yet when I see the managers sitting in an office, going through files, making a schedule; they make ten times what I do. How is that fair? They certainly don’t work ten times harder than I do.
chunks.label: Working hard as a server while managers make more
chunks.what_happened: The student works a physically demanding restaurant job for low pay and observes that their managers do less physical work while earning significantly more.

chunks.text:
The same goes for ceo’s of a company; they make 380 times what their average worker’s salary is, but is their job really 380 times harder? What is the purpose of boasting about his American Dream that hard work will get you far when those that work the hardest get the short end of the stick? The American Dream is advertised to get the country's lower class workers to do the dirty jobs that need to be done that no one else wants to do. Wealth comes more commonly through luck or inheritance, certainly not hard work.

I gain a lot of insight by serving the rich. They tend to be stuck up, judgemental, and usually have something to complain about. I work in a restaurant with ocean views and quality food and service. Yet, rich customers still tend to come in with smug looks on their face like they are too good to be there.
chunks.label: Critique of CEO pay and wealthy restaurant customers
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on executive pay disparity, the falsehood of the American Dream, and general attitudes of rich patrons at their restaurant.

chunks.text: I will never forget this one table, the second I approach them I get interrupted before I could even tell them my name. “Iced water with lemon on the side and a glass of chardonnay” she said, barely making eye contact. I noticed an extremely shiny necklace along with rings that probably cost more than my tuition. After I get their drinks, they make comments about things on the menu that they would never get. The lady finally orders but makes numerous changes to how the food is prepared, saying she doesn’t like spice but wants extra vegetables. When the food comes out, I hear her say “what is that,” in the snootiest tone I’ve ever heard. I explain to her that the fish pan seared, and she says it doesn’t look right, since her husband got the blackened. “I wanted what my husband got,” she says immediately. I have to hold in my emotions and take a breath before responding to people like this. “Your husband got the blackened grouper, which is spicy. I can bring out a side of blackened seasoning for you if you would like.” “No, you can just take it back.” I look at her and think about how dumb she is and how dumb I am going to look when I bring this plate back. “Of course, I’ll bring you a new one.” I tell the kitchen to make it on the fly, and she is brought a new fish within 5 minutes. I hand her the new dish and ask if she would like anything else. She says no but when I come back she says, “My fish is cooked strangely, I would like it well done.” When I asked her how she would like it cooked the first time she said medium. “And another glass of wine, with extra ice on the side. My ice has been empty for a while and I've seen you come back and forth without refilling it” she hands me her empty glass for ice and grossly smiles. “Yes of course,” I responded, biting my tongue. How rude, I think to myself. I walk away, tell the kitchen the fish is well done, and I nearly burn my fingers grabbing the new plate. The lady and her husband are enjoying their meal and I watch her beverages like a hawk, always keeping them refilled and checking up on them. “I want more butter” “We need more napkins.” “We need salt and pepper.” “We need more refills.” She has to be doing this on purpose. She waited until each time I arrived at the table and asked for everything one by one instead of all at once. I didn’t have time to run back and forth 5 separate times. No matter how much I had already on my plate or how busy I got, I still did everything with a smile. It took everything out of me to hand everything to her with a smile and in a nice tone of voice. When she finally asks for her check, the plate is cleared and the total comes to around $100 for the two of them. I pick up the check, and the tip is zero.
chunks.label: Serving an entitled, demanding customer who left no tip
chunks.what_happened: The student served a rude, wealthy woman and her husband who repeatedly sent food back and made separate demands, only to leave zero tip on a $100 bill.

chunks.text:
I made zero dollars serving what seemed to be an extremely privileged woman, who I needed extreme patience and diligence to serve. I gave her excellent service and she chose to selfishly get it for free. That woman seemed extremely well off, and clearly I am not since I am a 19 year old server, barely getting by. I often find myself frustrated when it comes to dealing with rich people who inherited their parents' wealth. They don’t know what it is like to struggle, and probably never will. They don’t know about basic human decency, or about the little things in life and how money doesn’t buy happiness. The fact that someone could group us in the same category as “middle class,” is absurd. Nobody wants to admit that there are more than 3 classes, and those who aren’t part of the top classes have little to no chance of moving up. There are hundreds of multi-billionaires in the U.S., yet for someone who makes the average salary ($35,672) it would take them 28,033 years or 400 lifetimes just to make $1 billion. Those who work harder jobs are essential in making this country run, yet are compensated little to nothing.

The distribution of wealth in this country makes people like the woman I served, continue to treat others in a horrible manner. She is a prime example of showing how selfish the rich are with their money, and how they’ll do anything to keep it to themselves. The higher powers have found a way to continue this scheme, all through the word of “middle class.” By saying that the majority of the country is in one class, they hide the fact that the majority of the country's wealth goes to the 1%, and those who have inherited wealth are better off than those who work hard. It is a shame that a girl like me has to see this the hard way, how I have to suffer through the treatment of those who will never know what it is like to be on the other side of this spectrum. I hope one day the real American Dream is exposed, and there is action taken to change the system of letting the rich take what should be distributed to those who work harder than them.
chunks.label: Reflections on wealth privilege, class, and the American Dream
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on being left no tip, the arrogance of the wealthy, class disparity in America, and calls for exposure of the flawed American Dream.

chunks.text:
America has not had the traditional forms of power held for most of its existence. As when compared to Europe, there has not any singular church to rule over the country as was the case in Europe for centuries, or a very large government to hold all the power as it was with nation-states in Europe or an extremely powerful military that could threaten to overthrow the government until very recently in 1940, relatively recent in the scope of 1776 to now. As G. William Domhoff points out then, there is only one way in which power can be accumulated in America, gaining economic power. This through the years has created its own social class of power elites in America that doesn’t put these people in positions as public policymakers like congressmen and women, but as corporate executives and members of the 1% that begin to decide everything through social circles that tend to involve board members of 80%-90% of all corporations in the United States.

These corporations while at first may have been limited to a few large media companies like big television networks like NBC and ABC and big newspapers like the LA Times and New York Times, the power elite’s control over the media has grown since then. With the boom of the internet and social media over the past 20 years, the power elite has been put in a better position to influence public policy and the general public’s opinion on policy through the usage of algorithms that have been put in place on social media like on Facebook which has created polarization on both sides of political debates.

G. William Domhoff defines in his work, “Power in America,” the three indicators of power as who benefits, who governs, and who wins. In these indicators, the corporate executives are able to hold positions of economic power that they financially benefit from. But also benefit from the political power they are able to hold in the usage of their funds for donations to campaigns of candidates that they either already influence or align with the beliefs of the power elite in turn putting the power elite in charge of the policymaking process allowing them to govern. As mentioned before, Domhoff points out that 15-20% of corporate directors that sit on 2 or more boards of directors that make up 80% to 90% of the largest corporations in the US into what is a very well-connected corporate community. Facebook, Twitter, and Instagram consist of these very large corporations now and likely have board members that are part of the “inner circle” 15-20% that influence the entire corporate community. This allows the corporations and in turn, the power elite to put who they desire in office to put in policies that benefit these large corporations and 1% of society more than the majority of Americans meaning that these power elites continue to win with those they put into office.

How does the power elite manage to win over public opinion on policies that should seem clear to not benefit the general public that is actually in control of the election process in America? This is where the influence of social media comes into play for politics. In an article written by Taiana Bucher, she evaluates the new algorithms that Facebook is putting into place and how these algorithms create misleading information to users in terms of the news they believe they are receiving. In her article, Bucher points out that Facebook models its homepage so that down the middle is a column titled, “News Feed” which is split into two types of Top News and Most Recent. Top News is what is primarily shown in the News Feed which the algorithm for determining what is, “Top News” is related to pages people interact with the most and like the most. Misleading the readers then to think that everything that pops up in their News Feed is the actual News when in reality, it is just news catered to your interests which can lead to the common misinformation we regularly read about when someone ends up only interacting with news sources of one political viewpoint. This is how the power elite gains public support for policymakers that would not normally be supported by the people. Passive misinformation can happen this way where the target audiences the power elite wants to reach can use this algorithm and others like it on other social media platforms to have users engage with news sources that consistently pump out information those users agree with and could spin that information to have that policymaker sound like they agree with what the general public wants.

This has put America on a trajectory where information and news are not dictated by fact, but by those who have the most engagement on their respective social media sites. This is a future that Stephan Lewandowsky and his other writers in their article about the era they labeled as the “post-truth” era have laid out and also fear that we are going towards. Lewandowsky and the other writers of the article look to the 2016 presidential election to show that this is already been proven to have worked with the popularity of what is said is more valued more than what is true. As they cite that an independent fact-checker known as PolitiFact found that during their respective campaigns, 70% of all statements made by Donald Trump were false as compared to the 26% of all statements made by Hillary Clinton during the campaign were false. Yet, Donald Trump was elected president of the United States over Hilary Clinton which Lewandowsky et. al. point to the fact that pro-Trump statements on Twitter were 4 times as prevalent as pro-Clinton statements on Twitter due to active efforts by pro-Trump Tweetbots that managed to skyrocket Trump’s interaction with the algorithm to get more viewership and in turn popularity on Twitter than what might be anticipated. Trump exists as one of the most obvious symbols of the power elite, who has been a one-percenter since the 1980s and has been the face of American wealth for over 40 years as a business executive. As a member of the power elite and probably a member of those inner circles of the corporate community that dictate the plans that are set into motion by these corporations, Donald Trump knew how to effectively manipulate the algorithms that were set in place to allow the very thing he did, which was win the election, through understanding how to just gain enough popularity through the usage of social media to influence an entire election for the US Presidency.

This alone is enough of a sign for how we have entered into the “post-truth” era of America. The fact that the highest office in America, which obviously in the past has been influenced by the power elite but never directly held by the power elite, was attainable through manipulation with an algorithm on a website and app used by the majority of American people should be a massive red flag to the people of America. Yes, misinformation can be combatted through diligent solo research on topics important to each individual but that alone is part of the problem. The fact that the people have to actively go out of their way to go to websites and news sources they don’t normally go to, to ensure that they aren’t being misinformed by the information they receive on sites like Twitter and Facebook that is catered to them by the algorithm. If an algorithm has a misinformation problem that literally placed a man from the power elite into the highest office of the United States that did not have the best interests of the majority population of America at heart and even showed it multiple times throughout his campaign, then maybe something should be done about the algorithms, not just the methods Americans should go about getting their information.

Some people have realized the influence that these algorithms can have when controlled in such a manner. That is why as Robert Gorwa writes in his article explaining platform governance, he cites the calls in Europe and many other countries too for these social media platforms to have a form of rules and regulations that must be followed. As it stands right now on the internet, there are no real laws or regulations for social media platforms when it comes to the information they provide, or don’t provide to their users in terms of the news. But, with the explorations in platform governance that Gorwa references, there may soon enough be a model for the United States to base their own platform governance laws on if what is being sought after in the EU is reliable and works to help solve misinformation and polarization issues that are so prevalent on social media platforms.

Social media’s influence cannot be ignored. It has influenced the entire American people through misinformation and the withholding of information that hasn’t ever been seen on this scale before. Yes, the power elite, who have always been in charge of media outlets have never spread misinformation on this level before, but that is because the usage of algorithms and the relative anonymity that is generally present on the internet means that they cannot be held liable largely for what occurs. If misinformation gets blamed for creating presidencies like Donald Trump where other power elites run and win, it can only be blamed on a math equation that was set up to help people see more of what that equation believes each user should see. Whether it was inadvertent or not, an algorithm has been set up across the primary American social media platforms that have been proven to be easily manipulated and when manipulated can jettison a man who nobody thought would ever be president into the highest office of the United States because of, in part, a Twitter algorithm. For better, or for worse these algorithms have significantly changed the lives of Americans, and the sooner we collectively realize the power and influence the algorithms have over us all and the information we do and do not see and that these algorithms are, to some extent, understood by the power elite to the point that they understand how they can be manipulated.
chunks.label: The power elite, social media algorithms, and misinformation
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological theories and academic articles regarding the American power elite, corporate influence, social media algorithms, and political misinformation.

chunks.text:
According to sociologist expert Dr. Nicki Lisa Cole, “collective consciousness can be defined as a fundamental, sociologically concept that refers to a set of shared beliefs, ideas, attitudes, and knowledge that are common to a social group or society.” (Cole 1) When looking at the readings, Microfoundations and The Cultural Logic and Collective Representations, there are contradicting ideas among the two. Microfoundations makes comparisons of homo sapiens and hominids to show parallels of consciousness. It also mentions the motives among society and relates them to doubt and fear. The Cultural Logic and Collective Representations discusses points of individuals in society creating their own realities. It also delves into science and how people trust the evidence behind it. After analysis of the two readings, Fligstein and MacAdams take a social approach to explaining collective consciousness, while Durkheim takes a scientific approach.

Microfoundations was able to elaborate the similarities between the human species and ape. Fligstein and MacAdams demonstrate parallels of consciousness through the comparison of tendencies of homo species. “Tools are typically regarded as a rudimentary element of culture and certainly all of the prior species in the Homo line have been shown to produce and use tools.” (Fligstein and MacAdams 36) This exhibits collective consciousness through a social approach by showing how the homo species are similar through their coordination and ability to adapt to their set surroundings. Fligstein and MacAdams also demonstrate parallels of consciousness through revealing how doubt and fear relate to collective consciousness. “... doubt/fear is the central motivating force in social life and yet produces little conscious awareness on the part of the individual actor.” (Fligstein and MacAdams 44) This demonstrates collective consciousness by showing that society is connected through the motivating force of doubt and fear.

The Cultural Logic and Collective Representations was able to elaborate collective consciousness by showing that individuals in society create their own reality. “A man does not recognize himself; he feels himself transformed and consequently he transforms the environment which surrounds him.” (Durkheim 73) This process alone shows that the psychic force can be changed through the individual, itself. The collective consciousness determines what is good or bad in a society. The belief system of the individual helps to create the interpretation of reality. Durkheim’s scientific viewpoint goes along the lines of collecting evidence and discussing what is right or wrong. Science is a belief system and we the people trust that process.

When members of a community share a sense of morality and identity through common experiences and beliefs that can identify as the collective consciousness. There are so many collective consciousnesses today, which explains why we get so overwhelmed with the world we live in. The collective consciousness furnishes the value system in which an individual believes. Fligstein, MacAdams take a different approach in explaining the collective consciousness than Durkheim. They do this by taking a more social perspective, while Durkheim uses a more scientific and religious perspective.
chunks.label: Analyzing readings on collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student compares readings by Fligstein and MacAdam versus Durkheim on the topic of collective consciousness, analyzing social versus scientific and religious approaches.

chunks.text: Self is an interesting concept which has been discussed in this course through many different perspectives. In 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, Harari discusses many topics that connect to sociology. The concept that connects to previous readings we did in class was the concept about self. Harari discusses that homosapians are story tellers and like to see life through a story. “We hope to find meaning by fitting ourselves into some ready-made story about the universe” (p. 302) He continues to say, “There is a storyteller in my mind that explains who I am, where I come from, where I am heading and what is happening to me right now” (p. 305) This can relate to Erving Goffman’s concept, The Presentation of Self. “These attributes of the individual qua performer are not merely a depicted effect of particular performances; they are psychobiological in nature, and yet they seem out of the intimate interaction with the contingency of staging performances.” (Goffman, p. 256)
chunks.label: Connecting Harari and Goffman on self
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the sociological concept of self and compares Harari's ideas about humans as storytellers to Erving Goffman's Presentation of Self.

chunks.text: Erving Goffman, The Presentation of Self, believes that we are actors in our own life. Our life is a stage and we are performers. However, our performances depend on the people involved. The people in our shows create what the social situation is and how we connect to the world. This can change by the way the other people are acting. “As performers, we are merchants of mortalities. Our day is given over to intimate contact with the goods we display and our minds are filled with intimate understandings of them” (Goffman, p. 255-256) As you can see Goffman sees the concept of self as performers. He uses the concept that life is a stage and people are acting in the play. The stage depends on the people, place and what is happening. This creates how people act. Sometimes, other actors create our responses and dictate the play while other times we do the controlling of the show.
chunks.label: Goffman's presentation of self
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Goffman's dramaturgical theory that life is a stage where people act as performers depending on the setting and audience.

chunks.text: Although these concepts are not exactly the same, they compliment each other. Harari believes that , “in order to understand ourselves, a crucial step is to acknowledge that the “self” is a fictional story that the intricate mechanisms of our mind constantly manufacture, update and rewrite” (Harari, p. 305). Both believe that people’s lives tell a story but the story is created by how people see themselves or respond to others. When someone is telling a memory, s/he is telling how they perceived the situation. Harari says that the story does not need to be complete but it must have two parts to the story. The story “must give me some role to play” (Harari, p. 280). “The story must provide me with an identity and give meaning to my life by embedding me within something bigger than myself” (Harari, p. 280). One can connect that Harari is an actor or performer in a story and this is how he perceives his life. Goffman also perceives “self” as an actor in one's story of life. Therefore one can see the connection between Harari and Goffman.
chunks.label: Comparing Harari and Goffman on narrative self
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how Harari's concept of self as a fictional story compliments Goffman's theatrical model of self-presentation.

chunks.text:
Harari’s beliefs compared to Durkeim

In class we have also spent time learning about society and how society connects people. We have studied sociologist Emile Durheim who explained how society defines morals and although these morals are defined, people are individuals who live within the morals. People have free will and make decisions on their own. Durkeim also believed that religion provided a meaning for life and collective representation is a form of religion that connects people. Harari discusses the fact that our democracy thinks there is free will and the customer is always right. However, with artificial intelligence (AI) and humans creating and using technology, data provided by AI is enhancing the decisions people are making and molding their minds. Harari also talks about religion and god. Although both philosophers discuss these concepts, their beliefs are different and show different ideas. This may be due to the differences in time but nonetheless the concepts show different aspects of humans connecting to the meaning of life.
chunks.label: Introducing Durkheim and Harari comparison
chunks.what_happened: The student outlines the differences and similarities between Durkheim's views on morality, society, and religion and Harari's modern perspective on AI and free will.

chunks.text:
Durkeim talks about “collective conscious” which is a “set of set of shared beliefs, ideas and moral attitudes which operate as a unifying force within

society”(The evolutionary origins of the collective consciousness powerpoint, slide 3). This concept is used to create morals in our society. Individuality is a good thing and people want to be themselves while living in this society. As a result, you are responsible for yourself and your choices. In our culture this is important and created from collective consciousness. Religion is also a part of collective consciousness and has brought people together. Collective representation is how collective consciousness is evident. Collective representation is when something symbolizes or represents a concept. An example would be the Christmas tree at Christmas time. People know that the tree represents the holiday celebration. Everyone may not know the reasons but they do understand the representation. The collective belief of the Christmas tree is to celebrate the holiday. Some other ways collective representation is evident is through the beliefs and morals of the religion. For example, women are supposed to dress a certain way and men and women are supposed to be a couple. This concept is one that Harari does not agree with. First I will explain Harari’s beliefs and then compare them to each other.
chunks.label: Durkheim's collective consciousness and representation
chunks.what_happened: The student describes Durkheim's theories of collective consciousness and collective representation, illustrating them with examples like the Christmas tree.

chunks.text: Harari talks about our world changing from a free world to a world controlled by data through AI. He brings up a concerning concept which changes what Durkheim believed about society. In today's world there is computer technology and information that is spread through AI. Harari is concerned that AI will begin to control society and create collective consciousness through the computer. The beliefs may not be shared but seen so much that the person looking over the information starts to believe in what they are seeing or reading. For example, if one is looking at their phone on instagram and watching surf videos, instagram as well as google will start to show advertisements that connect to surfing. It could be a trip to a surfing area, a surfboard or wetsuit advertisement, etc. This may not be something the person is looking for but will connect from the AI data on the phone and unconsciously decide they need the item. This is not a connecting force within society but could come to that if the power of these companies becomes too big. The question here would be do we truly live in a free world? Is our world starting to be taken over by the AI with all of the computer technology that is being implemented?
chunks.label: Harari on AI and collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Harari's concern that AI and data algorithms control information, using social media surfing ads as an example of shaped desires.

chunks.text:
Harari like Durkheim believes that religion has collective representations but those representations should not always be placed as part of the religion and what God wants or what is morally right. Harari explains that maybe the 3rd commandment which states not to use God's name in vain means that people should not use God “to justify our political interests, our economic ambitions or our personal hatred” (Harari, p. 202). Many times people say God says what is right or wrong. Harari believes that human suffering should be the reason for morality and should be how people decide what is right or wrong.

Durkheim and Harari believe that our present culture is one that promotes the customer's always right attitude but Harari is concerned with this concept changing and big companies who control the data and algorithms controlling people’s thoughts. This is something one needs to look out for. The corporations need to think about the meaning of life when creating AI.

Although Durkheim and Harari believe in religion, Durkheim believes that religion gives a meaning of life. Harari believes that people do not need religion to act morally or have a meaning to life. People are moral beings and need to understand human suffering when making decisions in life. Harari believes that the spiritual quest brings people the meaning of life. Meditation and looking for answers provide life’s meaning.
chunks.label: Harari versus Durkheim on religion and morality
chunks.what_happened: The student contrasts Durkheim's belief that religion gives meaning to life with Harari's view that morality should be based on reducing human suffering rather than religious dogma.

chunks.text: Harari has many connections with past sociologists. His book, 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, has some connections to the past but also connects some concerns for the future as the world relies more on technology. Like Goffman, people are actors in their own play while our collective consciousness ties us together when we should look more into our own thoughts and how what one does supports the success of society and reduces suffering. One needs to understand that the story of life is being made and people are learning as they continue through their journey.
chunks.label: Conclusion on Harari, Goffman, and society
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by synthesizing the connections between Harari, Goffman, and Durkheim regarding individual performance and collective life.

chunks.text:
From Emile Durkheim, to George Herbert Mead, to Yuval Noah Harari, sociological concepts of the past and today intertwine to create divine thoughts and ideas that challenge one another. No individual sociological thinker is the same because sociology itself is made up of the multitude of minds: creating what we know today as our world and our collective consciousness. Yet there are always inconsistencies – moments of inequities between perspectives that demonstrate how to be a sociological thinker, and how one cannot latch onto a single idea. For myself, it is sometimes hard to grasp and difficult to accept that the ideas I built my life upon were created out of a need for security and a lack of individuality. That goes for religion, collective representation, the authentic self, and the fiction that our world so easily plays into.

Emile Durkheim states that the religion of society is important to study because “the idea of society is the soul of religion” (The Cultural Logic of Collective Representation pg. 72). Durkheim concludes that religious rituals in early Homo sapiens came about from new and untouched emotion from Morotopithecus. As the emotion in our early species was created, it brought with it the capacity for symbolic thought and the connection between the neocortex and the amygdala in psychology. Durkheim believes that by studying patterns of religion in society and how that pattern was created, it is easily viable to see how new types of religions and collective representations can come about.

Yuval Noah Harari, in his book “21 Lessons for the 21st Century” and specifically in God in Part 3, details how the sociology of today impacts everything we know and do. He acknowledges the work of Karl Marx and many others, concluding that their theses helped to lay the foundation of what our world believes is true, and what we have created out of our minds that is a fallacy. Harari states that humans make God both a “cosmic mystery” and a “worldly lawgiver” (pg. 202). The idea of religion, more specifically God, is such an inconcrete thing, yet we make it the most concrete part of our lives and our collective. Each religious person makes God the answer and explanation to their own ignorance. Harari mentions that religion creates a set of rules that followers must, for lack of a better word, follow to be the best version of themselves that God will accept the most. Yet, these same set of rules also govern what humans are allowed to get away with. Harari uses the example of how some religions believe that drinking alcohol is a sin, yet a Christian woman may say that God said it was okay to have another glass of wine. These inconsistencies within people, and therefore what those people believe in, make religion and what we believe of God to be a rocky subject.

That is not to say that Harari disagrees with the foundations of religion that Durkheim is arguing. In fact, it is fairly correct to say that what Durkheim is arguing about religion being created out of a need for explanations is very much what Harari is qualifying. Yet, the differences in the time period and how much our world has changed throughout the decades, and even longer, reveals distinct thoughts that are separate from each other. Religious institutions that created guidelines to follow are still very much intact today, yet Harari argues that they show no difference than guidelines of government or social entities. “These laws were certainly very helpful in establishing and maintaining the social order for thousands of years. But in that, they are not fundamentally different from the laws of secular states and institutions” (Harari pg. 204). Harari says that to him personally, wondering about the greatest mysteries of the universe has no connection to following a set of guidelines for a leader that were most likely made up by “imaginative Homo sapiens.”

When considering this about Harari, what he and Durkheim conclude about religion is connected, yet they diverge paths. Durkheim states the collective consciousness is the body that allows religion to thrive and continue because people need something to believe in. Harari is arguing that we may be a more successful community of individuals that can better maintain a social order without a religious entity hanging over us. Considering the collective consciousness, Durkheim believes that the study of religious rituals has further pushed collective life into existence and collective representation, the manifestations of collective consciousness. Harari takes a tone of disapproval towards the collective consciousness, and values its negative effects of how religion and non-secularism has been forced upon the collective society, causing more harm to our mental wellbeing and what our minds can process. Durkheim wants to study why religion is a concept made of thin air, and Harari wants to dispel that same air and dissect it for what it is. Both authors believe that religion is somewhat of a construct, but they individually want to hold that construct accountable in their own particular manners.

According to George Herbert Mead, our persons are separated into two entities: the self or mind and the body. Our body is material, or rather what we can see, while our self is something that cannot be accessed just by looking at it. However, humans cannot get an experience from our whole body, like for example, we cannot see our backs or internal organs. The body does not have the capacity to experience the entirety of itself, but the self is a thing that is constantly open. Our body serves as the object and is incomplete knowledge, but our self can be both object and subject and is being constantly communicated. The parts that constitute the self, or rather make it up, are known as the “me” and the “I.” “I” is what humans say in direct response to outward communication and is the subject, where “me” is the mindset, a human has in responding to themselves and serves as the object. The “me” shows similarities to James’ Social Selves concepts. “Me” is what is born out of the collective consciousness, and an example of this would be a student wanting to raise their hand because of “I,” but their “me” says that the answer may be too trivial or political.

Science fiction is a concept that humans are remarkably familiar with. It is incredibly common to flip channels on the TV and find battles between robots and aliens, or crazy machines that travel to different dimensions. Humans enjoy this type of genre because we are the only species on earth that can understand the concept of fiction and therefore further communicate it. Harari highlights that the main problem that comes with fiction, but specifically in Part 4 with Science Fiction, is that it “confuses intelligence with consciousness” (Harari pg. 253). In movie scenarios, Harari states that there is always the main character who has a layer of their authentic self that “remains untouched” from the bindings of the “matrix” and “technological manipulations” (pg. 254). The cliché of movies creates a protagonist that watchers are drawn to because of the unlocked and untouchable part of themselves. The movie ends with the main character breaking out of said bindings and finding his own authenticity, which he then realizes has just been a myth created by the even greater “matrix” that is real life.

Both Mead and Harari explain that each human individual has a “self” that is the innermost and realest part of ourselves. It is something that we can access, but of course is very personal and sometimes difficult to comprehend. However, this authenticity that we believe to be untouched is still socially structured. “There is no authentic self waiting to be liberated from the manipulative shell (Harari pg. 254)” because there is no authentic self – it has already been manipulated. Our minds have no distinction between external cultural systems that we are a part of and internal beliefs that we hold. Mead and Harari qualify that we are subject to thinking that a part of ourselves is authentic because it agrees with the security we need to survive and have meaning in life. Science Fiction aims to explain that humans are constantly avoiding being trapped within the confinements of society, yet the confinement occurs from the human brain and from our own control. We are the “matrix” and therefore are what we fear being a part of. Our “self” is both the object and the subject, and therefore it is subject to the authenticity we create within it.

Durkheim and Mead have both immensely delved into how the human brain’s symbolic thought has led it to create an authenticity that is impacted by external factors, and therefore is an internal subject. Durkheim mentions that the collective consciousness of society exists independently from humans and provides us with categories of thought to understand and follow. The collective consciousness forms moral values that we follow to be considered an individual that is accepted within society. Our “I” and “me” factor into how we are and how we want the rest of our community to see us, which are two very separate concepts. The mind-body duality and emotions that brought about religious rituals are still relevant in present time, showing that as society evolves, it does not always change.

Harari’s Part 3 and 4 of his analytical novel stretch the thought processes from what we have learned from sociological thinkers like Durkheim and Mead into how we understand our minds and external world today. He underscores that God in every religion is a divided belief of a superhero and triumphant leader, and that concepts of science fiction often have deeper meaning, like everything else in society. He connects all his ideas together in a formative matter that leaves the reader able to question everything they know about their life: the good and the bad. He challenges and negates the collective consciousness and encourages everyone to strive for a world that we create with individuality and diversity.

Our sociology modules have given me the ability to change how I see society, how to better fix it for tomorrow, and learn to understand that not everything we believe is a reality. Sociology demonstrates how humans are cogs in a broken clock, but if that clock is built for something different, our lives may have more fulfillment. Thanks to Durkheim, Mead, and Harari, we can better reveal how the security and individuality that we so often strive for within the society we live in is missing key components: truth and humanity.
chunks.label: Analyzing Durkheim, Mead, and Harari on society
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on sociological theories from Durkheim, Mead, and Harari regarding religion, collective consciousness, the self, and science fiction, discussing how these modules shaped their view of society.

chunks.text:
There are many standards that people try to live by in today's world. These standards influence the way that you look at yourself and others. In particular they can make you act in a way that wouldn’t be considered yourself. This belief of having an ideal image and your actual image relates to your self-conception.

In Erving Goffman’s article “Presentation of Self” he talks about how people try to relate or be more like the people that they look up to. He uses the example of stage performers and how people will try to compare themselves to a performer. This is because of peoples need to adjust their image in order to be more in common with their ideal image. Goffman then explains how the ideal image is based off of society while your self image is based off of the real you.

The concept of adjusting to what social norm is also mentioned in George Herbert Mead’s article “The Self, the I, and the Me”. In Mead’s article he explains how the other people can affect our self-conception. He explained how certain people have more of an affect on you than others. Mead also developed a theory that the “me” is what is learned from a social setting and the “I” was the response to the “me”.
chunks.label: Sociological concepts of self-conception and social influence
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how societal standards shape self-conception, referencing Erving Goffman's ideas on ideal versus actual images and George Herbert Mead's theories on the 'I' and the 'me'.

ne4dc0481.title: Analyzing Theories of Systemic Racial Inequality

chunks.text:
The contradictions between Racial Formations and Equality, and similarities between Discrimination: in a Low-Wage Labor Market: A Field Experiment and Immigration

Michael Omi and Howard Winant’s concept of racial formations presents a contradictory claim to Harari’s concept of equality. In contrast, there are similarities present in Devah Pager, Bart Bonikowski, and Bruce Western’s field experiment in racial inequalities in the workforce and Harari’s concept of immigration. Omi and Winant’s work titled Racial Formations, asserts that racial inequality is a predominantly modern issue. This contradicts Harari’s claim in lesson four Equality, that inequality is a far older occurrence. It is the basis of each concept which differs. Devah Pager, Bart Bonikowski, and Bruce Western’s work titled Discrimination: in a Low-Wage Labor Market: A Field Experiment, presents similar claims to Harari’s ninth lesson Immigration, both contend that there are differences in treatment among different races within the workforce. Each concept presented can be compared to another in some way, but the most important consistency among the concepts is that they all encompass the idea that systemic racism is a present day issue. Not only that, but systemic racism has become a far larger issue than most people realize, affecting things such as immigration, the job industry, and everyday life.

Omi and Winant’s work titled Racial Formations, makes the assertion that “Race consciousness, and it’s articulation in theories of race, is largely a modern phenomenon.” Omi and Winant argued that racial inequalities stem from occurances of the modern world. The authors clarify what is meant by “modern phenomenon” by further explaining the time period of racial inequalities emergence, “When European explorers in the New World ‘discovered’ people who looked different from themselves, these ‘natives’ challenged then existing conceptions of the origins of the human species, and raised disturbing questions as to whether all could be considered in the same ‘family of man.’' From this perspective, racial inequality was the product of different races colliding and forming a class system. Omi and Winant view the formation of racial inequalities as a form of chain reaction. One could say this claim promotes the idea that discrimination is not a natually occuring part of human nature. This can be inferred because the authors marked the occurrence which led to the formation of racial inequality.

This contradicts with Harari’s claim in lesson four Equality, he claims, “Inequality goes back to the Stone Age.” Harari argues that racial inequality goes farther back than known history. He supports this claim with this statement, “Thirty thousand years ago, hunter-gatherer bands buried some members in sumptuous graves replete with thousands of ivory beads, bracelets, jewels, and art objects, while other members had to settle for a bare hole in the ground.” Harari implies that this concept could support the idea that discrimination is a naturally occuring part of human nature. Harari states that the formation of class systems is a normal practice for humans. This would mean that because humans inherently create class systems which produce racial inequality, one could even say that humans are inherently racist. When Harari’s argument is criticized in this fashion, his ideas seem far-fetched. According to the author's concept, “ Hierarchy was not just the norm but also the ideal. How could there be order without a clear hierarchy between aristocrats and commoners, between men and women, or between parents and children.” Harari is questioning what the world would be like without classes and hierarchy. He is almost critical of a world without such structures. This claim supports the idea that the formation of classes is a normal practice for humans. However, like many of his other concepts that pose questions, Harari offers no apparent answer to this issue.

Although this may seem like a trivial contradiction, it is actually a fundamental difference. It is the basis of each concept which differs. This distinction is the source from which racial inequality comes from in each concept. This one integral difference causes the concepts to clash. Omi and Winant assert that Racial Inequality is a modern phenomenon, in contradiction Harari argues that Racial Inequality has existed since the Stone Age. One can infer that Omi and Winant’s concept does not support the idea that discrimination is a part of human nature, and that Harari’s concept may support this idea. Harari poses a question of where we would be without such hierarchy, which again supports the previously stated inference. While Omi and Winant again present the opposite claim to Harari by including a summary of the biological aspect of racism which has proven to be unfounded countless times. Yet this aspect of racism is still being pursued to this day. Both of the pieces offer adequate evidence to support their claims.

Pager, Bonikowski, and Western’s piece Discrimination in a Low-Wage Labor Market: A Field Experiment presents their findings on the Racial Inequalities within the Workforce. According to the piece, “Economic theory predicts the decline of discrimination through market competition, but several features of contemporary low-wage labor markets may sustain or renew racialized decision making.” This means that the issue of racial inequality in the workforce is a system which feeds into itself because of those who sustain it. The author goes on to say that, “Shifts in the composition of both low-wage jobs and workers have potentially created new incentives and opportunities for employers to enact racial preferences in hiring.” Some Employers view Racial Inequality within the Labor Force to be an “incentive”, meaning they benefit from it. Those who benefit from this arrangement work to continue its occurrence. This supports the prior observation of this issue being a system which feeds into itself by those who benefit from it.

Harari’s ninth lesson Immigration holds that although Racism has shifted to Culturalism, it is still present within the workforce. It has a negative effect on multiple minorities and races. It is stated within this piece that, “Numerous countries turn a blind eye to illegal immigration or even accept foreign workers on temporary basis because they want to benefit form the foreigners’ energy, talents, and cheap labor.” The hierarchy which controls immigration allows this racial inequality to occur. Harari is alluding to the fact that immigrants are paid less than legal citizens. He goes on to say that they are allowed entry into the United States because they will be used as cheap labor. This system is continued by the hierarchy which profits from such an unjust arrangement.

To compare the two concepts, both present the assertion that racism, or modern racism (Culturism) does in fact have an effect on the job industry. Pager, Bonikowski, and Western’s piece Discrimination in a Low-Wage Labor Market: A Field Experiment holds that Racial Differences within the workforce are majorly due to systemic racism. The purpose of the piece was to highlight the differences in treatment among different races in the workforce. Harari’s nineth lesson Immigration asserts that countries ignore illegal immigration because immigrants are used for cheap labor. Therefore, immigrants are only “allowed” entry into the United States because they can be used as cheap labor. Both of the pieces allude to the differences in treatment among different races within the workforce. It is evident within each concept that there is indeed mistreatment of some races within the labor force. It is consistently implied that the system which produces the racial inequalities in the workforce feeds into itself because of those who sustain it for their own profit or well being. This is a key facet of each concept.

In closing, it is apparent that though the similarities and differences among each concept seem small, they involve fundamental aspects of each claim. Discerning such similarities and differences from each concept can prove to be a difficult task when approaching them from a broad perspective. The difference between Hararis concept of Equality and Omi and Winant’s concept of Racial Formations, is a matter of how Racial Inequality came to be. Harari asserts that it has existed since the Stone Age, and Omi and Winant assert that it was formed in the Modern World. In contrast, Pager, Bonikowsk, and Western’s piece Discrimination in a Low-Wage Labor Market: A Field Experiment, and Harari’s concept of Immigration have similarities. Both argue that there are differences in treatment among different races within the workforce. The pieces imply that racial inequality is the product of a system which feeds into itself by those who profit from it. As I have stated previously, each concept presented can be compared to another in some way. The most important consistency among the concepts presented, is that they all hold onto one steadfast truth, systemic racism is a present day issue that has become far larger than most people realize, affecting things such as immigration, the job industry, and everyday life.
chunks.label: Analyzing sociological concepts of racial inequality
chunks.what_happened: The student compares and analyzes theories and readings regarding racial formations, equality, low-wage labor market discrimination, and immigration from authors such as Omi and Winant, Harari, and Pager et al.

chunks.text:
There is a vast distinction between the skin colors of white and Black. One is considered privileged, the other prejudiced; and for those who consider themselves civil activists and politically inclined, then it is relatively easy to ponder a guess at which race is considered which. However, the differences between the races of white and Black for some people is much less obvious. Some may not see any difference at all, other than the obvious contrast in skin color. Others could believe the groups should be switched, and that white people are prejudiced, and Black people are privileged. A third group may think that both words are relevant and just for both races. But a privilege and a prejudice only exist because of the other. More or less, the two are codependent on each other, and they both stem from centuries of white privilege that spans throughout history and is far-reaching, all over the world.

The argument of this reflection is not to change the opinions of those who do not see their ignorance, but rather to change their ignorance into something that fuels a yearning for them, as humans, to be better. The color of skin, or rather a difference in the majority of a specific color of skin, is never celebrated for its difference, but is ridiculed, opposed, and put into a box where its beautiful and defining factor of color is drained to be replaced by a need for survival in a society that exists on that same ridicule and opposition. But for society itself to survive, its foundation of racism, hatred, and bigotry must be the first to go.

I am white, and so is my entire family. We have never felt the blunt force of racism that is so engrained into American culture today, and we probably never will.
chunks.label: Introduction on race, privilege, and personal background
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the distinction between Black and white skin, the codependence of privilege and prejudice, the persistence of racism, and their family's white background.

chunks.text: One evening, my mother and I bought groceries at Walmart, and had a few bags-worth of bananas, crackers, and some form of candy. There was a man in front of us who was also carrying his groceries out towards the exit door. Some superstores like Walmart will have an employee standing at the exit doors to check that a customer’s receipts match up with the items in their cart or hands that they have purchased. Keep in mind, my mother and I had a few bags in each of our hands, while the man had only one or two. The thing I forgot to mention was that this man was Black. As we all approached the exit door, a female Walmart employee stopped the man to check his receipt. She tediously looked over all the items, took her time scouting his bag(s), and then let him proceed through the exit. As my mother and I approached the employee, she simply smiled and said “You’re good. Have a nice night, ladies.”
chunks.label: Walmart receipt check incident
chunks.what_happened: The student and their mother were exiting Walmart with several bags and were allowed through without a receipt check, while a Black man in front of them with fewer bags had his receipt and bags tediously examined by an employee.

chunks.text:
What is wrong with this picture? That is the first question that I asked myself. How is it that one customer has to be thoroughly checked to make sure that they have not stolen anything, but two people with double the bags and items do not? It is safe to say that this is a consistent pattern that most people would admit that they have noticed first hand in their life; and most of the people that admit that would be Black. The man at Walmart did absolutely nothing threatening, or moreover did nothing to make the Walmart employee believe that he was doing something illegal. So why is it that she felt the need to question that? The answer is a few things: the man’s skin color, the employee’s skin color, and my mother and I’s skin color.

I am thankful for the political movements that are constantly occurring around the world today, specifically Black Lives Matter. If I were not exposed to this, I would not even have noticed first-hand the situation that happened at Walmart. Being white in America means that the country and its institutions are programmed to be catered to what is best for you. A white person in America is not punished, hate-crimed, or downgraded because of their skin color. They never have to feel what it feels like to be the only Black person in a room, or to have their family members brutally killed by police for seemingly being “thugs.” I acknowledge that I have never had to feel that, and that I never will. The goal is that all white people, hopefully, will one day acknowledge that too.

The instance at Walmart, and so many other instances like it, demonstrate how white entitlement is still so mainstream in American culture. White privilege is defined as conferred dominance and unearned benefits that give white people more power and respect in society, merely because of the color of their skin. Because of white advantage and authority, white people can argue with authority without repercussions, gain more generational wealth, and be more likely to be hired (Pager Discrimination Study). The mere concept of white privilege already indicates that there are a group of people, in a given society, that are not white, and are therefore underprivileged. The privilege in “white privilege” does not refer to a higher amount of wealth or resources, it refers to the prerogative that is given when the color of one’s skin is white. White people that are in lower income households or in poverty condemn white opportunity as a falsity, when in reality the privilege is referring to the skin color and how that promotes a white person in society.

Peggy McIntosh, activist, and author of "White Privilege: Unpacking the Invisible Knapsack,” claims in her article that all white people are racist. Speaking as a white person, it is quite common to hear that this claim is inherently “racist” towards white people. To say that all white people are racist would be racist towards white people, right? Wrong. McIntosh states that this racism towards people of color from white communities is a distinction between racism and prejudice. She offers that white people are not always intentionally racist, but that the institutions that they have grown up in, as well as white privilege, have perpetuated the underprivileged livelihood of people of color. Institutionalized racism refers to the meaning that schools, government, churches, and communities as a whole have created a system of prejudice that is outfitted towards white people, and exclusive towards people of color.

McIntosh shows how white entitlement works by using the example of male privilege in today’s 21st century society. “It seems to me that the obliviousness of white advantage, like obliviousness about male advantage is kept strongly inculturated in the United States so as to maintain the myth of meritocracy, the myth that democratic choice is easily available for all.” (McIntosh, 36). Men are conditioned to not see where their immunity lies and how it effects all others who are not males, and therefore not included in this privilege. The same goes for white privilege and its prejudice towards communities of color like Black, Latinx, and Asian. McIntosh’s rationale for the majority of white people’s racism would be because the concept of white advantage is the explanation for why white people are only aware of its positive qualities, and not its negative. Privilege highlights that white people are the top tier of the hierarchy of society, and because they have never been below it, they will never understand what it means to be a person of color.

Another important concept to discuss is that of racism against a majority group, in this case white people. As I mentioned earlier, it is routine for white people to frequently think that they are prejudiced against, or that people of color blaming white people for society’s problems is a form of racism. The exact definition of racism is “prejudice, discrimination, or antagonism directed against someone of a different race based on the belief that one’s own race is superior.” (Lexico). To say that white people are the victim of racism is to say that Black people are treated as royalty. The fact that America was built on the slaughter of Native Americans and the slavery of Black Americans underscores that white people are the group that has always been on top, even since the founding of the New World. Racism is not qualified when concerning white lives, because white lives have never been threatened because of their skin color. The structure of racism is a system that defines skin color, so the only way white skin is considered a positive is if black skin is first considered a negative. Reverse racism, the idea that plans like affirmative action and programs for people of color were created as a form of anti-white behavior, only exists if the concept of race itself reverses.

With white privilege comes its labels; and white people have always been seen as respectful and trustworthy individuals living their lives showing the same respect and trust to the society around them. The definition of Black people, however, is quite the opposite. “...other groups [of color] were likely being made inconfident, uncomfortable, and alienated.” (McIntosh, 34). The Black man at Walmart, like countless other Black stories, was a victim of racialization. Racialization, from Omi and Winant, is the top-down political process where a dominant group defines symbolic boundaries for subordinate groups. Because the white employee at Walmart saw that the man was Black, she characterized him as a person of dishonesty and malice.

The meaning of skin color is constantly being communicated through the collective consciousness and is shifting over time, just as the collective consciousness shifts. After the Civil War in 1865, Black people were freed from their slavery, but they were still perceived as lowly individuals that were less than human. In fact, part of the foundation of racism was built on the fact that many white people saw Black people as a different species, such as that of a farm animal in a field. After the Civil Rights Movement in 1968, a little over 100 years later, Black people were seen more as dangerous and violent than powerless. Because civil rights groups like the Black Panthers and activists like Martin Luther King Jr. came about, there was backlash from the collective society about how safe Black people really were to be around.

The collective consciousness refers to the set of symbolic and shared beliefs that a society holds that informs a sense of identity. In other words, the collective consciousness is made up of everyone around us and can in turn be heavily biased towards the majority of the population. When considering this, the collective consciousness in America is made up mostly of white communities, therefore the collective consciousness emphasizes white privilege. The collective consciousness of being white is a racial formation that has been agreed upon by society. To continue, the collective consciousness brings about collective representation, and collective representation in America is American ideals of freedom and unity. But this same freedom and unity are not relevant topics when it comes to race, because neither occurs. The racism that is formed by the benefits of white privilege is an understanding that Americans have adopted because it is something that has always been there and has always been communicated. The collective consciousness, by being white in total, exposes the systemic racism that no white person has ever cared to notice or condemn the actions of. Hopefully not until now.

White privilege exists. The racial formations that have been created through white privilege exist. Black oppression exists. White and Black opposition exists. As Americans, we have lived our lives by stepping on the backs of people of color because the America that we live in serves us, and us only. Maybe if the man in Walmart wasn’t black, my mother, I and the Walmart employee were not white, this would be a different story. But it is not. The argument of this reflection hoped to encourage all of us, every single one of us, to do better – for each other. It is time to no longer step on the backs of people of color, but to extend a hand out towards them, and finally break apart the institutions of racism that have fought so valiantly and unacceptably survived. This is the chance for every Black parent to not have to tell their Black child to fear the world around them, but rather to embrace it with open arms. And this is the chance for every white parent to tell their white child that the world should not hand anything to them because of their skin color, and that they should embrace that with open arms. This is our chance as Americans, as humans, and as people of privilege and prejudice – to be a society of peace and pride.
chunks.label: Analysis of white privilege, racism, and societal change
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes the Walmart incident through sociological concepts, discussing white privilege, institutional racism, sociological texts, collective consciousness, and the need for societal change.

n84ea5d89.title: Growing Up in a Technological Revolution

chunks.text: Harari continues his explanation on the assault of autonomy by describing democratic systems and how they have been hijacked in today’s society. HE claims that people do not vote with their heads, but with their guts. This adds into the collective consciousness as it explains that we may not always act in accordance with what we truly want but with how we are expected to feel. For example, someone with personally conservative views may vote liberal because society claims it is more virtuous and they may abandon what they believe to fit the expectations projected onto them.
chunks.label: Harari on autonomy and voting
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Harari's ideas about how democratic systems are hijacked and how social expectations influence how people vote.

chunks.text: In the middle of the chapter, he talks about the concept of truth. He claims that the only definitive truth left is the top results of google. The assault on definitive truth he claims is driven by large AI powered corporations. These corporations are only incentivized by turning a profit. So long as they can bend the rules to make that profit, they will. Even if it is at expense of the personal liberty. Harari claims that we have reached a turning point in terms of technology controlling everything, including what we think. Take for example advertisements. People claim that the devices are listening to them, which turned out to be true. However, they do not even need to listen to you to determine what to advertise to you. Google follows every click and search meaning they know if you have a dog. If they know you have a dog they know to advertise dog food to you. This again goes back to the collective conscience; this has now become the expectation. The few people who are skeptics of large corporations and data are far outnumbered by those who don’t see it as an issue.
chunks.label: Truth, AI corporations, and targeted ads
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Harari's claims regarding truth, AI corporations, Google tracking user data, and targeted advertisements.

chunks.text: My generation is the first to truly grow up in a technological revolution. Computers were always there as well as large corporations competing for our data. There will come a time where this is an acceptable way of life. Large corporations will eventually successfully change the collective conscience.
chunks.label: Growing up in a technological revolution
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on their generation growing up during a technological revolution and how corporations will shape the future collective conscience.

n0f592fcc.title: Analyzing Human Emotion, AI, and Religion

chunks.text:
In The Neurology of Religion, Maryanski and Turner argue that emotions are the simplest and purest form of the human consciousness. They emphasize the importance of emotions for the expansion of the process of acquiring knowledge and understanding it through thought, experiences, and/or the senses for ancestral hominids. This was accomplished by many points of evolution in the brain; this is to say that the brain did not undergo a sudden dramatic change. Rather, more and more connections between different areas of the brain started developing. They say the use of emotion enhances memory, for example a hominid finds two trees one has sweet delicious fruit in it, the other shoots seeds out of the trunk when it is touched protecting the fruit. The hominid would associate the two trees with emotions. The hominid could obtain the yummy fruit from one tree and would associate this tree with happiness. The other tree that shoots seeds out would be associated with pain, and fear, thus initiating memory for the hominid to know which tree to climb. With the introduction of memory came the introduction to rationality, helping us make decisions based on thoughts we incorporate with choices often based on the memory. Emotion leads to these behavioral accomplishments and is the most basic concept that makes them up. Whether Harari read Maryanski and Turner’s work or not he shares this common idea and compliments their work with his own.

It is because Harari believes emotions to be fragile, pure, and basic that he believes they are able to be so easily manipulated and even broken or coded. Harari wants to warn the world of relying too heavily on technology as he is afraid of a future where an AI will dominate humans. To attain this an AI would need to have emotions, as we have discussed emotions lead to all sorts of more complex feelings and behaviors. It is also true that emotions lead to the feeling of superiority over lesser things. Humans consider themselves the superior species due to a greater grasp of emotions as it is embedded in the neurological working used to build a far more advanced society than any other animal. So who is to say if an AI were to grasp emotions that they would not get a sense of superiority to humans eventually. There are already cases where humans are inferior to AI’s. Harari even gives the example of chess, “A closer look at the world of chess might indicate where things are heading in the long run. It is true that for several years after Deep Blue defeated Kasparov, human-computer cooperation flourished in chess. Yet in recent years computers have become so good at playing chess that their human collaborators have lost their value and might soon become utterly irrelevant” (Harari, 2019, 32). This is a great example because it provides a good perspective as to how fast computers are learning the game that Harari defines as “one of the crowning glories of human intelligence” (2019, 33). In other words chess was considered a superior way of testing human intelligence and now computers are exponentially gaining on them. As a matter of fact, a new AI produced by Google called AlphaZero was able to overtake the leading chess algorithm in only four hours. It is now unclear if any human will ever be able to reign supreme in chess again.

Harari fears giving AI emotions regardless of the fact that emotions are needed in order for an AI to help humans because an AI needs to value human life. Emotions would be the logical next step in the evolution of machines. If we want a machine to be able to unlock more complex functions such as the human brain, emotion is a vital step for that goal assuming an AI will process emotion the same way as the human brain. To code emotion into an algorithm is essentially the same as manipulating human emotion, Harari demonstrates how easy that task is with an example of musical arts in modern popularity. “Of course, personalized art might never catch on, because people will continue to prefer common hits that everybody likes. How can you dance or sing together to a song nobody besides you knows? But algorithms could prove even more adept at producing global hits than personalized rarities. By using massive biometric databases garnered from millions of people, the algorithm could know which biochemical buttons to press in order to produce a global hit that would get everyone swinging like crazy on the dance floors. If art is really about inspiring (or manipulating) human emotions, few if any human musicians will be able to compete with such an algorithm, because they cannot match it in understanding the chief instrument they are playing on: the human biochemical system” (Harari, 2019, 29). This excerpt shows how easy and common it is to manipulate emotions. Despite Harari, and The Neurology of Religion having completely different topics, Harari was still able to complement the work with aspects of his own. On the other hand, Harari found an aspect of Maryanski and Turner’s work to be wrong in his opinion and disagreed with it.

The point of disagreement Harari has with Maryanski and Turner’s work is their view of religion and the role it plays in society. To understand the role of religion we first have to look at how religion was formed through human evolution. As we have already discussed, through the development of emotions humans started to become neurologically superior to other species which led to a greater social divide between humans and other species. For example, humans have to perform work to maintain their social connections; this is due to the sheer emotional depth in interactions. Simply put, everything has meaning to humans in our interactions whether that meaning has a negative or positive connotation. Other mammals have bio programmers, automatic connections that can be thought of as their animalistic instincts. An elephant doesn’t have to learn to stick with the herd, it is sort of a natural law that mammals have to stay socially active. Whereas humans, while some find comfort in social situations, are a less socially dependent species. It is seen as normal for an adult human to have a house of their own and not seek a family. It is their personal choice. Furthermore, humans have become more intellectual because our emotional depth has developed. We are able to feel the weight of a decision and how it might affect not just ourselves but others as well. As we became more emotional we began to paint materialistic things with different emotional significance. This gave a greater importance to different objects, family heirlooms, ancestral artifacts, etcetera. As time passed on these objects that were held dear, protected, and made into tall-tales they became religious. They took an objective truth and through time these objects and the stories with them became fact. Maryanski and Turner say that religion became an absolute truth for humanity and if we look back in history a lot of major policy decisions were made from religious persuasion. Maryanski and Turner praise the formation of emotions for being the keystone in human development that sparked the making of a far more complex society. They believe emotions will and should be the driving force behind important decision making. Furthermore, if religious decision persuasion is a byproduct of emotional thinking then Maryanski and Turner would be supporters. This is where the disagreement between Harari and the other authors comes. Perhaps it was acceptable in the past however for the 21st century Harari feels that religion should ultimately play a different role in policy making.

The different roll should be not one at all. Harari covers this in one of his chapters in his book where he explains why he believes religion should have little to no role in policy making. Harari’s reasoning for this varies from religious ideals being outdated for modern society to religious influence having their religious motives above their intentions.
