Touching on outdated ideals Harai provides the example, “When Ayatollah Khamenei needs to make a crucial decision about the iranian economy, he will not be able to find the necessary answer in the Quran, because seventh century Arabs knew very little about the problems and opportunities of modern industrial economies and global financial markets. So he, or his aides must turn to Karl Marx, Milton Freedman, Frederick Hayek, and the modern science of economics to get answers” (Harari, 2019, 133-134). This perspective is that a lot of religious ideals were founded to solve olden problems and often times do not fit today's issues hence we cannot rely on religion to solve political issues as today we are facing issues unheard of in the past. Harari suggests that religious scriptures can be used to justify modern solutions; however, when faced with a modern policy issue it would be very difficult to find a direct answer in scriptures. He suggests it is significantly easier to seek an answer outside of scripture and to then go back, find common ideas and twist the scripture to justify your answer claiming that you seeked the answer through religious means. Harari says “twisting the scripture degrades it, “from a source of true knowledge to a source of mere authority” (Harari, 2019, 134). Religious influence is a powerful thing, followers will whole-heartedly support the actions of their religious movement just because the leader of the movement is of their religion. This is to say that in America if two candidates were running for office and despite the opponent being more qualified Christians would still likely vote for the less qualified candidate simply because he is of their religion and his actions will reflect that of Christian ideals. Harari touches on this himself when he talks about the Pope leading a holy mission against global warming, because he is the highest Catholic leader. Catholics will support this movement while evangelicals will oppose it simply because he is Catholic. Harari states, “This is already beginning to happen. Opposition to environmental regulations is incorporated into the fire-and-brimstone sermons of some American evangelical pastors, while Pope Francis is leading the charge against global warming in the name of Christ… So perhaps by 2070, the environmental question will make all the difference in the world whether you are evangelical or Catholic. It goes without saying that evangelicals will object to any cap on carbon-emissions, while Catholics will believe that Jesus preached that we must protect the environment” (2019, 136). Harai even says that this will reflect in other areas such as the cars each side of the conflict will drive whether gasoline powered or electric cars. The influence of religion can be a dangerous thing, if an idea turns into a religious dogma there is instantly a significant following because leaders will preach that the religious icon believed in it as well. Not only is this disrespectful to authentic scripture that is being mis-purposed but it is also creating a possible dangerous power struggle. Harari ultimately feels that it would be best if religious intentions and ideas were left out of major policy making.

Through Harari, Maryanski and Turner’s work we were able to see the way sociologists relate to each other’s work. It is clear that both sides were discussing completely different things. With Maryanski and Turner talking about the evolution and development of the modern human and Harari talking about where the 21st century will take us and how to prepare for it. Despite this sociologists always relate to one another whether by disagreeing or agreeing. This actually builds a stronger argument as it shows they are capable of comprehending other’s work and using that to further push thier own point.
chunks.label: Emotions, AI, and religion in sociological texts
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes and compares arguments by Maryanski and Turner regarding emotion and evolution with Yuval Noah Harari's perspectives on artificial intelligence and the role of religion in modern policy making.

chunks.text: Despite the many technological advances the world has seen, humans still need relationships and camaraderie. However, the more we develop technology, the more isolated we become. For society to truly become better connected, there needs to be a return to in-person interactions and communities.
chunks.label: Technology, isolation, and the need for in-person community
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how technological advances lead to isolation and argues that people still need relationships and in-person community interactions.

chunks.text:
The pervasive commercialization of personal relationships has proliferated in today's consumer-driven society. In the present-day era, people engage with others to acquire various benefits such as social recognition, financial gain, or emotional backing from them. To scrutinize this trend and examine its impact on our communal lifestyle through Erving Goffman's concept of "impression management," is a major objective for this document. This essay proposes that impression management tactics have become increasingly popular approaches utilized by individuals seeking advantages amidst the commodification of interpersonal connections within contemporary consumer-led societies.

Social interactions that are turned into commodities, where people act in a way to acquire social advantage or profit has been on the rise lately. Such behavior allows individuals to display themselves as appealing and is referred to as impression management - displaying oneself selectively so they can get desired reactions from others. Erving Goffman developed this concept when he theorized about social interaction, emphasizing its symbolic context with participants fully aware of their actions' significance and how others might perceive them.

There exist numerous instances that provide evidence for the notion of impression management. One such instance is the "Instagram influencer" trend, where individuals upload sanitized and glorified versions of themselves to their audience's delight. Instagram influencers meticulously select hashtags, filters, as well as lighting in order to portray an expert image of themself. By generating content that captivates both visually and intellectually, they are capable of drawing attention from a vast social media audience.

To delve deeper into the effects of commercialized personal connections on our society, it is noteworthy to analyze technology's function. The upsurge in social media and other technological developments have enabled us to maintain perpetual communication with others which wasn't always possible before; however, this comes with both favorable and unfavorable outcomes for our social existence. The favorability within this interconnectivity comes from the practically instantaneous communication it provides, yet this has created a culture of desensitization and overstimulation within the youth of the technological age.

Looking at it from a different perspective, enhancements in technological innovations have enabled flawless interaction with people located all over the world despite their geographical whereabouts. This has presented novel avenues for social engagement and enabled us to cultivate meaningful bonds despite differences in culture or background. However, conversely speaking, the perpetual obligation to portray an ideal image on online platforms can be overwhelmingly taxing leading to a potential disposition towards unease and inner hesitation.

Moreover, the strides made in technology have paved fresh pathways for people to generate revenue from their interpersonal relationships. To exemplify, those who hold sway on social media platforms can take advantage of opportunities and accumulate a substantial sum by endorsing various commodities and amenities among their supporters. This has generated an innovative kind of career that capitalizes upon people's private connections enabling them to procure livelihoods through it.

Nevertheless, this conveys an inquiry regarding the veracity of these individual associations. Could a bona fide affiliation with someone exist if they are remunerated to endorse their merchandise? This is a multifaceted matter that necessitates further investigation; nonetheless, it emphasizes the plausible detriments when personal alliances become commoditized.

In its entirety, the commercialization of human affiliations is an intricate occurrence that manifests both favorable and undesirable consequences for our communal existence. Through investigating the significance of presenting oneself in a positive light and technology as influential factors, we can commence comprehending this tendency's influence while devising tactics to establish genuine and substantial bonds with one another.

An additional example is the method wherein individuals who are in committed bonds frequently utilize methods of deceit to display themselves as "the ideal duo" on their various social media profiles. This strategic portrayal, meant to elicit acknowledgement from others who similarly compare relationships through these displays, allows such pairs of people to exploit personal connections. This is similar to other aspects of our existence which can be commercialized under pressure for superior perfection and validation.

In today's age of commodified personal interactions, individuals are compelled to exhibit themselves favorably in order to impress others. The presentation of oneself extends beyond the realm of social media and is evident across other social contexts as well. A prime example being job interviews where first impressions occupy a paramount position in securing employment opportunities for candidates. Impression management has therefore become indispensable amidst the proliferation of social media platforms like Twitter, Facebook, and LinkedIn alongside an acute emphasis on presentability while stepping out into public spaces - making it a critical aspect synonymous with contemporary societal living patterns.

In the field of mental health research, there is a particular domain that examines how commodified social interactions affect individuals. Research indicates that feelings of anxiety and depression may escalate due to constant pressure to project an optimistic front on social media while simultaneously comparing oneself with other people's seemingly perfect lives. Consequently, personal connections can become commercialized in ways where competition for acceptance becomes necessary and online presence has to be monitored incessantly - leading towards heightened stress levels and loss of positive emotional experiences.

One of the consequences that arise from commodified personal connections is the likelihood for social disparity. Those who possess a talent for presenting themselves positively and accumulating more approval may be granted better access to resources and prospects. Take, for instance, well-known figures on various online platforms with an extensive fanbase; they can readily convert their popularity into sponsorships or endorsements - unlike those without much following whatsoever, as such individuals may miss out on these opportunities in its entirety. Consequently, creating a gap where people who adeptly commercialize their personal ties stand to profit while others are left at a disadvantage.

The commercialization of interpersonal connections could potentially have an adverse effect on our perception of sincerity and bona fide human interactions. In scenarios where social exchanges are motivated by self-interest, there may be reduced opportunities for genuine dialogue or emotional intimacy. People might feel compelled to portray themselves in a particular manner to earn acceptance or evade criticism, thereby resulting in less sincere communication and superficial bonds between individuals.

Considering the potential ramifications that may ensue, it is imperative to contemplate on our approach towards social interactions and what motivates us to pursue them. While the inclination to capitalize on personal relationships could stem from present-day consumerism, taking a proactive stance against this tendency becomes our responsibility as individuals. Our priority should always be cultivating sincere human connections without any ulterior motives in mind rather than prioritizing private benefits over them. By accentuating building genuine bonds and esteeming connection beyond societal standing, we yield an opportunity for more gratifying social lifestyles that are imbued with significance.

As we come to an end of this paper, it is important that we reflect on the commercialization of personal connections in modern-day consumer-oriented societies by making use of Erving Goffman's theory on social conduct. The exchange or selling of such links has resulted in individuals purposely presenting themselves favorably before others. This analysis demonstrates how impression management has become a critical tool for achieving benefits such as positive feedback from society, emotional support and material wealth within current day societal set-ups. Nonetheless, further research must be carried out to fully understand the impact associated with commodified interpersonal interactions.
chunks.label: Commodification of relationships and impression management
chunks.what_happened: The student presents an academic essay analyzing the commercialization of personal relationships and impression management through Erving Goffman's sociological concepts, social media, and consumer society.

n6053e6e8.title: Questioning Religion and the Future Workforce

chunks.text:
As we have all read what Harari had to say within his book “21 Lessons for the 21st Century” as well as the numerous readings within the many modules throughout our time in this Sociology class. There have been numerous points made that I am sure I was not the only one who were intrigued to learn about but with that comes some gray area. While we have read the brilliant concepts from authors including Durkheim, Mead, Goffman, Foucault, Harari and the list just goes on and on, it would be inadequate to say that there is no overlap in some of these concepts. Now rather that overlap be inconsistent or consistent with one another would be hard to tell with just a single glance at this material.

The first reading that I would like to bring to your attention is one of the first readings if not the very first one we were given, The Neurology of Religion which was written by Maryanski and Turner. This reading goes into quite some detail about the adaptions that had to happen for humans to reach the spot where they are today. Great Apes back in the early ages adapted in ways that seem far beyond understandable to me. These Great Apes were able to have rationality which only came about according to Maryanski and Turner because they had the ability to have emotions. When one is able to have emotions or has emotions in general it can allow for things such as stronger relationship bonds to form which would be needed for these Great Apes to eventually became the humans they adapted to. Emotions also enable one to think symbolically which when you look at the bigger picture this is what ultimately allowed societies, religions, and families etc. to be able to exist today. This then becomes quite consistent with the theory of collective consciousness (Durkheim) as a whole.

With the Great Apes now not only being able to symbolically think as well as form these stronger bonds it will only continue to increase the size of one’s emotional capacity which made it possible for spoken languages as well as cultures to come about. As a part of all of this comes religion, and according to Durkheim society would not have to about if it wasn’t for religious forces. The belief that there is something beyond the life we lie here on Earth. This can be quite scary to think about especially since there is no evidence that there is anything after death for all we know it could be total darkness or we could all come back as bunnies…just something to think about!

Back on the topic, religion gives something to the collective to believe in so the inevitable fate that awaits us all isn’t as scary. Harari on the other hand believes that while religion can help bring people together as well as give people what seems to be a sense of identity it also makes those who have different beliefs not be able to see eye to eye, which in all honesty is the truth in my opinion. Religion (chapter 8) according to Harari might not cure the many diseases that infect this world or build the bombs that we use/used in many wars, but religion does decide who you are and how you see others around you. It decides if you see someone like you generally see yourself or if you see them as the “other.” Religion has taken how many perceive people within the world to a whole new level. He expresses this by saying that there are “beautiful” religious traditions as well as there being “ugly” religious traditions. He then goes into detail talking about how these religious traditions divide people and that though we are all the same there are these “small differences” that determine how one will be treated. An example he gives of this would be how LGBT people are faced with what is ultimately a life-or-death situation depending on where they live. In Iran I don’t know if it is considered illegal to be gay and/or lesbian within the country but it is not rare for someone to be killed or most of the time they would be maltreated due to that fact that they liked the same sex as them.

While both of these concepts of religion talk about how it shapes us in many ways, one can see the obvious difference between the two. Durkheim focuses on how religion shaped us into who we are and how it brought us together and allowed us to think symbolically and become the humans we are today. Harari focused his concept on how religion is what is ultimately tearing us apart. How religion today has it’s negative as well as positive impacts but the negative in my opinion outweighs what these positives are especially since nobody truly knows which religion is the most accurate and there is a good chance that we may never know seeing how it is tearing many of us apart and causing wars. These are kind of similar in the sense that they both build off of each other that while we needed religion to build us together it is also the thing that could break us apart.

Now the next reading I would like to bring light to is “Micro-foundations” by Fligstein and Macadam’s. Within this reading they both talked about how many humans thrive to have a purpose within their lives. This is similar to Durkheim’s theory that religion is really made so that we can avoid this “existential fear” because though it may not have anything to do with religion having a sense of purpose for your life can make the inevitable death, we all know a little too well a bit easier to bear. One goes through the same process of being confused and they may feel as though their life is ultimately meaningless whereas coming together as a collective and having these jobs can help them avoid that situation as a whole. Even if you take away the outlook on without jobs there would be no purpose or that life would not be as valued as it should be, our daily interactions with other humans continuously make us feel loved. Spending time with those around you regardless of if they are strangers give everyone a sense that they are not alone especially if it is during a bad situation.

Harari on the other hand in the chapter called “Work” discusses the topic that there is a decent chance that the workforce we have in our head in a few years may not be anything like we would think. These AI machines are beating humans at their own jobs which obviously would make sense being that they have algorithms and can learn things a lot faster than any human can. These algorithms could grant these private companies as well as the owners with more money and things that will enrich them even more. So, if the rich continue to only get richer than the poor will ultimately since their economic value will decrease as well as their political power. Also, since these machines will be getting to know you almost more than you know yourself it can allow for these companies to not only manipulate you but also make decisions for you. If this becomes the case, we will end up relying on them more than ever and it will become harder to stray away from these things.

Though not having a job would not be the best thing in the world it would be beneficial when you are looking at the bigger picture. Having these AI’s take over some of these jobs could lead to improvements as well as better results in total. An example of this could be where Harari discussed the AIs would take over some of the doctors’ jobs which could help with new treatments and things of that nature to be known throughout the whole world within minutes since all the AI’s will be programmed the same.

According to Harari when changing to robots doing majority of the work there will be dangers with algorithms. When you put these robots on the same system though it can help in a numerous number of ways there is also the chance that there will be mistakes but when all these machines are on the same system every one of them will make the mistake which can ultimately lead to some catastrophic results. Say the future did hold what Harari used as his topic for the chapter called “Work,” and we take it back to the example of the doctors and hospital staff being replaced with these programmed robots. Personally, I would find it quite terrifying to be about to undergo surgery and all I see is a robot there to comfort me knowing that there is even the slightest possibility that I may not make it out alive of that operating room. Regardless of the jobs being lost nothing can compare to the soothing aura of a nice man or lady being there and reassuring you that everything will be alright. I would be exactly like Fligstein and MacAdam’s said… I would feel meaningless that one I already don’t have a job so my life purpose that I worked hard for my whole life is thrown out the window but I also would feel terrified that I may get to experience the inevitable fate everyone is waiting for because the robot messed up an algorithm and now I am dead. With all of this being out in the open and knowing that Fligstein and MacAdam’s has a theory on how we as humans ultimately need a purpose in life it does leave one wondering what the future has in store for all of us.
chunks.label: Analyzing sociological readings on religion and work
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on course readings by Harari, Maryanski and Turner, Durkheim, and Fligstein and McAdam, analyzing concepts of religion, existential fear, collective consciousness, and the impact of AI on work and human purpose.

chunks.text:
People are continuously faced with social interactions throughout our day-to-day lives. Thus, we subconsciously practice the front stage theory and the looking glass theory. The front stage theory is a facade, or a performance, that people put on when surrounded by new people. The looking glass theory is how we think others feel about ourselves. Although the front stage and looking glass theory are comparable in that they both focus on how people view us in social interactions they differ in the ways that we alter our personalities in given situations.

The front stage theory is a social space, created by Goffman, that provides a framework for understanding the many layers of identity presentation and social interaction. When participating in the front stage theory, representation of the public persona is created when faced with social situations. In doing so, they carefully choose their actions and appearances to leave the right impressions based on the audience. For example, when meeting someone for the first time you’re not as vulnerable due to the pressure of people watching your every move. The performance aspect of social interactions is emphasized heavily in Goffman's theory, which highlights how people intentionally control how they appear in different social contexts.
chunks.label: Introduction to front stage and looking glass theories
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces and explains Goffman's front stage theory and Cooley's looking glass self theory, comparing how both relate to social interactions and public persona.

chunks.text: The Looking Glass theory compares to the front stage theory because of the idea that you are constantly putting on a performance to have a reaction from others. I have experienced these theories during Fall Recruitment for a sorority. As I was going around to different houses, I was constantly using my front stage self to be liked by different girls in each chapter. I projected my own image onto other people, in hopes that they might reflect it back to me. In addition, I experienced the looking glass theory when conversation flowed naturally because I felt as if the different girls, I talked to enjoy my presence.
chunks.label: Participating in sorority recruitment
chunks.what_happened: The student visited different sorority houses during Fall Recruitment, using a front stage persona to be liked and experiencing the looking glass theory when conversations flowed well.
chunks.feelings: felt as if the different girls enjoyed their presence

chunks.text:
The dynamic interaction between an individual's internal self-concept and outside social cues is made clear by Cooley's theory. Cooley clarifies how people negotiate the challenging terrain of identity development among a network of social influences by highlighting the significance of social interactions and interpersonal perceptions. This viewpoint emphasizes the significant influence of social dynamics on a person's self-concept, underscoring the significance of empathy and understanding the formation of identity.

In contrast, these two theories go against each other because the front stage theory deals with how you individually alter your personality towards a certain group of people, whereas the looking glass self is focused on how you alter your personality based upon how others perceive you. For example, I enjoy eating capers on my pasta. When practicing the front stage theory, I would choose to eat something else when I am around new people. However, if I practiced the looking glass theory, I would choose to eat the capers on my pasta around new people, but I would be constantly second guessing myself and assuming the people I am with are judging me.

As a result, during interpersonal interactions, the constant conversation between one's internal self-perception and outside social feedback produces an awareness and understanding of identity. Essentially, Cooley's theory stresses the passive reception and acceptance of social feedback in creating individual self-concept, whereas Goffman's theory emphasizes the active performance of self in social circumstances. Moreover, people actively build their social image to negotiate a variety of social circumstances, whether it is through the planned performances in Goffman's framework or the imagined reflections in Cooley's theory. When combined, these divergent viewpoints provide complicated insights on the intricate relationship between social impact and human agency in social environments and the complicated and diverse nature of identity formation. In contrast, Cooley's theory highlights the passive reception and internalization of social input in shaping individual self-concept, but Goffman’s theory highlights an individual change for approval of others. This view emphasizes the reciprocal nature of social interaction and the importance of social dynamics in forming identity formation.
chunks.label: Contrasting front stage and looking glass theories
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Cooley's and Goffman's theories, contrasts how each addresses identity and social feedback, uses a hypothetical example of eating capers on pasta, and concludes on identity formation.

n6106e873.title: Analyzing Global Inequalities in Maternal Healthcare

chunks.text:
Rural areas are infamous for lacking resources in departments such as education, healthcare, and transportation in comparison to urban areas. This phenomenon is commonly due to a lack of money in these areas. As countries develop, one might assume that those living in poorer parts of the country would receive more money and better services. However, that rarely happens. So, what happens to the mothers who have no or limited maternal healthcare? How does that affect the child’s health and its chance of survival? How is the mother’s physical and mental health affected? Socioeconomic differences cause women to receive varying levels of healthcare, and studies have shown that women in rural, impoverished, or uneducated areas are more likely to receive inferior care. In this paper, I will discuss the effects socioeconomic differences have on the mother’s physical and mental health, infant mortality rate, and infant injury and explain why all mothers should receive equal healthcare. Socioeconomic differences in maternal health care align with the unit in class regarding race and oppression, specifically Collins’s The Matrix of Domination. In this work, she presents the idea that all women are discriminated against in comparison to men solely because of their gender. From this, one can imply that women do not receive quality maternal healthcare as it is not a service that men require. The healthcare quality one receives is based on institutional biases such as race, class, and gender. According to Collins, black women are the most disadvantaged in society as they are discriminated against due to their race, gender, and sex, which all intersect to form a matrix of discrimination. Collins also states that the world’s Eurocentric view causes society to see people as two races- black or white- meaning that any woman who is not white is considered black. This issue is significant as women of color tend to also be in lower social classes, challenging them with more socioeconomic struggle. These struggles include education, access to resources, family size, and workplace occupations, which all impact their health. Some countries, such as New Zealand, have maternity care that is government-funded and free for all women (Dawson et al., 2021). The system is composed mostly of midwives. However, women do have the option to pay to see specialists, such as an obstetrician. Despite all women having free access to maternal healthcare, there are still inequalities. Approximately 3,800 women in New Zealand voluntarily completed a survey regarding their health care experience with additional data detailing their residential locations. The results showed that transport, housing, poverty, racism, and lower education levels were all barriers to equitable health and the outcome of the mother and the baby. The most vulnerable groups of women tended to be the most unsatisfied as younger, highly deprived, and remote rural women were most affected by inequality. They had fewer accessible services as healthcare centers were distributed based on population. Additionally, they had difficulties getting transportation to better facilities in urban areas. Women identifying as Pacific or Māori had more struggles as they said that cost was a factor in obtaining maternity care other than the standard midwife appointments, such as antenatal care (Dawson et al., 2021). New Zealand has a better maternity healthcare model than most developed countries. For example, in the US, maternal healthcare is not provided to all women and is far from free. However, there are still issues with New Zealand’s healthcare system. The lack of quality services given to women in areas with less economic resources is an issue as a zip code should not determine healthcare. Health is a human right and should not be taken from someone due to circumstances out of their control, such as the availability of health centers near them. This is especially true as public transportation is often not provided to women in rural areas. Additionally, one's money should not dictate their health, but even in New Zealand, money became a factor. Women in more urban areas with more clinics available, also tended to have more money (Dawson et al., 2020). This meant that if they had pregnancy complications, they had access to and were able to pay to see a specialist (Dawson et al., 2021). That implies that women with more money have more of a right to be healthy, receive more care, and have healthy babies. Socioeconomic differences in New Zealand caused mothers to be unsatisfied with their physical healthcare, and an Italian study showed socioeconomic differences also cause decreased mental healthcare (Cena et al., 2020). Perinatal depression (PND) is one of the most commonly seen pregnancy complications and is known to produce severe effects on both the mother’s mental health and the development of the fetus. This study examined factors of age, nationality, previous abortions, previous pregnancies, how many of the woman’s children were alive, if the woman planned the pregnancy, and if the woman had resources for reproductive technology. 1,471 women from eleven healthcare centers in Italy filled out a 10-question survey in addition to an unstructured clinical interview to study these factors. The study determined that PND was present in all socioeconomic groups. However, the women from whom it was their first pregnancy that also had at least temporary employment had a lower risk of PND. Conversely, the risk of PND was highest in women with a lower education status and work or economic stressors. Similarly, postpartum depression (PPD) was found only in women who had several or severe economic problems (Cena et al., 2020). The results of this study showed that women who had economic problems were most likely to have depression associated with their pregnancy (Cena et al., 2020). Not only did this put them at greater risk for PND, but socioeconomic disadvantages directly correlated to antenatal depression (AND) and PPD. Women who had not had already had children were more likely to have better mental health since they did not have the economic stressor of multiple children. Not only is this a problem for the mothers, but it is also a problem for their children, who can face decreased fetal development as a result (Cena et al., 2020). Once again, health should not be determined by where a person lives. Mental health disorders can affect people for years, and it is not right that people should have to suffer with them due to not having adequate care. The effects of a mother's mental health on fetal development should not be overlooked, as, in 2019, 7.6 million children died before they reached the age of 5, 47% of which was due to neonatal mortality (Chauhan et al., 2021). Over half of those deaths were in developing countries. This was a direct result of the mothers not receiving proper maternal healthcare services, specifically antenatal care. Currently, the leading cause of neonatal mortality is antenatal, natal, or postnatal care, which practices such as vaccination and institutional deliveries could decrease. When researchers surveyed 6,01,509 households in India, results showed utilization of maternal healthcare varied greatly among socioeconomic regions based on antenatal care, safe delivery, and postnatal care. Women experiencing their first pregnancy in urban areas with access to mass media sources who did not work were the most likely to receive proper health care. These women were less likely to lose their children as a result of early neonatal mortality. Women that received early neonatal, postneonatal, and antenatal care were the most likely to have surviving children. This chance was not affected by demographic differences. However, socioeconomic differences were a significant factor in the children’s health. Uneducated women living in rural areas and with no exposure to the mass media experienced higher rates of early neonatal mortality. However, they still fared better than mothers in scheduled castes or scheduled tribes with very little access to healthcare (Chauhan et al., 2021). This study showed that the use of maternal healthcare services severely affects the chances of early neonatal, neonatal, and post-neonatal mortality (Chauhan et al., 2021). The use of these services is in turn affected by socioeconomic features such as location and economic status. Women with a lower socioeconomic status received less and lower quality healthcare. This directly correlated to a higher chance of infant mortality. That correlation supports the idea that proper healthcare needs to be normalized everywhere. In the 20th century, women should not be losing children due to a lack of resources, especially due to predetermined circumstances. For instance, the women in scheduled castes and tribes are born into them (Chauhan et al., 2021). They frequently have no chance to leave, and even if they did, would not leave, as that is all they have known. However, that leads those women to have a much higher chance of losing their children. In a world where countries have the money to stockpile nuclear weapons continuously, there should be enough resources to prevent mothers from losing their families. Socioeconomic groups greatly contribute to both infant mortality and injury. In a study done in the UK, researchers studied brachial plexus (BP) injury in infants (Merrison et al., 2020). BP injury involves damage to the supraclavicular brachial plexus resulting in long-term self-image, mobility, and function issues. The study was conducted in the peripheral nerve unit of a hospital serving Northern Ireland, Wales, and South England. Researchers surveyed the participants through a questionnaire. In the study, ethnicity data followed the categories used in the UK census. There was an increased risk of BP in patients who did not identify as white. Patients who classified themselves as Asians were 2.7 times more likely than whites to have a BP injury, and those considering themselves black were 6 times more likely than whites to suffer this injury. However, those weren’t the only groups affected by this injury. Except for Indians, all ethnic minority groups were at a higher risk than whites. Additionally, those from deprived areas were also at greater risk. While there were limits to the study, such as the self-reported questionnaire, language barriers, and a lack of a control population, the risk for BP correlated with several factors. These factors ultimately included biological factors, access to care, health education, inequity within healthcare, and language barriers (Merrison et al., 2020). This study showed that the healthcare system is very exclusive regarding race (Merrison et al., 2020). Women who were white and from an area with more resources were less likely to have a child with a BP injury. Additionally, BP injuries correlated with language barriers (Merrison et al., 2020). While it is difficult for a hospital to incorporate all languages, they should accommodate the major languages of their country, which this study showed is not the case. A woman’s ethnicity and native language should not stop her or her child from receiving adequate healthcare. This problem is significant in society today, since 13 years after researchers conducted the study, no one has made any changes to rectify the situation. These four studies support Collins’s theory of Eurocentric thinking. The healthcare institutions provided white women with the healthiest babies, while women of color suffered. Since race, class, and gender all operate on the institutional level, women of color also face discrimination due to their class which is often associated with their race. Socioeconomic differences such as location, education level, and the previous number of abortions are all things that are frequently out of women’s control but still greatly affect their lives. The brachial-plexus injury study expressed surprise that in 13 years, women and their infants had not received better care. Collins would not be surprised by this as she theorized that social change would require a “changed consciousness of individuals and social transformations of political and economic institutions.” Women, especially those of lower class and color, have been oppressed since the beginning of society and will continue to be as underprivileged groups are in the same situations, allowing each group to gain a varied amount of privilege or punishment. So, even though all women are discriminated against, white women are unlikely to do anything about it as they are still treated better than women of color. Yet, health, a basic human right, should not be dictated by one’s zip code or the color of their skin. References Cena, L.,Mirabella, F., Palumbo, G. et al. (2020). Prevalence of maternal antenatal and postnatal depression and their association with sociodemographic and socioeconomic factors: a multicentre study in Italy. Journal of Affective Disorders. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jad.2020.09.136.

Chauhan, B. G., Verma, R. K., Alagarajan, M., et al. (2021). Effect of maternal healthcare utilization on early neonatal, neonatal and post-neonatal mortality in India.

International Quarterly of Community Health Education. https://doi.org/10.1177/0272684X211004925 Dawson, P., Hay-Smith, J., Jaye, C., et al. (2021). Do maternity services in New Zealand’s public healthcare system deliver on equity? Findings from structural equation modelling of National Maternal Satisfaction Survey Data. Midwifery. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.midw.2021.102936 Merrison, H., Mangtani, A., Quick, T. (2020). The shifting demographics of birth-related brachial plexus injury: The impact of socio-economic status and ethnic groups. Journal of Plastic, Reconstructive, & Aesthetic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjps.2020.08.091.
chunks.label: Socioeconomic disparities in maternal and infant healthcare
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how socioeconomic, racial, and geographic inequalities affect maternal mental and physical health, infant mortality, and birth injuries, drawing on sociological theory and empirical research studies.

chunks.text: In 2014 for my 12th birthday my parents bought me the black LG Cosmos 3 slider phone. The only functions were texts, calls, and a brick breaker game. The main purpose of this gift was that my parents could make sure I was safe when walking home from school, but I saw it as validation for my new middle school maturity. I would text and call friends to hang out, and show it off to people that did not have a phone yet. Owning that phone gave me a small insight to what I believed adulthood was like, however, it could not show me what the adults at the time were doing, thinking, saying, or even wearing. The phone itself was the symbol of adulthood, rather than what the phone provided.
chunks.label: Receiving first slider phone
chunks.what_happened: For their 12th birthday in 2014, the student received an LG Cosmos 3 slider phone with basic calling, texting, and a game. The student used it to text friends, show it off, and feel a sense of middle school maturity.

chunks.text: Fast forward to 2020, I was entering my senior year of highschool, and my youngest sister, Heidi, was entering sixth grade. Rather than getting a slider phone like I had, she got a new iPhone 8. Over the span of just six years, the representation of a phone had completely changed. Heidi was excited, yet it wasn’t even that big of a deal, all of her friends already had phones, in which they had access to thousands of different applications they could download. Of those apps, the most prevalent ones proved to be social media. My sister instantly had access to the lives of not just her friends, but also her acquaintances, distant family, celebrities, and thousands of others.
chunks.label: Sister getting an iPhone
chunks.what_happened: In 2020, the student's sixth-grade sister Heidi received an iPhone 8 with access to thousands of apps, especially social media.

chunks.text: In today’s society, access to the information social media holds forces younger generations to mature quicker, and negatively impacts the constituents that define the Self.
chunks.label: Impact of social media on youth
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how access to social media forces younger generations to mature faster and negatively impacts their sense of Self.

chunks.text:
The changes I noticed in my sister after having a phone were outstanding compared to the changes I had after receiving my first phone. I barely changed, I still wore the same clothes, talked the same way, and had the same friends within a year of owning my first phone. Heidi, on the other hand started wearing completely different clothes, obtained many new friends, stopped talking to many others, completely changed the decorations and color of her room, got a very different haircut, and even had a large change in her everyday vocabulary, only in the first year of owning her phone. Along with the outstanding changes in her lifestyle, Heidi also obtained vast amounts of knowledge about society, including current events, the clothes people wear, the language adults use, to the shows and movies people watch, the places her friends go and the things they do, and so much more. All these changes and gained knowledge can be accounted for by the use of social media.

The intention of social media is to share what you do in your daily life, aiming to cultivate friendships and decrease loneliness, but the harsh reality of social media demonstrates vast differences from this purpose.The knowledge Heidi has been exposed to along with the changes she has undergone have taken a significant toll on her mental health. Her life on social media and her life in the real world intertwined, and has given her symptoms of anxiety and even depression at her young age. Social media has caused her to develop personality issues, the constituents that make up her sense of ‘self’ have been negatively impacted by the use of social media.
chunks.label: Observing sister's changes from social media
chunks.what_happened: The student observed dramatic shifts in Heidi's clothing, friendships, room decor, haircut, vocabulary, and societal knowledge within a year of owning an iPhone. Heidi developed symptoms of anxiety, depression, and personality issues.

chunks.text:
William James, famous philosopher, historian, and psychologist, loosely defines the Self as “all that he CAN call his, not only his body and his psychic, but his clothes and his house, his wife and children, his ancestors and friends, his reputation and works, his lands and horses, and yacht and bank account.” The Self is made up of several different aspects, but can be separated into four general constituents; the material self, the social self, the spiritual self, and the pure ego. By becoming aware of the feelings and emotions these constituents arouse, along with “the actions to which they prompt” (James 123), one can understand the self in its widest sense.

The constituents that make up the self each have their own impact on personality and the way we and others view ourselves. The material self is made up of many aspects, but “the body is the innermost part of the material Self in each of us” (James 123). Other aspects of the material self are what we consider a part of us, this includes close family and friends, the home we live in, to the clothes we wear and the commodities we earned with labor. The material self is one of the largest factors in determining and expressing our personality and Self.

Next is the social self which is “the recognition [one] gets from his mates” (James 123). The social self is a factor people find most important, but also the most stressful. The social self is how we interact with others, as well as how others see us. “A man has as many social selves as there are individuals who recognize him and carry an image of them in their mind” (James 123). The social self is very influential on the personality others believe we have, and your social self can vary greatly among the people you’ve interacted with. The social self fluctuates the most among the other aspects, and determines our personality to others.

The spiritual self, on the other hand, changes the least throughout our life. The spiritual self can be defined by our “moral sensibility and consciousness” (James 124), it is our “indomitable will” (James 124) that lays the foundation for our actions in society. “These psychic dispositions are the most enduring and intimate part of the self” (James 124), and take a lot to be changed. We cherish our spiritual self, as it is the most personal and powerful part of the self, and most of the time can not be shared with others.

Last is the pure ego, which can be defined as “a wholly subjective phenomenon” (James 125). The pure ego is the broadest out of the constituents, and ultimately determines our thoughts. The pure ego is said to exist prior to experience, and is unchanged by it as well. The pure ego plays a large part in our interactions and basically determines personality. “Each thought, out of a multitude of other thoughts of which [one] may think, is able to distinguish those which belong to [one's] own ego from those which do not” (James 125). The pure ego is the most stable among the constituents, and is untouchable due to how deeply rooted it is in one’s consciousness.

These constituents play huge roles in determining our personality. By understanding the emotions and actions they cause, the self can be defined. Along with defining someone’s self with these aspects, we can also understand how outside factors, such as other people's actions, impact the Self.

Most of these aspects of the Self are influenced by interactions with others, therefore, prior to the modern society we live in, these aspects of the Self could not be easily changed. The only forms of interaction could happen in person, compared to today where there are dozens of different ways to communicate. Whether it’s through a text, a call, a snapchat, a facetime, and so on, interaction has completely changed. This is taking the largest toll on the younger generations, such as my sister, who are introduced to this new modern interaction at such a young age. More specifically, the access to social media greatly impacts the development of the Self.

The development of personality and the Self happen slowly throughout a person’s life. The most influential time of development is during youth, when the brain is not yet fully developed. The Self is developed through experience, as one can immediately realize they’re feelings and reactions to certain events, and take in those memories to slowly develop aspects of the Self and personality. Social media has unhealthily sped up this process in younger generations by exposing them to mature concepts at such a young age.
chunks.label: William James's constituents of the Self
chunks.what_happened: The student explains William James's concept of the Self and breaks down its four constituents: the material self, social self, spiritual self, and pure ego, noting how modern digital interaction rapidly speeds up youth development.

chunks.text:
At the age of 11, Heidi became exposed to such content. She had multiple social media apps that showed her broad concepts such as what adults wear and say, to more controversial concepts such as political news to different sexualities. This information was quickly taken in and took part in her development. Heidi also was exposed to negative content such as cyber bullying and content posted to make others jealous or feel a need to change. This content all came together to disturb the development of each aspect of the self.

Social media had the biggest impact on her social self. By having a profile on an app, you can create an instant social self. She became very stressed over this concept, and would change the photos and information on her profile constantly. She tried to seem more mature in order to seem cooler, which led to confusion between her social self and how she acts in person. This idea of social media also greatly impacted her material self. For me, the phone itself was the only part of my social self, but for Heidi the content on her phone became a part of her material self. Profiles, posts, and communications on different apps belonged to her person, and she treated these apps as if they were a part of her. She would work harder on perfecting her personality shown on her social media, rather than in person. The development of Heidi’s spiritual self was sped up by her access to social media. Morals are slowly learned by experience over time, however Heidi was exposed to a large amount of content that basically determined her morals instantly. She would watch YouTube or TikTok videos that displayed strong moral decisions, and from these videos she quickly developed the sense of her spiritual self. Her pure ego was also impacted this way, as she was exposed to so much varying content in such a short amount of time. Her brain was constantly being overloaded with thoughts and impacted the development of the most important aspect of her Self.

All of the content Heidi was exposed to impacted each constituent of the Self, which in turn increased the emotions and reactions to those constituents. This overload of emotion put great strain on the development of Heidi’s self, as well as her mental health.
chunks.label: Sister's self-development impacted by online content
chunks.what_happened: Starting at age 11, Heidi was exposed to mature and negative social media content, obsessively curating her online profiles and absorbing morals from TikTok and YouTube videos, which strained her mental health.

chunks.text: Being able to access such a large magnitude of mature content puts great strain on the development of the Self, especially when the ones viewing this content is a young person. Social media had forced Heidi, and multiple other younger people, to mature quicker and develop the Self faster. This exposure will continue to mature the younger generations faster, and will impair the development of the Self.
chunks.label: Conclusion on social media and maturing youth
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that exposure to mature online content strains the development of the Self and will continue to force younger generations to mature too quickly.

Collective consciousness is a collection of beliefs, ideas and sentiments shared by members of a community. Religion has grown all across the world and spread through groups of people wanted to share their beliefs.

Concurring to the “Neurology of Religion”, the human brain got to be more cleverly able to think with the complexity as we created enthusiastic profundity. Along with the movement of the human intellect, the collective consciousness was able to create as well.

There are unknown distinctive considerations almost the collective awareness and its unwavering quality. In spite of the fact that, it has been broadly backed and acknowledged over time numerous events have been found. Numerous European nations once got to be persuaded of the presence of a pixie known as a changeling, who would seize children from their families and supplant themselves with another version of themselves after stories had been shared inside communities for a long time. The point is that there does not have to be something tangible or even the ability for someone to see in something to believe in it. Agreeing to the “Micro foundations” perusing, the primary known illustrations of the collective consciousness were when burial and craftsmanship culture had risen. With the movement of the human intellect through history, their memory was upgraded and permitted for people to have complex contemplations have form religions. As our brains have matured so has our capacity to consider what others say and how to respond has ended up being known as the collective consciousness. In spite of their being a number of diverse shrewdly primates, people are set up differently because of their capacity to fundamentally think for the overall group and consider what is best for everyone. chunks.label: Sociological analysis of collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses the concept of collective consciousness, citing Emile Durkheim, historical examples such as beliefs in changelings and burial rituals, and course sources.

chunks.text:
How we as humans perceive ourselves is a very interesting concept. Have you ever wondered why you or a given entity will act a certain way in accordance to the environment of that said entity? Likewise, have you wondered how different social interactions can affect the way you would consider yourself to “normally behave”. There are numerous reasons and scenarios that could influence one’s behavior. Multiple sociologists have put their minds to the cause and through a broader view of the “Self” they have touched on the conception of self perception. It is through their writings and ideals that we will dissect how we as humans view ourselves and in some cases why we change ourselves and our behaviors to appropriately fit the occasion.

The idea of conception of self perception is simply formulating an idea of how we view ourselves. We then get an idea of the reasoning behind our actions through looking at concepts provided by sociologists, psychologists, and looking at examples of social interactions. There is an embedded system in our neurological working that self-consciously tells us how we should act, react, and where to place ourselves socially in a group. However, I am essentially challenging the idea that humans are in complete control over their actions and reactions. But, “How can anything other than the way I perceive myself, be the real me? Who is more me than me?” You are you, however, it is through a system of selves and social shields for certain situations that the “really real you” has manifested its residing. Perhaps it is more correct to say that the pure self is not what put these selves in place, but that past experiences have developed a better social construct. Whether it is in the soul, heart, or brain there is a pure self that defines who we are. The decisions we make in social interaction are affected by past experiences from which the pure self has learned and will integrate over time. At the end of the day the “you” that you perceive as “you” is only a part of the overall self that has been developed to fit a social interaction. So how does this occur?

George Herbert Mead is a sociologist who uses the idea of the different selves to emphasize his own idea of the “I” and the “Me”. He explains the selves as essentially being the different “you’s” you have for social situations. He demonstrates this idea when he says, “We carry out a whole series of different relationships to different people. We are one thing to one man and another thing to another… We divide ourselves up in all sorts of different ways with reference to our acquaintances. We discuss politics with one and religion with another. There are all sorts of different selves answering to all sorts of different social reactions.”, (Mead, 164). In this way, there are multiple parts to the self. Those parts make up what is referred to as the pure self, and these selves allow us to think of ourselves in whatever way we want to perceive ourselves in social situations. Think of it like this: one will act accordingly in the given environment. One doesn't act the same going in for a job interview as for a family Christmas get-together. This is because the self has evolved from previous experiences. Accordingly, we know when to be more professional with our actions and when it is ok to be more laid back. It is because of this fact that the “you”, as you perceive yourself, is not what is in control of your social interactions. In fact a form of the pure self known as the social self is in control and is what drives us to act a certain way. The social self is the identity gifted upon an individual from the reactions of others, giving birth to social tendencies as an individual. Through this we learn what is and is not appropriate in a social situation. This is also why those who have more experience with social interactions are less socially awkward than those who have not learned from the social self. The social self is just one example of the different “selves'' that make up the pure self; however, it is the self most responsible as to why we react the way we do during social interactions.

Despite the acceptance of the different selves that give insight into social interactions, there remains a belief that “I am as a human in control of my actions”. Essentially, the disbelief in the driving self provided through learned experiences. This type of logic is somewhat narrow minded. For example, when something scary happens the natural tendency is to run away. What triggered the tendency to run? The more narrow minded person would say, “I ran away because I wanted to get away from the scary thing, because I wanted to”. The sociological answer attributes the response to “fight or flight”, a response brought about from the parasympathetic nervous system when we perceive something to be dangerous. The key word here is “perceive”. The self told you it would be best to run from the unknown thing because past experiences have conditioned you to perceive the thing as scary. The reason the idea of humans being in absolute control of their actions/reactions is improbable is because nobody lives in a vacuum from reality. In other words, the idea suggests someone who has no knowledge of human interaction would react the same as someone who has grown up in society. To put this in perspective let’s look at two scenarios. Two children grow up differently, one child is in a fruitful middle class family home. This child loves Mickey Mouse, his parents get him Mickey Mouse themed merchandise, he watches the movies, etc. The child grows up seeing Mickey Mouse as a child friendly idol. In contrast, the other child is isolated from society living his whole existence in a box with no stimulation from anything or anyone. What if one day both the isolated child and the family child are surprised with their arrival at Disney World? The family child is blindfolded and the isolated child is in his box upon entrance to the Magic Kingdom. What happens when the outside world is revealed and there stands Mickey Mouse? Isn't the answer ridiculously obvious? The child who grew up knowing Mickey Mouse would be excited while the isolated child would shrink back into his only known world that is the box from fright of this freaky human sized animalistic being. No matter what you believe is true, this is basically the outcome that would happen. Sociological belief would predict this outcome. The family child knew who Mickey Mouse was. He was taught through experience that Mickey Mouse is his friend. The isolated child never heard of Mickey Mouse so he was frightened by the unknown and would attempt to run and hide. However, the belief in the idea that humans are in complete control and social background has nothing to do with their reactions presumes the two children should react the same. According to this reasoning, past experiences are not reflected in “in the moment” decisions which is the flaw in this type of thinking. The two children in this scenario would undoubtedly not have the same reaction.

The obvious question is, “why?”. “Why does our environment and background affect our behaviors? Why do we feel compelled to act a certain way when faced with certain situations?” There are a few concepts that can answer this question, and they are all rooted in self-perception. The way we view ourselves is a driving factor in how we present ourselves. There are essentially three ways of viewing yourself: there is how you directly view yourself, how others view you, and how you perceive others to view you. To put this in perspective, for a moment pretend You are a 10 year old child. You race your mom and she lets you win without you realizing it. She comments, “wow baby you’re so fast!” This starts to make you think you must be the fastest person in the world and this is how you view yourself. From your mom’s perspective, of course, she knows she let you win and you are most definitely not the fastest person in the world, this is someone else’s perspective of you. However, due to the fact you can’t read minds you have no idea this is the true perspective. All you know is that you left your mom in the dust and she is very impressed with you. This is your perspective of how you think others perceive you. Self perception is a powerful influencer on how to present yourself. As stated earlier humans are unable to read minds so we are only going to focus on self perception of yourself, through your own eyes and how you think others perceive you.

Firstly, self-perception through your own eyes is the subject of William James, a psychologist who uses sociological ideas to explain how we perceive ourselves. James describes the breakdown of the “self” into three key parts that help relate how you see yourself. James says the self is broken down into the social self, spiritual self, and material self. In short summary, the spiritual self is the personality, the social self is you defined in a social situation, and the material self is you expanding the self onto inanimate objects such as clothes, or a soccer ball. (For example, when you score a goal you say “I made it in!” when really the soccer ball made it in). James’ describes the idea of the self as, “We see then that we are dealing with a fluctuating material; the same object being sometimes treated as part of me, at other times as simply mine, and then again as if I had nothing to do with it at all. In its widest possible sense however, a man’s Self is the sum total of all that he CAN call his, not only his body and his psychic powers but his clothes and his house, his wife… All these things give him the same emotions. If they wax and prosper, he feels triumphant; if they dwindle and die away, he feels cast down-not necessarily in the same degree for each thing. Understand the Self in the widest sense, we may begin dividing the history of it into three parts, relating respectively to:

1.Its constituents

2. The feelings and emotions they arouse-- Self feelings;

3. The actions which they prompt-- Self-seeking and self-preservation”, (James, The Self and its Selves, 123). The constituents according to James are the material, spiritual, and social self, along with the pure ego (most closely relating to the soul). Through this we see that James’ breakdown of the self into its constituents is used to provide self perception in which the self occurs over a three-step process: stimuli is received through one of the constituents, it is transferred into the brain, and the product is produced as behavior. This is how perception of ourselves through our own eyes is made. However, perception of ourselves based on how we think others see us is a different process.

Secondly, self perception based on how we think others see us, is uniquely explained by psychologist, Charles Horton Cooley. Cooley’s views are very sociological and emphasizes how we rely heavily on social acceptance when making a decision. A good example of this is the decision making process that happens when choosing an outfit to wear in public. For the most part, humans feel inclined to choose outfits that will yield compliments. When picking out an outfit many of us begin to fantasize about people saying “wow nice look today!” The pride generated by such a compliment will in turn cause us to continue to choose outfits that we think others would enjoy rather than one that may not result in such credit. This excerpt from Cooley’s, “The Looking-Glass self” sums it up the best, “A self-idea of this sort seems to have three principal elements: the imagination of our appearance to the other person; the imagination of his judgment of that appearance; and some sort of self-feeling, such as pride or mortification. The comparison with a looking-glass hardly suggests the second element, the imagined judgment, which is quite essential. The thing that moves us to pride or shame is not the mere mechanical reflection of ourselves, but an imputed sentiment, the imagined effect of this reflection upon another’s mind. This is evident from the fact that the character and weight of that other, in whose mind we see ourselves, makes all the difference with our feeling, We are ashamed to seem evasive in the presence of a straightforward man, cowardly in the presence of a brave one, gross in the eyes of a refined one and so on. We always imagine and in imagining, share, the judgement of the other mind. A man will boast to one person of an action say some sharp transaction in trade--which he would be ashamed to own to another.” (Cooley, The Looking-Glass Self, 142) As evidenced in the excerpt Cooley’s ideals are heavily reliant on the idea of social interaction. Stating that our actions can be rooted back to how we think others might think of us. With the introduction of his idea of self perception Cooley also introduced a new sort of Self. This reinforces the idea that there are a series of selves that control our thinking when taking an action or making a decision.

Through the minds of William James, and Charles Horton Cooley, we were able to see the two different self perceptions in action. It is by breaking down the self into three selves all accounting for “you” in different areas of sociality, and by introducing a new or different self that we should consider how others might perceive us. The concepts work together but also apart from each other to show that we as humans are not as decisive on our own as we may think. Regardless of what you might think of this philosophy, there is no doubt that at some point in the reading of this paper there was realization or a connection that was made. These concepts were formed from critical thinking of life experiences to better understand how our “selves” behave in situations. Perhaps after reading this idea new ideas have started to form. We are a forever evolving species. Our neurological network is always learning and improving.
chunks.label: Sociological perspectives on self-perception and behavior
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes sociological and psychological theories of self-perception, discussing thinkers like George Herbert Mead, William James, and Charles Horton Cooley to argue that human behavior is shaped by past experiences and social interactions.

chunks.text:
Have you ever seen a woman working as an electrician? How about a mechanical engineer? The answer is probably yes being that it is the 21st century, however, that does not mean that women do not face the same discrimination that they faced decades ago just because of their gender. Sometimes these women become subject to a concept called defensive othering, which is when they know that they are a part of a subordinate group, however, they believe that they are not a part those judgments and discriminations. Although this now allows the one subordinate group to subjugate another, sometimes it is necessary to do so in a male dominated field just for a woman to thrive. I have faced a similar situation being a woman who is a deckhand. I understand from both sides what it is like to be discriminated against and what it is like to be a part of defensive othering. In a field that is predominately male, sometimes it is crucial to do so.

Women have come a long way when it comes to the careers they are able to pursue. A job that we have begun to conquer is engineering. Now more than ever there are woman engineers excelling in their field, but they still have a long way to go regarding the bias that they face. Obviously, it was not so easy for them to get to where they are today. Along with the massive amounts of education that they have to go through, they also had an extra step to take, which was persevering over the tremendous hurdles of everyone telling them that they will never make it as an engineer. In the past, women always had to live up to the standard of being the beautiful housewife, who would cook, clean, and live for her husband. It was not classified as normal to even have a job, let alone a job that was deemed as “manly”. This made it so much harder for them to accomplish their goals. Of course, these stereotypes and judgments can be ignored, but for how long until it becomes unbearable?
chunks.label: Defensive othering and women in male-dominated careers
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the concept of defensive othering and reflects on the history and struggles of women working in male-dominated fields like engineering.

chunks.text: For my first year and a half of college, I was a coastal engineering major. It was me and two other girls as the only females in my engineering classes. Most of the time, we got the feeling that the guys thought that they were better than us, just because we are girls. Eventually we learned that we had to join the mentality that they had just so we did not feel subordinate to them. Although it was contradicting in that it was going against feminism, it is what we had to do to thrive in our male dominated classes. Not only did we stop feeling inferior to the men in the class, but we also saw improvements in our grades. It is necessary to adapt to the environment that you are in so that you can succeed.
chunks.label: Adapting as a female engineering major
chunks.what_happened: During her first year and a half of college, the student and two other female students in their engineering classes adapted to the male students' mentality to avoid feeling subordinate and improve their grades.
chunks.people: two female classmates, male engineering students

chunks.text: The same concept occurred at my job. At home, I am a deckhand on a ferry boat, and I started when I was 16. Not only was I discriminated against by some of the passengers, but also by my male colleagues. Through the years, I have heard things like, “Give that to him, it’s too heavy for you to lift” or “Why is there a little girl running the boat? Where is the captain, I do not feel safe”. These are comments that both my female colleagues and I hear constantly from passengers, and we know by now that it is something that is going to be difficult to get around. On the other hand, we quickly figured out a way to fit in with our male coworkers, while still being able to adhere to being feminine. Although it may not be something that we are proud of, defensive othering is what has helped us develop our confidence and flourish at our jobs. Another part of the company is the job of the ticket girls. The ticket girls tend to be more girly and feminine than the girls who are deckhands. They also have fewer and less vigorous tasks as ticket girls. A way in which us female deckhands use defensive othering is by comparing ourselves to the ticket girls. By creating a sense that we accomplish more, and have more demanding tasks, we have found that the men at our job will not see us as equal to the ticket girls but hold us at a higher standing because we are acting in a similar way to the men. Again, it is not something to brag about, however, if it is not done then, it is tough for us to gain any confidence in what we are doing, which then makes it extremely difficult for any of us to move up in rank.
chunks.label: Defensive othering while working as a deckhand
chunks.what_happened: Working as a ferry boat deckhand, the student and other female deckhands faced discrimination from passengers and male colleagues, and used defensive othering against ticket girls to gain confidence and male coworkers' respect.
chunks.people: passengers, male colleagues, female colleagues, ticket girls

chunks.text:
The concept of defensive othering is not only seen in careers, but in many other places as well. For example, in some sports that are deemed as “men’s sports”, the women that participate create a shield that protects them from being discriminated against. The shield that they create is their attitude, which they modify to act like their oppressor. These women believe that if they act like the “dominant class” which would be men, that they will not be subject to the bias that all women face. For them to prove themselves to the dominated power, they need to reinforce that the stigmatizing labels, such as girls not being as strong or physically coordinated as men, are true of other women, but not for them. Although the concept refutes many of the things that feminists have worked for, it is a coping mechanism that has helped groups that are subject to the stigmas. It gives the group a sense of confidence that they would otherwise not have if it were not for this coping mechanism. As controversial as this concept may appear, there are many situations in which it has helped people of subjugated groups thrive in an environment that in the past, would not even allow them in.

Clearly, I can speak from experience when I say that I have become a member of defensive othering. Being a deckhand, an engineering major, and a woman, I must find some way to succeed in places where men see themselves as superior. It is a conflicting topic for me knowing that on some level, it is wrong because it reverses what feminists have worked their entire lives for, but on the other hand, it allows me to find my place in positions that I can feel superior and accomplished. Being a part of a group that participates in defensive othering lets me to put myself in the shoes of other people that are in situations that are like mine. It is now evident that minorities partake in this behavior as a coping mechanism.

Sometimes, there are situations where it is necessary to become a part of defensive othering. It becomes a mechanism to thrive and survive in places that have a clear dominant group. Many people have already discovered that this is the case because they feel inferior to the so-called dominant group, based on stigmas that developed from the past. Although it is morally wrong in some cases, people need to find ways in which they can succeed in the areas in which they feel they are the minority.
chunks.label: Defensive othering as a coping mechanism
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how defensive othering functions in sports and other environments as a controversial but necessary coping mechanism for subordinate groups to survive and succeed.

n8787df04.title: Minimum Wage Work at Custard Chain

chunks.text: I have experienced Marx’s theory of the property-owners becoming richer while the laborers become poorer at my last job. I worked for a custard chain that was already grossly overpriced, despite starting all of its employees at minimum wage. After having been at my job for approximately six months, the custard prices increased. However, my co-workers and I did not receive raises. Instead, it negatively affected our income. Some of our regular customers who would typically tip us were frustrated that we were not allowed to charge them as we typically would. Due to this, they did not leave a tip.
