While those tips weren’t a significant portion of our income, we performed an equal amount and level of work, while the company received more, and we experienced an income loss. Furthermore, our job was not glorious enough that we would have gone and worked for free. Therefore, we were frustrated by our job, and the company continuously got more money, while its employees remained a slave to their jobs.
chunks.label: Working at a custard chain during price increases
chunks.what_happened: The student worked at a custard chain where prices were increased, but employees did not receive raises. Customers tipped less due to the price changes, causing the employees to lose income while performing the same amount of work.
chunks.people: the student, co-workers, regular customers, employer

chunks.text: Those who hold the most funds have their money increase in value, while laborers continuously feel their money getting taken away. Despite how stingy a worker is with their income, they will always have to work to earn more. While this leaves them a slave to their work, their work is not satisfying enough to make them happy. However, they work so much that they do not have time left for the activities they do enjoy, leaving them weary and depressed.
chunks.label: Reflection on labor exploitation and worker exhaustion
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how laborers continuously lose money while the wealthy gain, leaving workers unhappy, enslaved to their jobs, weary, and depressed.

chunks.text:
Is the United States Becoming a Nation of Less Diversity Than We Think?

You don’t have to be an expert to see that the United States has had its fair share of a discriminatory past. Yet leaders and citizens today call the US a “melting pot”, a place where everyone is welcome, and people of all different cultural backgrounds come to thrive. But how true is that statement? Sociology studies and ideas have come to show that maybe the US isn’t as inclusive and welcoming as we might have thought. Two of these sociology topics that highlight this discrepancy is a research study done on discrimination in a low-wage labor markets and an observation of low, middle, and upper classes by Mantsios.
chunks.label: Questioning diversity in the United States
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the narrative by questioning whether the US is truly an inclusive 'melting pot' and references two sociological works examining discrimination.

chunks.text: The research study that was done was conducted by three scholars of sociology in order to investigate the discrimination in a low-wage labor market. The research study was to study whether or not discrimination is present in the low-wage communities of New York City when applying for a job in those areas. The research method that is used to address the research question is both quantitative and qualitative methods. For the quantitative research the researchers conducted an experiment based on having white, black, and Latino applicants submit resumes. The qualitative research was based on what the applicants resumes contained. The findings address the question of whether there was discrimation because it shows which percentage of applicants got the job and whether or not there was bias involved. It showed that black applicants were half as likely as equally qualified whites to receive a callback, or a job offer. A real-world example of this type of discrimination is when going into a restaurant a lot of times you may see that the hosts and waiters a lot of time are white, while the cooks and “back-stage” employees are of different racial backgrounds. The descrimination “mechanisms” that were observed during the interview process were categorical exclusion, shifting standards, and race-coded job channeling. Categorical exclusion is the immediate or automatic rejection of the black applicant in favor of a white candidate. Shifting standards is described as evaluation being actively shaped or constructed through a racial lens. Lastly, race-coded job channeling is a process by which minority applicants are steered toward particular job types. This research study in whole showed that racial discrimination is still so prominent in todays world.
chunks.label: Low-wage labor market discrimination study
chunks.what_happened: The student describes a sociological research study on racial discrimination in low-wage job markets, explaining its methodology, findings, and discriminatory mechanisms.

chunks.text: Gregory Mantsios comes to bring to light class oppression, class privileges, and the class nature of society within the United States. Mantsios talks about the ins and outs of three families living in the United States and their class within society. The first family seems very affluent, and their activities don’t really match “middle-class” it’s more upper class (salary is very high). This family does very expensive trips overseas regularly, are very well-respected in their community, and the father’s job is an executive at a good company. The second family does seem more “middle-class” because they spend time together and vacation, but not as luxurious as the first family (salary is middle-class). The third family seems more lower-class as the father and mother work a waitressing and janitorial job. Their salary is also very low. The main argument of Mantsios is that there is not a pretty picture of our country. Despite what we would like to think about our nation, opportunity and life in the United States is highly dependent on our race, gender, and the class we are born into. Also, as individuals we are hurt by injustice, but as a society we tolerate it. One real-world example that happens a lot in our world is that people born into more upper-class or prominent families go into positions of power like the government. This leads our government to be not as diverse in backgrounds, class, and beliefs as it should be. In order to fix these issues, there needs to be a radical redistribution of power and wealth. Just like the research study Mantsios’s research showed that discrimination whether racial or societal, the United States is not as much of a “melting pot” as we would like to seem. The research study showed a different type of discrimination, but in its basics, they are the same and show our country in a really negative light.
chunks.label: Mantsios's analysis of class in America
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Gregory Mantsios's observations of three families across different social classes, discussing how opportunity is shaped by class, race, and gender.

chunks.text: Discrimination remains a pervasive issue in the United States, despite progress made in civil rights movements. Systemic biases persist in various forms, including racial, gender, LGBTQ+, and economic discrimination. Addressing this complex issue requires multifaceted approaches. Firstly, fostering education and awareness about unconscious biases is crucial. Implementing anti-discrimination laws and enforcing them rigorously is essential to hold individuals and institutions accountable. Additionally, promoting diversity and inclusion in workplaces and communities can help dismantle discriminatory practices. It's imperative to amplify marginalized voices and prioritize policies that uplift underrepresented groups. Lastly, fostering empathy and understanding through dialogue and empathy-building initiatives can contribute to creating a more equitable society. By tackling discrimination comprehensively and inclusively, we can strive towards a future where all individuals are valued and treated with dignity and respect.
chunks.label: Addressing systemic discrimination in society
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by reflecting on pervasive systemic biases in the US and proposes multifaceted approaches to reduce discrimination and foster equity.

n00aa9c77.title: Adapting to the Gaze of Others

chunks.text: As humans, we all feel a constant need to be approved by those around us, as we need their approval in order to approve of ourselves. We are always being observed by those around us and observing others, whether we realize it or not. The way that others perceive us has a large impact on our lives, so our social self will adapt to different environments, ensuring that we are able to have others view us as a positive member of society so that we are able to view ourselves in the same light.
chunks.label: The need for social approval and perception
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how humans need approval from others to approve of themselves, how people observe each other, and how social selves adapt to different environments.

n1e59c28f.title: Breaking Gender Norms in High School

chunks.text:
Have you ever been outcasted because something that you liked was deemed too masculine or too feminine for you to like? Many people face a time in their lives where this occurs. Whether it be a boy that likes the color pink and to play with dolls or a girl who likes the color blue and to play football. Society has created these ideas that each gender must follow an extremely rigid set of rules to be seen as “normal” within the society. When someone does something outside of these rules people are hesitant to accept their actions because it has been ingrained in their minds that their actions are “wrong.” Every day we unknowingly do things because of these societal set of rules. When we alter our natural behavior to fit into what society deems acceptable, we are “doing gender.” We are taught by society that there are specific actions and behaviors that we have that are directly related to our sex even though science has proven that there are not very many biological differences between males and females. The perceptions of male and female that society has taught us since we were young enables us to be more skeptical to try things outside of the rules of our specific gender.

Despite the presence of gender roles and rules of masculinity and femininity, the world we live in today has been more progressive towards the idea that gender is socially constructed and can be done in different ways. Society has become more welcoming to the idea of women working in male dominated fields and men fulfilling home duties which in the past were viewed as abnormal and strange. People are more equipped to challenge the rules of gender because of the sociologic research done to prove the socially construction of gender. When people start to realize gender is a social construct, it is much easier to question the sexist thoughts that we have been taught. One is able to tell themselves that their perception of what is acceptable as a man, or a woman has only been constructed by society not science and that if they are to defy the gender norm they are not biologically or inherently different than their peers. I am not trying to argue that our society has completely overcome the sexism that gender norms have inflicted, but I believe there has been significant progress in questioning gender norms. Although gender roles/norms are still present in society today, there has been more acceptance with defying the rules of gender.

In the past, the roles of men and women were very different than those of today. We can see how far feminism and breaking gender roles has come since the late 1800s by looking at Charlotte Perkins Gilman’s article titled “The Yellow Wallpaper.” In this article, Gilman describes a fictional experience of a woman going through a depressive episode. She explains how her husband, who is a doctor that diagnosed her illness, has been dismissing all of her opinions and not allowing her to do the things she likes to do like writing. The readers can tell that the husband is belittling her and has a dominance over her. The woman in the story feels like she owes the husband because he has taken care of her and given her a house to live in, but she is also aware of how poorly he treats her and that it is not fair to her. The readers start to get frustrated with the woman because they know she deserves to be treated better but she continues to make excuses for the husband. Gilman wants her female readers to see that they are actually the woman in the story, and it is time to stand up for themselves. She wants them to fight the gender rules that say that women are supposed to stay at home and are not supposed to do anything without the approval of a man. During this time period, women were not viewed as equal citizens, but Gilman’s article was a very influential piece in helping women realize they deserve equality. The gender rules during this time period were so rigid that they were embedded in the justice system. Women did not have rights to own property or vote and were seen as objects in the eyes of the law, not people. Defying the gender norms as a woman in this time period would be as simple as wanting to make your own decisions. Women that did not want to be controlled by a man and did not get married would be outcasts in society. They would often fail to be able to support themselves because the system was built to benefit the man, not the woman. Fortunately, things are vastly different in today’s world due to the persistence and fight of the women before us. Now, a woman owning her own house and making a livable income is possible and seen as something pretty normal. The societal view as to what a woman can do has majorly shifted from the late 1800s to now.

Women have come very far in gaining rights to work our way to being seen as equal to men, but there are still areas and environments where women are still seen as inferior and not belonging.
chunks.label: Social construction of gender and historical context
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how society enforces rigid gender norms, analyzes Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 'The Yellow Wallpaper' and 19th-century women's oppression, and reflects on modern progress.

chunks.text: When I was in high school, while taking a weight training class I faced several moments of resistance to me defying gender norms. This weight training class was predominantly male, and I also had a male teacher. On the first day of class, I could feel a lot of stares and it made me feel like I did not belong. I was not doing gender in the way that was typical in society. Instead of taking a class that was deemed more feminine, like art or dance, I wanted to take a class where I could get stronger and learn more about weightlifting which was deemed masculine. After the initial hesitance to having a female in their class, the other boys in the class came to accept the idea that a girl could do well in the class. I took this opportunity to enlighten the boys in my class and show them that girls can be strong and interested in weightlifting too. Despite the original pushback from my classmates and teacher, I was still able to make strong relationships with the people in the class. As the class went on, I got really close with the teacher and made some really close friends. In this experience, I was able to see firsthand the hesitancy society has instilled in people to a person breaking gender norms, but I also saw that people are capable of overcoming their learned perceptions. Although I did face some isolation by breaking a gender norm, my experience was very different from other women that came before me. When women in the late 1800s did something against the gender rules that society had set for them, they were completely outcasted from society or would face major punishments. I use this example to show that there are still gender norms that need to be defied in today’s society to improve equality, but I also want to shed light on the fact that my experience in defying gender norms is vastly less consequential than those of the women of the late 1800s.
chunks.label: Taking a high school weight training class
chunks.what_happened: The student enrolled in a predominantly male high school weight training class, initially experienced stares and resistance, but eventually gained acceptance and became close friends with her teacher and classmates.
chunks.feelings: felt like she did not belong, felt isolated

chunks.text: Although I have focused mainly on women defying gender roles in this paper, men also face scrutiny when they defy gender roles. Similarly to women, the intensity of the criticism men face in today’s world seems to be less than in the past. For example, when boys would do cheerleading in the 1980s-90s they would be ridiculed for doing something that was “only for girls.” They would be accused of being “gay” for doing cheer because they were acting too feminine. They would also be told that they were only doing cheerleading because they were too weak to play a “real sport.” The boys that did cheerleading would face a lot of hate because of the hegemonic masculinity that was ingrained in so many people. The fact that these boys were doing gender in a different way resulted in so much pushback.
chunks.label: Historical criticism of male cheerleaders
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the scrutiny, ridicule, and accusations of weakness that boys faced when cheerleading in past decades due to hegemonic masculinity.

chunks.text: I have been involved in cheerleading for most of my life and I have seen how these criticisms that men face when they come into the sport have evolved. I have had several male coaches that cheered during the time where they were teased for cheerleading but have told me that overtime as more people learn about cheerleading and as it grows in popularity, society has started to change their perspective. In my experience, males have been very welcomed into the cheerleading community. In today’s world, people are more inclined to see the boys that do cheerleading for their talent and the strength that it takes to be a cheerleader, instead of focusing on how they are defying a gender norm. At my high school, the boys that cheered on my team were loved by our student section and from my perspective it seemed like they did not get teased or harassed for being cheerleaders.
chunks.label: Cheerleading experience with male coaches and teammates
chunks.what_happened: Drawing on her lifelong participation in cheerleading, the student spoke with male coaches about past teasing and witnessed male cheerleaders being welcomed, respected, and loved by the high school student section.
chunks.people: male coaches, male cheer teammates, student section

chunks.text:
I definitely believe some people face more scrutiny when they come into cheerleading, depending on the open-mindedness of their community, but overall, I think society has come to more widely accept male cheerleaders. Over time, as people become more educated, they are able to grow and come to realize that their perceptions of others should be made based on the individual, not the generalization that society has created for a specific group of people.

Defying gender roles or norms that are harmful is important for the growth of society.

People should not have to alter their natural behavior and interests to fit into society’s box that defines how they should act based on their sex. Defying gender norms and doing gender in your own way can be seen as an ongoing accomplishment as described by Candance West and Don H. Zimmerman in their article “Doing Gender” since it has the ability to alter society. In the past, women worked to defy gender norms to gain their human rights. Society has also shifted to become more accepting of men participating in activities previously deemed feminine. In today’s world, society has become more accepting of people defying gender norms because they are becoming more aware that gender is something we have learned and do each day, not something we are hardwired to do. Making this realization allows for people to understand that the roles men and women are supposed to play are made up and socially constructed. Although society has come a long way from the late 1800s when sexism was embedded into the judicial system, we still face hesitancy and pushback when someone defies a gender norm.
chunks.label: Importance of defying gender norms
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes how societal perceptions evolve, citing 'Doing Gender' by West and Zimmerman, and concludes that challenging constructed gender roles promotes equality despite ongoing resistance.

n8552e094.title: Analyzing Labor in Fast Food Chains

chunks.text: Digging deeper into labor in the fast-food industry, George Ritzer came up with the concept of McDonaldization. McDonaldization is the general overlook at how rationalization affected the food service industry. Companies like McDonalds found ways around human labor to make more profit while saving time and money. Industrialization played a huge role in this, especially with the use of mass factory production that cut down on the need to pay employees. Another aspect of McDonaldization is the way fast food chains have created a sufficient, cheap process in order to sell as many products in as much time as possible. Ever been to a fast food restaurant and gotten your food in under two minutes? This is thanks to the “Medialization” of fast food. Cheap products combined with cheap labor and profitable prices is the recipe for success for fast food businesses like McDonalds, Wendy’s, etc.
chunks.label: The concept of McDonaldization
chunks.what_happened: The student explains George Ritzer's concept of McDonaldization, describing how rationalization, industrialization, and cheap labor allow fast-food companies to maximize profits and efficiency.

chunks.text: McDonaldization is a prime example of what Marx talks about in capitalism, especially referring to estranged labor. Because of the McDonaldization of the fast-food industry, employees’ labor became even less valuable to companies. Most fast-food establishments pay their workers minimum wage in exchange for their work, which is nowhere near the kind of profits the companies are making off of their product. An average McDonald’s makes around 2.7 million dollars per year. An average employee making $11/hour working 40 hours a week earns about 0.8% of that store’s profit. This is where Marx’s estranged labor comes in, because the product doesn’t belong to the working-class laborers, it belongs to the power elite companies and company owners who are profiting from their cheap labor. Because capitalism is such a foundational part of the American economy, estranged labor is never going to be done away with. It’s everywhere you look. Not just McDonaldization, but in all types of stores. The girl at the mall folding clothes in Urban Outfitters isn’t making profit off you buying their outrageously overpriced shirts. The factory workers for American Eagle sewing clothes together aren’t getting paid based on how many sweaters get sold. Estranged labor is all around us.
chunks.label: McDonaldization and Marx's estranged labor
chunks.what_happened: The student connects McDonaldization to Karl Marx's theory of estranged labor in capitalism, comparing fast-food employee earnings to corporate profits and noting similar dynamics in retail.

chunks.text: When looking at Karl Marx ideas of capitalism regarding low-wage labor and estranged labor, the idea of McDonaldization fits right in as an example of how laborers are not profiting from their work. In turn, the power elites who run these massive fast food companies are becoming more and more wealthy at the expense of the working class who are just trying to stay afloat—therefore trading their labor for cheap wages. Marx opened the doors for people to see the problems with capitalism, especially in the labor market, and George Ritzer’s concept of McDonaldization fits perfectly into it.
chunks.label: Synthesizing Marx and Ritzer on labor
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by summarizing how McDonaldization exemplifies Marx's critiques of capitalism, low wages, and the exploitation of the working class by power elites.

n1a3f6e49.title: Performing Assigned Roles in Racial Hierarchies

chunks.text:
In America, from the day we are born, we learn that there is a power dynamic - a race-based hierarchy we must all follow. This power dynamic determines life opportunities, privileges, and obligations. In “The Presentation of Self,” Goffman explains that social interactions are a massive performance in which everyone has a role to play, whether major or minor. In“Racial Formations,” Omi and Winant present racial formation, which has since been ingrained into this performance to determine the role each character receives. In American society, one’s race decides their character role, which will determine how society views them.

The white race has been seen as the dominant race, performing the dominant role, for centuries now. It will take more than an individual character to change that, as a single individual trying to disrupt the hierarchy will just be placed at the bottom of the power structure. To change the practices that have been in place since hypo-descent, and eradicate subordinate roles, we must collectively decide to change the performance and character roles as a country.
chunks.label: Racial hierarchy and performance roles in American society
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on race-based power dynamics in America, referencing theories by Goffman and Omi and Winant to argue that race dictates social performance roles and collective effort is needed to change the hierarchy.

chunks.text:
Have you ever been turned down for a job that you were extremely qualified for? Have you ever made less money than a coworker with the same credentials? If this sounds outrageous, it is way more common than you may think. Since 1990, white applicants received 36% more callbacks from a job interview than black applicants, and 24% more than Latino applicants with the same level résumé (Quillian). There has been a racial bias in the hiring process for decades. People are turned down for jobs they are highly qualified for based on their racial background and upbringing. Determination of whether or not a person gets a job and the wage they make should not be based on the color of their skin.

Race has been a determining factor in many different cases on whether someone gets a job or not, whether or not people want to admit that. It also plays a factor in how much money they make from a job compared to their white coworkers. In a study done by Jud and Walker, a survey was conducted on 1,215 blue-collared males aged 18-28—consisting of 1,001 whites and 214 blacks—looking at their IQ, schooling, and earnings. The results were separated into low-social status and high-social status categories and then into black and white subcategories. The social status was based on the father’s occupation and Duncan Index, where it was showed if they made the average or less than the score for their job, they were placed into the low-social status category. Schooling had a big impact on the earnings the person made, which was lower in the black low-social status community where they began to be discriminated. Work experience was another impact on the individuals earnings, where blacks again were at a loss because they tend to have less work experience than their white competitors. The discrimination shines through when it was shown that low-social status blacks made $1,159 less than the low-social status whites on average. This shows that people of color with the same credentials as whites still make less money, based on their skin color. If discrimination was eliminated, black earnings could boost over twenty-five percent (Jud and Walker). The study explained above highlights the idea that racial discrimination is still a very real thing and that it can determine the amount of money someone gets paid for the same job as someone that is white in the same social class. If an individual is hard-working and gets their job done correctly, there should be no reason some make more than others. Discrimination in the workplace could easily be eliminated and it would allow for equality between races.

When employers are looking for job applicants, they tend to stray away from inner-city blacks, whether or not they have the correct credentials for the job and look for white neighborhoods. Inner cities tend to have a bad reputation, being seen as a place of widespread poverty, drug use, crime, etc. but not every person who lives in these areas represents that stereotype. Employers may see a person is from a bad area and assume they will be a poor worker or will act out in an inappropriate way, while this is not always the case, but if it was true, it could be because of the lack of work experience the individuals have due to the discrimination they face day-to-day. In a study done by Neckerman and Kirschnman, they observed interviews conducted on Chicago employers and the tactics they use in their interviewing processes. They focused on three areas while looking into the employer’s strategies: selective recruitment, job interviews, and employment tests. Selective recruitment is the idea of looking for certain types of people that meet their standards and could be based on “statistical discrimination” or race to predict the characteristics of the person they would be interviewing. Due to this process of selective recruitment, black and Hispanic applicants tend to have less of a chance, based on the bias that is present in today’s world that they may not be a good worker. Social class and where someone resides may also impact their chance of getting a job, because those who live in low-income areas have a bad reputation, whether or not they live up to that reputation. Job interviews conducted by a white male on a black male tend to be more prejudiced based on the fact they may not have much in common and race plays a role in the characteristics a person might have. Social cues and mannerisms impact a job interview as well, such as looking at a person’s posture, eye contact, or voice articulation. Black applicants tended to score lower on that scare, partly due to the difference in education or experience they have had. Prejudice and discrimination are seen amongst different races because they may not have been through similar experiences that they can comfortably have a conversation about, so in a job interview this makes it difficult to have an easy-flowing time. Employment tests are meant to test a job applicant on the skills and criteria of the specific job they are applying for, but that is not always the case. Some employers have outside-the-box questions that may not be obvious to someone with less experience or education, which makes it unfair. A skill test would allow everyone to have the same chance at the job since every individual is capable to complete the same tasks. Not all employers implicate employment tests and rely on selective recruitment or the job interview, which again discriminates racially due to the fact people of color are already at a disadvantage. The study found that most employers did selectively recruit by projecting their interviews in big neighborhoods outside of inner cities. They expected low-income blacks would be poor employees and instead of trying out an interview, they looked elsewhere for applicants. The stereotype that is held over a certain race plays a big role in their chance of getting employed, which is not fair due to the fact not every person is the same. A respondent of the study stated, “The blacks that are employed are just not as good, not that there aren’t good blacks, but it’s a smaller percent than it would be of whites, for whatever reasons, cultural things, or family background, whatever”, highlighting the argument that because of a person’s skin color and background, they have a smaller chance of getting employed compared to their white competitors (Neckerman and Kirschnman). The respondents comment hints on the topic of cultural and family backgrounds and how that plays into a person’s opportunities. Those who come from a “rougher” background are given less opportunities to show their worth because they are discriminated against from a young age. Just because someone comes from a broken home does not mean they will create one, in a lot of cases it motivates the person to do good in the world and strive for greatness. Job interviewers and employers tend to look over that and look purely based on their backgrounds. Another thing that employers look for is job experience and because of that, many blacks do not stand a chance due to their lack of opportunities to find work experience.

A black job applicant has a harder time getting hired than their white job applicant competitors due to the low confidence level many employers have in their race. Stewart and Perlow explore the idea of racial discrimination within the workplace and show how unfair it really is to people of color.

Certain jobs have more employees of a certain race, so it makes it difficult for others to get hired. If a black male applied for a job that is typically ran by whites, they get turned down more often than not. Evaluator’s attitudes towards blacks tend to be fogged by the stereotypes that come along with the race, meaning they may rate their qualifications lower than those of a white person purely based on the reputation their race holds in society (Stewart and Perlow). Going back on an idea from earlier, those with the same qualifications may be seen and scored differently based on the color of their skin. Just because someone is a race that has a bad reputation in society does not mean they live up to that name, and many employers do not take the time to truly investigate that. The disadvantages that come with the hiring process for a person of color impacts their future greatly, because if they cannot get a job, they will not gain the experience they need to move forward in a career. Some people may fall under the impression that blacks are lazy, not intelligent, or commit crimes due to the stereotype that is place upon them. Every person has the option to be a hard worker and be positive in the workplace, so why should their race stop them from that opportunity?

Seeing things from a different perspective, McIntosh expresses that white privilege is a thing, and it is extremely common for people to overlook. White people on a daily basis decide to ignore the privilege they truly hold over people of color. She explains the certain conditions she lives under as a white woman and how her African American co-workers and friends do not get the same privileges. Some of the things she listed were not having to worry about where she moves to and that she will get along with her neighbors, she is able to go shopping without the assumption she is stealing or committing a crime, she does not have to worry about what will happen if she is pulled over by a cop, and she is able to apply for a job and be confident that she will be hired. Many of these things are taken for granted by the white race, because it may seem like a very normal thing to them, but to those of a different race they have to fear things will go negatively purely based off of the color of their skin. It has been seen in the news recently about an unarmed person of color being pulled over by a cop and it ends in a fatality because the officer was in fear they were in harm’s way, when in reality, they were not. This stereotype placed on the race not only has made it harder for them to succeed and get a career, but it has put their lives in danger. The writing done by McIntosh highlights all of the little things white people take for granted every day that blacks wish they did not have to deal with. It is extremely unfair for someone to be at a disadvantage in many aspects of their life just because of the color of their skin and their background.

Do you now realize how lucky may be to be given the opportunity to start a career? Racial bias in the work industry and employment process puts large groups at a disadvantage, whether they are extremely qualified or not. Employers should eliminate this bias and give every applicant an equal chance at a job if they are just as qualified as their competitors. The elimination of racial bias in employment would allow for so many more people to get jobs and create a future for themselves and their loved ones. White privilege is extremely apparent in today’s world while everyone should be seen as equals.

Works Cited

Jud, G. D., & Walker, J. L. (1977). How racial bias and social status affect the earnings of young

men. Monthly Labor Review (Pre-1986), 100(000004), 44. Retrieved from https://search-

proquest-com.liblink.uncw.edu/trade-journals/how-racial-bias-social-status-affect-

earnings/docview/227888816/se-2?accountid=14606

Neckerman, Kathryn M., and Joleen Kirschenman. “Hiring Strategies, Racial Bias, and Inner-City

Workers.” Social Problems, vol. 38, no. 4, 1991, pp. 433–447. JSTOR,

www.jstor.org/stable/800563. Accessed 29 Apr. 2021.

Stewart, and Perlow. “Applicant Race, Job Status, and Racial Attitude as Predictors of Employment Discrimination.” Apps.webofknowledge.com.liblink.uncw.edu, apps.webofknowledge.com.liblink.uncw.edu/full_record.do?product=WOS&search_mode=GeneralSearch&qid=1&SID=8EdMi5syPd2iqsZMCBy&page=1&doc=1.

Quillian, Lincoln, et al. “Hiring Discrimination Against Black Americans Hasn't Declined in 25 Years.” Harvard Business Review, 15 June 2020, hbr.org/2017/10/hiring-discrimination-against-black-americans-hasnt-declined-in-25-years.
chunks.label: Racial discrimination in employment and white privilege
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological research and readings on racial bias in the hiring process, wage inequality, and white privilege, ending with a Works Cited list.

chunks.text: Growing up I would consider my friends, their families, and my own family to be middle class, but after reading “class in America “by Mantsios, that seems to be far from the truth. He argues that the middle class makes up just a tiny percent of Americans, which is surprising because I tend to think most people I know are in the middle class. this goes to show how twisted our perception of class has become, and how much Americans really don’t understand how segregated our social class system is.
chunks.label: Reflecting on Mantsios and social class perceptions
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on reading Mantsios's text about class in America and how it challenged their prior assumptions about the middle class and social mobility.

chunks.text: Mantsios states in his fourth reality that, “From cradle to grave, class standing has a significant impact on our chances for survival”, which I honestly didn’t think was true before. This statement reminds me if when I was younger, riding in the car, and we would pass homeless people and I would ask “why are these people asking for money?”, and usually whoever was driving would reply with “they don't need money they could just go out and get a job.”
chunks.label: Asking about homeless people from the car
chunks.what_happened: When the student was younger riding in the car, they would pass homeless people and ask why they were asking for money, receiving the response that they could just get a job.

chunks.text:
Meanwhile, I know that some people do put themselves in that situation, but most grew up into it and are stuck in this lower class of having nothing. I feel like my generation has grown up in the collective consciousness that you can make anything happen if you put your mind to it, and sadly that's not necessarily true.

The chances of making it from the bottom to the top are pictured as one in a million. Why, you ask? It's because the people at the top hold the power and continue to hold the power. Domhoff defines this group of people as the “power elite”, throwing light on the fat that they control many organizations and have their best interest in mind. This also meaning that this group has the power to appoint certain people to certain rolls and jobs that hold high importance. This ensures that the high-power roles are filled by people who will be in their favor when making decisions. Although, the power in America seems to be decided by a Democratic vote, it is exposed that in reality the power roles are already chosen by the same people who hold them.

As a nation we decide to disregard that social classes prevents people born into a lower class to be able to achieve the status of being in the upper class. It is clear that people who hold the power like their power and do not want to give it up, keeping the same cycle of people who dominate control. The truths of social class have been sugarcoated in the classroom and have brought us up to believe that the social class we were born in doesn’t refrains us from achieving the social class we strive to be in, when it is proven that it in fact does.

“Power in America.” Who Rules America: The Class-Domination Theory of Power, whorulesamerica.ucsc.edu/power/class_domination.html#power_elite.

Mantsios, Gregory (2006), “Social Class in America”
chunks.label: Reflecting on class mobility and power elite
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses generational beliefs about success, examines Domhoff's concept of the 'power elite', critiques societal myths around upward mobility, and lists citations.

na876ade3.title: Reflecting on Identity and Perception Abroad

chunks.text:
What does it mean to see yourself through someone else’s perspective? A question that many people ponder upon. Along with everyone else I was in search for an answer. Why was it that my view of myself changes when I am around certain people? It has been believed that this could be because your self-esteem has gotten lower, or you just have the wrong friends, which could potentially all feed into the answer.

The looking glass self, a concept created by Charles Horton Cooley, is what effects how one may feel about themselves. Just like how one may see their peers around them it is most likely completely different from how they believe they are. Perspective and perception play a huge role within the way anyone views themselves. Cooley states within the looking glass self that it is ultimately the way we see ourselves socially, it is our social self.
chunks.label: Introduction to looking glass self
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the question of seeing oneself through others' eyes and presents Charles Horton Cooley's concept of the looking glass self.

chunks.text: Throughout my eighteen years of living, I have encountered numerous amounts of people from a variety of different backgrounds. When meeting these people, it came to my attention that there were always certain people I would much rather be around, and they all have something in common. Anyone who has ever approached me with good energy or just seemed like they were happy to be in the same place I was made me feel as if I belonged. They showed no negativity towards me so I knew that they couldn’t have seen me in a negative manner.
chunks.label: General patterns of encountering people
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects broadly on meeting people over eighteen years and how positive interactions made them feel like they belonged.

chunks.text: To get a little more in depth there was a time back in the summer of 2017 where I went to Europe. I got to see four beautiful places, London, Paris, Brussels, and Amsterdam though I had an amazing experience overseas and I would love nothing more to go again there were some things that made me see myself differently while being there. Obviously, going to a completely different continent would mean that I was also going to experience different cultures as well as different people. One of the days I was there I was in the airport at London and a woman continuously kept watching me and just looking at me as if she were confused. She then decided to come up to me and ask me if I was Norwegian, I told her that I was not, but she was more than convinced that I was someone from Norway. I have never been asked something like that before probably because some people believe it is rude to ask, “what are you?” but it opened a door for me and started to make me question whether people see me and assume that I am from a certain ethnic group and/or race. It then opened my imagination up to the idea that some people might assume I belong to a said race or ethnic group and judge me poorly from it. It messed with my mind for a while and still sometimes does. This woman also then continuously wanted to hear me speak because I sounded like I “was from Texas” and she had never seen a girl who looked the way I did speak the way that I do. This then led me to think I sound absolutely ridiculous and that everyone probably agreed with her because my voice really doesn’t match my looks.
chunks.label: Encounter at a London airport
chunks.what_happened: While traveling in Europe during the summer of 2017, a woman in the London airport stared at the student, asked if she was Norwegian, and commented on her Texas accent.
chunks.feelings: messed with my mind, think I sound absolutely ridiculous

chunks.text: I have also had many friends within my life to which I have made some crazy memories with but there are barely a handful that make me feel good about myself. The way that they all look at me and care for me like no one else has and always come to me with open arms and big smile on their face shows me that they have no intentions other than pure ones. They make me feel like my authentic self when I am around them and from the way they continuously act they show me that I am worth so much and that I am valued.
chunks.label: Valuing supportive friends
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on having a handful of true friends whose care and positivity make them feel authentic and valued.
chunks.feelings: good about myself, authentic, valued, worth so much

chunks.text: They came along after I hit a hard place in my life. A guy that I saw the world of and who I at first thought saw the same of me really changed how I saw myself. He treated me as if I had no purpose in my life and as if I did something so horrible to hurt him. After being around someone who treats you in a negative manner for so long it takes a toll on how you see yourself. I started to believe that no matter what I did nothing I would ever do would be right. He made me believe by the way he treated me that I did not deserve to be loved and that my worth amounted to absolutely nothing. This then led to me feeling like everyone perceived me the way I perceived myself at that time which made me feel even worse about myself. I assumed everyone had lost hope for me just as I had lost hope for myself because a man who had no idea what he was doing with his life treated me so badly that I figured it must’ve been the way that I was that caused this. It wasn’t until I met my friends that I mentioned before that changed how I perceive myself and how I assume others perceive me.
chunks.label: Toxic relationship with a guy
chunks.what_happened: The student went through a difficult period where a guy she deeply cared about treated her terribly, making her feel worthless until new friends helped change her self-perception.
chunks.feelings: no purpose, worthless, did not deserve to be loved, lost hope, worse about myself

chunks.text:
Charles Horton Cooley believes that there are these “three principal elements” that tend to create what he calls “the looking glass self” they are the imagination of how we believe another person sees us, the imagination of the judgement that we think comes along with their perception of us, and then the feeling we then get from those things which can range from prideful and happy to worthless and depressed. The concept itself is about how we view our self-image which can be greatly influenced by the interactions we make with people around us and by what society deems as acceptable.

An example of this concept could look a little something like this. I am going to meet up with some people within a club I have recently joined. I personally think I am a very friendly person and are quite easy to talk to so I can hold a conversation though I am nervous about going to meet these new people I trust that my social skills can potentially help me avoid any type of awkwardness and spark a connection with some of these people. I get there and I am trying to make casual conversation, so everyone isn’t sitting there looking bored or in all just ready to leave. In response to trying to break the ice the only responses I seem to get are either very short sentences, or no response at all. Everyone avoids really keeping eye contact which I find is a key piece to making conversation and showing interest. I then begin to feel anxious because I believed in my social skills but now it is seemingly like they are currently failing me. Whereas if these new people I would’ve met would have held eye contact as well as try to carry on the conversation my views on my social abilities would not have changed. Depending on if a positive response would have been given, I would still have faith in my abilities and the self-image I have for myself would have remained the same. Since all I received was a majority of negative responses rather than be words or just body language it then led me to see myself differently and feel as if they wanted nothing to do with me when we met, and it seemed as if they did not even want to have a conversation with me in the first place.
chunks.label: Hypothetical example of club meeting
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Cooley's three principal elements and provides a hypothetical scenario of attending a new club meeting where cold responses make someone feel anxious.

chunks.text: With the knowledge you now have about the looking glass self we can now relate them back to the experiences I spoke on before. When in the London airport I went in assuming by the looks of me as well as how I acted that one would be able to view myself for what I was. I am a biracial female who is half African American as well as Caucasian. When I was approached by this woman of a race and/or ethnic group I wasn’t sure of and was asked whether I was Norwegian it nonetheless confused me. In her eyes I was of Norwegian descent, but I was nowhere near being that. It then made me believe that other people probably saw me for something I wasn’t as well. Then when she commented on my accent and how my voice did not match what she would’ve assumed I would have sounded like it really made my self-image change I become very self-conscious of how other people saw me because of the way my voice sounded. I thought to myself “do I sound like a country hillbilly to everyone?” which I have found out is true but that is irrelevant at this moment. In all hearing that my voice sounded like it belonged to someone quite different from me really affected me because from that moment forward, I felt like everyone thought I sounded crazy.
chunks.label: Analyzing the airport encounter
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes the London airport experience using the looking glass self, explaining how being asked if she was Norwegian and told she sounded Texan caused self-consciousness about her biracial identity and voice.

chunks.text: Looking back on the time that I was getting treated terribly and feeling like I didn’t deserve anything good to happen in my life I see now that I felt this way because that man was my “biggest mirror” he was who I cared about the most and would do anything under the sun for. I say he was my biggest mirror because he was what determined how I felt about myself and then it eventually went to how I thought everyone saw me. Getting treated rudely by one of the only people who truly understood you will make you question quite a few things. My “biggest mirror” within this looking glass concept was giving me the idea and really persuading me all together that I was the problem then I did become the problem because I allowed him to make me see things the way he wanted me to.
chunks.label: Analyzing the toxic relationship
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the past relationship, explaining that the man acted as her 'biggest mirror' and made her believe she was the problem.

chunks.text: What does it mean to see yourself through someone else’s perspective? The looking glass self is how one does so. You get around these people rather you just met them or if they have been in your life for a while but the way the interactions go, they place ideas in your head of how that person or those people perceive you. If you are continuously getting treated horrible by someone or the way, they give off body language is negative then that will lead to you having a negative look on yourself as well as feeling down as well. Now if you are continuously praised by these people and you are shown nothing less than their love for you this will make the idea you have of yourself take a positive turn. Surrounding yourself with people who are positive when interacting with you will enable you on your journey to have a better self-image. One is not defined by how others act towards you but it can often seem like it due to Cooley’s concept the looking glass self.
chunks.label: Conclusion on social perception
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by summarizing how social interactions shape self-image and emphasizes the value of surrounding oneself with positive people.

n53a38f26.title: Realizing the Reality of White Privilege

chunks.text:
Racism is heavily discussed about in schools and very prevalent today in America, but the way I have learned about it has altered my view on what the pressing issue is. In Peggy McIntosh’s’ article, “white Privilege”, she takes a step back to realize from a young age most Caucasian children socially learned and adapted to the mindset that “racism as something which puts others at a disadvantage”, not noticing that white Americans were the ones who needed to realize they are at an advantage. Emile Durkheim defines the “collective consciousness” as a set of shared beliefs, ideas, and morals and also says that individuals have the same morality to fit in. The collective consciousness that appears here is the shared idea that white people are not the thing that needs to be fixed, it is that African Americans need to be fixed(helped). Since this is set in our minds, we are oblivious to the things Caucasian people do regularly that black Americans have to worry about. McIntosh debriefs her life as a white person and points out issues she doesn’t have to worry about, like if people think she is financially reliable, or if she moves that her neighbors respect her, or even if she joins a group of sorts she wouldn’t be singled out by her race.

McIntosh uncovers something I never even thought about but is so looked over and ignored by white Americans. As children grow up it is a social ideal that they need to be more aware of how poorly and unfair African Americans are treated, which is true. But as white people, like me, age in society, they don’t realize that some of the things they do daily, black Americans have to be afraid of judgement, rejection, and the possibility of being harmed.

McIntosh, Peggy. White Privilege: Unpacking the Invisible Knapsack. Louisville Anarchist Federation and No Borders, 2000.
chunks.label: Reflecting on white privilege and collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Peggy McIntosh's article on white privilege and Emile Durkheim's concept of collective consciousness, reflecting on how white Americans often overlook their own advantages compared to African Americans.

nfaac5b72.title: Analyzing Religion's Changing Role in Society

chunks.text:
Religion has been at the roots of society since human civilization was formed. Overtime religion has grown and transformed dramatically. There are estimated to be about 10,000 religions practiced worldwide. The most practiced religions are Christianity, Judaism, Islam, Hinduism, and Buddhism. Religion has allowed for many people to form a community within their society. Emil Durkheim explains in his piece “The Cultural Logic of Collective Representations” that religion was a crucial part of the formation of society and aided in the creation of the collective consciousness. Yuval Noah Harari touches on the function of religion in today’s society in his book 21 Lessons for the 21st Century. Harari highlights how religion does not play as much of an influential role in today’s society because of the great advancement made by the human race through technology and complex thinking. Although Durkheim and Harari have differing views on the role of religion, both sociologist’s points are pertinent. Durkheim’s beliefs are more relevant to the beginnings of society, while Harari’s beliefs are more relevant to today’s society. Religion was crucial in the formation of society, but it has now become more obsolete and not necessary for societies to operate.

Emil Durkheim brought forth the idea of the collective consciousness to sociology. The collective consciousness can be defined as a set of shared beliefs, ideas, and moral attitudes that unify a society. It defines what is “good” and “bad” in a society as well as the kind of morality an individual must exude in the society. This shared belief is necessary to maintain moral order. Without it, society would not exist since everyone would have different ideas of how society was supposed to function. For example, one person could believe that hurting another person for personal gain is perfectly fine, while another could believe that hurting another person in any aspect is very wrong. Without a consensus and agreement between the people, everyone would have different moral codes leading to major conflict and a community would be unable to form. Collective consciousness forms by humans interacting with each other in some pattern. The religious rituals that were performed by early civilization – which is a coordinated sequence of events that relate to a higher power – brought the community together because they were coming together for a common purpose. This common purpose could be a range of things whether it be to have good crops in the next season or to grant good health among all of the people in the community. Participating in these rituals facilitated communication and social gathering. These rituals allowed for collective life to become tangible which aided in the development of the collective consciousness. Durkheim argues that when the collective life reaches an adequate amount of intensity, religious life is the direct consequence. Since religion plays such a critical role in the development of the collective consciousness, Durkheim also argues that the fundamental categories of thought, science, and social institutions have religious roots.

Yuval Noah Harari has quite a different take on the role of religion in society. Harari’s book 21 Lessons for the 21st Century focuses much more on religion in today’s world unlike Durkheim’s piece which focuses more on the birth of society. Harari argues the fact that religion has become less relevant to society’s function since human’s have advanced so much. Today’s society has integrated so much technology and science into people’s lives. With this advancement, people are exposed to much more information and scientifically supported explanations for things that may have previously only been explained by religion. With access to this information, people have the option to believe in the new discoveries or in the religious explanation. They are not limited to having to blindly believe in what religion says because it is the only explanation that society has been able to come up with. For example, religion used to tell people that sacrifices were the only way to have a good rain season and a good harvest, but now society has discovered the science needed to keep crops alive so that sacrifices are deemed unnecessary. Also, as the human race has grown, more religions have been born with different beliefs. These religions help bring together regions of people but having different religious beliefs has also led to many conflicts in the modern day. According to Harari, the entire human race is the society and having many religions does not help unify the community, but often polarizes people. Harari also refers to categories of issues that the world faces today including a technical aspect and a policy aspect. The technical aspect refers to the way things are done in the world and the policy aspect refers to how governments create policy to address problems in the world. Harari uses the example that if Egypt was struck by a plague of locusts, they could pray to Allah, but they would also call upon scientists to develop stronger pesticides and insect resisting wheat strains. In this situation, religion can play a role in the solution but modern-day solutions through science are also utilized. Harari also uses an example where he states that if a crucial decision needs to be made about the Iranian government, they turn to the modern scientists of economics to get answers because the 7th century Arabs did not have knowledge about modern economics that they could’ve put in the Quran. After coming to a solution using the ideas of Karl Marx, Milton Freidman, and Fredrich Hayek, they would also use a Quranic verse to support the economic decision. Here, Harari is trying to point out that religion is no longer the best or only way to make decisions since there are other resources for people to utilize.

Durkheim and Harari have different views on the importance of religion in our society, but both sociologists have convincing points for their arguments. Durkheim believes that religion is what founded society and allowed for people to come together and form the collective consciousness. He argues that a society would not be possible without religion. On the complete other end of the spectrum, Harari believes that religion is not necessary for our society to function. Since the world has made such advancements in science and critical thinking, religion is not the only thing governing how or what people think. Despite the fact that both of these arguments are very different, they are both still valid and they can also be tied together. Religion was necessary for society to be born because it brought people together and allowed for them to form a collective consciousness. Without this collective consciousness, people would not be able to live in harmony together or have universal standard morals. Early civilizations used religion as a way to explain things that they could not explain on their own. They also used religion as a comfort for the unknown. Many fear the uncertainty and unknowingness of death, but the belief of going to heaven puts them at ease and makes it less scary. This is still present in today’s world. Science and technology have not been able to figure out what happens to one’s soul once they die, so religion is used as a way to explain it. Although, science and technology have been able to provide evidence for other instances where religion was used to explain the unknown. In today’s society, technological advancement has allowed for more information to be discovered. When new information is discovered, it disproves previous beliefs, like those that are embedded within religion. As new ideas are brought into the world and challenges religion, it also can create conflict. The same can occur between different religions who have different beliefs. Religion in today’s world can definitely bring forth conflicts, but it can also bring a sense of community and identity to people. Interacting with people who believe in the same things you do, helps solidify and reassure your ideas and gives you a community of people that you can turn to. Harari and Durkheim both touch on this topic. Durkheim’s views reflect how religion effected society when it was created, but Harari’s views reflect how religion does not affect society nearly as much in today’s society.

Religion has majorly influenced our society in the way that it functions and the understood universal moral code. According to Durkheim, religion allowed people to come together because of a common belief which then resulted in the formation of the collective consciousness. With the formation of the collective consciousness, a society had the ability to form. As society has advanced through science, technology, and more complex thoughts and ideas, the role of religion has shifted. According to Harari, religion does not play as critical of a role in the function of society because people can rely on science and technology to give them explanations for things instead of religion. Religion can still be used today as something that someone can identify and feel a sense of community, but religion is not necessary for the functionality of society today.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of religion's role in society
chunks.what_happened: The student compares the sociological theories of Émile Durkheim and Yuval Noah Harari regarding the role of religion in early versus modern society.

nee7e13a6.title: Contrasting Theories on Technology and Power

chunks.text:
At first appearance Harari has a multitude of social theories on anything from warfare, religion, and education to ignorance, science fiction, and fake news; however, the crux of each of Harari’s discussions are data: big data, artificial intelligence, and its owners. Harari proposes that our future in social organization and strategic action will be based upon data, artificial intelligence (AI), and society’s reaction to AI. These reactions will shape our future.

In accordance with Harari, technology, big data, and AI are the driving forces of the future, which will not only shape industries and international trade, but humanity and global society. We must look to a future based on big data and AI and plan for it now. As AI matures, jobs once held by humans will transition to AI. As AI matures and algorithms become more complex, jobs once considered as irreplaceable, such as attorneys will be taken over by AI. The role of humans in the workforce will shift to that of maintenance of the data and AI.

Harari suggests that in response to the continued maturation and development of sophisticated AI and its increasing prevalence throughout all arenas of society, AI has the potential to establish a new class system of humans, which he calls “superhumans”. Superhumans are those individuals possessing technical skills, giving them the capability to manage AI and big data. Harari professes that these superhumans will be the leaders of the world, set apart from the rest of society due to their due to their exceptional technological savvy.

As AI develops Harari proposes that it will soon develop human creativity and emotion. This will continue to drive humans from jobs. Harari seems to pose this as positive; I am still looking for the positive in this scenario. With AIs advancement comes the geographic fallout as well as the large technically savvy countries will bankrupt the small struggling nations.

Harari turns to technology and its impacts on truth, personal finance, and fake news by the use of technologically created algorithms. Algorithms determine the order data appears during each Google search. The ability to control algorithms allows superhumans to control what we research and ultimately think and purchase. As such, these algorithms will dictate the responses to your Google searches, your loans, and you will assist in the ease of getting your daily fill of the internet’s fake news.

In accordance with Harari, what our schools are teaching today will be insignificant in the future. Students are taught volumes of data from historical events and dates, to current events. Why, we are just teaching our students data, which is easily accessible from anywhere. Harari goes on that these children need to be taught critical thinking skills, how to communicate and collaborate; the data is there for them to find; there is no need to memorize it. The children of the future need to learn how to work with the data through critical thinking and analyzation. Again, it is those that have learned the technological skills and are savvy that will be leaders of the future.

Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdam discussions are more of the social movements and how social movements are started and their changes on society than the use of technology for the future. Fligstein and McAdam focus on what creates and drives a social movement and elicits strategic changes. They have conducted research and studied how “actors” who were relatively powerless were able to take action and lead a social movement. Where Harari focuses on changes through AI and data, Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdam continue to look to social movements and their abilities to shape the future.

The key components to Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdam’s theory are through strategic action fields (SAFs) which include incumbents/challengers/governance units. Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdam consider SAFs as the field on which the actor’s function within society for social reform and change. This field is where they function in unison in accordance with the field rules.

Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdam’s theory on social organization and strategic action is based on the relationship of members of each strategic field and the interconnection of fields. Fligstein and McAdam’s propose that these fields are made up of members which continually vie for position and increasing reputation and power. There are numerous interconnected, overlapping, and often interdependent fields which contain actors that move on and off these field making moves for ownership of power. All the actors are continuously making moves on field to adjust their position and impact the actions of the other actors. Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdam believe that each field includes both incumbents and challengers. Incumbents who have been on the field for quite some time and challengers who have less authority and are vying for higher status. Most fields also have a form of oversight or governance which is used to ensure that rules are followed throughout the field. It is the entire group, the actors, governance, challengers, and incumbents that make up the each SAFs.

Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdam consider that social organization and strategic change may take place in part due to the back-and-forth churn for power within the SAFs. Moreover, Fligstein and McAdam do not consider that one or a small handful of superhumans hold the knowledge, but that the intelligence of the SAFs is obtained through the collective knowledge of the SAFs. The power of each SAF is created and momentum of each SAF is attained through the churn that takes place and the interactions within the SAF. As such, the skills are a collective of the highly developed group knowledge rather than that of an individual actor.

As noted in detail above, Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdam’s see social movements and change dictated through an elaborate system of strategic action fields (SAFs). These SAFs are a highly sophisticated hierarchical group that collectively possesses the knowledge and power to both initiative and action social change. On the other hand, Harari, sees the power of the future of our society in the hands of a smaller subgroup, the superhumans. Harari, sees not a collective, but a more highly specialized smaller group of individuals, the superhumans which possesses the required savvy to manage the worlds technological advances.

Harari focuses on the future being driven by big data, who understands it, who can manage it, and most importantly who owns it. Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdam do not make mention of big data. Harari continues to discuss the development of and advancements within artificial intelligence (AI) and its impacts to our future. Harari notes the impacts to education, career, creativity, and many other aspects f our society. Again, Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdam do not make mention of the impacts of AI.

Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdam are focusing on the social movements and changes of the past, how they were orchestrated and their ideals of the collective SAF conscience. They are less interested in predicting the future itself, but in predicting the functionality of the way in which society responds and shapes the future.

Harari takes a focus on where we are today based on the past and given that rate of development where will we be in the future and what does that mean for us. He takes a the past and the present and projects it upon the future.

Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdam do not appear to look forward as much as to the past. Harari takes the growth in data, technology, and AI, and projects what the impacts may be in the future. Knowing the rapid speed that technology has already changed the world Harari touches on what that may look like in many of the aspects of society. He addresses what our changes will be in the workforce, education, warfare, creativity, and even our religion. Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdam stay focused on the way changes will take place choosing not to discuss the changes they see coming or the impacts these changes may have on the future of society. Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdam simply remain focused on the structure of how the changes may be initiated. Harari takes his theories and projects them into the future. He takes that plunge into given the past, given where we are today, where will we be in the future. Harari speculates what can we expect for the next generation. He discusses this at length also addressing steps society needs to take to not to be successful in the future and prepare for what may be coming in all aspects of life. He discusses what each of us needs to do and how society needs to prepare to be successful in the future. Harari see the future lead by a small microcosm of superhumans while Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdam seem to see the collective as the crux of social movements.
chunks.label: Comparing Harari with Fligstein and McAdam
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes and compares Yuval Noah Harari's ideas regarding big data, artificial intelligence, and superhumans with Neil Fligstein and Doug McAdam's theory of strategic action fields and collective social movements.

necad621c.title: Gender Dynamics at a Female-Majority Campus

chunks.text:
The concept of “women as other” or “second gender” is something that has caught a lot of attention and more people are recognizing that it has been around for centuries and needs to change. Although it is still present on campus at UNCW, it is different than what I have experienced before. Because the majority of the student population is girls, there is a somewhat different dynamic on campus because it is not what we are used to seeing in the work place, or even in other educational places.

“Women as other” is a concept that has been getting more attention recently, but some people still do not understand what it is, or why it is a problem. Otherizing women is essentially putting them into a box, or certain roles (wife, mother, daughter) and not allowing them to create their own identity. Men are assigning the roles to women in their life and teaching them what they are supposed to doing. The women are not allowed to do or be anything outside of what the man assigns her to. This has been going on for ages, and it is very hard to pinpoint a time of when exactly it started. A woman becomes “other” when she submits to the males idea of the worlds, and accepts the world from their point of view. When the women gives up on trying to get the male to see the world from her perspective. She will become the other easily because it is what the rest of the world expects to happen, and the male is expected to be dominate, thus she gives into him, and the rest of society. Not only does this create issues with what women believe they are capable of doing, it also permanently places women on the outside, and makes them the “other”. Because they are being defined by men, they are becoming what is called the “second gender”.

The concept of “second gender” is very similar to otherizing, but it puts women in a lower place on the social totem pole than men. At one point in time, women were seen as the defective human, or the incomplete man. These thoughts lead to people thinking, and agreeing with the idea that being a man was virtue, and that women were inherently wrong. Once this idea was accepted by society, it made it very hard for women to create their own self or be something outside of a relationship with a man. It also led to the idea that women were trapped in their own body, and only making emotional decisions, thus they were not allowed to make important decisions that men were expected to make.

Women have been experiencing these issues for an extended period of time, and it has come to the point where it is almost expected for them to feel as if men are looking down on them. In the work place, educational spaces, and just normal everyday areas women are subjected to these views constantly. Women being treated differently in the workplace can be easily explained by the idea that women are nurses and men are the “real” doctors. The women are stereotyped into having a lesser job, or not being as important.

The aforementioned stereotypes are what people grow up learning and experiencing so they accept it and think that it is normal for women to be lesser, or not have an important role in public society. These stereotypes also arise because of the previous lack of women in the workforce. They were the minority and thus treated differently because of that. Now if we look at the campus of UNCW, you can see the juxtaposition between gender ratios in the workplace and on campus. With a gender ratio of almost 70% female and 30% male, there are significantly more females enrolled than males, and this creates a different dynamic that no one is used to being in. Women are now the majority, but men still treat them as the “other” or “second gender” and still do not allow them to create their own personalities outside of the typical stereotypes.

The men on campus all see the gender ratio as something good for them, some of the ones that I have talked to think that it makes their life easier. They can be talking to multiple different girls at the same time because there are such fewer males than females on campus. Although they might see it as something beneficial, it really is not. The amount if women on campus creates a lot of tension between all of them because they are all going after the same group of guys. Not only does it create competition, it also creates a lot more comparison. Comparison between women is another thing that has been around for decades, but it arose from stereotypes that have been created for them to fit into; These stereotypes can also be referred to as the “beauty myth”. The beauty myth gives us the idea that for women, the being beautiful should be the most important thing, and that women’s value is based on only their beauty, and actions that meet the standards created for them. The beauty myth came about as a backlash to feminism. Men wanted to undermine the power that they were gaining and ensure that they would never beat out men.
