Women are so subjected to it because society has accepted it and plays into it, this can be seen in the entertainment industry, where women are portrayed according to the male gaze. Consumerism and the expansion of media has also influenced this a lot and created a narrower picture that women are expected to meet and it has escalated the problem.

Both situations, women being the minority or the majority, there are issues that are created and there is no true way to get around them. There is also no way to make sure that everyone is happy with how they are being treated in the workplace, or in an education space and this makes solving the issues that we know are so prevalent and have been around for so long extremely more difficult than previously thought.

Although there are things being done to combat these stereotypes and ideas that are been around for centuries, there has been a lot of damage done by them, and they will continue to be practiced and accepted because it has been engrained into society and passed on from one generation to the next. The only way for these ideas and concepts to stop being socially accepted, is to start teaching the next generation about them in a way that will allow them to realize why things like “women as other”, “second gender”, and “the beauty myth” are harmful to a whole, and start providing resources and help that will allow them to change the ways people are treated. The gender stereotypes that were created by all of these concepts are slowly starting to change, but not enough to make it were there are no more gender expectations. People now have the freedom of expression and open interpretation which allows them to be the person they want to be, not what others expect of them.
chunks.label: Gender concepts and UNCW gender dynamics
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on sociological concepts such as 'women as other', the 'second gender', and the 'beauty myth', discussing how UNCW's female-majority gender ratio affects interactions, competition, and enduring gender stereotypes.

n9ed3fe0e.title: Comparing Views on Capitalism and Technology

chunks.text:
Yuval Noah Harari is known for his popular books; “Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind,” and “21 Lessons for the 21st Century.” In class, we read “21 Lessons for the 21st Century,” where Harari unpacks and addresses a lot of the social issues our society faces today. Harari has a more modern perspective on our current society and has some very interesting and somewhat radical perspectives. Harari views capitalism as something people follow like a religion. He believes capitalism is reliant on people's belief in it. Harari believes that capitalism is greatly threatened by algorithms and AI and warns us about them. Algorithms collect data and give computers instructions that make them work smarter. The advancement of these computers is frightening because there are no regulations as to how this technology advances. The sci-fi television shows we watch with crazy robots and dystopian societies are becoming less of a fictional topic, and more of something we may see everyday. With the advancements in technology, workers in our capitalist society are becoming threatened, because AI could do the work they do more efficiently, and cheaper. These private companies will gain immense amounts of power, for they will have to pay fewer people, which could result in many people being out of a job. This large amount of power granted to these private companies and their higher up employees is frightening, and unfair. Overall, Harari sees capitalism as something that may be overtaken. While both Harari and Marx lived in different time periods, they do have similar views. Harari’s views are more futuristic, whereas Marx’s views are dated due to the fact that he was alive 200 years ago. I would argue and say that regardless of this massive time gap, Marx's opinions and views are universal, considering they are still heavily discussed today. Both of these men see Capitalism as fragile and bound to come to an end. Harari believes that algorithms and AI will bring capitalism to an end. Marx believed that tension amongst the differing socioeconomic classes would cause the end of capitalism, and society would adopt socialism. Both Harari and Marx recognized the unfair treatment of workers in the Capitalist system. Harari discusses how unfair, unequal, and scary the amount of power private companies have truly is. Marx also mentions how unfair this distribution of power is. He also shined light on how these workers work hard, at their employers beck and call, to produce products. Product they will never receive the profit from. Overall, both of these great thinkers see Capitalism as a flawed system that is bound for failure. Karl Marx and Yuval Noah Harari are both highly respected intellectuals with some radical and mostly prolific ideas. Marx’s ideas are very controversial and have been for a long time. There is one undeniable truth, and that is that Marx’s ideas are highly influential, important, and timeless. Almost 200 years later and his ideas and theories are still discussed, disputed, and even used today. Harari on the other hand, who is still currently alive, also has very interesting and thought provoking ideas and theories about our society. He does a wonderful job using what we know now as the basis for predictions about how our future will look. Both Harari and Marx share similar views about Capitalism. They both see it as a doomed system that will fail eventually, as well as unfair and cruel to the workers the private companies within the system thrive off of. Marx has his own political ideology, with some followers still to this day. Modern day forms of communism stem from his writings. Harari is not a political theorist, he is a great thinker and philosopher that has used information he has gathered from the world around us to draw conclusions and state observations. After reading and studying the work and ideas of both of these men, I have gained a new perspective on Capitalism as well as the socio-economic class system here in the United States. Works Cited “Capitalism Definition & Meaning.” Merriam-Webster, Merriam-Webster, https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/capitalism. Harari, Yuval N. 21 Lessons for the 21st Century. Vintage, 2019.

Harari, Yuval N., et al. Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind. Harper Perennial, 2018.

Marx, Karl, 1818-1883. Alienated Labor. Private Property and Communism. Critique of the Hegelian Dialectic. Three Essays Selected from the Economic-Philosophical Manuscripts. [Place of publication not identified],[publisher not identified], 1947. Marx, Karl, and Friedrich Engels. The Communist Manifesto. New York: Penguin Books, 2011. Print.
chunks.label: Comparison of Harari and Marx on capitalism
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the ideas of Yuval Noah Harari and Karl Marx regarding capitalism, technology, and labor, concluding with a works cited list.

nea95a30b.title: Conforming to Unrealistic High School Standards

chunks.text:
Have you ever found yourself envying an attractive actress? It’s nothing to be embarrassed about, it is a common emotion when faced with popular actresses who are stunningly beautiful and live these glamorous lives. However, I guarantee I can describe the character’s general appearance. She probably had flawless skin, a flat stomach, large breasts, and a small waist that tapers out into a larger buttock region, yet her legs are thin enough to leave a gap between her thighs. Was I close? Predicting to physical features of a common actress or celebrity is not as difficult as you think in the age that we live in. In a time that is supposedly accepting of all people no matter their size, shape, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, or any other factor that makes them unique among others, there remains an underlying standard for women’s beauty that becomes increasingly more complex as the world of social media expands. Society claims to be increasingly concerned with the health of our bodies yet continues to objectify and judge women based on their physical features, which leads to all kinds of health issues including depression, anxiety, body dysmorphia, and eating disorders.

The topic of beauty standards and mental health is not a new topic to society, but rather one that has become increasingly more popular as our society transitions into the era of “Postmodern Beauty.” This new era is incredibly detrimental to the development of the personality, self-image, and overall mental of women of all ages. As a woman myself, I have seen and experienced firsthand these starling effects and I am frustrated at the fact that I have no choice but to mature in a culture that is based on uniformity. As children, we see each other as equals, with no real awareness of the shape and size of our bodies. We are fascinated with what the world has to offer and see our bodies as the simple vessels for life that they are. However, at some point, a switch is flipped, and you recognize that the orientation in which you present yourself is subject to the judgment of everyone around you. Some individuals gain great confidence or simply remain ignorant in acknowledging the judgment. For others, this is an all-consuming force that slowly chips away at their self-esteem and can cause catastrophic changes in their lives.
chunks.label: Beauty standards and mental health
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the concept of impossible beauty standards for women in modern society and explains how social media and the judgment of others harm women's self-esteem and mental health.

chunks.text:
As a child growing up in rural Pennsylvania, I had little knowledge of social media and therefore was not aware of the standards to which I was supposed to conform to, however, I failed to recognize the nonelectronic influences around me. My parents did a wonderful job at raising my siblings and I to appreciate ourselves, nature, and all the experiences we had been blessed with. Although we protested for phones and other electronics our friends boasted about at school, they remained firm in shielding us from the inevitable detriment of these technologies. However, they could not hold off forever, so when each of us started our freshman year we got phones. I thought I was finally going to be able to make friends and be cool, popular, and all of the things that a 13-year-old valued. But I quickly found out that being close friends with my sibling and the way I dressed was “not cool” and my body measurements were considered “obese.” My spark of hope died out quickly as I listened more closely to the comments my “friends” made about my clothes, my personality, the way I spoke, my acne, and above all my body. Comments I had previously dismissed as jokes as I was oblivious to the harsh truth that being unique and experiencing normal bodily changes were ridiculed.

In my first 2 months as a Freshman, I found my group of friends no longer talking to me, excluding me from group activities, and pictures, and making crude comments about my appearance behind my back. I began to regress from my social and outgoing nature. I threw myself into school and sports and became infatuated with social media and what was acceptable. I stopped eating breakfast and what little food I ate for lunch I ate alone in my English teacher’s classroom to avoid judgment. I became consumed with the looks I got in the hallways and overanalyzed every conversation I had throughout my day trying to figure out if I looked how they wanted me to. By the beginning of my sophomore year, I had lost almost fifty pounds and I was constantly tired and hungry. People commended me for my weight loss, but it still wasn’t enough to get back the friendships I had lost. Then the pandemic hit. Suddenly no one saw me every day, I couldn’t bury my thoughts in school or athletics because everything was shut down. I was left alone with my thoughts, social media, and most importantly my family. In such a constructive environment I began to dig myself out of the hole of my negative self-image and pulled away from the harsh environment of social media. I gained back some of my weight in muscle and became more comfortable being alone with myself and accepting my uniqueness.
chunks.label: High school bullying and body image struggles
chunks.what_happened: After getting a phone in freshman year, the student was bullied and excluded by friends about her appearance, causing her to restrict her eating and lose nearly fifty pounds until the pandemic allowed her to recover at home with family.

chunks.text: Society is structured with the façade of encouraging each and everyone to be different yet is only truly accepting of those who fit the mold of “perfection.” Although I was able to heal from such a dark time in my life I still deal with constant anxiety and self-esteem issues that will never really go away as long as I live presently in our society. I have seen this need to conform in many other women in my life as well. I have spoken to peers who have spent hundreds of dollars on lip fillers at 17 years old and more recently a friend expressed her excitement as her breast enhancement surgery was just scheduled for the upcoming month, she is only nineteen. Women are constantly striving to attain the perfect body encouraged by multiple factors in American society from influencers such as the Kardashians to weight loss supplement advertisements to the simple plastic doll known as Barbie. These “health” and “beautiful” bodies are riddled with unrealistic measurements and the expectation that women have thin limbs and a flat stomach while also sporting curves in “all the right places” and large buttocks and breasts. Genetically this is nearly impossible and results in continued dissatisfaction in your own skin. Sometimes the need to fit in can become so powerful it prompts women to take drastic measures such as surgeries or diets that often end in eating disorders, worsened body dysmorphia, and festering mental health issues.
chunks.label: Societal pressures and drastic physical modifications
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the ongoing pressure women face to conform to unrealistic body shapes, mentioning peers getting cosmetic procedures and the role of influencers and media.

chunks.text:
I am drawn to the complexity of this topic, not only from personal experience and the fear of raising children in such a harsh society but also from the elaborate take Naomi Wolf presents in her piece “The Beauty Myth.” Wolf defines the beauty myth itself as a commodified, censored, and unreachable physical ideal to which women must adhere. In other words, it is the idea that women should present themselves in a beautiful way while men should always have access to these beautiful women. This myth functions as a means of controlling the actions and appearances of women and keeping them under the control of society. It is a despicable idea rooted in the ideas of eating disorders, inferiority, and domestic violence, each of which is incredibly toxic in the grand scheme of how women see themselves. While Wolf claims the myth of beauty is an order that dictates behavior rather than appearances, it is clear that the behavior provoked produces actions contributing to the beautification or enhancement of the appearance of the affected individual. An example of this myth in effect was seen after the Industrial Revolution. As women began to emerge from their stationary place in the home they infiltrated secondary education, legal rights, the circle of trade, and the liberal professions. Men sought a means to weaken them and given that they already gained physical control of themselves they imposed beauty standards to weaken them mentally, contracting the rise of feminism. While this was imposed by all of society, it was pushed heavily by males in order for them to remain in prominent positions and keep women complacent in their servitude to men. In our modern age, the beauty myth has shifted substantially in the sense of what is its main source of power and momentum.

As Wolf outlined in her piece men played the largest role in imposing this idea of strict beauty standards on women, motivated by remaining in power above them. However, I believe in the 21st century men are not responsible for the mass imposition of standards on women. It is the collective effort of both men and women to oppress other women. Men still strive to stay ahead of women as per the age-old tale of gender supremacy. The complexity comes when you consider how women oppress each other. If you think about it, which gender is inherently obsessed with the action of gossiping, a process of speaking poorly about someone based on a judgment they have made? When women discuss other women more often than not, they are critiquing the way the woman at hand has presented herself to society, referring implicitly to her physical features. Women partake in the breaking down of one another for the same reason men do, to gain more power over the oppressed, and do so through many means from physical speech to social media to pushing diet culture through society. This makes it increasingly harder for women to escape this maltreatment as it approaches them from all angles, attesting to the chain reaction of anxiety depression, body dysmorphia, and eventually eating disorders that lead to larger medical issues. Somehow society has taken the nontangible idea of “beauty” and invested so much, attention, time, energy, and resources into it allowing it to manifest and effectively kill these women from the inside out through their own behaviors and call it “healthy.” Men and women will always have an underlying imbalance in power, but it would be to unsensible the imbalance women create within their own gender group.
chunks.label: Analyzing Naomi Wolf's The Beauty Myth
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Naomi Wolf's text on the beauty myth, discussing its history since the Industrial Revolution and arguing that in modern times women also actively oppress each other through gossip and competition.

chunks.text: Upon reevaluating Wolf’s idea of “beauty myth” I am prompted to reflect on my time in high school. My “friends” gossiped about my clothes, my skin, and my weight for the purpose of putting themselves ahead of me socially and ensuring that I would not be able to infiltrate their group, all of whom fit the mold of the “Barbie Doll” figure. I altered the way I acted by restricting my eating to change my appearance in an attempt to win over their approval. I recognize now that men had nothing to do will the change in my behavior, they were solely provoked by the insecurity of other women fighting for their own spots in the small social environment of our high school. A simple change in the environment I spent my time in daily shifted my outlook on my body and image, reinforcing the idea that without the presence of societal pressure from others the beauty myth is nonexistent, or has no power over an individual. If we are really looking for someone to blame, we should blame ourselves because even those oppressed are guilty of oppressing others. Wolf does an excellent job outlining this fact throughout the rise of feminism to the 21st century, requiring only the elaboration of the reader’s own place in society to recognize this malicious pattern.
chunks.label: Reevaluating high school through sociological theory
chunks.what_happened: The student connects her high school experiences of exclusion and disordered eating to Wolf's ideas, concluding that female peer insecurity drove the oppression rather than men.

chunks.text: Our society is extremely contradictory in expressing and acting on their values. We claim to be increasingly concerned with the health of our bodies yet continues to objectify and judge women based on their physical features, which leads to all kinds of health issues including depression, anxiety, body dysmorphia, and eating disorders. We produce diets, advertisements, influencers, and even toys that project the need for an unrealistic body type to truly be “beautiful” in American society. This means, for women, there is no true escape from these detrimental standards. I would like to end on a positive note of hope for a future free of oppressive standards but in honesty, there does not seem to be a way to shift a pattern of oppression that spans thousands of years and continues to reproduce itself in new ways as technology continues to advance. Peace and equality among gender would be ideal yet unrealistic, however, peace and support among women could go a long way in helping to ease the impact of this oppression, allowing for the cultivation of body positivity and positive self-esteem among all women.
chunks.label: Conclusion on societal contradictions and female solidarity
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that while societal beauty standards are unlikely to disappear, women supporting rather than oppressing one another could mitigate the harm.

ncbb47706.title: Critiquing Religion and Exploring the Self

chunks.text:
After reading 21 Lessons for the 21st Century by Yuval Noah Harari, I have found that he not only relates to some of the things that we have talked about in this class but he also seems to disagree as well. I believe that he would agree with Mead’s way of finding ones true self but would disagree with Durkheim’s view on religion. Well he would not fully disagree but I do not think that they wold see eye to eye on a few things regarding religion.

In Harari’s book he made a chapter that is title religion. In this chapter he talks about religion and how it contributes to our society. He believes that religion does serve as a foundation for the society we live in today, which is very similar to Durkheim’s view on it. However, he does in fact believe that religion could be a negative thing as well. In this chapter he asked this question “So how relevant are religions such as Christianity, Islam, and Hinduism? Can they help us solve the major problems we face?” (Yuval Noah Harari) To follow up his question he then made a list of three problems that are relevant to the 21st century. These three problems included technical problems, policy problems, and Identity problems. For each of these problems he gave an example to give more base to his argument against religion. The example for a technical problem was a farmer’s solution to severe droughts that are caused by global warming, then for policy it was what measures should the government come up with to prevent global warming. Lastly, for identity problems he gave an example that basically asks if you should even care about what the farmers problems are or if you should only care about your people. Out of these three problems Harari believes that religion only plays a part in identity problems and does not really help in the others. In fact, he believes that religion contributes to the problem instead of solving it at all. He says that traditional religions have lost their vantage to science because unlike religion scientist can learn from their mistakes. Them learning from their mistakes gives them the ability to gradually learn to do things like grow better crops and develop cures and better medicines. Because of this traditional religions are starting to lose authority in these technical fields as they lean more toward scientific approaches.

Religion towards the economy also does not seem to do much according to Harari. He says that religion would not give us the answers that we need to be able to solve any economic problems that we are faced with. This is because people back then have no idea how to tackle modern day problems that we are faced with now because they never had the chance to experience them. Without that experience how can the Bible or Quran provide answers that are needed. Instead of these books being a source of true knowledge Harari believes that are nothing more than a source of authority. He thinks instead of relying on religion that we should rely on Karl Marx, Milton Friedmen, Friedrich Hayek, and modern science of economics (Yuval Noah Harari) to get the solutions that are needed. Also, he speaks on how religion separates people. It does this by giving people a firm structure of what they should do in life. This may cause a very religious person to view something differently than another religious person. Because of this religion does not really have too much to add to policy debates and economics. Instead, it causes more argument and disagreement between people because they are more bias towards one side of an argument because of their viewpoints.

Now, I do believe that Harari does in fact believe that religion is a building block for the society, but I also believe that he thinks we should not rely on it as much as we did before. He believes that it is doing us more harm than it is good and that we should start relying on more modern things like science. I think that Durkheim would disagree on relying on science. The reason I say this is because Durkheim believes that society needs religion. Religion is a critical part of society; without it we would not have the society that we have today. He believes that religion provides purpose for people, authority, and means for communication. It acts as a magnetic force that pulls people toward one another. With that being said, I believe that they would agree that religion does help a person’s identity problems, but I think that Durkheim would not want to stray from religion like Harari would suggest. Without religion, the strong foundation of our society, we would fall apart. That’s where the disagreement would come in hand. Durkheim’s a firm believer in religion, while Harari does believe it was necessary in a sense back then and may have helped then, but that it is not much of a solution for problems that we are faced with now.

In 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, Harari speaks about meditation and how important it is to him. Through meditation he was able to learn more about his self and other humans by observing his sensations. Through meditation he was able to fully understand his emotions and find peace within his self. He found his true self. He stated that he did not have to accept any story, theory, or mythology, and that all he had to do was observe reality as it is. That is how he found the answers he was looking for, not through religion or other people but through himself. Therefore, I would say that he would agree with Mead’s concept of the self. With both the external component of the self that has to do with social interactions, and the internal feelings that are needed to understand yourself. By meditating Harari is starting to learn more things about the society we live in today and his self as well. This has opened his mind and helped him to find answers that he could not have found before. Mead’s theory of self is very similar to this, and it was the first thing I thought about when reading this chapter. Through meditation Harari is about to find the “I” aspect of himself, he realized that the only mind he can truly observe is his own. He said that he now meditates every day for about 2 hours. During this 2 hour he observes reality for what it is. I believe that can kind of tie into the “me” or external aspect of the self. I say this because the external aspect focuses on reality and the social aspect of life and how it affects us. I know meditation is not social because while doing so he is not out talking to other people. However, he is finding answers about other humans through his mediation. I believe he is doing so by thinking back on social interaction he may have had while meditating and by doing so he not only learns more about himself but others that he may interact with daily. Harari also states that “consciousness is the greatest mystery in the universe.” (Yuval Noah Harari). He believes that if we do not find the time to learn more about ourselves that algorithms and AI will eventually take over leaving us useless. In order to find ourselves Harari wants us to look deeper, and to recognize and understand our feelings and sensations. Once we find ourselves then we may understand one another and start to agree on things. If we can not do so however Harari does believe that the algorithms will end up doing that for us as well and that there will be nothing left for humans do to. We would be nothing but an empty shell that relies on machines to tell us what to do, what to buy, and how to think. This is why he wants us to look deeper into our mind and to gain self-awareness and a self-image. Which goes hand and hand with Mead, who also believes that our self is found through the conscious as well. They both would agree that the self is not something that is evident at birth because Harari did not even truly understand the person he was until he started meditating. Mead believes that the self comes over time and is found by experiences that you have throughout your life. Harari needed the experiences in his life to lead him to the path he is on now. With out doing the things that he has he would not have found out how to meditate and he would not have found his true self.

In conclusion, Harari’s book has presented many strong points with lots of evidence to back up his claims. He shares similar beliefs with both Mead and Durkheim in a way. I believe that his view on meditation and him find his self would cause him to agree with Mead’s concept of self. While his view on religion would support Durkheim’s in a way but would contradict it as well. Durkheim believes that religion is a strong base of society, and that society needs religion, while Harari agrees, but also believes that religion can cause more harm to the society than it can good.
chunks.label: Analyzing Harari alongside Mead and Durkheim
chunks.what_happened: The student compares Yuval Noah Harari's 21 Lessons for the 21st Century with sociological theories by Mead and Durkheim, discussing perspectives on religion, science, meditation, and the self.

n20e47d82.title: Challenging Societal Gender Roles and Power

chunks.text: When discussing sex and gender roles amongst society, it tends to lean towards a male power conversation. Women have tried to push their idea of feminism around the world attempting to prove that they are worth just as much as men and are just as capable to hold the same jobs, participate in the same tasks, and the list goes on. The collective conscious comes in to play when expressing how society has this view on gender roles and how a male and female should act in their unique ways. It is important for people to try and stand up against these said norms in an attempt for equality.
chunks.label: Views on gender roles, feminism, and equality
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on male power in discussions of gender roles, efforts by women to promote feminism, society's collective consciousness regarding gender norms, and the importance of challenging these norms for equality.

chunks.text: Similarly to James, Erving Goffman theorized the idea of “The Presentation of the Self”, which essentially compared personality to a stage. He claimed that your “front stage” is your façade, while your “back stage” was composed of your true, raw self, unfiltered. In your “backstage” is where you prepared your presentation for your “front stage”, which is what the world would see. For example, when you are out at a bar with your friends, your “backstage” prepares your fun, silly, energetic part of your personality to put on your stage. However when you come home alone at the end of the night to your bed, you are your raw true self: “the backstage”. Goffman used the analogy of the stage to put emphasis on the fact that our brain is always putting on an “act”. He said that in no matter what social context, our backstage is always working to prepare the front stage to perfection.
chunks.label: Goffman's presentation of the self
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Erving Goffman's theory of the front stage and backstage using hypothetical examples of going to a bar with friends and returning home.

chunks.text: Interestingly, Goffman and James’ ideas have the capacity to go hand in hand. The “social self” is essentially a combination of the front and back stages. The back stage defines the role you are playing in the particular social context, while the front stage performs the different social self you must be playing. The idea of knowing your audience is especially important in both James and Goffman’s theories. Without social awareness, how could the backstage possibly know which social self to present on it’s stage? Without knowing the context of the musical, how can a marketer know which audience to target their show towards? An additional point in Goffman’s theory of the stage has been recently related to the use of social media. Current sociologists compare his theory to the idea that social media is also a stage—one who’s play never stops running. Your image is curated by your backstage in order to portray yourself how your followers want to see you. James would say that your defined role in social media determines the kind of content you are putting out for your followers.
chunks.label: Comparing James and Goffman to social media
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the intersection of James' and Goffman's theories regarding audience awareness, front/back stages, and their modern connection to social media.

chunks.text: Even though William James and Erving Goffman’s theories were multiple decades apart, their similarities are uncanny. Personality is a big component of both theories, especially the variations of personality that are portrayed throughout your day to day basis. James’ main idea about role identification in the social self directly correlates to the function of the backstage in Goffman’s theory of the stage. Essentially, the job of the backstage is to identify your role in context, so the front stage can present the appropriate version of the social self. Whether that be a loving, compassionate, helpful husband in the morning, or a strict, powerful, controlling boss during the work day, your backstage is always working to identify the role you are playing to put forth the correct identity.
chunks.label: Synthesis of James and Goffman theories
chunks.what_happened: The student synthesizes the uncanny similarities between James and Goffman's ideas on personality, roles, and the function of the backstage.

chunks.text: Tap, Tap, tap… straighten posture, shift weight, keep eyes down, no, keep your eyes up, be confident, smile, look approachable. These are the many thoughts that circle a woman's mind while walking down the street. Billboards and magazines of the ideal woman's physique at every turn, unable to escape the perfection of the surrounding. Above the want for gentle eyes, silky hair, and radiant skin, there's one factor that far outweighs the desire of my appearance and want of the “male gaze.” The thought so frequently pops into my head of what it would be like to have the respect and stature as that of a man. Since the beginning of time, women have been dissimilar, supplementary and seen as “other” to the male sex. With no independent history, culture, or belief system, women have been in the shadow of man, supporting one's goals, aiding in their needs, and providing in any way achievable.
chunks.label: Women's internal pressure and historical status as other
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on societal beauty standards, walking down the street, and how women historically have been treated as 'other' and placed in men's shadows.

chunks.text: Since coming to UNCW I have visited the Recreation Center an average of four days a week give or take. Wednesday, February 8th, 2023, I approached the Rec Center eager to start my workout. After completing my five sets on the leg press, I approached the young man on the squat rack and asked, “Hey man, how many sets do you have left?” He responds, “Oh, I just started a new workout, so four to five sets.” With a smile on my face, I answered, “Okay. May you please let me know when you’re done? Thank you!” After walking away, not two minutes go by, and the young man sees what I assume to be his friend and gives him the rack. Although a little shocked, and thrown off by this interaction, I brushed it off. I then approached the only other squat rack in the gym and proposed to the man the same question. After being looked at from head to toe, he informs me that he has two sets left. Walking away, I watch the same event transpire. Giving another man the rack, my jaw drops in disbelief. Staring at the situation before me, I was puzzled. Thinking of all the possible reasons why one would not allow another a simple request, I struggled to come to a single conclusion. A couple days went by, and I spoke to one of my male friends that lives in my dorm, who also actively attends the gym. That’s when it hit me. I questioned, “How do I earn the respect of a man?” His head tilted abruptly, paused for a minute and mumbled, “I don’t know.” As a man who often makes jokes about gender differences whether that be “women can’t drive” or “women wear clothes for men, not for themselves,” he was not pleased with the treatment I was experiencing at the gym.
chunks.label: Ignored at the gym and talking with a dorm friend
chunks.what_happened: The student visited the UNCW Rec Center, where two different men gave away squat racks to other men after she asked for them. Later, she discussed gaining men's respect with a male dorm friend.
chunks.feelings: eager, a little shocked, thrown off, disbelief, puzzled
chunks.people: two men at the gym, male friend in dorm

chunks.text: Raised in a divided home with a dominating father and a goal driven mother, I saw the many conflicts that not playing your “gender role” creates. My father informed me from a young age of a woman's role in society. The caretakers of the household and appeal to the man's eye. Since 2nd grade, I have desired a career in the medical field, specifically, a medical doctor. These desires were constantly shot down as my father would say, “You shouldn’t become a doctor, you won’t have time for family, for your kids. Why not be a nurse?” He attempted to condition me to dress, speak, and portray myself as something to be advertised and admired by others. I can’t tell you the countless times I've heard, “that isn’t ladylike.” In comparison, my mother taught me that I am capable of anything permitting I put in the work… until I wanted to join the military, then all bets were off. Women that stray from their gender role and lack the desire to conform are put in undesirable positions in regard to relationships and profession. If surrounded in a male dominated environment, there will always be something to prove, because after all who wants the girl on their team.
chunks.label: Growing up with conflicting parental gender expectations
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up with a dominating father who discouraged her medical career ambitions and enforced traditional ladylike roles, while her mother encouraged her until she wanted to join the military.

chunks.text: Simone de Beauvoir, writer, activist, and social theorist focuses many of her pieces on women, most notably, “Second Sex.” She voices how women are viewed in comparison to men and how naturally speaking women are the inferior sex and always have been. In 1949, Beauvoir explained women's place, when expressing, “They live dispersed among men tied by homes, work...to certain men-fathers or husbands-more closely than to other women ” (pg-261). As a tactic of control, men have kept women separate, focusing their attention to the kitchen, the house, and the children. Without any purpose independently, there is an attachment that is created that ensures that a woman would not survive without the economic stability of a man. Due to the lack of financial contribution, women have had to compensate with their appearance, cooking skills, and physical affection for a man. A woman's purpose has been to serve, whether that be their husbands or their fathers, but never themselves. Self-interest is a pleasure not given, as every other member in their household takes priority. In addition to that, on page 260, Simone quotes the famous Aristotle, “The female is female by virtue of a certain lack of qualities” (Woman as Other). In this section of the piece, Beauvoir quotes many respected men in their fields, all of them displaying women as something to be conquered, lesser, and defective. Right off the bat, women have been almost pitied for their ignorance and have played the role of the underdog for far too long. Without quality education, resources, and equal opportunity how would one expect a man and a woman to possess the same qualities, skills, and experiences at that time. Marilyn Frye had an excellent analogy for comparing oppression to a bird in a cage. Being caught in metal bars or wires, restricts one's ability to spread their wings and flourish. No matter how many times one chirps or chitters, the barrier set in place by the bars allows the system (men) to observe with leisure, benefiting from the beauty, while the decoration remains trapped inside.
chunks.label: Simone de Beauvoir and Marilyn Frye on oppression
chunks.what_happened: The student explains feminist theories by Simone de Beauvoir and Marilyn Frye regarding women as the 'Second Sex' and the birdcage analogy of oppression.
chunks.people: Simone de Beauvoir, Marilyn Frye, Aristotle

chunks.text: As time has gone on and women have strayed from their household duties, there is a new problem underway. In an attempt to control women, there is a new war in place, women against women. Naomi Wolf provides insight on the new struggles women encounter when stating, “...attractive, successful working women, there is a secret “underlife” poisoning our freedom ; infused with notions of beauty… self-hatred, physical obsessions, terror of aging, and dread of lost control” (pg. 1). Every place you go there is an illustration of this in society. Women often speak of getting botox, liposuction, fake tans, and other aesthetic procedures. Girls in high school are even infected with this desire, as they chase the appearance and attention of the women they see on social media. The gossip of putting others down for their bodies, continues, as the standard of beauty increases. If you haven’t heard, the attraction scale has changed from the 1-10 rating to 1-30 to account for breasts, face, and derriere. Pornography has climbed to the top of the ladder for mainstream media. As women have begun to advance in society, attend college at higher rates than men, fight for higher level positions of power, one more factor of control had to be computed to once again seclude and create a barrier of division between women across the country, and the world.
chunks.label: The beauty myth and division among women
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Naomi Wolf's ideas on beauty standards, aesthetic procedures, social media pressure, and how beauty standards create competition among women.

chunks.text: Through experience and evaluation of the society around me, I have come to realize that the concept of earning the respect of a man is unattainable. Upon seeing an individual, there are certain perceptible characteristics including age, race, and sex. Before a word even slips off one's tongue, perceptions have already been made based on their physical appearance and overall presentation. Women around the world continue to feed into this perpetual sequence by upholding the standards of the beauty myth. Conforming to the expectations will forever yield the same undesirable results. Women often talk about how upsetting it is to be treated with such lack of kindness and respect by men but take it without refusals like they’ve been conditioned to. I too have played my own part in this debacle, however in recent times I have gained a deeper perspective regarding the identification of where these issues stem and the potential solutions to these problems. This pattern continues because the men and women in this society that are raising their children are doing a poor job of straying from the collective consciousness and the double standards held to each sex.
chunks.label: The impossibility of earning male respect under current norms
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how physical judgments, conforming to beauty standards, and parental conditioning prevent women from gaining respect from men.

chunks.text: My mother still tells me to not go out at night, still asks me if I have pepper spray on my keychain. My stepfather, a man's opinion I hold in high regard, told me that I should not step off campus alone, that I should bring a “friend”, but we all know when he said that he meant male friend.
chunks.label: Parents giving safety warnings about going out
chunks.what_happened: The student's mother reminds her not to go out at night and checks for pepper spray, while her stepfather advises her not to step off campus alone without a friend.

chunks.text:
This is the problem of our generation and the generations before us. There is an undeniable power struggle of respect between men and women and mothers and fathers have aided in this neglect. Children are only as skilled as we give them space to be. Having different standards for your opposite sex children causes boys to think girls are not capable, not competent, and not trusted. That is why when a woman does something as well or better than a man, all eyes are on her. The beauty myth and expectation of performing one's role denies a woman her full potential. Discouragement from family, friends, and peers does not create a supporting environment to breed success. Whereas a man has been raised to believe he will accomplish great things and be an author of his own destiny. This superiority complex plays a role in our everyday interactions. Whether that be the classroom, grocery store, household, or the gym, one does not escape it.

In addition to that, without respect for one's wishes and values held dear to them, consent has become a major dilemma of this parental and societal failure. Without the necessary backing from a young age, regarding the utility of men and women, the “other” sex has been exploited and made as a tool to serve man's sexual desires and cravings. The thrill of the chase, the anticipation of the capture, this animal behavior has been tolerated for far too long. Regardless of the regulations that have been established in workplaces, women still face many issues of respect from their male coworkers, customers, and employers. What appears to be a never-ending cycle is in fact just another representation of the lack of respect across the country and the world for women as the “incidental” being. A man should be equally afraid of a woman as he is a man, and a woman should know that she is capable of more than being just another pretty face.

In conclusion, women have been thrown into a box of seclusion and limitation since the beginning of time. The expectations set in the Stone Age still hold true today and the generations to come will continue to encounter these issues of unbalanced respect. Without the change of the collective consciousness spread throughout society regarding the role of a man vs the role of a woman and parental standards, the fight of oppression will always be a losing battle. As the fight goes on, measurements will be taken to continue to control women whether that be their role, job opportunities, appearance, or the community within us. The ability and respect of an individual should not be determined by what is between their legs, but between their ears.
chunks.label: Conclusion on gender roles, consent, and societal change
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that gendered double standards, consent violations, and ancient expectations must be broken through changing collective consciousness and parental upbringing.

nb6b583d4.title: Facing Pressures of the Beauty Myth

chunks.text:
The beauty standard is taught from a young age to be in an important component of many people’s lives, especially in women and girls. “The Beauty Myth”, while still relevant today, embodies that ideal in which women should want to be beautiful and are expected to especially if they want to attract a man. Previously in society women did not have much choice when it came to what they could do to be beautiful, the men in their life would decide that for them. Throughout history the “beauty myth” has not been an issue but time has changed and after the industrial war this is an obstacle for many. There are multiple reasons and concepts of how and why “The Beauty Myth” exists and its effect on normal women in the United States. In the rest of this essay, I will dig into what those concepts are and how the beauty myth has grown to become more harmful than it has ever been.

Naomi defines “The Beauty Myth”, as the increase in beauty standards and importance of beauty while at the same time women making progress in equality. Although many women might not like to admit it, a big population wish they were more beautiful. This toxic collective consciousness shared by women is influenced by what is presented by big corporations that want to make women feel the need to be “more beautiful” and therefore buy things that can help them achieve that. The saddening thing about this is that society pushes this myth even though it is not true in the way that women need to be more “beautiful” . In fact, this “beauty myth” is pushed to make women appear weaker and for men and other beneficiaries look more powerful, which will be talked about later.

Through the course of American history beauty standards have changed and since the Industrial war has then grown into “The Beauty Myth”. Before then, women did not have the constant reminder by technology of what “beauty” looks like. During this time, in order to find a spouse as a woman you had to have fertility and be willing work in the home and take care of the children. It is evident this standard has since changed for the worse. Because after the industrial war not everyone in the family was expected to work and hold the same important of importance in providing for the family, women became domesticated in the household. Wolf explains that not long after that took place, “since the Industrial Revolution, middle-class Western women have been controlled by ideals and stereotypes as much as by material constraints.” (Wolf, 4) By this time women were exposed to photos and images of what women should want to look like all because of technology. As technology has advanced and is commonly used by people every day this issue of an idolized beauty has gotten worse and encouraged by “men's institutions and institutional power.” (Wolf, 3)

As there has been a push by society for women to engage in beauty, this also came with a huge “backlash” of a certain level of beauty women feel necessary to attain. Many people agree and believe women should be able to do whatever they want to feel beautiful and actually are encouraged to but even feminists according to the school of psychological sciences proclaim that “intense social pressure to pursue beauty disempowers women” ( Leeat Ramati-Ziber, Nurit Shnabel, Peter Glick) Well then why do women focus on beauty so much if it is actually maker them appear weaker? It is mainly because beauty and specifically beauty products are targeted to make women feel more confident and more beautiful. Someone might ask well then if its advertised to help you feel better about yourself why would that be bad? And that is because of who is behind all the selling and advertising of these beauty products. It is big corporations who are just trying to make money and most of the time are controlled by men. These people know that society pushes “The Beauty Myth”, which then allows men to profit off of women’s insecurities and twisted mindset that they need to be more beautiful.

This journal called, The beauty myth: Prescriptive beauty norms for women reflect hierarchy-enhancing motivations leading to discriminatory employment practices, goes into further detail of not only how “beauty norms” leave women with less power but how they influence women to be discriminated against. The introduction of this journal makes a good point of exactly how women’s progress has also allowed beauty standards to develop to replace “traditional ideologies” that gave men a type of power over women. They explain how these expectations of women’s appearance, set by society reflect a correspondence to sexist hierarchy organizations that want to prevent the growth of women empowerment.

Along with the deceiving way sexist hierarchies have made profit off of women using beauty products they have also imposed great discomfort for women by producing harmful beauty products for a men’s benefit. For example, Chinese mothers forced foot-binding on their daughters to increase their chance of marriage. Another example is corset tops and high heels which can cause internal organs to move and damage to feet, but make women appear more attractive and allow assistance for instability on their feet. It is obvious that these practices used by women were encouraged because in some way it made men feel more powerful.

While the practices talked about previously were harmful, most of them are no longer encouraged by society but over the past decade eating disorders have been higher than ever in the United States. If you open a magazine, turn on the T.V., or even go shopping you will notice that most women included are thin. Especially in today’s society women have idolized and obsessed over the idea of being “skinny” and “thin”.

The Beauty Myth and Female Consumers: The Controversial Role of Advertising, is a chapter in a journal that goes into greater detail of how “The Beauty Myth” effects the dangerous market targeted towards women. In the beginning of this journal, it states major concern for the increase in eating disorders and body dysmorphia occurring in American females and what exactly the cause of that could be. The first suspecting cause is the promoted food and dieting in American Culture and that even taking a look in food magazines that “food advertisements focus more on dieting than on quality.” (Stephens, Hill, Hanson, 139) This reveals just how unsafe our society has prioritized being “lean” and that even food magazines talk about cutting down on food. The next issue possible causing this is the images of girls and girls that are looked up to and the kind of body they have. This idea of being “small” and “tiny” has become a trend for American girls and is then set by fashion models, Miss America, and girls in pornographic magazines. Because the beauty standard of what a woman’s body should look like is represented everywhere, most women feel the guilt that they do not look like that and can turn to harmful ways of looking the way they do. The dieting industry has grown because of this, even though they have been hit with lawsuits claiming the dangerous effects, the trend of being thin boosts the products that they sell.

In this journal included a survey done by Wooley and Wooley (1984) and it provided trouble data about women and the toxic body dysmorphia that continues to excel. In the survey they used 33,000 females and their ages ranged from 15 to the age of 35 and they were asked about their opinions about their body’s and how they managed weight control. The results are shocking because only 25 percent of the women were “overweight” but 75 percent of them believed that they were considered fat.

This research ties back to advertising and how they know that if they use an “attractive” and “skinny” girl in their ad that the women consumers are more likely to buy because they feel the need to look like this. There is a cultural idea that women have to look a certain way and when women are dissatisfied with the way they look they are more susceptible to giving in to products that will make them look the way they want to. This is where you can start to see the cycle, that there is someone who is money and power-hungry using women’s insecurities and wanting to conform to societies beauty standards as an advantage to help them.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces and analyzes the concept of the beauty myth, discussing its history, corporate advertising, patriarchal power dynamics, and academic studies on body dysmorphia and eating disorders.

chunks.text: Growing up as a female in the United States I have experienced many of these pressures to achieve the beauty standard. It is extremely hard as a teenager growing up and trying to remember I don’t need to change to society’s standards but yet they are shoved in my face almost every day. Seeing these “perfect” girls all over my social media makes me feel like I am not “beautiful” even though the collective concept of beautiful has been altered to be an unhealthy standard for women to aspire to meet.
chunks.label: Experiencing social media beauty pressures
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up as a female in the United States feeling societal pressure and seeing images of seemingly perfect girls across social media, which makes the student feel not beautiful.

chunks.text:
As technology has advanced in America the ways men and power-hungry corporations can promote unhealthy beauty standards is baffling. Even in the news there is talk of how celebrities can “Photoshop” and change they way they look so that the public will only see an unrealistic picture of what they look like. This then sets expectations high for regular girls and women to appear like that as well. Now in 2021, you never know if anything you see is ever a real raw image and the probability that it is is very slim. Since society has pushed this “beauty Myth” unconsciously, it has prompted people to feel the need to look perfect and that it is necessary in order to be beautiful. The scariest part, like I said earlier, is that society is not necessarily doing this on purpose but the people who help promote it know exactly what they are doing.

All of these journals and articles lead back to a basic concept of “The Beauty Method.” That although women feel more empowered in society than ever they also feel at their weakest. And with thr incline of exposure of the misunderstood meaning of “beauty” , this has become harmful to women everywere. When the “beauty myth” was first introduced the media and online networks were not like how it is today. Now the women and models we see on posters and television are most likely not a real image. There are so many ways an image can be altered in the slightest ways to make you think it is reality. Naomi Wolf informs in her article that “beauty is the last one remaining of the old feminine ideologies that still has the power to control those women whom second wave feminism would have otherwise made relatively uncontrollable” ( Wolf, paragraph 4)

Overall, the “beauty myth” is at its highest peak than ever. As Wolf explained, economies depend on the representation of women within the beauty myth, meaning that women are being trapped in this ideology that the economy profits off of only because of how it negatively effects women. The reason I believe it has gotten worse is from what I have said before technology and the ability it has to spread images and create false images. This allows the people holding the power more power by creating a false and unattainable measure of beauty to ultimately leave women coming back for something more again and again. The ultimate and pressing reason the “beauty myth” is causing more damage than ever is because of the physical and emotional impairment it has imposed on women. The high development of eating disorders, body dysmorphia, and the feeling women experiment of never being “beautiful enough” in the recent years just goes to show why this ideal is harmful. The pressure society puts on women is outrageous and if these beauty expectations keep growing it will become extremely detrimental to women’s health.
chunks.label: Reflection on modern media, technology, and health impacts
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how modern technology, Photoshopping, and unattainable media standards continue to reinforce the beauty myth and harm women's physical and mental health.

n1ad48a7d.title: Performing Different Roles Across Everyday Life

chunks.text:
Looking at me, I would say to my parents I am talkative and goofy, to my close friends that I’ve known a while I am pretty sarcastic, new friends consider me funny, my teachers would categorize me as quiet and diligent, and people I am meeting for the first time would consider me extremely quiet and potentially shy. Why do I have so many facades and appearances? Why do I act in such opposing ways when around friends, strangers, teachers, and parents? I present myself to different people differently in any given situation. Why do we all choose to be a different character around these different groups of people and in various settings?

“All the world’s a stage,” according to Shakespeare and that’s so true. It is understandable why it is so difficult to get to know who people truly are and why they act the way they do. This is because we are all actors and life is our stage. In the application of “Presentation of Self,” a person is an actor / actress and their “act” is dependent on the situation and who is present. We project the image that we want based on the specific setting. What we project is the image of ourselves that we want others to see. It may or may not be part of our “true” self. Our friends, family, teachers, anyone we meet are constantly looking and judging to see who we really are. Who is the “true” Carly?

Our roles are an important part of how we act. We have various roles as we go through each day. We have roles that are ascribed, these are roles that were chosen for us, such as daughter, female, Hispanic, adopted. Then we have roles that we have choses such as student and hopefully nurse. It is through the performance we give that we express ourselves within each of these roles. This plays a large part in our behaviors and interactions throughout the day. I do not act the same in the role as daughter as I do in the role as friend, acquaintance, or student.

In front of my parents, I play the role of daughter. It is in the role that I am most likely my “true self”. This may be the one role that is at this time in my life, this easiest role to play. They are the only people that love me unconditionally. As such, I am not inclined to need to search for the appropriate character, the role comes naturally. I feel very comfortable, so I am able to just be myself. In front of them the performance is very limited. Would everyone agree that I’m being one hundred percent myself? Probably not. They would probably assume that I act a certain way to please my parents. To some extent they are correct. I won’t talk to them like I would talk to my friends, because there is a certain amount of respect that you owe to your parents. Other than the way I talk to them, I would say I am myself in front of them. Since I have been in front of them and have known them since before I could really “perform” one could argue that I am not performing. At an early age I learned that if I misbehaved in front of my parents, there would be trouble. Things were much better for me if I just waited until they turned their heads. It was at that early age that we were already beginning to learn how to “act” in front of our parents. The daughter role is the easiest of my roles.
chunks.label: Presentation of self and daughter role
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on having different facades and characters in different social roles, focusing specifically on how natural and comfortable it feels to play the role of daughter in front of her parents.

chunks.text: For the years of my high school I had been basically living “re-runs” or syndicated television shows or living in the movie “Groundhog Day” when it comes to the roles I need to play. I was living with my parents and my sister and going to the same the school. So I played the roles of daughter, sister, close friend, not-so-close friend, and student on a daily basis. So, for those four years of high school, and most likely the three years of middle school as well, I did not have the need to make that many adjustments to the “acts”. It was a comfortable time. Now and then a new friend or situation would show up, but for the most part, things remained relatively constant.
chunks.label: Routine roles in middle and high school
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how routine and constant her social roles were while living at home and attending middle and high school.

chunks.text: Thing took a dramatic shift when it was time to hit the road to Wilmington, NC. I had several “discussions” with my new roommate over Snapchat before it was move in day for college. Over the internet is hard to determine how you need to act, what character you need to play. As I moved my stuff into my room, my parents were with me, along with my roommate and her mom. Who was I to be? On one hand, I was Carly, the daughter; and on the other, I was not sure who I was because Snapchat was not very helpful. Now this is every actor / actress’s nightmare, it is like forgetting your lines. My problem was, I had no lines. I had no directions on who I needed to be.
chunks.label: Moving into college dorm with roommate
chunks.what_happened: The student moved her belongings into her college dorm room in Wilmington with her parents, meeting her new roommate and the roommate's mother after having chatted on Snapchat.

chunks.text: Now, turn your attention to center stage, things take a sharp turn. I was walking to one of my first days of college classes. One of my friends in our group had just told a crazy story about something that happened to her in her senior year of high school. As we were all laughing hysterically, I reached the place that is to be the spot for my class. I am entering the stage playing the role of a classmate. Suddenly, my back was little bit straighter, and I ran my fingers through my hair. Quietly I entered the building and found my classroom. I opened the door as gently as possible to ensure no one heard me so they would not turn around. I slipped into my seat and opened my bookbag and pulled out my laptop, ready for class. I sat quietly waiting on my professor. During class, I tried not to make eye contact with the professor.
chunks.label: Walking to and attending first college class
chunks.what_happened: The student walked with laughing friends to one of her first college classes, then entered the building quietly and slipped into her seat to wait for the professor without making eye contact.

chunks.text: When in class I am a student and that is my role. As such, my character is quiet, and my demeaner studious. I am meeting the expectations of the teachers. This drives much of my behavior. They have the expectations that students are here to learn, and that education is first on their list. Teachers tend to keep personalities out of their evaluation of students. As such, with my teachers, I remain quiet and scholarly, blending into the crowd.
chunks.label: Student role expectations in class
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how classroom expectations cause her to act quiet and studious around teachers.

chunks.text: The role of close friend is harder for me. I act differently given each of the friends. I think this is when different sociological concepts come into play as well. I think that in front of each one I act differently because of how I originally presented myself. When I met each of them for the first time, I was at a different stage in life, so I acted differently in front of each of them. The type of performance they put on when I first met them also influenced how I acted. My one good friend I met in sixth grade, at this point in my life, I was still unsure about who I really was so my performance conveyed someone who was colder and more closed off because I didn’t want to be judged. Her performance at the time was similar, so we got along and never had any cases of mistaken identity. My other good friend I met junior year of high school, by this time I was more comfortable with who I was and was able to be more myself when meeting her. Our dynamics are different, but they both work because we know our roles and how to perform in front of each other.
chunks.label: Navigating roles with close friends
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how her performances differ between two close friends based on her own maturity and presentation when she first met each of them in sixth grade and junior year of high school.
chunks.people: friend from sixth grade, friend from junior year

chunks.text: When meeting new people I am definitely perceived as quiet and probably shy. With new people I am unsure of the role I am supposed to play, so until I watch them for a while and get a feel of their part. Once I get to know them and we become friends I become more open and my performance changes. With my newer friends, they perceive me as an easy going and funny person and for the most part accept me. However, I also know that there is a risk of falling out of acceptance. As such, with my friends, I am able to be funny, but because there is always that chance of additional judgement, I stay sarcastic; it keeps me in control. I am also nicer because that level of comfortable enough to jokingly be mean hasn’t been reached yet. There are always the possibilities of roles getting changed though.
chunks.label: Presenting self to new acquaintances and friends
chunks.what_happened: The student explains why she acts quiet and cautious around new people and uses sarcasm to stay in control around newer friends.

chunks.text: With my parents, they love me and want the best for me. They don’t judge me and have unconditional love for me, but they perform in front of me, they aren’t their true selves because they have the role of being in charge. My parents keep me on my toes and hold me accountable for what I say and do. Without this performance though, there would be an imbalance in the relationship.
chunks.label: Parents' performance and accountability
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how her parents put on their own performance of authority and unconditional love to maintain balance in their relationship.

chunks.text: On social media it’s an entirely different story. Only the good parts of life are really shared on social media, I think people use it as a little bit of an escape. They like to look at the pretty things in life. This however is toxic because there is no immediate physical presence of anybody and people aren’t really invested in what’s happening with you.
chunks.label: Social media presentations and toxicity
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how people present curated versions of themselves on social media as an escape and why that lacks genuine connection.

chunks.text:
Everybody has a different role they play in different situations and these roles only work if the performers are able to recognize the different roles. For example, in a group of close friends I am sarcastic, at home I am talkative and goofy, and yet to my teachers quiet and diligent. This is due to my “presentation of self,” this is the idea that in the immediate presence of others, people put on a performance. How do you know who someone really is, when all you can do is examine appearance and current “role performance”? In each setting you could find yourself putting on a different performance, being “a different person”.

When you are alone and when no one is around, the stage is gone. It is at this time that you jump off the stage. You can remove all the facades that you have had to carry around throughout the day. It is at that time that you take a deep breath and realize that you are you. Are you funny? Yes. Are you sarcastic? Yes. Are you goofy? Yes. Are you quite? Yes. Are you diligent in your studies? Yes. Are you shy? Yes. Are you an actress? Yes. You become all of those things. So, are you truly acting? Maybe, but these are all parts of what make up you. They are pieces of who you are when you are with others and in other situations.
chunks.label: Concluding thoughts on roles and identity
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that all her different roles and facades across situations are authentic components of who she is as a complete person.

chunks.text:
“If you had a million dollars, what would you do?” I asked myself the very same question. Once you’ve covered all the things you’ve wanted to do and help the people who are important to you, you’ll still have more money than you know what to do with. Have you ever wondered how we are trillions of dollars in debt but power elites hold over 40% of that wealth? How are world hunger and poverty rates at an all time high and yet there are billionaires who have the resources and power to end it and still havent? Most recently with the COVID-19 pandemic, somehow the rich just kept getting richer. According to the institution for Policy Studies, U.S billionaires got 62% richer during the pandemic and are now up to 1.8 trillion dollars. How is it possible for the power elites, or top 1%, to maintain power? Why is it that the rich keep getting richer and the poor are getting poorer?

The power elite is a group of upperclassmen that hold the most power and influence over the decisions of policy makers. There are 3 groups of people who hold power in the power elites. There is the social class, the corporate community, and the policy planning network. The social upper class not only have immense wealth but also have influence over their own class-meaning they set the rules. The corporate community are people that are on more than one board of directors, holding many seats in largest corporations in the United States. The last group, Policy makers are people who have a direct impact on government policy.

The world has been facing a surge in economic inequality. Recent events like the COVID-19 pandemic and the war in Ukraine exacerbated and accelerated the impact. The rich in America use Capitalism as a tool to continue to profit off of the hard working people of America. Americans are well accustomed to the “rise & grind” mentality also known as Hustle culture. The government has been utilizing the working classes' efforts to overcome poverty the way a hamster is constantly running on a wheel. A conscious and free life is what distinguishes humans and animals. Under Capitalism, it subverts that nature by alienating the worker because unless you are at the top, all jobs are in some way or another alienating you. The more a worker works, the less that belongs to them to call their own.

According to Marxist theory, alienation is a condition of workers in a capitalist economy resulting from a lack of identity with the products of their labor and a sense of being controlled or exploited. Commodity fetishism is the condition in which production is no longer seen as a social endeavor but as the simple exchange of money and commodities-the labor is severed as soon as it is connected to money. Due to this, the laborer does not get recognition for the effort or energy put into that commodity/product. Commodity fetishism is a direct result of alienation as people become obsessed with having the newest and coolest commodity. An example of this would be getting the latest iphone when it drops. The power elite control what is deemed valuable in order to turn the highest profit margin.

Domhoff talks about why the working class has such little power in America and it boils down to 3 major reasons such as: Internal division, political frustration, and union defeat. The working class is so divided especially when it comes to race. In the beginning, African Americans had no social power or influence due to their enslavement-meaning there was no way to organize workers. Once they gained their freedom, prejudices in the white working class kept the 2 groups apart. The working class was unable to develop their own political party due to the electoral system greatly disadvantages third parties, so they had no other choice but to pick between Republican and Democrat. In both parties, they had no influence due to the power of the wealthy. The American system is a free market, based in Laissez faire liberalism, so American employers fiercely opposed interference with private property. This caused the working class to not have much luck organizing themselves through unions as employers were able to call upon the government to strike down unionizing. Employers were able to do this as they had great influence with politicians and the backing of a free market.

After the Great Depression, the United States enacted a Keynesian economic policy. Keynesian policy created the conditions for high rates of economic growth through the 1950s and 1960s. Keynesian economics focused on putting more money into the economy and was equitable for all classes. This was not good for the power elites so they wanted to enact Neo-liberal economic policies. They were able to get rid of Keynesianism as it was not helping the economy anymore as America was already experiencing stagflation. Stagflation is a combination of high unemployment rates and high inflation. The power elite enacted Capitalism once more to fix this by raising interest rates and mass deregulation of the economy/ market to counter inflation and unemployment. This is how they were able to pass Neo-liberal economic policy that worked for them and lined their pockets that are still in motion to this day.

In the present day, the American working class is still unable to garner power and unionize to enact policies that work to help the lower classes. An example of this would be Starbucks employees still trying to unionize for democracy in the workplace and facing major backlash from the company and lack of media attention to their cause. Starbucks themselves is trying to twist the narrative into being a healthy and supportive employer that offers lots of benefits. Starbucks workers are calling for improvements to said benefits and a democratic say in what's going on in their workplace and having the protection to do so. Workers are making less every year as wages don't go up due to inflation, they are calling to unionize as they see this matter as “life of death” because what happens at work will directly impact their families and quality of life. Inflation means less money and by choosing to unionize, workers are aiming to take back some control from employers so they can have a say.

A huge and consistently rising issue Americans faceis the cost of living. Minimum wage is $7.25 an hour but it is not possible to live in an U.S county if you are not making $14.50 an hour according to the Economic Policy Institute. That is twice the current federal minimum wage. Minimum wage has been the same since 2009, which is the longest the U.S has gone without an increase. The federal minimum wage has lost 21% of its value since the last time Congress raised it in 2009.
