If Congress had continued to raise the minimum wage in line with the times, the minimum wage would be around $22.

Americans quit their jobs at a record rate in November of 2021. 4.4 Million Americans which makes up 3% of workers voluntarily left their positions, this movement has been called the Great Resignation. Economists have called this phenomenon an employee exodus which displays a deep dissatisfaction and discontent with present and previous employment situations. The pandemic has enabled the American working class to rethink their work/life balance,working conditions, careers, and long term goals. Many workers voiced their plights of feeling overworked, underappreciated, and underpaid as the top 3 reasons why they have chosen to leave their jobs.

The reality of American society is that the fates of many are at the hands of the few. The Rich have a hand in every American's plate and way of life. Ironically the American way of life has always been marketed to the world as the Land of second chance and new beginnings. Many people took a leap of faith and believed in chasing the “American Dream”. Through understanding these very harsh truths about the reality of the disproportionate power gap and highlighting that the power elites are really the ones who get a say on everyone's lives. However, we are starting to see improvement in the working class fighting back against oppressive forces and corporate agendas. Although there are many faults and necessary improvements to be made in our society, there is hope spread amongst the younger generations to unite together and raise awareness to the very skewed distribution of wealth and actively working to bring the change needed.
chunks.label: Wealth inequality and the power elite
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on economic inequality, Marxist theory, the power elite, historical and economic policies, labor struggles such as Starbucks unionization and the Great Resignation, and hope for change.

chunks.text: I overheard my parents complaining about me to one another, friends, and other family all the time. My siblings and I always joked about how our house had “rice paper” walls. Let me tell you, nothing, and I mean nothing is more irritating than hearing your parents talk down about you. Letters came in the mail from schools and programs for troubled youth. I was constantly being punished for one thing or another. I was always to blame for any and everything. The “common denominator,” as I previously stated. Anytime me and any of my brothers bickered, my parents would automatically assume I was to blame.
chunks.label: Overhearing parents' negative remarks and facing punishments
chunks.what_happened: The student constantly overheard their parents complaining about them to others and was frequently blamed and punished for issues at home, including bickering with siblings.

chunks.text: At school I was the teacher’s pet. Perfectly behaved. We had citizenship sticker charts and I had the most stickers in my class. I was always on the honor roll and my teachers could not seem to praise me enough.
chunks.label: Being a well-behaved student at school
chunks.what_happened: At school, the student was well-behaved, earned top citizenship stickers, made the honor roll, and received constant praise from teachers.

chunks.text: The first “principle element” of the Looking Glass Self is the “Imagination of our appearance to the other person.”
chunks.label: First element of the Looking Glass Self
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the first principle element of Cooley's Looking Glass Self concept.

chunks.text: My parents left very little up to imagination. I knew exactly how they viewed me when private conversations were very loudly spoken just a room over (New York Italians do not know how to be quiet). My countless number of nicknames referring to my attitude problem very much reinforced the things I overheard. The many positive reinforcements for my behavior and the special treatment I received from teachers really solidified the idea that they believed I was good. I was viewed as two different children at home and at school.
chunks.label: Contrasting perceptions from parents and teachers
chunks.what_happened: The student heard their parents' loud negative comments and nicknames at home, while receiving positive reinforcement and special treatment from teachers at school.

chunks.text: The third and final principle is the presentation of yourself for others based on how you believe and imagine someone sees you. Because I had conflicting views as to how others viewed me, I had two ‘presentations” so to speak.
chunks.label: Explaining the presentation of self principle
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the third principle of the Looking Glass Self regarding how one presents oneself based on perceived views of others.

chunks.text: Based on my parents' negative view, I acted negatively. I was the problem child. I acted out. I argued, fought, yelled, screamed, and threw fits. I was a terror. Any chance I had to cop an attitude, I did. Nobody needed to provoke me. I was a horrible listener, disrespectful, and mean. My attitude was “if they think that was bad, I’ll show them bad.” Every adult other than my parents thought of me positively. I was the golden child. So, at school, or at a friend's house I was perfect... A good listener, respectful, and well mannered. I was more than happy to lend a helping hand, sometimes without being asked. I had good grades, and never had to be disciplined by my teachers. I was the student teachers put next to the new kid on their first day. My friend’s parents always happily welcomed me into their homes. I am my grandparent’s favorite grandchild. I was truly two different children. Two extremes. My teachers were always baffled to hear that I had an attitude problem at home, whereas my parents were always confused as to why I wasn’t that way at school. Ultimately, I reciprocate the energy I receive, still to this day.
chunks.label: Acting out at home versus being well-behaved elsewhere
chunks.what_happened: The student acted out negatively and disrespectfully at home in response to their parents' expectations, while behaving as a helpful, respectful, and high-achieving child at school, at friends' houses, and with grandparents.
chunks.people: parents, teachers, friend's parents, grandparents, new kid

chunks.text:
Overall, the concept of the Looking Glass Self has affected me throughout my childhood, and still affects me to this day. The three core principles of the theory have been clearly demonstrated throughout my life. I was seen as good for some people and bad for others. Consequently, I acted good and bad. The conflicting views of me from my parents against the views of other adults caused me to act in two different ways. It is really hard to have a clear cut view of yourself when there are so many different perceptions. Nowadays, my relationship with my parents has completely changed and I am not ill behaved and a pain anymore. The clearest demonstration of the Looking Glass Self for me and others recently is via social media. There is a clear and pressing urge to impress. You want others to view your life as exciting and intriguing. It is all a facade.

Nobody’s life is perfect. It is truly thought provoking and crazy to think about how we all act in certain ways and base it on others opinions. You are constantly told to just live your life and not care what others think but we are truly a reflection of others opinions whether we want to help it or not. Claiming you don’t care about others opinions is simply untrue. It is inevitable. Throughout my life I have been acting a way in order to appease the opinions and thoughts I assume others have about me.
chunks.label: Reflections on Looking Glass Self and social media
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how the Looking Glass Self has shaped their behavior and self-perception, how their relationship with their parents changed, and how social media compels people to maintain a facade based on others' opinions.

chunks.text:
Works Cited

Cooley, Charles Horton. “The Looking-Glass Self.” Social Media & the Self: An Open Reader, 1902, https://doi.org/10.32376/3f8575cb.73d69f51.
chunks.label: Works cited entry
chunks.what_happened: The student provides a citation for Charles Horton Cooley's work on the Looking-Glass Self.

chunks.text: Real men don’t wear nail polish. This is a statement often said by traditionalists and even some who claim to be progressive. The societal structures put in place have created rigid gender stereotypes and expectations for the entire population to conform to. In reality, gender is not a binary logic and it’s not easily defined into two categories. Children are taught at a young age about what is masculine and what is feminine and that they should lay claim to one depending on how they were born. In reality, most people are not comfortable accepting that men can be feminine and women can be masculine because of how we’ve been conditioned.
chunks.label: Gender stereotypes and societal conditioning
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on traditional statements about nail polish and how societal structures teach children rigid gender binaries and expectations.

chunks.text: As a man who wears nail polish I have received many compliments and also criticisms along with brash assumptions being made about me. This social anomaly has posed new social problems for me when moving to college and engaging with people that I've never met before. In one specific instance, a close female friend that I had in the first semester revealed to me that she thought that I was gay until I started dating my girlfriend. Considering that this was someone I considered a close friend, I was shocked to hear that she made that assumption about me. This friend also made numerous comments about me wearing nail polish and would refer to me in a demeaning manner as a “Fashionista”.
chunks.label: Friend assuming student was gay due to nail polish
chunks.what_happened: A close female friend at college revealed to the student that she had assumed he was gay until he started dating his girlfriend, and she repeatedly made demeaning remarks calling him a 'Fashionista'.

chunks.text: I’ve also encountered people passing judgments on me because of the fact that I wear nail polish since I’ve moved to UNCW. Most people see it as something that only women and gay men do because it’s “too feminine” and “soft”. Many of my male friends have a hard time believing that I was a captain of my varsity Soccer and Basketball teams in high school because I’m seen as feminine and not athletic. However, this is not to say that some people do understand that painting my nails can be a form of self expression and creativity and by proclaiming that nail polish is only available to women can be a very harmful idea. I've found that in a heteronormative and hegemonically masculine environment, being a man and painting your nails leads to symbolic violence from your peers.
chunks.label: Judgments and doubts from male friends at UNCW
chunks.what_happened: Since moving to UNCW, people have passed judgments on the student for painting his nails, and his male friends have struggled to believe he was captain of varsity soccer and basketball teams in high school.

chunks.text:
When women engage in what is thought to be traditionally masculine activities like being highly competitive in sports or being the breadwinner of the house it contradicts the idea of “Doing Gender”.

West and Zimmerman present “Doing Gender” as a concept for how we are conditioned to conform to traditional gender roles in our heteronormative society. Essentially, we are taught what is okay and what is not okay for our assigned sex to do in order to be an effective member of our society. We are taught that certain genders are expected to do certain roles and gender is merely a social construct. West and Zimmerman argue that humans are not born performing their gender but that it’s taught through social experience and parental influences. We use “Doing Gender” as a way to easily recognize and organize ourselves in today’s society. One’s sex category and external identifiers determine the social expectations for their gender which ultimately create the act of “Doing Gender” according to West and Zimmerman.

Hegemonic Masculinity is a sociological concept that covers the idea that men are to act as the dominant gender in society in order for their role to be legitimized. The widespread ideas that men are to be tough, aggressive, and competitive are what support Hegemonic Masculinity. Hegemonic Masculinity supports that men should be the logical and independent gender while women are the dependent beings. “Feminine” traits such as painting your nails or being emotional are seen as weak if a man engages in them under hegemonic masculinity. While the practice of hegemonic masculinity attempts to benefit men in our society it ends up doing quite the opposite. Men who force themselves into these roles suffer from internalized mental health issues and the encouragement of this practice leads to an increase of sexual violence.

The subordination and objectification of women is also a factor of hegemonic masculinity that should be recognized. By placing men as the dominant gender, this concept of hegemonic masculinity effectively places women as the subordinate. Women are oftentimes seen as places for emotional support by men who support hegemonic masculinity. This idea also supports the “women as trophies” outlook that some men hold. This explains why painting your nails and caring about your appearance can be seen as trying to appeal to the dominant and ultimately being weak.
chunks.label: Sociological concepts of Doing Gender and Hegemonic Masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the concepts of 'Doing Gender' from West and Zimmerman as well as 'Hegemonic Masculinity' and their societal impacts on men and women.

chunks.text:
When applying the concept of “Doing Gender” to my experience of being seen as homosexual or unathletic for painting my nails, the situation becomes easily understandable. Since we are taught from a very young age on how to “Do Gender” we are conditioned to look for certain traits to help us legitimize and identify other’s roles in our society. My friend on campus, even being as progressive as she is, could not accept that painting my nails is a form of creativity and self expression. Instead she interprets my decision as an expression of femininity because that’s what “Doing Gender” has taught her to do. She associates certain traits to certain genders and sexualities so her system of identifying is essentially disrupted when a straight male paints their fingernails. The conditioning of “Doing Gender” can be combined with the ideas of Hegemonic Masculinity in order to see feminine traits as weaker traits.

Hegemonic Masculinity when applied to my situation, explains why some see me as unathletic and soft. This idea of masculinity influences my male friend’s decisions when they make the assumption that since I’m not a domineering male, I’m essentially weak and unathletic. The mix of hegemonic masculinity and doing gender can help reveal how the two are related through the lens of my own experience. The act of painting my nails leads others to believe that I am “doing the gender” of a female which brings about the assumption that since I am engaging in what is seen as “feminine” qualities that I am weaker and less athletic according to hegemonic masculinity.
chunks.label: Applying sociological concepts to personal experiences
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how the concepts of 'Doing Gender' and hegemonic masculinity explain the reactions and assumptions made by his female friend and male friends about his nail polish.

chunks.text: The concepts of hegemonic masculinity and doing gender can be used to dissect and help explain the reactions that different people have to a male painting his fingernails. I have come to reveal that the action of a straight male painting his fingernails creates a contradiction that isn’t easily digested when looking through the lens of “Doing Gender”. Additionally, The feminine act of wearing nail polish in the minds of hegemonic males creates the perception that it’s a sign of weakness and fragility. These ideals are not applicable to every single person in our society of course but they do help form most social contexts in the United States. We have to change how we think of gender, sexuality, and traditional roles as a society in order to make strides against these constructs. Educating others and creating a diverse community in which others can be provided with perspective and understanding is an important first step. These are not problems that can be solved overnight but social change is ignited through institutions and also social experience so shifting the narratives of your own community can help immensely.
chunks.label: Conclusion on gender constructs and social change
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes how societal perceptions link nail polish to weakness and argues that education and shifting community narratives are essential steps toward social change.

chunks.text:
Gender roles have been attributed to biological differences in men and women. The concept of gender roles was introduced by John Money, coining it as the actions that reveal the status as a boy, man, girl, or woman. It is universally known that men are integrated in society to provide for their family, be in charge, and always portray bravery. Women were meant to be the caretakers of the household and follows the man’s orders. All throughout history these stereotypes have existed but recently, the stereotypes are slowly disintegrating. It is no longer black and white, meaning that masculinity and femininity is fluid. Society has labeled what is considered masculine and feminine which pressures the fulfillment of the roles. Recently, the two distinguished categories are blurring together and switching. In the broadest sense, they provide normal behavior, attitudes, and hierarchy values. People have found ways to resist the gender roles by new ideas such as women’s rights, nationalism, and socialism. Gender roles have been made important towards society because they organize the necessary tasks in early human society. Doing gender furthers into the effects of the roles in males and females. The male role represents that men should dismiss emotions, while the female role encourages the feeling of being overly emotional.

The December 2020 Vogue magazine cover holds an image of Harry Styles wearing a Gucci jacket and a dress. Styles says, “I find myself looking at women’s clothes, thinking they’re amazing.” Not only was this British pop singer the first-ever make cover star but also wore women’s wear. The designer, Harris Reid, and Harry focus on gender fluid clothing, making a statement. Days later, Candance Owens, a conservative author and commentator, posted on social media causing a spiral. She mentioned how disgusted she was with the Vogue cover and used the phrase, “bring back manly men.” The attacking of Harry Styles continued for a whole month since the release of this magazine saying the dress is not masculine which is ruining society. In response to Owens, Harry posted an image of his cover with the caption saying, “bring back manly men.” Some supported Styles while some supported Owens, as well as the other way around. This occurrence brought inspiration to the song writer Charlotte Sands who wrote the song “Dress” about Harry’s cover. An actor, Billy Porter, also created backlash by saying, “I’m not dragging Harry Styles, but he is the one you’re going to try and use to represent this new conversation? He doesn’t care, he’s just doing it because it’s the thing to do.”

Doing gender is the things we do to lay claim to a sex category where gender is performed. It is a psychologically ingrained social construct that surfaces everyday interaction. Differences are created between girls and boys and women and men. These contrasts are socially made through interactions, but some people think of it as “essential” and innate biological differences. The female group has the stereotype of having kids and wearing make-up, dresses, and heels. The males are made out to be the protector, holding doors for women, and having a male stoic strut. Men are meant to not wear make-up, women’s clothes, and high heels. These actions are behaviors that are expected in society. The body is a resource, but gender is not in the body because there are no essential gender characteristics. The control of your appearance is the outward appearance and how your sex identifier is presented. The model of socialization suggests that it is a lifelong process of learning and then relearning the gender expectations. Doing gender is breaking the gender rules but can also be where you passively obey. An example of doing gender is considered a social construction. When a door is opened for a female by a male, it is being polite and a gentleman. Society exhibits how we should act, dress groom, speak, and conduct ourselves on the assigned sex. Females are expected to be nurturing, polite, and accommodating while men must display strength, competitiveness while not displaying emotion.

Masculine and feminine qualities is labeled on how society is performed. People are expected to perform a gendered role and are held hostage by the sex identifier. Gendered stereotypes are slowly changing but there are still a lot of gendered expectations. The stereotypes are now open to interpretation which assists in freedom of expression. The dress symbolized breaking away from the stereotypes, tolerance, and creativity. It aimed to stir a debate among the industry because Harry Styles believes that establishing barriers just limits ourselves. People view the cover as going against societies norms where some are in support while others find it unnatural. As Owens believes that it is not manly, actress Jameela Jamil said, “Harry Styles is plenty manly, because manly is whatever you want it to be” and not what was decided a hundred years ago. This British singer broke all the doing gender norms and is still continuously breaking them. Not only does he dress feminine but does not want to constantly display emotionless behavior as men have been painted to be. Clothing should not make a person masculine or feminine and historically, dresses have been worn by men for over a thousand years. For example, the British in the Middle Ages wore skirts and tights, and the ancient Greeks and Romans wore togas. Too many believe that in order to be “manly” you have to act and dress a specific way. The pantsuit, which is originally catered towards men, is now acceptable for women. There is an unconscious negative bias that men express towards femininity which is known as toxic masculinity. Not only has the fashion aspect has altered with doing gender but so has the jobs. The workforce was once consumed of men but now has been transitioning into women taking the roles of “manly” jobs.

Doing gender has always been in society but in this day and age, the stereotype is being challenged. Men and women are surrounded by the idea of fitting a specific role that is integrated mentally and physically. A way these categories are changing are by blurring the masculinity femininity line. Harry Styles made a strong statement towards this by the outfit choice of wearing a dress. Controversy appeared, creating support and disgust. Although it is more common with the fluidity of gender, it wavers back to default only because society has not fully embraced the erasing of stereotypes. Besides the ability to wear any type of clothes, jobs have also altered. For example, men were primarily the doctors while women were the nurses, but that is no longer the case. The male to female ratio in the workforce began without being equal which now sets back the women. Finding equality overall can only be accomplished if femininity and masculinity are not as analyzed. Gender blurring introduces the concept where a man behaves as it is expected of women, while a woman’s behavior follows the male character than the female one. While the two-category culture is pressurized, doing gender is still relevant today. They do however hold no real significance to human society because they were made up which means that they can also change. Doing gender can exhibit many forms but can also stay compact in the two categories, creating a never ending cycle.
chunks.label: Gender roles and Harry Styles' Vogue cover
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the sociological concept of doing gender, gender roles, and the controversy surrounding Harry Styles wearing a dress on the cover of Vogue magazine.

chunks.text: When you were a child, I'm sure you wore silly costumes and the most obscure outfits without thinking twice about it. Going to school in wacky outfits, playing dress up with siblings, and back-to-school clothes shopping were considered the highlights of childhood. Yet, the older you get, the more you feel the pressure of society to look, act, and dress a certain way. You stop playing dress up and no longer wear your old favorite shirt with bananas on it. We as individuals are expected to constantly fit into the molds society has made for us and adapt to the changing trends. While men and women are both held to obscure standards in the world, especially regarding beauty, women get the blunt end of it.
chunks.label: Societal beauty standards from childhood to adulthood
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how childhood freedom in appearance transitions into intense societal pressure and beauty standards as people age, particularly affecting women.

chunks.text: As a female growing up in an ever-changing world with constant changes in appearance, I experienced the blunt end of the beauty myth. Going back to middle school, I vividly remember I was drastically different than the majority of the other girls. I was existing for myself and no one else until I came to realize what society expected of me. I began to face high amounts of bullying based on my outward appearance and began to feel excluded from my fellow peers. I took those years in middle school to change everything about myself before I entered high school. I changed my hair, my clothes, my makeup, and the way I dressed to please others. I felt the weight of society's expectations and felt as if in order to be happy, I had to fit in.
chunks.label: Middle school bullying and changing appearance
chunks.what_happened: In middle school, the student faced bullying and exclusion because of her outward appearance. She subsequently changed her hair, makeup, and clothes before entering high school to fit in.
chunks.feelings: excluded, felt the weight of society's expectations

chunks.text: Once I entered high school, I aimed to be more fit and active in the community so I began coaching youth soccer. I used to play back in middle school and the passion carried on into high school and college. I am very knowledgeable about the sport and am very involved. Since I am a female, I have often gotten snarky looks and slick side comments about my ability to coach as a woman. I was no stranger to hearing “Should we request a new team?” and “I don't think she will be as good as the male coach we had last year”. I even found that I was constantly doubting myself. Based on the ideas I had in my mind of the ideal female soccer coach, I would constantly compare and ridicule myself. I felt like maybe I didn’t look as athletic as I should or maybe I wasn’t as fast as I should be. The ideas and pictures that have been instilled in my mind and in society caused me to overthink. The beauty myth had infiltrated my life, making me feel unworthy. I felt like I had to overcompensate in attitude and energy to make up for what I felt I was lacking in outward appearance.
chunks.label: Insecurities and criticism coaching youth soccer
chunks.what_happened: The student began coaching youth soccer in high school and faced snarky comments and skepticism regarding her coaching ability as a female. She felt insecure about her appearance and athletic ability, pushing herself to overcompensate.

chunks.text: In my very first year of coaching, I worked alongside a male counterpart. He was there to show me the ropes, strategies on how to interact with the kids, and effective teaching methods. Oftentimes when at practice, the parents as well as the male children tended to flock to him. I would do my best to conversate and interact with them, but no matter how hard I tried, it was not enough. I realized this is because of the stereotypical idea that sports are a male-dominated field, reigning supreme while having vast knowledge and ability. Once I began to coach independently, I relayed to the parents I have previously played and coached and was adamant about having good communication with them. While they did trust my word, I could tell that they were still skeptical. They felt like since a woman was coaching the team, the instruction their kids were receiving would not be as good as if a male counterpart coached. In other words, they felt cheated.
chunks.label: Coaching with a male counterpart and independently
chunks.what_happened: During her first year of coaching, parents and male kids gravitated toward the male counterpart rather than her. When she later coached independently, parents remained skeptical and seemed to feel cheated having a female coach.

chunks.text:
Simone De Beauvoir perfectly encapsulated my situation and how women are portrayed. Beauvior described women as “others''. Women are constantly being seen as inferior to men, falling into an entirely different category that is deemed not as worthy. Women are held to high standards in regard to beauty and “womanly skills”. No matter what status or ability a woman has, she is still not as recognized as her male counterpart. Yet, while women are incredibly powerful beings, they are deemed incapable of doing traditional male skills, events, or activities. “As is indicated by the common use of man to designate human beings in general; whereas woman represents only the negative, defined by limiting criteria, without reciprocity” (Beauvoir, 1972). The male population has dominated many of the more successful jobs, roles, and titles in society. This leads to a majority of men having more advantages, higher wages, retention of success, and more. Men have more power, influence, and supremacy in society, therefore, women are put on the back burner, becoming a group of “others”'.

The idea that men are the default power holders dates back to the beginning of time. Take sports, government officials, and first responders for example. When we look at these fields and their lasting influence on America, we see that a majority, if not all, are dominated by the male population. This is the driving factor in the suppression of women. Beauvoir paints an elaborate picture of gender inequality and how women are perceived as less adequate in society. Both writings from Wolf and Beauvoir emphasize how women are considered less than and objectified. These readings really put into perspective how unjust and unfair women are treated in our world. Women have fewer rights, higher rates of objectification, and a smaller rate of success in career fields in the majority of the world.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of gender inequality and Beauvoir
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Simone de Beauvoir's concept of women as 'others' and Naomi Wolf's ideas, examining how male dominance across careers leads to the subjugation and objectification of women.

chunks.text: With all this being said, I can often be part of the problem. Society has drilled these beauty standards, roles, and ideas of women into our minds and we are taught from a young age a woman’s “place in society”. I tend to look at fellow women and judge them based on conventional beauty standards. I tend to experience a feeling of shock when I see a woman do a tough job that is traditionally completed by males. I know these thought processes are common for a majority of the population. I saw it firsthand from my experience coaching soccer. Those parents gave into the “women as other” concept and I let the beauty myth engulf me.
chunks.label: Internalizing societal biases and beauty standards
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how she herself internalizes societal expectations by judging other women's appearances and being surprised by women doing traditionally male jobs, connecting it back to her soccer coaching experience.

chunks.text: The way women are perceived and treated in our society impacts the way we operate as a whole. Women are considered maids, cooks, and moms. Men are seen as the breadwinners, the successful, and the strong. This creates a large gap and divides in our society that ultimately continue the cycle of gender views for decades to come. In order to break this precedent, we must stop viewing women as others and instead provide them with equal opportunities. It is necessary to ensure equality and fairness in order to demolish outrageous beauty standards and promote the success of the female population.
chunks.label: Conclusion on gender roles and equality
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by summarizing traditional gender stereotypes and calling for equal opportunities and the elimination of unfair beauty standards.

n337006f1.title: Reflecting on Nationalism and Global Unity

chunks.text:
Nationalism has influenced many conflicts, many victories, and even many unresolved issues. It not something that is engraved in our human biology but is rampant throughout people in countries around the world. The flags that represent countries become a collective representation for nationalism and can inspire for the better or even for the worse.

Instead of dismissing the idea of Nationalism as a whole Harari suggests that the world finds a way to come together to solve problems. I think that this world has gotten used to having pride in your own country to the point where we don’t realize the many thing we could do if we shared and collaborated as a whole. This would be changing the way we use nationalism and not using it as a way to be better than everyone else.
chunks.label: Nationalism and global collaboration
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the influence of nationalism, its representation through flags, and Harari's suggestion that the world collaborate to solve problems rather than using nationalism to feel superior.

nf375b739.title: Perception and Identity on Social Media

chunks.text:
How does social media shape the way we view ourselves?

Cooley’s theory called the “Looking glass self” is mainly about how we think others view us, but not how they actually view us. It is more of a personal perception in our heads. If you think about it like a light switch in our brains, like when it’s on you try to force the people around you to view you a certain way and even when they dont view us in this way, as long as we think they are happy. When the light switch is off, you don't care how other people view you, but it also depends on who you are surrounded with or talking to. For example, You might tell your friends that you drank so much last night and were so drunk, but would you tell your professor these things?.. No, because you want your professor to view you in a different way, like a different version of yourself.

When thinking about Social Media, there are infinite options of how you can portray yourself. Many people are one person online, so everyone can view them the way they want to be seen, but behind the screen they are completely different and could have a completely different lifestyle. We tend to post the best versions of ourselves on social media, even if it's not who we truly are. You always see famous influencers posting about all these new things they just bought or this super fun day they had and all these positive things, but that’s not who they are all the time, it's how they want you to view them. No one ever posts about anxiety, depression or things surrounded by negativity, but because we have this human tendency to want everyone to see us in a certain way, we show our best sleeves all the time for people to see online. In reality, we post on social media to shape an image of ourselves in other people's eyes. The big picture around this whole idea, is that we don’t want others to see us how we see ourselves, so we make us this version of ourselves online, so viewers will see that and not the real you.

William James created the theory of “The Self and its Selves”. He believes there are 5 main parts: The Self, the material, the social, spiritual, and personal identity/pure ego. The social self is most important because it is the recognition you get from your friends.We have this tendency and desire to be noticed by our friends or people around. The social self makes you change yourself based on the social situation you are in. For example, friend groups are an example of the social self because it provides you with a positive social identity and feeling of a sense of belonging. Overall, this part of self, is how we are seen and recognized by others. This theory means a man has many social selves and there are people who recognize him and carry that image of them with them. Although, we only care about certain groups' opinions.

Again, Social Media takes a big part in this. We all have a social self, the self the world sees, the part of us that we want everyone to know.Its the words we use to present ourselves and the overall image we present to the world. This social self is an image we control, it is portrayed by us, and it confirms that people don't see the bad moments or the vulnerable parts of us. Social media allows us to present ourselves in a whole different way, than you would normally present yourself, which at times can be scary. In a way the social media self is your social self, you have been portraying different groups and people.

When comparing these two theories they have similarities and differences. To start one similarity between both of their theories is the emphasis on the role of social interactions in the development of the self. James and Cooley both talk about how our self-perception is shaped by how we are perceived and assessed by others. A difference between the two theories is the way they both defined the self. Cooley defined the self in a means of how we feel, like self feeling. Whereas, James on the other hand defined the self as different parts.

In conclusion, I think Cooley's theory is more rational because it is relatable to how the world is today. Social media has a negative impact on the way we view ourselves and causes us to portray a person online that isn’t the real us. The “Looking glass theory” is how we feel about ourselves because of the way others view us. I would choose this theory, because it relates to me personally. I feel like I am constantly worried about what people think of me and it portrays how I think of myself.
chunks.label: Theories of self and social media
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Cooley's 'looking glass self' and William James's 'The Self and its Selves,' analyzing how both theories apply to how people present themselves on social media and connect to the student's personal tendency to worry about what others think.

nddea99f3.title: Rationalization and Alienation in Modern Capitalism

chunks.text:
While rationalization and estranged labor both touch on aspects of the human experience in today's capitalist society, they approach the subject from different angles. Rationalization studies the objective changes of social institutions that comply with logical principles, and estranged labor focuses on the individual's personal experience of alienation within the labor process. Despite these distinctions, both ideas provide insightful understandings of the difficulties and intricacies of modern socioeconomic systems.

There are similarities and differences when comparing rationalization and estranged labor. These ideas emphasize how people simply become parts of a huge, emotionless machine in today's capitalist society, which has the alienating consequence of destroying uniqueness. However, rationalization focuses more on the objective rearrangement of social processes and structures, while estranged labor highlights the subjective feeling of alienation among workers.

In addition, rationalization is frequently presented as having two sides, whereas estranged labor typically highlights the negative consequences of capitalist exploitation. While it does promote economic growth and technological advancement by bringing about previously unattainable levels of efficiency and organization, it can also result in the loss of deep personal relationships, the uniformity of culture, and a breakdown of established social institutions.

Imagine an assembly line setting in a modern manufacturing facility, where employees have been tasked with operating machinery to make consumer devices. During the day, every employee completes the same tedious tasks without interruption. Due to management's strict enforcement of result goals and quality standards, they have little control over the speed at which they work or the outcome.

Workers who experience estranged labor feel disconnected from the products of their labor, which they rarely see in their completed form. The completed devices are transported off to distribution locations without their input or recognition, which separates them from the rewards of their labors. Because they become little more than parts of production, the repetitive nature of their jobs creates a sense of boredom and disempowerment. A lasting sense of alienation may result from the employees' feeling more and more cut off from their jobs, their coworkers, and even their sense of purpose.

Rationalization principles guide the factory's operations. To simplify the assembly line, the production process is carefully planned, distributed among workers, and optimized for efficiency. Standard Operating Procedures are carefully followed to guarantee accuracy and reduce mistakes. Additionally, management uses data-driven research and performance metrics to satisfy market expectations and continuously enhance efficiency. Rationalization lowers costs and boosts output, but it also dehumanizes workers by treating them like interchangeable parts in the industrial process.

The contrast between rationalization and estranged labor in this scenario highlights the complex structure of present-day industrial capitalism. Although rationalization promotes production and efficiency, it also makes workers feel more alienated, reflecting the deeper disputes that exist in capitalist systems between the needs of the economy and the well-being of people.

Both rationalization and estranged labor are useful lenses that view the processes that make up modern industrial capitalism, but they have advantages and disadvantages of their own. Marx's concept of estranged labor highlights the gap between people and the outcomes of their efforts and successfully portrays the subjective sense of alienation that workers feel inside capitalist institutions.

However, Weber's idea of rationalization offers an organized structure for examining how social systems are reorganized in line with logical principles. It provides insightful information about how different aspects of society are rationalized. Rationalization has come under fire for putting efficiency and predictability ahead of human values and creativity, which has resulted in the alienation of the world and the collapse of established social systems.

Rationalization and estranged labor reveal distinct aspects of a common phenomenon: the degrading effects of capitalism on people and communities. We can better understand the intricate details and mysteries present in current capitalist society and the urgent need for substitute models that put the well-being of people before achieving the goal of profitability by analyzing these ideas in unison.
chunks.label: Comparing rationalization and estranged labor
chunks.what_happened: The student compares the sociological concepts of rationalization and estranged labor under modern capitalism, illustrating them through a hypothetical assembly line factory example.

chunks.text: Race is a social construct that is used to separate people with different features into groups. This way to characterize others is used as a way to create social ranks in society. These “ranks” are used to give power to one group of people, while keeping others down. An example of this in society would be the undying issues between whites and blacks. Still to this day you can see discrimination of blacks in almost everything. Blacks have come a long way by fighting for rights that they should have been born with, all because of their skin tone. They are discriminated and have always been discriminated in the US because of their race. Because of a social construct that was created by humans to separate each other. So, I always ask myself, why? Why is it that we still hold on to something as trivial as race, something that does not biologically separate humans in the slightest?
chunks.label: Race as a social construct
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the concept of race as a social construct used to create social ranks and discrimination in society, questioning why it persists.

chunks.text: Growing up in an African American household I have always asked myself that same question. I always wondered why my dad would always give me talks about the world and how it would be a bit harder for me than white people. Or why I had to do certain things differently just so I would not get in trouble. As a kid I did not understand any of this I would just sit there and listen. Once I started going to school that is when I started to finally develop an understanding of what he was trying to warn me about. I started learning about things like slavery, segregation, and racism in class. I Started learning about ways blacks were kept in a lower position and were treated and something less than human.
chunks.label: Father's talks and learning in school
chunks.what_happened: Growing up, the student's father gave talks about how life would be harder and how to behave to avoid trouble; the student later began understanding these warnings while learning about slavery, segregation, and racism in class.

chunks.text: Eventually I started seeing these things happen in our society today, a society that is supposed to be equal and fair to all. It is far from fair and have never been fair in the slightest. Yes, blacks may have more rights now and can do many things that they would have been punished for years ago. However, there are still many ways that blacks are held back by their race in this society.
chunks.label: Continued inequality in society
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on witnessing racial inequality in modern society and notes that Black people are still held back despite having more rights than in the past.

chunks.text: The first example of discrimination because of race would be the workforce. Blacks are constantly being discriminated in the workforce and have trouble getting jobs. In one of our readings for this class we read an article called, “Discrimination in a Low-Wage Labor Market: A Field Experiment.” This field experiment was carried out to determine if there was still discrimination in the workforce. During this experiment there were whites, Latinos, and blacks that were all give equivalent resumes that applied to hundreds of jobs to see who would have a higher chance of being hired. Needlessly to say whites came out on top getting hired the most while blacks were dead last. In this field study they even saw ways that the employers would reject blacks. For example, some of the employers would use a person qualification against them. Certain qualifications were weighed a bit more for a person depending on their race. In the article they talk about a black man that was rejected because he had little to no experience that was needed for the job. However, his white and Latino counterparts were not rejected like he was from the job even though they had the same amount of experience. In the article it was also stated that not only did whites beat out blacks in a 2-1 ratio but that a white male with a criminal record did about the same as a black male with a clean record. Not only do blacks have trouble getting jobs over their counter parts they also are more likely to face racism than any other race in the workforce. There are also less black CEOs than white CEOs. For example, Fortune has 500 companies and only 4 of them have a black CEO, only 4. Businesses are still relatively low in diverse leadership and studies show this.
chunks.label: Workforce discrimination and course reading
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses racial discrimination in the workforce, detailing a course reading about a field experiment on hiring practices and citing statistics on Black CEOs.

chunks.text: My next example of discrimination would be the incarceration rates of African Americans in the US. I was reading an article from CNN a few days ago and in that article, it was stated that black Americans are incarcerated almost five times the rate of whites. I did not find this information to be surprising at the slightest. In America blacks have always had higher numbers of imprisonment than any other race. In fact, African Americans make up 30 percent of the United States population but the make up 60% of the prisons (“It’s 2020. Why Is Workplace Discrimination against Black People Still a Problem?”). The US had a war on drugs that was used to crack down on illegal drug use and trafficking. This so-called war on drugs was really used to incarcerated African Americans as it mainly focused on black communities. The Human Rights Watch found that blacks were not anymore likely to use drugs than whites but still suffered higher arrest rates. During this time in America many blacks were threw in jail for petty crimes but were given lengthy sentences. Imprisonment is also a problem in black youth in America as well. Studies show that African American juveniles are being put into juvenile detentions at astonishingly high rates. The Sentencing Project shows that while African American juveniles make up 16 percent of the United States youth population, that a whopping 37 percent of their cases are transferred to criminal court. While 58 percent of African American youth is sent to adult prisons. (“It’s 2020. Why Is Workplace Discrimination against Black People Still a Problem?”). These studies show just how much more blacks are incarcerated than any other race in the United States today.
chunks.label: Disproportionate incarceration rates
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses racial disparities in incarceration and the criminal justice system, citing articles and studies regarding the war on drugs and juvenile detention.

chunks.text: Another way blacks are discriminated in the US is through voting. Voting is a right that blacks did not even have and was something that my ancestors not only fought for but died for. Throughout US history there were always laws that were put in place to prevent African Americans from having a fair vote. Voter suppression is a real problem in the US that still has yet to be resolved. Voter suppression is a tactic that was always used to keep certain people in power. It causes unfair elections by not giving everyone an equal chance to vote for who they would like to. African Americans used to deal with literacy polls, poll taxes, all-white primaries, more just because they wanted to vote. Blacks had to deal with these voting restrictions for 95 years until the Voting Rights Act was established in 1965. It took that long for the government to make voting fair for blacks. If you look at our government it is mainly made up of whites, our first black president was the 44th president. This shows just how unfair the voting is in America.
chunks.label: Voting rights and voter suppression
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses the history of voter suppression, the struggle for voting rights, and the lack of diversity in US government leadership.

chunks.text: These are just few of the many ways that blacks are discriminated in the US. Blacks are discriminated in almost everything they do. There is always someone who holds on to the past and believe that another person is superior because of their skin color. Things like that should not matter in modern day society. It should have never matter. How we look on the outside should not characterize us as a person, nor should it give someone else power over us. I should not have to fear being pulled over by cops, or have more trouble getting a job, or have to worry about my vote not counting. It is 2021 and black people are still fighting for rights in the US, is that not sad? All because of the social construct that was put in place to give power to people that believe they are the closest to what they believe God is.
chunks.label: Persistence of racial injustice and personal fears
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the ongoing nature of discrimination in modern times, expressing frustration over having to fear police encounters, job discrimination, and disenfranchisement.

chunks.text: In conclusion, race is in fact a social construct that is used to divide people amongst each other while making one group superior to all others. So, to answer my own question I would have to say that a trivial thing such as race is held onto so that people of the so called “superior” race can maintain their power in society above others. People use race for any and everything. Race is used to determine if you get a job, if you can get into a school or not, if you are going to prison, or to determine the person you are. Race should not be something that determines any of this, but sadly it is. We are all and undoubtingly human no matter our skin tone, hair texture, and facial features. So, I do not believe that race should be used as a social hierarchy, everyone should be treated as equal no matter what.
chunks.label: Conclusion on dismantling racial hierarchy
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that race is maintained to preserve power and argues that everyone should be treated equally regardless of physical features.

chunks.text:
Throughout history, the wealthy have always had more luxuries than the lower class. They have luxuries in not just designer items but services that make their life much more efficient. The sociologist Max Weber would refer to the development of services as rationalization, which is when emotional decisions replace efficient procedures that make items more accessible for some consumers but, in turn, dehumanize the people who work for these corporations. Through the growth of rationalization in the modern world, companies that rely on consumers must also evolve. This growth can be shown through limited-item grocery stores developing into million-dollar corporations. To do this, grocery stores have implemented rationalization by having certain arrangements of items, consistent training, and new-age technology that adapts to consumers who are making them more money. Since adding these systems, it has affected the working class because they are the workers being dehumanized and turned into machines since that is the most consistent service.

Many people feel the need to get things done fast to keep up with the fast-paced life in the US but cannot afford services that will allow them more time to focus on their careers. Some grocery stores have developed so people do not need to walk inside the store to buy items. Wealthy people would rather pay someone to get an item directly than walk into a store to find it themselves. Grocery stores now have adapted to the people who want this leisure by creating grocery delivery, curbside delivery, and personal food shopping services. These services allow the wealthy to pay to get items more quickly to live a leisurely life, while the lower class must adapt to providing these services.

People still choose to go inside the grocery stores or cannot afford these luxury services, so, through rationalization, they have used people's predictability to set up their stores in the same arrangement. All stores in a specific corporation are set up the same way, so it is more convenient for consumers to go through them regardless of their area. They also have items such as cleaning supplies and drugstore items, so consumers only need to go to one place for everything. This accessibility allows customers to navigate the store quickly and find all the necessary items, enabling corporations to make more money from consumers by adapting to them. For example, people who need a dairy or meat item when going grocery shopping, stores set up those items to be placed in the back of the stores, people must walk through the aisles to get to the item they are searching for. Having to walk through makes them buy more because they see items through their walk, and do not even consider needing them until they see them. Once people finish shopping, they must go to checkout, which is set up so consumers can buy more. There are always small, cheaper items such as gum or a soda that are easily accessible while the customer is checking out, which makes them consider needing them as well. All these set-ups throughout the store are purposely in place to get more customers to subconsciously buy more items, which allowed grocery corporations to grow.

Another aspect of rationalization in grocery stores is that all workers are trained in the same way to allow consistency for consumers. This training can dehumanize working-class people by making them all act the same way. Through training courses, they are taught to act always of service to customers, specifically answer phones, and be in a specific uniform. Having to act the same robotic way towards every customer takes away from the personable experience lost through rationalization. Many consumers enjoy the reliability of getting in and out of the stores with no unexpected scenarios, but that is not naturally realistic in life. Naturally, nothing can be predicted entirely, but through the modern world, rationalization has made unexpected obstacles to getting something done much less likely, and even workers with strict training are not doing well enough.

Even employees are not efficient enough for people anymore, they have adapted to better technologies. Introducing new technologies, specifically self-checkout, has made even buying items at the store more efficient but takes away from human jobs and the personability behind them working. Now, with the establishment of grocery delivery services, people limit their interaction with other humans who are just robots working for them. People in higher classes use this type of service the most because they can pay more for a more efficient process. While the lower classes cannot pay for these efficient services, they must be the ones who do them.

Through analyzing rationalization being used for the growth of grocery stores it is shown how there are many advantages for wealthy people but disadvantages for those part of the working class. Overall, even though rationalization has made the modern world much more efficient, it has also turned the working class into machines.
chunks.label: Rationalization in grocery stores and class disparities
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Max Weber's concept of rationalization, explaining how grocery stores use predictable store layouts, standardized worker training, and automation to cater to wealthy consumers while dehumanizing working-class employees.

n9f192bcd.title: Conforming in Private Christian High School

chunks.text: Is the conception of the self based off the way we perceive ourselves or from the perspective of others; and do the environments we are placed in influence our behaviors? Although, it might seem that we are constantly critiquing ourselves it is seen that the emergence of modernity has shaped the notion of self. One knows who they are, how to act, and when to act in particular ways because of others and their influences. It is a common thought that we are self-aware, but I posit that we are not because within the situation it is difficult to fully grasp this idea. In a report it stated most people believe they are self-aware, yet only 10%—15% of people actually fit the criteria. In western society, it has been noticed that the majority of identities these days come from the perspective of how others perceive us rather than the raw portion of our personalities and what makes us unique for who we are. To understand this concept, one must examine the constituent parts of the self and how they are related to human behavior within different environments.
chunks.label: Concept of the self and social influence
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the concept of the self, questioning whether identity comes from internal perception or the views of others and environment.

chunks.text: In high school I went to a private Christian school where we would wear uniforms and take the most challenging courses in order to be a college preparatory school. While in this setting I was surrounded by everyone who seemed to be there for the same reasons. One, they had money to afford a prestigious school, two, parents wanted their children to be around other Christians so when they left for college they would have a solid foundation, and lastly in order to receive an education that was top tier in the area. As a background as to why I went to this school in the first place is because my family has a legacy there. All of my siblings went to high school at Asheville Christian Academy and my father served on the board. In a sense I did not have the choice whether I wanted to attend. This perspective does not disregard my gratefulness for having the opportunity to attend a college preparatory school though. Yet, from my experiences I have felt that there were moments that did not encompass my true “self.”
chunks.label: Attending Asheville Christian Academy
chunks.what_happened: The student attended a private Christian high school because of family legacy, wearing uniforms and taking college prep courses alongside wealthy Christian peers.

chunks.text: Because I was surrounded by the same type of people in high school where we quite literally all looked the same due to the fact, we wore uniforms I think it created a stereotype in which I found myself often times having to pretend to be more Christian than I was in order to please my friend group and teachers who were very religious. For example, each Tuesday the entire high school would have a convocation and chapel. This included a time of worship in which we would all sing. In order to please others, I would sing along even if I didn’t feel emotionally connected to the words or meaning of the song.
chunks.label: Pretending during high school chapel
chunks.what_happened: During weekly Tuesday chapels, the student sang along during worship despite not feeling emotionally connected, pretending to be more religious to please friends and teachers.
chunks.people: friend group, teachers, high school students

chunks.text: This situation at high school to conform to the stereotypes of Christianity and present myself as something that I was not emotionally engaged with is a pure example of Goffman’s idea of the presentation of the self. This idea presents that we are always presenting ourselves. He uses a stage as an analogy is where our interactions are produced. The front stage is where we are being presented and must be polished. So, in my situation my idea of the front stage was to act as if I was religious in front of my friends, family, and teachers so that I could appease them. Then, the backstage is where things come together. Before school I would need to prepare myself to act in this way so that everyone would think I was just like them. It was like a coat that you put on and then take off. If I had not bought into feeling the need to act like someone, I was not then I feel like I could’ve had the opportunity to discover my true self in high school rather than in college.
chunks.label: Applying Goffman's presentation of self
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes high school conformity through Goffman's front stage and backstage concepts, noting how preparing to act religious prevented discovering their true self.
chunks.feelings: feeling the need to act like someone I was not

chunks.text: Now that I am in college here at the University of North Carolina Wilmington as a freshman I have experienced what I would say would be a culture shock. Coming from the background of always being surrounded by the same people in high school I have found that college is much different than that. I have met many people who are from many different backgrounds. I have felt that I have been more able to express who I am and explore who I really want to be. Yet, there are times that I wish I could find a church group because my family always asks me about that when I come home, because I would like to please them and the standards that they have for me. Here at college, I have experienced that one often gets looked down upon for being religious as from experiences with one of my friends who hates on people who are semi-religious. I have a couple of friends who are like me but ultimately it is difficult to find the right people, but this is by choice rather than being forced.
chunks.label: Experiencing culture shock at UNCW
chunks.what_happened: As a freshman at UNCW, the student met diverse people and felt freer to express themselves, while navigating family expectations about finding a church and a friend who looks down on religious people.
chunks.feelings: culture shock, wishing to please family
chunks.people: college peers, family, friends, friend who hates on semi-religious people

chunks.text:
I think the difference between high school and college is that in high school I didn’t have as much of a choice as to who I was around, but here at college there is more diversity allowing me to be more open and find myself. Although, I do still struggle sometimes with the presentation of the self and having my identity being influenced by others, I think this in turn plays into James’ idea of the self and how we are perceived.

This has a direct correlation with James’ idea of the self. He breaks it down into 3 different parts. The material self which includes clothes, property, friends, and family. I experience this in the way that I am constantly making sure that the clothes I wear fit into what everyone else has. The social self which is my role and reputation is seen through the lens that I want to fit in with my friends here at college and go with the flow. And lastly the pure ego which is the core of my spiritual self and the life force that creates my reactions is what I know is deep down my moral spectrum that won’t allow me to do anything bad during my time here at college. Through the different perspectives of the self, I personally agree that I resonate with all of these on a daily basis to appease the people that are around me.

I also resonate with Mead’s idea of the I and the Me. He explains how the Self is experienced out of internal dialogue between the “I” and the “Me. Therefore, the “I” is the subjective reaction of the mind to the stimuli. So, in my experiences many of the external forces of others and the people I surrounded myself with was the “I” in these situation. Yet, the “Me” is the objective evaluation of the “I” reaction. So, the “I” came from my natural reactions, and the “Me” would be like an off and on the switch to act accordingly based on my environment. Therefore, the nature of myself can be seen as the nature of the language of society and the particular settings that I have been located in.

Through the presentation of the self, the idea of the self, and the I and the Me I have been influenced many times to conform to what society has told me to do. Yet, in order for one to combat the issue of conforming to society and finding identity in our true selves we need to believe in ourselves and act accordingly for what we think is right for yourself not what society says. Based on my experiences, I am still learning how to do this and how to surround myself with people that I feel like I can be myself in.
chunks.label: Theoretical reflection on self and conformity
chunks.what_happened: The student contrasts high school and college, applying James's parts of the self and Mead's 'I' and 'Me' to explain ongoing personal conformity and the search for authentic identity.

chunks.text: Based on, “The Social Selves,” by James, Our collective thoughts belong to ourselves, however we can alter them to change in human interactions and in the different ways we present ourselves to the world around us. We are the same human, however we are always fluctuating because of the idea of the self and its selves. This becomes evident as we grow older and wiser; we are the same person, however, we are increasely more knowledgeable and experienced with our life. We need to be able to distinguish these different thoughts into what is self and what is its self.
chunks.label: Reflecting on James's 'The Social Selves'
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses William James's concept of the social self and explains how people change their self-presentation and thoughts across interactions as they grow older and more experienced.

chunks.text: In Cooley’s, “The Looking Glass Self”, Our self lives in a particular mindset or idea that we put together, our imagination makes up those ideas. The way we feel pride and shame comes from our imagination or reflection from someone else’s mind. This shows that you are always looking at yourself, and you see yourself in everyone you meet because you are constantly thinking about yourself, if you know it or not. Sometimes we are ashamed of who we become or ashamed of ourselves and you see that in others. This brings the idea that the looking glass self is present and this is how we perceive ourselves and others around us.
chunks.label: Reflecting on Cooley's 'The Looking Glass Self'
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Cooley's looking glass self, describing how feelings like pride and shame originate from imagining how others perceive us.

n147c098b.title: Challenging Traditional Gender Roles and Beauty

chunks.text:
Have you ever fallen into the idea of the beauty myth? Although it is something we as humans do almost every day, understanding it is a different story. The beauty myth can be described as, according to Wolf, as the order that dictates behavior and not appearance but rather the beauty of a women based upon the duty to base the identity and value of it. The idea being that beauty is subjective and that beauty women do not disagree with men. This idea falls victim to the idea that women are only seen for the they appear rather than their personalities: everyone has their own idea of beauty.

The idea of the beauty myth has been something I have been interested in since we read about it.
chunks.label: Understanding the beauty myth concept
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces Naomi Wolf's concept of the beauty myth and reflects on its societal definitions and implications for women.

chunks.text: Throughout my life, in school I have always been told that ‘men are the bread winners’ and women should always look presentable for their man. However, at home it was always the opposite, my father would tell me that man or woman, it does not matter if you are happy and at a good job it does not matter who the “breadwinner” is.
chunks.label: Contrasting messages from school and father
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up hearing in school that men are breadwinners and women must look presentable, while at home their father taught them that gender does not matter as long as one is happy at a good job.

chunks.text: Yet, it still surprises me that to this day men and women are still so polar and the idea that men success is based on if he is with a beautiful woman.
chunks.label: Reflecting on gender polarization
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how men and women remain polarized and how men's success is tied to having a beautiful woman.

chunks.text: I know from personal experience that I have been catcalled. Catcalling could mean when you are walking down the street and a man says something to you, it is most likely an uncomfortable experience and extremely awkward.
chunks.label: Personal experience with catcalling
chunks.what_happened: The student experienced being catcalled by a man while walking down the street.

chunks.text: Being told from a young age that men will always make the money and women are just supposed to stay in the kitchen, watch after the children and clean honestly sounds like a good deal until something sparks in you and you want to make your own money. My whole life I always wanted to be a CEO or own my own my business like my father did, however, people always told me that owning your own business was for men and only men could handle those jobs. My father always believed in me and wanted me to succeed in whatever I did. However, down the line I decided that teacher was for me, I love teaching, children and being able to make a difference in one person’s life. Even with that profession, comments are always made about that idea.
chunks.label: Career aspirations and father's encouragement
chunks.what_happened: The student wanted to be a CEO or business owner like their father despite people discouraging them, received constant support from their father, and eventually decided to become a teacher.

chunks.text:
After learning about the beauty myth in class it made me realize how often and prevalent it is. For starters, a stereotype that has always stuck with was that being a stripper is morally wrong. However, being a stripper could make you money extremely fast and if someone wants to do that and loves what they do, there is no reason to degrade them for it. I also completely disagree with the idea that men are breadwinners and women should not disagree with men. Not only is that false but the idea that women are less than men is extremely unfortunate. I feel as if man or woman we should all have equal opportunities and dreams to do what we want to do no matter the stereotype.

To go into further detail, the beauty myth is the almost a backwards way of men trying to reinforce their male dominance. However, the beauty myth has nothing to do with women at all and everything to do with a men’s institution and power. The overall idea is that women should be beautiful, and men should have access to it. Furthermore, beauty is subjective, and women are subjected into the “beauty myth” by feeling the pressure to adhere to the unrealistic social standards of physical beauty. Another point to be made would be that now, social media has completely changed the idea of being beautiful. Women are constantly comparing themselves to what they see online, some in which are due to the idea that men love beautiful women.

I believe there are many new insights to this topic, which is why it fascinated me so much since we read about it. I believe that although this is happening and the idea that women are valued as less. As a woman we should stand up understand that we are all beauty in our own ways and do not owe ourselves or our beauty to anyone. I also feel as if women should be starting their own business and companies, fulfilling their dreams with no reproductions about what a man might say or react to our decisions. The beauty myth is such an eye-opening topic, especially for women, and understand what it truly means I feel like everyone should do in order to fully understand.

The beauty myth is something completely assumed by a myth, hints the name, it is all a myth. Men should not be valuing their success on how beauty their women are, they should be appreciating what women do and putting their value into their own success. I feel as if that no matter a person, their value is based on many things, and what they do in this world is a main one. If you decide you hate life and want to sit at home all day, obviously your success is less than someone who prides themselves on being a hard worker and making each day their all-time best. However, success is the spectrum, and that person sitting at home all day on their couch may say going to the store was a success and they are proud of themselves. Success is what you make of it, and no one should belittle someone even if they feel like they are more successful. In my opinion, I feel like my parents are the most successful people, not only from their jobs but from the people they have become. Inside and out, they are successful in my eyes based off how they raised me, I would say my brothers and I are all extremely hard workers and will always make the most of any situation we are in, good or bad.
chunks.label: Critique of gender stereotypes and the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses stereotypes about women, male dominance, the role of social media in beauty standards, female empowerment, and what defines true success.

chunks.text: After taking this class, I can proudly say I have learned so much in ‘finding meaning’. Although I have taken a sociology course in High School, I have forgotten the importance of it and how extremely interesting it is. Learning about beauty is something I had to take a step back on and understand deeper, I left class and wanted to learn more about it. Therefore, I had to do my own research on the topic. I learned so much from diving deeper and have a good understanding of what the beauty myth truly is.
chunks.label: Independent research after sociology class
chunks.what_happened: After learning about the beauty myth in their college sociology course, the student left class motivated to do independent research on the topic to understand it more deeply.

chunks.text: In conclusion, according to Wolf the beauty myth is the idea that as women increasingly focus their attention on their physical appearance, their focus on equal rights and treatment takes a lower priority. The idea is that men base their success of the beauty of their women and women should obey them and never disagree with them. However, women should be proud of who they are and work for what they want no matter if a man tell you to or not.
