nab0cc2cc.title: Examining Shared Beliefs and Social Systems

chunks.text:
Harari states that all different species and societies are formed around beliefs and traditions that have been around for centuries and they have distinct social systems. However, the social systems aren’t something that is genetic is based on what communities you are brought up in. In chapter 6 he compares how the Germans have been organized into six different systems which were the Hohenzollern empire, Weimar Republic, The Third Reich, German democratic republic, the federal republic of Germany, and the Democratic reunited Germany. In some of these communities, the beliefs were all different because they were made up of different thoughts and ideas and that’s why they ultimately separated. They still all somewhat have kept to their original routes and ways even though the Germans went through that much change.

He also compared primates to how some of human society’s work and to evolve, for example, a gorilla pack is more like a dictatorship where there is a leader that is above all the others and then the females follow behind. Then Chimps work together more like a democratic group where there is open to more possibilities to teamwork and not just being ruled by one and less violence because if a gorilla is challenged by another they make that problem go away more so with violence. The main point in that is within those two groups things may change and rules may change but the way of doing things will stay the same.

Harari's arguments also connect with Emile Durkheim's view on the collective consciousness which is a set of shared beliefs ideas and moral attitudes which operate as a unifying force within a society. While over time in different society’s although things change and all different communities keep up with time and technology they are always going to hold on to the strong beliefs and being set in certain ways and that’s why Harari’s and Durkheim views are similar and can be compared to each other.

Harari states that in any civilization or group, anything can be manifested into a common belief in a society’s system especially if the society is for it. His statement says “Human groups are defined more by the changes they undergo than by any continuity, but they nevertheless manage to create for themselves ancient identities thanks to their storytelling skills.” Similarly, Durkheim, believes that all societies have the collective concessions to enforce and bind individuals to the moral order that a society creates. These relate to each other because even a single person within a community must follow the traditions and beliefs that have been set up by that certain society. In almost any society there is always some form of consequence for disrespectful acts, and the severity of your actions is based on where you are and what rules have been put in place.

Another comparison between Harari and Durkheim is when Harari discussed different anthems. He stated that if you take out the specific name of the country in almost every anthem it would be hard to tell where and what regions the anthems come from. Most anthems have to do with pride and loving and supporting their communities but some people take their county pride and use it to be harmful and negative towards others.

This relates to Durkheim because he believes that the social is something that we collectively create together by a shared sense of reality, morality, and identity-based on commonly shared experiences. Both of these people believe that communities need to feel a, sense of unity together to thrive, even if it means being prideful.

When discussing religion Harari seems to shift the meaning of religion more so on modern-day religion and how some religions have matured around science and technology. He believes that in modern-day society religion had created three types of problems. The first being technical problems which would be problems caused by natural events and how back in the day you would go to the church and ask the priest how to handle stations. Most would tell you to turn to prayer and wait for God to solve the problems instead of action themselves. The second problem is policy problems which would come into conflict with problem-solving especially if you are in a very strict religion. Say if you have a medical problem but your religion restricts you from reaching out for modern-day help because it would cause you to potentially “sin” against your religion, would you choose to adhere to the policies that your religion has put in place or take care of the problems head-on and risk possibly sinning. The third problem that he states is identity problems which can be scary because a lot of times people will hide behind religion or use it as a mask even for things that have been done wrong. Like someone using religion as an excuse to back up a wrongdoing no matter how evil it is.

Unlike Harari, Alexandra Maryanski and Johnathan H. Turner believe that religion was important to society because it was necessary to bring people together based on a collective belief created/manifested by a group of people who value their religion and the rules of it. Because of a stronger development of emotions, the range that people feel about their specific religion becomes greater, therefore, they needed something to believe in and base their hope in. This contrasts with what Harari said because he doesn’t quite get the importance of religion and how people like to stay on the path and follow the “rules and guidelines of their own religion. He thinks that people like that need to try and find a way to evolve their religion with modern-day technology and medicine.

While Maryanski and Turner believe and understand that religion is different in every society and community because of the beliefs that have been followed by that group they respect that and embrace it. They also believe in the ability to form relationships became very prevalent as the capacity for symbolic thought increased. They seemed to understand the critical role that religion played in the forming of civilizations more than Harari did.

Another example of a contrast between the two is when Harari talks about how some traditions from different religions can make many people behave unfairly and cruelly to others to the point of committing harmful and potentially causing death towards others just because they don’t have the same beliefs and views. This is one of the reasons he sees religion as a problem because it can blindside so many people from realistic thinking. He states that “when it comes to solving rather than stoking the global problems of the 21st century they don’t seem to offer much.” So, Harari is basically is saying that people who run to religion as a safety net are just really avoiding the bigger problems at hand.

However, Maryanski and Turner believe that if a group of people from a community come together and share a belief such as using prayer as a form of protection, then they will be able to collectively create a “protective power”. This is considered collective effervescence, which is the feeling of the energy that someone gains from doing something as a whole. They state that religion is the “soul of society” because it has the ability to bind societies together to form a community. They can go through this not only when they feel protected by their god, but just doing something as a community can give this effect.

In conclusion, the points made by Harari throughout this book were very interesting. Upon reading this I was faced with many points that made me stop and think for a second. When Harari talks about how the future is going to be based on artificial intelligence and technology is very scary for someone who is rising up into those future generations. As he said, many jobs will be at risk which could cause a downfall in the economy. He really makes you sit back and look at the bigger issue with today’s society and that the world needs to focus on evolving as a whole to solve today's problems. Not saying that everyone needs to be the same but the world needs to come together and help each other out instead of being so against one another and being more open-minded.
chunks.label: Analyzing Harari, Durkheim, Maryanski, and Turner
chunks.what_happened: The student compares and contrasts theories on society, collective consciousness, and religion from Yuval Noah Harari, Émile Durkheim, Alexandra Maryanski, and Jonathan H. Turner, and reflects on Harari's predictions about artificial intelligence.

chunks.text:
The third lesson I learned, was that leadership is a collaboration and a process. A major thing I learned from Leadership for a Better World by Susan R. Komives was that leadership is not a position that someone with power or money has to gain more power over people. Instead, leadership is a process of learning about yourself while collaborating with others. This lesson ties to the previous lessons learned about becoming more self-aware about one’s strengths and weaknesses and creating a concrete connection between leaders and followers. In this book, Komives further explains this through the Social Change Model of Developmental Leadership. With this model, social change was explained to me as people learning about themselves, their society, and the group they are a part of to comprehend how they can cooperate to achieve a goal.

At the beginning of the semester, I viewed leadership as a position that people of power or a large amount of money have. I believed leaders were more like managers that assign certain tasks to people to achieve their goals. By taking this course, I have gained more knowledge about what leadership is, who can be a leader, and the different ways to become a better leader. Leadership in itself is not a position held by someone with power or money. It’s also not a manager using people to complete a goal. Instead, leadership is a process in which someone acts as a teacher or guide to help others alike achieve a common goal. This leader, or group of leaders, can be anyone for any amount of time. In the book A Long Walk To Water, written by Linda Sue Park, the main character is a young boy named Salva Dut. His story represents how leadership takes courage and motivation to create change, even if it is from a young boy in a difficult situation. Aside from positive leaders, there are some negatively motivated leaders. However, if you can connect with others and guide them to a common goal, you are technically a leader.
chunks.label: Reflecting on leadership concepts and course readings
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on course readings, concepts of leadership as a collaborative process rather than mere power, and examples such as Salva Dut from A Long Walk to Water.

chunks.text: One thing I have learned about leadership this semester based on experiences outside of the classroom is that good leader and follower relationships are essential. While being a full-time student at UNCW, I decided to look for employment near campus to obtain some extra income. One day, my roommate and I decided to visit a local bakery. We walked in, only expecting to pick up some pastries. However, we were able to apply and were hired that same day. The first day, I noticed how nice the manager was and how the other employees interacted with each other. Overall, I believed it would be a lovely place to work. However, I soon learned that wasn’t entirely true. Although nice, the manager was very disorganized when it came to paperwork, schedules, communicating, and leading his workers. This created a very negative connection between him and me. Due to this, I decided to find work elsewhere. I soon applied for Starbucks and received an interview within the week. During the interview, I discovered the works are labeled partners rather than coworkers, how the business is run, and how I would be a part of this corporation. I was also informed that my manager is a good example of a leader. Although she manages the store and does tell people how to work, she also leads her partners, answers any questions, creates connections with almost every customer, and will work alongside the other partners to help alleviate the workload and any stress.
chunks.label: Working at a bakery and interviewing at Starbucks
chunks.what_happened: The student and their roommate got hired at a local bakery, but the student left due to the manager's disorganization. The student then interviewed at Starbucks and learned about their collaborative leadership style.
chunks.feelings: believed it would be a lovely place to work, negative
chunks.people: roommate, bakery manager, other bakery employees, Starbucks manager

chunks.text:
My biggest takeaway from Leadership 211 is that leadership is not a position, it’s a process. I first believed that leadership was a position or role that one takes to lead others. With this course, I learned that is not true. Although a leader tends to be the one person who takes initiative to lead and seems to control a group of people, they are guided by their followers. Leaders must go through a process of becoming self-aware and understanding their goals, strengths, weaknesses, and how they lead. They also learn to understand and connect with others to create a group of loyal and supportive followers who can help them become a better leader. Leadership is not a position. Leadership is a process of growing and connecting with other people to reach a common goal.

Works Cited

Clifton, Don. Clifton Strengths for Students. Gallup. 2017. Yuzu.

Komives, Susan R., Leadership for a Better World. Publisher. 2009. https://ebookswhiz.com/pdf/leadership-for-a-better-world

Northouse, Peter G., Introduction to Leadership, 5th ed. SAGE Publishing. 2008. Yuzu.
chunks.label: Course takeaways and works cited
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes their main takeaways from Leadership 211 regarding leadership being a process rather than a position, and provides a works cited list.

chunks.text:
Women and men are seen as two different types of people in society. In society, women are viewed as objects more than humans. However, men in society are told they have to be tough and not to express their emotions all of the time. Women in the earlier decades were “made” to be housewives where their roles were to cook, clean, take care of the kids, and tend to their husbands. Men were to work a job so they could make money and provide for their family. Many concepts about gender roles have changed over the years and women are seen less as objects now that it is normal for them to work full-time jobs.

Gender roles have been a set-in stone stereotype between masculinity and femininity. Up until the later 90’s, women have been housewives and never been able to show their full potential in the workforce. In the reading The Yellow Wallpaper by Charlotte Perkins Gilman, Gilman talks about how a wife is “sick,” diagnosed by husband and brother, physicians, even though she feels fine. They control her and will not let her work or even write, trapping her inside the house. The men in her home manipulate her to be bed bound for a reason of “sickness” when she is not. This shows how the man thinks he is doing good for the woman, but it really makes women feel inferior and useless. In the reading Women as other by Simone de Beauvoir, Beauvoir talks about how women are looked at as less knowledgeable because they are female. A woman cannot think independently without being questioned of their knowledge. Women are objects in the eyes of men and what a man instills, compels the woman to believe. This history is no longer a reality with the growth over the past couple of decades. Women are finally gaining their equality.

Over the year’s women have been able to overcome previous gender norms and feel as though they are more important and independent. In today's society we have females in positions of power whereas in the 19th century this would have not been reality. We also have women CEO’s and leaders to inspire the future generations that previous norms have been disbanded and anything is possible.
chunks.label: Gender roles and readings on women's inequality
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the history of gender roles, discussing texts by Charlotte Perkins Gilman and Simone de Beauvoir, and notes how women have gained independence and equality today.

n0d9e5049.title: Navigating Discomfort in Awkward Social Silences

chunks.text:
Sometimes, awkward and uncomfortable experiences or beliefs that connect a group of people, are seen as normal for other groups, or even society as a whole. Having a group of people come together and share values, beliefs, ideas, and morals attitudes is seen as a relatively positive concept. However, there’s always a negative, or a less pleasant side. For some groups, this may be morals that other groups or society as a whole don’t agree with. For others, it might be awkward or uncomfortable shared experiences that influence and alter their beliefs. In this case, why do these experiences continue to happen if they are so awkward and uncomfortable?

A shared belief among socially anxious people and introverts, is that silence is awkward. This belief can be shared with other people as well, including extroverts. It’s something that happens frequently between strangers, friends, or family. However, awkwardness and being uncomfortable are just a normal feelings that humans encounter every so often. These awkward silences typically last for only a few short moments or even a few minutes. They also happen commonly between strangers you most likely won’t interact with again. Overall, it might be an irrelevant moment in most people’s lives.

Most of the time, awkward silence happens with strangers. Since they are unfamiliar, this interaction allows the people to create their first impressions of each other. In some cases, such as having an interview or meeting with someone significant, having this awkward silence could be detrimental. First impressions of strangers are typically unimportant, however, in those cases they are seen as crucial. This first interaction with important people can determine if you are able to obtain things such as being hired for a certain job or possibly new connections that could be helpful in times of need. There are multiple other instances where people encounter awkward silences with strangers.

Most people will avoid awkward situations or situations that make them uncomfortable. An example, for some people might avoid getting on a crowded elevator full of strangers. On the other hand, sometimes you are talking with someone on the elevator and having a private conversation, but someone joins. Neither you nor the person you are talking with want this stranger to listen to this conversation, so you both stop talking. This creates an awkward silence. This stranger might feel most awkward because they unintentionally interrupted your conversation.

On another note, some people don’t like awkward silence because they feel the need to fill that space. Some extroverts feel the need to constantly have people to talk to. When they are still around people, but unable to do that, it makes them uncomfortable. This also applies to the person in a group who tends to be the entertainer. In the group, they are usually the extroverted person who is always telling jokes to make everyone happy and makes light of most situations. When they are around a new group of people or in a setting that requires silence, it makes them uncomfortable because it’s not what they are used to.

These moments typically don’t last very long and seem insignificant in our overall life. Most people may not pay any mind to it. However, for those who do pay more attention to it, it can be difficult. Introverts and socially anxious people typically stay within their friend groups or familiar people, but at times they want to interact with new people. When they start talking to new people and the conversation begins to shift to awkward silence, it affects them the most because they were actively trying to meet new people and it didn’t go over well. For extroverts and entertainers, the silence is something that creates discomfort because it’s something they aren’t used to. Overall, this awkward silence just creates an uncomfortable situation that most people would much rather avoid.

David Emile Durkheim was a French sociologist and philosopher who was born on April 15, 1858 and died on November 15, 1917. He was known as the father of the French School of Sociology for incorporating empirical study with sociological theory. In 1983, he presented the concept of collective consciousness (also known as collective conscience), in his book “The Division of Labor in Society.” This is a concept that describes a set of beliefs, ideas, and moral attitudes that are shared within a common group or society. The collective consciousness is manifested by society through collective representations. Collective representations are symbols, artifacts, or narratives that embodies the beliefs, ideas, or moral attitudes of a group or society as a whole.

Collective representation can include symbols such as a wedding ring, artifacts such as football, or narratives like “the customer is always right.” For a group of people with social anxiety or who are introverted, they dislike silence in social settings. This is because the silence creates a feeling of anxiety, discomfort, and awkwardness. These experiences of encountering strangers, meeting new people, entering crowded spaces, or wanting to interact with others but not being able to, happens all the time. Since those experiences kept happening, socially anxious and introverted people, as well as extroverts and entertainers, started to view silence as awkward. This led to the narrative that silence is awkward continues to present itself whenever a situation becomes too quiet and the interaction between people is interrupted or disappears.

Through the collective consciousness, the narrative of silence being awkward has presented itself in many people’s lives. This begins when one person experiences silence and describes it as awkward. Then, one person encounters another person, or other people with the same experience and belief. What started as a singular, personal experience, is now recognized as a more common event. When this group comes upon conclusion or opinion about the event, it becomes a collective representation of silence.

Sometimes, what connects a group of people is something that is seen as negative or unpleasant. Commonly amongst socially anxious people and introverts, they experience and dislike awkward silence. These instances can happen with friends and family, but most frequently, its between strangers. There are situations where the awkward silence lasts a few moments and seen as irrelevant later-on. Examples include meeting someone for the first and only time, getting on an elevator with other people already on it, or going to a social gathering and making small talk. However, there are situations where an awkward silence could detrimental. Examples of this would be meeting someone important or having a job interview. Along with socially anxious people and introverts, some extroverts and entertainers of the group find silence to be awkward as well. Most common situations for them would be talking to new people and not being able to hold a conversation, or they are in a setting where they must be quiet. This silence makes them uncomfortable because it’s not what they are used to. Durkheim’s collective representation explains this narrative that silence is awkward amongst the group of socially anxious people, introverts, extroverts, and entertainers.
chunks.label: Collective representation and awkward silence
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on why awkward silence is perceived negatively by various groups and analyzes this phenomenon using Durkheim's concept of collective consciousness and collective representation.

nc8983163.title: Navigating Inequality in Male Friend Groups

chunks.text: Why as women in a friend group of men we are technically in, still somehow out unless there is a convenience to them? As women, we are only seen objectively even if we are in close relations with men. Whether it be in a relationship way, or even just a friendly way, we as women will never and have never been seen as equal in a society ruled by men. We as women continuously fight to be equal and to just be seen by men as something worth more than using or looking at. That is why I would like to discuss how women are othered by men, objectified, and put under a beauty myth even in friendships with men. No matter what title you have with a man, there is a consistent inequality and that is what I would discuss.
chunks.label: Inequality and objectification in friendships with men
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces her essay topic, reflecting on how women are objectified, othered, and subjected to the beauty myth even in friendships with men.

chunks.text: In my personal experience, I am the only straight female in my friend group, with there being only two other women. As you may be already thinking, I definitely hear and am a part of what men my age feel and say about women. I think when we think about inequality between women and men, we don’t discuss how crazy it is that it even exists between friendships, not just professional and love lives, and day-to-day strangers. These are people in my life who I count on and depend on, but when it comes down to it I am not equal to them in the slightest. There are a few examples to show this and what I have personally experienced.
chunks.label: Being the only straight female in friend group
chunks.what_happened: The student describes her position in her friend group, noting she is the only straight female alongside two other women and male peers who treat her unequally.

chunks.text: To start off, my guy friends basically treat me like their no strings attached girlfriend. They are very flirty and make comments that as guys in a friend group, you should not be making. They only do this with me and don’t do this with my other two friends who are lesbian. I believe this is because of the standard of beauty they have in their heads. Stereotypically, I have features that fall under the normal standards of beauty women follow. However, my lesbian friends don’t follow those standards and are beautiful in a not your typical women's way. So, in my friend group, the guys are definitely more friendly with me than they are with my other friends just because of how I stereotypically look. They flirt and everything like that, even though we are clearly just friends, and do it just because they can’t see me as just a human being to them but someone they need to be sexual and flirty towards.
chunks.label: Guy friends flirting due to conventional beauty standards
chunks.what_happened: The student's male friends treat her like a no-strings-attached girlfriend, making flirty comments toward her while not treating her lesbian friends the same way.

chunks.text: This leads me to my second topic, they see me as nothing but an object and when they do see me as more since we are just friends, it is almost demeaning. This is probably the most frustrating thing out of all of the things that they do, but anything that has to not do with my experience when complimenting me is “actually”. One of my guy friends when I make a joke always has to burst out laughing, even if it isn’t the funniest thing he has heard, and says that I am “actually” really funny. The first time he said it I didn’t mind it, but over time it gets frustrating to be seen as actually something. That's also not the only thing said, I am also “actually” smart, interesting, or in general anything that gives me any sense of value, but I can’t help but feel like that value is taken away with the word actually is then added to it. Even when they see what is good about me, they are shocked by it and add surprise to it just because I am a girl, they don’t do this to any of the guys in the group it is just me. So why is it a shock to them that as a girl there is more worth to me than how I look? This is why it is so incredibly frustrating to try and be equal when the closest thing they can say to make me equal isn’t even worth saying.
chunks.label: Backhanded compliments expressing surprise at student's abilities
chunks.what_happened: The student's male friends express shock whenever she is smart or funny by qualifying compliments with the word 'actually,' treating her like an object.

chunks.text: My last example is the fact that they reach out or hang out when it is convenient for them. My guy friends are never the ones to arrange any kind of hangout unless they are getting something out of it besides just hanging out with me, or they need someone. I invite them places quite frequently and so do the other girls in my friend group. Yet, the only times that they really want to hangout out are asking us to hang out is when there is a party where there are girls, or something along the lines of it being convenient for them and them physically getting something out of it. Secondly, when we do hangout and aren’t up and going somewhere, they expect me to listen to all of their issues with other girls and give them advice, whether they listen or not they don’t say anything else about the discussion and they don’t even bother to ask me about my life or anything, they only care about whether something involves them or not. If it does not involve them then they do not care the slightest. This is why it feels like I am just separate from the group and only a part of it when they get something out of it for their own satisfaction.
chunks.label: Guy friends only reaching out when convenient
chunks.what_happened: The student's male friends only invite her out when it benefits them, and they expect her to give emotional advice without asking about her life in return.
chunks.feelings: feels like I am just separate from the group
chunks.people: guy friends, other girls in the friend group

chunks.text: It is important to look at the topics that go along with gender equality, starting with Simone de Beauvoir's theory of othering. Beauvoir describes othering as men seeing women as “the other”. Basically saying that men are the dominant group and then there are just women, who are under a completely different, lower category compared to a man. Men are subject and women are presented as an object to men and nothing else. Making women the “other” in the eyes of men. An example of othering for women would be in the workplace men listen to men before they listen to women for advice or answers because they see them as the other and would rather hear from a man from their own group. Women are seen as that objects that it nothing for than their bodies so women aren’t listened to.
chunks.label: Simone de Beauvoir's theory of othering
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Simone de Beauvoir's concept of othering, discussing how men treat women as objects and dominant subjects in society.

chunks.text: My second concept to discuss is Naomi Wolf’s beauty myth. Wolf describes the beauty myth as the absolute need to be a certain way as women and the completely unrealistic and sometimes dangerous lengths women go to try and be this stereotypical definition of beauty. Men only feed into this myth along with social media as well as telling us what we should and shouldn’t look like. An example of this is seeing a model on Instagram who is obviously in very good shape, who has perfect features, long hair, and things of that nature, and we as women feel the need to fit into that section of beauty in order to make a way in society. With this not only does it make women insecure and put other women down, it completely has altered the male mind as well as what women should look like in society too.
chunks.label: Naomi Wolf's beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Naomi Wolf's concept of the beauty myth and how societal pressures and social media affect women and men's expectations.

chunks.text: My final concept is from Sigmund Freud and how men are towards women and why. Sigmund Freud says that men are drawn to women who look and/or act like their mothers. As men they want someone to take care of them and nurture them and listen to them and then go off and do whatever else they want to do. For a mother-child relationship that is okay because that is what moms do for their children, however, it does not work as well in a love relationship. For example, men like to boast about themselves to women they are romantic with, and have them glorify and praise them just like when a child does something they are proud of they want their mom to look immediately and be proud of them.
chunks.label: Sigmund Freud's theory on men and mothers
chunks.what_happened: The student reviews Sigmund Freud's theory that men seek mother figures who will nurture and listen to them.

chunks.text: Using this topic of Sigmund Freud in my experience goes along with my experience that my guy friends only talk to me when it is convenient for them. They will talk to me when they want something and then they don’t talk to me any other time. Also, they come to me begging for advice or when they need someone to talk to, but usually don’t return that kind of action back. As Sigmond Frued said, I am basically just a mother to them who they can come to when they need something or when they need help and that is about the limits of how they act towards me most of the time.
chunks.label: Applying Freud's concept to student's friend dynamics
chunks.what_happened: The student applies Freud's theory to her own friendships, analyzing how her male friends use her as a maternal figure for advice and convenience.

chunks.text: Moving on to my second situation within my friend group, the beauty myth plays into my friend group and how they treat me because of it. As I was saying, there is a standard for women in society, and the constant pressure put on women is created through this beauty myth. With this beauty myth, men are 100% involved in it and those are the standards of women they are shown meaning that is the standard of women they believe is achievable even though a good majority of the time it is not. My friends are friends with me specifically because of how I look and are a lot friendlier to me only because I am a part of whatever they consider the beauty to them. However, this beauty myth only objectifies women, and like in my friend group I am only seen objectively and for nothing else, so they treat me as if I am nothing more than a pretty face just because of their view on all women.
chunks.label: Applying the beauty myth to friend group interactions
chunks.what_happened: The student connects the beauty myth to her friend group, explaining that her male friends objectify her and treat her as merely a pretty face.

chunks.text: Lastly, Simone de Beauvoir and her theory on othering. I am 100% seen as other in my friend group than the men. They see me only as an object as they are subjects and anything that I say or do that adds value to me leaves them shocked because I am not a man and I am just the other to them. They see me as just a ditsy girl who if I do something a normal human being would do they see it as a shock because I am “actually” something, as opposed to them, which it wouldn’t be impressive if one of them did it because of course as a man they can do everything.
chunks.label: Applying Beauvoir's othering to friend group behavior
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how her male friends treat her as 'other,' reacting with surprise when she shows intelligence or humor because she is a woman.

chunks.text: In conclusion, being in a friend group full of men doesn’t make you feel like you are fully in the friend group, just someone who is there and worth nothing more than what they objectively see you as and what they choose to think and see about you on the inside. In society, I think many women have experienced this and have been made less than a group of men just because that is how men genuinely view them yet in reality women are capable and worth the same amount as any man is too. As women, we just want to be seen and be given the equality of men because it has always been this horrible challenge to even be considered as anything to men unless they are objectifying you. Women and male friendships are very much a part of that topic as well even though it isn’t discussed as much as we may discuss other relationships between men in women. So, the point I am trying to make is there is a clear divide between men and women and although in our society we try to find to change it, there will always be some form of inequality between men and women just because of how men are psychologically and how society projects women.
chunks.label: Conclusion on gender inequality in male-female friendships
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that male-female friendships reflect broader societal inequalities and objectification, summarizing her thoughts on the gender divide.

n763e8bb2.title: Examining Racial Bias in American Media

chunks.text:
This paper will seek to supply an argument that explores the issues in today’s media and how the media fails to properly provide black people with the attention and resources they need. For generations racial bias has affected the way America is run, who holds the power, and whose face will be shown to the public masses. This generalized bias has slowly formed white privilege over the years, and it is clear within America’s media who the main addressed audience is truly meant to be.

There seems to be a clear, unavoidable connection between racism and social media because social media can pave an easy way for people to share their prejudiced views from the safety of being behind a screen (ScienceDirect 2018). With privilege preexisting in the media, so many products, news, events, etc. generalize and assist white people more than they do black people or portray white women as more beautiful or superior to black women. Also, the ability for anonymous messages and posts behind the screen can end up leading to racism, hate crimes, microaggressions and so many more things that could be used to oppress black people. Furthermore, the media can end up fueling the preexisting beliefs harbored by people with privilege and cause even more separation between different social groups. When being portrayed in the media, almost always, whites can ensure that they will be portrayed in a fine light and more people will trust what they have to say, but that usually fails to be the case with how society views black people on a screen. This relates back to Peggy McIntosh’s point of never needing to harbor a fear of whether her race will allow people of power to trust her or not (McIntosh 32). Social media is definitely not the only place of imagery where we see privilege written all over it, even paper magazines will almost never fail to include a majority of white people in order to appeal to the larger public mass.

The idea of racial bias exists inevitably within social media today because of what most of modern society considers to be appealing or beautiful. The media has been structured on what privileged individuals desire to see and will be interested in. Through science, everyone can begin to see how everyone’s brain holds a certain level of bias, but when confirmation bias begins to form as racial bias because of past privilege and history, then the media will reflect it and America will continue to fail to grow as a country with empathy (ScienceDirect 2018). With white people having the means to control history and how it can be told, they are also able to control the media and how it is portrayed to the public. With control over the media, white people have the ability to use their superiority to skew how black people look to the public, especially when it comes to violence or sports (Carter-Francique 2016). Those who control the media can pick and choose what is revealed to the public and what is not, whether it will be fully truthful or not, and whether it will be prejudiced or not.

A huge example of something that white people use to try and study blackness would have to be music and movies which both hold immense amounts of racial bias. However, the given stereotypes that white people develop for black people within music or movies can be problematic because they make black people out to be so different from themself and try to assign people to fit into a different “box” from their own. Humans have this innate desire to want to make things make perfect sense and to be able to fit everything into a category or theoretical box so that they can come to a conclusion about where a person belongs. However, when people look different and act differently, and cannot be related as well to them, humans will usually outcast those who are different or treat them as lower than themself, even if they do not realize they are. These “boxes” and developed stereotypes through media such as music and movies have helped facilitate white privilege more than ever because it can put the differences of black people on display; and although it can fascinate some and help some understand, many will still look down upon black people despite their clear accomplishments. Hip-hop, rap, and crime have been three of the biggest areas for stereotyping black people by white people and it only became more problematic when white people were allowed to publish their personal views of these stereotypes in the media.

Racial bias can often come from heavy amounts of confirmation bias that is already held by those who are privileged based on the color of their skin. If white people have grown up around mostly white people, and they have been raised to enjoy being around white people, they may begin forming a racial bias towards white people because that is who they know to be safe. Also, if someone is raised in a home where the caregivers only trust white people and speak terribly about people of color, that person is likely to begin forming a racial bias that black people are worse than white people. Similarly, if someone only sees white people around their neighborhood and they hear from the media to steer clear of black people roaming around their neighborhood, they may form a racial bias and choose to believe that all blacks are dangerous and cannot be trusted roaming around anywhere. This begins to spark racial biases between both groups white and black, and because of the knowledge a group of people think they now know, they form a confirmation bias about the group’s race, and they become completely polarized from each other.

Another example where racial bias is used is in the sports industry. Black people, and especially black women have been severely oppressed when it comes to being an athlete (Carter-Francique 2016). Black women must face the reality of holding the least amount of privilege out of any race or gender, so many of them for generations never even dreamed of trying out for a sport. Sports media represented dominant groups in order to appeal to the public eye, causing whites to rule the athletic field for years. Upper-class white men were given the power to play, watch, and share sports because of the public’s belief that they were superior. Sports began to cause even more marginalization towards black people because whites were given the power to assume that black people were less capable in performing athletically than white people.

Unfortunately, the media fails to represent black people and provide enough necessary resources that apply to black people’s needs, rather than just whites. However, the media has had these flaws for such a long duration, and they are seen as such micro flaws to the public, that the public fails to recognize and stand up to the media on this issue. McIntosh clearly states that she never has to worry about going to the store and not have a choice for “blemish cover or bandages in “flesh” color (McIntosh 33). This is just one example of an ad you would be able to see in the media that favor white people. Commercials on tv for hair products mostly for women, but sometimes even men, will reach to the white public because their hair is considered “more beautiful” or much easier to take care of. Black people’s Bantu features, and bodies are not celebrated, they are forgotten and overlooked by the media industry. The media has celebrated white professionalism and white models in order to ensure that the public believes that “white” is the goal and the face of the media itself.

There is evidence within the lives of the citizens of America that so many are only willing to take a “middle ground” when it comes to accepting who owns privilege, and who does not. The media never rushes to tell stories about what black people had to go through years ago in slavery, or how turmoil within the Underground Railroad should illustrate how capable and worthy they are to be considered as a human being in the same way white people are (Johnson 2015). Ultimately, these historical events have been spoken about; however, change within a society built on racism is not expounded upon often within the media. Furthermore, when the media does happen to discuss historical issues, they can still often be told by the white perspective and can only force more stereotypes on black people that they might wish to leave behind and be able to grow from. In the media industry, there is such a large platform, that it seems to be one of the easiest places for people to subtly bring about social injustice and not get caught or face challenges. Media holds ideas of white superiority and power, especially sports and social media. If someone is black and is portrayed in sports media, they may be seen as more intimidating or fear-striking than someone who is performing and is white which can point back to racial bias.

In conclusion, racial bias and stereotypes towards black people are deeply embedded into society’s media. Due to these stereotypes being inevitable, black people have had to accept that their needs would always have to be second behind whites, and the media would never put them on display for the public to follow. Generations of conformational bias have caused the public to be more fearful of black crime, to avoid counting black people’s resources as unimportant compared to their own and categorize black people into a “different box” from their own allowing for oppressive behavior to occur.

The domination of white privilege throughout America has silently kept the “micro” issues in the dark so that people have become so numb to them, they hardly recognize there is any problem at all. For change to occur within the media, there must ultimately be identification of white privilege by those who are behind and in front of the camera. White privilege is not an invisible, negotiable topic, it is the reality of everyday American society that must face change. Peggy McIntosh further explains this is her list from White Privilege where she describes basic everyday things, she will never have to be fearful of. It would be easier to ignore the racial bias people harbor every day or in the media, or easy to ignore the privilege that white people own, especially if someone is in fact a white person; however, without recognition and empathy, America will continue to suffer as a whole.
chunks.label: Racial bias and white privilege in media
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how American media reinforces racial bias, white privilege, and stereotypes across sports, music, film, and advertising, referencing scholars like Peggy McIntosh.

chunks.text:
21 Lessons for the 21st Century Through a Sociological Perspective

Yuval Noah Harari is an israli historian and professor of in the Department of History at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem. He has also written many books such as: Homo Deus: A Brief History of Tomorrow, Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankin, and 21 Lessons for the 21st Century. A key theme in his belief system is that human society has mostly been driven by our capacity to believe in fiction. Our collective belief in fictions, which we give meaning to, establishes a cooperative basis for existing as a community. Among his bestselling books is 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, which goes into greater detail about this key belief among other things. In 21 Lessons for the 21st Century Harari explains his opinions on various social dynamics and dilemma’s using historical and sociological evidence. While some of his points complement the writings of the authors who we read in class, Harari holds some opinions, which outlined in his book, contradict certain writings. In other words those opinions hold little sociological ground. This semester we have covered a wide array of topics, the origin of man, class in America, race and enthinicty as well as our conception of self. Through deeper analysis we can conclude to what extent the content of this semester corroborates Harari’s opinions or whether it does at all. More broadly, we can determine, of his opinions, what contradicts or complements what we have read and learned in class. The conclusions of this analysis will serve as a good foundation for identifying where sociology played a role in the formation of his ideologies.

Class systems have existed throughout time as a means to subjugate individuals through diminishing their worth and propping up a minority as a result. These systems sow inequality into a community which yields a hierarchical placement of people in the upper, middle or lower classes. The Caste System in India works similarly, you are placed, from birth, in a caste which automatically assigns characteristics to you accordingly. These characteristics are not equal to others, but determine your freedom and worth throughout your life. Ancient Greece and Rome had similar systems but like India’s they were blatant at keeping people down. In the United States, a kind of caste system exists but is not as obvious. Gregory Mantsios explains in his essay, “Class in America”, Americans are too afraid to distinguish the economic differences between their fellow citizens and the power of oppression in the class system largely keeps people in the class they were born into. The class a person is born into affects their life more than they know, and their unwillingness to recognize it propagates the reach and longevity of the system. This inequity takes two prominent forms, power and wealth, which are the mechanisms used to either give or prohibit the assumption of power. It is almost as if the country is a large company with a few very powerful and rich executives with most others serving as worker drones. Yuval Harari’s arguements, in part 4 of his book called Truth during the Post-Truth chapter, complement Mantsios’ analysis. In this chapter Harari explains that humans have always been living in a post-truth age, this is in line with his key belief that humans naturally believe falsehoods or fictions. Fake news if you will is necessary for classism to work, instilling false beliefs in a lower class can garner submissiveness and compliance. The American Dream is a prime example of how hope and fiction collide to produce a misguided but effective belief for the lower class to cling to. The dream itself states that anyone can achieve monetary success so long as they putforth the necessary effort. This is provably false, statistically and sociologically, it can be observed that not anyone can achieve success due to barriers like race, creed, economic satus, and a host of other variables. It is conveneient a lie however, because many people believe it and as such comes a variety of other sub beliefs that reinforce the class system. Beliefs like, the United States fosters an even playing field and no one can have too much money if they earned it working hard. Harari’s post truth argument also finds an important role in rendering Americans ignorant of the facts. Words like socialism and communism get used interchangeably by politicians despite being different ideologies, so as to scare Americans into believing the U.S will slip into communism should policies be enacted to give the middle and lower classes more or even as I see it. By falsely claiming basic quality of life policies for average Americans are akin to socialism or communism creates a negative association and infringes on the misguided, inherent, belief that everyone should make it on their own, in effect reinforcing the class system. In part 4 of his book Yuval Harari’s writings about post-truth and fake news serve as a foundation for allowing what Gregory Mantsios described in his essay about class in America. False ideals and fictions believed by the public supported and continue to support the class system in the United States by obscuring individuals perception and understanding.

A civilization is defined by Merriam-Webster as, “the condition that exists when people have developed effective ways of organizing a society and care about art, science, etc.” It seems from the definition that we as a collective of civilizations each with our own cultures, values and appeciations. At one time there existed merely one civilization of humans on earth. A small tight-knit community of people who shared common beliefs and acted their individual roles to help better the community. However, over time that civilization has grown exponentially and branching wildly in varying directions. Through this, it has become many distinct civilizations existing with each other but not exactly together. Harari argues in the civilizations chapter that we emerged from one and remain one, where it concerns human civilization. He claims that we are one civilization, something which might have been true thousands of years ago but as the world became more complex people divided themselves into smaller groups effectively making new ones. Each country is like its own civilization and because each has it own set of values, beliefs, et cetera, when they collide with others conflict can emerge in the form of xenophobia or war. It can be observed that when differing beliefs come together, each end will mostly try to rein supreme, which means they not only hold on to their beliefs but actively advocate for it over others. Many Americans, for example, fear immigration because they believe members from a civilization merging with theirs would infringe on or change the ideals they subscribe to. In our race and ethnicity module, Tomas Almaguer describes in his essay, the process of racialization. A process in which a group will ascribe ethnic or racial characteristics and identities to a group that they do not belong to themselves. Almaguer describes that Puerto Ricans and Mexicans had preconceptions of eachother according to the way race is defiend in those countries. They had taken to establish a conception based on more than that which they have been exposed to in their country. I think this contradicts what Harari presumes about civilizations because there appears to be no global lens through which to look. Although Harari argues that we are all members of the same civilization, we do not acknowledge each other like we are members of the same community, something that is integral to existing as one.

Yuval Harari’s book 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, outlines many interesting opinions and highlights some observable facts within society. Many of his points seem to rest on sociological ground as well as statistical ground. His post-truth argument is especially interesting as it has a significant role to play in both small and large things. Its application to class in America bolsters Gregory Mantsios’ overall point that Americans do not realize the rampant inequity that plagues their country and creates an uneven playing field. However, not all of what Harari says complements what we have learned in class. His assertions about the existence of a global civlization seem to contradict what Tomas Almaguer writes in his Essay, “Race, Racialization, and Latino Populations in the United States.” He writes that individuals create images for themselves about others in a racial group that they do not belong to according to how race is defined within their country. Regardless of whether we live in a single civlization or not this concept severely limits the extent to which it exists. Nevertheless, 21 Lessons for the 21st century provides insight and greater context to many of the topics discussed this semester, reinforcing my understanding of sociolical thinking and analysis.

Sources

“Civilization Definition & Meaning.” Merriam-Webster, Merriam-Webster, https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/civilization.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of Harari's 21 Lessons
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces and analyzes Yuval Noah Harari's book '21 Lessons for the 21st Century' by comparing his arguments about post-truth and a global civilization to course readings on social class and racialization.

n41a61e3d.title: Labor Estrangement During the COVID-19 Pandemic

chunks.text:
What are the most terrifying aspects of a pandemic? Initially, nearly all individuals will not hesitate to simply answer the above question as the possibility of becoming deathly ill, and even dying. Although the previously mentioned consequence of a pandemic is indeed terrifying, there are numerous other aspects of widespread diseases that can be very detrimental to human life as well. During the Coronavirus pandemic that the world is currently still facing, many challenges have arisen that affect people's everyday lives. The COVID-19 virus has proven to be very injurious to human lives in relation to their health, their finances, their labor, and much more. Throughout this paper I will discuss how the Coronavirus pandemic estranges individuals from their labor, fully destroys people’s relationship with their work, and can even harm a person's overall identity.

In class, we educated ourselves about capitalist societies in module seven. Throughout this module we read two discourses about humans in relation to these societies. In the writing, “Estranged Labor,” Karl Marx does an in-depth analysis about how labor in a capitalist society can be alienating for the worker in numerous aspects. Through the action of labor, workers can be isolated from the product, the process, each other, and themselves. The individual worker does not possess the product that is being produced, and therefore the more that they make, the less they actually own and the more segregated they become. In addition, the worker is solely performing the labor as a mechanism to survive and not for their personal contentment. This idea of labor being forced is also explained in “The Spirit of Capitalism and the Iron Cage” by Max Weber. Weber elucidates how people rationally devote their entire lives to making money, which expands upon how the labor merely serves the purpose of providing individuals with revenue. Since the labor is not voluntary, the worker remains unsatisfied and is alienated from the process. The forced labor can also estrange people from their own bodies and their human potential because their life activity is only a manner to physically exist. Finally, there is also the potential for the worker to become isolated from other workers in capitalist societies. Marx explains how this separation from each other occurs due to the competitive manner and the breakdown of labor in this economic system.

This complex alienation that workers face occurs naturally in a capitalist society. Therefore, the detachment is already present within working citizens' lives. However, the estrangement becomes exaggerated and worsened through the presence of a crisis, such as a pandemic. The COVID-19 virus has been extremely damaging to human life in relation to their labor. This virus has been researched and was discovered to be spread from person-to-person through respiratory droplets. Due to this, the most efficient way to prevent the virus from rapidly spreading during the early stages of its emergence was to shut down unnecessary industries and restrict individuals from leaving their own homes. Therefore, this led to the forced shutdown of some companies and the failure of other businesses because they could not make enough profit to survive. The pandemic led to a record number of people becoming unemployed, more than ever before.

Numerous studies have been conducted that show the implications of this virus on the world. One of these studies is titled, “Experiences of Latinx Individuals Hospitalized for COVID-19, A Qualitative Study” and was written by thirteen certified researchers. This inquiry interviewed sixty citizens of Latin America, both male and female, to divulge how the Coronavirus pandemic directly affected these individuals. This investigation revealed that only 9% of the people were able to work from their houses, only a fifth of them were able to get money for a leave due to illness, and nearly 40% of them lost their job entirely due to the pandemic. In addition, of these individuals who lost their jobs and had to adjust their work environment, slightly more than 70% of them were deemed essential workers. Aside from numerical discoveries from the examination, the information also concluded that the COVID-19 widespread disease generated economic fears and disadvantages, social drawbacks, and labor issues (Cervantes et al. 1). The social downsides described in this article are a result of humans being forced to remain in their own homes. The forced social distancing, due to this virus, prevents individuals from interacting and leads to them becoming extremely isolated. Although not all of this isolation is related to labor, it still significantly impacts people and their connections to other humans, society, and even their own self-perception. Together, these implications can inflict damage upon a person’s overall identity.

The above study performed in Latin America also unveils the effects from the Coronavirus specifically in relation to labor. The individuals in this inquiry experienced estrangement from their career, impacts on their relationship with their work, and consequences on their overall identity as well. The approximate 10% of people who continued working, but solely from home, experienced increased isolation from their co-workers due to the transition from in person employment to online employment. This isolation is added onto the previous segregation these people already faced, as described by Karl Marx. The nearly 20% of workers who received paid leave, as well as the 40% who lost their jobs entirely were fully stripped of the chance to form a relationship with their labor. In addition, having no occupation takes away an individual's ability to rationally devote their life to working, as described in “The Spirit of Capitalism and the Iron Cage” by Max Weber. Together, the increased alienation and unemployment then go on to harm an individual's overall identity. This is because they are no longer able to achieve a level of occupational status, which is the social ranking that derives from the labor one does.

Another study conducted in relation to COVID-19 also demonstrates how the illness leads to complications between an individual and their relationship with their labor. This analysis is titled, “Forecasting major impacts of COVID-19 pandemic on country-driven sectors: challenges, lessons, and future roadmap” and was written by seven reliable researchers. The findings of this article reveal how the virus has been brutally challenging for citizens of the world by specifically examining the effects of the disease on India. The main challenges revealed through the article are economic damages, the shutdown of education centers, disaster in the healthcare industries, harm to international and local businesses, and impairment to the transportation, power, and oil industries (Kumar et al. 20-21). The damages done to all of these industries and aspects of life can be unified through the common theme of isolation. Shutting industries and education centers down leads humans to become segregated from other individuals, as well as aspects of their own life, such as their education and work. In addition, all of the harmful economic effects and the effects on businesses have led industries to fail and shut down. The article even states that, “Due to maintaining social distancing, the sales of the industry stop and all the companies are facing financial loss and closure” (Kumar et al. 9). This shows how the Coronavirus has caused companies to cease to function and individuals to lose their jobs. As previously mentioned, when individuals no longer have a profession, they also no longer have the chance to maintain a relationship with their labor. The elimination of this occupational relationship, as well as the greatly increased alienation from their coworkers, harms a person's social identity.

However, the forced shut down of businesses not only takes people away from their own careers, but it also takes them away from other businesses. This then ruins their opportunity to go out and spend their money at these places. Throughout module seven, we learned about commodities in addition to humans' relationship with their labor. Commodities are essential to society because they captivate people and provide them with a motivation for their labor, which also shapes the productive and consumptive social world humans reside in. Commodities also give people a chance to develop their own identities, by allowing them to purchase materials that supply their life with meaning. However, in order for these commodities to exist there must be both a workplace and workers to produce them. Therefore, when businesses shut down and people lost their jobs due to the Coronavirus, the number of commodities diminished also. This directly impacted both individual human identities, as well as society as whole.

A third study conducted by qualified researchers reaffirms the harm done by the pandemic. This examination is titled, “Association of job loss, income loss, and financial burden with adverse mental health outcomes during coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic in Thailand: A nationwide cross-sectional study” and analyzes the effects of the Coronavirus on Asia. For this particular investigation, the researchers examined nearly 2,500 adults who were actively employed with full time jobs during the shutdown of the nation. The conclusions of the study were summarized by the loss of professions, income loss, and financial issues due to the outbreak of the disease. The conclusions continued on to prove how these economic complications then went on to create higher levels of stress, anxiety, and mental health problems in individuals (such as depression). The analysis directly states that “participants who reported losing their job had 51.9%, 56.9%, and 84.7% prevalence rates of depressive symptoms, anxiety symptoms, and perceived stress… income loss showed a slight association with depressive symptoms” (Ruengorn et al. 4). This quotation from the study discloses how individuals' mental health was harmed as a direct result from the elimination of a relationship with their labor. Overall, this shows how when a person is severely alienated from their work and loses the association they have maintained with their labor, their health suffers as a result. When a persons’ mental health is diminished their quality of life is also harmed, which can alter their self-perception and overall identity as well.

Therefore, the Coronavirus pandemic has been proven to estrange individuals from their labor, fully destroy people’s relationship with their work, and even harm people's overall identity. Although the above studies were conducted by examining individuals in Thailand, India, and Latin America, the damage done to the people within these locations resembles the destruction done to the rest of the world as well. This detriment has stemmed from the shutdown of nations throughout the world, which has led to changes in work environments, destruction of companies, and more unemployment than ever before. These alterations have caused people to become more isolated from numerous aspects of their work, such as their co-workers and the process of their labor. People who fully lost their jobs no longer have the opportunity to have a connection with their occupation and as a result have had impacts on their identity as well. The negative implications from COVID-19 on peoples working identities can then change the way people feel about themselves and adjust the way they act in society, which will further impair aspects of the social world humans reside in down the road. Pandemics have much more harmful characteristics than the simple health consequences they provide. The Coronavirus, as well as other widely spread diseases, can harm individuals' identities, economical aspects of the world, and socialization within the world as well.
chunks.label: Pandemic effects on labor alienation and identity
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes sociological texts and research studies to discuss how the COVID-19 pandemic worsens alienation from labor, disrupts workers' relationships with their jobs, and harms individual identity.

n092069dc.title: Navigating Gender Stereotypes in Competitive Dance

chunks.text: From the moment a child is born they are proclaimed as either boy or girl and unknowingly, so is their social identity. Sex can be classified as a characteristic of the body while gender is the set of roles that are taught. Therefore, it’s fair to say that they are distinctly different. Our society instils upon the idea about how men and women should and should not behave which result in harsh gender stereotypes. For centuries, society has been driven by masculine men over dominating women and making patriarchal institutions a natural way of life. Sex and gender are highly debated topics and by breaking down their fundamentals and discussing their differences, society can better understand them.
chunks.label: Sex, gender, and societal stereotypes
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the distinction between sex and gender, and how society instills gender stereotypes and patriarchal institutions.

chunks.text: As a woman, I have had moments in my life where I have recognized and experienced gender-based stereotypes. My entire childhood and early adulthood I was a competitive dancer and was primarily surrounded by women. I was taught at a very young age that dance was not a sport because it was just a “girls sport.” I had played plenty of sports throughout my youth and had never been scrutinized for participating because they were “boys sports” such as baseball and soccer. My father was also a huge factor in my development of gender-based stereotypes. He is a very strong-opinionated masculine man who insisted on telling me what I could and could not do because I am girl and was one of the people in my life who guided me to think the sport, I played was not valid because it was a “girls sport.” One of the most detrimental things about these so called “girl sports” is that body image plays a huge role. In sports heavily containing girls like dance, cheerleading or gymnastics you will almost never see a girl who is seen as “fat.” All these sports involve tiny, thin little girls because that is what is what society expects of them. The saddest part of this expectation is that it leads to issues like body dysmorphia or eating disorders. This type of stigma is very different, however, if you look at male dominated sports like football all you expect of them is to be strong whether they were seen as heavy or not. As much as I love the sport that is dance, I cannot deny the pressure that came with maintaining a socially accepted body.
chunks.label: Competitive dance and gendered body expectations
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up as a competitive dancer surrounded mostly by women, facing dismissal of dance as a mere 'girls sport' from her father and navigating pressure around body image.

chunks.text: The media has become one of the most influential ways to distribute information and give insight to people’s personal affairs. Whether it’s a movie, magazine, podcast or television show, gender stereotypes are made and are discriminated. The media portrays men and women in extremely different ways. Women are portrayed as being beautiful and desirable and primarily sex symbols while men are portrayed as being overly masculine a dominating. If you were to look up a music video for a song, say Lil Wayne, I almost guarantee you will find women in either provocative clothing or doing something sexual. The women are almost like moving props to attract an audience or just a selling point to the video. With that said, its also notable to mention that the lyrics to these types of music videos are just as equally shameful. The genre of rap has been one of the most negative media outlets for gender stereotypes because its one of the most popular types of music amongst this generation.
chunks.label: Gender stereotypes in media and rap music
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how media and rap music videos portray men as dominating and reduce women to sexualized props.

chunks.text: As said in the previous paragraph, I used to be a dancer and one style I did was hip hop. The style of hip hop is heavily based around rap music, and I remember being a preteen/teen in middle school dancing to songs like “Baby Got Back” or “Hot in Here.” To make matters worse I would sometimes have to do provocative movements just because it went along with the lyrics.

chunks.text: Collective consciousness is a sociological concept that refers to a set of shared beliefs that are common to a specific social group. As part of being a female, women learn these gender stereotypes and tend to just accept them and go on their lives. The first wave of feminism took place in the late 19th century and their initial attempt was to organize a national movement for women's rights. Feminists drew in sight from abolitionists and the French Revolution. Often sides were dominated by men in the often did not allow women to speak freely in front of a male dominated audience and women were often mocked for speaking out of turn. One of the most popular topics of the feminist movement was women suffrage and not a lot of people agreed with these values, but the activists believed that their goals would not be impossible without the right to vote. The 19th amendment would soon be able to be ratified however it only guaranteed white men women directed vote while on the other hand black women and other people of color were denied that act until decades later. The goal of feminism was to challenge the inequalities of women that were faced on a daily basis in at this time they were well met and continued to progress throughout history
chunks.label: Collective consciousness and history of feminism
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on collective consciousness, the history of first-wave feminism, women's suffrage, and the exclusion of women of color.

chunks.text: Most of society seems to think that sex and gender are very much the same but by analyzing it from a sociological perspective it can be agreed that sex denotes biological features and gender denotes social factors. Gender is the social interpretation of sex, and it is conceived of masculinity and femininity. Cultures interpret the anatomy of a body rather than the cultural characteristics of the person. Author De Beauvoir Claims that “one is not born but rather becomes a woman and that social discrimination produces in women moral and intellectual effects so profound that they appear to be caused by nature.” This means that females become women through a process where they acquire traits and learned behavior. They are casually constructed and have a role and bring individuals into existence and shape the way men and women are socially.
chunks.label: Sociological perspectives and De Beauvoir on gender
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes the social construction of gender, citing Simone de Beauvoir's theory that one is not born but becomes a woman.

chunks.text: You come into this world with a sex, but society influences whether you choose to be masculine or feminine. When we are born our sex determines how we will be treated and what we will achieve. The way we view sex can determine how we will be treated and more so through outlets like media and society. Society defines a set gender role and enforces it. In life we are born with a sex but are given the choice of gender and through that we choose how to express ourselves. Outside influences such as media and society or friends make us conform to these gender roles. In today's generation it is becoming more acceptable to be who you truly are but it was not always like that and we need to learn where and when these gender roles were set and how much they impact our lives.
