But how do each of these topics relate to each other? And how do societies begin to actively work to fix the damage done by these issues? In predominately white cultures in Europe and North America, the issue of white privilege is currently receiving a lot of attention due to more efforts made to expose and resolve issues of racism in western societies. Numerous studies have been done on racism and white privilege especially in the United States since it currently holds the position of hegemonic power in the world. One of the main difficulties in ending the power these issues have over society is that they are so deeply ingrained in society and government that to tackle one topic, it to have to deal with all of them. The issue addressed today is the presence and effects of racism and white privilege in current western society, how it is currently shaping the future of these cultures, and what has proven effective in changing how issues, like racism, are treated.

White privilege: this term is defined as “the set of social and economic advantages that white people have by virtue of their race in a culture characterized by racial inequality” by the online dictionary and thesaurus Merriam-Webster.com. The concept of white privilege is one that often makes people uncomfortable, mainly white people, and therefore is not an easy topic of conversation. Because white people do not perceive their inherent advantages as such, they do recognize that it affects every single racial and ethnic minority around them in an increasingly negative light.

One distinction that should be made is that occasionally when used in discussion, the term white privilege can be confused with the term white supremacist, which is defined by Merriam-Webster.com as “a person who believes that the white race is inherently superior to other races and that white people should have control over people of other races”. While white supremacy in western culture is viewed as the more serious offense against racial and ethnic minorities, white privilege can be seen in almost every facet of western society; governmental institutions, education, housing, social media, etc. With regards to general society, white privilege can be seen in how minorities are treated by authority figures. A most recent example being the recently exposed cases of police brutality in the United States, including the murders of George Floyd and Brianna Taylor

While the United States is often at the forefront of the news when the topic of racism and white privilege comes up, most predominately white cultures still have these issues. Michael J. Mascarenhas talks about the intersection between white privilege, the environment, and racism, in Ontario, Canada in his work Where the Waters Divide: Neoliberal Racism, White Privilege and Environmental Injustice. None of these issues are singular events that can be solved individually, they have been integrated almost completely into each other. Mascarenhas illustrates how racism and environmental injustice go hand in hand through his research into the contemporary type of racism that Canadian and First Nation people are seeing today. He states that this new type of racism “thrives in highly racialized societies that espouse racial equality, but in which whites… will not tolerate either being inconvenienced in order to achieve racial equality, or be denied the full benefits of their whiteness”. (Mascarenhas, 8).

In Mascarenhas’ study, he interviewed twenty-seven First Nation people, including two Chiefs, water treatment plant workers, and community activists. He observed that Each of them faced the same fundamental racism in their everyday lives and when white Canadian citizens felt that their “rights” were being threatened by the First Nation people, they used “two of the oldest racial stereotypes of Indigenous Peoples—lacking motivation and intelligence “to work to survive.” (Mascarenhas, 11). According to Mascarenhas, the difference between the two groups was that the shortcomings of the First Nation people were due solely to choices of the individual instead of results from a society organized around particular types of racism.

The work Everyday Racism’ in a Culture of Political Avoidance: Civil Society, Speech, and Taboo by Nina Eliasoph takes a deeper dive into what racism looks like through the more focused channel of how people talk about racism and race in situations that are not specifically devoted to that topic. Eliasoph looks at the benefits of having race conversations in everyday life and how when people treat these topics with sincerity, but not awkwardness or fear, much more progress in communication can be made. Communication is indeed one aspect of daily life that most people do not understand the power of or how to properly use it. The question of why most white people find it difficult to discuss racism or race during normal social conversation is because most people can be classified as “passive bystanders”. (Eliasoph, 486). Similar to the situation that occurs when a large group of people see someone be attacked and do nothing because they believe that someone else will do something, passive “bystanders notice the action and do not actively support it but do not do anything to oppose it, either.” (Eliasoph, 486).

In the conclusion of Eliasoph’s work, she broke down how each of the categories discussed in her work, beliefs, social structures, and conversation, were observed to either encourage or limit open dialogue about race. While personal beliefs did not impact the conversation as much as anticipated, the concept of polite conversation did inhibit people from speaking freely about racism. Eliasoph noted that when social structures, like school/education, asked people to not speak on their thoughts of race but rather question the types of speech surrounding racial topics that the conversation flowed much more freely and the thoughts were then uncovered with less resistance. The last topic Eliasoph tackled is the global side of the discussion. Since racism is so ingrained into every society and culture in one way or the other, talking about it also involves talking about many other issues in the world including sexism, homophobia, ableism, sex trafficking, the drug trade, police brutality, etc. and when people are uncomfortable talking able one, they will be uncomfortable talking about any of these topics.

Color-Blind Racial Attitudes: Microaggressions in the Context of Racism and White Privilege by Jared Edwards tackles the issue of microaggressions. The term microaggression is used to describe “a comment or action that subtly and often unconsciously or unintentionally express a prejudiced attitude toward a member of a marginalized group (such as a racial minority)”. Edwards talks about the historical context of racism in the United States, beginning with the slave trade that took place predominately in the southeast of the country. Though the true history of overt racism began with the early colonizers and the continual slaughter of the Native Americans, most history books lead the race discussion with the peak of slavery after the revolutionary war. But, in continuation, Edwards also mentions the Internment camps used during World War Two for the mass imprisonment of Asian American people due to the discrimination and distrust of Asian people.

In the conclusion of Edwards’ argument, he talks about how every culture, group, society, etc. is unique and if we try to ignore or wash over this fact, we will face our own downfall. The experience that each group and more specifically each individual has in life will be different than anyone or other group could experience. “However, when we choose to truly explore our differences and really see others with their identities and experiences intact, then we can move toward true acceptance and valuation of diversity.” (Edwards, 15).

The concept of true and complete acceptance of all differences while comforting on some levels is realistically impossible, and Edwards does address this unnamed concept of a utopia. This statement is backed through Color-Blind Racial Attitudes, otherwise referenced as CoBRAs, which Edwards defines as “the values expressed by those who claim to see all people as the same without acknowledging, or even noticing, racial identity” (Edwards, 12). However, CoBRAs and white privilege meet at an interesting point, because if people are completely blind to the differences of the minority groups around them, whether racial, sexual, or gender groups, then they hold to the same bases of the concept of white privilege; They will not be able to recognize the disadvantages that the other groups face and the challenges that they have to overcome. Like any controversial matter, education and honest discussion are the most effective tools for changing our perspectives.

In conclusion, while western culture has made great pushes towards racial and gender equality in recent years through the activism and work of the people in these cultures, there are millions of more steps to take forward. None of these issues are new, but all are extremely important for every person to be educated in. Like the discussions of racism mentioned at the beginning of this essay, discussion about differences between different individuals or groups is not a comfortable one. Problems including white privilege and white supremacy are so securely rooted in the culture and society of the United States that to undermine these structures would be to destabilize the foundation of western social order. The reality of racism and sexism is that they are so ingrained into the world, that in order to wholly disassemble them, there will have to be a complete restructuring of every government and social concept.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of racism and white privilege
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes racism, white privilege, and intersectional injustice in western society using literature by Mascarenhas, Eliasoph, and Edwards.

nabc37c1e.title: Examining Power and Class in Higher Education

chunks.text: Power and class in America have always shaped the social, political, and economic parts of the nation. It also has caused significant problems throughout the nation like political influence, economic disparities, and educational inequalities. This essay will explore the origins, effects on society, and challenges associated with reaching equality for everyone.
chunks.label: Introduction to power and class essay
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces their essay discussing the origins, social effects, and challenges of power, class, and equality in America.

chunks.text: The roots of the power and class dynamics in America can be traced back for a very long time. The institution of slavery which happened for years laid a foundation for racial distributions and systematic oppressions in America that even shape the nation to this day. Both power and class share pretty similar relationships but power is defined as the ability to influence or control others, class splits hierarchical divisions within society based factors like wealth and education. Even after the abolition of slavery, some discriminatory laws like the Jim Crow Laws and redlining maintain racial disparities in wealth, education and opportunity. Amidst this, America's foundation relies on equality, its economic structure, and also free market principles. In America, people seek to own property, earn high incomes, and be very wealthy. All of these values are unequally distributed and may be all used as a power indicator. While the idea of capitalism promises equal opportunity and progress, it very often fails to meet these ideas because of top figures of society. Many higher class individuals, corporate executives, and people with higher salaries shape the public discourse and they determine the distribution of resources. Conversely, the working class and lower middle class and lower class communities face things like economic insecurity, limited access to resources, and sometimes poverty.
chunks.label: Historical and economic roots of class inequality
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the historical roots of power and class dynamics through slavery and discriminatory laws, as well as the unequal distribution of resources under capitalism.

chunks.text: In addition, the center of power and class usually extends to the political realm where individuals and special groups have a large influence due to campaign contributions, sponsors, and corporate interests. The money in politics has become far more beneficial to the wealthy underachieving some principles that America has stood for and often amplifies the voices and opinions of the lower class and less fortunate communities. “The Rich” are into a social upper class that has developed institutions by which the children of the rich are also put into that upper class world view. The dominance of some cultural norms and values also intersects with power and class in America because mainstream media, entertainment industries, and educational institutions play a huge role in shaping public perceptions, reinforcing stereotypes, and perpetuating social hierarchies.
chunks.label: Power and class in politics and culture
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how wealthy individuals influence politics through campaign contributions and how media and institutions perpetuate social hierarchies.

chunks.text: A real world scenario between these would be at a prestigious university, where power and class are a very relevant thing, the administrators and staff have significant influence over most campus policies, academic programs, and resources. They come from very privileged backgrounds and have many connections which give many opportunities and it shapes the university's reputation. Within the campus there are students who also have the same benefits through generational money or have family connections who got them into this prestigious school will one day have a great chance at being successful one day through prestigious internships, and networking through other alumni. Meanwhile, the middle and lower class students at most college campuses may face many problems with paying for college, private tutors, and networking to find jobs once they graduate. This is an example of the power and social class benefits that many Americans have over the others. This illustrates how power and class intersect with many things that go on in today's world, shaping people's experiences and opportunities.
chunks.label: Hypothetical scenario of privilege at university
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes a real-world scenario of class dynamics at a prestigious university, contrasting privileged students and staff with middle and lower class students.

chunks.text: As a result of these inequalities in educational experiences, and life connections, ultimately, acquiring high level jobs and earning high income salaries becomes an obstacle for those less fortunate. This perpetuates the economic divide to provide a more established foundation leading to successful futures between those who have had power and class to influence their lives and those who have not.
chunks.label: Effects of educational disparities on future success
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how disparities in educational experiences and connections lead to inequalities in career outcomes and perpetuate the economic divide.

chunks.text: In conclusion, power and class are very important concepts for understanding societal structures and many dynamics. These dynamics are not solely determined by economic capital but are also shaped from factors like race, gender, and ethnicity Furthermore, by acknowledging these issues between social classes and power, we can strive towards a more equal social change.
chunks.label: Conclusion on addressing class and power inequalities
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by summarizing how power and class intersect with race, gender, and ethnicity, calling for acknowledgment to achieve equal social change.

n86444f0d.title: Rethinking Wealth Power and Social Class

chunks.text:
Mantsios states in the very beginning of his work that people do not like to talk about social classes, at least they do not like the connotations that come with some of the terms about their class. But, when a new name or more “gentle” term is applied to the group, everyone is more willing to talk. On the other hand, people are coming to recognize that the title of one’s class, whether it is economic or gender specific etc., they are no indicative of a person’s inherent worth. This idea is most definitely not new, but something that must be reintroduced to each generation. In continuation, the basic summary of Domhoff’s piece is that power and financial prowess will always go hand in hand. While this statement is true in many aspects of contemporary American society, the physical obtainment of money is not longer what people want to see. Society is beginning to judge those by not if they have money, but what they do with it. The truth is that people are seeing that bad people with a lot of money but no support are not going to get very far. Money is an arbitrary thing, and once the collective decides that a certain person’s wealth, no matter how much, is going worth respect, the finances lose all grounds.

In regards to both of the readings, nothing is as simple as society likes to believe. One can poses an exorbitant amount of money, but if they do not command the respect of their peers and society, they hold very little power. The classes that people are defined away into continually change but each new generation must come to their own understanding of that these classes actually mean and what their generational relationship with intrinsic value is going to be. Yes, both reading make excellent points, but society is a living organism that will always change and adapt to the surrounding influences.
chunks.label: Reflecting on readings about social class and power
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses readings by Mantsios and Domhoff regarding social class, money, and power, concluding that money alone does not command respect or inherent worth in society.

chunks.text:
Since the dawn of humanity and the civilizations that they built, there has been inequality between groups. These inequalities were split down many social lines like gender identity, sexuality, ethnicity, etc. but one of the most common and still existing inequalities that humanity faces today is the effects of income inequality. In western society, income is equal to power and social standing, therefore whoever has the most money has the most influence in society. But, the role of technology is the fate deciding factor in how social standing and inequality affect humanity in the future.

In conclusion, since the 1% of society are almost in control of western civilization through their financial gains, it would be easy for them to monopolize the rest of society by buying out the technology companies that they do not already own in order to control the personal data that everyone else willing submits to these companies. In the opinion of Harari, the only way to prevent this from happening is through the regulation of data ownership. The best way to move forward with that plan is to educate the populous and use the power posses by the majority to stop the 1% from completely controlling their lives.
chunks.label: Inequality, technology, and data regulation
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the history of inequality, noting how income grants power and how technology and data ownership by the 1% could lead to total control unless regulated and resisted through education.

n855e0a4f.title: Disconnect and Alienation in Social Media

chunks.text:
As humans we are naturally social being. Social interactions play a big part in how we identify and form our view of self. It is a fundamental need to feel like we belong and have intimate relationships with others. With the emergence of social media, you can be connected with thousands of others at a click of a button. This might sound like a useful tool, but it has its consequences.

You would think in a world with social media we would feel more connected, but this is not the case. It has actually done the opposite; people feel more alienated than ever. This is because hundreds of online friends cannot provide you with the same feeling of belonging as a small intimate offline group can. We are becoming more disconnected by using social media as the main way to communicate and interact with each other. In order for us to feel like we belong it has to stem from the offline world. The body and self, interact and affect each other. To take away physical sense and the body from social interaction plays part in why online relationships are not able to provide you with the same feelings.

Social media is a slippery slope. If we want to create meaningful relationships and feel like we belong we have to stray away from social media. People don’t realize the drastic affect social media can have our sense of self and should be educated on it.
chunks.label: The impact of social media on human connection
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on human social nature and argues that social media causes alienation and disconnect because online relationships lack physical presence and cannot fulfill the need for belonging.

nb602d967.title: Examining Power Elites and Racial Privilege

chunks.text:
The “power elite” makes up only a small percentage of the U.S. population. It is the rich socialites, Corporate executives, and prominent think tank members. These few people control a majority of all decisions made by political leaders. They use their money and influence to control the classes below them. Political leaders are not included in this “power elite,” as they are the main ones asking these elites for support for their campaigns. This makes them borderline puppets that the “power elite” use to push their agenda.

White privilege is a system developed in the United States as a means of justifying slavery and discrimination. It is extremely subtle in the ways it supports white people over other racial groups. Some examples of white privilege would be a white man being more likely to get a job over a minority or white people being put in “nicer” neighborhoods than other minorities. These practices further segregate races while giving white people an unfair advantage in life.

Some argue that it is on the part of white people themselves to tear down the workings of white privilege. Others contest that it is not their fault for being born white. Therefore, they have no obligation to fight that agenda. Looking to the power elite for an answer in this contest leads one to believe that they are the ones controlling it. A majority of the power elite consists of white men. The very people that white privilege serves are the ones with the most power to end it. The power elite controls all the policies that systematically promote white privilege.

Both these concepts share the promotion of people based mainly on birth right rather than by working for their spot. In the case of the “power elite” nepotism is a huge factor in who is in the “in” group and who is out. If someone is the child of a wealthy pharmaceutical CEO, odds are they will be invited to the same social events as his father when he hits the right age. This helps to condition their brain to promote the same culture for themself when they inevitably take control of their family's estate. It’s all about building up the foundation that protects themselves. When it comes to white privilege, it is a lot broader who is in the “in” group and who is out. Every white person in America is in the “in” group. Being born white is not nearly as exclusive as being born into money, but there are still a good amount of benefits that come with it. There is also the opportunity for motivation to keep the system in place. So, there is very clearly the process of elite white people to keep both systems in place to secure their high standings in the world. They do this by first protecting their position as elites, then using that power to keep white privilege as a system in place.

In comparison, white privilege is a much less direct process than holding power as the “power elite” is. Gaining and perpetuating white privilege is a very subconscious process. It can be summed up as being born white and reaping the benefits. The main workings of white privilege are just general prejudices deeply ingrained in the collective consciousness of the general population. Gaining and perpetuating the process as a “power elite” involves a lot of careful planning and luck. The lucky part is being born into the position and the careful planning is the lobbying you do to political leaders to keep yourself safe.

Real life examples of both these concepts can be found in high level office jobs across America. The diversity levels of high level jobs across America are so low that there are actual laws in place to try and even out the graph. This shows how white privilege perpetuates an advantageous life situation for white people. Some can argue that white people work for, and earn that spot. Even so, they have lives that are systematically designed for them to make it to the top. The “power elite” live for these high ranking office positions. These are not jobs like receptionists or printers. These are the board directors who sit for the boards of multiple different companies just to ensure the success of them all.

These two concepts are important to one another to stay afloat. White privilege gives the “power elite” a safety net to keep themselves in positions of power. While the “power elite” manage policies to maintain their own position and the systematic reproduction of white privilege. To tear down this horrible accumulation of power it takes white people to recognize their own privilege and for people to recognize where the power in our country is actually located. People need to bond together to tear down the “power elite” currently dictating our lives.
chunks.label: Analyzing the power elite and white privilege
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the concepts of the power elite and white privilege, comparing how they operate, how they perpetuate inequality, and how they reinforce each other.

n7e7dd2af.title: Struggling Against Restrictive Masculinity and Expectations

chunks.text: It is an essential part of everyone's life regarding gender. Many things in the world are assigned based on people's gender, which is called gender, in many ways in which they are given certain things based on their gender. The roles of certain people, when humans were hunters and gatherers, were determined by the gender they fit into. The men would be the ones that would provide for their families and tribes through a variety of activities, such as hunting and thereby achieving the necessity for them to survive. Women became more independent as time went by, and as such, they became more independent, pushing back against the traditional barriers imposed on women by men. Fighting for the right to vote, the right to work, and being respected and honored just like men, they wanted to be viewed and treated as equal. You can argue that women have always enjoyed this; as you see in historical texts, women have always wished to be regarded not just as objects but as people. Women have always wanted to be valued as people. We need to remember that the stories they would write imagine a world where the only strong women are that they would see as a utopia. Yet, in our world, where we are forcefully dodging gender norms, all of that is merely a distant dream as we can't break away from how we handle gender.
chunks.label: Gender roles in history and society
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the historical roles of men and women from hunter-gatherer times to the present and women's fight for equality.

chunks.text: Regarding gender, it means that a specific gender will act in a particular way based on what they can expect. There is no doubt in our minds that when it comes to our everyday lives, regardless of who we are and where we come from, we all judge people based on their appearance. Having done it myself, I can attest that it's something I do repeatedly. Whenever I pass a group of people holding skateboards, I think to myself, well, they must be skateboards, or it might be a guy with a tank top and massive arms; that is what I would assume myself, he is on steroids, and he must be a gym guy; those are the things I would consider myself. There is a sense in which that is almost how doing gender is; we may see a man with a woman and know the man as the more prominent and dominant figure in the relationship, which is almost the way it is. There are also many ways in which men can be viewed in a gender-biased light just as much as women are in many respects. An example of this would be the example I just gave, where the man was viewed as more dominant than the woman in the relationship. In the idea of gendering men, men are seen as people who are emotionless, strong, and masculine. Men in this generation feel that they can never express how they truly feel because people would push them aside for being girly or not genuinely being heard. After all, men are supposed to be strong.
chunks.label: Perceptions and expectations of masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how people judge others based on appearances and gender expectations, specifically focusing on how men are pressured to be masculine and emotionless.

chunks.text: In many ways, I have experienced gender firsthand. When I tried to open up to some of my friends, all they did was sit there and make fun of the things that had happened and acted like it wasn’t a big deal and that I was joking, but I wasn’t, and I realized that I could never truly open up to them.
chunks.label: Friends mocking opening up
chunks.what_happened: The student tried to open up to some friends, but the friends made fun of what happened and acted like it was a joke.

chunks.text: The same thing happened with my ex-girlfriend; when I tried to let down my walls and show her the real me, she started to drift apart from me, all she wanted was for me to be the stoic, cold man that would listen to her problems and protect her, and at the time I saw nothing wrong with that. Once she broke up with me, I was left with so many built-up emotions, and I had no idea what to do, so I just pushed them down with the rest because I had no idea what to do since I was supposed to be strong and emotionless.
chunks.label: Breakup with ex-girlfriend
chunks.what_happened: The student tried to show his real self to his ex-girlfriend, who drifted apart and broke up with him because she wanted a stoic partner, leaving him with repressed emotions.

chunks.text: Then one night, I was driving home from a volleyball tournament, and I was listening to a podcast, and for some reason, I started to feel; I had no idea what it was, but it was just so overwhelming, I eventually turned off the podcast and sat there for a couple of seconds in silence while that feeling was swallowing me I couldn’t understand. At that moment, I broke down in tears for the first time in my life. Things from my childhood were brought up, and I realized how sad I indeed was for almost all of my life, but I was told to forget about it and push them down, and from that moment on, I decided never to let myself get to that point ever again. Most men suffer from things like that for their whole lives just because they feel the need to fit the role of a man set by society.
chunks.label: Emotional breakdown while driving home
chunks.what_happened: While driving home from a volleyball tournament, the student became overwhelmed with emotion and broke down in tears for the first time in his life.

chunks.text: My cousin, a lesbian, does not fit the role set by society for women and has faced intense backlash from many people. She is very masculine; she has a substantial amount of muscle. She plays rugby for the Ohio State team and has this big mullet that, in my opinion, looks awesome, but to most people, they feel like she is weird because she does not fit the role and look of a woman. She doesn’t match what society calls the beauty myth. The beauty myth is society’s standers of beauty for women; an example of this is that women need to have the least amount of hair on their bodies as possible, which is why women will shave their legs, their armpits, any part of their bodies that grows hair they will try to either shave it wax it or use a product like Nair to remove it chemically.
chunks.label: Cousin facing backlash for masculine appearance
chunks.what_happened: The student's lesbian cousin plays rugby, has significant muscle and a mullet, and faces backlash from people because she does not fit society's beauty myth for women.

chunks.text: Everything in this world fits into what we call collective consciousness; doing gender is a big thing that feeds into this idea. Collective consciousness is what sociologists define as the shared beliefs between people which work as a force within society. In latent terms, it is the flow of community, the unwritten rule of what everyone believes is right and wrong. Doing gender stems from this idea that a woman should be caring and sweet and fit beauty standards, and men should be brutish and emotionless with the intent to provide. And if you were to go against these gender roles, you would go against the flow of the collective consciousness, which will, in turn, create you into a sort of outcast. There has been a big push in the last couple of years for men and women to leave these toxic roles in the past and treat everyone as equals, yet those who do still are viewed as outcasts for doing so.
chunks.label: Collective consciousness and gender roles
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the sociological concept of collective consciousness and how breaking gender roles turns people into outcasts.

chunks.text: There are times when I will paint my nails, and people will look at me with disdain for the simple fact that I am a man who likes the look of his nails when they are black.
chunks.label: Receiving disdain for painted nails
chunks.what_happened: People look at the student with disdain when he paints his nails black.

chunks.text: Just as my cousin is an outcast for being a woman with a mullet, this is a world that says it is open to everyone, yet they never said that it would accept everyone for who they indeed are.
chunks.label: Society's failure to accept individuality
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by reflecting on how society claims to be open but does not truly accept people who defy gender norms.

n86ed57b8.title: Rationalization and the Commodification of War

chunks.text:
When thinking of past worlds, you tend to greatly understand the reason behind them, why they were fought, what was gained. Modern wars? Not so much. If asked why the United States was involved in World War Two, the answer would be simple, to fight the Nazis; but if asked why the United States is fighting Iraq, most Americans would draw a blank. In chapter eleven of 21 Lessons For The 21st century, Harari depicts how much war and its reasons have changed over the years; much like the concept of rationalization which driven humans away from their roots.

According to Harari, wars used to make sense politically; the United States fought Mexico for land, Japan grew more powerful as it fought China and Russia, and Britain became the Earth’s top empire through tiny wars all across the planet. These wars were successful, they had purpose, the United States grew by over 2.3 million square kilometers. This has changed though, wars in the Middle East are not successful and there are no clear winners or a purpose. As society grew and we modernized what had meaning, we also modernized war. Much like mostly everything in society, war has become a commodity; it has lost its meaning and purpose and now serves capitalism. Back in the premodern age, the only money you made was through the land you captured, but now its through profits on guns, machinery, and instruments used to cause more war; no one wins this way, war just continues. Just as society has been modernized, war has also been rationalized.

Harari examines premodern wars to modern wars, proving to his readers how war has been modernized into a commodity to feed the growing economy and money hungry elites. War is no longer about gaining land and growing your empire but gaining money so war can continue with no clear winner or goal.
chunks.label: Modernization and commodification of war
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Harari's book, discussing how premodern wars had clear goals like territorial expansion while modern wars have been rationalized and turned into commodities to serve capitalism.

n89996997.title: Challenging Myths of the American Dream

chunks.text:
Mainstream media and politicians elude from the fact that we live in classes. As a nation we like to think we live in a classless society, and that class does not matter. This is far from the truth. Gregory Mantsios mentioned this among other “myths” about our society. He mentions four main ones. These “myths” are essentiality beliefs of our collective consciousness as a nation. The first belief I already expanded on which is that the U.S. is a fundamentally classless society. The second belief is that we are a middle-class nation. The third belief is we are all getting richer. The fourth belief is Everyone has an equal chance to succeed. Our class system contradicts every single one of these beliefs. As a nation there are huge differences in class, the gap between classes is great. Distribution of wealth is completely skewed, the middle class holds a small percent of the nation’s wealth, and that percent is falling. As a nation we are taught to believe we have an equal chance to succeed, but there is no doubt that class standing helps people succeed while it hinders others. We are also taught to believe that our government is democratic and fair. While this is mostly true, some people have more power than they should. This group is called the Power Elite. Domhoff talked of the Power elite and their influence on federal government.

As a nation it is a part of our culture and collective consciousness to believe in things such as the American dream, but it is just an illusion. Not everybody can achieve the American dream especially those living in poverty. Our class system contradicts many beliefs as An American.
chunks.label: Myths of a classless society and the American dream
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on societal myths about classlessness, wealth distribution, equal opportunity, the power elite, and the illusion of the American dream based on sociological concepts.

nc2284720.title: Analyzing Power Dynamics and Oppression Systems

chunks.text:
Throughout all of history there has been a struggle for power whether it be for an individual, group, or organization. This power does not come without pushing others down, and can be seen by examples of slavery, racism, or other types of prejudice. Groups such as African Americans, Asians, Native Americans, and women have had to push against being denied basic human rights in America along with being socially outcasted because of a feature they cannot control. Even in the modern day it is discussed about if there is true equal opportunity for everyone and whether certain groups are targeted for actions more than others in instances of applications, policing, and discrimination.

One group of people that continue fighting the systems set in place today are feminists. They have combated and resisted ideas pushed on them in the past such as the nuclear family, caretaking responsibilities, and the meaning of femininity. A representation of this is shown in The Yellow Wallpaper by Charlotte Gilman. The husband in the story, John uses his power as the head of the household to keep his wife in the house telling her she cannot read, write, or go outside because it will make her condition very bad. She is reluctant to argue about it with him and does as she as told, therefore conceding her basic wants to someone who is seen in society as higher than her. Any woman at the time would not dare disobey her husband and would continue to stay in the marriage even if it was abusive. A woman’s role during this period was to be submissive and listen to their husband because a man knows what’s best. This power dynamic is what allowed John and many men to remain in power while oppressing women by doing so.

This display and want for power are what the matrix of domination is about. The matrix describes that this oppression is done through institutions or communities and grants each person certain privileges and penalties. These are all dependent on your standing in society and how each individual respond to it when forced upon them. African American women for example have not only been more subject to racism, but sexism as well. Just as in The Yellow Wallpaper, they have been told that they cannot do things because of either their race or gender because it is the opposite of who has been in power most history. One thing the matrix also analyzes is the difference in consequences because of those factors. A white feminist in the 1800’s would not have been punished as hard as a black feminist would have been because of this race disparity.

Every person is subject to some kind of prejudice because of how society or an individual views them. It is the response of the individual that matters by not conforming how the dominator wishes them to act. The feeling of superiority is what keeps discrimination and matrix of domination in place, meaning that there is no true equality until it is dismantled. This process is not something that can change fast because it is a result of the collective conscious of a society and similar mindsets are passed on for generations.
chunks.label: Reflecting on power struggles, feminism, and matrix of domination
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the historical struggle for power, feminist resistance, Charlotte Gilman's The Yellow Wallpaper, the matrix of domination, and how societal discrimination persists.

chunks.text:
Race has no basis in genetics whatsoever; it is entirely socially constructed. Just because race is not in our DNA does not mean the effects of it are not real. The meaning of slavery has changed over time; slavery used to be a period of bondage that an ancient person might pass through; today, when we think of slavery, we picture the enslavement of Africans in the United States. Slavery has been transformed into a racial issue over time and has triggered widespread racism all across the globe. Europeans created the idea of race to differentiate between those who did and did not look like them. This idea of different races separated and belittled certain groups of humanity, making them appear not even human anymore. Categories such as ‘savage’ for Native Americans, ‘subhuman’ for Africans, and ‘white’ were created, instilling the idea of race. These categories separated groups of humans by skin color and dehumanized those of darker skin. By claiming Africans as ‘subhuman,’ whites were able to strip them of their humanity and treat them as animals because that was how they were seen: like animals. As Europeans immigrated over to America, they took their ideas of race with them, developing an entirely new culture created by racism. As industrialism grew in America, so did the need for inexpensive labor; the Americans turned to the ‘subhumans’ in Africa. Whites kidnapped and sold Africans like animals, forcing them into slavery. Dark skin became an easy identifier for whether someone was a slave or not. The whites justified their enslavement of Africans with religion, economics, and science. They claimed that this race of subhumans could only be led from sin by a white master and that science proved that people of darker skin were not humans. These erroneous fundamentals helped shape and build American culture and society; the United States of America is founded on racism.

Although Americans have come an incredibly long way from slavery, racism is still very much so prevalent in our society. American racism is no longer involves slavery or blunt dehumanization, but unjust inequalities not noticed by most. Things such as jobs, education, and luxury are catered more towards white Americans, leaving African Americans struggling. Yes, white Americans do have to deal with struggle and loss, but that pain will never be a result due to the color of their skin. As harsh racism of the past has begun to fade away, a new form of racism is taking its place: white privilege. White privilege is the advantages given to a white person due to their society or culture being founded or controlled by race. For many white people, the advantage they have due to their skin color is hard for them to comprehend and see. Often, white people are dismissive of the idea of white privilege and like to pretend it does not exist. The dismissal of white privilege makes it stronger and harder to fight. The more people who can recognize and understand their privilege, the more likely it is that this form of racism can be eliminated. Making racism illegal will not stop it; the best way to prevent racism is to exploit the racists that what they are doing is wrong and how it is wrong. Only by recognizing that the United States was built off racism and that white privilege thrives in society today; we will be able to take more steps of getting rid of racism completely. White privilege is a modern-day form of socially constructed racism to provide unfair advantages to those with white skin.

In class, we studied how racism and slavery began and evolved over time; with no roots in genetics, racism was completely socially constructed. Humans created race to dehumanize other humans with different skin colors. This allowed for the white race to gain power over other races and exploit them for labor. White people labeled those with darker skin complexions as animals and inhuman to justify their horrible mistreatment and racism. Slavery and other extreme forms of racism may no longer be present in the United States, but racism still exists in America. The United States of America’s society and culture was founded on racism and that the white race is superior. These ideas are still structuring American society today, even with the advances taken to eradicate racism and establish equality for all. White people are still given unfair advantages in American society due to their skin color. Things such as work, power, and education are unfairly leaned in favor of white people, making it extremely hard for people of color to access these things. White privilege is an existing system within American society the promotes and upholds racism. It encases the idea that white people will never have to deal with struggles or tragedies due to the color of their skin. Society created white privilege to keep its old racist structure in tack while the idea of equality for all became more widespread.

The concept of white privilege is often denied or misunderstood by white people. They can see that people of color are struggling but they look at themselves to see that they are also struggling. Due to their own struggle, white people tend to think that they cannot possibly have an advantage over anyone because they are struggling too. These people fail to comprehend that they are not struggling due to the color of their skin. White privilege is not saying that white people have never had to deal with struggle; it is saying that white people have never dealt with struggle due to the color of their skin. Whites often feel that white poverty is neglected “in order to portray poverty as a problem of black and brown” people (Blacksher). It is beliefs like that which drive white people from accepting that white privilege exists. The “deflection, discomfort, and denial of such advantages have been called white fragility,” which is when white people are unable or unwilling to recognize or accept that they have an advantage due to the color of their skin (Blacksher). White fragility dates back to when white people used science, religion, and economics to justify their poor treatment of people of color. Saying something along the lines of ‘white privilege does not exist, I am just as poor as he is’ is just as much as a dismissal of racism as ‘it does not matter, those are animals, not people’ is. By refusing to accept the existence of white privilege and American roots in racism, white people prevent the uprooting and eradication of racism.

Although not all white people have open arms to accepting the concept of white privilege and its existence, some white people have. Studies have found as white people have been more exposed to the advantages provided to them due to race, feelings of “guilt and shame are common reactions,” (Pinterits). Many white people have been able to come to terms with their own privilege and accept that they are advantaged because of their skin color. Instead of white fragility, they associate with white guilt. Although white people alive today are not responsible for creating racism and American society, with failure to recognize their privilege, they must maintain it. A common response to white privilege may be “apathy, or avoidance,” (Pinterits). Avoiding the subject ultimately could be due to feelings of discomfort or that they feel threatened by the discussion. Often when white privilege is pointed out, some white people feel like they are being attacked or called racist, but it’s the refusal to have the conversation about white privilege which makes someone more racist. People who are more willing to talk about the privilege they hold because of their skin color are more inclined to make an effort or change to get rid of their privilege and strive for equality. Feelings of white guilt are entirely normal when talking about white privilege; what really matters whether someone is just going to continue to feel guilty or if they are going to make a real effort to combat white privilege. After conducting her study, Pinterits was able to determine that different white people had “various behaviors to address white privilege and engage in anti-racism and social justice work.” This shows that not all white people are unable to come to terms with their own white privilege and that some are willing to make a change. Yes, many white people are unwilling to talk about or recognize their own privilege. Still, on the flip side, some white people are ready and able to have a conversation about white privilege and what they can do to make a difference.

Recognizing white privilege is one of the first steps towards gaining total equality. Some are able to comprehend they have an advantage due to the skin color but end up stuck, not knowing what to do next. Knowing how to see privilege is a powerful thing. By knowing what white privilege looks like, people are more likely able to recognize the personal privilege they hold and the institutions and rules that support that privilege. Being able to recognize white privilege is “useful for helping identify internalized, often invisible, forms of racism. It could also provide tools for unmasking a structural exclusion that ensures that people of color get the short stick every time,” (Aouragh). As a white person being able to not only see your own privilege but the privilege of others and the systems that maintain that privilege is fundamental. With that, you can use your privilege to call out unjust systems and behaviors in order to help people of color reach equality. Things such as white fragility and silence stunt the growth of anti-racism and prevent other white people from speaking out. By recognizing and speaking out about their white privilege, white people are able to help promote ideals of equality and fight the racist American society and culture put into place hundreds of years ago.

Eradicating white privilege in America is one of the first steps of ridding the United States of racism. As a country that was built and founded on racist beliefs and ideologies, it will take time to unravel all the hate and prejudice that has been intertwined into American culture. In class, we went over how the United States of America was structured after racism and fitted white people as the power elite. Race was created so whites could dehumanize and exploit people of color. Whites justified their actions by claiming that people of color were not human or that only a white master could lead people of color from sin. Although these ideals have been thrown out in the United States today, racism and the system that maintains it is still in place. White privilege provides unfair advantages to white people due to the color of their skin. Still, if we contain to fight for equality for people of color and recognize our own privilege, we can end racism and build a better and more accepting society and culture for all humans to live.

Works Cited

Aouragh, Miriyam. “‘White Privilege’ and Shortcuts to Anti-Racism.” SAGE Journals, SAGE Journals, 26 Sept. 2019, doi-org.liblink.uncw.edu/10.1177%2F0306396819874629.

Blacksher , Erika, and Sean A Valles. “White Privilege, White Poverty: Reckoning with Class and Race in America.” The Hasting Center, The Hastings Center, 25 Feb. 2021, doi-org.liblink.uncw.edu/10.1002/hast.1230.

Pinterits, Janie E. “The White Privilege Attitudes Scale: Development and Initial Validation.” EBSCOhost, American Psychological Association, July 2009, web.b.ebscohost.com.liblink.uncw.edu/ehost/detail/detail?vid=0&sid=56157bfc-d108-4351-b112-2e775f38780e%40sessionmgr103&bdata=JnNpdGU9ZWhvc3QtbGl2ZQ %3d%3d#AN=2009-10122-007&db=pdh.
chunks.label: Racism, white privilege, and historical roots
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the social construction of race, the history of slavery in America, and how modern concepts like white privilege, white fragility, and white guilt function today, concluding with an academic bibliography.

chunks.text:
Many people face a societal pressure to fit in and be the “norm” while still being unique in their own way. They wish to be themselves and make choices around their morals, while still looking to fit in a group and some level of social approval. This is because there is a “self” in each person, which is who you are and what you believe. There are different interpretations of how that self in each of us works and the impact society has on someone when they develop with different factors all around them.

George Mead was a philosopher who believed that because of communication, it allowed the self in everyone to have confliction for further development in every interaction. These experiences can then cause for a change in self, depending on the kind of previous experience along with how others are representing themselves in the current moment. That is this “I” in us which is formed from a reaction while the “Me” is then what is decided because of it. Erving Goffman was a social psychologist who also believed that society had an important role for how someone develops. He claims that when we are alone, that is when we really respond and prepare for the next social encounter, so it does not go poorly and allow for continuous acceptance in that group. Goffman compares us to performers that only wish for the show that is interaction to go well because of this, which also requires time to process how it went and then make for further changes. This ties into what Mead explains between the “I” and “Me”, where there is always feedback being given to one another for thought and analysis of what to keep and what to change for similar situations.

With those still wanting to fit in, the individual will want to show off or highlight their own special behavior because it is our natural calling. Every person’s thoughts are different in some way because of who we are as people and what we do, and as time goes on this gap widens because of our experiences. Erving Goffman and George Mead both offer reasonable claims for how this process works, and ultimately agree on one core concept; Self reflection is the cause of change.
chunks.label: Theories of the self and social interaction
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the tension between individuality and societal pressure to fit in, comparing George Mead's concepts of the 'I' and 'Me' with Erving Goffman's theatrical model of social interaction.

n58602927.title: Navigating Height and Traditional Femininity Standards

chunks.text: Do you let other people’s opinions affect you? Most people would answer this question by saying “No, I don’t let other people’s opinions control me”, and most of the time that would be a lie. Growing up you hear multiple people’s opinions from your own families to strangers, but now in the 21st-century social media, brings on even higher expectations from a larger amount of people. With society's expectations women need to be pretty, petite and always need to look presentable. A lot of people would think in current times everyone would be more accepting of diversity, but that is not always the case. Women are still expected to be well dressed and fall into certain standards that males will like. People tend to be judgmental and a lot of the time it will get into your head. This can lead to a lot of overthinking or anxiety in women.
chunks.label: Societal expectations and opinions about women
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how societal expectations and others' opinions regarding beauty and behavior cause anxiety and overthinking in women.

chunks.text:
For as long as I can remember, I was always the tallest girl among my peers. In every elementary school class picture, I was in the middle of the back row because that is where the tallest person goes. Consistently I would hear the same statements over and over again. Oh, what I would do to be your height! You should embrace your height, it is so beautiful! The reaction from other adults is not the same as what I received from people my age. I would consistently hear negative comments from both boys and girls around my age. When coming from a taller family, you grow fast and always have to get new clothes, so I grew up wearing a lot of oversized clothes and was never a “girly-girl.” I consistently wore tee shirts and athletic shorts. If I ever wore a dress and had my hair done it was because I was told to by my parents. Girls would

speak down on me because I was intimidating and different than them. Boys would do the same because they were insecure. How could a girl be taller than them, right? Society has instilled this expectation that males should be tall and powerful, but if a woman is of the same stature, she’s intimidating and “too masculine”.
chunks.label: Growing up tall among peers
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up as the tallest girl among her peers, wore oversized athletic clothes, and received contrasting reactions from adults and peers, with peers speaking down to her.

chunks.text: From a young age, a lot of girls are told to be “ladylike” and that they should dress to impress. I grew up with a large group of boys my age and we would all physically fight and play sports together. I started playing basketball competitively at a young age. Eventually, I got tired of hearing I was good at the sport, “for a girl.” Boys my age would tell me that girls should not play basketball, so I started playing volleyball, which is traditionally a girl sport. I let society's standards of females control me and my decisions.
chunks.label: Switching sports due to peer comments
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up playing sports with boys and played competitive basketball, but switched to volleyball after boys told her girls should not play basketball.

chunks.text: Specifically, in middle school is when I started realizing people talking about me and eventually started receiving comments to my face. I would receive rude comments about my height and how that made me ugly or less feminine. At this time in school, a new boy moved into my neighborhood and started riding our bus to school. Immediately he was the person all the guys were new friends with. The new boy started a new nickname for me, Sasquatch. He and the other boys then proceeded to laugh and poke fun at me. Many of the people in his friend group started calling me that on top of making jokes about me being a giant. I was young so I would just laugh it off with them but realized later how much it affected my mental health. This led to all the little comments swarming around in my head constantly. I started feeling insecure in my body and did not put myself out there as much. I started slouching over a lot to make myself feel shorter because I was not comfortable in my own height. The feeling of this teasing-induced anxiety was always in my body and on my mind. I started to believe that I was not enough because of a few characteristics that were not feminine enough for others in society, one of those being genetically tall. I started seeing myself how others did and slowly started to change myself to society's standards of women.
chunks.label: Middle school bullying over height
chunks.what_happened: In middle school, a new neighborhood boy and his friends teased the student on the bus by calling her Sasquatch and a giant, which led the student to slouch and try to change herself.

chunks.text: Candace West and Don H. Zimmerman wrote a paper on “Doing Gender”. They explained how certain characteristics and activities tend to identify with a certain gender. For example, being tall, powerful, participating in sports, and having short hair is more masculine. On the other side being beautiful, petite, dressing up, and having long hair is more feminine. When one is doing gender, they are behaving the way society expects them to, like others with the same external features and gender. When one has female features, they try to act like their mom, sister or the person raising them of the same sex. They start wanting to wear the same makeup and clothing as their adult counterpart does.
chunks.label: Concept of Doing Gender
chunks.what_happened: The student explains West and Zimmerman's sociological concept of 'Doing Gender' and how society prescribes masculine and feminine characteristics.

chunks.text: Naomi Wolf talks about the “beauty myth” and how women are controlled. Men control the beauty myth, by using a standard of beauty to stop women from advancing in careers and other parts of life. If a woman fits a specific set of beauty standards, she is called dumb because one cannot be pretty and smart. A women’s job in society's rules is to marry a man and take care of their kids while the man works for money. Wolf talks about how women fear each other because of their different qualities, this makes them self-conscious. They eventually get stuck in a cycle of trying to be what a man wants.
chunks.label: Naomi Wolf and the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Naomi Wolf's concept of the 'beauty myth' and how societal standards are used to control and divide women.

chunks.text: The concept of “The Looking-Glass Self” was explained by Charles Cooley. He explains that it is how one sees themselves when looking in a so-called mirror. When looking at oneself they do not just see themselves based on their own opinion. The looking-glass self is how you see yourself with all the outside opinions about you. Outsiders’ opinions affect how they see themselves and eventually will affect how they act and stuff they do.
chunks.label: Charles Cooley and the Looking-Glass Self
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes Charles Cooley's sociological concept of the looking-glass self, explaining how outside opinions shape self-perception.

chunks.text: When I was younger, I did not follow the female standards of “doing gender.” I would keep my hair short, play competitive sports, and would wear colors and shirts that were sold for males. I did not feed into the expectations that women were held to. Women are supposed to be emotional and depend on men. While men are strong, emotionless, and a protector of others. As a kid, I did not want boys in my class to help me with things because I could do it myself. When I would wear clothes meant for boys and keep my hair short, it did not make me any less feminine. In school, teachers would ask frequently “Do we have any big strong boys that want to help move stuff?”. This was inadvertently teaching young girls that they couldn’t be strong enough to help move a desk, or whatever it may be. I was always the biggest in my class, so this question made me think because of my gender I could not complete a simple task. I was still a girl and little characteristics should not have affected how I was treated.
chunks.label: Defying gender expectations in school
chunks.what_happened: As a child, the student wore boy-marketed clothes and kept short hair, refusing help from boys, and experienced teachers asking only 'big strong boys' to help move furniture in class.

chunks.text: When Wolf wrote about the beauty myth, she said that the men controlled its expectations of it. This causes women to compete in trying to earn acceptance. This results in women talking down to one another, trying to be prettier than each other. That should not be the case, however, women should be building each other up. In personal experience, other girls would try to pick on little things about me so they would get more attention than me from a boy. They did not like how I was close with the boys I grew up with, a lot of them would talk poorly of me.
chunks.label: Competition and criticism from other girls
chunks.what_happened: Other girls talked poorly of the student and picked on her to compete for boys' attention because the student was close with the boys she grew up with.

chunks.text: The looking-glass self that Cooley talks about is a big thing in our world today. When people bully someone or talk bad about them it gets in that person's head. Eventually, it leads to that person seeing themselves how those other people see them. Personally, people talking about how I was too tall and did not wear cute clothes got to me. I started seeing myself as an outcast and did not believe that any of my friends liked me. I felt unlovable with all the comments made about me. Consistently I talked down to myself, I started to slouch to be shorter, which then turned into me doing heavy makeup, then finally changing my personality and style. People’s opinions clouded my mind and I started to believe they were right about me. My personal looking glass self was textbook defined, I did let outsiders define how I saw myself.
chunks.label: Internalizing negative comments through the looking glass
chunks.what_happened: After being criticized for her height and style, the student internalized the negative comments, slouched, began wearing heavy makeup, and altered her personality and appearance.

chunks.text: Women are disproportionately affected by “doing gender” and the “beauty myth” which eventually turns into their looking glass self. Society’s standards for women get into their heads, making them change for the outside perspectives. As I grew up the standards started affecting me more and no one should feel like they need to change who they are because of other people’s opinions. Women should start building each other up instead of tearing each other down. In today’s day and age, everyone should be able to do what they want without standards for a certain gender affecting their actions. When a girl is tall, competitive, and likes playing sports it does not make them any less of a female. The multiple times I was told being tall made me less pretty should not happen. Everyone is biologically different, and no beauty myth should affect how one feels about themselves.
chunks.label: Concluding thoughts on gender and beauty standards
chunks.what_happened: The student synthesizes the sociological theories with her conclusion that women should support one another rather than letting societal beauty standards and gender expectations dictate their self-worth.

chunks.text: Picture that from the time you are born, your worth in society is already determined. Throughout elementary and middle school, you are catcalled on the street by men who are ten times your age. Your mom tells you that boys push you and tease you because they like you. When you enter high school, you are pulled out of the classroom because your shirt exposed your shoulders and that would distract the male students. Your male teacher has wandering eyes because he is trying to “protect” you. When you enter college, you have a 1 in 6 chance of being sexually assaulted. Once you graduate from your university, you finally have your first real job in the big world. You find out that your male coworker is making three times what you are, and he doesn’t even have a college degree. You find the man of your dreams, and everything is going well. You get married and have your first child, and it is a dream until everyone tells you that you should quit your job that you have worked so hard for to become a full-time stay at home parent, while your husband supports the family. After you have your second child, your mother-in-law tells you that you should probably start working out to get rid of that “baby weight”. Every night, you are critiqued by your husband when he gets home from work because there are dishes in the sink and dinner is not ready. When you are sixty years old, you find out your husband, who you have sacrificed so much for, is having an affair because you are no longer “attractive” in his eyes. You want to make it work but he runs off with a woman twenty years your junior. Your children are grown and now families. You see your child going through a similar cycle that you once fought to break. For many women, this is a reality. Sociology provides multiple theories that help explain and narrate why women experience one or multiple of these scenarios throughout their lifetimes, and why women have always been perceived as “other”.
chunks.label: Hypothetical lifetime scenarios of female inequality
chunks.what_happened: The student presents a hypothetical timeline of a woman facing objectification, inequality, and unfair expectations throughout life, explaining that sociology can help theorize why women are perceived as 'other'.

chunks.text: Growing up, I considered myself to be a “tomboy”. I wore my brothers’ clothing, never put time into doing my hair, opted out of painting my nails, and did not pick up mascara until I was sixteen. I never understood why my grandmother would badger me about my appearance and ask me if I had done my hair that morning. By the time I was a sophomore in high school, I had switched out leggings for jeans, bought shirts that were tighter, and straightened my hair every morning. While I was unaware at the time, I was falling into specified gender roles. After my braces came off and I lost a few pounds, boys started to notice and give me attention. I was never used to that, and I became comforted with the gratification from them. I thought that as long as men found me attractive, I would be successful. As I was beginning to think I was comfortable with my appearance, my body dysmorphia skyrocketed as a result of the constant feeling I had to be at a certain weight, with a certain face-shape and body that boys wanted. I was no longer putting effort into my appearance for myself, but to seem attractive to males. While I still find myself doing some of those same things, I am more aware of the fact that I am choosing to be comfortable rather than trying to seem appealing to men.
chunks.label: Shift from tomboy to gendered expectations
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up as a tomboy but altered her appearance in high school to gain attention from boys, which led to body dysmorphia and a focus on appealing to men until becoming more self-aware later on.

chunks.text: American culture has monetized on attractive women, using them in advertisements to sell alcoholic beverages and fast-food specials. Music videos almost always display what society has deemed as an “attractive woman,” with minimal clothing, an attractive hairstyle, and makeup done to draw in attention to the song, which in turn leads to more people viewing the video. Video games almost always portray female characters as having small waists, a large bust, and big, puppy dog eyes. It is quite unlikely to find an American film, video game, or music video that does not include a woman who is half-clothed with attractive features.
chunks.label: Media monetization of attractive women
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how American culture and media monetize attractive women in advertisements, music videos, and video games.

chunks.text: It is important to know the difference between sex and gender. Sex is assigned at birth, as male or female, by the genitalia of the baby. Gender is a set of behaviors that is learned socially and associated with the assignment of sex. For example, women tend to have longer hair, while men have shorter hair. Women wear skirts or dresses, while men typically wear pants.
chunks.label: Distinction between sex and gender
chunks.what_happened: The student defines sex as assigned biological genitalia at birth and gender as learned social behaviors and expectations.

chunks.text: Simone de Beauvoir explains women as other. She says that the category of other is as original as consciousness itself. No group has ever defined itself as the One without setting an opposite group as the Other. Man thinks of himself without woman, but woman does not think about herself without man. Women are nothing other than what men decide; thus, giving women the label “the sex” which ultimately means that men see women as a sexed being. Man is the subject and the absolute, and woman is the Other. De Beauvoir explains that there have always been women, as far back as history can trace, and women have always been subordinate to men. Women’s dependence has never been a consequence of an event, it just was.
chunks.label: Simone de Beauvoir on woman as Other
chunks.what_happened: The student outlines Simone de Beauvoir's theory of women being defined as the subordinate 'Other' relative to men.

chunks.text: Goffman provided a definition for the action of doing gender between girls, boy, women, and men. It is creating differences between those four categories, which are not natural, biological, or essential. Goffman also elaborates on “role conflict”, which occurs when a person of a particular sex can see clearly that they are out of place, and if they were not there, the current troubles they are facing would not exist. The example provided is a female physician, who is respected for her skill and addressed with the appropriate title of her qualification, but is still subjected to evaluation based on normative conceptions of appropriate attitudes and activities based on her sex category. The female physician’s sex category is used to discredit her participation in vital activities and her involvement in medicine is used to dishonor her commitments as a wife and mother.
chunks.label: Goffman's doing gender and role conflict
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes Goffman's concept of doing gender and role conflict, using the example of a female physician being scrutinized based on sex roles.

chunks.text: Cahill looks at the experiences of preschool children that were recruited into normally gendered identities. He argues that children are primarily concerned with being known as socially competent, which in turn leads them to claims of gender identities. Eventually, little boys appropriate the gender ideals of physical strength, while little girls begin to value appearance by managing themselves as ornamental objects. Through this, these children learn that the use of sex categorization is mandatory rather than optional. The act of “doing gender” is unavoidable because of the social consequences. If doing gender is done properly, we sustain, reproduce, and render the institutional arrangements that are based on sex category.
chunks.label: Cahill on gender socialization in children
chunks.what_happened: The student reviews Cahill's study of preschool children learning gender identities to appear socially competent and reinforcing sex categories.

chunks.text: Perhaps, if we were aware at a younger age that our gender would set us on a certain path in life, whether that means we become successful or our abilities are undermined, it could change the course for how a little girl views herself and grows into a woman. Had I been aware that I was not “different”, but rather fitting into the societal standards of a woman, I may have accepted my preferences and not changed myself for the appeal of others. De Beauvoir explains how women became inferior to men. Goffman and Cahill are only few of many sociologists that have studied why genders perform certain actions in order to establish themselves. But now, some men now wear skirts and high heels, with elaborate make-up and hair. Women no longer feel the pressure to have long hair or dress in skirts. Sociologists have provided various theories and explanations as to why each gender falls into their own stereotypes, but as time goes on, and society moves forward, each group pushes these boundaries and gives sociologists new perspectives to understand and explain.
chunks.label: Reflections on gender standards and societal change
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how earlier gender awareness might have changed their own self-acceptance, recaps the sociological theories, and notes evolving gender boundaries in modern society.
chunks.people: Simone de Beauvoir, Erving Goffman, Spencer Cahill

n6f7844f8.title: Reflecting on Religion and Collective Consciousness

chunks.text:
Religion is a common part of our society’s collective consciousness. Like many, I believe in my religious faith and I feel that my belief is genuine. I thought I chose to be religious on my own but apparently, that’s not completely true. As humans we are predisposed to be religious as a reaction to existential fears. Whether we think we are acting on our own or not, our behaviors are affected by cognitive conditions that have developed over millions of years.

The first evidence of religion was dated to around the same time we gained the capacity for abstract thought. The reason for this is because we gained the awareness to be able to ask the scary big questions, like “what happens after you die?” Because of the complete uncertainty to questions like this, they are the basis of existential fears. Religion provides us with comfort and answers to exertional fears. This prevents us from living in fear and uncertainty. Without the development of complex emotions, abstract thought could not exist. The capacity for emotion and the intelligence of a species are directly correlated. Modern humans have a wider range and capacity for emotion compared to our ancestorial species of the great ape. For instance, our amygdala is twice in size compared to that of the great ape.
