The growth of our ability to feel a wide array of emotions along with the connection of neural networks over time helped us gain our capacity for language and abstract thought.

Despite how special religion can make you feel, it is a normal behavior that has been around as long as we have been able to speak. Religion is not solely a decision you make as an individual, but a behavior in reaction to our natural fears of existence.
chunks.label: The evolutionary and cognitive basis of religion
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on religion as part of human collective consciousness and explains how it evolved to comfort existential fears alongside abstract thought and complex emotions.

chunks.text:
The phrase “money can’t buy happiness” has been around for generations and is even disagreed on by many. While it is dependent on the person, the message is that all the materialistic things in the world cannot give satisfaction. Currency is the universal way to determine worth in a society, and it is adjusted based on the time, abundance, and skillset needed to produce something. A person’s livelihood is dependent on what they can produce for the society and that society determines its value.

A dependency on how a product is sought after is what allows another person to eat, sleep, and live comfortably. This is what Marx says is the only reason for people working and what Weber claims to keep people trapped inside of the system. Workers are driven for the sole purpose of getting money and contributing more to capitalism rather than what may actually be beneficial. Capitalism takes control over the lives of the people and the incentives are not healthy as products are made just for money instead of connecting the society together. Some workers do become connected with their work and see their product as more than an object, and something that the consumer will become attached to for years. This can be seen across the world in examples such as fashion, children’s toys, and cars.
chunks.label: Capitalism, money, and worker motivation
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the phrase 'money can't buy happiness' and discusses sociological perspectives from Marx and Weber regarding capitalism, wages, and worker attachment to products.

chunks.text: I spent over a decade of my life at a summer camp that I wanted to and became a counselor there. I had personally become attached to the business and was willing to work there for any wage they would pay me, even if another job would offer more.
chunks.label: Working as a summer camp counselor
chunks.what_happened: The student spent over a decade at a summer camp, became a counselor there, and grew attached enough to work for any wage.

chunks.text: These occupations that work with people rather than products draw attachment from workers and will still attract them, even if the pay is low. Teachers in America including my aunts have protested for higher pay since they are shaping the future of the country, and feel they are not represented based off their worth. It’s for certain that less impactful jobs that benefit society get paid more than teachers, who are more of use, but that is capitalistic values.
chunks.label: Value and pay of people-oriented jobs
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how occupations that work with people draw attachment despite low pay, mentioning aunts protesting for higher teacher pay under capitalistic values.

chunks.text: Everyone has unique skillsets and minds and it is applying that best to what they want to do. Whether we like it or not, we have values on what we can do and create. It is up to the individual to use and market those skills best while in a capitalistic system, all so they can live. The labor people do for the majority of their lives is not set in stone and the value of it will change throughout time, but it is done more so the purpose of living rather than beneficial.
chunks.label: Marketing individual skills in a capitalist system
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how individuals must market their unique skillsets in a capitalist system to survive, concluding that labor is driven by the purpose of living rather than benefit.

chunks.text:
The discussion of gender, the influences, the struggles, and the importance of has been a focal point of philosophers and sociologists throughout history. There have been distinct differences in how gender is viewed in many societies, ranging from the Native Americans to the Japanese and to the Egyptians. One of the largest issues that have surrounded this topic is between the difference of gender, therefore gender expression, and biological sex which has led to even more oppression of women and minorities.

Simone De Beauvoir’s work titled Woman as Other describes how, for as long as documented history can tell, the idea of a woman has always been tied to the idea of men. In the discussion of this duality, it puts the idea of a woman as being solely linked to their biological sex and therefor their genitals. The Beauty Myth that Naomi Wolf writes about discusses how femininity and beauty are the two qualifiers for womanhood, how, by the decree of society, the only way that a woman can possibly hold value is by being deemed beautiful and feminine. Both of these assumptions about what is means to be a woman not only place unforgiving qualifier on what it means to be a woman, it destroys what people over centuries have been trying to accomplish: defining womanhood by the ideas of women. The only people who should be defining what a woman is, is a woman, regardless of what their birth assigned sex is, or her portrayal of femininity, or her ideal beauty goals. Yet, people who do not and are unwilling to understand this concept still oppress women and minorities, including Transgender people.
chunks.label: Sociological perspectives on gender and womanhood
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses historical and philosophical views on gender, citing works by Simone de Beauvoir and Naomi Wolf to argue that womanhood should be self-defined rather than dictated by biological sex or societal beauty standards.

n1ffb8c0a.title: Navigating Eurocentric Ideals and Beauty Standards

chunks.text:
The Western Ideal of Beauty and Its Impact on Black and Asian Women

Beauty standards are challenging enough to meet, and can lead to negative self-esteem in all women. But declines in mental health, self-esteem, and self-worth have a more serious impact on Black and Asian communities due to the added internalization of racism. Omi and Winant explain in Racial Formations about the beginnings of racism as an institution in society meant to establish a dominant race - White Europeans. The process of racialization resulted in a racial hierarchy in society, where white people were superior over other groups of color through socially-constructed meanings added to race. This “superiority” of the white race has translated over into beauty standards, as physical features associated with the ideal are Eurocentric. This leads to more problematic consequences for Black and Asian women, as they internalize these beauty standards and learn to dislike physical features associated with their race that they not only see in themselves, but also in other members of their racial group.
chunks.label: Eurocentric beauty standards and internalized racism
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the concept of Eurocentric beauty standards and explains how historical racialization leads to internalized racism and lower self-esteem among Black and Asian women.

chunks.text: This internalization of racism and beauty standards translates directly into how Black and Asian women approach and experience potential romantic relationships with members of different racial groups. This was investigated by a group of social scientists at the University of California, that interviewed a group of eighteen university students. A goal of the study was to gauge the impact of Western beauty standards and racism in media on interracial attraction. Scientists saw a common theme held by the majority of the sample, that supported that beauty standards portrayed through media heavily impact what racial groups are believed to be most attractive. The sample also concluded that through media perpetuation of Western beauty standards, white people are portrayed as more attractive and successful compared to minorities, who are usually portrayed in congruence with offensive racial stereotypes. Media also tends to portray white people more frequently than minorities, which also has an impact on how familiar people are with other racial groups (Silvestrini, 2019). These stereotypical and sparse portrayals of minorities in popular culture and media impact the public’s judgements and familiarity with different racial groups. This leads to internalized racism as people choose to not pursue relationships with other specific racial groups because of negative, preconceived personality traits associated with certain physical features. This internalized racism is even present among minority groups, especially in Black and Asian populations as their traits deviate more from the Eurocentric standard. These variations are common among the features of people who identify within populations due to interracial attraction. Those who come from mixed-race backgrounds are found to be more highly valued as potential partners in Black and Asian populations, because they are closer in resemblance to the Western model. Due to the role of beauty standards and internalized racism in interracial attraction, Black and Asian women may start to see themselves as undesirable romantically, which can further translate into feeling completely undesirable.
chunks.label: Impact of beauty standards on romantic attraction
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological research regarding how media representations and Western beauty standards influence interracial attraction and romantic desirability for women of color.

chunks.text: Besides the usage of cosmetics and forms of dieting, another way that women can change their appearance to conform is through cosmetic surgery. This is the most expensive form of physical alterations, but it has become more common, with the United States, South Korea, and Brazil being the leading nations in this industry. In a study performed by Dr. Alexander Edmonds from Britain and Dr. So Yeon Leem from South Korea, the relationship between plastic surgery and racial phenotypes were analyzed to explore popular procedures in different countries, and show that race can be measured. This research was conducted through interviewing surgeons in all three countries, and analyzing medical and historical literature about the initial purposes of cosmetic surgery. In their study, they highlighted different surgical procedures that were especially popular in all three nations. In the US, they found that rhinoplasties were very common among patients that wanted to elongate and thin their noses. Rhinoplasties are also very common in South Korea and Brazil, as well as higher rates of skin-lightening procedures (glutathione injections). Another popular procedure more specific to South Korea is the double-eyelid procedure, which is a surgery that adds a crease to the upper lid of the eye that changes the appearance of the Asian monolid. These cosmetic procedures all result in patients appearing more Western, as common features of the Eurocentric beauty model are a whiter skin-tone, a smaller and thinner nose, and double-eyelids. The researchers discovered, however, that on the surface, the marketing and methods used in plastic surgery do not advertise Westernization of features directly. While plastic surgery is initially meant to help individuals look more similar to Europeans, a term referred to as “passing”, that has changed over the years as more Black and Asian people have received procedures, or are of mixed-race. In the US and South Korea, reference images of plastic surgery have changed to better fit the race of the individual seeking a certain trait. This is due to the science of anthropometry, which centers on the study of measurements and proportions of the human body. Through the usage of anthropometric facial analyses, surgeons are able to integrate Western features more naturally into the faces of Black and Asian women, and therefore create more accurate reference images that do not utilize solely European or white models. Through the usage of anthropometry, the marketing message of the plastic surgery industry has changed from the concept of “passing” to building upon the natural beauty of Black and Asian women (Edmonds & Leem, 2020). While the shift in message and methodology within the plastic surgery industry says otherwise, the core of the cosmetic industry in these countries remains the same in its intentions. The plastic surgery industry still relays the message to women that their “imperfections” should be corrected to correlate with beauty standards. The existence of anthropometry also shows that race cannot solely be deemed a social construct. While racial meanings are socially-constructed, as Omi and Winant propose, the differences between races can be scientifically measured through analysis of racial phenotypes. These differences in racial phenotypes are then medicalized, and operated on - providing a substantial livelihood to plastic surgeons all around the world. While the US and South Korean cosmetic surgery industries capitalize off of the idea of racial enhancement, researchers found another concept that drives the Brazilian cosmetic surgery industry. The concept of a “meta-race” refers to the perfect mixture of African and Eurocentric skin tones and features. This model however implies that there can be an excess of African traits present, and that those traits must be balanced out by Eurocentric ones (Edmonds & Leem, 2020). Cosmetic procedures are expensive and come with risks having to do with health complications and/or the surgeon who performs them. Overall, cosmetic surgery may stand to correct the superficial, but on the inside low self-esteem and internalized racism persist as Black and Asian women see their racial features as unattractive and abnormal.
chunks.label: Cosmetic surgery and racial phenotypes
chunks.what_happened: The student reviews academic research on cosmetic surgery in the US, South Korea, and Brazil, examining how racial phenotypes are medicalized and modified to approximate Eurocentric ideals.

chunks.text: Internalization of the Western ideal of beauty not only is detrimental to women of color on an individual level, but also on a societal level. On the individual level, Black and Asian women face lower self-esteem and self-worth that can impact the quality of their relationships and careers. This can also lead to other serious mental and physical health conditions, such as eating disorders, anxiety, and depression. As women of color internalize beauty standards, they also tend to internalize racism. This leads to poorer relationships with others of their racial/ethnic groups and a lack of appreciation for their culture in general. As these attitudes are combined in society, internalization of beauty standards serves to threaten diversity as a whole. With more assimilation towards Eurocentric ideals, the world loses the uniqueness of culture that contributes to its overall beauty. Diversity in body types, skin tones, and facial features should be celebrated, as there is much more diversity than there are women that completely fill this standard.
chunks.label: Broader consequences of beauty standards and need for diversity
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by summarizing the mental, physical, and societal impacts of internalized beauty standards and arguing for the celebration of diversity.

chunks.text:
A topic that has existed and is debated by many for centuries on end is religion. People formed groups based off their opinion of what god(s) they think are real and live their entire lives around religious beliefs. Religious texts such as the Bible and Quran are scriptures that people read and follow that listen to their teachings, which causes confliction as societal values may digress from the values that were centuries ago. These people form a collective conscious of their own by following specific practices such as prayers or fasting. One question that must be asked from this is did the people choose a religion from their values, or did they choose values because of their religion?

One thing Harari mentions that helps understand this question more is the uprising of the LGBT community in the mid-20th century. Harari mentions Ted McIlvenna who founds the Council on Religion and the Homosexual to help protect non heterosexual members in the modern from discrimination. This becomes a war against the longest traveling of collective consciousness in religion where these religious texts are used as reasoning for discrimination. These religious people then fight what they consider a modern-day crusade to combat a more modern collective conscious that is looking to loosen ties with traditional values. Examples such as this are what create generation defining experiences and make people of similar ages more relatable to each other, as they are more likely to have similar experience and takeaways from them that cause unification. Harari says that we all have universal ethics for things such as stealing and murder which is why there has not been as much debate among those topics, but religion looks to take it further and claim ideology on more from this ground. However, when generalization happens of what a religion says to practice, a dislike for one topic may become a dislike for the entire religion and influence other morals.

Whether an individual believes in a god or not, they still have a moral compass that will dictate their actions and what is seen as acceptable. Religion is just another factor that looks to justify their actions with the collective conscious either adding support or clashing with them. Likeminded people will always be able to find each other in the world which is why people will always attract a crowd to them throughout life, regardless of how they are. History has also shown that religion is something that cannot just disappear slowly, thus allowing every generation so far access to values that may even be for completely incomparable societies than ones that have existed.
chunks.label: Religion, collective consciousness, and morality
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses the role of religion, collective consciousness, and universal ethics, referencing Harari and historical conflicts between religious texts and modern values such as LGBT rights.

chunks.text:
Before colonization took the world by storm, we lived in isolated groups that most the time shared the same color of skin, religion, and shared set of beliefs called our collective consciousness. Now days we live in diverse communities with varying religions, races, and beliefs. Despite this difference we still manage to share certain ideals and views as Americans. We have made great strides towards racial and gender equality. Our society has changed a lot, but nevertheless change is slow. America is known as the land of opportunity. Then why are the same people that founded this country still the ones at the top? That does not sound like opportunity to me. This is because the white Europeans that founded this country established a system and society that operates and benefits their selves. Despite what we are taught to believe, we still live in a white European centric masculinist society. This is why whites benefit from something we call white privilege.

Erving Goffman says the self is made up of a structure of social encounters. White privilege plays a part in this development of identity. It has drastic effects on our society and the people in it. It results in a change of how whites and minority groups view themselves self, in different ways. Not only does white privilege change your sense of self, but it also actively prevents minorities from having equal opportunity as whites, while helping whites succeed. What does this mean and in what situations does white privilege take place? This can be from education, to politics, and also wealth disparities. As white privilege has become more of a focal point to our society in recent years, there is plenty of fresh research that applies to how white privilege brings down minorities while keeping whites at the top. Throughout this paper I will expand on how white privilege changes our sense of self, the structure of white privilege, and also how it affects certain groups when it comes to wealth education political action and other fields.

Whether we like it, or not racial and gender stereotypes are a part of our society’s collective consciousness. We might not realize it but subconsciously we have been taught to associate certain qualities with certain groups of people. These stereotypes play part in us “playing our roles”. In every social situation we identify the situation and try to fit a role. Since everyone is aware of how people expect them to act whether because the color of their skin or gender, people feel pressured to fit those stereotypes. Our sense of self changes based our reaction to these social reactions. For example, whites are handed unearned benefits at every turn. If a person is continually treated this way, it will have an effect on how they view themselves. This privilege can lead to unearned feelings of entitlement and superiority. This change of identity also takes place in minority groups in a different way. If you are taught your whole life that you are lesser than others just because of the color of your skin or your gender, you might start to believe it. This leads to subordination, self-hate, and an unjustified feeling of being inferior. This process is more subtle than it sounds, people might not even be completely aware they are being treated differently or the effect it has on their sense of self. The fact we are becoming more aware of white privilege is already a good indicator that we are headed in the right direction. Even so our collective consciousness of shared beliefs is deeply rooted into our society and will take a long time to make a permanent positive change.

In class we talked about the Matrix of domination. Where there are people being oppressed there will also be oppressors. There are three main levels of oppression that people can experience: the level of personal biography, group or community oppression, and then systemic oppression. White privilege is an example of systematic oppression towards minorities and women. White women fall into an interesting group of being an oppressor and being oppressed simultaneously. Another interesting group to look at is women who are also minorities. They are systematically oppressed not only because their skin color but also because they are women. Nobody has it harder than women of color in our society. Knowledge plays a huge role in how oppression operates. People who are less knowledgeful and educated are more easily influenced and taken advantage of. At points in history both minorities and women were denied education. This lack of knowledge and keeping these oppressed groups uneducated fosters subordination. Till this day these groups are denied a voice and equal attention. Our society focuses on the power elite white men, this gives them more control and a bigger voice. One example of this “attention” is how media and news stations tend to only care and report when something happens to a white person. If we want to change how our society oppresses women and minorities, we have to start giving them central attention and an equal voice.

There are endless examples and situations in which white privilege takes place. There are also plenty statistics to back these claims of unequal treatment. White privilege is involved in wealth disparities, health disparities, lack of equal education, unfair political action, unequal incarceration, and among many more. When it comes to wealth disparities there is a huge gap in pay between white men and non-white men. For example, Black women are on average paid 21,000 dollars less than their white counterparts for the same job (NPWF 2018). Not only is there a pay difference but whites are more likely to get better jobs than minorities or women that are just as qualified. There are also distinct differences in healthcare between races. For example, “Black women in the United States are more likely to die from pregnancy or childbirth than women in any other race group” (NPWF 2018). Black women are also three to four times more likely to experience a pregnancy-related death than white women (NPWF 2018). Another place where minorities are put at a disadvantage compared to whites is our incarceration system. For example, “Black men constitute 6 percent of the US adult population but are approximately 35 percent of the prison population and are incarcerated at a rate six times that of white males” (Marit Rahavi 2014). Another staggering statistic when it comes to incarceration is that “US incarceration rates for white men are 678 per hundred thousand and 91 per hundred thousand for white women. The incarceration rate for black men is a staggering six times greater than white men, and almost three times higher than for black women” (Moser 2020)

Even though we have made significant progress towards equality, we still have a long way to go. Whites continue to reap unearned benefits while minorities and women are continuously put at a disadvantage by our society. Through health disparities, wealth disparities, unequal incarceration rates, and in countless more situations. This treatment does not just prevent them from succeeding but it also affects their sense of self. Nobody deserves to feel like less just because the color of their skin or gender. White privilege has been an issue for a long time and will continue to be one unless we make an effort from both sides to make a change. This entails giving racial minorities and women more attention and a bigger platform. We should also make an effort to get qualified women and racial minorities into positions of power, especially in the government. It will take active awareness, while accepting that white privilege is a real and relevant issue.

chunks.text: At birth, you are assigned your sex by the appearance of your genitalia. This assignment affects your gender, which is a socially learned set of behaviors associated with your sex. The roles of gender were developed by the collective consciousness, which men made. Gender roles have reinforced ideas such as men going to work while women stay home with the kids or working subservient jobs since the beginning of time. The concept of gender has been used to hold women back from advancing in society and stop them from changing the collective consciousness. Charlotte Perkins Gilman and Simone de Beauvoir’s works display how gender roles have prevented women from reaching total equality.
chunks.label: Gender roles and societal oppression of women
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how sex assigned at birth shapes gender roles developed by men to hold women back, referencing Charlotte Perkins Gilman and Simone de Beauvoir.

chunks.text: In The Yellow Wallpaper, Gilman shares a story about a woman who is struggling with being oppressed. The woman has been told that she is sick by her husband when she actually realizes she’s being held back from her full potential. She is not allowed to write or even think too hard without being met by harsh criticism. By telling his wife that she is sick, John keeps his wife confined to the gender role of being an obedient housewife. Likewise, in Women as Other, Beauvoir asserts that men are essential in the lives of women, but women are not necessary to men; “He is the Subject; he is Absolute. She is the Other.” It is the woman’s role to be an object for the man instead of being her own person and member of society.
chunks.label: Analysis of Gilman and Beauvoir's texts
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the themes in The Yellow Wallpaper and Women as Other regarding how women are kept oppressed and treated as objects or the 'Other.'

chunks.text: Both works display how assigned gender roles have held women back and isolated them from contributing to society. Although gender may help us identify who we are, gender roles are harmful and prevent people, especially women, from impacting the world.
chunks.label: Conclusion on the harm of gender roles
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that gender roles hold women back, isolate them from contributing to society, and are harmful.

chunks.text: There are times when two people are talking, and their thoughts just seem to click. This is no coincidence. Humans have been assigning spiritual and conceptual meanings to the natural world since they first started forming abstract thoughts. This is the basis for animist religion which has shaped how humans view the natural and synthetic world. Due to this shaping of the perceived world, things like social stages can form. A social stage is the shared idea of how an individual “actor” should perform in a given social setting. So, for these two ideas to be possible they need to work as a collective unit. These two concepts work together through social actors playing into animism, creating their own animistic “props,” and doing the opposite of what is expected from the animistic setting.
chunks.label: Interplay of animism and social stages
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces how human abstract thought and animist religion shape perceptions of the world, leading to social stages and how social actors interact with them.

chunks.text: Animist religion is a part of every person's daily life. Whether it be knocking on wood or wishing on a dandelion, these are both examples of animist religion. Ever since humans developed the capacity for abstract thought, they have been searching for ways to give their own lives meaning. Animist religion is a great way of accomplishing that because it gives spiritual meaning to otherwise meaningless aspects of life. This enables environments to be seen differently than what they physically present themselves as. For example, a beach is a collection of sand and shells next to an ocean. These things by themselves mean nothing more than a functioning ecosystem. Through the practice of animist religion, a beach can mean a day full of fun, relaxation, and bonding with others. This is the social stage that animist religion has created for the beach. It becomes bigger than each individual object and becomes a universally understood social environment.
chunks.label: Animism creating social stages in daily life
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how animism gives spiritual meaning to daily life and physical environments, using a beach as an example of a universally understood social stage.

chunks.text: Social stages can also lead to the development of animism that might not already exist for a certain setting. For example, a police station compared to a doctor's office. These locations share many rudimentary objects in common such as a front desk. But a front desk at a doctor's office feels much more welcoming than a front desk at a police station. The social stage set at these locations are drastically different. At a doctor’s office, the social actors are nurses and physicians whose primary goal is to make a person feel welcome. While the social actors at a police station consist of police officers and detectives. These figures are playing a much more intimidating role, so naturally a person will feel less welcome there. Both these locations also share rooms in the back where a person goes to be one on one with different social actors. Obviously, the contents of these rooms differ, but that is not the only thing that makes the emotions a person feels inside these rooms so different. When a police officer takes someone back in the police station, they are doing it in an intentionally intimidating manner to provoke cooperability out of whoever they are going to speak to. When a nurse leads an individual to their room, they do it intentionally soothingly to ensure that the person feels safe. These are a couple of examples of how social actors influence the animism of different social settings.
chunks.label: Social stages shaping feelings at police stations versus doctor's offices
chunks.what_happened: The student compares a doctor's office and a police station to illustrate how different social actors intentionally shape the atmosphere, animism, and emotional experience of a setting.

chunks.text: Social actors can also do the opposite of what is expected from the animistic beliefs surrounding an object to play into different social stages. Going into a social setting knowing what is expected of you is a powerful tool. The obvious course of action is to use that knowledge to play the part socially assigned to you. Another less tapped option is to do the opposite. Some strong public speakers use this method to grab their listener’s attention. A great example of this being done in practice is an elementary school BMX anti-bullying campaign. When the average person hears about speakers coming to talk about the problems of bullying, they will be expecting a put together person coming in with a well-prepared speech. In the case of this specific anti-bullying campaign, it could not be any more different. Instead of a designated speaker it is a group of people all doing stunts on BMX bikes while talking about the problems with bullying in between sets. It may not be the most informative way of going about it, but it is one of the most memorable.
chunks.label: Subverting expectations through an anti-bullying campaign
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how social actors can subvert expectations to grab attention, illustrating this with an elementary school BMX anti-bullying campaign.

chunks.text: The power that social actors hold is immense. Especially when said actor is aware of the potential they have to manipulate their surroundings to benefit their performance. Understanding animism and how it can be applied to daily life can take a person's social acting to another level of convincing. It is evident that trying to comprehend animism without the help of social acting is a dead end, and vice versa. You cannot have one without the other.
chunks.label: Conclusion on social acting and animism
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by summarizing the immense power social actors hold when aware of animism and asserting that animism and social acting depend on one another.

nb2213e1b.title: White Privilege and Sense of Self

chunks.text: The sense of self develops over time, along with social encounters. White privilege plays part in the social structure in which the self forms and naturally reflects in the character of white people. For example, if someone is treated special, they will begin to believe they are special. These repeated social interactions will affect how you view yourself. This can lead to unearned feelings of entitlement and superiority. On the flip side other groups of people are put at a disadvantage. This also affects the sense of self in different ways. Instead of unearned feelings of confidence, you are brought unjustified hate. As a society we have learned these stereotypes over time and they have become part of our societies shared attitudes, a part of our collective conscious. Our society has a strong set of beliefs and it can take a long time for them to change. For thousands of years white men took power and used it to establish a system that benefits them. Our society still reflects that to this day in the form of white privilege and systematic disadvantages for other groups.
chunks.label: Development of self, white privilege, and societal beliefs
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how the sense of self develops through social encounters, explaining the impact of white privilege and systemic disadvantages on self-perception and society's collective consciousness.

chunks.text:
In a world fueled by consumerism and marketing tactics that influence where the working class allocates their money towards, there is a large aspect of how different products are marketed to the different social classes. Commodity fetishization is a Marxist idea that differentiates the value of a product from the labor that went into creating that product. This idea is highlighted in many capitalistic market structures where the idea of what a product is worth comes from the status of possessing that product. This idea aligns strongly with the social classification of members in a capitalistic society. Social classification is the make up of how a group is organized and looked upon from the perspective of education, race, wealth, and many other factors. In this paper, the descriptions of social classification and commodity fetishization will be focused on the structures within the United States.

Moreover, as human actions have progressed from fulfilling basic needs like food, water, shelter, and community we have created many false values around products that do not directly have value associated with them from a physical view. This idea of value is pushed upon the working class from the power elites through the processes of marketing and brand recognition. This practice has only furthered the wealth disparity between the power elites and the working class by creating the idea that the working class so align their thoughts of value with the illusory value that the power elite created around these products. With this the working class continues to spend their money on products with little to no functional value while lining the pockets of the power elite who own the means of production of these products.

Continuing on, the example of Apple products is a great representation of the practices of the working class playing into the game of the power elites. Apple operates on a very short product life cycle process where an updated product to an existing device is released every year to a year and a half. The product that was released a year ago will have the majority of the functions as the new product but by successful marketing and commodity fetishization people still purchase the new product. This is also led on by third-party companies like tele-service providers who advertise and encourage customers to lease devices then trade them in for the next new model. This practice allows the power elite to control how working class consumers spend their money to further the elites gain.

In addition, the practice furthers the wealth disparity between the power elites and working class by making the working class continuously spending money on products that in turn do not have a larger value than the ones before. If the working class continues to spend their money on frivolous items then they do not have the opportunity to invest in practices that will raise their income and generational wealth. By controlling how the working class spends their money then the power elites are able to keep a stable lifestyle and not worry about change. If the wealth distribution changes and shifts to a healthier middle class society then the power elites will not be able to sit comfortably on the throne they have built.

In conclusion, commodity fetishization will always be used as a method of controlling the working class in turn adding to the pockets of the power elites. The idea of the value of a product does not come from it’s functional activities but the value assigned to it through marketing and the ideas that the power elite want the working class to think of it as.
chunks.label: Commodity fetishization and class disparity
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses commodity fetishization, social classification, and how marketing and products like Apple devices allow the power elite to extract wealth from the working class.

chunks.text:
Race falls into one of the many categories in the matrix of domination. It is used to prevent certain groups from advancing in society and contributes to creating the disparities caused by the matrix of domination. The idea behind the matrix of domination is that unrelated privileges such as race, gender, and sexuality shape and organize social order. Tomas Almaguer and Patricia Hill Collins show us that despite what category you fall into on the matrix of domination, whenever its racial or ethnical, if you are not the top dog on the matrix you will be oppressed.

In Race Racialization, Almaguer debates whether Latinos fall into the category of race or ethnicity. Race is defined by oppressors and is used to control social balance and hierarchies while ethnicity is created by members of a community to make a collective identity. Almaguer hints that the US government has constantly gone back and forth between Latinos being a racial or an ethnic group. The answer is simple really, Latinos are both. Latinos share their religion, culture, and language with one another, but they also share the oppression from the dominate caucasian group. There is so much debate where Latinos belong because they are both a racial and ethnic group, there is not a wrong answer.

The matrix of domination is social order based off of race, gender, and other categories created by the dominant white male group to oppress and force other groups into subservient roles. Patricia Hill Collins exhibits how this social hierarchy inhibits the white male population from seeing the discrepancies suffered among the subordinate groups. Old white men are unable to complete accurate social studies on inequality because they have never been victim to it. You cannot properly conduct research on inequality if you have a natural bias or if you have no idea what inequality looks like.

Almaguer and Collins present how it does not matter if you fall into the race, ethnicity, gender, or sexuality groups in the matrix of domination, you will be met by oppression and inequality. The higher up you are on the matrix the more immune you are to not only suffering from inequality but seeing it.
chunks.label: The matrix of domination and racial categories
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological concepts including the matrix of domination, oppression, and debates on whether Latinos represent a race or ethnicity based on readings by Tomas Almaguer and Patricia Hill Collins.

n6ed13c87.title: Collective Beliefs and Sources of Authority

chunks.text:
As humans we allow our societies to be ruled by what we chose to believe in as a group. Whether it is religion or liberalism, we establish these ideas as the collective consciousness and shape our society based off them. In chapter three of Harari’s book and in the work Microfoundations by Fligstein and MacAdams the idea that collective beliefs build and govern our society.

Harari presents the idea that human authority has always come from a shared human idea, such as mythology. Humans use ideas like religion and liberalism to justify authority. He suggests humans now are moving towards establishing technology as the new source behind authority. Harari’s idea that authority is maintained by human beliefs is closely tied to Fligstein and MacAdams’s idea that humans are different than apes because we can share collective meanings with one another.

Both works associate with the idea that collective consciousness shapes human authority and decides what is right and acceptable in our society. Religion, liberalism, and technology are all forms of collective consciousness that control humans and their motives.
chunks.label: Collective consciousness and authority in Harari, Fligstein, and MacAdam
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how collective beliefs shape society and govern authority, drawing on readings by Harari and Fligstein and MacAdam.

chunks.text:
Nationalism is an interesting social trait of human beings. While tribalism and group loyalty are inherent to social creatures it is completely unnatural to feel loyalty to a large group outside of a small social group whether that be a village, family or a social circle. It would seem that the sense of nationalism is an effect of the collective consciousness among those who reside in that country. This would explain why it occurs despite being an inorganic part of the human psyche.

In microfoundations we explore the origins of humanity’s collective consciousness and it is concluded that the main factor behind this collective thinking is the development of language. This is something that I find interesting when considering nationalism because languages are one of the largest barriers between cultures and it would seem that this is not coincidental when searching for the source of nationalism. Of course with a shared language and shared geographic location comes a shared culture to include things such as religion, morals, codes and social/political hierarchies, essentially, the collective consciousness that is associated with that nationality.

This occurs to the point where this nationality becomes intertwined with a person’s “self” as a result of it being reinforced by the collective consciousness. A shared language and culture makes it easier to associate and identify with members of the same country. It would appear that nationalism is really just the tribalism we saw in early homosapiens just on a large scale as a result of growing civilizations.
chunks.label: Nationalism and collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the sociological origins of nationalism, discussing how collective consciousness, language, and culture scale tribalism up to large nations.

nf8986dfa.title: Reflecting on Modern Labor and Alienation

chunks.text:
One of the most hard pressed issues in today’s political climate is our economy. America is always seen as the embodiment of capitalism and economic mobility amongst its citizens. This would be what the collective consciousness deems, however given the sheer size of our population, the intricacies/bureaucracy of our government and the disparity between classes it is not always the key to freedom as we envision it. Economic success does not always equate to satisfaction.

Both of the readings addressed how long ago, there was a connection between producers and consumers, giving people a sense of purpose through their work. Today the worker is often so far removed from the end product of their labor that their work becomes nothing more than a way to earn a check. Turning life into a repetitive and monoughtenous cycle.

I believe that the working environment today cannot be compared to what it was when labor was not estranged. Given our large population and the overwhelming demand which it creates, systems need to be streamlined. A trade off between efficiency and satisfaction. However in certain industries, craftsmanship is valued over efficiency. Looking at trades such as woodworking, brewing, glass blowing etc, and hand made products is much more desirable than one made on an assembly line. These also just happen to be the places where workers tend to be the happiest and I don’t think that that is a coincidence.
chunks.label: Reflections on capitalism, labor, and satisfaction
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how the economy and capitalism affect workers, referencing course readings about the alienation of labor and contrasting streamlined modern production with trades where craftsmanship brings greater satisfaction.

ne97d4b48.title: Gendered Expectations in a Dive Bar

chunks.text: So why is it that over years and years of women fighting back during the first wave feminist movement surrounding the right to vote, the second wave feminism movement focusing on equality and anti-discrimination, and the third wave feminism? It may seem like efforts to break away from things such as the beauty myth have done nothing but women’s work against this fight hasn’t gone unnoticed. Although it has taken time women need to continue to overlook the societal standards of the beauty myth placed on them by men that objectify and subordinate women.
chunks.label: Introduction on feminist movements and the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the waves of feminism and explains that women must continue to resist societal beauty standards placed on them by men.

chunks.text:
With that being said one of my experience that occurred based off my looks was my first job. My first job ever was at a dive bar. When I applied for the job, I was applying for food prep before it goes out to the tables and taking it to the tables because that is what my friend Alyssa

did there and I wanted to do the same, working with her. In my interview process that wasn’t the case. I had the male manager interview me and instead of offering me the job working back of the house he offered me the position to be the hostess. The hostess greats costumers once they enter the restaurant and set the tone for the visit there. The manager implied that this job was better for me because I was pretty, and they needed someone pretty to work the door and set a good mood for the costumer’s experience at our bar.
chunks.label: Hired as a hostess because of looks
chunks.what_happened: The student applied for a food prep job at a dive bar to work with her friend Alyssa, but the male manager interviewed her and made her a hostess instead because she was pretty.

chunks.text:
With working at a dive bar, it is also no surprise that the kegs our customers go through is like a revolving door constantly needing to be changed. At my bar our kegs were stored in a cooler with two shelfs and bottom shelf only about a foot above the ground and the top shelf about 4 feet above the ground. For those that don’t know an average keg that is full of beer weights about 100 pounds and empty they weight about 30 pounds. As a girl most people don’t expect for me to be able to pick up a 100pound keg let alone put it on the top self 4 feet above the ground.

I was never once asked to go change a keg. At our bar it was normal to yell keg change and our manager would always go to the big guys that worked in the kitchen and the men would go and change the keg. Why did me and all my bartenders as women never get asked to change them because we were “weak”? Or we would get comments from our manager like don’t change the keg you’re going to “blow your back”. How come comments like that never got said to any of the men. With that being said, me and the girls really turned a blind eye to that and would still go change and change the keg anyways. Nobody at my work knew I lifted at the gym everyday let alone picking up 100 pounds was practically nothing for me to pick up without hurting myself. I was more than capable of changing a keg on both the bottom and top shelf. Not just

that but the guys would be busy in the kitchen why wait until the cooks would have a break to change the keg when you have women who are more that capable to change a keg. The manager would simply say no because we were women.
chunks.label: Manager refusing to let female staff change kegs
chunks.what_happened: At the dive bar, the manager always called men from the kitchen to change heavy beer kegs and told the female staff not to do it, but the student and other female workers changed them anyway.
chunks.people: manager, kitchen staff (big guys/men/cooks), female bartenders (me and the girls)

chunks.text: I’ve introduced this topic of the beauty myth so what exactly is it? Naomi Wolfs Beauty Myth is based off of a modern version of social reflex it is a concept that society has created this ideal image of a women, but this standard is not for or in support of women. Women become concerned with things such as their hair, makeup, body, and their clothes based on the concepts surrounding beauty created by men. Naomi Wolf also stated that “The quality called “beauty” objectively and universally exists.” Women must want to embody the beauty myth because it is necessary and natural for society. It has existed since the earliest societies in our time and still follows through till present day. The myth has been used as a power structure against women and a fight against feminism while it sets unrealistic beauty standards for women. As women we become so focused on what we look like and how society makes us look.
chunks.label: Explaining Naomi Wolf's beauty myth theory
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Naomi Wolf's concept of the beauty myth as an unrealistic power structure that causes women to compete against and tear down each other.

chunks.text:
We then focus on tearing each other down based off of which one of us is more attractive rather than bringing each other as a community

So how does any of this theory of the beauty myth fit into my life as a woman …well it happens to be part of my everyday life. Earlier I explained that rather than getting a job helping with food in back of the house I was told I wasn’t suitable for that job and that front of the house as a hostess was for me because I was pretty that was just part of it. Sadly, enough in that aspect of my job I let myself become consumed with the beauty myth. The words I get payed to stand here and look pretty came out of my mouth almost every single shift and In, a way it was true. I

was given that job working the door not based off of experience or a good resume it was 100% based off of the fact that a majority of people would agree that I fit into beauty standards. Not just that but anytime anyone pretty would come in for an interview I would get territorial and go mean girl on them. I saw it as competition for my job position and thought anyone remotely attractive could come in at any moment and sweep my job out from under me. I never thought of that before now I just saw it as my job being replaced but after learning the beauty myth I saw it as a threat because of standards imposed on women in todays’ society due to the beauty myth because of men.
chunks.label: Feeling territorial toward pretty applicants at work
chunks.what_happened: Working as a hostess, the student realized she was hired purely for her looks, frequently saying she was paid to stand and look pretty, and she became territorial toward other attractive women interviewing for jobs.

chunks.text: As I have mentioned it is no secret that there are certain expectations in how a woman should act, what she should look like, and what she should wear. Since the earliest times in history the men in society have imposed a commodification on women’s beauty for their own benefit. Such beauty standards on men’s behalf subjected and objectified women’s bodies to the point where women we’re against each other in this system of power that then benefitted men. Even though such pressure is present in today’s society women need to continue to overlook the societal standards of the beauty myth placed on them by men. Some women might not even notice that they are falling into and being objectified by the beauty myth. It is one of those things that has been present in society for so long that it’s hard to find the line of true reality sometimes. Just like me I, knew that certain beauty standards existed in society, but I never knew it to the extent of the theory of the beauty myth. Let alone did I expect to have beauty standards imposed on me at my first job ever just at the age of 17 years old. As a woman we are more than just a pretty face or nice body. If we don’t work to stand up for ourselves nobody will.
chunks.label: Reflections on standing up against beauty standards
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how male-imposed beauty standards pit women against each other, noting her own surprise at experiencing this at age seventeen and urging women to stand up for themselves.

chunks.text:
The conception of self is a very thought-provoking concept. This conception refers to our unique and personal perceptions or a picture of who you truly are as an individual. Our self is different for everyone and while we tend to alter our personalities in various situations, our true self remains constant no matter what.

The conception of self is a concept in which individuals throughout the world have varying viewpoints about. Even though people have varying beliefs, they all believe the self exists whether it is something we can see or not. As people’s bodies and surroundings change, new opportunities are opened for the self to form.
chunks.label: The conception of self
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the conception of self, describing it as an individual's unique perception of who they are and noting that while viewpoints vary and bodies change, the self remains constant and continues to form.

chunks.text:
Overtime various social norms have formed and taken a hold of individuals lives. Society has built up individual’s collective conscious and made them believe that some individuals are superior to others. We have a voice in the back of our heads that constantly tells us that we are better than everybody us. We have been raised in a world where this is normal to think. Society has formed concepts about what is considered to be normal and we feel like we have to live up to them and strictly follow them

Yuval Noah Harari goes into depth about concept of humility and how society needs to be reminded that we are not the center of the world. In his book, 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, Harari states, “most people tend to believe they are the center of the world, and their culture is the linchpin of human history.” We are born into an egotistical society, where we view others as less than us. If someone has different opinions or values as we do, we tend to look down on them. This is similar to the concept of superiority when it comes to gender. Simone de Beauvoir wrote in Women as Other, “we should regard women’s nature as suffering from natural defectiveness”. This demonstrates how men are considered to be the superior gender and females are looked down on.

Growing up, we are drilled with social norms that we are expected to follow and live by. The idea of superiority is making the widening the gap between various groups of people and cultures. In the end, we are all humans. We need to differentiate between what is true and what society has been telling us to believe.
chunks.label: Reflecting on social norms, superiority, and societal expectations
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how society creates norms and beliefs about superiority, referencing texts by Yuval Noah Harari and Simone de Beauvoir to critique egotism and gender hierarchy.

n4a367ebf.title: Analyzing Hegemonic Masculinity in Violent Media

chunks.text:
Patriarchal masculinity is the belief that power is derived from violence and men hold the indisputable right to power. Therefore, it is only natural for media to reflect this attitude in movies, TV shows, video games, and more. However, showcasing the patriarchal standard of power in media has created a form of commodity fetishism that has directly linked itself to hegemonic masculinity.

Commodity fetishism, coined by Karl Marx, in simple terms, refers to the overconsumption of goods and services. Although it also suggests more, it showcases a sense of superiority and an ignorance of how these goods and services come to be in the mind of the consumer. In relation to media, commodity fetishism reflects the ever-growing sources of entertainment that seek to satisfy the public’s gluttony. With the forming of new streaming platforms, the death of cable, and an infinite but also finite choice of selection. However, media cannot simply entertain; it is inevitable that it must also send a message to viewers. Due to patriarchal pressures, media oftentimes represents the desires of men both seeking and in power. As such, the creation of films like John Wick, Nobody, The Beekeeper, Taxi Driver, and many more serve the purpose of feeding a white male audience blood and guts through a screen. All of these films share a similar, if not the same, plot: a white male character, at first glance, lives an everyday life but is later revealed to be a deadly foe to those who have wronged him. As stated before, power has always been promised to men, not as something they should seek to gain, but as a right. With this in mind, it becomes apparent that the target audience of these films are white males who feel suppressed by their surroundings and wish to escape through violent means. The men showcased in these films are rage-filled.

In Nobody, the main character begins off as a meek, quiet husband who appears to be jealous of his much more successful wife. And when he takes his wrath out on people he deems morally corrupt, he becomes addicted to the violence. On the surface, this plot is insignificant and could potentially provide a fruitful discourse. However, problems arise as the film continues and displays the main character’s acts of violence as fun and exhilarating. Another commonality of these films is the lack of female characters. Not only do these movies have very few female characters, but the ones that appear have no personality and exist solely to further the plot. The most obvious example of this is seen in the first John Wick movie, where the beginning plot point is the death of John’s wife, Helen. Despite Helen’s supposed importance to the plot, she is rarely named and is given no characterization apart from her relation to John. The two examples highlighted represent a significant problem in this genre of movies: either women are underrepresented, or they are made out to be threats to masculinity. Unfortunately, as seen with the numerous other media creations, gluttonous viewers will never be satisfied. So, an endless cycle of repetitive media will continue to feed the delusions of power-hungry men.

However, men are not born bloodthirsty; instead, these standards are thrusted upon them with the use of hegemonic masculinity. In essence, hegemonic masculinity is patriarchy manifested. It is the father telling his son not to cry like a girl, the teacher telling a girl that the boy pulling on her pigtails likes her and that “boys will be boys.” Boys learn to crave violence as that is all that they are taught. At the same time, girls are given baby dolls with hushed whispers of their value lying solely in their wombs. Boys, in return, are given toy guns, roughhousing, and told to “suck it up.” As such, the effects of hegemonic masculinity arise in the formative years of a boy’s life. Starting in adolescence, boys are pitted against each other; in return, they learn to seek out male validation to ensure their social standing among men. Moreover, men are tasked with replacing their fathers as head of the household. Replacing one’s father, to many men, is an impossible task. As Oscar Wilde once said, “Every woman becomes their mother. That’s their tragedy. And no man becomes his. That’s his tragedy.” Such strenuous conditions lead to violence amongst men as they cannot wash their bloodied fists or learn to soothe their smoldering rage. Due to this powerlessness, many men have not grown as people and are stuck in a perpetual state of boyhood.

In conclusion, violent media is often used to intensify the bitterness of powerless men while also glorifying acts of cruelty. Media accomplishes this goal through the use of hegemonic masculinity to showcase stories of white men who desire a release. Thereby creating a form of commodity fetishism directed towards a white male demographic.
chunks.label: Media, commodity fetishism, and hegemonic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how violent media feeds commodity fetishism and hegemonic masculinity among men, examining film tropes and childhood gender socialization.

chunks.text:
With all the different influences of the world and people telling you to just be yourself, it is hard to figure out who that true self is. We all have a true self but depending on what social setting we are in determines which part of ourselves is shown. The conception of self has been molded by the different collective consciousnesses we are a part of. James and Mead both discuss the numerous perceptions of self we have. The collective consciousness gives us a false sense of self because we define ourselves by the society, we are a part of.

In The self and its selves, James divides the self into three parts; 1: its constituents- material, social, spiritual and self-preservation, 2: self-feelings, 3: self-seeking and preservation. The social self is a big part of we because it can have numerous parts, such as, family, friends, co-workers, church, school, etc. We put on a different persona when we are in each of these different groups of people. This is because as humans we have a greater range of emotions. Our greater range of emotions increases our fear of not being liked and of what others think of us. Mead relates to James’ conception of self by saying we are mainly our social selves. Our personality is shaped by those we surround ourselves with. People may have trouble discovering their true selves because they feel like they have multiple selves.

Humans were not all born exactly the same and then shaped by society, but the people we are around do have a big part in shaping who we become. When humans started becoming social beings, they started to care more about how others perceived them. The collective consciousness we are a part of plays a big role in our personalities because we all want to feel like we belong, so we mold ourselves to the people we surround ourselves with. So, if the collective consciousness didn’t exist, who would we really be?
chunks.label: Theories of the social self and collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on concepts of the self and collective consciousness, discussing theories by James and Mead regarding how social settings and groups shape our personas and personalities.

chunks.text:
“One’s self concept is a collection of one’s beliefs about themselves” (Wikipedia). I am going to discuss where the self-concept comes from and how it is formed. Numerous scholars as discussed in class have different opinions on this. The concept of self is an important topic to discuss because how we define ourselves can affect self-esteem, increase social comparison and affect body-image.

The first study I want to discuss is Self-Concept and Self-Esteem: How the Content of the Self-Concept Reveals Sources and Functions of Self-Esteem. In this article, the authors discuss the four domains of self-image, “competence, morality, social acceptance and energetic dispositions”, (Kinga, Lachowicz-Tabaczek, Justyna, Śniecińska, pg. 24). A study was conducted to find out which of these domains had the most effect on self-esteem. The results found that self-evaluation involving acceptance of others was a clear predictor of self-esteem more than the other domains of self-concept (Kinga, Lachowicz-Tabaczek, Justyna, Śniecińska, pg. 24). Susan Harter researched the correlation between Self-Concept and level of Self-Esteem and human development (Kinga, Lachowicz-Tabaczek, Justyna, Śniecińska, pg.26). She found that kids who were more successful in sports, school, social status, etc. had higher self-esteem (Kinga, Lachowicz-Tabaczek, Justyna, Śniecińska, pg.26). This can correlate to James’s concept of self, he believed we are mainly our social selves. The authors give credit to James for the development of self-concept. “The direct relation of the self-concept and self-esteem was postulated over one hundred years ago by William James (1980/1952) who stated that self-esteem is a product of an individual’s own sense of their achievements and aspirations,” (Kinga, Lachowicz-Tabaczek, Justyna, Śniecińska, pg.25). The article goes on to talk about further research after James done by Jennifer Crocker with her model of contingencies of self-worth. According to Crocker, “The subjects of their research most frequently indicated appearance, others approval, outdoing others in competition, academic competency, love and support from family, virtue and God’s love,” (Kinga, Lachowicz-Tabaczek, Justyna, Śniecińska, pg.25). Crockers research further makes James’s point that self-concept is greatly impacted by the social self. The authors also discuss Mead and Cooley, other scholars we discussed in class who believed, “social functioning and self-concept are directly connected”, “ Thus an individual’s self-concept and self-concept and self-esteem reflect how they are perceived and evaluated by others,” (Kinga, Lachowicz-Tabaczek, Justyna ,Śniecińska, pg.25). These facts discovered by researchers show a great correlation between self-concept and self-esteem. We define our self-concept by other people which can put a lot of pressure on our social status and can affect our self-esteem. The authors go on to explain how higher self-esteem can give you a sense of belonging. Although, increasing self-esteem is difficult because, “According to the sociometer theory, proposed by Leary and his colleagues, self-esteem reflects the degree of acceptance by a group,” (Kinga, Lachowicz-Tabaczek, Justyna, Śniecińska, pg.25) If you don’t feel accepted by a group this could lead to lower self-esteem, which can lead to greater risk for anxiety and depression which is a prominent issue in our current society. “Watson and colleagues (Watson et al., 2002) observed high correlations between self-esteem and positive and negative affectivity as well as between self-esteem and depression and anxiety,” (Kinga, Lachowicz-Tabaczek, Justyna, Śniecińska, pg.25). So those with a lower self-esteem may have more of a risk for anxiety and depression. Another point James made was all the different social situations we find ourselves in, school, friends, church, work, family, etc. Feeling like you have to be a different person in each of these situations can put a lot of stress on a person, also increasing the chances of anxiety and depression. From the first person that defined self-concept, James, and these recent authors, the way we develop our self-concept tends to come mostly from other people, which is not good for our self-esteem. “This idea of self-esteem is consistent with the conclusions drawn by Baumeister and associates (2003) that self-esteem determines, among other things - initiation of activity, readiness to take up challenges, and perseverance in task executions,” (Kinga, Lachowicz-Tabaczek, Justyna, Śniecińska, pg.26). As you can see from these quotes self-esteem can have positive effects, but we need to change how we define our self-concept because that leads to low self-esteem.

In the article, Relationships between the frequency of social comparisons and self-concept clarity, intolerance of uncertainty, anxiety, and depression, the authors discuss factors such as anxiety and depression. This study found correlation between anxiety and depression and social comparison. Social comparison can greatly affect our development of self-concept. Those who feel like they have more control of a defined self-concept tend not to compare themselves to others as much as those who have lower self-esteem (Butzer, Kuiper). Social comparison can turn into a downward spiral of negative thought about yourself. When we look to others to define our self-concept then it is hard for us to have a clear sense of who we are. The looking glass self was an idea that we discussed in class, formed by Cooley. The looking glass self consists of three parts, “the imagination of our appearance to the other person, the imagination of our appearance to the other person, the imagination of judgement and pride or modification”, (Cooley). The more an individual adheres to social comparison the more they will see themselves as the looking glass self. Comparison with others leads to wanting more and more that others have and wanting to be more like those around you. Constantly having to conform yourself to the world is exhausting and leads to dissatisfaction. Especially in current times it is much easier to compare yourself to others when we are surrounded with numerous social media platforms that constantly have people’s lives in your face. Most people post on social media when they are at their best not their worst. This idea was also discussed by Goffmon’s Presentation of Self. He draws upon ‘the stage’ as an analogy of the presentation of self. In his analogy the front state is how you act in front of important people such as a professor or someone interviewing you for a job. The back-stage-self is who you are when you are around those you are most comfortable with (Goffman). Posting on social media could be an example of your front-stage-self. Therefore, comparing yourself to others on social media gives you a false sense of who others really are and gives you a false sense of who you are because people compare themselves to people performing on front stage.

Lastly, I want to discuss how misinterpretation of self-concept can lead to a negative body image. Vartanian makes a great point of, “Without a clearly defined sense of self, individuals might seek external sources to provide coherence to identity,” (Vartanian, pg. 94). He discusses the issues that come up when the body defines the self, especially in women. As I discussed previously the media has a huge impact on how we perceive ourselves because we think we are supposed to conform ourselves to the perfect model image we see. This concept can be defined as the Beauty Myth, which is that women’s “worth” is in how they look (Wolf). Vartanian discusses this, but specifically regarding body image. He conducted a study that resulted in “lower self-concept clarity predicted a greater degree of internalization of social standards for women, but not for men,” (Vartanian, pg.94). This article relates to Mead’s, The Self the I and the Me. He discusses how an experience of the body and an experience of self are two separate experiences. The body is just a vessel for the and the self is, “a reflection of the whole social process,” (Mead). The body can do many things on its own without incorporating the self. There comes a risk when the self becomes a reflection of the body. Everyone is made different and there are some things you cannot change about your body. So, measuring your worth by your appearance or shape of your body can lead to many unhealthy habits. According to Vartanian, “Internalization of societal standards of attractiveness play a major role in the development of body image issues and disordered eating,” (Vartanian, pg.95). Those who have a lower clarity of self-concept are more likely to fall into these negative patterns of internalization of unrealistic social standards of attractiveness. Vartanian goes on to explain a study which tested different characteristics that make people more likely to have a lower self-concept clarity. He found that factors that contribute to social-standard interiorization and self-concept clarity are conformity, public self-consciousness and body weight contingency (Vartanian, pg.117). This means that, “low self-concept clarity might lead to a general tendency to conform and a tendency to base one’s self-worth of of one’s body weight, which in turn lead individuals to adopt social standards of attractiveness as personally relevant beliefs, values or goal,” (Vartanian, pg.117). Conformity to these standards could lead to eating disorders such as Bulimia, “the strongest predictor for Bulimic behaviors was body image and dieting concerns for both men and women,” (Vartanian, pg.117). As you can see from this study low self-concept clarity can lead to an unhealthy view of yourself based on unrealistic standards from society, which in turn can lead to negative body-image and life-threatening eating disorders. This is a big factor into why our society needs to dismantle self-concept being based on others and find healthier ways to create a positive self-image.

This idea of self-concept was defined long ago by James, but it's uncertainty and prominence in our society today is creating an unhealthy environment for many people surrounding mental health and body image. We must evaluate where self-concept comes from and how to find a clear self-concept. Some ways to do this include promoting positive body-image, reducing the help-seeking stigma around mental illness, reducing social-media use and endorsing positive feed and developing ways to increase self-esteem. These are a variety of ideas, but I believe they would effectively help society define self-concept more clearly, in turn increasing self-esteem so that it's less likely that they will fall into social comparison. It may take further research to implement these ideas and changes that need to be made in many different areas including, a more positive media, school systems and parents teaching and raising children to have a clear and positive concept of self. I believe this would decrease the percent of people who suffer with low self-esteem, decrease mental illnesses and eating disorders.

In conclusion, implementing ways to more clearly define self-concept may not be the only solution to decreasing low self-esteem, social comparison, and negative body-image in our society. Although, I believe finding clarity in who you are from an internal source rather than an external source can make an individual more confident in who they are and more successful in life.

Works Cited

Butzer, Bethany, and Nicholas A. Kuiper. “Relationships between the Frequency of Social Comparisons and Self-Concept Clarity, Intolerance of Uncertainty, Anxiety, and Depression.” Personality and Individual Differences, vol. 41, no. 1, 2006, pp. 167–176., doi: 10.1016/j.paid.2005.12.017.

Lachowicz-Tabaczek, Kinga, and Justyna Sniecinska. "Self-Concept and Self-Esteem: How the Content of the Self-Concept Reveals Sources and Functions of Self-Esteem." Polish Psychological Bulletin, vol. 42, no. 1, 2011, pp. 24. ProQuest, https://search-proquest-com.liblink.uncw.edu/scholarly-journals/self-concept-esteem-how-content-reveals-sources/docview/1323962494/se-2?accountid=14606, doi:http://dx.doi.org.liblink.uncw.edu/10.2478/v10059-011-0005-y.

Vartanian, Lenny R. "WHEN THE BODY DEFINES THE SELF: SELF-CONCEPT CLARITY, INTERNALIZATION, AND BODY IMAGE." Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, vol. 28, no. 1, 2009, pp. 94-126. ProQuest, https://search-proquest-com.liblink.uncw.edu/scholarly-journals/when-body-defines-self-concept-clarity/docview/224872979/se-2?accountid=14606, doi:http://dx.doi.org.liblink.uncw.edu/10.1521/jscp.2009.28.1.94.

Wolf, Naomi. The Beauty Myth: How Images of Beauty Are Used against Women. Vintage Books, 2015.
chunks.label: Self-concept, self-esteem, social comparison, and body image
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes sociological and psychological literature regarding the origins and effects of self-concept, discussing its links to self-esteem, social comparison, body image, and mental health.

n606f323c.title: Choosing Money Over True Career Passions

chunks.text:
Capitalism is abundant in our lives and is a driving force in America to this day. Karl Marx and Max Webber both go into depth on the framework of capitalism existing within our society and how it has been developing overtime.
