Estranged Labor and The Spirit of Capitalism and the Iron Cage emphasizes the idea that capitalism within societies contribute to inhibiting individuals from pursuing their dreams and passions.

In the Spirit of Capitalism and the Iron Cage, Webber uses the concept of the iron cage to refer to how individuals tend to devote their lives to making money. If they do not live up their standards and the standards of society that our collective consciousnesses have formed overtime, then they have failed. Karl Marx goes into detail about the concept of alienation in his writing Estranged Labor. Marx believed that in the capitalistic society, the workers are exploited. Workers are treated as though their labor is property and can be sold or bought. Both of these authors point towards that capitalism puts shields on individuals eyes and leads them to making life changing decisions based on the money rather than what they truly want to do.
chunks.label: Capitalism, Marx, and Weber's concepts
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses capitalism in America and explains theories by Karl Marx and Max Weber regarding the iron cage, alienation, and how capitalism inhibits individuals from pursuing passions.

chunks.text: I have seen capitalism and the concepts mentioned by Webber and Marx all throughout my life but have looked right past it for the longest time. I remember these ideas being evident is in my brother’s life recently. Shortly after getting out of college, my brother was offered two jobs; one was a job that he was super interested in but did not pay the most and the other was not very captivating but paid very well. My brother chose the second option and is in a spot now where he is blinded from the concepts within capitalism that are exploiting him. His collective consciousness and society have thrown these concepts at him and causing him to miss out on other opportunities. He is surrounded by people telling him to take the higher paying job, when they should be encouraging him to pursue his dreams and aim for what he loves.
chunks.label: Brother's career choice after college
chunks.what_happened: The student observes how their brother graduated from college and chose a higher-paying, less interesting job over an interesting lower-paying job, influenced by societal expectations.

chunks.text: Capitalism is going to continue to exploit us as individuals and workers. Many people do not realize what capitalism to doing to our society. Americans need to wake up and realize that society has dictated so much of our life and we are allowing it to continue to do so. Society should not prevent us from doing what we love, it should push us to pursue our dreams. Our passions should be what drive us, not our money.
chunks.label: Critique of capitalism's societal impact
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how capitalism exploits workers and argues that people should be driven by their passions and dreams rather than money.

ndc380414.title: Reflections on Gender Equality and Oppression

chunks.text:
Gender equality is one of the most ongoing hot topic issues in modern society. Across the world, women are still fighting for equal opportunity and to put an end to the patriarchy and toxic masculinity, which is harmful to both men and women. Although society has improved, our progress as a society was a hard-fought battle starting with the first wave of feminism.

In the reading, Gilman creates the diary entry of a woman who is an “other,” as defined by Beauvoir. In the entry, the woman claims that she is ill but her husband and brother, who are both physicians, dismiss her illness as womanly issues. The woman goes on to say that she is frustrated with her husband and brother and feels like an outsider in her own home. She describes how her husband controls everything she does, not letting her read or write or even pick out their bedroom. Sadly, it is obvious through the diary entry that the woman does not realize that she is being oppressed and that the way her husband is treating her is the reason she is ill. The woman described in the reading is a visual representation of how a woman becomes an “other.”

In conclusion, both readings aimed to push the feminist movement. By creating a dialogue about female oppression and opening the eyes of women who feel like “others” but do not know why. Thanks to the efforts of the early feminist movement, society has improved for the better. However, society still has a long way to go until equality among the genders is achieved.
chunks.label: Gender equality and course readings on feminism
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the ongoing struggle for gender equality, analyzes a reading by Gilman depicting a woman's oppression as an "other," and discusses how early feminist movements pushed for societal progress.

n509ca878.title: Reflecting on Inequality and Immigrant Stereotypes

chunks.text:
People always dream of a world where every individual is treated equally, regardless of their race, gender, religion, sexuality, and socioeconomic status. We want this to be true, but sadly, equality does not truly exist in today’s world. As innovations in technology and transportation increase, along with political unrest and injustice, we are made aware of how large of a gap really exists between certain areas of the world, with some of the largest gaps being used against immigrants.

In chapter 4 of “21 Lessons for the 21st Century”, Harari discusses how equality has recently become ideal in society, as we have begun to try to reduce gaps between groups of people based on gender, religion, race, and class. While people today have greater equality than people did 100 years ago, there is still a long way to go before total equality is achieved. In chapter 9, Harari makes the statement that globalization is both a blessing and a curse, as it has reduced cultural differences, but has also made us that much more aware of our differences. These differences cause some people to become upset with those who they deem to be “odd”. Immigrants flee their home countries to escape war, famine, natural disasters, political unrest, and violence, but they are often not greeted with open arms.

In our fight for equality, are we right to close the borders to those who need help? Does this not go against our views of having freedom for all? Is our nation really built upon liberty and justice for all people, or is it only for people who look and act a certain way? We need to take a step back and consider the bigger picture. People who immigrate often do not make a country “bad”. Immigrants often take up jobs that no one else wants, like farmers and custodial staff, landscape specialists and construction workers. Immigration is what makes our country diverse. We need to do away with the stereotype that all immigrants are thugs, sex offenders, and drug dealers in order to work towards our goal of equality for all. We cannot pick and choose who gets treated equally, especially due to something that one cannot control, like their origin and race.
chunks.label: Reflections on equality and immigration
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the lack of true equality in the world, discusses Harari's book '21 Lessons for the 21st Century', and argues against negative stereotypes of immigrants.

chunks.text: Does nature verses nurture really make a difference? Can individuals be completely different even though they had the same childhood? Although it may seem like a bunch of madness, the answer is yes. Individual’s environments are not the only thing that shape them to be who they are, it is also a matter of genetics. Genetics greatly impact individuals’ social aspects and how they cope with the different environments they are in. The argument of nature versus nurture is a very interesting and important topic and it has a lot of evidence holding it to be true.
chunks.label: Nature versus nurture debate
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the concept of nature versus nurture and asserts that genetics and environment both shape individuals.

chunks.text:
I have seen a great and clear example of this throughout my life. My dad and his brother are both adopted and come from different families, meaning they have completely different genetics. My dad is a couple years younger than his brother, but they were pretty close growing up. My dad did not have the best childhood, as his adoptive mother died when he was nine and she was the one who wanted to adopt my dad and his brother in the first place. Because of this my dad and his brother were left with just their dad (my grandpa) raising them as well as my dad’s oldest sister who stepped in when she could. My grandpa was not the kindest to my dad and his brother and would often tell them how he never wanted them, how useless they were and how he did not love them, and no one ever would. This had a great impact on the development of my dad and his brother’s personalities and social ques, and they struggled because of it. Both my dad and his brother would act out and do things they should not be when their sister was not around to take care of them. Although my dad acted out, he was still a good student and played many sports to help him have an outlet for his bad home life. This is the point where you could start to see a difference between my dad and his brother and how their genetics (nature) made them cope with their environment (nurture) in different ways.

My dad got good grades in high school and was great at track. On the other hand, my dad’s brother (my uncle) started using drugs and getting into trouble with the law. My uncle was in and out of jail while my dad was in high school, and he continued to be while my dad was in college. My dad had decided that after high school, he wanted to go to college and try to be as successful as he could be. He wanted to attend North Carolina State University, as that is where all his older siblings attended college. This, however, was not in the cards for my dad because he had gotten a scholarship to run track at Western Carolina University and his dad forced him to go there. At Western, my dad struggled with doing his work during his first semester as he had had no structure in his life before then, but after his first semester he got his head in gear and was very successful in college. He joined a fraternity and made lots of friends and got a very good job out of college. All the while, my uncle was still in and out of jail for many different things. After college, my dad began to work at his job and continued to get promoted and transferred to an even bigger company where he could make more money. He is still at this company today, and he is very successful in supporting my family and plans to continue this. Soon after my dad graduated, my uncle began committing major crimes and was put in jail for 25 years. He just got out a couple months ago and is still trying to work on being a functioning member of society, with the help of my dad and his sister.
chunks.label: Dad and uncle's contrasting upbringings
chunks.what_happened: The student recounts how their adopted dad and uncle grew up in an unsupportive home after their adoptive mother died. While the student's dad found an outlet in sports and academics and built a successful career, their uncle turned to crime and drugs and spent 25 years in prison.
chunks.people: dad, uncle, grandpa, adoptive grandmother, oldest aunt

chunks.text:
My dad and uncles story relates back to nature verses nurture in a couple ways. The concept of nature verses nurture is a long-standing debate about the balance between two competing factors which determine fate: genetics and environment. Genetics being the nature aspect and environment being the nurture aspect. Individuals develop inherited characteristics through their genetics that come out in the right environment. For example, in my dad and uncle’s case, their different inherited characteristics were brought out by their poor childhood environment. My dad took his pent-up sadness and anger and turned it into motivation to be successful, whereas my uncle took these factors and turned to drugs and committing crimes.

Another example of these social differences between my dad and his brother includes their relationships within their family. My dad resented his father, but never meant any ill intention towards him. My dad made a life for himself and wanted to prove to his dad that he could be successful and loved since he had heard otherwise his whole life. This mentality differs from my uncles because when he had nothing left after turning to the streets, he decided to steal from my grandpa’s business and cut off communications with many people in his family. Even after being in and out of jail all his life, giving him plenty of time to think about how he really wanted to turn his life around, as soon as he got out of the structured prison life he had, he turned back to drugs and crimes almost immediately.

Finally, my dad and uncle’s situation exhibited a clear example of nature versus nurture in the fact that nothing has changed as my dad and uncle have grown up. Even after spending many, many years in prison, having lots of time to change his mind set about how he wanted his life to be once he got out of prison, he was not able to make this mental change. This really solidified for me that it really is a matter of nature versus nurture going on with my dad and his brother. My uncle could not change his ways, even with the help of my dad and his sister and their level headedness. My dad and his sister tried their hardest to motivate him to be better. Even with the most convincing arguments, my uncle reverted to his original ways because of how his brain is wired, his genetics would not allow him to cope with his childhood environment like my dad’s genetics allowed him to. This is important to the argument because even over time, my uncle never and his genetics took over.
chunks.label: Analyzing family differences through nature versus nurture
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how their dad and uncle responded differently to the same abusive environment based on their genetics, noting their dad used adversity as motivation while the uncle reverted to crime even after prison.

chunks.text: I never really knew much about my uncle growing up and even the things I did know I did not really think anything of because I was so young. As I started getting older and learning more things about my uncle as well as him and my dad’s childhood, I began to question how their lives ended up so different despite having the same childhood. Everything started to make sense as I learned more and more about my dad and uncle’s childhoods as well as what nature versus nurture entails.
chunks.label: Understanding family history through sociology
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how learning about their dad and uncle's childhood helped them understand how nature versus nurture explains their vastly different lives.

chunks.text:
The Appeal of Greek Life to Young Men: A Sociological Analysis

Why are fraternities such an appealing aspect of upper-level education for young men? It seems that every university across the nation has implemented Greek life as a means to promote a “brotherhood” among their environments. The largest college campuses in the country are riddled with different sectors of Greek houses. Furthermore, fraternity parties are the big events in town on the weekends. Of course, college students love to party, the only issue is that men who are not in the fraternity cannot participate in fraternity parties or events. So how is it that Greek life at large universities has taken such a big stand in developing the social aspect of a college? It has to do with certain societal norms and concepts illustrated by ideas like “doing gender” and “hegemonic masculinity,” and the appeal carries significant relevance to Brian Stoudt’s “In or Out” dilemma involving the Rockport boys.
chunks.label: Introduction to fraternities and gender theory
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the appeal of fraternities on college campuses and sets up sociological concepts such as doing gender, hegemonic masculinity, and Stoudt's study of the Rockport boys.

chunks.text: Prior to coming to university, I had minimal knowledge of what a fraternity is. I knew that pledges (people who have pledged to the fraternity and are going through their initiation) are hazed for weeks on end. There are stories of people having to do some outrageous things in order to show their allegiance to the fraternity. When I arrived at UNCW for my first semester in the fall, I learned about “rush week.” This is when students attend dozens of fraternity events at numerous different houses, and decide which frat seemed best for them. I had a blast, attending parties here and there and meeting new people. However, every time I would meet a new person, the conversation always ended up with, “hey man, are you rushing?” It was almost like that becomes your new personality trait; as if rushing a fraternity made you a more appealing person. When rush week ended, parties became closed to the general public, meaning only females, and the pledges could attend. The whole process changed my point of view on fraternities entirely.
chunks.label: Experiencing rush week at UNCW
chunks.what_happened: The student arrived at UNCW for their first fall semester, learned about rush week, and attended fraternity parties where everyone asked if they were rushing.

chunks.text: Sure, it was fun to go to these parties and experience college a little bit, but would it have been worth it to rush? After seeing some of my peers go through the process, I reassured myself I made the right decision. Some of them would miss class, some were exhausted all of the time, others disappeared from my daily routes to class, and all of them wore suits for a semester. Who would want to give up half of their first school year to wear suits in 80-degree weather, get bossed around, and do unspeakable things for a semester? Perhaps people would say it is worth it after the semester when they get to party, but this is where I formed my dilemma. What is so appealing about suffering for a semester to most college guys? Why does it become a personality trait, and why is it a huge part of college in the first place?
chunks.label: Observing peers going through fraternity pledgeship
chunks.what_happened: The student watched peers endure the pledging process, noticing they wore suits in hot weather, missed class, were constantly exhausted, and got bossed around.

chunks.text: Doing gender is a sociological concept by Candace West and Don Zimmerman that refers to the ways in which people actively perform their gender roles and behaviors in a social setting. The idea is that gender is not just the sex we were born as, but rather something we need to learn and perform to fit the societal role. During this process, people will actively participate in maintaining gender through their actions and interactions. We each learn to behave in accordance with what society deems normal for what a gender is and should be. People are ultimately rewarded through these norms and face negative backlash for failing to conform to these roles. Doing gender for a guy may be holding the door open for a lady or carrying the heavy groceries in from inside. Doing gender for a woman may be cleaning up around the house and being emotional support for men.
chunks.label: Explaining the concept of doing gender
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Candace West and Don Zimmerman's sociological concept of doing gender and how individuals perform traditional gender roles.

chunks.text: Hegemonic masculinity is another sociological concept that refers to the dominant form of masculinity that is idealized and reinforced in a particular culture or society. It represents the specific set of traits and behaviors that are socially valued and associated with being a "real man". Hegemonic masculinity is characterized by traits such as strength, toughness, and independence, as well as the ability to control and dominate others. Another important aspect of hegemonic masculinity is not showing emotion. This idealized form of masculinity is often associated with power and privilege, and it is reinforced especially through media, sports, entertainment, and society itself. Men who conform to this ideal are given status and respect, while those who do not adapt may face negative consequences such as discrimination or marginalization.
chunks.label: Explaining hegemonic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student describes hegemonic masculinity as an idealized dominant form of masculinity characterized by toughness, emotional restraint, and power.

chunks.text: In Brian Stroudt’s “In or Out,” he conducts a social experiment in an all-boys prestigious private school called “Rockport.” The boys in Rockport are part of a culture that values traditional forms of masculinity, which includes traits such as physical strength, aggression, and toughness. In order to be accepted and respected within their peer group, the boys must conform to these masculine norms and expectations. They engage in activities such as playing sports, fighting, hazing, and bullying as a way of demonstrating their masculinity and asserting their social status. The boys often make sexist jokes with teachers and pick on the boys that aren’t “manly enough.” However, the study also reveals a few outliers in the school. For example, some boys show plenty of emotion and view woman as equals. Some reject the masculine ideology all-together. A few have even criticized the school for not learning the teachings of some famous women. Although, there are a few outliers, many support the hegemonic masculinity and culture created at this school and embrace it.
chunks.label: Discussing Brian Stoudt's Rockport study
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes Brian Stoudt's study 'In or Out' on the culture of masculinity, bullying, hazing, and outliers at Rockport private school.

chunks.text: I know I am a culprit of doing gender myself. As a straight male, I was raised to conform to the traditional societal roles of being a man. My mom taught me to be a gentleman, hold the door, and help females with the heavy lifting. I always make sure I shake someone’s hand and look them in the eye as well. When I am older, I know that I must have a successful job to provide for my family (because that is the traditional job of the male).
chunks.label: Being raised with traditional male roles
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on being raised by their mother to be a gentleman, hold doors, shake hands, make eye contact, and prepare to provide for a family.

chunks.text: Fraternities are clearly endorsers of this philosophy. As an all-male institution inside of a university, they must show certain characteristics to the school. These fraternities must uphold a standard to the community to stay alive and recognized by the university. Therefore, fraternities attend community events, hold fundraisers for charity, and set a moral code on campus. These ideas promote doing gender in a way where men must be successful and prosperous. They must act without recognition from the community. This is why fraternities often make their pledges wear suits around campus; to show that they are part of a successful brotherhood. You will never see a fraternity brother act like a female, where female clothes, or fail to promote characteristics of a male.
chunks.label: Analyzing fraternities and doing gender
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how fraternities reinforce doing gender through suits, charity work, moral codes, and promoting male success.

chunks.text: On a larger scale, hegemonic masculinity is perhaps the most prominent concept upheld by fraternities. I, myself, don’t believe I support hegemonic masculinity throughout my everyday actions. However, I am someone who has played sports my entire life. Football is especially one of those sports where you must compete and dominate your opponent.
chunks.label: Playing sports and competitive football
chunks.what_happened: The student played sports throughout their entire life, especially football where they had to compete and dominate opponents.

chunks.text: Fraternities often engage in rituals and competitions to assert dominance and be more “manly” than their counterparts. For example, fraternities will often engage in excessive alcohol consumption, or compete for women. In this way each brother can compete to win. They often treat woman as sexual objects rather than people. Alcohol use attests to their tolerance and if they can hold their beer better than others or have more to get them drunk. Furthermore, hazing is a huge part of the process. The pledges must go through hazing to see if they are man enough to be a part of the fraternity. They must pass the test to the rest of the brothers. The higher-ups in the fraternity are also asserting their power over the newer members by making them do things for them through hazing. Each of these aspects are fundamental features of fraternity life, and they cater directly to the sociological concept of hegemonic masculinity.
chunks.label: Connecting fraternities to hegemonic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how fraternity behaviors such as heavy drinking, competing for women, and hazing exemplify hegemonic masculinity.

chunks.text: Brian Stroudt’s social study of the Rockport boys in his “In or Out” is perhaps the most effective comparison to fraternity life. The Rockport boys show numerous examples of using hegemonic masculinity to gain an edge over their classmates, while each of them is being taught every day how to be a man (doing gender). The teachers are noted making sexist jokes with the boys, while many of the boys exclaim that woman are more of sexual gratification and trophies to be competed over. The all-male institution is very similar to a fraternity; mostly because the boys compete with others in athletic competitions and school. It is also mentioned that many of them haze the younger students to see if they can be a part of the elite group at the school. The entire theme of the school is to be prestigious and superior and make it the highest level of education that they can. Many of these students will end up pledging to a fraternity to achieve the same status and competition as they did at Rockport. Whether they were being hazed, competing for girls, or supporting the successful agenda, they are each devoting themselves to hegemonic masculinity. Furthermore, they are all athletic, successful, and are working towards building a future for their upcoming families, all of which are traits for doing gender.
chunks.label: Comparing fraternity life to Rockport boys
chunks.what_happened: The student compares the competitive, sexist, and hazing culture of the Rockport boys to university fraternity systems.

chunks.text: Fraternities are breeding grounds for the traditional aspects of male society. The reason they are so appealing to young men in universities is due to the male instincts involved with the institution. Whether it be upholding the general roles of what it takes to be a man, being involved in a brotherhood, or competing with other men to assert dominance and eventually build relationships, the aspects of doing gender and hegemonic masculinity are being presented. Brian Stroudt’s study of the Rockport boys is a perfect example of why fraternities are built the way they are. Why would someone want to engage in a fraternity, even with knowing the hazing and toxic masculinity are involved? It is because these aspects are fundamental to the primal instincts of men. There are positives and negatives, but no matter the case, these sociological concepts will cater directly into the unconscious instincts of men. It may be one of the few traditional male institutions remaining in our consistently-changing world.
chunks.label: Conclusion on Greek life and masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that fraternities endure because their practices cater to traditional and unconscious male instincts.

n2580ffdb.title: Beauty Standards in Fast Food Work

chunks.text: In 2016, I began my journey as a working woman in the United States by taking my first job as a cashier at Kentucky Fried Chicken. At that time, I was a sixteen-year-old, blonde haired, blue eyed, white girl and had never thought anything significant about my appearance. That was until my first day on the job. My manager assigned me to the front cashier position immediately rather than the back of the store. I was confused and inquired about his decision to put a first-time cashier front and center with the customer, not really knowing what I was doing at the time. He simply replied that “I appeared much more approachable than my other coworkers.” Therefore, in my manager’s opinion, it was more important to have someone to greet the customers that was more in line with societal beauty standards, than it was to have someone that was more qualified.
chunks.label: First day working as cashier at KFC
chunks.what_happened: On the student's first day as a cashier at Kentucky Fried Chicken, the manager assigned her to the front position instead of the back. When she asked why, he told her she appeared more approachable than her coworkers.

chunks.text:
Unfortunately, my story is not unique. Many women in all levels of the workforce have had similar experiences in their careers.

In 1991, author Naomi Wolf wrote about a concept that she called “the beauty myth”. As described by Wolf, the beauty myth is the unrealistic beauty standards society demands of women to achieve if they want to be accepted by society. In her writing, Wolf claims that this unrealistic beauty standard was created and enforced by men and exacerbated by the media and the marketplace. Furthermore, Wolf argues that the beauty myth was created to silently and indirectly keep women oppressed in society. In the 21st century, however, there are more women entering the workforce than ever before. The oppression created by the beauty myth is now translating to gender inequality in the workplace. While gender is a protected class under United States law, the beauty myth creates a barrier for women in the workforce because these unrealistic beauty standards make it more difficult for women to be hired and promoted into well paid careers. These unrealistic beauty standards can be argued as being an even bigger obstacle than racial bias for women of color in the workforce as personal appearance is not a protected class under current United States law.

First, the beauty myth creates a barrier for woman in the workforce because these unrealistic beauty standards make it more difficult for women to be hired and promoted as has been proven in scientific studies. Of these studies, one conducted by Leeat Ramati-Ziber and Nurit Shnabel of Tel-Aviv University and Peter Glick of Lawrence University, aimed to investigate whether such beauty standards make it more difficult for women to be hired and move up into higher-level career positions.

Another scientific study conducted by Ramati-Ziber, Shnabel, and Glick, examined appearance-related discrimination towards women who seek out higher positions within a workplace context. The study provided evidence that there are more appearance standards imposed on women in the workplace than those placed on men. Women who seek out higher positions are more likely to be required to strive to these levels and maintain an attractive appearance far greater than those placed on men. The study included a sample of 206 undergraduate students at an Israeli University. Of the participants, 93 were women and 113 were men. Their ages ranged from 22 to 39 years of age. The study was initiated by measuring the sexism of each individual participant using a questionnaire. The questionnaire asked participants to assign either a female employee or male employee to a list of 12 different occupations. These occupations included low-power and high-power positions. The jobs also fell within six masculine domains. The participants were then asked to indicate the amount of money and time an employee working in each occupation should invest in his or her appearance for each month as part of their professional duties.

This study found that participants in this survey demanded a much higher appearance-related investment from female employees in high-power positions as opposed to men in the same positions. Thus, making it harder for women to receive promotions within the same job classifications as men due to these added beauty requirements. “In other words, sexists made especially strong, discriminatory beauty-investment demands toward precisely those women who most directly threaten gender hierarchy. That is, women who were in more powerful, masculine occupations.” (Ramati-Ziber et al., 2019). This quote explains the findings of this study and relates to “the beauty myth”. Wolf stated, “Recent research consistently shows that inside the majority of the West's controlled, attractive, successful working women, there is a secret "underlife" poisoning our freedom; infused with notions of beauty, it is a dark vein of self-hatred, physical obsessions, terror of aging, and dread of lost control.” (Wolf 1). The “secret underlife” poisoning women that Wolf is referring to is the pressure of discriminatory beauty-investment that is placed on women in the workplace and is proved by the above study.

The next study we need to look at was conducted by Ramati-Ziber, Shnabel, and Glick, which examined if individuals with job interview experience would impose a higher beauty standard tax on women who were interviewing for high and low-level positions. This study looked at a sample of 55 men and 45 women with a mean age of 45 years old, all with experience in conducting interviews within the hiring process. The participants were asked to give their professional impression of a candidate after they were shown a picture of a female candidate and determine in their opinions, the level of position for which the candidate should apply. The only differences between the pictures of the candidates were the presence of or lack of fingernail polish as well as straight or non-straight hair. The study found that these hiring-level employees that do in fact hire outside candidates, penalized women for not meeting beauty standards. Even though these hiring managers had large amounts of experience in interviewing candidates, they possessed negative attitudes towards women perceived as not meeting these beauty standards and especially towards women who were applying for the more powerful positions.

The findings of this study relate to the “The Beauty Myth” when Wolf said “It is no accident that so many potentially powerful women feel this way. We are in the midst of a violent backlash against feminism that uses images of female beauty as a political weapon against women's advancement: the beauty myth.” (Wolf 1). The findings of the study relate to this quote from “The Beauty Myth” because the results of the study prove Wolf’s statement to be correct. The findings of the study prove that female beauty is being used by people with job interviewing experience to prevent women from being hired into higher positions.

Additionally, the beauty myth is shown to have such a profound influence on the way women are treated in the workforce that it is a bigger obstacle than racial bias is for women of color in the workforce. A study conducted by N. Michelle Hughes and Cedric Herring aimed to investigate if skin tone and the beauty myth affected the way African American women are treated in the workplace.

The study examined a sample of 393 employed African American women. The study began by collecting demographic information and recording the physical characteristics, such as skin tone and hair texture of each participant. The study then asked all the participants to fill out a self-reported questionnaire aimed at determining if they ever felt “hassled at work” or been unfairly denied a promotion based on their appearance.

The study found that although skin color does play a role in how African American are treated at work, the results found that shockingly, regardless of skin tone the more “attractive” the appearance of the women, the more likely they reported being hassled at work and denied promotions. “The results suggest that the more attractive a woman is judged to be, the more likely she is to report being hassled at work” (Hughes & Herring 177). This quote describing the results of this study truly shows how deeply rooted the beauty myth is in creating barriers for women. It is so deeply rooted that it even is, according to the study, a more deciding factor in female workplace treatment than racial bias. The result of this study further reinforces how important it is that the beauty myth be addressed and undermined to benefit women of all races and ethnicities.

Now that it has been determined through research that the beauty myth is negatively impacting women in the workforce and creating barriers for female advancement, the question remains as to the best solution. It is a complicated question to answer. Under current United States law, gender is a protected group in employment, and it is illegal to discriminate against an individual based on gender. However, there is no law that protects an individual from being discriminated against based on their appearance. An excellent example of this is the restaurant Hooters. Hooters has had a very appearance-based discriminatory hiring practice since the inception of the company. For a woman to work as a waitress at hooters she is required to be deemed attractive with a thin body and large breasts. A woman who works at Hooters is required to wear specific makeup, painted fingernails, and have only “natural” colored hair. The hiring practices that Hooters utilizes, which are solely based in ideal beauty standards, should not be legal.

To stop the beauty myth from continuing to undermine and oppress women in the workforce, appearance must become a protected group under US employment law. In her article “APPEARANCE MATTERS: A PROPOSAL TO PROHIBIT APPEARANCE DISCRIMINATION IN EMPLOYMENT”, author Elizabeth M. Adamitis emphasizes the role that beauty plays in our society and how beauty is considered as a legitimate consideration in employment matters. “Further, the focus on appearance serves to perpetuate and foster harmful societal inequities.” (Adamitis 195). This quote from Adamitis directly relates to the beauty myth because she is sharing the same opinion that Wolf expresses in her writing, that the focus on appearance in employment is to intentionally create workplace inequality between men and women. Furthermore, Adamitis writes, “Women are often both considered and expected to be more attractive than men.” (Adamitis 199). This quote is relating to both study five and three described above because the statement is consistent with the findings of both studies.

In conclusion, the beauty myth has created many inequalities for women in the workforce. The beauty myth affects all women and makes it harder for women to get hired or to advance to high power positions during their career. Although gender discrimination is against the law, appearance discrimination is not. This allows employers a way to discriminate against women without having to cite their gender as the reason. The best solution to fix this unequal treatment it to also make appearance a protected group under law.

Work Cited

""the Beauty Myth: Prescriptive Beauty Norms for Women Reflect Hierarch- Enhancing Motivations Leading to Discriminatory Employment Practices": Correction to Ramati-Ziber, Shnabel, and Glick (2019)." Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, vol. 119, no. 2, 2020, pp. 343-343.

Hughes, N. Michelle, and Cedric Herring. "FAIRNES ON THEJOB: SKIN TONE, THE BEAUTY MYTH, AND THE TREATMENT OF AFRICAN AMERICAN WOMEN AT WORK." Reinventing race, reinventing racism 50 (2012): 177.

Adamitis, Elizabeth M. "Appearance matters: A proposal to prohibit appearance discrimination in employment." Wash. L. Rev. 75 (2000): 195.

Wolf, Naomi. The Beauty Myth: How Images of Beauty Are Used against Women. London: Vintage, 1991. Print.
chunks.label: The beauty myth and workplace discrimination
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Naomi Wolf's concept of the beauty myth, cites academic studies showing appearance-based discrimination against women in hiring and promotion, discusses Hooters' hiring practices, and argues that appearance should be a legally protected class.

n55fa1b1b.title: Analyzing Power, Privilege, and Artificial Intelligence

chunks.text:
George William Domhoff’s ideas stated that class had a large role in life, especially in the workforce. His main idea is that the “power elite” controls the workforce. The power elite describes the leadership group of the upper class. An example is the Bush family as many people in this wealthy family held positions of power. The power elite has a clearly stated policy agenda which included anti-tax, anti-union, and deregulation. Therefore, they knew what they wanted to accomplish, and they maintained these goals. The power elite is the intersection of economic, government, and military institutions as they are people with different positions of power in the country with goals in all aspects of the nation. The power elite also explains why the working class does not have much power. The origins of why the working class has less power are rooted in slavery which creates a division between whites and blacks. This division benefits the power elite as it makes it harder for labor unions to form. The working class is then further divided between skilled and industrial or unskilled workers. These great divisions throughout the workforce make it hard for the working class to unite and form labor unions. This is good for the power elite as they are anti-union and want to maintain their rule. Also, they want to be able to continue to live and control the workforce as they please, rather than having to listen to the demands of labor unions. Altogether, Domhoff’s ideas underscore the role of class and that the workforce is controlled by a group of people known as the power elite.

However, Harari describes the role of artificial intelligence in the workforce. Robots and algorithms are beginning to replace human hands in the workforce as they take over many jobs. Losing a job to artificial intelligence could actually be quite beneficial. Artificial intelligence reduces human error in the workforce, making things safer and more efficient. Also, everyone could have their own personal doctor, therefore, you could receive faster and better healthcare at any time. There would also be less discrimination for hiring as there is no race in artificial intelligence. Another benefit is that humans would be able to focus on meaningfulness as artificial intelligence could detect your mood and be able to efficiently change the song coming out of your sound system to better reflect and synthesize with your emotions. A large benefit for the lower class of America as artificial intelligence becomes more prevalent in the workforce is universal basic income. Universal basic income (UBI) suggests that the governments tax the billionaires and corporations that control the robots and algorithms. This money should then be distributed to provide everyone with a generous payment that covers their basic needs. This eliminates the worry of not having enough money to provide for your family due to simply poor treatment due to class or race as each person gets what they truly need. Despite having a multitude of benefits, there are also some concerns regarding artificial intelligence in the workforce. For instance, these robots and algorithms are able to learn you better than you can understand yourself, therefore, they understand what advertisements and agendas you would be more willing to follow or support. This could be harmful as these advertisements and agendas may have a hidden false statement or negative effect. Essentially, algorithms are going to become tools or great control that can effectively help or harm humans as they take over the working class.

Domhoff and Harari’s ideas on power and the workforce differ as Domhoff sees the power in a group of people while Harari sees it in artificial intelligence. As artificial intelligence takes control, we see fewer disparities between classes as universal basic income provides each person with the amount of money they need in order to have their basic needs. Universal basic income also provides a type of control similar to checks and balances so that there isn’t a human power elite. This is because the wealthy people and corporations who control the artificial intelligence are taxed greatly in order to provide the public with generous stipends that create universal basic income. Domhoff’s ideas are greatly supported by division in the workforce due to race, however, Harari’s ideas don’t allow that. Harari’s ideas state that the use of artificial intelligence in the workforce would decrease discrimination as robots cannot be discriminated against. Robots do not have races, therefore, there cannot be racism or discrimination. Their ideas also differ as the power elite has a clear, set agenda while algorithms may manipulate their advertisements and agendas in order to make the public do what they want as they know humans better than humans do. All in all, Domhoff and Harari’s ideas differ as they find the power within the workforce in different things which causes differences in income, division, and racism in the workforce.

Now let’s talk about similar ideas:

Peggy McIntosh’s ideas regarding white privilege compliment Harari’s ideas of ignorance hindering social justice. McIntosh explains that white privilege can be defined as advantages whites have in everyday life that they do not recognize. An example is that bandaids do not match colored skin which reinforces that there is a standard for what flesh color should be. Also, representation on TV can be very misleading for people of different races. Think about it, who typically plays a smart, athletic, successful role, and who plays the comedic relief role? While this is changing slightly today, we typically see white people in more serious roles on TV while colored people more commonly play a less serious or more violent role, depending on the film or show. Another thing that white people may take for granted is the treatment they receive from society. For instance, most white people will not be followed or watched in a grocery store while colored people might. Similarly, most white people do not fear interactions with law enforcement becoming violent while colored people do. These are all privileges that white people subconsciously live with and reinforce every day. White privilege typically goes unnoticed to white people as they are taught to ignore it, they are taught that this system is “normal” and “fair”, that there is no need to acknowledge it.

Harari has similar ideas to McIntosh, he uses the idea of “the knowledge illusion” to further explain that humans are much more ignorant than they think. The knowledge illusion explains that humans believe the knowledge of others is their own. In other words, people believe that they share the knowledge contained by others. This encourages the idea of groupthink. Groupthink is essentially when people follow the same beliefs or values. It can be beneficial but also quite harmful. Groupthink makes a group feel like their idea or belief is concrete as so many people agree with you and it allows the idea to spread extremely effectively. Harari underscores that when a group agrees with your stance on an issue, you will lose sight of the issue, therefore, becoming ignorant to the roots or origin of a problem. People find understanding conflict to be too difficult to understand, they attempt to break it down into four methods, including downsizing, personalizing, conspiracy theories, and dogma. Downsizing an issue refers to looking at it on a smaller scale. For instance, people attempted to understand the Syrian civil war as if it were between two foragers. The Assad regime was thought about as one person and the rebels were thought of as another person and one is termed “the bad guy” and the other “the good guy”. Personalization is when humans focus on one human story that represents the entire issue. This is a method used by charities quite often. For instance, in an experiment people were asked to donate money to a poor seven-year-old girl named Rokia. She was from Mali and received many donations when just her story was presented to the public. However, when the researchers presented her story along with statistics about the issue of poverty in Africa, they received significantly fewer donations. Conspiracy theories describe when humans create fantasies in order to help them understand the world. For example, when trying to understand the global economy, it is simpler to explain it as twenty multibillionaires “pulling the strings behind the scenes, controlling the media, and fomenting wars in order to enrich themselves”. No one understands the world, therefore, no one can effectively “pull the strings”. Finally, dogma is humans putting their trust in one supposedly all-knowing theory, institution, or chief. They then follow this dogma wherever it takes them, allowing them to feel like they do not have to form their own opinions or ideologies as they are presented to them by the dogma. These methods allow humans to become ignorant of the actual issue as they manipulate it.

Both McIntosh and Harari’s ideas highlight that ignorance causes social justice issues to not be solved. McIntosh explicitly states that ignorance is the root of white privilege as people are taught to not recognize it. This is similar to how Harari’s ideas of ignorance relate to the difficulty of solving social justice issues. Like I previously stated, people find understanding conflict in the contemporary world to be extremely difficult so they find methods to focus on one thing that aids them in understanding the issue. However, this power just distorts the reality of the issue rather than bringing clarity to what needed to be done in order to solve the problem. Social injustice is embedded in the system and clouded in the minds of the public. People are taught to not recognize social injustice like racism and discrimination therefore they cannot be solved. Altogether, both McIntosh and Harari’s ideologies underscore that ignorance is a large factor in social injustice that causes the public to not recognize the issues, therefore, change cannot occur.

Overall, Harari’s ideas are both challenged and reinforced by different ideologies. Though Harari may have differing ideas on power, racism, and income in the workforce, he has similar ideas regarding ignorance in social justice. Learners and readers must think critically as they will often learn from people with both similar and different ideas to each other and the student themselves. It is important to be open-minded while learning in order to be able to fully learn about each side before making your final decision as to which ideology you believe is correct.

I believe that Domhoff, McIntosh, and Harari all make excellent points and none of their ideas should be discredited. While Domhoff’s ideas challenge Harari’s, his ideologies are still valid, they are simply different and it is up to the reader to use critical thinking and previous beliefs and knowledge to decide who they support. McIntosh’s ideas underscore Harari’s, therefore the reader can recognize that these ideas may be commonly supported.

To conclude, though Harari and Domhoff have contradictory ideologies regarding power in the American workforce, they still present valid arguments that the reader must deeply ponder in order to gain their own understanding and beliefs. McIntosh’s ideas complement Harari’s ideologies focusing on how ignorance affects social justice issues by distorting the truth and blinding humans from the greatness of the issue. Harari’s work may have both reinforcing and challenging ideas, but he still produced amazing work and it is imperative that people read and understand his work using critical thinking skills to form their own beliefs and ideas in relevance to his work.
chunks.label: Analyzing ideas of Domhoff, Harari, and McIntosh
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes and compares sociological theories on power, the workforce, artificial intelligence, white privilege, and ignorance from Domhoff, Harari, and McIntosh.

chunks.text:
The concept of gender is not something assigned to us at birth, but rather a socially learned set of behaviors, a role we develop in the collective consciousness. Most of us are used to our societies being gender binary, where we believe sex assigned males should be masculine and sex assigned females should be feminine. In “The Yellow Wallpaper” and “Woman as Other” Gillman and Beauvoir express their concerns about how women are treated as the secondary gender to the men.

In “The Yellow Wallpaper” we read what appears to be Gillman’s journal entry about her life. Gillman talks about how she is sick, but her husband and brother essentially just tell her she is fine and do not seem to listen to her. Gillman is somewhat confined to this house and is in a way neglected by her husband who does not seem to care to greatly about her well-being. Her illness is caused from the oppression and mistreatment she gets as a woman and it is driving her to the point of depression from the lack of equality she receives for simply being a woman. Then in “Woman as Other”, Beauvoir writes in detail about how women are not seen as equals to men and women are just seen as inessential while men are essential. Beauvoir labels women to be “the other” in contrary to the men who are “the one” and how the other must submit to “the one” and be subservient to them. However, unlike other groups who are considered “the other” women have always been that way and there was no event that caused them to submit to the men and they are not even a minority, there are as many women as there are men.

The gender concept is something that has changed a lot over time, but in most of our world today women are still seen as an inferior gender to men. Both Gillman and Beauvoir are expressing their unhappiness with women being a gender just like men, yet they are not seen as the same. As the world evolves, we could see gender binary societies wither away and one day everyone may look at the concept of gender and see us all as the same as Gillman and Beauvoir wanted.
chunks.label: Gender roles and readings on women's oppression
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on gender as a social construct and discusses themes of female oppression and inequality in texts by Gilman and Beauvoir.

chunks.text:
One of the main aspects of humanity that separates us from other species is our sense of self. The self is what makes somebody unique; it is our perception of who we are to ourselves and to others in social settings. This perception of self is something that has come about and is a direct result of the development of a collective consciousness.

One of the key things we gained from a collective consciousness was the ability to communicate and socialize. It also happens that our perception of self is reliant on communication and social perception. In The Self, The I, and the Me, Mead states that linguistic behavior is the only form of behavior where an individual is perceived as an object to themselves. This social behavior is also how the individual is able to get a sense of how others may perceive them. This is key because within a social setting as a result of the collective consciousness, there are standards which are formed among a group and a person will adjust themselves in order to meet those standards. Goffman supports this in The Presentation of Self by comparing us to performers, saying that rather than conforming to these standards with the moral issue in mind, we conform for the purpose of creating an impression that we fit in with the group.

Said at the most simple of levels, our presentation of self stemmed from communication which also helped to develop the collective consciousness. It is the collective consciousness that formed our social norms and procedures. These standards which are in essence, the collective consciousness, and are what shape our sense of self and the performance we put on to adhere to these social standards.
chunks.label: Collective consciousness and presentation of self
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how the development of collective consciousness and communication shapes the sense of self, drawing on concepts from Mead and Goffman regarding social perception and conforming to group standards.

n0768255f.title: Analyzing Racial and Economic Income Gaps

chunks.text:
Final Paper: Income Gap Between Races and Injustice Done to Minorities

As society has evolved and time has continued to tick on, many things around the world have changed greatly. Although this is true, there are still many issues that have plagued our world for so long that we do not seem to see being resolved. Arguably the most terrible problem we continue to discuss is racism. Racial inequalities and disparities have been prominent for so long, and even though it has gotten much better, it is still a big problem our world faces to this day. One of the areas we can still see racial disparities clearly is in the workplace and differences in income or a wage gap. There is much research on the difference in income between races and the racial gap minorities are faced with. I will look at and discuss how the income gap breaks down, what this means for different races, and how this can be a hardship minorities have to face.

In class, we discussed the sociology of race and the history behind race in America. Race shapes opportunity and perceptions of difference in America today. From the times of slavery to now, race is something that has been an important factor for each individual’s life every day. Even though slavery is no longer present and seen as inhumane, race still divides our society and creates boundaries or separate groups of people. In “The Matrix of Domination”, Collins created a system to show the symbolic order racial, along with other, disparities created between all of us and how one’s configuration defined their rank in order of preference. This is something we still see prominent today where a white male is more likely to receive higher pay or even get hired for a job over a male of color. This matrix is extremely prominent in the field of work and is the driving influence behind these racial disparities that create wage gaps/differences in income.

Economic disparities is an area widely researched, mostly analyzing statistical differences between racial groups and their correlating incomes. The main factors looked at are differences in wages and employment rates between whites and blacks or other minority groups. These gaps show the racial inequalities when it comes to economic income and the obstacles minorities are faced with in everyday life still to this day. In “Race and Economic Opportunity in the United States: An Intergenerational Perspective”, Chetty et. al study the sources of racial disparities in income in America and find three main results. They find the black-white income gap to be driven by wage and employment rate differences between black and white males. They also find differences in parental marital status, education, and wealth explaining some of the problem and finally the black-white gap persisting even among boys who grow up in the same neighborhood. This research shows studies of the causes of the issue and what it means for different races. Many different studies and mathematical analysis are done in order to make the argument for the wage gaps we see between whites and blacks as well as other minorities. As time goes on, we may see the gap between some races begin to diminish, but there will continue to be these economic differences and some races will meet this injustice more than others even as time goes on. This even shows how people of different races who may have grown up very close to each other, have similar backgrounds, or meet the same qualifications for a job will still see an income gap between the one who is white and the one who is black. This research leaks over and is the foundation for many other studies done in the area of income gap and how it breaks down or what it may mean for different races.

Income inequality and wealth disparity is the main focus for the racial group gaps. All the studies will look the differences in numbers for income across races and determine their findings on the economic gap between races. Ho-Hing et. al in “Economic Inequality and African Americans: A Comparative Analysis” also look at and discuss similar findings on economic inequality between whites and blacks. They analyze the relationship between inequality coefficient and variables such as income, consumption, and wealth. Doing this they confirm a long-lasting relationship between the two and the income gap seems to remain somewhat consistent. This shows that economic differences have been lasting for a long time now and do not seem to be getting better at all. Proving the existence between racial and economic inequality is something all studies easily demonstrate, but these prove to show the issue has been this way for a long time and show no signs of improving as time goes on. Even though the income gap seems to be somewhat the same through the duration of this research’s study, the disparity between races in wealth has grown. This shows that the continued rise in inequality is making more challenges minorities are being faced with just in order to be capable of living a sufficient life while being faced with racial inequalities. Income differences and gaps in wealth will continue to prove to be a more than difficult obstacle for minorities to have to face unless we can move towards a world where we do not see these economic gaps between races.

A big thing we would like to figure out is how to resolve these racial inequalities when it comes to income gaps. Something that helped drastically in years past was the expansion of minimum wage. In “Minimum Wages and Racial Inequality”, Derenoncourt et. al show how minimum wage has actually helped the racial gap in income differences a great amount today. Minimum wage allows for all workers to at least be paid a certain amount no matter their race or any other disparities. Although this does not help with hiring rates between races, if someone is to get hired, they at least have to be paid a given number. If this were not present, the economic gap would be even greater across races since people would not be required to pay minorities a certain amount. Although this is true, we still see big racial inequalities today even though they are not as large as they may be without minimum wage. This leads to the question of if minimum wage can help fix this problem even more. Even though we cannot just continue to raise minimum wage more and more without business’ revenue increasing, raising minimum wage if feasible is something that could help reduce the economic gap across races to hopefully be a smaller number. The obvious answer would clearly be to just stop exhibiting racism and pay everyone equally based off skill and performance done in work, but that is not something so easily done as it is told. Racism is an attribute many people will continue to possess due to their beliefs and be able to cover up for in many ways in order to make it seem right or reasonable so just abolishing racism is not something we can do in a quick, swift manner or else it would have been done long ago. However, looking into minimum wage may be a smart area to consider in order to figure out how to make minorities be able to receive fair pay based off their abilities and not their race.

All three of these sources discuss the issue of economic gaps seen due to racial inequalities and analyze data to convey their research to the audience. The income gap is very large between whites and minorities such as blacks and does not seem to be getting very much better. This is driven by systematic racism and continues to provide barriers for minorities to face that should be nonexistent. Unfortunately, this has been an issue for a very long time, and even though some aspects have helped minimize it to a degree, the gap remains wide and does not seem to be closing anytime soon. The income gap even proves to exist in people who grew up in nearby areas and meet the same qualifications for a job and perform equally, the only difference is the color of their skin. These sources all tie together to prove the long existing relationship between race and income as well as the gap this relationship has provided for many years and seems to likely continue in the future. Today we see an income gap of nearly 30,000 dollars between the average white and black family, which is white families almost receiving double what black families annually receive. Racism is an issue very highly spoken of today, but for whatever reason we continue to see it effect people in so many different ways that make some of our lives so much harder than others for no good reason. Being born into a certain race should not have such a grave impact on how much money you make and how well you are able to provide for yourself and your family. This does not mean all white people make more than all people of color and that no one of a minority race makes a large amount of money, but when you look at the averages the gap is very wide and proves the racial inequalities we continue to see today.

There is much research done on this subject and most of it is very insightful in understanding the issue, but the most important areas are those that look at how the correlation is present and what can be done to help fix it. The articles I looked at show sources of racial disparities in income, the relationship income inequality and wealth disparities, and minimum wages impact on racial economic disparities. These are important by showing why we see the issue as well as the effects it has on different groups and areas that can maybe help these groups face less hardships than they already do. If the income difference continues, we will only see minorities be forced to live lives harder than they need to be and continue to have larger gaps in wealth. Every single person is affected by racial inequalities, whether they benefit or harm them. Hopefully, we can find solutions to end this problem and diminish the economic gap across races in order to live more equal and fair lives in the future.

In conclusion, the existence of an economic gap between races is very prominent and it causes minorities to be faced with many more hardships than someone of a majority. This makes minority races receive on average lower incomes leading to larger economic gaps simply due to their race. Racism is something we still see very clearly today in our society and even though it has gotten better, it is still a huge issue we struggle with. Economically is one of the many areas effected due to racism and an area that has a great deal of importance on someone’s life. Considering areas like minimum wage could potentially help the issue get better some, but in order to make it dissolve and create a world where there is no economic gap at all based off race, we would need to see us each become better individuals and realize that race is not something that should have this type of impact on everyone’s life. Collins described the issue perfectly with the matrix of domination and the matrix is still something we see very existent to this day with race being arguable the leading factor among the other disparities used in the configurations.

Works Cited

Chetty, R. et. al. (2020). Race and Economic Opportunity in the United States: An Intergenerational Perspective. Quarterly Journal of Economics. Retrieved from: https://academic.oup.com/qje/article/135/2/711/5687353?login=true

Collins, P. (1990). The Matrix of Domination. Retrieved from: patricia_hill_collins_black_feminist_thought_in_the_matrix_of_domination.pdf (oregoncampuscompact.org)

Derenoncourt, E. et. al. (2021). Minimum Wages and Racial Inequality. Quarterly Journal of Economics. Retrieved from: https://academic-oup-com.liblink.uncw.edu/qje/article/136/1/169/5905427

Ho-Hing, D. et. al. (2019). Economic Inequality and African Americans: A Comparative Analysis. Journal of Applied Economics and Business Research. Retrieved from: http://www.aebrjournal.org/uploads/6/6/2/2/6622240/joaebrseptember2019_166_176.pdf
