chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes scholarly literature and sociological concepts regarding racial income inequality, wealth disparities, and the role of the minimum wage.

chunks.text: What makes us different from other species of animals? Humans are social beings. As talked about in the first module, changes in brain structure created a greater range of emotions in humans which lead to the development of language, making it easier to communicate. Culture bound humans together and stories and rituals were able to pass down because of language, this took rise to the collective consciousness. This created communities, civilizations and nations. The collective consciousness is the first topic we discussed, but it correlates to Harari’s second section of 21 Lessons for the 21st Century. In order to solve all the global issues of the twenty-first century we must reform the collective consciousness.
chunks.label: Collective consciousness and human evolution
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how brain changes, language, culture, and collective consciousness formed human communities, linking these class concepts to Harari's book.

chunks.text: According to Harari online communication has led to a false sense of community, where people feel closer to people halfway across the globe then right next door. You would think this means that technology has helped make the whole world connect and become one big community, but the person you were messaging on Facebook is skeptical of letting you or someone from your country into their country. As humans evolved and became more social beings a collective consciousness was formed, determining social norms of society. Over time people have formed different religions and cultures that unite them together. In modern times, preconceived beliefs about specific religions and cultures are separating the global society.
chunks.label: Technology, false community, and division
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Harari's perspective on online communication creating a false sense of community, noting how modern prejudices divide global society despite technological connectivity.

chunks.text: Harari believes that Europe opening its gates to refugees or not can be attest to the rest of the world’s tolerance and values of freedom. If the global civilization reverted back to the collective consciousness of people as a whole instead of their own excluded communities maybe we would realize whether we are across the globe or across the street, we as humans are all intertwined together as a global community. This is the key to solving the most difficult global issues; unity, created by a common collective consciousness of all humans across the globe.
chunks.label: Global unity through shared collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Harari's points about refugee tolerance and argues that global unity through a shared collective consciousness is needed to solve global issues.

nbdafe371.title: Technological Shifts in the Modern Workplace

chunks.text:
We live in a society today where technology is advancing with every blink of an eye. With the advancements in technology comes the need for faster, more updated, and more advanced operations, leading to a huge shift in the modern workplace. The first aspect of this essay is analyzing the concept of “McDonaldization” by Ritzer. This concept describes the process of fast food with four important components. Efficiency, control, calculability, and predictability. It highlights how much fast food cares about cost and speed. The next aspect is from the source “The Third Wave” by Alvin Toffler. Toffler addresses the third wave of technologies and their advancements. In this paper I will explore how McDonaldization and technological advancements help companies and operations, but actually have harmed the workforce and the working class.

While both articles are different in their own sense, they share a very common theme. Both scholarly sources address the need for efficiency and order. McDonaldization, which is heavily focused on fast food services and hoped for consistent costs with predictable results. In terms of technology, it is designed to predict data and complete. The need for that technologically allows for McDonaldization to fall into place. Both concepts work hand in hand to make sure sales and prices are up. These two concepts allow for a global workplace with standards across the board. It makes sure products are consistent in size, price, and quality. McDonaldization also expands beyond just fast food. We could apply this concept to schools, corporations, and the healthcare system. Everyone in these fields is working with major technological advances while also trying to be consistent in their services and speed. While both these concepts help create fast and predictable work results, it also damages the natural workplace and the contribution from individuals.

The concepts of McDonaldization and technology completely transformed the labored workforce. Even though we have had great advancements in these fields, it has been harmful to the people. These advances have led to substantial job misplacements. While these technological advancements are new and exciting, it is eliminating jobs for the working class. Jobs that used to be operated by people are now just robots and computers. Each year we see more and more jobs go digital. Because of this decrease in work, it is harder for people to find jobs with a lower education, leading to a large decline in economic equality. Workers are let off for these new technological advances but are given no resources in order to find a new job. These technological advances and McDonaldization do not aid these workers but instead just replace them.

A real-life scenario and example of the effect of McDonaldization and technology is the transition from cashier services to only self checkout. In most grocery stores in America, the check out went from having 6 lanes open with cashiers assisting to check out shoppers to there being 6 self checkout lanes and maybe one cashier. This shift towards self- service is a direct example of companies wanting the fastest and most predictable services with the lowest labor costs. Another example is the advancements in fast food services. If you walk into most fast food stores today, they will have a self ordering kiosk. These kiosks allow people to place their personal orders without human interaction and lessen the chances of messed up orders. By placing these kiosks in fast food restaurants, corporations are attempting to have control over the pace of the restaurants and the labor force. This is not just in fast food, but can also be seen in retail, banks, schools, healthcare, and more. Everyone is working towards the more efficient and least costly results in the work field, oftentimes not putting workers in mind.

In conclusion, the concepts of McDonaldization and technological advances, while effective in allowing for businesses to boom and have consistent results, are very damaging to the workplace and the working people. As more machines and computers take over more jobs, we see individuals losing their jobs and struggling to find new jobs more than ever. We see this shift most often in places like fast food and grocery stores, but can truly be seen happening almost everywhere. Everyone is wanting to advance and make money without thinking of the repercussions it will have on our economic state and the individuals who would be affected the most by these shifts. As jobs advance and continue to be replaced, we can expect an even bigger economic diversion between the rich and poor. McDonaldization and technological advancements can be very helpful and crucial to our society. However, it is crucial for the government and business owners to recognize this significant drop in jobs and the effect it has on our social and economic inequality. By recognizing this shift, resources and plans can be set into place to assist the working class.
chunks.label: McDonaldization and technology's impact on workers
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the sociological concepts of McDonaldization and technological advancements, arguing that while they increase efficiency and predictability for businesses, they eliminate jobs and harm the working class.

chunks.text:
We have given culture and society too much power over our lives. Society has formed concepts about what is considered to be normal and we feel like we have to live up to them and strictly follow them. The fear of stepping out and going off the path that society is leading us down is controlling us.

Gender norms have become more and more evident overtime. Society is controlling how we act, how we dress, how we speak, and so much more when it comes to gender. We do not want to stand out and be ourselves because we are scared it will be too far off from the gender norms and we will be considered an outcast. As Simone de Beauvoir wrote in Women as Other, “we should regard women’s nature as suffering from natural defectiveness”. Simone’s writing demonstrates how men are considered to be the superior gender. We have grown up in a culture and society that tells us that women are not good enough or women cannot live up to the high standards society holds for men. This article seemed a little dehumanizing to women and reminded the reader of the gender norms culture has formed over the years.

Not only do we grow up being drilled with gender norms, but we also grow up being taught, sometimes unconsciously, the differences between various races and the privileges that tend to come along with each one. Many individuals look right past the very evident interconnection between gender and race. The idea of black feminism mentioned in The Matrix of Denomination by Patricia Hill Collins brings these concepts together and refers to how they are all intertwined with one another. Collins states, “the significance of seeing race, class, and gender as interlocking systems of oppression is that such an approach fosters a paradigmatic shift of thinking inclusively about other oppressions.” When it comes to black feminism, not only is gender a rising issue, but race as well. Black feminists are argued to be the most oppressed, which provides them with a unique knowledge and understanding. Advocates for black feminism are stripped from privileges other individuals such as men or white women are given. Many individuals do not notice or pay any attention to the differences in treatment and have been brain washed to think it is normal.

Our society is leading us further down a path of gender and social prejudice. While each culture and society are unique from one another, they seem to be all brainwashing individuals in some way. We are all humans, no matter what our gender and no matter what race we are. No human is superior to another, even though society may try to tell us that sometimes.
chunks.label: Societal control, gender norms, and intersectionality
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how society and culture enforce gender norms and racial differences, citing writings by Simone de Beauvoir and Patricia Hill Collins to discuss oppression, black feminism, and human equality.

n008dc2d5.title: Disconnecting Bodies in a Digital World

chunks.text:
As our world continues to make advances in technology, we see ourselves and our communities becoming more and more distant from their self and their body. Something we all seem to be intact with everyday is our self, however the thing that we seem to forget about sometimes or not be in tune with is our body. In his book “21 Lessons for the 21st Century” Harari discusses in part two chapter five titled “Community” how today we live in an online world that disconnects us from our bodies and true offline experiences. Harari argues that as technology has advanced over all these years, we have begun to live more and more online and drifting apart from our real world or offline experiences that simply remind us that humans have bodies.

Harari argues how as humans roam more into the offline community, they are disconnecting themselves from the offline one and the feelings and experiences we get through our body. This more prominent use of the body is something that used to have a much vaster role in everyday life before technological breakthroughs. This argument supports Mead’s argument of the body and self in “The Self, the I, and the Me”. Mead argued how the body and the self are experienced differently, the self indirectly but completely and the body directly but incompletely. He also argues that the body was the vessel for self. This runs into Harari’s argument about the difference in experiences humans are having and how that of the body is seeming to decrease. Harari supports this argument by showing how online interactions decrease the body’s direct experiences so it can not be experienced completely due to the lack of interaction in the offline world.

The increase in technological advances has led to many great accomplishments for mankind, but also many unintentional drawbacks in human experience and human communities. Our communities need to be directed away from the online realm and more into the offline one for our bodies to properly experience life in the way they once did. This shift will lead back to humans utilizing their bodies properly and returning to a community we can all learn to appreciate much more.
chunks.label: Technology, the body, and online disconnection
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses ideas from Harari and Mead about how technological advances and living online distance humans from their bodies, offline experiences, and community.

n6a4f8ffd.title: Sociological Perspectives on Religion and Self

chunks.text: 21 Lessons for the 21st Century is an insightful book written by Israeli author Yuval Noah Harari. It addresses the political, technological, scientific, and sociological problems of today, as well as how humanity should face them in the coming future. According to Harari, we have no idea how the world will look in the year 2050. Harari offers priceless advice, perception, humor, and rationale in his quest to navigate the challenges of the twenty-first century In doing so, his goal is to provide some historian-based perspective so we as a people can begin trying to form some semblance of understanding going forward. The balance between introductory concepts and more abstract notions was carefully written and made for a thought-provoking read. However, since Harari comes from a more modern time, some of his ideals do not coincide with previously learned concepts, many of which were conjured hundreds of years ago. Still, as many sociological and philosophical concepts are for the most part unchangingly universally accepted, most of Harari’s writing agrees with theories learned in previous lessons. This essay seeks to examine how sociological concepts align with the insights of Harari.
chunks.label: Introduction to Harari and Sociological Concepts
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces Yuval Noah Harari's book '21 Lessons for the 21st Century' and explains the goal of examining how its insights align with sociological concepts.

chunks.text: Most of the lessons we have learned in class were confirmed by Harari’s writing. The following is just one example, but arguably may be the strongest alignment. In module one, when the class was introduced to sociology, we reviewed Emile Durkheim and his perception of the significance of religion to human societies. According to Durkheim, “If religion has given birth to all that is essential in society, it is because the idea of society is the soul of religion” (p. 72). Here, Durkheim credits religion as the foundation of human civilization and society. He continues on by saying, “It is true that since collective sentiments can become conscious of themselves only by fixing themselves upon external objects; they have thus acquired a sort of physical nature; in this way they have come to mix themselves with the life of the material world…” (p. 72). When humans apply spiritual meaning to work, it becomes tangible. Durkheim names religion as the cause for objects in the material world, which constitutes human society.
chunks.label: Durkheim's Theory of Religion and Society
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Emile Durkheim's sociological perspective on religion as the foundational core of human civilization and society.

chunks.text: To add onto Durkheim’s theory, in module one, the class explored The Neurology of Religion by Alexandra Maryanski and Jonathan Turner. The authors concluded that meaningful, abstract thought (for example, religious behavior and collective representations) can be explained by Darwinian natural selection. Hominin neuroanatomy evolved, making humans more social and able to form stable groupings. The adaptation of the brain of the ape Morotopithecus makes forming stronger social ties much more effective. “Humans are very disposed to give emotional significance to special situations, including their emotionally charged social relations” (Maryanski & Turner, 135). The authors connect the experience of emotion to social bonding, which is extremely important among humans for development in several different aspects (for example, cognitive, social, emotional, verbal, etc.).
chunks.label: The Neurology of Religion by Maryanski and Turner
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how Maryanski and Turner argue that hominin neuroanatomy evolved through natural selection to enhance emotional significance and social bonding.

chunks.text: While Harari does not delve into the neurological and evolutionary aspects of society like Maryanski and Turner do, he instead stresses the importance of emotional and social bonding with others several times in the book. “In order to flourish we still need to ground ourselves in intimate communities” (p. 86). “...humans are social animals, therefore their happiness depends to a very large extent on their relations with others. Without love, friendship and community, who could be happy? If you live a lonely self-centred life, you are almost guaranteed to be miserable” (p. 206). He argues that social relationships are one of the most significant aspects of human health and wellbeing. Therefore, healthy and strong communities or societies cannot be formed without intimate connections between its members.
chunks.label: Harari on Emotional and Social Bonding
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Harari's view on the necessity of intimate communities, love, and friendship for human happiness and social health.

chunks.text: Furthermore, the importance of religion in social bonding is emphasized in 21 Lessons for the 21st Century. Harari states that “Homo sapiens is a post-truth species, whose power depends on creating and believing fictions. Ever since the Stone Age, self-reinforcing myths have served to unite human collectives… By bringing people together, religious creeds make large-scale human cooperation possible. They inspire people to build hospitals, schools and bridges in addition to armies and prisons” (p. 240-241). He goes on further to argue that religion is the most effective tool in bringing humans together over a shared passion. It is successful in forming strong social ties with humans. So, not only are social bonds extremely important to humans for successful societies, but they may as well have not even been possible if not for religion as a shared passion. It is religion in some form or another that brings humans together, regardless of the connection they previously had. Religion is the universal connector, because of the importance of assigning meaning to phenomena.
chunks.label: Harari on Religion as a Social Connector
chunks.what_happened: The student explores Harari's perspective that shared religious myths and creeds enable large-scale human cooperation and form strong social ties.

chunks.text: Thus, Harari and Maryanski and Turner stress the importance of religion and social bonding when it concerns human civilization development. According to Maryanski and Turner, the evolution of the brain led to the inherent human ability to attribute emotional significance (usually with a religious subcontext) with a natural phenomena (usually rationally unexplainable by humans). This emotional significance transfers to meaningful relationships with human communities. Durkheim’s theory of religion being the foundation to society is only further proved by Maryanski and Turner’s research. In addition to this, Harari states that religion is extremely effective in strengthening cooperation and unity. With religion as a common uniter, humans can deepen their social and relational bonds, resulting in stronger communities and healthier individuals.
chunks.label: Synthesizing Harari, Durkheim, and Evolutionary Theory
chunks.what_happened: The student synthesizes the views of Harari, Maryanski, Turner, and Durkheim, highlighting how religion and social bonding drive human community development.

chunks.text: While many of Harari’s ideas are in harmony with the theories and concepts explored in class, there is definitely a major conflicting idea regarding the philosophy of the self. In module two, we explored “The Self and Its Selves” by William James. James describes the “self” by dividing it into separate components. The material self is all that an individual possesses, whether it be their body, their money, their friends and family, or their reputation. The social self is the perception of the individual as seen by others. The spiritual self consists of one’s emotions and drives. Most importantly, the pure ego is the unchanging soul of the individual, which is stable regardless of one’s environment or experiences: “The sense of personal identity is not, then, this mere synthetic form essential to all thought. It is the sense of a sameness perceived by thought and predicated of things thought-about. These things are a present self and a self of yesterday…” (James, 1890). In this quote, James argues that the pure ego is true and consistent, unchanged by thoughts, perceptions of experiences, or emotions. He simplifies the different versions of the self by synthesizing one’s essence into a single, unmalleable soul.
chunks.label: William James on the Self and Pure Ego
chunks.what_happened: The student reviews William James's concept of the self, specifically the pure ego as an unchanging, stable soul.

chunks.text: However, Harari contradicts James’s rationale in Chapter 21, Meditation. He reflects on what it means to live and be after explaining how the practice of meditation simplified his mental state to the here and now. Harari explains how it is human nature to become fascinated by the mystery of life after death and what that means to us as conscious beings. Many believe that “‘...the soul endures from birth to death and thereby holds life together…’”, but Harari argues that you cannot “observe a soul”, and the soul cannot be constant, because there is nothing that “endures from birth to death”. “The body keeps changing every moment, the brain keeps changing every moment, the mind keeps changing every moment” (p. 318). In this argument, Harari interconnects the mind and the soul- claiming that since the mind is perpetually changing in some form or another, the soul cannot possibly be a constant.
chunks.label: Harari's Meditation Chapter Contradicting James
chunks.what_happened: The student examines Harari's perspective from his meditation chapter, which rejects the idea of a constant soul because the mind and body are continuously changing.

chunks.text: Therefore, according to Harari, if the human mind is constantly adapting to new experiences and information, there is no possibility that the soul can be constant. The soul may not even exist because it is not observable, and we should not view the mind and soul as separate because they are too connected to ignore. Harari focuses on the perception of life and how physical sensations affect human bodies, not the abstract meaning of the self and one’s cosmic purpose. He pays strict attention to the observable, immediate senses. Since this is the only truly empirical evidence of human existence, it should be prioritized over the abstract pondering of eternal life and spirituality. Meanwhile, James attributes the human personality with an inherently permanent personal essence. It is untouched by experience or environmental input. The soul remains the same, even beyond physical death. James and Harari clearly disagree on the philosophical approach of human life and spirituality, especially when it concerns death.
chunks.label: Contrasting Harari's Empirical View with James's Essence
chunks.what_happened: The student contrasts Harari's emphasis on immediate, observable sensations with James's theory of a permanent personal essence.

chunks.text: When reflecting on Harari’s perception of human sociology and the “lessons” he insightfully posits in 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, it can be confidently said that most of Harari’s ideas are consistent with the learned class material thus far. To recapitulate, Harari’s argument about the significance of religion and its social bonding power completely coincides with the research and theories of Maryanski, Turner, and Durkheim. Each of the three authors’s research or opinions perfectly complement each other. However, Harari’s opinion on what takes place after death does not agree with the theory of William James, who postulated that the pure ego is the ever-present and unchanging soul of a human being that transcends time and physical presence on Earth. It must be taken into consideration that James’s theory is considerably older, and Harari’s opinion stems from a personal experience (which he reflects on in Chapter 21, Meditation). Though, this disagreement is one of the few inconsistencies between opinions and is the most noticeably major. Reading 21 Lessons for the 21st Century successfully proves how sociological theories can approve or disprove each other, and is a powerfully stimulating opportunity to compare and contrast some of the most influential thinkers of human society.
chunks.label: Conclusion on Sociological Theories and Harari
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes the essay by summarizing where Harari aligns and disagrees with the theorists discussed and reflecting on comparing influential thinkers.

n96f0526f.title: Exploring the Origins of Collective Consciousness

chunks.text:
Within every society, social group, religion, and culture there is a shared set of belief systems, ideas, attitudes, and customs. These shared traits are apart of something known as the collective consciousness. Although collective consciousness can be observed anywhere in the world, many still seek to find the origin of collective consciousness. In the readings Neurology of Religion and Microfoundations, two theories are presented, the neurology theory and the microfoundation theory, that both argue that the origin of collective consciousness stems from evolution and the development of abstract thinking in Homo sapiens.

In conclusion, although each reading used different theories, both readings use evolutionary evidence to support the argument that the collective consciousness stems from the evolutionary development of abstract thought in human beings. Knowing that abstract thought is a trait unique to humans and that abstract thought is the foundation of collective conscious, implies that collective consciousness is what make us human.
chunks.label: Collective consciousness and human evolution
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses the concept of collective consciousness and reviews readings arguing that it originates from the evolutionary development of abstract thought in humans.

chunks.text: I will be providing an example of how gender roles in school can affect how the people around you characterize you. There are multiple parts of your life that the social evaluates to form assumptions about your gender and sexuality.
chunks.label: Introduction on gender roles
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces their topic of how gender roles influence assumptions about gender and sexuality.

chunks.text:
Eventually, Kenan found out that Garrett was interested in him and thought he was gay and stopped talking to him. Garrett’s suspicions died down until Kenan texted him apologizing for not talking to him and referring to Garrett as a “great friend”. This caused Garrett to once again believe that Kenan was attracted to him. Though they do not talk to each other much anymore, Garrett’s thoughts continue.

Garrett’s obsession with Kenan was the basis for his assumptions about him as he wanted to believe there was an opportunity for a relationship. Garrett created a picture in his mind of Kenan as feminine and gay.
chunks.label: Garrett's assumptions about Kenan
chunks.what_happened: Kenan stopped talking to Garrett after learning Garrett thought he was gay and liked him, but Garrett renewed his assumptions after Kenan apologized and called him a great friend.

chunks.text:
This leads me to discuss gender, or more specifically, doing gender. Most people view gender as whether you are male or female. While that is true, gender is created by how you act, masculine or feminine. Sex is described by the presence of genitalia at birth while gender is determined by your behavior. If you want to be female, you have specific guidelines you must follow in order to be interpreted as feminine by the social. Females are supposed to wear make-up, dress nicely, have long hair, be organized, wear jewelry, be emotional, etc. Similarly, males also have “rules” they must follow to be characterized as masculine. Males must dress in more comfortable clothing, be tough, do physical labor, engage in contact sports, be confrontational, act more nonchalant, etc. These gender roles allow humans to individualize themselves and categorize each other.

Gender is something that a person does in order to fit how they want society to view them. If someone wants to be viewed as feminine, they partake in “feminine” activities such as getting their nails done, putting on makeup, shopping, etc. They also enter a feminine persona when in the social such as being more submissive, emotional, and polite. Females are supposed to be helpless and need a man to take care of them. Males are supposed to disregard things such as school, jobs, and people. They are supposed to be tough and heartless. Someone who wants to be described as male would workout, have muscles, be hostile, cuss, put women below them, etc.

Extracurricular activities can also determine whether you are viewed as male or female. For instance, sports such as volleyball, cheerleading, swimming, or dance are viewed as feminine sports. While sports such as football, basketball, baseball, or wrestling are viewed as masculine sports. Males get made fun of for partaking in “feminine” sports as they are seen as weak for not choosing a contact sport. Women may be called “dykes” for partaking in a “masculine” sport. However, women are more commonly seen playing in “masculine” sports in attempts to empower themselves and other women. Also, things such as theater, band, and choir are viewed as feminine and typically result in bullying for males that take part in them.

Hegemonic masculinity is also something important to discuss. It is simply the proper term to describe the ideal masculine traits. It emphasizes that males are supposed to be brave and feel no pain, physical or emotional. It also reinforces the role of being a protector that is assigned to males, they are supposed to keep women and children safe. They are also expected to take care of and provide for their families. Men are supposed to be self-sufficient and not rely on anyone.
chunks.label: Sociological concepts of gender and hegemonic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological definitions of gender, gender performance, expectations for men and women, and hegemonic masculinity.

chunks.text:
Males are often told to grow up “strong and straight” in order to fit the idea of hegemonic masculinity.

This information relates to Garrett’s situation as he evaluated Kenan’s actions in order to make assumptions about his gender and sexuality.

Garrett argued that Kenan was feminine due to his clothing. For example, Kenan would sometimes wear colorful khaki shorts with collared shirts. This led Garrett to assume that he was feminine or gay as he believed that was something a gay boy would wear. Garrett often wore similar shorts which was also a cause behind his characterization of the clothing. Also, Kenan wore a pink shirt which Garrett believed was a feminine color, therefore, characterizing Kenan as feminine.

Similarly, Kenan’s actions caused Garrett to suspect that he was gay or feminine. The social media app TikTok was new and extremely popular at this point. Kenan would make dancing TikToks which Garrett viewed as feminine instead of funny or talking videos that he viewed as masculine. However, Kenan made these TikToks to be ironic and as a method of creating jokes with his female friends.

Also, the way Kenan talked and what he said was another reason for Garrett’s assumptions about him. Kenan used words and phrases that were common among females such as “period”, “shawty”, “girly pop”, “bae”, etc. Garrett thought he was being serious when he was again just being ironic.

Another thing is Kenan is very religious. He spends a lot of time at church, posts bible verses, and often tells people to turn to God in hard times. Garrett viewed this as Kenan relying on others and often said that straight men were not that religious. However, Kenan simply was grounded by God and found something he was passionate about to live by. His family in general was very religious and he had strong family bonds that also bounded his relationship with God.

Kenan is a strongly kind-hearted person. He is extremely polite and kind to everyone which caused Garrett to characterize him as feminine due to most men being rude. Kenan’s manners and kindness came from the way he was raised. He was raised by the typical southern bell and had a great relationship with his family. He was also raised in the church as I have previously stated. Along with males typically being characterized as rude, Garrett mistook Kenan’s kindness as him being attracted to Garrett and attempting to be flirtatious.

Garrett also thought that the typical features of masculinity that Kenan embodied were methods of hiding his true sexuality. For instance, Kenan played multiple sports and did well in them such as football, lacrosse, basketball, and soccer but Garrett always said that was him attempting to divert attention from things that may make people think he was feminine. Another example of this is Kenan’s posts and statements about him working out. Garrett thought that he was making it so public that he works out and goes to the gym so often in order to make the idea that he is masculine concrete in the minds of society.

Overall, Garrett assumed Kenan was gay or feminine as he interpreted his actions, clothing, words, and personality did not conform to typical masculine ideals. Despite many explanations from people around him such as Kenan is a star athlete, simply wants to dress nicely, came from a religious family, or that he was raised to have good manners, Garrett believed he was simply attempting to cover up his true sexuality.
chunks.label: Garrett evaluating Kenan's gender and sexuality
chunks.what_happened: Garrett analyzed Kenan's clothing, dancing TikToks, slang, religiousness, and kindness as signs of being feminine and gay, while interpreting Kenan's athletic accomplishments and workouts as cover-ups.

chunks.text:
It is important to recognize that most guys are often made fun of for being gay but males find two generally attractive girls kissing to be “hot”. However, if these girls were deemed unattractive, they would also be made fun of.

A similar concept of going against gender roles being attractive or unattractive can be seen through the Boy Scouts of America allowing girls to be a part of the organization. Some females may be looked down on or viewed as masculine for joining, while a beautiful girl would be welcomed. Also, some girls may find this organization to be empowering, while others may find it to be negative as males that are a part of the organization may make them feel like they do not belong or that they should not be there.

Finally, gender roles play a crucial part in every experience people participate in as they decide how society views you due to multiple aspects about you. Everything you do, say, wear, etc. is another piece of evidence the people around you employ to formulate how they characterize you. Their assumptions may be true or inaccurate depending on their interpretation of your actions. People may celebrate your actions and relate them to your desired gender role, or do the opposite and make you feel bad or less than.
chunks.label: Reflection on double standards and gender roles
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on societal double standards regarding gender nonconformity, using examples like girls joining the Boy Scouts, and concludes on the pervasive influence of gender roles.

n1b4ac8d1.title: Analyzing Labor Alienation and Cultural Assimilation

chunks.text:
Yuval Noah Harari analyzes modern society along with the many problems of the 21st century in his book 21 Lesson for the 21st Century. Harari goes through many different issues seen today, such as problems with jobs, equality, religion, and immigration. Readers can see many different similarities in the other sociological approaches of other sociologists, politicians, and real-life scenarios along with many differences. When it comes to similarities, Harari has similar ideas to those of Karl Marx. Marx criticizes capitalism because it is alienating the workforce which is like Harari’s argument that artificial intelligence has the possibility of alienating the workforce along with other harmful effects. Harari’s analysis of immigration then differs from the experience of Yelena Khanga as she was never able to fully assimilate even according to Harari’s three-step process of immigration.

Throughout 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, Harari includes many examples of how advancing technology and how artificial intelligence is affecting modern society. Granted, technology is the main topic of discussion with its effects on all aspects of the world today. When this is applied to jobs and the workforce, Harari refers to it as the “AI revolution.” Even if a solution is found to the issue of the job market being taken over by artificial intelligence, humans will constantly have to find new jobs after their job is taken over. Harari says, “The AI revolution won’t be a single watershed event after which the job market will just settle into a new equilibrium. Rather, it will cascade of ever bigger disruptions. Already today few employees expect to work in the same job for their entire life. By 2050, not only the idea of a job for life but even that of a profession for life might seem antediluvian.” (Harari 32)

Harari believes that artificial intelligence will only benefit humans by creating more jobs on top of leaving more opportunities for humans to take jobs that they enjoy and take jobs that influence creativity. This still does not solve the problem at hand according to Harari. The inability to be dedicated to a single job could cause a great disconnect between the worker and the industry which Marx elaborates further in his writing. Change is stressful, hectic, and can cause chaos in some people’s lives. This problem must be addressed even though Harari sees the overall situation as beneficial.

Marx's writing, Estranged Labor, relates to Harari’s argument in a few different ways. The main idea of this writing is that capitalism is alienating the workers from the industry and from the product itself. There are many ways in which the worker is alienated. The worker is alienated from the product because the product is meant for the capitalist and not the worker. The worker is alienated from the process because often, the work is tedious and repetitive. This specific example can be seen as a similarity to Harari’s argument to one of the benefits of artificial intelligence being the fact that they are taking over the “boring” jobs. Marx then goes on to other ways in which the worker is alienated including being alienated from each other as work is becoming more isolated.

Marx makes an interesting point knowing that Estranged Labor was written in 1844, almost 180 years ago. The date this writing is published is only interesting because of the idea of alienation in modernity. Society is so complex and is only becoming more complex as time goes on, which Harari also elaborates on during his discussion of the future of artificial intelligence and the future of society. Marx also says, “the worker becomes all the poorer the more wealth he produces, the more his production increases in power and range. The worker becomes an ever-cheaper commodity the more commodities he creates. With the increasing value of the world of things proceeds in direct proportion the devaluation of the world of men. Labor produces not only commodities; it produces itself and the worker as a commodity and does so in the proportion in which it produces commodities generally.” This quote stands out because we can see a similar pattern when it comes to the integration of artificial intelligence going along with Harari’s argument earlier. The worker becomes ever cheaper the more technology he creates.

Harari and Marx have similar outcomes in their arguments about issues with the workplace even though they have different reasonings. Harari reasons that artificial intelligence is the reason for the disconnect while Marx reasons that capitalism is causing the alienation of the workers. Both argue that a disconnect between the workers, the workplace, the products, and even other workers is bad for the economy overall.

Later in Harari’s book, he talks about immigration. At the beginning of the chapter about immigration, Harari identifies three basic conditions that must be met to consider immigration or immigrant to be successful. The first condition is that the host country allows the immigrants in. The next condition is that in return, the immigrant must embrace at least the core norms and values of the host country, even if that means giving up some of their traditional norms. The third and final condition is that the immigrant assimilates to a certain degree and becomes equal and full members of their host country. Of course, this is a very general overview of the immigration situation around the world, but it works well as a summary.

One of the most important conditions is the third and final one saying that immigrants that make a sincere effort to assimilate into society will become full citizens of the host country. This can be considered the most important because the effort the immigrants put forth is key. Assimilating into a new country and a new culture is never impossible but can be extremely difficult in some situations.

Yelena Khanga has a unique and interesting story concerning racism and immigration. Khanga is an Afro-Russian, Jewish woman born in Moscow while the Soviet Union was still active. Khanga’s grandfather, Oliver Golden, was one of the few African Americans who escaped racism by migrating to the Soviet Union before World War II. In the area in which she grew up, Khanga was the only black person except for her mother. Born in 1962, one would expect her to experience some sort of racism during this time. Khanga later claims on her episode of the podcast This American Life that she never experienced any sort of social or institutional racism when she was growing up. She was always questioned about her looks and her race while growing up, but Khanga argues that she never experienced racism and only ever experienced ignorance as she was the only black person in her town. A specific example of Khanga experiencing ignorance rather than racism with her boyfriend back in Russia. Khanga’s boyfriend came up with the nickname “Monkey” while they were still dating. Khanga claims that this was not racist at all because her boyfriend had no intent to be racist or insulting.

The very beginning of this podcast, which is titled Get Back to Where You Once Belonged, listens to the hosts watch a clip out of a Soviet film from 1936 called Tsirk. This clip was during the climax of the film and includes a group of Soviet citizens make a show of accepting a mixed-race baby into their society. Being right before World War II and about 30 years before the Civil Rights Movement, this was very well before its time. This portrayal of the lack of racism in the Soviet Union was a very interesting and powerful segue into the story of Yelena Khanga.

Khanga is now a Russian journalist and television personality. When she first moved to the United States, it was almost impossible for her to assimilate to the African American culture. According to Harari, if the immigrant puts forth the effort to assimilate, then the country will treat them as one of their own citizens if they are willing. Even though Khanga put forth the effort, she could never fully assimilate to African American culture because she could never understand what these African American men and women were going through in terms of racism. It was extremely difficult for Khanga to date or create any meaningful relationships because the hardships of African Americans at this time had such a strong influence on African American culture.

Khanga’s experience is a unique example of how Harari’s basic conditions for immigration is not accurate for all people looking to emigrate to another country or all countries that are accepting immigrants. Though Harari’s three basic conditions are very general, it still does not apply to everybody’s situation. Khanga was never able to fully assimilate to African American culture in the United States.

Harari’s book, 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, included many interesting ways to analyze problems in our world today and problems that one must keep an eye out for in the future. A lot of these concepts would totally agree with other sociological approaches from other sociologists, politicians, writer, and even real-life scenarios and situations. Some people may also disagree with a lot of these concepts and believe that Harari is not completely accurate. No one is right or wrong in this subject as everything is based on perspective.
chunks.label: Analyzing Harari, Marx, and Khanga's narrative
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Yuval Noah Harari's book '21 Lessons for the 21st Century', comparing his arguments on technology and alienation with Karl Marx's 'Estranged Labor', and evaluates his theories on immigration using Yelena Khanga's life story from a podcast.

n27c59cb9.title: Analyzing Collective Consciousness and Intersectional Oppression

chunks.text:
Durkhiem goes into detail and explains that overall we as humans typically have some of the same values. However, there are values that are held in some cultures but not in others leading to a different collective consciousness in each culture. These differences have been linked to genocides,wars and oppression throughout all of human history. For example, the Rowandan Genocide of 1994 can be linked back to the different cultural practices of each group involved and can also be attributed to the different values held by colonial europeans that ultimately lead to the conflict.

Collins furthers this idea of different cultural collective consciousness. She talks about how different minority groups cannot be fully understood until their lives are studied with all the different groups they belong to are applied. She talks about how African American women often find empowerment by being the head of the household, where as in the eurocntric view of the family, its often seen as a shameful or bad thing to have and only mother. These different views lead to the matrix of domination. Minority groups who have different values and who view things differently are often oppressed and looked down upon by those in the majority. These groups that are most oppressed belong to interlinking minority groups and because of that, theres a compound affect on how they are treated by others.

Collective consciousness come from the demographic groups that we fall under. No one belongs to only one group of people. Its these webs of interlocking demographic groups that people belong to that build their personal collective consciousness. Because humans have an innate desire to be better than one another there is oppression against the minority groups and people who fall into multiple minority groups are the ones who are oppressed the most. Even today as the world sways toward a more progressive future, those groups are being marginlized and oppressed almost the same amount they were one hundred years ago.
chunks.label: Sociological concepts of collective consciousness and oppression
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Durkheim's and Collins's theories regarding cultural values, collective consciousness, interlocking minority groups, and the roots of societal oppression.

chunks.text:
While social media platforms have caused a revolution of new methods of communication and capturing technologies, it has also led a vast number of individuals into constant battles with their mental health. Not only has social media led to internal battles for individuals but it has also contributed to the growth of racial discrimination. Social media has allowed people to share their opinions and beliefs about these controversial topics. Many individuals have been left wondering whether the negative impacts social media outweigh the positive. Social media platforms can lead to very destructive life patterns. While social media can be related to the spread of racial discrimination, it has also strengthened concepts such as the gender role that society has formed. Throughout this paper I will discuss how social media can pull us in and contribute to the spread of racial discrimination, strengthen our concept of gender roles, and also have a huge impact on one’s mental health and identity.

While we identify ourselves as male or female from the day we are born, society and our interactions within it on a daily basis influence our idea of gender and what we associate with. The role of gender and sex has always been a very controversial issue across our world. Are men superior to women? What is the difference between one’s gender and sex? These are just a few of the question’s individuals have been grappling with for a long time. In order to provide some clarity to those questions, most people stumble across the following assumptions; one’s sex is identified at birth and is either male or female while one’s gender is more complicated. Gender is best described as either masculine or feminine. In the Yellow Wallpaper by Charlotte Perkins Gilman, it goes into depth about how the character felt like she had to act and behave in a particular way and that her husband was superior. The character begins to describe her house in much detail but the minute her husband approaches, she feels as though she has to stop what she is doing in fear that he would not approve. In a separate article, Women as Other by Simone de Beauvoir, Aristotle states “We should regard women’s nature as suffering from natural defectiveness.” Both of the previous articles have parts that feel dehumanizing to women within the society. The articles make women think they are less than men. While that may have been true in past generations and societies, it should not still be the case today. Just because someone is female does mean that they are capable of what a male is capable of. Society has drilled this idea of gender superiority into our minds. Not only that, but they also convinced us that we have to act a certain way depending on our gender in order to fit into society.

Social media content also has an overwhelmingly big impact on the concept of gender roles. Kids grow up constantly engaged on these social media platforms and whether they realize it or not, their minds are consistently forming ideas of what is considered normal by society. Gender role stereotypes are abundant on these platforms. Social media is full of celebrities and even media models. In many cases, their posts contribute to these standards because others look at their posts and tell themselves that they need to look like that. For many women, they feel as though they need to be tan and skinny and have it all together. They also feel like they have to buy cute and expensive clothes to fit in. Majority of men feel as though they have to be lean and muscular. When the truth is that these are impossible standards that we do not need to commit our time to. We need to realize that it does not matter what we look like or how we dress.

Not only do we grow up being drilled with gender norms, but we also grow up being taught, usually unconsciously, the differences between various races and the privileges that tend to arise with each one. There is also an interconnection between gender and race when it comes to society norms. The idea of black feminism mentioned in The Matrix of Denomination by Patricia Hill Collins brings these concepts together and does a good job referring to how they are all intertwined with one another. As Collins states, “the significance of seeing race, class, and gender as interlocking systems of oppression is that such an approach fosters a paradigmatic shift of thinking inclusively about other oppressions.” When it comes to black feminism, not only is gender an evident issue, but race is as well. Black feminists are argued to be the one of the most oppressed. This provides them with a unique understanding and knowledge. Advocates for black feminism are stripped from privileges other individuals such as men or white women are usually given. Many individuals do not notice or even pay any attention to the differences in treatment these groups receive and have almost been brain washed to think this is all normal.

In some cases, social media can appear to be contributing to the spread of racial discrimination. One scenario that is a great example is the fact that majority of celebrities and models in the past have been white. In the past majority of companies post an advertisement on social media platforms, most of the posts include a white celebrity or model. Although that is beginning to shift in the right direction, I still do not believe that we are where we should be. While we have the ability to use social media for the better and use it to make a difference, we first need to come to the realization that there is a change that needs to be made. Our society is leading us further down a path of gender and social prejudice. While each culture and society are unique from one another, they seem to be all brainwashing individuals in some way. Not only in a negative way but social media can also have impacts on society in a positive way. Especially over the past year with everything that has been going on in the world, people have been using social media platforms to help spread the word and raise awareness. Many individuals are also using these platforms to take the opportunity to inform themselves on these topics or even help reach out to others. After the death of George Floyd, social media platforms such as Instagram blew up with posts on the topic. Many brands, influencers, organizations, and even celebrities took this time to do what they could to help and make a difference. In some cases, it was something small like posting their throughout and trying to raise awareness on the issue. Some even registered for peaceful protests and encouraged others to do the same. Social media has the power to make a huge impact on this issue of racial discrimination but ultimately it comes down to whether or not we can realize there is a problem and then decide to do something about it. We need to move past the stigmas that society has engraved in our minds and come together.

As social media becomes more relevant, it begins to take over certain areas of people’s lives. These platforms can become very controlling and often contribute to the standards that society forms around the concept of body image. People rely so heavily on these apps to determine what we are supposed to look like. We often find ourselves caught up in the trap of comparing ourselves to others and feeling overwhelmingly judged by others. According to Julie Andsager, “Social media messages have the potential to present much more diverse representations of female and male bodies because they are mostly produced and disseminated by individuals”. As a society, we are approaching a point where we are allowing social media platforms to take over. These platforms are full of unrealistic body images due to overly edited and even photoshopped images. Many individuals, especially young females feel as though they have to live and look like the other females that fill up their social media feed. It is shocking how many individuals are willing to go to extreme measures in order to work towards changing their appearance. This need for change can often result in eating disorders. While social media is not the cause of eating disorders, there is a link between the two without a doubt. Today’s society is seeking approval from others in order to feel better about themselves and their appearance. This dependency and added pressure to appear perfect can act as a trigger for disordered eating.

Not only do social media platforms contribute to the rise of eating disorders, but it also plays a big role in the increase of mental health illnesses. Some of the most common mental health issues that arise with social media use are depression and anxiety. People tend to feel as though they have to have everything together on social media. Majority of individuals find themselves in a constant battle with anxiety partly because of these platforms. A study done in 2019 by Common Sense Media showed that teenagers spend an astonishing 7 hours and 22 minutes a day using mobile devices. That is not including time spent online for schoolwork. I would assume that since that study has been conducted, that number has increased. Not only do people spend a surprisingly vast amount of time on smart phones each day, but there have also been new anxiety disorders arise through the excessive use of social media. Social Media Anxiety Disorder has become a fairly common mental illness. It is related to Social Anxiety and is when we become too attached and dependent on social media. It can often lead to other mental illnesses like Obsessive-compulsive disorder or depression if not dealt with in a proper and healthy way. Social media has built up these false claims that we should not struggle with mental illness and in some cases can make many individuals feel as though something is wrong with them if they are struggling with depression or anxiety. They often feel as though they have to put up walls and think they can only post about certain things. As a society we need to break the stigmas that arise with social media platforms and mental health disorders. If we allow these issues to grow, they will eventually take over aspects of our lives if they have not already.

Social media platforms have led a rather large number of individuals into constant battles with their mental health. While social media has provided people with a space to share their opinions and beliefs about these controversial topics, it has also created a space where people often feel overwhelmingly judged or find themselves constantly judging others. Social media platforms can lead to very destructive life patterns f we do not take the proper steps in order to prevent that from happening. While these platforms can be tied to the spread of racial discrimination, it can also be used to slow the spread if we are willing to make the change. We have allowed it to strengthened concepts such as the gender roles that society has engraved in our minds. Social media can reel us in and contribute to the spread of racial discrimination, strengthen our negative concepts of gender roles, and also have a big impact on one’s mental health and body image. If we do not come to the realization that something needs to be changed that there is a problem within our society, things are going to continue to get worse. Individuals are going to sink into darker and more dangerous battles with mental illnesses and identity issues. Individuals will continue to feel stuck in a trap of judgment when using social media platforms. We need to shift our perspective from allowing society norms and social media to shape us to making the decision that these things do not have to have control over us if we do not let it.

chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how social media and societal norms affect mental health, gender roles, body image, and racial discrimination, referencing academic texts and concluding with a Works Cited list.

chunks.text:
A name or ideal that has been a focal point for human beings which goes as far back as we know is God. The idea of God is something we have no real proof of besides us deducing he must be the cause of things that cannot be explained scientifically. In 21 Lessons for the 21st Century, Harari argues in part 3 chapter 13 that God is something that is a mystery of existence, yet many people fall into some belief on the matter. The concept of that enables us all and Harari to even be able to have our beliefs or disbeliefs in God is our collective consciousness. The collective consciousness’ formation allowed religious beliefs to be carried out and without it, most people would likely not even be aware of a God at all.

Harari argues that we do not need God to lead us to live a moral life and how God is something that differs so greatly in everyone’s minds. According to Harari, the whole concept of God is something derived from our inability to explain many events without it being the work of some godly being. For us to even be able to have our different religious beliefs and groups, the collective consciousness is a necessary aspect. Durkheim argues for the idea of the collective consciousness to be a set of beliefs or ideals which act as a unifying source within society. The whole idea of God is something that is enabled by the collective consciousness and a prime example within likely every society. Without the development of language, we could not possibly have the collective consciousness which would therefore prohibit God from even being known to many. The different religions that Harari talks about and how they differ are different collective consciousness’ within different societies, which connect back to his argument about using God’s name to invoke a moral life in some way based off the specific religion.

The whole unknown idea of God that we all are aware of is only possibly spread due to the collective consciousness’ existence. Depending on the religion or beliefs someone aligns themselves with will determine the way they use God’s name to try to live a moral life. Harari’s argument is derived from the existence of the collective consciousness explained by Durkheim. While we all have our own individual beliefs in God, we can still live a moral life in our own ways without invoking his name to do so.
chunks.label: Collective consciousness and the concept of God
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Harari's and Durkheim's arguments regarding the concept of God, morality, and how collective consciousness enables religious beliefs to form and spread.

n5a8796dc.title: Perceptions of Class and Media Influence

chunks.text:
Money has been, and always will be, associated with power. Social classes are groups within a hierarchy, based on wealth, income, education, and occupation. In the United States, there is a simple three class system: the upper, middle and lower class. As people are grouped into one of the classes, they adopt that class’s collective consciousness. Social media can also have a great impact on

In “Class in America”, Gregory Mantsios breaks down the myths that are associated with class. He makes the connection of class, wealth and education. People born into the upper class have access to better education, live in better areas, and will most likely remain a member of the upper class for their entire lives. People born into the middle and lower classes typically go to large public schools, live in less desirable areas, and will also most likely remain within their class for the rest of their lives. “The Class-Domination Theory of Power”, written by G. William Domhoff, discusses power in relation to wealth and the collective consciousness of those within each class. Members of each class have very different ideas and priorities. They differ on issues such as taxation, conservation, and welfare.

Mainstream media plays a part in forming our collective consciousness. Ads are created that target the lower and middle classes. These ads cause people to believe that some products are used and prioritized by members of the upper class in order to trick consumers into spending money on them, while the upper c

lass profits. Social media allows people to post content showing a “typical day in their life”, causing people to believe that people who are wealthy live a lavish lifestyle filled with expensive cars, clothes and food.

The concept of class will forever be an uncomfortable topic of discussion.

The concept of class is an uncomfortable topic of discussion. Social classes are parts of a hierarchy, based on things like wealth, education, and occupation. Three classes exist in the United States: the upper, middle and lower class. With each class comes differing ideas and priorities.

Mainstream media plays a large part in forming our collective consciousness. Members of the upper class are idolized and thought to be what we should aspire to be. Rather than focusing on how unfair it is that these people get paid so much more than everyone else, we are taught to glamorize their lifestyles. Members of the middle class are largely represented in media, typically in movies and TV shows, as most people are able to better identify and connect with the characters if they have similarities to themselves. Media portrays members of the lower class as being dirty, reckless and uneducated. Media creates stereotypes of people belonging to each of the social classes, which then influences our collective consciousness.

In “Class in America”, Gregory Mantsios states that street life and the lavish lifestyles of the rich are models for what to avoid and what we should aspire to be. The United States has some of the most well-hidden poverty in the world, as designer clothing is marketed to target members of the middle and lower classes in order to “allow them to experience luxury”. Designer products allow people to put on a show tIn “Power in America”, G. William Domhoff says that money is a vessel for domination and control of other social classes. Those with the most money are able to set the terms and conditions under which others must follow.

Class will forever be an uncomfortable topic of discussion. Mainstream media has a great effect on the collective consciousness of people belonging to each of the social classes. We need to work toward social equality, rather than striving to be rich, in order to improve the lifestyles of the less fortunate.
chunks.label: Reflecting on social class and media
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological concepts of class hierarchy, power, and collective consciousness, drawing from texts by Gregory Mantsios and G. William Domhoff, and examines how mainstream and social media perpetuate class stereotypes and consumerism.

chunks.text:
Will it ever be possible to fully understand and dismantle oppression in our world? It is necessary to understand terms such as intersectionality and the matrix of domination to attack this question. These ideas help break down what oppression and domination are and how they can be stopped. One must understand their own experiences with oppression and even their own experience with privilege before one can begin to contribute to the dismantling of oppression.

This would be a good time to describe my own experience with oppression, more specifically the lack thereof given my situation as a heterosexual, white, male. The privilege was prevalent, and subconscious throughout my childhood as I was oblivious to most kinds of oppression and what was going on in our world, outside of my own life.
chunks.label: Understanding oppression and personal privilege
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the necessity of understanding oppression, privilege, and terms like intersectionality before attempting to dismantle oppression, acknowledging their own privilege as a heterosexual white male.

chunks.text:
I came to this conclusion at a time I can only describe as an embarrassingly late age when I found out that Uncle Terry, my dad’s best friend from his childhood who is also black, wasn’t my uncle. Thinking back on the time I have spent with Uncle Terry; I recall a time when he told me about “the talk” that he had with his parents when he was younger. “The talk” was given to inform him and his siblings how to deal with the police if they ever were to encounter them. He described it as a very serious, hard, and sad talk to have with his parents.

Hearing this story was astounding for me at the time because I felt that I never really had a reason to fear the police.
chunks.label: Uncle Terry's conversation about the talk
chunks.what_happened: The student recalls learning that their father's Black childhood friend, Uncle Terry, was not a biological uncle, and remembers Terry telling them about having 'the talk' with his parents about how to handle encounters with the police.
chunks.people: father, Uncle Terry, Uncle Terry's parents, Uncle Terry's siblings

chunks.text:
As I got a little older, learned more about current events and oppression in our world, I realized that racism was only one of the many levels of oppression in our society.

This realization of mine was me grasping the idea of intersectionality. Intersectionality is a term that was coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw who was a pioneering writer on civil rights, critical race theory, and Black feminist legal theory. Crenshaw defined the term to describe how many individual characteristics intersect with one another and overlap. These individual characteristics include race, gender, sexuality, class, religion, and anything else that is used to define a person. She defined and introduced this theory in 1989 with her paper “Demarginalizing the Intersection of Race and Sex: A Black Feminist Critique of Antidiscrimination Doctrine, Feminist Theory, and Antiracist Politics.” Crenshaw used intersectionality to convey that being black and being a woman is not independent of one another. Intersectionality has become more widely known over time and has become mainstream over the past ten years.
chunks.label: Explanation of Crenshaw's intersectionality
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how learning about oppression led to understanding Kimberle Crenshaw's concept of intersectionality and how overlapping identities function.

chunks.text: I know that my Uncle Terry has been approached by police in his life, though I am not quite sure how it played out, his situation could be described using intersectionality. Not only was he black, but he is also a man which may be thought of by the police to be more of a threat than say a black woman or even a white man. Since intersectionality includes all aspects of one’s character, even height could be a factor. Terry is around 6’3”-6’4” which definitely would have played a role in that situation. Intersectionality also counts privileges on top of oppression. A privilege that I know Terry has is that he is highly educated which would also have influenced his situation. His position of oppression most likely outweighs his privilege in this scenario.
chunks.label: Applying intersectionality to Uncle Terry
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Uncle Terry's hypothetical or past encounters with police using intersectionality, considering factors like his race, gender, height, and education level.

chunks.text: People can be privileged and oppressed at the same time, just adding to the complexities of domination and oppression in our society. The Intersecting Axes of Privilege, Domination, and Oppression was adapted from Kathryn Pauly Morgan, “Describing the Emperor’s New Clothes: Three Myths of Educational (In)Equality.” The graph is made up of two sides, one listing the axes of privilege and the other listing the axes of oppression. For example, the axes include genderism, sexism or androcentrism, racism, eurocentrism, heterosexism, ableism, educationalism, ageism, politics of appearance, classicism, language bias, colorism, anti-Semitism, and pro-natalism. This graph does a great job breaking down the many levels of privilege and oppression without overlapping the social identities.
chunks.label: Morgan's axes of privilege and oppression
chunks.what_happened: The student describes Kathryn Pauly Morgan's graph depicting intersecting axes of privilege, domination, and oppression.

chunks.text:
Patricia Hill Collins was another person who played a major role in analyzing problems with oppression. She is a distinguished sociology professor at the University of Maryland, College Park. She integrated ideas of intersectionality and coined the phrase “matrix of domination” in her writing “Black Feminist Thought in the Matrix of Domination.” In her writing, she emphasizes how Afrocentric feminist thought “demonstrates Black women’s emerging power as agents of knowledge. By portraying African American women as self-defined, self-reliant individuals confronting race, gender, and class oppression.”

Collins integrates intersectionality in her writing by portraying African American women as agents of knowledge. According to the idea of intersectionality, few people are entirely a victim or entirely an oppressor. Some individuals display privileges and oppression. Collins is emphasizing how African American women are one of the few people with so much oppression based on their identity. She also emphasizes how this position that African American women are in is necessary and must be used to produce Black feminist thought. This is very difficult to accomplish because it also requires an African American woman to overcome the widely known, Eurocentric ideologies. It is necessary because as much as white feminists point out their oppression as being a woman, they unintentionally refuse to see their privileges of being white. This reinforces the idea of the matrix of domination and intersectionality and how race and gender cannot be independent of one another.
chunks.label: Patricia Hill Collins and Black feminist thought
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Patricia Hill Collins's concept of the matrix of domination and the role of Afrocentric feminist thought in confronting oppression.

chunks.text:
Through Collins’ analysis of the matrix of domination, she includes the multiple levels of domination. The three levels people experience oppression are the level of personal biography, the group or community level, and the systemic level of social institutions.

The level of personal biography focuses on the unique experiences, unique identities, and the relationships that follow. A situation of domestic violence is an example of oppression on the level of personal biography. These situations tend to have multiple points of view for interpretation. The level of personal biography is an example of how domination does not only occur through top-down processes.

The level that is shared by a group or community is the next example of how domination experiences and how oppression is resisted. This is where the cultural context of domination is found as groups can be defined by race, religion, age, class, and gender. Collins often focuses on this level of domination to emphasize the Afrocentric feminist group’s perspective.

The final level, and largest, is the systemic level in social institutions. This level includes all the examples of domination that occur in social institutions such as schools, churches, and the media. This is the level most people would think of when the topic of domination and oppression should arise.
chunks.label: The three levels of domination
chunks.what_happened: The student breaks down the three levels of domination defined by Collins: personal biography, group or community, and systemic social institutions.

chunks.text: Collins concludes her paper, “Black Feminist Thought in the Matrix of Domination,” by emphasizing the importance of dialogue and empathy. There is, what seems to be, an infinite number of perspectives and standpoints. Collin’s includes a quote by Elsa Barkley Brown where she claims that eventually such dialogues may get us to a point at which “all people can learn to center in another experience, validate it, and judge it by its standards without need of comparison or need to adopt that framework as their own. [In such dialogues], one does not need to ‘decenter’ anyone to center someone else; one has only to constantly, appropriately, ‘pivot the center.’” This quote emphasizes that it is important to be able to share one’s own unique experiences. On top of this, it is important to listen to other unique perspectives, learn about them, and respond.
chunks.label: Dialogue and empathy in Black feminist thought
chunks.what_happened: The student explores Collins's emphasis on dialogue and empathy, referencing a quote by Elsa Barkley Brown on centering other experiences.

chunks.text:
Much progress has been made to dismantle oppression in society and make way toward equality for all, but there is still much that needs to be done. Oppression, prejudice, racism, sexism, or anything that involves the domination of an individual or group, is so much more complex than it seems. Before we can attack these ideals and dismantle oppression, one must gain a better understanding of what oppression means and the many levels of domination and resistance. One can gain a better understanding through ideas and theories such as the matrix of domination and intersectionality.

Even though the solution to this problem may be far in the future, it is still very possible. The best way to continue to make progress toward equality is through children and young adults. Adding more classes that go farther into the depths of oppression in our society. These classes would include ideas that Patricia Hill Collins and Kimberlé Crenshaw emphasize in their papers along with many other ideas and concepts against oppression. One must point out examples of oppression instead of trying to ignore or forget. It is also important to point out privileges one has because of their characteristics.
