Identifying examples of oppression and privileges in one’s own life is the beginning of dismantling oppression in society today.
chunks.label: Steps toward dismantling oppression
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by proposing educational solutions, including teaching intersectionality and the matrix of domination to children and young adults to dismantle oppression.

nd81f79c4.title: Constructing Race Through Historical Imperial Conflict

chunks.text:
In Racial Formations it is stated that the reason behind racial conflict was political and social factors rather than biological ones. Coming back to the idea that race is a result of differences between collective consciousnesses, it references how when Europeans were met with Natives in the New World the very fact that the natives existed had challenged their beliefs about the world. They thought themselves as children of god and that since these natives, whose collective consciousness did not align with their worldly views, were not. This world view gave them the explanation they needed in order to deny the humanity of these newly discovered races.

This example of conflict goes to show how race is defined and molded by the collective consciousness. One collective consciousness came into contact with another and their beliefs were challenged by the existence of it. As a result these imperialists followed their collective beliefs to come up with the assumption that this new race was one they had to convert and show them the correct path. This mindset became fact to them as well as the rest of their collective.
chunks.label: Reflections on Racial Formations and collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on concepts from Racial Formations, discussing how European imperialists encountered Natives in the New World and used differences in collective consciousness to deny their humanity and justify conversion.

n2efc8c63.title: Understanding Race as a Social Construct

chunks.text:
The concept of race is a relatively new idea, coming to fruition as European colonizers came across natives who had a different physical appearance. Humans now group themselves into different “races”, often based on inherited traits, despite there being no basis of race linked to genetics. The concept of race and racism can therefore be connected to the collective consciousness.

The collective consciousness also causes us to stereotype people that identify with certain races. Omi and Winant state that we often become disoriented when people do not act within their “race”, leading to microaggressions like saying “You don’t sound black” or “You’re so articulate”. These things are rarely said to white people, but are said to people of color due to the misconception that people of color are less intelligent.

Acts of racism and microaggressions can easily become part of the collective consciousness. Without anyone to stand up against these acts, they continue occurring, being passed around different groups worldwide.
chunks.label: Race, stereotyping, and the collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how race is a social construct tied to the collective consciousness, leading to stereotyping, microaggressions, and perpetuated racism.

n8b786d3a.title: Intersections of Race, Gender, and Sexuality

chunks.text:
When we are born, we are automatically assigned certain roles that we have no control over. The main things predetermined are race and gender. Along with these main features, everyone eventually grows into the third main category which is sexuality. In “The Matrix of Domination” Collins described how race, gender, and sexuality together create an intersection to a certain configuration for each individual that are rank ordered. The matrix of domination explains Omi and Winant’s argument in “Racial Formations” that race is a big factor determining how you are seen and treated by society.

Omi and Winant discuss how race has determined how you are seen and treated by others for a long time. They talk about how people of minority races may be seen as lower class and treated poorly by others and how some people may be seen as higher class from their race alone. The idea of this is not something anyone has any control over but rather their fate in the matter was decided upon birth. Even though some races may differ slightly, the concept of being a different race will alter how you are looked at by others regardless of how close you may be to another race.

The idea of the matrix of domination supports this argument. The matrix states how if you are white, black, or some other race you will automatically fall into a different configuration depending upon the other two categories as well. Collins concept of the matrix shows how if you are a minority race, you will automatically be lower on the rank order and be a lower preference in many things. Although there are still other factors that determine your configuration with the matrix, you will rank higher or lower due to being a majority or minority race.

Race is something everyone has that will be a big factor determining symbolic order based off racial disparities. Omi and Winant’s argument of different races having different experiences in their society can be supported by Collins concept of the matrix of domination. Everyone’s order in the world’s preferences will be partially decided by race and along with gender and sexuality, your configuration can determine how easy or difficult your life may be. Race is a big part of the matrix and whatever race you happen to be born into, can drastically change your whole life ahead of you.
chunks.label: The matrix of domination and racial formations
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological concepts from Collins, Omi, and Winant, explaining how race, gender, and sexuality create intersecting configurations that influence how people are ranked and treated in society.

n05f2adab.title: Analyzing Gender Bias in Modern Society

chunks.text:
As a whole the human race is unified under our biology, but that's the extent of our unity. The world is split into thousands of different groups and it would seem unlikely that gender is a major divider, seeing as how it's the most basic and closely related to biology a division can get. However, gender is one of the most taxing and heavily debated topics of recent history. There are many arguments to be had over the gender topic such as what the actual phrase “gender” really means, or how one decides what gender they belong to. But one has been on the forefront of politics and pop culture for the last one hundred years. The roles in which gender plays in society is a topic that has been written about and discussed for hundreds of years, and there's no end in sight. In 1760 the industrial revolution began. Women, who were key members of the farm to table industry, or the cottage industry (societal complex where goods were made in the home and sold elsewhere) were overlooked for jobs in the factories and instead stayed home to educate and to care for children.During the First and Second world wars we see that women all over the world were the only able bodied individuals that were able to help provide for the soldiers who were off fighting a war. During those times the world saw the rise of Rosie the Riveter, a fiction character that was created to encourage women to join the workforce and manufacture war supplies. Again, women working in a factory in the year 1942 assembling tanks and bullets is nowhere near what women were doing in 1842. A Lot has indeed changed since then, in the year 2021 it's been a little over a century since women in the United States gained the right to vote. Ever since then, women have been working their way into the workforce and into positions of power. In the 2020 election, the United States constituents voted their first woman vice president into office. This job is ofcourse a far cry from the typical job a woman would hold in the year 1921. Not only are women in elected offices now, but women have also made great strides in the workforce.

These events bring the discussion to the present day. Women in countries like Saudi Arabia are still fighting for their rights to drive cars, and they’re lightyears away from being able to vote. Meanwhile, women in the United States are still fighting for equal pay while performing the same job as men. The United States has yet to elect the first woman president. In countries around the world some women are still fighting for the right to vote, or even drive cars. Although women in some parts of the world have made great strides towards living in equality, there is a long road ahead. Just think, it took women in the US from the year 1776, when the colonies gained independence, to the year 1919, when the 19th amendment was passed allowing all citizens of the United states who were females to vote. That 143 years of no representation in their own governing body. The fight for equality still continues today, we can see it in workplaces in 2021, and while women may be able to vote in the US, discrimination still takes place.

While women do have the ability to obtain and hold jobs at a higher level, many women struggle to be selected for those positions. In many of the world's top businesses there is an “implicit gender bias” that holds women back from being accepted into higher level positions (Rogus-Pulia et al., 2018). The “implicit gender bias” is ingrained to the subconscious of men who are already in positions of power that make the decisions when it comes to hiring new people (Rogus-Pulia et al., 2018). Gender stereotypes are often known but not noticed. This plays into what “The Beauty Myth” (Wolf, 2015) is all about. The Beauty Myth is that women are held to higher standards when it comes to physical attractiveness simply because they are a woman. Those are the types of stereotypes that affect women in today’s world. When it comes to hiring new employees, women also face a greater level of stereotyping than their male counterpart applicant would (Rogus-Pulia et al., 2018). There's also the age-old stereotype of having a “woman’s job” or a “man's job”. Meaning that for so long men were the predominant gender in that job so it's now unconsciously seen as a man's job to hold. For instance, when you picture a coal miner, do you picture a woman wearing a hard hat covered in soot? No. Most people would describe a big burly man who was covered in coal with a pickaxe. Or when asked to picture a teacher, nurse or babysitter do you picture a woman? Yes. Most people would say that they picture a woman in one or all of these professions. That simple thought experiment underlines one of the key points of this study. To put it in more mathematical terms: “When at least 75% of the occupants of a job are men, the job is assumed to require stereotypically male, agentic qualities, and when at least 75% are women, the job is assumed to require stereotypically female, communal qualities (Cejka & Eagly, 1999; Glick, Wilk, & Perreault, 1995).” (Rogus-Pulia et al., 2018). This is an example of the walls that are put up between true equality for women in the workplace. Men in higher positions are often unaware and or ignore/directly use their bias against women and because of that the chances for women to advance in the workplace are diminished significantly. Training and more effective hiring practices should be used in the workplace. It will take a conscious effort to reverse the already ingrained implicit bias against women and there hasn't been much effort made.

The bias doesn't just stop in business. In the S.T.E.M. fields of study, there is much evidence to suggest that gender bias still exists there as well. However, the evidence for the suppression of women here doesn't come from the hiring process (but as i've previously underlined, I’m sure it still exists), it instead comes from the education that is needed to obtain a successful career in the STEM field. In data taken from a 2015 study, there is a major red flag when it comes to women’s advancements in their education in the STEM fields (Robnett, 2015). In particular, female students who are progressing through their education drop in numbers the closer they get to obtaining their doctorate degrees (Robnett, 2015). The bias in education stops women from even getting to attempt a career in their field of study. Robnett’s article suggests that the most bias comes from their male peers. The pressure and intimidation that exists in the field of study is enough to drive down the numbers of women who think they can make it in the stem field, leading to obvious results like less female representations in physics, engineering and other higher level STEM professions (Robnett, 2015).

There is however, a bright side to the studies' conclusions. When peer support networks were well established, the gender bias had significantly less effect on the number of women that were attempting to make a career in the STEM field (Robnett, 2015).” This pattern suggests that the consequences of gender bias are lessened if girls and women also have a supportive peer network in their area of study (Robnett, 2015).” Support within the field of study was proven through mathematical data to have a positive effect on the success of women in education (Robnett, 2015). If these systems were employed outside of just the educational realm, the results could be groundbreaking for the advancement of women in the world.

All of these studies and examples build on the idea that gender was and is still a major issue for the advancement of our society. Like many great authors like Gilman, Beauvoir, Stroud, and Wolf have said, women face a variety of inequalities in the world. One common factor seems to the ideology of men being superior to women. This concept has fostered the growth of institutional practices that are built to put down women. For example, the concept of a man's job or a woman's job. That idea alone is the basis of issues that can arise for women in education, the workplace, and in trying to develop a sense of self. In practically all areas of life, whether it's getting a job, having an education, or simply trying to live as a human in society women are put down by men who have a deeply embedded superiority complex.

The fight for the equality of women in the world has been going on for a long time. The results of this fight differ in different areas of the world. In the US women are seen as equals to men in the eyes of the law but are not treated as such when it comes to being fully accepted in the workplace or in academia. Women in Saudi Arabia are seen as lesser humans and are treated as such. Regardless of the religious ideology that is passed around, women are humans and should be treated as such. This isn't a process that we should just simply sit back and let time do the work. As I mentioned earlier, there are ways to support women in the pursuit of equality. The Robnett study done in 2015 showed promising signs that support groups that identified the bias against women and had cross gender support, benefited female students in their sense of belonging in the STEM field (Robnett, 2015). There simply isn't enough being done by the other half of the population, and the reason why is apparent. Men who grow up in a society that already has a male superiority complex established, are of course, by nature, going to grow into that superiority complex and hence further infatuate the issue. Overall, there needs to be more education around the fact that males have a tendency to overlook and try to overpower their female counterparts, in means that aren’t necessarily physical. There also needs to be more education of the situations that women find themselves in, in other parts of the world. While the United States has made great strides in the advancement of women in society, there are many places around the world that have women in the same situation that they were in hundreds of years ago.

In the US, we have the resources and knowledge to actually do something about the mistreatment of women. Underlining the issue at a young age should be the first step in teaching young adult males that it is their obligation to treat their female peers and counterparts as equals without any form of bias. Furthermore, there should be more done in the legislation of making sure that males and females are treated equally when it comes to hiring processes and workplace equality. The wage gap is a concept that has been talked about for many years now yet no legislation on the matter has been passed. It ought to be the governing bodies responsibility to enforce true equality, especially in countries that are built on the equality of all, for example, the United States. However, it is not surprising that legislation like this has yet to be passed, remembering that a large portion of the congress and senate are males. Women are biologically just as equipped as men; we have the science and years of performance data to prove it. Yet there is still enough evidence for me to write this paper about how unequal the world really treats women.
chunks.label: Gender inequality in history, STEM, and society
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the history of gender roles, workplace bias, underrepresentation of women in STEM fields, and the need for societal and legislative change.

n3f43a6df.title: Navigating Veteran Identity in College Classrooms

chunks.text:
An in-depth look at the unique sub-culture of U.S. Military veterans from a sociological perspective

Tattooed, with short-cropped hair and walking with a self-assured swagger, veterans are easily identifiable in contemporary society. Emphasizing honor, duty, and patriotism while also encouraging tattoos, aggressiveness, and foul language, veteran sub-culture can be as unique as it is vexing to those who’ve never experienced it first-hand. Unlike most other professions in modern society, military service molds for its adherents a new identity and culture that sticks with its individuals for life. Through training, deployments, combat, and camaraderie, veterans have developed similar values, beliefs, and sense of self identity in stark contrast to who they were before. Service in the United States Military, more so than any other culture or sub-culture, is able to forge a new and lifelong culture out of innumerable different individual identities and cultures.
chunks.label: Introduction to U.S. military veteran subculture
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the distinct characteristics, values, and shared identity of U.S. military veterans from a sociological perspective.

chunks.text: A few weeks ago in my introduction to Film Studies class, we watched a very avant-garde film which featured a live childbirth scene. This scene was graphic and didn’t hold anything back: a series of direct shots of a child being born, with very little editing done to conceal any of the viscera or vivid imagery that went along with such a process. Needless to say, this scene turned some stomachs amongst the students viewing it; so much so that one of my classmates vomited during the scene. In response to this, the film was stopped, and the lights were turned on to ensure the safety of the unfortunate student who had succumbed to the graphic images shown on screen. It was at this moment that I unknowingly and subconsciously reacted with an act that would be widely considered uncouth and inappropriate in most civilian circles: I cheered.
chunks.label: Cheering in Film Studies class
chunks.what_happened: In a Film Studies class, a classmate vomited during a graphic childbirth scene, and the student subconsciously cheered when the lights came on.

chunks.text: Is this because I’m a sadist who enjoys seeing pain in others? Is it because my own pride is dependent upon seeing others fail where I succeed? Is it because I’m unable to read social situations appropriately and chose the wrong reaction to such an event? The answer is much more nuanced and involves many layers of enculturation.
chunks.label: Pondering the reaction to the classmate
chunks.what_happened: The student questions why they cheered and attributes the reaction to deep enculturation rather than sadism or social inability.

chunks.text: Drawing on my own personal experience from the Marine Corps, there is a saying: pain is weakness leaving the body. This saying permeates throughout all aspects of life in the Marine Corps – be it physical training, sleep deprivation, or studying for tests. Consequently, when Marines see others enduring physical pain but pushing through, it is seen as the individual experiencing pain become stronger. There is no better example of this than the infamous “Indian run”. This particularly grueling exercise involves a group of around twelve Marines running in a single file line, with the Marine at the front of the line holding an ammunition can usually weighing around thirty pounds. While still running, the Marine at the front will pass the can to the Marine behind them, then to the Marine behind them, until it reaches the Marine at the back of the line. The last Marine will then sprint to the front, carrying the can the entire time, and start the process all over again. This process can last for miles, and many Marines end up vomiting from the physical strain. However, more often than not, the exhausted Marine will get back in line and continue the training. This process of overcoming physical pain and pushing through what was believed to be the absolute physical limit is often met with cheers and rallying cries from onlookers, because it is perceived to be the act of becoming stronger in real time.
chunks.label: Marine Corps culture and the Indian run
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the Marine Corps ethos that pain is weakness leaving the body, describing the grueling 'Indian run' exercise and why onlookers cheer when runners push through exhaustion.

chunks.text:
So by cheering at my fellow student for getting sick at a film, was I being insensitive? Or, much more plausibly, was I enacting a response engrained in me by the culture of “shedding weakness through physical hardship”? Much like active military culture, veteran culture holds toughness, aggressiveness, and tenacity as sacred values.

This focus on resilience and steadfastness plants deep roots within the souls of those served in the military, carrying over into the veteran culture. When in active military service, veterans witnessed the real-world necessity of these values played out, further deepening their importance in the minds of veterans. Veterans have witnessed first-hand the effects of great triumph of high achievement and the disastrous consequences of giving up, which are incredibly unifying ideals when uniting so many from a variety of different cultures and upbringings. These ideals cement themselves so concretely in the hearts of veterans that they leave an indelible mark on the psyche of the veteran even after leaving service.
chunks.label: Connecting military values to veteran culture
chunks.what_happened: The student connects their reaction in class to the military value of overcoming physical hardship, discussing how toughness and resilience carry over into veteran culture.

chunks.text: The French scholar Emile Durkheim observed that any given society develops what he called a “collective consciousness”. This consciousness is the amalgamation of what is to be highly regarded in a society and what is to be avoided – what is morally good and what is morally wrong. Furthermore, this consciousness, as Durkheim points out, is what unifies individuals into a society, merging individuals into a stream of relatively common thought. This unifying cohesion of what values ought to be held sacred can further manifest itself in collective representations, that is, tangible representations of intangible ideas. A cross, for example, may appear simply to be two bisecting lines, but believers may see it as a representation of the Christian faith. A crescent moon and star may seem to be two celestial bodies next to one another but may represent Islam and all of its pillars to others. These symbols are indeed representations of the collective consciousness, signifying what values and beliefs are desirable to the culture that holds them.
chunks.label: Durkheim's collective consciousness and representations
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Emile Durkheim's sociological theories of collective consciousness and collective representations using religious symbols as examples.

chunks.text: Collective representations of the collective consciousness of military culture are abundant and clearly encompass military values. Many symbols will often include skulls, rifles, predatory animals, and stars, representing lethality, weapon mastery, tenacity, and patriotism, respectively. These symbols often conjure up images of brutal wartime prowess, like the skull and southern cross of the Marine Raiders, or historical patriotism, like the screaming eagle of the 101st airborne division. These representations of the collective consciousness are often held as holy relics to the veterans who served in those units, manifesting itself on t-shirts, buttons, or tattoos. They are seen as icons, representing a long and proud history in which they played a role; a sacred tradition they got to be a part of. It is through these symbols of the collective military consciousness that veterans develop and maintain their unique culture, as despite their time in active service being over, it remains a part of who they are.
chunks.label: Military symbols and veteran identity
chunks.what_happened: The student describes specific military insignia and symbols, showing how they embody the collective consciousness and sacred traditions of veterans.

chunks.text: Veteran sub-culture can safely be described, therefore, as a continuation of military culture. A culture that breaks down the potential clash of ideals of so many individuals from so many different societies and philosophies and rebuilds them as a unified identity. Through the pain and hardship and subsequent victories and achievements of the rigorous military life, a collective consciousness is born among those who served in the United States military unlike any other in contemporary societies. Through symbols and representations depicting a warrior culture and bonds of brotherhood, veterans maintain their values of honor, toughness, aggressiveness, and tenacity into their civilian lives. As Emilie Durkheim pointed out, this collective consciousness solidifies the values and aspirations of veterans stronger than any other culture so far seen in modern society.
chunks.label: Conclusion on veteran subculture
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that veteran subculture sustains a uniquely powerful collective consciousness rooted in military hardship, brotherhood, and shared symbols.

n2270216b.title: Reflecting on Racial Formation and Identity

chunks.text: Everyone puts their self-identity in something. It could be your job, the sport you play, your friends, etc. These are all things you invest your time into because they interest you and you usually want to be identified by what you do. Race is a completely social constructed identity, but not something you can pick. Over time certain races have developed stereotypes. These stereotypes can often be what people define themselves by. The problem with this is it has developed a collective conscious thought that some races are superior to others. While your skin color doesn’t make you better or worse, the beliefs of society have affected what others believe about themselves.
chunks.label: Identity and socially constructed race
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how people form self-identity and argues that race is a socially constructed identity that has led to stereotypes and harmful beliefs about racial superiority.

chunks.text: In Racial Formations, the author describes racial formation as, “the process by which social economic, and political forces determine the content and importance of racial categories, and by which they are in turn shaped by racial meaning.” An example of this is how slavery created a sense of superiority in white people. They believed that African Americans were a “lesser human”, so they used them as slaves. Obviously, no race is superior, but this article says that white is seen as pure. This shows that a social consciousness of white being “superior” was developed, which is the reason we still have stereotypes for different races today. This article relates to The self and its selves from module 2. The author discusses how we have 3 different forms of self, the main one being social. This means that we are affected by what others think of us and how we are treated by others. So if for a large part of history African-Americans were treated as lesser than they are going to start to feel lesser than.
chunks.label: Course readings on racial formation and social self
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses course readings on racial formation and the social self, connecting them to the historical impact of slavery on racial stereotypes and internalized inferiority.

chunks.text: In conclusion race developed as the collective consciousness developed. Slavery had a huge impact on the collective consciousness believing our race can identify ourselves. Race developed by the social and became something we define ourselves as. Just like gender, we should not be prone to certain stereotypes based on race. The only way to change this view is to change the collective consciousness.
chunks.label: Conclusion on race and collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that race and stereotypes developed alongside collective consciousness, arguing that changing these views requires shifting the collective consciousness.

n23fd4f03.title: Chasing Dream Jobs in Capitalist Society

chunks.text: Everyone has a dream job, but not that many people do that job because it is simply just a dream. While it would be awesome to have your dream job, it usually doesn’t provide enough money for you to make a living. This is because of our capitalist society.
chunks.label: Dream jobs and capitalism
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how dream jobs often do not provide enough money to make a living because of capitalist society.

chunks.text: A quote from Confucious is, “ Choose a job you love , and you will never have to work a day in your life.” A quote from my Dad is, “Choose a good paying job that you like, so you can do the things that you love.” The idea of having a job you love makes perfect sense, but we live in a consumer society that has changed this quote around. People now measure success and happiness by how many things you have or how many extravagant things you do. The quality of life shouldn’t be measured by things, but if you are content where you are and have people you love surrounding you. Yes, work is probably going to be hard no matter what you do, but why do something everyday that you don’t enjoy?
chunks.label: Comparing quotes on work and consumer society
chunks.what_happened: The student contrasts quotes from Confucius and their father about choosing a job, reflecting on consumer culture and measuring quality of life.

chunks.text: The Iron Cage discusses how society has transformed into a capitalist society over time. Early societies were based on tradition and culture. As work ethic increased, these traditions decreased. As work became the center of society, this “iron cage” of capitalism developed, trapping consumers into the idea that commodities measure success. This relates to Marx, who discusses Commodity Fetishism. Which is the concept that the consumers decide the value of the commodity. The value of the work doesn't matter in a consumer society. This leads to people who do very hard work not being able to make a living because they don’t get any credit, the commodity does. He also talks about alienated labor, which is work in isolation. This is viewed as valueless in our society because if there is not a commodity it doesn’t matter in a market economy.
chunks.label: Sociological theories of capitalism and labor
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the concepts of the Iron Cage, commodity fetishism, and alienated labor in relation to how consumer society values commodities over workers.

chunks.text: In conclusion both of the authors discuss how our society bases value around commodities. The collective consciousness of capitalism has formed the idea in our society that work is not to make a living anymore but it has become our way of life. This ultimately pulls society apart because instead of working together to survive everyone is working against each other to higher their own status in society. The collective consciousness of capitalism must be dismantled in order to create a society in which tradition and culture unites people together to work for the greater good of the society as a whole.
chunks.label: Conclusion on dismantling capitalist consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that capitalism divides society and that its collective consciousness must be dismantled to unite people around tradition, culture, and the greater good.

n24a97c24.title: Hegemonic Masculinity in Marine Corps Culture

chunks.text: Do the strong only survive in the military? Circumstances may enable us to rethink otherwise. Considering our beliefs and out thought process it may be accurate to assume that in the United States Marine Corps, that this era of masculinity continues to play a role in this establishments. In many of these military groups we can conclude that having the mindset of hegemonic masculinity theses service members are affected from boot camp all the way to their end of service date. These service members are categorized on their positions and roles as leaders and followers, or as in military terms either a motivator or a shitbag. Both groups utilize their masculinity for physical and mental demands. These demands will either lead them to success or failure and although these categories have their benefits and disadvantages, both groups find a way to continue through their service and either make it skating through their career or excelling in their short time in service. Regardless of their time in the service marines will be a product of hegemonic masculinity.
chunks.label: Hegemonic masculinity in the Marine Corps
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the concept of hegemonic masculinity within the United States Marine Corps, explaining how service members are categorized as either motivators or shitbags from boot camp to the end of their service.

chunks.text: From the beginning of a service members career individuals are required to enter military boot camp training. During the transition from civilian to servicemember, men are put into platoons with a maximum of 100 other males in which they will use their performance of mental and physical abilities to gain positions within the platoon such as squad leader, guide, or scribe. These positions are important because they are a reflection of the drill instructors and a representation of the marines in the platoon as far as their discipline and motivation. These positions are known as the go getters or the motivators. In order to obtain these positions at the beginning marines conduct a physical fitness test to include a 1.5 mile run along with pull ups and crunches. The results of their physical fitness and motivation will ultimately land them a spot at one of the desired positions. These marines will display their masculinity by expressing their motivation through loud screaming, authoritative action towards other platoon members, and through their knowledge of basic marine corps manner. Their masculinity and authoritative actions will be highly viewed as alpha males within the platoon. During their roles above the common marines, they are able to scan to platoon to see who of which are the go getters of the platoon and who are the stragglers. Although these marines in these roles try to motivate other members, they display what needs to be done to successfully make it through the cycle to either join the bandwagon or become an outsider or viewed as they call a weak body.
chunks.label: Masculinity and leadership roles in boot camp
chunks.what_happened: The student describes how recruits in Marine Corps boot camp demonstrate physical fitness and motivation to earn alpha leadership positions or risk being viewed as stragglers.

chunks.text: As Marines leave boot camp and get to the fleet the masculinity does not end. Physical fitness continues to be the basis for promotion boards. Within these promotion boards the marines that are seen as most fit, knowledgeable, and confident with leadership skills are competing against other marines in a series of tests for disciple and knowledge. The marines that are chosen are ultimately the alpha males when it comes to the model marine. These model marines are the ones that fit in that motivate others to do well and also look down on those who don’t follow the same path. These marines that are chosen for boards like this thrive in Marine Corps martial arts programs and earn extra MOS jobs that go beyond their normal jobs. Although much of these attributes for these alpha males benefit them and their career, it can also have a negative effect for comradery for fellow marines.
chunks.label: Model marines and promotion boards in the fleet
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how hegemonic masculinity and physical fitness standards continue in the fleet through promotion boards and martial arts programs, potentially harming camaraderie.

chunks.text: For the marines that are not primarily a part of the hegemonic masculinity group they are seen as a different type of marine. Since the model marines are classified as go getters the others are classified and put into a group as they call the skaters or the shit bags. These types of individuals do not fit the model type marine. They are not as fit, not as mean, and not as lean as they are imagined to be from civilians looking in. These marines are often always looked down on and frowned upon because of these standards that they do not uphold. For example, marines that have a difficult time trying to stay within the Marine Corps height and weight standards are viewed as shitbags. If they do not meet the height and weight standards, they are subject to be put on a program called BCP which is an acronym for body composition program. This is a 6-month period of monitored and documented physical fitness and dieting get the individual back into the fit marine. During this time the marine is taken away from their jobs to go PT and can lead to insufficient manpower within the work center. From fellow marines this program is highly frowned upon. Although these marines may be the most efficient and most beneficial to their work department just them being overweight it classifies them into something that they might not be.
chunks.label: Treatment of marines who do not meet standards
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how marines who fail to meet physical fitness or weight standards are labeled as shitbags or placed on the body composition program, facing stigma despite their actual work contributions.

chunks.text: In the article written by Brett Stroudt, “Your Either in or Out” he utilizes the Rockport school as an institution where it is either fight or flight. Since Rockport is a Male only institution, the boys needed to find other ways to be viewed as Alpha males. The boys could either conform or get confronted. The boys at Rockport have it worse than of a school that would be Co-ed due to cliques and groups picking on one another. They use examples such as not being able to wear a purple shirt in fear of being ridiculed and teased. By not conforming to the schools’ traditions as far as shaving their heads as freshmen or during freshmen Friday do whatever the upper classmen say to do, they are looked down on upon or seen as resistant to the group which will ultimately lead to more teasing and more distant from fellow classmates. In some ways Hegemonic Masculinity has benefited them. It teaches them comradery with the groups and helps them build relationships to network through school and then on to college. With hazing and conforming to the needs of upper classmen they are able to build trust and build a foundation of acceptance.
chunks.label: Hegemonic masculinity at the Rockport school
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Brett Stoudt's article about an all-male school, discussing how boys must conform to peer traditions, avoid teasing, and build camaraderie through hegemonic masculinity.
chunks.people: Brett Stoudt, boys, upperclassmen, freshmen, classmates

chunks.text: In conclusion I believe that servicemembers of our military face these theories of hegemonic masculinity from the beginning to the end of their career. In my own opinion I believe that when it comes to hegemonic masculinity it is more beneficial to conform but only to a certain point of advancement. For those marines who want to make a full career out of the military it benefits them greatly for promotion advancement and job advancement. They will be able to move through the ranks much quicker and stay on the path of success for the full 20 years until retirement. For the other marines that only do a few years in the military it is not so beneficial to be the go getter or the masculine type of marine. These marines will end their service and move onto something else such as school or back to work as a civilian. I believe that hegemonic masculinity will continue to play a crucial role in the Marine Corps.
chunks.label: Conclusion on conforming to military masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student shares conclusions on how conforming to hegemonic masculinity benefits career marines seeking rapid advancement compared to those serving short enlistments.

nb8291143.title: Navigating Social Media and Body Image

chunks.text:
Social Media and Its Influence on Body Image and Mental Health

Social media is a new type of media that is entirely user generated. The most popular forms of social media are Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, and TikTok. As new forms of social media are created and gain popularity, along with technology advancements in smartphones, people have an increased level of accessibility to these platforms. What impact does this increased accessibility have on people, especially teenagers? How does it affect one’s sense of self, their body image, and their self-esteem? Social media can be beneficial, as it allows us to easily and quickly do things like connect with friends and family and stay updated with current news, but the effect it may have on one’s mental and physical health can be detrimental.

The concept of body image can be defined in a number of different ways. One of the main definitions is that body image is the way that a person sees their physical appearance, and the feelings and emotions that come from that perception, whether they be positive or negative (Jiosta). One’s body image reflects society’s social norms, thus pertaining to the concept of the collective consciousness. People will always strive to look their personal best, but the beauty norms of society often portray people who are tall, thin, tan and with clear skin as being the “ideal” model for what we should all look like. This can lead to things like tanning, buying expensive clothes, shoes and makeup, and working out and dieting excessively. Many people alter their appearance to fit into these high beauty standards. In a study done by Meier and Gray, it was found that an increased exposure to social media can be connected to “weight dissatisfaction, a drive for thinness, thin ideal internalization, and self-objectification among female high school students”.

Traditional media, like newspaper and magazines, has had a negative impact on people’s body image for decades, according to Fardouly and Vartanian. Social media is different from traditional media as it allows users to display themselves, rather than just seeing celebrities and models. People put forth their best self on social media. Not many people want to broadcast the “undesirable” aspects of their lives on social media. Photos can be edited, filtered, and altered to make them seem more attractive. These images do not portray who you are normally, but rather show an enhanced version of yourself. This leads to an increase in body dissatisfaction, as people feel as though they can more closely relate to peers on social media rather than models and celebrities in traditional media.

As new forms of social media arise, we begin to notice the major differences between social and traditional media: the use of likes and who runs each platform. Social media is peer and user generated, which traditional media is generated by major corporations and paparazzi. Social media focuses on interaction, while traditional media does not (Kim). Likes and comments are a form of instant gratification, which can lead to an obsession with this type of feedback. The amount of views, likes and comments on posts can lead to negative feelings about ourselves and our appearance. Comments are a quintessential part of social media, as they guide perceptions on what is deemed “ideal”. We strive for this instant gratification and modify our beauty standards to fit within the societal norm in order to receive more positive feedback from our peers.

In an article written by Tiggemann and Anderberg, the trend of “Instagram versus Reality” is discussed as being a form of online social activism. This trend shows two side by side photos of the same person. In the first photo, the person is their ideal self, wearing nice clothes and makeup with their hair done. This photo is edited and taken from flattering angles. In the second photo, the person shoes their “natural” self, without makeup or filters, posed in a more natural and comfortable way. This trend is very important, as it allows people to realize that what is posted on social media is entirely different from who people are when no one is looking. “Instagram versus Reality” serves as a way to remind people that what is posted on social media is often not the truth, but rather a lie and a coverup to make people seem more put together and “perfect” than they actually are, This exposure to “natural” photos leads to lower facial and body dissatisfaction, and an increase in body appreciation and positive body image. According to Tiggemann and Anderberg, positive body image is a multidimensional construct that refers to love, respect and acceptance of one’s body. People realize that their body is serving its purpose: keeping us alive. An increase in body appreciation can lead to greater self-esteem, self-care and adaptive eating. Once people begin to realize the truth behind social media, they will start to become more satisfied with their own bodies.

The negative effects of social media have generally been connected to the process of social comparison (Tiggemann and Anderberg). People who are the targets for comparison on social media are usually peers, whereas in traditional media, the targets are models and celebrities. The comparison with peers often results in body dissatisfaction, as people who do the comparison see their peers to be “normal” people that they can relate to more closely than they could with models and celebrities. This body dissatisfaction is often detrimental to one’s mental health and confidence in their appearance.

Social media provides a very narrow view of one’s life. Not many people choose the broadcast the chaos and disorder of their everyday lives on social media. Erving Goffman proposes the idea that people are “performers”. In his writing, “Presentation of Self”, Goffman states that each person has a front and a backstage. The backstage is made up of actions that people do “behind the scenes”, when no one is looking. Think of the backstage as your true self, without filters. The front stage is made up of actions that others can see, or the character that you show your “audience”. The front and backstage theory can be applied to social media. The backstage is your true, everyday self, while the front stage is how you appear on social media platforms. This appearance that people put on display is often very different from who they actually are as a person.

Social media can also be used as a platform for bullying. It is easy to make a fake account with none of your personal information and to use that account to bully others. Social media provides a “curtain” for bullies to become anonymous. It is much easier to say hateful things to others behind a screen than to their face. According to Peled, cyberbullying is defined as electronic posting of mean messages about a person, often done anonymously. Types of cyberbullying include fraping, dissing, trolling, catfishing, phishing, stalking, blackmail, the sharing of photos and videos that one wants to keep private, shunning, and sexting. Fraping occurs when someone makes a social media account pretending to be someone else, Dissing is done in an attempt to ruin someone else’s reputation. Trolling is trying to provoke a reaction from someone else. Catfishing involves stealing someone’s identity to create profiles used to deceive someone. Phishing is a tactic used to trick or manipulate someone into revealing personal information, like bank account numbers, addresses, and social security numbers. Blackmail is a threat to reveal someone’s secrets. Many of these bullying tactics would never be done face to face with the victim, so social media provides a perfect platform for these types of bullying. Cyberbullying can lead to mental health disorders like anxiety and depression and may also cause body dysmorphia and eating disorders. Victims of cyberbullying may also become lonely, have low self-esteem, gain phobias of school, and show poor performance in school or at work.

Social media will forever change the way people interact with one another. What was once face to face interactions is now done online. This causes people to put forth a version of themselves that is entirely different from who they are. Real life shows the raw, natural, and unedited version of who you are, whereas social media allows you to filter how you are seen to others. The use of social media is a great way to stay updated with current events and to connect with people around the world, but it also provides the perfect platform for anonymous bullying. Social media can also have a negative impact on one’s self-esteem, their body image, and their mental health. As we use more and more forms of social media, we need to remind ourselves that what we see on these platforms often is not one’s true self. We are able to select the best version of ourselves to put forth, rather than putting forth who we truly are. We need to stop comparing our physical appearance to that of others. Once we realize that each and every person has an appearance and personality that is unique and perfect, we will be able to build a more positive and accepting environment.
chunks.label: Social media influence on body image and mental health
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological research and theories on how social media impacts body image, self-esteem, cyberbullying, and mental health.

chunks.text: The collective conscious is present within all groups and societies. In “The Cultural Logic and Collective Representations”, Emile Durkheim states that ideas that correlate to the diverse elements of language form collective representations. These collective representations are what make up the collective consciousness. As people interact with one another, sharing ideas and beliefs, the collective consciousness begins to form. Although the collective consciousness is not something that we can see, it can be observed by collective representations. The collective consciousness has been around since the beginning of modern civilization, guiding people to follow practices and ideas that those around them believed. The idea of collective consciousness was created by Durkheim and can be connected to Aaron Mahnke’s podcast “Lore”, as people that interact closely with one another have the same beliefs and ideas.
chunks.label: Durkheim's collective consciousness and Lore podcast
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces Emile Durkheim's concept of collective consciousness and collective representations, connecting it to Aaron Mahnke's podcast 'Lore'.

chunks.text: Collective representations are evident in Lore’s podcast episode titled “Black Stockings”. Myths and lore were created as a coping mechanism. In Ireland, the belief of creatures called “changelings” existed until the late 1890’s. Changelings were fairies who would act as a replacement for a “kidnapped human”. The fairies would take the kidnapped person to the fairy world and leave a fairy in their place. The person would be considered “kidnapped” if they began to behave differently than they had previously, or if they were different from those around them, like people born with mental disabilities. The fairies were thought to be a curse that took away luck, so the families of those believed to be replaced would do many things to try to get the fairy to leave and return their loved one. These methods included holding the person above a fire and forcing them under cold water. These extreme practices would often lead to the death of the person believed to be a fairy. The people of Ireland were afraid of what these fairies would do, and it is human nature to hate what we fear. The collective conscious of the people in Ireland at this time overpowered basic human instinct, as they believed that they were harming the changelings rather than their loved ones. The Irish all shared this belief, it became integrated into their collective consciousness.
chunks.label: Irish changeling beliefs from the Lore podcast
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes an episode of 'Lore' about Irish beliefs in changelings, explaining how collective representations and fear led people to harm loved ones they believed were fairies.

chunks.text: The collective consciousness varies widely from group to group, as we can clearly see the difference in cultures around the world. Both Durkheim and Mahnke prove that the collective consciousness exists to enforce societal rules and a greater moral order. Humans constantly feel the need to fit in to survive, and those who are seen as different may be seen as dangerous to society. Ignorance is used as an excuse to fuel hatred for things that are outside of the societal norm, and this ignorance is shared amongst people in tightly knit groups.
chunks.label: Societal conformity and collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how collective consciousness varies across cultures and operates to enforce societal rules, conformity, and shared hatred of differences.

nc4b9953f.title: Critiquing the Sexualization of Young Women

chunks.text:
Why are women scared of taking up space? How does being feminine equal being submissive? Why do men like younger, attractive, submissive women? These interconnected questions are, of course, generalized- but the idea of women being associated with powerlessness is a historical and ever-present motif. Usually, explanations for the sex-related power dynamic issue consist of “it’s biology”, or “that’s just the way the world works”. These rationalizations are comfortable to our society because they are easy to grasp. Thinking of women as human beings just as complex as men is somewhat revolutionary, because we (even women) haven’t had this concept ingrained in our minds like we have with misogyny. Some women accept the submissive role that has been placed on them-- either subconsciously or because their beliefs align with it. Those are personal decisions for women to make for themselves, and as long as they are not allowing themselves to be taken advantage of, their lifestyle choices should not be criticized as long as they are happy and healthy. The problem is the expectation for all women to submit to this subordinate position. Generally, society assumes women will align themselves with the submissive role in which they are associated with, and this is problematic beyond the surface-level connotation.

Though the specific roles of women in society have changed over time, there still lies the foundational belief that they should be nurturing mothers and obedient to their male counterparts. The underlying idea is that women exist to serve others, but mostly men. This shapes expectations for women to consistently conform to how they are perceived by others, especially correlating with desires shaped by the male gaze. When reflecting on aspects of the male gaze, it is clear that men subconsciously view child-like traits as desirable. What makes a woman conventionally attractive often correlates with being younger, which leads to sexualization of sexually immature girls and young women. This objectification often starts at a young age, causing the affected girls to feel pressured to mature faster than they are mentally prepared for, and is quite a pedophilic ideology.

Of course, “being younger” encompasses a broad range of attributes, and is not specific in itself. When one assumes what a desirable woman would look like to a hetereosexual man, many features come to mind: a mostly hairless body, petite, weak, etc. These are general assumptions and obviously do not represent every man’s desires, but there is a common factor in those attributes: they often correlate with younger ages. Almost all grown women have body hair, and the average height of a woman in the United States is 5 feet, 4 inches (Barhum, 2018). So, the average American woman does not align with these desires, and it is unrealistic to expect them to do so, since these are natural developments.

If grown men should be attracted to grown women, then why are these natural physical characteristics of women considered undesirable? After all, the growth of hair is a secondary sex characteristic, signifying the development of sexual maturity. When ads for women’s razors became more popular in the early 20th century, “... an ideology of unsullied chastity, women were reduced to a primarily sexual identity, or to the identity of a child” (Ewen & Ewen, 1982, p. 237). Womens’ societal standards for attractiveness (in this case, the removal of body hair) often compare to that of a child. The idea that a woman is purer or sexually tamed also stems from the desire of her having no body hair. Either way, the disappearance of leg, armpit, and pubic hair growth is equated with beauty and proper hygiene, even though it is completely natural, healthy, and a symbol of sexual maturity.

Another patriarchal concept, virginity, is another way of controlling women and seuxalizing young women and girls (often inexperienced and more likely to be taken advantage of). The following sexual descriptions are generalizations and preferences that clearly do not represent all men, but seem to be a common denominator regarding sexual enjoyment. Many sexual fantasies involve the fascination of virginity and being the one to take it away. “Stealing innocence” is associated with the feeling of dominance. There is also a common category in pornography which is referred to as “barely legal”, meaning just above the age of consent and no longer a minor. This term is disproportionately used in reference to women, and suggests the freedom to exploit and sexualize very young women without the feeling of guilt or wrongdoing. This is why Billie Eilish, the iconic 19-year-old singer and songwriter, dressed in baggy clothes for so much of her career: she wanted the attention to focus on her work and not her appearance, but she was sexualized at a young age anyway, and many people on the Internet spoke about her turning eighteen so that they could freely sexualize her without the same backlash. Eilish’s personal experience with objectification is just one example- many older men prey on girls and make excuses for the age gaps by passing her off as mature, which unfairly gives her an expectation to act older than she really is.

This allure of taking away innocence derives from the association of being in control when men have more power. They are commonly expected to take a dominant position and exercise this strength over their partner. Because of this expectation, men prefer something they can control: “...females are more desirable to males when they carry traits associated with low power such as youthfulness and faithfulness” (Nature). Since innocence, purity, and naivety often correlate with inexperience and youthfulness, this can lead to the sexualization of girls and young women, most of the time without their consent and at an age that they are not yet sexually mature enough for. It perpetuates objectification and the pressure of the male gaze, even before girls reach sexual maturity. While preferences should not be criticized (to an extent), it is crucial to reflect on any desires from which they may stem- such as sexual frustration, jealousy, anger, violence, pedophilia, etc., and how this endangers young women, especially minors.

Another common practice of controlling girls that is rooted in sex-based misogynism is dress code, especially in school settings. Girls are convinced from an early age that only certain types of clothing are acceptable to be viewed by peers and adult staff in a learning environment. Oftentimes, the dress codes are aimed towards traditionally “feminine” clothing options, like leggings, sleeveless shirts or tank tops, and shorter shorts or shirts. There are usually many more restrictions to what female students can wear than male students. From personal experience, this is extremely frustrating, because (even at a very young age) as a female we are pressured to show skin or wear form-fitting clothes. However, we are shamed for wearing these clothes to school, in a place where we should feel comfortable and safe. No matter what kinds of clothes we maintain wearing, we are subject to criticism in one form or another.

Not only do dress codes contradict societal pressures for females, they also persist rape culture. “...girls are...blamed for the violence, in particular sexual violence, done to them…” (Katz, 2021). The misogyny and control that is enforced by the dress code teaches girls that their bodies are sexualized, and that this is their fault for choosing to dress that way. The dress code thrives through the fear of ridicule or objectification, but the dress code itself makes girls feel embarrassed, ashamed, and objectified already. It also teaches boys that they are not expected to control themselves by making girls dress as to “not distract them”, and perpetuates the blame of sexual violence on girls. It operates around their comfort level, which clearly shows the prioritization of boys’ school experience over the girls. It is also unsettling how male staff’s comfort is protected from girls dressing more “provocatively” as well as the boys’ comfort. But perhaps the most concerning aspect of enforcing dress codes is the implementation of them at such an early age for most girls, often in elementary school, and how the microaggressions they bring about continue into adulthood.

Still, it does not just come down to how women change their physical appearance to fit the male gaze. Women, mostly girls, first experience harassment or sexual assault at an early age. The majority of women (27%) first experienced sexual harassment between the ages of 14 and 17, but a total of 30% of women first experienced harassment before the age of 14 (Stop Street Harassment). Over half of women who have been sexually assaulted in some form or another were children when it occurred. Plus, “[Of rape and sexual assault,] nearly 99% of perpetrators are male” (U.S. Dept. of Justice, 2002). This is an extremely dangerous aspect of misogynism and pedophilia. There is clearly an imbalance of safety based on sex-related desires, which disproportionately targets and affects adolescents and teenagers. It is unquestionable that sexualizing girls past what they are mature enough for is more dangerous than perceived by society. It is deeper than just microaggressions and leads to true sexual violence, which, if left unchecked, is potentially harmful in a number of ways.

Even when analyzing only a few aspects of misogyny and objectification in society, such as the topics previously discussed, it is clear the similarity: control. Unfortunately, this constant urge for control is rooted in misogyny, power imbalances, and in extreme cases, sexual violence and pedophilia. How disturbing is it that women must be concerned about their safety and wellbeing just for being female, especially at such a young age? Why is the blame placed on girls for “growing up too fast”, which is actually a result of how they are oversexualized by the male gaze? It is time, and has always been time, for the urge of domination to eradicate.

Works Cited

Barhum, Lana. “Average Height for Women Worldwide.” Medical News Today, MediLexicon International, 6 Mar. 2018, https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/321132.

Basow, Susan A. “The Hairless Ideal: Women and Their Body Hair .” CiteSeerX, Lafayette College, 1991, https://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/download?doi=10.1.1.901.6904&rep=rep1&type=pdf.

Kaplan, Matt. “Men Prefer Less Powerful Women.” Nature News, Nature Publishing Group, 26 Jan. 2010, https://www.nature.com/articles/news.2010.37.

Katz, Claire Elise. “You're Wearing That? from School Dress Codes to Rape Culture.” Blog of the APA, 24 July 2021, https://blog.apaonline.org/2021/07/28/youre-wearing-that-from-school-dress-codes-to-rape-culture/.

“Statistics.” Stop Street Harassment, 19 Dec. 2016, https://stopstreetharassment.org/resources/statistics/.

“Sexualized Violence Statistics.” Stop Rape: Response & Prevention, https://stoprape.humboldt.edu/statistics.
chunks.label: Societal objectification and control of young women
chunks.what_happened: The student examines how societal expectations, beauty standards, school dress codes, and the male gaze sexualize and control girls and young women.

chunks.text: Thus, McIntosh’ argument goes along with how James describes how we become who we are. He describes it as changing interests and groups is how we present ourselves which them would make sense that we are taught to do this. We are taught to act a certain way in front of parents, teachers, and friends. However, we do not always notice that we do this, just like we do not always notice that someone is at an advantage or disadvantage by the way that they present themselves.
chunks.label: Connecting McIntosh and James on social presentation
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how McIntosh's argument relates to James's views on identity and presentation. They reflect on how people are taught to act differently around parents, teachers, and friends without always noticing advantages or disadvantages.

nd771be10.title: Media Portrayals of Extreme Wealth Disparities

chunks.text: In mainstream media typically there are two models of people shown. Those who are living in poverty on the streets and those that own three vacation homes with no room in between. In my own personal experience, the biggest example I can think of is reality TV. Have you ever seen a reality TV show that follows the life of an average income working family? The answer is probably no. Reality TV usually only follows the lives of the extremely privileged or the extremely misfortunate. In the reading Class in America, Mantsios argues that the use of these two sole models of people in mainstream media is one way that the media perpetuates the idea that America is a classless society.
chunks.label: Media portrayals of social class in reality TV
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how mainstream media and reality television only depict the very rich or the very poor, referencing Mantsios's reading on social class.

chunks.text: In conclusion, based on the readings the collective consciousness that America is a classless society and wealth determines success is a false perception pushed onto Americans by the mainstream media, which is controlled by the wealthy upper class who benefits from this false perception as it allows them to maintain control without the public noticing. The reality is America has many classes not just lower, middle, and upper.
chunks.label: Conclusion on class perception and media control
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that the idea of a classless American society is a false perception promoted by the wealthy upper class through the media.

n2e2f8c11.title: Reflecting on Power Elite and Wealth

chunks.text: These two authors have similar concern about the powerful elite class of people that are so much wealthier than the rest of the world. Domhoff explains that this power elite group has control over the current wealth of the world and Harari explains that once the item that determines wealth changes to internet data, the same group will dominate the world’s wealth once again. This is the shared information and concepts that are in both Module 6 and the current Module 8.
chunks.label: Comparing authors on the powerful elite class
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how two authors, Domhoff and Harari, share concerns about the powerful elite class dominating current and future wealth across course modules.

chunks.text: While much of military training is centered on physical fitness and tactical proficiency there is much more that goes into producing a capable warfighter. You can take any person off the street, teach them how to hold a rifle and have them do push ups until they collapse but that won’t make them any more capable in battle. The reason why the Marine Corps training pipeline is so effective in producing capable warriors from the everyday citizen is because along with the physical training it has instilled a completely separate collective consciousness among its members. This is a process that begins in bootcamp and continues on until the day that a service member is discharged from active duty. Throughout this paper I will discuss how the Marine Corps infantry training pipeline creates a subculture with its own collective consciousness and why it is necessary in order to facilitate combat effectiveness.
chunks.label: Introduction to Marine Corps collective consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the thesis that the Marine Corps infantry training pipeline creates a subculture and distinct collective consciousness necessary for combat effectiveness.

chunks.text: The best way to show the sociological development of an infantryman is to follow the training pipeline in chronological order, starting with boot camp. One of the most significant changes which takes place at this step is the removal of what Goffman refers to as the self in his writings. From the moment a recruit steps off the bus they become an object. The words I, me, my, he, us, they and them become “this recruit, that recruit, those recruits and these recruits.” Referring to yourself or any other recruit as a person is met with swift punishment from the drill instructors. Next all heads are shaved and everyone is put into the same uniform. Once everyone is uniform, every single part of your life is now regimented, from the time you wake up in the morning down to what utensils you are allowed to eat with. By removing all sources of individuality, the recruit becomes an object. Their sense of self is no more. This is necessary for breaking down civilian habits and creating a blank canvas to resculpt the recruit into a warrior which values the needs of the organization above their own wants and needs. Another key part in shaping a Marine is the language which is permitted. For example as I mentioned before a recruit is not allowed to refer to themselves or any other recruit as a person but there are also many other forms of prescribed language which is used to mentally condition the recruit for aggression. For one, a recruit is never allowed to speak in a voice any lower than yelling as loud as they can. The word “kill” is used as a response and chanted before recruits complete mundane tasks such as washing their hands before eating and curse words as well as insults are hurled at the recruits non stop by the drill instructors. Other phrases such as “slay bodies”, “kill bodies” and “stack bodies” are widely used by Marines for the same purpose. Overall the purpose of bootcamp is to create the most stressful environment possible to acclimate recruits to and to remove their individuality in order to create a Marine who values his peers wants and needs as well as the organization’s needs over his or her own (Novaco 1991).
chunks.label: Depersonalization and conditioning in boot camp
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how boot camp systematically removes recruits' individuality, regulates language and routine, and conditions them for aggression and obedience.

chunks.text: Now that the individual has been broken down and had their civilian collective consciousness replaced the formation of the Marine Corps collective consciousness can begin. While this replacement does begin in bootcamp, for the infantryman it really begins to take root in the school of infantry, which is where infantry Marines receive their infantry specialty such as machine gunner, rifleman, mortarman etc. While these hard skills were the main objective of training there were many soft skills and mental conditioning methods which were implemented on the side. One of these being furthering our desensitization and conditioning to violence. In order to achieve this combat instructors would often recount their war stories and during our classes we would be shown graphic videos of executions, death and gore to normalize it. I found this aspect of the training interesting because it was something that happened on the side with little to know extra thought but the changes it made in our heads was substantial. Marines began to be entertained by these videos and at times would seek them out on their own accord. Weapons training and desensitization aside, what I found to be the most important aspect of SOI (school of infantry) was the camaraderie and trust it formed between us.
chunks.label: Desensitization to violence in SOI
chunks.what_happened: During training at the School of Infantry, combat instructors shared war stories and showed graphic videos of death, executions, and gore to normalize violence among the trainees.
chunks.people: the student, combat instructors, fellow Marines

chunks.text: This is perhaps the most vital trait of an infantry Marine and is imperative to war fighting because cohesion is essential for unit performance as well as overcoming stressors. You can ask any war vet and they will tell you that they put the Marines to the left and the right of them above themselves, and going into war knowing that is extremely reassuring. The amount of trust gained in military training has been tested across multiple military occupations and in the end it was found that infantry training yielded the highest levels of cohesion(Orme 2020). This is no surprise when considering the substandard living conditions which trainees go through together.
chunks.label: Importance of unit cohesion and trust
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses sociological research and observations regarding how extreme stressors and living conditions build camaraderie and trust in infantry units.

chunks.text: To name just a few events which brought my platoon closer to each other was a field operation in which we were awake to the point of visual and auditory hallucination and a 13 mile hike with over 150lbs. of gear on us in gale force winds. There is something about “embracing the suck” with fellow Marines which creates bonds which are often as close as family.
chunks.label: Platoon bonding through extreme training events
chunks.what_happened: The student's platoon bonded during grueling experiences, including a sleep-deprivation field operation leading to hallucinations and a 13-mile hike carrying over 150 pounds of gear in gale-force winds.
chunks.people: the student, fellow Marines in the platoon

chunks.text: Once a Marine has completed their infantry training and has gained their respective military occupation specialty they are shipped off to their unit. The general principles of being a Marine such as discipline and putting the organization first should be set in stone by this point. The unit or “the fleet” as it is called is a place where skills are refined and the Marine fully settles into their new ways. The platoon they belong to becomes their new family and in some cases even more than family. The fleet is also where you begin to have more exposure to the Marine Corps traditions including some of the less traditional ones such as hazing. One widely known tradition among infantrymen is “pinning and bloodstriping.” Pinning takes place when a Marine reaches the rank of Lance Corporal and it is when the newly promoted Marine wears their new rank without pin backings for 24 hours. For those 24 hours any Marine who is a Lance Corporal or above punches and jams the pins into the Marines chest. Blood stripping is when a Marine reaches the rank of Corporal and becomes a non commissioned officer. It is the same principle as pinning but instead of stabbing a Marine with pins they knee the side of the new NCO’s legs until they can no longer walk. To the average collective consciousness this would be seen as undesirable and something to be avoided, but for Marines this is a cherished tradition which has been passed down through generations of infantry Marines. There is also the tradition of celebrating the Marine Corps birthday every year which is a sacred event among Marines, more so than any other holiday. Another key part of the average Marines collective consciousness is the elevation of Marines such as Chesty Puller and John Basilone as gods. John Basilone is literally the God of machine gunnery to Marines and Chesty Puller is a larger than life, undying, killing machine who is used as the pinnacle of leadership. Another tradition which is noteworthy, is the structure of rank.
chunks.label: Fleet traditions, rituals, and hierarchy
chunks.what_happened: The student describes the traditions within Marine fleet units, including pinning, bloodstriping, birthday celebrations, deification of historical heroes, and the rank structure.

chunks.text: While superior ranks are to be fully respected and obeyed to a level beyond any example in the civilian world, senior Marines are also held to the standard that they must treat their juniors better than they would treat themselves. This does not mean that you must be kind and never yell at your juniors but for example when I was a section leader, we would never let our junior Marines see us sleep or eat, meaning that you don't eat until all of your guys are fed, you don’t sleep until all of them are sleeping, and you wake up before any of them wake up.
chunks.label: Serving as section leader
