Even if here are only two religions in the entire world, humanity will still be in conflict as one group will always try to dominate the other.

Now how do Durkheim’s views of the collective conscious and Harari’s views on the collective consciousness tie together? Well simply Harari’s views build upon Durkheim’s views of the collective consciousness regarding religion and apply them to our modern society. Durkheim states that religion forms off of the collective conscious when a group of individuals with the same believes come together and allow it to bind them together, while Harari explains how religion is in fact harming our society yet will most likely stay in our society based off the collective conscious. Religion in society gives people comfort and a sense of being, however as Harari argues, it is harmful. It separates people into different groups, and with the separation of groups, tensions begin to form between the groups. These groups end up in conflict with one another because each full heartly agrees that they are correct, and that any other group trying to spread their religion is either false or working for whoever the evil deity in their religion is. With this Harari is ultimately right, religion divides us and causes many world issues. Fighting occurs, conflict between different religion, and the constant belief that you are better than someone else of a different religion because you are believer in the true religion. However, with this, religion will ultimately stay in our society. It comforts people and give many with no meaning a sense of meaning. By having and worshipping with a group of who all believe the same as you, it gives you comfort and makes you feel like you have a place to stay. This plays into the concept of the collective conscious. When a group together with he same beliefs and values, the collective consciousness forms dictating the morals of the society, helping the people in the group come together. So therefore, religion is needed in our society even though it’s ultimately bad for society. It splits us apart and is one of the leading causes of wars and conflicts in the world’s history. Most likely religion is here to stay, unless everyone joins the same religion, or if religion ultimately ends.
chunks.label: Collective consciousness and religion in society
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Emile Durkheim's concept of the collective consciousness alongside Yuval Noah Harari's writings on religion, discussing how religion and shared beliefs shape societies, create conflict, and influence modern life.

n413474d0.title: Mental Health Stigma in the Military

chunks.text:
As far as mental health goes in the military, they want the members to talk about it, but they also punish them for utilizing the available resources. Why would they continue to think that people would want to utilize their resources if they will inevitably be punished for it? This goes to say that many service members participate in the front stage and back stage concept of how they present themselves. It is used as a way to protect their careers from the harm that mental health institutions inflict. And how the concept of “the looking glass self” has an immense impact on the actions of those serving.

Many service members, especially on active duty, experience some form of mental illness, such as anxiety to depression and everything in between. Most will deal with it in the comfort of their own homes and not seek professional help, because they know about the repercussions of utilizing the help. This causes a lot of members to turn to a really dark place that is hard to get people out of. If that happens, it is crucial to help them, or the worst of things could occur.

The back stage element that they participate in is trying to cope with their mental health without professional help. This does not work for everybody, but most will try it in the beginning. A lot of unhealthy coping mechanisms that many participate in include drinking, drug abuse, self-harm, and many more. There are also some healthy coping mechanisms such as working out and hobbies. Most tend to participate in both, which puts the impression that they are doing fine. People will say things like “Oh he’s been working out, so he must be doing okay.” Which is exactly what the person wants the public to think.

The backstage is where all of the hard things tend to boil over and cause bad things to happen, but as long as they put on a good face at work then they are fine, according to higher-ups. The front stage is what gets all of the glory in the military. If they can put on a good face and do their job well, then they are good to go in the eyes of the military. But if they have a slip up, the impression starts to do a 360. That is when the back stage starts to merge with the front.

This causes problems within the service member’s career. If one is to go to the mental health clinic, for even one visit, they can not deploy or go TDY, which is going to another stateside base for work. And that causes a lot of issues, because most of people’s problems are on their home station and they would like to get away on occasion. Not to mention, if the problems include money, then they are losing out on a lot from a deployment. This also goes on for six months after the last appointment with the clinic, so it is not a little bump in the road. It takes a long time for the restriction to fall off of their record.

The front stage and back stage also applies to the mental health clinic. They put on this face of wanting to help and provide for active-duty members, but when an individual actually gets into the room, they do not help as much as they should.
chunks.label: Military mental health and front/back stage
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the stigma and career penalties associated with mental health resources in the military, applying the concepts of front stage and back stage.

chunks.text: Which I know from personal experience. The therapist that I had pretty much said I was cured, because I had not had a panic attack in a couple of weeks. Clearly that was not the case. They can go on and say it is because they are understaffed and have too many patients, but they should be able to at least act like they care when someone is back in the room with them.
chunks.label: Therapist dismissing panic attacks
chunks.what_happened: The student attended a therapy session at a mental health clinic where the therapist declared the student cured simply because they had not had a panic attack in a few weeks.

chunks.text:
The mental health problem also contributes to the concept of “the looking glass self”. It is believed by many that if an individual is seeking help for mental health, then they are weak or not fit for duty. Whether or not people actually think this of those that seek help is not the point in this situation. The members will still think that this is how they will be viewed and it deters them from utilizing the resources available. Active-duty members also do not want to scare off any potential friends or lovers with the notion of their mental health issues.

Not everybody will run from a person that clearly voices their issues, but that is not the case for all individuals. Some people just simply do not want to deal with the uncertainty or emotions in a person or do not know how to in some situations. On the other hand, some people can not always be to blame, they just simply have not been around enough people with mental health issues, so they have no idea on what to say or how to respond. Either way, this causes the members to not want to voice their problems, so they keep it locked away in themselves.

The “looking glass self” concept has a lot to do with the collective consciousness of society as a whole. If there was not a huge negative stigma around mental health, then everybody would feel comfortable about talking about it. But since there is that negative feeling surrounding it, most will hide the fact that they have problems or not associate with somebody that does. The collective consciousness around mental health is a negative one, but with all of the new conversations being brought up, it is turning into a more positive tone.

Hopefully at some point the mental health epidemic will no longer be a huge problem for many active-duty members. That they will change the policy of the six-month restriction, in most cases, so that the members will actually seek help with the available resources. Making it so that the back stage and front stage of the active-duty members will not be as divided and unhealthy and the “looking glass self” will be seen in a more positive light.

Until then, the conversations still need to be had and the higher-ups in workplaces need to step up their game and actually get to know their subordinates. That will ensure that they will actually notice when somebody is not acting themselves, so they can intervene before it is too late. Because once it is too late, the whole base will be under a lockdown. Nobody will want to talk about their issues, because they do not want it to be a big deal that is broadcasted to everybody in the workplace. Not to mention the hardships that it will put the family and friends of the individual through.

Making the talk about mental health more common and comfortable will cause many more to open up about their problems. It will end the negative notation in most societies and, hopefully, lower the suicide rates among active-duty individuals. Continuing to provide resources will also help with the climbing rate of mental health diagnoses and help to control them, so nobody feels left out of the conversation.
chunks.label: Looking glass self and mental health stigma
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how the looking glass self and collective consciousness affect service members' willingness to seek mental health care, advocating for policy and cultural changes.

chunks.text:
There is a collective consciousness surrounding the expectation to attend college after completing high school. This should make you think, was I given a choice of a different path other than college? Why did I decide to attend college instead of a trade school? Did I choose my career based on my own passions and interests? Or instead on the salary I would receive? These questions may show that you like many others followed a path that was expected. To attend school, college, and then start a career that you should stay in until retirement.

Relating to this is a journal titled, “Estranged Learning” by Jean Lave and Ray McDermott. The authors describe Marx’s writing as a “delivered phenomenon (McDermott and Lave 2006).” They believe that his idea of estranged labor has the power to make readers realize the relation between labor and profit. Furthermore, it is stated, “in critiquing the theories of political economy available in 1844, young Marx unwittingly wrote a quite devastating critique of the theories of learning available in 2002 (McDermott and Lave 2006).” Thus, showing that Marx’s idea of estranged labor that was based on a pre modern society still fits todays now modern society.

The journal goes on to use Marx’s work “Estranged Labor” as a template for what the authors are calling Estranged Learning. The new creation changes the concepts of Marx’s writing to focus on the education system and theory. For example, Marx’s original words are, “Political economy starts with the fact of private property, but it does not explain it to us (McDermott and Lave 2006).” To focus on education this is rewritten to say, “The educational establish starts with the fact of standardized knowledge, but it does not get explained to us (McDermott and Lave 2006).” The education system in our pre modern society is allowing and continuing the existence of estranged labor. The authors put this in very simple terms “labor produces commodities, learning produces commodities, labor produces the laborer as a commodity, learning produces the learner as a commodity (McDermott and Lave 2006).” Once again showing that the collective consciousness surrounding education is cause of estranged labor practices.

There is also relation to Mark Andrejevic’s writing titled “Estranged Free Labor.” Andrejevic talks about the online economy. He states that “the online economy relies upon consumers’ willing submission to increasingly detailed and comprehensive forms of monitoring (Andrejevic 2013).” All of this is due to the growth of online culture. The writing also then talks about the privacy issues that are created due to the everyday use of technology. The relation to estranged labor has to do with the fact that you do not receive a wage from online activity, however a wage is generated for others by it. The example Andrejevic gives is custom advertising, that is bought and sold to companies. He refers to a Wall Street Journal investigation and report that surrounds data mining. According to this study companies can pay $1 per thousand movie lovers. The economy relies on the buying and selling of this information to generate sales. This also increases the value of social media platforms.

This use of the online economy creates a form of estranged labor. Consumers of social media and online sites are turned into a commodity that can be bought and sold. This is purely the idea of estranged labor that is given to us by Karl Marx. The difference is, these sales and transactions often happen without the acknowledge of the consumer.

Another relationship between modern society and estranged labor can be seen in a journal titled “Estranged Labor, Habitus, and Verstehen in the Rise of Extreme Endurance Sports” by Colleen P. Eren. According to this journal the number as well as participants of extreme endurance sporting events has grown rapidly since the 1970s. Examples of extreme endurance sports are triathlons, marathons, Iron-mans, and military-style obstacle courses. These events have millions of participants as well as spectators. Eren points out that previous studies have been done to analyze this growing phenomenon but not have analyzed it “from a microsociological perspective, looking at individual characteristics of participants (Eren 2017).” It is these characteristics that allow Eren to associate these sporting events with Marx’s idea of estranged labor.

Eren goes on to describe the participants of these events. She describes the number of amateurs involved to be extraordinary. A specific example of this is the increase of marathon participation in the United states from 1976 to 2013. In 1976 there was 25,000 participants and then 2013 there is a dramatic increase to 541,000 participants. Eren also points out that there is an unequal class distribution of those participating in extreme endurance sports. She is compelled by the number of participants that “have at least a bachelor’s degree, occupying well-compensated white-collar and professional jobs (Eren 2017).” An example given is that in 2016 at the Rock and Roll Marathon series the average income of a runner was $112,000 with 79% having at least a bachelor’s degree.

Eren also reports that in the 20th century there was a workforce trend away from high activity and manual labor. Instead, there was an increase in white collar and service industry workers. Eren claims that the growth in immaterial labor has an influence on extreme endurance sports. She is able to theorize this due to Marx’s idea of estranged labor. Due to estranged labor the worker is not involved in the process of making the product. This often takes away a person’s creativeness, activity, and interaction with others. The person then makes up what they are lacking in their job by participating in an extreme endurance sport. Eren also argues that there is lack of physical energy used in today’s labor, psychically for middle- and upper-class professionals. Therefore, extreme endurance activities are used to increase physical involvement.

Extreme endurance activities allow participants to feel less confined by the collective consciousness of estranged labor. As stated before, due to estranged labor, passions are often put aside in order to receive the best salary. The participation in these events allow the individual to find passion about something else. The increase of stationary jobs is also due to estranged labor in this modern society. These events are used to increase physical movement as well as bring purpose to the individual that may not have at their job. Participants in these events get to have moment of not working towards a profit that benefits someone else but instead have feeling authentic profit for themselves.

Karl Marx coined the term estranged labor in 1844 based off a pre modern society in Europe. However, this term can still be used to describe the modern society of the United. States. Due to a collective consciousness surrounding college and careers estranged labor is continuing to happen. Evidence of this can be seen in our own education system, as shown by McDermott and Lave in “Estranged Learning.” Estranged labor is also produced by the online economy. Consumers of social media are being bought and sold as commodities in order for these companies to make a profit. This can be seen by Andrejevic’s work titled “Estranged Free Labor.” Lastly, a result of estranged labor is shown by Eren and her journal, “Estranged Labor, Habitus, and Verstehen in the Rise of Extreme Endurance Sports.” There has been an increase participation in extreme endurance events that Eren accounts to estranged labor.

After exploring causes and results of estranged labor you should think about how it specifically has and can affect you. Did a collective consciousness motivate you to go to college instead of a passion? Are companies using you as a free commodity to boost their advertising? Do you want participate in marathons to make up for lost physical movement? But most of all, what can you do to change it?

Work Cited

Andrejevic, Mark. “Estranged Free Labor.” Digital Labor: The Internet as a Playground and Factory, Routledge, 2013, pp. 149–164.

Eren, Colleen P. “Estranged Labor, Habitus, and Verstehen in the Rise of Extreme Endurance Sports.” Journal of Sport and Social Issues, vol. 41, no. 5, 2017, pp. 384–401., doi:10.1177/0193723517719663.

Marx, Karl. Estranged Labour, Marx, 1844, www.marxists.org/archive/marx/works/1844/manuscripts/labour.htm.

McDermott, Ray, and Jean Lave. “Estranged Labor Learning.” Critical Perspectives on Activity: Explorations Across Education, Work, and Everyday Life, edited by Peter Sawchuk et al., Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, 2006, pp. 89–122
chunks.label: Analysis of estranged labor in modern society
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Karl Marx's concept of estranged labor and reviews scholarly literature applying it to modern education, the online economy, and extreme endurance sports.

chunks.text: Class and Power in America: Exploring Dynamics of Socio-Economic Influence Sociology Doctor Elliot Aaron Williamson 5/3/24 Introduction: In the Unite­d States, different groups of pe­ople have power and mone­y. This impacts how society works. Class and power are ve­ry important parts of the social system. They de­cide how resources and chance­s are shared. They also show who has advantage­s and disadvantages. This piece looks at how class and powe­r connect. It explains how they shape­ American life. From how wealth and status are­ divided, to the ways power works in place­s like schools and jobs, looking at class and power gives insights into the­ American experie­nce. By studying the past, prese­nt, and future, we can understand the­ forces behind socio-economic influe­nce in America's society and politics. What is socio-economic influence? Money and powe­r shape how people live­. Some groups have more of the­se than others. This lets the­m make rules and call shots. They can ge­t resources and jobs. Their life­ chances are bette­r than those with less money and powe­r. Groups with less money and power have­ fewer choices. The­ir voices are not heard as much. Whe­re you stand in life depe­nds on your social class. Someone's social class is based on the­ir income, education, and job. Classes with more­ money and power are at the­ top. Classes with less money and powe­r are at the bottom. There­ is an uneven spread of we­alth, status, and chances in society. Social class makes the difference. Those occupying higher social classes often wield greater economic resources and social capital, affording them increased opportunities for advancement and influence. Concurrently, power, both institutionalized and informal, serves as a mechanism through which socio-economic influence is exercised, enabling certain individuals or groups to assert control over economic resources, political institutions, and cultural narratives (Domhoff, 2013). Whether through corporate lobbying, media ownership, or elite networks, the pe­ople with money and power ofte­n have big advantages. They ge­t more opportunities that add to their we­alth and status. Meanwhile, others with le­ss money and power struggle. Unde­rstanding this pattern requires looking at how mone­y and power impact society. We must se­e how class divides link to systems that privile­ge certain groups over othe­rs. Dynamics The dynamics of socio-economic influence are multifaceted and complex, reflecting the interplay of various factors that shape individuals' and groups' access to resources, opportunities, and power within a society. At its core, socio-economic influence encompasses a web of interconnected relationships, institutions, and processes that determine the distribution of wealth, status, and influence. One key aspect of this dynamic is social stratification, which refers to the hierarchical arrangement of individuals and groups based on factors such as wealth, occupation, education, and social status (Macionis & Plummer, 2012). This stratification system creates distinct social classes, each with its own set of privileges, opportunities, and constraints. Moreover, socio-economic influence is often reinforced and perpetuated through mechanisms of power and privilege, which enable certain individuals or groups to exert disproportionate control over economic resources, political institutions, and cultural narratives (Domhoff, 2013). This can manifest in various forms, including corporate lobbying, media ownership, and elite networks, all of which serve to amplify the influence of the economic elite while marginalizing disadvantaged groups (Gilens & Page, 2014). How society can be positively, or negatively affected The exploration of "Class and Power in America: Exploring Dynamics of Socio-Economic Influence" holds the potential for both positive and negative impacts on society. On one hand, a thorough examination of socio-economic dynamics can empower individuals and communities by fostering awareness of systemic inequalities and informing efforts to address them. By highlighting the interplay between class, power, and privilege, this exploration may catalyze social movements, policy reforms, and grassroots initiatives aimed at promoting equity and social justice. However, if not approached with care, such an exploration could also perpetuate harmful narratives or reinforce existing power structures, further marginalizing vulnerable populations and hindering efforts towards societal progress. Therefore, it is essential to engage in this exploration with a commitment to inclusivity, empathy, and critical inquiry, ensuring that the insights gained contribute to positive societal transformation. Conclusion In conclusion, the dynamics of socio-economic influence constitute a multifaceted tapestry woven from the intricate interplay of social stratification, power dynamics, and patterns of social mobility. Social stratification, manifested through various hierarchies based on factors such as income, education, and occupation, lays the groundwork for unequal access to resources and opportunities. Concurrently, power dynamics, whether institutionalized or informal, shape the distribution of influence and control over economic, political, and cultural domains. Furthermore, patterns of social mobility, influenced by factors like intergenerational wealth transmission and structural barriers to advancement, dictate the extent to which individuals can transcend their socio-economic circumstances.
chunks.label: Analysis of class and power in America
chunks.what_happened: The student presents an academic paper analyzing the dynamics of socio-economic influence, social stratification, power, privilege, and social mobility in American society.

chunks.text:
Collective Consciousness comes from the natural selection of low class and “non-group-forming" to make a more social and group oriented to ensure survival. Survival is partly based on your ability to work together. It’s been proven that if you are in a group your chances of survival are higher than if you were alone.

The collective consciousness is a shared understanding of social norms not the moral conscience. The social norms are shared morality, beliefs, and ideas that everyone uses to go about their day and how they go about their social interactions. A good example would be the way people are supposed to dress, girls and boys wear their respective clothing.

To go with Collective Consciousness, there is something called collective mindsets. These mindsets are a collection of all our background knowledge. This knowledge changes as we progress with life and our culture progresses.
chunks.label: Collective consciousness and collective mindsets
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the concepts of collective consciousness, social norms, survival through groups, and collective mindsets.

n73bb01b6.title: Struggling to Survive on Minimum Wage

chunks.text:
Sometimes people go into a profession because they know it’ll be stable income that they can use to provide for themselves and their family. They might not be happy with their job but if it’s the only job they can get and the only job that’ll pay the bills, that’s where they may stay. Working for a wage has become most people’s motive to get up in the morning, not because they enjoy it, but in order to live, they have to.

Depending on what profession someone is in, their worth becomes defined and ranked by society. Then based on their rank they are paid more and seen as more essential to the betterment of society. So as much as someone may hate their job, as long as they are getting paid, they will continue to go to work in order to make a living. A person’s basic needs are food, clothing, shelter, and water, but in today’s society money has become almost as important as the rest of these, because without money you can’t always get those basic needs. As things are priced, nothing is priced based on the living wage. The market determines the value of what is being produced, and the people that actually work to produce stuff aren’t included in the decision. This allows things to become overpriced without anyone really having a say. Unless a person can produce something for society to use for its own gain, they almost have no worth in the end. The more you can produce for society, the more you are compensated for your work.

On a smaller scale, when someone is making the first big steps in their life, they start taking on new expenses that they didn’t have to pay for originally. If you aren’t as fortunate, you’ll only be earning minimum wage. However, even though minimum wage is defined as the amount you’d had to be paid to live comfortably, in order to actually live comfortably you’d have to almost work full time or have two jobs. The price for rent and other utilities is so expensive that minimum wage struggles to fully cover it.
chunks.label: Working for wages and societal valuation under capitalism
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on why people work jobs they dislike to survive, how society values and compensates production, and the inadequacy of minimum wage.

chunks.text: My brother has been dealing with some of these things firsthand and it can really take a toll on someone who is already lacking knowledge when it comes to paying important expenses.
chunks.label: Brother struggling with expenses
chunks.what_happened: The student notes that their brother has been dealing firsthand with high living expenses and the struggles of paying bills.

chunks.text:
Even if minimum wage were to be increased, the prices for rent and other expensive will increase as well so there will not be a true way to escape this system. In order to live comfortably you have to sacrifice a lot of your happiness and free time in order to earn enough money to pay for everything that you need.

Capitalism only works in favor of those at the top of the food chain. Unless you already have enough to buy everything, you have to work your entire life in order to continue to afford some of the market’s high prices. Waking up every day in order to make sure that you earn enough money to live comfortably is not an ideal way of living and unless the power is given back to the working class, this will not change anytime soon.
chunks.label: Critique of capitalism and minimum wage
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how increasing minimum wage will not solve rising prices and argues that capitalism only favors those at the top while hurting the working class.

nf09c7dbb.title: Navigating Social Media and Beauty Standards

chunks.text:
Over the years, social media has grown into a platform that people tend to portray themselves on. However, when filters and photoshopping come into play, women begin to create a new beauty standard that is unrealistic. While social media platforms such as Instagram are increasing their body positivity posts, some are still not ending with positive effects. These negative effects lead women to have unrealistic beauty standards as well as trying to change themselves physically. Leading to the question what effects does social media have on the beauty standard in women? The effects of social media on the beauty standard in women include but are not limited to the formation of eating disorders, cosmetic surgeries, and strict fitness and diet goals. However, there are limitations on this subject because social media does not result in only negative effects. In recent years, social media has had an increase in positive posts in regard to body positivity, embracing one’s experiences and doing what makes them happy instead of what makes others happy. Depending on the mentality of the woman and the environment they are in can change how they are affected by beauty standards in social media negatively or positively.

While Afful and Lazuka as well as their colleagues argue that social media has a large impact on women and beauty standards, Susruthi Rajanala, Mayra B. C. Maymone, and Neelam A. Vashi argue that the society one lives in and participates in has a higher impact. Maymone et al points out that when people find themselves more attractive, they are happier and have a better well-being. (Maymone et al. p. 1). This causes people to go about cosmetic surgeries to enhance themselves. Today’s beauty standards are also linked to wealth and how well someone is doing in their life. Therefore, people tend to have these cosmetic surgeries to please others if not for themselves. Maymone et al. Explained that when women underwent specific surgeries, they were deemed more likeable, social, and trustworthy. Most of the cosmetic surgeries mentioned in this article refer to facial cosmetic changes rather than bodily changes. Certain features in the face can transform a person into becoming more approachable or trustworthy because of how they look. Some women undergo cosmetic surgeries to appear more professional looking in their workforce (Maymone et al. p. 2). The reasons for women undergoing cosmetic surgeries are very dependent on the environment they are surrounded by. If they believe that they do not look the part, they would appear more likely to have a surgery performed to help them in that aspect. If they feel that they look more professional, they may perform their job more effectively if they feel good while doing it. While this is not always the case, in my own experience I have felt more confident and done a better job at whatever I was doing if I felt that I looked better. It is important to notice the environment that a woman is in and whether that will affect the need to look a specific way. If the environment suggests that perfecting one’s appearance through weight loss, dieting, or cosmetic surgery is positive, then the women in that environment are going to feel pushed towards that decision. However, if the environment looks positively at being healthy, and not pushing people towards the contrasting culture, the women in that environment would not feel as pressured to make those changes. The examples and studies viewed by Maymone et al. Support the argument that social media as well as the environment can pressure women to surgically change their appearance to fit the beauty standards on social media.

While this is not part of a source, the importance of real-life examples in my own life supports the argument as well that social media has an effect on beauty standards in women. We tend to follow celebrities and influencers on social media. Whether they are models, singers, speakers or millionaires we compare our lives and our bodies to them. While some of the celebrities have begun to push the idea of body positivity and not give in to diet cultures and cosmetic surgeries, instances come up where they are paid to promote a product. Some give in to promoting the product and others decline in order to not go against what they stand for. Some celebrities have faced their own experiences with diet cultures and eating disorders growing up famous. They are pressured to look a certain way even more than the average person. More recently, they have opened up to these experiences in order to show normal people that they are not perfect. Celebrities become older, they have children, and they struggle to lose the weight from carrying a baby. In this day and age, they are more than likely pressured to get a cosmetic surgery to remove the extra fat from carrying that baby. Some may decide to take part in receiving the surgery while others will continue to pursue a healthy but not toxic lifestyle. They may get back to the body they had before, or they will not. Celebrities are slowly making it known that they do not have to portray themselves as perfect and flawless on social media. I personally believe that they are realizing that it is better to show their “human” side in order to abolish the unrealistic beauty standards that are shown on social media. In my own experiences, I have caught myself comparing my life in how interesting it is to my peers or celebrities and influencers as well as comparing how I look in comparison. It makes you think that if you can just figure out what their trick is to look a certain way then you will be happy. However, that is not the trick to being happy. I think people are also realizing that and doing what makes them happy regardless of how others are living their lives or how they look. Celebrities and influential people are also posting more about doing what makes you happy and not what makes other people happy. This is important because it contradicts the argument about social media having negative results on women. More recently there have been an increased number of body positivity posts that do not include pressure to live a specific life style and to embrace what makes you happy.

In conclusion, my argument was supported by my sources as well as showing the possible limitations in the studies that I used. Social media does cause the formation of eating disorders, the want for cosmetic surgery, and negative fitness and diet culture in women. While it was shown that social media had a large part in these effects, it was also observed that the environment one lives in can play a part in beauty standards as well. Celebrities and influential people on social media are normally the people showing unrealistic beauty standards for the average person because of the edited and photoshopped pictures. This is normal for celebrities to do because they have professional pictures taken constantly. However, more recently celebrities have been opening up with their own experiences with eating disorders, beauty standards, and how they are expected to portray themselves. Since they are doing this, they have also started posting more on social media about body positivity especially after having a baby, and unfiltered photos in their posts. I think that celebrities and influential people that we look up to making this change in social media and beauty standards will be better for women and they will appreciate their bodies more instead of wanting to change it in order to cater to other people’s expectations. Therefore, social media is not only producing negative effects on women, but slowly increasing the positive effects through positive posts on social media instead of promoting unhealthy methods of becoming what you want to look like.
chunks.label: Social media effects on women's beauty standards
chunks.what_happened: The student presents an academic essay analyzing literature and societal trends regarding how social media and the environment influence beauty standards, cosmetic surgery, and body positivity for women.

nad9fe8d2.title: Navigating Female Sexualization in Video Games

chunks.text:
An Analysis on the Sexualization of Women in the Media

Representation in the media matters. At a young age, children internalize messages from the pop culture they consume and perform imitations of the personalities they view as role models. This is extremely difficult for young girls who are often exposed to sexualized characters in the entertainment industry. As opposed to interesting and developed female protagonists, women are subjected to sexual and two-dimensional personalities, used to enhance the male gaze. The media aids in perpetuating concepts like the beauty myth by constantly portraying tall and thin women as the epitome of beauty, leaving those who do not fit the standard, without a voice. But why are women used solely for their bodies in these industries, as opposed to the intelligence and unique set of skills they offer? Short answer, sex sells. Under a patriarchal society in which males dominate these industries, women are objectified under the beauty myth and seen as a product to sell and make money from.

The media further objectifies women, by using the beauty myth as it’s template. Naomi Wolf describes the beauty myth as a political weapon that places women in a hierarchy based on their appearances, forcing them to fight each other for resources allocated by men. Essentially, men want beautiful women; women want to be beautiful. However, with the addition of the media, the standard of beautiful becomes impossible to obtain. Take for example, the Kardashians, these women are the face of pop culture, in commercials, hosting SNL, or the face of a designer brand, they dominate every social media platform. The Kardashian women have become the epitome of the sexy woman, with full lips, big breasts, tiny waists, and of course big butts. The problem with these depictions arises when these women promote their bodies as a natural outcome of exercising and dieting, and not from plastic surgery. This encourages the illusion that all women can and should look like this as, men find an hourglass body extremely attractive. When women do not fit this standard, they feel unworthy and excluded, despite their talents. The beauty myth allows the media to display one body type, which is just not attainable to average woman without developing an eating disorder or getting plastic surgery.
chunks.label: Sexualization of women and the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how media and pop culture objectify women, enforce impossible beauty standards like the beauty myth, and cater to the male gaze.

chunks.text: Looking back on my experience with my first Wii game, I understand why I will never find a character I can identify with; I don’t fit the beauty myth and the game isn’t for my enjoyment. Like most video games, this game marketed towards men and men want beautiful women on their screens. The beauty myth provides the creators with the categories of the sexy Zero Suit Samus or the sweet Princess Peach character, while the belief that women are a “second sex” justifies this objectification. Unlike the men in the game, Samus is given unrealistic body standards which goes on to show how dethatched and disillusioned these creators are to the average female body. Looking at this puzzle through the lens of the beauty myth and women as a “second sex,” highlights the way this sexualization is justified and created to reinforce gender norms, leaving those who do not fit this tiny waist, tall, big breasted category, without a platform to express themselves. My feelings of unease towards the game were really feelings of exclusion that my brothers could not understand, as they chose characters that personified their proudest traits.
chunks.label: Playing first Wii game with brothers
chunks.what_happened: The student played their first Wii game with their brothers and noticed the female characters like Samus and Princess Peach were sexualized or unrealistic, making it impossible to find a character they could identify with.

chunks.text: Representation contributes greatly to youth development by allowing children to visualize themselves as role models. Marvel movies like Black Panther and Shang Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings allow Black and Chinese kids to feel like superhero’s, however, these movies are still relatively new, showing Hollywood is just now starting to break barriers. As long as the entertainment industry is dominated by men, it will be marketed towards men who desire beautiful women on their screens. In the video game industry, which is extremely male dominated, even games that are targeted towards a young audience like Super Smash Bros. Brawl, will feature sexualized depictions of women to sell more games. With the view of women as a “second sex,” women’s bodies are objectified into products that can be sold for profit. The beauty myth just makes things easier for creators by providing them with the mold for the perfect money-making product. Young women deserve representation in the media that depicts an average body type, and showcases women for their intelligence and unique set of skills, as opposed to the two-dimensional eye-candy that is consistently displayed in pop culture.
chunks.label: Importance of representation in media
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the importance of positive representation in youth development and critiques how male-dominated industries continue to sexualize women instead of showcasing realistic role models.

nadbc746d.title: A Mother's Shift from Passion to Wages

chunks.text: In my own life an example of this can be seen in my mother. She went to college and graduated with a degree in early childhood development. She spent many years working in this field and really enjoyed it because it was something that she was passionate about. However, after having children she chose to not go back to work because her wage from the passion filled career barely covered the cost of day care. Now that her children are older, she has chosen to go back to work. However, not in her previous field that involves her degree, instead corporate America. While she does enjoy her work, the purpose of it is no longer the passion she felt in the past but the wage she receives. While her job may not hold the same sentiment, it does give her a sense of meaning that she craved when staying at home.
chunks.label: Mother's career shift and return to work
chunks.what_happened: The student's mother worked in early childhood development, stopped working after having children because daycare was too costly, and later returned to work in corporate America for the wage and a sense of meaning.

chunks.text:
This personal example also supports Marx’s idea of estranged labor and that a job satisfies ones feeling of existence.

Karl Marx introduces the idea of estranged labor based off the pre modern society of a European village. However, these ideas can also be seen in modern society as well as my own personal life. The collective consciousness involving going to college is just way that estranged labor is being brought into the modern market. In my own life I can see how estranged labor is present. Nevertheless, I feel it may be possible for some to have a career without estranged labor, like working for a nonprofit. This type of work involves passion and most of the time comes with a low salary. Thus, going against Marx idea that the people only do the work in exchange for a wage.
chunks.label: Reflecting on Karl Marx's estranged labor concept
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Karl Marx's theory of estranged labor in relation to college, corporate work, and nonprofit careers driven by passion rather than just wages.

nccf6dfe3.title: Critiquing Online and In-Person Social Interactions

chunks.text: Both Harari and Goffman argue negative impacts that social media can have in their writing. Harari believes that people are focused too much online interactions instead of in person connections. Goffman argues that these online interactions can unfavorable due to the lack of understanding between the two parties when communicating online. Unlike Goffman, Harari also goes into detail about how specifically Facebooks tries to bridge groups but instead does the opposite.
chunks.label: Harari and Goffman on negative impacts of social media
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Harari and Goffman's arguments regarding the negative impacts of social media and online interactions.

chunks.text:
There is no doubt that men and women are different. Thanks to the continuous feminism waves that have taken place in different periods, women have been able to slowly crack the collective consciousness of patriarchy and sexism. The right to vote, the right to own land, equal educational opportunities, and many more rights have made the gender discrimination gap smaller and smaller. But why are eating disorders still more prevalent in women than men? Why does America spend more than 20 billion dollars every year on beauty products (Wolf 1991)? Why is there still a pay gap between men and women? Why do most employees prefer to have a male boss rather than a female one? Of all the barriers that women have been able to tear down, there is one restriction that still controls women and stops them from being truly free: The Beauty Myth. As of today, unrealistic beauty standards keep women in a constant fight with their identities, therefore not able to concentrate in achieving their personal and professional goals. Mass media plays an important role in the creation and distribution of the idols that girls and women aspire to look like.

On module three from our Sociology class, we discussed the differences between sex and gender. We analyzed the collective consciousness that surrounds men and women and how society expects them to behave. We talked about how men are expected to be the head of the household, support a family, be physically strong, hide their emotions, and show leadership and security. We also learned how women are expected to give birth, raise children, and be silent and prudent. It is normal for women to cry or be emotional, because women are expected to be weak. But even after all the feminist revolutions, why are women still not viewed equally among men? The Beauty Myth is what still keeps women restrained from achieving their full potential. Our society is still immersed in a collective consciousness that evaluates women based on appearances rather than knowledge or experience.

From the beginning of human civilization, physical differences determined what kind of tasks men and women should perform. Men would use their strength and stamina to do hard labor such as farming, hunting, and constructing. On the other hand, women were valued based on fertility and their ability to raise kids. It was like this for centuries; fertility was considered women’s main asset, and a fat, full woman was actually considered a sign of good health. It wasn't until the 16th century, around the time that the printing press was invented, that the proliferation of media began spreading all kinds of ideas across Europe and America. By the 19th century, the press had already spread the idea of how the perfect woman should look. In an effort to look more attractive, women began to put themselves through painful diets and uncomfortable corsets that would create a skinny waist and voluptuous hips and breasts. For decades, women were seen as second class humans. In medieval Europe, a woman's goal was to get married and fully depend on her husband’s income. Women were hardly judged by their appearance and only gained value by their husbands.

As years passed by, the Beauty Myth kept growing as the printing media began spreading faster. Then the Miss America pageant emerged. As the world began to praise and admire these models, girls and women began to think about the desirable body a woman should have. Having a perfect body became synonymous with compliments, success, and freedom. However, having the perfect model body was only achievable by extreme diets and exercise that marked the beginning of eating disorders. Going through the 20th century, the spread of mass media allowed the diffusion of the perfect female body. Magazines, television, and advertisements began to only show perfect models that represented the American beauty standards. Those who did not meet those standards would work as hard as they could to achieve the dream body.

Nowadays, the media continues to be a great influence on girls and young women. If we look closely at the way women are portrayed in the media, we can see a pattern on how these women are presented. Perfect hair, highlighting makeup, hourglass bodies, and high skirts is what women in the media look like. This is especially true on sport shows and events. The clothing these women would be wearing is most of the time extremely revealing and highlights their body’s curves. The sexualization of the body is part of the Objectification Theory (Roberts & Gettman, 2004) that goes hand in hand with the Beauty Myth because it creates a disconnection between mind and body that makes women more conscious about their bodies.

According to the self-objectification theory, when women create this third perspective of themselves, it makes them more self conscious which allows feelings of shame and anxiety to overpower. Women would continuously compare themselves with beautiful models which, in return, lead to feelings of discomfort and mortification. This eventually would stop them from participating in activities like going out, wearing a swimsuit, or even going to school and work. A study made by Fredrickson and colleagues (1998, as cited in Roberts & Gettman, 2004) and Gapinski, Brownell, and LaFrance (2003 as cited in Roberts & Gettman, 2004) consisted in examining men and womens’ reactions to their bodies in a swimsuit and a sweater. The results showed that women had a higher level of body shame compared to men while wearing a swimsuit. This traces back to the stereotypes present in the media. Girls grow up with images of what the perfect woman looks like, and a swimsuit that highlights perfectly seen areas can trigger self-consciousness and lead to poor mental and emotional health.

The ironic part about the Beauty Myth and the self-objectification theory is that almost every “perfect” woman portrayed in the media is a product of computer alteration. Legs are stretched out, skin is highlighted or darkened, and even some models are digitally created by the morphing of several models. It is ironic because all these magazines talk about how to get the perfect body by natural processes while the models depicted as “real” are not even authentic (Consalvo, 1997, as cited in Roberts & Gettman, 2004)

Women who set up goals to unrealistic standards are hardly ever going to meet this desire. According to research, only a minority of women in the US are actually overweight, however, the majority of women claim to feel overweight (Crandall, 1994, as cited in Roberts & Gettman, 2004). Women pursuing an unrealistic dream creates this ongoing cycle of anxiety and frustration that can stop them from doing what they really want. These feelings of worthlessness and low self esteem, according to the Beauty Myth, have been set up by the patriarchy to convince women they do not deserve more. This explains why in the 21th century, where everybody has equal access to education and connections, there is still a pay gap between men and women.

According to a study made in Poland, there are a couple of theories that could explain the pay gap in this country. From prejudice taste by employers and clients, to the assignment of roles based on gender. The study collected, analyzed, and compared women and men’s wages from 1991 to 2015. During this time period, researchers made sure to consider education level, job experience, and wage level when comparing gross and net income. This study not only found out that there is a considerably big pay gap between men and women, but it also found that this pay gap tended to be greater in higher levels of employment. But how can citizens from a first world country in the 21st century still allow this phenomenon to happen? The research concludes that is mainly because it is socially accepted. The population in Poland still follows the Christian-catholic, which considers family as their highest value. Therefore, men are privileged over women with higher pay rates because they are still considered the main providers of the family. Women have accepted this secondary role because it is part of the collective consciousness of Poland’s society (Calogero, Borought, & Thompson, 2007).

All of these articles and researches show how deep the Beauty Myth is in our collective consciousness. Women have been taught that their body image is their ticket to a life of acceptance, success, love, and money. But when the market saw the opportunity to profit from girls and women’s insecurity, the mass proliferation of the “perfect” and “natural” woman created an unrealistic goal that continues to feed itself and grow from womens’ anxiety. The mass expansion of the perfect model has created unreachable expectations by the rest of society that now young women feel they need to reach. This has led to feelings of insecurity and incompetence that can affect the way women are seen because it sets very high standards. The self devaluation of women has allowed them to accept lower wages.

The Beauty Myth is the last, but the strongest barrier that women need to tear down in order to be truly confident and free. Feminism is women’s strongest ally, but there are still a lot of prejudices surrounding feminism for women. Women will finally gain power once society and themselves accept that femininity and beauty does not equal competency and civility. The Beauty Myth portraits women as beautiful and young, basically inert. But the modern woman is not inert, it is changing, progressing, and expressing their individuality (Wolf, 1991).
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of the Beauty Myth and gender inequality
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the Beauty Myth, gender roles, media representation, self-objectification theory, and research on gender wage gaps discussed in their sociology class and academic literature.

chunks.text:
Why do men feel pressured to haze or be hazed as means of validation of their identity? Throughout various communities and groups across society, particularly pertaining to those associated with masculinity, hazing has served as a means of inclusivity and acceptance, causing men to feel forced to accept means of humiliation and degradation in order to feel a sense of accomplishment and meaning within a group. In addition, older members of such groups arguably feel the need to haze as a means of securing their masculine roles as tough, strong, and dominant leaders, thus engaging younger members through the process. Although many have begun to combat and resist the idea of hazing, the same ideas and principles associated with hazing can still regardless be found and applied throughout masculine culture, thus suggesting a deeper cause. Overall, despite efforts being made to better understand and eliminate hazing, the base of the problem lies within the forced view from society on masculinity, holding that men should be expected to play the dominant role of being tough, strong, and emotionless in order to fit in.

Due to the fact that men are expected throughout society to play the role of being tough, strong, dominant, and emotionless, this further causes them to fall subject to this flawed norm of society, with abuse and humiliation through hazing serving as validation. In order to combat these situations of abuse and humiliation as a means of validation, it is crucial to understand and oppose the norms brought on by hegemonic masculinity implicitly pressured through society.
chunks.label: Hazing and hegemonic masculinity in society
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces how societal expectations of masculinity push men to haze or be hazed to gain validation, and argues for opposing hegemonic masculinity.

chunks.text: One example in which this can be applied includes my experience in our varsity boys' soccer team in high school. Over the course of my time on the team, we would frequently play a series of games and activities we referred to as “consequences.” The idea of the game was to force whoever lost to perform a specific punishment or “consequence.” The activity was originally created as a “team bonding activity;” however the activity soon grew into a means of hazing and humiliation, particularly from the upperclassman. Over the years, the consequences created and forced onto the losers, typically lowerclassmen, became more and more outrageous, unbearable, and disgusting, mainly serving as a means of entertainment and a feeling of power for the seniors, who always conducted the activities. However, regardless of the punishment, members of the soccer team would almost always face up to the humiliation and degradation of the various consequences in order to feel viewed with validation. In contrast, members who did not face up to the consequences would frequently be regarded as “weak,” “scared,” or “unmanly,” while also frequently being harassed and targeted in future engagements of the activity. Additionally, players would also encourage you after completing a consequence, saying things like, “you’re the man, I can’t believe you did that, that took guts,” further conditioning you into thinking of yourself with a false sense of validation and “manhood.” On a soccer team built upon the foundation of brotherhood, love, and serving others, this situation of hazing acted as the total opposite, further negatively reflecting on the values and ideologies of masculinity. In order to avoid feeling viewed differently from other members of the team, as well as to feel a sense of accomplishment and validation among other members, players would give into this toxic ideology of not being “weak,” while instead being “courageous” and “strong” to further feel accepted.
chunks.label: High school soccer team consequences hazing
chunks.what_happened: During high school varsity soccer, the team played games called 'consequences' where losers suffered humiliating punishments from upperclassmen to prove their manhood and gain acceptance.
chunks.people: varsity boys' soccer team members, upperclassmen, seniors, lowerclassmen

chunks.text: An additional example from my experience that can be applied includes the idea of hazing within fraternities. In contrast to sororities, which usually contain almost no hazing, fraternities across the nation commonly use situations of hazing towards their pledges, ranging from mild to extreme instances. Common examples include forcing pledges to drive brothers to and from various locations, performing a specific set of chores, and wearing often absurd or specific outfits, with more extreme examples including performing a set of pranks, as well as the forced consumption of various narcotics. Fraternities often haze as a means for their pledges to prove that they are “man enough” to do whatever it takes to become a brother of the fraternity, while also weeding out those who are unsuccessful when performing these specific tasks. I have also noticed a large difference relating to the personality of some of my friends before and after completing their pledge process. Specifically, many of them seemed to be conditioned through hazing to express a style of masculinity built upon the foundation of acting “strong, tough, competitive, and emotionless” to not appear as an outcast. For example, one of my friends whom I have known since high school previously used to be much more energetic, lively, and full of emotion before he decided to pledge his current fraternity. However, over the course of the process, he gradually began to develop a more careless attitude, often hiding his emotions and developing a new sense of self in order to fit in better as a man within his fraternity. This ideology found within hazing not only causes pledges to feel a sense of rejection if not accepted, but further conditions the idea that in order to find a sense of meaning, purpose, and masculinity, one must be willing to not act as “weak” and instead be “courageous” through often demoralizing and degrading activities.
chunks.label: Observing fraternity hazing and friend's personality change
chunks.what_happened: The student observed fraternity hazing practices and witnessed a high school friend become emotionally distant and careless after going through the pledging process.
chunks.people: fraternity pledges, fraternity brothers, student's high school friend

chunks.text: The concept describing that men hold stereotypical roles of being dominant, strong, courageous, aggressive, invulnerable to threats and problems, and emotionless relates to the idea of hegemonic masculinity. Brett G. Stroudt describes this idea when analyzing a private, mostly white, boy's boarding school named Rockport. According to Stroud, the school essentially served as a “breeding ground” for hegemonic masculinity, as the roles found within the ideology were frequently reinforced through each other, mostly due to their privilege as white males. The roles reinforced further taught the boys to hide their emotions publicly and instead share them in private with women. He further states that the reinforced roles also create a dichotomy between privacy and emotions as being related to women and needing to be kept out of a public, objective, rational classroom, further suppressing and lowering the standards of women (stroudt). Overall, when society begins to accept this ideology, this can become problematic as it thus assigns a stronger more powerful role towards men, while also assigning a lower, limiting role towards women.
chunks.label: Hegemonic masculinity in academic literature
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the concept of hegemonic masculinity, drawing on Brett G. Stroud's analysis of boys' boarding school culture and its effects on views of women.

chunks.text:
I believe that situations of hazing, as described through my high school soccer team as well as within college fraternities, serve as excellent examples that can be explained through hegemonic masculinity. Essentially, allowing oneself to haze or be hazed in order to feel a sense of accomplishment and validation is built upon the foundation of the stereotypical roles described through hegemonic masculinity, such as toughness, emotionlessness, and courage. For example, over the course of our soccer team playing “consequences,” members who lost essentially agreed to engage in the humiliating punishments as this strengthened their sense of masculinity and validation among themselves and other players, while also avoiding the reputation of being viewed as “weak” and “cowardly.” Additionally, fraternity pledges also feel led to give into hazing as this will allow them to feel “strong” and “courageous,” while also becoming a part of a group that will help them find meaning among others who potentially view them with these roles. Oftentimes, leaders of groups like these, because of the dominant roles they play, believe it is important to express their role through hazing in order to be viewed by themselves and others as “strong, fearless, and emotionless” leaders, further contributing to the spread of hegemonic masculinity.

Groups such as fraternities and athletic teams also allow and encourage the reinforcement of these specific hegemonic masculine traits, as members within these communities are surrounded by others who believe the same way and are never challenged on their beliefs. Fraternities, for example, typically are very exclusive, picking and choosing exactly who they believe will serve as an asset within that group. Fraternities would not choose someone who they believed would act out against the hazing process or damage their reputation. Thus, within a selected group of mostly privileged men from similar backgrounds, these hegemonic traits are able to spread and reinforce easily. In relation to the soccer team, however, the process of hegemonic masculine reinforcement is slightly different. Although members are not specifically chosen due to these traits, oftentimes male athletes regardless still express similar hegemonic masculine traits, and when selected onto a team surrounded by others who share the same traits, these values are thus reinforced and encouraged. This ultimately leads to situations of hazing becoming more common, as members thus feel safe within their communities to practice it without repercussions.
chunks.label: Analyzing sports teams and fraternities through hegemonic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how high school soccer and college fraternities reinforce hegemonic masculine traits and encourage hazing behaviors.

chunks.text: In sum, members within these selected, often privileged, communities typically allow themselves to haze or be hazed as this helps to build a sense of validation of their masculine traits to themselves as well as additional members. However, many members within these communities are unaware that in an effort to pursue this sense of validation, these traits are implicitly built off the flawed foundation of stereotypical hegemonic masculine roles. I personally have found evidence of this through examples including our “consequences” activity on my high school soccer team, as well as through witnessing college fraternity pledges endure humiliation in order to feel validated. Overall, how can one stop the reinforcement of hegemonic masculinity through means of hazing? One crucial tactic includes helping to spread awareness of the topic of hegemonic masculinity, further leading others to resist the support of its toxic traits, which are often applied and encouraged through means of hazing. In relation to groups such as fraternities and athletic teams, I believe it is possible to embrace a healthier definition as well as healthier values associated with masculinity, particularly those apart from hazing. This ultimately allows groups such as these the ability to lead one to find a more plausible and respectable sense of self, meaning, and validation.
chunks.label: Conclusion on ending hazing and reshaping masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes how hazing validates flawed masculine norms and argues for spreading awareness and adopting healthier masculine values.

chunks.text: Harari, in the book often looks to the future. He mentions, at one point, that in 2100 the rich could have the ability to be better than those who don’t have money because with the way technology is advancing, people will be able to buy themselves “enhanced bodies and brains.” The gap between the rich and the poor will continue to widen, and it won’t be able to close again. Domhoff discusses the ways of the upper class and how they are the groups that work in the higher up areas, such as corporations and federal government positions. Working people don’t hold power in this world because they don’t have money. They work to survive and buy groceries so they can eat. The working class, in 2100 won’t have the ability to buy themselves enhanced bodies and brains. They are already set apart by the upper class, so imagining a world where the gap is bridged even wider is intimidating already.
chunks.label: Reflections on Harari, Domhoff, and future class inequality
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Harari's predictions about future technology widening the gap between rich and poor, as well as Domhoff's analysis of upper-class power.

n2ebd30fc.title: Understanding Unconscious Privilege Through Sociological Theory

chunks.text:
In Peggy McIntosh’s article titled White Privilege she explains that she noticed how men often are unaware or don’t admit they are more privileged than women. When she became aware of this, she often became aware of the privilege that white people have over people of color, and how white people are often unaware of this privilege as well. In Mead’s The Self the I and the Me he explains his theory of self and how it relates to a person’s learned behaviors and their conception of self.

Peggy explains that she believes white people are carefully taught not to a acknowledge their privilege. This makes them unaware that they even have it, and only by become aware of it can they do something to change it. In Mead’s theory of self, he explains that the self has two sides, the “me” and the “I”. The “me” represents an individual’s learned behaviors and attitudes as well as their expectations of people. The “I” is a person’s response to others. This helps to further Peggy’s argument because it explains that a white person’s “me” is their learned behavior of not acknowledging their privilege therefore they have no expectation of others to admit their privilege. Once a person becomes aware, they become more inclined to expect others to notice as well. Peggy goes on to say that becoming aware of the privilege will help to change the circumstances surrounding it.

In Peggy McIntosh’s article titled White Privilege she speaks about how becoming aware of her white privilege also made her more aware of all the things she was able to do without discrimination. Mead’s theory of self helps to explain why people are often unaware of the

privilege that they have.
chunks.label: Analyzing Peggy McIntosh and Mead's theories of privilege
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Peggy McIntosh's article on white privilege and connects it to George Herbert Mead's sociological theory of the 'I' and the 'me' to explain how people learn not to acknowledge their privilege.

n61c24474.title: Pressures of Living Up to Masculinity

chunks.text: Are society standards for men fair? What about them makes them fair? And why are men put into these standards?
chunks.label: Questioning societal standards for men
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces questions regarding whether society's standards for men are fair and why men are held to them.

chunks.text: All my boyfriend’s life he has had to live up to not only society’s standards but his unrealistic and unfair expectations from his family. He must prove to his family every single day of his life how tough he is and how masculine he is. He is putting himself through mental and physical strain to prove these things. If he shows he’s sick, not being self-sufficient, or doesn’t work and make money then he appears weak according to the standards of modern society and his family as well. There are some examples of why he isn’t masculine or “tough” and shows weakness. He constantly must prove to his family he is masculine and strong by doing some of those examples listed above.
chunks.label: Boyfriend's struggle with family expectations
chunks.what_happened: The student describes how her boyfriend endures mental and physical strain to constantly prove his toughness, work ethic, and masculinity to his family.

chunks.text:
Is this fair? I ask that again because in today’s culture there is consistent back and forth on what the actual definition of what a “man” is if there even is one. Why must men like my boyfriend out themselves through a personal battle with something that has no definite answer? The reason is because the definition varies from person to person.

Men are often judged based on their masculinity and how strong or weak they are.
chunks.label: Reflecting on the definition of a man
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the unclear and shifting definition of what constitutes a man in modern society and how men are judged by masculinity.

chunks.text: When my boyfriend must act “tough” and strong around his family it is an example of hegemonic masculinity. To better understand what hegemonic masculinity means, it is defined as, “the dominant frame for how men should be in Euro-American societies.” Hegemonic masculinity is what my boyfriend must prove to his family every day within his home. For example, says that he is sick, or isn’t self-sufficient his family will ask him, “are you okay?” or “This isn’t like you to not be doing something or working.” If he shows himself crying to his family, they assume something is drastically wrong because they think men shouldn’t cry based on society’s standards.
chunks.label: Boyfriend facing hegemonic masculinity at home
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how her boyfriend must display hegemonic masculinity around his family, who question him or assume something is drastically wrong if he is sick, resting, or crying.

chunks.text: This isn’t true at all in my opinion. When men are seen crying, it can be for any number of reasons not just weakness. Men can have suppressed emotions just like any other person. When holding back emotions, the works just like a dam, yeah it can hold a good number of things but if the flow isn’t controlled then it is bound to burst open.
chunks.label: Thoughts on men suppressing emotions
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on why men crying is not weakness and compares holding back emotions to a dam waiting to burst.

chunks.text: Discussing with my boyfriend his struggles with proving his masculinity within society standards and his family expectations and the struggles he faced daily to show them he’s a strong person and not weak really opened my eyes that he’s not the only male struggling with this on the daily basis.
chunks.label: Discussing masculinity struggles with boyfriend
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses masculinity standards and family expectations with her boyfriend, which opens her eyes to the widespread nature of these struggles.

chunks.text: Many of us were raised in a sort of blinded society. Meaning that crying and showing emotions were shunned or perhaps best saved for the privacy of isolation. Men are surrounded by loved ones and people that they trust that may often compel them to hide their tears, to appear strong and unbroken. There are many men that must prove that they are strong and worthy of their family, their friends, and society. The idea that “big boys don’t cry” is a complete wash. To me, I think it’s unfair and I think men should be able to express their feelings and emotions the way they want them to and how they feel now. Also, not having to hide their emotions and feelings to be seen as strong people. Releasing emotions, like crying or being sad for example does not define how strong or masculine a person is, in my opinion. Also, being sick or taking a rest day and not doing anything should not show others that you are not self-sufficient or busy.
chunks.label: Critique of emotional repression in society
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on societal conditioning against emotional expression in men, arguing that crying, resting, or being sick does not make someone weak.

chunks.text: Learning about the struggles he faced proving his masculinity every day, really opened my eyes and made me realize that society’s standards aren’t fair to men as they are to women. Women can express their emotions, cry, and laugh, and be angry all in the same day, and it’s just seen as a hormonal imbalance, or they are just having a rough day. For example, with my boyfriend I have days that I am very emotional, I will be crying one minute next then I am angry or upset which could be about anything and I am told its okay to cry and let it out. Men on the other hand if they express their emotions like I stated above they are seen as weak, and too emotional. For example, as described above, if my boyfriend shows emotion, he is asked multiple questions if he is okay, or if something serious is wrong or it’s not like him to act like this but I’m told its okay to cry and let it out. The differences here are absurd.
chunks.label: Comparing boyfriend's and student's emotional expressions
chunks.what_happened: The student contrasts her own freedom to be emotional and receive comfort with her boyfriend's experience of being questioned and scrutinized whenever he shows emotion.

chunks.text: In a society that is always trying to fight for equality, we don’t see much fighting for this subject at least it isn’t shown in widespread public media. What society needs to understand is that there is not a clear definition of weak or strong. I don’t think some people understand what really goes on in people’s lives behind closed doors. Some people only see others as happy but really, they could be struggling but they don’t show it because they don’t want to be seen as weak or too emotional to others. The only real definition is found within each person. It is all based on one’s own thoughts and recollections of themselves. Society as a whole can define who we are as people, only we can do that. Breaking the mold on what makes a man a ‘man’ is the first step. Like everything else, this will take time to reach the minds of every man, having them just know that they are an important part of the lives around can help them make their own definition of what being a man truly is. Then, I think the next step is to let people be who they want to be and express how they feel without people feeling like they are going to get bashed for showing emotion. Then we as a society will be headed in the right direction.
chunks.label: Call for redefined masculinity and equality
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the lack of attention to emotional inequality for men, arguing that individuals should define strength for themselves and express emotions freely.

n7256e210.title: Understanding the Consequences of Workplace Alienation

chunks.text:
Alienation in the Workplace and how it Affects a Worker.
