Have you ever been unsatisfied with your work? Feel as though your job doesn’t stimulate your creativity? Does your job give you a sense of purpose? These feelings are not uncommon with in the workplace, and many people around the world experience alienation within their place of work. Karl Marx, a German sociologist, explained these feelings and the concept of alienation in “Estranged Labor”.

Karl Marx believed that the feeling of alienation comes from a person labor. He describes four different types of alienation and why this alienation is experienced by the worker. What Karl Marx does not explain however is how this alienation effects the worker outside of their workplace. How it affects their social life and their mental wellbeing. After further research into this matter, it is clear that alienation within the workplace has a distinct negative effect on a person life outside of the workplace.

The four different types of alienation that Karl Marx describes are the separation the worker has to the product, the estrangement that the worker feels during the production process, alienation from the human identity, and finally alienation of man to man. These feelings of alienation all stem from different things but they all occur within the workplace, and they all have a negative effect on the worker. A study titled “The effects of work alienation on organizational commitment, work effort, and work-to-family enrichment” focused on the powerlessness and the meaninglessness aspect of alienation. Karl Marx's concept and theory of alienation is predominantly in regard to the worker, and it focuses on how the capitalist production process is what makes the worker feel alienated. Marx believed that alienation is the result of being within a society where there are social classes, and that wage labor resulted in a feeling of alienation. Marx also believed that our society was divided into two classes, the first one being capitalist, and the second one being the laborer’s. He argued that labor is an essential part to a man's core concept of himself. When a worker creates something, he puts himself into that object, but alienation occurs because the production of that object is not his. As the worker creates more this feeling of alienation grows. In our economy work is about surviving, and we do not work for the sake of ourselves. For the labor, their work is not driven from the core concept of themselves but instead driven by survival. The alienation that occurs when a worker feels alienated from the human identity, or as Marx called it "species being”, occurs when the labor feels separated from their basic humanity. Referring to the idea that labor is the essential part of a man's core identity, Marx believed that we are what we create. Due to capitalism, private ownership, and the division of labor however a worker has no ownership over his creations. This division between the capitalist and the labor creates another form of alienation between man and man. Due to the labor producing goods for others it separates the worker from the person who truly "owns" the goods being produced. Therefore, creating a divide between man and their fellow man.

The purpose of this study was to analyze the effects of work elimination on organizational commitment, work effort, and work to family enrichment. They had three hypotheses that they studied the first one is that work alienation will be negatively related to passive performance at work, the second one is that work alienation will be negatively related to active performance at work, and the third and final one is that work alienation will be negatively related to life outside of work. The way that they test their hypotheses was by using surveys collected among a national sample of midwives in the Netherlands. They chose to do midwives because of their growing scarcity as well as the fact that most midwives are the primary caregivers within their families. This study in particular is important because it recognizes that work and family are no longer separate life demands but that they are becoming increasingly related, therefore also recognizing that work has an effect on life at home. The three things that the study was looking at is organizational commitment, work effort, and work to family enrichment. Organizational commitment is the emotional feeling that an employee has towards the organization that they are employed to, workers who experienced this are more likely to stay with the organization because they are able to identify with it. This is also an important feeling for the worker to experience because it positively influences the employees’ health and their well-being. Work effort is when employee extends their work beyond what is written in their employment contract. Feelings of powerlessness or meaninglessness can affect the performance of a workers work effort. The two aspects of alienation, powerlessness, and meaninglessness are negatively related to organizational commitment and work effort. This is due to the fact that having control over the way that work is done is likely to increase organizational commitment and work effort within the worker. Available studies show that there is a negative relationship between meaninglessness and job performance. A lot of them also show that meaninglessness is negatively related to a worker’s commitment to their work. Meaninglessness and job satisfaction as well as work effort also have a negative relationship. The study found that work powerlessness and meaninglessness both have a significant negative influence on organizational commitment of workers. This means that when workers feel that their work has no meaning and when they have no power over their work, they are less committed to their job or their employer. The data of the study also shows that when the worker feels that they have no meaning in their work or when they feel powerless at work, they are less willing to put effort into their jobs. Finally, the study showed that work meaninglessness does in fact have a negative effect on work family relationships, it found that when the worker felt that their work was not important, they also experienced less positivity in their family life.

Another study titled "on the personal consequences of alienation in work" aimed to study the consequences of feeling alienated at work. They conducted the study by examining a random sample that consisted of working males in a Swedish community. The consequences that are usually allotted to work alienation consist of hostility, political withdraw, a sense of powerlessness, and the seeking of a status. Alienation can be considered the wrongful denial of a man to his potential. This concept connects to mark's idea that a man's labor is his core concept of self. When a man is consistently working in an environment or a job that is unfulfilling it can have very serious social affects. The consequences of unfulfilling labor do not just consist of the refusal of a personal fulfilment but also consists of trouble within a person's political life, as well as their social life and many other aspects outside of the workplace. Alienation within the workplace not only affects a worker at their job but also at social events, political affairs, and their home life as well. The theory is that the effect of alienation in the workplace trickles into a person's social and personal life therefore affecting those aspects as well. The feeling of powerlessness also has a negative effect on the worker's mental well-being. This study in particular raises questions about what can alleviate the feeling of alienation. Things such as becoming a member the worker's occupation, friendships with fellow workers, especially those who work face to face. The friendship idea in particular has been found to help alleviate the feelings of being alienated within the workplace. This study in particular found that there was little evidence that length alienated work to being less engaged in political and social matters. However, the study also raised interesting questions about what factors could have played a role in these findings. Like whether or not outside friendships contributed to the worker's well-being.

While looking further into Karl Marx’s theory of alienation I realized that it is still a very prevalent issue to this day, and that lots of people are studying the effect that it has on workers who experience it. Marx contributed a worker’s creations or their work to their sense of purpose, explaining that a man’s core concept of self was what he creates. Feeling as though one has no control or ownership over their creations and their work leads to alienation. This occurs because of the separation between the two classes the laborer, and the capitalist. The laborer has no ownership over what they create therefore creating a divided between the worker and their work. As human beings we find purpose in our work, and we work for our own self-fulfillment, but in today’s society most people have to work for survival. Working only because you have to in order to survive does not give a sense of fulfillment and leads to the separation between the worker and their job. Feelings of alienation contribute and led to feelings powerlessness and meaninglessness within and outside of a person’s job. Even though the studies had different results in regards to how alienation affects the worker outside of the workforce, they both found that it did have some type of affect. The first study found that those who felt a feeling of meaninglessness within their jobs, also felt less positivity within their home life. That there was a direct negative correlation between feelings of alienation to negative feelings outside of work. Feelings of alienation also affect the workers work effort, when they feel as though their job has no meaning, they are less willing to put effort into their jobs. Alienation not only effects a person while at work but also outside of their job, such as in their home life and their social lives. The second study found that friendships within the workplace can help to lessen or alleviate feelings of alienation, especially when the friends are those who work closely with you. In conclusion alienation within the workplace has a negative effect on personal aspects of a worker’s life, such as their family and social lives.

SORCES

Tummers, L.G. & Den Dulk, L. (forthcoming 2013). The effects of work alienation on organizational commitment, work effort and work-to-family enrichment. Journal of Nursing Management

On the Personal Consequences of Alienation in Work. www.jstor.org/stable/2091817.

Bennett, Elizabeth A. “Alienation and Its Consequence: An Exploration of Marxism, Hikikomori, and Authenticity via Relational Connection.” The Humanistic Psychologist, vol. 48, no. 3, 2020, pp. 257–270., doi:10.1037/hum0000153.
chunks.label: Workplace alienation and its effects
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Karl Marx's theory of alienation in the workplace and reviews empirical sociological studies examining how work alienation affects workers' commitment, effort, family life, and social well-being.

chunks.text:
Battle of the sexes. Male versus female. Man versus woman. A large discussion that seems never-ending. There are many opinions people out there that say a man is better than a woman. There are things that men can do that a woman can’t do. This is true, there are things that a man can do that a woman can’t do, but there are also things that a woman can do that a man cannot. The popular saying when it comes to this is the fact that a woman can have children, but a man cannot. While true, this is not the only example out there. A woman can do a lot but there is a long history where women were seen as the weaker of the sexes. Progress has been made, but there is evidence that shows that women are still being treated unfairly compared to their male counterparts. In this paper, I will discuss the gender roles that women are stereotyped with, which can be seen in relationships, in the workplace, and how these roles are still seen today.

Relationships Between Men and Women

Men, in relationships, are generally seen as the dominant figure. They are the “man of the house.” Men provide for their families while women are expected to stay home and take care of the children. This is a gender role that is still acknowledged today by many people and religions. Another example is how a man protects a woman, and the woman allows herself to be protected. This can be seen throughout children’s stories of the princess being saved by a prince. Kids learn through these stories at a young age, that women need men to save them from the “big, bad, and scary things.” They grow up learning these things and go about it by believing they need a man to thrive or by challenging the social norms.

This then brings up the point of learned gender roles in a learning community. There has been recent research that shows a focus on the “separate sphere” model. This is where men are seen as the provider or breadwinners. Women are seen as caretakers. A man’s “domain” is the workplace while the home is the woman’s. Going back to the children’s stories, a man is expected to save the woman. Men and women in a relationship are expected to look a certain way. Usually, in the dating scene, people make assumptions, and they have ideas as to what a relationship should be like. The man should be taller, older, and they should make the first move. Men get praised for having many sexual partners while women are condemned for doing the same. These stereotypes remain the same. Men are expected to propose marriage and to be taller and older than their female counterparts. Women are expected to listen to their partner and stick to the social gender norms (Yu & Duan, 2021). There are stereotypes for women everywhere, these form at home, at school, and in the workplace.

Hiring and Job Selection

When hiring for a job, hiring committees can often be quite selective. Committees look at achievements, personality, work ethic, and they have to look at geographical locations. They need a person that fits the job, so they look at everything, including relationships. Women are seen as a big part in a family. Because of this gender role, where women prioritize their family, hiring committees are less likely to offer a job to a partnered woman because of the chance of a geographical move. Males and single females were the target audience, instead (Rivera, 2017).

Gender stereotypes have messed with the hiring scene for women because men are depicted as being better at most things than women, so they are the target interviewees. Already, from the start, women are not being considered because they have a family and are in a relationship. They are stereotyped to be family women when that isn’t always the case. Aren’t women allowed to have goal and aspirations? Or does that stop when they have a family? It doesn’t stop. Women dream and they can be ambitious while having a family. A geographical move is a small price to pay for a good working job that they applied for in the first place.

Sexual Harassment in the Workplace

In a workplace, women are known to have to put up with more concerning issues than a man. These issues can come in the form of sexual harassment and discrimination. Women are considered to be more vocal about these issues in the recent years. For the most part, women will speak up about what they have been through, but when it comes to a person in a higher-up position committing an act, women are more likely to lose their voice. Sexual harassment has the power to harm the victim’s wellbeing in total. This can affect their physical and mental wellbeing, which is also seen as a problem because women and mental health in a sentence are seen as a bad thing (Foley et al., 2020). Women are seen as being ruled by their hormones and their emotions. They cannot work and have a hard day because they need to give their one hundred percent to keep up with the males in the workplace.

Then, there is the flexibility and unequal pay aspect where women are known to accept lower pay in exchange for flexibility in their schedule. This adds fuel to the “unequal pay” fire that was built years ago, and that is still a problem today (Cooper et al., 2021). Women, because they were seen as a part of man, and in need of a man, are taught to keep their mouths shut. While this situation has improved today, sexual harassment in the workplace is still a major issue. Unequal pay is a problem in every industry. The music, acting, and sports industry is where we hear about it the most. Female actresses have come out to speak about the fact that they are paid a considerable amount less than their male counterparts.

Women’s sports teams are hardly spoken about and there are many problems within the industry when it comes to treating both genders fairly, more than just payment. There was a recent issue that came up involving the WNBA weight room where the women received yoga mats and six pairs of weights, while the men received many workout benches, dumbbells, and bars for their gym. It was considerably larger than the women’s gym (Fernandez, 2021). While men’s sports are considered to be the most popular out of the two, women’s sports are still important and shouldn’t have to be considered less than by the organization.

Gender Roles in Early Childhood

“Despite their growing presence in the labor force and educational institutions in the last few decades, women remain socially marginalized and underrepresented within, as well as, outside of households in low-income countries (Islam & Asadullah, 2018).” Every year, in many countries, women are married off before they reach adulthood and according to UN Women, one in three women experience a form of physical harassment. Along with this, “the United Nation’s Girl Education Initiative identified it as one of the five challenges towards achieving gender equality in education. Biased textbook contents not only limit women’s worldviews and career choices, but they also distort their self-image and the image of the opposite gender group.” So, women are taught this in “biased textbooks,” instead of learning that they have the ability to get good jobs and help their families in more ways than one.

Looking at the situation from an academic standpoint, opinions and ideas differ greatly. In some countries, like the United States, school is encouraged, and girls attend earlier than boys. They feel safe in this place and are able to learn which is said to be easier for women. However, in other countries where traditional thinking is encouraged, “boys need careers and girls need husbands,” which is a type of “truth” that teachers in schools say in Africa. This way of thinking still being around won’t go away. In some cultures, like the Mexican culture, a woman is told to serve her husband. She makes him food while he works. She washed clothes and cleans the house while he rests from the workday. This is a truth, but it is important to acknowledge that the gender norms develop in early childhood. It comes from school, the television, and from the family that a child is born into. It comes from culture and familiarity.

Gender Roles in Religion

Religion is a part of every kid’s life, whether they believe in God, gods, goddesses, divine beings, or nothing. Religion always has something to say about what a woman’s place is. In the Christian bible, a woman’s place is next to her husband. There is a man of the house, a head of household, a man to care and provide for his family. There is a woman to grow the family and care for the children. Women in Buddhism have stricter guidelines than men in their religion. Only men can reach the highest level of spirituality because women were reluctantly given the ability to become ordained. These are guidelines that many traditional religious families follow, and they teach their children who grow up and do the same. Kids learn these gender roles everywhere and this is why women are still being held back from being seen as equal (Salgado, 2015).

Women have had it rough. This is seen throughout history and it is still seen today in the world. Men and women are different physically, yes. Men and women have different parts and ways of thinking. There are scientific methods and studies that have proven men are stronger than women. Studies that show women react in different ways to a crying baby than men. This is also the twenty-first century. A female president was almost elected. There is now a female Vice President, the firs ever. History has been made and history will continue to be made. No, women and men aren’t equal, yet. Men and women both have different strengths, but women should not be treated as an extension of a man. Women are not less than men. There are gender roles that are expected of women, but those roles do not have to be followed.

Conclusion

Women are told how to act and to know their place. There has been improvement, but equal pay has not been accomplished. Men are still seen as higher up than a woman. There is inequality in the workplace, in relationships, in school, and that is clearly seen today. Women are still seen as the weaker of the two sexes. We can look at Simone de Beauvoir and read her perspective of women being seen as other. We can look to Christianity and Buddhism where woman are subordinate. We can look to school systems where teachers tell kids to know their place. Where woman are seen as obstacles to a man. Where men are sole providers for their families. No matter how many people say that inequality is no longer an issue, there are many situations where women still have to prove their worth to a man. There are still points to be proven and changes to be made.
chunks.label: Gender roles and inequality facing women
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the history and persistent realities of gender roles and inequality facing women, analyzing relationships, hiring practices, workplace harassment, pay disparity, early childhood socialization, and religion.

n881d7034.title: Transitioning from Rural Conformity to College

chunks.text: For the last 19 years of my life, I have lived in a small rural community where there are open fields filled with cows for miles. I graduated from a small High School with about three hundred other students. I have had the same group of friends since elementary school. Our parents are all friends, and everyone knows everyone. As a group we all went to parties together, on family vacation’s together, and spent 8 hours a day at school together for over 10 years. Saying that it made me sad leaving such a close-knit group like this and going our separate ways to universities all across the state would be an understatement. Making new friends and only being able to see the people you spent your entire life with on special occasions was something that has changed me as a person forever.
chunks.label: Growing up in rural community and leaving friends
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up in a small rural community with the same close-knit group of friends since elementary school before they separated to go to different universities across the state.

chunks.text: College life is a major adjustment to everyone. It comes with ups, and it most definitely comes with downs.
chunks.label: Reflecting on the adjustment to college life
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how adjusting to college life involves ups and downs for everyone.

chunks.text:
Watching my parents leave after dropping me off at a huge school where I

knew no one was where this new life of mine began.
chunks.label: Parents dropping the student off at college
chunks.what_happened: The student watched their parents leave after dropping them off at a large university where they knew no one.

chunks.text: Like I previously stated, growing up in a small community where I knew everyone and was close to my friends and family was nice… However, it was also very restricting and didn’t leave much room for self-expression and confidence. Growing up in a community like this you are expected to look a certain way, act a certain way, and certainly always say; yes ma’am, no ma’am, please, and thank you. From an outsider’s point of view small communities look perfect, and everyone seems nice. This in fact is not the case. Once you’re inside the community you’ll see that you must portray a character that in often cases isn’t the person you want to portray. Growing up I really didn’t understand this or notice it. However, when I got to High School this idea became extremely prevalent. In order to stay in the “in crowd” I had to dress a certain way and act a certain way. I kept up with all the fads, played high school as well as club sports, and participated in as many clubs as I could. Although I acted one way at school in a very high stress social setting, I acted completely different at home around my parents. This went on all through high school. However, once I got to college, I realized that none of this mattered. It doesn’t matter what you wear, how you look, or what you drive.
chunks.label: Pressures of conforming in high school versus college
chunks.what_happened: The student navigated the strict social expectations of their small community and high school by acting differently at school and home, but realized in college that those pressures no longer mattered.

chunks.text:
With this idea in mind Mead as well as James are onto something big with their ideas.

Mead’s logic is that we as humans are made up of three different parts, “The Self, the I, and the Me.” Each one of these parts works together in harmony to create each of us as individual human beings. To break this logic down we can look at each of these constituents separately. The self. The self is what we as humans experience on the outside as a result of the internal dialogue that happens between the “I” and “Me” inside your body. The I. The I is the immediate reaction that your brain makes based on your surrounding environment and social

setting. The me. The me is the internal self-evaluation on your reaction to the “I”, think of it as the self-objectification of your reactions to situations. In further detail the “I” in all of us stems from our emotional responses as well as our reactions which can be compared to a reflex or gut instinct. The “Me” is what overtime we learn from different social settings. Our “Me” learned to be laid back around our friends and family and anxious or nervous in large groups of unfamiliar faces. Mead continues to tell us that the self is experienced indirectly but completely whereas, the body is experienced directly yet incompletely. In laymen’s terms this means that our mind experiences emotions and the world around us, but it can’t physically experience sensations like touch. However, our body physically experiences sensations such as touch but it will never be able to completely experience the world around us. Mead has compared the body to a vessel that carries the self and allows for it to experience the world. With all this being said, the main point that Mead is trying to get across is that people base their self-images on their social situations and interactions that they may have with those around them.

William James, the “Father of American Psychology,” has a logic of “The Self and it’s Selves.” Looking into this logic James explains that the self is made up of four constituents: the material self, the social self, the spiritual self (personality), and the pure ego (the soul). Looking at each of these constituents separately you can see how they all work together in the same way as Mead’s self, I, and me to create individual human beings. If we look deeper into each of these constituents, we can understand that the material self is physical or tangible objects such as your family, your friends, and your clothes. Your social self however is how other people view you. Are you loud? Are you kind? Are you overall a good person? Your spiritual self is your personality or what you see yourself as. These can be things such as your inner emotions, the

things you value most in life, or even how you see yourself in the mirror. And lastly your pure ego or the soul, James looks at the pure ego as your personal identity that comes from your collective stream of consciousness or the personal feelings that one feels at any moment in time. Overall, James recognizes oneself as having many different parts that can all be different at different times depending on the social situation or setting you are in at any point in time.
chunks.label: Theories of Mead and James on the self
chunks.what_happened: The student explains George Herbert Mead's concept of the Self, I, and Me, as well as William James's theory of the constituents of the self.

chunks.text: After looking further into both Mead’s and James’ point of view and understanding the fact that each one of the social situations that your put in can alter the way you view things, I can compare this to my high school experience. Wanting to be popular. Acting different ways around different groups of people. Playing sports and participating in clubs to prove a point. Wondering what people think of me. Never feeling comfortable just being myself. All these things are simply the constituents of the self and its many selves.
chunks.label: Reflecting on high school social pressures and self-consciousness
chunks.what_happened: The student recalls striving for popularity in high school, changing behaviors around different groups, joining clubs and sports, and struggling to feel comfortable being themself.

chunks.text:
Everyone experiences this and the experience itself may be different for each individual but in a way, we are all made up the same and are impacted tremendously by our social settings. Moving to college and taking classes to understand how our society works together to create the world we live in has taught me that individually we are all different yet one in the same. Our views, opinions, and biases come from others. With that being said, the only person who can really know a person and how they think is, yourself. People may see you in a certain way or having a certain personality, but you will always see yourself in a different light.

In conclusion, Mead believes that one is made up of “The Self, the I, and the Me” and the social self is tremendously impacted about social settings and the things that a human experiences. James believes that one is made up of “The Self and it’s Selves” and that the four constituents of the inner self are once again, impacted by social settings and experiences.

Humans are trained in social settings and are expected to act differently around different sets of people. This logic can be applied to everyone in society and it’s something that everyone should not only know but understand as a part of growing up.
chunks.label: Conclusion on social settings shaping the self
chunks.what_happened: The student synthesizes the course concepts, concluding how social settings shape human behavior and self-perception.

chunks.text:
The sociological paradigm known as the Matrix of Domination is where many are forced to deal with oppression due to their race, social class, gender, sexual identity, age, and religion. The more you meet, the more you are caught up in the matrix. One could describe the matrix as a spider web if they liked.

(1)Woman + (2)Person of Color + (3)Transgender + (4)18 to 25 years old = Deep Within The Matrix

According to Collins, “The Matrix of Domination stems from Eurocentric, masculinist thought which are institutions, paradigms, and any elements of the knowledge-validation procedure controlled by white males and whose purpose is to represent a white male standpoint.”

Before diving deeper into the Matrix of Domination, it is important to discuss Collins’ explanation of the role of black feminist thought. Afrocentric feminist thought rejects additive approaches to oppression by utilizing knowledge to resist domination and empower those dealing with oppression (Collins, 1990). This not only helps shift the way we think about oppression but also allows us to better assess the “truth” behind many current debates (Collins, 1990). Collins expresses that black feminist thought views the system of oppression as being part of the intense structure of domination. She also states that domination operates by seducing, pressuring, or forcing African American women and other members of subordinated groups to replace individual and cultural ways of knowing with the dominant group’s specialized thought. The author relays that dominant groups aim to do this because they realize that gaining control over this dimension of subordinate group’s lives, simplifies control. This paper will examine how the Matrix of Domination affects minorities by specifically discussing Black Transgender Women, Transgender people of color, and Latina warehouse workers. The more minorities you are a part of, the more predisposed you are to oppression.

Now, onto one of the topics at hand; the Matrix of Domination and Black Transgender Women. Black Transgender Women are probably the best “agents of knowledge” because they receive the least privilege, meaning that they have dealt with all aspects of the matrix for the longest time. During the Summer of 2020, six black transgender women under the age of thirty-two were killed over a period of nine days. As stated by Foreisteire, “...hate crimes against transgender and gender non-conforming individuals have been on the rise for years, with the number of murders in 2020 already almost surpassing that of 2019. Of the 26 victims so far this year and the 27 victims last year, the majority have been Black transgender women under the age of 30.” The reasons that Black Transgender women are killed at such crazy rates is due to the mix of homophobia, transphobia, sexism, homophobia, etc. which are ideas that stem from Eurocentric, masculinist thought (Foreisteire, 2020).

Navigating Community Institutions: Black Transgender Women's Experiences in Schools, the Criminal Justice System, and Churches, written by Louis F. Graham, further displays the oppression that Black Transgender Women face. This study aims to bring attention to the issue by collecting the life histories of ten black transgender women between eighteen and twenty-four years old, all living in Detroit, Michigan (Graham, 2014). It explores the institutional violence, harassment, and discrimination they face, specifically at schools, churches, and within the criminal justice system (Graham, 2020).

Some statistics that shed the light on the negativity this specific group of people face are explained within this article. For example, Graham quotes that, “In 2001, the Gay, Lesbian, and Straight Education Network (GLESN) conducted a School Climate Survey and found that 82 % of LGBT students reported being the victim of sexual, physical, or verbal harassment; over 90 % indicated that they regularly heard anti-LGBT comments at school; and nearly 25 % heard these comments from school personnel (Bauer, 2002).” Also, the bullying that occurs in school towards transgender people is so intense that it leads many to develop numerous mood disorders and suicidal ideations. The mood disorders one can develop from the environment Black Transgender Women endure can range from Major Depressive Disorder to Anxiety Disorder to Panic Disorder and more.

When one feels like this or is getting bullied, they are often told by a counselor or friend to turn to their community for support but when it comes to Transgender people of color, even that may not be an option. The majority of the time, Transgender people of color are not accepted by their own cultures because how they identify goes against their cultures’ set of beliefs. In turn, they feel alone and isolated.

Another big issue Transgender people of color have to deal with is fetishization. Transgender people of color’s experiences of sexual objectification: Locating sexual objectification within a matrix of domination, written by Flores, Watson, Allen, Ford, Serpe, Choo, and Ferrel, interviewed fifteen Transgender people of color about their experiences with sexual objectification (Flores, Watson, Allen, Ford, Serpe, Choo, & Ferrel, 2018). The authors state that, “results suggested participants’ sexual objectification experiences were shaped by the intersections of cissexism, sexism, and racism, and that participants experienced various levels of privilege and oppression based on their specific identities,” which once again, ties in with the Eurocentric, masculinist thought (Flores, Watson, Allen, Ford, Serpe, Choo, & Ferrel, 2018). It is well known that Transgender people of color face more unequal treatment, assault (whether it be physical or sexual, and harassment than any other group whether it be White Transgender people, Lesbian or Gay people, etc. These findings also show that “TPOC, especially TPOC women may be at-risk for oppression-based victimization (Flores, Watson, Allen, Ford, Serpe, Choo, & Ferrel, 2018).”

As a result, when one takes a look at the everyday lives of Transgender people of color or specifically, Black Transgender Women, they see exactly how dominated these people are. Due to ideas created hundreds of years ago of what is socially “correct” or what “should be”, these people are predisposed to overall, poor quality of life just because of others’ opinions and actions.

Another example is Desperate Fortunes: Latina Warehouse Workers in the "Matrix of Domination", written by Danielle J. Lindemann and Teresa M. Boyer, applies Collins theory to data from focus groups with immigrant Latina “perma-temp” warehouse workers. A “perma-temp” is a temporary employee who works for an extended period for a single staffing client. One main topic of this article and the one above is Intersectionality Theory. Basically, “Women of color who were involved with these movements understood that race, class, gender, and sexuality could not be explored and addressed separately; rather these categories are part and parcel of interlocking systems of oppression (Lindemann & Boyer, 2019)”. The study states that if one, “...apply(ies) insights from intersectionality theory to the topic of migrant organizing, and contends that class, race, and gender are collectively key to understanding the labor market experiences of immigrant women.” This is basically the “matrix” that leaves those controlled.

Another issue that these factory women have to deal with is harassment within the work environment. This article tells of one story where the managers and supervisors see these women as objects and sexual beings and how they were only hired if they met the supervisors’ “level of desirability”. Not only did they have to deal with that, but they had to deal with pay inequality as well.

If one looks over all of the information provided, one can draw the conclusion that the further into the matrix one falls, the more they seem “predisposed” to oppression. If you are a woman, you may have to deal with not being paid the same amount as a man for the same job when you have the same qualification. If you are a woman of color, you are even more likely to not be chosen for a job compared to a white man, a man of color, or a white woman. The pattern becomes worse and worse the farther you fall into the matrix. It seems that if one is not a straight, white male, the fewer opportunities you will be given and the higher the chances of you being bullied, assaulted, harassed, treated unfairly, etc.

This leads to my last important point. America prides itself, saying that it is a country of “equal opportunity for all of its citizens” but, how can that statement be true if you are born as or identify as any one of the categories that isn’t a straight, white male? The answer is simple: It’s false. You can not control what you are or how you feel and it is unfair that one may have to deal with extreme forces of oppression because of things out of their control.

In conclusion, the more minorities you are a part of, the more predisposed you are to oppression. Black Transgender Women are the best “agents of knowledge” because of how far they are in the matrix and because of all the dangers they experience and face. Latina factory workers are forced to deal with terrible work environments and are harassed simply because of who they are. This is all one sad, modern-day, multi-century truth.

Take a look at the news and read the titles: the Black Lives Matter movement; the Black Trans Lives Matter movement; the Stop Asian Hate movement; the Stop Immigrant Hate movement; the LGBT movement; the Gender Equality movement. Speak up and be a part of the change. Don’t let what is unacceptable, continue. Don’t be an oppressor and don’t allow yourself to be oppressed.

Work Cited:

Flores, M. J., Watson, L. B., Allen, L. R., Ford, M., Serpe, C. R., Choo, P. Y., & Farrell, M. (2018). Transgender people of color's experiences of sexual objectification: Locating sexual objectification within a matrix of domination. Journal of Counseling Psychology, 65(3), 308-323. https://doi.org/10.1037/cou0000279

Forestiere, A. (n.d.). America's War on Black Trans Women. Harvard Civil Rights-Civil Liberties Law Review. https://harvardcrcl.org/americas-war-on-black-trans-women/.

Graham, L. F. (2014). Navigating community institutions: Black transgender women's experiences in schools, the criminal justice system, and churches. Sexuality Research & Social Policy, 11(4), 274-287. doi:http://dx.doi.org.liblink.uncw.edu/10.1007/s13178-014-0144-y

Hill, C. P. (1990). Black feminist thought: Knowledge, consciousness, and the politics of empowerment.

Lindemann, D. J., & Boyer, T. M. (2019). Desperate fortunes: Latina warehouse workers in the “Matrix of domination”. Labor Studies Journal, 44(2), 161-183. https://doi.org/10.1177/0160449X18767317
chunks.label: The Matrix of Domination and intersectional oppression
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Patricia Hill Collins' Matrix of Domination and reviews academic studies regarding the intersectional oppression faced by Black transgender women, transgender people of color, and Latina warehouse workers, concluding with citations.

chunks.text:
In Yuval Noah Harari’s book titled 21 Lessons from the 21st Century he talks about how with the development of artificial intelligence (AI) and the advancements in the field of AI, they could eventually replace humans in the work force. The better AI is at understanding human emotions and behavior the more suited they could become for human jobs. In Karl Marx’s “Estranged Labour” he talks about different forms of alienation a person can experience in the workplace, one of which is “species-being” alienation. If AI does take over the work force it could potentially make this form of alienation more severe.

In Karl Marx’s “Estranged Labour” One of the forms of alienation is “species-being” which explains that for human beings our life purpose is their work. He explains that creating things is part of the identity of a human being, and that a person is what they create. In modern society this alienation occurs due to divisions of labor, making the worker distanced from the act of creating things. If AI were to take over the workforce this form of alienation would become more severe. Going off of what Karl Marks says about the human identity being what they create, if artificial intelligence takes over jobs then humans will lose their form of identity because they will no longer have the opportunity to create.

Harari’s book titled 21 Lessons from the 21st Century he explains how the development and improvement of artificial intelligence could lead to AI becoming them main form of worker in the workforce. If this does occur the alienation that occurs because of the distance between a worker and his ability and opportunity to create will deepen. Potentially leading to humans losing their identity.

. . .

. “.” (): . .
chunks.label: AI in the workforce and Marx's alienation
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Yuval Noah Harari's ideas on artificial intelligence replacing human labor and connects this to Karl Marx's concept of species-being alienation, explaining how losing the opportunity to work and create could strip humans of their identity.

na6f58806.title: Navigating Pressures of Youth and Gender

chunks.text: As we as people get older and there are more generations there are on this earth, the more and more we hear about the rise of mental health issues in people, namely young people. I feel as if there are some bigger reasons for this than just what meets the eye. I feel as if society has been imposing some standards on young people that would make them feel this way, and that could seriously affect their concept of self. I feel as if there are some things that need to be fixed in this society so that people will ultimately be beneficial for people and their mental health.
chunks.label: Introduction on mental health and societal standards
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the rise of mental health issues among young people and argues that societal pressures negatively affect people's self-concept.

chunks.text: As I was growing up and going through school, we as kids got to see many things that we maybe should not have. Sometimes these were on the news, hearing about all the bad things that were going on in the world. Sometimes it was in our own school, with the near-constant fist fights, people wearing things that are definitely not appropriate for a business-like environment, and even the occasional fight that turns a little more violent than usual. While those things might not have been affecting on people's mental health strongly, the things that really did were the things that were being imposed on everyone. People telling you that you have to do well in school and that your whole life depends on it. Some people gave up on that, however, and decided to just try to be popular at the time, which brought around its own set of stresses. You had to be up to date on everything going on and try to match the fads so that in the eyes of others you seemed “cool.” The atmosphere of the school made it so you felt you had to be good at everything or you were a useless member of society and that is a lot of stress to put on children who are ranging from ages 12 to 18. Then there are the pressures that are put on each gender that seem to be present. For females at any age, it seems from the people I have talked to as if people expect them to be calm collected but at the same time be soft and caring and basically asking them to meet a certain mold. For men it is also a mold just a vastly different mold than the one for women. Men are supposed to be the strong ones who show no emotion and be successful in work even if school was not pushed as hard on some. Basically, the main point I am trying to show is that there is a lot of pressure and stress put on people these days and there is a solid chance that these things a contributing to the seeming rise of mental health issues in this society.
chunks.label: Pressures and environment while growing up in school
chunks.what_happened: The student describes their experiences growing up in school, witnessing frequent fights, and experiencing intense pressures to excel academically, fit in, be popular, and conform to gender roles.
chunks.people: school peers, people the student talked to

chunks.text:
One concept that might be applying to this situation is the looking glass self by Charles Cooley. This concept is mainly focusing on this current technological age, and it states that we basically perceive ourselves as we feel like other people in our lives perceive us. A good example of this concept is that if someone perceives that their coworkers think they are a weird and awkward person they might start to become a weird and awkward person. The same is also true for the opposite feelings. This is why it is important as a parent to make your child feel like a certain type of person, normally a nice caring person.

Another concept that might apply to this is the concept of the beauty myth by Naomi Wolf and the idea of hegemonic masculinity by Connell. The beauty myth is the concept that women feel that they must adhere to a certain set of unreachable beauty standards, and it is something that controls them. An example of this is that a mother is projecting onto her daughter that she must dress in a certain way to make her appear attractive. The concept of hegemonic masculinity is the concept that men are supposed to be stronger than women and they do this by being aggressive and use violence and they should show no other emotions besides this. The most common example of this concept is that people telling boys that real men do not show emotion and that they should just deal with it.

All of the concepts: looking glass self, beauty myth, and hegemonic masculinity all apply to the situation in the second paragraph where it was talked about how there was a lot of pressures and expectations of people that might be leading to an increase in mental health issues in today's society. The concept of looking glass self brings the reason to the table that people might have a poor concept of themselves because of the increase of social media and the need to appeal to people on those social medias and if you feel like people are not liking what they see on that then that might make you feel not liked which would increase the rates on mental health issues. The concept of the beauty myth also brings forward why there might be an increase of mental health issues in women and more particularly younger women. This is because if someone is always telling you that you must dress and fit a mold as a child you might feel as if you are not able to be your own person and develop your own style. Getting rid of this feeling of individuality can make it more likely to feel useless and this may develop into something more serious. Lastly, the concept of hegemonic masculinity brings forward why there might be an increase of mental health challenges in younger men and men in general. This is because being forced to hold in emotions and not show anything can be quite detrimental to one's mental health and the act of holding in emotion could lead to increased rates of mental health problems.

As stated throughout the paper it seems to be there is an increase in mental health issues across the United States. I feel, as shown in this paper, that the main reason for this increase is the toxic culture this country has started to develop. Namely the prevalence of beauty myth among women and with the increase of social media this seems to be affecting women more than ever and it is leading to lower self-esteem and more mental health issues. Also, the prevalence of hegemonic masculinity is definitely a contributing factor to the increase of mental health issues among men because the holding in of emotions can be very detrimental. Another contributing factor with the increasing use of social media is the concept of look glass self. This is because if you do not feel like people on social media are not liking you then you may develop a negative view of yourself which is not good for mental health. I feel like these are some really important things that people in the US need to talk about and address, so we do not hurt people unnecessarily and we can together create a happier society that can function well together without bringing each other down.
chunks.label: Sociological concepts and concluding thoughts on mental health
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the concepts of the looking-glass self, the beauty myth, and hegemonic masculinity, connects them to modern social media and gendered pressures, and concludes with a call to address these cultural issues.

chunks.text:
A person’s home life and upbringing can be a determinate in their conception of self. People brought up in a positive well caring home may have a more positive caring conception of self. This is due to what they are taught growing up as well as what they are exposed to regularly in their environment. In Mead’s The Self the I and the Me and Goffman’s the Presentation of Self they explain further into what can influence a person’s conception of self.

In Mead’s theory of self, he explains that the self has two sides, the “me” and the “I”. The “me” represents an individual’s learned behaviors and attitudes as well as their expectations of people. The “I” is a person’s response to others. A person who grew up in a healthy environment where morals and a positive perception of themselves and others was taught, will most likely have a more optimistic concept of self. They will expect the best of themselves and others because that is what they have been taught. Goffman explains that people are trying to meet the standards that are put in place for them. In a healthy home those standards are put into place and therefore are strived to achieve.

Mead and Goffman both explain in depth what makes up an individual’s conception of self as well as what can affect it. a person who had a healthy and caring upbringing is more likely to have a more positive conception of self. This is due to morals being taught and how their home life influenced their perception of others. It also is due to a standard being put in place for them to achieve.
chunks.label: Theories of upbringing and conception of self
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how home life and upbringing influence an individual's conception of self, referencing sociological concepts from Mead and Goffman.

chunks.text: Why does an intelligent woman have to be an unattractive woman? Why does an unintelligent woman have to be an attractive woman? Society has told women that men prefer a pretty girl to a smart girl. We have become so superficial as to judge someone on their appearance rather than their qualities. Women spend thousands to look and feel beautiful from cosmetics and plastic surgery. Now more than ever, our social media is full of half-naked skinny women glowing with a fresh tan and smiling with perfect white teeth. Do we ever ask ourselves; I wonder what her story is or what her aspirations in life are? No, the women who see that image will go to the gym or starve themselves, get a spray tan, and whiten their teeth. The men will awe the beautiful woman and think about how perfect she is. Over the years, women have faced yet another oppressing technique masked in competition with one another to be desirable; the beauty myth. Women have become so infatuated with how they look the matter of education, genuine connection, and identity are disregarded. Men have given themselves the power to mentally abuse women and persuade them into believing if they sit still and look pretty, they will be feminine and desired. Women with the intelligence and bravery to stand up for their rights disrupt males' institutional power, thus being cast as undesired and masculine.
chunks.label: Societal beauty standards and oppression of women
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how society equates female intelligence with unattractiveness and values women solely based on superficial beauty, describing this as an oppressive beauty myth designed to maintain male institutional power.

chunks.text: A bit of background for relevance; I am a tall, white, skinny, blonde woman. I am also majoring in biomedical engineering, which includes courses filled with mostly men and a few women. Growing up, my parents prioritized my education and taught me about my image's importance. How to carry yourself, which clothes to wear, how to interact with others, and everything a young woman learns. However, they never taught me that men would solely view me as a tall skinny unintelligent blonde. How that young men assume I was in the wrong class because this was Calculus 3, and what business would I have there? How older men would look at me and say, "You should smile more. It makes you look prettier." My life consists of men telling me how I should look, and if I do look that way, I should be content with life.
chunks.label: Being judged on appearance in academic spaces
chunks.what_happened: The student describes her background as a tall, blonde biomedical engineering student, noting that despite her parents emphasizing education and image, young men questioned her presence in Calculus 3 and older men told her to smile more.

chunks.text: One instance that still resonates with me is an interaction with one of my high school teachers. He asked, "What do you want to be when you grow up?" The most mundane and run-of-the-mill question people even ask it to kindergarteners. I responded with doctor or lawyer because I knew I wanted to have an A-list career. His response was genuinely demoralizing, saying I should lower my standards, maybe be a teacher or a nurse, something that would suit me better. He didn't know I was taking sophomore-level classes in 8th grade; he didn't know I had been on the Honor Roll since kindergarten; and he didn't know I was on the mathlete team. He only saw a pretty face that needed to mold into a category that fits the standard.
chunks.label: High school teacher discouraging career ambitions
chunks.what_happened: When the student told her high school teacher she wanted to be a doctor or lawyer, he told her to lower her standards and suggested teaching or nursing, ignoring her high academic achievements and judging her only by her appearance.

chunks.text: As a young woman, I fully developed by age 15, which meant my parents needed to warn me of how to dress and carry myself yet again. Always dress to impress, but you must leave things up to the imagination. They failed to mention if you show no skin, you're a prude, but if you show too much skin, you're asking for it. So how do I, as a woman, find my true identity amongst the roadblocks, devaluation of my knowledge, and sexualization of my body?
chunks.label: Parental advice after developing physically
chunks.what_happened: After developing physically by age 15, the student's parents warned her about how to dress modestly to impress without revealing too much, leaving her to question how to find her identity amid conflicting expectations.

chunks.text:
Naomi Wolf wrote a piece exposing the beauty myth and evaluating its effect on women. The beauty myth stems from the sexual liberation of women during the industrial revolution after women abandoned the feminine mystique of domesticity. At that point, the only feminine ideology left was beauty, thus creating this intangible idea of impossible standards for women to achieve. This standard, created by men's institutionalized power, pulls women's focus away from political issues such as equality and turns it towards beauty. Women now constantly compare themselves to skinnier, younger, and more developed women. Therefore, according to Wolf, eating disorders have grown exponentially, and cosmetic surgery is the fastest-growing medical specialty. Women will do whatever they can to be the most beautiful, desired, and fit the beauty standard. Have you ever wondered why older women get Botox and plastic surgery to look younger? When someone ages, male or female, they grow wiser, meaning age indicates intelligence. However, women must not be intelligent because they would threaten men's power, making them unattractive to men.

Men further instill this myth by not dating a girl more intelligent than them because if women were free from this hold, their power would contest men's power considerably. In her paper, Wolf mentions a caricature from 1960 of an "Ugly Feminist" which shows a masculine woman smoking a cigar. Society is making women believe that if they portray themselves as unintelligent, conceal their feelings, and don't cause any disturbance in male dominance; they are considered beautiful and feminine. On the other hand, if you are portraying intelligence and awareness of the oppression of women, you threaten male dominance; therefore, you are considered ugly and masculine. We must ask the question, why do women allow this to happen to them? The answer is more complex than just ignoring it because women are now permanently psychologically affected by the beauty myth. The only way for women to break free from the myth is to see the world through a different lens. Something challenging to achieve when our economy relies on the income from cosmetic companies resulting in the standardized beautiful woman plastered on every magazine, television, and billboard.
chunks.label: Analysis of Naomi Wolf's beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Naomi Wolf's work on the beauty myth, analyzing how historical liberation led to restrictive beauty standards and male power dynamics that psychologically harm women.

chunks.text:
If I were to look back on my personal experiences, I could understand why people view an unattractive woman as intelligent and why people view an attractive woman as unintelligent. Brilliant women stand to disrupt the male institutions and challenge their dominance. In turn, men accuse them of being ugly because men fear the power of a woman free from the shackles of the beauty myth. If women gain complete confidence and trust their knowledge, it will carry them much further than the makeup on their faces and the Botox in their cheeks.

My fellow male classmates don't think I am capable because I am intelligent and beautiful, which they are intimidated by. My high school teacher attempted to discourage me because he was worried a witty woman would achieve more remarkable accomplishments than him, thus hindering his dominance. The problem is not the woman but the insecure men attempting to oppress women to feel better about themselves. My identity is not how many men like how I look but the intelligence and connections I possess.
chunks.label: Reflecting on personal experiences through theory
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects back on past interactions with male classmates and her high school teacher, concluding that their dismissive behavior stemmed from intimidation of an intelligent and beautiful woman rather than her own shortcomings.

chunks.text:
Sense of humor is another excellent example of the beauty myth. Men's sense of humor, when determining if they find a woman funny or not, is based on whether or not the woman laughs at his joke. On the other hand, women would choose a good sense of humor if the male told a good joke. In elementary school, the teacher would ask, "Are there any strong boys here that can help me carry this?" Notice how the teacher never asked if any strong girls could help because women should sit still and look pretty. In our society, instances of the beauty myth range in all age groups.

Women need to see that men don't say derogatory things to them because they are true but because they are worried women will become as powerful as them, if not more powerful. Women can be conventionally beautiful and just as intelligent as someone who isn't conventionally beautiful. The same goes for a woman who isn't considered a classic beauty and can be just as unintelligent as a woman who is a classic beauty. Standardized beauty is another way for men to approve or disapprove of a woman's behavior and intelligence. Women are not less because they are women but because female beauty is used as a political weapon to oppress them.
chunks.label: Everyday examples and concluding thoughts
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes double standards in humor and elementary school gender roles, concluding that beauty standards are weaponized by men to oppress women and maintain dominance.

nbaa9b155.title: Conforming to Gender Norms in High School

chunks.text: Have you ever adjusted your identity just to fit the norm? Most people at some point in their life have changed something about themselves in order to fit in. We grow up and think that we must fit our specific gender stereotypes. As a girl you are expected to wear pink, play with dolls, wear dresses, and have long hair. If you want to play a sport and you’re a girl, its suggested that you either dance or cheerlead. We shouldn’t be conditioned at such a young age that certain styles, colors, interests, or athletics fall into gender categories.
chunks.label: Gender stereotypes and societal expectations
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the concept of adjusting identity to fit gender stereotypes and argues that children should not be conditioned into gendered categories.

chunks.text:
Up until high school, I was what was known as a “tomboy”. I grew up on a farm, so I enjoyed activities such as hunting, fishing, and riding four-wheelers. Part of these hobbies came from being part of a family of all boys. All of my cousins were boys, and I also had a younger brother. We would play different sports like basketball, football, and baseball. I was always just hanging out with my family and never understood these activities weren’t typically participated in by girls.

Not only did I act the part of a tomboy, I also dressed like it. I was always wearing baggy t-shirts and athletic shorts. Dresses, skirts, and sandals were not part of my wardrobe. Additionally, I wouldn’t wear colors such as pink or purple. All of my clothes were either blue, black, or grey. Many of my mom’s friends or my family members would always tell her to dress me in pink so I would look more like a girl. However, my mom didn’t like pink or bright colors anyways, so I never had to worry about that.
chunks.label: Growing up as a tomboy
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up on a farm with male cousins and a younger brother, engaging in outdoor hobbies and sports while wearing baggy clothes rather than feminine attire.
chunks.people: younger brother, cousins, mother, mother's friends, family members

chunks.text: When I got to high school, I was districted to a school in the city. I decided that I needed to switch up my look so I would fit in. I changed out my typical tomboy look for skirts and crop tops. I even dyed my hair blonde and started growing it out. It worked and I made friends quickly, but it didn’t really feel like me. I wanted to get involved with something that actually felt true to my interests, so I tried out and made the women’s basketball team at my high school. It was the best decision I made but I was quickly brought back down again. All of the guys on the men’s team would tell us that women’s basketball isn’t a real sport. I was the team captain so I tried to help the other girls get past these comments, however I couldn’t really get over them myself. I started to question if they were right. Additionally, some of the guys in my grade would tell me that I was “too pretty to play basketball,” and that I should do something that was “more girly” such as cheerleading. Even though I loved playing basketball, I ended up quitting my junior year because I was tired of all the remarks about my looks and ability to play a sport as a girl.
chunks.label: High school appearance change and basketball
chunks.what_happened: Upon attending a city high school, the student changed her appearance to fit in, joined the basketball team, but ultimately quit junior year due to sexist comments from male students.
chunks.people: friends, women's basketball teammates, men's basketball players, male classmates

chunks.text: Candace West and Don Zimmerman wrote an article titled, “Doing Gender.” It talks about how gender is an ongoing accomplishment in your everyday interactions. Your sex is your biological differences that you were born with. However, your gender is the societal expectation of you based on your sex. Therefore, doing gender is behaving as expected based on your biological identifiers.
chunks.label: Concept of doing gender
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the concept of 'doing gender' from Candace West and Don Zimmerman's article.

chunks.text: Naomi Wolf wrote about the “Beauty Myth.” The beauty myth is essentially an idea that is designed to control women by telling them that their identity is in their beauty. This makes women become more obsessed with how they look than pursuing a strong leadership role. This makes it hard for women to come together and make a community since they aren’t striving for power together. It is a tactic used by men and political authorities to keep women virtually submissive. They want women to believe that a woman is more desirable if she is domesticated and beautiful.
chunks.label: Naomi Wolf and the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes Naomi Wolf's 'Beauty Myth' and how it is used to control women and prevent them from pursuing power.

chunks.text: When I was growing up, I wasn’t “doing gender” to societies standards. Society has set standards for girls and boys. Girls are told in order to be a real girl you need to have long hair, wear dresses, paint your fingernails, wear makeup. They are also told to be emotional and subservient. As a boy you are told to have short hair, wear suits, and not to wear makeup. They are told to be stoic and dominate. If you don’t follow these expectations, then you are told you aren’t a real girl or boy. As a child I was typically taking part in activities and wearing clothes that were typically reserved for boys. This is why I was always called a tomboy. However, I never wasn’t a real girl. These were activities that I truly enjoyed. We shouldn’t grow up and be told by society that we can’t dress a certain way or do certain activities because of our sex. We shouldn’t have to prove that we are a real girl or boy by doing gender. These expectations keep people from being their true authentic self.
chunks.label: Reflecting on childhood and doing gender
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on childhood experiences through the sociological lens of 'doing gender' and societal standards for boys and girls.

chunks.text: When I was in high school, I played directly into the beauty myth. I became obsessed with how others viewed me. I wanted everyone to like me so bad that I changed myself to the point where I didn’t recognize myself anymore. I changed my hair color because I thought it would make me more desirable. Additionally, when my ability to play basketball was doubted, I didn’t try to stand up for myself. I would just brush it off when I could have done more about it. Even when I was told I shouldn’t play basketball because I didn’t look the part, I didn’t even try to disagree. It all led me to quitting. This is exactly what Wolf meant when she talks about how women won’t be able to form a community because they become more obsessed with their beauty than their fight for power.
chunks.label: Applying the beauty myth to high school
chunks.what_happened: The student connects her high school experiences of changing appearance and quitting basketball to Wolf's beauty myth.

chunks.text: Society tries to control women in multiple ways. They try to question their beauty so that they won’t try to fight for more power. They also try to convince women that they aren’t a true woman if they participate in activities or dress different than the norm. This became apparent to me throughout my whole life. The beauty myth along with doing gender have forced me multiple times to adjust my identity in order to fit societies standards. We need to change societies expectations that a woman’s identity is in her beauty to hinder her drive for power. We also need to teach the younger generations that they can participate in any sport, activity, and dress however they want. Just because a girl doesn’t want to wear skirts and dresses doesn’t make them any less of a real girl. We also need to teach society as a whole not to judge others based on their appearance. The number of times I was told I should dress differently eventually did drive me to changing my appearance. We shouldn’t be convinced to change our appearance to fit societies standards. I am a real woman no matter what activities I choose to participate in and how I decide to dress.
chunks.label: Conclusion on societal standards and empowerment
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that society should stop judging appearance and pushing gender norms, affirming her own identity as a real woman.

n166a4bde.title: Analyzing Modern Racism and Religious Politics

chunks.text:
Racism and Religion – How it all Fits. Or does it?

Harari has many adamant and powerful positions which discusses in his book: 21 Lessons for the 21st Century. With his impassioned arguments, he shares similar views with other authors, economists, and philosophers, as well as shares quite contrary views with some people. This essay will highlight just a few of those similarities or differences, between Harari and other writers and thinkers.

One example of this is on the subject of racism, specifically, how it has evolved and changed over time – to modern day. Michael Omi and Howard Winant, in the excerpt “Racial Formations”, from the book Racial Formations in the United States: From the 1960s to the 1980s, assert that as race is a social construct, it was developed and evolved from just having differences in people’s skin color. In fact, the authors in this article argue that the use of racism in this new, modernized, evolved way, is very much deliberate and a way to oppress groups of people. The way this is done is by attributing specific negative characteristics or behaviors, to certain groups of people – based on skin color, or country of origin, for example. As Omi and Wyant write: “Skin color ‘differences’ are thought to explain perceived differences in intellectual, physical, and artistic temperaments, and to justify distinct treatment of racially identified individuals and groups” (Omi & Winant, page 23). Race became a way to explain societal issues and failures, blaming issues on negative and racist stereotypes of African Americans. The authors here argue that this shift in ‘racializing’ groups of people is a more modern day development. This attributing of negative traits to people of color is something that the authors assert has further perpetuated a system which is full of systemic racism, which is also then absorbed by our society. People then tend to accept and believe what they are hearing and seeing on various forms of media, as to how some groups of people may act. This is a way for human beings to explain problems, to disassociate themselves from ‘bad people’ or ‘bad things’ and to further oppress groups of people.

Similarly, Harari believes that racism is alive and unfortunately, well; however, he argues that the way it presents has evolved from being based upon biological differences, to focusing on an individual’s culture. Even with this evolution, racism is still very much about judging an individual or group of people based on assumptions, stereotypes, and bias. This is similar to Omi and Winant’s beliefs.

In his book, Harari dives into the issues and beliefs surrounding immigration. Immigration of a “foreign” person who does not come from there, into a new country. Using the context of immigration, Harari points out how racism has evolved into something different today. This evolution of racism began with the time period where it was both publicly, and widely accepted, that white people were the superior race. Of course through history and all of the events that took place, Harari points out, there was a shift in this “Racism was seen not only as morally abysmal but also as scientifically bankrupt” ( Harari, p 149). However, in its place came a new type of racism, or a new demonstration of it. While the morality factor, as well as scientific evidence, discourages people from stating that a person of color is inferior because they are ‘biologically’ different, there is now the belief that based on where a person is from (location-wise, or national origin), there are negative stereotypes and assumptions that can be attributed to that group of people. This is racism, just in a different disguise, according to Harari. As he writes: “Saying that black people tend to commit crimes because they have substandard genes is out; saying that they tend to commit crimes because they come from dysfunctional subcultures is very much in” (Harari, page 152).

Harari’s stance on this evolved form of racism is very much aligned with Omi and Winant’s position. Harari does take it a step further than Omi and Winant, where he points out that this ‘new’ form of racism may look on the surface like it is less racist than the former. However, as Harari discusses, in the context of immigration – if the pressure is to get the immigrants to become more like ‘us’, then it really is no better: “…present day culturists might be more tolerant than traditional racists – if only the ‘others’ adopt our culture, we will accept them as our equals. On the other hand, that could result in far stronger pressures on the ‘others’ to assimilate, and in far harsher criticism of their failure to do so” (Harari, page 153). This perfectly illustrates the issue with viewing this new racism as a better or more tolerant form. It still remains the same: judging individuals based on assumptions and stereotypes, and using negative attributes to label an entire group of people – merely based on where they are from, what their ethnic background is.

On another topic, religion, Harari differs in his view from Max Weber. While the issue of religion and its involvement in our policy making or social interactions is separate and different from religion, there is of course some overlap.

Max Weber, in his article titled “The Spirit of Capitalism and the Iron Cage”, writes that religion is something that not only ‘can’ create social change, but that it has historically been used, and can still be used, and should be used. In fact, Weber argues that the Puritan people were “called” (Weber, p 105) to their particular work, whereas today, people are instead “forced.” Weber further argues that the religious calling, spirit and reasoning behind one’s work, historically, is what made it something meaningful, significant, and powerful. In contrast, today’s modern day Capitalism, Weber argues, is devoid of that religious foundation. Without it, Weber asserts that this creates a lack of values, no sort of satisfaction from work, and really a lack of anything good. In this way, Weber asserts that this has led humans to simply be motivated by the making of money, rather than working for some higher purpose, to benefit society or other human beings. Interestingly, Weber believes that religion is actually where capitalism first originated from. However, modern day capitalism, in his view, has strayed from where it began. Rather than being “called” to a particular work, and doing so as a result – currently, we are now just doing the work, to make the money. This, Weber believes, moves away from the religious foundation, which is to our detriment as a society.

Harari’s position on the interplay of Religion and policy making and politics is vastly different from Weber’s. Contrary to Weber’s stance, Harari asserts the belief that there really is no appropriate place for religion in the making of policy, or social change, in our society. Harari argues that the involvement of religion is dangerous, in large part due to the fact that there are so many different religions. Whose is right? Whose is better, or best?
