Every religion thinks their religion is the “right” one. So, Harari argues, how does that possibly fit into policy making and politics. While his views do not necessarily directly contradict with Weber’s belief that religion can motivate a person to operate in a spiritually-led way, his views differ overall -in that he believes religion does not have an appropriate place in the political and policy relations in our society and world. As Harari highlights about human nature and thinking: “National, religious and cultural tensions are made worse by the grandiose feeling that my nation, my religion, and my culture are the most important in the world -and therefore my interests should come before the interests of anyone else, or of humankind as a whole” (Harari, page 183). This sums up his concern pretty perfectly, pointing out that while each religion believes itself to be the best, the most correct, then this would lead to disagreement in actions, policy, and beliefs – due to the simple fact that there are multiple different religions.

Within his argument, Harari focuses a lot on the concept of humility. This concept is something he says is lacking in the use of religion within politics and policy making in our world. There is no humility when each religion believes their own to be true, to be the best, to be superior to others, and the “right” one. This perfectly illustrates the issue involving religion on the biggest stage – world human relations and policy making. In contrast, Weber is arguing that Christianity in particular, has been, and should be, the moral compass to determine how to motivate individuals and groups, and within the making of policies and effecting social changes.

As you can see, even where Harari may align his views with other notable thinkers and writers, there is considerable difference between him and others. Harari’s book helps to set forth his positions in totality, and presents the arguments with sufficient substance and reasoning. The two topics of religion and racism are two topics which have received considerable attention, thinking and writing from various individuals over time – and this continues to be the case today. As a result, we can see that Harari has some similar views – for example – with Omi and Winant; whereas, he differs significantly in views on religion (in some aspects at least) from those views of Max Weber. Religion and race/racism are topics which are complex and extremely laden with human emotions, and deep conviction.
chunks.label: Comparing Harari, Omi and Winant, and Weber
chunks.what_happened: The student compares Harari's ideas on racism and religion with the perspectives of Omi and Winant as well as Max Weber.

chunks.text: The collective consciousness is made up of people with shared beliefs and morals. There are hundreds of groups who believe in a number if things. People who believe in God, gods, goddesses, and other divine beings. They make up these religions that are their own collective consciousness. They have shared ideas. They have a reliance on religion, beliefs, traditions, and rituals.
chunks.label: Collective consciousness and religion
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the concept of collective consciousness and how religious groups share common beliefs, morals, traditions, and rituals.

chunks.text:
Two sections are spoken about in these two readings majorly. These are race and gender. Being black or white and a woman. Collins really points out the fact the being a black woman is extremely different and that unless an individual is a black woman, they cannot understand what they go through. She highlights in the reading that a white woman is “penalized by their gender but privileged by their race,” where the “privilege” is then highlighted in MacIntosh’s article.

The Matrix is a paradigm that outlines and explains oppression that surrounds race, gender, and class. There are other models of oppression, “interlocking ones creates possibilities for new paradigms.” These interlock by being a black female or a white male. A white female or a black male. Collins highlights important aspects of what it is like being a black female person and how different their way of thinking and living is. MacIntosh recognizes that she is a privileged female and that she has these benefits because of her skin color.
chunks.label: Analysis of readings on race, gender, and oppression
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses readings by Collins and MacIntosh, explaining concepts of race, gender, privilege, and the matrix of domination.

naf290ba0.title: Navigating Spaces as a Black Student

chunks.text: My brothers are two of six African American students in their entire private high school. I was a pre-professional ballet student for four years away from home, and yet I was one of two African American students my entire time there.
chunks.label: Being a minority in ballet and school
chunks.what_happened: The student was one of two African American students during four years of pre-professional ballet, while their brothers are two of six African American students at their private high school.

chunks.text:
What is the reason for this? Is it really that only predominantly white people can afford a private high school? No, it’s much more than that.

The systemic issues in our society continue to benefit and support white people automatically, while oppressing people of color, which is known as “white privilege”. Many people have denied this term stating that: their life hasn’t been easy, that they’ve had to work hard, or that they are poor. That’s not what it means. White privilege is like an “invisible package of unearned assets'' (McIntosh, pg. 30) that white people receive just because of their skin color. White privilege is not something that can be taught or learned, it is automatically given to any white individual. It does not matter the age or gender, you still have white privilege.

So why do so many people resist to acknowledge it? Well it comes down to fear and refusing to see it. The fact that many people with privilege don’t try to see how they fall into that category, because it simply doesn’t impact them. Then, there are people who know that the system exists but they don’t want to change it because that same system gives them benefits. Instead, white privilege is used by the dominant group as a way to further racialize African Americans.

Whether it pertains to housing, lending, education, medical disparities, interaction with law enforcement or simply just everyday bias - African Americans disproportionately end up being negatively impacted in all of these categories. As a result, you see more people of color: receiving inadequate education (and therefore often leading to inadequate employment later on), incarcerated, suffering in poverty, labeled as criminals or “thugs”, and more. This provides the exact ammunition for those holding the power to attribute those things to being African American, rather than due to institutionalized racism and white privilege.

Racism is an ongoing issue that has yet to be resolved but there are not enough people doing anything about it. You can learn about the different cultures instead of judging and making comments about it, and accept and respect people's differences and beliefs. Schools should teach about it more, people should discuss it with others, get to know someone before making assumptions about them; these are all good places to start. Instead, for example, most schools provide a whitewashed education; rather than teaching students in Wilmington about the 1898 Wilmington massacre, we learn all about what white people did, and how Columbus was a hero.

When people are trying so hard to not be racist they might try to make some jokes or claim that they don’t see color to come across as an inclusive person. However when someone says, “I don’t see color” it is the same thing as saying I don’t see our differences and that's not necessarily good. Everyone doesn’t believe the same things or think the same way, so yes there are differences and it’s how you react to those differences that determines if you are racist or not. There are some people who try to avoid the topic of racism altogether because they believe that if we don’t talk about it then it won’t be an issue any longer, but as a society we are not at that point yet. Instead of avoiding the topic we have to learn how to embrace and accept the differences that make each of us who we are. A big part of this is the school systems fail to educate students properly. School systems need to incorporate a more diverse system for learning considering most people get their education from school, if it is not being learned in school people are most likely to grow up unaware of how important racism is in society and are less likely to learn about it as they get older which is a problem.

Racism is not something that should be ignored or silenced. There are plenty of people who try to silence the ones fighting for equality, and unfortunately the system and power of white privilege allows that to happen; this is one of the reasons there hasn’t been enough impactful change to systemic racism. Those people who are trying to silence the others are often wearing the privilege of being white, and are often the same people who don’t believe that racism is still a problem. Frequently these are the same people that claim they “don’t see color.” This is a common theme I have encountered throughout my experience. A majority of those people are also white, and because they are white they have never had to experience the oppression that people of color have to deal with every single day. Instead, they have the benefit of white privilege. White people automatically have one less obstacle to overcome in daily life. It doesn’t mean life is easy and simple for white people, but it does mean that there is not the added layer of skin color to make things more difficult.

So how does white privilege really make things easier for white people? As a result of racializing and stereotyping, it is often easier for them to find and keep jobs no matter their previous experience. They do not have the hurdle of being stereotyped at the outset just due to their skin color, and this provides an advantage. Some interviewers won’t even allow a black person to come in for an interview or will offer them a lower position that they could work, even if their resume shows they have a lot of experience and are better for the job (Pager Discrimination article). This is an example of the interviewer being racist because they don’t want to hire someone who is black. Or you can look at what happens in the education system. As a result of racializing, it is more likely that a brown or black skinned student will be overlooked, labeled, or worse. One bad incident early on can start a cycle which makes it harder for these students to receive the same education or experience the same opportunities.
chunks.label: Reflections on white privilege and systemic racism
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how white privilege works as systemic oppression, critiques colorblindness and whitewashed education, and references sociological readings on employment discrimination.

chunks.text: My family has to make conscious decisions of where we are going and what the risks may be. Driving through certain geographic areas at night may not be smart, so we try to avoid that. We have learned from a young age what to do when a police officer pulls us over, or interacts with us, to be sure that we don’t do or say anything that could be used against us. None of my friends have had to go through that same “talk”. This is not something that we should have to teach young children, telling them to be careful how you act around certain people, and having to constantly be in fear of their life.
chunks.label: Family precautions and police talk
chunks.what_happened: The student's family makes conscious decisions about safe travel and learns how to act if stopped by police, a talk none of the student's friends had to experience.
chunks.people: the student, family, friends, police officer

chunks.text:
I’m a proud black person. I’m a proud white person. Two very similar sentences with very different meanings. Saying that you are a proud black person is saying: I am proud to be me despite society being largely against who I am. It is the idea that you had to fight for equality in this country and that it was never something that you just had. It is empowering. It’s saying I am proud that I have overcome the oppression, racism, hardships, and constant negativity that you receive just for having brown or black skin. It shows that even after being criticized by the beauty standards and by white supremacists, I still love me for me and wouldn’t want to change. However, saying “I am proud to be white”, is not the same. As discussed above, merely by being white, there are automatically certain things that you can do that a black person can’t do. There was nothing that you had to risk your life over or spend decades upon decade trying fighting for something, like equality. From the start everything is automatically easier. With that being said there is a difference between being confident with how you look or your ethnicity and saying you are proud of what your culture has done in the past.

White privilege is an insidious creature, living in us and among us, continuing to foster a destructive system - rather than change it. With education, awareness, willingness to be anti-racist, and advocacy, it is possible to shift this dynamic; we can shift the dynamic so that white peivikege is instead used to make impactful changes to a racist system. This would then ultimately eliminate white privilege. While there is still a percentage of the population who would not want that, we should hope that there is enough power in the percentage of people who do. If awareness of the issue is raised, and changes are made in how people of color are racialized - there is hope to change the longstanding institutionalized racism that this country was built on.
chunks.label: Reflections on racial pride and eliminating privilege
chunks.what_happened: The student compares the meaning of saying one is proud to be Black versus proud to be white, and reflects on using education and anti-racism to dismantle systemic racism.

chunks.text: Growing up and to this day, I might frequently be considered a “tomboy.” A tomboy is a girl who exhibits characteristics associated with masculinity and prefers hanging out with the guys and ditching the “girly girls.” Why is there a special category for girls who enjoy wearing pants and playing in the mud versus masquerading in pretty dresses as princesses? Society creates neat categories for humans to fit into, and gender is a significant category. However, human beings “do” their gender in unique ways. So, a person might feel confused or upset if they see an individual who doesn’t automatically fit into their schema for the typical man or woman. Tomboys act outside the bounds of what a typical girl is expected to do. Such behavior tends to be more accepted than identifying as non-binary or transgender; nevertheless, it receives pushback.
chunks.label: Defining tomboys and gender categories
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the concept of a tomboy and reflects on how society creates strict gender categories that receive pushback when breached.

chunks.text:
My neighborhood was full of kids back in elementary school, and we would all hang out together after school and on the weekends. There were more guys than girls, and I was inclined to want to do whatever the boys were doing. I was good friends with the girls, too, but making up dances and playing with barbies did not sound all that appealing to me. I wanted to have nerf gun wars and lightsaber fights and play video games. I don’t know if it was ever an official name that we called ourselves, but the boys and I would always hang out in this storage room at my house called The Boy’s Club. I felt cool because I was the only girl allowed in there (even though it was my house).

Don’t get me wrong; there were times when I played dress-up and had the stereotypical sleepovers with my girl friends. I never felt like I would rather be a boy, but it felt more comfortable and more like me to hang with the guys. I would wear my hair up in a ponytail, burp like a beer-drunk man, and sit with my legs open (an unladylike position). My mom was not fond of this. I can’t tell you how often she told me to stop doing these things because girls don’t behave like that.
chunks.label: Childhood neighborhood play and The Boy's Club
chunks.what_happened: During elementary school, the student hung out with neighborhood boys in 'The Boy's Club' storage room playing video games and nerf wars, while her mother scolded her for unladylike behavior.
chunks.people: neighborhood kids, neighborhood boys, neighborhood girls, mother

chunks.text:
Candace West and Don Zimmerman examine gender from the lens of a performance or as something human beings are always doing in the context of social interactions. They clearly define the terms sex, sex category, and gender. First, sex is “a determination made through the application of socially agreed upon biological criteria for classifying persons as females” (i.e., genitals at birth or chromosomes; West and Zimmerman 127). Sex may seem as though it is concrete, but there is a myriad of chromosomal typings and physical displays of these typings that can make even sex ambiguous. Second, sex category is “achieved through application of the sex criteria, but in everyday life, categorization is established and sustained by the socially required identificatory displays that proclaim one’s membership” as males or females (West and Zimmerman 127). Identifiers such as hair length or body language help others categorize someone as one sex or the other because the sex of a person, or biological characteristics, is not typically readily available for everyone to perceive. One can be categorized as male and be seen as masculine even if a person lacks male sex criteria if their performance of gender is adequate. Gender is “the activity of managing situated conduct in light of normative conceptions of attitudes and activities appropriate for one’s sex category” (West and Zimmerman 127). Notice that gender is described as an activity that one does and is meant to signify and validate a person’s sex category. These three terms are complex and interconnected and must be analyzed together to understand how someone moves through the world as a gendered being.

Through visual clues, one might determine that my sex category is female. This determination is made by my stature, body language, voice, etc. I do not readily display my sex characteristics, but these clues help others visually identify me as a female. However, the way I “do” gender is ambiguous and depends on the context. West and Zimmerman state that displays of gender are context-dependent. I may perform a more feminine gender or a more masculine gender identity in different social interactions.
chunks.label: West and Zimmerman's concepts of gender performance
chunks.what_happened: The student explains West and Zimmerman's definitions of sex, sex category, and gender, applying them to how the student's gender is perceived and performed.

chunks.text: Returning to the neighborhood kids, I performed my gender differently when I was with the Boy’s Club than with the girls. The kids may have perceived my sex category to be female and, thus, I was treated as such, but the way I did my gender depended on the people. I was still feminine when I was with the boys, but I leaned into my more masculine traits when playing with them. Whereas with the girls, I remained more feminine. I roughhoused with the boys and was generally more assertive in this group. I was calm and passive with the girls. The boys accepted me into their group, but I was still a girl, so I couldn’t be hit or teased as much as the guys.
chunks.label: Performing gender differently with boys versus girls
chunks.what_happened: The student acted more assertive and roughhoused when playing with neighborhood boys, while acting calm, feminine, and passive when hanging out with girls.

chunks.text:
According to West and Zimmerman, our environment also impacts how we perform gender. We do gender by gathering resources from our surroundings. For example, I may have been doing gender in a more masculine way on the playground with the boys, but if I had to use the bathroom, I would choose between the girl’s and boy’s bathrooms. Due to my sex characteristics and the sex category others perceive me as, I use the bathroom designated by the stick figure with the triangle dress. However, as evident by gender-neutral bathrooms, bathrooms do not need to be separated based on sex characteristics. “Gendered” environments such as separate bathrooms reinforce the gender binary, strengthening our socialized schemas. I would be chastised if someone perceived my sex category as a woman and saw me go into the men’s bathroom.

Even before birth, humans are placed into a category. An expecting mother might show an ultrasound picture of her baby boy to her friend, who might say, “wow, he looks like he’s going to grow up to be a big, strong man.” Conversely, if shown an ultrasound picture of a baby girl, the friend might say, “awh, look how cute she is. She’s going to be a heartbreaker.” As far as we know, fetuses are not socialized to perform gender to match their sex category while they’re in the womb; however, around preschool age is when children are taking on their socialized gender identity behaviors. West and Zimmerman discuss how little boys focus on how they affect the world physically and socially via physical strength. Little boys want to interact with the world and get their desired outcomes.
chunks.label: Environmental gender cues and early socialization
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how physical environments like bathrooms reinforce gender binaries and explains how children are socialized into gender roles from early childhood.

chunks.text: In contrast, little girls focus on how they interact with the world via their appearance. They want to fit in by looking how they think little girls should look. This observation matches how I behaved in elementary school with the boys versus the girls. I roughhoused with boys to get what I wanted, and I played dress-up with the girls. I was still socialized as a girl, but, like most children, I didn’t completely follow the rules (no matter how much it annoyed my mom).
chunks.label: Navigating childhood gender expectations and mother's annoyance
chunks.what_happened: In elementary school, the student engaged in roughhousing with boys and dress-up with girls, failing to fully adhere to girl socialization despite annoying her mother.

chunks.text: Tomboys are just a tiny exception to the gender binary in Western society. This term is used to designate a girl/woman who acts like a boy/man. Of course, human beings do their gender in various nuanced ways. Some are not born with the sex characteristics that match their gender identity and may identify as transgender. Some may not identify with any gender and describe themselves as non-binary or gender non-conforming. There are many examples of how humans convey their identity in their social interactions, and we must consider this when thinking about how we place people in categories. I’ve received a lot of judgment for being a tomboy, and others who do not strictly adhere to gender roles do too. When we think about gender as a performance and not as something that belongs to us, it takes away the idea that we have to be the thing that people perceive us to be. It is easier said than done to persuade people not to perceive our sex category. However, society can move toward accepting with open minds rather than judging.
chunks.label: Reflections on gender performance and social judgment
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on experiencing judgment for being a tomboy and argues that viewing gender as a performance can help society become more accepting of non-conforming identities.

n3a9aa372.title: Analyzing Technopoly and Rationalization in Society

chunks.text: In a modern constantly changing society, two ideas, Technopoly and rationalization, are out to shape the future. Technopoly is primarily about putting technology on the face of the world and advocating for it to solve any problem. This idea values making things the same, focusing in, and pursuing for things to go faster than before. With anything there are consequences. For there has been a notice of a decline in critical thinking, traditional values, and the way people work together. From this, problems can arise that will be addressed later on. Though there are numerous pros and cons, many organizations push for technopoly, hoping it will make society better. On the other side of things, Rationalization is a broader shift pushing for organization and efficiency among everything possible. This means replacing traditional ways with a more rational approach to make things better overall. Ultimately, Rationalization aims to make society and the world run smoother and more predictable. Though both ideas have similar goals to enhance society, they take a different approach to get things done in their own way. For now, it is important to try to understand their effects on society and how they navigate society today for the brighter future everyone hopes for.
chunks.label: Introduction to Technopoly and rationalization
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the sociological concepts of Technopoly and rationalization, noting their goals to shape and improve society through different approaches as well as their potential consequences.

chunks.text: Technopoly is about a culture that views technology as the best and ultimate solution to any problem that society is facing. This is because with technology comes valuable characteristics. Standardization, specialization, and efficiency are a few of the key parts and often most favored. These traits are often believed to benefit the shaping of society. However, with this are risks and cons. Just like any action there are consequences, some positive and others negative. For example, AI has grown in popularity over the years. Although AI has benefited healthcare systems and businesses, and used in education, unfortunately, this causes a decline in critical thinking development and skills. When there is technology that can do the thinking without a person, the person’s mind works less and doesn’t use the opportunity to think without the use of technology. This is where problems start to arise. With technopoly there has been a leading loss of critical thinking, traditional values, and different work ethics. In addition, there is a loss of societal values that can lead to social inequality, loss of privacy, and issues among the workforces. In spite of the risks, institutions, organizations, etc., take the risk and promote technopoly to “better” society. Alvin Toffler described how technopoly and the key components of standardization, specialization, and efficiency benefit society. He describes them in three ways being agriculture, industrialization, and information. This is ultimately to better efficiency, convenience, access to information, problem solving, economic growth and overall enchanting quality of society.
chunks.label: Analyzing Technopoly and its societal impacts
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Technopoly, citing its traits of standardization, specialization, and efficiency, mentioning Alvin Toffler and AI, and evaluating both its benefits and negative impacts on critical thinking and traditional values.

chunks.text: Rationalization is a concept from Max Weber as it pertains to the process in which traditional modes of thought, action, problem solving etc, are replaced with more rational, systematic, and efficient ones. Assembly lines come from this idea. Instead of individual craftsmen making individual items, the rational system of an assembly line came where each person specialized in a specific part of making an item. One of the traits rationalization strives for is efficiency. The division of labor divided up among the workers promotes and reaches the goal of increased productivity and efficiency. Keep in mind that rationalization is a broader concept that reaches a multitude of spheres in society, not just assembly lines. This includes economic and culture driving by not only the pursuit of efficiency but, calculability, predictability, and a sense of control. Ultimately this leads to increased productivity and organization. Similar to technology this can lead to a chance. Unlike technopoly the changes are not necessarily about the same 3 traits but more so about how traditional values, beliefs, society structures, are improved by the idea of rational systems. What ultimately makes rationalization different is how the idea is more focused on how rationalization contributes to more and different aspect of society including social organization and culture
chunks.label: Explaining Max Weber's concept of rationalization
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Max Weber's theory of rationalization, using the example of assembly lines to explain how efficiency, predictability, calculability, and control replace traditional methods across various spheres of society.

chunks.text: In the scheme of things understanding how fast society changes is critical with how Technopoly and Rationalization compete to shape modern society. While technopoly promotes technology as the ultimate problem-solver, emphasizing standardization and speed consequence occur. These consequences damage humans in a way as there has been a great decline in critical thinking, problem solving, and creativity. On the other hand, there is rationalization. For that idea seeks organization and efficiency, while also carrying a risk of having a lack of variety and everything being more uniform. Both concepts aim to improve society while they differ in approaches and consequences. Understanding these concepts is crucial in figuring out which way is best to have the upper hand in order to promote a brighter future, where there is a balance of efficiency with ethical considerations for everyone in society.
chunks.label: Comparing Technopoly and rationalization for future balance
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by comparing Technopoly and rationalization, arguing that understanding their differing approaches and risks is necessary to balance efficiency with ethical considerations for a brighter future.

n4587cac7.title: Confronting Social Media and Beauty Standards

chunks.text: Many women are, and most likely will always be, immediately judged based off their physical appearance. This causes an immense amount of pressure that begins to take a toll on women’s social, mental, and emotional wellbeing. To start, I am 22-year-old women living in today’s society, where technology and social media use are at an all time high. With these great inventions unfortunately brings great consequences as well.
chunks.label: Pressure on women from appearance and technology
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the judgment women face regarding physical appearance and the consequences of widespread technology and social media.

chunks.text: I have grown up with technology and social media and I have come to realize that it is not the healthiest for me. I have always struggled with fearing I do not live up to standards of beauty and never will. For me, this has always caused some sort of depression and anxiety, that truly does stem from my physical appearance. It may sound cliché, because a lot of people I know struggle with these issues, but it is something that affects my everyday life, and has for years now.
chunks.label: Struggling with beauty standards and mental health
chunks.what_happened: The student has grown up with social media and continuously struggled with fears of not meeting beauty standards, leading to daily anxiety and depression.

chunks.text: Before taking this class, I did not know that there was such thing as the “beauty myth,” but after learning more about it, I realized how prevalent it is today, especially with the effects of social media.
chunks.label: Learning about the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student explains learning about the concept of the 'beauty myth' in class and recognizing its prevalence today.

chunks.text: I, like most people my age, have TikTok and Instagram. I am constantly seeing beautiful women who fit into this beauty standards, but it is hard to separate fake social media filters and reality. The constant exposure I see to this sort of content makes it hard for me to feel confident in myself.
chunks.label: Using TikTok and Instagram
chunks.what_happened: The student uses TikTok and Instagram and finds it difficult to feel confident when constantly seeing filtered, beautiful women.

chunks.text: I also have a younger sister who is almost 15 years old. I am starting to see some potentially damaging effects that social media has on her and her young friends. I’m sure that these girls feel similarly to how I feel; much pressure to conform to these unrealistic expectations of society. I fear that they will struggle with the same issues I struggle with. These unrealistic expectations can lead to very serious issues such as body dysmorphia, eating disorders, very low self-esteem, anxiety, and depression.
chunks.label: Observing social media effects on younger sister
chunks.what_happened: The student observes the potentially damaging impacts of social media on their 15-year-old sister and her friends, fearing they will face similar struggles with unrealistic expectations.

chunks.text: In an attempt to not let myself fall into the trap of social media and the “beauty myth,” I have tried to distract myself with different things. I have put limits on my social media, to try to limit the amount of time spent on it. I also surround myself with positive people, such as my family and friends. It is important to take care of your own mental health before you worry about anything else.
chunks.label: Coping strategies against social media pressure
chunks.what_happened: The student sets limits on their social media use and surrounds themselves with friends and family to distract from negative beauty standards.

chunks.text: On the contrary, social media has some potential positive aspects to beauty stands that could help young women know their worth and not worry about fitting into the unrealistic standards of beauty in today’s society. When Naomi Wolf wrote her book, it was published in the 1990s, a time before the expansion of social media. Today, women are trying to crush the “beauty myth” using social media. For example, there are a lot of “body positive” movements that encourage young women to be comfortable in their own bodies. Many of these advocates use social media to show the many representations beauty has to offer. This in turn, can lead to self-love, healing, and help.
chunks.label: Positive aspects and body positivity on social media
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how social media can host body-positive movements and self-love advocates to push back against the beauty myth.

chunks.text: Now, is there a “beauty myth” for men, even though it was created by them? The short answer is no, not necessarily. Men are held to a certain standard, but not a certain “myth” or physical standard. For example, men are not supposed to show emotion because this can lead to people thinking of them as weak, but they are expected to be the leader of the household and be strong. A lot of times, if men show emotions, it is considered feminine, but recently, society has started to stray away for this idea. These stereotypes cause men to become subject to toxic masculinity. The term “toxic masculinity” can also be known as hegemonic masculinity, where hegemonic means dominant. This is a legitimate male role in Western society, and it is a practice for men to show superiority against other men and women. Men have intangible standards whereas women have physical standards. This idea of toxic masculinity encourages men to stay cold and dominant to focus on success and prosperity. Women could be considered “property” to them, or it may be encouraging men to possess women. This idea then leads more into the idea of men having power over women, therefore oppressing women even further.
chunks.label: Societal standards for men and toxic masculinity
chunks.what_happened: The student examines whether a beauty myth exists for men, discussing toxic and hegemonic masculinity, emotional repression, and male power over women.

chunks.text: Throughout Naomi Wolf’s book, she explains and provides many examples as to why and how women are judge based on the “beauty myth.” She begins to explain how this myth is composed of emotional distance, politics, finance, and sexual repression. To further explain the point of oppression with women, she states that the beauty myth isn’t about women at all. It is all about men and the institutional power they hold. Western women have always been controlled by ideas and material stereotypes, but I feel that as social media usage has increased, the “beauty myth” and transformed it. In this perspective, I feel that the “beauty myth” is still prevalent, if not more, but with the emergence of social media, it may be transforming into a beauty myth that is being reinforced by other women.
chunks.label: Naomi Wolf's arguments and social media evolution
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Naomi Wolf's book on institutional power and reflects on how the beauty myth has transformed through social media and reinforcement by women.

chunks.text: As much as I hate to admit it, the first thing I tend to notice about a person, especially other women, is there physical beauty and appearance. I think the notion of the “beauty myth” changes a little here because I am not looking to have power over other people, I am simply comparing myself to them. I think this is a natural thing that all people are subject to do.
chunks.label: Comparing oneself to other women
chunks.what_happened: The student notices the physical beauty and appearance of other women first and compares herself to them.

chunks.text: After looking and exploring through a different lens and writing about my own experiences with social media and the “beauty myth,” I quickly realized that the emergence of social media has increased my negative implications of the “beauty myth.” With the unrealistic societal expectations, it is hard to be confident in myself, especially when every time I open a social media app, I am bombarded with beautiful with who are “societally beautiful.” I do think that Naomi Wolf’s idea of the beauty myth has transformed and changed with society. I think that this myth was started by men to have power over women, and I still believe that is the case, but I also believe that this myth is being enforced by other women as well. I don’t think it is trying to be forced in a negative way, but many women are trying to fit into societal norms to fit in with society. This idea of the “beauty myth” pins women against each other in a competitive way, when actually, women need to encourage other women and stand up to the men that oppress them. Social media is a part of life now, and it always will be, so it is important that we find effective ways to keep our generation and generations to come in a positive mindset, so they know that they should not fall into societies trap of “the beauty myth.”
chunks.label: Concluding thoughts on social media and the beauty myth
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes how writing the essay revealed the beauty myth's negative effects, how women reinforce it against each other, and the need for mutual support.

n2d63c073.title: Reflecting on Gender Inequality and Roles

chunks.text: We can see this idea that men think they know best in “The Yellow Wallpaper,” where Gilman writes about this woman who is sick. Her husband has diagnosed her with nervous depression. He often dismisses her wants to work and write because he believes she needs to rest and not do anything. She has to hide her journal from him, which she becomes very good at, and because she is used to this, she is often defending her husband in the story. He is careful, loving, and gives her special direction. The woman learns to hide her writing, becomes so fixated and obsessed on this wallpaper, which her husband does not notice, and drives herself into insanity.
chunks.label: Analysis of The Yellow Wallpaper
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses the plot and dynamics of Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 'The Yellow Wallpaper,' focusing on how the husband dismisses the wife's desires and leads her to insanity.

chunks.text: Women back then were often dismissed, and their worries were not important. Now equality is still in issue. While we have come a long way from just being housewives and being unable to attend school, there are obstacles that need to be overcome. Women are not only what men decide they can be, one is not superior to the other (although arguments can be made), they differentiate greatly, and women have done many great things to overcome the societal norms of a woman and their roles in life. Girls can go to school and have jobs. Equal pay is still an issue that needs to be overcome and hopefully will be one overcome soon.
chunks.label: Reflections on gender equality and progress
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the historical dismissal of women and examines ongoing gender equality issues such as equal pay, noting both progress made and remaining obstacles.

nc3f89cb7.title: Performing Scripts in a McDonaldized Society

chunks.text:
As people we strive for authenticity, yet societal pressures can cause us to shape ourselves into something that we are not. We often judge ourselves based on other people's opinions and reactions towards us. One concept that shows our interactions with other is the “Presentation of the Self" as described by Erving Goffman. However, as society becomes increasingly influenced by the principles of McDonaldization, the distinction between Goffman's 'front stage' and 'backstage' is fading. This is because people are changing themselves to fit a certain standard. Through the McDonaldization of our everyday lives, “the backstage” is becoming obsolete and individuals are being forced to “put on a show” that aligns with corporate ideas for the sake of efficiency. When you combine both of these ideas it becomes apparent that we are all actors in a play that is scripted by societal norms that leaves no room for authenticy. The “Presentation of the Self" as described by Goffman uses the analogy of “the stage”. This idea is that individuals make an effort to control or manipulate the way others see them, as if they are an actor on a stage. We try to control how others see us by putting on a show for them. The role we play can depend on who we are with, where we are, and what we are doing. First, we have work to try to understand the situation and then act accordingly. This space is what Goffman refers to as the “frontstage”. He also believes in what he calls the “backstage”. This area is supposed to be where you are most calm and relaxed. But even when you are backstage you are still putting on a show for someone. This is because Goffman does not believe in a true self. He believes that our identities are created through various social interactions. So even when you are in the “backstage” there is still something making you feel like you need to act a certain way. This is something that we are seeing more of as time goes on. McDonaldization contributes to the blurring of the line between the "backstage" and "frontstage." There is an emphasis that is placed on efficiency and standardization in McDonaldization. It is making individuals become more and more expected to stick to predetermined scripts and behaviors, both in public and private spaces.

McDonaldization is a term used by George Ritzer and is all about pumping out goods and services quickly and easily. The main attributes of McDonaldization are efficiency, calculability, predictability, and control. This means that they operate with speed, quantifiable products, consistency, and strict regulations. One example of this is fast food chains. They are fast, predictable, and leave no room for a personalized experience. Another place where this concept is found in the real world is in the healthcare industry. You can see McDonaldization in the use of protocols and guidelines for treatments. There is also an emphasis on quick patient turnover as well as the fact that healthcare facilities are designed for efficiency and uniformity. With this idea, the focus is put on customer interaction. This is because this is a system that works to control how people interact. This is why the McDonaldization of our everyday lives is diminishing our authentic self-expression.

Both concepts showcase how workplaces today are choreographed with standardized routines to control impressions and experiences. McDonaldization takes rationalization into consumerism by trying to control how people interact and accomplish social tasks. This aligns with Goffman's theater metaphor where social interactions are viewed as a performance on a stage. In McDonaldized organizations, the employees have to carefully follow a scripted role wih specific behaviors. This is them putting on the "front stage" performance that Goffman is talking about. The backstage areas are strictly off-limits and in today's world it is almost like that backstage never existed.

When we look at how McDonaldization connects to Goffman's stage concept, we see how they both contribute to making people feel like they cannot truly be themselves. McDonaldization is about making things quick and predictable, like in fast food restaurants, which affects how we behave and interact with others. But McDonaldization does not just affect how society works or how people act. It also messes with their heads which makes it harder for to be yourselves. The constant need for everything to be fast, predictable, and controlled makes everyone feel like they have to act the same exact way. Whether we're at work, or just in a store buying something, we are pressured to follow the same rules. This can lead to feeling like we are not being true to ourselves. Goffman's idea of the stage compares social life to a theatrical play. In life, we are constantly on a stage where we act out certain roles depending on the situation. Together, these two ideas show how societal pressures and standardized rules can limit our ability to express ourselves truthfully. It is important to remember to be authentic and true to ourselves, even in a world that sometimes feels scripted.
chunks.label: Goffman's presentation of self and McDonaldization
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Erving Goffman's presentation of the self and George Ritzer's McDonaldization, analyzing how standardization and societal pressures force individuals to act in scripted roles and eliminate authentic self-expression.

chunks.text:
​Why do men have to ask the girl on the first date? Why are men expected to pay? Why are they expected to carry the conversation all night? Why do men talk about their successes and riches? Gender roles tell them they have to. Society has drilled it into their brains that this is their role as a man. These dominant actions such as asking a girl on the first date, paying for the meal, opening all the doors, etc. are men fulfilling their gender roles. Gender roles play an immense part in how people of the opposite sex act around each other. Men take on a dominant role and tend to take charge when around a woman. Women are the opposite. Women fall into a submissive role and are viewed as innocent and polite. They are expected to sit there and talk about makeup, nails, hair, etc. Men tend to look at the beauty on the outside and how well a woman would be able to take care of a child, while a woman views success and power as attractive in men. A heterosexual couple goes through all of the stages of a first date. This shows all of the dominance in men and submission in women. They successfully fulfill their gender roles with the company of one another.

Men portray this dominant role and women take on the submissive role on dates because they are “doing gender”. Men taking on the dominant gender role indirectly, and sometimes even directly, suppresses women’s power and authority. Women are given no control and no decision besides if they want to accept or decline the date invitation. Every other decision and action is given to the man. This oppression towards women is something that goes unnoticed by most people, especially women. It is considered normal and is something that society has said to be expected. Society wants women to think that a man treating them this way is “respectful”, but in reality, it is degrading. It is viewed as “romantic” or “chivalrous” for a man to act this way towards a woman, but in actuality, that could not be further from the truth. It is how men were taught by society to treat a woman in order to declare their superiority.

Think back to a heterosexual couple going through all the stages of a first date. Watching across the street as a man argues to himself if he should go ask this woman out on a date or not. He eventually walks up to her and begins a basic conversation. He asks her how her day was, if she’s single and he compliments her. He asks her out on a date, and she says yes; the only decision made by her. He decides on the time and the place of the date and picks her up from her house. He walks up to her front porch to greet her and then opens the car door for her to get in. Once they arrive at the restaurant he opens the car door again, as well as the restaurant door, and begins to talk to the hostess. They are led to the table by the hostess, and then the man pulls out the chair for her to sit down. This is where the date officially begins.

He carries the conversation most of the night by talking about how athletic he is, how much money he makes, how much power he has, and how successful he is. She sits there silently, continuing to acknowledge every word he says to show her listening abilities. Every once in a while she would mention a few things about her hair or her makeup, or even how she helps to take care of her younger siblings. When they are done at the restaurant, he opens the passenger car door for her and drives them back to her house. Once again he opens the car door and proceeds to walk her up to her front porch where he gives her a goodnight kiss. This is where the date officially comes to an end.

As West and Zimmerman explain in their piece “Doing Gender”, sex is something that is assigned at birth, while gender is a socially learned set of behaviors associated with a society. This includes social expectations and the idea of masculine versus feminine. The “existential function of the social'' argues that a belief system is needed to make sense of symbolic material. Gender is a role that is developed by the collective consciousness. The characteristics of your body that determine your sex, signal to you and others the role that you should be playing in society. Sex is simply a characteristic of the body, but gender is the set of roles we learn to play when we understand that gendered roles exist, and are hard to escape.

According to the authors, gender is done by “laying claim” to a sex category. This can include short versus long hair, clothes, makeup, attitude, and actions. “Doing Gender'' is the performance of a gender role. It reinforces an idea of gender through actions in a particular social setting. “Doing gender” comprises the set of tools that anchor the experience of self to the body. By “doing gender”, fitting into societal expectations becomes a lot easier. It is typically unavoidable and is something that everyone experiences. It is the differences between girls and boys and women and men that are not biological or essential. These differences create the infinite amount of roles that the genders are fit to play into. These roles are necessary for the world to not feel like it is crumbling, and for people to feel like they belong. As shown in the heterosexual date, men play into their dominant gender roles when around people of the opposite sex, such as women. By taking charge of asking on dates, opening doors, and carrying the conversation the man is doing gender. He is playing into his dominant masculinity. The typical male and female gender roles can only occur in heterosexual couples, not homosexuals. If two people of the same sex are going out one of them will likely obtain the dominant role and one will obtain the submissive role, however, this means that one of them will not be doing gender. On this heterosexual date, the man is reinforcing the idea of gender through his actions on this date. The woman sits there quietly, listening to him talk and letting the man take control. Every once in a while she talks, but only to show what a suitable mother she would be to their children if they ended up together. The man took command over all aspects of the date, besides the decision of if she would like to go or not. By the man “doing gender” throughout the date, he indirectly suppresses the woman’s strength and authority. These dominant actions subconsciously oppress the woman without her even realizing that it is occurring.

“The Yellow Wallpaper” by Charlotte Perkins Gilman is a prime example of a woman being oppressed without knowing oppression is occurring. Gilman is treated very negatively by her husband. He controls her, makes her decisions, and acts as a father figure towards her. He fulfills the dominant gender role directed towards men and pushes her into a compliant gender role. Although the husband may think that he is doing what was best for her, he wasn’t. Gilman was unknowingly being oppressed by her husband. She was observant of what was going on but was not aware that it was not considered to be normal. These dominant actions against them were considered “normal”, as it was the only thing women knew. Women did not have any way to conceptualize their oppression, because there was no language for it.

The heterosexual date is another example of this. The woman on the date is being unknowingly suppressed. When the man does gender by approaching her, asking her on the first date, holding doors open, paying automatically, and taking charge of the conversation, the woman is being oppressed. It pushes the woman into the passive and nurturing gender roles that they are told they need to fulfill. The woman’s gender roles are being polite and motherly, and when the man takes dominance he forces her into this. This is viewed as normal, so the woman does not even know this is occurring. She sat there quietly letting the man take full control, because it is what she was told since a young age was expected, and even romantic. By men and women consistently doing gender, women are pushed into the submissive role, giving men control.

Gender roles are needed in society for it not to fall apart. The ideas of masculine versus feminine create roles that are meant to be played by the fitting character. These roles given by society do not stay the same. “Doing gender” has changed over time, it does not have to stay consistent. The roles expected of each gender depend on the society in which it is taking place. In modern times gender roles have begun to overlap with each other. Men are allowed to be feminine and women are allowed to be masculine. Whereas it used to be that the men doing gender could only be masculine, dominant actions and women doing gender would have to be feminine and submissive. Women used to be unaware that they were being forced into submission by men’s dominant actions, but that is changing. Nowadays with feminist movements becoming more prevalent, women are becoming more aware of their oppression. The issue of having no language to conceptualize their oppression is no longer a problem in the modern world. Women are banding together and working to fight against this oppression. Women now make the first move, ask men on dates, pay or split the bill, etc. They are no longer being forced into submission, but instead, they are taking charge. By doing gender, society is kept in control by separating genders and the characters that they are supposed to be playing. When men act into their dominant role, it indirectly suppresses women’s power and independence. This oppression towards women goes unnoticed because it is viewed as normal in society. This is changing every day and women are becoming more and more aware of this oppression. Soon, women will successfully take a stand against this oppression, and it will no longer exist.
chunks.label: Gender roles and oppression on dates
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how traditional heterosexual dating norms reflect sociological theories of 'doing gender' and female oppression, referencing West and Zimmerman and Gilman's literature.

chunks.text:
In our society, it is evident that certain groups are put into stereotypical categories and are therefore treated differently. One aspect of this that is not discussed as frequently is what occurs when these groups internalize these stereotypes and even continue to perpetuate them. A prime example of this is how women purposely fall into certain roles of femininity in order to pertain to what is considered normal in society. While women have come a long way in terms of obtaining rights and being able attain similar opportunities as men, many still fall into the trap of still trying to pertain to the male gaze. So the question remains, if we are truly equals, then why do women feel the need to portray themselves in a way that is deemed acceptable by society?

It is safe to say that times are very different today than they used to be. A little under a century ago, women were fighting just for the right to vote in America and to not be treated as property of men. Nowadays, women are scientists, doctors, filmmakers, and have opportunities to pursue basically any field of interest that they wish. Although things have never been better for women, our society is constantly being inundated with subliminal messages regarding femininity. In stores we see handbags in glittery pink that say “You go girl!”. On TV there are commercials for barbie dolls with tagline that read, “you can be whatever you want!”. Everywhere you look, there are false messages about female empowerment, with subtext that essentially tells women that they can do what they want, but they need to remain feminine to do so. Female comedians constantly get glammed up before they go on stage and will most likely face judgement if they don’t, yet when male comedians go up before a crowd of thousands in sweatpants, no one bats an eye. Women are constantly told that they have to play by a certain set of rules if they intend on being as successful as men are.
chunks.label: Stereotypes and expectations of femininity
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how women internalize and perpetuate societal stereotypes and expectations of femininity despite progress in rights and opportunities.

chunks.text: I have seen firsthand how women respond to societies messages, and therefore perpetuate them in their own lives. In high school, there were always strict policies involving the dress code, but they almost always only applied to women. Girls were barred from wearing a multitude of different items as to not be too “distracting” to other students. Yet there seemed to be nothing that pertained to the boys at all. This therefore make women feel uncomfortable int their own skin, and that they are not allowed to wear what they want.
chunks.label: High school dress codes
chunks.what_happened: The student observed that dress codes in high school were strict and almost entirely enforced on girls to avoid being 'distracting' while ignoring boys.

chunks.text: I have also seen examples in college as well. In Greek life culture at colleges, including UNCW, women in sororities are all expected to be extremely feminine and dress up glamorously, especially when attending events or parties. The parties are only allowed to be held by the male sororities and the girls are only expected to do things such as holding fundraisers in cute outfits. The parties are all on the men’s terms and are about them being able to meet girls. Despite how counter to feminism this might seem, girls still continue to join these sororities and do not seem to question many of these outdated traditions.
chunks.label: Greek life and gender expectations
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how sororities at UNCW and other colleges conform to traditional, outdated gender roles and male-centered party cultures.

chunks.text: In my own experience, I tried to attend a party with a male friend and was told that only I was allowed in because I was a girl and that they needed to have a certain ratio of women at the party.
chunks.label: Denied entry with a male friend
chunks.what_happened: The student tried to attend a party with a male friend and was told only the student could enter because of fraternity gender ratios.

chunks.text:
I have heard even worse stories at other college campuses, where only girls who met certain beauty standards were allowed into parties. One fraternity even went as far as having a secret scale at the door of the house and would not let in girls who weighed above a certain number. Sororities are large communities, and they would be able to change things if they worked together and refused to continue playing by other people’s rules. But the sad truth is that most of them do not and keep adhering to old customs in order to continue to remain popular and relevant.

Another example of women adhering to toxic femininity was found through Matthew Ezzell’s research of the female rugby players at Competitive University. After observing the rugby team’s habits, he noticed that many of the players engaged in defensive othering as well as other toxic habits. The girls portrayed a strong sense of femininity both on and off the field, to combat possible notions that they were not girly enough, due to the tough nature of the sport. There are many stereotypes surrounding tough female athletes and the rugby girls did everything they could to not fall into them. They would dress glamorously, wear makeup while on the field, and engaged in similar forms of normative identification. They wanted to fit into the feminine narrative, while maintaining a status of being competitive and hardened players. This created a hard scenario for the girls, because not only did they have to prove themselves on the field, but they had to remain feminine and “pretty” while doing it. By doing this, the rugby players were perpetuating the notion that women can only achieve success if they are simultaneously pertaining to the male gaze. This feeds into the subordination that women constantly face and sets a standard for other women to follow suit, or risk being othered.

The example of the rugby girls helps to paint a clear picture of how women internalize their role in society. While trying to climb the social ladder and become a relevant part of their school, the girls unintentionally undermined feminism as a whole. Not only did the girls feel a strong need to fit certain standards, but they also put down other women and shamed them if they felt they didn’t belong. This is very dangerous. The actions of the majority of a group have a strong influence on its members because it is simply human nature to want to fit in and do what others are doing. This idea of being feminine, dressing up, needing to speak a certain way, are all things that have fallen into the collective consciousness of women in general.

All in all, this perdiciment that women in our society are currently in is very complicated to say the least. While there is a great deal of empowerment going on, there is also a struggle for women to stay in certain positions unless they act a certain way. Over a long period of time, women have had to fight every step of the way to achieve the same things as men. Even after that, women feel the need to control themselves so they fit into a category that is palatable and accepted. It is hard to say how this issue could eventually be resolved, but it seems that one of the main things that has to happen is that women need to work together more to fight this silent sexism. I feel that only after this, will women be able to take down these stereotypes that have followed us over centuries, and be able to rise above them. If more people take steps to show others that they don’t have to fit into a box in order to be successful, others will most likely follow in suit, and will no longer have to be under the pressure of constantly conforming to society’s expectations.
chunks.label: Analysis of toxic femininity and conformity
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on rumors at other campuses, Matthew Ezzell's rugby study on defensive othering, and concludes on the need for women to challenge silent sexism together.

n227e3662.title: Analyzing Privilege and Othering in Hiring

chunks.text:
In our societal discourse, two intertwined concepts often arise in discussions of race and identity. White privilege and defensive othering. While both concepts touch on issues of power dynamics and social hierarchies, they manifest in distinct ways and serve different purposes within conversations about race and identity. By examining these concepts through a comparative lens and illustrating them with a real-world scenario, we can better grasp their nuances and evaluate their effectiveness in addressing systemic inequalities. White privilege refers to the societal advantages, benefits, and immunities that white individuals experience simply by virtue of their whiteness. These advantages are often invisible to those who possess them, as they are ingrained within societal structures and norms. White privilege encompasses various aspects of life, including access to education, employment opportunities, healthcare, and the criminal justice system. It operates on both an individual and institutional level, shaping the experiences and opportunities of white individuals while simultaneously a huge disadvantage to people of color.

Defensive othering, on the other hand, is a psychological and sociological phenomenon characterized by the reflexive tendency of individuals or groups to distance themselves from marginalized or stigmatized groups. This distancing often takes the form of reinforcing stereotypes, prejudices, or hierarchies to protect one's own identity or sense of belonging. Defensive othering can manifest overtly through discriminatory actions or more subtly through microaggressions, implicit biases, or denial of systemic injustices. It serves as a mechanism for maintaining power and privilege by perpetuating narratives of superiority and inferiority. Consider a real-world scenario in which a job opening becomes available at a prestigious company. The hiring manager, who is white, receives applications from two candidates: one white and one Black. Both candidates possess similar qualifications, experiences, and skill sets. However, due to the pervasive influence of white privilege within the hiring process, the hiring manager unconsciously favors the white candidate. This preference may stem from shared cultural backgrounds, implicit biases, or a desire to maintain the status quo within the company. As the hiring process unfolds, the white candidate is offered the job while the Black candidate is passed over, despite being equally qualified. This outcome exemplifies the operation of white privilege, as the white candidate benefits from systemic advantages that afford them greater opportunities for success. Meanwhile, the Black candidate experiences the impact of systemic racism, facing barriers to employment based on their racial identity.

In response to criticisms of the hiring decision, the hiring manager engages in defensive othering. They dismiss claims of discrimination, attributing the decision solely to the white candidate's qualifications and fit for the role. They may downplay the significance of race in the hiring process or assert that the company values meritocracy above all else. By engaging in defensive othering, the hiring manager deflects accountability and perpetuates the myth of a level playing field, thereby reinforcing existing power dynamics. Both white privilege and defensive othering offer valuable frameworks for understanding and addressing issues of systemic inequality and discrimination. However, their effectiveness can be evaluated and critiqued in various ways.

White privilege provides a lens through which to examine the pervasive nature of racial advantages and disadvantages in society. By acknowledging and interrogating one's own privilege, individuals can work towards dismantling systemic barriers and advocating for equity. The concept of white privilege may be met with resistance or denial from those who benefit from it. Additionally, focusing solely on individual privilege may obscure the broader structural and institutional forces that perpetuate inequality.

Defensive othering highlights the ways in which individuals and groups perpetuate systems of oppression through their actions and beliefs. By recognizing and challenging defensive othering, individuals can disrupt harmful narratives and foster greater empathy and understanding. Defensive othering can be difficult to address, as it often operates at a subconscious level. Moreover, individuals may be resistant to acknowledging their own complicity in perpetuating discriminatory attitudes or behaviors.

In conclusion, white privilege and defensive othering offer complementary frameworks for understanding the complexities of race and identity in society. While white privilege illuminates the systemic advantages afforded to white individuals, defensive othering exposes the mechanisms by which privilege is maintained and reinforced. By critically examining these concepts and their manifestations in real-world scenarios, we can work towards building a more equitable and just society for all.
chunks.label: Analyzing white privilege and defensive othering
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the concepts of white privilege and defensive othering, analyzes a hypothetical hiring scenario to illustrate them, and critiques their effectiveness in addressing systemic inequality.

n359f0f0f.title: Analyzing Power Structures and Ritual Sacrifice

chunks.text:
The concepts and aspects of sociology are ones that cannot be definitively explained in a single phrase or statement. There are many different sociologists and other individuals who claim to have found specific reasoning for an aspect of how our society can be understood, but each of these opinions and perspectives can overlap and complement each other, or disagree entirely. After reading 21 Lessons for the 21st Century by Yuval Noah Harari, and getting to learn about his opinions on certain sociological topics and how he believes they play a part in our society today, it is easy to use his commentary in a comparison between other authors and evidence that have been discussed in class. There are both similarities and differences between Harari’s writing and that of the many readings we have covered this semester; mainly a similarity in the topic of society’s system or matrix, and a difference in the effects of rituals when used by individuals to strengthen and create religion.

One of the similarities between Harari’s theories and other sociological perspectives is in relation to the topic of how our society is set up and how its structure affects the grouping of humans and our interactions with those different from us. The concept of “The Matrix of Domination” can be related to Harari’s insistence that the system of our society is still affecting certain groups negatively, especially minorities.

“The Matrix of Domination” is based on the idea that there are multiple circles of oppression that exist and overlap into how each individual is viewed and treated in society. The three circles of oppression are class, race, and gender; each with its own effect on the individual. The beginning of the matrix in society is believed to be partially due to the Eurocentric masculine biases that spread around the world in the time of colonialism; as Europeans discovered new territories and populations of people that proved to be different from any of the ideas that they used in their society previously, they created new concepts of categorizing individuals into groups that led to some being more privileged than others in society. The privilege that individuals had was very proportional to their power and standing in society; depending on where an individual fit in each circle of oppression, they could either fall into the group of the oppressors (those with more power and a higher standing in each circle of oppression, more participation and say in controlling society) or the oppressed (with less power and lower standing than the oppressors, very little say and participation).

These beliefs and biases very quickly became a central part of how the matrix of domination shaped society. The matrix can be split into multiple levels, but the main three involve personal biography (an individual's own collection of experiences, values, emotions, and unique identity within their social space), group or community (based on similarities in stance in class, race, religion, political views, etc.) and systemic or national (the formatting and way of functioning for institutions such as schools, churches, media, and other organizations). Altogether the levels of domination combine to create a symbolic system that we all live in and are sorted in based on how much power we can obtain or hold. This idea of a large system or matrix that in part depends on the power and influence of certain individuals can be connected to a similar idea of Harari’s, where the formatting of society has caused us to be more susceptible to unconscious prejudices.

According to Harari, the arrangement of our society has a large effect on how we go on to form smaller and smaller groups within society, and how those groups then interact. He goes on to state that this structure of society is also a large part of why social justice issues such as discrimination and racism are so prominent and challenging to face and change. Because society is set up with a structure of hierarchy and power that is centered among the higher groups and individuals, this makes it possible for perspectives and biases to be leveraged into the system; trickling down into the rest of society as unconscious biases that then impact us when making everyday decisions. Harari summarizes this in the remark that “most of the injustices in the contemporary world result from large-scale structural biases rather than from individual prejudices…” (pg. 232); meaning that though we may not actively think and act in a biased way, there is no denying that part of our consciousness already has those biases because of how society and those with power have shaped the way we think.

However, this does not mean that there is no opportunity for us to pursue an even more equal and inclusive society despite our present societal structure (or matrix). The reason that we do not already have a more nondiscriminatory society is because our society has formed its truth around the opinions and wants of the people who hold the power in society; both tangible and intangible. Harari mentions these people of power as “the global elite” and that in order for there to be an explanation to change society’s current structure, we must look at how we are being affected by the truths of these individuals that surround us. He states that, “If you really want truth, you need to escape the black hole of power… [and] revolutionary knowledge rarely makes it to the center, because the center is built on existing knowledge,” (pg. 226). Most people will be content to live in the information at the center of society, because that is the truth that they have been known and living with, whether or not it is the most just perspective. In order for us to live in a society with less discrimination, there needs to be continual adjustments made to the structure of society and to who is holding the power.

On the other hand, a difference between the sociological writings we’ve explored in class can be seen in “The Cultural Logic of Collective Representations” and in Harari’s writings, specifically amid the topic of religion and religious rituals. Though both seem to agree that religion can play a large part in how people bond within their social and physical communities, there is an added aspect that Harari details about the drawbacks of religion as a coordinating force, depending on how and which rituals are used to enhance the strength of the religion within an individual.

At the beginning of the semester, some of the first things we discussed were about the nature of religion and how it has played a part in our emotional and social development as a species. In Emile Durkheim’s “The Cultural Logic of Collective Representations”, religion is largely described as something that occurs in our brains where we begin to attach meaning to certain objects or activities. Each object or activity begins to have its own separate meaning for the entirety of those who believe in the religion, evolving into things such as using wedding rings, eating communion bread, and going to church every Sunday. Religion provides us with the ability to coordinate ourselves socially into agreeing on what certain things mean for each and every one of the beliefs we have that make up whatever religion we choose to follow and believe in everyday, and each of the small differences in beliefs and rituals has led to the creation of different societies and cultures that have evolved out of different religions or even further into separate religious denominations. Ultimately, rituals are very important in the creation and function of religion because rituals provide a deeper meaning or reasoning for individuals to do them so as to participate and believe in the religion. Without rituals, it’s harder for people to physically act and feel emotionally bonded over the same beliefs as others.

Harari’s take on religion is somewhat similar in the fact that religion can and is used as a binding force between individuals that leads to communities. He also mentions the important role that rituals play in religion; defining them as “a magical act that makes the abstract concrete and the fictional real,” (pg. 287). Rituals serve as a binding force for those who partake in them, but Harari brings up that rituals are not always strengthening religious beliefs in a positive manner, and that “of all rituals, sacrifice is the most potent, because of all the things in the world, suffering is the most real. You can never ignore it or doubt it,” (pg. 291).
