Sandel, Michael J. “Justice: What’s the Right Thing to Do?” Farrar, Straus, and Giroux, 2009.
chunks.label: Analysis of Sandel's Justice and moral philosophy
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Michael Sandel's book 'Justice,' comparing Sandel's communitarian approach to utilitarianism (Bentham) and liberal neutrality (Kant and Rawls).

n61457351.title: Projecting the Future of Modern Families

chunks.text:
Projecting the Future of the 2035 Families: Trends and Transformations

Dakota Williams

University of North Carolina at Wilmington

SOC-345: Sociology of the Family

Dr. Douglas Engleman

October 24, 2025

Projecting the Future of the 2035 Families: Trends and Transformations

Sociologists examine family change not only by documenting past and current trends, but also by imagining reasonable futures based on these patterns. The American family has been rapidly changing due to shifting cultural norms, economic conditions, and policy responses. For example, marriage rates and age at first marriage have changed (Herre et al. 2025, para. 10). Mothers' labor force participation has risen, while single-parent and one-person households have increased. Likewise, blended and cohabiting families have become more common, and a growth in households identifying as same-sex couples. There is current evidence to project how these trends may reconstruct what a "typical" family life looks like by the year 2035.

Multiple evidence-based trends can help us understand what 2025 to 2035 might look like, for example, regarding marriage and partnerships. After decades of declining marriage rates and increasing ages at first marriage, and a resulting drop-off in marriage counts due to the 2020 pandemic, marriage counts have recovered for the time being (Herre et al. 2025, para. 23). Trends in the data still show a smaller percentage of people marrying at an earlier age, and the share of people currently living unpartnered or cohabiting, rather than marrying, is greater than in the mid-20th century. Recent analysis has found marriage rates in the low ratings across the entire US. Still, the marriage rate is offset by a much greater share of adults who are either unmarried or cohabiting without marriage (Buck et al., 2024, para. 6-8)

Women's involvement in labor has increased mostly during the late 20th century, and even though the overall female labor force participation rate has been changing in the 2010s and early 2020s, mothers of children of school age still experience relatively high labor force participation rates, and many families depend on two earners in the family. Recent Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data show that about three-quarters of mothers of children under 18 are in the labor force (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2023, para. 9)

The amount of children living with a single parent rose steeply in the decades after 1960; by the 2010s–2020s era, approximately one quarter of children had spent time in a household with a single parent, and one-person households accounted for an increasing share of all households. However, some recent data show slight declines at times in the share of single-parent households (Barrett, 2022, para. 3-5). Blended families and cohabiting couples are more typical today than in earlier generations. Households headed by married same-sex couples and by same-sex cohabitating couples are also common today and increasing (Scherer, 2022, para. 1-4)

Marriage is becoming less of a universal life experience and is now just one way to experience cohabitation among many forms that are sanctioned. For instance, many adults who form long-term partnerships will continue to delay legal marriage until later in life, once they have established careers or financial resources. Others will cohabit long-term without legal marriage, particularly when there are weakened legal and economic incentives to marry, or when couples actively prefer cohabitation over marriage to maintain flexibility (Fry, 2025, para. 2). Levels of overall marriage at any age will be lower than in mid-twentieth-century America.

By 2035, most mothers will be engaged in paid work, but the nature of that work will be more diverse. The continued increase of remote and hybrid workplaces, greater acceptance of flexibility in employer expectations, and technological shifts will enable parents to combine paid work and caregiving responsibilities with greater flexibility. Nevertheless, wage inequality, employer-provided benefits, and unequal access to quality childcare will still constrain the choices of mothers in less-than-ideal financial situations (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025, p. 2). The data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics on labor force participation rates for mothers with school-aged children, including findings from a recent survey indicating a significant amount of interest in telework, would also support these assumptions (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025, p. 2-3). Data show that women who are married, pregnant, or have children under age 3 are less likely to be employed in their marriages (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025, p. 14). This is because mothers are still seen as the family's caregivers and are expected to be at home taking care of the child, rather than the man.

Blended families and cohabitating multigenerational living arrangements are likely to be common adaptations to economic pressures and shifting social norms. Some young adults will remain in or return to their parental homes for more extended periods, while some older adults will live with adult children due to economic constraints, health needs, or preference. Rising census data on one-person households, cohabitation households, and multi-type households indicate this pluralization of family structures (Barrett, 2022, para. 3)

By 2035, households headed by same-sex couples will represent an appreciably larger share of family types, as they have continued to grow alongside the expansion of legal recognition and social legitimacy in the 2010s and 2020s. There are legal and social barriers; diversity in race/ethnic backgrounds, income, and parental status will only increase. Further evidence from census records of the continued increase in same-sex married households indicates this trend should persist. (Hays & Minkin, 2025, para. 3-10)

The future of families will differ. Families with higher incomes and better education will have more opportunities to avail themselves of flexible working hours, good child care, and housing that supports family stability and choice. On the other hand, lower-income families will continue to suffer from the same limitations as before; they will have unstable jobs, housing insecurity, and difficulties in finding affordable childcare that will not be available in their neighborhoods, which will lead to the rise of complex living arrangements and children with different fathers in some areas (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025, p. 4-6)

The shape of 2035 families will be altered by three important domains that can amplify trends: public policy, cultural change, and the technology/labor market. The expansion of publicly funded childcare, full paid maternity leave, and subsidized housing in the United States would mean that families from lower-income to high-income would have more options: in case of an economic risk, earlier childbearing would be less risky, mothers could still be in the labor force with lesser sacrifices, and single parents would get more help. On the other hand, if these policy areas stagnate, inequalities will worsen and choices will be reduced, which in turn will make it unavoidable for complex household arrangements to become survival strategies (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2025, p. 6-14). If the public continues to take in different types of families, social institutions like schools, hospitals, and employers will adapt, thereby eliminating stigma and making it easier for unconventional families to live day to day.

The​‍​‌‍​‍‌​‍​‌‍​‍‌ American family by 2035 will probably not go back to being a single dominant type. Instead, families will have plural, layered arrangements, resulting from delayed marriage. Maternal labor force participation will be high but uneven; the number of single-parent households will remain steady; more blended families will exist; and the visibility of same-sex families will be greater. The most important questions for scholars and policymakers are which policies and cultural changes will reduce inequality and, at the same time, help shape stable, healthy family lives in diverse households? Real-world evidence, as shown in data, suggests that the only thing left is society's choice in response to those trends.
chunks.label: Projecting the future of 2035 families
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes demographic trends, statistics, and sociological research to project how American family structures, marriage, labor participation, and policies will transform by the year 2035.

chunks.text: In this paper, I will share my views on marriage and how I think my views are similar and different from others. I will also talk about how we all interpret marriage differently, then I will talk about what this means for the overall society, and how we will look as a society in 2035. I am an oddball compared to most people in our class.
chunks.label: Paper introduction
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the paper's focus on marriage views, society, and predictions for 2035.

chunks.text: My parents had me in high school; they were together for a few years after I was born, and then my mom took me and her out of that environment. To sum it up, I came from teenage parents who were never married, and they split when I was very young. My mom and I moved out, and she became a single mom. My dad wasn’t super consistent in my life when I was young due to many reasons. Having gone through all of that has really impacted the way I feel about dating and how picky I need to be for a husband. My mom and dad dated different people as I grew up; some were nice, some were not so nice. Seeing my mom being treated in abusive ways made me realize what I did not want in a relationship or marriage. It made me feel as if marriage was going to be impossible for me, and I was going to end up alone with a hundred cats. Growing up, I never had an ideal marriage in my head, even in modern times, I don’t because to me, families look different in so many ways.
chunks.label: Growing up with teen parents and single mom
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up with teenage parents who split up, lived with a single mother, experienced an inconsistent father, and witnessed abusive relationships involving their mother.
chunks.feelings: fear of ending up alone with cats, feeling marriage would be impossible
chunks.people: mother, father, partners of mother and father

chunks.text: This class has really gotten me thinking lately about my future with my boyfriend. Personally, I want to have a husband and 2-3 kids. I want my husband and me to both have jobs that we love and are passionate about, and I want us to have a balanced chore list instead of it all relying on me. My boyfriend and I have been discussing marriage and how we feel like we are getting to that point. The only reason why my boyfriend and I would be able to get to that point is because he is in the military. Financially, we would be supported, and we could live on base, so there aren’t as many barriers impacting us compared to others our age.
chunks.label: Discussing marriage with military boyfriend
chunks.what_happened: The student and their boyfriend have discussed marriage and their future together, supported by his military benefits.

chunks.text: I feel that currently there is a somewhat Midterm Paper By: Bryanna Yarborough SOC 345 - 001 balance of people my age getting married and then people my age not wanting to get married. I really don’t know where we are as a society when it comes to marriage and family because I see both sides being represented pretty equally. Some of my friends have been in a relationship for years, and they are at the point where they want to get engaged and married, but they also want to be financially stable before they take that step. Since divorce rates are higher, some people want to have a nice, stable job that pays them enough in case they need to support themselves after a divorce. I also have some friends who are not ready for marriage, but they live with their significant other. They figured that if they are always spending time at one place, then why both pay for expensive apartments and not split the costs.
chunks.label: Reflections on peer marriage and cohabitation
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how friends and peers balance getting married or cohabitating to save costs.

chunks.text: Throughout this class, I started to think about how the military might affect the statistics on marriage. I am around Marines a lot, and I have seen some of them get married really young so they can have that extra financial support of BAH. It makes me wonder if military marriages are affecting the statistics in any way. There are some people marrying their best friend in the military to get double BAH, and there are some people getting married to someone they barely know. I wonder if this could affect the statistics of how many same sex marriages are in the United States, and if this is making the divorce rate go up. I would really like to see research and the statistics on military marriages.
chunks.label: Observing military marriages
chunks.what_happened: The student is around Marines often and has seen young people marry for military BAH benefits.

chunks.text: Since, unfortunately, I am not able to predict the future due to my indecisiveness, I decided to look into what people are predicting the next few years will look like based on the research. ​ Looking at the Pew Research Center, I think the numbers will continue to decline. More people are cohabitating, not having kids, etc. I think part of the cause for this is due to the cost of everything. If a couple can barely survive working two full-time jobs, then why would they want to have kids? They would be in an even more financial burden with the cost of all of Midterm Paper By: Bryanna Yarborough SOC 345 - 001 the crazy things that babies need, hospital bills, and so much more. People are barely able to stay afloat as is, so they’re not going to want to bring someone else into this world. I believe this is another factor in why the divorce rates are increasing. People are supposed to be loving their partner, spending time with them, and being able to relax in their home. Instead, people are going from a stressful work environment to a stressful home environment, too. Their home environments could be stressful due to their partner not working, their home being a mess, or even because they simply can’t pay their bills, even though they and their partner are working full-time jobs. Looking at the Pew Research Center, it shows the statistics of families declining but there are newer forms of families. For example, “in 1970 67% of Americans ages 25 to 49 were living with their spouse and one or more children younger than 18. Over the past five decades, that share has dropped to 37%” (Pew Research Center). The data also shows that 0.7% marriages in 2015 were for same sex couples, but in 2021, that percentage went to 1.1%. Through this center and their research also shows how the percentage of married with kids has declined, but the percentage for cohabitating with kids, unpartnered with kids, cohabitating no kids, and other family members has increased. All of these statistics show that even though marriages have declined, the different forms of families have expanded. The acceptance of interracial and same sex couples is becoming more accepted by people.
chunks.label: Analysis of Pew Research Center data
chunks.what_happened: The student examines Pew Research statistics regarding declining marriage rates, financial strain, and new family structures.

chunks.text: In conclusion, I think the decline of marriage will keep going down because of financial burdens. If somehow we can fix our economy, then I think there will be an increase in marriages, but for now, that number is still going to keep going down. In addition to that, I believe that the different forms of families are going to keep increasing. I believe this will keep increasing because some of those family types are easier financially. Like I said above, many people I know Midterm Paper By: Bryanna Yarborough SOC 345 - 001 live with their significant other because rent and mortgages are very expensive nowadays. Other things like your other bills, groceries, and gas are also very expensive. When the cost of those things starts to decline, then in the future divorce rates will go back down and marriage rates will go back up. A huge factor in divorces is usually related to money and being burnt out. If prices go down, then it will create a less stressful home and work environment, which means that families will most likely stay together rather than be stressed and give up.
chunks.label: Conclusion on economy and marriage trends
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes that financial burdens drive declining marriage rates and increasing divorce rates.

The author of “Justice: What is the right thing to do?” is an American political philosopher and professor at Harvard University named Michael Joseph Sandel. This book is a New York Times bestseller that explores political philosophy and moral dilemmas by applying theoretical and analytical thinking to real-world issues. Sandel invites the readers to engage in reasoned debate about justice and the common good in society. He challenges the shallowness of debates focused solely on personal gain or individual liberty, arguing for a third basis: the impact on the common good. In “Justice: What is the right thing to do?”, it focuses on and examines different philosophical approaches to justice, including those of Aristotle, Kant, Mill, and Rawls, to understand contrasting ideas. While engaging with complex philosophy, the book is written in a lively and accessible way, making it suitable for a broad audience interested in making sense of politics, morality, and their own beliefs.

Chapter 1, “Doing the Right Thing,” of “Justice: What is the right thing to do?” talks about the central question of justice: how should we decide what’s right? He uses real-world problems and dilemmas to depict this, for example, his trolley problem, Hurricane Charley, or the Afghan goatherds. He uses these examples to show three main approaches to justice: maximizing welfare (utilitarianism), respecting freedom (libertarianism), and promoting virtue/common good (Aristotelian traditions). The runaway trolley dilemma proposes the question of saving one life or saving five when the solution is in hand. The brakes on the trolley stop working, and there are two groups on the track. You can pull the lever and move the trolley to the right, killing one worker and sparing five. A little bit later into the story it proposes another question: if you are just watching from a distance and see a bigger man standing there, you could push him onto the tracks and avert this disaster. In my opinion, I would not push this man onto the tracks, knowing in doing this I just killed him and put myself into a bigger situation. I would just let the train go, knowing I could not do anything aligning with my morals. It would be on my guilty conscience that I just killed this man when I could have removed myself from the situation and not done anything. Obviously this is a hard and terrible situation, knowing you could have people but at the loss of others.

In chapter 2, “The Greatest Happiness Principle/Utilitarianism,” it speaks about utilitarianism, defining justice as maximizing overall happiness or pleasure. Sandel explores strengths like simplicity and impartiality and weaknesses like knowing utilitarianism can justify sacrificing individuals, ignores rights, and undervalues higher ideals. Like, for example, the lifeboat story when there were four stranded sailors, and when the cabin boy got sick, the group killed and ate him. They claimed they did this out of necessity to survive and promote the general well-being of keeping the majority alive. Bentham, an English moral philosopher, founded the doctrine of utilitarianism to maximize happiness. Mill contradicts this idea, thinking refinement emphasizes quality of pleasures and liberty as essential to well-being. Chapter 3, “Do We Own Ourselves?/Libertarianism,” goes hand in hand with this. Libertarianism holds that individuals own themselves and their labor, so government oversight should be minimal—protecting life, property, and contracts. Sandel examines issues in the book like taxation as it is seen as forced labor, drug laws, and military conscription. For libertarianism, taxation is seen as forced labor because “if you are taxed, you can always choose to work less and pay lower taxes; but if you are forced to labor, you have no such choice.” Basically saying that people are forced to pay the government money, and it should be voluntary; if they wanted to pay and help the community, they would. The tension arises between absolute self-ownership and the social responsibilities that come with living in a community. Personally, it's hard for me to lean one way completely because in certain situations I could agree with either. I do think that taxes should be something everyone has to pay and should not be voluntary because it helps the majority, but I also don’t think some people should be sacrificed unwillingly to help the majority.

Chapter 4, “Hired Help / Markets and Morals,” asks whether everything should be up for sale. Sandel considers markets in controversial areas like military service substitutes, surrogate motherhood, and organ sales. He argues markets aren’t neutral: they can corrupt or degrade the value of certain goods and can create inequality by allowing the wealthy to “buy” advantages. One story that gets brought up to demonstrate this is “Pregnancy for Pay,” which is about a family paying a surrogate to have their baby since they can’t. It comes up with the question of if they are paying for the baby itself, which is baby-selling, or paying for the service of having the baby. Mary-Beth is the surrogate for the Sterns, and eventually when she has the baby for them, she tries to take it, but they go to court and fight for custody of the child. The baby ultimately went to the Stern family for the child's sake. In my opinion, I think they were paying Mary Beth for the service of having the child and the burden of carrying it to term for them, not for the baby itself. Also, I think it is a good idea that the child ended up in the custody of the Sterns because they had a contract set and paid Mary Beth; not only that, but she tried to flee with the child.

“What Matters Is the Motive/Immanuel Kant” is the name of chapter 5, and it focuses on how Kant shifts focus from consequences to motives. Thinking that the only truly moral actions are those done from duty, guided by reason, and acting only on principles you would have as universal laws, treat people as ends, not means. Justice, in Kant’s eyes, requires respecting human dignity, not maximizing welfare or efficiency. He believes that actions represented as good in themselves are necessary: “Kant contrasts hypothetical imperatives, which are always conditional, with a kind of imperative that is unconditional: a categorical imperative” (pg. 112). I don't fully believe in Kant's ideas; for example, if an axe murderer was coming after my friend, I would lie about where they were. I would want my friend to survive, and I would not want to be the reason they got found and killed. There are reasons to lie sometimes, which Kant doesn’t believe. In Chapter 6, “The Case for Equality / John Rawls,” Rawls argues that justice is fairness. Using the “veil of ignorance” thought experiment, he claims people would choose two principles: equal basic liberties for all, and inequalities are just only if they benefit the least advantaged, involving social and economic equality. Kant and Rawls agree on the importance of universal principles, autonomy, and justice over consequences. Rawls ideas challenge libertarianism and utilitarianism by emphasizing fairness over luck or efficiency.

In Chapter 7, “Arguing Affirmative Action,” Sandel examines debates over affirmative action in college admissions. He outlines three justifications: correcting past injustice, promoting diversity, and promoting meritocracy. Critics argue it violates fairness or demeans achievement. For example, the Hopwood study is based on Cheryl Hopwood, a white applicant who was denied admission to the University of Texas Law School despite strong academic credentials. She argued that the school’s affirmative action policy discriminated against her, since minority applicants with lower grades and test scores were admitted. In my opinion, I think there are many different things that go into college applications that could be bigger than test scores and academics. Like their essay, extracurriculars, athletics, etc. Even if they were even on that standpoint and just differed in academics, I think the school is still entitled to choose who they want if they want to include more diversity. She did not have to go to this college, and college is a choice and privilege for many people. The discussion highlights deeper questions: what counts as merit, and should admissions reflect individual achievement or social purposes?

In chapter 8, “Who Deserves What?/Aristotle,” it kind of goes along with chapter 7, saying that Aristotle sees justice as giving people what they deserve, but this depends on the purpose or telos of the good being distributed. For example, the purpose of a university is cultivating knowledge, not rewarding legacy or wealth. Justice thus requires reasoning about virtue and the common good, not just neutral principles. In the book, they talk about the story of Callie Smartt, a high school freshman with cerebral palsy. She was a cheerleader during the football season, but at the end she got kicked off for not being able to perform the gymnastics and tumbling required to be on the team. “Callie’s story raises two questions. One is a question of fairness. Should she be required to do gymnastics in order to qualify as a cheerleader, or is this requirement unfair, given her disability?” (pg. 149). My response to this question would be that it's not fair to kick her off the team when she has an abundant amount of school spirit and shows her worth of staying on the team. Just because she cannot do flips or tricks, she can still cheer the team on while her other cheerleading teammates fulfill the requirements.

Chapter 9, “What Do We Owe One Another?/Dilemmas of Loyalty,” explores moral duties rooted in ties of loyalty, community, and identity, such as family, country, or religion. Sandel contrasts universal moral principles with particular obligations, for example, patriotism and solidarity. He raises the question: are we only bound by impartial and unbiased principles, or also by the “moral weight” of our personal attachments? Part of this chapter asks the question of if the government and people should apologize for the sins and wrongdoings of our predecessors. Even if we did not personally harm those, and it was the previous generations, we should still acknowledge and apologize for it. For example, slavery—although slavery is not a thing anymore, racism still exists, and we can acknowledge that so that history does not repeat itself. Finally, the last chapter, “Justice and the Common Good,” argues that justice cannot be morally neutral. Decisions about justice inevitably involve debates about virtue, purpose, and the common good. Sandel critiques liberal neutrality, like Rawls and libertarianism, and concludes that a just society must engage in moral and civic dialogue about what kind of people and community we want to be. This chapter brings up one point about justice and the common good, talking about how John F. Kennedy and Barack Obama had very opposing ideas about religion in politics. John F. Kennedy felt that even though he was Catholic, he was not going to base any of his ideas or concepts on religion, knowing people would disagree. On the other hand, Obama thought that his Christianity should be involved in his politics, since the majority of America would be influenced and believe the same as him. Personally, I think religion has no place in the government or politics, especially in America, knowing that we have such a diverse country and not everyone believes in religion or the same religion at all. I do understand where Obama was coming from, though, because both he and JFK were doing what would get them the most votes.

In the end, “Justice: What Is the Right Thing to Do?” pushes readers to wrestle with difficult questions about morality, fairness, and the common good. By exploring contrasting philosophies and applying them to real-world dilemmas, Sandel shows that justice is never simple and cannot be reduced to one principle alone. Instead, it requires thoughtful reflection, open debate, and a willingness to balance personal freedom with responsibility to others. His work ultimately challenges us not only to think critically about what is right but also to consider the kind of society we want to build together.
chunks.label: Review and reflections on Sandel's Justice
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes and reflects on each chapter of Michael Sandel's book 'Justice: What is the right thing to do?', discussing philosophical frameworks like utilitarianism, libertarianism, Kant, Rawls, and Aristotle, alongside various moral dilemmas.

chunks.text: Rawls challenges the reader to imagine designing a society without knowing our place in it. Referring to this idea of the “veil of ignorance” which he argues, we would all choose principles that would guarantee our basic rights and ensure that inequalities would work to benefit the least advantaged. And I completely agree with that argument, and it really makes you think about this situation in an entirely new way. It forces you to confront the bias that goes on in your head that you may not even realize is there.
chunks.label: Reflections on Rawls and the veil of ignorance
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Rawls's concept of the veil of ignorance and explains how it confronts internal biases.

chunks.text: In my own life experience, I come from a very diverse area in Baltimore, Maryland. I live 5 minutes outside of the city so over my life I have made friends who live out in the country with big houses and a bunch of land and have friends that are clumped up in small apartments barely having room for their families. Friends who are growing up never even thought of going to college as an option. I think growing up seeing both sides of the spectrum helped give me a perspective for both sides and makes me feel very grateful.
chunks.label: Growing up near Baltimore with diverse friends
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up near Baltimore, befriending people from wealthy country homes as well as those living in cramped apartments who never considered college an option.

chunks.text: This exercise and my life experience make me appreciate and respect policies like affirmative action. That if education is meant to reward merit but also serve the purposes of society, universities considering diversity and fairness is completely justified and something I would like to have in my own society to ensure a sense of fairness for all.
chunks.label: Support for affirmative action
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how personal experience and Rawls's exercise lead to an appreciation of policies like affirmative action in education.

chunks.text: Another idea that stuck out to me is Aristotle’s idea of “telos”. Which meant that everything in life has a specific purpose. An example would be that the telos of a flute is to make music. But for humans and society, it is to live well and fulfill our maximized potential as social beings. Aristotle argues that justice is giving people what they deserve based on their purpose. Arguing the people should get opportunities in ways that help them fulfill their true purpose. He explains how we must consider the common good, allowing a community to thrive and for its members to live good, fulfilling lives. Aristotle's approach is different from utilitarianism and libertarianism in the way that it is not maximizing pleasure or protecting freedom. Justice is about helping people and society as a whole find their purpose and succeed. The differences between these three ideas can be expressed through this example. If your school is picking a captain for a basketball team a libertarian would argue to let the students vote. A utilitarian would argue to pick the player that will give the team the best chance at winning. And Aristotle would argue to pick who deserves the role, who will help the team grow as a whole. But with this idea comes the issue regarding who decides someone's true purpose? And whoever that is, how do you know that there is no bias towards that discussion? This especially is concerning because Aristotle excluded woman and slaves from politics because he believed that the telos of political life was reserved for men. Which in my opinion completely discredits his ideas because he is extremely incorrect. And with a society so large and diverse how could anyone ever reach an agreement regarding moral purposes.
chunks.label: Aristotle's telos and justice theories
chunks.what_happened: The student examines Aristotle's concept of telos compared to utilitarianism and libertarianism, critiquing Aristotle's exclusion of women and enslaved people.

chunks.text: Reading Sandel has challenged me to think critically about justice as a more in-depth concept. And reading all of these different ideas and theories has helped me to develop my own ideas. Helping me think about freedom, fairness, and purpose. I think there is a little bit of truth in all of these theories, but I do not completely reside with just one. Each contains some ideas that I may agree with and plenty that I do not. But I do see that justice requires major public reasoning about what we, as a society, value and why. And the importance in considering all perspectives and places of reasoning to better understand. In such a diverse society that process is not easy, but is absolutely necessary if we are to all understand one another and work toward the common good. Justice is less about answers but being able to question, communicate, and reflect on what kind of society we want to be.
chunks.label: Conclusions on reading Sandel and justice
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how reading Sandel helped them develop their own views on justice as an ongoing dialogue and reflection for the common good.

chunks.text:
Throughout this first part of the semester, we focused on Michael Sandel’s book titled “Justice: What's the Right Thing To Do?”. Throughout this book, Sandel discusses several topics within the conversation of justice and what is morally correct. Within his book, Sandel covers topics ranging from utilitarianism all the way to Rawls' difference principle. Utilizing the concepts discussed within this book, we were able to have deep conversations and evolve our understanding of morality and justice. This book further connects historical theories and ideas, as well as occasionally more modern ones, and then relates them to current issues and debates within our society. Furthermore, we were encouraged to utilize the principles within this book to take a stance on current issues and form our own opinions on such issues.

Throughout the book, there is a common theme about “who deserves what”, explaining how justice should be determined or distributed. Although each chapter is a different explanation of how to distribute justice, and an understanding of such according to different historical philosophers and sociologists, Sandals sets his major guidelines of justice in the first few chapters according to historical philosophers. Sandel draws primarily from Aristotle, explaining how he simply defines justice as “giving individuals what they deserve”. He goes on to further explain and break down this concept by explaining that we determine what individuals deserve this by defining the values and virtues of our society that are worth rewarding. Sandel continues by contradicting this statement by explaining that the view of modern philosophers who define the morally correct way to define our rights of justice cannot be reliant on any particular virtue. So what is justice, and how should society break down the ways we determine who deserves what? This question is the backbone of the book, and there are a few major interpretations I have taken from the book to interpret my own understanding of justice.

Within the book, the utilitarianism and libertarianism concepts are essentially pitted against one another. From my own understanding as well as what I have gathered from class discussion and the video of Sandel’s students, I believe most people align with a combination of the two perspectives. Furthermore, I feel as though the evolution of utilitarianism, developed later on by John Stuart Mill, is far more rational. His understanding expands utilitarianism beyond just “what maximizes pleasure and happiness” into “what maximizes happiness for the greatest number of individuals without negatively impacting or hurting other individuals”. Additionally, if you add in part of the libertarianism concept of “individuals should be free to decide with limited, if any state control” into Mills' Idea, you form a more rational understanding of these three. Despite their polarity, they are concepts emerging from similar issues and therefore feed into each other. The morally right decision to make is one that causes you the most pleasure while not hurting anyone else. In this discussion, one should also be free to make decisions with limited governmental control, considering it is your discussion. This understanding of combining the three major principles additionally aligns with most of my decisions regarding the political climate.

To further explain my belief system formed from these three major concepts within the book, I will relate it to current political debates. Firstly, this concept aligns with my stance on abortion. To my understanding, through these principles, the state should not regulate abortion until 16 weeks. I believe that giving individuals the right to be able to choose for themselves what they want to do regarding their own personal situation is the morally correct decision. Whether an individual decides to get an abortion or not does not directly negatively impact anyone else (it is their own body and their own decision). Furthermore, being given the decision positively impacts them and allows them to choose for themselves. However, I have set up the guideline for myself to limit them to around 16 weeks (with potential for exceptions because there are always exceptions). This time frame typically marks the start of the fetal nervous system development and, therefore, potential for fetal pain. At this point and beyond, I personally believe it may be morally wrong to get an abortion because of the potential pain felt by the baby and how developed it has become. This would further fall into the concept of utilitarianism by Mills, where he states that so long as it does not “harm other parties”. Overall, I believe that I can apply the logic and morality I have developed to multiple political and moral debates and take a stance on them.

The last major topic is the idea of equity versus equality, and how that would function within our society. The major perspective brought up in the book is Rawl’s, which brought forward the idea of everyone having equal opportunity as well as the demand for social and economic inequalities to benefit those least advantaged. I believe from my own logic, the most important perspective of those two parts is the latter. Although I believe it is important to have equal opportunities, I fear as though with the way our society functions, that will be difficult to conjure. I believe most efforts should be placed in changing the system in a way that allows for ( most likely after the fact) the social and economic benefit, mainly to the least advantaged. I see this likely occurring in the way we organize taxation, possibly creating more equitable means (instead of simply equal). More real-world interpretations of this concept are specifically the issue of taxation. As stated specifically in Sandel's lecture (within the YouTube video), is it morally right to create more equitable stances through means of taxation? Although this concept is very controversial, I believe and, according to Rawls' perspective, it would be morally correct. Taxation is a way to “even the playing field”. Taxation like this could allow for almost a redistribution of wealth in such a way that it benefits though socially and economically disadvantaged. I would not necessarily consider it “taking” from those with more money, but simply a means to create more equitable stances. I do acknowledge that this may contradict my earlier development of the utilitarian and libertarian perspectives. The contradiction lies specifically within the ideas that if this taxation redistribution occurs, it would be directly harming those with higher economic and social standing. As stated in Sandel’s lecture, it could be considered “slavery” (free labor/work without compensation). I believe that regardless of whether there is a slight redistribution or not, a party is already harmed. Furthermore, I argue that those individuals in the top economic percentile may have only gotten there through insincere means, specifically through the exploitation of those in the lower classes. I argue that maybe it is important to consider how they obtained that wealth, especially when considering the redistribution of it.

Another major debate discussed was the topic of affirmative action. The question of is it morally correct to prioritize certain factors while accepting individuals into the workforce and college admissions? From my understanding of this debate, I recognize that the factors that they are adding (despite just merit) are factors of minority groups. I argue that this adds into Rawls’ perspective about ensuring inequalities benefit those less advantaged. I argue that those merits are already biased with the results regarding the unfair distribution of funds to different school districts, and affirmative action could be a means to balance the afteraffects of those inequalities. These inequalities are also deep ridden and come from bias of language, funds, opportunities, etc. If there are no attempts to balance the inequalities through aiding those least advantaged, then the system will continue to be corrupt and unfair. Without the implications of affirmative action, this bias continues into college and secondary education then continues to bleed into the workforce. I argue that it is what causes generational disadvantages, further setting in stone the unfair class system.

Overall, throughout this book, I have noticed the evolution and development of my stance and morality on such difficult topics. Through this reading, I have been able to shape my understanding of morality and justice while also applying it to the current political situations. It is important to allow yourself to feel empathy and understanding for others' situations and think more critically about the root of these very sensitive debates and issues. It is important to discuss issues such as abortion, gun control, and the wealth gap. Individuals need to develop their own rationale on such a topic. The media present that the social climate is currently very divided on such topics, but I believe that more individuals are most likely on the middle ground of these topics but it is necessary to debate and have conversations to be able to discover that fact. This book has allowed for my own personal exploration of such topics especially alongside the aid from the class discussions we have. This book has continued to allow me question the systems we have set place in society, wondering how corrupt is the economic and social workings of our world?
chunks.label: Reflections on Sandel's book Justice and societal issues
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Michael Sandel's book Justice, examining philosophical concepts like utilitarianism, libertarianism, and Rawls's difference principle, and applies them to societal issues such as abortion, taxation, and affirmative action.

chunks.text:
Families in the United States have evolved significantly over the years. The nuclear family is no longer the only type of family accepted in society. Diverse families have become more common, including same-sex families, single-parent households, and interracial families. There are more women in the workforce and more men taking on caregiving roles. Marriage rates are declining, and people are deciding to have children later in life or not at all. Ten years from now, these things will only be more prominent.

Marriage rates are declining and will only keep doing so. Only 47% of households are made up of married couples. In 1970 it was 71% (Census Bureau, 2024). People are starting to wait to get married for many reasons. Cohabitation is a lot more common. People are not waiting for marriage to move in together. If people do not need to be married to live together or to even have kids, there will not be as much of a rush to get married. Divorce rates are high. Around 40% of marriages will end in divorce, which is not too promising (Bailey, 2025). It is smart to be more cautious because weddings are expensive and so are divorces. People want to wait to be financially stable before getting married. Weddings can be expensive, and a lot of people look at them as more of a symbol of achievement and success and less as a right of passage. (Walsh, 2021).

People are also waiting to have children or are planning on not having any at all. Just from 2012 to 2023 the total number of children people planned to have dropped from 2.3 to 1.8 (Hays, 2025). Having children is expensive. People are reaching financial goals, like moving out of their parents’ house and getting married, later in life, which means they are having children later because self-sufficiency is harder to achieve. This is because mortgage rates are up and so is unemployment. (Medaris, 2024). Childcare is expensive and most families cannot afford to have one parent not working. Some couples are scared to have children because of climate change. About 39% of young people are hesitant to have children because of climate concerns, according to a study by Caroline Hickman, et al. Some women are even scared to reproduce since Roe v. Wade was overturned. They feel their reproductive rights are being threatened and bringing a daughter into that world is scary for them (Medaris, 2024). About 44% of adults below the age of 50 say they most likely will not have any kids at all (Brown, 2021). Women also may not want to take on the responsibility. When having kids, most of the negative sides affect the mother. She is more stressed, has lower life and relationship satisfaction, and has career disadvantages (Reich-Stiebert, 2023). Women are normally the parent that takes on emotional role, which can take a toll on someone. The social and political climate does not seem like it is going to change within the next ten years, so the fertility rate will most likely stay the same or even decline even more.

Family structures will become less traditional. More women are entering the workforce and in turn, more mothers are entering the workforce. For a lot of families, it is hard to support a family with one income, so mothers entering the workforce is not always out of want, but sometimes necessity. Mothers in the workforce have a harder time than non-mothers and men. They suffer a penalty that other women who are not mothers and men do not. They are perceived as less committed and incompetent compared to their coworkers, held to a higher standard, and paid less. Mothers are less likely to be promoted or recommended for hire. Their starting salaries are 7.9% lower than non-mothers whose starting salaries are 8.6% lower than fathers (Correll, 2007). People have started recognizing that being a mother is not a woman’s entire identity, so the motherhood penalty will be less prominent in the future. This also has to do with the fact that more men are taking on the caregiving role and staying home. It is becoming more normalized for a woman to be the breadwinner and the man to stay home. In the future it will be even more common, which will cause people to respect women in the workforce even more.

Single parenting households are on the rise. The United States has the highest rate of single parenting in the world. About 23% of children live in a single-parent household (Kramer, 2019). The decline in marriage rates is a contributing factor and the rise in divorce rates. It can also be a lot easier being a single parent now because of help from community and extended family. It is common for a grandparent to help raise a child because of the amount of help needed. In the future this will be more normalized because it does take a village to raise a child. Even if the child is not part of a single-parent household, there is still a possibility that both parents work, so there is still help needed in taking care of the child. This opens up into complex family structures. Sometimes a household consists of both parents, children, and grandparents. This can be more economically efficient, and it gives the parents an extra set of hands to help raise their children.

Same-sex marriage, another non-traditional family structure, has been legal in the United States since 2015. Since then, same-sex families have been on the rise. There has been a lot of public support for this movement. Despite all the support from the public, the Supreme Court has been asked to look at overturning Obergefell v. Hodges, the case that legalized same-sex marriage (Irwin, 2025). This does not mean that same-sex marriage will no longer be legal, but since the Supreme Court is reviewing it, it shows that society is not completely okay with same-sex marriage. In ten years, society might not feel the same. Same-sex families will still be normalized. It has only been ten years since it was legalized, and it is already a lot less stigmatized.

In ten years, marriage will not be something that people do just because they think they should. There will be more people deciding not to get married because it is a lot more normalized for people to do so. Fertility rates will be lower because not as many people will want to have kids or as many kids. Having children is a big step, financially, and making sure being stable enough to have children will become an even bigger priority. Family types will still be diverse, including same-sex families, interracial families, and single-parent families. Less traditional households will be seen more because it will become less stigmatized for parents to ask for help. The typical American family will not be traditional or conventional. The structure of family is always evolving and so is society, so the future is promising.

nf616b752.title: Reflecting on Grief and Mental Illness

chunks.text:
When I first heard about my midterm assignment being based on the book, ‘A Boy Broken’ by Douglas Engelman, I was thinking it would be sadder with a family dynamic of son and father, but I never expected it to hold. as much power as it did. Engleman’s book carries more than just sadness; it carries love, truth, and suffering. While reading this book, I not only opened my mind up to the possibilities of mental illness and loss, but also what it means to have hope, to be strong, and to keep going when the future seems so terrifying.

Engelman starts the story by sharing his fatherhood to a son who suffers with mental illness. The book shares about Engelman’s son having a psychotic breakdown. This means his mind stopped working the way it usually would. His son begins to see things and hear things that are not there or real. This unfortunate circumstance changed Engelman’s entire family dynamic that day. Engelman describes how he learns about how his son's future will now be altered; he shares how he tries to help him, talks us through the raw difficulties, treatments, therapy, and the hope he held on for things to get better.

Ultimately, yes, they have good moments, some even giving more hope that his son will get better, the book takes a terrible turn and horrifying ending with his son unfortunately being killed in a car accident. Left with grief, sadness, and questions, this led Engelman to search for what this all meant for his life moving forward.

I learned several things while reading Engelman’s, A Boy Broken, that I think any person would agree are important, especially for teenagers growing up and those who still seem to get stuck with the short end, figuring out how hard life can be.

Starting off, mental illness is a severe problem someone deals with every day, and it is not to be dismissed.
chunks.label: Reflections on reading 'A Boy Broken'
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces and reflects on reading their professor Douglas Engelman's book, 'A Boy Broken,' summarizing the book's story about his son's mental illness and death, as well as the initial lessons learned.

chunks.text: Before this book, I had dabbled in some anxiety prescriptions and investigated therapy for myself, however I was unaware of how serious mental illness could be and how much of your life it could take over, not just for you but for those around you as well.
chunks.label: Past experience with anxiety and therapy
chunks.what_happened: Prior to reading the book, the student had tried anxiety prescriptions and looked into therapy for themselves.
chunks.feelings: unaware of how serious mental illness could be

chunks.text:
Engelman dives into his son’s mental illness and how it affects his family life, also how this was not something he could just “snap out of.” Mentally ill people not only are affected by themselves, but they affect those around them, the loving family, and friends by their side. Not grasping the idea of this can lead to misunderstanding, judgement, and fear. Seeing Engelman learn to listen, try to empathize with his son, and give him unconditional support even when it is scary and showed me how important it is to show grace to everyone and give kindness to all.

Another lesson for me was that grief comes with life but does not have to end everything for you. Engelman deals with a tremendous loss towards the end and even the beginning of the book by losing his son to a mental illness. The end of the book led to Engelman’s sadness, confusion, and guilt. He tries his best to make sense of everything, he goes back and forth with questions in hopes of finding an answer, and he tries to find meaning. How to keep going in a way that supports not only his son, but others as well. He learns how to accept the idea that everything going on is out of his own hands and he cannot control it, no matter how hard he tries. I learned that grief, as horrible as it is, is not something that will last overnight. Grief is something linear, one day you feel good, and the next day you feel the same emotions twice as hard, like it had just happened again. Grief is something that changes you, something to carry with you every day, but also something that forces you to grow, something that helps you view life differently than before.

Lastly, I was reminded of the importance of hope. The book is dark, but not all dark. It has moments where you feel optimism, moments where Engelman's son seems as though he is starting to get better, when small victories are apparent. These joyous moments made the hardest parts somehow feel heavier, because you see what it could be, which makes your losses hurt more. Hope gives you the strength needed to push yourself through to keep going. Engelman had a choice when his son was diagnosed. He chose to help him fight, even though his son’s future was unclear, showing that hope was helping him choose for his family.

I was conflicted while reading this story, feeling all kinds of emotions, hope, love, loss, grief, pain, empathy, and optimism. Feeling for Engelman’s family, wondering if his son understood, if he was getting treated correctly. I was terrified when his son would get scared or begin to suffer more. I felt so much love and admiration for Engelman, knowing he was doing his best to understand, and giving his son the vulnerability, honesty, and love still given to him so deeply.

I will be honest, I did get angry while reading, not at anyone in the story but just at society for not understanding mental illness as they should. Sometimes, those who are sick do not get the care they need, when treatment comes too late or is wrong.

Something I felt connected by with the story was understanding when Engelman searched for answers as to why this had to happen and how he could have stopped it. Truthfully, I feelmoments like these more frequently than I would like to admit. I’m unsure as to why I feel like I am the root cause of a problem, but due to this feeling, I tend to always look for a way to fix things or to help things get better, in hopes that instead of ruining things, I am the reason they get better.

Some questions I was able to think about asking Engelman and his family while reading was, was it easy deciding to support your son with his mental illness? If someone you love was diagnosed with a mental illness, what are the limits with support? Would you still care for yourself?

Engelman sometimes struggles with feeling like he could have done something differently, does he ever have peace with what he did do? Did he forgive himself for the things he could not do?

As Engelman is my professor this semester in class, was your son the only reason you starting teaching sociology with a mental illness?

Thankfully in my situation, I have never had to lose someone to death just yet, out of curiosity and the upmost respect, how do you go on with life? How do you still honor your son, but still live your life?

This book showed me that life throws you curveballs and puts you through horrible tragedies to teach you something unclear at the moment but will eventually benefit you later on.

People we love get hurt in ways we would never imagine, and we end up in situations we cannot fix. I did learn though that even though we are unable to fix things sometimes, we are always able to choose how we respond, you can choose to be kind, you can choose commitment, and you can choose hope.

This book showed me that every family is different, and how every family deals with things, such as mental illness, is different. Love holds a lot but is not always enough. In this case, Engelman and his family needed understanding, professional advice, honest and sometimes hurtful conversations, and the courage to stay even when it is hard. Loss does not change how strong your love can be, love stays when it gets hard, love is honest, love is loud in a world that seems so quiet.

A Boy Broken by Douglas J. Engelman is a strong but heartfelt book. It does not hide emotions; it does not pretend; it is loud. It gives you the reality of a demanding situation with an unsure future. It shows you the insight of what it looks like to go through pain, to stay when it is hard, to love when it hurts too much, and to still have hope when the world seems so shattered.

I strongly feel as though this book gave me the knowledge to be more aware of others mental illness, their family life, society and the misconstrued belief of grief and loss. It reminds me that we may never truly know what someone else is going through. It reminds me to still give kindness to those who hurt me, to not judge others, and always lend a hand whenever I can. Most importantly, this book taught me that time is not guaranteed, and that I need to cherish my small victories and little moments, while I still can. Engelman’s story will be carried out with me, even after drafting this essay.
chunks.label: Lessons and takeaways from the book
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects extensively on the themes of the book, including mental illness, grief, hope, societal reactions, questions they have for their professor, personal habits of wanting to fix things, and the lasting impact the reading has on their outlook on life.
chunks.feelings: conflicted, hope, love, loss, grief, pain, empathy, optimism, terrified, admiration, angry

n2f94a5da.title: Reflecting on Morality and Distributive Justice

chunks.text:
In “Justice: What’s the Right Thing to Do?” by Michael J. Sandel, there is a deep dive into the reasons we think the way we do about situations that we can reject or agree to. Sandel lays out different philosophical approaches in a manner that is intriguing to read and understand. Sandel does so by referencing utilitarianism and libertarianism, Immanuel Kant, John Rawls, and Aristotle. He encourages the reader to think deeply about where their thought process comes from and where it can go.

Sandel brings up the first argument of utilitarianism vs. libertarianism with a few examples, one of them being the trolley incident. The basis of it is that you are a trolley driver in one instance, and there are five workers working on the track ahead of you. Do you kill the five workers on this track, or switch to another track that only has one? In another instance, you are watching the scene unfold but see a heavy man next to you, also watching the scene. You could push him onto the track and save the five workers. This is a moral dilemma, and the answer that you seek could be rooted in utilitarianism or libertarianism. Jeremy Bentham’s utilitarianism would say that the answer would be whatever creates happiness or utility for the masses. In Sandel’s book he says, “There are no possible grounds for rejecting it. Every moral argument, he claims, must implicitly draw on the idea of maximizing happiness” (pg. 19). The utilitarian would sacrifice the one to save five. On the other hand, libertarianism, supports individual freedom. Sandel says, “Their central claim is that each of us has a fundamental right to liberty – the right to do whatever we want with the things we own, provided we respect other people’s rights to do the same,” on page 30.

The utilitarian theory would be held up in society in the real-life example of COVID-19. The coronavirus affected everyone in the world greatly, a pandemic that reached all corners of the Earth. Due to the highly spreadable nature of the virus, whole countries were put into quarantine. This quarantine shows the utilitarian value of maximizing utility, as the quarantines were put in place to stop the spread of COVID-19, and minimize the amount of people sick. All of the policies put in place during COVID-19 were done so to protect people from getting the virus, therefore increasing the amount of utility.

Sandel brings up Immanuel Kant’s philosophy, looking at his moral philosophies as well as how he agreed or disagreed with libertarianism and utilitarianism. Kant’s philosophy was majorly focused on the intention behind actions. His categorical imperative, which he stated was to, “Act only on that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law” (pg. 60), which means to only do something with the knowing that it is correct or right. Sandel relates this to making a promise you know you cannot keep. In his second formulation Kant says, “Act in such a way that you always treat humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, never simply as a means, by always at the same time as an end” (pg. 61). This means Kant says it is morally right to treat people as an end, not as a means to an end. Kant also brings up how in this same vein, lying by any means is morally wrong.

This brings up the question of whether it is still morally wrong if you are lying to protect the person you are lying to or lying for the benefit of another. In Kant’s theory, it is morally wrong. As in the book, Sandel’s example is even if there was a murderer at the door for your friend and you lied and told them they were somewhere else, it would still be morally wrong. My own criticism of this theory is that lying is not morally wrong in all situations. I believe it would be morally correct to lie to the murderer than tell them your friend is right behind you. I believe it’s the same as if you would lie for your own good, or for your own safety. I would do my best to keep my friend safe by lying to the murderer and I would feel happy that I lied to keep that person safe. I would feel like my decision was morally correct.

Sandel also brings up philosopher John Rawls. The big picture for Rawls was justice from fair terms. He explains in Sandel’s book that his hypothetical contract has two principles of justice which are, “…basic liberties for all citizens, such as freedom of speech and religion…it permits only those social and economic inequalities that work to the advantage of the least well off members of society” (pg. 70). Rawls was also into the idea of a “veil of ignorance” that created an equal playing field for all. The theory is that if you are behind this “veil of ignorance” that it makes it so your biases are unknown, you don’t know the outcome of your life. It creates a more fair and equal opportunity for everyone this way. John Rawls was very focused on benefitting the least advantaged. The “veil of ignorance” was a way to do so as you don’t know what kind of life you will lead.

Another aspect of this, is that the people in high parts of society can help those who are not as well to do. The argument is why should people who have worked long and hard to acquire that sort of status and income have to give it away. I think that if someone has worked for the money they have, they don’t have to give it away. I also think that it takes a lot of contribution as well as time and effort. It’s tricky when it comes to the point of influencers and celebrities making large amounts of money though. In the book, there is a reference to the pay difference between the chief justice on the Supreme Court, and Judge Judy, the latter making more than 10 times the amount the chief justice does. I feel like this is where things get weird. I don’t think it’s necessarily right, but since Judge Judy has a show, she makes an incredible amount of money. She is a celebrity, like Oprah and David Letterman, which doesn’t come easy, but the amount that these people are making compared to schoolteachers and justices is a lot. I think it shows an interesting divide in wages in our country.

Sandel also discusses Aristotle’s theories and what he believes justice is. Aristotle believed in the telos of the argument. He believed that the telos was the defining factor. The telos is the purpose of the argument. Sandel also writes in his book, “For Aristotle, politics is about something higher. It’s about learning how to live a good life” (pg. 95). The telos, or purpose, of politics is to live a good life. Politics is an essential way to express your opinions and vote for someone you see fit to lead your country. To Aristotle we are doing our duty as citizens when we engage in political discourse.

An example of Aristotle’s telos in real life is the allocation of art supplies. According to Aristotle, the best supplies would be allocated based on the purpose of its use. Sandel says in the book, “Aristotle claims that in order to determine the just distribution of a good, we have to inquire into the telos, of purpose, of the good being distributed” (pg. 93). The purpose would be better suited to an artist that had the best artistic ability, not someone who doesn’t know how to use the supplies. This is due to the artist with the best ability using the supplies to their best ability. The purpose is better suited to the artist with the best ability. The telos of the supplies is to be used to create art, which the artist can emulate.

Sandel’s work explains the different theories of justice through utilitarianism vs. libertarianism, Immanuel Kant, John Rawls, and Aristotle. These theories and philosophers create and answer the question of Sandel’s, “What’s the Right Thing to Do?” Us as people have differing opinions on this, but they can stem from these philosophers, based on what we believe is morally wrong or right. Through these different theories we can gather whether we would choose utility for all, or our individual freedom. We can understand if we agree with certain philosophers who believe lying is morally wrong at all times, that a “veil of ignorance” will provide an equal playing field for all, and that telos is the center of an argument. My personal opinions reflect my lived experience, and Sandel’s book helped me expand my thoughts on certain subjects in ways I had never thought of before. He brought up subjects that could be considered sensitive subjects, however he explained them in the ways of these philosophers which gave me new and different ideas than I had had.
chunks.label: Analysis of Sandel's theories of justice
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Michael Sandel's book 'Justice: What’s the Right Thing to Do?', examining philosophical theories from utilitarianism, libertarianism, Kant, Rawls, and Aristotle, while reflecting on hypothetical dilemmas and wage divides.

n52c1e307.title: Reflecting on Morality, Class, and Duty

chunks.text:
I think some of the critiques with utilitarianism can be valid as well. One of the points that Sandel brings up is the violation of individual rights and reducing morality to a mere calculation. While I think I tend to lean in a more utilitarian way of thinking I think these are some great points. I think in some scenarios there’s more than just simply making the most amount of people happy. We need to look at the motive and intention behind certain situations. I also believe what one person might consider happiness might be different from what another might consider happiness. It’s all subjective. Another topic that Sandel addresses is libertarianism. He uses philosophers like Nozick to explain the specifics of what libertarianism is. The example that I resonated with is Michael Jordan. As a die-hard basketball fan who is also a Chicago Bulls fan, I thought that using Michael Jordan as an example really put this theory into perspective. During the 90’s, Jordan brought the NBA much more viewership and appealed to the global market. With this new spike in viewership, I think it was only fitting that Jordan be the highest paid player in the league. Nozick presents the idea that making Jordan pay 30% of his salary(taxation) is equivalent to stealing or forced labor.

The main critique to this argument is the poor are more in need of the money and that Jordan isn’t playing alone on the court. For this scenario, I lean both ways but I’m slightly going to side with Nozieck. The Chicago Bulls didn't see nearly as much revenue when Michael Jordan decided to retire abruptly and play major league baseball. Almost all people were spending money to see Michael Jordan play, not Scottie or the rest of his teammates. While I do agree it wasn’t fair how big the discrepancy of pay was between Michael and his peers, I understand why it was the way it was. Now in terms of taxation, I don’t think it’s stealing to tax someone and help the poor out. The more money you make the more you're gonna get taxed. This is a system that I believe is fair because of how hard it is for lower class people to climb and succeed in this world. I also think most people who become billionaires did something unfair and immoral to achieve that amount of wealth(not all of them). I understand the frustration of people who made their money legitimately and worked extremely hard for their wealth, just for 30% to be given to people who may not work nearly as hard. But I think it is moral to help our fellow neighbors and be selfless.

As someone who knows people in the military, the drafting vs volunteering discussion was very interesting to me. Now my initial reaction to this type of discussion is in favor of the volunteer army. From my perspective, I myself could never see myself in the military fighting for my country and millions of others are just like me. But reading this allowed me to be more enlightened on the discussion. The best critique that I heard about this argument was about lower income people. Lower income people have less of an opportunity to go to college or get economic opportunities so when the military approaches these kids with promises of benefits and pay, it’s really not much of a decision.
chunks.label: critiques of utilitarianism, libertarianism, and military draft
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on course readings by Sandel and Nozick regarding utilitarianism, taxation using Michael Jordan as an example, and the debate between volunteer versus drafted military service.

chunks.text: One of my co-workers just graduated high school and I was talking to him about what his future plans after high school are. He told me he was going to the military in hopes that it will pay for his education in the future.
chunks.label: co-worker joining the military
chunks.what_happened: The student talked to a co-worker who had just graduated high school about his future plans, and the co-worker explained he was joining the military to pay for college.

chunks.text:
This is a situation that so many people have to go through who don’t have the money to afford college. People born into a higher class are less likely to go through this situation. Wealthier citizens are less likely to serve in the military for this reason. Another argument for this scenario was the civic duty one. Sandel agrees that as American citizens it is our civic duty to serve our country if asked to. Hearing these arguments definitely make me ponder on the topic but I still would favor the volunteer army over a drafting one.

The idea of lying is wrong no matter the situation is something that I thought was very interesting. In the reading, the scenario is someone with an axe approaching the door looking for your friend, and asking you where he is when you know where he is. You can either lie or tell him exactly where your friend is. Kant believes that it is right to tell this person where your friend is. For this concept I really have to disagree with Kant. I think there are so many situations where telling the truth is less moral than lying. In the scenario brought up in the reading, if you tell the person where your friend is, and then he murders him, that makes you directly responsible for your friend's death. I think that lying to not hurt someone’s feelings would be considered moral.
chunks.label: reflections on military service and Kant on lying
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how economic inequality affects military recruitment and civic duty, and then critiques Kant's view that lying is always morally wrong.

chunks.text: I remember when I was a kid, I really wanted the new NBA 2k for christmas. When Christmas came around, I ran to the tree excited to open what looked like the new 2k. I opened the present and it was the newest Madden instead of what I wanted. Deep down I was disappointed but when my parents asked me with a smile if I liked it, I had to lie to them. I don't think that made me wrong for not wanting my parents to feel sad.
chunks.label: lying about a Christmas present
chunks.what_happened: As a child, the student opened a Christmas gift expecting NBA 2k but received Madden instead, lying to their parents that they liked it to spare their feelings.

chunks.text:
Kant feels this way because he perceives lying as intentionally manipulating another person, which is true in a sense but I think lying to save a life or spare feelings is a moral thing to do.

One of the biggest discussions in the reading was the obligation of solidarity. Sandel believes that solidarity is essential for justice. I agree with Sandel when it comes to this stance. The topic about reparations is one that I’ve actually had conversations with people with before. I think that countries that have a dark history should apologize and give reparations. Even if the people apologizing weren't directly involved, they are a part of the community that benefitted. I also think apologizing can prevent certain bad things from occurring in the future as well. I think the mentality of “I don’t owe anyone anything” is ignorant and immoral. I think as a community we owe each other respect and a helping hand if needed.

In terms of politics, Sandel brings up an interesting question about whether the government should be morally neutral. I remember talking in class about whether the government is overly influenced by Chirsitanity since our country is majority of the christian faith. As somebody who is a Christian myself, I tend to agree with laws and people who have my religion in mind when making policies and laws. But I also respect other religions and technically America is not allowed to favor any religion over another because of the first amendment(freedom of religion). Tying this concept with utilitarianism, a utilitarian would think it’s moral to have a christian based government since it would maximize the happiness of most Americans. While a libertarian would be in favor of the government stating neutrality. I think I side with libertarians more in this matter if I put bias aside because it is more fair to Americans., .
chunks.label: reflections on morality, solidarity, reparations, and government neutrality
chunks.what_happened: The student evaluates Kant on manipulation, supports Sandel's view on solidarity and reparations, and reflects on class discussions concerning government moral and religious neutrality.

n1d4157c0.title: Navigating Mental Illness in the Family

chunks.text: Douglas Engleman's A Boy Broken is not a book that skirts around pain. It looks straight at what it is to love someone who is seriously struggling with their mental health and to be part of a family that is trying to hold itself together through that pain. Reading this book hit close to home for me because I’ve seen what happens when mental illness enters a family. It doesn’t just affect one person. It changes everything; the way people talk, how they act, how they feel about each other, and even how they see themselves.
chunks.label: Introduction to A Boy Broken
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Douglas Engleman's book A Boy Broken and how mental illness impacts an entire family.

chunks.text: Engleman’s story about his son made me think a lot about my own brother. He’s struggled with serious depression for years, and it hasn’t been a quiet struggle. There have been multiple suicide attempts. There have been nights when everything felt like it might fall apart.
