There have been stays in psychiatric wards, moments of fear I’ll never forget, and stretches of time where our family felt like it was barely holding itself together. As in Engleman's book, the pain in our house wasn't just my brother's pain; it became everyone's. My parents were scared, tired, and not sure what to do. My dad hadn't had to handle much mental illness before all of this, so he was learning along with us. That meant not just learning about hospitals, meds, or symptoms, but learning how to sit with something that doesn't have any easy answers.
chunks.label: Brother's struggle with severe depression
chunks.what_happened: The student describes their brother's years-long battle with depression, multiple suicide attempts, and psychiatric hospitalizations, which heavily strained the family.

chunks.text: When one of us is hurt, the whole family feels the pain. My brother's pain did not stay his own; it invaded the way the rest of us lived. My parents' relationship was strained. There were many fights that were not really about each other but about fear. My mom and dad handled things differently. My mom had to talk about everything and hold on to things. My father was more subdued at first, as though he didn't know what to term what he was feeling. As time passed, he had to adapt, to learn how to be there in the life of someone whose mental illness he didn't quite understand. Engleman describes the same sort of learning in his book. A father who was suddenly and unexpectedly propelled into the world of mental illness, trying to learn, to assist, and not lose himself in the process. That resonated. I watched my dad slowly change over the years. I think the possibility of losing my brother compelled him to change in ways he never thought possible.
chunks.label: Parents' differing coping mechanisms
chunks.what_happened: The student recalls how their parents' relationship was strained by fear and how their dad gradually adapted and learned to handle mental illness.

chunks.text: With a family like this growing up, there is a lot that goes unspoken. When someone in the house is struggling with something as heavy as depression, everyone starts walking on eggshells, even without realizing it. You start to try not to say anything incorrectly, not to bring any more stress. Sometimes you do not say anything at all. There were moments when I felt like I had to be the "good" one, the one who did not cause trouble, who did not add to my parents' stress. Reading about the emotional toll on Engleman's family, I saw my own. When tragedy is happening to someone you love, you start compartmentalizing parts of yourself to make room for their pain. It's not something people tell you to do. You just do.
chunks.label: Walking on eggshells and being the good child
chunks.what_happened: Growing up in a home affected by depression, the student felt pressure to walk on eggshells and be the 'good' child to avoid adding stress.

chunks.text: One of the most powerful things in the book was how Engleman describes holding on to hope. Hope sounds easy to have, but when you’re in a situation like this, it’s anything but that. It’s hard. You’re constantly hoping this time things will be different. That the treatment will work. That the phone won’t ring in the middle of the night with devastating news. That your family will finally get a break from the hold of mental illness. I know that weight. When my brother was in the hospital, there was this mix of hope and fear that existed in all of us. It was exhausting to keep hoping and, at the same time, be ready to be disappointed. I saw how my parents were exhausted from holding that hope too. It did not necessarily equate to the fact that they no longer cared; if anything, they cared so much that it hurt. But it wore all of us down.
chunks.label: Exhaustion of holding hope during brother's hospital stays
chunks.what_happened: The student and their parents navigated an exhausting mix of hope and fear whenever the brother was hospitalized.

chunks.text: Reading about a family experiencing so much also made me consider the other end of it, the guilt of being the person in the hospital. I had my own inpatient stay for anorexia. It was a hard, scary process, and even though I was trying to survive my own battle, a part of me couldn't help but think about how it was affecting my parents. I remember being in the hospital bed and thinking about how my mom was probably at home, blaming herself, and my dad was probably trying to be strong and act like he was fine when he wasn't. That guilt stayed with me. Even while I was getting help, I felt like I was making more problems for them. It's something that Engleman's book depicts so perfectly, not so much guilt on the part of the one struggling, but the reality that families are all intertwined in a manner where one person's pain always pulls on the others.
chunks.label: Hospitalization for anorexia and feelings of guilt
chunks.what_happened: The student was hospitalized for anorexia and struggled with feelings of guilt about how their illness affected their parents.

chunks.text: When mental illness comes into a family, relationships change. Some bonds grow stronger; others are tested. I’ve seen my parents fight in ways they probably wouldn’t have if they weren’t carrying so much pain and stress. I’ve seen my dad be shut down emotionally because he didn’t know how else to handle everything. I’ve seen my mom break down because she felt helpless. And I’ve felt my own role shift between being a sister, a supporter, and at times, someone struggling myself. Engleman doesn’t sugarcoat this reality in A Boy Broken. He shows how love can exist alongside exhaustion, frustration, and fear. That felt honest to me. Love doesn’t disappear when someone is sick, but it gets tested.
chunks.label: Shifting family roles and parental stress
chunks.what_happened: The student observed their parents argue, their dad shut down emotionally, their mom break down, and their own role shift between sister and supporter.
chunks.feelings: pain, stress, helpless, exhaustion, frustration, fear

chunks.text: Another thing the book gets right is the quiet form of grieving that families do. It's not always necessarily about losing a person physically, though sometimes it is, but losing how life used to be. Life wasn't always easy before my brother got sick, but it didn't have the fear factor underlying it. When depression took over his life, it took something from the rest of us as well. There is grief in watching someone you love lose themselves to their illness, even when they are standing physically in front of you. There is grief in knowing that your family will never quite be what it used to be again. I saw my parents change. I changed too.
chunks.label: Quiet grieving over changed family life
chunks.what_happened: The student watched their family and parents change as depression took over their brother's life, creating a sense of grief.

chunks.text:
There is another important element to this story, the guilt that lies in each and every person's heart. My father was guilty for having no clue how to handle mental illness. My mother was guilty for not being able to fix everything. I was guilty for being both a part of the family trying to cope with the pain of my brother, and, at one point, the source of my parents' further worry with my own issues with mental illness.

Engleman speaks of his paternal guilt, of what he could have done differently. That kind of guilt is one that I comprehend, not just secondhand from my parents, but firsthand. I do know what it is like to feel like a burden, even when people tell you that you are not. I know what it is like to want your pain not to cause pain for the people who love you.
chunks.label: Family-wide guilt over mental illness
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the guilt experienced by their parents and themselves for their own struggles and brother's illness, feeling like a burden.

chunks.text:
What struck me about the way Engleman writes is that through everything his family goes through, they never stop attempting to learn and grow. My family has done the same thing. My dad, with no mental health experience, learned little by little to talk about it. He learned to ask more questions. He learned to sit in the lack of control. It wasn't perfect, but it was progress.

I've also learned to talk about things I once kept secret. I didn't tell people for a long time what was going on with my brother or with me. I thought silence would make all of it easier. It didn't. What I've learned is that families can't navigate pain like this alone. It takes learning, support, and a great deal of painful honesty.
chunks.label: Family learning to communicate and break silence
chunks.what_happened: The student's father learned to talk about mental health, while the student stopped keeping their family's and their own struggles secret.

chunks.text: Reading A Boy Broken was not simple as it mirrored so much of my life. It made me understand, though, that these stories need to be told. Mental illness is not just a personal battle; it's a family story. It touches every member of the family. It tests love but also shows how deep that love goes. The book also reminded me that hope, pain, and guilt can exist together. It's not tidy, it's messy, but it's real. And even though the pain may never go away, families can evolve and change as a result of it.
chunks.label: Reflection on A Boy Broken and mental illness
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how the book validates the reality that mental illness is a family struggle involving hope, pain, and guilt.

chunks.text: When mental illness enters a family, nothing is the same again. I've lived it. I've seen my brother battle depression and survive more than once. I've seen my parents work to stretch themselves to the breaking point to hold everything together. I've lain in the hospital myself, bearing both the weight of my own illness and the guilt of what that did to the people that I love. Engleman's story is so deeply personal, and yet it's not just his story; it's a story with which so many families connect, mine included. It shows the devastation, the learning, and the love that still holds on even when it's tested to its limits.
chunks.label: Summary of family experience and connection to book
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes how their lived experiences with family mental illness connect deeply to Engleman's story.

chunks.text:
In chapter one Sandel discusses price gouging. He introduces three main ways people think about justice utilitarianism, libertarianism and promoting virtue. He points out that even though prices are based on consumer spending, there are needs and wants in a free market. For example, insulin is extremely overpriced by manufacturers such as Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk. The lack of competition in the market allows them to set high prices and extract significant profits. In this case, “buyers under duress have no freedom”. This allows readers to realize that questions of justice are not just abstract theories but real issues that affect daily life and politics.

In chapter two I learned a lot about utilitarianism. When combined with other moral philosophies it is good but by itself can be very dangerous. Sandel discusses throwing Christians to lions because the people in the audience outweighed the people being thrown in. When Sandel writes about torture I believe the utilitarianism point of view makes a strong argument when it comes to saving the lives of others. I believe if someone kidnapped just one person and wouldn’t tell anyone where they are they deserve to be tortured for the information. This is equivalent to violating the rights of a minority if it benefits the majority. The police want to know where the person is and the only way to figure it out is torture. I question at what point someone’s rights should be violated if it benefits the majority and how this should be determined.

In the Ford Pinto case, it shows how a utilitarian cost-benefit analysis might decide to pay settlements for injuries rather than fix a safety defect. I feel like when it comes to exploding gas tanks on cars that no one should ever be allowed to drive them. Of course, the company would take a loss but it’s their fault in the first place. Unless the people driving them consent to the risk before or after buying them. This is another example of how, “buyers under duress have no freedom”. You buy a car then find out it explodes wouldn’t you want your money back? I feel like the best option in this case is for Ford to take all the cars back and fix them. Then sell them again. All the people who bought one and figured out it was exploding should have been able to get their money in exchange for the car.

In chapter three I found different than the other chapters. It introduces Robert Nozick and his argument for a minimal state focused on protecting individuals from force, fraud, and theft, asserting that individuals have rights over their own bodies, talents, and the fruits of their labor, even if it leads to unequal distributions of wealth. Sandel discusses individual liberty, self-ownership, and the importance of voluntary transactions in a just society. This chapter helped me understand the reason for unequal distribution of wealth and why it is necessary. Sandel notes that market exchanges are not always as voluntary as libertarians suggest, particularly when there are vast inequalities. Severe economic necessity can create unfair bargaining conditions that undermine the idea of truly free exchange.

In chapter four Sandel discusses markets and morals. Sandel makes the point that if an army is 100% volunteer there are still people who have no other option but to join because of personal circumstances like poverty or homelessness. He argues what choice do they really have if the only job for them is the army. Sandel challenges the idea of a completely neutral state by arguing that involving markets in these areas can erode civic virtues, such as solidarity and shared responsibility, and may not always lead to the greatest good for the greatest number.

Chapter five focuses on the philosophy of Immanuel Kant. This philosophy makes the argument that justice is rooted in human dignity and autonomy rather than consequences or markets. The categorial Imperative is Kants moral principle. It teaches you about universality, which is only acting on principles that could become universal law. Another concept in Kants moral principle is humanity as an end. This is treating humanity as end and not as a means. This reminded me of treating others the way you would like to be treated. Sandel writes about Kant’s belief that utilitarianism leaves rights vulnerable and misunderstands morality's true nature by basing it on variable consequences and desires. This kind of goes back to the Christians and the lions where their rights where overshadowed by the majority’s desires.

In chapter six Sandel discusses John Rawls’ theory of justice. This is where I start to understand difference principles from a more theoretical point of view. Rawls difference principle holds the belief that, "only those social and economic inequalities are permitted that work to the benefit of the least advantaged members of society” (Sandel pg. 152) should be implemented. For example, higher doctor salaries that improve healthcare in impoverished areas align with Rawls’s principle, while those that only benefit the wealthy do not. Rawls emphasize looking at the overall system of a society like taxes and their effects on the poor rather than just looking at individual salaries. Sandel makes the point that affirmative action should not be viewed as a reward for merit or virtue. According to Dworkin, universities set their criteria and standards based on their specific goals, and there is no inherent right to be admitted based on any set of qualities. Justice in admissions involves selecting students in a way that best advances the university’s mission and societal goals, not simply rewarding individual merit.

In chapter eight Sandel introduces Aristotle's "honorific" and "teleological" approach to justice. He discusses that Justice isn’t just about equal treatment, it’s about giving each person what they deserve to help society achieve its proper goal, like excellence or moral growth. In our society the goal is to ensure human survival and wellbeing. When people act against these goals, judges and juries help uphold justice by holding them accountable. I learned that one of the purposes of the state is to cultivate good character among its citizens by allowing them to have political dialogue and encouraging citizens to pursue careers consistent with their nature and the state's understanding of the good life. There are countries that don’t allow free discussion of politics like North Korea. The lack of freedom in North Korea makes me question if the government is cultivating bad character among its citizens? These people have no control over their lives because of the government, so how could they present good character towards the country?

In chapter nine Sandel discusses what one person owes to another. He does this by examining moral individualism and collective responsibility. One of Sandel’s examples involves a French bomber that has been ordered to bomb is own village. Sandel asks, “What do you make of the pilot’s stance? Do you admire it or consider it a form of weakness?” I think about the other villages the pilot may have bombed. Why are his friends and family worth more than the friends and family of others. This is why I view the pilot’s decision as weak. If you can kill the friends and family of others what’s stopping, you from killing your own. If you were to say because I love them then I would call you selfish for killing people who were also loved by others. This chapter reinforces Sandals previous arguments in the book that that a just society requires a moral engagement with, rather than an avoidance of, the moral questions about the good life and collective values.

In chapter ten Sandel discusses how cultivating a just society requires civic virtue and solidarity to promote citizens' shared concern for the community and its inherent moral purposes. Sandel introduces debates about abortion. This is where I realized that some debates are unavoidable moral and religious controversies like abortion. People who are religious are pro-life and people who believe abortion should be legal are pro-rights. I feel like these two different sides debating will not result in any progress made to each side’s beliefs on the subject. In a case where progress cannot be made, is it better to avoid moral questions? This is where maximizing freedom is important because without freedom you cannot follow the other steps to cultivate a just society.

In conclusion, Sandel discusses moral philosophies from multiple perspectives, carefully avoiding bias and unnecessary controversy. He presents each theory fairly, allowing readers to see both its strengths and weaknesses. By making counterarguments, Sandel helps the reader understand the pros and cons of each moral philosophy he introduces, showing that no single approach has all the answers. He also includes real-life examples, historical cases, and current events, which allow for deeper thinking about the rights and wrongs of each complex moral dilemma he writes about. This method makes abstract ideas easier to understand and connects philosophy to everyday life. Through his balanced approach, Sandel encourages readers not only to grasp different views of justice but also to reflect on their own beliefs, question their assumptions, and engage in thoughtful debate about what it truly means to live in a just society.
chunks.label: Reflections on Michael Sandel's Justice book
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on and summarizes various chapters and moral theories presented in Michael Sandel's book Justice, sharing their thoughts on concepts like utilitarianism, libertarianism, Kantian ethics, Rawls, Aristotle, and civic virtue.

n2b828c07.title: Analyzing Mental Illness and Family Systems

chunks.text:
Through the memoir, Engelman recounts detailed and at times terrifying descriptions of his son's psychiatric breakdowns, including terrifying hallucinations and the constant threat of relapse. These descriptions are not just narrative but portals into the everyday life of serious mental illness. The writer's account of the "ups and downs" that characterize the journey of struggle with mental illness is all too recognizable to anybody who has witnessed a loved one’s struggle through psychological distress. Engelman's willingness to account for the disarray, confusion, and devastation of each episode highlights the cost of emotional anguish that such episodes exact on both the sufferer and the support network. By pursuing the point of desperation, hope, and strength that occurs, the memoir enables readers to understand the nuance of mental illness as it plays out in the moment, so that the story is not merely that of an individual family but a symbol for many others who fight similar struggles.

The power of the book lies in its refusal to sentimentalize or trivialize the experience of mental illness. Engelman presents to us the reality of watching a child endure diseases that defy easy explanation and quick fixing. His account resists the shame that so often clings to mental illness without negating the real challenge of figuring these problems out as a family. By showing the truth of everyday uncertainty, emotional exhaustion, and moments of hopelessness, Engelman provides an image of mental illness that is both genuine and compassionate. He invites readers to move beyond stereotypes or misconceptions and instead bear witness to the courage and perseverance it takes for both the patient and the family members. In doing so, the memoir is an effective instrument of empathy, opening up a discourse regarding the need for care, consciousness, and cultural change when it comes to mental healthcare.

The Burden on Family Systems

Maybe the most powerful aspect of "A Boy Broken" is its description of how mental illness affects entire family systems. Engelman does not at all isolate the experience within his son's personal struggles but illustrates how his son's illness reconfigures the emotional, logistical, and psychological environment of everyone around him. The family will be forced to navigate their lives each day, now colored by doubt, vigilance, and worry, a climate in which each member's needs and wants can become secondary to the resolution of the crisis.

Mental illness has ripple effects far beyond the person. Families are forced to recreate their schedules, expectations, and even sense of self. Plans once taken for granted can be replaced by fear, worry, and a general sense of uncertainty. Engelman's story shows that wives, brothers, and sisters, and mothers all feel feelings of guilt, helplessness, or bitterness as they work to care for the family member in trouble. This emphasis can lead certain members of the family to feel left out or excluded, as their own emotional demands take a back seat to the pressing demands of the mental health crisis.

Secondary trauma affects the cost sustained by those who care for someone with serious mental illness and is a recurring theme. Engelman speaks of deep sorrow and concern, not only for the health of his son, but for stability in the family and as a husband and father. Predictability and normalcy in the family generally lead to family mourning for the loss of an "ordinary" life. His observations closely reflect scholarly interpretations of family systems theory, which suggests that when one part of the system is debilitated by chronic illness or psychological distress, the entire system must compensate. In some instances, this adjustment also brings about beneficial restructuring, as families become more empathetic, communication becomes more robust, and new coping mechanisms are developed in response to adversity.

Moreover, Engelman's openness about revealing instances of conflict, misunderstanding, and exhaustion among family members shows the very human instances of caregiving. He is practical in understanding that caregiving for one who has a serious mental illness is not merely a labor of love but occasionally a source of frustration, fear, and tension. These accounts cut through cultural myths of unyielding strength and unbreakable togetherness, providing an honest account of the frailties and complexities that emerge during periods of adversity.

The memoir also provokes reflection about wider social issues. Family members also have to cope not only with the in-house issues of sickness but with external pressures—such as stigma from neighbors, friends, or even within the healthcare system. Engelman shows how these external pressures serve to build isolation on the part of families, intensifying distress and making the journey even more challenging. And yet, among these challenges, families can also find unexpected resilience. In mutual support, in moments of connection, and in a determination to keep going, many families—like Engelman's—build a new, though imperfect, path ahead.

Lastly, Engelman's honesty in the book is an important service to readers in that it reveals both the burdens and the bonds that psychiatric illness may impose upon a family. His book is an important contribution to mental health literature, extending consideration beyond clinical or personal records to encompass the entire family system and how it learns, breaks, and heals under stress.

The Search for Meaning Through Stoic Philosophy

With the death of his son in a car accident, Engelman embarks on a difficult path of discovery, finding solace in the philosophical principles of Stoicism as a way of coping with and surviving loss. This solution is a great model not just for insight into the situation of loss but also for living with integrity and purpose even in the middle of overwhelming loss. Engelman's tale demonstrates the Stoic idea that even things like becoming ill or dying by mishap are typically beyond our control in the external world, but our responses to such things lie within our control.

Death and suffering are met head-on with conviction by the Stoics. Grieving is acknowledged as a human, natural emotion and not something repressed or denied, but Stoic philosophers insist on resignation in pain as part of the tapestry of life. For Engelman, the process is embracing the pain and not refusing to acknowledge it, as one focuses on positive aspects: taking care of loved ones who survived, seeking assistance, remembering past experiences, and attempting to tell the truth after destruction.

One of the fundamental tenets of Stoicism outlined in the memoir is what is within our control and what is not. We have no control over altering fate, warding off all disaster, or halting mortality, but we do control engaging with trouble with intelligence and compassion. Engelman's ability to confront his grief head-on, and to make productive inferences from it on his own behalf and others', serves to validate the philosophy in life.

In addition, Stoic thought promotes the cultivation of gratitude for what is lost as opposed to mourning what is lost in absence. Seneca, another leading Stoic, promoted consideration of the beauty of being together and how those no longer with us shaped us, as compared to allowing absence to cheapen lived moments and the plenitude of memories. This helps to convert mourning into an even deeper love of the ephemeral nature of life.

Engelman's own case also reveals that Stoicism is not a denial of emotions, but a healthy working through of them in the moment. Mindfulness practice, present moment living, and acceptance of impermanence are all coping mechanisms for loss. Accepting what can’t be changed becomes part of an everyday coping mechanism to continue onward. By interweaving these practices, Engelman shows how philosophical examination can help us transform loss into wisdom and resistance and new purpose, neither forgetting but internalizing it as a necessary part of the human experience. Thus, "A Boy Broken" is not merely a survival guide to tragedy but a guide to drawing on loss as fuel for growth, empathy, and self-awareness. Engelman's embracing of Stoicism provides the language and protocol to those who are traversing through grief.
chunks.label: Analysis of Engelman's memoir on mental illness and Stoicism
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Engelman's memoir, discussing how mental illness impacts family systems and how Stoic philosophy offers tools for navigating grief and loss.

n089f0a76.title: Predicting the Future of American Families

chunks.text:
Since the late 1970s, America has seen a steep increase in dual earing households, single parent households, same sex relationships, and a decline in marriage rates as a whole. This change can be attributed to many things or even viewed as a domino effect. This begs the question: What would the average family in the United States look like 10 years from now? Personally, I believe we will see this trend to continue due to the implementation of more women than ever before being able to walk about from relationships that do not serve them or joining the work force, as well as same sex relationships being slowly more accepted than in the past. The combination of these factors will make it so we see an overall decrease in families with For starters, I don’t think there will be as many families to start with in 2035. Obviously, you don’t need to be married to raise a family, but it is how a great majority of families start. With fewer marriages, there will be fewer families. ‘In 2024, only 47.1 percent of households had a married couple, which is only second to the lowest marriage rate in 2022, where the all time low was represented by 46.8 percent. Compared to 75 years ago, you could see as much as 78.8 percent of households were those of married couples. Since 2010, the rate of married couple households has never risen back to above 50 percent. This can partly be attributed to not only men but also women marrying later in life. As stated on USAfacts.org, “Both men and women are marrying later in life. In 2024, the average age for a first marriage was 30.2 years for men and 28.6 for women. The Census has tracked marriage ages since 1890. In that time, the youngest median ages of marriage were in 1956, when it was 22.5 for men and 20.1 for women.” Another factor in the decrease in marriage rates is that since the 1980s, the life expectancy has increased. The rush to marry decreases when there’s more life to live compared to other generations. The combination of a longer life expectancy and lower rates of marriage can both factor into the future. Following current trends, it looks like 2035 won’t have as strong of a push to marry overall, greatly impacting how many families there will be in 2035.

Daul income families are on the rise due to the overwhelming current cost of living. This is no new trend. We first saw women join the workforce in the late 19th century to cope with a lack of men available to work during the war period. This trend never slowed down, and we can now see that about half of the families today are a part of a dual earner household structure. Additionally, dual earning families have a higher likelihood to have fewer children as compared to single earning household structures. This is often because married couples of dual earning households are more often to be career driven whereas having children could put a halt to this drive. Cloudninefertility states: Both men and women in the current society are highly ambitious and want to priorities their careers. They are more focused on investing their energy, time and money in achieving their career goals. They do not want to impact their career by taking time off for parenthood and potentially limiting their opportunities for career advancement. Bearing a kid and raising them means less freedom and flexibility. DINK couples usually like their freedom and want to enjoy the spontaneity of travel, leisure, etc and do not want to be constrained by responsibilities. They want to invest time and money in self-care, personal development and relationships rather than looking after kids.” Overall, with a dual income career driven couple, its less likely to see more children in their future. This contributes to my belief that we will see less families overall in 2035. However in the rise of dual income household structures, it is also important to consider that there are households without this option, single parent households.

The rise of single parents can never be pinned down to just one specific reason, there are too many factors, lifestyles, situations, and stories to make a blanket statement on how this comes to be. However, one large outcome of being a single parent household is that it is extremely more likely to see fewer kids once the parent of the household is single. The cost to raise a child is no small feat and having a single income of a single parent, the cost to have multiple children may not be possible. There has been a steep increase of single parents from earlier years to now. More specifically, the percentage of single parent households structures is 25 percent of total families as compared to the previous 9 percent, as seen in the 1960s. As stated in niussp.org, “For decades, the share of U.S. children living with a single parent has been rising, accompanied by a decline in marriage rates and a rise in births outside marriage (Livingston 2018). The percentage of US children living in single-parent households nearly tripled between 1960 and 2023, increasing from 9% to 25% (US Census Bureau 2023). In the same period, the share of households with fathers missing more than doubled, increasing from 11% to 25%” This is why I believe the increase of single parent households will contribute to the decrease of families with children in 2035. Furthermore, with an increase of same sex marriages, there is less opportunity to have children.

Same sex relationships have always been around, but not widely accepted until recent years. In fact, same sex marriage wasn’t fully legalized until June 26, 2015. With same sex couples, there are limited ways that a child can become a part of the family. These options can be incredibly expensive and even if it is a feasible cost there is still incredible amounts of discrimination that these couples face. This contributes to the difficulty of bringing a child into the home but it also contributes to the decision for some of These couples to not pursue a family with children. A recent study of LGBTQ individuals experience in the foster/adoption process stated after rigorous research that “In light of their interest in foster care and adoption (Goldberg, 2012), LGBTQ people should be regarded as highly valuable assets by the child welfare system and adoption agencies (Brooks & Goldberg, 2001; Mallon, 2011), yet they continue to face challenges at various stages of the adoption or foster care process. Such challenges may delay the placement of children in their home, or the legal adoption of those children, and/or result in disruption of those placements.” This barrier contributes to a decrease in families with children, and I predict this trend will unfortunately continue to increase into the year 2035.

Works Cited

Chamie, Joseph. “America’s Single-Parent Households and Missing Fathers - N-IUSSP.” N-IUSSP, 13 Jan. 2025, www.niussp.org/family-and-households/americas-single-parent-households-and-missing-fathers/.

“Dink (Double Income, No Kids) Trending and Fertility Declining!” Www.cloudninefertility.com, www.cloudninefertility.com/blog/dink-double-income-no-kids-trending-and-fertility-declining.

Goldberg, Abbie E., et al. “LGBTQ Individuals’ Experiences with Delays and Disruptions in the Foster and Adoption Process.” Children and Youth Services Review, vol. 106, Nov. 2019, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.childyouth.2019.104466.

News, PBS. “What to Know about the Supreme Court Ruling That Legalized Same-Sex Marriage 10 Years Ago.” PBS News, 26 June 2025, www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/what-to-know-about-the-supreme-court-ruling-that-legalized-same-sex-marriage-10-years-ago.

“Same-Sex Parents and Their Children.” Humansyst.org, 2020, www.humansyst.org/Human%20Systems/Consumer_Updates/Same-sex_Parents_and_Their_Children.aspx.

USAFacts. “The State of Relationships, Marriages, and Living Alone in the US.” USAFacts, 14 June 2023, usafacts.org/articles/state-relationships-marriages-and-living-alone-us/.
chunks.label: Trends shaping the future of American families
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes demographic trends including marriage rates, dual-income households, single-parent homes, and same-sex couples to predict family structures in 2035, concluding with a works cited list.

chunks.text:
Michael J. Sandel is a well-known modern-day political philosopher, famous for his speeches and for redefining how people discuss and view traditional economic markets, according to The Decision Lab. Most of his speeches took place in lecture halls and stadiums, where he discussed economic markets, political issues, and moral & ethical codes. Sandel has authored many books about these subjects, including “The Tyranny of Merit,” “What Money Can’t Buy,” “Equality,” and others. However, this paper will analyze his book “Justice: What is the Right Thing to Do?” He explores moral codes, justice, and analyzes philosophers to define justice when discussing philosophical and ethical dilemmas.

Sandel’s Justice: What is the Right Thing to Do? This prompt raises an important question as it sets the tone for the direction and discussions within Sandel’s work, as he breaks down and analyzes various aspects of how philosophers and people approach this prompt. He asked: what do we consider justice to be? Sandel explores this question through three lenses: welfare maximization, freedom requests, and virtue cultivation. In the next section, Sandel introduces a philosopher who further explores into these identifiers as well as countering with critiques and addressing limitations with their ideologies.

Jeremy Bentham an English philosopher is known as the father of modern utilitarianism where he was known to critic both judicial and political instructions through defining fundamental concepts of ethics (John P. & Brian, 2025). Moreover, Bentham held the belief that the ultimate moral principle is the maximization of general welfare, collective happiness, and the overall balance of pleasures over pain. This reflects the utilitarian perspective, which advocates for decisions that yield the most favorable outcomes for the majority. Utilitarianism advocates for wealth distribution, positing that those with greater financial capacity can aid those in less favorable economic conditions, subsequently improving their overall welfare. Another example, pulled from his book, Sandel presents the lifeboat case, a scenario involving four English sailors adrift in a small lifeboat in the South Atlantic, who were then rescued days later (Sandel 18). Upon their rescue, only three of the four members had survived, as one crew member confessed to having eat a fellow crew are due to starvation; the surviving sailors were then taken transported back to England to be tried for their crimes (Sandel 18). Sandel presented this scenario to illustrate that Bentham and other utilitarians would condone the sailors’ actions, as their philosophy prioritizes maximizing overall happiness. The sailors in question were affected from extensive famine. If sacrificing one sailor benefits the survival of the other crew mates, their actions are morally justified. Those who condemn the sailors’ actions would be unjust. In the following section, Sandel will present a counterargument and philosophy to the utilitarian perspective. While clarifying these philosophical stances, ideals, and specific aspects of utilitarianism, as this perspective presents a contrary viewpoint. Moreover, this contrasting viewpoint challenges the core principles of utilitarianism in moral judgement.

The utilitarian perspective, which prioritizes communal satisfactions and happiness, is at odds with individual rights, as it does not respect them. This stands for a core principle of libertarianism, as their philosophical positions emphasize self-ownership, given that individual have dominion over their individual rights, personhood, and efforts, “I am entitled to the fruits of my labor.” Libertarians advocate for a free market, minimal government intervention & regulations, oppose wealth redistribution, and prioritize individual liberties and the maximization of individual happiness. For instance, libertarians do not support a neoliberal economy because of their opposition to government involvement in the market; they view government spending and taxation as slavery. From this perspective, which is based on individual ownership and labor, taxation is a violation of these principles because of the government’s confiscation of an individual’s income without producing or contributing to said labor. This association is further emphasized because libertarians view taxation as a coercive practice by the government, with potential punishments including financial penalties, assets taken, and/or incarceration for those who do not pay their taxes.

However, Sandel critiques the libertarian viewpoint, challenging its fundamental principles and the bases of societal and systematic justice. Initially, he contests the notion that taxation equates to slavery. He counters this belief with several arguments, for instance, in the United States (US); should and individual contest the taxation of their earnings, they are eligible to vote on reforms. This argument specifically argues taxation as slavery, as those enslaved cannot advocate for their interests or their labor. The following argument proposes that individual accomplishments are not the product of personal effort or hard work. Instead, success may arise from chance, or an individual’s background, as an individual’s talents and skills vary across communities, and some of these factors are considered in achieving success. Sandel’s argument is that success is not achieved indefinitely; rather, the individual, the community and one’s surroundings foster success, and the resulting benefits should be attributed to that community. In essence, Sandel further argues that libertarianism places excessive focus and priority on the self, individual ownership, and absolute freedoms. This ideology overlooks societal duties, restricts the perspective of freedom & rights, devalues communal support, and does not acknowledge that people are part of a broader social structure.

To clarify and explain the fundamental principles of some philosophical perspective discussed in Sandel’s “Justice: What’s the Right Thing to Do?” When discussing the concept of justice, I ask myself similarly to Sandel’s question, which stance would serve as a greater or a morally just perspective to follow. Additionally, how is justice perceived within our society? My personal beliefs and ethical framework are aligned with utilitarian principles, which prioritizes the maximize of overall well-being. I prioritize collective support and reject individualistic expectations, as well as any actions that marginalize others to achieve self-ownership. My stance is in favor of wealth distribution, which is based on the idea that the wealthy continuously accumulating wealth, justifying it with the mindset of “self-owned success,” which hinders efforts to alleviate the suffering of others. I find the current mindset and systems, such as capitalism, that perpetuate wealth accumulation problematic, and closing this gap will require several generations. In addition, that wealth is preserved through exploitative methods where individuals, specifically workers, are required to provide labor with little to no returns. This worsens community suffering while solely promoting and upholding the happiness of a single person. However, I acknowledge the disadvantages and drawbacks of the utilitarian perspective, such as the ultimate disregard for individual rights and its failure to recognize human complexities and our placement in society. The utilitarian approach emphasizes the outcomes of actions and their effects on collective happiness, potentially overlooking those who do not align with the majority’s views. Additionally, some individuals may be unwilling to relinquish their independence rights because of personal values, beliefs, morals, and experiences. In addition, utilitarianism focuses on the overall happiness of the group, weighing the pleasure and pain instead of the moral rightness or wrongness. Those who judge society from a utilitarian perspective risk framing their discussions and decisions about collective happiness, neglecting the inherent morality of actions done for the benefit of the majority. This introduces complexities in justice and in deciding the fairness of personal decisions. Integrating philosophical ideologies into our systems requires acknowledging their limitations in providing a comprehensive framework for society. While I support utilitarian principles, I also agree with certain aspects of libertarianism related to government involvement and individual labor rights. The prioritization of one philosophical perspective over others restricts the understanding and nuance of intentionally flawed systems, societal norms, and individual behaviors within their prescribed roles. An individual’s experiences influence their decision-making and moral compass, considering values vary across national, cultural, communal, and individual lines. Each viewpoint possesses inherent strengths and weaknesses, and its applicability is limited by the context; however, by analyzing and dissecting these perspectives, we can acquire a clearer understanding of what justice may entail.

Justice: What’s the Right Thing to Do, by Michael J. Sandel confronts a multifaceted question relating to societal justice and how it operates within our society. Throughout the text, the author examines this theme from various philosophical perspectives. The primary focus of this paper was libertarian and utilitarian perspectives, which resonated most strongly with me in Sandel’s writing. Examination of these aspects within the book not only educated me of these perspectives but also highlighted their alignment with my personal moral and ethical stances. Reading Sandel’s work enhanced my comprehension of diverse justice explanations, while simultaneously receiving clarity on my own personal moral framework.
chunks.label: Analyzing Michael Sandel's book on justice
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes Michael Sandel's book 'Justice: What is the Right Thing to Do?', examining utilitarian and libertarian philosophies, discussing their own moral alignment with utilitarianism, and reflecting on how the reading clarified their personal ethics.

n9f21d29d.title: Navigating Family Stigma and Mental Illness

chunks.text:
What stood out to me was the tension between love and helplessness. Douglass loved his son deeply, but he couldn’t control the illness. He couldn’t fx it. That helplessness is something many families face when mental illness enters the picture. Society often expects parents to have the answers, but the truth is, situations like this are confusing, overwhelming, and unpredictable. Reading this book also made me think about how mental illness is treated in society. Douglas felt like he had to lie about his children’s struggles because of stigma. That stigma still exists today. People still keep mental health quiet out of fear of being judged. Families end up isolated, not because they want to be, but because they feel like no one will understand. The book also made me think about identity and loss. When Douglas explained feeling like his son had become a stranger, it struck me deeply. That kind of grief isn’t often talked about. It's not losing someone physically, but emotionally. And it can last for years. Douglas’s honesty in sharing these feelings made his story even more powerful to me.

As I read, I also thought about how strong families can be in the middle of pain. Douglas didn’t always have the answers. He felt lost and ashamed at times. But he still showed up for his son. He learned, advocated, and kept hoping, even had to show tough love at times. That kind of strength isn’t loud, it’s quiet and steady, and it often goes unnoticed. This book also showed me how much support families need when facing mental illness. Douglas had to figure everything out by going to the library on his own. There wasn't a clear path or enough resources to guide him. While things have improved in some ways today, many families still experience that same lack of support. Mental health care often focuses on individuals, but families are a huge part of the story. They’re the ones trying to hold everything together when things fall apart. By the end of A Boy Broken, I didn’t just feel like I had read a book, I felt like I have been trusted with someone’s real life. I walked through confusion, hope, heartbreak, love, and even tons and tons of important information. The story doesn’t need dramatic language to be powerful. It’s powerful because it’s honest.

On a personal level, it made me think about my own family and how complicated it can be to love someone through something you don’t fully understand. Even when the situations aren't the same, the emotions, fear, helplessness, frustration, love, are all universal. That’s why this book matters. It doesn't just speak to families dealing with schizophrenia; it speaks to anyone who has ever loved someone they couldn't save. In the end, A Boy Broken is a story about love, lost, and resilience. It’s about a father doing everything he can in a situation bigger than him. It’s about a son whose life was shaped by illness but also moments of connection and hope. And it’s about a family carrying the pain that most people never see. This story reminded me why it’s so important to approach mental health with honesty and compassion. It’s easy to talk about menta illness in terms of symptoms or statistics. But Douglas’s story gives it a human face. It shows the daily reality: the denial, the fear, the grief, and the moments of hope.

Reflecting on this book has changed the way I think about mental health and family. It made me more aware of how stigma can isolate people, how love can hold on even at hard times, and how loss can be both exprected and devastating. It also made me respect the strength it takes to share a story like this. It’s one thing to live it, another to let others in. I am grateful I got to read this story and learn from it. A boy Broken isn’t just book, it’s a personal testimony of a father’s love, pain, and courage/. It left me with a deeper understanding of what it means to love someone through their struggles, and how even in loss, that love never disappears. This story reminded me how powerful things can be, even in the darkest and most painful moments of life.
chunks.label: Reflections on reading A Boy Broken
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on reading the book 'A Boy Broken' by Douglas, discussing the impact of mental illness on families, stigma, grief, resilience, and personal takeaways regarding love and compassion.

chunks.text:
As we progress in the United States, we stray farther and farther from traditional Western ideals. It is already apparent that men are no longer considered and expected to be the only source of income and the “breadwinners” of a household. Today, more women than ever before are in the workforce, and their life goals often do not include being a stay-at-home mother, nor do these goals perceive marriage as the end-all be-all. As a society, we are shifting our focus away from basing our entire lives on getting married, having children, and starting a family.

When comparing current marriage trends to the past, it is evident that fewer people are getting married, and those who do eventually get married do not do so until later on in life. The legalization of gay marriage also shifted the way society views marriage. Instead of it being a legal recognition of a union between a man and a woman, it can be applied to any two persons in any scenario.

Declining Marriage Rate:

Why are we seeing a decline in marriage? To simply answer the question, in today’s society, people are more career-driven. Marriage no longer marks the start of adulthood. Going to school, graduating, and becoming successfully employed are goals now put ahead of settling down with a partner and starting a family. Recently, individuals are seen not even wanting to think about marriage until they are well off enough financially and can provide a nice life for themselves. Welcoming a partner into one’s life takes attention away from their job. It jeopardizes mental well-being for those who are doing just fine remaining single. When in a relationship, marriage especially, you have to put your partner's needs above your own, and this can become difficult when an individual has devoted their life to their job.

With so many women involved in the workforce today, the societal pressure of getting married to a man so that you can be taken care of and provided for is lifted. Women can now easily provide for themselves. The traditional ideal that pictured men as providers and women as dependent on the men to provide made it seem as though marriage was a necessity and an expectation. If you were older and unmarried, you were originally viewed as having failed at life. Nowadays, with women focusing on their education, careers, and overall independence, the pressure to get married is now not as intense. It is abundantly evident that men and marriage are not necessary to live a fulfilled life. If one is happy single, why risk that happiness in order to gain a partner?

Another reason that can be attributed to declining marriage rates is the fact that people do not view the label of marriage as necessary to prove their love and commitment to one another. At the end of the day, it is quite literally just a piece of paper. The legal recognition of a union between two individuals does not affect the relationship itself. Those in long-term cohabitation relationships may see no real reason to get married. It has been evident throughout their whole relationship that they love and care for one another and want to spend their lives together as they have been doing over the past years. There is no real reason that they would need to go out and get married. Other factors, like the price of having a wedding, also deter people from getting married, as well as the fear of divorce.

Single parenting creates another reason that people either choose not to marry or get married later on in life. A single parent raising a child places all of their attention on raising that child. There is no time to go out and meet someone, much less get to know them on a deeper level, when raising a child at home. Single parents may also not feel comfortable bringing essentially a stranger around their young children.
chunks.label: Societal shifts in marriage and declining marriage rates
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on changing gender roles, economic factors, career priorities, cohabitation, and single parenting that contribute to declining marriage rates in society.

chunks.text: From personal experience, though my mother was married to my father at one point, at two years old, they got a divorce. My whole upbringing, and to this day, I never saw my mother with another man. Growing up, I would ask her why she did not try to find someone new, and her response was always that I came first, and she did not feel comfortable bringing random men into the house to meet me. It was not necessary for her to find another partner and remarry. A single parent with a child in the house places that child and their needs above all else (most of the time). Now that I have been out of the house for some time, I still ask my mother why she does not try and find love again, and as I stated above, as people are completely fine with being single, that is also her mentality. She says that she has been single for almost twenty years, and she does not even want to stress about another person coming into her life. She is content with the way her life is and does not need some man coming into her life and creating stressors she would not otherwise have while remaining single.
chunks.label: Mother remaining single after divorce
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up with a single mother following their parents' divorce at age two. The student frequently asked their mother about dating, but the mother chose to stay single to focus on raising the student and avoid stress.

chunks.text:
This perspective can also be applied to single mothers who were never married, thus why single parenting impacts the declining marriage rates.

LGBTQ Couples:

As we have seen, the declining marriage rates are impacting original marriage ideals, and the legalization of gay marriage has also shifted views of what a traditional marriage looks like. No longer is marriage seen and accepted between only a man and a woman, but now we see marriage between any two people who love each other and want to take that next step. This shift challenges society’s heteronormative view of marriage by focusing the idea of marriage more on love, commitment, and connection. The commonality of same sex marriages normalizes diversity within families and demonstrates that the foundations of marriage are focused on love and trust rather than gender and heteronormacy.

Conclusion:

Taking into consideration all of the points brought up previously in this paper, it is very evident that marriage trends ten years from now will look different from what we see today. Not only will there be fewer marriages due to seeing it as a non-necessity, and not prioritizing marriage as a whole, but we will also see more diverse, LGBTQ marriages in the future.

Instead of marrying for security, people will marry intentionally, and later on in life, if at all. Marriage is no longer a contributing factor to the age-old “American Dream”. Individuals will not be getting married just to be able to say they did. If a person meets a great partner and feels the overwhelming need to get married, they will. Previous pressures and rushing straight into the act will be a thing of the past. People will be seen getting married later on in life because they want to, not because they need to. Marriage is a choice, not an obligation.
chunks.label: Impact of single parenting, LGBTQ marriage, and future trends
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how single parenting and LGBTQ marriage reshape views on marriage, concluding that future marriage trends will reflect diverse, intentional, and optional unions.

chunks.text:
Trends of family styles, models, and interpersonal functionality have vastly changed over the course of the past few decades. Women have joined the workforce at an increasing rate to attain social and economic gain, young adults have prioritized education and a career over marriage- which has contributed to higher rates of single-parent households-, and lesbian/gay couples are more common than ever before. In combination with the increased cost of living in recent years, these trends can be used to forecast how American families will likely function in the year 2035.

There are multiple factors contributing to the steady decline of first marriage rates amongst Americans in the past few decades (Brown et al., 2022). Young adults have been prioritizing a higher education and/or their career over marriage in their early 20s, societal expectations to marry early (or at all) have been less pressurized, and young adults have been waiting to marry until they feel financially stable (Trevino, 2022). The current decline of the economy, including an increase in the cost of living, creates an incentive for the lower class to put off marrying or not marrying at all (Furstenberg, 2015). A decrease in religious expectations to marry removes the sexual appeal towards marriage and in general removes pressure to marry for some Americans; this trend will continue as society progresses and decentralizes religion further. These factors can also contribute to a couples’ decision whether or not to have children, biological or otherwise. Overall, the American birth rate has dropped a whopping 20% from 1980 to 2007 (Kearney et al., 2022); factors previously discussed, such as prioritizing higher education, are responsible. Marriage rates and birth rates have a symbiotic relationship in saying that when marriage becomes socially normalized later in life, many do not try to become pregnant until later in life. Therefore, it is not unreasonable to say that the average family in 2036 will consist of older parents who married later in life or decided to not marry at all; they most likely have one or two children, if any.

The decline in marriage until later in life combined with the trend of cohabitation rather than marriage are two factors that will contribute to the increase of blended families by 2035. On the other hand, marrying for true love rather than for financial benefit- which has traditionally been the case- has decreased divorce rates since the 1980s (Coontz, 2005). I believe the typical family in 2035 will overall be happier than the typical family from 2025 for several reasons; the upward trend of young adults not marrying until their late 20s on average (or not marrying at all) provides individuals with the opportunity to not be socially forced into early marriage for possibly financial reasons. When young adults view marriage as a social institution that comes after being financially stable and educated with a career, there is more opportunity for success (Coontz, 2005). It is not a secret that a happy home environment generally produces happy and well children compared to those from a socially dysfunctional one.

Same-sex marriage has experienced an upwards trend since its legalization in 2015, and the number of same-sex households (married and unmarried) continue to rise. Although I think the “average”, as in most common, relationship would be straight, it would not be surprising if some Americans in 2035 thought of a gay couple when asked to picture the average relationship. In regards to masculinity, the erosion of the belief that the more masculine appearing or acting partner is responsible for traditionally male roles and traits will continue. The Second Shift Change described by Hochschild in which women began being active members of the workforce while remaining responsible for caretaker tasks will evolve as we have already been seeing. Women may enter the workforce while men stay at home, take care of the children, and do household tasks. This motion and the stigma of males being the breadwinner are becoming more and more common as time goes on, and will continue to do so. With that being said, the typical family in 2035 will most likely have both partners of the relationship in the work force. Economically, we have experienced stagnant wages for decades while the cost of living continues to increase. This only provides more of an incentive for Americans to pursue a higher education, not marry, and not have kids; furthermore, Furstenberg (2015) proposes that unless American wages increase or our tax system is modified to better benefit workers of lower paying jobs, there is no incentive financially for the lower class to marry young (if at all). In a climate where lower-income families have lower rates of marriage in the present day, the typical family in 2035 may not involve marriage altogether, making blended families more common (Furstenberg, 2015).

The biological mother position will have slightly shifted and become more multifaceted. Given that there will be a greater population of same-sex households, blended households, and single mothers, the biological mother may devolve from its traditional traits, one of which being the primary caregiver. Because mothers will continue to be active participants in the workforce and stigma around employed women still being homemakers more so than the male, The rate of single mothers rising also means increased aid of community (family, friends) to raise children, making the family dynamic even less traditional than before; the projected growing disparity between cost of living and wages will also expand this concept. Given that there will be a greater population of gay couples that do not have a biological mother role and less couples will be having children, the biological mother will be less common and more diverse. However, social change does not occur overnight, so in ten years the average couple will have a biological mother.

To conclude, the trends we see in the past few decades such as a decline in marriage and higher rates of blended families will continue into the year 2035. Although the population of single parents have been increasing in recent years, the rising cost of living will increase cohabitation rates, whether that be with a significant other, family, or friends. Another result of this economic change is that the majority of families will be dual-income, meaning the mother is a part of the labor force as well. There would be more instances in which the mother works while the father becomes a homemaker if not for the projected economic shift raising the cost of living while keeping wages stagnant. Social movement and the overall stray from the traditional nuclear family, including its gender roles, will continue; the father of the average household will contribute to household tasks such as dishes and laundry as well as taking care of the children. More families who do not have biological mothers, such as same-sex couples, will be a part of the movement in which both parents contribute equally to family life while working; couples who adopt actively make an assumption that each person will care for the child and continue caring for the home equally, or at least what they perceive to be fair (Moore, 2008). The average family will be dual-income, unmarried until later in life (if at all), and have one or two kids; the trends we have seen in past decades will continue into the next one.
chunks.label: Forecasting American family trends for 2035
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes societal trends regarding marriage, birth rates, gender roles, and economic factors to forecast the structure of American families in the year 2035.

nb44f9778.title: Navigating Class Registration and Campus Parking

chunks.text: One example of a dilemma that arises for me and every college student is registration for classes. I know that there have been many instances where I have tried to register for a class that fits both a need for my degree and a want for my interests post college, but the class is full, and I must scramble frantically to try and find a replacement class. There is the argument of whether registration priority should go to seniors first as they need to put the finishing touches on their degree or the current system which goes by GPA regardless of what year you are.
chunks.label: Registering for college classes
chunks.what_happened: The student has repeatedly faced full classes while trying to register for courses that fit their degree and interests, forcing them to scramble for replacements.

chunks.text:
A utilitarian would want to maximize a college student’s happiness and would use a system which would prioritize certain classes for their degrees. An example would be prioritizing Criminology classes for Criminology majors so they would not have to worry about it filling up. In a 35-person class have 30 spots of that class dedicated to Criminology majors and use the same pattern for other majors. It would ensure each student gets the classes they need and want for their degree and have spots for other majors to take a class they might find interesting. There would also be the case of using a hybrid schedule for the classes that are in high demand to fit schedules of students to ensure their happiness.

A libertarian would likely not change the current system by much if at all. They would defer to individuals’ rights to all choose the class and would not want to hinder a certain major or grade to benefit another. They would want all people to have an equal opportunity to get into a class to try and change that would infringe on an individual’s rights. The wealth distribution example that Sandel uses in the book would be very similar to this as it is not fair to the wealthy to have to give some of their money because they are wealthy. It would be unfair to those students whose GPA is highest to have to give up their position in registration because there are others with lower GPA’s who cannot get into the classes they need.

In my opinion, there needs to be a mix between what a libertarian would do and a utilitarian. I would alter it more than a libertarian would but not quite the same way a utilitarian would do. I would say that seniors would get priority as they have the most need to get certain classes as they need to graduate but I would sort the grades by GPA, so the seniors with the highest GPA would get their preference, and then the seniors get their choice and that cycle continues. Freshmen would go based on their high school GPA to reward those who put in the work to get into college. In my opinion this is the fairest way to complete registration as it considers the need of seniors to have them graduate while also rewarding academic success. There will also be more open spots for each level of course as seniors will be less likely to take a 200-level course as it will have been open to them in earlier years.
chunks.label: Philosophical perspectives on class registration
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes how utilitarians and libertarians would approach course registration and proposes a compromise based on class standing and GPA.

chunks.text: Another dilemma that arises for most college students is on campus parking. We have a system where you must pay a certain fee to park in a zone for the entire academic year. There are many students that will park in zones that are far away from their classes and must walk long distances and will end up being late for class. Areas such as the Trask lot and Hamilton lot are not feasible zones as they are near no buildings in which students have classes. It presents an issue for all off campus students that are over one mile from campus, especially since there is an uptick in students enrolled this year compared to previous years.
chunks.label: Issues with campus parking
chunks.what_happened: The student describes the campus parking zone system and the challenges off-campus students face with distant lots and enrollment increases.

chunks.text:
A utilitarian would prioritize the overall happiness of college students parking versus the needs of students. They would likely try a system of prioritizing those that are farthest from campus such as people that might live outside of Wilmington. They would create more park and ride situations than the ones that exist as the only one is the parking lot behind the Taco Bell across from campus. They might even incentive park and ride situations by making them much cheaper or even taking money off students’ tuition to make it more attractive. Overall utilitarians would try to make as many students happy as possible even if they have other students that want to park close even if they do not need it.

A libertarian would want to prioritize the usage of the free market and would value each student having an opportunity to buy a parking pass. They would have the prices raised to see which students really value convenient parking as they would feel it is unjust for prices to all be the same as the zones with more convenience should be more expensive. They would leave it up to the students to decide who wants to pay for more premier parking rather than have a higher authority decide who gets what parking. A potential downside for this method would be wealthier students being able to afford the parking and it would leave other students scrambling for parking alternatives and making more students late for class.

I would use a system that matches students closest to the zone for their degree, and it would also be a first-come first serve method. If a student has most of their classes in Bear Hall then I would have the off-campus student park in commuter zone one which is the closest student parking to Bear Hall. I would have that system for student parking on a first come first serve basis. I would also have more parking for students as it seems that there is teacher parking in every building but not enough parking for students. It would help to divide the vast students across campus as well as to keep them as close as possible to the building they have the most classes in. My system that I feel is best would utilize the libertarian view of first come first serve while also having utilitarian views of maximizing the happiness of students whom have to park from off campus housing.
chunks.label: Philosophical perspectives on campus parking
chunks.what_happened: The student considers utilitarian and libertarian approaches to parking allocation and suggests a first-come, first-served system tied to major buildings.

chunks.text: In the book, Sandel uses examples such as which system for supplying the military is the best or using pregnancy for pay. He discusses how the systems have changed over time from the civil war system to use of conscription, to the volunteer army we have today. The utilitarians and libertarians would both prefer the volunteer system for different reasons because of maximizing utility, and the personal freedom it gives. The libertarians would allow surrogacy as it is a person’s personal freedom to be able to decide to have a child elsewhere if they could not have one themselves. The utilitarians would also support surrogacy as it maximizes happiness for a couple that cannot have a child that wants one. Overall those two issues that Sandel uses in the book happen to have utilitarians and libertarians agree on which method is the best as it aligns with both of their views for different reasons.
chunks.label: Sandel's examples of military service and surrogacy
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Sandel's book examples concerning volunteer military service and paid pregnancy under utilitarian and libertarian views.

chunks.text: In conclusion, my arguments are ones that hit close to me as well as other college students. Registration is something I have had issues with from the start as there have been instances I have had to scramble to find classes to take after the ones I wanted filled up. It is a system that had always seemed unfair to me as I should be able to get into Criminology classes with no issue.
chunks.label: Frustration with class registration
chunks.what_happened: The student recounts persistent issues with registration, having to scramble for classes after desired Criminology courses filled up.

chunks.text: The parking issue is one I have had to deal with as I park in the Trask Lot and it is a manageable walk, but this year has been rough as there are many more students on campus parking this year and I find myself hunting for parking in the Hamilton Lot as the Trask Lot is always full.
chunks.label: Hunting for campus parking
chunks.what_happened: The student usually parks in the Trask Lot, but due to increased student enrollment this year, they often find it full and must search for parking in the Hamilton Lot.

chunks.text: Overall, these issues might not be life or death, but they are near and dear to me and diving into how utilitarians and libertarians would solve these issues has been insightful for me to understanding how they both think.
chunks.label: Conclusion on philosophy and campus issues
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by reflecting on how analyzing these campus issues through utilitarianism and libertarianism provided useful insight.

n7a292f53.title: A Veteran's Perspective on Moral Duty

chunks.text:
Throughout this reading, we have visited a plethora of topics, discussed a multitude of social, moral, and other issues, and compared every avenue of approach utilizing our own lived experiences and facts. Michael Sandel creates passages of information based on facts, lived experiences, hypotheses, theologies, and a vast array of other sources of contribution. As a Professor at Harvard, Sandel provides us with a variety of moral and social dilemmas throughout this book. As a class, we have dived deep into his realm and spent extensive time discussing and presenting his ideas. We have taken the time to draft our own interpretations and draw conclusions to the best of our ability. A key feature throughout this reading is to not only recall the amount of history that has been written about, but also how it has transcended into the very present-day society we live in.

As we know, social justice comprises two interconnected categories, personal and political aspects. Sandel provides an intimate exploration of every perspective across all categories in Justice. In the beginning chapters, Sandel discusses the early stages of moral reparations that will cascade in keeping with the theme throughout the entire book. He compares and contrasts different beliefs, principles, and their outcomes. Most of the philosophical and theological questions posed offered no true, definitive response. In part, this is due to the nature of such inquiries, as there are so many details and contexts contributing to each one. While exploring these topics in class discussions, student presentations, discussion posts on Canvas, and throughout my own reading, I have drawn many conclusions and still have many questions to be discussed and elaborated on further.

Referring back to the reading regarding Marcus Luttrell and the historic event of the Afghan goat herders, his team, and the mountainside in Afghanistan. They stumbled upon each other, along with a 14-year-old boy. Luttrell and his team cast a vote on whether or not to let them go or kill them, and he cast the deciding vote to release them. They did not have a rope to tie them up. The risks of releasing them were all known - they could easily report back to the Taliban and associates of Osama Bin Laden right down the mountainside. This would 100% compromise their position, and they would likely be overrun by insurgents within the hour and killed. Unfortunately, that was exactly what occurred, and all of Luttrell's teammates were killed; he was the only one to survive. He admits that his vote was mostly based on his Christian faith, and that is why he voted against killing them. However, he quickly regretted his decision as his teammates were all killed in action shortly after the goat herders were released, and notified the Taliban of the SEAL's position. In addition, the insurgents also shot down a helicopter that was aiming to rescue the SEALs who were pinned down, adding an additional 16 casualties.
