Overall, not killing the three goat herders cost 19 American lives, nearly 20 as Luttrell barely survived. We discussed this in class, and the perspective I provided as a United States Army veteran myself was insightful to the real moral dilemmas service members face every day. Some opinions were shared in class once Dr. Engelman asked us, "Would you have killed them or let them go?" I believe everyone in class said they would have released the goat herders, especially sympathizing with the fact that they had a 14-year-old boy with them. I offered the opinion that I would have killed them had I been in Luttrell's position. I provided substantial information regarding this decision and a perspective that no one else in the class has lived. While I understand the impacts of this decision, and being that Luttrell himself faced a moral dilemma in this situation that affected him so greatly, he couldn't execute them, this is still a heavily circumstantial issue. There is a concept in the military called "violence of action." You are relentlessly in pursuit of making a decision within the least amount of time possible. This is necessary in order to mitigate loss of life. Unfortunately, in response to the point of my classmate, children were often used by insurgents for a variety of attacks and casualties on American troops while in combat in Afghanistan. There is also regard for your training, especially as a prestigious Navy SEAL such as Luttrell. Speaking on this issue is definitely no easy feat, as is in keeping with most of the topics within this book. However, it is imperative to understand where your degree of responsibility lies in situations such as this.

Another topic of Sandel's book that was frequently visited throughout our classroom presentations and discussions is that of military service being a civic obligation, where it lies on the scale of virtue, patriotism, and moral duties. Above all, the vast majority of our conversations related back to accountability in some way, whether it was collectively or as an individual. Dr. Engelman promotes us to think in ways that acknowledge our individual responsibility and understand and interpret how it transcends into society. Civic virtues and obligations are two wings that contribute not only to military service, but also to our conversation of patriotism. As we elaborated on in class and discussed during our presentation, patriotism is another aspect that Sandel incorporates that is difficult to navigate. The relation to our moral compass and the battle between the grounds of one's own character contribute extensively to how we interpret the world, but also how we show up in it. If we do not believe we are obligated to serve others, the likely outcome of that would be a thought process consistent with inaction and beliefs consistent with not viewing military service as a civic obligation. This concept also applies to other areas in society, as we discussed in the book regarding our involvement, or inaction, in saving someone else's life, or even just having the courtesy to help someone across the road. This is an interesting topic that Sandel visits and compares throughout the book. It is most relevant to the practices of libertarianism in the sense of the prevalence of one's own rights. What particularly stood out to me was the fact that so much of what he elaborated on applies to our present-day society.

As we continued to dive deeper into the philosophical meanings behind what is honorable, virtuous, and noble, we see a common theme in the differences of opinions and adopted practices. When this topic arose while discussing the 'learning by doing' portion of another team's presentation during class, it sparked more interest in accountability. They asked the discussion question, "Do you think that practicing good behavior eventually leads someone to feel virtuous emotions (like gratitude/justice) genuinely?" The responses to this question were intriguing and led me to speak on this topic. In particular, with regard to character, virtues, and one's moral compass, it makes sense that a person is either of good behavior naturally or they aren't. What I mean by that is, someone who is practicing good behavior in order to feel virtuous would do it naturally, as it is a core component of who they are as a person. It is not necessarily something that you would 'learn' or 'exercise.' The same concept applies to selflessness in the conversation regarding service and civic obligation, as previously mentioned. While one student explained his positive notions regarding selflessness in society, I politely disagreed. The world can be a very cruel place, and with spending any amount of time in regular society, you can witness that firsthand. We also see it on social media every day. I argued, via my own personal and professional experiences, that people are more selfish today than selfless. The art of understanding and respecting humanity has been lost, and in this current era, people are only worried about themselves and are less worried about anyone else. Decisions are based on emotion versus logic, science, facts, etc. This practice further deepens the divide we all see and feel every day in 2025. As I stated in class, people are going to pursue the easy wrong over the hard right by nature. This is not to excuse their behavior, however, but to acknowledge the fact that people in society do not possess the same amount of intrinsic desire to be of good moral character without an external emotional influence pushing them to that decision. The example I gave was the social media trend where people do things for those who cannot afford to, but the entire point of it is that they record it and put it on social media. While I am not saying it is wrong to celebrate someone doing a good deed, we are living in a society that only cares about the views, likes, and how they are able to further monetize something, instead of just being a good person and doing the right thing because it comes from the heart of who they truly are.

The viewpoints provided in this book have been nothing less than interesting, intriguing, and insightful. We have discussed and interpreted different historical philosophers, public figures, and others of the like. This has been a pivotal movement in bringing our class together and fostering a safe and healthy open platform for us to discuss our differences in opinions and experiences. I aim to continue doing so with the goal of further educating myself and also learning from Dr. Engelman and my classmates.
chunks.label: Reflections on Sandel's Justice and course discussions
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Michael Sandel's book Justice, the moral dilemmas explored in class such as Marcus Luttrell's decision in Afghanistan, and philosophical topics like military service, civic obligation, virtue, and selfishness in modern society.

n6f0d793b.title: Understanding a Relative's Mental Illness Diagnosis

chunks.text:
As the reading deepens and the story goes on, the Engelman family begins to come to an understanding of their son’s illness. They can begin to learn what is real and what is hallucinations in his mind. As Dr. Engelman goes to more and more doctor's visits; he is able to gain a deeper connection to what his son is experiencing. He learns more about the diagnosis everyday alongside Doug and it begins to re-strengthen their relationship again. But this isn't to say the relationship was filled with love and understanding. There was often tension and confusion and frustration that would arise from all corners of the household. Family sometimes serves as a strength and sometimes serves as a tension holder. As his illness varies, they all vary.

The moments of lightness and compassion are what make this story such a true tale of the lives all lived. Dr. Engelman is bluntly honest about his feelings, and his confusions and his frustrations could very easily seem as if they took over his time with Doug after diagnosis, but the moments of understanding and love stick out so beautifully. Love prevails through all emotions, making the small moments of true happiness and love shine through the pain and suffering of this family. As the reader bounces back and forth between raw emotions and hopeful expectations, the book entails a true encapsulation of what this experience could look like in so many other lives.

In the end of Engelman’s heart aching story of love and sorrow, the worst tragedy to lay upon this family was the fatal car accident stealing their precious son's life. A life taken too quickly. After all of the emotions his family faced day in and day out, nobody could have warned them of the pain they were about to encounter. Loss is a painfully encapsulating debilitating emotion. For a father; unimaginable. The loss of a loved one is an emotion most people know too well and it is something that will never, for the rest of their lives, go unfelt. Looking at your faith and your perception of the world is a trap most people find themselves stuck in for months and sometimes years at a time after this life altering event. Death is an emotion humans were not wired to deal with all too easily. Whether it comes to stay in the moment or it comes back later, it never leaves.

Many people, when they find themselves living with the grievance of a loved one, are disabled in the real world until they can formally accept what is happening. After enduring the relationship and diagnosis of Doug’s death was not any different than the emotion of helplessness. Left to question all of the actions he's made in his life and all of the different ways he and his son interacted and loved one another. The cyclical emotion of loss, helplessness and confusion continued into his personal life, but because of this he became a more thoughtful person. Whether the dwelling of the loss or the dwelling on actions before death were the emotions at hand. Dr. Engelman was able to look back on his and the life of his sons with a different perspective. He was able to understand better the effects his actions caused Doug and the effects that his life had on his own. Gaining better insight day after day was one of the things that allowed Engelman to gain some peace and clarity after his son's passing. Leaning on his faith and learning that not all events have to happen for a reason is one of the strongest senses of clarity he was able to gain in the toughest time in his life.

The reader is able to gain a better perspective on what it is like to be in a family with a troubling diagnosis of a loved one. We are sent through a rigorous combination of emotions that shows us the raw and real experiences of a family. This story allows the readers to make connections to their own lives and for some it may be a helpful outlet. Learning that other people may be going through a similar experience can help in so many ways.
chunks.label: Reflections on Engelman's book and grief
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the story of the Engelman family, Doug's diagnosis, the car accident that took his life, and the nature of loss, grief, and family dynamics.

chunks.text: I was able to resonate with this story and was blessed enough with this reading to be able to understand diagnosis in my life better. My grandmother on my moms side recently went through a diagnosis with bipolar disorder. Throughout our lives there has always been an overarching tension between my grandmother and this side of the family. I was always told as a kid that my mom just didn’t have a great relationship with her mom and I started to see more and more of that the older I grew older. Over the past couple weeks my mom grew very anxious of the unresponsiveness of my grandmother. She called for a wellness check and shortly after she was admitted to a mental institution in Georgia. She was very quickly diagnosed with bipolar disorder and was given strict medication. After reading A Boy Broken, I was able to feel a generous amount of alleviation to the anger I held toward my grandmother. I realized that all of the emotions I held were because I didn't understand what was going on, it frustrated me that I didn’t know and continued the cycle. I feel grateful for the moments of generosity I had for her actions towards my mother and was able to feel safe in knowing that those moments shined through just as much as Dr. Engelman's actions of light and breakthrough did. Although I wasn’t able to be as knowledgeable as Engelman during most of the time, It made me feel safer to know that all of my emotions weren’t something only I experienced.
chunks.label: Grandmother's bipolar diagnosis and mental institution admission
chunks.what_happened: The student's grandmother was diagnosed with bipolar disorder after a wellness check led to her admission into a mental institution, helping the student process and relieve family tension and anger.

chunks.text: Overall, this novel showed great discomfort and vulnerability of a father and his journey with his son through a debilitating diagnosis. Throughout the novel the reader is able to gain better insight on what it would be like to experience a seemingly broken family to an outsider. But when taking a deeper look, we are able to realize that all people experience the same emotions and not one of them can be held in greater disdain than another. A heartbreaking story that shows raw human emotions allows people to see that there is more to a person than a diagnosis.
chunks.label: Concluding thoughts on the novel
chunks.what_happened: The student concludes by summarizing the novel's depiction of vulnerability, family struggles, and shared human emotions beyond a diagnosis.

n3643f28e.title: Living with Epilepsy and Hospital Stigma

chunks.text:
Sociology of mental disorder points out that stigma has many factors which influence its severity and sources in a given community. Doug's journey with schizophrenia exemplifies how an individual, on a micro level, is impacted by these community or society level shifts in stigma. Doug’s experiences have reminded me of many of my own, and I’ve considered how the two might relate to certain concepts from the aforementioned text.

Stigma impacts both Doug and those around him throughout his journey both directly and indirectly. Doug ends up being targeted for repeated robberies at a place he stays which houses other patients; it's likely he was targeted due to a symptom of schizophrenia that results in the patient being “gullible”. Doug's family also puts up with constant pressure from the responsibilities of a caregiver, but also pressure from whether or not to reveal the nature of Doug's condition to their neighbors and extended family out of fear for how that might change their relationships. While in the latter example there is no form of harassment or bullying taking place which would constitute what one might think of as prejudiced, stigma is more often an internalized process which impacts one's decisions and leads to such isolation of specific groups.
chunks.label: stigma and Doug's journey with mental illness
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on sociological concepts of stigma related to mental disorder, discussing examples from Doug's life and his family's experiences.

chunks.text: I have spent some time in mental hospitals when I was a teenager for suicidal intent, and recall a similar kind of stigma. Even though I was on the inside of the hospital there was still a palpable sense of defensiveness between the patients; when we came in, and whenever someone new came in or was admitted, they specifically warned patients not to get anyone's contact information and that this isn't a place to socialize. While that is a good warning considering the circumstances, it made us feel like we were in danger from everyone else in the facility. There was one particular patient who was 17, it was a juvenile unit, and during my stay he was having his 18th birthday which meant he was transferring to the adult unit; the nurses frequently warned him about the adult unit and pushed him to leave the hospital altogether before he would be transferred there. These warnings and feelings of danger come from the outside stigma of “people with mental disorders are inherently dangerous”.
chunks.label: teenage stay in a mental hospital
chunks.what_happened: As a teenager admitted for suicidal intent, the student experienced hospital staff warning patients not to socialize and cautioning an older teen about transferring to the adult unit.
chunks.feelings: defensiveness, feel like we were in danger

chunks.text: These stages of grief experienced by caregivers reminded me of many events from my life and how they have impacted my family members. The one that I would say creates the emotions most synonymous with grief is epilepsy. They go through a lot of stress and effort managing my seizures and repeatedly saving me from them; my brother has had to kick through my door multiple times and my mother once broke a window to get to me. On the rare occasion when they don't do these things fast enough they have found me blue from oxygen deprivation. Although this isn't a mental disorder they certainly qualify as caregivers; they're always ready at a moment's notice to run upstairs or to wherever they heard me fall, and if they don't know where I am for a long enough period of time they get anxious and call me or contact me. I was diagnosed with epilepsy when I was 15 and early on in the process my neurologist said that some people are able to grow out of epilepsy until age 25 (I’m 26 now). I never had hoped that that would happen for me, however my mother always clung to it as a chance that I wouldn't need this constant supervision and other interruptions to my life. Retrospectively, she does seem to have gone through a very similar process of denial and grief.
chunks.label: family caregiving and grief over epilepsy
chunks.what_happened: The student was diagnosed with epilepsy at age 15, leading their mother and brother to repeatedly save them during seizures while their mother held out hope they would outgrow it.

chunks.text: When searching for Doug, it is mentioned how the homeless seemed so invisible before, but now that he is somewhere in that crowd you realize how many homeless people there are.
chunks.label: homelessness and stigma in Doug's narrative
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on scenes from a book where Doug interacts with homeless individuals, highlighting how widespread stigmas about homeless people can be untrue.

chunks.text: Later, while having lasagna with Wendy and Doug, he mentions that he met a nice group of homeless people who could tell he didn’t know his way around the streets so they offered to help him out; the event led to a revelation that a widely held stigma, in this case against the homeless, is untrue. This moment reminded me of an experience I had which led me to the same revelation; I was sitting in a park on Market Street, trying to gather myself after a stressful day, and a man who I had passed by a few times on the street downtown before walked up and sat on the bench beside me. I thought nothing of it at first, but I was as anxious as I am with all people. Then he spoke to me about how he is God and he thought I was some incarnation of a spirit of some kind that he didn't fully explain the nature of. I was somewhat unnerved by this as the two of us were alone, so I downplayed it and treated the God and spirit stuff as a conversation topic; we talked about his family as well, but he was more interested in the former topic. It was at this point that he took out a knife, which I was very frightened by. He didn't threaten me with it but rather just did tricks with it; one of which was to reach behind and in between my legs, throwing it up and then catching it in front of me. He was constantly laughing and smiling, a very pleasant and kind man, but seemingly unaware of social norms. He gave me a stress ball which I still have 3 years later. At the time I was very scared, however retrospectively this experience made me realize that anyone is capable of being that manner of pleasant and kind person despite their circumstances.
chunks.label: encounter with a man in the park
chunks.what_happened: While sitting on a bench in a park after a stressful day, the student talked with a man who claimed to be God, did knife tricks between the student's legs, and gave the student a stress ball.
chunks.feelings: stressed, anxious, somewhat unnerved, very frightened, very scared

chunks.text:
Understanding the circumstances of Doug and Jeff, the man from my experience, through a symbolic interactionist lens enables us to better understand why they might be considered outsiders by society’s standards. Symbolic interactionism states that an individual is able to choose their own behavior according to or despite the influences of society, and those societal influences are largely communicated by subtle ”symbols”. Individuals struggling from certain mental disorders or other conditions may have a harder time discerning or deciphering these symbols and are therefore more likely to ”act of their own accord” according to symbolic interactionism.

One thing that came to mind from the textbook was William Cockerham's seven phases of experiencing mental disorder; though the phases are not intended to be a road map or to be experienced in a specific order. Beginning with alienation from place, Doug was considered by his teachers to be very pleasant in school, but when his symptoms hit that strain led to such outward effects as social alienation, certainly what could be described as troublesome emotions. With regards to recognizing symptoms, he gains improved insight later on in his journey once he started seeing Julie at Mercy Hospital in Pittsburgh, but was very resistant to acknowledging the existence of his condition early on in this journey; that isn't to say he never did prior to his work at Mercy but rather he truly accepted it at that stage which allowed for a very successful recovery. Madness as a method of coping says one uses symptoms to cope with life circumstances or interacts with others with different perceptions of reality, the latter qualifier is certainly observed throughout the book such as the instance where Doug is sitting in the car and claims that there is a girl in the backseat, a recurring hallucination, and recounts having sex with her. Regarding the definitive outburst there is a very clear instance of this towards the beginning of the book when Doug has been brought home and Wendy finds him very distressed, yelling at no one in the backyard. For removal from place, when Doug is being targeted by the kids at Madden and can’t go home he resolves to remove himself from the situation by self isolating until he feels ready to come back. For the rendering of accounts, the closest symptomatic thing he does to an attempt to excuse, justify, or explain his symptoms is to say that the people he sees and voices he hears are in fact there. The paradox of normalcy occurs throughout his journey; there are moments such as the “lasagna night” after he came home from being missing for several weeks, or normalcy can also be found in how he says, “What’s up?” and attempts to maintain a casual atmosphere.

Doug’s experiences, my own, and those of our families are demonstrative of such concepts as stigma, the seven phases of mental disorder, and the process of grief experienced by caregivers. What is stigmatized, why it is so, and to what severity are all constantly shifting in a given community; this influences individuals in life-changing ways. Similarly, people are capable of finding ways to adapt to current societal expectations and requirements regardless of such counter forces.
chunks.label: sociological analysis of mental disorder and stigma
chunks.what_happened: The student analyzes behaviors and phases of mental disorder using symbolic interactionism and William Cockerham's framework, summarizing key themes of stigma and caregiver grief.

n68fcbaaa.title: Grappling with Moral Dilemmas and Justice

chunks.text:
Michael Sandel’s “Justice: What’s the Right Thing to Do” is not only a text looking at philosophical ideas but it also acts as a conversation to create dialogue from the reader. The experience of reading this text resembled a classroom discussion instead of studying political theory because Sandel leads readers to confront difficult moral dilemmas.

When I first picked up Sandel’s book, I expected a discussion of right and wrong. Sandel bases his investigation on actual life situations which include emergency price hikes during disasters and military draft requirements and marriage rights for same-sex couples. These examples demonstrate that justice exists as an actual life experience which people experience during their regular activities. For me, this immediately shifted how I thought about ethics. The concept of justice operated as a real political principle which people used to discuss during their news debates and everyday dialogues.

Sandel starts by discussing utilitarianism which Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill developed as a theory that justice should create the most happiness for the largest number of people. The basic principles of utilitarianism drew me in because this philosophy evaluates decisions through only how much happiness the decision will bring, which was interesting for me to explore since the philosophy seems pretty simple and fairly democratic but when you put yourself in these positions it’s hard to say if you would follow through with it.

The examples Sandel presented in his argument really made me think critically about what I would do. The author presents the runaway trolley scenario to determine if killing one person would be ethical to save the lives of five others. The utilitarian approach supports this decision yet I couldn’t help but to think about what if the one person was a partner or family member, (or even me!) and the five others were strangers. Would I still approach the scenario with the utilitarian ideal? I doubt that I would let me or people close to me die and let 5 strangers live. Even though the five strangers most likely have people close to them that share the same feelings I have for people close to me. This example really demonstrated to me that I value human dignity and moral limits more than achieving the best possible results. I now think about scenarios like these all the time. For example, what if there WERE active shooters on campus and I saw a friend running for his life towards my car that I would be driving, but at the same time there is a group of 5 others further away. And somehow I wouldn’t be able to save the five strangers AND my friend. What would I do? It's hard to say, maybe I would attempt to save all and fail to save any. It is a hard thing to grapple with but I thought that example was interesting.

Sandel moves from utilitarianism to libertarianism which focuses on individual rights together with free markets and limited government intervention. The protection of free market exchanges and personal property rights serves as the foundation for justice according to Robert Nozick. I respect the libertarian commitment to individual liberty as a core principle. I think it's important to not look at yourself and others as “tools” to get somewhere as a group. Of course there are exceptions but generally speaking it feels more moral to respect each other's liberty.

Sandel presents examples which demonstrate how libertarian principles produce unacceptable results. The practice of selling kidneys for financial survival raises doubts about transactional fairness according to the author. The text showed me that my dedication to freedom exists in the same way as my dedication to equality. The social and economic environment determines our choices according to my perspective on extreme libertarianism. Justice demands that people understand the current social imbalances which exist in society.

Perhaps the most difficult but rewarding part of Sandel’s book is his discussion of Immanuel Kant’s philosophy. Kant rejects utilitarianism because he believes in the importance of duty and autonomy and treating people as ends in themselves. The initial aspect of Kant's writing style that caught my attention was his use of abstract terms which was a challenge to understand. Sandel used Kant’s philosophy to explain dignity which helped me grasp its significance.

Kant would oppose lying to save a life because it uses the deceived person as a tool. My initial impression was that this approach went too far. Kant explained his position through demonstrating that justice requires permanent rules which should not be altered by any situation. I myself do not follow these permanent rules really at all in my life. I mean, when you really think about it, someone who follows the laws would be kind of an asshole to be around or at least I think so. Sometimes it is good to not tell it straight up and to put a subject in a different light so it is easy for the person to process. Nevertheless, Kant’s view, while strict, pushes me to take responsibility for honesty and integrity more seriously.

The concept of "justice of purpose" which Sandel describes as Aristotle's perspective drew my interest the most. Aristotle argues that justice is about giving people what they deserve, based on the purpose of a practice or institution. For example, who should get the best flute?Aristotle says the best flute should go to the best flute player, because the purpose of a flute is to make beautiful music.

This idea provided me with a fresh look about how people discuss things like politics. Groups disagree because they have different views about what institutions should achieve as Sandel explains. In my experience, human beings create disagreements about justice because they hold different perspectives about what makes life significant. This knowledge has allowed me to become more patient and have more humility during debates because it demonstrates that people will not understand each other unless they first define their terms.

Sandel presents an interesting part in the book which explores what money should buy and what it should not. The author shows how markets now penetrate domains which used to fall under moral and civic rules by giving money to children for reading and by selling immigration slots. While markets are efficient, Sandel warns that they can corrupt the values at stake.

This resonated deeply with me. The way Sandel presented his argument forced me to think about whether civic goods should receive the same treatment as commercial products. The value of friendship, civic duty and education disappears when they become subject to commercialization according to my personal perspective. Sandel assisted me in understanding my discomfort about market expansion into all areas of life because it transforms both our acquired goods and our personal identity.

Sandel establishes his preferred approach to justice by focusing on the common good in his final section. Sandel stands apart from libertarians who focus on freedom and utilitarians who focus on results because he places primary importance on civic values and ethical choices. He believes we need to explore the moral and religious elements which establish the basis of justice.

The final part of the book had the most impact on me. The current era of political division makes people want to embrace non-partisan principles which stay away from all moral conflicts. Sandel believes authentic democratic practice demands citizens to join public discussions about their preferred social structure. I agree. I have a fear of political debates yet I understand that staying away from them leads to increased social separation between individuals. Through Sandel I learned to view disagreements as essential because they help us understand our core values and make us listen to different perspectives.

I thought I would also talk about these three essential lessons from the book that will remain with me after reading the book.

Firstly, justice exists in real-world application rather than theoretical concepts. The trolley problem and military service and same-sex marriage present more than abstract dilemmas because they show how philosophical ideas affect both state policies and personal decisions.

Secondly, freedom and equality need to exist in a state of equilibrium. The absence of concern for inequality in libertarian freedom creates an unjust system while utilitarian equality without dignity consideration results in dehumanizing effects. To find the right answers you have to have the right balance.

And Finally, the common good needs dialogue to operate effectively. Human beings will always disagree about moral issues, but we have the power to handle these disagreements through respectful dialogue. Things like political violence which we have seen recently only oppress people and cause harm to our system of democracy.

The book does not contain straightforward solutions. This book was refreshing from most of my books that I get for my classes. Rather than stating different views and arguing for which one is the most effective, this book presents different moral traditions which enable readers to evaluate their personal ethical values. For me, it was a journey of questioning assumptions, confronting stereotypes, and appreciating the complexity of justice. The book provides its most valuable contribution by allowing readers to improve their involvement in ongoing discussions rather than providing opinions to existing debates. The world today is controlled by fast-paced eye-catching statements, yet Sandel shows us that justice needs patience and humility and most importantly requires dialogue even when it is uncomfortable.
chunks.label: Reflections on Sandel's Justice and moral philosophy
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Michael Sandel's book 'Justice: What’s the Right Thing to Do', exploring utilitarianism, libertarianism, Kant, Aristotle, market ethics, and the importance of civic dialogue.
chunks.feelings: interested, challenged, uncomfortable, patient, humble, fearful of political debates, refreshed

nb4697144.title: Growing Up with a Disabled Sibling

chunks.text:
This was such a tragic and moving story. To follow along on your journey with Doug was an enlightening experience. Before this class, I would have never thought how many people mental disorder affects. I mostly just thought about it in an internal way; how it affects the person themselves. Now I know that the family has to step up in severe cases, providing support however they can. Every step in this story, when you found out Doug was hearing voices, to getting him care, to waiting for him to get better, to seeing him gain insight, backslide time and time again, but eventually end up in a good city, with friends and even a girlfriend was really inspiring. It must have been so scary knowing something detrimental could happen at any point, but still trusting he will do good for himself. Doug must have been a very strong willed person to learn coping skills and get his life together so soon after the diagnosis.

Reading about his premature death after all the things your family went through was devastating. It must have been exhausting not only to be his caregiver, but to lose that role in the blink of an eye. What’s even worse is that this probably happens to so many people. Car accidents are far too common and take so many lives. This book really made me think about all the bad things that can happen to someone. Not only that, but how those events impact other people, especially with regards to mental health. Experiencing something like that reshapes how you see the world. You had no further interest in business, and just wanted to find meaning by telling your story. Melissa had Scott for support but ended up moving closer to her mother. The good thing was that at least you guys had a good bond for a few years after Doug’s death. I know that death can either tear people apart or bring them closer. This seemed like one blessing in a river of sorrow.
chunks.label: Reflections on Doug's journey and loss
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on reading an author's biographical book about caring for a family member named Doug with schizophrenia and his tragic premature death.

chunks.text: I really resonated with how you discussed being a caregiver to Doug. I’ve seen firsthand how intensive a role of a caregiver is. My little sister is disabled. She is nonverbal, has limited mobility, and has a lot of health concerns. She has a number of medications to control her seizures, mood swings, and vitamins to keep her relatively healthy. She can’t do things normal kids do. When we found out she was disabled, my mom jumped right in to all the doctors’ appointments and diagnostics. It has been nine years since my sister was diagnosed with 13.31q deletion syndrome. My mom has been the primary caregiver the whole time and I’ve seen it affect her in so many ways. Like you said in your book, she has faced the mental consequences of being a caregiver. She has less of a social life, and she has sacrificed her hobbies and career to take care of my sister. Because of this, she has been struggling with her anxiety disorder, self-confidence, and depression. However, she loves my sister and makes the most of it. After 10 years of caregiving for my sister, my mom is able to communicate with her nonverbally. Sometimes it even seems like they are reading each other’s minds. My mom celebrates the little victories now, like when my sister eats a new food or has the energy to walk around.
chunks.label: Mother caregiving for disabled sister
chunks.what_happened: The student witnessed their mother become the primary caregiver for the student's severely disabled sister, seeing how it affected their mother's career, mental health, and social life over ten years.

chunks.text: Knowing what I know, it is interesting to see how the caregiving relationship is for someone with a mental disorder. Being a caregiver to Doug is unlike my experience, where my mom and sister interact every day. A long distance caregiving relationship is very different. In both cases, you are making sure the person is taken care of. While my mom can physically look at my sister and keep her safe, you did not have that luxury. He wasn’t a child with a disability, but a grown man with schizophrenia. I did not even know people could be caregivers for that. It had to have taken a lot of trust between the two of you to get to where you were in his last few months.
chunks.label: Comparing caregiving dynamics
chunks.what_happened: The student contrasts the author's long-distance caregiving for an adult with schizophrenia to their own family's daily in-person care for a disabled child.
chunks.people: the author, Doug, mother, little sister

chunks.text: Another thing I resonated with was Melissa. I am the oldest child, followed by four disruptive siblings. Two of my younger brothers are impulsive and have anger issues. My youngest brother has ADHD and my little sister, as I said before, is severely disabled. I’ve always been the “easy” one. I like to follow rules, be nice to people, and get straight As. I also have a strong personality, like how you described Melissa. I will eventually be moving far away from my family as well, putting distance between my parents and I, as did Melissa. I have also struggled with depression and anxiety and felt invisible. It’s interesting to see how being the “glass child,” or even the eldest girl, can affect people’s personality and mental health in similar ways. I’ve been comparing my experience with others for a long time now. It is definitely comforting to know that others experience similar things as me.
chunks.label: Growing up as the eldest glass child
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up as the oldest sibling alongside four disruptive or disabled siblings, striving to be the well-behaved child while struggling with anxiety, depression, and feeling invisible.

chunks.text:
In the first few steps of yours and Doug’s journey with schizophrenia, there was a lot of discovery involved. When he first admitted to you his hallucinations, it was shocking. The element of stigma came into play immediately there, when you said you were a little bit scared of him. This made me realize our society associates schizophrenia with danger and fear. I’m not sure when I learnt this, but if I saw someone talking to no one on the street, I would walk faster. It is bad that in our modern society, we still have a long way to go with regards to understanding and tolerance. The insert you put about stigma was very helpful in understanding how transformative this experience was. When you realized Doug was hallucinating and possibly schizophrenic, you didn’t really know what to do other than send him away. That does make the most sense initially. What do you tell friends, family, and neighbors? I would be scared of people acting weird around me or walking on eggshells. Stigma is so prevalent in our society.

I thought this book offered really unique insight to schizophrenia. In the past, I’ve only read or heard about mental disorder firsthand. I have watched videos and movies on schizophrenia in the past, but I enjoyed reading an outside view on someone with schizophrenia. You never really knew what he was thinking, but you got him help and stood by his side through it all. I was so curious about what he did when he left Madden, why he left Madden and whether or not the neighborhood boys were actually threatening him or not. It was also very interesting how you included the “Grief” section and compared each stage to what you went through. I didn’t know that was possible for someone who was still alive.
chunks.label: Reflections on schizophrenia, stigma, and grief
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how the book portrays schizophrenia and examines societal stigma and the stages of grief applied to a living person.

chunks.text: It made me think of my sister again, and I began to associate my own experiences with the stages of grief. I remember experiencing denial when my sister gained then lost around 25 words. She couldn’t even speak sentences yet when her disability caught up with her. I did not accept that she was disabled for a very long time. It was about until she was five, and was now going off to elementary school and couldn’t speak or play. She was developmentally still a baby. At this point I was in middle school, and the anger came in. I was so angry that I couldn’t have one normal sister. I have 3 brothers and was so excited to play with her and grow up with her. I felt like I got that ripped away from me. Bargaining was when I decided to be a doctor so I could cure people like her. I had heard about stem cells and that was it, I decided to cure chromosomal disorders. Depression was when I couldn’t even look at her. I still feel guilty about it. I love her to death, but it was just too hard to see her in her bed all the time. Finally, acceptance, which I believe I just reached this past summer. I started to help my mom with her medicine and caregiving, and I feel like I finally saw my sister for exactly who she was. I stopped wanting her to be normal after that. I’ve reached the point where she would not be my sister if she didn’t have her disability.
chunks.label: Stages of grief over sister's disability
chunks.what_happened: The student went through denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and finally acceptance regarding their sister's severe disability, eventually helping with her care.
chunks.feelings: in denial, angry, excited, depressed, guilty, loving, accepting
chunks.people: the student, little sister, mother, three brothers

chunks.text:
I did not know what to expect when I read this book. It ended up taking me on so many unexpected twists and turns. It would get scary then uncomfortable then flat out difficult. From him first admitting his hallucinations (although not admitting that they were hallucinations) to him leaving his group home and going off the grid for three weeks. I think the “Tough Love” and “In The Wind” chapters had to be the most scary to experience. You have to approach this new dynamic so carefully, but also support Doug’s growth as a person. Navigating that must have been tough. Then when he decided he wanted to go back to Pittsburgh, you had to respect his autonomy. This surely did not seem like the most stable decision but you both had to find compromise.

My favorite chapter was definitely “Mercy” because everything was looking up. I could tell you felt it and he did as well. He finally found a good connection with a therapist, and it opened him up. He gained insight, found friends, and was being more social. After everything you guys had gone through it had to have felt like a win. On top of that, him getting to go to a wedding and see his family one last time was refreshing. The way you described him being the “highlight” of your day was adorable. I loved this book because I do not normally read biographical works. I usually stick to fiction, but this was a nice change in my routine. It was a very riveting book and I believe I got some lessons from it. One was to hug my siblings. The other is to give people more grace and acceptance. Our world could use more empathy.
chunks.label: Final reflections on the book's impact
chunks.what_happened: The student reviews key chapters of the book, praising its narrative arc and explaining the lessons of empathy, acceptance, and sibling love they took from it.

n89acaec5.title: Confronting the Stigma of Mental Illness

chunks.text:
“A Boy Broken”, written by Douglas J. Engelman in June of 2023, is a story about a father’s experience after his eldest son, Douglas Jr., is diagnosed with schizophrenia. The story takes the reader through firsthand events leading up to the diagnosis, the diagnosis itself, and how the Engelman family moved forward after not only Douglas Jr.’s (Doug’s) diagnosis, but also his death that occurred eight years later.

In his work, Engelman (2023) shares his personal firsthand experiences with schizophrenia in order to help readers better understand the mental disorder. His goal, as I interpreted it, was to assist others who have been affected by a mental disorder diagnosis, whether it be personally, as a caregiver, or simply affecting someone close to you. He rawly describes his emotions, which allows others to relate to and not feel so ashamed or just upset with themselves when they feel those same emotions. He discusses the stigma surrounding mental disorders and why this stigma has to be broken in order for society to move forward. And, in order for individuals and their families to confidently be able to reach out for help and support during one of the hardest times of their lives. Engelman (2023) describes this stigma as “inhibiting recovery and a favorable life outcome for the person with mental illness” (p. 29).

Theories and Stigma:

Theories like the symbolic interactionist and labeling contribute to the overall stigma and perception of mental illness or disorder. Once born, individuals are expected to conform to the societal ideals of “normal” behavior. If a person goes against these societal norms, values, and beliefs, they face the consequence of being labeled “deviant”. Edwin Lemert, an American sociologist, divided this “deviant” label into two separate terms, primary deviance and secondary deviance. Primary deviance “is associated with non-normative behavior” (Engelman 2023:26). Engelman provides schizophrenia as an example. So, Doug being diagnosed with the mental disorder already put him in a box, labeling him deviant, though it was not his choice to not be “normal” according to society, just an unfortunate circumstance. Secondary deviance is when an individual assumes their deviant identity and acts out because of society’s prejudice towards them. In the book, we did not see secondary deviance in Doug; in fact, he worked diligently to be one of the ten percent with schizophrenia who go on to live a normal life.

Another American sociologist, Bruce Link, connected stigma to labeling theory. He claimed that “stigma of the label ‘mentally ill’ is internalized and imposes social stresses on the individual, to which the person adapts by implementing coping strategies such as concealing the condition…or the outright withdrawal of the individual from social interaction” (Engelman 2023:27-28). The stigma surrounding those who are deemed mentally ill makes an already difficult situation even more difficult for both the individual and their family. A Canadian sociologist, Erving Goffman, explained how stigma applied to the mentally disordered leads them to restricted social opportunities, and changes in self-identity” (Engelman 2023: 28). It is also brought up in the text that stigma impedes one’s ability to recover from a mental disorder.

Later on in this paper, it will be discussed how Doug overcomes this stigma associated with his schizophrenia diagnosis and goes on to receive treatment, respond very well to that treatment, land himself a job, and be able to live on his own (like many others with the disorder cannot).

We see the author and his family also react to the stigma caused by his son’s diagnosis. Originally, Engelman (2023) tried to hide Doug’s diagnosis due to fear of what others would think of him as a parent, even though the diagnosis had nothing to do with his parenting. Engelman then dove into how he questioned if the diagnosis was his fault. If he had not divorced Doug’s mother, if he had not moved away, if he had been more present. But all of these what-ifs are not an explanation for how or why Doug ended up being diagnosed with the disorder. The only fact that truly mattered was how the author helped his son deal with the disorder.

If it had not been for his unwavering support and love for his son, I do not think Doug would have been a part of that small ten percent that comes out on top, and is able to live normally (for the most part). It is truly admirable to be able to, what I felt was, experience just how much a father loves his son, how far he is willing to go, how much he is willing to do. And, in the end, it worked out beautifully; all of both Engelman and Doug’s hard work paid off.

Doug’s Story:

At age twenty, Doug was diagnosed with drug-induced schizophrenia. Doug’s first psychotic break was witnessed by his sister Melissa. He was outside on the back porch, repeatedly yelling the phrase “Why do they have to die?” for ten minutes (Engelman 2023:6). Melissa was worried, so she called the police. Officer Thomas arrived on the scene and talked it out with Doug. The author reached out to Officer Thomas in hopes of finding answers to his questions. The officer relayed his belief that Doug may be schizophrenic and that he should be checked out by medical professionals.

The author’s first experience of realizing his son may be schizophrenic occurred when he picked Doug up the morning after the incident to go to breakfast. While in the car, Doug mentioned that two people, Wendy and Dave, were always with him. Doug said that Wendy was in the car with them when it was only the author in the driver’s seat and his son in the passenger seat. While in the car, Doug experienced severe pain in his abdomen. He claimed that Dave and Wendy could put their hands inside of him, and that was what was causing it.

Doug’s Uncle Harry, on his father’s side, was also diagnosed with schizophrenia in his early twenties. The family history, and as the author mentioned later on, Doug’s frequent smoking of marijuana could be attributed to the development of his disorder, but this question was not specifically answered.

Doug’s first experience in the medical field was at Loyola Medical Center’s Mental Health unit. His father dropped him off for intake there, and he was taken right into a thirty-day program. This is where Doug was first medicated for his disorder, and he was responding well, saying it was “helping him think straight” (Engelman 2023:63). His first days at the facility were spent in solitary where he was heavily medicated. He then underwent individual and group therapy sessions, and eventually exposure to the rest of the patients in the facility.

After the month at Loyola, Doug was moved to John J. Madden Mental Health Center. Madden allowed Doug more professional care, more exposure to experimental anti-psychotics, and more therapy (Engelman 2023:65). Once in the care of Madden, Doug had his first experience with a group home, where he ended up staying for nine months. During his stay at the group home, Doug experienced ups and downs. His money was taken from him, and later on, he was threatened. This threat caused Doug to return home to the author’s house one day, claiming he needed to leave Madden.

Three weeks after coming back to Madden from his father’s, that one night, Doug disappeared. It was not until three weeks after his disappearance that Doug reached out to his father. For three weeks, Doug was out on the streets, staying at Franciscan Outreach during the nights. After the phone call, Engelman (2023) went directly to pick up his son and brought him home. They had dinner, talked, and decided it would be best for Doug to move out of the group home.

Doug ended up moving into an apartment with an older man. At this apartment, Doug landed himself a job. After over half a year at this place, Doug decided he wanted to go back to Pittsburgh, where he was surrounded by family that he was missing.

When back in Pittsburgh, Doug had moved back in with his mother and was serviced by Chartiers Mental Health/Mental Rehabilitation Center. He stayed with his mother for two years before moving out and moving in with his sister Melissa, which lasted only for a year.

Eventually, the author came to Pittsburgh to help with Doug’s situation along with his sister and mother. They found Doug an apartment where he faced some challenges. He was continuing to abuse weed and alcohol even though he knew it was bad for him to partake in them with his diagnosis. And he was not staying consistent with his medication. While at this apartment, and hanging out with old friends Chuck and Bob, Doug found himself frequently in trouble with the police. It was in his best interest that he move, so he did.

When Doug moved apartments, he ended up moving to a new mental health facility, Mercy Behavioral Health. It was at Mercy where Doug began to flourish more than ever before. His new therapist, Julie Gatti, helped him in ways he had not been helped before. Engelman (2023) noted that “It was clear she had reached him in a way that no one else had previously” (p. 123). Doug was getting a handle on his substance abuse during this time, and his progress with his overall diagnosis became even more prominent.

Doug stayed in the area but moved into his own home, where he was approved for Section 8 housing. He had made such a nice life for himself, even regaining employment at his old high school job where he installed carpeting. With all of these amazing opportunities happening to Doug, he gained “a sense of purpose and optimism” that his father, the author, had not seen in years.

The last time the author saw Doug in life was at Doug’s Uncle’s wedding. Doug was doing great.

The last time Doug and his father talked over the phone on December 16, 1988, things were really looking up for him. He called just “to say how great I’m doing. How happy I am” (Engelman 2023:135). Doug had plans to go back to school, but sadly, three days after their last call, Doug was killed in a tragic car accident.

Summary:

During the eight years of living with schizophrenia, Doug became one of the ten percent to live a somewhat normal life. Tragically, that life was cut short.

This book delivers a sense of hope to its readers, whether they have experience with mental disorder or not, hope for families made up of mentally disordered individuals. With hard work and determination, people can overcome and be more than their disorder.
chunks.label: Review of A Boy Broken
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes and reflects on Douglas J. Engelman's book 'A Boy Broken,' discussing theories of deviance and stigma alongside Doug's journey with schizophrenia.

chunks.text: While reading the book, I felt certain aspects on a personal level. When I had my first depressive episode, I was too scared to admit it to my mother. I did not want her to blame herself that I no longer wanted to live. Eventually, I had to admit it to her.
chunks.label: Confessing first depressive episode to mother
chunks.what_happened: During their first depressive episode, the student was afraid to admit to their mother that they no longer wanted to live, but eventually told her.

chunks.text:
So, I think this book and how the author dealt with and supported his son through his entire diagnosis and life can help others struggling to get over the “shameful stigma” and reach out for support. If I had not already had my conversation with my mother, I most definitely would have after reading this book.

Source:

Engelman, Douglas J. 2023. A Boy Broken. Kindle Direct Publishing.
chunks.label: Concluding thoughts and citation
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the book's value for overcoming stigma and seeking support, concluding with a formal citation for the text.

n89c03863.title: Redefining the Future of Family Structures

chunks.text:
This generation is all together skipping that or waiting a longer period because they want to be sure of the decision, and the social expectations have lightened up as far as getting married, starting a family, and living happily ever after. I think that this will continue as a part of the continuing social progression, and legislation will be forced to catch up with the majority's sentiment. I think that divorce laws will loosen up in things like No-Fault divorce, and the amount of time that you need to be “separated” before being able to officially file for divorce.

To support yourself, and potentially a family in this economy, it would be ideal for both partners to have full-time jobs. I see this continuing, as everything is continuing to get more expensive. The economy ebbs and flows, but right now and for the foreseeable future, inflation is only going to get worse. With both parents working, to be able to afford daily basics, there is no one in the house that is left to watch the children at home. Some families must choose between scraping by because one parent (usually the mother) must stay home or scraping by because childcare costs so much. I think with increased accessibility to teleworking, this will be less of a problem as far as childcare is concerned.

Even with companies that allow teleworking, there is still some period where employees must physically be in the office. If there is no option for teleworking for some reason, then we are back to square one, with no one to watch the kids. There is the option of a childcare facility, but the rates for those places can be an extra financial burden on top of other general living expenses. The average range of childcare facility costs in the United States is $400-$1,500 a month. Families who can afford childcare are considered luxurious, and almost unattainable.

In recent years, there has been a shift in social ideas about single parenthood. There will always be a racial and gender factor that will slightly change these ideas, but people are starting to see that single parenthood isn’t always negative. In 2018, a study found that one third of single parents are Black, and 71% of single parents are mothers (Livingston, 2018). Even though mothers take up a lot of real estate in single parenthood, fathers are becoming more prevalent in this group too, due to the shifting ideas that it is okay for a father to be a nurturing and caretaking parent. The setting of single parenthood is also a big part of this trend; some single parents are in multigenerational homes; others are single by choice. The “by-choice” situation was seen to emerge in the 1980s, and I predict that this trend will continue through 2035. This generation is hyper fixated on being as independent as possible, because we all have trust issues and horrible relationship trauma. We also have parents who had messy divorces, or stepfamilies that cause drama. I even have a close friend that for a while, he dreamed of being a single father and traveling the world with his future kid. This generation's ability to romanticize lifestyles that aren’t as common or as lucrative will be a determining factor for the increase in single parenthood.

Further on non-traditional domestic arrangements, I feel blended families will be a large increase within the next 10 years. If about 50% of marriages end in divorce, then 50% of people have the decision to either remarry, stay single, or possibly cohabitate with a new long-term partner. A blended family is defined as a family where one or both parents have kids from a previous marriage, get together in a long-term relationship. These parents can also decide to have their own children or adopt in this new arrangement. I think that there will be a lot more instances of cohabitation instead of remarriage. This generation is grossly untrusting as it is, if individuals take the leap to get married and it does not work out, there will be less people who sign up to repeat the process.

A lot of people are also finding out how truthful the phrase “It takes a village” can be. I think with the state of the economy, we will see a lot more kinship systems. Some people in these systems other than the parents may be providing financially for the child or children, but I think mostly these systems will be used to reduce financial strain on the biological parents. When you have a tight-knit system of people that you trust with your child, you won’t need childcare. If the people in these networks are willing to watch these children for an extended period, or in consecutive days, this allows the parents more time to work, which leads to the parents being able to save up more money for future experiences with their families.

If LGBTQ+ couples will still have the right to be married and have children in the next 10 years, I think that we will see more openly lesbian and gay families. They will be adopting children, as that is an option at the forefront of their minds, because biological kids aren’t the typical route unless someone has kids from a previous marriage. I’m not sure if “increase” is the right word, I just think that more families will be open about this arrangement they have. If legislation passes that removes this right, I think we will start to hear about it less as time goes on, but there will still be a large chunk of the population who have lesbian, gay, or gender-nonconforming parents. There will still be children being adopted by LGBTQ+ families, but there will be a bit of fabrication on the documents. Things like lavender marriages will be what is presented to the outside, but the people parenting the child will be a part of the community.

Overall, I think that we will have a hard time strictly defining “family” in the next 10 years, and that is not a problem. We will continue to move away from the heteronormative, white “picture perfect” family that was only viable in the 1950s because of women’s lack of rights and freedom to be an independent person and their expectation to be baby incubators who also cook and clean at home and aren’t expected to be anything except for content with their lives. Not everyone and everything is meant to be the same, and the push for individuality without fear of social consequences has been more prominent over the last 10 years has done wonders, and I can only assume that it will continue to be that way in the next 10 years, assuming we still have the right to.

References

Ahmed, F. (2023). Generation Z’s thoughts on dating, marriage, and mating.

Brown, S. L., & Lin, I.-F. (2022). The graying of divorce: A half century of change. The Journals of Gerontology: Series B, 77(9), 1710–1720. https://doi.org/10.1093/geronb/gbac057

Illumine. (n.d.). How much childcare costs by state in USA. https://illumine.app/blog/how-much-childcare-costs-by-state-in-usa

Yorks, J. (2022). Singled out no longer: The changing narratives and types of single‐parent families. Sociology Compass, 16(2), Article e12951. https://doi.org/10.1111/soc4.12951
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of future family structures
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on shifting social expectations around marriage, the economic strains of childcare, the rise of single parenthood and blended families, kinship networks, and LGBTQ+ families, concluding with a reference list.

chunks.text:
In practice, this maps onto how many of us already reason when stakes are high. Hospitals triage. Governments budget. Even in ordinary life I allocate time and attention where they do the most good—helping a teammate who’s struggling before polishing a slide that’s already fine, or donating to a malaria charity that demonstrably saves lives rather than a vanity cause that merely makes me feel generous. Utilitarianism tells me I’m not cynical for thinking about numbers; I’m responsible.

Mill’s insistence on qualitative differences in pleasures—his “better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied”—also matters. It answers a caricature Sandel notes: utilitarianism is not addicted to shallow pleasures so much as committed to human flourishing broadly conceived. If reading, making music, or building a fair institution predictably deepens lives, then a utilitarian can rank those goods higher because they reliably produce more and richer happiness.

The best objections bite—and change how I apply utility

Where Sandel presses hardest is also where my own view softened. The first worry is about rights. If maximizing the balance of happiness could justify punishing an innocent person to quell a riot, we sense the calculus has gone wrong. Similarly, we recoil at throwing the “fat man” off the bridge in the trolley problem even if it would stop the train. These cases remind me that some actions are wrong not only because of what they cause but because of what they are—they use a person merely as a means. Mill tries to address this by building rights into the utility calculus (societies that protect rights do better overall), but the thought experiment exposes a limit: in extreme cases, rights look like side constraints, not merely rules of thumb.

The second worry is about measuring the unmeasurable. Sandel discusses cost-benefit calculations that put dollar values on human life—the Ford Pinto case has become emblematic. While some valuation is unavoidable in policy (every speed limit and drug approval implies risk trade-offs), Sandel is persuasive that certain ways of doing the math can degrade what we value. If a spreadsheet treats a vulnerable group’s suffering as a small externality, we haven’t just made a calculation; we’ve missed a moral reality. This pushes me toward rule utilitarianism: instead of justifying each act by its immediate payoffs, I favor rules that, if generally followed, predictably maximize well-being while protecting persons against being sacrificed in the name of efficiency.

Libertarianism, obligation, and why negative rights matter yet don’t settle the question

Sandel’s neighboring chapter on libertarianism made me appreciate the moral power of negative rights—the idea that others are obligated not to interfere with what I own and how I live, so long as I don’t harm them. Libertarianism dignifies consent and bodily autonomy: no one may conscript my life plans for their purposes.

I agree with that much. Yet utilitarianism warns me not to stop there. Libertarian freedom can ignore structural harms that are invisible if we fixate only on non-interference. A society that refuses to tax wealth to fund basic healthcare might pride itself on respecting self-ownership, but the predictable misery that follows is a moral cost we can count. This is where Sandel’s examples involving civil rights and equal access resonate: sometimes the best way to protect everyone’s negative rights over time is to invest in conditions that enable real options now. Freedom without capabilities rings hollow.

Rawls’s difference principle as a friend, not a foe, to utility

I read Rawls’s veil-of-ignorance device as a utilitarian ally. Behind the veil, we don’t know whether we’ll be born into wealth or poverty, health or disability. In that uncertainty, it seems rational to choose social rules that maximize the floor, not just the average. Rawls’s difference principle—arrange inequalities so they benefit the least advantaged—can be reframed as a risk-averse version of maximizing expected well-being. Large gains for those already well-off often return less happiness than smaller gains for those in severe need, because of diminishing marginal utility. So a safety net isn’t charity; it’s a predictable way to make the overall sum of well-being larger, in line with utilitarian aims, while also respecting persons by ensuring basic capabilities.

Admissions, merit, and telos: what are colleges for?

Sandel’s line that “admission is not an honor bestowed for superior merit or virtue” forced me to examine a comfortable story. If a seat at a university is simply a prize for individual excellence, then fairness looks like perfect rank ordering by scores. But Sandel reframes the practice through Aristotle’s telos: to decide who should be admitted, first ask what the institution is for. If a college exists to create certain kinds of learning communities, to train citizens, to pursue research, and to serve the public good, then it may justly select a class that advances those purposes, not merely the highest test scores.

From a utilitarian angle, this isn’t a betrayal of fairness; it’s a broader outcomes question. A class with genuine diversity of background and experience often yields better learning and better service to the public—consequences that matter. But Sandel’s caution helps: if we treat admission as pure social engineering, we risk instrumentalizing applicants for institutional goals. The sweet spot, I think, is to align individual opportunity with the mission’s social payoffs—a rule-utilitarian compromise that avoids fetishizing “merit” while preserving respect for applicants as ends in themselves.

Markets and the Baby M case: the utilitarian case for guardrails

Sandel’s discussion of surrogacy (and Elizabeth Anderson’s critique) captures another utilitarian tension. On one side, allowing willing adults to enter contracts like surrogacy can increase overall happiness: infertile couples find families, gestational carriers are compensated, and the arrangement is consensual. On the other side, certain market logics can corrupt meanings and produce subtle harms—turning parenthood into a commodity, exerting pressure on economically vulnerable women, or treating a child as the object of purchase. A purely act-utilitarian defense—if both parties consent and the outcome is net positive, it’s fine—can miss long-run effects on dignity and social trust.

My takeaway is again rule-based. A regulated surrogacy regime—cooling-off periods, independent counseling, clear parentage rules, bans on coercive contracts, fair compensation, and robust protections for the surrogate’s health—predictably produces better outcomes over time than either prohibition or laissez-faire. It keeps faith with the utilitarian aim (more families, less suffering) while honoring the non-fungible values at stake.

Obligations to strangers: the demanding edge of utility

If there is a part of utilitarianism that scares me, it is how demanding it can be once we recognize the scale of need. In the spirit of Peter Singer’s “shallow pond,” Sandel gently pushes readers to see that distance and numbers don’t erase obligation: if I would ruin my shoes to save a drowning child nearby, why wouldn’t I forgo luxuries to save children far away? A consistent utilitarianism challenges my comfort. It demands giving effectively, voting for policies that reduce global suffering (pandemic preparedness, climate mitigation), and shouldering fair taxes to fund programs that prevent predictable harms.

This is where a utilitarian lens becomes not only personal but political. Cost-effective health interventions (vaccines, bed nets), emissions policies that prevent catastrophic harms, and housing rules that reduce homelessness all pass a straightforward maximizing test. Sandel’s broader tour of justice reminds me that this is what politics is for—to make the trade-offs explicit, to argue about the values we honor, and to choose the rules that leave the fewest people worse off.

Where I draw the line: utility with side constraints

So where does this leave my self-description? I’m still a utilitarian because I think outcomes matter morally, and pretending otherwise often just hides whose outcomes we’re ignoring. But I’m a utilitarian who has learned from Sandel to value three constraints:

Rights as real limits, not just heuristics. We should adopt rules that refuse to sacrifice basic liberties even when a short-term calculus tempts us. Societies that keep those side constraints tend to do better anyway—and, more importantly, they respect persons as inviolable.

Telos as a guide to design. Before maximizing, ask what the practice is for. You can’t optimize a university, a marriage, or a court unless you honor its purpose. Otherwise, utility talk becomes blind to meaning and invites corruption of value.

Distribution matters. Because of diminishing marginal utility, how benefits and burdens are distributed is central to the sum of well-being. Rawls’s veil formalizes that insight, and it dovetails with utilitarianism’s concern for those at the bottom of the heap.

These constraints don’t abandon utility; they discipline it. They push me toward rule utilitarianism and toward institutional design that predictably raises human welfare while protecting the values we cannot price.

A few places I’m still wrestling

Sandel encourages critique, not closure, so I’ll end with the tensions I haven’t fully solved:

Measuring what matters. We can count lives saved or years in school. But how do we incorporate dignity, belonging, or meaningful work without either hand-waving or reductionism? Mill’s “higher pleasures” gesture in the right direction; I’m still looking for better proxies that policymakers can use without cynicism.

Preference formation. Utilitarianism often treats people’s preferences as the inputs. But many preferences are shaped by unjust structures or advertising. Should a planner maximize current preferences or the preferences people would hold under fair conditions? Rawls’s and Aristotle’s emphasis on education and virtue here is not a luxury; it’s the precondition for sensible maximization.

Partiality and personal ties. If I must always choose the option that produces the most total good, how much partiality to family and friends is morally permitted? A rule utilitarian answer—allow partiality up to the point where it predictably sustains valuable social roles—seems right, but the boundary is fuzzy.

Speech and offense. Libertarian non-interference protects expression; utilitarianism asks us to weigh harms. In polarized environments, it’s hard to separate transient discomfort (which may be the price of learning) from genuine degradation. Sandel’s classroom method—argue in good faith, name the values at stake—models a practice whose telos is mutual understanding, not victory.

Conclusion: maximizing with humility

Sandel’s book didn’t convert me away from utilitarianism; it matured it. I still think the core moral demand is to reduce suffering and increase flourishing impartially. But I now see more clearly that the best way to do that, over time, is not to run a ceaseless act-by-act calculus. It is to adopt rules and build institutions that honor persons, respect purposes, and attend to fair distribution—because human beings are not just containers of pleasure and pain but agents whose dignity and relationships generate the very goods we want to maximize.

Calling myself a utilitarian, then, is less a declaration of a calculator’s creed than a promise about attention: to count everyone, to face trade-offs honestly, and to choose policies that predictably leave fewer people worse off. Sandel’s tour through Rawls’s fairness, libertarian freedom, Aristotelian purpose, and market limits equips me with the humility to do that work better—aware of the edges where numbers mislead, where rights must stand firm, and where the telos of a practice tells us what “the most good” even means.
chunks.label: Reflections on utilitarianism, Sandel, and justice
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on reading Michael Sandel and evaluates utilitarianism, discussing its limits, rule utilitarianism, libertarianism, Rawls's difference principle, affirmative action, surrogacy, demandingness, and unresolved moral questions.

chunks.text:
Marriage as a Selective Institution: Education, Cohabitation, and the future of the Traditional Family by 2035

Olaf Sanchez-Parada

Department of Sociology and Criminology, University of North Carolina Wilmington

SOC 345-Sociology of the Family

October 24, 2025

As we examine the trends of the nuclear family in the United States over the past two decades, certain trends point to a decline in marriage rates, accompanied by the rise of an individualistic society, and a growing preference for cohabitation over traditional marriage. This paper does not aim to judge whether the decline of the nuclear family, that historically has been encompassed by a male breadwinner and stay at home mother, is right or wrong; instead, it seeks to explain how these trends may evolve into 2035. By analyzing studies linking education level to marriage rates, the increasing participation of women in the workforce, the rise of the individualistic self, and the rise of cohabitation, this paper argues that marriage is becoming a rare and more selective institution, accessible primarily to those with economic stability.

Education has a complex relationship with marriage. A 2010 Pew Research Center study found that in 2008, 64 percent of college graduates were married compared to just 48 percent of individuals with a high school diploma or less. Both groups were equally likely to aspire to marriage, but those with less education placed more emphasis on financial stability before marrying (The Decline of Marriage and Rise of New Families, 2010). More recent research complicates this picture. Ahn and Winters (2025) found that higher education can delay marriage, particularly for adults aged 25 to 34, but it also increases marital stability, reducing the prevalence of divorce, separation, or widowhood (Ahn & Winters, 2025). Current trends point that the delay in marriage is also due to the rise in cohabitation. Today the rise of cohabitating with a partner before transitioning to marriage is becoming more of the norm. This trend as pointed out by Sassler and Daniel (2020) is more popular among college educated women.
