However, this transition of singlehood to marriage with cohabitation as the anchor point, has a thin line of separation and as referenced by Sassler and Daniel (2020) is primarily dependent on economic stability. The argument could be made that financial instability makes it harder for couples, even those who are college-educated to successfully transition from cohabitation to marriage. The rise in cohabitation has not only led to a decline in marriage but has also led to the new trend of couples choosing to have children within cohabitating relationships rather than waiting for marriage. The work by Sassler and Daniel (2020) highlight how between 2006 and 2010, childbirth from cohabitating women was at 23 percent. This percentage increased from 14 percent in 2003 (Sassler & Daniel, 2020). This trend helps paint the picture that for many couples in the U.S. having children has become a more prominent factor in forming partnerships than forming those same partnerships through marriage. The rise in cohabitation, whether due to economic pressures, evolution of social norms, and the decline of nonmarital births viewed as taboo by society, have made the raising of children within cohabitating couples socially acceptable.

This delay in marriage, combined with the increasing acceptability of childbearing withing cohabiting couples, interacts with the fertility patterns presented in the study by (Nitsche & Hayford, 2020). Their study highlighted fertility trends which show that highly educated women, particularly those desiring larger families, are more likely to remain childless, largely due to the fact that postponed marriage narrows the window for childbearing. Highly educated men who marry later also face higher rates of childlessness, though the effect is somewhat smaller. These findings suggest that higher education provides individuals with greater strategic freedom and independence, allowing them to prioritize careers and personal goals, but ultimately at the cost of a delayed family formation. Ultimately, higher education shapes marriage and parenthood in ways that make them more selective and strategic. While fewer highly educated individuals marry or have children at younger ages, those who do are more likely to form stable unions and make deliberate partner choices, signaling a shift from marriage as a universal milestone to a targeted life strategy (Nitsche & Hayford, 2020).

Current research shows that this delay in marriage has also contributed to a comprehensive shift in society that researchers call the Second Demographic Transition (SDT). This shift in society emphasizes that personal choice, emotional fulfillment, and lifestyle preferences play a heavier role in family formation than traditional institutions like marriage. This shift in society from societal to individualistic norms is central to the SDT theory. As individuals pursue self-actualization and freedom. SDT helps explain both the decline in marriage and marital fertility and the simultaneous increase in childbearing and childrearing within cohabiting couples. I think that by 2035 marriage rates will continue to decline and cohabitation among partners and blended families will be the norm. This personal belief is supported by the study of Manning (2015) which highlights how in 2015, only 5 percent of unmarried single pregnant women got married before their child was born, ensuring the child was not born out of wedlock. This is a significant change compared to 1970 when 30 percent of single unmarried pregnant women got married before the child was born (Manning, 2015). From a blended family perspective, the study by Manning (2015) also shares how 37 percent of children in cohabiting families live with their step or half siblings. Manning also shares how this trend is more prevalent in cohabiting families than families with married parents.

Overall, current data demonstrates how the level of education plays a key role in shaping how cohabiting couples transition into marriage as the economic outcomes associated with the formation of the family. As pointed out by Manning (2015) research demonstrates how parents in cohabitating households usually have a lower educational level than their married counterparts. This gap in education is closely tied to differences in income and wealth. As noted by Manning (2015) there is a 50 percent lower median income in cohabiting parent households compared to married households. Other disparities surface such as cohabiting parent households are also more prone to experience poverty, have scarce access to homeownership, and lack health insurance. All of which lead to financial burdens and undermine the long-term stable resources for children. These patterns aim towards the idea that education is a key factor in determining both the feasibility and strategic value of marriage. Couples with a higher education are more likely to obtain the economic and social resources needed to successfully transition from cohabitation to marriage, while those couples with a lower education level tend to remain in cohabitating relationships due to economic constraints and disparities. This trend falls right into place with the SDT framework, that emphasizes individuality, delayed marriage, and the prioritization of personal goals over traditional societal expectations. Given these trends, by 2035, marriage will no longer be a traditional institution but will evolve into a selective and strategic one. One where couples with a higher education and income will use these resources to consolidate economic stability, plan to intentionally have children, and form stable relationships. On the other hand, couples with lower education will tend to cohabit without moving to marriage. As both family formation and patterns of fertility are increasingly influenced and shaped by education and economic capability, this reflects a comprehensive shift in society that no longer views marriage as a universal norm but one that is a targeted strategic life choice. A choice that by 2035 will be selective to just those who can afford it.
chunks.label: Sociological analysis of marriage, education, and cohabitation trends
chunks.what_happened: The student presents an academic paper analyzing demographic trends, research studies, and sociological theories regarding education, cohabitation, and marriage leading up to 2035.

n396491da.title: Finding Purpose in Student Government Debates

chunks.text:
In Michael J. Sandel's book titled Justice: What’s the Right Thing to Do? Sandel invites the reader to consider a multitude of different philosophical approaches through different philosophers. Michael J. Sandel, a Harvard lecturer, is incredibly well sought after due to his lectures being in high demand because he is so well informed on the topics he discusses. His book, Justice, was on the New York Times Bestseller list for its thought provoking and hard-hitting topics. Those topics span from Immanuel Kant to Aristotle and focus on things such as moral standings, libertarianism, utilitarianism, and more. In Justice: What’s the Right Thing to Do, Sandel presents the reader with many different perspectives on human life and the value of it.

Immanuel Kant is one of the first philosophers that Sandel mentions. Kant was born in 1724 and passed away in 1804. He was born in Prussia to a Protestant family that focused on doing good works for the church and religion. Kant was an academically inclined individual who tended to look for ways to continue his learning. Kant’s first job was as an unpaid lecturer whose salary came from the number of people he taught. After a few years of working for the university, he became a well-known lecturer and was a highly regarded individual. His lectures were focused on topics such as geography, anthropology, law, and logic. During his time teaching, Kant began writing philosophical works to explain his beliefs to the masses. One notable work is his book titled Groundwork.

In Groundwork, Kant begs the question of what is truly of moral worth. Kant states, in his categorical imperative, that humans should “act only on that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law.” (pg. 120) When Kant mentions a “maxim” he is regarding the rule or principle of an action. In short, Kant believes that we should act only as we would wish for things to become a universal truth. In my personal life, I have told countless lies to my loved ones that have ranged from “I never said that” to “I don’t know who did that.” If I apply Kant’s philosophy to my personal life, I am not acting according to his maxim because I would hate for all my friends and family to lie to me all the time. A universal law of lies would create distrust between myself and the people I hold closest to me. That would not be considered justice.
chunks.label: Introduction to Sandel and Kant's categorical imperative
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces Michael Sandel's book Justice and explains Immanuel Kant's background and categorical imperative, reflecting on how telling lies in personal life contradicts Kant's maxim.
chunks.people: Michael J. Sandel, Immanuel Kant, loved ones, friends, family

chunks.text: Another example of this philosophical approach in my personal life would be watching people pick flowers from a public park. I went to New York City this summer and witnessed multiple people in Central Park pick flowers off a bush. If everyone in the world acted in that way, would it be morally right? No, because the slope of one person taking a flower off the bush to everyone taking flowers off the bush would leave all the flower bushes in New York City barren. Humans would not gain anything from having empty flower bushes, so the action of picking a flower is not morally right in Kant’s view.
chunks.label: Witnessing flower picking in Central Park
chunks.what_happened: During a trip to New York City in the summer, the student saw multiple people picking flowers off bushes in Central Park and considered the moral implications.

chunks.text:
Immanuel Kant is also known for his views that tend to overlap with libertarianism. Specifically, the right to self-governance. He believes that we, as individuals, have the right to do whatever we want as long as we do not harm others. This thought process is juxtaposed by the utilitarian idea that the people should always do what is the best for the group rather than the individuals themselves. A modern example of these opposing ideas would be taxing. Libertarians would claim that we shouldn’t tax the rich because they earned that money and nobody has the right to redistribute what they earned. However, utilitarians would say we should tax the rich because the people with less money need the money more. Their stance would be that it would help with the overall happiness of the group if the majority, the poor, got paid more.

I had learned about libertarians and utilitarians in my history courses at high school but never thought this deeply about them before. Sandel poses many good points of view on both sides, and I believe that I fall closer to the libertarian view. I think everyone has a right to self-governance and the right to live life as themselves. Thinking back on the thought experiment about the lonely kid under the city that Sandel talks about in his book, I find that to be wrong. No matter how happy the upper city is, that kid deserves the right to be happy as well. That is an idea that would oppose utilitarians because I would be voting against the happiness of the majority for the freedom of the little boy. Although I am more libertarian, I do believe in taxing the rich.

Further into the book, Sandel begins a chapter on John Rawls. Rawls was an American philosopher who was born in 1921 and died in 2002. During his time alive, he advocated for the idea that justice is not based on what is morally right, like Kant, but rather “what principals we would agree to in an initial situation of equality.” (pg. 140) Rawls created a thought experiment titled the “Veil of Ignorance” which means that people do not know their social status, their genders, or their education and from there, they create an unbiased foundation of justice. Sandel explains it as, “Since no one would have a superior bargaining position, the principles we would agree to would be just.”

In the thought experiment, Rawls creates the idea of an “original position of equality” where “Rawls invites us to ask what principals we- as rational, self-interested persons- would choose if we found ourselves in that position.” (pg.141) When I allowed myself to sit with this experiment for the first time, I was uncomfortable. I have empathy for everyone, but I realized I don’t spend much time thinking about those less fortunate than me on a daily basis. While I was thinking about if I was in an original position of equality I came up with some points that I would value for basic human justice. My list was filled with things like free healthcare (at the very least, affordable healthcare), access to education, access to healthy foods and clean water, and a safe place to live. Through Rawls thought experiment, anyone can put themselves in the shoes of another person and realize that some things are just inaccessible for the less fortunate.

Looking at my life from the perspective of the veil of ignorance has made me feel a lot of privilege for my way of life. I have access to things such as insurance, safety, healthy foods, livable wage, a fun job, and good friends. A lot of thought experiments in Sandel’s book lead to feelings of being uncomfortable because they push the reader to think about people less fortunate than themselves. The examples of the kid under the city and the veil of ignorance are just two of the ones I wanted to explore in this reflection.
chunks.label: Reflecting on libertarianism, utilitarianism, and Rawls's veil
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses Kant's libertarian ties, compares utilitarianism and libertarianism on taxation, reflects on Sandel's kid-under-the-city example, and evaluates John Rawls's Veil of Ignorance thought experiment and personal privilege.
chunks.people: Immanuel Kant, Michael J. Sandel, John Rawls, good friends

chunks.text: Sandel also mentions Aristotle near the end of the book and mentions Aristotle's idea of “Telos”, meaning purpose or end. Aristotle believes that everything in nature has a purpose or an end, for example: a watch has the purpose of telling time. Aristotle's view of justice is based around the idea of giving people what they deserve based on their actions. Digging deeper into the watch example, a person facing justice would be the one wearing the watch or the one reading the watch because the person wearing the watch has the purpose of telling time. Looking into Aristotle's idea and adding it to my own narrative, I immediately think about my purpose or “telos” in Student Government. The purpose of student government is to represent the student body of UNCW. If we represent the student body, then we oversee advocating for the students and making decisions for our peers based on what we know. From that perspective, the purpose of a student government member is to be the best representative of the student body they can be.
chunks.label: Aristotle's telos and student government purpose
chunks.what_happened: The student explores Aristotle's concept of telos and reflects theoretically on the purpose of UNCW's Student Government Association and its representatives.

chunks.text: Student Government meets every week on Tuesdays. Those meetings can span from thirty minutes to two hours and thirty minutes. Last year, during my freshman year, we had a meeting discussing the tuition increases for out-of-state students. This discussion went on for hours as senators debated on whether an increase was a viable option. On one hand, the increase would mean more money for the university to expand as well as keeping up with other UNC campuses. On the other hand, the out of state students may be less likely to apply to UNCW. When it came to voting, I felt it was my duty to vote for increasing tuition due to the fact it would better the campus as a whole, granted that money is allocated properly to all students. My telos, as a student government member, was to serve the student body to the best of my ability that night.
chunks.label: Student government vote on out-of-state tuition
chunks.what_happened: During their freshman year, the student attended a lengthy Student Government meeting debating an out-of-state tuition increase and ultimately voted in favor of the increase.

chunks.text:
After finishing the book, there were a lot of points I was left to reflect regarding what justice means to me. Reflecting on Kant, Rawls, and Aristotle has left me with a clearer picture of philosophy and of what I believe is right. There truly is no right way to think of justice but there are new ideas about being fair. All three philosophers have great philosophies about justice and Sandel leaves it up to the reader to decide on which one they agree with the most. I personally feel that Rawls has the fairest idea of justice with the veil of ignorance. His idea of being ignorant of a person's path in life has really stuck out to me.

Moving forward I plan on being more empathetic to those who are less fortunate than myself. Rawls thought experiments have really changed the way I see things, especially situations overseas and out of the country. I was aware of the situations people were going through overseas, but I was ignorant of how truly terrible it can be as an everyday living situation. Even expanding past Rawls, before this class I was ignorant of how much effect a New York City flower or lying could have on a universe of truth. Sandel's book Justice: What’s the Right Thing to Do? Has challenged me to expand my horizons of thought and has encouraged me to think more outside the box than usual. This book and the ideas posed have been meaningful and transcendent and taken together, all three philosophers will impact the way I see justice. Justice is a personal and a communal effort that more people need to be aware of.
chunks.label: Concluding thoughts on justice and course impact
chunks.what_happened: The student synthesizes the ideas of Kant, Rawls, and Aristotle, noting how the book and class expanded their views on empathy, fairness, and justice.
chunks.people: Immanuel Kant, John Rawls, Aristotle, Michael J. Sandel

n62cadb30.title: Observing Modern Shifts in Family Structures

chunks.text:
The Future of Families Through the Eyes of a College Student Bailey Brown Department of Sociology SOC 345: Sociology of the Family Dr. Douglas Engelman October 17, 2025 The Future of Families Through the Eyes of a College Student Over the past 80 or so years, we have seen several changes in the typical family structure. What used to be common in the 40s and 50s is much different from what we see today, or is it? The traditional nuclear family has expanded and can seem somewhat unfamiliar, but when taking a closer look, it appears that society’s ideas have not ventured as far as we think. While stigmatizations have changed quite a bit, society still tends to be set in what could be considered traditional. Marriage and Divorce Rates The stigma surrounding divorce has subsided greatly compared to what it was before World War II. Sheela Kennedy and Steven Ruggles (2014) share that individuals who are forty or older tend to have higher divorce rates, especially after World War II. This can be attributed to the fact that divorce was no longer highly stigmatized, but also the legality of divorce changed significantly (Kennedy & Ruggles, 2014). We can see during this time that women were allowed to enter the workforce at a much higher rate than before. This access to jobs meant access to money, which meant that a woman could have financial freedom. Women now had access to leave their husbands and be financially stable on their own terms. We have seen a decline in divorce rates among women who are age twenty-five or younger (Kennedy & Ruggles, 2014). This decline can be associated with the lack of marriage in the first place. Kennedy and Ruggles (2014) mention that in 2008, over forty percent of the population was not married by the time they turned thirty. A lot of this has to do with individuals being more selective in their partners compared to the past. Couples before World War II got married to fulfill societal roles, whereas now, we see couples dating or getting married to fulfill individual goals. I believe that divorce rates could swing either way. In one instance, I think that religion is becoming increasingly popular again. In the event that this popularity continues to increase, we could see an increase in traditional marriages once again, with a lower divorce rate. We may also see a decrease in divorce rates because couples are simply not getting married. Cohabitation is common and is beginning to possess the same rights as couples who are married. In this instance, I think we will see that marriage becomes less important, and therefore, divorce rates would decline. In another scenario, I could see divorce rates rising. You rarely see people being stigmatized for divorce; instead, it is applauded for the fact that you are strong enough to remove yourself from whatever situation it may be. There is a lot more freedom when it comes to divorce in the fact that a woman or a man can initiate a divorce. With those ideas in mind, I can see divorce rates increasing. Honestly, there is no perfect answer for how that will change in ten years. It could be exactly what it is today, or it can change completely. Traditional Nuclear Families: Stay away or make a comeback? We have seen a big shift away from traditional nuclear families. Society is much more open to cohabitation, same-sex marriages, and single parents. Cohabitation has increased drastically since World War II. We are now seeing that marriages typically begin with cohabitation instead of living separately until marriage (Smock, 2000). I have noticed an increase in cohabitation among college students living with significant others. Cohabitation has become very similar to marriage, which in turn makes it “good enough” for those who aren’t quite ready for the responsibilities that come with marriage. In 2035, I believe that cohabitation will become the norm for people. I almost want to say that the number of people cohabitating will be much greater than those who are actually married. Another nontraditional family type is same-sex couples. In 2011, only seven states in America legally allowed same-sex marriages (Chamie & Mirkin, 2011). This has since changed with the Supreme Court’s ruling in 2015 that legalized same-sex marriages in all fifty states. Previously, same-sex marriage was not only legally unavailable, but there was a great deal of stigma that came with it. Now, we see much more acceptance; however, there are certainly opposing groups that do not believe in same-sex marriage and do not believe it should be legal. I think that if we continue the path we are currently on, same-sex marriage will remain legal and most likely continue to hold similar statistics as it does now. With that being said, I still firmly believe that we will have a group of people who will continue to oppose the allowance of same-sex marriages. While these rates are increasing, we also see an increase in single parents, specifically single mothers. Single parents were not common prior to World War II, as families were trying to fulfill societal roles. Now, we see an increase in divorces or never-married couples because individuals are more likely to prioritize themselves. With these separation rates, it is more likely that a child will be under the care of a single parent. Mothers tend to get custody of the children, whether that be court-ordered or because the father does not put in the same effort. This, of course, can go both ways. In 1984, 25.7% of families were single-family households, accounting for one-fourth of the population (Hanson & Sporakowski, 1986). In the college age group, it is common for a teen pregnancy to occur and the mother to be the primary caregiver. Through my own experience, I have noticed that the majority of my friends who live with single parents live with their mothers. I do not see this changing a whole lot in the next ten years. We have normalized divorce, which increases the number of single-parent households. I will not say that the number of single-parent households will increase, but I do think that it will continue to stay at a similar level compared to what it is now. So, what will the world be like in ten years?

Overall, I think that the structure of families will continue the path that they are on now. We will continue to see divorce rates increase or plateau because of how society has normalized it. An increase in divorce rates can be a leading cause for single-parent families. I also think that we will continue to see a rise in same-sex marriages. Since it has become legal, we have seen an increase. I do think that this will continue as it becomes less stigmatized and more normalized. I don’t see us reverting to past traditions and normalizing marriages as something to satisfy societal roles. We have opened the gates by allowing women in the workforce and pushing towards egalitarian roles. I believe that egalitarianism will become the most popular format for families moving forward. I think certain things need to be fixed to achieve an egalitarian society, but if we continue to push, we might get there. Things like fixing the wage gap, finding better solutions to childcare, and allowing Americans to have a better work-life balance. It is very prevalent that egalitarian relationships are subjective, and the definition of egalitarianism is dependent on the couple. While we will never know what the future will bring, I predict that these could be some of the possible outcomes. Of course, we see rapid changes in history, meaning we have the potential to experience these norms changing without having any insight currently.
chunks.label: Future changes in family structures and norms
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on historical and future changes in family dynamics, analyzing trends in marriage, divorce, cohabitation, same-sex marriage, single parenthood, and egalitarianism.

ncf53129c.title: Finding Purpose After Overwhelming Family Loss

chunks.text: As someone who had not really been informed about schizophrenia before, only through maybe a few films, I found this book insightful. I was able to gather information that I will be able to take with me through the rest of my life. As I never know what may happen in my life, I can eventually be in close relation with someone who has schizophrenia, and I now have a better understanding of it. Through the way the author told the story, you can see his true determination to understand his son and his son’s diagnosis, as well as making sure his treatment plan was good. If ever I were to have this issue, I know that I can refer to this book to have a more informative way to navigate it. The reading also helped me understand how much marijuana and alcohol can affect individuals with schizophrenia. As I knew it could affect schizophrenic individuals trying to deal with their mental disorder, I did not necessarily understand how hard it could be not to participate in these situations. Most young adults are getting the first chance to experiment with these things, and schizophrenic individuals are just expected not to participate. It can be another isolating factor whenever socializing as well especially at parties.
chunks.label: Reflections on schizophrenia book
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on reading a book about an author's son with schizophrenia, explaining what they learned about the condition and substance use.

chunks.text: Having a passion for turning your work into something meaningful is something that the author and I have in common. I have had experiences in my life that have impacted me so deeply that it has moved me to want to make a change. Similar to the author, whenever his son passed, he felt the need to one day share his story. I have a story to tell of my own, and reading this book has reignited something within myself.
chunks.label: Connecting author's purpose with personal story
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on relating to the author's desire to turn personal pain into a meaningful story to make a change.

chunks.text: I lost my brother in 2020 and my dad in 2021, and there is so much I went through that I can use to help others in the future.
chunks.label: Loss of brother and father
chunks.what_happened: The student lost their brother in 2020 and their father in 2021, enduring hardships they hope to use to help others.

chunks.text: When the author spoke about going to college when he was an older adult and discovering a purpose for something, it helped me reassure myself that I am on the right path. The author’s path did not happen overnight and eventually he was able to put into words what he wanted to say. I feel many of the things I struggle with in my own life would be able to be let go if I could write and be as openly honest as the author. As I have grown into the young lady I am today, I am still learning the right words I need to put together to tell my story. The author’s dedication made me want to continue to pursue my education and try harder to be better.
chunks.label: Reflecting on education and telling personal story
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the author's path through college and writing, finding reassurance for their own educational and personal journey.

chunks.text: My father was killed, and when my brother died, I kind of fell apart.
chunks.label: Grief over father and brother's deaths
chunks.what_happened: The student's father was killed and the student struggled deeply and fell apart after their brother died.

chunks.text:
The author mentioned speaking to a priest who told him to basically stop playing victim, because he did not die, and I feel, after reading that, I have to switch up my own mentality a little bit.

Overall, the story, “A Boy Broken”, is informative for all and not just people dealing with family members who are experiencing schizophrenia. It tells a complex story of family and how family dynamics can function when there are mental disorders present. To be able to read something so personal from someone makes me respect their ability to even be brave enough to do that. We face a lot of judgment in life, and being able to tell your story truthfully for the sake of others is so brave. To tell such personal details of my life can be scary, but being able to stand in what you know is the truth can be more powerful than anything. In the future, as I grow and maybe have a family one day of my own, if they ever have to face certain challenges, I will be able to approach them differently than I did before because of reading this book. We as a society indeed have a long way to go before mental disorders are not stigmatized anymore, but being honest about an experience can help other people within their own or someone in their family. Hearing personal stories from individuals and their experiences, I feel, is one of the best ways to really learn and understand. Inevitably, to be able to change societal standards and ideas surrounding mental disorders will take a lot of effort, and I feel like we are going to continue to backslide on any of the progress that we may have had recently.
chunks.label: Reflections on mindset, storytelling, and stigma
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the author's advice regarding mindset, praises the bravery of sharing personal stories, and considers societal stigma surrounding mental disorders.

nf3dad4a9.title: Caring for a Grandfather with Dementia

chunks.text: Early in the book, Engelman explains the caregiver role to give the reader an understanding of what this role implies and what you may expect in that role. Throughout the book, Engelman uses his personal experience with Doug and how much it means to be a caregiver. He talks about how caregiving can be both rewarding and extremely stressful. He loves his son deeply, but there are times when he feels frustrated, angry, and overwhelmed. To give a reference to these feelings is when Doug called about being robbed because he gave someone money for a dime bag of pot, which, in return, he never got his pot. Engelman felt frustrated because he used his weekly allowance on pot but also having pot could have gotten him kicked out of the mental institution he was staying at.
chunks.label: Caregiver role in Engelman's book
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how Engelman depicts the caregiver role and feelings of frustration and guilt when caring for his son Doug.

chunks.text: Later, he explains the feeling of guilt during those frustrating situations because he wanted the best for Doug so that one day he could reach the 10% of schizophrenic individuals who become fully independent. These frustrating moments throughout Engelman’s story reminded me of how my dad gets frustrated with my grandfather because he hides his TV remote and money and forgets where he puts them, so he assumes someone stole his items. When my dad tries to help, my grandfather won’t tell him much and gets agitated and hangs up the phone. This is very tolling on my dad because he has a full-time job and a family to provide for while having to deal with these frustrating situations over the phone. My grandfather stays in Ohio while we live in North Carolina, but luckily my dad’s sister lives up there, so he can coordinate with her when he needs additional help. Like Engelman, when he would receive phone calls from Doug, I see it within my dad that same expression of whether it’s good news or another problem to solve.
chunks.label: Dad managing grandfather's confusion by phone
chunks.what_happened: The student observes how their father deals with stressful long-distance phone calls from their grandfather, who hides items, forgets, and assumes people are stealing from him.
chunks.people: the student, father, grandfather, father's sister

chunks.text: Engelman and his wife Wendy started reading into schizophrenia to get a better understanding on how to approach it and give Doug a fighting chance.
chunks.label: Engelman navigating Doug's hallucinations
chunks.what_happened: The student describes how Engelman and his wife learned about schizophrenia and navigated Doug's hallucinations.

chunks.text: As Engelman and his son are both at ground zero with trying to figure out how to approach this Engelman learns how to talk with Doug without upsetting him but also pushing the limits because Doug kept everything close with what was going on like his hallucinations of Wendy being in the back seat of the car when they were going to McDonalds for breakfast. That really connects with what I’ve seen between my dad and my grandfather. When my grandfather calls in a confused or angry state, my dad tries to calm him down, but sometimes he loses patience. I have also seen it in person once when we were visiting him because while in his room he was talking about some man that gets into fights with and out of nowhere, he goes” he is standing right there” but there was no one there. Just like Engelman with Doug my dad had to figure out how to approach in which in this situation my dad moved the door which the shadow from the light was gone and my grandfather then replied, “he’s gone, where did he go”. It was hard to see that and explain what is going on.
chunks.label: Visiting grandfather during an episode of hallucination
chunks.what_happened: The student visited their grandfather and saw him hallucinating a man in the room, which the student's dad managed by moving a door to change the light's shadow.

chunks.text:
Throughout this book Engelman helped me see how caregiving changes people. It forces them to be patient, resourceful, and resilient. Traveling through this rough journey with his son Engelman became more understanding and reflective. He learned to see the world differently by noticing how society treats people with mental disorders, and how families are often left to carry such a burden alone. Being able to personally connect to Engelmans story has made me realize how my dad’s life has changed since becoming the primary caregiver of my grandfather. He has become more patient but also compassionate not just toward my grandfather but others as well. It has also taught me a lesson that caregiving isn’t just about taking care of someone but also learning to love them through their tough times.

The most heartbreaking part of Engelman’s story was the passing of Doug in a car accident, but something that I was truly saddened by was when Engelman and Wendy went to Doug’s apartment after the funeral, where they saw nothing but positive things. Doug’s apartment was organized and clean, and he had a planner on his nightstand in which Engelman told him it would be helpful to have. Also, in that planner, Doug had a reminder to call the Pittsburgh admission office because he had gotten to a point where he was ready to go back to college. When Engelman and his wife, Wendy, also saw this in Doug’s apartment, it showed how much progress Doug had made and that he was on the right track to be a part of the 10% of schizophrenia patients who go back to being fully independent.

Despite the unimaginable grief, Engelman finds a new purpose by going back to college, where he wanted to learn how to be an author to write Doug's story, but later changed his major to study sociology, from the advice of a professor he had. This change made it possible for Engelman to help others understand mental illness, showing the incredible strength and resilience. After reading A Boy Broken and having Engelman as my sociology of mental disorders professor, it gives me a new understanding of the class and mental disorders. It has shown me that healing can come from sharing our pain; it creates connection, understanding, and comfort for others in need.
chunks.label: Reflections on caregiving, grief, and learning
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how caregiving transformed both Engelman and their father, discusses Doug's tragic passing, and explains what having Engelman as a sociology professor taught them about resilience and healing.

n2c02d44a.title: Navigating College as a First-Generation Student

chunks.text:
Justice: What’s the Right Thing to Do? by Michael J. Sandel investigates age-old queries of ethics, justice, and the duties we owe to each other. Sandel takes the reader on a whimsical tour of competing moral paradigms. Including utilitarianism, libertarianism, and Kantian duty to Aristotelian virtue, through the ten chapters. These theories are theoretical, but practical and relevant to human experience. As a first-generation college student, growing up and seeing others struggle, I am interested in how these ideas illuminate not just questions of law and public policy but also personal decisions in my own life. Sandel’s reading really drives home the point that justice is not only a philosophical idea, but also material practice, influenced by freedom, fairness, and responsibility.

Sandel opens with the example of price gouging following a huge hurricane event, offering three different approaches to justice: maximizing welfare, respecting freedom, and promoting virtue. The struggle between advocates of the free market and those against it, shows us how crises bring to the forefront the concept of self-interest versus civic duty.
chunks.label: Introduction to Sandel's theories of justice
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces Michael Sandel's book 'Justice' and explains how its exploration of ethical theories connects to public policy and personal life.

chunks.text: Growing up, I often saw people economically exploited, like when landlords raised rents or employers reduced hours and workloads as the economy was failing.
chunks.label: Witnessing economic exploitation growing up
chunks.what_happened: Growing up, the student often saw people economically exploited when landlords raised rent or employers reduced hours during economic downturns.

chunks.text:
These everyday injustices reflected Sandel's argument: markets don't ensure fairness, especially where people are most desperate. This chapter speaks profoundly to me because it brings to the forefront of why I came to criminology and law: to better understand the rules and structures that protect people who are vulnerable, not just people with money or power.

The narrative of the marooned sailors who vanquished and devoured the cabin boy personifies utilitarian thought of sacrificing one for three. While utilitarianism values the outcomes with reference to the "greatest good for the greatest number," it and efficiency can displace the worth of the dignity of individuals. As a first-gen student, I feel society sometimes sees other first-gen students and me with a utilitarian logic; institutions regularly value individuals based on statistics. Such as graduation rates, income levels, test scores rather than an individual’s unique battles and resilience. Utilitarian thinking has merit in the public policy space; the utilitarianism logic often considers individuals as simply numbers. Sandel pushes us to consider whether efficiency is important enough or does justice mean something more?

Sandel makes his first foray into libertarianism, with a focus on individual rights and a limited role for government. Libertarian thinkers such as Robert Nozick even contend that redistributive tax policies are tantamount to "forced labor." While I find great-to-strong admiration in the libertarian insistence on personal freedom. I tend to value my own independence, by sympathizing with the libertarian tendency to own my choices, my own life experience provides insight into the blind spot that libertarianism holds. Specifically, I would never have had the opportunity to think about pursuing post-secondary education if it weren't for financial aid, scholarships, and support from family and community members. Without the help from scholarships and financial aid, my studies could not be done. All forms of cash transfers or redistribution are in fact not theft, but rather the most basic forms of inspiration for me.

The chapter's emphasis on markets, whether for paying soldiers or surrogates, begs the question of what money should and should not buy. I felt strongly connected to this discussion when Sandel asks whether the volunteer army is voluntary or if poverty conditions coercively pull people into military service.
chunks.label: Reflecting on utilitarianism and libertarianism
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how economic exploitation relates to Sandel's work, critiques utilitarianism and libertarianism using their background as a first-generation student on financial aid, and reflects on markets.

chunks.text: I grew up seeing friends enlist in the military because college did not seem to be an option. Their choice was less motivated by patriotism than by necessity and survival.
chunks.label: Friends enlisting in the military
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up watching friends enlist in the military out of necessity and survival because college did not seem like an option for them.

chunks.text:
This connects me back to why student loan debates, minimum wage debates, and education access debates are moral issues as the justice we seek requires conditions for having meaningful choices. Not merely free choice.

Kant redirects the discussion when he asserts that ethics relates to motives, not consequences. His claim that individuals must always be treated as an end and never as a means is no small task but is also an extraordinary challenge. As someone who is trying to go to law school, I also find Kant’s view to be particularly striking. The legal system often vacillates between utilitarian efficiency which is cost-effectiveness and Kantian dignity making sure that each defendant’s rights are honored. Personally, Kant's emphasis on intention makes me aware that my success in college is not really about earning grades or bulking up my resume for law school; it’s about why I choose to pursue an education; for me, it’s about the honor of doing so for the sake of my family and an opportunity to serve for justice for those who doesn’t.

John Rawls establishes the "veil of ignorance," tasking us to think about how we would establish a society without the context of having a social position. His principles equal basic liberties and the difference principle feel fair and real to me. As a first-generation student, I know the sense of being weighed down, to know what it may feel like competing like you are in a race, while everyone else has socially-based head starts. I found that my peers have had it better getting into the best of the best schools, because they could afford it. Although my parents have helped and supported me, financially I could not be here without financial-aid or scholarships. Rawls legitimizes that feeling by stating inequality is only fair if it benefits those in an inferior position. That is why programs such as need-based scholarships are a good, real-world approximation of Rawlsian justice. Need-based scholarships do not provide charity, but pursue justice.

Sandel examines concepts of justice through the discussion around affirmative action, considering perspectives of fairness, merit and diversity. This debate strikes a personal chord with me, because I have witnessed privilege and disadvantage in admission processes.
chunks.label: Reflections on Kant, Rawls, and affirmative action
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on meaningful choice, Kantian ethics, Rawlsian justice, and the affirmative action debate in relation to their aspirations for law school and first-generation background.

chunks.text: Some classmates had the advantage of a tutor, legacy, and financial support. I relied upon my persistence and community support.
chunks.label: Contrasting admission advantages with peers
chunks.what_happened: The student relied upon personal persistence and community support to get into school, whereas some classmates had the advantage of tutors, legacy status, and financial backing.

chunks.text:
Affirmative action, in my mind, is not about disregarding merit but it is about broadening our understanding of merit. A student who has Systemic Barriers demonstrated resilience and potential that cannot be captured through test scores alone. In this case, justice understands context.

In Aristotle’s virtue-based theory, the virtue of justice is understood as giving people what they are due, which entails understanding the telos, or the purpose of social roles and institutions. This chapter challenged me to consider what may be my telos as a student and future lawyer. Is my education exclusively for my personal achievement of moving ahead in my life; or does it have a collective telos of fulfilling my community?
chunks.label: Reflecting on merit and Aristotle's telos
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on systemic barriers, broadening the understanding of merit, and considers their own purpose and telos as a future lawyer through Aristotle's virtue ethics.

chunks.text: I have witnessed through my sorority experience how rituals and service projects develop character and virtue, leading me to recall that being part of a community means more than fulfilling self-interest.
chunks.label: Participating in sorority rituals and service
chunks.what_happened: The student participated in sorority rituals and service projects that helped develop character and virtue within a community.

chunks.text:
Aristotle's emphasis on the good life leads me to reflect on education and law not merely as mechanisms to earn an income, but as vehicles to serve justice itself.

Sandel focuses on moral obligations based on community, history, and consent. It raises in my mind the obligations I have to the family who sacrificed everything for me to go to college and to the community that created me. Being a first-gen college student isn't just an individual accomplishment; it is a community accomplishment. I am bearing the weight of my family's hopes, and I also feel a commitment to pay it back to my family or at least my community. Justice, then, is not a project of universal principles, but also the honoring of particular obligations.

The last chapter contends that justice cannot be morally neutral; it must attend to questions about the good life. Sandel questions the principle of governance neutrality and argues that societies debate virtues and values no matter what. As I reflect on my engagement in public life, this rings true to me.
chunks.label: Reflecting on communal obligations and the good life
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on obligations to family and community, the weight of family hopes as a first-generation student, and Sandel's argument that justice cannot be morally neutral.

chunks.text: As a student ambassador at my community college and now as a member of Greek community life. I have witnessed the flourishing of communities when we talk significantly and openly about values, like fairness, honesty, and service.
chunks.label: Serving as student ambassador and Greek life member
chunks.what_happened: The student served as a student ambassador at community college and joined the Greek community, witnessing communities flourish by openly discussing values like fairness and service.

chunks.text:
For me, justice and the good life mean a commitment to education that enhances the voices of those silenced by inequality.

Sandel's first ten chapters are more than a quick primer in moral philosophy but also a mirror in which one can see personal experience. Being a first-generation college student, I have found myself hovering at the chain of these theories. Hovering over utilitarian calculations of cost and benefit, libertarian visions of freedom. Kantian respect for dignity, Rawlsian demands of fairness, Aristotelian invitations to virtue, and communal responsibilities of solidarity. Justice, as Sandel illustrates, is not a remote problem to be solved but a question to ask about the kind of society we want to build and the kind of people we want to be. My course through college is not so much one of individual improvement but one of taking that question into my own life. Striving for a vision of justice that honors both freedom and community, rights and responsibilities.

Reference

Sandel, M. J. (2009). Justice: What’s the right thing to do? (1st ed., pp. 1–118). Farrar, Straus and Giroux.
chunks.label: Conclusion and reference list
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes how Sandel's philosophical theories provide a mirror for their college journey, and concludes with an academic reference for Sandel's book.

n9324fd47.title: Navigating Mental Health and Family Support

chunks.text: The overarching themes of this story are plentiful, but one that sticks out to me most is family. Your perseverance in supporting Doug is admirable, as is your honesty with your shortcomings. I think that most individuals struggling with intense mental disorders do not have reliable support systems, financially or emotionally. The fact that Doug had a family that cared about him so much is so rare and special. As you discuss in the book, support systems are crucial for someone experiencing a severe mental disorder.
chunks.label: Importance of family support for mental disorders
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the book's themes of family and support systems for individuals dealing with severe mental disorders.

chunks.text: I really enjoyed the book’s emphasis on social stigma and the labelling theory as it relates to mental disorder. Specifically, I found the discussion of public stigma and self-stigma, both definitionally and anecdotally, interesting. As we’ve discussed in class, stigmas heavily influence mental health and the way that we view others who are suffering from disorders. Deviance from the norm, in any format, is often seen as “weird,” and we prefer to distance ourselves from those who don’t behave in a “normal” way. These kinds of public stigmas make people who suffer from mental disorders feel ‘othered.’ This may also affect their self-stigma. They may internalize this ‘otherness’ and use it to further distance themselves from society. Because of this, their relationships may deteriorate, they may not be able to hold jobs, and they may experience a decline in social class.
chunks.label: Social stigma and labelling theory
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how public stigma, self-stigma, and labelling theory impact people suffering from mental disorders and can lead to deterioration in relationships and social standing.

chunks.text: Another part of the memoir that I found especially interesting was when you were explaining the stages of grief as it relates to finding out about Doug’s schizophrenia. This serves as a reminder that grief comes in many formats, not just after death. One of my favorite classes that I’ve taken at UNCW has been Sociology of Death and Dying. In that class we heavily explored the stages of grief, and how grief can be experienced as a result of many different events. I enjoyed how you explained each stage through the lens of how you were processing the news of Doug’s diagnosis. I also liked that you pointed out that you couldn’t see the stages clearly at the time, but upon reflection years later you were able to group parts of your story into distinct emotions and stages. I am sure that your grieving process upon the news of Doug’s death manifested itself in different ways. People grieve differently, but ultimately, similarly. While the stages are interesting, it is also important to note that they are not linear, and they never really “end.”
chunks.label: Reflecting on stages of grief
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the memoir's depiction of the non-linear stages of grief following a schizophrenia diagnosis, connecting it to concepts learned in a UNCW sociology class.

chunks.text: I appreciated the rawness of your explanation about your guilt in trying to hide your son’s schizophrenia from others. I feel like this is something that many people with someone close to them who has a mental disorder goes through, but feels like they can’t talk about. The stigmas around mental health made you feel like, at least for a while, you couldn’t share your son’s struggle with your friends and family without being judged.
chunks.label: Guilt and stigma in concealing mental illness
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the author's guilt about hiding his son's schizophrenia from others due to social stigmas.

chunks.text: While I, specifically, have not dealt with someone close to me experiencing a severe mental disorder, I do have an uncle who experienced a severe drug addiction throughout my childhood. I know my parents attempted to shield me from this in many ways, which I’m sure you did for your younger children as well. He has been sober and living alone for several years now, and my dad’s role in his recovery is not lost on me. My dad also displayed unconditional love, perseverance, healthy boundaries, and caretaking for his brother during his lifelong struggle with substance abuse.
chunks.label: Uncle's addiction and father's support
chunks.what_happened: The student grew up with an uncle who had a severe drug addiction, while the student's parents attempted to shield them from it and the student's dad supported his brother through recovery.

chunks.text: In that way, this novel kind of reminded me of the film “Beautiful Boy.” “Beautiful Boy” is based on a memoir written by a father as well. That movie, much like this book, details a father’s struggle with his son’s mental state, although in “Beautiful Boy,” the son is experiencing severe substance abuse and drug addiction. Additionally, there are ‘scenes’ in both in which the son goes missing and the father is helpless in his search for him. In both stories, the father figure searches for meaning among the grief he is experiencing by feeling like he is losing his son to something beyond his control. Both are profoundly moving and beautifully depict the relationship between fathers and sons. Furthermore, both are important in sharing real-life stories about struggles with mental health and substance abuse.
chunks.label: Comparison to the film Beautiful Boy
chunks.what_happened: The student compares the book to the movie and memoir 'Beautiful Boy', highlighting similarities in how fathers cope with their sons' struggles with addiction and mental health.

chunks.text: Anecdotally, I was diagnosed with Generalized Anxiety Disorder and Panic Disorder when I was 16 years old. This seems like a pretty common occurrence for young women my age. That was my first glimpse into the world of mental health. As someone who was raised in a very conservative, Southern Baptist household, I was always taught that you could pray away sadness and anxiety. It wasn’t until I was in high school that I realized that the anxiety I felt on a daily basis was not the norm. I filled out a questionnaire at the pediatrician’s office and was in therapy within a month. My experience with therapy was less than ideal. I have also been on medicine at different points in my life, with varying success.
chunks.label: Personal diagnosis and treatment of anxiety
chunks.what_happened: Diagnosed with Generalized Anxiety Disorder and Panic Disorder at age 16, the student sought therapy through a pediatrician's questionnaire and subsequently tried medication.

chunks.text: All this to say, discussions about mental health are essential. Especially, as the Epilogue covers, during the present time, when so many young people struggle. I relate to your passion in wanting to make conversations about mental health more accessible and more normalized, especially in the school setting. No one should feel “othered” or stigmatized because of struggles with their mental health. Accurate and factual information is also important, as no one should be made to feel as if they could ‘pray it away.’
chunks.label: Importance of mental health discussions and factual info
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the importance of normalizing mental health conversations in schools and replacing harmful beliefs like praying anxiety away with factual information.

chunks.text:
Overall, I really enjoyed reading this memoir. I enjoyed the way that the story was easy to follow, but interspersed with theories, statistics, and real-life information about mental disorders. Often, it seems like people are content to be ignorant about certain topics until it happens to them. Apathy is the norm when it comes to mental health, until an individual is personally affected by it. This memoir is a glance into the life of someone who didn’t have much of an awareness about mental health, but who used his son’s experiences as a catapult to educate himself about disorders, social stigma, and treatment.

Your experiences, as told through this memoir, are important in many ways. It should serve as an example to readers, how you can use adversity to learn, grow and change. Mental health is something that we should all take an interest in, because it affects so many people in our everyday life. It may one day affect someone close to me. It is an important topic to be interested in, educated in, and to care about and advocate for. Voting is an essential way that we, as a society, can change the policies around mental health and mental health treatment. Being more aware of the problem is the only way that we can take necessary steps to fix it. If social structures are some of the main factors that lead to mental disorders in certain populations, the question becomes: what can we do to fix it? How can we better serve populations most prone to mental disorders? How can we break down gender norms and make space for every individual to feel comfortable to share their emotions and seek treatment? How can we better serve our unhoused population who have mental disorders?
chunks.label: Societal action and advocacy for mental health
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the memoir's educational impact and discusses the need for society to address mental health through education, breaking gender norms, helping unhoused populations, and voting.

chunks.text: This class, and specifically, reading this memoir, have made me even more passionate about mental health awareness. Mental disorders can happen to anyone, at any time. Negative events, drug usage, even age can bring upon mental disorders on anyone. It is important to be knowledgeable about mental health and to be able to provide support to those we love who may be struggling with it. Additionally, I am a Criminology major and plan to work in Victim Advocacy in the future. I will be dealing with individuals with mental health issues who have been through traumatic events. Knowing about mental disorders is so useful and important for everyone in our generation and beyond. This memoir was an honest and important glimpse into your life, which was shaped and changed by your son’s journey with schizophrenia. It serves as a reminder that it could happen to anyone. It inspires readers to be more empathetic, to realize that we don’t always know what others are going through, and to advocate for mental health.
chunks.label: Course impact and future criminology career
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how the class and memoir reinforced their passion for mental health awareness and connects it to their future work in Victim Advocacy.

n91a98d40.title: Living with Family Mental Illness Diagnoses

chunks.text: Right from the off, the bit about visiting Uncle Harry in the mental hospital made me remember when I visited my grandmother at the assisted living facility where she spent her last years. At this point she had dementia, and when we visited her it was a holiday (I can’t remember which one,) but she thought it was a different one. My mom and my aunt made sure my sister’s and my exposure to her was limited, so we wouldn’t see her decline. As time went on, my aunt kept visiting her, but at the end, my grandmother couldn’t recognize her.
chunks.label: Visiting grandmother with dementia
chunks.what_happened: The student remembers visiting their grandmother, who had dementia, at an assisted living facility. Their mother and aunt limited the children's visits so they would not see her decline.

chunks.text: In a similar vein, my grandmother had psychotic breaks when she stopped taking her bipolar medication, and at one point tried to kill her dog because “the angels told her to do it.” That episode was what led to my aunt taking the dog away from her for his own safety, and I can only imagine how terrifying it is to witness a psychotic break firsthand.
chunks.label: Grandmother's psychotic break and the dog
chunks.what_happened: The student's grandmother had psychotic breaks when she stopped her bipolar medication and once tried to kill her dog, so the student's aunt took the dog away.

chunks.text: The first paragraph of Chapter 2 is one that I understand better than I would have liked. My mother has never hidden from me the struggles of her childhood and life when my grandmother was in decline. She has told me about the times when she was punished for things that didn’t make sense to her, and when my grandmother did things that were harmful to herself, others, and things of value, sentimental or financial. My mom remembers how during one particular psychotic break, my grandmother put a cabinet with family photos out on her porch for the entire winter. Every photo in there got destroyed. My mom and my aunt tried their best to keep my grandmother safe and comfortable in her later years, and I was kept out of the loop because I was 7 or 8 at the time, too young to truly appreciate their struggle. It was only when I was in high school that my mom told me more about everything regarding her mother.
chunks.label: Mother's stories of grandmother's decline
chunks.what_happened: The student's mother told them about being punished as a child and about the grandmother's harmful behavior, such as leaving family photos on the porch all winter. The student was too young at the time to understand.

chunks.text: The part about social reaction to conditions and behavior of mental illness being what makes the illness stigmatized makes a lot of sense from a sociological perspective. As I’ve said before in class, humans love an other. Whether it be by physical traits or mental traits, we love categorizing things around us. It may have something to do with subconscious evolutionary traits that served to keep us safe from predators or unknown dangers, but in the context of mental disorders, it is the unknown of the individual that scares us. Even when we see someone on the sidewalk talking to themselves, we don’t know if they are just talking to themselves or if they are going to act on a thought that could bring harm to others or themselves. That is another thing about humans: we fear the unknown. As was pointed out in the book, society likes its routines and acceptable behaviors. To act outside of those norms is unacceptable and therefore deserving of punishment, be it actively or passively. To borrow a term I first heard from the autism community, people with mental disorders from a young age learn to “mask” in order to limit, or hopefully avoid, that stigma surrounding mental disorders, the goal being to fit in enough to avoid bullying or mockery.
chunks.label: Stigma, othering and masking
chunks.what_happened: The student explains that mental illness is stigmatized because people sort others into groups, fear the unknown and punish behavior outside norms, so people learn to mask.

chunks.text: On page 41, where it says that children reflect directly on their parents, it called to mind how my grandmother on my dad’s side viewed everything pertaining to him and his family. Anything that was wrong with his children had to come from my mom’s side of the family. His struggles in school were never willingly acknowledged by her, and she was always telling my parents how they were parenting wrong.
chunks.label: Paternal grandmother blaming the mother's side
chunks.what_happened: The student's paternal grandmother blamed anything wrong with the children on the mother's side of the family and criticized the parents' parenting.

chunks.text: The good news is, as social media and mainstream media have more of an impact on people’s perception of mental health, that perspective may become less prevalent as people understand that mental disorders are a product of many factors coming together instead of just one or two things.
chunks.label: Media and changing views of mental health
chunks.what_happened: The student hopes media attention will help people see mental disorders as having many causes.

chunks.text: Even the statement at the start of page 48 is something I’ve experienced myself with my diagnoses. After spending the first 19 years of my life trying to be normal and failing miserably, having the answers to questions it had never occurred to me to ask felt amazing. Understanding that I was different and that there were ways that I could work with it made life more tolerable. I still remember that when my parents received word of my diagnoses, their general reaction can be summed up as, “Yeah, that makes sense.” I was lucky that the child they “lost” was an enigma, and the child they gained was a more complete picture. I was also lucky that as a result of the diagnoses, they were willing to work with me on academics and general life skills, instead of leaving me to wing it.
chunks.label: Getting diagnosed at 19
chunks.what_happened: After trying to be normal for 19 years, the student received diagnoses that answered questions they had never thought to ask. Their parents said it made sense and helped with school and life skills.

chunks.text: Reading about Doug having Julie in his life made me glad, since it looks like he had someone in his life besides his family that he felt comfortable not only being around but also opening up to. One thing that I’ve learned, both through classes and personal experience, is that having the right therapist can be helpful in self-improvement, and the wrong therapist can be detrimental. Having someone that he was looking forward to sessions with sounds like it was a big part of his understanding and coming to terms with his situation.
chunks.label: Doug's therapist and finding the right one
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Doug's therapist Julie and how the right therapist helps and the wrong one can hurt.

chunks.text: The section of Doug’s death and funeral again felt similar, to me, to when my grandmother died. The pain of losing a loved one, the transition from carer to mourner, even now still casts a shadow. Admittedly, my mom and aunt went from carers to grieving daughters, but that’s still not easy. I don’t know how it was for Dr. Engelman, but for my mom and aunt, my grandmother’s death also brought with it a sense of relief. Death brought with it an end to my grandmother’s suffering, and also meant that my mom and aunt wouldn’t have to make any difficult choices regarding my grandmother’s care. The toughest one they faced, since my grandmother at this point had advanced dementia, was whether or not to put her on a feeding tube.
chunks.label: Grandmother's death and the feeding tube decision
chunks.what_happened: Doug's death reminded the student of their grandmother's death. Their mother and aunt went from carers to mourners, felt some relief, and had faced deciding whether to use a feeding tube.

chunks.text:
Reading this book gave me a better perspective of how some of the things my family has gone through are more common than someone might think in the moment. I understand that the book was about a father’s experiences with a schizophrenic son, but they also share similarities with a woman who goes from having bipolar disorder to having dementia, and also with a young man who had to wait until he was nineteen to learn that so many of the things he went through growing up were not normal, but they also were not his fault. The fact that these similarities can be shown between mental disorders of very different types and levels of care leads me to wonder how many other similarities there are between different disorders, and how much can be gained by opening up and sharing experiences with other people.

I know that when Dr. Engelman told us about this assignment, he told us that he didn’t want praise or acclaim, but he still deserves credit where it is due for being there for his son when he needed him. Mental disorders can drive wedges between family members, and lead to some relatives avoiding the “crazy” family member, but he stood by his son and helped to the best of his ability. This book is written with the benefit of hindsight, but it is easy to look back on events and say, oh, I should have done this, I should have said that, stuff like that. In the moment, Dr. Engelman did what he could for his son, and it is a credit both to him and his son that his son was able to make the progress he did before he died.

Doug had a support system in place that was able to help him come to terms with who he was and learn to adapt to situations. It sounds like his parents, his sister, even “Saint Julie,” all played very important roles in getting his life back on track. The fact he went from psychotic breaks to having a girlfriend and friends that helped him shows how much a person’s life can change for the better when circumstances allow it.

This book was an interesting read in terms of understanding life with a family member dealing with a mental disorder from the perspective of the carer. It gave me a newfound appreciation for what my mom and aunt went through with my grandmother and also made me realize how lucky I was that my parents were accepting of my diagnoses and that society is less stigmatizing of people with ASD. This book was, quite honestly, enlightening, both for an outsider trying to understand the challenges of living with someone with mental disorders, and also from the perspective of someone finding out that they are not alone in what they are dealing with.
chunks.label: What the book taught about mental illness in families
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on what the book showed about caring for a family member with a mental disorder and their appreciation for their own family.

chunks.text: Michael Sandel is an American political professor and philosopher. Michael Sandel teaches at Harvard and intends to get his students to answer the thought-provoking questions of our society and justice system. Sandel is known for his topics on democracy, justice, and ethics, and in this book specifically, he also proposes the ideas of past philosophers. I believe that many ideas that philosophers had then, are extremely relevant and common now, so I will be writing about those specific ideas that Sandel poses in this book.
chunks.label: Introduction to Sandel
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces Michael Sandel and the book.

chunks.text: This book in particular, was not an easy read for me. I have never pondered on topics revolving around justice prior to this class and this book. Considering I am a Tourism, Recreation and Sport major, I don’t necessarily think about topics like price gaps, utilitarianism, telos, and veils of ignorance. However, I quickly realized how embedded these ideas and concepts are in our society today and how relevant they really are. I intend to go into greater detail into some of these specific topics in this paper but first I want to give my definition of justice that I had before learning about what it really is. Before reading this book and being a part of the social justice class, I thought justice was a way to give fair treatment and consequences. On page 19 of the book, Sandel writes, “To ask whether a society is just is to ask how it distributes the things we prize- income and wealth, duties and rights, powers and opportunities, offices and honors. A just society distributes these goods in the right way; it gives each person his or her due.” After reading that for the first time, I realized that justice entails much more than I imagined.
chunks.label: The student's first idea of justice
chunks.what_happened: The student describes finding the book hard and how their definition of justice changed.

chunks.text: Two topics that Sandel brings up in this book repeatedly are utilitarianism and libertarianism. Utilitarianism, founded by Jeremy Bentham, states that the highest principle of morality is to maximize happiness. This basically means that we should do whatever is best for the majority. Libertarianism on the other hand, says that everyone has a right to liberty and we have the right to do whatever we want with what we have, as long as we respect the right of other people to do the same. One example of this debate that is brought up in the book is wearing seatbelts. Libertarians would say that forcing everyone to wear seatbelts is infringing upon their freedom however a utilitarian would probably say that it is safer and better for the majority if everyone wore them. I would like to say that I would be a utilitarian but I know that I am stubborn and tend to want to do whatever I want so I think I would more so be a libertarian. For example, if the government decided to legalize drugs like narcotics, I wouldn’t necessarily partake but I couldn’t stop another adult from using them in privacy.
chunks.label: Utilitarianism versus libertarianism
chunks.what_happened: The student explains both views using seatbelts and drug laws and says they lean libertarian.

chunks.text: I want to switch courses a little bit and talk about Aristotle. One major idea that came from Aristotle was “telos,” meaning the final purpose or function of something. One specific thing Aristotle mentioned while on his topic of telos was the telos, or purpose, of the government. He thought that the purpose of the government was to provide laws to aid in safety, morality, virtue, and more. He thought that the government should be guiding us and helping us thrive in life. I most definitely agree with Aristotle on his idea about the telos of politics, or the government. I believe that our government is put in place to provide more answers than questions, to provide aid and help, to reassure, to keep us safe, and to do what is in the best interest of our nation and our society. I wanted to bring this specific point up because I wanted to talk about how the purpose of our government today is exponentially worse than what Aristotle experienced and mentioned. I truly believe that with our government, we are in one of the worst spots in history. Our nation is completely divided and are even going to extremes to hurt one another because of opinions and political views. For example, the situation with Charlie Kirk recently. He was killed because of his opinions that someone found as hateful. I think our government tends to be more focused on money than it is focused on the nation’s safety and overall virtue. Our nation is more divided than ever and it’s disgusting to see. It is hard to believe we are so far off from what Aristotle said was the purpose of the government. Another topic that relates to our government and its “telos” is patriotism.
chunks.label: Aristotle's telos and today's government
chunks.what_happened: The student compares Aristotle's idea of the purpose of government with a divided government today.

chunks.text: Patriotism can be a controversial topic because of how our nation is today, as I mentioned before. One common question asked is, why are we obligated to our own country more than others? While I didn’t necessarily choose to live in America, or to even be born at all, I believe that because I was born into this nation, that I should help uphold its values and I should do my best to do what is right for those around me. I think this also involves speaking up for change when our government is failing us. I believe that being able to feel patriotic about where you live is to truly believe in and experience goodness. We should be able to reap the benefits of a flourishing and thriving nation, not the other way around. It seems common today to have either no patriotism at all and to only have hate for where you live and what the people governing it are doing. On the other side, it seems common as well to have too much patriotism that you are a mindless follower of whatever you’re handed. I brought up this topic of patriotism because it is something I feel very passionately about and I truly believe our society will not improve if we don’t start recognizing when something is good and respectfully challenging something when it’s not.
chunks.label: Patriotism and obligation to country
chunks.what_happened: The student explains their view of patriotism and speaking up for change.

chunks.text: Another concept that I found to be very interesting about this book was the idea of our dilemmas of loyalty.
