Sandel poses the question “can loyalty override universal moral principles?” on page 236. My answer to this question would be yes. I once watched a video about parents answering the question “would you kill someone for your child?” and a shocking amount of parents said no. At least that was shocking to me. I would kill for any of my sisters or anyone close to me. If their life depended on me killing someone else, I would most definitely do it because I am loyal to them.
chunks.label: Loyalty and moral principles
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses whether loyalty can override moral principles and says they would protect family.

chunks.text: For example, my older sister was caught shoplifting once and I was young at the time but I was with her. I was asked if I saw her take the items and while I had, I said no because I felt a strong sense of loyalty to my sister. It was strange because while it’s a very small example, I knew that what she did was wrong and I didn’t agree with her decision at all but my loyalty was overriding my morals at that point. The topic that Sandel posed was very complex and interesting to me while reading so I wanted to write about my thoughts in this paragraph.
chunks.label: Covering for older sister's shoplifting
chunks.what_happened: When the student was young, their older sister was caught shoplifting while they were with her. Asked whether they saw it, the student said no out of loyalty, even though they knew it was wrong.
chunks.feelings: strong sense of loyalty, felt strange

chunks.text: I want to circle back to Aristotle and bring up his views on justice, and our identities generally. Aristotle believes that we have a set identity when we are born and it is our purpose to fulfill that. On the other hand, Kant and Rawls believe that Aristotle’s way of thinking leaves little room for choice and freedom. While I disliked many of Rawls and Kant’s ideas throughout the book, I agree with the both of them on this topic. I believe that we should have the ability to choose freely what we pursue, where we work, who we become, and the kind of people we want to be. I think that Aristotle’s identity for humans is bland and it would cause us to only ever do what is considered to be the right thing to do or the good citizen’s choice. I think that you can’t actually have an identity without mistakes. I think that you cannot fulfill your purpose without trying and failing at things. This would be my answer to whether or not our duties can be traced to an act of will or choice, a question Sandel wrote about in the section “Justice and the good life” in chapter 9.
chunks.label: Aristotle, Kant and Rawls on identity
chunks.what_happened: The student argues people should freely choose who they become and that identity needs mistakes.

chunks.text: In this paper, I chose to write about the philosophical topics from the book that Sandel posed. I found it to be transforming to sit and think about where my loyalties lie, what justice looks like, what the telos of something is, what patriotism means, and our identities in relation to justice. While I have my views on abortion, price gouging, same-sex marriage, and more similar topics, I wanted to focus on the points that really stuck out to me from this book. Overall, justice is seen in our everyday lives in small and huge ways and this book helped me get an idea of what it looks like and what some issues we face look like!
chunks.label: Conclusion on justice
chunks.what_happened: The student sums up what the book taught them about justice.

n2e14a654.title: Predicting the Future of American Families

chunks.text: Throughout American history, the family has been the foundation of moral order and social stability. However, over the past few decades, it has shifted dramatically. We have seen a decline in marriage rates, a rise in single-parent families, and a new wave of diverse family structures. These changes represent cultural changes towards individualism, gender equality, and economic change. Many sociologists question what is lost when the traditional family structure weakens. As we look towards 2035, the difference between conventional households and modern family trends will define the new era of American family life. These modern family trends tend to emphasize flexibility and self-expression, where traditional households are grounded in commitment, stability, and shared values and viewpoints. These traditional viewpoints tend to be the strongest foundation for raising children and sustaining family and community life.
chunks.label: The changing American family
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the shift away from traditional families.

chunks.text:
Over the last fifty years, marriages in America have shifted from being viewed as a social and religious obligation to a personal choice or lifestyle preference. According to the Pew Research Center (2023), marriage rates have fallen to new historic lows. With these declining rates, there has also been a new average age for first marriage, now 30. The reason for this shift is economic uncertainty, educational priorities, and a new cultural focus on personal fulfillment rather than collective responsibility. From a sociological viewpoint, this shift in declining marriages is a result of individualism (Cherlin, 2010).

By 2035, we can expect marriages to remain relevant but less tied to religious and communal expectations. There will be a rise in long-term partners and cohabitation among many Americans. However, research shows that stable marriages and two-parent households are better environments for young children. They tend to have better education, better well-being, and long-term economic stability (Wilcox & Marquardt, 2025). Even though our culture still gravitates toward flexible family arrangements, the traditional family and traditional marriage will remain the most stable and prosperous.
chunks.label: Decline of marriage and its future
chunks.what_happened: The student explains falling marriage rates and predicts marriage in 2035.

chunks.text:
The nuclear family model, in which men traditionally worked and women managed the household, has largely disappeared. In 2024, more than 70% of mothers with children under 18 were in the workforce (U.S. Department of Labor, 2024). This statistic shows both the economic necessity and the progress that women have achieved. By 2035, all families will likely depend on two incomes, making dual-earner households the norm in the United States.

This new shift has created an interesting condition: on the one hand, we have growing equality between men and women in the labor market, which continues to contribute to empowerment and financial independence; on the other hand, it hinders traditional family roles and increases stress on work-life balance. This new expectation that both parents must try to contribute equally to income and still be active in childcare is what Sociologist Arlie Hochschild called the “Second Shift.” Which is the unpaid labor of homestead and childcare responsibilities.

In a traditional household, labor is often divided more clearly. Each partner assumes specific responsibilities that support the family’s stability and lifestyle. While this modern gender flexibility is valuable, sociologists have found that households that maintain clear role expectations, whether traditional or egalitarian, tend to experience fewer problems and more satisfaction than those without structure (Wilcox 2020). In 2035, we may have new hybrid family models that balance traditional clarity with modern equality. Things like remote working and flexible scheduling could make it easier for families to share household and economic responsibilities.
chunks.label: Dual-earner households and the second shift
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses working mothers, divided labor and the second shift.

chunks.text:
In recent years, there has been a significant rise in single-parent and blended families. This is one of the most visible modern trends changing American households. In 1960, 9% of children lived in single-family homes; the figure is about 25% (U.S. Census Bureau, 2023). Economic and cultural factors have been the biggest reasons for these high divorce rates, nonmarital births, and delayed marriages. These families display resilience but often face significant sociological challenges. Research has shown that children raised by a single parent tend to face higher rates of poverty, lower academic performance, and increased behavior problems compared to those children raised in a stable traditional family. (McLanahan & Sandefur, 1994).

Through blended families, remarriage and cohabitation are expected to be even more common in 2035. These living arrangements bring unique strengths, such as expanded support networks, but also require navigating very complex and emotional times. These patterns underscore the value of family and stability in long-term commitment. Families grounded in faith, communication, and mutual sacrifice tend to manage change and transitions better than families guided by personal satisfaction. While modern, diverse families will continue to be the norm, the traditional household will remain the benchmark for consistency and child development.
chunks.label: Single-parent and blended families
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses the rise of single-parent and blended families.

chunks.text: The legalization of same sex marriage happened in 2015, and it marked a significant turning point for American family life. By 2035, it is expected that same sex families will be normalized within society. Sociologists say that this change expands the definition of the family, promotes acceptance, and reduces stigma. However, this evolution reflects a redefinition of family away from the biological and gender roles toward emotional and contractual ties. This recent trend shows how much our culture is shaping our understanding of family.
chunks.label: Same-sex marriage and family
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses same-sex families after 2015.

chunks.text:
Technology will play a significant role in shaping the family in 2035. Things like artificial intelligence, remote work, and digital education are already altering how families interact. From one perspective, these tools can create more opportunities for parents to be more involved with their kids when working remotely. However, factors such as screen time, digital isolation, and the lack of face-to-face communication pose a significant threat to intimacy and family bonds. Economic pressure will continue to affect families with rising housing costs, student debt, and childcare expenses, all of which discourage marriages and the idea of having children among the young generation (Pew Research Center, 2023).

Traditional households, which tend to have clear roles, strong community ties, and shared faith, are more likely to be affected by these new threats. A family that prioritizes family meals and rituals creates a personal connection, which serves as a counterbalance to the digital world. By 2035, families that limit technology in their homes and daily lives could live a healthier, more connected life with all the modern conveniences and a deeper level of relationships.
chunks.label: Technology and economic pressure on families
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how technology and costs will affect families.

chunks.text:
In 2035, the typical family will come in all shapes and sizes. There will be dual-income families, single parents, cohabiting couples, same sex parents, and blended families, all of which will remain present. Research still suggests that these families will maintain structure and stability while sharing moral values, and they will thrive. The traditional household in 2035 will look significantly different from one in 1950. It might have two working parents or rely heavily on technology, but it will still work.

Modern families will continue to work with flexibility and equality, but they will rediscover that freedom without order leads to instability. As these social norms fluctuate, family values will likely experience renewed appreciation among Americans. However, the sociological evidence will remain clear. Children and communities will benefit most from stable, committed two-parent households that prioritize responsibility and structure. Traditional households will continue to serve as a model of resilience and clarity in a rapidly changing world.
chunks.label: Conclusion on the family in 2035
chunks.what_happened: The student predicts family types in 2035 and argues for stable two-parent homes.

n5bdbaf86.title: Reflecting on Grief and Family Trauma

chunks.text: When I first began reading A Boy Broken by Douglas Engelman, I didn’t realize how much it would pull me in and affect me emotionally. The story felt heavy right away, almost like I was stepping into someone else’s pain. Engelman writes, “like someone trying to describe a nightmare, he weaves a disjointed, chaotic narrative, trying to bring me into this world of his…a reality that he sees, hears, and feels” (Pg. 13). That line stuck with me because it perfectly described how the story feels. The story is messy and heartbreaking but very real. It’s like you’re right there with Douglas and Doug Jr. trying to make sense of everything that has gone wrong. Reading about Doug’s struggle with pain, confusion, and loneliness made me think about how deep emotional wounds can shape someone’s entire life. Even though the story is dark, it also shows a quiet kind of strength where even when someone feels completely broken there’s still a part of them fighting to heal whether they know it at the time or not.
chunks.label: First impressions of A Boy Broken
chunks.what_happened: The student describes how the book pulled them in from the start.

chunks.text: As I read deeper into the book, I found myself feeling a mix of sadness, frustration, and empathy. The way Engelman writes makes Doug’s emotions so raw that it’s hard not to feel them. His words aren’t just telling his story, but they pulled me into the chaos of his mind where he is trying to make sense of pain that’s too big to even understand. Engelman writes about how he is sitting there listening to Doug Jr. describe impossible, frightening things that are impossible for him to imagine. This statement was gut wrenching for me because it showed how helpless Engelman must have felt, wanting to comfort Doug Jr. but realizing that some pain can’t be fixed with words. It made me picture how lonely that kind of suffering must be. It is crazy to think that with these circumstances, the people who care most about you can’t even truly understand what’s going on inside your head no matter how hard they try. What struck me most about this was the feeling of quiet in those moment’s, the pauses between Doug Jr.’s words where I kind of felt the weight of everything he’s been holding back and keeping to himself. This reminded me that sometimes the silence in a person’s story says more than the words ever could. I think Engelman’s writing captured that silence perfectly. The brief intermissions per say, between Doug Jr.’s emotional explanations allowed a space to feel. During those points, I felt heartbreak, empathy, and humility.
chunks.label: Emotional response to Doug's story
chunks.what_happened: The student describes feeling sadness, frustration and empathy while reading.

chunks.text: As I continued reading, I kept finding myself thinking about how real it all felt especially because I knew it was their reality. I just kept thinking wow this was my professor’s life at a time. That thought made the experience feel so different and honestly kind of strange at the time. It is one thing to read about trauma and heartbreak but it’s another thing to realize that the person who wrote it actually lived through that pain. It made me see Engelman not just as a teacher but as a person who had survived something unimaginable and then had the courage to share it with others. Knowing that this was his real life and his family’s real experience gave the book a heavier weight for me while reading. It also made me think about how many people I see daily walk around carrying stories that I’ll never know. It also made me respect Engelman much more than I already did because he was brave enough to put his perspective and his son’s story out into the world for others to read. It made me think about how much strength it takes to turn personal pain into something that can help others understand and feel. The more I read, the more I realized that this book wasn’t just telling a story, but it was also teaching empathy. It was reminding me that behind every person even those who seem put together, there may be a whole world or battlefield we don’t know about.
chunks.label: Knowing it was the professor's real life
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on reading a story their professor lived through.

chunks.text: Another thing that really stayed with me was how this story made me think about the way we process grief and trauma. Everyone experiences pain differently, but Engelman showed how hard it can be to actually express that pain especially when words never seem to be enough. It reminded me of times when I’ve seen people struggling silently, putting on a brave face while carrying things that no one else can see. Reading this made me more aware of how important it is to listen without judgment, even when I don’t fully understand what someone is going through. I think one of the most powerful things about this book is how it shows that healing isn’t a straight shot and there is no right way to do it. Engelman didn’t try to make the story neat he let it be as chaotic as it was in real time for him, Doug, and their family. This made the story feel even more real for me. I think it’s really rare to read a book these days where an author doesn’t hide being the perfect language or a happy ending. This book shows the reality of trying to move forward while still carrying a weight. Reading about all the different perspectives through the book surrounding the difficult situation at hand made me think about how healing isn’t about forgetting it’s about finding a way to live with the pain and still choosing to keep going.
chunks.label: Grief, trauma and healing
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on how the book shows grief and healing.

chunks.text: Toward the end I was really intrigued reading the short section about Engleman’s daughter Melissa. Even though it was brief, it carried so much emotional weight and added a different kind of depth to the book. Up until that point, most of the focus had been on Doug Jr. and his struggles, so reading about Melissa gave me a different perspective on how the whole family was affected. What struck me most about this part of the book was how Engelman captured the way Melissa seemed to process things differently than everyone else in their family. Her presence in the story reminded me that pain doesn’t just touch one person it spreads throughout everyone who love them especially family members. I thought it was interesting that Melissa’s portion was not drastic or long, yet it still showed how individuals cope with loss and confusion in their own way. Melissa’s message on the stairwell felt really close to home. It was such a simple act, but it carried so much emotion behind it. This was a reminder that grief doesn’t always have to be loud to be felt deeply.
chunks.label: Melissa's part of the story
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the section about Melissa.

chunks.text: By the time I finished A Boy Broken, I realized this book left a mark in me that went far beyond just reading a story. It didn’t feel like any other book I’ve had to read for any other of my classes, it felt like an experience. I wasn’t just reading about Engelman’s family, I was sitting in their pain, walking through their memories, and trying to understand the weight they all carried. In my opinion, what really made this book great was how honest it was. Engelman let the truth out and allowed for it to sit and mingle. The book was raw and uncomfortable but then again that’s what grief and trauma really are. What stood out to me most throughout the entire book was the never ending amount of compassion and love that was present even through the sadness. Engelman’s words showed how love never really goes away, it changes form but it’s always there. This book made me see love as fragile but also incredibly strong, something that can survive even when everything else feels broken.
chunks.label: What the book left with the student
chunks.what_happened: The student describes the book's honesty and its message about love.

chunks.text:
I also want to express how reading this book had me reflecting on how Engelman’s story connected to the world outside of his. It really made me realize that everyone out there carries heavy things and we often overlook or judge them without realizing what they’re living through. I definitely think that after reading this I need to be more understandings and patient with others but also with myself. I think everyone has their own story, their own pain, and their own way of trying to heal and Engelman’s book showed me that but also made me feel that. That is the best part of this story, the way it is an experience, and you truly feel throughout it all.

Honestly, I am grateful that I got to read this story and I am also grateful that Engelman was willing enough to share the truth even through the painfulness. Through Engelman’s vulnerability, he not only gave his son’s pain a voice but also allowed readers like me to see how love and grief can coexist. I think it is incredible to be courageous enough to write out your story, the good, the bad, and the messy all for the sake of helping others. This book was not an easy read, but it was a meaningful and thought provoking one. This book has taught me many things, but my biggest takeaway is that even in a dark place there can still be light.
chunks.label: Lessons about empathy and gratitude
chunks.what_happened: The student describes what they learned and thanks the author.

n9ee5b358.title: Evolving Family Structures in Modern America

chunks.text: Family dynamics in the United States have been changing throughout the past one hundred years. Beginning with the integration of women in the workforce, and most recently the rise in diverse family structures, it is quite clear that the “typical” family in the United States is shifting. There has been a steady decline in marriage rates alongside a rise in divorce rates. While this can partially be attributed to women gaining the right to divorce their husbands without fear of repercussions, there are many other factors, such as economic pressures, cultural values, and social media’s influence. In addition, gender roles continue to shift and are a controversial topic of conversation. Many believe that all marriages and/or relationships should be egalitarian, while others believe that traditional gender roles should be adhered to. This paper will discuss the ways in which family dynamics have shifted in the United States, as well as examine what the “typical” American family could look like in the year 2035.
chunks.label: Changes in American family life
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces changing family dynamics in the United States.

chunks.text: Throughout the past one hundred years, marriage and partnership trends have begun to change and fluctuate. As mentioned, the decline in marriage rates has been a topic of conversation. Many wonder why exactly there is a decline. The marriage rate decline is due to a multitude of factors. Firstly, the cost of living has gotten so expensive that many couples choose to avoid a long-term commitment. Secondly, it is now far more normalized for a woman to value her education and career over getting married and having children. This is mainly because women no longer have to rely on a man to support them financially. Due to this, women are choosing not to get married and instead focus on their education and career. Thirdly, because the divorce rates are so high, it discourages couples from getting married in the first place. Lastly, today, cohabitation is far less stigmatized than it has been in the past. Therefore, getting married may feel “pointless.”
chunks.label: Reasons for the decline in marriage
chunks.what_happened: The student lists reasons marriage rates are falling.

chunks.text: Parenting and household structures have begun to see a shift as well. Women are no longer forced to stay in unhealthy relationships, which has resulted in an increase in single-parent households and co-parenting. Similarly, blended families have also become more normalized. As new styles of parenting come about, so do transformations of gender roles and work-life balance. With the steady increase in technology, new and innovative ways to care give are offered. For example, online homeschooling, AI, and digital monitoring (i.e., parental control apps, location tracking, baby monitors, etc). There has been a steady rise of women in the workforce, and this is a result of many factors. One being that fathers are being held more accountable than ever before. Therefore, it is becoming normalized to be a stay-at-home father while the mother is the breadwinner. Another factor is online job opportunities. Even if a mother desires to be a stay-at-home mom, she now has the freedom to work from home (and vice versa for stay-at-home dads). Essentially, the egalitarian lifestyle has developed into a feasible option for many households; however, it can show itself in more ways than one.
chunks.label: Parenting, work and gender roles
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses single parents, blended families and women in the workforce.

chunks.text: Many cultural and economic factors influence a family dynamic. These can be race, class, economic pressures, and the reliance on extended family and community support, just to name a few. The economic pressures that a family is placed under play a vital role in the overall family dynamic. In the United States, housing, healthcare, and childcare costs are pretty much unfeasible for the vast majority of families. This commonly results in families relying on extended family for financial support. This could be living with them, asking them to watch the children, or even helping pay for groceries, gas, doctors’ bills, etc. Thus, leading to changes in the definition of “family.” While the “typical” American family may seem like a married couple living with their children, that is simply a common stereotype. As mentioned, many couples never marry, have children together, and cohabitate. Other families may live in a multigenerational household consisting of immediate family (husband, wife, and children) alongside grandparents, aunts, uncles, and cousins. As mentioned by Andrew Cherlin, marriage has gone through an era of deinstitutionalization, accompanied by the normalization of same-sex unions as well as cohabitation. Thus, leading to the era in which America is currently experiencing. “That marriage has undergone a process of deinstitutionalization—a weakening of the social norms that define partner’ behavior—over the past few decades. Examples are presented involving the increasing number and complexity of cohabiting unions and the emergence of same-sex marriage.” (Cherlin 848).
chunks.label: Economic and cultural pressures on families
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how costs and culture change who counts as family.

chunks.text: When discussing diverse family dynamics, LGBTQ families and their inclusion into modern spaces are a hot topic. Now more than ever before, LGBTQ couples and families are being provided greater visibility when it comes to family norms. For many years, it was an extremely taboo topic that caused great controversy. While the controversy has not necessarily ended, LGBTQ individuals, couples, and families are able to integrate themselves into spaces without the fear of legal repercussions. There continue to be people who are against this; however, there is an undeniable amount of social acceptance that accompanies the legal protections. In addition, LGBTQ couples are provided with more pathways to parenthood than previous generations. Although they cannot conceive naturally, adoption and surrogacy are options that are no longer restricted by means of public policies that were inherently and clearly discriminatory.
chunks.label: LGBTQ families
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses the growing visibility of LGBTQ families.

chunks.text: As mentioned previously, technology has made a significant impact on family life. Not only does it aid parents in everyday tasks and help them monitor their children’s safety, but it also provides a space for virtual family gatherings (Zoom), communication through apps (groups on Facebook), as well as smart home tech. This is something that seems to have taken flight during the COVID-19 pandemic and has since integrated itself into the everyday life of a person and their family. Just twenty years ago, the idea of video-chatting seemed foreign. Nowadays, it is just another way of easy communication with one’s family, no matter how far apart they may be.
chunks.label: Technology in family life
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how technology connects families.

chunks.text: The “typical” family in 2035 is on track to look far more diverse when compared to a family fifty years ago, or even today. While I do not foresee an extreme change in just ten years, there seems to be a great possibility of a continuing shift in priorities when it comes to marriage and having a family. By 2035, the “typical” American family will, on average, lean towards the egalitarian model. The traditional nuclear model will continue to fade with an increase in single parents, co-parenting, cohabitation among partners, blended families, multigenerational households, and LGBTQ families. The nuclear model will not be obsolete but will exist alongside a much more diverse range of family models. Furthermore, with an increase in opportunities for women, the marriage rates will continue to decline. With women no longer having to marry in order to live comfortably, they may feel as if marriage and a family would hold them back from achieving their long-term goals.
chunks.label: The typical family in 2035
chunks.what_happened: The student predicts a more egalitarian and diverse family.

chunks.text: In conclusion, the “typical” family in the United States has changed significantly throughout the past one hundred years and is only continuing to evolve. While family is a concept that most strive to have, the ways in which it is created are ever-changing. Women’s integration into the workforce has caused a decline in marriage rates simply because women no longer must rely on men. Since then, cohabitation, single parenting, and co-parenting after divorce have become far more normalized. With these family dynamics becoming less taboo, individuals and couples have been more inclined to simply go against historic social norms when it comes to starting a family. Furthermore, the concept of LGBTQ families is no longer criminalized and/or prohibited by law. With this has come opportunities for these couples to become parents through adoption and surrogacy. While many American citizens look down upon and judge those who do not subscribe to the nuclear family model, it is no secret that other family models are becoming more prominent. This is an increase that will continue to happen within the next ten years. By 2035, the “typical” American family will be continuing to shift and strive for more egalitarian models alongside a growing acceptance of diversity, technology, and flexible familial roles within the household that aim for connection and equal responsibility. This change not only reflects a shift in social structure but also an important cultural shift in America.
chunks.label: Conclusion
chunks.what_happened: The student sums up how the American family has changed.

n7af26960.title: Caregiving for a Mother with Bipolar

chunks.text:
A Boy Broken by Douglas J. Engelman - Mid-Term Reflection

What does it mean to keep hope in the face of relentless despair? A Boy Broken reveals this through a father’s journey and sociological perspective of the trials, rewards, and tribulations of his son’s life with schizophrenia. The stigma of mental illness is a long lasting, penetrating topic that can inhibit one’s recovery and fall on the family of the people suffering. Most of the time the perspective of the family is not thought of but from personal experiences, I too know how it feels to live this reality. Some people may make mistakes on this hard course of the unknown through loss, grief, caregiving, and tough love; this story does provoke deep emotions, especially to me, as I was not always prepared in these situations. The mental health of all family’s needs to be acknowledged and made aware of helpful ways to use their experiences for the better and to help others in society diminish the stigma.
chunks.label: Introduction on stigma and families
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces the book and the stigma families face.

chunks.text: The story starts with the end, the shock of coming back to reality, the narrow acceptance of a father hearing of the death of his son, Doug. In the words of Engelman, “...is now just a body…I imagine it cold, broken, and lifeless on a stainless-steel table in the darkness of the hospital morgue.”. But let's start with the beginning of this journey. In April 1991, 7 years before the death of his son the events began, Doug was on his sister Melissa’s porch repeating “why do they have to die?” This wasn’t normal for Doug and scared his sister. She didn’t know what to do, she had never experienced anything like this, she called the authorities, Officer Thomas. Officer Thomas alluded that Doug may be schizophrenic, their uncle Harry had been diagnosed in his 20’s, this could be true. Of course, hearing this as a parent and seeing your child in dirty clothes, preoccupied, and having a psychotic break you don’t want to believe it.
chunks.label: Doug's first psychotic break
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes how Doug's illness began in the book.

chunks.text: Doug explained to his father that there are two people who were “always with him”, a guy named Dave who taunts him about being gay, and a girl named Wendy. This reminds me of when I first began seeing the signs that my mother had bipolar disorder II, I was just nearing my last years of high school, I had never seen any other signs or even known about the illness. I experienced lots of emotions when I found out she was suffering, and I was really the only main one there for her, I didn’t know what would come. I remember I had to either involuntarily commit her, or there would be worse consequences in the justice system, for the first time at just 16 years old. I heard the cop in the background talking bad about my mother and how he knew her in the past, displaying the same awful stigma that most law enforcement leads with. When really, he didn’t know her, what she was going through, or anything of the sort for that matter. Another moment when we began arguing a lot, I felt like it was because she wasn’t herself, but she told me “I’m the same, I have always been this way”; this made me come to the realization that I too was making her into the disorder herself and not seeing who she really is. “I can’t see her…but I believe you.”, people struggling with mental illness bring us into their chaotic world, and what it’s like but the major thing they need is someone that is going to listen and be there for them. We feel like we know this person so well, and hope that it was all just temporary. My experience as a child with a parent with a mental disorder may differ but it is also all in the same.
chunks.label: Mother's bipolar diagnosis and involuntary commitment
chunks.what_happened: In high school the student first saw signs of their mother's bipolar II disorder and, at 16, had to have her involuntarily committed while a police officer spoke badly about her. Later arguments made the student realize they were seeing her only as the disorder.
chunks.feelings: many emotions, unsure what would come

chunks.text: Doug confided in his father by telling him of the diagnosis, at the McDonalds, an important moment and it brings back feelings of their past, divorce, childhood; Doug being left repeatedly by his father during his young, estranged relationship with Bobbie, Doug's mother, until now where his father had to silently promise to never leave him again, to commit. I wish the conversation could have been as open and honest, in my experience but it wasn't. It hit me like a truck, just as it does for lots of families in society, especially because I have a little brother that was too young to understand, and I had no idea how to explain it to him. I bottled all my emotions in, and I didn't want to talk to anyone, no one understood, and I was going through my own battle during all of this all alone, but she is my mom. Although I have experienced all these feelings and instances of this book, it still helped me, and I know it helps others.
chunks.label: Learning about the illness without an open talk
chunks.what_happened: Unlike Doug telling his father openly, the student never had an open conversation about their mother's illness. It hit them hard, they could not explain it to their little brother, and they kept their feelings to themselves.
chunks.feelings: hit me like a truck, bottled up, alone

chunks.text: Now what? That’s the question everyone is left with. People with mental disorders “most likely lack insight into the existence of the illness and may even reject the idea of a cure.” This all plays into stigma, society sees people as socially deviant or exhibiting behavior out of the norm of their culture, stereotypes, and values. “Stigma is a “socially constructed” determination of disgrace and disapproval that can lead to profound disadvantages by those bearing the stigma.” A theory apart included in stigma is the symbolic interactionist theory, which explains that “the meaning of actions and social objects are not inherent in those objects but rather, are formed through interpretation and definition in social interaction”. There are numerous different views that can describe stigma, Georges Herbert views stigma as society norms providing the framework for his own actions. Charles Horton Cooley explains that they come to see themselves as others see us. And Lemert believes that a person sees themselves as deviant, that society has created by making ‘rules’. Again, stigma can be a barrier to recovery from mental illness, creating public and self-stigma. When a person is labeled as a mental illness it triggers negative stereotypes like fear and danger, when they really aren't. This can lead to changes in one's identity, some even say “it was how he was raised”. Altered family relationships are created from stigma; it provides a negative social framework where family has to reorganize their day-to-day routines. They must help cope with the idea that their family members will no longer be seen as acceptable in society, they feel the need to change them. “Burden falls on the family, both become the object of stigma, strained and distant relationships.” Doug’s father even hid him from his neighbors, society, everywhere, and everything to hide the fear and reality of telling the truth. He started creating false stories about what he wished Doug and Melissa’s life was really like, he hid them because of their mental illness and because of what he thought it would reflect on him, his family, and his parenting. Living with a mental illness and seeking counseling is stigmatized, the fear of rejection from many from pursuing opportunities and dreams prohibits them. There was shame and denial, both his children had a mental disorder, even though Doug was doing good he still wanted to hide the mental illness. He didn’t start sharing the real Doug until it was too late. Doug was in and out of group homes, mental facilities, therapy, apartments, it was a lot for his father and family. I feel it was probably hard on Melissa also because most of the attention was on Doug when she was going through her own mental situations.
chunks.label: Stigma theory and hiding the illness
chunks.what_happened: The student explains stigma theories and how Doug's father hid his children's illness.

chunks.text: When a parent or child experiences a loved one being diagnosed with a mental illness, there is a sense of loss, it seems like the person is different, but still there. There are events out of the norm that we are unprepared for, and they believe they could have prevented it in some way in this long process of grief. “Unlike death, there is no “object” to mourn”, they are still there with them, but the person is unrecognizable, or even unlikable but the family has to commit to care and support. Therapists even have a tough time addressing the grief of family members. Grief started when Doug told his father about his diagnoses as they sat at the McDonalds. “My little boy, now a broken man, was a stranger, my son was gone.” Grief includes 1. Denial, 2. Anger, Doug was angry at himself as a parent, angry at God, and angry at Doug for the substances he may have used before this. 3. Bargaining, Doug’s father thought if Doug would just do what the doctors told him, he could be a part of the tiny fraction of survivors. “But this is what grief like ours does. It resists acceptance. It allows anger to consume love. And it allies hope to obscure reality.” 4. Depression, there is loss of hope that manifests, this is the quiet stage, last there is 5. Acceptance, understanding the reality of what everyone is really going through, a productive and joyful life is possible and there is potential for more positive outcomes and relationships.
chunks.label: Grief after a mental illness diagnosis
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the grief families feel and the stages of grief in the book.

chunks.text: When you are a close family member of one with a mental illness, you can become a caregiver. Doug's father never saw it as caregiving, and neither do I with my mom, but that’s what it is. My mom takes care of herself for the most part, but there are times when this is needed. “Overall, caregivers describe feelings of isolation, financial difficulties, relationship problems, and physical complaints related to their caregiving roles.” There is lots of investment, time and energy that goes into caregiving and can even offer a sense of purpose. But like most we are often scared and anxious of what could happen when we are not there. Families that don’t have it so well and lack certain resources experience even greater stressors, discrimination, and economic insecurity. Doug went to Loyola mental facility where they prevented family interaction, he then transferred to Madden and stayed in a group home for 6 months, this was a good thing for Doug, the meds were helping push the images away, although they were still there.
chunks.label: Families as caregivers
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how family members become caregivers.

chunks.text: I have seen my mom go through many health evaluations until they settled on Latuda. The only thing about this medicine is that she's been taking it for over 10 years and if it gets out of her system, she will most likely have a manic episode. Family members don’t know the direct stress of people suffering, what is going on in their head. We are there for the evaluations, the therapy, the ups and the downs, and losing everything and starting all over again. Again, and again, but there are good parts and good can come out of it. There are downs but the ups are so much greater that they pull us out of this rut into something much better, my faith in God has helped realize we cannot control these situations, and we cannot change the person, but we can give them grace, learn their triggers, and not challenge them when they are in need.
chunks.label: Mother's medication and the family's ups and downs
chunks.what_happened: The student watched their mother go through many evaluations before settling on a medication she has taken for over 10 years. The family has gone through therapy and ups and downs, and the student's faith helped them accept what they cannot control.

chunks.text: But sometimes they need a little tough love, Doug was allowed a weekly allowance and received disability that his father managed most of the time. When Doug was at the group home, he was having some challenges and often stated that his money was being stolen. He even tried to buy a dime bag of marijuana but got conned out of his money. Doug had to learn some responsibility. His father was upset with him that he was smoking on his meds and wanted to go off. But he gave Doug grace, it couldn't have been amazing for Doug, “Do you have any idea how shitty life is here? Nothing to do. No real friends. I just wanted to feel good for a little while.” This was understood and although Doug would buy weed again, he learned not to be so trusting, as he was vulnerable. This tough love helps strengthen their relationship. But then Doug showed up out of the blue one night, saying he couldn't go back to the group home, and he wanted to leave because there were guys that “were going to kill him” because they thought he was gay. Doug’s father said he could not stay there, this made him upset, but he knew it was for the best. Until Doug didn’t show up to the group home and went missing for three weeks.
chunks.label: Tough love and Doug going missing
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes Doug's time in the group home and his disappearance.

chunks.text: I know that during the manic episodes with my mom, they didn’t occur frequently, but they did last a little time. Often, I would go without talking to her and had to stop by her house to check on her. One thing she thought was that all the electronics were bad, she was being tracked. During these times, I was really the only one my mom would trust, until I wasn’t. It saddened me when she would see me as the enemy or think that things were happening that weren't. But I had to learn the right approach, arguing with her and not accepting was not going to help. Things were said that I think about on the regular, I wondered did she mean these things, there was no way she didn't know she was saying. Dealing with these bouts changed me, for the better and for the worse sadly. Sometimes I would have no idea where my mom was, I would have to look for her, who was going to be there for her. All while I was trying to establish my life and finish college. Her childhood was very tough, and her siblings were not close, their mother and father also suffered from their own mental illness. My mom is also the only child that helps my grandmother with her mental disorder.
chunks.label: Mother's manic episodes during college
chunks.what_happened: During their mother's manic episodes the student checked on her, sometimes had to search for her, and was at times seen as the enemy when she believed electronics were tracking her, all while finishing college.
chunks.feelings: saddened, changed for better and worse

chunks.text:
Doug's father searched for him high and low until he received a call from Doug at a homeless shelter, ah the relief to hear their voice, to know that they are okay. Doug's father cherished the late-night ride back through the city. Yeah, you're probably pissed, but they are okay.

Through Doug's journey on the streets, he did pretty well, it had changed him for the better, but he learned that he was very fortunate to have help from Madden and security at the group home. Doug decided to get an apartment with another resident and become more independent. Then Doug decided to move back with his mom in Pittsburg, staying in his programs of course. But his mom was battling her own mental health issue, so he tried to move in with his sister and work at an art studio, he had frequent run-ins with the Dermont police. He moved from Dermont to Mercy behavioral health facility, where he met his therapist Saint Julie. Saint Julie understood Doug in a different way no one else had and Doug trusted her, this would be different. “Doug began to show indications of introspection and mature thought that he had never been able to express before his therapy with Julie". Doug had moved back to Pittsburg and became more open in social interactions with women. “Doug has gained greater insight into his disease; he developed greater understanding of the influence drugs had on his mental health and was able to remain abstinent.” Doug found a woman he really liked; with more confidence she liked him for him. She didn’t even realize he had mental illness, they had a true connection, and this was great for Doug. Doug's father was so happy for Doug and Doug knew he was doing great; things were on the up and up. Until Doug passed away on December 19, 1998. Dougs father went back to see Doug's apartment after the funeral in Cary. He thought it would be a mess, disorganized, and unclean. But instead, it was organized, clean and he even had a Christmas tree with a present from his dad and presents for his little siblings. He was taking care of himself, and he was happy, his dad was happy. “This would be his legacy; this was proof that this once broken young man was putting the pieces of his life back together. I have recalled that visit, viewing my son's life through his habitat, hundreds of times. It has helped me so often to think about how he had grown, about my journey with him, and the person that he had become through his disease and recovery.”
chunks.label: Doug's recovery, death and legacy
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes Doug's recovery, death and what his father found in his apartment.

chunks.text: Today, my mom is doing great, she is still here improving her life for the better, in a good area. I can say that seeing our family members with mental illness do good and better is the best thing, we were a part of the journey. It was long, it was hard, there were tears and smiles, but we made it. Every day we continue to make it and keep going.
chunks.label: Mother doing well today
chunks.what_happened: The student's mother is now doing well and improving her life, and the student says the family made it through together.

chunks.text: This book made me cry, smile, and relive trauma from my past experiences. I wish this book was here for me at that time, but it has done its job in helping me, one person, and I hope it continues to help everyone else in society.
chunks.label: What the book meant to the student
chunks.what_happened: The student says the book made them relive their past and that it can help others.

nb9f5ccdc.title: Navigating Reproductive Health and Societal Standards

chunks.text: As a woman in this society, I run into many obstacles related to my health and have to make decisions or deny “help” to better my health. Women are stuck between a rock and a hard place in today’s society. There are debates about what we should do with our bodies, more accurately, what to do with our wombs. Women’s reproductive rights are the highlight of governmental arguments, how abortion is murder, how it is not murder, how it needs to be an option for women and young girls who have been raped, how women have to be sentenced for aborting their baby, etc.. We have limited access to contraception, and would have to go to a health professional to spend hundreds of dollars. There are arguments that have arisen where women should or should not be about to have contraceptives over the counter. In society it is clear that women are not responsible for our own reproductive rights.
chunks.label: Women's reproductive rights debate
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces debates over women's reproductive rights and contraception.

chunks.text: According to Sandel, utilitarianism focuses on getting the ultimate happiness for all, and libertarianism focuses on individual liberties and the protection of their rights. Utilitarianists would look both ways, in supporting ways and going against abortion. A utilitarian supporting abortion would focus on the suffering of a pregnant woman because she is going through an unwanted pregnancy. In order to end her suffering, abortion would be considered a good solution. The woman would be struggling mentally and economically, which can lead a life that is unpleasant for her child. It is argued that the child would grow up in a household that is not full of life, but unstable. In order to prevent that, an abortion must occur. A utilitarian going against abortion would focus on the harming of the woman’s fetus. Killing a fetus can cause harm to many, but mostly to the mother. The mother will have to endure the pain during the procedure, but after the procedure too. Many women, and society, do not understand that abortions take a toll on the body and can cause us many reproductive issues. Just like utilitarianists, a libertarianist would argue two sides for abortion. A libertarian focuses on pro-life and pro-choice. The pro-life argument shows that the fetus has a right to be alive, and to continue growing in its mother’s womb. It considers abortion to be an act of violence on another human being. The pro-choice argument states that a woman is her own, she has the right to do anything she wants with her body. A woman's liberty is violated, if she is forced by the government to keep a baby that she does not want. Under this argument, the government cannot and should not tell a woman what she needs to do with her body.
chunks.label: Utilitarian and libertarian views on abortion
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how both theories argue for and against abortion.

chunks.text: For contraceptives, utilitarianists and libertarianists have different arguments. A utilitarianist would support the idea of contraceptives, if they are accessible to women, or to all. Contraceptives can help women prevent unwanted pregnancies and have intercourse safely. It can be beneficial for women’s reproductive health. It can allow our menstrual cycles to be less painful and lighter. It allows companies to make profit off of women and it allows us to prevent pregnancies, which benefits society as a whole. A libertarianist would believe that contraceptives should be available everywhere, and that it should be accessible without having the government involved. Women should be able to have control over what we put in our bodies, instead of being prevented from doing so.
chunks.label: Views on contraceptives
chunks.what_happened: The student explains both theories' views on contraceptives.

chunks.text: In my eyes, abortion is not beneficial in any way. If a man and a woman want to have intercourse, they have to take precautions to avoid pregnancy. In cases that a woman gets pregnant because of the lack of contraceptives, the baby should be kept. It was the parents actions that allowed them to get pregnant, abortion is not the key. I agree with the libertarian view, where abortion is harmful because the baby is a human being. The fetus, no matter how many weeks old, is being taken out of its only life source and that is the mother. After an abortion occurs, not only does it kill the fetus but it messes with the woman’s reproductive health or health in general. When women and men make choices that put them in this predicament, there is no going back and it kills a poor innocent human being. The government does not agree with abortion, but wants to charge women to get on birth control. If they want to prevent abortions, contraceptives should be available to women. When they are available to women, we would no longer be at risk for a pregnancy that we may not be ready for.
chunks.label: The student's view on abortion and birth control
chunks.what_happened: The student argues against abortion and for free access to contraceptives.

chunks.text: Healthcare has been advancing over the years. There has been more technology, more education on life changing procedures, but the one thing that isn’t being advanced is women’s healthcare. Women are struggling to find professionals who would be willing to listen to what we have to say is happening to our bodies, or what we are experiencing. Healthcare professionals are not taking into consideration how women feel when we are getting check-ups, implants, or any other medical procedures. Every woman has shown that we are not in any way comfortable with healthcare professionals, we believe that they are doing what they do because it is just a job to them. To add to this belief, pregnant women have to deal with these professionals who do not want to take care or help in any way possible. Many women have stories about how Gynecologists and other healthcare professionals have wronged them, or have done procedures that caused them discomfort and pain. Women go through life-changing things, one of those things is becoming a mother. Society feels that if women can go through life changing things, they will be able to not take breaks with their child. Many companies do not allow maternity leave or paternity leave, and if they do, it is not a long time. The time for maternity or paternity leave varies by company, and sometimes it is unpaid. Many companies do not view maternity leave as something necessary, and it enrages society and new mothers.
chunks.label: Women's healthcare and maternity leave
chunks.what_happened: The student argues that women's healthcare and maternity leave are neglected.

chunks.text: Healthcare, according to the utilitarian view, is supposed to help women and their well-being. Healthcare being something for the public as a whole benefits everyone, there is nothing that can prevent healthcare from being useful. According to the libertarian view, healthcare is a service and not an individual’s right to have. It is believed that women should not pay for our healthcare services, but have to pay for others who are not able to pay for their own. Women not only have to worry about our own healthcare, but we also have to worry about other individuals taking their money through insurance.
chunks.label: Theories on healthcare
chunks.what_happened: The student explains utilitarian and libertarian views on healthcare.

chunks.text: Maternity leave through the lens of a utilitarian and libertarian differ in many ways. Utilitarianism views maternity or paternity leave as a beneficial thing for the mother and baby. The leave should be paid, and that gives mother and baby time together. It helps their health, giving the baby time with its mother and allows the mother to heal after giving birth. When the mother spends more time with her child, the more they have a stronger bond. It also helps reduce any mental health issues that could have arisen if she was to work straight after giving birth. Libertarianism views are against paid maternity or paternity leave, it is believed that the leave should not be a mandatory thing as they are interfering with the work space.
chunks.label: Theories on maternity leave
chunks.what_happened: The student explains utilitarian and libertarian views on maternity leave.

chunks.text:
Healthcare and maternity leave have to be available for all women. I believe that women’s healthcare should be advanced and affordable. They should also have the say in what professionals think is best for them to do, women most likely go with what the professionals say. More recently that has not been the case, and women have gone with their gut feeling. Healthcare should be more than a way to get money, but also have the patients in mind. Maternity leave is something that all women should be given the opportunity to do. Women need the chance to be with their child and to be allowed to better themselves before going back to work. I agree with the views from the utilitarianists for maternity leave, because it is important for both the baby and the mother. If a mother has to directly go into work after giving birth, there will be no or weak connection between her and her baby. It also can interfere with her mental status and stress levels.

After talking about what women go through on a daily basis, it leaves me defeated. Women have to endure a lot of discussions and mistreatment from healthcare professionals, co-workers, and even from society. Sandel’s book had allowed me to gain a deeper understanding more about how utilitarians and libertarians would think about abortion, contraceptives, healthcare, and maternity leave. It had also questioned how I felt about each topic, and how it can hurt or help society. I now understand these debates and conversations benefit many people, many get hurt or insulted, but there is always someone being benefitted.
chunks.label: The student's conclusions
chunks.what_happened: The student argues for better healthcare and paid maternity leave and sums up the book.

na1a9474b.title: Observing Disconnected Families as a Server

chunks.text:
Recently, society has seen a shift in marriages or long-term relationships, and who the breadwinner is and who does the household chores. In the past, men were primarily the breadwinners, while women were housewives and would cook, clean, and care for the house. This dynamic has shifted going into the 21st century, and more women have entered the workforce. Some men have also shifted to stay-at-home dads, but the question of relationship equality still exists. Many old norms and traditions are still held up today, even though society is pushing towards an egalitarian relationship model. Many couples are also refraining from getting married or having kids. With all of these factors up in the air, it leaves many possibilities for a relationship to lean towards in the future. While these were some bigger factors, some smaller, seemingly insignificant influences also have a big impact.

Currently, we live in a society that is rapidly developing newer and more advanced models of technology. Technology is growing faster than society can keep up with, and it impacts society on large and small scales.
chunks.label: Changing relationships and technology
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces changing roles in relationships and the growth of technology.

chunks.text: Whether or not we realize it, technology has an extreme impact on families and their dynamics. I see this personally at my job every day. I work as a server in a local restaurant, and oftentimes when I go to greet a table, everyone at the table is on their phones. I’m not judging by any means. I’m on my phone more than I like, but throughout the entire dining experience, everyone is on their phones rather than talking. I believe that this is negatively affecting the family dynamic, and unless it is addressed, it may continue to harm families and cause many issues in the years to come.
chunks.label: Seeing families on phones while serving
chunks.what_happened: Working as a server at a local restaurant, the student often greets tables where everyone in the family is on their phone instead of talking for the whole meal.

chunks.text: This is not just my opinion; sociological researchers are also concerned about this issue. Lee et al. (2022) examined how parental efficacy and methods, along with mobile device usage in children, negatively impact a child’s relationship with technology and the family dynamic. The researchers' findings indicated that overconsumption and reliance on mobile devices are more likely to lead to negative outcomes. They mentioned that children holding mobile devices constantly will interfere with their daily lives, thus affecting their relationships and daily lives (Lee et al., 2022). This has many implications for how families may look and operate in 2035.
chunks.label: Research on mobile devices and families
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes research on how mobile devices affect children and families.

chunks.text: Small things can have big implications on family dynamics, as seen with mobile devices. Things like quality time are extremely important to build strong and deep connections. Not having deep connections in relationships can lead to other tough situations, like Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs). One ACE that is most commonly seen in families is substance use and abuse. According to Jabbari (2023), substance use and abuse can be affected by unhealthy family dynamics, especially in adolescents. Sometimes adolescents are looking for a way to escape or to regain a sense of control over their lives, which often manifests in them sneaking out or using substances. Jabbari (2023) also suggests that those in stressful family situations tend to gravitate towards unhealthy coping mechanisms, which impacts their health. Unhealthy family dynamics impact everyone in the family individually, as well as the whole unit.
chunks.label: Weak family connections and childhood adversity
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how weak family connections can lead to adverse childhood experiences.

chunks.text: So how does all of this play into the future dynamics of American families in 2035? There are a couple of different ways that families could go. One dynamic is a detached, unemotional, power struggle dynamic. This is the worst possible case scenario. This dynamic depicts a family that is not close, spends no time together, and is constantly fighting for attention. The parents would be fighting for equality in breadwinning, which would leave no room for quality time for their children. These children would grow up without a strong foundation, and if their parents suddenly tried to discipline them, then it would create an unhealthy dynamic. This dynamic would create the most strife and distance within the family.
chunks.label: A detached family in 2035
chunks.what_happened: The student describes the worst-case family dynamic.

chunks.text:
Another dynamic would be a semi-balanced family dynamic. This dynamic would still have some strife and cause some issues between the parents themselves and the parents and children. In this dynamic, there is more of a balance with breadwinning and less competing. Both parents may work or only one, but they are working together to be financially stable. If only one person is working, it may cause some issues with providing for the family and the splitting of household chores. This may also cause strife with their children, especially if one parent is more present than the other. Even with some of the strife, this would be more optimal than the example in the previous paragraph.

The last dynamic depicts the most perfect dynamic in the ever-changing society that we live in. This would mean that no matter what each parent is doing, whether they are both at work or just one, they are both equally contributing to housework and taking care of their family. Their relationships with their children would be close and trusting. There would be no unhealthy dynamics like substance abuse or abuse. This would be the most optimal, but this seems to be harder to reach.
chunks.label: Semi-balanced and ideal family dynamics
chunks.what_happened: The student describes two better family dynamics.

chunks.text: In conclusion, many factors impact a family’s dynamic. There are large-scale and small-scale factors. All of these factors combined can have a multitude of effects. Ultimately, there is no way to predict a “typical American family in 2035.” Society changes so much in ten years, and it’s difficult to predict everything. Technology is changing constantly, and social media is impacting how we view society and how we should handle family dynamics. Families can be complicated, but I’m hoping that the last scenario is what we are heading towards as a society.
chunks.label: Conclusion
chunks.what_happened: The student says the 2035 family is hard to predict.

chunks.text: For starters, something that caught my attention straight away was a piece of the setting taking place in Pittsburgh. I am from Pittsburgh and was born and raised in Burrell, about 30 minutes North East of the main city before moving to NC in 2015. I was younger, about twelve, when I moved but I still remember all the memories I have of the city and the surrounding areas. It was almost eye opening to me because I never really experienced anyone who was struggling with mental health nor was I ever exposed to it in school being so young. Obviously, I was not born at the time, but most of my family members were and in a way it was almost like I didn’t know mental health existed and when reading, it made me realize just how different everyone’s lives are, even when living in the same area.
chunks.label: Connection to Pittsburgh
chunks.what_happened: The student notes that they grew up near Pittsburgh and never saw mental health struggles as a child.

chunks.text:
Chapter three actually became one of my favorite chapters for how honest and raw it felt while reading. I really appreciate how you weren’t afraid to share the truth about how you felt regarding Doug. Specifically when you wrote “We were afraid of Doug. Truly afraid” on page 37. It takes a lot of strength to write something negative about yourself because even if you don’t feel that way in the present, it was true in the past.

Another part of chapter three that made me feel this way was on page forty two when you mention the shame and denial you faced surrounding Doug. How even when he moved back to Pittsburgh, you kept up the “masquerade” and how it was actually easier for you. Even when he was doing better, you still felt the need to embellish. I feel like this is something people may judge for or think negatively on your part, however, I feel I would be in a similar position. I wouldn’t want to talk about how my child is struggling even if it was to someone I am close with.
chunks.label: Shame and denial in chapter three
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the author's fear of Doug and on keeping up appearances.

chunks.text:
It reminds me of when people would ask me about my dad.

To make a very long story short, my dad passed away my senior year of high school in 2021 after a battle with ALS. People would always ask me how he was doing, how I am doing or my mom, sister, etc. I would always just lie because it was hard to talk about. I wasn’t necessarily ashamed, but I didn’t want people knowing how much my family was struggling at the time.
chunks.label: Hiding how the family was doing after father's death
chunks.what_happened: When people asked about the student's father, who died of ALS in their senior year of high school, the student lied because it was hard to talk about and they did not want people to know how much the family was struggling.
chunks.feelings: not ashamed, but did not want people to know

chunks.text:
Overall, I thought chapter three was an incredible chapter and where the book fully got me locked in until the end.

While reading the book, I actually began to annotate a lot of quotes or phrases that I really began to like. For one, on page fifty three at the end of the chapter, you wrote “the ability of families to reach the point of acceptance offers the greatest potential for positive relationships to develop, and a positive life-course trajectory for their child.” I thought this was very well written and very transformative toward the emotion of the story. When reading the story, naturally it will have a somber tone and be a tougher read, but once you write with your past self having acceptance and a will to learn, it transforms with a bit more light in a dark time. I thought it was very well written.
chunks.label: Favorite chapters and quotes
chunks.what_happened: The student describes the chapters and quotes they liked.

chunks.text:
Again in the following chapters, specifically chapter five where you give some more academic information about caregiving and then pertaining it to your story in the following few chapters was very well detailed and laid out to me, showing how you always want the best for your son. Being in class and talking about how support is such a vital factor when dealing with someone who is suffering from a mental disorder, it is amazing to read about it happening in real time. The way you write about helping Doug with his miscellaneous finances like cigarettes or snacks but also teaching him some responsibility as well as navigating through his disease was a great example of the importance of support in a meaningful way.

I do also want to note that you do an incredible job at sharing what it is like to be exposed to schizophrenia. Before reading this, I had never once been exposed to the true reality of the disease, minus fictionalized and dramatic movies. From beginning to end of the book, I learned something new in almost every chapter and I feel a bit more prepared than I would be if I were to ever experience it with someone in my life. I am aware that everyone is different and experiences things differently, however, even having a bit of knowledge as well as someone’s first experience can be helpful.
chunks.label: Caregiving and learning about schizophrenia
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on support, caregiving and what they learned about schizophrenia.

chunks.text: Reading about how Doug might have schizophrenia based on him having a concerning conversation to himself, to him opening up to you about Dave and Wendy, to eventually seeking help and getting on some medications. People think that medications are a fix all when in reality they aren’t and are just a support towards a variety of setbacks. Reading about Doug’s paranoia in his group home and then him essentially going missing was scary to see. That feeling of helplessness would be gut wrenching, I could not imagine the fear. I also like how you, these events were happening in real time for the first time. Being able to read about how your past self also became exposed to a new symptom or struggle the same time I did was really interesting to me, but it also made me feel sad for you. You had no idea what was going to come next and had little background with the disease. I can say the same thing when reading about Melissa’s struggles with her mental health too.
chunks.label: Doug's symptoms and the father's helplessness
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on Doug's symptoms, his disappearance and Melissa's struggles.

chunks.text: I have been exposed to depression in my life with my dad and my sister following his passing, but reading a bit about your experience shows how everyone battles things differently. Reading about Melissa’s death at the end of your book actually made me want to call my sister and just talk to her. I know you aren’t exactly sure what happened to your daughter, but it made me feel like I have taken my sister for granted at times.
chunks.label: Depression in the family and wanting to call sister
chunks.what_happened: The student has seen depression in their father and in their sister after his death. Reading about Melissa made them want to call their sister.
chunks.feelings: felt they had taken their sister for granted

chunks.text:
There are so many aspects to your book and your journey that I could touch on, but I want to move on towards the end of the book which is just awful and heartbreaking to read. When reading the last few chapters, before the epilogue, I was sad to hear about Doug falling slowly back into a hole that he was working to get out of. However, it shows the true reality of life and the disease. Him having issues with the police or having those inconsistencies you mention towards the end of chapter 8. Within chapter nine, you bring up his psychological evaluation as well as the updates and progress logs. I really appreciate you adding those in because it helps to better show how Doug was doing in this time.

Reading about Doug gradually getting better and wanting to improve really flipped me into a happier tone, almost forgetting what was about to happen. Anytime you have someone you care about, you always want what is best for them, so I can’t imagine how you felt when writing the end. It's incredibly unfair how Doug’s life ended. All of his hard work to better himself, just to pass away at his highest point. It's heart wrenching, but real and shows that life doesn’t care about who deserves what. I'm glad you included an epilogue because I feel those are where the most important or detrimental parts of a book take place in terms of the overall book. I am glad you left your book on a more positive note, sharing the ways you saw Doug improving. Whether it was the tidiness of his home or finding his plans for the future. Finally, with you mentioning how all the wonderful memories are enough to keep you from feeling like you truly lost him. I really enjoyed reading that and it made me a bit happier for you but still feeling sad, especially after reading about the loss of Melissa. I couldn’t imagine the pain of losing your second child.
chunks.label: The end of Doug's life and the epilogue
chunks.what_happened: The student reflects on the last chapters and the epilogue.

chunks.text: I am truly truly sorry for what you went through and the struggles and the long, hard journey you endured in the eight years surrounding Doug’s disease and Melissa’s own mental health struggles as well as the lasting effects their deaths have on you. I also want to say thank you for sharing your journey. You wrote such an incredible book and truthfully, it became one of my favorites for how truthful and vulnerable you write. . I plan on recommending it to anyone who I feel could benefit from your words. Your journey really opened my eyes to how brutal life can be and how important mental health is. I know at the end of the day, I am just a student in your class, but that's why I took this class. I wanted to learn more about mental health and its importance. Your book provided the best first hand account of this and I look forward to the rest of the course.
chunks.label: Thanks to the author
chunks.what_happened: The student thanks the author and says what the book taught them.

nf8878a48.title: Analyzing Family Structures and Social Policy

chunks.text: Over the course of the past century America has shifted from a relatively homogeneous culture placing priority on assimilation and the nuclear family to a more diverse society defined by stratified social identities. Towards the end of the civil rights movement the codified laws which would be created in the name of forcing an end to segregation would see many positive outcomes but in practice some mandates have often fallen short due to inconsistent enforcement and uneven social integration. To contrast, the most homogeneous societies of the world are also the ones with the best success of welfare implementation, as social consensus and shared norms can simplify policy coordination. In the United States, however, the ongoing struggle to balance cultural diversity with cohesive national identity has placed increased pressure on traditional family structures. This family structure shift stems from the struggles of maintaining a non-homogenous national identity and prospects of the shape this could take tend to form around two schools of thought.
