chunks.label: Diversity and the American family
chunks.what_happened: The student argues that diversity has put pressure on traditional family structures.

chunks.text: Firstly, the once normative traditional American family with a husband, wife, and kids has now become the counterculture and can be predicted to see a return due to the weakness of maintaining collective values in an increasingly diverse society. Most trends fluctuate so seeing a return to form based on strong family bonds free of ambiguity is a viable option. Many today believe rapid social changes have progressed too forcibly due to the application of political agendas on social thought instead of organic cultural evolution. Current debates over family values, gender roles, and cultural identity have been often too politicized. This changes what would otherwise be normative social adaptations into an ideological battleground. This politicization risks obscuring genuine discussions about how best to gauge a balance between equality, stability, and personal freedom within modern family life.
chunks.label: Return of the traditional family
chunks.what_happened: The student predicts a return of the traditional family and criticizes politicized debates.

chunks.text: The crux of the issue can be understood when looking at the codified laws being proposed to combat inequality in the workplace and household. The ultimate logic for dictating a replacement of social norms is not clearly defined in many instances allowing for perpetual violations of the ultimate cause being fought for. This issue is not new as various civil rights laws like the Title 7 of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Equal Pay Act of 1963 suffer from the same issue of legal ambiguity. One good example of modern equality legislation passed in the UK in recent years. Laws like the Equality Act of 2010 (UK) often leave ambiguous explanations on how it intends to change social norms. The ultimate change achieved by these types of legislation are inherently weak because even though it defines new standards to meet, things like failing to define sexual orientation clearly end up not enshrining the social leap it was intended to. This applies to the US because there was intent on implementing an adapted version which never came to fruition.
chunks.label: Ambiguous equality laws
chunks.what_happened: The student argues that equality laws are too vague to change norms.

chunks.text: The sociological thinker Durkheim comes to mind when defining the problems of practicing ambiguous policies. To quote Sociology of Law by Milovanovic on Durkheim social philosophy, he states “Durkheim assumes that society, left to itself, will evolve from the traditional to the complex form,” existing in “a state of equilibrium.” However, “when these adjustments do not take place,” he notes, “a state Durkheim referred to as anomie” emerges, an idea “many criminologists embed or assume in their explanation of crime.” (Milovanovic 2022, p.67) This state of anomie (normlessness) can be seen much more vividly than ever before, perhaps resulting in accepted application of normlessness as the norm. Something as simple as the man paying on the first date or asking another on a date is being actively torn down making what was already a difficult hurdle for people to make now being thrown into question; a socially accepted procedure for centuries. This state of anomie, or normlessness, according to Durkheim’s philosophy, is also linked to suicide. In a time when the application of equitable laws is at an all-time high, this may correlate with rising male suicide rates from 18.1 per 100,000 in 1968 to 22.8 per 100,000 in 2023, an increase of 26% (National Institute of Mental Health) potentially reflecting a displacement of their societal roles.
chunks.label: Durkheim, anomie and changing norms
chunks.what_happened: The student links Durkheim's anomie to changing dating norms and male suicide rates.

chunks.text: To understand the place that counter-traditional relational ideologies will take in the coming years you need to first break down the aspects these groups use to define themselves. The future of gay couples in America is undoubtedly an important one and many social thinkers believe these social advancements are being normalized much like racial integration once was. There are many debates within LGBTQ+ movements about how internal representation and behavior have influenced public perceptions, sometimes hindering support. There is no better way to tear down a movement than to evoke societal reactions to perceived displays of misconduct. The civil rights activists did a very good job at showing how strongly spoken they were to the public and everything from the way they dressed to the way they organized and conducted themselves saw them winning social acceptance, changing predominant beliefs. Homosexuality being sexual in nature has seen problems of acceptance due to displays of social misconduct and demands of image reorientation are needed in order to spark lasting transformative change. Recognizing how image and perception influence public acceptance is essential as these factors directly impact whether policies aimed at family equality achieve genuine integration or remain symbolically progressive.
chunks.label: LGBTQ families and public image
chunks.what_happened: The student discusses how public image affects acceptance of LGBTQ families.

chunks.text: Along the more contemporary lines of reform, if Europe is to be used as a model for America in the coming years there are plenty of positive and negative takeaways to understand before new laws become formalized. Positive takeaways include laws like Norway's Paid Parental Leave and “Use-It-or-Lose-It” quotas which sees all parents being entitled to paid leave even reserving a portion for fathers. This is a good example because not only does it shift workplace norms but it also helps the parents fulfil their family duties at home. One other example would be Germany's Anti-Discrimination Act (Allgemeines Gleichbehandlungsgesetz, AGG) which nets some benefits like providing a clear legal framework for victims of workplace discriminatory practices and a focus on encouraging proactive HR policies. The categorizations within this remedy based approach helps reduce confusion in interpretation allowing for clear paths for enforcement.
chunks.label: European policies to learn from
chunks.what_happened: The student describes Norwegian and German laws as good models.

chunks.text: Regarding examples not to follow France’s Gender Parity in Politics Law (2000) and EU’s Directive on Work-Life Balance (2019) provide a good contrast. With France’s law it explains a requirement for political parties to present 50% female, 50% male candidate nomination. Results here are thoroughly superficial as the issue of political representation among women in France, even though statistically improved, still lacks a qualitative effect with women being placed in local non-competitive districts for party compliance purposes. The EU directive on work life balance sees a different set of issues. It is designed to encourage flexible working arrangements and parental leave across EU states but because it is another EU law designed to be applied in countries with completely different internal interests application and enforcement suffer putting into question the integrity of the law’s legitimization. The United States can learn from this aspect especially in a time where federal legal precedent is used to apply to states which fail to share social values of other states. Laws are always best applied at the state level first and foremost because they’re more likely to reflect the communities interests. When it comes to family representation nothing could be farther away than a federal mandate.
chunks.label: Policies not to follow
chunks.what_happened: The student criticizes French and EU laws and argues for state-level laws.

chunks.text: The failure of social legislation to alleviate pressures on families forces new generations to adapt resulting in individualized social nets to form at an advanced rate. While this can be economically beneficial by eliminating financial dependence on others, phenomena like the single mother epidemic and the rise of less conventional blended families present their own instabilities. It would be a disservice of governance to supplement these situations without first addressing the systemic roots of unideal living situations. True reform requires legislation that strengthens the social foundations of family life. This can be achieved by focussing on wage inequality, affordable childcare, and accessible housing (the Blackrock problem) rather than policies that merely treat the symptoms of deeper structural imbalance. Without this shift, future generations will continue to bear the private costs of public inaction, mistaking adaptation for progress. Social change is slow so in the year 2035 the differences from 2025 are going to be negligible even if federal mandates are created today the process of trickling into the social consciousness will not be completed.
chunks.label: Conclusion on social policy and families
chunks.what_happened: The student argues for policies on wages, childcare and housing.

nedefc495.title: Predicting the Future of the Family

chunks.text: Looking to the future of society based on what is seen now, what would a typical family in 2035 look like? To begin, let's look at where society is now. First, let's think about society's views on family and marriage. Marriage right now is seen as a goal for most. It is a goal that for some is seen as attainable, others it is seen as something that isn’t. For most, marriage means that they are marrying and then co-habituating with someone. Though this isn’t always the case. Many are leaning towards co-habitation before marriage, and this is leading to a question of is marriage as valued as it once was? The answer is complicated. Given this economic state, seeing marriage as a goal is common, but seeing it as attainable is not. Saving for the cost of what it takes to be married with a “proper” wedding and having that be the measure of that goal to many seems like it isn’t worth doing. This is why a rise in co-habitation and living together before being married and longer engagements etc. is becoming more common. This is because marriage is shifting away from being seen as a “status” symbol to be achieved for only monetary value. (Coontz, 2015) We are seeing people’s marriage values shift to being focused on love and what each can bring into the shared relationship. (Coontz, 2005) This is seen especially between classes and particularly between the upper to middle and the lower class. The lower class cannot view marriage with a lens of status increase since they are not able to have financial stability enough to be able to offer or add increasing monetary value to each other. (Coontz, 2015)
chunks.label: Marriage today and its value
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how marriage is seen today and why cohabitation is rising.

chunks.text: This brings the next point forward of the workforce and how that can relate to families and their family planning, childcare, earnings, etc. The workforce influences families in a major way. First is the income that couples receive with and without children. Without having children, there is a gender pay gap that was slowly closing. However, it has begun to widen again. It also increases when children are brought into families as well with fatherhood bonuses being given to them to provide further for the family, versus penalties mothers face when they need to take time off after giving birth, or to care for their children etc. (Budig, 2014) So, with earnings factored into a couple's marriage and family this affects their want to have children and how they do their family planning and how many kids that they may want to have. This affects the type of care and the amount that these parents can do for their children. Which ties back into family structures and the impact being a working parent has on them. Because of the workforce’s impact parents are having to decide how to best provide care for children, this means deciding if one of them will be working whilst the other stays home, if both will be working, if they each will do both which would mean each is working and caring parttime. If one parent stays at home it is most likely assumed to be the mom, which can come with its own issues of mom doing more labor at home and feeling overworked and that labor not being recognized, and if it is the father at home, there is a huge stigma that they only sit around and do not care properly for their child. If they both choose to work, there could be the issue of the mom having to deal with the “second shift.” Meaning she must come home from her nine to five job and then come do household chores and childcare etc. on her own. (Hochschild & Machung, 1989) Which causes an imbalance of how much each parent contributes to the home. If they both decide they want to try and do both in equal measure, they often will find that they are always losing out on either free time at home catching up on things or find that they must be absent from work often. It is hard to find a balance between doing both care and working. (Hochschild & Machung, 1989)
chunks.label: Work, pay and childcare
chunks.what_happened: The student explains how the pay gap and the second shift shape families.

chunks.text: This brings back our original question based on what is seen now: what might the typical family in 2035 look like? Based on what has been seen It is safe to say that our typical family structure still will likely look like a nuclear one. It is safe to try and predict that as we see that other family structures are struggling to become made or are thought of as normative. Two parents and their children are likely still going to be the normative family, if they choose to have any. However, it may not hold the traditional gender roles or traditional differential sex parent make up. I think we are growing more acceptive of LGBTQ parents having children and still seeing that as a family. However, things such as polyamorous families and couples, kinship and village networks, etc. are still not seen as proper families or the norm. It is likely there will be a push towards trying to provide and be equally involved in relationships, the household, and parenting. What that looks like will likely be different for each family like how it does now. The way that this will likely be done is by investing greater effort into finding balance within work and personal life and time as we are seeing a trend now of that.
chunks.label: The typical family in 2035
chunks.what_happened: The student predicts a nuclear family with changing roles.

chunks.text: In conclusion, based on the trends we are seeing now, even though it may be hard to make airtight predictions due to different influences and how fast we can see trends ebb and flow based on them, it is safe to assume within the next ten years we can expect more continued growth and change within these different areas. Particularly in the areas of what and who we consider a family, gender roles in marriage and families, childcare, how parents respond to the work force, etc. These changes, although they may not be big, will hopefully be continuing a track of growth that we are seeing and not a regression of where trends are now.
chunks.label: Conclusion
chunks.what_happened: The student sums up expected changes in the family.

n9dff474a.title: Telling a White Lie While Babysitting

chunks.text: Michael Joseph Sandel is a very accomplished and acclaimed American political philosopher and professor at Harvard University. Michael Joseph Sandel is very well known for his internationally bestselling book called “Justice: What’s the Right Thing to Do?” Throughout this book, Michael Joseph Sandel expands on his ideologies about morals, ethics, laws, and politics. He connects real-world events to different theories of justice, like utilitarianism and libertarianism, as well as different philosophers' ideas, such as Kant, Aristotle, and Rawls. Michael Joseph Sandel's book serves as a clear, engaging, and well-written piece of literature that challenges readers to reflect on their own beliefs and moral compasses. Michael Sandel's book “Justice: What’s the Right Thing to Do” also laid the foundation for a lifelong career dedicated to involving the public in moral, ethical, and civil discussions.
chunks.label: Introduction to Sandel
chunks.what_happened: The student introduces Michael Sandel and his book.

chunks.text: In Michael Joseph Sandel’s book “Justice: What’s the Right Thing to Do?”, he states that there are three approaches to justice. A society distributes different things we prize, including income and wealth, duties and responsibilities, powers and opportunities, and offices and honors. A society that is just distributes these things fairly and equitably, giving each individual his or her due. Michael Sandel states, however, “The hard questions begin when we ask what people are due, and why” (pg. 17). The first idea of justice is maximizing welfare. Maximizing welfare is centered around the ideas of promoting prosperity, improving our standard of living, and producing the overall greatest good for a society. Michael Sandel further explains this ideology by connecting it to the philosophical approach of utilitarianism. Utilitarianism is a moral theory that emphasizes the importance of the greater good. If an action promotes the greatest happiness and well-being for the greatest number of people, then it is right. Individuals who follow the utilitarianism approach often evaluate their actions by asking themselves Does it improve the overall quality of life and welfare? While utilitarianism sounds simple enough, it also has its negatives that come along with it. Utilitarianism can overlook individual rights and justify acts of injustice as long as they result in a greater good for a majority of people. While I do personally think that utilitarianism can be an effective tool for maximizing happiness and welfare, I do think it has a few drawbacks that raise some ethical and moral concerns.
chunks.label: Maximizing welfare and utilitarianism
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the first approach to justice and its drawbacks.

chunks.text: The second approach links justice to freedom. In this section of Michael Joseph Sandel's book, he explains that a wide range of theories emphasize respect for individual rights and decisions. Sandel states that “The idea that justice means respecting freedom and individual rights is at least as familiar in contemporary politics as the utilitarian idea of maximizing welfare.” For example, the U.S. Bill of Rights sets out certain liberties—including rights to freedom of speech and religious liberty—that even majorities may not violate. And around the world, the idea that justice means respecting certain universal human rights is increasingly embraced (in theory, if not always in practice). (pg. 19). This approach is broad and uses both libertarian and egalitarian views. On one side, Sandel states that libertarians argue “that justice consists in respecting and upholding the voluntary choices made by consenting adults” (pg. 19), while egalitarians argue that “unfettered markets are neither just nor free. In their view, justice requires policies that remedy social and economic disadvantages and give everyone a fair chance at success” (pg. 19). Both the libertarian and egalitarian arguments linking justice to freedom have strong points as well as limitations. I personally think that I agree more with the egalitarian argument. I think that in order for everyone to truly be free, we need to address the more deeply rooted structural inequalities and biases, and social injustices that are among us. I believe that justice is truly served when everyone has equal access to different opportunities and chances at success.
chunks.label: Justice as freedom
chunks.what_happened: The student explains libertarian and egalitarian views and agrees with the egalitarian one.

chunks.text: In the third approach, Michael Joseph Sandel connects justice to virtue and the good life. This approach highlights the idea that justice isn’t only about the outcomes but also about promoting certain moral values and ethics within a society. Sandel goes on to explain that different moral and religious ideologies have shaped political movements and arguments for decades. One example of this is Martin Luther King Jr., who drew his visions and ideas of what justice looks like from different moral and religious perspectives. The approach that connects justice to virtue and the good life shows us that debates and different opinions about what justice is are often intertwined with the different values a society chooses to uphold.
chunks.label: Justice and virtue
chunks.what_happened: The student explains the third approach to justice.

chunks.text: All three of Michael Joseph Sandel's approaches to justice—maximizing welfare, linking justice to freedom, and connecting justice to virtue—show just how complex it is to determine what justice really is and what it looks like. Sandals' explanations of the three approaches to justice really make me think about the deeper values and individual morals that shape our choices and decisions. Everyone has a different perspective on what justice should look like, and these different approaches encourage us to think about what justice is to us. Sandel provides us with an example of how our moral reasoning leads us to the decisions we make. In the example of The Runaway Trolley, Sandel states that “Suppose you are the driver of a trolley car hurtling down the track at sixty miles an hour. Up ahead, you see five workers standing on the track, tools in hand. You try to stop, but you can’t. The brakes don’t work. Suddenly, you notice a side track off to the right. There is a worker on that track, too, but only one. You realize that you can turn the trolley car onto the side track, killing the one worker but sparing the five. Now consider another version where you are an onlooker. The trolley is about to crash into the five workers. You feel helpless to avert this disaster—until you notice, standing next to you on the bridge, a very heavy man. You could push him off the bridge, onto the track, into the path of the oncoming trolley. He would die, but the five workers would be saved” (pg. 20). I found the example of the runaway trolley to be very interesting because it truly does raise a moral and ethical puzzle. Individuals will have different ideas on what choice is correct, and this example goes to show that everyone has different moral principles, dilemmas, and perspectives on what is considered right and wrong.
chunks.label: The trolley problem
chunks.what_happened: The student summarizes the trolley example and what it shows about moral reasoning.

chunks.text: Michael Joseph Sandel shows us how different individuals face different moral dilemmas, which further reveal the way people view topics “about right and wrong, justice and injustice. Some people favor abortion rights, and others consider abortion to be murder. Some believe fairness requires taxing the rich to help the poor, while others believe it is unfair to tax away money people have earned through their own efforts. Some defend affirmative action in college admissions as a way of righting past wrongs, whereas others consider it an unfair form of reverse discrimination against people who deserve admission on their merits. Some people reject the torture of terror suspects as a moral abomination unworthy of a free society, while others defend it as a last resort to prevent a terrorist attack” (pg. 27). While it may seem like our moral convictions are fixed by our upbringing or faith, I believe that our morals can change. Throughout our lifetimes, we are faced with different situations that challenge our personal principles and morals. Sandel states that in order for justice to be discovered, different debates, dialogues, and ideologies must be had, and sometimes our minds can be changed. Throughout the book, Sandel brings up the different perspectives of Aristotle, Immanuel Kant, John Stuart Mill, and John Rawls to encourage us to further examine our own morals and to figure out why we think the way we do.
chunks.label: Moral disagreements and changing morals
chunks.what_happened: The student argues that people's morals can change.

chunks.text: Immanuel Kant (1724-1804) offers us one of the most powerful accounts of duties and rights. Kant’s account depends on the ideology that we are rational beings worthy of dignity and respect. Kant’s groundwork relates to the question of “What is the supreme principle of morality?” and in the course of answering that question, it addresses another hugely important one: “What is freedom?” (pg. 104). Kant's opinion on freedom challenges our understanding of morality because he believes that true freedom is acting according to the principles we have given ourselves. Kant rejects utilitarianism because he believes that it leaves rights vulnerable, and just because something benefits the majority doesn't make it morally right. Kant also believes that every individual deserves respect because they are rational beings capable of reason and making choices. Kant also believes that freedom is our obedience to impulses that we don’t get to choose. To act freely is to act autonomously according to the moral laws we give ourselves. I do personally have some critiques of Kant’s philosophy. I believe that his ideology is almost too rigid at times. Kant believes that moral rules are absolute, especially when it comes to lying. I personally believe that lying is ok in some instances.
chunks.label: Kant on duty and lying
chunks.what_happened: The student explains Kant's view of freedom and disagrees that lying is always wrong.

chunks.text: One personal example of where I believe that it was ok for me to lie was when I was babysitting. The little girl and I were painting together, and she asked me if her painting she made of her and her parents was good (it was not). I obviously lied and said yes because why would you tell a little girl that her painting was not the best? I believe that in this situation, it was ok for me to lie in order to spare the little girl's feelings. While Kant would argue that all lying undermines morality, I believe that in some instances lying is ok. Morality requires flexibility, context, and empathy.
chunks.label: Lying about a child's painting while babysitting
chunks.what_happened: While babysitting, a little girl asked the student whether her painting of her family was good. The student said yes to spare her feelings, which they think was an acceptable lie.

chunks.text:
Sandel's book on justice provides us with different philosophical ideologies and perspectives that we can use to help us face our problems today. He compares different views on what justice is, like libertarianism and egalitarianism, and draws on different philosophical perspectives, like Immanuel Kant's. I found Kant’s perspective on morality and freedom to be quite interesting, but also too strict at times. All these different ideologies and perspectives make me really think about what justice and morality are and should look like in our daily lives.

Reference:

Sandel, M. J. (2009). Justice: What’s the right thing to do? Farrar, Straus and Giroux. Kindle edition.
chunks.label: Conclusion and reference
chunks.what_happened: The student sums up the book and lists the reference.
